title: Data Science vs. Statistics: Two Cultures?
Abstract: Data science and statistics have long been intertwined disciplines, each contributing significantly to the world of data analysis and interpretation. However, as data science has evolved and become increasingly prominent, a narrative has emerged suggesting that it is at odds with statistics, with two distinct cultures emerging. One perspective views data science as an artisanal craft, emphasizing creativity, intuition, and collaboration, often reliant on machine learning techniques and powerful computing resources. This approach prioritizes producing actionable insights and predictive models over rigor and theory. In contrast, statistics is seen as a disciplined field, adhering to a strict framework of hypothesis testing, probability theory, and statistical inference. Proponents of statistics argue that its methodological rigor and emphasis on statistical significance are essential for ensuring that conclusions drawn from data are both valid and reliable. The tension between these two perspectives is examined in this paper, with a particular focus on the role of statistics in data science, the implications of data-driven decision-making, and the consequences for the way in which data is analyzed, interpreted, and presented. Through a combination of theoretical discussions, empirical analyses, and case studies, this research aims to provide insight into the nature of the tension between data science and statistics, with a view to promoting a more nuanced understanding of the complex relationships between these disciplines.

title: Estimation and Inference of Treatment Effects with $L_2$-Boosting in High-Dimensional Settings
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel methodology for estimating and inferring treatment effects in high-dimensional settings using$L_2$-boosting. The $L_2$-boosting algorithm is an ensemble learning technique that combines a series of weak models to form a strong predictive model. We leverage this algorithm to develop a weighted treatment effect estimator that can handle high-dimensional covariates and interactions between them. Our approach is motivated by the need to improve upon existing estimation methods, which often suffer from high prediction error and poor inference due to the curse of dimensionality. In high-dimensional settings, traditional regression-based estimation methods may not accurately represent the treatment effect, leading to biased inference. Our $L_2$-boosting based estimator, dubbed "BoostTE", addresses this challenge by iteratively refining a model based on both covariates and the treatment exposure. Through extensive simulations and real-world applications, we demonstrate that BoostTE outperforms existing approaches in terms of accuracy and robustness. Furthermore, we develop a novel inference framework for the BoostTE estimator, which allows for the estimation of uncertainty and statistical significance. Our results highlight the potential of $L_2$-boosting as a powerful tool for the estimation and inference of treatment effects in high-dimensional settings.

title: SenseNet: 3D Objects Database and Tactile Simulator
Abstract:
SenseNet: 3D Objects Database and Tactile Simulator represents a novel, comprehensive framework designed to facilitate advancements in the field of haptic communication and robotic manipulation. This framework integrates seamlessly with three-dimensional (3D) object databases, allowing for the creation and manipulation of intricate models that can be accurately rendered in various software applications. The database itself is built upon a versatile architecture that is easily scalable and adaptable to accommodate diverse models and varying user needs.

Further development of this framework involves pairing the database with a tactile simulator, providing a multi-modal interface that enables users to interact with simulated objects and environments via physically tangible interfaces such as gloves or haptic feedback devices. The simulator accurately simulates tactile sensations such as texture, pressure, and temperature, thereby creating immersive experiences that closely mimic real-world interactions. This integration of simulated objects and multi-modal interfaces facilitates a wide range of applications in fields such as manufacturing, healthcare, education, and training.

The proposed framework can also act as a valuable tool for reducing real-world experimentation and training costs, while also improving the quality and safety of the work. Experimental evaluation of the SenseNet framework showed promising results in terms of tactile perception and accuracy, demonstrating the potential for significant advancements in its future development.

title: ZOOpt: Toolbox for Derivative-Free Optimization
Abstract: ZOOpt is an open-source software toolbox for derivative-free optimization, specifically designed to handle non-linear, non-convex, and high-dimensional problems. Its primary goal is to provide a unified framework for various derivative-free optimization algorithms, allowing for efficient and flexible implementation across different applications. This toolbox encompasses a wide range of methods, including evolutionary computation, surrogate-based optimization, Bayesian optimization, and variants of multilevel models. ZOOpt enables users to leverage these individual algorithms, as well as to combine them seamlessly to suit their specific problem requirements, thereby empowering the optimization of complex systems where analytic gradients are either unavailable or computationally expensive to calculate. By incorporating several components, such as problem-independent interfaces for function evaluation, parallel computation, and diverse algorithmic backends, ZOOpt seeks to provide a versatile, extensible, and efficient platform for tackling complex optimization tasks with a focus on real-world applicability. Overall, ZOOpt offers a unique and streamlined optimization framework that leverages domain-agnostic and problem-agnostic design principles to efficiently handle large, stochastic, and high-dimensional search spaces.

title: Towards Building an Intelligent Anti-Malware System: A Deep Learning Approach using Support Vector Machine (SVM) for Malware Classification
Abstract: In the realm of cybersecurity, developing effective anti-malware systems has become increasingly crucial due to the escalating rise of advanced malware threats. Traditional signature-based detection methods have limitations in recognizing and mitigating new and unknown malware variants, thus necessitating the adoption of artificial intelligence and machine learning techniques. Towards this end, this research proposes a deep learning-based approach leveraging Support Vector Machine (SVM) to improve malware classification efficiency. The proposed system integrates various feature extraction methods, including opcode analysis and neural network-based techniques, to obtain a comprehensive understanding of binary code characteristics. Malware samples collected from public datasets are preprocessed, and relevant features are extracted and used to train the SVM classifier. Experiment results demonstrate the superiority of the proposed system over state-of-the-art methods in terms of classification accuracy and training speed. Furthermore, the exploration of various kernel functions and regularization parameters provides insights into the impact of hyperparameter tuning on the system's performance. Additionally, the qualitative analysis via confusion matrix and ROC curve offers further insight into the system's robustness and discriminative power in recognizing malware variants. By capitalizing on the strengths of deep learning and SVM, the proposed system represents a significant step forward in the pursuit of building intelligent anti-malware systems that remain vigilant against evolving malware threats.

title: Learning Relevant Features of Data with Multi-scale Tensor Networks
Abstract: This paper presents a novel framework for extracting relevant features from complex data leveraging the capabilities of multi-scale tensor networks. The proposed method, called Multi-Scale Tensor Network Feature Learning (MSTNFL), efficiently captures various patterns and relationships within data by representing it as a hierarchical tensor network structure. This multi-scale representation enables the extraction of features at different granularities, allowing for a more comprehensive understanding of the data. The approach first learns a coarse-grained representation of the data through a graph-based construction of the tensor network, followed by a refinement process that infuses finer details through local updates. A set of heuristics is also proposed to prune the tensor network and reduce redundancy, making it scalable for large datasets. MSTNFL is benchmarked on several machine learning datasets, demonstrating significant improvements over state-of-the-art models in terms of representation quality, generalization performance, and computational efficiency. Furthermore, the proposed method outperforms these models in downstream tasks such as classification, regression, and clustering, showcasing its potential in various applications including computer vision, natural language processing, and bioinformatics. The computational efficiency and interpretability of the learned features can also facilitate data exploration and visualization, highlighting the utility of MSTNFL in real-world data analysis and decision-making scenarios.

title: Neurally Plausible Model of Robot Reaching Inspired by Infant Motor Babbling
Abstract: This paper presents an innovative, neurally plausible model of robot reaching inspired by infant motor babbling. Building on the established connection between humans and robots, we draw parallels between the early stages of motor development in infants and the reaching behavior of robots. Our approach is grounded in the seminal concept of motor babbling, a crucial stage of infant learning characterized by systematic experimentation with various motor options, ultimately leading to efficient movement patterns and improved motor skills. We propose an architecture for a robot reaching system that captures the essence of this neurodevelopmental process by incorporating similar iterative testing and refinement mechanisms. By decoupling error-based learning from traditional closed-loop control schemes, our framework enables robots to explore an open space of potential reaching movements without explicit guidance from an external model. This leads to an increased likelihood of discovering successful approaches to reaching a target, facilitating a more natural and intuitive robotic reaching behavior. Experimental results demonstrate the viability of this approach, allowing a robot to progressively refine its reaching movement over time, with performance continuing to improve even in the absence of additional training data. The framework's ability to mimic human motor learning highlights the potential for more effective human-robot interaction and potentially enables robots to adapt to various novel situations, thereby broadening their operational capability and enhancing overall performance.

title: Restricted Boltzmann Machines for Robust and Fast Latent Truth Discovery
Abstract: This study proposes the application of Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs) to enable robust and efficient latent truth discovery in complex systems. The research emphasizes the critical need for effective latent truth discovery in various domains such as recommendation systems, decision-making, and opinion aggregation. However, the increasing complexity of these systems poses significant challenges in accurately extracting true underlying patterns. By introducing an RBM based latent truth discovery framework, this study demonstrates significant improvements in capturing robust and accurate latent structures, while also reducing computational time and requirements. The proposed framework involves multiple stages of RBM training and fine-tuning, allowing it to effectively navigate the complexities of high-dimensional real-world data. A rigorous set of experiments on multiple benchmark datasets highlights the superiority of the proposed RBM-based framework over state-of-the-art competitors, including its ability to remarkably sustain performance in the presence of noisy inputs and incomplete data. By harnessing the power of RBMs in latent truth discovery, this study makes ground-breaking contributions to the field of pattern recognition and unsupervised learning, fostering the development of more reliable and efficient solutions in real-world applications. The outcome promises to empower the automation of complex decision-making processes with higher accuracy, and enable sound conclusions to be derived from the intricate patterns hidden within vast datasets. Overall, this framework offers a potential paradigm shift in approaching the extraction of latent truths across diverse domains, sparking new avenues of exploration and innovation.

title: Using Deep Neural Network Approximate Bayesian Network
Abstract: This paper explores the integration of deep neural networks with approximate Bayesian networks, a probabilistic graphical model, to leverage the strengths of both methodologies and overcome their individual limitations. The integration aims to develop a more robust and interpretable method for learning complex interactions within multivariate data. Beginning with an overview of the theoretical foundations of approximate Bayesian networks and deep neural networks, the research delves into a theoretical framework that presents a probabilistic graphical model where the parameters of the neural network are modelled as latent variables in the Bayesian network. By incorporating an approximate inference method using variational principles, an efficient and scalable approach is derived for approximating the posterior distribution over the model parameters. The proposed method is evaluated on a range of simulated and real-world datasets, including both classical regression and binary classification problems, exhibiting superior performance when compared to standard deep neural network models and demonstrating improved interpretability through novel insights into the interactions between model parameters. The integration also reveals potential applications in anomaly detection and sensitivity analysis of model parameters, contributing to the growing body of research in the fusion of probabilistic and deep learning methodologies.

title: Non-invasive biomarkers of fetal brain development reflecting prenatal stress: an integrative multi-scale multi-species perspective on data collection and analysis
Abstract: This study embarked on a comprehensive exploration of non-invasive biomarkers of fetal brain development, focusing particularly on their reflection of prenatal stress through an integrative multi-scale multi-species perspective. The aim was to develop a discerning understanding of the various biological pathways involved, ensuring that prenatal stress translates to distinct biomarkers that signify changes in fetal brain development. Utilizing a multi-modal approach that encompasses analytical proteomics, metabolomics, epigenomics, and neuroimaging techniques allowed researchers to delve into different layers of prenatal brain development. From computational modeling and systems biology to in vivo studies on model species such as rats and mouse, the methodology encompassed diverse investigative pathways to ascertain the reliability and validity of biomarkers for fetal brain development, even in the presence of prenatal stress. Integrating structural and molecular alterations discovered in model species into clinical investigations provided critical insight for translating findings to the human context, thus linking human studies that explore perinatal developmental trajectories in healthy subjects and test subjects revealing signs of prenatal adversity, effectively examining the hypothesis that specific combinations of functional imaging modalities, genetics and biochemistry can signal stress's deleterious effects on brain development before, at and after birth.

title: Early detection of Crossfire attacks using deep learning
Abstract: Crossfire attacks pose a significant threat to network security, leveraging compromised nodes to launch coordinated attacks and disguise malicious activity as legitimate user behavior. However, early detection of such attacks is a challenging problem due to their ability to evade traditional intrusion detection systems (IDS) and their reliance on machine learning algorithms that can be trained to mimic normal user behavior. This research proposes a novel approach to detecting crossfire attacks using deep learning techniques. The proposed system employs a two-stage architecture, consisting of a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) for feature extraction from network traffic data and a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) for classification of the extracted features into normal or crossfire attack behavior. The training dataset is comprised of simulated and real-world network traffic data, including benign traffic, crossfire attacks, and other types of cyber threats. The system's accuracy is evaluated using metrics such as precision, recall, F1 score, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC-ROC) to assess its effectiveness in detecting crossfire attacks. Preliminary results indicate that the proposed system is capable of detecting crossfire attacks with high accuracy and outperforms state-of-the-art IDS solutions. The proposed approach can be applied to various network architectures and has the potential to enhance the security of complex networks by providing early warning of potential crossfire attacks. The system's ability to adapt to changing network conditions and cyber threats makes it a valuable asset in the fight against crossfire attacks.

title: Unstable modes in projection-based reduced-order models: How many can there be, and what do they tell you?
Abstract: This study focuses on the analysis of unstable modes in projection-based reduced-order models, with the goal of providing a comprehensive understanding of their occurrence and implications. The behavior of unstable modes in reduced-order models can significantly impact their accuracy and reliability in capturing the dynamics of the original system. A key question that arises is how many unstable modes can coexist in a reduced-order model, and what information can be gleaned from their presence or absence. This inquiry is essential for developing effective reduced-order model frameworks that can optimally capture the dynamics of complex systems. Employing a combination of theoretical analysis and numerical experimentation, this research delves into the fundamental characteristics of unstable modes in projection-based reduced-order models, including their distribution, detectability, and interpretability. The study also examines the interplay between the number and characteristics of unstable modes and the properties of the original system, such as dimensionality and nonlinearity. Ultimately, this research aims to reveal the relationships between unstable modes, system properties, and reduced-order model performance, providing valuable insights for the design and validation of reduced-order models in various fields, including fluid dynamics, structural mechanics, and control systems. By shedding light on the role of unstable modes in reduced-order models, this research contributes to the development of more accurate and reliable reduced-order model frameworks.

title: Machine Learning for Building Energy and Indoor Environment: A Perspective
Abstract: This paper provides an in-depth analysis of the applications of machine learning in optimizing building energy consumption and indoor environmental quality. With the increasing global focus on energy efficiency and sustainable living, machine learning algorithms have emerged as a powerful tool to improve the performance of building systems. By leveraging the vast amounts of data generated by various building systems, machine learning models can learn patterns and correlations that are not immediately apparent to humans. Computer-controlled building systems equipped with data analytic capabilities derived from machine learning offer enhanced predictive capabilities that contribute to smart buildings and smart cities by leveraging real-time data analysis and predictions that forecasted critical conditions impacting the building operation. The proposed solution to optimize energy consumption is through the use of energy consumption forecasts, which can alert the management to optimize resource and prevent expensive penalties. Furthermore, the indoor environment controls rely on occupants feedback that feed into advanced artificial intelligence and data analytics models. As an additional outcome, smart systems integration together with machine learning opens new employment opportunities and increases the appeal of sustainable design to consumers.

title: Transfer learning for diagnosis of congenital abnormalities of the kidney and urinary tract in children based on Ultrasound imaging data
Abstract: The use of deep learning techniques, particularly transfer learning, has revolutionized the field of radiology by enabling medical imaging analysis with unprecedented accuracy and efficiency. However, its application in diagnosing congenital abnormalities of the kidney and urinary tract (CAKUT) in children, a condition that is difficult to detect using conventional ultrasound imaging techniques, remains relatively unexplored. This study proposes a transfer learning-based approach for CAKUT detection from ultrasound imaging data. We employ a pre-trained convolutional neural network (CNN) model, specifically designed for medical image analysis, and fine-tune it on a dataset of ultrasound images of children's kidneys and urinary tracts, labeled with CAKUT and normal conditions. Our results show that the proposed approach achieves a high diagnostic accuracy of 95% for detecting CAKUT, outperforming traditional machine learning methods. The technique's ability to extract relevant features from ultrasound images, combined with its transfer learning capabilities, renders it an effective tool for radiologists to quickly and accurately diagnose CAKUT in pediatric patients. The implications of this research are twofold: it can improve the quality of care for children with CAKUT and provide a viable solution for low- and middle-income countries, where access to state-of-the-art medical equipment and expertise may be limited.

title: Effects of Home Resources and School Environment on Eighth-Grade Mathematics Achievement in Taiwan
Abstract: This study aimed to investigate the effects of home resources and school environment on eighth-grade mathematics achievement in Taiwan. Using a comprehensive dataset from the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) 2012, we selected a sample of 3,457 Taiwanese eighth-grade students from 125 public schools. Our results showed that students' home resources, including parental educational level, household income, and home computing devices, significantly predicted their mathematics achievement. Specifically, students from households with higher parental educational levels and household incomes consistently demonstrated higher mathematics scores. Moreover, students with access to home computing devices also performed better in mathematics. In addition, we found that a supportive school environment, characterized by a positive school climate, low student-teacher ratio, and adequate instructional resources, positively influenced students' mathematics achievement. Notably, schools with stronger school-parent partnerships and higher levels of teacher professional development tend to have better mathematics achievement. Our findings also highlighted the interactions between home resources and school environment in shaping students' mathematics achievement. Specifically, students from households with higher parental educational levels and household incomes benefited more from a supportive school environment in achieving higher mathematics achievement. Implications for education policy and practice in Taiwan are discussed, emphasizing the importance of fostering a collaborative partnership between parents, schools, and policymakers to support students' mathematics learning.

title: Learning Continuous User Representations through Hybrid Filtering with doc2vec
Abstract: This research explores the development of continuous user representations in online systems, particularly focusing on harnessing the potential of hybrid filtering techniques to effectively combine structured and unstructured data. The integration of doc2vec, a variant of the popular word2vec algorithm for text document representation, is proposed to capture semantically meaningful user characteristics from unstructured user-generated content. By capitalizing on the strengths of both structured filters such as demographic information and unstructured filters provided by doc2vec, this hybrid approach promises to significantly enhance the accuracy of user profiling. Empirical studies delve into the implementation of the proposed hybrid filtering method on a range of datasets, validating its efficacy against various benchmarks and comparing it with current state-of-the-art methods. The primary outcome of this research is a more robust and comprehensive representation of users, incorporating both explicitly-provided and implicitly-derived attributes, which has positive implications for various applications requiring personalized interaction such as recommender systems and social network analysis. Moreover, the extended representation enables researches to understand users' interactions on the level of a single user rather than a group, leading to potential improvements in user segmentation and profiling applications.

title: Deep Reinforcement Learning for List-wise Recommendations
Abstract: List-wise recommendations, a type of personalized recommendation, have become increasingly important in modern e-commerce systems, where users are presented with a ranked list of items tailored to their preferences. Deep reinforcement learning has been gaining popularity in recent years for its ability to learn complex policies in challenging environments. This paper investigates the application of deep reinforcement learning for list-wise recommendations, where the goal is to learn a policy that can produce a ranked list of items, maximizing user engagement and satisfaction. A multi-agent reinforcement learning framework is proposed, where each item in the list is treated as an agent interacting with the user. The framework employs a actor-critic approach, where the actor learns a policy to select items for the list and the critic learns to evaluate the quality of the list. To handle the cold start problem, a pre-training stage is introduced, where the model is trained on user behavior data to learn general knowledge about user preferences. The pre-trained model is then fine-tuned in an online setting, where the model interacts with real users and receives feedback in the form of item click-through rates. Comprehensive experiments are conducted on a large-scale e-commerce dataset to evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed framework, demonstrating significant improvements in recommendation accuracy and user engagement compared to state-of-the-art baselines. The results of this study highlight the potential of deep reinforcement learning for list-wise recommendations, opening up new avenues for personalized item discovery and user satisfaction in e-commerce systems.

title: Molecular enhanced sampling with autoencoders: On-the-fly collective variable discovery and accelerated free energy landscape exploration
Abstract: Molecular enhanced sampling with autoencoders offers a promising approach to accelerate the exploration of complex free energy landscapes in molecular systems. By leveraging the unsupervised learning capabilities of autoencoders, this method enables on-the-fly discovery of collective variables that effectively describe the relevant conformational fluctuations of a system. Unlike traditional collective variable identification techniques, which often rely on pre-defined educated guesses or time-consuming manual search procedures, autoencoders can autonomously learn a representation of the system's conformational space that is tailored to its specific characteristics. This adaptive ability significantly enhances the efficiency of enhanced sampling simulations, allowing for the systematic exploration of the free energy landscape with minimal human intervention. Furthermore, the deep neural network architecture of the autoencoder enables the identification of hidden and non-trivial degrees of freedom that escape traditional analysis methods, such as molecular dynamics simulations or statistical mechanical calculations. By unlocking these new perspectives on the free energy landscape, molecular enhanced sampling with autoencoders opens up exciting opportunities for mechanistic insight into complex biological processes, catalytic reactions, and other advanced scientific questions, ultimately driving breakthroughs in our understanding of the intricate behavior of molecular systems.

title: Orbital Period Changes in WZ Sagittae
Abstract: WZ Sagittae, a highly magnetic cataclysmic variable white dwarf-star binary system, is a prime example of the complex interplay between binary orbital evolution and the accretion process. This study focuses on the analysis of orbital period changes in WZ Sagittae, leveraging a carefully curated dataset of 148 precise epoch times spanning 115 years. By applying a sophisticated period analysis technique, namely the PRECEDING method, the authors have successfully identified and characterized a complex pattern of orbital period variations. The results indicate the presence of a notable modulation in the orbital period, with an amplitude of approximately 1.88 seconds, which is aligned with the 6.25-day superhump periodicity commonly observed in cataclysmic variables. A meticulous examination of the orbital residuals reveals a monotonic increase in the orbital period, with an average rate of approximately 0.013 seconds year^-1. Furthermore, this study demonstrates that the mass transfer rate is a crucial factor in driving the orbital evolution of WZ Sagittae, thereby shedding new light on the complex physics governing this enigmatic binary system. The outcome of this research significantly adds to our comprehension of cataclysmic variable binary evolution and the intricacies of mass transfer processes in highly magnetized white dwarf-star systems.

title: A dynamic network model with persistent links and node-specific latent variables, with an application to the interbank market
Abstract: This paper proposes a dynamic network model that incorporates both persistent links and node-specific latent variables to accurately capture the complex dynamics of interbank market interactions. The model accounts for the heterogeneity among banks by allowing each bank to have its own set of latent variables, which influence its behavior and connections with other banks. Persistent links are introduced to capture the long-term relationships between banks, while also accounting for potential ruptures or changes in these relationships over time. The proposed model combines elements of dynamic network models, stochastic blockmodels, and node-specific latent variable models to create a flexible framework for modeling the interbank market. By leveraging the rich structure afforded by this model, we demonstrate the ability to identify key clusters of highly interconnected banks, detect subtle changes in network dynamics over time, and examine the impact of node- and link-specific features on network behavior. The model is rigorously validated on a dataset of interbank transactions from several European countries, and its performance is compared to that of baseline models.

title: A Real-time and Registration-free Framework for Dynamic Shape Instantiation
Abstract: This paper presents a novel, registration-free framework for real-time dynamic shape instantiation in 3D environments. The proposed approach harnesses recent advances in deep learning and geometric processing to enable instantaneous and detailed shape reconstruction from sparse input data. By leveraging a novel combination of neural networks and iterative closest point algorithms, the system achieves remarkably accurate results with minimal computational overhead. The key contribution of this work lies in its ability to bypass elaborate registration processes typically required by existing methods, thereby significantly reducing the overall processing time. Real-time simulations, which previously necessitated simplified and grossly inaccurate models, can now be faithfully recreated with sophisticated shapes. Moreover, the system's capacity to dynamically generate shapes is particularly useful for a wide range of applications, including computer-aided design, virtual reality, and physics-based video games. The proposed framework is extensively validated using a diverse set of test cases, encompassing various types of shapes, resolutions, and dynamic input scenarios. Comparative analysis with existing registration-based methods demonstrates the superiority of the proposed approach in terms of both speed and accuracy, thereby underscoring its potential as a practical and efficient solution for the real-time instantiation of complex 3D shapes.

title: Theory of Deep Learning III: explaining the non-overfitting puzzle
Abstract: Deep learning models have achieved remarkable success in various fields, yet they still seem to defy conventional understanding of overfitting. Traditional wisdom dictates that overly complex models, often resulting from low training data or high capacity models, are prone to overfitting when they memorize noise in the training data rather than learning generalizable patterns. However, in the context of deep learning, a counterintuitive phenomenon has been observed, where models can avoid overfitting despite possessing an exponentially large capacity and having access to single-digit levels of training data. This phenomenon, colloquially known as the "non-overfitting puzzle," has sparked intense debate and research in the field, with many attempts to theoretically explain this enigma. One line of inquiry focuses on the role of activation functions, specifically how they influence the representational capacity and generalization performance of neural networks. Another perspective emphasizes the importance of optimizers and regularization techniques in guarding against overfitting, citing evidence that carefully tuned hyperparameters can significantly influence a model's susceptibility to overfitting. This research seeks to elucidate the non-overfitting puzzle by exploring the interplay between model structure, optimization methods, and regularization strategies, shedding fresh light on the intricate dynamics governing the performance of deep learning models. Through a combination of theoretical analysis, empirical exploration, and architectural experiments, we aim to provide novel insights into the mechanisms driving the impressive generalization capabilities of deep learning models.

title: PAC-Bayesian Margin Bounds for Convolutional Neural Networks
Abstract: This study extends the theoretical framework of PAC-Bayesian theory to convolutional neural networks (CNNs), a type of deep neural network commonly used in computer vision tasks. A key challenge in deep learning is understanding the generalization performance of complex models with many parameters, where a good fit to the training set does not necessarily imply good generalization performance. Traditional methods for estimating the predictive performance of CNNs often rely on empirical measures, such as cross- validation, leaving room for significant overestimation of model quality. Building on previous PAC-Bayesian work, we derive novel margin bounds for CNNs that provide a probabilistic guarantee of the model's generalization performance in terms of the effective margin, taken as a measure of the predictive accuracy of the model. Our approach does not require access to the test data, thus making it a significant improvement over existing methods that are based on empirical risk minimization. The theoretical results provide new insights into the interplay between model capacity, data complexity, and the effective margin in deep neural networks, leading to improved understanding of the risk of overfitting and underfitting. Furthermore, we demonstrate the practical usefulness of our margin bounds using experiments on real-world vision datasets, where our probabilistic predictions outperform state-of-the-art bounds for classical neural networks.

title: Deep Learning for Fatigue Estimation on the Basis of Multimodal Human-Machine Interactions
Abstract: Fatigue estimation from human-machine interactions has been increasingly significant in various industries, including transportation, healthcare, and manufacturing, as it can lead to improved safety, efficiency, and well-being. Traditional fatigue estimation methods rely heavily on a single modality, such as physiological signals, behavioral patterns, or self-reported measures, which can be subjective and error-prone. However, recent advancements in deep learning have shown great potential in utilizing multimodal data to improve the accuracy and robustness of fatigue estimation models. In this study, we propose a novel deep learning framework for fatigue estimation from multimodal human-machine interactions. Our framework combines convolutional neural networks (CNNs), recurrent neural networks (RNNs), and graph neural networks (GNNs) to extract features from physiological signals, behavioral patterns, and interactions with a human-machine interface. Specifically, we develop a multimodal fusion module to integrate information from different modalities and a fatigue estimation module to predict the level of fatigue based on the fused features. We evaluate our framework on a real-world dataset collected from a driving simulator experiment, demonstrating its superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods. Our results indicate that incorporating multimodal human-machine interactions can significantly improve the accuracy of fatigue estimation, enabling the development of more effective and user-centric fatigue management systems.

title: Community Detection in Partially Observable Social Networks
Abstract: This paper delves into the realm of community detection in partially observable social networks, a complex and challenging task given the incomplete information available. Traditional community detection methods often rely on global network structure and node attributes, but in partially observable social networks, the lack of information can hinder the process. To address this issue, we propose a novel community detection approach that leverages both local and global information. Our method, drawing from ideas in network embedding, graph convolutional networks, and clustering techniques, aims to infer missing links and community structures simultaneously. We achieve this by first learning a low-dimensional representation of nodes using locally informed embedding and subsequently apply graph convolutional networks to aggregate global information and refine community assignments. Experimental evaluations on real-world and synthetic datasets demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in detecting communities in partially observable social networks. Our results show significant improvements over existing methods in terms of community quality and robustness to missing links. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of partially observability on community structure and provide insights into the relationships between network structure, observability, and community detection performance. By shedding light on the consequences of incomplete information, our work offers a comprehensive understanding of community detection in partially observable social networks and opens avenues for future research in this area.

title: Towards co-evolution of fitness predictors and Deep Neural Networks
Abstract: The co-evolution of fitness predictors and deep neural networks represents a critical component in the ongoing pursuit of developing more efficient and effective machine learning strategies, particularly within the realm of evolving artificial neural networks. Given that the optimal performance of deep neural networks heavily relies on the pre-evaluation of fitness functions that often require manual tuning of various hyperparameters, establishing an evolutionary synergy between these two pivotal components significantly enhances overall efficiency. By integrating learning mechanisms for both fitness functions and neural networks in a mutually intertwined and adaptive framework, it becomes possible to incrementally update and refine the associated components as the system progresses, allowing for real-time responsiveness to various evolving complexities. The objective of this research is to critically investigate the co-evolution of these fundamental elements by integrating them within a unified framework, harnessing powerful optimization strategies such as genetic algorithms and swarm intelligence procedures for evolving both fitness functions and neural networks in a highly interdependent yet dynamically adaptable manner. Ultimately, our aim is to guide the development of more comprehensive, flexible, and performance-driven deep neural network models capable of adapting to increasingly intricate data distributions and effectively addressing the growing requirements associated with Big Data applications.

title: Compare, Compress and Propagate: Enhancing Neural Architectures with Alignment Factorization for Natural Language Inference
Abstract: This work presents a novel neural architecture that incorporates alignment factorization to enhance natural language inference, specifically in the task of recognizing textual entailment. By leveraging the key idea of alignment between the premises and hypotheses in a given text pair, our method, dubbed Align-Transform-Unify (ATU), effectively captures complex semantic relationships pertinent to entailment prediction. ATU achieves this by first comparing the input text pairs, followed by a compression step aimed at extracting essential context, and finally propagating the obtained features through a unifying transformation module dedicated to aligning the relevant semantic information. The proposed architecture is demonstrated to outperform state-of-the-art models on three benchmark datasets for natural language inference, including Stanford Natural Language Inference (SNLI), Multi-Genre Natural Language Inference (MultiNLI), and Natural Language Inference (NLI) using diverse ensemble methods. Moreover, we explore the strengths of alignment factorization and abstraction through a series of experiments showcasing variable input lengths, training paradigms and data combinations. In doing so, the findings validate the efficiency and robustness of ATU and support its potential applicability in a vast range of real-world textual entailment tasks, particularly those involving large-scale language models.

title: Parameter-free online learning via model selection
Abstract: Our research focuses on devising a parameter-free online learning approach for model selection, an area crucial in machine learning where the choice of model significantly influences the performance of the learning system. Existing methods often rely on specific parametric assumptions, which may not be suitable for various real-world scenarios. This has led to a gap in understanding how models adapt and generalize online without imposing such constraints. In this investigation, we combine theoretical and applied insights to address a fundamental question: can we construct a parameter-free online learning framework that allows model selection without imposing explicit constraints on the underlying data distribution? To achieve this, we leverage the concept of discrepancy, which quantifies the difference between empirical and population loss functions. Specifically, we derive a novel adaptive model selection criterion based on discrepancy, incorporating a provably efficient algorithm to minimize it online, while ensuring that the loss remains bounded over time. Our results demonstrate that this adaptive approach can effectively adapt to changing environments and outperform parameter-constrained methods, making it an attractive solution for practical applications where adaptability is essential. By eliminating the requirement for explicit parameter tuning, our parameter-free online learning framework via model selection offers a powerful tool for tackling complex real-world problems where adaptability is critical.

title: Towards automated patient data cleaning using deep learning: A feasibility study on the standardization of organ labeling
Abstract: This study explores the feasibility of using deep learning for automated patient data cleaning, specifically the standardization of organ labeling, which is a critical task in medical image analysis. Existing deep learning models can identify various organs in medical images, but their performance degrades when these images have inconsistent and unclear labels. The proposed approach utilizes transfer learning combined with active learning to address the limitation of annotated data, where human annotators label a subset of images and the deep learning model infers labels for the remaining images. By evaluating the performance of deep learning models on a dataset of annotated images with inconsistent labels, this research aims to determine the potential of the proposed approach in achieving high accuracy in standardizing organ labels, which can facilitate faster clinical trials and improve personalized medicine. The results show that the combination of transfer learning and active learning can improve the performance of deep learning models in standardizing organ labels, thus validating the feasibility of this approach for automated patient data cleaning. Abstract: The proliferation of online news sources and financial market volatility has created a pressing need for effective sentiment analysis in financial news to inform investment decisions. title: Learning Structural Weight Uncertainty for Sequential Decision-Making
Abstract: Sequential decision-making is a fundamental task in various fields such as robotics, finance, and healthcare. However, many decision-making models fail to accurately capture the underlying uncertainty associated with system dynamics, leading to suboptimal choices. A key aspect of system dynamics is structural weight uncertainty, which arises from partial knowledge of the system's underlying structure. Ignoring this uncertainty can result in aggressive adaptation that may cause instability in the decision-making process. To address this challenge, learning structural weight uncertainty is essential for making better decisions. We propose a novel approach to learning structural weight uncertainty using a probabilistic framework that models weights as a Markov-dragon distribution. The Markov-dragon distribution introduces a set of fixed points, from which a sequence of weights can grow or shrink to adapt to the underlying noise. This approach enables effective adaptation by scaling the weight assignments based on the severity of the predictions, resulting in more resilient and trustworthy decision-making. Additionally, our approach is amenable to online learning and efficient in terms of computational cost. Experimenting with standard problems, we demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in learning structural weight uncertainty, and its performance benefits in terms of learning speed and decision-making accuracy compared to state-of-the-art models.

title: Face Synthesis from Visual Attributes via Sketch using Conditional VAEs and GANs
Abstract: Our work explores the novel task of face synthesis from visual attributes via sketches. This aims to bridge the gap between sketch-based face generation and high-fidelity face synthesis. Traditional face synthesis methods heavily reliant on complex 3D face models, facial landmarks, or direct photorealistic renderings often fall short in replicating diverse and intricate facial characteristics. To circumvent these limitations, we propose a conditioning framework combining the versatility of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) and the probabilistic generative power of Conditional Variational Autoencoders (VAEs). The conditioned VAE, specifically designed to address the challenge of limited sketch input, learns to disentangle and capture facial attributes while maintaining delicate facial features. By integrating this disentangled representation with a GAN-based facial generation module, we create a synergistic system that leverages the complementary strengths of both architectures to produce photorealistic face images from sparse sketches. Our comprehensive quantitative evaluation encompasses both qualitative and quantitative metrics, highlighting remarkable improvements in generating anatomically accurate and diverse faces with varying attributes. title: Particle Clustering Machine: A Dynamical System Based Approach
Abstract: This study introduces a novel approach to particle clustering, referred to as the Particle Clustering Machine (PCM), utilizing a dynamical system-based framework to detect and categorize clusters within a particle population. The PCM integrates concepts from machine learning and dynamical systems theory to effectively model the emergent behavior of particles interacting within a shared environment. By representing particle populations as interconnected dynamical systems, the PCM generates a network that automatically identifies the spatial structures and temporal patterns forming within the system. Based on the theoretical foundation of complex networks and stability analysis, the approach leverages the unique properties of the network, such as degree distribution, clustering coefficient, and spectral properties, to infer the presence and characteristics of clusters. Empirical evaluations conducted on both synthetic and real-world datasets suggest that the PCM can accurately detect and describe particle clusters with unprecedented robustness and efficacy relative to existing machine learning methods. Furthermore, the approach facilitates a deeper understanding of the inherent dynamics of particle aggregation and its dependency on system properties, opening up avenues for the optimization of clustering algorithms in a wide range of applications, including particle physics, astro-particles, and materials science. title: Dendritic error backpropagation in deep cortical microcircuits
Abstract: Dendritic error backpropagation in deep cortical microcircuits is a novel approach to understanding neural computation in the brain. Analysis of the cortical microcircuit architecture shows that both feedforward and feedback connections play a critical role in this computational process, facilitating the flow of information through bidirectional circuits. Furthermore, simulations demonstrate that the developed dendritic error backpropagation scheme can be integrated with stochastic synapses and neuromodulatory inputs, leading to more robust and flexible neural representations. These findings have critical implications for understanding how the cerebral cortex enables complex processing in early sensory analysis, decision-making, and memory formation. title: f-Divergence constrained policy improvement
Abstract: This paper focuses on policy improvement in reinforcement learning constrained by the f-divergence metric, which is a generalization of the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence. The f-divergence provides a more flexible framework for evaluating the difference between two probability distributions, making it a suitable choice for constrained policy improvement. The goal of constrained policy improvement is to find a policy that maximizes a reward function while satisfying a distributional constraint, which is typically enforced using an f-divergence upper bound. We propose a novel approach for constrained policy improvement using f-divergence upper bounds, where the policy is optimized using an alternating optimization scheme that iteratively updates the policy and the f-divergence upper bound. Our method, referred to as f-divergence constrained policy improvement (FDCPI), leverages the properties of f-divergence to efficiently explore the policy improvement space and constraints. FDCPI is capable of handling large and complex environments while efficiently navigating the trade-off between policy improvement and distributional constraint satisfaction. Through a series of experiments, we demonstrate the efficacy of FDCPI in various reinforcement learning domains, showing competitive performance against state-of-the-art methods. Our experimental results provide strong evidence for the potential of FDCPI in real-world applications and contribute to the advancement of constrained policy improvement techniques in reinforcement learning.

title: Deep Reinforcement Learning for Unsupervised Video Summarization with Diversity-Representativeness Reward

The proposed framework relies on a reinforcement learning architecture, where an agent learns to select the most pertinent segments from a video based on a custom-designed reward function that balances between two primary objectives: maximizing diversity and maintaining representativeness. This duality ensures that the generated summaries are both diverse, covering a broad range of key events and actions, and representative, conveying the essential information and storyline of the original video. By using a state-of-the-art video encoder and a carefully curved reward function, the agent learns to navigate the complexities of video structures, weights, and preferences of the content. The model is evaluated on several benchmark video datasets, demonstrating noticeable enhancements in terms of numerical metrics such as F1-score, BLEU, and MSVD, which indicate higher peak engagement and correlation to the human perception of video content quality. title: Characterizing optimal hierarchical policy inference on graphs via non-equilibrium thermodynamics
Abstract: This work explores the application of non-equilibrium thermodynamics principles to the inference of optimal hierarchical policies on graphs, a problem of significant interest in complex system modeling and analysis. Traditional approaches to hierarchical policy inference often rely on equilibrium-based methods, which may not adequately capture the dynamics and inefficiencies inherent in real-world systems. In contrast, non-equilibrium thermodynamics offers a framework for analyzing systems far from equilibrium, where energy and entropy transport play crucial roles. We develop a novel inference framework, rooted in the non-equilibrium thermodynamic concepts of entropy production and free energy, to estimate optimal hierarchical policies on graph-structured systems. Our approach involves formulating the policy inference problem as a non-equilibrium thermodynamic process, where the optimal policy corresponds to the minimum free energy configuration. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method on a range of synthetic and real-world graph systems, showing significant improvements in policy accuracy and efficiency compared to conventional equilibrium-based methods. Furthermore, we provide analytical insights into the relationship between entropy production and policy optimality, shedding light on the thermodynamic underpinnings of complex system behavior. The proposed framework has potential applications in a variety of domains, including network science, control theory, and econophysics, where understanding and optimizing complex system behavior is paramount.

title: Non-negative Matrix Factorization: Robust Extraction of Extended Structures
Abstract: Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF) has emerged as a powerful tool for extracting interpretable and meaningful representations from high-dimensional data. A crucial challenge in NMF is the extraction of extended structures that exhibit a non-local and hierarchical organization, such as long-range correlations and multi-scale patterns. This is particularly relevant in datasets that exhibit complex dynamics and relationships, where local features alone may not suffice to capture the essence of the data. conventional NMF methods often struggle to recover extended structures due to their reliance on local approximations and the inherent sparsity of the non-negative factorization. To address this limitation, we propose a novel NMF framework based on a combination of non-local and hierarchical features. Our approach incorporates a multiscale diffusion process to capture long-range correlations and a hierarchical representation learning mechanism to distill the essence of multi-scale patterns. Furthermore, we introduce a robust optimization scheme to deal with noise and outliers, allowing our method to effectively extract extended structures even from noisy and incomplete data. Through a range of experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets, we demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in discovering extended structures and comparing our work to other standard models, we have achieved impressive performances and robust results. title: A Unified Bayesian Inference Framework for Generalized Linear Models
Abstract: This abstract describes a novel Bayesian inference framework for Generalized Linear Models (GLMs), encompassing both likelihood-based and Bayesian perspectives. Through the implementation of Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) and variational Bayesian methods, the framework enables researchers to employ approximate inference techniques, mitigating computational limitations associated with the traditional Bayesian model. title: SBEED: Convergent Reinforcement Learning with Nonlinear Function Approximation
Abstract: This paper presents a new approach to convergence-critical reinforcement learning known as SBEED, which incorporates global nonlinear function approximation into a variant of natural actor-critic methods. SBEED uses the entropy method to measure a comprehensive exploration bonus, using a combination of the TD-error and the sample state-action visitation count, hence achieving true probabilistic distribution over exploration states. Unlike past methods, SBEED converges under significantly weaker assumptions which enable the use of policy-based deep reinforcement learning in a model-free fashion with provable convergence. Furthermore, our experiments demonstrate that utilization of nonlinear function approximation significantly outperforms past approaches, such as the natural actor-critic method and SARSA using linear function approximation. title: Large-Scale Experiment on the Importance of Social Learning and Unimodality in the Wisdom of the Crowd
Abstract: This paper presents a systematic large-scale experiment investigating the critical roles of social learning and unimodality in the emergence of the wisdom of the crowd phenomenon. The findings of our study reveal that incorporating unimodality significantly enhances the collective decision-making accuracy, substantially reducing error rates when working with unimodal data. title: Boosting the Actor with Dual Critic
Abstract: This work presents a novel approach to reinforcement learning by introducing a dual critic architecture designed to improve the actor's performance in complex decision-making environments. The dual critic framework combines two separate critics, one learning the state value function and the other learning the state-action value function, to provide more comprehensive and accurate value estimations. By leveraging this dual critic setup, the actor can benefit from enhanced guidance and more informed decision-making, ultimately leading to improved policy performance and faster convergence. A key aspect of this approach is the ability to learn a more reliable and informative critic, which translates to more confident and accurate actor updates. title: A Stochastic Trust Region Algorithm Based on Careful Step Normalization
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel stochastic trust region algorithm that integrates careful step normalization to effectively balance global convergence and fast local convergence rates. The proposed algorithm, STN-TR, operates on a trust region framework that iteratively updates the model parameters through minimization and explores the solution space through careful normalization of the step size. To achieve fast local convergence, careful normalization maintains the step size within a predetermined range and prevents oscillations around local minima. On the other hand, STN-TR leverages stochastic gradient descent for efficient exploration of the global landscape. By utilizing a combination of batch-averaged gradient information and randomly sampled mini-batches, the algorithm adapts to both globally sparse and locally dense regions of the model, leading to improved convergence rates. As a result, STN-TR exhibits robustness and flexibility in handling diverse types of optimization landscapes, including those with ill-conditioning and partial linearity. Using extensive numerical experiments and comparisons with state-of-the-art algorithms, this study demonstrates the efficacy of the proposed framework, showcasing its ability to provide faster convergence and improved solution quality on a wide range of test problems. The method has applications in various machine learning domains where trust region optimization plays a pivotal role, highlighting its potential for efficient model training and optimization. title: Using abstract elastic membranes to learn about quantum measurements

title: Deep Learning Interior Tomography for Region-of-Interest Reconstruction
Abstract: Deep learning has revolutionized image reconstruction techniques in computed tomography (CT), allowing for faster, more accurate, and higher-quality imaging. Unlike traditional interior tomography methods that rely on mathematical models and iterative methods, DeepInterior leverages the power of deep neural networks to directly learn the mapping between raw measurement data and reconstructed images. title: Scalable Multi-Domain Dialogue State Tracking
Abstract: This paper proposes a scalable multi-domain dialogue state tracking framework that leverages advancements in deep learning and graph neural networks to accurately track user preferences and intents across multiple domains. The framework comprises three key components: a domain-agnostic dialogue state tracker, a domain-specific feature extractor, and a graph neural network-based fusion module. The domain-agnostic tracker is trained to predict high-level dialogue states that can be shared across domains, while the domain-specific feature extractor captures domain-specific nuances and trends. The graph neural network-based fusion module then aggregates the outputs from both components to obtain a comprehensive understanding of the user's intents and preferences across all domains. title: Learning Deep Similarity Models with Focus Ranking for Fabric Image Retrieval
Abstract: Deep similarity models have revolutionized the field of image retrieval by enabling accurate and efficient matching of images based on their semantic content. title: Quantum Lower Bounds for Tripartite Versions of the Hidden Shift and the Set Equality Problems
Abstract: This paper investigates the lower bounds of quantum algorithms for solving tripartite versions of the Hidden Shift and the Set Equality problems, two classic problems in quantum information processing and query complexity. We provide a formal definition of the tripartite Hidden Shift problem and its generalization, as well as the tripartite Set Equality problem, and explore the implications of these problems for quantum query complexity. By analyzing the tripartite Hidden Shift problem, we demonstrate that a tripartite version of the Discrete Log problem in the Hidden Shift problem, which is known to require quantum super-polynomial time, seems to require a more complex approach to obtain polynomial-time bounds. Our work, while not conclusive, suggests that a polynomial-time quantum algorithm for the tripartite version of this problem might be unfeasible. We use known reductions from Set Equality problems to other problems, such as Boolean Circuit, and analyze the tripartite version of those problems. Furthermore, we find a relationship between our setup and the decision version of the Element Distinctness problem, as studied in the context of quantum query complexity. Our findings can serve as a starting point for future study on quantum lower bounds for these important problems in quantum information processing.

title: Non-linear motor control by local learning in spiking neural networks

title: Significance of Softmax-based Features in Comparison to Distance Metric Learning-based Features
Abstract: This research delves into the realm of deep learning and explores the significance of softmax-based features in comparison to distance metric learning-based features in various machine learning applications. title: Learning Deep and Compact Models for Gesture Recognition

The goal is to create models that strike a balance between accuracy and model complexity, enabling their deployment on devices with limited computational resources. Traditional deep learning models, such as convolutional neural networks (CNNs), have exhibited impressive performance in various computer vision tasks, including gesture recognition. However, these models often result in large memory footprints and slow inference times, making them impractical for real-time applications on edge devices. To address this challenge, we propose a novel approach that combines knowledge distillation and compact model design to craft efficient and accurate gesture recognition models. Our approach involves distilling knowledge from a large pre-trained teacher network to a smaller student network, while applying various compact model design techniques to minimize the model's size and computational requirements. Through extensive experiments on several benchmark datasets, we demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, showcasing significant reductions in model size and inference time without compromising recognition accuracy. Our results highlight the potential of deep and compact models in enabling seamless gesture recognition on resource-constrained devices, paving the way for novel applications in human-computer interaction, robotics, and beyond.

title: The Multilinear Structure of ReLU Networks
Abstract: This study provides a comprehensive analysis of the multilinear structure inherent in ReLU (Rectified Linear Unit) networks. By leveraging tensor algebraic techniques and graph theory, we demonstrate that the activation patterns within ReLU networks give rise to a multilinear structure that can be decomposed into a low-dimensional subspace. This structure captures the key information flow within the network, enabling a significant reduction in the dimensionality of the activation space. Furthermore, we show that the multilinear structure allows for a more accurate and efficient prediction of the network's output, as well as improved interpretability of the results. Our findings are validated through extensive experimental results on a variety of benchmark datasets, including MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100. By shedding light on the underlying multilinear structure of ReLU networks, our work contributes to a deeper understanding of neural network dynamics and highlights the potential benefits of leveraging this structure in neural architecture and optimization. Our results also show that the multilinear structure of ReLU networks can be exploited to develop more efficient and interpretable deep learning models, which is a crucial step towards the broader adoption of artificial intelligence in real-world applications.

title: Beyond Keywords and Relevance: A Personalized Ad Retrieval Framework in E-Commerce Sponsored Search
Abstract: This paper presents a novel personalized ad retrieval framework for e-commerce sponsored search that moves beyond traditional keyword-based and relevance-focused approaches. Our framework, dubbed 'PersonaMatch,' utilizes a user-centric and context-aware strategy to match users with products that cater to their individual preferences and shopping behaviors. By leveraging a combination of machine learning algorithms, natural language processing techniques, and user profiling details, PersonaMatch aims to improve the accuracy and effectiveness of product recommendation ads in sponsored search results. To achieve this, our framework first constructs a comprehensive user profile that incorporates demographic information, search history, browsing behavior, and purchasing patterns. Next, it integrates this user profile with product information and semantic knowledge graph data to identify relevant and personalized ad matches. A hybrid recommendation strategy is then employed to prioritize product advertising offers that are not only relevant to the user's search query but also align with their distinct shopping personas. Empirical evaluation of our proposed framework on a large-scale e-commerce dataset demonstrates significant improvements in ad click-through rates, conversion rates, and overall user satisfaction in comparison to conventional keyword-based ad retrieval approaches.

title: Objective evaluation metrics for automatic classification of EEG events
Abstract: This study aims to develop a framework for objective evaluation metrics to assess the performance of automatic classification models in event-related electroencephalography (EEG) analysis. Current evaluation methods rely heavily on subject-specific metrics, such as area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), and do not account for the variability in EEG signals across different subjects and electrode placements. To address this limitation, this research proposes a novel set of metrics that incorporate data-driven approaches to quantify the accuracy of the classification models. Specifically, we developed metrics that evaluate the performance of the models across different electrode combinations, training protocols, and task categories, allowing for a more comprehensive assessment of the model's capabilities. Using publicly available EEG datasets, we conducted a performance comparison of four machine learning algorithms on event-related potentials associated with visual, auditory, and motor responses. Our results demonstrate that the proposed metrics provide significant insights into the strengths and weaknesses of the classification models, which can enhance the development and deployment of effective EEG-based neurotechnology applications. The findings of this study have important implications for researchers working on event-related potential analysis and contribute to the development of more robust and generalizable evaluation metrics for automatic EEG classification.

title: Generation of Bose-Einstein Condensates' Ground State Through Machine Learning
Abstract: This study explores the application of machine learning algorithms to generate the ground state of Bose-Einstein Condensates (BECs), a state of matter predicted by statistical mechanics. By leveraging the inherent complexity of BECs, our research utilizes machine learning techniques to iteratively approach the ground state, effectively reducing the computational cost of solving the mean-field Gross-Pitaevskii equation, a widely used mathematical model in BECs research. Our approach combines a variational ansatz, which constructs a set of candidate wave functions, with a machine learning-driven optimization process, based on the minimization of the energy functional. Training on a set of numerical solutions obtained via the full Gross-Pitaevskii equation, our model learns to approximate the ground-state wave function through its own learning process. A novel architecture, based on a combination of convolutional and recurrent neural networks, is employed to enhance the capacity of the ansatz to capture the complex structure of the ground state. The experimental results demonstrate an order-of-magnitude decrease in computational time relative to brute-force direct methods, making the proposed framework an attractive tool for large-scale computational studies of BECs in condensed matter physics.

title: Finite-sample risk bounds for maximum likelihood estimation with arbitrary penalties
Abstract: Maximum likelihood estimation is a fundamental component of statistical modeling, yet its performance can be drastically altered by the choice of penalty in penalized likelihood estimation. In this paper, we derive finite-sample risk bounds for maximum likelihood estimation with arbitrary penalties. Our results reveal that the optimal penalty depends not only on the true underlying distribution of the data but also on the spectral properties of the Hessian matrix of the log-likelihood function. By leveraging recent advances in learning theory and the theory of convex optimization, we are able to establish non-asymptotic risk bounds for penalized maximum likelihood estimation that hold with high probability. Our bounds are general enough to encompass a wide range of penalty functions, including L1, L2, and elastic net penalties. We demonstrate the applicability of our results through numerical simulations and illustrate how our risk bounds can be used to choose the penalty parameter in practice. Furthermore, we derive a data-driven method for selecting the optimal penalty, which relies on a finite-sample estimate of the spectral norm of the Hessian matrix. Our method is simple to implement and requires minimal prior knowledge of the underlying data distribution. By providing a finite-sample performance guarantee for maximum likelihood estimation with arbitrary penalties, our work contributes to a more comprehensive understanding of the trade-offs involved in penalized likelihood estimation and paves the way for more robust inference in high-dimensional statistical models.

title: Recent Advances in Recurrent Neural Networks
Abstract: Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) have been instrumental in modeling sequential data for a wide range of applications, from speech recognition to natural language processing and time series forecasting. Despite their popularity, traditional RNNs have been plagued by vanishing and exploding gradients, which hinder the effective training of deep models. To address these limitations, recent advances have focused on developing novel architectures and training algorithms that enhance the performance and stability of RNNs. One significant breakthrough has been the introduction of gated feedback mechanisms, such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) and Gated Recurrent Units (GRU), which improve the flow of information through the network and allow for the efficient processing of long-term dependencies. Another area of research has focused on exploring different learning objectives and regularization techniques, including teacher forcing, sequence-wise optimization, and early stopping, which facilitate more effective and efficient training procedures. Additionally, recent work has investigated the use of attention mechanisms to selectively focus on relevant regions of the input sequence, further improving the accuracy and interpretability of RNN-based models. These advances have not only enabled the development of more accurate and robust RNN models but also have opened up new possibilities for a wide range of applications, from automatic speech recognition and machine translation to sentiment analysis and recommendation systems.

title: Application of Convolutional Neural Network to Predict Airfoil Lift Coefficient
Abstract: This research paper explores the application of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) in predicting the lift coefficient of airfoils, a critical parameter in aerodynamics. The increasing demand for efficient and accurate aerodynamic analysis has led to the integration of machine learning techniques, such as CNNs, into Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) simulations. A dataset of 3D airfoil geometries and corresponding lift coefficients is employed to train a CNN model, allowing it to learn the complex relationships between geometry characteristics and aerodynamic performance. The trained CNN model is then used to predict the lift coefficient of new, unseen airfoil geometries, demonstrating a high degree of accuracy and reliability. Additionally, a sensitivity analysis is performed to identify the most influential geometry features contributing to the lift coefficient, providing valuable insights for airfoil design and optimization. The results show that the CNN model can predict the lift coefficient with a mean absolute error of 0.012, significantly outperforming traditional physics-based methods. Furthermore, the application of CNNs to airfoil analysis opens up new avenues for aerodynamic research and design, enabling the optimization of airfoils for various aerodynamic applications. The research contributes to the development of more efficient and accurate aerodynamic analysis tools, ultimately enhancing the performance of aerospace vehicles.
