title: Reinforcement Learning with Analogical Similarity to Guide Schema Induction and Attention
Abstract: Reinforcement learning has emerged as a promising approach to schema induction, allowing agents to discover meaningful patterns and relationships in complex, high-dimensional environments. However, discovering these patterns is a daunting task, especially when data is noisy or ambiguous. To alleviate this challenge, this work proposes a novel approach that leverages analogical similarity to guide both schema induction and attention in reinforcement learning. By utilizing the cognitive process of analogy-making, our method enables agents to identify relevant patterns and relationships between different entities and environments, allowing for a more effective and efficient exploration of the state space. The proposed approach consists of an analogical similarity-based exploration strategy, which encourages agents to focus on regions of the state space that share similar characteristics with previously visited states. This strategy complements an attention mechanism that selectively highlights the most relevant features and relationships within the agent's perception of the environment. Through a series of experiments and evaluations, we demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed approach in a variety of scenarios, including both simple and complex environments, showcasing its ability to efficiently discover meaningful patterns and relationships and ultimately achieve better performance in reinforcement learning tasks. Overall, this work presents a significant step forward in the integration of cognitive principles and reinforcement learning, highlighting the potential of analogical reasoning to guide schema induction and attention in complex cognitive systems.

title: Active Robotic Mapping through Deep Reinforcement Learning
Abstract: This research explores the application of deep reinforcement learning in active robotic mapping, enabling robots to efficiently gather environment information and construct a faithful map. Current mapping approaches often rely on exhaustive exploration, which can be impractical and time-consuming, particularly in large or complex environments. In contrast, our proposed active mapping framework uses an on-policy actor-critic method to sample the environment in an informed and exploratory manner. The framework integrates a state-of-the-art deep reinforcement learning algorithm with a geometrical mapping approach, allowing the robot to select actions that maximize the likelihood of encountering new features and landmarks while minimizing the traversal of redundant spaces. To evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed method, we conduct a series of experiments in both simulated and real-world environments, including a large warehouse and a cluttered outdoor scene. Our results demonstrate that the proposed active mapping approach can significantly reduce the mapping time and improve the accuracy of the constructed map compared to traditional approaches. Furthermore, our framework can adapt to changing environments and situations, making it suitable for real-world deployment. The potential applications of this research include areas such as autonomous robotics, terrain exploration, and search and rescue operations.

title: Multi-timescale memory dynamics in a reinforcement learning network with attention-gated memory
Abstract: This study delves into the intricate dynamics of a reinforcement learning network that incorporates an attention-gated memory mechanism, seeking to elucidate the role of multi-timescale memory processes in decision-making and learning. By implementing a novel attention-gated memory architecture within a deep reinforcement learning framework, our model is able to selectively concentrate on task-relevant knowledge from varying temporal scales, thereby fostering more efficient and adaptive learning. Theoretical analyses and numerical simulations reveal that the proposed network exhibits a complex interplay between short-term and long-term memory, wherein the attention mechanism plays a pivotal role in dynamically allocating memory resources according to the demands of the tasks at hand. Our results demonstrate that this multi-timescale memory architecture significantly enhances the network's capability to learn and generalize across various reinforcement learning environments, including those that are characterized by temporally distant rewards. Furthermore, we provide an in-depth exploration of the emergent memory dynamics within the network, shedding light on the importance of attention-gated memory in shaping the trade-off between exploration and exploitation in decision-making processes. The insights gained from this study have the potential to significantly advance our understanding of intelligent decision-making in complex environments, and may inform the development of more sophisticated and adaptable artificial intelligence systems capable of mastering a wide range of real-world tasks.

title: Corpus specificity in LSA and Word2vec: the role of out-of-domain documents
Abstract: This study investigates the impact of out-of-domain documents on the performance of two popular word representation models: Latent Semantic Analysis (LSA) and Word2vec. While both models have been successful in capturing semantic relationships within a given corpus, they often rely on internal contextual information, which may not always be reliable or representative of the entire domain. The role of out-of-domain documents in augmenting the representational power of these models is examined by manipulating the proportions of in-domain to out-of-domain documents within the corpus. Our analysis shows that the incorporation of out-of-domain documents can improve the semantic coherence of LSA models, whereas Word2vec models exhibit a more nuanced behavior, with some domains benefiting from the additional data and others being negatively affected. These findings have significant implications for the application of these models in real-world tasks, such as text classification, sentiment analysis, and information retrieval. We also discuss the potential benefits and drawbacks of incorporating out-of-domain data, as well as the trade-offs between domain-specific and generalizable representations. This research provides new insights into the role of corpus specificity in LSA and Word2vec, and sheds light on the importance of evaluating these models in the context of their respective domains of application.

title: Kernel Robust Bias-Aware Prediction under Covariate Shift
Abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to kernel robust bias-aware prediction under covariate shift, a scenario where the distribution of the input data changes between training and testing phases. Our proposed method, Bayesian Kernel Covariate Shift Adaptation with Bias Correction, combines a Bayesian kernel approach with an adaptive covariate shift correction mechanism to handle the bias introduced by the distribution mismatch. The method incorporates a novel bias-aware covariance estimation strategy, which leverages the Bayesian framework to quantify the uncertainty associated with the covariate shift correction. Additionally, our approach employs a robust kernel learning method to minimize the impact of noise and outliers in the input data. We perform extensive experiments on several benchmark datasets to evaluate the performance of our proposed method under various scenarios of covariate shift. The results demonstrate significant improvements over existing algorithms in terms of accuracy and robustness. By adaptively adjusting the bias correction term and the kernel parameters, our approach is able to achieve superior performance on both seen and unseen data, showcasing its efficacy in handling covariate shift in real-world applications. The proposed method has potential applications in fields such as computer vision, natural language processing, and healthcare, where covariate shift is a common challenge.

title: Robust Covariate Shift Prediction with General Losses and Feature Views
Abstract: This paper addresses the critical problem of predicting covariate shifts in machine learning models, particularly under general loss functions and diverse feature views. Covariate shift occurs when the underlying distribution of the training data differs from that of the test data, leading to a significant decrease in model performance. Traditional covariate shift prediction methods often rely on restrictive assumptions, such as linearity in the relationship between the mean and variance of the covariates. By contrast, our proposed approach leverages a novel meta-learning framework that generalizes to various loss functions and feature representations. This framework exploits the relationship between the underlying distribution of the test data and the empirical distribution of the training data, estimating the covariate shift using a learned neural network. Our approach is based on a two-stage learning procedure: first, a domain-invariant feature extractor is learned to minimize the spectral norm of the Jacobian matrix of the learned embedding with respect to the input features; second, a shift predictor is trained to forecast the covariate shift based on the extracted features and a set of auxiliary tasks. Experimental evaluations demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach across multiple loss functions and feature views, achieving superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods in predicting covariate shifts for various machine learning models, including neural networks, decision trees, and support vector machines.

title: Discriminative and Geometry Aware Unsupervised Domain Adaptation
Abstract: The rapid growth of deep learning has empowered various applications, however, most models are trained within isolated domains or datasets, leading to performance degradation when applied to unknown target domains or seen environments with different distributions and sources. Therefore, unsupervised domain adaptation has emerged to bridge this gap and transfer knowledge across different domains. This paper, termed Discriminative and Geometry Aware Unsupervised Domain Adaptation, presents a novel framework that combines the advantages of discriminative feature learning and geometry aware adaptation methods. The framework consists of two main steps, where the first step revolves around learning a discriminative feature representation that is invariant to domain shifts, while the second step is geared towards incorporating geometry aware adaptation techniques to adjust for domain-specific geometric variations. The proposed framework leverages the geometric information of source and target domains together with the discriminative feature learning capability, which exhibits remarkable adaptability and robustness under various domain adaptation scenarios. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmark datasets, including Office-31, DomainNet, and VisDA-2017, validate the efficacy of the proposed framework in achieving state-of-the-art performance in unsupervised domain adaptation tasks, demonstrating the potential of this research approach in facilitating real-world applications in computer vision and beyond.

title: Debiased Machine Learning of Set-Identified Linear Models
Abstract: This paper addresses a crucial challenge in machine learning: debiasing linear models for set-identified parameters. Set-identification occurs when a specific parameter can take on multiple values, and exact identification of the true value is impossible. In such cases, conventional machine learning methods may produce biased estimates, leading to inaccurate conclusions. We propose a novel approach to debias the set-identified linear models, focusing on the properties of the set-identified region. Our method uses an empirical likelihood-based weighted meta-learning strategy to derive unbiased expectation and variance estimates from the obtained set-identified model predictions. In doing so, we demonstrate sufficient conditions for exact debiasing, providing insights into the relationship between the set-identified region and the likelihood of each potential parameter value. Furthermore, extensive experiments are conducted to evaluate the effectiveness and the robustness of our approach on synthetic and real-world data sets. Results show that our method not only achieves unbiased estimates but also outperforms existing models in terms of precision and reliability in predictive performance, showcasing the competitive superiority of our approach in set-identified linear models. Our findings offer important implications for both researchers and practitioners, providing a practical guide to deriving unbiased and precise likelihood estimates using the novel debiasing strategy.

title: Parallel Active Subspace Decomposition for Scalable and Efficient Tensor Robust Principal Component Analysis
Abstract: Tensor Robust Principal Component Analysis (Tensor RPCA) is a crucial technique for decomposing massive noisy and incomplete multi-dimensional data into low-rank and sparse components. As the size of modern data grows exponentially, the existing algorithms for Tensor RPCA often suffer from the curse of dimensionality, prohibiting their scalability in real-world applications. To overcome this limitation, we propose an innovative parallel active subspace decomposition (PASD) framework for scalable and efficient Tensor RPCA. Our approach leverages the fact that real-world data often resides in a lower-dimensional subspace, and exploits this subspace to reduce the computational complexity. We first identify the active subspace of the original tensor using Principal Component Analysis (PCA), and then perform the low-rank and sparse decompositions in parallel on this reduced subspace. Our PASD framework significantly improves the scalability and efficiency of Tensor RPCA, by minimizing the computational cost and memory requirements. To demonstrate the efficacy of PASD, we conduct extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets, showcasing its superiority over state-of-the-art methods in terms of speedup, memory usage, and decomposition accuracy. Our results indicate that PASD is a promising solution for large-scale Tensor RPCA problems, paving the way for its adoption in various applications, such as computer vision, recommender systems, and finance.

title: Estimation and Inference on Heterogeneous Treatment Effects in High-Dimensional Dynamic Panels under Weak Dependence
Abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of estimating and making inferences on heterogeneous treatment effects in high-dimensional dynamic panels in the context of weak dependence, particularly in the presence of serial correlation and cross-sectional heterogeneity. A major limitation in current empirical research arises from the omission of key variables, underassessed uncertainty due to misspecified parameterizations, and computational constraints when dealing with high-dimensional datasets. By focusing on the local linear moment condition that incorporates both static and dynamic treatment effects, we propose an estimator that can effectively deal with high-dimensional and finite samples, making the estimation more feasible and accessible. As a critical step in achieving model adequacy, the empirical coverage probabilities and finite sample bias of the proposed estimator's confidence intervals are rigorous in numerical illustrations based on different data generating processes, suggesting that it outperforms its competitors in dealing with weak dependence and dimensionality. Moreover, the empirical analysis demonstrates that the proposed method enables model analysis of endogenous regressors to support valid inference across a range of practically relevant applications.

title: Random Feature-based Online Multi-kernel Learning in Environments with Unknown Dynamics
Abstract: This paper presents a novel online multi-kernel learning algorithm that relies on a random feature-based approach to adapt to environments with unknown dynamics. The proposed algorithm leverages a generative model to learn a probabilistic representation of the data, which is then used to construct a multi-kernel classifier. By incorporating a random feature transform, the algorithm can effectively approximate the data distribution and adapt to changes in the environment. Our approach differs from traditional online multi-kernel learning methods, which typically rely on spectral filtering or convex optimization techniques that can be computationally expensive and sensitive to the choice of kernel. In contrast, our algorithm is based on a sparse and efficient representation of the data, enabling it to handle high-dimensional data streams and online updates. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on a range of tasks, including classification and regression problems with varying degrees of nonlinearity and complexity. Notably, our algorithm outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy and robustness, particularly in environments with sudden changes in dynamics or when the true distribution of the data is significantly different from the initial assumptions. Our contributions include a computationally efficient online algorithm for adapting to unknown environments and a novel application of the random feature transform in the context of multi-kernel learning.

title: Social Bayesian Learning in the Wisdom of the Crowd
Abstract: Social Bayesian Learning in the Wisdom of the Crowd is a novel approach to understanding how individuals contribute to collective decision-making processes when uncertain. By leveraging the asymmetric and yet complementary nature of social and individual Bayes' updates, this framework explores an integrative method that enables the iterative fusion of subjective probabilities, creating an evolving collective knowledge base. Through modeling human subjective updates and the cognitive biases associated with individual confidence and trust evaluations, developers can identify robust factors facilitating group decision-making under uncertainty. Within this study, the analysis examines the interplay between social learning and information diffusion within a simulated Wisdom of the Crowd model and evaluates how patterns of confidence, reliability, and influence predictably emerge as group members act upon updates from others. Findings suggest the superiority of collective judgments resulting from iterative and probabilistic aggregation processes to traditional methods when confronted with open-ended, uncertainty-rich environments. Furthermore, by developing well-informed algorithms integrating both cognitive biases and adaptive learning strategies, the proposed model aims to enhance prediction performance while highlighting areas of improvement in human perception and calculation. The convergence between Bayesian perspectives and mechanisms, integrating interdependent inferences from subjective uncertainties, hence allows a truly integrated model of how group knowledge collaborates dynamically.

title: Minimizing Polarization and Disagreement in Social Networks
Abstract: This paper explores the issue of polarization and disagreement in social networks, where individuals with homogeneous beliefs and values often congregate, reinforcing their existing views and creating an environment conducive to dogmatic thinking. By leveraging insights from social psychology, network analysis, and computational modeling, we identify key factors contributing to the perpetuation of polarization, including echo chambers, algorithmic filtering, and confirmation bias. Our investigation reveals that social media platforms, often designed to maximize user engagement, inadvertently perpetuate polarization by highlighting conflictual views and demarcating individuals from opposing perspectives. To mitigate this issue, we propose a novel approach to redesign social network architectures that foster interaction and dialogue across ideologically disparate groups. This approach incorporates diverse algorithmic strategies, including activity-based ranking, community detection, and recommender systems, specifically crafted to stimulate cross-cutting discussions, counterbalance extreme views, and promote knowledge sharing. The architecture's efficacy is evaluated using a series of computational simulations and real-world social network data, demonstrating its ability to diminish polarization and increase engagement among individuals with diverse backgrounds and opinions. By creating a more inclusive and interconnected social media environment, this research aims to contribute to the development of healthier online communities, fostering civil discourse, and promoting social cohesion in the digital age.

title: Toward Continual Learning for Conversational Agents
Abstract: Conversational agents have been designed to mimic human-like conversations with users, and their performance has been shown to improve significantly with the incorporation of machine learning techniques. However, the current state of conversational agents' learning is primarily based on supervised learning paradigms which require large amounts of labeled data. The limitations of this approach become apparent when agents are faced with real-world scenarios where context, intent, and user behavior can change constantly. Continual learning for conversational agents is essential to cope with these challenges, where the agents can learn from the users without relying on additional human annotations. This research focuses on developing a framework for continual learning that allows conversational agents to learn from the users over time, adapt to new user behaviors and preferences, and improve their overall performance. We adopted a combination of online learning and transfer learning strategies, allowing the conversational agent to leverage knowledge from previous interactions while accommodating new information from continuous dialogues. Our approach involves the use of an incremental neural network that captures user and context-dependent information through a set of contextualized embeddings. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in real-world conversational scenarios, showcasing significant improvements in performance and user engagement. Furthermore, we discuss the implications of this work, pointing to the potential for applications in numerous areas including customer service, emotional support, and human-computer interaction.

title: Gradient Regularization Improves Accuracy of Discriminative Models
Abstract: Gradient regularization has emerged as a promising technique in improving the performance and robustness of discriminative models. While traditionally regularization techniques have focused on reducing overfitting by penalizing large model weights, gradient regularization introduces a regularization term directly related to the magnitude of the gradients of the loss function with respect to model parameters. This technique has been shown to effectively reduce overfitting and improve model generalization, particularly in deep learning models where gradient information is more insightful. By constraining the magnitude of the gradients, gradient regularization encourages models to produce more stable and less erratic updates, thereby increasing the likelihood of early convergence to a more optimal solution. Furthermore, gradient regularization has been observed to have a positive effect on the interpretability of model updates and can potentially provide deeper insights into the underlying data and decision-making processes of the model. In this work, we investigate the efficacy of gradient regularization in boosting the performance of discriminative models and explore its applicability across different model architectures and datasets. Our findings highlight the benefits of integrating gradient regularization as a standard component in model training and demonstrate its potential to revolutionize the field of discriminative modeling.

title: On the Challenges of Detecting Rude Conversational Behaviour
Abstract: Detecting rude conversational behaviour is a significant challenge in human-computer interaction due to the context-dependent and culturally nuanced nature of rude interactions. Researchers propose various computational models to detect rudeness, often relying on handcrafted features and machine learning approaches. However, current approaches have limitations, including ignoring contextual information, failing to capture subtle nuances, and being culturally biased. To address these challenges, this study develops a novel framework that incorporate multimodal inputs, including speech, text, and visual cues, to detect rude conversational behaviour in real-time. Employing a context-aware and rule-based approach, this framework tackles the lack of contextual information in traditional models. Furthermore, it integrates a sentiment analysis module with a multimodal fusion strategy to capture subtle nuances of human emotions. Additionally, to address the cultural bias challenge, the framework employs a multimodal diversity approach, enabling it to adapt to different cultural contexts. Through a large-scale database of real-world conversational data and user evaluations, this study demonstrates the efficacy of the proposed framework in detecting rude conversational behaviour, achieving state-of-the-art performance on a set of standard metrics. Implications of this research not only contribute to human-computer interaction but also provide valuable insights for the design of more empathetic conversational systems.

title: Rapid Adaptation with Conditionally Shifted Neurons
Abstract: Rapid adaptation in neural networks is a fundamental aspect of information processing and cognitive development, allowing organisms to efficiently and effectively respond to changes in their environment. However, the neural mechanisms underlying this adaptation process remain poorly understood. One promising avenue of research involves conditionally shifted neurons, which are cells that exhibit variable excitability in response to internal and external stimuli. This study explores the phenomenon of conditionally shifted neurons in the context of rapid adaptation, examining both the theoretical and experimental aspects of this phenomenon. Using a combination of computational modeling and electrophysiological recordings, we investigate how conditionally shifted neurons rapidly adjust their excitability to optimize information processing in the presence of changing inputs. Our results demonstrate that conditionally shifted neurons can adapt extremely rapidly to changes in input patterns, often within a matter of milliseconds. Additionally, our analysis reveals that the properties of conditionally shifted neurons, such as their excitability threshold and temporal dynamics, play a critical role in determining the speed and effectiveness of adaptation. These findings have important implications for our understanding of neural information processing and the development of novel artificial intelligence algorithms that can adapt to changing environments, and highlight the potential of conditionally shifted neurons as a key component of future neural prosthetics and brainachine interfaces. By shedding light on the neural mechanisms underlying rapid adaptation, we hope to inspire future research in this area and contribute to the development of more sophisticated models of neural information processing. The theoretical and experimental results presented here provide a foundation for further investigation into the role of conditionally shifted neurons in rapid adaptation, and pave the way for the development of novel artificial intelligence algorithms and neural prosthetics that can accurately and efficiently process complex information.

title: What do we need to build explainable AI systems for the medical domain?
Abstract: The development of explainable artificial intelligence (AI) systems is a growing need in the medical domain, where trustworthy decision-making is crucial for patient care and treatment outcomes. To build explainable AI systems for medical applications, we need a multidisciplinary approach that combines advances in machine learning, computer vision, natural language processing, and clinical expertise. This requires the integration of techniques such as feature attribution, model interpretability, and transparency methods to provide insights into how the AI system arrived at a particular decision. Furthermore, establishing a shared understanding of explainability and its requirements between AI researchers, clinicians, and patients is essential for the successful deployment of these systems in real-world healthcare settings. We also need to address the challenges associated with ensuring the fairness and accountability of AI decision-making processes, which can be particularly critical in high-stakes medical applications. Overall, building explainable AI systems for the medical domain requires a coordinated effort from various stakeholders, including AI researchers, clinicians, policymakers, and patients, to develop and validate the required techniques, tools, and regulations that ensure the safe and effective use of AI in healthcare. The development of explainable AI can lead to improved patient outcomes, increased trust in medical AI systems, and cost savings for the healthcare system.

title: Visualizing the Loss Landscape of Neural Nets
Abstract: Deep neural networks have become increasingly successful in various machine learning tasks by leveraging complex, nonlinear relationships between input features and model parameters. However, training these models poses various challenges due to the non-convex nature of their loss landscapes, which are composed of intertwined local minima, flat regions, and sharp saddles. Understanding the structure of these landscapes can provide valuable insights into the optimization algorithms used to train neural nets, as well as their generalization abilities. Recent studies have employed visualization techniques to map the loss landscapes of neural networks trained on specific datasets, often revealing intricate patterns and relationships between model parameters. However, the vast majority of these studies focus on small to moderate-sized datasets, limiting the general applicability of their findings. In order to advance our understanding of neural network loss landscapes, this work develops novel visualization techniques capable of efficiently mapping the landscapes of large, complex models trained on high-dimensional data. By employing dimensionality reduction methods and visualization tools, this research aims to shed light on the relationships between local minima, flat regions, and saddles in the loss landscapes of deep neural networks, ultimately informing the development of more efficient and effective optimization algorithms.

title: Improved Inception-Residual Convolutional Neural Network for Object Recognition
Abstract: This research presents an innovative extension to the Inception-Residual Convolutional Neural Network (Inception-ResNet), a deep neural network architecture designed for image classification tasks. The proposed architecture, termed Improved Inception-Residual Convolutional Neural Network (IIRCNN), focuses on addressing the limitations of the original Inception-ResNet model by incorporating a dual attention mechanism and introducing a novel layer, dubbed the Fusion-Conv block. The dual attention mechanism allows the network to selectively focus on salient features of the image, thereby enhancing its discriminative power. Meanwhile, the Fusion-Conv block facilitates the fusion of feature maps from different layers, enabling a more comprehensive and robust representation of the input image. The proposed architecture demonstrates remarkable improvements in object recognition accuracy compared to its predecessor, achieving state-of-the-art performance on popular benchmarks including ImageNet and CIFAR-10. Quantitative evaluations also reveal the IIRCNN's superior resistance to overfitting and its ability to generalize well across diverse datasets. Furthermore, extensive ablation studies and qualitative visualizations are provided to offer insights into the effects of the proposed components on the network's performance.

title: Handwritten Bangla Character Recognition Using The State-of-Art Deep Convolutional Neural Networks
Abstract: Handwritten Bangla character recognition is a complex task that has garnered significant attention in recent years, especially in the realm of regional language processing. This paper explores the feasibility of applying state-of-the-art deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs) for classifying Bangla handwritten characters. A comprehensive literature review reveals that existing approaches in Bangla OCR face challenges such as variability in writing styles, limited dataset size, and the presence of nuances in Bangla script. To bridge this knowledge gap, the study presents a comparative analysis of three pre-trained DCNN architectures, including VGG16, ResNet50, and MobileNet, for Bangla character recognition. The proposed approach involves data augmentation, pre-processing, and transfer learning techniques to improve the robustness and accuracy of the models. Experimental results reveal that the ResNet50 model yields the highest accuracy of 96.8% on a publicly available Bangla character dataset, outperforming other competitors. Furthermore, the study investigates the impact of dataset size on the performance of DCNNs and recommends appropriate data augmentation strategies for improving model generalizability. The findings provide crucial insights into the application of DCNNs for handwritten Bangla character recognition, paving the way for potential applications in Bangla text-based applications, including data entry, document analysis, and language translation systems.

title: Connecting Software Metrics across Versions to Predict Defects
Abstract: This study explores the concept of connecting software metrics across different versions to predict defects in software development. It delves into the world of software analytics, where the incorporation of metrics and modeling techniques can significantly improve the accuracy of defect prediction. By analyzing version control systems and metrics such as code size, complexity, and rate of change, researchers can identify patterns and trends that foretell potential defects. Machine learning models, including those based on Random Forest and Support Vector Machines, are applied to historical data to detect correlations between metrics and defects. Furthermore, techniques such as transfer learning and model interpretability are employed to enhance the accuracy and robustness of the defect prediction system. The outcomes of this research indicate that connecting metrics across versions enhances defect prediction performance compared to analyzing a single version. The findings also suggest that incorporating additional contextual information, such as commit messages and author experience, can further boost the accuracy of defect prediction. This research contributes to the growing body of knowledge on software analytics, providing a framework for developers to leverage software metrics to anticipate and mitigate potential defects, thereby improving overall software quality.

title: Accurate Bayesian Data Classification without Hyperparameter Cross-validation
Abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to Bayesian data classification that circumvents the need for hyperparameter cross-validation, a common yet computationally expensive and often biased method. The proposed framework is founded on a hybrid methodology that combines the robustness of a hierarchical Bayesian model with the efficacy of a two-stage technique, allowing for the simultaneous estimation of both the hyperparameters and the model parameters without the need for cross-validation. The approach leverages a clever interplay between model selection and parameter estimation, thereby circumventing the typically computationally expensive and potentially misleading cross-validation step. The methodology is demonstrated on a battery of synthetic and real-world datasets, showcasing its superiority over traditional Bayesian methods in terms of both predictive accuracy and computational efficiency. Results indicate that the proposed framework can accurately classify data without the need for cross-validation, suggesting its potential for widespread adoption in real-world machine learning applications. Furthermore, this methods avoids overfitting issues from hyperparameter cross-validation thereby improves the accuracy for generalization.

title: A Multi-Scale and Multi-Depth Convolutional Neural Network for Remote Sensing Imagery Pan-Sharpening
Abstract: This research paper presents a novel architecture for remote sensing imagery pan-sharpening, titled as A Multi-Scale and Multi-Depth Convolutional Neural Network (MSMD-CNN). The proposed network is designed to improve the spatial resolution of multispectral imagery while preserving high-quality features of the panchromatic images. Key to this design is a hierarchical structure that incorporates multiple scales and depths of feature extraction. The multi-scale component employs different receptive fields to capture contextual information and facilitate the identification of meaningful spectral and spatial relationships among pixels. By establishing multiple depth connections within the network, contextual dependencies and hierarchical representations of scenes are effectively fostered. At each depth, pan-sharpening processes the relevant information extracted at the preceding depth, and the outputs from each depth are progressively combined to obtain enhanced spatial resolution. In contrast to competing models, which focus primarily on local relationships among pixels, MSMD-CNN more thoroughly analyzes spatial and contextual information to enhance its performance. When coupled with dataset training and validation, this network showcases elevated performance over other traditional and deep learning methods by correcting both global and local variances in geospatial data. The pan-sharpened outcome's consistency and detailed level of information retrieved demonstrate that MSMD-CNN is effective for a wide variety of geospatial applications involving image classification, object detection, and context analysis and also shows a strong alternative to traditional merging algorithms.

title: Learning to Customize Network Security Rules
Abstract: This research delves into the realm of network security, particularly focusing on the ability of machines to autonomously configure and customize network security rules. As networks become increasingly complex, managing and maintaining their security is a daunting task. The need for automation in security has grown, driving the development of artificial intelligence and machine learning techniques to tackle this challenge. Our research explores the application of these techniques to build a system that can learn from both normal and anomalous network traffic, thereby enabling it to autonomously generate customized security rules. To achieve this, we employ a multi-stage approach that consists of data collection, feature engineering, and neural network-based modeling. Through a systematic evaluation of the proposed system, we demonstrate its efficacy in detecting and preventing various types of network-based attacks, including DDoS, SQL injection, and cross-site scripting. Our results show that the system is able to learn and adapt quickly to new and emerging threats, thus ensuring the integrity and security of the network. Furthermore, we investigate the trade-offs between security and performance, as well as the challenges of scalability, demonstrating the potential of our approach to handle large-scale networks with diverse security requirements.

title: Siamese LSTM based Fiber Structural Similarity Network (FS2Net) for Rotation Invariant Brain Tractography Segmentation
Abstract: This paper presents a novel deep learning approach for rotation invariant brain tractography segmentation, leveraging the capabilities of Siamese LSTM and Fiber Structural Similarity Network (FS2Net) architectures. In brain tractography analysis, accurate segmentation of the brain's white matter tracts is crucial for understanding neurological disorders and developing treatments. However, the existing state-of-the-art methods often struggle with rotation invariance, which is vital for comparing and validating results across different subjects. To address this challenge, we propose the Siamese LSTM based Fiber Structural Similarity Network (FS2Net), a rotation-invariant neural network architecture designed to segment brain tractography by learning structural similarities. The FS2Net incorporates a Siamese LSTM module for model-agnostic feature extraction, followed by an encoder-decoder architecture using convolutional neural networks (CNNs) with residual connections. The proposed network learns to capture the underlying coherent structures in brain tractography, yielding state-of-the-art performance in rotation invariant tractography segmentation. Through extensive experiments on public datasets, the proposed approach demonstrates its superiority over existing rotation invariant deep learning algorithms, showcasing its potential for broad applications in clinical neuroimaging analysis and population-wise brain connectivity comparison. The proposed FS2Net model offers an essential improvement over previous methods, providing more accurate and robust brain tractography segmentation, ultimately paving the way for improved disease diagnosis and treatment.

title: Topic Compositional Neural Language Model
Abstract: Recent breakthroughs in developing more comprehensive and sophisticated neural language models have led to significant advancements in natural language processing applications. However, the existing models such as BERT and RoBERTa have several limitations, including a lack of compositional understanding, inability to generalize to unseen situations, and unscalability for long-range dependencies. These limitations are largely due to the fact that these models primarily rely on pre-trained word-level embeddings, which are static and unresponsive to contextual cues. In response to these challenges, compositional neural language models have emerged as a new paradigm for designing more effective and robust models of language. These models leverage a two-stage architecture, where the first stage generates composable low-level syntactic structures and the second stage uses these structures to generate meaningful utterances. Importantly, the compositional approach allows for better generalization, adaptability, and modularity, making these models more scalable and responsive to varying linguistic contexts. In this research, we explore the strengths and potential applications of compositional neural language models, including their improved contextual understanding, better capturing of long-range dependencies, and enhanced applicability to downstream NLP tasks, particularly text classification, question answering, and machine translation. Our experiments with comprehensive datasets demonstrate the compelling performance of these models, with significant gains over state-of-the-art baselines, highlighting the potential of compositional neural language models as a more comprehensive and adaptable alternative to traditional neural language models.

title: Mass and Age of Red Giant Branch Stars Observed with LAMOST and \emph{Kepler}
Abstract: The red giant branch (RGB) stars offer a unique window into the evolution of low mass stars in the Milky Way. Recent advances in space-based photometry, such as the \emph{Kepler} mission, and targeted spectroscopic surveys, such as the Large Sky Area Multi-Object Fiber Spectroscopic Telescope (LAMOST), have afforded an unprecedented opportunity to investigate the properties of RGB stars on a large scale. This paper aims to leverage the synergy between these datasets to accurately determine the mass and age of RGB stars. We will systematically examine the stellar parameters of over 40,000 RGB stars with LAMOST spectroscopic data, utilizing a robust spectroscopic analysis method that combines the strengths of multiple line indexes and comparison with state-of-the-art stellar evolutionary models. The subsequent mass and age assignments will be refined through detailed comparisons with \emph{Kepler} space-based photometric data, enabling precise determination of the evolutionary stage of these stars and yielding substantial improvements in our understanding of stellar populations. Furthermore, we will use these precise stellar parameters to investigate the physics of red giant stars, the properties of their atmospheres, and the implications for galactic evolution. By bringing together the precision of LAMOST spectroscopy with the high-precision photometry of \emph{Kepler}, this study will significantly enhance our understanding of the stellar life cycle and the evolution of our galaxy.

title: Deep Architectures for Automated Seizure Detection in Scalp EEGs
Abstract: This abstract explores the application of deep learning architectures for automated seizure detection in scalp electroencephalography (EEG) signals. Scalp EEG recordings are widely used for diagnosing and monitoring seizures in patients with epilepsy, but the process is often time-consuming, labor-intensive, and prone to human errors. Recent advances in deep learning and computational power have made it possible to develop sophisticated architectures that can learn complex patterns in EEG signals and identify seizure activity with high accuracy. A comprehensive review of existing deep learning models, including convolutional neural networks (CNN), recurrent neural networks (RNN), and long short-term memory (LSTM) networks, reveals their limitations and potential areas for improvement. The proposed work designs and evaluates novel deep architectures that integrate multiple features, such as time-frequency transforms, spectral features, and spatial filtering, to enhance seizure detection performance. The research utilizes a large dataset of scalp EEG recordings from patients with epilepsy and investigates the impact of different hyperparameters, training protocols, and evaluation metrics on the overall performance of the proposed models. The results demonstrate significant improvements in seizure detection accuracy and reliability, paving the way for the development of cost-effective, non-invasive, and real-time seizure detection systems that can potentially revolutionize the diagnosis and management of epilepsy.

title: Automatic Analysis of EEGs Using Big Data and Hybrid Deep Learning Architectures
Abstract: The advent of big data and advancements in deep learning technologies have paved the way for the analysis of electroencephalograms (EEGs) to become more sophisticated and accurate. This paper explores the application of big data and hybrid deep learning architectures in automatic EEG analysis, aiming to improve the diagnosis and treatment of neurological disorders. The study presents a novel framework that integrates both feature extraction and selection techniques with a hybrid deep learning architecture, leveraging the strengths of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and recurrent neural networks (RNNs). By leveraging vast EEG datasets collected from various sources, the proposed framework is able to learn complex patterns and features that are indicative of specific neurological conditions, such as epilepsy and Parkinson's disease. The results demonstrate the superior performance of the hybrid deep learning architecture in classifying EEG signals when compared to traditional machine learning algorithms. Moreover, the framework's ability to learn from large amounts of data allows for the generation of personalized diagnostic models, catering to the specific needs of individual patients. The study contributes to the growing body of research in the field of neurophysiological signal processing, paving the way for the development of more accurate and reliable diagnostic tools. The proposed framework has the potential to revolutionize the field of neurological diagnosis, enabling earlier and more effective treatment of neurological disorders.

title: Differentially Private Matrix Completion Revisited
Abstract: This work revisits the problem of differentially private matrix completion, where the goal is to recover a low-rank matrix from a partially observed input matrix while preserving the privacy of individual entries. The existing methods for differentially private matrix completion often rely on iterative algorithms that incur high computational cost and may not achieve satisfactory recovery accuracy due to the stringent privacy constraints. To address these limitations, we propose a novel framework that integrates differential privacy with non-convex optimization techniques, enabling the use of more efficient algorithms while maintaining robust recovery guarantees. Our approach involves deriving privacy-preserving variants of popular non-convex optimization algorithms, such as gradient descent and its randomized variants, and shows that these variants achieve similar convergence rates to their non-private counterparts. Furthermore, we develop novel analysis techniques to establish the privacy guarantees of our framework, leveraging tools from differential privacy and non-convex optimization. Through extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets, we demonstrate the efficacy and efficiency of our framework in recovering accurate low-rank matrices under differential privacy constraints. Our results highlight the potential of integrated differential privacy and non-convex optimization techniques in solving high-stakes machine learning problems, where accuracy and fairness are paramount.

title: PixelSNAIL: An Improved Autoregressive Generative Model
Abstract:
This paper introduces an improved autoregressive generative model, PixelSNAIL, designed to revamp the limitations of existing sequential models for image synthesis. PixelSNAIL significantly advances the capabilities of its predecessors, WaveNet and Transformer, in tackling the task of generating high-resolution natural images. The model's primary contributions lie in employing a novel hierarchical architecture and leveraging sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) mechanisms.

At its core, PixelSNAIL leverages explicit discretisation to facilitate parallel computation, thus achieving higher processing speeds compared to earlier alternatives. It utilises a spatially-adaptive attention mechanism, enabling better exploitation of local context within images. Furthermore, the incorporation of a hierarchical generation process empowers the model to adopt varying levels of detail in generation tasks, thereby demonstrating its ability to balance and adapt to complex, high-resolution images. Quantitatively, PixelSNAIL exhibits superior results in terms of Frechet inception distance (FID) score, especially when compared to existing, state-of-the-art autoregressive models such as StyleGAN, and other methods like Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) on multiple benchmark datasets. In visual terms, PixelSNAIL consistently produces high-quality, diverse, and realistic images with considerable detail and realism. These advancements propel PixelSNAIL as a leading contender for long-range autoregressive generative tasks, pushing the boundaries of computational generative models in image synthesis.

title: Directional Statistics and Filtering Using libDirectional
Abstract: Directional statistics and filtering have been increasingly applied in various fields, such as computer vision, geographic information systems, computer-aided design, and environmental monitoring. However, these applications often face challenges related to the handling of vectors and directional data in complex spatial domains. libDirectional is an open-source C++ library developed to address these challenges, offering a comprehensive set of tools and algorithms for directional statistics and filtering. This paper explores the efficiency and effectiveness of libDirectional in four key areas: estimation of directional distributions (including mean direction and principal axes), filtering of directional data (using established and novel anisotropic kernel methods), computation of directional geometry (covering topics such as radial distances, polar histograms, and orientation fields), and integration with established data structures in spatial databases (serving to leverage libDirectional for analysis of large datasets). The implementation, algorithms, and test results for all four topics are thoroughly examined and compared to established competitors. Furthermore, we discuss several prospective applications, illustrations, and an object-oriented programming manner which illustrate the usage of the functions from libDirectional for handling directional data.

title: Extrapolating Expected Accuracies for Large Multi-Class Problems
Abstract: This paper presents a novel methodology for extrapolating expected accuracies of deep learning models on large multi-class problems, focusing on mitigating the difficulties associated with scaling up existing techniques. Empirical evidence demonstrates that current accuracy prediction methods, such as naive Bayes or logistic regression-based approaches, are inherently biased toward worst-case performance estimates for large, complex data sets. Existing techniques have been shown to break down near the regime of interest, namely under 10^-3 error. To address this challenge, this research leverages theoretical results relating test and training performance to a carefully chosen universal 'distance' measure, serving as a theoretical basis for prediction. This distance measure stems from two well-known metrics, the probability of misclassification and the Bayesian $K$L divergence, which are tailored to accommodate the characteristics of multi-class classification problems. By combining insights from these metrics, the efficacy of deep leaning models is characterized in terms of the number of classes and sample ratio between individual classes. Furthermore, this framework provides the theoretical tools to understand the key determinants influencing accuracy in large multi-class problems, addressing limitations inherent in previous approaches. Extensive experimentation demonstrates the validity and applicability of the extrapolation framework, examining multiple state-of-the-art architectures and several widely used benchmarks in the deep learning community.

title: Learning More Universal Representations for Transfer-Learning
Abstract: Transferring knowledge across different tasks and domains has emerged as a cornerstone in deep learning research, with the aim of leveraging previously learned representations to accelerate the learning process of new, yet related tasks. While the ability to generalize to unseen tasks has demonstrated unprecedented success, the fundamental challenge of universal representation remains elusive. Despite the advancement in pre-trained models, their applicability and effectiveness are predominantly task-specific, limiting their ability to adapt to a wide array of tasks. This has motivated the pursuit of more robust, generalizable, and transferable representations that can consistently aid in the learning of diverse tasks. Towards this end, we explore the architecture and mechanisms that govern the learning of universal representations, highlighting key considerations such as inductive bias, domain adaptability, and task flexibility. By distilling the essence of representational learning and leveraging insights from cognitive science, information theory, and empirical evidence, our work seeks to elucidate the intricate dynamics at play in learning universal representations, providing a more comprehensive understanding of transfer learning. This research endeavors to pinpoint the core factors that govern the acquisition of generalizable representations, which could ultimately revolutionize the field of deep learning and accelerate progress in various application domains by harnessing the power of pre-trained universal models.

title: Deep learning for universal linear embeddings of nonlinear dynamics
Abstract: This paper investigates the applicability of deep learning techniques for uncovering universal linear embeddings of nonlinear dynamics within complex systems, facilitating the interpretation of intricate relationships through a simplified linear lens. The existing body of research has shown that a subset of nonlinear systems can be accurately modelled using linear equations following a certain transformation. Yet, discovering these transformations remains a non-trivial challenge due to the inherent complexity entailed in these systems. This study aims to address this limitation by developing and fine-tuning a novel deep learning-based method for identifying suitable linear embeddings from data-driven nonlinear dynamics. Employing a range of datasets generated from fundamental oscillators and real-world systems, the efficacy of our approach is evaluated against traditional methods, such as Koopman theory and kernel methods. Through extensive experimentation and comparison, we demonstrate the superior universality and adaptability of our learning model in unearthing the correct linear embedding for a broader class of nonlinear dynamics, thus shedding light on intricate time-evolution patterns within those systems. These findings possess the potential to significantly streamline the analysis and prediction of nonlinear phenomena in various disciplines, fostering a deeper understanding of underlying generative mechanisms and prompting new avenues for theoretical exploration.

title: On the estimation of correlation in a binary sequence model
Abstract: This paper delves into the problem of estimating correlation in binary sequence models, a crucial task in various fields such as computer science, engineering, and statistics. Binary sequence models are widely used to represent and analyze digital data, and understanding their correlations is vital for extracting meaningful patterns and characteristics. However, estimating correlations in binary sequences poses significant challenges due to the inherent inherent properties of binary data, such as its non-normality and finite support. The existing correlation measures, which rely heavily on continuous assumptions, often fall short in dealing with binary data, resulting in biased estimates and suboptimal performance. In the absence of standard correlations, frequency-based metrics have been proposed, but these are hardly generalizable and lack rigorous mathematical foundations. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a novel framework for estimating correlations in binary sequences, grounded in the principles of information theory and stochastic processes. By leveraging recent advances in machine learning and statistical inference, the proposed method is shown to outperform existing approaches in terms of accuracy and robustness. Empirical evaluations on a diverse set of synthetic and real-world datasets confirm the efficacy and interpretability of the proposed method, shedding new light on the complex relationships within binary sequences and opening up fresh avenues for data analysis and modeling.

title: Combining Representation Learning with Logic for Language Processing
Abstract: Representation learning and logic have been emerging as promising paradigms for improving language processing tasks such as language understanding, generation, and question answering. However, their integration remains a largely under-explored area in the field of natural language processing. This paper aims to bridge the gap by proposing a novel approach that combines the strengths of representation learning with logical reasoning to enhance language processing capabilities. Our approach leverages a type of neural network architecture that can effectively integrate logical rules into the learning process, thereby enabling the model to learn more semantically meaningful and accurate representations of language. Through the use of a task-agnostic evaluation framework, we demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on a range of language tasks, including sentiment analysis, named entity recognition, and question answering. Results show that the integration of logic-based reasoning enhances the performance of deep neural networks in capturing subtle nuances of language, leading to improved accuracy and reduced error rates. Notably, our approach also exhibits better generalizability and interpretability compared to traditional neural network-based approaches. These findings highlight the importance of combining representation learning with logic for effective language processing and have significant implications for the future development of more sophisticated language understanding models.

title: Neural network augmented inverse problems for PDEs
Abstract: This paper presents a novel framework for solving inverse problems associated with partial differential equations (PDEs) by incorporating the power of neural networks. Traditional methods for solving inverse problems involve imposing strong regularization on the sought solution or employing complex and computationally expensive optimization schemes, which can significantly limit their effectiveness. Conversely, our approach leverages the learning capabilities of neural networks to efficiently approximate the solution to the inverse problem, thereby overcoming some of the inherent difficulties associated with traditional methods. Specifically, we propose a hybrid strategy that combines deep learning techniques with established methods for solving PDEs, such as finite element methods and gradient-based optimization algorithms. Our framework allows for the incorporation of prior knowledge about the physical system being modeled and provides a flexible and computationally efficient means for tackling a wide range of inverse problems, including those involving non-linear and non-unique solutions. Comprehensive numerical experiments demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in identifying coefficients, initial conditions, and boundary values associated with various PDEs, including the popular advection-diffusion equation and the Navier-Stokes equations. Our results show that the proposed neural network augmented framework significantly outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy, computational efficiency, and robustness to noise and model uncertainty.

title: A Light-Weight Multimodal Framework for Improved Environmental Audio Tagging
Abstract: This paper presents a novel, lightweight multimodal framework for improved environmental audio tagging that leverages the strengths of acoustic and visual features to classify sound events accurately in various environmental settings. In real-world applications, such as surveillance and monitoring systems, accurate audio event classification can significantly enhance the detection and identification of potential security threats, wildlife species, or even signs of human-emitted gas leaks. However, current audio tagging approaches often rely heavily on computationally intensive deep learning models that are impractical for deployment on resource-constrained devices or real-time streaming scenarios, where low latency is critical. To address this challenge, our proposed framework draws on the concept of multimodal fusion, incorporating spectrogram representations of audio signals with corresponding RGB or thermal video frames. By leveraging both auditory and visual information, the proposed framework can improve the robustness and accuracy of audio event classification in noisy or degraded environments. Experimental results demonstrate that the lightweight multimodal framework outperforms state-of-the-art approaches by achieving a notable increase in precision while yielding substantial reductions in processing overhead and latency. Moreover, the framework's adaptability and real-time processing capabilities make it particularly suitable for embedded systems, smartphones, or other edge devices that require rapid, ambient sound recognition and response.

title: Momentum and Stochastic Momentum for Stochastic Gradient, Newton, Proximal Point and Subspace Descent Methods
Abstract: The increasing complexity of modern machine learning tasks has led to the development of various optimization algorithms that can efficiently handle large-scale data. This study provides a comprehensive analysis of momentum and stochastic momentum techniques for several popular descent methods, including stochastic gradient descent (SGD), Newton's method, proximal point descent, and subspace descent. Momentum and stochastic momentum are often used to enhance the convergence rate and stability of these algorithms, but their effects are still not fully understood. We investigate the theoretical properties of these techniques and their interactions with different descent methods. Our results show that momentum can improve the convergence rate of Newton's method and subspace descent, while stochastic momentum can reduce the variance of the gradient estimates in SGD and proximal point descent. However, we also find that stochastic momentum can lead to increased variance in Newton's method and subspace descent, particularly when the step sizes are large. We provide numerical experiments to support our theoretical findings and demonstrate the benefits of using momentum and stochastic momentum techniques in different optimization scenarios. Our study contributes to the understanding of momentum and stochastic momentum in various descent methods and provides practical guidelines for selecting the most appropriate technique for specific machine learning tasks.

title: Multiple Instance Deep Learning for Weakly Supervised Small-Footprint Audio Event Detection
Abstract: This research paper presents a novel deep learning approach for weakly supervised small-footprint audio event detection. Existing audio event detection methods are often limited by their requirement of precisely labeled audio data, which is time-consuming and cost-prohibitive to obtain. Furthermore, these methods often suffer from large model sizes and computational complexities, making them unsuitable for resource-constrained devices. In this work, we propose a Multiple Instance Deep Learning (MIDL) framework that addresses these challenges. Our approach treats short audio segments as instances and utilizes a convolutional neural network to extract features that capture both local and non-local dependencies within each instance. We then employ a hierarchical classification scheme to aggregate the instance-level predictions and obtain a final audio event label. By leveraging both weak annotation supervision and small-footprint model design, our proposed framework achieves state-of-the-art performance on several benchmark datasets while significantly reducing model complexity and computational requirements. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of MIDL in adapting to variable audio duration and addressing the challenges posed by imbalanced data distributions. The proposed approach has the potential to revolutionize audio event detection in applications where resources are limited, such as smart home devices and wearable sensors.

title: CNN Is All You Need
Abstract: This research paper delves into the prospect of achieving state-of-the-art performance in various computer vision tasks solely utilizing Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), thereby eliminating the necessity for more complex models or specialized architectures. Recent advancements in deep learning have led to significant breakthroughs in object detection, segmentation, and generation, largely owed to the incorporation of additional modules and components. However, the rise of 'shallowness' and efficient neural networking has fostered renewed interest in CNNs as standalone models capable of tackling these complex tasks. Through a detailed analysis of the structure, parameterization, and optimization techniques, this study demonstrates the feasibility of employing a CNN-based pipeline, despite its simplicity, to achieve comparable or even superior results to competing methods that often involve multiple complex components. A set of experiments conducted across various benchmarks and applications, including image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation, validate the proposed CNN-based approach, providing evidence for its effectiveness and robustness. By shedding new light on the capabilities of CNNs and systematically evaluating their performance in different scenarios, this research contributes to the ongoing discussion around the role and potential of simple neural network architectures in achieving high-quality results in computer vision tasks.

title: The information bottleneck and geometric clustering
Abstract: This research explores the intersection of information bottleneck theory and geometric clustering, revealing a novel framework for compressing and categorizing high-dimensional data. Building on the concept of the information bottleneck method, we present a geometric clustering process that leverages the intrinsic structure of data to enhance compression efficiency and data interpretability. By employing the information bottleneck principle, our approach identifies the optimal transformation of high-dimensional data into a lower-dimensional space while minimizing the loss of mutual information with the class labels. The geodesic distance metric, a ubiquitous concept in information geometry, serves as the underlying structure for data clustering, ensuring that similar data points are compactly grouped in the embedding space. Our proposed approach, dubbed "InfoBottleneck Geometric Clustering" (IBGC), is instantiated in a simulated environment and applied to multiple benchmark datasets, including the MNIST handwritten digit and the CIFAR10 images dataset. Results demonstrate that IBGC effectively balances the tradeoff between compression and accuracy, offering comparable performance to state-of-the-art methods while preserving structural information in the emergent feature representation. The work provides a general framework for high-dimensional data analysis, promising applications in unsupervised learning, dimensionality reduction, and data visualization.

title: On Convergence of some Gradient-based Temporal-Differences Algorithms for Off-Policy Learning
Abstract: This abstract presents a comprehensive analysis of the convergence properties of several popular gradient-based temporal differences (TD) algorithms for off-policy learning in reinforcement learning. The proliferation of off-policy learning methods in recent years has necessitated a deeper understanding of their theoretical foundations, particularly concerning their convergence characteristics. A multitude of studies has demonstrated the efficacy of gradient-based TD algorithms, but an in-depth examination of their convergence properties has been lacking. This research endeavours to bridge this knowledge gap by systematically investigating the convergence properties of variants of vanilla TD(Q), Q-learning with linear function approximation, and TD with LSTDQN (least-squares temporal-difference learning with quadratic regularization). Utilizing a combination of analytical and numerical techniques, the study evaluates the impact of different weighting schemes, step-sizes, and exploration strategies on the convergence of these algorithms. The findings of this research provide novel insights into the convergence behaviour of gradient-based off-policy temporal differences algorithms, shedding light on their capacity to learn optimal policies in complex reinforcement learning environments. By enhancing our understanding of these methods, this work will contribute to the development of more effective and robust reinforcement learning algorithms that can be widely applied in a range of domains.

title: A Composite Quantile Fourier Neural Network for Multi-Step Probabilistic Forecasting of Nonstationary Univariate Time Series
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel composite quantile Fourier neural network (CQFNN) model for multi-step probabilistic forecasting of nonstationary univariate time series. Traditional forecasting models often struggle to capture nonstationary patterns in time series data, resulting in inaccurate predictions. To address this issue, CQFNN integrates the strengths of Fourier neural networks, which can efficiently model periodic patterns, and quantile regression, which can provide reliable probabilistic forecasts. In CQFNN, we first employ a Fourier neural network to extract periodic features from the time series data. Then, we feed these features into a quantile regression module, which generates a set of quantile forecasts for different confidence levels. This enables CQFNN to capture both the location and dispersion of the forecast distribution, thereby providing reliable probabilistic forecasts. We conduct extensive experiments on various benchmark datasets and demonstrate the superiority of CQFNN in comparison to state-of-the-art methods in terms of forecast accuracy and robustness. Furthermore, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the model's performance under different scenarios, including nonstationary patterns, heteroscedasticity, and misspecified models. Our results highlight the potential of CQFNN as a powerful tool for multi-step probabilistic forecasting of nonstationary univariate time series in real-world applications, including weather forecasting, financial forecasting, and system monitoring.

title: An empirical evaluation for the intrusion detection features based on machine learning and feature selection methods
Abstract: This study presents a comprehensive empirical evaluation for the intrusion detection features based on machine learning and feature selection methods. The primary objective of this research is to explore the efficacy of machine learning algorithms in identifying and classifying network intrusions, and to compare their performance with traditional rule-based intrusion detection systems. Using a real-time intrusion dataset, this empirical analysis employs a range of machine learning techniques, including Support Vector Machines (SVM), Random Forest, and Gradient Boosting, to identify the most relevant features that differentiate between normal and anomalous network traffic. In addition, this research investigates the impact of feature selection methods, such as Correlation-based Feature Selection (CFS) and Mutual Information (MI), on the performance of machine learning models. The key findings of this study indicate that the combination of machine learning algorithms and feature selection methods can significantly enhance the accuracy and efficiency of intrusion detection systems. The experimental results demonstrate that the selection of relevant features can lead to a reduction in the dimensionality of the feature space, thereby improving the scalability and computational efficiency of the intrusion detection system. Overall, this study contributes to the development of more robust and effective intrusion detection systems, which can provide enhanced security for computer networks and defend against sophisticated cyber threats. The findings of this research can be applied in various industrial and commercial settings to improve the security and reliability of computer networks.

title: An Artificial Neural Network-based Stock Trading System Using Technical Analysis and Big Data Framework
Abstract: This study proposes and implements an artificial neural network-based stock trading system that combines technical analysis and big data frameworks to make informed investment decisions. The proposed system utilizes stock market data from various exchanges and industry sources, incorporating features from established technical analysis indicators such as moving averages, relative strength index, and Bollinger Bands. By leveraging big data technologies, the system is able to process and analyze vast amounts of data from multiple sources in real-time, enabling the detection of subtle trends and patterns that may elude investors relying solely on traditional technical analysis methods. An artificial neural network is used as the underlying model, trained on a comprehensive dataset comprised of stock prices, trading volumes, and technical indicators. The proposed system is tested and validated on a set of historical stock prices using the walk-forward optimization technique, demonstrating its ability to generate significant returns while minimizing losses. The experimental results show that the proposed system outperforms traditional buy-and-hold strategies and other AI-based trading systems, highlighting its potential to become a valuable tool for investors seeking to optimize their portfolios and stay ahead of the market.

title: Memory-Efficient Deep Salient Object Segmentation Networks on Gridized Superpixels
Abstract: This study proposes a novel deep learning approach for salient object segmentation by leveraging gridized superpixels to significantly reduce memory requirements while maintaining high accuracy. Gridized superpixels represent an efficient data structure that partition the image into a regular grid of superpixels, simplifying the computational complexity and memory needs associated with densely connected superpixel representations. Building upon this gridized superpixel framework, we design a deep neural network architecture that efficiently captures long-range contextual information and focuses on learning local patterns that are indicative of salient objects. Our approach involves a hybrid encoder-decoder framework that combines spatial, channel, and contextual attention mechanisms to selectively weigh the contributions of different spatial locations, channels, and contextual cues. Notably, our framework incorporates a spatial attention mechanism that adaptively learns to focus on regions of interest, and a channel attention mechanism that simultaneously recalibrates channel-wise features to retain critical information relevant to salient objects. Experimental evaluations on various standard benchmark datasets demonstrate that our gridized superpixel-based framework outperforms the state-of-the-art methods under strict memory constraints, achieving superior accuracy- efficiency tradeoffs while requiring minimal computational resources and memory. Our proposed framework is particularly beneficial for real-world applications where timeliness and memory efficiency are highly valued, such as real-time object detection, autonomous vehicles, and surveillance systems.
