title: DeepIEP: a Peptide Sequence Model of Isoelectric Point (IEP/pI) using Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs)
Abstract: DeepIEP, a novel Peptide Sequence Model of Isoelectric Point (IEP/pI), leverages the power of Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) to predict the IEP/pI of a peptide sequence. Traditional methods of IEP/pI calculation are largely based on empirical formulas and rely heavily on the pKa values of individual amino acids. However, these methods often fall short in accurately predicting the IEP/pI of complex peptide sequences due to limitations in accounting for interactions between amino acids. To address this, the DeepIEP model employs a combination of LSTM and GRU RNN architectures to learn the patterns and relationships between amino acid sequences and their corresponding IEP/pI values. By analyzing a large dataset of known peptide sequences and their associated IEP/pI values, the model is able to learn and make accurate predictions with a high degree of precision. This work demonstrates the potential of RNNs in revolutionizing the field of computational proteomics and provides a powerful tool for researchers and researchers, enabling the rapid and accurate calculation of IEP/pI values for a wide range of peptide sequences. Furthermore, the DeepIEP model's ability to take into account complex interactions between amino acids makes it particularly well-suited for predicting the IEP/pI of complex peptides and proteins, such as those found in biological membranes and cellular compartments.

title: Consensus-based Sequence Training for Video Captioning
Abstract: This research paper explores the application of consensus-based sequence training for video captioning, a task that aims to generate accurate and concise captions for videos. Conventional sequence-to-sequence models have been widely adopted for video captioning, but they often suffer from mode collapse and lack of diversity in generated captions. To address these limitations, we propose a consensus-based sequence training approach that integrates multiple sequence generators to produce diverse and informative captions. Our approach involves training multiple sequence generators in parallel, with a consensus mechanism that aggregates their outputs to produce a final caption. The consensus mechanism is trained to optimize the overall quality and coherence of the generated captions, ensuring that they accurately represent the content of the video. Our experimental results demonstrate that the proposed consensus-based sequence training approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art video captioning models in terms of caption diversity, coherence, and accuracy. Additionally, our approach is found to be more robust to noisy and ambiguous video inputs, making it a reliable solution for real-world video captioning applications. We also conduct an ablation study to investigate the impact of different consensus mechanisms and sequence generator architectures on the performance of the proposed approach, providing insights into the design and optimization of consensus-based sequence training for video captioning.

title: Co-Morbidity Exploration on Wearables Activity Data Using Unsupervised Pre-training and Multi-Task Learning
Abstract: This study explores the application of unsupervised pre-training and multi-task learning for the analysis of wearable device data in the context of co-morbidity identification. The rapid proliferation of wearable technology has enabled the collection of large-scale, high-frequency data on individuals' daily activities, potentially offering valuable insights into the complex relationships between different health conditions. However, the extraction of meaningful co-morbidity patterns from these vast datasets remains a significant challenge due to the presence of class imbalance, noise, and feature dimensionality. Our research proposes an innovative methodology that initially leverages the power of unsupervised pre-trained representations to learn generalizable features from the wearable data. Subsequently, a multi-task learning framework is designed to jointly train a set of diverse tasks, including disease classification, activity recognition, and wearable-derived physiological signal extraction. The integration of these tasks allows the model to capture nuanced relationships between seemingly disparate indicators of disease presence, ultimately facilitating the identification of predictive co-morbidity patterns. A rigorous evaluation of our approach using benchmark datasets demonstrates its superiority over state-of-the-art methods in terms of both co-morbidity discovery accuracy and feature interpretability, underscoring the promise of our methodology for real-world applications in precision medicine and disease prevention.

title: Tensor Regression Networks with various Low-Rank Tensor Approximations
Abstract: Tensor Regression Networks (TRN) have gained significant attention in recent years due to their ability to model complex relationships between high-dimensional input and output variables. However, the curse of dimensionality often renders traditional regression models inefficient in such scenarios. Inspired by the recent breakthroughs in tensor decompositions, this study delves into the realm of combining TRN with various low-rank tensor approximation techniques to ameliorate their scalability and generalizability. By incorporating low-rank tensor approximations, such as the Tucker and CANDECOMP/PARAFAC (CP) decompositions, we aim to reduce the parameter space complexity of TRN while preserving its rich feature extraction capabilities. Experimental investigations using several benchmark datasets and tasks are conducted to validate the proposed framework's performance. Our findings indicate that the incorporation of low-rank tensor approximations significantly enhances the scalability of TRN, rendering them more suitable for handling large-scale high-dimensional data. Moreover, we demonstrate that the choice of tensor decomposition technique has a substantial impact on the model's predictive performance, underscoring the importance of careful selection. By leveraging the synergy between TRN and low-rank tensor approximations, we provide a powerful tool for tackling complex regression tasks in various domains, including but not limited to computer vision, natural language processing, and recommender systems.

title: Exploring the Space of Black-box Attacks on Deep Neural Networks
Abstract: Black-box attacks on deep neural networks (DNNs) have gained significant attention in recent years due to their ability to pose a threat to the security and integrity of DNN-based systems without requiring access to the network's internal architecture or weights. Despite their potential implications, the space of black-box attacks remains poorly understood, with existing research primarily focusing on developing new attack methods rather than gaining a comprehensive understanding of the attack landscape. This paper aims to bridge this gap by providing a thorough exploration of the space of black-box attacks on DNNs. Through a systematic analysis of existing attack methods, as well as a comprehensive review of the literature, we identify key characteristics and commonalities among black-box attacks, including their reliance on transferability and adversarial examples. Our analysis also highlights the limitations and vulnerabilities of existing defense mechanisms, which are often reliant on knowledge of the network's internal structure or the ability to observe its output. Furthermore, we discuss the implications of our findings for the development of more robust and secure DNN-based systems, and propose a framework for future research that bridges the gap between theory and practice in the study of black-box attacks on DNNs. By providing a broader understanding of the space of black-box attacks, our work contributes to the development of more effective defense mechanisms and more secure AI systems.

title: Robust Loss Functions under Label Noise for Deep Neural Networks
Abstract: Deep neural networks have achieved remarkable success in various machine learning tasks, but they are notoriously sensitive to label noise in training data. Label noise refers to inaccuracies or inconsistencies in the class labels used for training the model, which can significantly degrade the performance and robustness of deep neural networks. In this paper, we propose a novel framework for designing robust loss functions under label noise for deep neural networks, with the goal of enhancing their robustness and generalizability. Our approach involves developing a set of novel loss functions that incorporate noise-regularization terms and noise-aware weighting schemes, which enable the model to learn robust representations and alignments in a noisy environment. We experiment with various types of label noise, including symmetric and asymmetric noise, random noise, and confounded noise, and demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed framework through extensive experiments on benchmark datasets, including MNIST, CIFAR-10, and SVHN. Our results show that the proposed loss functions achieve state-of-the-art or comparable performance under both clean and noisy data conditions, and outperform existing robust loss functions in many cases. We also provide a comprehensive analysis of the effect of label noise on model performance and robustness, which highlights the need for noise-aware loss functions in practical machine learning applications.

title: Sketching for Kronecker Product Regression and P-splines
Abstract: The integration of machine learning and spline-based regression models has emerged as a crucial area of research in computational statistics, enabling enhanced prediction accuracy and flexibility. This study explores the concept of sketching for Kronecker product regression (KPR) and P-splines, focusing on the theoretical foundations and practical applications of a novel sketching-based approximation technique for these models. By leveraging the scalable nature of sketching algorithms, we aim to improve computational efficiency in high-dimensional settings, thereby enabling the widespread adoption of KPR and P-splines in real-world data analysis tasks. Our approach is built upon the fundamental idea of approximating high-dimensional matrices using a much smaller set of representative rows, dubbed the sketch, which significantly reduces the computational complexity of traditional methods without sacrificing accuracy. This development draws inspiration from recent advances in compressed sensing and structured random matrices, and by casting KPR and P-splines in this mathematical framework, we are able to theoretically guarantee the convergence of the sketching approximation for a wide range of problem settings. Our experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed sketching-based approach, boasting substantial reductions in computation time and memory requirements, making it an attractive solution for practitioners seeking to harness the power of these sophisticated regression models in large-scale applications.

title: Multi-modal Geolocation Estimation Using Deep Neural Networks
Abstract: This study presents a novel methodology for multi-modal geolocation estimation using deep neural networks. The objective is to develop a robust and accurate system that can estimate a device's location based on various sources of information, including its visual, acoustic, and inertia data. A deep learning framework is proposed that integrates multiple sources of data from sensors and maps to estimate the location of a device. The system is trained on a large dataset of geotagged images, audio recordings, and sensor readings to learn the relationships between the input data and the device's location. The proposed framework consists of three modules: a feature extraction module that extracts relevant features from the input data, a mapping module that generates a probabilistic distribution of possible locations, and a decision module that combines the outputs of the two modules to produce an estimate of the device's location. The proposed system is evaluated on several scenarios, including urban, suburban, and rural environments, and is shown to outperform state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy and robustness. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in estimating device location using multi-modal input data, and highlight its potential applications in various fields, including smart cities, robotics, and the Internet of Things (IoT). Additionally, the study explores the potential challenges and limitations of using deep neural networks for geolocation estimation in real-world scenarios, and proposes several avenues for future work.

title: Timely Feedback in Unstructured Cybersecurity Exercises
Abstract: Timely feedback is a crucial component of effective learning in cybersecurity education, particularly in unstructured exercises where hands-on experiences play a pivotal role. Despite the evidence supporting its significance, the provision and effective utilization of timely feedback in such settings remains a significant challenge. This research investigates the impact of timely feedback in enhancing the learning outcomes of participants engaged in unstructured cybersecurity exercises. Through a mixed-methods approach combining both quantitative and qualitative data collection and analysis, this study identifies key factors associated with the provision and utilization of timely feedback, including the technological and pedagogical constraints that hinder its effective implementation. A survey of instructors and participants was conducted to examine the effect of timely feedback on learning attitudes, participation levels, and perceived skills development in unstructured cybersecurity exercises. Additionally, case studies were carried out to gather in-depth insights into the experiences of participants who received timely feedback during the exercises. The findings from this research demonstrate a statistically significant correlation between timely feedback and improved learning outcomes, including enhanced problem-solving skills, increased motivation, and improved cyber defense abilities. The study also highlights the importance of recognizing the role of timely feedback in fostering a culture of continuous learning and improvement in cybersecurity education. Overall, this research contributes to the growing body of knowledge on effective pedagogical practices in cybersecurity education and underscores the need for educators to prioritize the timely provision of feedback in unstructured exercises.

title: Horn-ICE Learning for Synthesizing Invariants and Contracts
Abstract: The development of robust software systems necessitates the integration of formal verification techniques to ensure their correctness and reliability. Horn clauses have emerged as a popular choice for specifying invariants and contracts in software, due to their simplicity and expressiveness. Invariant contracts, which are used to express properties about program variables, play a crucial role in formal verification, as they enable the detection of potential errors and the automatic generation of test cases. Recently, Instruction-Conditioned Embedding (ICE) techniques have gained significant attention for their ability to learn high-quality embeddings of program instructions, which can be exploited for various programming and natural language processing tasks. In this work, we propose a novel approach, termed Horn-ICE learning, for synthesizing invariants and contracts by utilizing the expressiveness of Horn clauses and the prowess of ICE techniques. By combining these two powerful tools, our approach enables the generation of accurate and robust invariants and contracts, which can be leveraged for a range of formal verification tasks, including property-based testing, assertion checking, and static analysis. Through extensive evaluation on a collection of open-source and benchmarked programs, we demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in generating high-quality invariants and contracts, outperforming state-of-the-art techniques on various metrics. Our Horn-ICE learning framework offers a significant step towards the automation of formal verification, enabling developers to write more robust and reliable software systems.

title: Mapping to Declarative Knowledge for Word Problem Solving
Abstract: This paper explores the application of mapping to declarative knowledge in solving word problems, a fundamental component of mathematical education. Current methods of solving word problems emphasize procedural knowledge, which focuses on the steps required to arrive at a solution without necessarily understanding the underlying mathematics. In contrast, declarative knowledge involves the comprehension and recall of mathematical concepts and relationships. By integrating declarative knowledge, students can develop a deeper understanding of mathematical concepts and improve their ability to solve word problems. Our research proposes a novel approach to teaching word problem-solving skills that leverages mapping to declarative knowledge. Using a combination of cognitive load theory and multiple representation learning, we aim to examine the effects of this approach on students' mathematical understanding and problem-solving skills. We present the design of an intervention study involving 120 middle-school students and the results of pre- and post-tests assessing students' understanding of mathematical concepts and their ability to solve word problems. The findings suggest that integrating declarative knowledge through mapping significantly improves students' understanding of mathematical relationships and their ability to apply these concepts to solve word problems. The paper contributes to the research on mathematical education by introducing a practical and effective approach to teaching word problem-solving skills and highlights the potential benefits of declarative knowledge in mathematical education.

title: Scaling GRPC Tensorflow on 512 nodes of Cori Supercomputer
Abstract: This research focuses on exploring the scalability of the Google Remote Procedure Call (gRPC) framework in conjunction with TensorFlow, an open-source machine learning library, across a large-scale distributed computing environment composed of 512 nodes of the Cori Supercomputer. To scale effectively, we examine the approaches to ensure seamless communication between nodes using gRPC's Remote Procedure Calls (RPCs) and implement various load-balancing techniques to optimize the utilization of the Cori Supercomputer's resources. Our experiments aim to evaluate the efficiency of different tensor partitioning strategies, including 1D, 2D, and 3D methods, to distribute tensors across the nodes and optimize performance. Additionally, we investigate the impact of different loss functions and activation functions on the overall performance of the distributed deep learning model. To assess scalability, we employ metrics such as wall clock time, memory usage, and throughput. Furthermore, we analyze the challenge of fault tolerance in a large-scale distributed system and propose a solution utilizing a combination of gRPC and Apache Kafka for efficient task queuing and recovery. By scaling TensorFlow on the Cori Supercomputer with 512 nodes and utilizing gRPC for efficient communication, our results demonstrate the possibility of training massive deep learning models at unprecedented scales and provide valuable insights for solving complex problems in the field of artificial intelligence and distributed computing.

title: RLlib: Abstractions for Distributed Reinforcement Learning
Abstract:
Ray's scalable distributed library, RLlib, facilitates the exploration and optimization of complex tasks in reinforcement learning environments through abstractions of the entire RL workflow. This research aims to delve into the inner workings of RLlib by examining its suite of algorithms and engines, both supervised and reinforcement, allowing for seamless experimentation and benchmarking of existing methods as well as novel paradigm shifts. A comprehensive analysis of the RLlib framework's hierarchical architecture reveals a clearly defined modular design which fosters a culture of collaborative development among the reinforcement learning community.

Through RLlib, users can rapidly orchestrate simulations of complex RL domains spanning multiple learning procedures, distribution methodologies, and agents. Our analysis covers RLlib's capabilities in distributed training, multi-algorithm tuning, automatic hyperparameter search, asynchronous execution, automatic failure detection and recovery, and aggregation of results, using existing implementations of various RL algorithms, including well-known model RL and actor-critic methods, as well as novel approaches. Furthermore, this research explores possible use cases to demonstrate the transformative power of RLlib. We thoroughly integrate state-of-the-art frameworks into RLlib for distributing reinforcement learning algorithms effectively and achieve decisive performance gains over its competitors.

title: IHT dies hard: Provable accelerated Iterative Hard Thresholding
Abstract: Iterative Hard Thresholding (IHT) has been a widely popular and influential method in sparse approximation, appearing in a number of diverse applications including signal processing, machine learning, and optimization, particularly in settings where the goal is to recover sparse solutions exactly from noisy linear observations. Despite its robustness and flexibility, IHT has been implicated in several issues, including slow convergence and the potential for poor initialization, which in turn can significantly degrade its overall performance in many applications. To address this problem, researchers have introduced various forms of accelerated IHT methods, the primary goals of which center around boosting the performance of the basic IHT process through the integration of acceleration and extrapolation techniques. This research makes several key contributions to this area by providing provable accelerated IHT algorithms. Specifically, we develop three advanced IHT-based methods, which combine low-complexity implementations with strong worst-case performance guarantees. We provide rigorous analyses to prove that these accelerated algorithms can recover sparse signals exactly, given noiseless linear observations, using a constant number of iterations that is much less than what is needed with the basic IHT formulation. Overall, the devised accelerated IHT techniques proposed here offer faster and more reliable recovery capabilities for users, making significant improvements in terms of computational efficiency and robustness.

title: Entropy-SGD optimizes the prior of a PAC-Bayes bound: Generalization properties of Entropy-SGD and data-dependent priors

This work investigates the connection between Entropy-SGD and PAC-Bayes theory, focusing on how Entropy-SGD updates the prior distribution based on data and its impact on the generalization performance of a machine learning model. Entropy-SGD, a stochastic gradient descent method, updates the model's parameters and the prior distribution simultaneously, balancing the exploration-exploitation trade-off by adapting the optimal size of the mini-batches used for training. Theoretically, this approach optimizes the prior distribution by identifying the most concentrated set of masses within the given support while minimizing the expected Kullback-Leibler divergence with the true prior. In practice, Empirical evidence from experimental results suggests that Entropy-SGD significantly improves generalization in real-world datasets, particularly for complex models and when the data is noisy and high-dimensional. A key takeaway from this work is that Entropy-SGD, by optimizing the prior through data-dependent priors, effectively provides a principled approach to selecting regularization parameters, hence increasing model generalization. Overall, the study highlights the strong connections between Entropy-SGD and PAC-Bayes theory, yielding insights into principled optimization techniques that may lead to better generalization performance.

title: HACS: Human Action Clips and Segments Dataset for Recognition and Temporal Localization
Abstract: The advent of deep learning techniques has led to significant advancements in human action recognition and temporal localization, with numerous applications in fields such as healthcare, surveillance, and human-computer interaction. Each video clip and segment is annotated with precise action labels, temporal boundaries, and object annotations, facilitating the creation of various machine learning benchmarks for tasks such as action classification, temporal action localization, and action segmentation. The dataset is carefully curated to account for key aspects of human behavior, such as action complexity, object interactions, and contextual relationships, offering a robust foundation for advancing the field of human action analysis. title: Who is Smarter? Intelligence Measure of Learning-based Cognitive Radios
Abstract: This paper explores the concept of intelligence measurement in learning-based cognitive radios, specifically focusing on determining who or what is considered smarter between the radio and its environment. Traditional radio systems rely on pre-programmed rules and algorithms to operate efficiently, but the dynamic nature of the radio environment renders these systems ineffective. Cognitive radios, on the other hand, can adapt and learn from their environment using machine learning algorithms, enabling them to optimize their performance in real-time. The paper investigates various intelligence metrics, including information-theoretic metrics, learning-based metrics, and resource allocation metrics, to evaluate the intelligence of learning-based cognitive radios. title: Zero-Shot Learning via Latent Space Encoding
Abstract: Zero-shot learning has emerged as a promising approach in machine learning, enabling models to generalize across unseen categories without requiring explicit training data. In this work, we explore the potential of latent space encoding for achieving zero-shot learning. By mapping the input space into a latent representation, our proposed method capitalizes on the inherent structure and relationships between classes embedded within the latent manifold. Specifically, we employ a variational autoencoder (VAE) to learn a disentangled representation of the input data, where each class is mapped to a distinct point in the latent space. This approach allows us to leverage the VAE's ability to capture nuanced patterns and discrepancies between classes, thereby facilitating zero-shot classification. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through extensive experiments on diverse benchmarks, such as ImageNet, CUB-200-2011, and Stanford Cars dataset. Results show that our latent space encoding scheme can achieve competitive performance with state-of-the-art methods, often outperforming them in scenarios with few shots or limited labeled data. Furthermore, we analyze the learnability of our model and identify key factors influencing its performance, providing valuable insights into the underlying mechanisms driving zero-shot learning. title: Quantum Learning Algorithms and Post-Quantum Cryptography
Abstract: The advent of quantum computing poses a significant threat to the security of current cryptographic systems, which have long been based on classical computational hardness. To counter this threat, post-quantum cryptography aims to develop new cryptographic algorithms that remain secure even against attacks from a quantum computer. However, the development of post-quantum cryptography is hindered by the relative infancy of quantum learning algorithms, which are essential for optimizing and training these new cryptographic systems. This paper provides an in-depth exploration of the state-of-the-art in quantum learning algorithms and their applications to post-quantum cryptography. Specifically, the paper surveys recent advances in quantum machine learning algorithms for optimization and learning paradigms, such as Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA), Quantum Alternating Projection (QAP), and Classical Approximate Quantum Computation (CAQC), as well as their applications to cryptographic problems, including key encapsulation, encrypted quantum computing, cryptographic hash functions, and oblivious linear function evaluation. Furthermore, this paper highlights the challenges and limitations of these algorithms and suggests future research directions for the development of more robust and efficient post-quantum cryptographic systems. By providing a comprehensive overview of the current state of the art in quantum learning algorithms and post-quantum cryptography, this paper aims to inspire and facilitate further research in this critical area of cryptographic security.

title: Scalable Prototype Selection by Genetic Algorithms and Hashing
Abstract: This abstract explores the potential of integrating genetic algorithms with hashing techniques to cope with scalability issues in prototype selection. Prototype selection is a crucial step in instance-based learning and k-nearest neighbors algorithms, where a small set of prototypical instances is chosen to represent the entire dataset. However, existing methods often fail to scale with increasing dataset sizes due to their high computational complexity. To address this challenge, we propose a novel hybrid framework that combines the strengths of genetic algorithms and hashing. Our approach uses a genetic algorithm to select a subset of instances from the original dataset, and then employs a deep hash function to map the selected instances into a compact hashed space. This enables efficient storage and retrieval of prototypical instances while preserving their essential characteristics. The proposed framework is evaluated on a variety of benchmark datasets with different sizes and complexities. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy, scalability, and computational efficiency, making it a promising solution for large-scale instance-based learning applications. title: A Real-Time Autonomous Highway Accident Detection Model Based on Big Data Processing and Computational Intelligence
Abstract: This study proposes a real-time autonomous highway accident detection model that leverages the integration of big data processing and computational intelligence. The preprocessed data are then analyzed using computational intelligence techniques, including supervised and unsupervised machine learning algorithms, to identify patterns and anomalies that may indicate high-risk accident scenarios. The model also incorporates a rule-based system that integrates domain-specific rules and expert knowledge to further enhance the accuracy of accident detection. By leveraging real-time data analytics and computational intelligence, the proposed model enables effective accident detection, early warning systems, and efficient allocation of emergency resources, thereby reducing the risk of accidents and improving highway safety. title: Machine Learning Cosmic Expansion History

title: Chaos-guided Input Structuring for Improved Learning in Recurrent Neural Networks
Abstract: Chaos theory has long been used to describe complex and unpredictable systems in various fields, including dynamical systems and physics. However, recent studies have explored the application of chaos theory in the field of machine learning, specifically to improve the learning capacity and robustness of neural networks. This paper proposes a novel approach that utilizes chaos theory to guide the input structuring for recurrent neural networks (RNNs). By introducing a measure of chaos, the algorithm adjusts the input data to maximize the complexity and diversity, thereby enhancing the RNN's learning capacity and generalization performance. The proposed method leverages concepts from topological chaos theory and applies it to the input space of RNNs. It identifies critical points of maximum entropy, which are used to perturb the input data, leading to more robust and efficient learning. Experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method, achieving significant improvements in learning accuracy, convergence speed, and adaptability in comparison to state-of-the-art RNN architectures. Furthermore, theoretical analysis and comparisons with existing methods provide insights into the underlying mechanisms and performance benefits of the proposed chaos-guided input structuring approach. title: Algorithmic Regularization in Over-parameterized Matrix Sensing and Neural Networks with Quadratic Activations
Abstract: Algorithmic regularization has emerged as a vital component in understanding the behavior of neural networks, particularly in over-parameterized models with quadratic activations and matrix sensing applications. This paper presents an in-depth analysis of the relationships between algorithmic regularization, over-parameterization, and neural network convergence. Specifically, we focus on the role of spectral normalization, weight decay, and gradient clipping as key algorithmic regularization techniques in over-parameterized matrix sensing and neural networks with quadratic activations. Through a mathematical framework and empirical evaluations, we demonstrate how these regularization techniques can lead to improved stability, generalization, and robustness of neural network models. Our results indicate that the choice of regularization technique and its combination with over-parameterization significantly impact the convergence and generalization capabilities of neural networks in matrix sensing applications. We also provide insights into the connections between gradient-based methods, neural tangent kernel, and algorithmic regularization, highlighting the potential for novel regularization strategies in future research directions. By bridging the theoretical understanding of algorithmic regularization with empirical evidence, this work provides essential knowledge for developing robust and generalizable neural network models, particularly in matrix sensing and quadratic activation regimes. title: The Robust Manifold Defense: Adversarial Training using Generative Models
Abstract: The Robust Manifold Defense: Adversarial Training using Generative Models proposes a novel approach to enhance the robustness of deep neural networks against adversarial attacks. Traditional methods of adversarial training rely on the use of malicious examples generated using white-box attacks, which can lead to overfitting and decreased performance. This work presents a manifold-based defense approach that utilizes generative models to create a diverse set of perturbations that are more realistic and challenging to evade. By leveraging the power of generative models, the proposed approach is able to generate a wide range of adversarial examples that preserve the original input's manifold structure, making it considerably harder for attackers to fool the network. Experiments on a range ofstate-of-the-art models and benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method, resulting in significant improvements in robustness against various types of attacks. Notably, the approach outperforms previous robustness-enhancing methods in several scenarios, highlighting its potential as a versatile and reliable solution for adversarial training. Furthermore, the modular structure of the proposed framework enables easy adaptation and integration with existing deep learning architectures, making it an attractive solution for real-world applications where robustness against attacks is critical. Overall, the manifold defense using generative models offers a fresh and promising line of research for enhancing the security and reliability of deep neural networks against adversarial attacks.

title: Actionable Email Intent Modeling with Reparametrized RNNs
Abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to modeling user intent from email interactions, denoted as Actionable Email Intent Modeling (AEIM). Our method focuses on repurposing Reparametrized Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) to learn predictive models that can accurately infer user goals from their email sequences. By leveraging the power of RNNs, we aim to identify a robust representation of user intent that can be used to improve email client experiences, automate email filtering and categorization, and drive business outcomes. Our AEIM model learns to capture underlying patterns and relationships in email activities, enabling the extraction of actionable intent from raw input data. Through a comprehensive analysis of email users' behavior, we demonstrate that AEIM model can accurately identify intent hidden within the complexities of email interactions. Our findings indicate that incorporating contextual information and continuous learning enables AEIM model to adapt and improve its predictions over time, making it a versatile solution for real-world applications. We comprehensively evaluate AEIM model using diverse datasets from various domains, validating its robustness and effectiveness in identifying actionable intent and its influence on decision-making processes. Our study contributes significantly to the development of effective email intent modeling methods and their practical applications in the digital age.

title: Deep Meta Learning for Real-Time Target-Aware Visual Tracking
Abstract: Visual tracking in real-world applications often encounters the challenge of adaptivity to diverse scenarios, variable lighting conditions, and varying target sizes, making it essential to develop a visual tracking system that can learn in real-time and generalize across different environments. Deep meta-learning approaches have emerged as a solution to this problem by leveraging the framework of meta-learning to quickly adapt to new unseen tasks across different target-aware scenarios without the need for extensive training. This study proposes a model-agnostic deep meta-learning framework called Target-Aware Visual Tracking (TA-VT), which employs a template learning mechanism and a meta-updating process to learn tracking policies across various target sizes, lighting conditions, and motion patterns. TA-VT is based on a two-stage meta-learning process, consisting of a learning process and an adaptation process, to efficiently refine the target model and learn a robust tracking policy that facilitates both accurate and consistent tracking performance across multiple target-aware scenarios. Through extensive experiments on a variety of visual tracking benchmarks, the efficacy of TA-VT is demonstrated in achieving state-of-the-art performance for various target sizes, dynamic motion, and varying lighting conditions, setting a new benchmark for deep meta-learning in real-time visual tracking. The proposed framework's ability to learn and generalize adaptively across unseen tasks showcases its practicability and scalability for diverse real-world applications.

title: Variational Bayes Estimation of Discrete-Margined Copula Models with Application to Time Series
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel Variational Bayes (VB) framework for estimating discrete-margined copula models, which are increasingly employed in modeling complex dependencies in multivariate time series data. The framework, dubbed VB-Copula, leverages recent advances in variational inference to address the computational challenges associated with copula-based models. By employing a Mean-Field Variational Approximation, VB-Copula efficiently approximates the posterior distribution of the copula parameters with respect to the latent variables, providing an effective scalable and accurate method for estimation. Our approach accommodates a broad class of discrete-margined copulas, including those with non-standard dependence structures, thereby allowing for more comprehensive and flexible modeling of time series data. We demonstrate the efficacy of VB-Copula through a comprehensive simulation study, which showcases its ability to recover the true parameters with high accuracy. Furthermore, VB-Copula is applied to several real-world time series datasets to illustrate its practical utility in modeling conditional dependencies, as well as forecasting and risk assessment tasks. Compared to existing approaches, our results consistently highlight the superiority of VB-Copula in terms of accuracy, computational efficiency, and scalability. Overall, the proposed framework offers a powerful tool for practitioners and researchers seeking to harness the strengths of discrete-margined copula models for time series analysis.

title: Towards Measuring Membership Privacy
Abstract: This research endeavours to develop and investigate various methods for measuring and assessing an individual's membership privacy, specifically in relation to their participation in group settings and associated affiliations. Our work is grounded in the theoretical underpinnings of membership and privacy, drawing on the concepts of Foucauldian surveillance, social exclusion, and power dynamics as they pertain to identity, belonging, and individual autonomy. We address a significant research gap in the current literature by providing a framework and metrics for quantifying personal membership information while accounting for contextual and socio-cultural nuances that influence perceptions of privacy. This research integrates insights from disciplines such as sociology, information science, and philosophy, aiming to address practical concerns and challenges related to data protection, transparency, and individual agency. We present case studies highlighting the implications of our approach, demonstrating how individuals themselves, organizations, and policymakers can assess membership-related privacy violations and facilitate more privatisation-aware social exchanges. The goal is to facilitate a more intricate understanding of privacy measurement that takes into account user experiences of membership and their contexts.

title: Strongly Hierarchical Factorization Machines and ANOVA Kernel Regression
Abstract: Strongly Hierarchical Factorization Machines and ANOVA Kernel Regression is a research study that proposes a novel approach to modeling complex relationships in large-scale datasets. By integrating the principles of Factorization Machines with the hierarchical structure analysis from Analysis of Variance (ANOVA), this study develops a new predictive modeling framework referred to as Strongly Hierarchical Factorization Machines (SHFM). Unlike traditional factorization machines that struggle to interpret and capture significant variable interactions, SHFM incorporates hierarchically structured feature interactions using ANOVA decomposition and Kernel Ridge Regression. This results in better interpretability and significant performance enhancements in handling high-dimensionality as well as large datasets. Shown through simulated and real-world experiments including the Sloan Digital Sky Survey and the IMDB dataset, SHFM demonstrates the capacity to explain complex, high-order interactions that other machine learning models encounter difficulty with. As experiments show, SHFM consistently generates comparable or better predictive performance over conventional factorization machines and baseline models while achieving high interpretability. As this study demonstrates, the proposed framework can support the community in predicting numerous real-world and complex modeling applications and drive practical exploration into interpretable machine learning models.

title: General-Purpose Visual Language and Information System with Case-Studies in Developing Business Applications
Abstract: This research paper presents an in-depth examination of a general-purpose visual language and information system, with a specific focus on its application in developing business applications. The proposed system utilizes a visual interface to streamline the development process, allowing users to create, modify, and execute applications with minimal programming knowledge. The system boasts a robust feature set, including automatic code generation, data modeling, and integrative connectivity with existing databases and software systems. A selection of case studies highlights the system's potential in various business domains, including financial services, e-commerce, and supply chain management. The research demonstrates the system's effectiveness in rapidly developing and deploying business applications, with notable improvements in productivity, reduced costs, and enhanced user experience. By employing a visual language, the system empowers non-technical stakeholders to participate in the development process, fostering seamless collaboration between technical and non-technical team members. Further, the system's capacity for data-driven decision-making promotes organization-wide adoption and facilitates business intelligence. The empirical results from the case studies demonstrate the system's applicability to diverse business settings, solidifying its position as a suitable solution for businesses seeking to accelerate their digital transformation efforts. Overall, the research underscores the potential of the general-purpose visual language and information system as a powerful tool for developing business applications.

title: Generative Adversarial Nets for Multiple Text Corpora
Abstract: Generative adversarial nets (GANs) have gained significant attention in the field of natural language processing (NLP) for text generation tasks, particularly for generating samples from a single text corpus. However, handling multiple text corpora with diverse styles, domains, and characteristics poses significant challenges for traditional GAN-based approaches. To address these challenges, this study presents a novel framework, MultiCorpus GAN (MC-GAN), that can generate coherent and diverse text samples from multiple text corpora. The proposed MC-GAN architecture comprises a generator that can learn the underlying distributions of multiple corpora and an adversary that can evaluate the generated samples based on their fluency, coherence, and styles. The framework incorporates a multi-task learning strategy that involves training the generator to generate text samples from multiple corpora simultaneously, while the adversary is trained to evaluate the generated samples from each corpus separately. Experimental results on several benchmark datasets, including 20 Newsgroups, IMDB, and Amazon Reviews, demonstrate the efficacy of MC-GAN in generating high-quality text samples that are comparable to those generated by traditional GAN-based approaches optimized for individual corpora. Furthermore, our analyses highlight the potential of MC-GAN in capturing the commonalities and differences between multiple corpora, thereby enabling effective style transfer and text augmentation tasks. The MC-GAN framework provides a scalable and efficient approach to handling multiple text corpora and has promising applications in various NLP tasks, such as text generation, language models, and natural language understanding.

title: SAGA: A Submodular Greedy Algorithm For Group Recommendation
Abstract: This paper introduces a novel algorithm, SAGA (Submodular Greedy Algorithm), specifically designed to tackle the complexities of group recommendation tasks. Group recommendation is an essential aspect of recommender systems that involves providing a curated list of items suitable for a given group of users. The problem is challenging due to its inherent inherent redundancy and diversity constraints, where the presence of an item in the recommended list for a group should be meaningful in addition to being relevant for each individual member. The SAGA algorithm employs a submodular maximization framework, which allows it to efficiently approximate the optimal solution given the vast search space. By using a greedy approach that leverages the properties of submodularity, SAGA selects high-relevance items that collectively provide the most value to the group. Our empirical evaluation demonstrates the robustness and efficiency of SAGA on various group recommendation benchmarks, showing its ability to outperform existing approaches. Furthermore, we extensively analyze the behavior of SAGA and provide theoretical insights into its convergence properties. The overall contribution of this work is a novel and adaptive algorithm that improves accuracy and efficiency in group recommendation tasks, making it an attractive choice for practical applications in areas such as e-commerce, news aggregation, and media streaming services.

title: Overcomplete Frame Thresholding for Acoustic Scene Analysis
Abstract: This paper presents an overcomplete frame thresholding approach for acoustic scene analysis, a field at the intersection of audio signal processing and machine learning. The existing overcomplete frame based methods for acoustic scene analysis employ thresholding techniques to selectively retain frames whose mel-frequency cepstral coefficients (MFCCs) demonstrate high energy. However, these standard techniques restrict the overcomplete frame processing to a narrow subset of the frame set, effectively overlooking the significance of other frames. As a result, a considerable information loss occurs, leading to reduced classification accuracy of acoustic scenes. The proposed approach leverages a variational autoencoder (VAE) to learn a lower-dimensional representation of MFCCs feature space. Thresholding takes place using a data-driven criterion, based on the MFCC reconstruction error determined by the VAE. The thresholded frames are then analyzed using a context-aware representation, where each frame includes a vector of MFCC coefficients and encoded audio segment information. These representations are fed to separate convolutional neural networks, which are specifically designed to recognize acoustic events in complex environments. Experiments conducted on well-known acoustic scene classification benchmarks show that the proposed method achieves state-of-the-art recognition accuracy, while significantly reducing computational costs associated with feature extractions.

title: NNDrone: a toolkit for the mass application of machine learning in High Energy Physics
Abstract: The ever-increasing volume of data in High Energy Physics (HEP) necessitates sophisticated algorithms to improve data analysis efficiency. To address this challenge, the NNDrone project develops a comprehensive toolkit based on state-of-the-art machine learning techniques. By applying neural networks to patterns within HEP data, the project aims to unlock novel correlations and patterns that conventional statistical methods may overlook. The NNDrone toolkit leverages the strengths of modern computing hardware, such as graphical processing units (GPUs) and tensor processing units (TPUs), to expedite the computationally intensive process of neural network training and application. Furthermore, the toolkit incorporates techniques for optimizing neural network architectures and hyperparameters, ensuring that the application of machine learning models can be adapted to meet the requirements of diverse HEP analysis tasks. By providing a standardized interface for integrating machine learning models into the existing HEP data analysis ecosystem, NNDrone facilitates collaboration and facilitates a range of opportunities for researchers to develop and apply innovative machine learning techniques to complex HEP problems. The ultimate goal of NNDrone is to revolutionize the field of HEP by empowering researchers to tap into the full potential of machine learning and drive breakthroughs that can only be achieved through synergistic integration of HEP data with AI-driven models.

title: On Connecting Stochastic Gradient MCMC and Differential Privacy
Abstract: This paper establishes a theoretical connection between stochastic gradient Markov Chain Monte Carlo (SG-MCMC) methods and differential privacy by providing general frameworks for analyzing private inference techniques. A key contribution is developing a class of differentially private stochastic gradient sampling algorithms, enabling efficient private inference in the context of large-scale Bayesian learning problems. Our approach combines the benefits of adaptive Markov Chain Monte Carlo algorithms and the guarantees of differential privacy. We demonstrate how the use of private stochastic gradient sampling allows for scalable posterior inference tasks under the constraints of differential privacy, resulting in minimally impactful perturbations that preserve the underlying model's accuracy and efficiency. This serves to identify novel characterizations of private inference and post-processing techniques, significantly improving our understanding of the fundamental trade-offs between posterior estimation quality and privacy guarantees, thus refining the bounds on performance under private stochastic gradient-based inference methods.

title: Deep Blind Image Inpainting
Abstract: Deep Blind Image Inpainting has emerged as a crucial tool in image restoration, particularly for restoring images with missing or damaged regions. This paper presents a comprehensive review of the current trends and advancements in deep blind image inpainting techniques. Recent deep learning-based methods have shown impressive results in terms of restoration quality and speed, with some algorithms capable of achieving state-of-the-art performance. However, these methods often require a priori knowledge of the image's content and a significant amount of training data, limiting their applicability in real-world scenarios where images may be highly diverse or lack clear patterns. To address this limitation, researchers have proposed several blind inpainting approaches that leverage self-consistency and iterative refinement techniques to adapt to varying input datasets. The proposed methods leverage deep network architectures such as Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), Variational Autoencoders (VAEs), and U-Net to learn the underlying structure and patterns within the input image, thereby facilitating coherent and artifact-free restoration. Despite their progress, existing blind inpainting methods still suffer from artefacts, particularly under scenarios with low input image quality or incomplete mask information. This paper discusses current techniques, their advantages and limitations, and highlights open challenges and future directions for advancing deep blind image inpainting. By understanding the existing landscape and future research opportunities, we can push the frontiers of image restoration and contribute to the development of more practical and accurate deep blind image inpainting algorithms for a wide range of applications.

title: Leveraging Long and Short-term Information in Content-aware Movie Recommendation
Abstract: This study develops an innovative content-aware movie recommendation system that effectively leverages both long and short-term information to improve user satisfaction. Existing movie recommendation systems often rely on simplistic approaches that focus on either short-term or long-term user preferences, neglecting the complexities of human behavior and preferences. To address these limitations, we propose a novel hybrid model that integrates the advantages of both short-term and long-term information through a dual attention mechanism. Our model, dubbed "LSTM-CTFA," combines the strengths of long short-term memory (LSTM) networks with the collaborative temporal factor analysis (CTFA) method to capture both the dynamic and static aspects of user preferences. Through a comprehensive evaluation using a large-scale movie dataset, we demonstrate that our proposed system significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of recommendation accuracy, diversity, and serendipity. Our results show that the LSTM-CTFA model is able to effectively exploit short-term fluctuations in user behavior while also accounting for long-term patterns and consistencies, leading to improved user satisfaction and engagement. The proposed system provides a more nuanced and comprehensive understanding of user preferences, enabling the development of more effective and personalized movie recommendation services.

title: Automatic Image Cropping for Visual Aesthetic Enhancement Using Deep Neural Networks and Cascaded Regression
Abstract: This paper explores the application of deep neural networks and cascaded regression in automatic image cropping for visual aesthetic enhancement. The proposed approach aims to identify the most visually appealing region of an image by evaluating various cropping ratios and compositions. Through a comprehensive literature review, we identify the limitations of existing methods, which often rely on manual annotation, simplify the cropping process, or fail to capture the complexities of visual aesthetics. Our solution leverages the strengths of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and recursive bounding box regression to predict the optimal cropping mask, thereby enhancing the image's visual appeal. A customized dataset, comprising high-quality images with pre-aligned and annotated cropping masks, is constructed for training and validating the proposed approach. The deep neural network architecture is designed to learn the relationships between image features, cropping ratios, and visual aesthetics, employing a novel hybrid loss function that balances regression and classification objectives. Extensive experiments demonstrate the efficacy of our method, achieving significant improvements over state-of-the-art techniques in terms of aesthetic quality evaluation metrics. Furthermore, our approach is demonstrated to be efficient, scalable, and generalize across various image categories and shooting scenarios. The proposed automatic image cropping method offers a powerful tool for image processing applications, such as portrait photography, advertising, and social media platforms, providing users with intuitive and visually engaging content.

title: Neural Collaborative Autoencoder
Abstract: This research paper presents a novel neural collaborative autoencoder (NCAE) framework that effectively integrates collaborative filtering and autoencoder architectures to model complex user-item interactions in recommender systems. By leveraging the strengths of both approaches, NCAE aims to improve the accuracy and robustness of predicted user preferences. In the proposed framework, a collaborative block processes the co-occurrence patterns among users and items, capturing the hidden collective behavior and incorporating it into the autoencoder's encoding process. A neural network's autoencoder architecture is utilized to learn a compressed and informative representation of the user-item interaction matrix, which exhibits strong regularizations properties due to the mutual influence of the reconstructed users and items. To adequately handle the limitations of the collaborative filtering approach such as the cold-start problem, the model incorporates an attribute embedding mechanism to incorporate additional side information about users and items, further enriching the discovered patterns. Comprehensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets are conducted to demonstrate the empirical performance of the NCAE, validating its efficiency and scalability as a viable solution for recommender systems in real-world applications.

title: Domain Adaptation Meets Disentangled Representation Learning and Style Transfer
Abstract: This abstract delves into the intersection of domain adaptation, disentangled representation learning, and style transfer. Domain adaptation enables a machine learning model to generalize well across different domains or datasets, addressing the problem of lacking training data. Disentangled representation learning, a type of self-supervised learning, aims to learn representations that are rich in meaningful and separable factors, such as attributes or styles. Style transfer, a related concept in computer vision, refers to the ability to transfer the style of an image to another image while preserving its original content.The integration of these concepts can facilitate more effective and robust adaptability across various domains. By learning disentangled representations and applying style transfer, machine learning models can better generalize across different environments and identify key factors that are invariant to domain shifts. The recent advent of novel neural architecture designs and optimization techniques has motivated further exploration in this area. This research aims to investigate how the fusion of domain adaptation, disentangled representation learning, and style transfer can be leveraged to develop more robust and efficient algorithms for cross-domain learning. We will explore the theoretical foundations and empirical applications of this harmonious combination, shedding light on its potential applications in computer vision and beyond.

title: Geochemical discrimination and characteristics of magmatic tectonic settings; a machine learning-based approach
Abstract: This research employs a machine learning-based approach to improve the geochemical discrimination of magmatic tectonic settings in convergent and continental rift settings. By integrating a comprehensive dataset of major and trace elements from oceanic and continental magmatic rocks, the study enhances our understanding of tectonically influenced geochemical signatures and their variations across diverse tectonic settings. A machine learning algorithm is utilized to differentiate between the geochemical characteristics of different tectonic settings, identify potential predictors, and quantify their significance in distinguishing between convergent and continental environments. The developed model showcases the suitability of employing artificial intelligence in deciphering the intricacies of magmatic geochemistry. The proposed approach facilitates a more detailed discrimination of tectonic settings based on key geochemical parameters, allows for the identification of distinct geochemical signatures within sub-sets of tectonic environments, and enables the differentiation between convergent, oceanic, and continental rift settings where existing empirical discrimination approaches often fail to yield clear results.

title: Stratified Transfer Learning for Cross-domain Activity Recognition
Abstract: This abstract presents a novel approach to cross-domain activity recognition, leveraging stratified transfer learning to improve the adaptability of deep neural networks across disparate datasets. Conventional transfer learning methods often suffer from the "source to target" gap, where the performance of pre-trained models degrades significantly when adapted to novel domains. To address this limitation, our proposed stratified transfer learning framework employs a multi-layered architecture that distinguishes between fine-grained features and coarse-grained relationships. The fine-grained features, learned through pre-training on a large source dataset, enable the model to capture subtle variations in activity patterns, while the coarse-grained relationships, derived from domain-specific similarity metrics, facilitate adaptation to target domains with limited annotated data. Our method computes a subset of informative features for each target domain based on the learned coarse-grained relationships and refines the pre-trained model using a novel domain-invariant loss function. This loss function simultaneously updates the model's weights and adjusts the domain-invariant representations, allowing the model to adapt to diverse activity recognition tasks in new domains. Extensive experiments on several public benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our stratified transfer learning approach, achieving state-of-the-art performance in cross-domain activity recognition and highlighting its potential for real-world applications in human activity analysis.

title: Null Dynamical State Models of Human Cognitive Dysfunction
Abstract: This research paper delves into the development and application of null dynamical state models to human cognitive dysfunction, offering a new perspective on the underlying neural mechanisms associated with cognitive decline. By defining a null system as one with no preferred mode of behavior, current understanding of cognitive function and dysfunction are conceptualized within the constraints of constraints based on dynamical systems theory. Research has demonstrated that cognitive processes can exhibit emergent properties and non-linear interactions, suggesting that even relatively small perturbations in brain dynamics can produce significant cognitive deficits. Through the use of advanced mathematical techniques, such as nonlinear dynamics and computational modeling, null dynamical state models are capable of capturing the complex interplay between neural activity and cognitive processing. This study aims to investigate the efficacy of null dynamical state models in modeling human cognitive dysfunction by analyzing the topology of neural activity, the influence of task context, and the effects of aging and neurodegenerative disease on neural dynamics. The results of this research are expected to provide novel insights into the dynamics of human cognition and contribute to the development of more effective therapeutic interventions for cognitive impairment.

title: Stochastic Multi-armed Bandits in Constant Space
Abstract: In high-dimensional environments, online learning strategies have become increasingly popular for solving tasks that have uncertain rewards or the knowledge of environment is limited. The stochastic multi-armed bandit algorithm is one of these methods that allows the learner to select which actions to take by exploring the uncertainty in rewards associated with different options, leading to optimal or close to optimal outcome. This paper discusses the theoretical limitation imposed by the requirement of constant storage space with respect to the number of actions available, so that users working under memory constraints could apply stochastic multi-armed bandit algorithms that enable them to benefit equitably from available observations by trying all eligible actions to find one with higher payouts. The proposed approach involves approximating the action-value function using incremental and data-ecient algorithms thereby giving effective recommendation even in extremely cold start settings. Our empirical evaluations demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed method on a selection of sequential decision tasks described by discrete states transitions for multiple arms which give up-to-date results comparable to optimal solutions based on full memory exploitation for selected experiments. The efficiency of our strategies, such as handling virtually bound data and achieving high accuracy for bandit arm recommendation, is sustained even in situations adverse to success, proving that our proposed approach could become an authentic solution for the issues of cold starts across a variety of online and recommendation systems in potentially distributed modes of execution.

title: Efficient Algorithms for t-distributed Stochastic Neighborhood Embedding
Abstract: The t-distributed Stochastic Neighborhood Embedding (t-SNE) is a popular dimensionality reduction technique widely used in unsupervised machine learning for visualizing high-dimensional data. However, the algorithm's high computational complexity and memory requirements have limited its applicability to large-scale datasets. In this work, we investigate the possibility of developing efficient algorithms for t-SNE by leveraging both distributed and parallel processing. Our approach is based on the concept of factorized approximation of the t-SNE objective function, which allows us to represent the similarity matrix as a product of two matrices. We further introduce a hierarchical parallelization strategy, specifically designed for factorized t-SNE, to partition the computational tasks across multiple processing units. By exploiting the properties of the factorized approximation and the hierarchical parallelization strategy, we demonstrate significant speedups and memory efficiency improvements over the original t-SNE algorithm. Our experiments, conducted on various high-dimensional datasets, show that the proposed algorithms can efficiently handle large-scale datasets while maintaining the accuracy and interpretability of the t-SNE visualization. We also discuss the implications of our results for the application of t-SNE in real-world datasets and outline future research directions for further improving the efficiency and scalability of the algorithm.

title: RIDI: Robust IMU Double Integration
Abstract: RIDI: Robust IMU Double Integration is a novel approach to enhance the accuracy of sensor fusion in orientation estimation, particularly in applications where gyroscope bias instability is a significant concern. The proposed algorithm builds upon traditional double integration by incorporating a robust estimator that weights the contributions of individual acceleration measurements based on their variance and convergence speed. This enables RIDI to effectively mitigate the effects of measurement outliers and accelerometers' bias estimation errors. By leveraging an adaptive window-based fusion strategy, RIDI adapts to varying levels of sensor noise and bias drift, accommodating a wide range of operating conditions and sensor configurations. The incorporation of a bias transfer mechanism allows RIDI to retain the advantages of double integration while effectively eliminating the accumulation of gyroscope bias noise. This is achieved through a decoupled online bias estimation and correction scheme, ensuring that the estimated orientation remains accurate and robust in the presence of sensor noise and hardware degradation. Simulation results demonstrate the superior performance of RIDI in comparison to traditional double integration and other state-of-the-art algorithms, emphasizing its potential in applications where reliable orientation estimation is critical, such as in autonomous vehicles, robotics, and virtual reality systems.

title: Kernel Regression with Sparse Metric Learning
Abstract: Kernel regression with sparse metric learning proposes a novel approach to address the challenges associated with high-dimensional data, particularly in scenarios where the number of features is much larger than the number of instances. Traditional kernel-based methods often suffer from the curse of dimensionality and computational complexity, hindering their scalability and applicability to real-world problems. The proposed framework leverages sparse metric learning to induce a low-dimensional representation of the data by identifying a subset of the most relevant features. By doing so, it effectively mitigates the curse of dimensionality and achieves significant reductions in computational costs. Additionally, the framework incorporates a two-stage kernel learning scheme, which involves a sparse kernel-based classifier and a support vector regression model. The proposed approach outperforms existing kernel-based methods by demonstrating superior prediction accuracy and improved robustness against noise and outliers. Moreover, the framework exhibits exceptional performance in scenarios with high-dimensional data, underscoring its potential in real-world applications, including image classification, time series prediction, and recommendation systems. By amalgamating sparse metric learning with kernel regression, the proposed framework sets a new benchmark for robust and efficient high-dimensional data analysis and modeling.

title: Android Malware Detection using Deep Learning on API Method Sequences
Abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to Android malware detection using deep learning techniques applied to API method sequences. Current Android malware detection methods primarily rely on static analysis of code or behavioral patterns, which may not capture all possible malicious activities. To address this limitation, we propose a convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture that processes sequences of API method calls to identify characteristic patterns associated with malware. Our approach involves collecting a large dataset of API method sequences from benign and malicious Android apps, where each sequence represents a series of API calls made by an app during execution. We then design an CNN model that learns to recognize these patterns and classifies them as either legitimate or malicious. The proposed CNN model employs convolutional and max-pooling layers to extract spatial features from the API method sequences, followed by a fully connected layer for classification. Our experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves high accuracy in detecting malware compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. The analysis also reveals that the CNN model is effective in identifying various types of malware, including trojans, ransomware, and adware. Ultimately, this research contributes to enhancing the security of Android apps by developing an accurate and efficient malware detection method that can be integrated into the Android operating system and used to protect users from malicious threats.

title: Network-Scale Traffic Modeling and Forecasting with Graphical Lasso and Neural Networks
Abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to network-scale traffic modeling and forecasting by combining the graphical lasso method with neural networks. Real-time traffic data from various sources, including sensors and GPS devices, is often incomplete, noisy, and sparsely available, posing significant challenges to traditional traffic modeling approaches. To address these issues, we propose a hybrid method that leverages the graphical lasso to identify the most relevant traffic variables and formulate a sparse traffic regularization term. This term is then integrated into a deep learning framework based on recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and long short-term memory (LSTM) units, allowing for accurate and robust traffic forecasting. The proposed method is evaluated on a variety of road networks and demonstrates improved predictive performance compared to state-of-the-art baseline models. The results show that the graphical lasso and neural network hybrid approach can effectively capture complex traffic dynamics and provide accurate short-term forecasts, even when faced with data sparsity and heterogeneity. Furthermore, the proposed method is scalable and can be easily adapted to different network configurations and traffic data sources, making it a promising solution for large-scale traffic modeling and forecasting applications.

title: Leveraging Native Language Speech for Accent Identification using Deep Siamese Networks
Abstract: This research paper explores the application of deep Siamese networks for accent identification in native language speech, a task crucial for speech recognition, natural language processing, and human-robot interactions. In many scenarios, a speaker's accent is a significant aspect of their identity and can influence perceptions of authenticity, trust, and intelligibility. However, existing approaches for accent identification often rely on manual annotation, machine learning models that demand extensive pre-trained data, or rely on second-language speech, making them unsuitable for native languages with minimal resources. To address this limitation, we propose an approach that harnesses native language speech for accent identification by designing a deep Siamese network that learns to encode speaker-specific accent features from pre-trained embeddings. Our approach leverages word embeddings, such as GloVe, and fine-tunes the deep Siamese network to capture accent variations in a local minimum. Experiments conducted on a dataset of 120 speakers with 5 accents demonstrated that the proposed model improves accent classification accuracy by up to 10% and reduces the number of false positives by nearly 20%, compared to state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, our study highlights the importance of incorporating linguistic and sociolinguistic factors into machine learning models for accent identification, as they significantly impact model performance and generalizability. The outcome of this research has the potential to aid language recognition, enhance human-robot interactions, and contribute to more informed and culturally sensitive language assessments.

title: Smart Fog: Fog Computing Framework for Unsupervised Clustering Analytics in Wearable Internet of Things
Abstract: This paper proposes a Fog Computing Framework for Unsupervised Clustering Analytics in Wearable Internet of Things, titled Smart Fog. The proliferation of wearable IoT devices has led to an explosion of data generation, which poses significant challenges for real-time analytics and decision-making. To address this issue, we design a hierarchical framework that combines the strengths of fog and cloud computing. Smart Fog leverages the processing capabilities of edge devices, such as wearable sensors and smartphones, to perform initial data filtering and pre-processing, while also harnessing the computing resources of nearby fog servers. A clustering algorithm with a novel weighting strategy is employed to identify patterns and anomalies in wearable data, facilitating real-time insights into users' health and activity levels. Our framework efficiently handles massive amounts of sensor data, ensuring reduced latency and increased contextual awareness. The scalability and adaptability of Smart Fog enable seamless integration with various IoT devices and multiple applications, including health monitoring, emergency services, and smart cities. Furthermore, the use of unsupervised clustering techniques minimizes the need for labeled training data, reducing the computational overhead associated with machine learning algorithms. Through systematic evaluation and comparison with traditional analytics methods, Smart Fog demonstrates its effectiveness in uncovering patterns and relationships within wearable data, with potential applications in various domains where real-time insights are critical.
