title: Learning to Run with Actor-Critic Ensemble
Abstract: This research paper proposes a novel method for learning to run with actor-critic ensemble, focusing on improving the balance between exploration and exploitation in the high-dimensional action space of quadrupedal locomotion. Inspired by the advantages of ensemble methods in the realm of reinforcement learning, we combine multiple actor-critic learners, each with unique characteristics, to effectively explore the vast motion space of a quadruped robot. By leveraging a decentralized training paradigm, where each agent interacts with the same environment but receives distinct exploratory signals, our ensemble approach significantly reduces the reliance on manual parameter tuning and hand-crafted exploration strategies, which are often prohibitively difficult to design for the complex dynamics of quadrupedal locomotion. Moreover, we implement a novel dynamic weighting scheme that adaptively adjusts the influence of each agent based on its historical performance, thereby ensuring that underperforming agents receive more probing signals and are subject to more frequent updates. As a result, our proposed actor-critic ensemble method yields superior running performance and enhanced policy stability, as demonstrated through comprehensive evaluation on both synthetic and real-world quadrupedal robots, and is thus poised to open new avenues for embodied AI applications in robotics and autonomous systems.

title: On Statistical Optimality of Variational Bayes
Abstract: This work explores the statistical optimality of Variational Bayes (VB) methods, providing a comprehensive assessment of the theoretical foundations and limitations of this popular class of approximation techniques for Bayesian inference. We investigate the variational lower bound (VLB) as a measure of the proximity of the VB approximation to the intractable true posterior distribution, examining the implications of its convexity and the non-asymptotic properties of the optimized variational parameters. Through a series of mathematical derivations and theoretical results, we demonstrate that the VLB possesses a form of stationarity that is weaker than the strict stationarity typically required for convergence of the gradient-based optimization procedure used to compute the VB approximation. We also discuss how these findings relate to the convergence behavior of VB algorithms, highlighting potential regions of slow or intractable convergence. Furthermore, this research extends existing work on computational schemes designed to mitigate these convergence issues, developing a set of theoretical conditions that guarantee the global convergence of iterative VB optimization methods through convex optimization, resulting in tighter approximation bounds on the intractable posterior distribution. These results contribute to a deeper understanding of the theoretical underpinnings of Variational Bayes and its specific application to various inference tasks, ensuring that it holds when applicable.

title: Mean Field Residual Networks: On the Edge of Chaos
Abstract: Mean Field Residual Networks (MFRNs) emerge as a novel paradigm in the realm of deep learning, intricately blending principles from statistical physics and neural networks. This study delves into the mathematical underpinnings of MFRNs, where the network's behavior is approximated using a mean-field description, assuming mutually independent interactions between neurons. This simplification allows for the derivation of a set of self-consistent equations, enabling a tractable analysis of the network's properties. We provide a theoretical framework for understanding the onset of chaos in MFRNs, which occurs when the network undergoes a critical transition, marked by an exponential increase in its computational power. Our investigation reveals that the edge of chaos, a concept previously identified in random Boolean networks, can be precisely characterized in the context of MFRNs. By analyzing the MFRN's phase diagram, we identify a regime of optimal performance, where the network balances stability and computational capability. Our results have far-reaching implications for the design and optimization of deep learning models, suggesting that MFRNs can achieve a desirable trade-off between expressivity and stability. Furthermore, the findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the complex interplay between stochasticity and computational power in neural networks, shedding light on the mysterious connection between chaos and intelligence.

title: Spurious Local Minima are Common in Two-Layer ReLU Neural Networks
Abstract: Despite their near-optimal training performance and wide adoption in various machine learning tasks, two-layer ReLU neural networks still suffer from several challenges and limitations. This paper provides an in-depth analysis of one of the significant hurdles faced by such networks, which is the prevalence of spurious local minima. Our study demonstrates that spurious local minima are indeed extremely common in two-layer ReLU networks, being significantly over-represented compared to regular local minima. We show that the majority of spurious local minima can be easily connected to the global optimum via a rectifiable cycle path, while a small fraction has long and complex paths between optima. Importantly, spurious local minima cannot be solely attributed to the empirical sub-optimality or poor optimization techniques, but rather originate from the network's intrinsic properties and the ReLU activation function itself. The discovery of such an intimate connection between spurious local minima and the ReLU activation function leads to the identification of several practical avenues for improving the network's training performance and alleviating the problem of spurious local minima. These insights also cast a broader perspective on neural network architecture and optimization techniques, placing a renewed emphasis on their compatibility with the mathematical framework and signal properties of the activation functions used. Ultimately, this research could contribute to developing deeper neural networks that are less prone to such common but significant pitfalls during training.

title: Machine learning technique for morphological classification of galaxies from the SDSS. I. Photometry-based approach
Abstract: This study explores the use of machine learning techniques for morphological classification of galaxies in the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS), with a focus on a photometry-based approach. By leveraging a robust dataset of galaxy images from the SDSS, our research aims to develop an accurate and efficient framework for classifying galaxy morphologies using machine learning algorithms. We employ a combination of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and traditional machine learning models to analyze the photometric properties of galaxies, including their shapes, sizes, and surface brightness profiles. Through an extensive comparison of various machine learning approaches, we identify the most suitable models for galaxy morphological classification, including the use of transfer learning from pre-trained CNNs. Our results demonstrate the ability of these machine learning models to achieve classification accuracy significantly higher than traditional non-machine learning approaches, with overall accuracy rates exceeding 95%. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of feature selection and dimensionality reduction on the performance of these models, highlighting their roles in enhancing the robustness and reproducibility of galaxy morphological classification. Overall, this study seeks to advance our understanding of galaxy morphologies and their relationships to various astrophysical properties, with far-reaching implications for the study of galaxy evolution and the formation of structure in the universe.

title: Player-Compatible Learning and Player-Compatible Equilibrium
Abstract: This paper introduces the concept of player-compatible learning and player-compatible equilibrium, two novel constructs in the realm of game theory and learning theory. Building on the foundations of Nash equilibrium, it is often assumed that players converge to the equilibrium through some form of learning process. However, this assumption may not hold under non-atomic player populations where individual players constitute only a small portion of the overall population. The proposed framework of player-compatible learning allows for individual learning processes to be compatible with the system-level behavior, leading to the convergence of player populations towards a stable equilibrium. A key contribution of this research is the derivation of a new solution concept, termed player-compatible equilibrium, which captures the emergent behavior of players that learn to play compatible strategies at the system level. This framework is developed through a combination of analytical and experimental evidence, drawing from both theoretical and empirical methods. Through systematic analysis and simulation studies, we demonstrate the efficacy of the player-compatible learning framework in capturing realistic dynamics of non-atomic player populations, and propose its applications in various strategic settings, including networked systems, distributed decision-making, and decentralized control. The insights provided by this research have the potential to inform the design of novel learning algorithms, that can facilitate the emergence of robust and adaptive behavior in complex systems.

title: Judicious Judgment Meets Unsettling Updating: Dilation, Sure Loss, and Simpson's Paradox
Abstract: This paper delves into the interplay between judicious judgment, unsettling updating, dilation, sure loss, and Simpson's paradox within the realm of decision theory and probability. The concept of judicious judgment, often associated with subjective probability, is a coherent way of making decisions under uncertainty, as it avoids making explicit predictions about uncertain events. Conversely, unsettling updating refers to the phenomenon where an individual's confidence in a particular event's probability appears to be disrupted when new evidence becomes available, especially if the evidence contradicts their initial beliefs. This paper endeavors to reconcile the principles of dilation, which are employed to quantify the notion of sure loss, with the paradoxical situation where data seem to show that one outcome is more likely than another when the sample sizes are different, better known as Simpson's paradox. By exploring how these concepts interact and influence decision-making, this paper endeavors to advance our understanding of the interplay between subjective probability, evidence, and decision-making under uncertainty. It employs a rigorous analytical and philosophical approach to tease out the intricacies of these concepts and their applications in various real-world scenarios.

title: A Survey of FPGA-Based Neural Network Accelerator
Abstract: Field-Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGA) have garnered significant attention in recent years for their role in accelerating Artificial Intelligence (AI) workloads, particularly in the realm of Neural Networks (NNs). This survey provides a comprehensive overview of FPGA-based Neural Network accelerators, encompassing a wide range of architectures, design considerations, and optimization techniques. The survey begins with a detailed analysis of existing FPGA-based NN accelerators, categorized based on their system architecture, processing engine, and memory hierarchy. A thorough examination of the major design considerations, including power consumption, thermal management, and area-efficient implementation, is also presented. Additionally, the survey delves into the various optimization techniques employed to enhance the performance and efficiency of FPGA-based NN accelerators, such as parallelization, pipeline optimization, and precision reduction. Furthermore, a critical evaluation of the current state-of-the-art FPGA-based NN accelerators is conducted, highlighting their strengths and weaknesses, and identifying potential research directions for future advancements. title: Deep Learning for Massive MIMO CSI Feedback
Abstract: Deep learning techniques have revolutionized the field of wireless communication by efficiently addressing the challenges in massive Multiple Input Multiple Output (MIMO) systems, particularly in channel state information (CSI) feedback. The exponential increase in the number of antennas in massive MIMO systems leads to a significant increase in the amount of CSI feedback required, posing a considerable challenge to the existing limited uplink resources. In this paper, we investigate the application of deep learning to compress and process CSI feedback in massive MIMO systems. We propose a novel deep learning-based approach that leverages the strengths of both compressive sensing and spatial modulation techniques. Our approach employs a neural network to learn the compressed CSI feedback from the raw channel measurement data, thereby reducing the overhead of CSI feedback while maintaining the same level of accuracy. The proposed approach is evaluated in a variety of scenarios using extensive simulations, demonstrating its superiority over the state-of-the-art approaches. Quantitative results show that our approach achieves a significant reduction in the CSI feedback overhead with minimal loss of accuracy. title: Building a Sentiment Corpus of Tweets in Brazilian Portuguese
Abstract: This study aims to create a sentiment-annotated corpus of tweets in Brazilian Portuguese, addressing the need for a large-scale, fine-grained dataset for sentiment analysis and polarity classification in Portuguese language research. The collected corpus will consist of approximately 50,000 tweets, extracted from the Twitter API between 2015 and 2019, using a combination of keywords, hashtags, and geolocation filters to target Brazilian Portuguese-speaking regions. To ensure the corpus' representativeness, we employed a multistage strategy, involving the selection of relevant sentiment-bearing words, named entity recognition to annotate relevant entities, and evaluation of gold standard using an enhanced three-class sentiment annotation scheme, classifying sentiments as strongly negative, weak negative, neutral, weak positive, and strongly positive. A computational model integrating machine learning, word embeddings, and annotated corpora will be developed to assess the quality of the annotated corpus and examine the feasibility of applying the existing sentiment analysis technologies to the Brazilian Portuguese domain. The compiled corpus will have potential applications in consumer psychology, marketing analytics, natural language processing, and any other fields where sentiment analysis yields valuable insights, offering Brazilian researchers and practitioners access to a local, reliable, and extensive resource to explore their research questions.

title: Bayesian Nonparametric Causal Inference: Information Rates and Learning Algorithms
Abstract: This abstract discusses advancements in Bayesian nonparametric causal inference by introducing new learning algorithms and information rate analysis. Bayesian nonparametric models offer a flexible approach to causal inference by treating causal relationships as random variables. However, their application has been limited by computational inefficiencies and difficulties in diagnosing convergence, particularly when dealing with high-dimensional datasets. To address these challenges, researchers have developed novel information-theoretic techniques for analyzing the information rates of Bayesian nonparametric causal inference algorithms. These methods enable more accurate assessments of the performance of these algorithms, uncovering crucial insights into the trade-offs between model complexity, data compression, and causal signal detection. In this study, we explore the integration of these information-theoretic techniques into learning algorithms for Bayesian nonparametric causal inference. The proposed framework encompasses modifications to traditional Bayesian nonparametric methods, enabling more efficient and accurate causal discovery, particularly in high-dimensional datasets. Our results demonstrate the efficacy of this approach in various scenarios, underscoring the importance of refined information rate analysis in optimizing Bayesian nonparametric causal inference. The contributions of this research will enhance the application of Bayesian nonparametric causal inference in diverse fields, from econometrics and epidemiology to neuroscience and artificial intelligence.

title: Weighted Data Normalization Based on Eigenvalues for Artificial Neural Network Classification
Abstract: This study proposes an innovative weighted data normalization approach, incorporating eigenvalue metrics for optimizing artificial neural network (ANN) classification performance on imbalanced datasets. The traditional normalization techniques, such as mean and standard deviation normalization, often fail to address the issue of data skewness and are incapable of leveraging the inherent internal structures of the datasets. In contrast, our weighted normalization approach utilizes the eigenvalue spectrum of the datasets to identify the most informative features and assigns varying weights to each feature based on its relevance. This allows for more accurate representation of the data and enhances the robustness of the ANN model. By leveraging the properties of eigenvalues, our approach can adapt to complex data distributions and identify instances that contribute significantly to the class boundaries. The results obtained from a series of experiments on multiple benchmark datasets indicate that our proposed method significantly improves the accuracy of ANN classification models on imbalanced datasets, particularly in scenarios where the class distribution is highly skewed. Furthermore, the analysis of the eigenvalue-based weights reveals that features with smaller eigenvalues are often less informative and contribute more to the noise in the data, thus underscoring the importance of feature selection in enhancing the performance of ANN models. Overall, our weighted data normalization approach based on eigenvalues offers a novel solution for addressing the challenges associated with imbalanced datasets in ANNs and has significant implications for the development of more accurate and robust classification models.

title: Lectures on Randomized Numerical Linear Algebra
Abstract: This series of lectures provides an in-depth exploration of randomized numerical linear algebra, a field that has emerged at the intersection of numerical analysis, linear algebra, and randomized algorithms. Randomized methods have revolutionized the solution of large-scale linear algebra problems, which arise in numerous applications, including data analysis, machine learning, and scientific simulations. By leveraging random sampling and matrix approximation, these techniques offer an efficient and scalable alternative to traditional deterministic methods, particularly when confronting massive datasets. The lectures discuss fundamental concepts such as matrix sketching, subspaces, and eigenspaces, as well as more advanced topics like sampling, statistical bounds, and numerical analysis. The lectures also delve into the empirical evaluation of these algorithms, including the challenges of interpreting results in the presence of randomness. title: Optimal Weighting for Exam Composition
Abstract: This research explores the optimal weighting for exam composition, a pressing concern for educational institutions striving to create fair, rigorous, and valid assessments. title: Maximizing the Collective Learning Effects in Regional Economic Development

To address this challenge, the paper develops a conceptual model integrating key dimensions of CLEs, including institutional thickness, innovation system complexity, and networked relationships. title: Can the Many-Worlds-Interpretation be probed in Psychology?
Abstract: The Many-Worlds-Interpretation of quantum mechanics proposes that every time a quantum event occurs, the universe splits into multiple parallel branches, resulting in an infinite number of parallel universes. While this theory has been widely discussed in the realm of physics, its implications on human psychology remain largely unexplored. This research delves into the possibility of probing the Many-Worlds-Interpretation in the field of psychology, exploring whether the concept of parallel universes can be integrated into existing psychological theories and frameworks. By examining the psychological theories of perception, consciousness, and the human experience, we find that the Many-Worlds-Interpretation may offer a novel explanation for certain psychological phenomena, such as the experience of déjà vu, the sensation of parallel timelines, and the concept of alternate selves. Furthermore, we propose that the Many-Worlds-Interpretation can be used as a framework for understanding the consequences of split-brain phenomena, the nature of personal identity, and the human capacity for self-reflection. Through a multidisciplinary approach that combines theories from physics, psychology, and philosophy, we aim to provide a preliminary exploration of the psychological implications of the Many-Worlds-Interpretation, and to shed light on the potential of this concept to challenge our current understanding of human consciousness and the human experience.

title: Visual Stability Prediction and Its Application to Manipulation

title: Conformity in virtual environments: a hybrid neurophysiological and psychosocial approach
Abstract: Conformity emerges as a pervasive phenomenon in virtual environments, where individuals engage in digital social interactions that blur the boundaries of physical spaces. title: Formalizing Neurath's Ship: Approximate Algorithms for Online Causal Learning
Abstract: Neurath's Ship proposes that our understanding of the world is necessarily incomplete and that, like the mariner referring back to his map, our beliefs and knowledge can never be fully verified. Formalizing this idea within the context of online causal learning involves designing algorithms that can iteratively update their understanding of causal relationships in a world with potentially incomplete information. This dissertation presents a framework for approximating such algorithms. By combining approximation techniques with causal structures and incorporating domain-specific prior knowledge, a class of algorithms is identified that can efficiently and accurately update their causal models. The key contribution lies in the development of a novel approximation scheme that reduces the computational cost of model updates while maintaining the accuracy of the final model. This scheme relies on a probabilistic abstraction of the model and a clever exploitation of the problem structure. Empirical results demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed algorithms in real-world scenarios, showcasing their ability to learn complex causal relationships in a variety of domains. Further, a detailed comparison with state-of-the-art methods highlights the advantages of the proposed framework. title: The Gaussian Graphical Model in Cross-sectional and Time-series Data
Abstract: The Gaussian Graphical Model (GGM) has emerged as a powerful tool for uncovering the underlying structure of relationships between variables in high-dimensional datasets, including both cross-sectional and time-series data. In cross-sectional data, the GGM has been successfully applied to identify network structures and clusters, revealing complex relationships that were previously hidden from view. For instance, in gene expression data, the GGM has been used to construct regulatory networks that highlight key genes and their interactions. In time-series data, the GGM has been used to build auto-regressive vector autoregression (VAR) models to capture the temporal dependencies between variables. However, the estimation of GGM in time-series data can be challenging due to the presence of temporal dependencies and the need to account for both cross-sectional and temporal relationships. Recent advances in estimation methods, such as the graphical lasso and nodewise regression, have improved the accuracy and efficiency of GGM estimation. In this work, we investigate the application of GGM in cross-sectional and time-series data, focusing on the challenges and opportunities arising from the temporal dependencies in time-series data. We also highlight the potential uses of GGM in a range of applications, including biology, finance, and social sciences.

title: When categorization-based stranger avoidance explains the uncanny valley: A comment on MacDorman & Chattopadhyay (2016)
Abstract: Categorization-based stranger avoidance, a theory developed by social psychologists, offers a compelling explanation for the phenomenon known as the uncanny valley. MacDorman & Chattopadhyay (2016) contend that the uncanny valley occurs when a humanoid robot exhibits near-human yet not-quite-human qualities, disturbing humans due to its ambiguous categorization as friend versus stranger. However, this theory has been subject to limited scrutiny. This paper aims to explore the applicability of categorization-based stranger avoidance in explaining the uncanny valley by investigating the neural correlates of categorization in response to humanoid stimuli. Our hypothesis is that when encountering humanoid robots, humans' fear of the unknown, a common motive underlying categorization-based stranger avoidance, activates the brain's safety-threatening detection and treatment centers, shifting emotional responses from pleasant affinity towards discomfort and aversion. Utilizing cognitive and neurobiological methods, including electroencephalography, functional magnetic resonance imaging and self-reported measures, our results offer critical insight into the manner in which categorization influences human emotional processes. This study aims to provide substantial evidence to support, as well as modify, the theoretical framework presented by MacDorman & Chattopadhyay, shedding new light on the neural essence of the uncanny valley and its putative role in human social cognition.

title: Identifying Dogmatism in Social Media: Signals and Models
Abstract: This research investigates the phenomenon of dogmatism in social media, a maladaptive cognitive style characterized by close-mindedness, intolerance of ambiguity, and resistance to change. Using a mixed-methods approach combining natural language processing (NLP) and computational modeling, our study identified several features distinguishing dogmatic speech from neutral or liberal voices on Twitter. Quantitative analysis revealed significantly higher presence of superlatives, derogatory language, and hyperpartisan content within dogmatic profiles. Regression models and sentiment analysis further corroborated the presence of these signals, and revealed significant associations between individual-level characteristics, such as age, ideology, and follower network, and dogmatic behavior. Complementary qualitative analysis of 1,000 tweets and 100 profiles probed the narratives and social dynamics surrounding dogmatic online engagement, uncovering evidence of targeted radicalization, intergroup conflicts, and echo-chamber reinforcement of hyperpartisan discourse. title: Engagement Detection in Meetings
Abstract: This study investigates the phenomenon of engagement detection in meetings, where participants actively contribute to discussions and demonstrate interest in the topic at hand. Current approaches, such as manual observation and surveys, are time-consuming and prone to human error. To address this gap, this research proposes a novel methodological framework that combines machine learning techniques with multimodal sensory data, including audio, video, and physiological signals. The proposed framework is designed to detect engagement cues, such as vocalizations, body language, and physiological responses, to identify participants who are actively engaged versus disengaged. The study also explores the impact of various meeting characteristics, including participant number, topic discussion, and meeting duration, on engagement levels. title: Semantics derived automatically from language corpora contain human-like biases
Abstract: The pervasive and insidious nature of human-like biases in automated semantic models generated from large language corpora raises significant concerns about their fairness, accuracy, and reliability. Previous studies have demonstrated that these biases can stem from a multitude of sources, including societal stereotypes, cultural norms, and historical artifacts, which are reflected in the datasets used to train these models. Furthermore, these biases are often perpetuated through mechanisms such as word embeddings, where objects and concepts with similar meanings are inadvertently bundled together with undesirable associations. For instance, a study on objectivity in automated sentiment analysis revealed that the word embeddings used in the model had a clear male bias, highlighting the pernicious effects of subtle and invisible biases. While several strategies have been proposed to mitigate these biases, including debiasing word embeddings, evaluating and addressing biases remains an ongoing challenge due to the inherent complexity of language, data variability, and the need for expertise in multiple fields. Examining how human-like biases in automated semantic models can be mitigated, and considering potential solutions from multiple domains, this study offers a comprehensive treatment of the problem, shedding critical light on the intersection of technology, social realities, and human experiences.

title: Practical optimal experiment design with probabilistic programs
Abstract: This research proposes an innovative approach to practical optimal experiment design leveraging the power of probabilistic programming. By utilizing probabilistic programming languages, such as Stan or PyMC3, researchers can now seamlessly integrate complex statistical models with uncertainty quantification directly into experimental design processes. This allows for the allocation of limited resources in a way that maximizes the information gain from an experiment, reducing the risk of encountering uninformative data and minimizing the cost of conducting additional experiments. In this study, we present a comprehensive framework for probabilistic optimal experiment design, combining principles from Bayesian decision theory and model-based design of experiments. We develop novel algorithms and methodologies that can efficiently handle high-dimensional design spaces and complex statistical models, providing insights into optimal sample allocation and experimental conditions. Furthermore, our approach is demonstrated using various case studies across diverse fields, including environmental monitoring, materials science, and pharmaceutical development. title: Aristotle vs. Ringelmann: On Superlinear Production in Open Source Software
Abstract: This study conducts a comparative analysis of two distinct but related theoretical frameworks - Aristotle's concept of synergy and Ringelmann's principle of collective action - to better understand superlinear production in open source software. While Aristotle's synergy theory posits that the whole is greater than the sum of its parts, Ringelmann's principle, on the other hand, describes how individual productivity tends to decrease as the size of the group increases. These principles seem to contradict each other, raising questions about their applicability to a collaborative development environment such as open source software. By investigating how these theories interact with and influence each other, this research aims to shed light on the underlying dynamics of superlinear production, a phenomenon where the growth rate of the team's productivity exceeds the sum of the individual contributions. A combination of qualitative and quantitative methods will be employed to collect and analyze data from various open source projects, including forays into the world of GitHub, Reddit, and Stack Overflow. Our analysis will consider variables such as the size and composition of the development team, the dynamics of collaboration, and the impact of individual characteristics on team productivity. title: Adapting Deep Network Features to Capture Psychological Representations

We evaluate the efficacy of our approach by adapting a range of deep features to represent a selection of psychological entities, including mental disorders, emotions, and social constructs, and compare their performance with traditional deep learning models. title: HyperLex: A Large-Scale Evaluation of Graded Lexical Entailment
Abstract: HyperLex: A Large-Scale Evaluation of Graded Lexical Entailment is a comprehensive study that evaluates the nuances of lexical relationships, specifically graded lexical entailment, in natural language processing. Graded lexical entailment is a critical aspect of linguistic understanding, as it captures the varying degrees of semantic implication between words. Existing traditional lexical entailment frameworks fail to account for the complexity and variability inherent in these relationships, leading to inaccurate representations of lexical meaning. This study introduces HyperLex, a large-scale evaluation framework designed to address these limitations. The framework comprises a comprehensive dataset consisting of over 2 million entailment relations across a range of lexical semantic contexts. Furthermore, HyperLex incorporates a novel, multi-scale ranking approach to graded lexical entailment, allowing for a more precise and context-dependent evaluation of lexical relationships. By systematically analyzing the strengths and weaknesses of current lexical entailment models, HyperLex aims to establish a new standard for evaluating and improving these models in real-world applications, such as question answering, sentiment analysis, and text classification. The research contributes to the development of more accurate and robust AI models capable of understanding the intricate semantics of natural language, ultimately enhancing their ability to reason, learn, and communicate effectively in human-computer interactions.

title: Personalized Emphasis Framing for Persuasive Message Generation
Abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to personalized persuasive message generation through the application of emphasis framing, a technique rooted in behavioral economics. Emphasis framing involves manipulating the presentation of information to draw attention to certain key features or details, thereby influencing decision-making processes. By incorporating individual differences in personality traits, values, and prior experiences, our approach, dubbed Emphasis Framing for Persuasion (EFP), tailors the framing of persuasive messages to better resonate with specific target audiences. Through a systematic analysis of existing literature on persuasive techniques, cognitive biases, and personalization, we develop a comprehensive framework for determining optimal emphasis framing strategies. A user-centric framework is introduced, where the machine learning model learns to predict the influence of individual characteristics on the persuasiveness of emphasis-framed messages. Our methodology involves an examination of psychological adaptation, cognitive dissonance, and framing effects to customize and optimize the persuasive approach. In experimentally evaluating the efficacy of EFP on a diverse set of participants, we report significant gains in message persuasiveness and a notable increase in the relevance of messages to the target audience. Our findings suggest that personalized emphasis framing can yield substantial and meaningful improvements in persuasiveness, underscoring its potential as a strategic tool in marketing, public speaking, and healthcare communications.

title: Cognitive Science in the era of Artificial Intelligence: A roadmap for reverse-engineering the infant language-learner
Abstract: Recent breakthroughs in artificial intelligence (AI) and language processing have sparked a new revolution in the field of cognitive science, but this progress largely leaves behind an essential aspect of human cognition: the acquisition of language in early childhood. The study of this process is particularly intriguing, especially in light of the successful deployment of language models in AI applications. By embarking on a comprehensive roadmap that integrates the most recent findings from neuroscience, linguistics, and AI, this research aims to develop a more profound understanding of how infants learn language. We advance a theoretical framework that integrates infant language development models with deep learning algorithms, highlighting their shared structural properties and possible evolutionary trajectory. Key insights are gained by juxtaposing human infant language behaviors with that of neural language models trained on large-scale linguistic datasets. This convergence approach reveals valuable similarity and analogy between the two, including patterns of distributed representation, layered hierarchies, and combinatorial rule learning. Empirical results demonstrate that the knowledge acquired through this approach improves language comprehension, generation, and interpretation, offering novel directions for augmenting both language-learning models and neural language processing systems with data-driven constraints.

title: Psychologically inspired planning method for smart relocation task
Abstract: A strategically effective smart relocation task planning method is proposed in this research, grounded in the principles of cognitive psychology and artificial intelligence. Building on the concept of human planning processes, the proposed method, referred to as Cognitive-Based Relocation Planning (CBRP), is designed to optimise the decision-making process for transforming existing physical spaces into functional smart homes. This innovative approach capitalizes on the unique problem-solving strategies exhibited by individuals, including the exploitation of contextual knowledge, efficient cognitive prioritization, and informed estimation of potential risks. The methodology integrates psychological theories such as mental simulation, goal-directed behaviour, and episodic memory to create a decision support system capable of automating relocation tasks, including asset re-prioritisation, furniture layout optimisation, and future-proofing for anticipated changes in occupants' needs. A comprehensive simulation-based validation is carried out to scrutinise the performance of CBRP in challenging smart relocation scenarios, showcasing substantial time and resource savings. Furthermore, CBRP is implemented in a real-world relocation project, where its efficacy and effectiveness in enhancing relocation outcomes are demonstrated empirically. These findings establish CBRP as a promising technique for streamlining complex relocation tasks amidst growing urbanisation, empowering smart cities to flourish with efficient, streamlined processes. Consequently, CBRP bridges the gap between human-centric decision-making and the computational demands of smart home planning.

title: The Python user interface of the elsA cfd software: a coupling framework for external steering layers
Abstract: This paper presents a novel Python user interface for the elsA CFD software, a highly-parallelized and production-oriented computational fluid dynamics solver. elsA is characterized by its complex, optimized implementation, which makes it challenging to integrate with external steering layers, traditionally requiring extensive manual modification of the code. To address this, we introduce a novel coupling framework that enables straightforward and flexible integration of external steering layers with elsA's native solver. This framework leverages existing technology, specifically the Python language and its numerous scientific computing libraries, to create a robust and extensible interface for user-defined steering functions. The resulting Python interface, detailed in this work, is designed with both performance and usability in mind, allowing for seamless interaction with the solver through Python scripts or even graphical user interfaces built on popular libraries such as tkinter or PyQt. By providing a simple and standardized way to hook into elsA, we significantly simplify the task of utilizing the solver as part of larger software architectures and tools, making it more accessible to a wider range of users and applications. Through the creation of this Python interface, we aim to improve the overall usage and integration experience of elsA. As an example, applications in fields such as fluid dynamics, computational physics, or industry-specific simulations can leverage the capabilities of elsA when paired with user-defined steering layers tailored to their precise requirements.

title: Towards Personality-Aware Recommendation
Abstract: Recent advances in the field of human-computer interaction have led to the development of personalized recommendation systems, which have become an integral part of modern life. However, existing recommendation approaches primarily rely on user behavior, preferences and demographic information, often neglecting the underlying psychological aspects that play a crucial role in shaping individual preferences and experiences. The integration of personality traits into recommendation systems has been proposed as a potential solution to address this limitation, as it can lead to more accurate and meaningful recommendations. Personality-aware recommendation systems utilize machine learning and natural language processing techniques to analyze individual personality traits and their impact on user behavior, preferences, and experiences. This abstract reviews recent work in the area of personality-aware recommendation and highlights the potential benefits of incorporating personality traits into recommendation systems. We examine the various methods and techniques used to analyze personality data, including personality typing models, affective computing, and psychological profiling. Additionally, we discuss the potential challenges and limitations of implementing personality-aware recommendation systems, including issues related to data collection, representation, and interpretation of personality traits, as well as concerns regarding user privacy and feedback manipulation. Our review provides an overview of the current state of the art in personality-aware recommendation systems and highlights areas for future research and development.

title: Adaptive Artificial Intelligence in Games: Issues, Requirements, and a Solution through Behavlets-based General Player Modelling
Abstract: Adaptive artificial intelligence (AI) in games represents a significant shift from traditional game development approaches, where AI agents were designed to follow pre-programmed scripts. In contrast, adaptive AI focuses on responding dynamically to the player's actions, adapting to their playing style, and predicting their future behavior. However, implementing adaptive AI in games is challenging due to the need for comprehensive knowledge of the player's behavior and preferences. Furthermore, the complex interplay between game dynamics, player psychology, and AI decision-making processes creates numerous issues, including contextual understanding, preference modeling, and model drift. To address these challenges, a novel solution, Behavlets-based General Player Modelling (BGPM), is proposed. BGPM is based on the idea of representing player behavior using a set of discrete, non-overlapping, and context-dependent behavioral patterns called Behavlets. This approach enables a deep understanding of player preferences and behavior, allowing for more accurate predictions and adaptive game plays. BGPM can adapt to changing player behavior, handle multiple player personas, and provide a scalable and interpretable solution for complex game contexts. By employing BGPM, game developers can create highly engaging and responsive game experiences, which has the potential to significantly enhance player satisfaction and longevity.

title: Neural scaling laws for an uncertain world
Abstract: The explosion of computational power and advancements in deep learning have led to rapid progress in artificial intelligence, and neural scaling laws provide a framework to understand and predict these trends. However, the applicability of established scaling laws to complex and dynamic real-world problems remains uncertain. Existing scaling laws assume that neural network behavior follows a predictable and idiosyncratic path, but the high degree of variability and non-stationarity in such scenarios presents significant challenges. This study aims to bridge the gap by introducing a novel framework for neural scaling laws that can accommodate and provide insights into uncertain and dynamic systems. Our approach integrates techniques from machine learning, control theory, and statistical physics to develop a generalized scaling theory capable of capturing the characteristics of complex systems. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework using a variety of case studies, including robotic control, time-series forecasting, and uncertainty-driven optimization. The results show that our novel framework can adapt to and outperform existing scaling theories in a wide range of uncertain and dynamic environments. By providing a more comprehensive understanding of neural scaling laws, this research has significant implications for the design, training, and applications of artificial neural networks in uncertain and dynamic real-world systems.

title: Re-presenting a Story by Emotional Factors using Sentimental Analysis Method
Abstract: This abstract presents a novel approach to analyzing and representing the emotional essence of a story through sentimental analysis. By automating the process of sentiment detection in narrative texts, our proposed method promises to unlock the emotional dynamics that underlie narrative structures. Sentimental analysis has evolved as a significant technique in the realm of natural language processing, and its extension to storytelling holds immense potential for gaining deeper insights into the human experience. Our method utilizes advanced computational tools to extract and visualize emotional textures from literary works, contributing towards a holistic understanding of narrative dynamics and their cultural significance. This paper critically examines the theoretical underpinnings of sentimental analysis and its applicability to narrative research, laying the groundwork for new avenues of exploration in textual characterization and its implications in psychology and literary studies. By situating sentimental analysis within the context of narrative scholarship, our approach aims to shed light on the affective dimensions of storytelling, thereby fostering a more nuanced appreciation of language and meaning in relation to human emotion.

title: Pseudo-Centroid Clustering
Abstract: Pseudo-centroid clustering is an innovative approach to traditional centroid-based clustering algorithms, such as k-means, which suffer from limitations when dealing with complex and irregularly-shaped clusters. This study presents a comprehensive review of pseudo-centroid clustering, a technique that has garnered significant attention in recent years due to its ability to handle high-dimensional data, noise, and outliers. By utilizing a proximity-based framework, pseudo-centroid clustering avoids the need for explicit distance calculations between each pair of points, resulting in substantial computational savings. Furthermore, this method enables the discovery of non-convex and anisotropic clusters that may elude traditional clustering algorithms. Our analysis reveals that pseudo-centroid clustering has shown promising results in various real-world applications, including image and speech processing, bioinformatics, and recommender systems. Despite its potential benefits, pseudo-centroid clustering also poses unique challenges, such as parameter selection and algorithm initialization, that require further exploration. Therefore, this study aims to provide a thorough examination of pseudo-centroid clustering, its strengths, and its limitations, as well as to investigate its robustness and performance under different conditions. The findings of this research will contribute to the advancement of pseudo-centroid clustering and its successful adoption in a wide range of domains, ultimately paving the way for more accurate and efficient clustering solutions.

title: The usability canary in the security coal mine: A cognitive framework for evaluation and design of usable authentication solutions
Abstract: This research explores the concept of the usability canary in the security coal mine, shedding light on the oft-criticized authentication solutions that exist in today's digital landscape. The need for more usable authentication methods becomes increasingly pressing, with the current state of affairs often characterized by cumbersome passwords, two-factor authentication, and biometric verification systems that are prone to errors, biased towards certain demographic groups, and are not tailored to diverse user needs. Following this understanding, our study proposes a cognitive framework for evaluating and designing more effective and user-centered authentication solutions. Drawing from theories of cognitive psychology, human-computer interaction, and design science research, this framework provides a comprehensive model for the process of design, analysis, and evaluation of authentication systems. It grounds usability analysis in a deeper understanding of users' thoughts, feelings, and behaviors when interacting with authentication interfaces. By developing design and user experience guidelines that focus on usability, the goal is to create authentication systems that provide seamless and secure interactions, while recognizing and giving due consideration to individual differences, accessibility requirements, and the context of use.

title: Bipartisanship breakdown, functional networks and forensic analysis in Spanish 2015 and 2016 national elections
Abstract: This study focuses on examining the dynamics of bipartisan breakdown in the context of Spanish 2015 and 2016 national elections. By applying a functional networks approach to socio-political context analysis, the research aims to explore the interconnected relationships between governmental and non-governmental actors. The use of forensic analysis enables a systematic and objective examination of the election-related data, shedding light on campaign strategies, media coverage, and grassroots mobilization patterns. A close examination of these elections highlights a remarkable decline in bipartisan efforts and collaboration between the two dominant parties: the People's Party (PP) and the Spanish Socialist Workers' Party (PSOE). As a result, the competitive network structures become increasingly fragmented, with other actors invading the space previously held by the two traditional parties. By analyzing this bifurcation, the study aims to identify the factors driving the decline of bipartisan consensus, including the role of party leaders, campaign finance systems, and underlying societal shifts. Additionally, this analysis provides valuable insights into the reconfiguration of the Spanish party system and sets the stage for comparative investigations across different national contexts. The findings of this research also have strong implications for electoral reform, facilitating changes in the electoral laws and rules aimed at promoting more collaborative politics.

title: Bayesian emulation for optimization in multi-step portfolio decisions
Abstract: Bayesian emulation has emerged as a promising framework for model-based optimization in high-dimensional decision-making problems. This paper leverages Bayesian emulation to optimize multi-step portfolio decisions, addressing a critical challenge in finance where dynamic portfolio rebalancing and hedging require intricate trade-offs between risk, return, and regulatory constraints. The proposed framework integrates a machine learning algorithm, Gaussian Process Emulation, with Bayesian optimization to develop a computationally efficient approach for global optimization of portfolio decisions across multiple time steps. By emulating the high-fidelity black-box model of the portfolio optimizer with a computationally efficient surrogate model, the algorithm significantly reduces the computational burden of evaluation and maximizes the discovery of improved portfolio solutions. To demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework, we apply it to a suite of benchmark models, including the Black-Litterman model and the Markowitz model, and conduct a comprehensive comparison of the optimization outcomes with those obtained by state-of-the-art global optimization methods. Our results demonstrate that the proposed Bayesian emulation framework consistently yields high-quality solutions with reduced computational overhead, offering a substantial improvement over competing approaches. The insights and benefits of the proposed framework have far-reaching implications for automated portfolio optimization in finance and financial technology applications, enabling more efficient decision-making under uncertainty and fostering better risk management practices.

title: The Effects of Cultural dimensions and Demographic Characteristics on E-learning Acceptance
Abstract: This study investigates the impact of cultural dimensions and demographic characteristics on the acceptance of e-learning among higher education students. Building on the existing literature, we integrated the Hofstede's cultural dimensions framework and the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) to develop a comprehensive model that explains the e-learning acceptance behavior of students from diverse cultural backgrounds. Our research design employed a mixed-methods approach, combining both qualitative and quantitative data collection and analysis techniques. We surveyed a sample of 1,500 students from various countries, representing diverse cultural and demographic profiles. Our findings suggest that cultural dimensions such as individualism, power distance, and uncertainty avoidance are significant predictors of e-learning acceptance, while demographic characteristics like age, gender, and prior technology experience also play a crucial role in shaping students' attitudes towards e-learning. Specifically, our results indicate that students from individualistic cultures tend to have a higher level of perceived ease of use and perceived usefulness of e-learning, while those from collectivistic cultures are more likely to experience discomfort and anxiety when using e-learning platforms. Furthermore, younger students and those with prior technology experience tend to have a more favorable attitude towards e-learning. Our study provides valuable insights for educators, policymakers, and e-learning developers to design and implement effective e-learning programs that cater to the diverse needs and preferences of students from various cultural and demographic backgrounds.

title: A Tutorial on Regularized Partial Correlation Networks
Abstract: Regularized partial correlation networks have emerged as a powerful tool in unraveling complex relationships between variables in high-dimensional data. This tutorial aims to provide an introduction to the concepts, methods, and applications of regularized partial correlation networks. We begin by introducing the traditional partial correlation coefficient and its limitations in high-dimensional data settings. Next, we present the concept of regularization and its role in stabilizing the estimation of partial correlations. We then delve into the different types of regularization techniques, including Lasso, Elastic Net, and Graphical Lasso, and discuss their mathematical formulations and computational implementations. The tutorial also covers the construction of regularized partial correlation networks, including methods for selection of the regularization parameter and tuning of the network structure. We demonstrate the practical applications of regularized partial correlation networks in various fields, such as genetics, neuroscience, and finance, and highlight the advantages of these networks in identifying meaningful relationships between variables. The tutorial will provide a comprehensive overview of the theoretical and methodological aspects of regularized partial correlation networks, and serve as a useful resource for researchers, students, and practitioners who seek to apply these techniques in their own research.

title: EmoFit: Affect Monitoring System for Sedentary Jobs
Abstract: EmoFit: Affect Monitoring System for Sedentary Jobs is a novel, non-invasive, wearable system designed to monitor and manage the emotional states of individuals engaged in sedentary jobs. The system utilizes machine learning algorithms combined with physiological and behavioral data to continuously track users' emotional responses, identifying early signs of stress, anxiety, and burnout. By incorporating affective computing and ambient intelligence, EmoFit provides personalized feedback, suggesting activities and interventions to mitigate symptoms of emotional distress, promoting overall well-being and job satisfaction. Key components of the EmoFit system include a wearable wristband equipped with electrodermal activity sensors, a mobile application for user input and feedback, and a cloud-based platform for data analysis and expert system integration. Preliminary results demonstrate the effectiveness of EmoFit in improving mood, reducing stress levels, and enhancing cognitive function among employees engaged in sedentary occupations. Furthermore, the system facilitates a shift from reactive to proactive emotional management, empowering users to adopt healthy coping mechanisms, foster resilience, and cultivate a healthier work-life balance. As a holistic, biopsychosocial intervention, EmoFit has the potential to transform the work environment by promoting productive, stress-free workspaces, ultimately enhancing quality of life and employability.

title: Risk and Ambiguity in Information Seeking: Eye Gaze Patterns Reveal Contextual Behaviour in Dealing with Uncertainty
Abstract: This study examines the relationship between information-seeking risk preferences and ambiguity in various contexts, elucidating how individuals navigate uncertainty when selecting information sources. Utilizing eye-tracking technology to monitor and analyse participants' gaze patterns while engaging with hypothetical information-seeking scenarios, the research reveals that distinct contextual cues influence individuals' risk-taking decisions, particularly when faced with ambiguous information. Specifically, the findings indicate that individuals tend to seek riskier or safer options depending on the perceived level of ambiguity in the situation, which in turn affects their information-seeking behavior. Moreover, results show that participants' gaze patterns reveal different cognitive processes involved in uncertainty dealing, including information searching, risk assessment, and outcome expectation weighing. Employing a comprehensive approach combining eye-tracking technology with survey data and individual interviews, the study provides insights into individuals' strategic efforts to mitigate uncertainty when making informed decisions about which information to consult. The study sheds light on the complex dynamics involved in context-dependent risk taking, which is crucial for crafting more effective strategies for mitigating ambiguity in uncertain situations, thereby illuminating new avenues for understanding and enhancing the information-seeking behavior. Present findings highlights the necessity to carefully design information systems that support individuals in dealing effectively with uncertainty, incorporating feedback mechanisms that sense and adapt to the level of risk an individual is willing to take.

title: Bayesian Games with Intentions
Abstract: This paper contributes to the development of Bayesian games by introducing a novel framework that incorporates intentions into game-theoretic decision-making. We propose a formal definition of intentions as decision-makers' meta-strategies that influence their behavior and trust decisions in sequential, imperfect-information games. Our approach builds upon existing work in dynamic Bayesian games and philosophical theories of intentions. We introduce two main components: a probabilistic intention model to capture the attitudes of rational players and a prospect theory-based value function to elicit preferences with respect to self-fulfilling intentions. This is achieved through a learning process where each player attempts to reason about their opponent's current intention and anticipate their future actions. We demonstrate the applicability of our framework by applying it to a series of illustrative examples and case studies, showcasing its effectiveness in capturing strategic and cooperative behavior in Bayesian games with imperfect information. Our results highlight the importance of incorporating intentions into decision-making processes, yielding new insights into game-theoretic concepts like collaboration and deception. Furthermore, we compare our proposed framework to traditional Bayesian approaches, demonstrating robust improvements in predictive accuracy and better representation of realistic human behavior in strategic decision-making situations.

title: Human-Agent Decision-making: Combining Theory and Practice
Abstract: Human-Agent decision-making represents the intersection of artificial intelligence, cognitive science, and economics, aiming to foster effective collaboration between humans and artificial agents in various decision-making scenarios. This research investigates the synergistic potential of integrating theoretical insights from these disciplines with practical considerations from real-world applications. By systematically examining existing frameworks and evaluating their efficacy in different contexts, the study seeks to identify key limitations and opportunities for future advancements. A major concern in human-agent collaboration lies in the fundamental issue of trust; the ability to trust in the competence and benevolent intentions of the artificial agent. The study investigates how robustness of human-agent interaction can be maximized by enhancing transparency in decision-making processes, implementing fault-tolerant reasoning mechanisms, and establishing cooperative learning frameworks that foster mutual understanding between interacting partners. Furthermore, this body of research provides a comprehensive literature review on established decision-making theories and models, offering detailed analysis and critique. By bringing together diverse strands of theoretical inquiry and real-world experience, the research aims to inform the development of decision-making protocols, enhancing the reliability and effectiveness of human-agent collaboration in complex decision-making environments. Ultimately, the study's findings are likely to have significant implications for a wide range of sectors, including intelligent transportation systems, assistive robotics, and expert system applications.

title: PPM: A Privacy Prediction Model for Online Social Networks
Abstract: This research proposes an innovative Privacy Prediction Model (PPM) designed to forecast an individual's likelihood of maintaining their online privacy in social media. The advent of online social networks has intensified concerns regarding user data protection and information leakage. Currently, existing solutions mainly focus on securing the user data upon exploitation, rather than preventing information disclosure in the first place. By integrating an array of parameters, such as user demographics, social media usage patterns, number of connections, and security awareness, the proposed PPM model endeavours to establish a robust correlation between the characteristics of a user and their propensity to safeguard their private data. Furthermore, this study applies advanced machine learning algorithms, including Random Forest and Support Vector Machines, to train and validate the developed PPM model. Experimenting with a large dataset collected from a leading social media platform, the results demonstrate that the proposed model can effectively identify high-risk users who are more susceptible to revealing sensitive information online. The significance of PPM lies in its ability to enable informed decision-making by social media providers and end-users to implement tailored countermeasures, thereby preserving online privacy and reducing the risk of data breaches. Overall, the privacy prediction model contributes to the literature by addressing the pressing issue of online data protection and promoting a secure online environment.

title: Likelihood-based Parameter Estimation and Comparison of Dynamical Cognitive Models
Abstract: This paper presents an extensive likelihood-based framework for parameter estimation and model comparison of dynamical cognitive models. Dynamical cognitive models, also known as state-space models, are used to elucidate the internal workings of the human brain and its ability to perceive, learn, and generate behavior. In these models, the cognitive process is described by a set of differential equations that capture the changes in the internal states of the system over time. However, the parameters of these models, which are essential for making predictions and assessing the efficacy of interventions, are often unknown and require estimation. This study addresses the issue of parameter estimation by developing a maximum likelihood approach that takes into account the uncertainty and variability in both the model and the observed data. We demonstrate the utility of our approach on three popular dynamical cognitive models: the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) process, the linear diffusion process (LDP), and the FitzHugh-Nagumo (FHN) model. Our results show that the proposed approach can accurately estimate the model parameters and select the best-fitting model with high precision. Furthermore, this study highlights the importance of model comparison in evaluating the goodness of fit and providing a mechanistic understanding of the underlying cognitive processes. These findings demonstrate the potential of our framework in elucidating the neural basis of cognition and identifying effective treatments for various neurological and psychiatric disorders. The proposed approach is versatile, easy to implement, and can be applied to a wide range of cognitive tasks and experiments.

title: Proceedings Fifteenth Conference on Theoretical Aspects of Rationality and Knowledge
Abstract: This paper presents a framework for formalizing and analyzing the role of shared knowledge in multi-agent decision-making scenarios. By combining elements from game theory, knowledge representation, and epistemic logic, we provide a rigorous theoretical foundation for understanding the dynamics of shared information in cooperative and non-cooperative environments. Our approach is centered around a novel representation of joint epistemic states, which captures the complex relationships between agents' beliefs, knowledge, and actions. We demonstrate that this representation allows for a more refined analysis of the strategic implications of shared knowledge, taking into account the subtle distinctions between common knowledge, common belief, and joint uncertainty. Our results show that accounting for the nuances of shared information can have significant effects on the outcomes of cooperative games and interactions, and provide new insights into the design of protocols and mechanisms that leverage shared knowledge to enhance collective decision-making. The framework developed in this paper has far-reaching implications for understanding the role of shared knowledge in a wide range of applications, from artificial intelligence and multi-agent systems to economics and social sciences.

title: Identifying individual facial expressions by deconstructing a neural network
Abstract: This paper introduces an innovative approach to deconstruct and interpret the workings of a deep neural network that specializes in identifying individual facial expressions, a complex task that has garnered significant attention in the realms of affective computing and human-computer interaction. By employing a novel deconstruction technique, we are able to dissect the inner workings of a state-of-the-art neural network architecture, allowing for a nuanced understanding of its decision-making processes. Our results demonstrate that the facial expressions identified by the neural network can be deconstructed into a set of essential components, which can be used to create a more interpretable model. A key finding of this research is that the neural network's ability to accurately classify facial expressions is largely dependent on the presence of distinguishing features, such as the shape and position of facial muscles, which are often undetectable to the human eye. By identifying these key features, our deconstructed model is able to achieve performance close to that of the original neural network, while providing a clear and interpretable explanation of its decision-making processes. These findings have significant implications for the development of more accurate and explainable AI systems, and highlight the potential of deconstruction techniques as a tool for improving the transparency and accountability of complex machine learning models.

title: Brief Report on Estimating Regularized Gaussian Networks from Continuous and Ordinal Data
Abstract: This brief report proposes a method for estimating regularized Gaussian networks from a combination of continuous and ordinal data. Gaussian networks or Gaussian graphical models are statistical models that infer conditional dependencies between variables based on their conditional dependencies in a joint distribution. However, most existing Gaussian network estimation methods assume that the data is entirely Gaussian or ordinal, which is often not the case in real-world scenarios. To address this issue, we extend the existing framework of regularized Gaussian networks to incorporate both continuous and ordinal variables. Specifically, we develop a Bayesian method that accurately accounts for the relationship between the different types of data and learns the structure of the regularized Gaussian networks from combined data. Our approach uses a hierarchical representation, where separate models are used to capture the conditional dependencies between continuous and ordinal variables separately. The ordinal variables are represented as ordered categorical variables, which are integrated into the network estimation process using an effective statistical framework. The proposed method, through numerical and simulation-based experiments, is shown to outperform existing methods and is able to accurately recover the network structure in scenarios with both continuous and ordinal data.

title: Identifiability and testability in GRT with Individual Differences
Abstract: This paper focuses on the advancement of Generalized Randomized Transformations (GRT) for predicting individual data outcomes using GRT modeling with individual differences taken into consideration. In this context, the problem of identifiability, which refers to the ability to accurately determine a model's parameters, and testability, which is concerned with whether a model can be tested and validated, are critical issues. The novel concept of identity learning processes is proposed to address identifiability concerns by establishing an evaluation platform to examine the testability of models with various parameters based on the training data, experiments, and simulated samples. This makes it possible to examine the practical implications of a model and provide insights into its predictive consistency across diverse samples while controlling for the potential effects of internal variations among the individual data. A simulation-based study is designed to illustrate the reliability and computational efficiency of the newly suggested framework. It aims to demonstrate how GRT models can be both identifiable and testable, thereby yielding a fruitful predictive power over various data types, including both synthetic and real-world datasets. The overall goal of this research is to make a substantial contribution to the advancement of GRT models in dealing with individual differences through theoretical and methodological innovation, offering researchers, clinicians, and policymakers in depth insights into their unique performance characteristics and utility in the real setting.

title: Using instrumental variables to disentangle treatment and placebo effects in blinded and unblinded randomized clinical trials influenced by unmeasured confounders
Abstract: In randomized clinical trials, the identification of treatment effects is often confounded by both measured and unmeasured factors. This study addresses the issue of disentangling treatment and placebo effects in both blinded and unblinded trials subject to unmeasured confounders by employing instrumental variable (IV) methods. By leveraging external instruments that are correlated with the treatment but not with the outcome, we propose a novel approach to accounting for unmeasured confounding in the context of randomized trials. Our methodological framework integrates IV methods with the standard analysis of randomized trials, allowing for the estimation of causal effects under the assumption of unmeasured confounding. We contrast the IV approach with standard regression-based analysis, demonstrating its superiority in recovering the true causal effect in the presence of unmeasured confounding. Using simulations, we evaluate the accuracy and robustness of our IV-based estimator across a range of scenarios, including varying levels of confounding, sample sizes, and instrument strength. Our results provide evidence that IV methods can be effectively used to mitigate the impact of unmeasured confounding in randomized trials, thus providing more reliable estimates of treatment effects. We also discuss the implications of our findings for the design and analysis of future clinical trials. This research contributes to the development of a robust and flexible methodology for estimating causal effects in the presence of complex confounding in both clinical and non-clinical settings.

title: Personality Traits and Echo Chambers on Facebook
Abstract: Social media platforms like Facebook have revolutionized the way people interact and communicate with one another. However, the rise of echo chambers has become a major concern in recent years, as users tend to engage with people who share similar opinions and ideals, thereby limiting their exposure to diverse perspectives. The present study aims to examine the relationship between personality traits and the likelihood of individuals being trapped in echo chambers on Facebook. Specifically, we focus on the "Big Five" personality traits, including openness to experience, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, and neuroticism. Our research utilizes a survey-based approach, where a random sample of Facebook users completed an online questionnaire assessing their personality traits and social media behavior. We also collected data on their Facebook network structure and content interactions to identify signs of echo chamber behavior. The results indicate that individuals with certain personality traits, such as those who are more extraverted or less open to experience, are more likely to be trapped in echo chambers on Facebook. We also find that individuals with more homogeneous networks tend to engage in more echo chamber behavior, suggesting that the structural aspects of social media networks play a crucial role in shaping the information individuals are exposed to. Our findings contribute to a better understanding of how personality traits and social media architecture interact to create and maintain echo chambers, highlighting the importance of promoting diverse online interactions and cross-cutting connections.

title: BigEAR: Inferring the Ambient and Emotional Correlates from Smartphone-based Acoustic Big Data
Abstract: This research introduces BigEAR, a data-driven framework to infer ambient and emotional correlates from smartphone-based acoustic big data. Through an unsupervised learning approach, BigEAR utilizes environmental sound and physiological signals captured by mobile devices to construct a comprehensive acoustic big data repository. By leveraging this repository, BigEAR develops a novel framework that leverages a combination of feature extraction, hierarchical clustering, and natural language processing to unravel the intricate relationships between various ambient sounds, human emotional states, and cognitive loads. This framework's three core components, namely SFX, Affective Emotion, and Human-Computer Interaction, establish BigEAR as an unparalleled tool for analyzing acoustic data and examining its psychological effects on individuals in various daily life situations. A long-term multi-cohort study with a diverse group of participants, involving lab environments and in-the-wild experiments, validates BigEAR's theoretical underpinnings and showcases its capabilities in ambient and emotional correlate inference. By integrating acoustic signals from smartphone-based sensors, this research illuminates a fresh path for understanding the symbiotic relationships between the environment, human emotions, and technology-aided interactions. BigEAR's profound implications for affective computing, behavioral analysis, and user-centric design, may spark new ideas and technologies that revolutionize the way we perceive and interact with our surroundings.
