title: Variable phase propagation velocity for long-range lightning location system
Abstract: A long-range lightning location system (LLLS) depends critically on its ability to accurately determine the time delay between the lightning discharge and the arrival of the associated electromagnetic radiation, typically in the very high frequency (VHF) range. However, variable phase propagation velocity during the lightning discharge process has long been recognized as a significant source of error in LLLS. This inherent ambiguity stems primarily from the changing characteristics of the electric charge distribution over the lightning stroke, impacts from the near-surface inhomogeneities of the soil and local topography, and additional propagation effects caused by ambient temperature, type of terrain, and different electromagnetic wave types, also due to non-uniform ionization and non-linearity that alters the phase velocity. Moreover, ionization over distances of kilometers leads to the changing density of the air which can have a significant influence on the speed of propagation of electromagnetic waves. As a result, any LLLS using a single phase velocity value may either severely over-estimate or under-estimate the actual propagation delays, resulting in suboptimal performance, producing system errors and reduced accuracy. Therefore, addressing variable phase propagation speed accurately is crucial for the general efficiency of a long-range lightning location system in order to improve the robustness in real world operations.

title: Comment on Influence of induced interactions on superfluid properties of quasi-two-dimensional dilute Fermi gases with spin-orbit coupling
Abstract: Our research explores the effects of induced interactions on the superfluid properties of quasi-two-dimensional dilute Fermi gases with spin-orbit coupling. We develop a theoretical framework that accounts for both the Fermi-Hubbard model and the spin-orbit coupled Bogoliubov-de Gennes equations. Analyzing the crossover from BCS to BEC behavior within this framework, we examine how induced interactions, which arise from the exchange of particles and antiparticles in the Fermi sea, influence the superfluid transition temperature, condensate fraction, and pairing gap. By incorporating spin-orbit coupling into the model, we take into account the effects of rotation and orbital angular momentum on the superfluid properties. Our calculations reveal that the induced interactions significantly modify the critical temperature and condensate density in the presence of spin-orbit coupling. Additionally, we observe that the rotational symmetry of the system breaks in the strong coupling limit, leading to novel topological features in the superfluid state. The emergence of Majorana fermions and the development of topological superfluid phases are also addressed within our theoretical framework. Our results demonstrate that the interplay between induced interactions, spin-orbit coupling, and quasi-two-dimensional geometry gives rise to rich and complex behavior in Fermi gas superfluidity, which has significant implications for the study of superfluidity in cold atomic gases and future quantum technologies.

This is particularly important in view of accelerating global internet growth, mobile multimedia services, urban crowd densification, and modern wireless applications that strain the system under heavy data loads. Our research also explores the role of crowd behavioral dynamics, using a combination of complex systems modeling and agent-based simulation techniques. title: Gas Accretion in Star-Forming Galaxies
Abstract: Gas accretion is a crucial process for the formation and evolution of galaxies, particularly in the context of star-forming galaxies. However, the observational evidence for gas accretion remains limited, and the theoretical understanding of this process is still developing. Observationally, signatures of gas accretion can be inferred from the presence of kinematically distinct gas clouds, the detection of Lyman-alpha emission from the intergalactic medium, and the observation of enhanced star formation rates in gas-rich regions. Despite these efforts, the character of gas accretion in star-forming galaxies remains poorly constrained, with the importance of different accretion channels and the impact of galaxy properties on the accretion process still uncertain. In this paper, we present a comprehensive study of gas accretion in star-forming galaxies using a combination of simulations, observations, and semi-analytic models. Our goal is to better understand the role of gas accretion in shaping the galaxy population and to provide insights into the underlying physical mechanisms that drive this process. We explore the accretion of gas in different galaxy types, including spiral and irregular galaxies, and examine the dependence of accretion on galaxy mass, size, and environment. Our results have implications for our understanding of galaxy evolution and the formation of the cosmic web.

title: Influence of the external pressure on the quantum correlations of molecular magnets

title: The Tyranny of Data? The Bright and Dark Sides of Data-Driven Decision-Making for Social Good
Abstract: This research paper explores the complex and multifaceted nature of data-driven decision-making in achieving social good, raising important questions about the concept of "tyranny of data." On the one hand, data-driven approaches have led to significant improvements in areas such as healthcare, education, and poverty reduction, allowing for more efficacious use of resources and better outcomes. The diffusion of data-driven innovations, such as mobile health technologies, has also expanded access to essential services, particularly in low-income and marginalized communities. However, beneath these successes lies a more sinister reality, where data-driven decision-making can perpetuate existing power imbalances, exacerbate inequality, and erode democratic decision-making processes. This paper will examine the dark side of data-driven decision-making, highlighting instances where its supposed objectivity has masked underlying biases and flaws, resulting in regressive policies that reinforce systemic injustices. Through a critical analysis of the interplay between data, technology, and power, this research aims to challenge the notion that data is an inherently neutral or objective force, and instead, underscore the need for a more nuanced understanding of the complex dynamics at play in data-driven decision-making. By acknowledging the dual nature of data, this research contributes to a more informed conversation about the potential of data to achieve social good, while avoiding its potential pitfalls.

title: A Joint Analysis for Cosmology and Photometric Redshift Calculation Using Cross Correlations
Abstract: Cosmological studies often rely on photometric redshifts for large-scale galaxy surveys, but the accuracy of these redshifts is crucial for cosmological parameter estimation. Traditional approaches to photometric redshift calculation involve supervised machine learning methods, which require extensive training data and can be sensitive to selection biases. The framework combines type Ia supernovae, cosmic microwave background, and baryon acoustic oscillation measurements with cross-correlation observables, including the galaxy-galaxy, quasar-galaxy, and quasar-quasar correlations. By analyzing the cross-correlation signal, we can indirectly recover the photometric redshift distribution, thereby bypassing the need for training data. This approach has the potential to provide more robust and accurate photometric redshifts, especially for high-redshift galaxies and in regions with limited spectroscopic coverage. We demonstrate the feasibility of this framework using a combination of next-generation cosmological surveys and forecasting tools, showing that it can reach the desired level of accuracy for the current and future surveys. The outcomes of this work will bridge the gap between photometric and spectroscopic redshifts, leading to more precise cosmological parameter estimation and a deeper understanding of the universe.

title: Statistics and structure of spanwise rotating turbulent channel flow at moderate Reynolds numbers
Abstract: This study investigates the effects of spanwise rotation on a turbulent channel flow at moderate Reynolds numbers, with a primary focus on the resulting changes to the flow's statistical properties and structural characteristics. An extensive dataset was produced using direct numerical simulations (DNS) of spanwise rotating channel flows at various rotation rates, Reynolds numbers (up to Re_tau = 1000), and Ekman numbers (ranging from 10^-2 to 10^-5). The mean velocity profiles, Reynolds stresses, and cross-stream integral momentum transport were analyzed to elucidate the effects of rotation on mean flow behavior. Investigation into the instantaneous flow topology, including the persistence of coherent motion in rotating flows, was facilitated through application of particle image velocimetry (PIV) and proper orthogonal decomposition (POD). The emergence of rotational Taylor-Görtler vortices and their role in the modification of the logarithmic mean velocity profile and Reynolds stress distribution was a key finding of this study. Furthermore, Lagrangian coherent structures (LCS) revealed the presence of complex rotation-induced structures that have a pronounced effect on fluid mixing and transport processes in the wall region. Through its comprehensive and detailed characterization of the statistical properties and structural complexities of rotating channel flows at moderate Reynolds numbers, this research provides new insights into the inherent mechanisms governing rotating wall-bounded turbulent flows, contributing to a deeper understanding of their complex behavior and associated applications.

However, the stability of DMSO was found to decrease at higher pyrolysis temperatures, suggesting a trade-off between yield and stability. These findings provide valuable insights into the optimization of DMSO production through the pyrolysis of polysiloxanes filled with nanosized silica and ceria/silica, and have the potential to influence the development of high-yielding and stable DMSO synthesis methods for industrial applications.

The reaction plays a crucial role in the proton-proton chain, contributing to the production of $^{14}$N during hydrogen burning in main-sequence stars and in the subsequent helium burning phase. However, the uncertainties associated with the reaction rate have led to varied predictions of $^{17}$O stellar abundances and yields. Recent measurements and theoretical calculations have resulted in revised rates that differ from previous estimates. As a result, recalculations of $^{17}$O stellar abundances and yields using the revised reaction rate have shown substantial variations, with implications for our understanding of stellar nucleosynthesis. This study aims to investigate the sensitivity of $^{17}$O stellar abundances and yields to the revised reaction rate, with a focus on its impact on hydrogen-burning and helium-burning phases. The results of this study are expected to provide valuable insights into the complex interplay between nuclear reactions and stellar evolution, ultimately facilitating a more accurate understanding of the formation of light elements in the universe.

title: Following The Cosmic Evolution Of Pristine Gas I: Implications For Milky Way Halo Stars
Abstract: The cosmic evolution of pristine gas, which has been tracked through the analysis of chemically primitive stars in the Milky Way halo, plays a pivotal role in understanding the galaxy's formation and evolution. By studying these halo stars, researchers have been able to reconstruct the gas's journey through the early universe, from its initial formation shortly after the Big Bang to its incorporation into the first stars and galaxies. The findings suggest that the Milky Way halo was shaped by a series of large-scale gas flow processes, including galactic stripping and mergers, which deposited large quantities of gas and metallic enrichment into the region over billions of years. These events not only fueled the growth of the Milky Way but also likely instigated the formation of some of its most metal-poor stars. Furthermore, by examining the chemical signatures of these halostars, researchers have been able to shed light on the complex interplay between star formation and gas recycling within the galaxy, revealing intriguing clues about the role of mass loss and metal pollution in shaping the pristine gas's evolutionary trajectory. The implications of this research extend beyond the Milky Way halo, offering valuable insights into the formation and evolution of galaxies in the distant universe.

By employing a combination of numerical integrations and spectral energy distribution modeling, our study aims to investigate the stability of the planet's orbit over multiple timescales, including orbital decay and atmospheric impact of stellar variability. We incorporate the effects of tidal interactions, magnetic winds, and stellar rotation into a state-of-the-art solar system dynamics code to consider the long-term implications of HD 131399Ab's orbit. Our results reveal that the planet's orbit exhibits complex, chaotic dynamics, driven by subtle variations in the quadrupole moment of the A-star and the effects of binary tidal forces within the close binary pair. By addressing fundamental questions about planetary system stability and long-term habitability, this research sheds new light on the intricate relationships between massive stars, multiple stars, and their associated planetary systems.

title: Predicting Urban Water Quality with Ubiquitous Data
Abstract: The rapid urbanization of cities worldwide has led to significant increases in urban water pollution, posing substantial threats to public health, aquatic ecosystems, and the economy. The recent proliferation of low-cost, miniature sensors and mobile devices has enabled the collection of ubiquitous water quality data, including parameters such as pH, temperature, turbidity, and dissolved oxygen levels. By leveraging these emerging technologies and integrating them with advanced machine learning techniques, researchers can create predictive models that forecast urban water quality with unprecedented accuracy. This paper explores the potential of ubiquitous data for predicting urban water quality, with a particular focus on the use of sensor networks, crowdsourced data, and artificial intelligence algorithms. The results of our study demonstrate the effectiveness of these approaches in identifying key factors that influence water quality, including temporal and spatial variability, and provide valuable insights into the underlying mechanisms driving urban water pollution. By developing and deploying predictive models that incorporate ubiquitous data, we can better anticipate and mitigate the impacts of water pollution, ultimately protecting human health and aquatic ecosystems in urban environments.

title: Does a Differentiated, Carbonate-Rich, Rocky Object Pollute the White Dwarf SDSSJ104341.53+085558.2?
Abstract: SDSSJ104341.53+085558.2 is a post-main-sequence white dwarf star with the unique characteristic of having a highly inflated radius, which is generally seen in white dwarfs that undergo significant atmospheric contamination. Recent studies have linked these inflated radii to the presence of a circumstellar disk or disk-like structure around these stars. In one such case, the contamination is believed to originate from a differentiated, carbonate-rich, rocky object that potentially transits the star, only to have the star's strong gravitational pull capture it and contaminate the white dwarf's photosphere. Meanwhile, white dwarfs that are less contaminated have radii consistent with purely stellar mass estimates. These findings have led to an ongoing investigation to identify and characterize the makeup and origin of such objects. Furthermore, the inflating radius provides observable markers of potential accretion that imply enhanced metal enrichment, thus allowing astronomers to study various dynamical processes at play within these heavily contaminated white dwarfs, including photoevaporation and gas-giant core accretion. In the case of this star, understanding the origin of its inflated radius is crucial in determining whether or not the theoretically predicted differentiated, carbonate-rich, rocky object is in fact contributing to the observed radius inflation.

title: Are Chinese transport policies effective? A new perspective from direct pollution rebound effect, and empirical evidence from road transport sector
Abstract: Chinese transport policies have been increasingly designed to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and mitigate pollution, yet their effectiveness remains a subject of debate. This study offers a novel perspective on the impact of these policies by examining their unintended consequences, specifically the direct pollution rebound effect, in the road transport sector. Our findings reveal a more complex relationship between policy interventions and emissions than previously understood, indicating that some policies, such as the promotion of hybrid and electric vehicles, have been effective in reducing emissions, but others, like the expansion of high-speed rail and road infrastructure, have exacerbated emissions through increased demand for energy and land use. Additionally, we identify two key contributors to the direct pollution rebound effect: the China's economic growth, particularly in the transportation services and logistics sectors. Our results highlight the limitations of relying solely on short-term measures to address the long-term energy and environmental challenges facing China's rapidly changing transport landscape. Ultimately, this study underscores the need for policymakers to consider the complex interplay of factors influencing energy and emissions in transport policy design and implementation.

title: Adjusting for Unmeasured Spatial Confounding with Distance Adjusted Propensity Score Matching
Abstract: This study aims to contribute to the growing body of literature on addressing unmeasured spatial confounding in empirical research by introducing a novel approach utilizing distance-adjusted propensity score matching. The methodological challenge of spatial confounding arises when the exposure or outcome of interest is influenced by unobserved spatially correlated variables, threatening the validity of estimates obtained from traditional regression analysis. In geographical contexts where spatial relationships are paramount, such as in environmental epidemiology or urban planning, incorporating spatial heterogeneity is crucial. To tackle this issue, the proposed method integrates distance-based weights into conventional propensity score matching, yielding improved estimates by incorporating the spatial proximity of treatment and control units. Our simulation study indicates that the distance-adjusted approach significantly outperforms traditional matching methods in mitigating spatial confounding bias and reducing statistical variance. Furthermore, real-world analysis of housing prices and local crime rates demonstrates the practical applicability and robustness of the distance-adjusted propensity score matching methodology. The proposed novel approach offers a robust, flexible, and scalable method for researchers to effectively adjust for unmeasured spatial confounding and produces reliable and generalizable findings in policy-relevant contexts, facilitating informed decision-making and evidence-based policy development.

Moreover, the results indicate that travel time, household size, and age have significant effects on demand, underscoring the significance of individual lifestyle factors. title: pg-Causality: Identifying Spatiotemporal Causal Pathways for Air Pollutants with Urban Big Data

title: Explaining the variability of WD 1145+017 with simulations of asteroid tidal disruption
Abstract: WD 1145+017 is a unique extreme helium white dwarf exhibiting erratic amplitude variations in its helium line emission signal, accompanied by near-periodic dips in brightness. Observations have suggested that this variability may be caused by the gravitational disruption of a small asteroid passing close to the white dwarf, resulting in tidal forces that alter the asteroid's structure and release material. However, no comprehensive numerical simulations of this process have been conducted to directly link the observed variability to asteroid disruption. In this work, we present the first numerical simulations of asteroid tidal disruption around a white dwarf, including the effects of self-gravity, stellar gravity, and orbital dynamics. Our simulations reveal that the tidal forces excited by the white dwarf's gravity can produce variations in the asteroid's size and rotation rate, leading to periodic dips in luminosity that are in good agreement with those observed in WD 1145+017. Furthermore, we explore the impact of various asteroid properties, such as its mass and composition, on the amplitude and characteristics of the variability. Our results demonstrate the potential importance of tidal disruption in shaping the light curves of WD 1145+017-like objects and may provide insights into the orbital and internal structure of small, disrupted bodies in white dwarf systems. These findings have significant implications for the study of stellar evolution and the search for exoplanetary material within white dwarf environments.

As observed, the magnetic field can either enhance or hinder thermal equilibration, depending on its amplitude, frequency, and direction, thereby underscoring the importance of precise control in shaping the fluid's thermal behavior. title: Constraints of the physics of low-mass AGB stars from CH and CEMP stars
Abstract: Understanding the properties of low-mass asymptotic giant branch (AGB) stars is crucial for elucidating the core structure and late-stage evolution of such stars. However, observational evidence for such evolutionary stages is scarce, as they lie on the Hertzsprung gap, where the observational signature of low-mass AGB stars is weak. On the other hand, carbon-enhanced metal-poor (CEMP) stars, which possess high lithium and carbon enrichments and a metal-deficient composition, are thought to be pristine photospheric samples of the atmospheres of low-mass AGB stars at their pre-third dredge-up evolutionary stage. By analyzing the carbon (C) and nitrogen (N) abundance ratios and their variability among the populations of CH and CEMP stars, we aim to establish the constraints on the possible range of third dredge-up efficiencies and internal mixing timescales for low-mass AGB progenitors. Using our comprehensive compilation of abundance ratios and their evolutionary trends in carbon, nitrogen, lithium, and other key s-process elements, we find that the third dredge-up is likely to begin around 10^3 years before the helium plasma flash, at a stellar mass close to 1.3 solar masses, in agreement with recent hydrodynamic evolutionary models of low-mass AGB stars. Our results suggest that a more rapid onset and extensive third dredge-up mix may be expected for these progenitors, which may facilitate mass loss through a thermal pulse or at the end of the AGB evolution, significantly affecting their post-AGB mass, surface composition, and subsequent interactions with the surrounding medium.

The effects can manifest as enhanced orbital instability, increased planetary transit probabilities, and possibly contributing to the formation of exoplanets via planet-planet scattering. Further understanding of these mechanisms can help predict the long-term evolution and potentially improve the detection and characterization of exoplanetary systems in binary and multiple star environments. Thus, in attempting to consistently integrate theoretical representations and established experiments, it is rational to examine current descriptions of interactions accounting for any deficiencies these deviations signify in predictive power or otherwise. Standard model-based predictions in these areas continue to face challenges and possible openings for explorations into new physics. Our results show that these pollution events can be linked to mergers of binaries in close proximity to the GGC centers, where intense dynamical interactions lead to mass transfer and deposition of Al-enriched material. title: Isogeometric finite element analysis of time-harmonic exterior acoustic scattering problems
Abstract: This study investigates the numerical solution to time-harmonic exterior acoustic scattering problems using isogeometric finite element analysis. Several numerical experiments are conducted to validate the performance of the hybrid NURBS-BEM approach, demonstrating potential applications in solving complex acoustic scattering problems and analyzing the acoustic properties of structures with arbitrary geometries. title: Effect of cavitation on velocity in the near-field of a diesel nozzle

title: Linear Convergence of Proximal Gradient Algorithm with Extrapolation for a Class of Nonconvex Nonsmooth Minimization Problems

This research extends the current understanding of the universality of TAM across cultural contexts, shedding new light on the areas of modification required to conform to local preferences.

title: Nonparametric Bayesian Factor Analysis for Dynamic Count Matrices
Abstract: Nonparametric Bayesian factor analysis has become a widely discussed approach in contemporary statistical research, capable of handling complex data structures that cannot be adequately described by traditional parametric assumptions. This study focuses on extending nonparametric Bayesian factor analysis to dynamic count matrices, providing a novel framework for modeling temporal dependencies within non-negative integer-valued observational data. Count matrices often arise in applications involving frequency-corrected data matrices common in genetics, spatial-temporal phenomena, and social or environmental networks. Traditional methods employing Bayesian factor analysis often encounter challenges due to model misspecification and inflexibility when applied to dynamic count matrices, prompting the development of novel techniques. By adopting a nonparametric Bayesian approach, our proposed framework avoids the restrictive parametric specifications while maintaining flexibility in modeling temporal dependencies within dynamic count matrices. Specifically, we model the dynamic count matrix as a product of a nonparametric Bayesian factor loadings and a set of time-dependent latent factors, taking into account the stochastic volatility exhibited by such data. A nonparametric prior is introduced to learn the latent structural patterns without pre-specifying the number of factors or their priors. The methodological advancements in this study contribute to a more robust approach for inferring the underlying structure of dynamic count matrices, providing new insights into their inherent dynamics and facilitating novel applications in data analysis, prediction, and decision-making. This research offers a comprehensive methodological framework, inclusive of theoretical derivations, simulation studies, and an application-based evaluation of the proposed nonparametric Bayesian factor analysis approach.

title: Evaluating Go Game Records for Prediction of Player Attributes
Abstract: Evaluating Go Game Records for Prediction of Player Attributes explores the application of statistical analysis and machine learning algorithms to a large dataset of Go game records for the prediction of player attributes such as skill level and playing style. A comprehensive review of existing literature on Go strategy, game theory, and data-driven approaches to predicting player performance is presented. A dataset of over 10,000 Go games is extracted from various online platforms, which includes game records, player information, and ratings. A range of feature extraction and dimensionality reduction techniques are utilized to select relevant attributes from the game records, such as move patterns, game outcomes, and player ratings. Various machine learning models, including decision trees, random forests, and neural networks, are trained on the extracted features to predict player attributes. The performance of the models is evaluated through a combination of metrics, including accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. The results demonstrate that supervised learning models can effectively predict player attributes from Go game records, with notable accuracy in distinguishing between different skill levels and playing styles. The study also investigates the effect of different feature extraction techniques and model architectures on prediction performance, providing insights into the most effective strategies for player attribute prediction in Go. The research has far-reaching implications for Go education, talent scouting, and performance analysis, highlighting the potential of big data and machine learning in facilitating the development of Go players and teams.

title: Simple, Robust and Optimal Ranking from Pairwise Comparisons
Abstract: This abstract explores the problem of ranking objects based on pairwise comparisons, a fundamental task in various fields including machine learning, data analysis, and decision making. Current methods for ranking from pairwise comparisons often rely on complex optimization techniques, which can be computationally expensive and prone to errors. In this work, we propose a simple, robust, and optimal ranking framework that addresses the shortcomings of existing approaches. Our method, inspired by the principles of preference aggregation, leverages a novel pairwise comparison model that estimates the underlying ranks in a data-driven manner. We show that this model is not only computationally efficient but also robust to noise and outliers in the comparison data. Theoretical guarantees are provided to ensure the optimality of the ranking solution. Empirical evaluations on various synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the superior performance of our approach compared to state-of-the-art methods. Our results highlight the potential of this framework in a wide range of applications, including collaborative filtering, recommendation systems, and document ranking. By providing a simple, robust, and optimal ranking solution, our work paves the way for more reliable and efficient decision-making processes in various domains.

title: Online Keyword Spotting with a Character-Level Recurrent Neural Network
Abstract: Online Keyword Spotting with a Character-Level Recurrent Neural Network is a crucial task in speech recognition that involves the detection of specific keywords from variable-length input speech segments in real-time. This paper proposes an innovative approach to achieve this goal utilizing a character-level recurrent neural network (RNN) architecture. The developed approach is capable of spotting keywords in continuous speech and generating the corresponding transcriptions in real-time, making it highly suitable for applications like voice assistants, real-time transcription services, and event detection systems. Experimental results validate the effectiveness of the proposed method in identifying keywords with high accuracy and low latency, even in the presence of background noise and varying speaking rates. Furthermore, we present a comprehensive evaluation of the proposed approach using various benchmark datasets and compare its performance with existing state-of-the-art methods. A detailed analysis of the experimental results reveals that the proposed method demonstrates improved keyword spotting accuracy and lower end-to-end latency compared to traditional keyword spotting approaches. The proposed approach also exhibits excellent adaptability to different speaking styles and background noise conditions, making it a robust and reliable solution for real-world applications. Our findings contribute significant advancements to the field of keyword spotting and provide valuable insights for researchers and practitioners seeking to develop efficient and accurate real-time transcription systems.

title: Estimation of the sample covariance matrix from compressive measurements
Abstract: The sample covariance matrix, a fundamental statistic in multivariate analysis, plays a crucial role in various high-dimensional data applications such as dimensionality reduction, discriminant analysis, and portfolio optimization. However, traditional methods for estimating the sample covariance matrix based on the infeasible model of observing the entire data covariates vector have shown significant inefficiencies in terms of computational and data storage complexities, particularly in the context of high-dimensional data streams. This paper addresses the issue of estimating the sample covariance matrix from compressive measurements, where the available data are obtained through a linear transform, known as compressive sensing or dimensionality reduction. We develop a computationally efficient and robust method, coined as the "Sparse-Compressive Covariance Estimator" (SCCE), that leverages the inherent properties of compressive sensing to exploit the sparsity pattern of the covariance matrix. The proposed method is computationally scalable and can be efficiently implemented on large-scale high-dimensional datasets. Through extensive simulations and real-data applications, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in terms of accuracy, computational efficiency, and robustness to noise and outlier contaminations. Results show that the proposed SCCE outperforms state-of-the-art methods in estimating the sample covariance matrix from compressive measurements, paving the way for its applications in various interdisciplinary fields.

title: Sharp Computational-Statistical Phase Transitions via Oracle Computational Model
Abstract: Statistical inference is a cornerstone of empirical sciences, with significant implications for various fields including machine learning, engineering, and econometrics. Recent advancements in the theory of computational-statistical phase transitions (CSTs) have been pivotal to a deeper comprehension of the close tie between computational hardness and statistical accuracy in a wide range of inference tasks. Nevertheless, comprehensively analyzing CSTs remains an object of study and a long-standing open question, with longstanding efforts having only led to limited results. The theory of phase transitions has been a cornerstone for investigations in physics throughout the years, also demonstrating its relevance to learning tasks. Inspired by recent papers from the Oracle computational model and the asymptotics of computational power of polynomial-size circuits, certain rigorous frameworks focusing on sharp CSTs do indeed create fascinating opportunities. We consider this topic of phase transitions for empirical models and establish theoretical results, specifically employing techniques introduced by the analysis of certain phase transitions and exploring the oracle computational model of approximations. This research underlines theoretical growth of this unique methodology and shows the relevance of its applications to statistical inference, pushing the frontiers of CSTs, significantly promoting a profounder, full-scale understanding of the existing problems. The theoretical outcomes presented are grounded in insights into learning phase transitions gained from prior research.

title: Learning Natural Language Inference with LSTM
Abstract: This paper contributes to the advancement of Natural Language Inference (NLI) tasks, which involve determining the relationship between a premise and a hypothesis. Recent studies have demonstrated the efficacy of recurrent neural network (RNN) models, particularly Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, in resolving NLI tasks. In this study, we investigate the potential of LSTM networks in learning NLI and explore various architectural modifications to enhance their performance. The proposed approach utilizes pre-training and fine-tuning strategies to fine-tune LSTMs on existing NLI benchmarks. To further improve performance, we incorporate attention mechanisms into the LSTM model to capture key elements in the premise and hypothesis. Our experiments indicate that the proposed method outperforms previous state-of-the-art models on standard NLI datasets, such as SNLI and Multi-Genre Natural Language Inference (MNLI). We also provide a detailed analysis of the attention weights, which reveals how the model focuses on specific components of the premise and hypothesis when making inference decisions. Additionally, we examine the performance of our model on different premise and hypothesis lengths, highlighting its ability to handle varying input lengths. Our findings demonstrate the effectiveness of LSTMs in NLI tasks and provide valuable insights for future research in the field, which could be beneficial for the development of more sophisticated language models.

title: Learning to Filter with Predictive State Inference Machines
Abstract: Predictive State Inference Machines (PSIMs) have been shown to provide accurate inferential representations of partially observed systems, allowing for robust inference and control under uncertainty. However, when considering complex systems where continuous streams of sensory data may overwhelm the inference process, the problem of data filtering becomes increasingly relevant. In this context, this work explores the theoretical foundation for learning to filter with PSIMs. To tackle this problem, we leverage the high-dimensional latent representation inherent to PSIMs as the basis for recursive, conditional state estimation. We derive a learning framework that incorporates a combination of predictive coding, attentional weights, and adaptive filtering, which collectively enable the PSIM to adapt to changing environments and selectively focus on relevant aspects of the input data. Experiments are conducted on challenging datasets where agents must simulate scenarios involving conflicting and rapidly changing sensor data to assess the efficacy of the proposed method in improving decision-making under uncertainty. Through an evaluation of the outcomes, our framework demonstrates improved robustness to data explosion, significantly diminished noise, and greater recognition of temporally unfolding patterns. By effectively learning to filter within the PSIM framework, agent performance improves within complex, high-dimensional, uncertain environments.

title: Improving Style Similarity Metrics of 3D Shapes
Abstract: This research paper introduces a novel approach to enhancing the style similarity metrics of 3D shapes, aiming to bridge the gap between appearance and functionality in computer-aided design (CAD) systems. Traditional methods for style similarity assessment rely heavily on geometric features, neglecting the complex relationships between shape elements. Our proposed framework, called StyleCon, leverages a combination of graph-based and neural network-based techniques to analyze and compare the structural and visual characteristics of 3D models. By capturing the hierarchical organization of shape elements and their spatial dependencies, StyleCon provides a more comprehensive understanding of shape style. Our experimental results demonstrate the superior performance of StyleCon in evaluating shape style similarity, yielding high preservation of shape semantics and geometry under various transformation scenarios. Additionally, we showcase StyleCon's versatility by applying it to tasks such as shape analogy identification, style transfer, and style-based shape retrieval. The contributions of this research are twofold: (1) the introduction of a novel framework for style similarity assessment that seamlessly integrates geometric, topological, and visual features, and (2) the evaluation and demonstration of StyleCon's effectiveness in applications that benefit from style similarity evaluation. Ultimately, StyleCon paves the way for more advanced CAD systems that can effectively utilize style similarity to automate complex design tasks and facilitate human- CAD collaboration.

title: Privacy Preservation in Distributed Subgradient Optimization Algorithms
Abstract: This paper focuses on addressing the pressing need for privacy preservation in distributed subgradient optimization algorithms, which have emerged as a promising approach for large-scale machine learning and big data analytics. As data privacy concerns continue to escalate, the need to protect sensitive information while preserving the benefits of distributed optimization methods has become increasingly urgent. We propose an innovative framework that integrates differential privacy techniques with existing distributed subgradient optimization algorithms to safeguard sensitive information. Key features of our framework include the development of novel gradient noise mechanisms that ensure statistical robustness, while minimizing the degradation in convergence rates. Our approach utilizes a combination of local differential privacy (LDP) and federated learning paradigms to overcome significant challenges in implementing scalable and robust privacy-preserving distributed subgradient optimization. We evaluate the efficacy of our proposed framework through extensive numerical experiments on various large-scale datasets, demonstrating its ability to strike an optimal balance between privacy, accuracy, and computational efficiency. By bridging the gap between privacy preservation and distributed optimization, this work aims to provide a comprehensive framework for securing the distribution and processing of sensitive information in complex machine learning and data analytics applications. Our results contribute significantly to the ongoing research in this area, illuminating new avenues for developing scalable and private distributed optimization methods that are essential for future-proof data-intensive computing.

title: Joint limiting laws for high-dimensional independence tests
Abstract: This paper investigates the limit distributions of high-dimensional independence tests under the null and alternative hypotheses. We establish joint limiting laws for a large class of popular test statistics, including the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD), the energy distance, and the distance correlation. Our result provides a unified framework for understanding the asymptotic behavior of these test statistics, enabling a direct comparison of their power under different alternatives. The joint limiting laws also facilitate the construction of asymptotic confidence sets for the independence structure between blocks of variables. We develop a bootstrap-based method to approximate the limiting distributions in practice, which enables accurate and robust power calculations. Our theoretical results are supported by comprehensive simulations, which demonstrate the good finite-sample performance of the established approximations. Additionally, we apply our methodology to real-world datasets and highlight its utility in identifying complex relationships between multiple variables. The joint limiting laws are shown to be surprisingly simple, involving only a product of simple one-dimensional distributions. As a result, many existing independence tests can be naturally extended to high-dimensional settings, while also providing new insights into the structure of multivariate dependencies. Overall, this research contributes to a deeper understanding of high-dimensional independence testing and provides a practical toolkit for statistically sound inference in large-scale datasets.

title: Sparse group factor analysis for biclustering of multiple data sources
Abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to biclustering of multiple data sources using sparse group factor analysis, which is an essential tool for identifying coherent patterns and relationships in complex, multi-modal data. Biclustering, which aims to reveal co-occurring patterns in both rows and columns of a data matrix, has numerous applications in various fields, including but not limited to, bioinformatics, finance, and marketing. However, the existing biclustering methods often struggle to handle datasets with multiple sources, as they are typically designed for a single data matrix or fail to capture the interdependency between multiple sources. Our proposed method leverages sparse group factor analysis, a technique that can effectively extract and represent the patterns in multiple types of data by incorporating the inter-source information. By integrating the inter-source relationship into the biclustering model, the proposed method is able to identify coherent biclusters across multiple data sources. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method through comprehensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets, showcasing its ability to identify meaningful biclusters that incorporate inter-source relationships. Furthermore, we provide a thorough analysis of the computational complexity and scalability of our method, highlighting its practicality and promise for large-scale multi-source data analysis. Overall, our work presents a decisive step forward in multi-source biclustering analysis, offering a powerful tool for interdisciplinary researchers seeking insights from diverse data types.

title: Common Variable Learning and Invariant Representation Learning using Siamese Neural Networks
Abstract: The ability of a learning model to generalize across varying environments, known as common variable learning (CVL), is a fundamental challenge in artificial intelligence. A subset of CVL, known as invariant representation learning (IRL), seeks to elucidate how neural networks learn representations that remain unchanged under different data conditions or distributions. Recently, Siamese neural networks (SNNs) have emerged as an attractive class of architectures for tackling the challenge of CVL/IRL. SNNs are composed of paired networks that are connected via a shared set of weights, enabling the learning of symmetries across input pairs. This paper presents a comprehensive exploration of CVL and IRL using SNNs, incorporating both theoretical insights and practical experiments. The proposed method leverages the symmetrical property of the SNNs to facilitate the learning of invariant representations. This is achieved through a novel weighted cross-entropy loss function that takes into account both the similarity and dissimilarity of pairs, thereby facilitating the learning of common variables. The method is validated through a series of experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness in learning invariant representations for CVL. The results provide new insights into the role of SNNs in CVL/IRL and contribute to the development of more robust and generalizable AI models. Overall, this work offers a novel approach to understanding and evaluating the CVL/IRL capabilities of neural networks.

title: Matrix Completion Under Monotonic Single Index Models
Abstract: Matrix completion under monotonic single index models has drawn increasing attention in recent years, particularly in the realm of recommender systems and missing data imputation. This research endeavors to bridge the gap between the theoretical understanding of matrix completion methods and their practical implementation by considering the monotonic single index model, a variant of the single index model. Under this framework, the entries of the underlying matrix are organized in a manner that satisfies a monotonic relationship with a common index variable, often presumed to capture some form of underlying semantics. By leveraging this information, we aim to propose novel matrix completion approaches that can effectively harness the monotonic structure of the data. In doing so, we investigate the theoretical properties of these methods and examine their empirical performance against existing techniques. Furthermore, we investigate various strategies for learning the index variable in the context of noisy and partial observations, utilizing techniques from both linear and non-linear dimensionality reduction. Through extensive numerical experiments and the analysis of real-world data, we demonstrate that the proposed approaches exhibit superior performance and robustness under different regimes of noise and data availability. These findings contribute to a deeper understanding of matrix completion under monotonic structures and lay the foundation for the development of scalable and efficient methods for recommender systems and other applications involving high-dimensional data.

title: Feed-Forward Networks with Attention Can Solve Some Long-Term Memory Problems
Abstract: Feed-forward networks with attention have gained considerable attention in recent years due to their ability to process sequential data in a more efficient and effective manner. However, their ability to tackle long-term memory problems has remained largely unexplored. In this research, we investigate the extent to which feed-forward networks with attention can solve some long-term memory problems, particularly ones that involved sequential data with long-term dependencies. We propose a novel architecture that combines the benefits of feed-forward networks and attention mechanisms to process and retain information from different time steps. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed architecture outperforms traditional feed-forward networks and attention-based models on several benchmark datasets, particularly on tasks that involve long-term memory, such as linguistic reasoning and memory-based question answering. The proposed architecture is also found to be computationally efficient and scalable to handle large datasets. Furthermore, we conduct an ablation study to analyze the contribution of individual components of the architecture, highlighting the importance of attention in solving long-term memory problems. Our results provide new insights into the capabilities of feed-forward networks with attention and demonstrate their potential in tackling challenging problems related to long-term memory. We hope that our findings will pave the way for further research in this exciting and rapidly evolving area of deep learning.

title: A Stochastic Majorize-Minimize Subspace Algorithm for Online Penalized Least Squares Estimation
Abstract: This paper presents a novel stochastic majorize-minimize subspace algorithm designed for online penalized least squares estimation, where the parameters of interest are updated using noisy and incomplete data as it arrives in real-time. The proposed algorithm is particularly suitable for large-scale datasets, where computational efficiency and reduction of memory requirements are crucial. By leveraging the divide-and-conquer strategy and utilizing the available sketch of the data, the algorithm efficiently estimates the model parameters without having to store or process the entire dataset simultaneously. Furthermore, the proposed method incorporates penalties to estimate models that have a high degree of regularization, such as L1 or L2 regularization, or those that have additional structure, such as sparsity or group-sparsity. The resulting estimates are shown to be scalable in real-time environments with limited computational resources and allow for flexible and robust online updating without sacrificing computational efficiency or increasing storage requirements. This algorithm extends the applicability of penalized least squares estimation to applications involving large datasets, time-evolving parameters, or restricted computational resources. Its efficacy is demonstrated through simulation results and real-data experiments, highlighting its potential for widespread adoption in various fields, including signal processing, machine learning, and communication systems.

title: Error Bounds for Compressed Sensing Algorithms With Group Sparsity: A Unified Approach
Abstract: Recent advancements in compressed sensing have shown that group sparsity models can effectively leverage the underlying structures of data in various applications, including signal processing and imaging. However, the theoretical performance limits of group sparsity models remain unclear due to the lack of robust and versatile error bounds. This paper proposes a unified approach to establishing error bounds for compressed sensing algorithms under group sparsity constraints. Our approach utilizes a novel combination of mutual coherence and restricted isometry properties, which allows for flexible adjustment to diverse scenarios of group sparsity. The proposed error bounds capture both the deterministic and stochastic aspects of measurement matrices, enabling them to be widely applicable to a broad range of applications. Furthermore, we present sharp bounds that outperform existing results in terms of achievable reconstruction accuracy and computational complexity. A series of experiments on both synthetic and real-world data sets demonstrates the superior performance of our unified approach, highlighting its potential for improving the reliability and precision of compressed sensing algorithms in practice. Overall, this study presents a framework for robust and efficient compressed sensing of group-sparse signals, capable of coping with the intricate structures of complex data.

title: Robust Scene Text Recognition Using Sparse Coding based Features
Abstract: This paper presents a novel approach for Robust Scene Text Recognition (RST) using sparse coding based features. Traditional scene text recognition methods often struggle to account for variations in font style, size, and orientation, as well as noise and blurriness inherent in real-world visual environments. In contrast, our proposed approach taps into the power of sparse coding to learn compact and meaningful features from image data. By employing a hierarchical sparse coding framework, we effectively decompose complex image patches into lower-dimensional feature representations, highlighting the most salient and informative components. These features are then fed into a deep neural network for classification, where we incorporate a novel attention mechanism to selectively focus on regions of the input image most relevant to the recognition task. Extensive experiments on a range of benchmark datasets demonstrate the superiority of our approach in terms of accuracy and robustness compared to state-of-the-art counterparts. Our contributions include the introduction of a principled feature extraction framework grounded in sparse coding principles, and the development of an attention mechanism tailored to the specific demands of scene text recognition. This work showcases the potential of sparse coding for scene text recognition and provides a compelling starting point for further research in this area. title: Testing for Differences in Gaussian Graphical Models: Applications to Brain Connectivity
Abstract: This paper addresses the fundamental issue of testing for differences in Gaussian Graphical Models (GGMs), a widely used framework for modeling and analyzing network structures in complex systems, particularly in brain connectivity studies. The comparison of GGMs across samples or populations is crucial for understanding variations in network patterns, yet current methods are often hampered by limitations in statistical power and difficulties in accurately estimating the differences between sparse high-dimensional graphs. To mitigate these challenges, we propose a novel test statistic that measures the difference between two GGMs, leveraging the strengths of both the graphical lasso and cross-validation techniques. Our approach allows for the flexible specification of a null distribution, allowing users to select from a range of hypotheses, from simple equality between models to more nuanced comparisons. The performance of the proposed test is thoroughly evaluated using both simulated and real datasets, where it is demonstrated to exhibit substantial gains in power compared to existing methods. Furthermore, we showcase the practical application of our test through analysis of the functional brain networks of individuals with schizophrenia and healthy controls, providing insights into the possible underlying alterations in brain connectivity associated with this condition.

title: Democratizing Children's Computation: Learning Computational Science as Aesthetic Experience
Abstract: This thesis contributes to the democratization of computational science by reconceptualizing the way it is learned by children, shifting the emphasis from technical proficiency to aesthetic experience. Through an arts-based research methodology, this study sets out to challenge the prevailing wisdom that computational science needs to be learned as a complex and abstract subject. Drawing on diverse theoretical perspectives including hacker culture, embodied cognition, and childhood studies, the thesis argues that children's engagement with computational science can be facilitated by tapping into their creative and playful potential. By designing and implementing a series of interactive workshops that combine traditional art forms, such as origami and poetry, with computational thinking tools, this research aims to create a novel learning environment that cultivates children's appreciation for the beauty and complexity of computational patterns. Through case studies of children's participation in the workshops, the thesis will explore how aesthetic experiences can foster an appreciation for the emotional and tactile qualities of coding, thereby promoting a more inclusive and holistic understanding of computational science. Ultimately, this study seeks to contribute to the development of a more participatory and creative approach to learning computational science, one that values diversity and encourages children to explore the inherent beauty and playfulness of computational patterns.

title: Tight Bounds for Approximate Carathéodory and Beyond
Abstract: This paper provides tight bounds for the approximate Carathéodory problem, a fundamental problem in discrete geometry and convex optimization, where a vector x in a high-dimensional space is represented as a convex combination of a subset of m affine-independent vectors in R^n. We derive a tight (1 + ε)-approximation algorithm with a polynomial dependence on the error parameter ε, which is the best possible in the context of Las Vegas algorithms. The algorithm also yields a new result on approximate Helly numbers, where we show that for any family of convex subsets in R^n, the approximate Helly number is at most O(log k/ε), where k is the size of the family and ε is the error parameter. These results have significant implications for the design of efficient algorithms in various areas, including geometry, optimization, and computational complexity. Our approach involves a careful analysis of the trade-offs between approximation and dimension reduction, as well as the application of random sampling techniques. We also discuss some further applications and extensions of our results to nearest points and near-convex hulls, and outline some open questions and areas for future research.

title: Optimal Selective Attention in Reactive Agents
Abstract: The ability of reactive agents to select the most relevant information in dynamic and uncertain environments is critical to their success in real-time decision-making. Selective attention enables agents to focus on key stimuli, prioritize tasks, and allocate limited resources efficiently. However, current reactive agent architectures often struggle to balance exploration and exploitation, leading to inadequate information processing and suboptimal decision-making. This research explores the concept of optimal selective attention in reactive agents, aiming to develop a novel framework that integrates sensory processing, cognitive architecture, and machine learning techniques. The proposed framework, called "OptiSA," utilizes a hybrid approach that combines attention-driven sampling, reinforcement learning, and Bayesian estimation to effectively manage uncertainty and adapt to changing environments. By leveraging the strengths of these techniques, OptiSA enables reactive agents to prioritize tasks, filter irrelevant information, and make more informed decisions. A series of experiments and simulations are conducted to evaluate the performance of OptiSA on various tasks, including navigation, obstacle avoidance, and goal-oriented exploration. The results demonstrate that OptiSA outperforms traditional reactive agent architectures in terms of efficiency, accuracy, and adaptability, providing a significant step towards the development of more robust and autonomous reactive agents.

title: Structured Pruning of Deep Convolutional Neural Networks
Abstract: This research contributes to the area of deep learning and neural network efficiency by presenting an in-depth exploration of structured pruning as an effective approach for reducing the computational complexity of deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs). Structured pruning involves identifying and systematically removing redundant or weak connections in a network, often in a structured pattern, such as removing entire rows or columns from weight tensors. The proposed approach uses a combination of forward and backward pruning techniques to remove connections that have minimal impact on the network's performance, thereby reducing the number of parameters and computations required to process input data. A thorough analysis of the pruning strategies is conducted, highlighting the impact of different pruning patterns on the network's accuracy, parameter efficiency, and computational requirements. Moreover, the paper presents a comprehensive comparison of different neural network architectures, including state-of-the-art models, and evaluates their sensitivity to structured pruning. Empirical results demonstrate that structured pruning can achieve significant reductions in computational requirements and parameter count, leading to efficient implementation on various hardware platforms, including embedded systems and high-performance computing systems, without compromising on the network's accuracy and performance. The findings of this research have significant implications for the development of highly efficient and deployable CNNs for real-world applications in computer vision, image processing, and other areas.

title: Taming the Noise in Reinforcement Learning via Soft Updates
Abstract: This paper tackles a critical challenge in reinforcement learning - the noise inherent in the decision-making process. The conventional approach of updating model parameters using hard updates at each time step leads to unstable and noisy policies, which can result in significant performance degradation. In an effort to mitigate this issue, we explore the adoption of soft updates in reinforcement learning. Our methodology introduces a novel variance-reduced variant of the soft update algorithm, termed Variance-Reduced Gradient Soft Updates (VRG-SU). By leveraging a combination of gradient descent and the exponential moving average of previous updates, VRG-SU achieves improved stability and reduced variability in policy updates. A novel exploration-exploitation trade-off strategy based on the uncertainty of the updated policy is also proposed to promote more informed decision-making under the soft update regime. Our experiments demonstrate the efficacy of VRG-SU on a range of benchmark tasks, including Cartpole, Mountain Car, and MuJoCo domains. By significantly reducing the impact of noise in reinforcement learning, VRG-SU offers a promising approach for the deployment of more robust and adaptive agents in complex environments, with far-reaching implications for applications in robotics, game playing, and autonomous systems.

title: When Coding Style Survives Compilation: De-anonymizing Programmers from Executable Binaries
Abstract: This paper presents a novel approach for de-anonymizing programmers by analyzing the coding style preserved in executable binaries. Previous work in de-anonymization has focused on source code analysis or static code analysis, which may not retain the unique coding style characteristics associated with a programmer. Drawing on the fact that coding style influences compilation, we demonstrate a method to indirectly de-anonymize programmers by examining the characteristics embedded in executable binaries. Our proposed framework leverages a range of coding style attributes, including whitespace usage, naming conventions, commenting practices, and code organization patterns. By comparing these attributes across different program binaries produced by the same programmer, our technique identifies unique profiles that distinctly represent their coding style. Experimental results reveal that the proposed method is highly effective in de-anonymizing programmers, achieving a success rate of 92% when tested on a large-scale dataset of open-source projects. This research underscores the potential of analyzing executable binaries as a means to infer programmer identity and has significant implications for software development security, intellectual property protection, and programmer attribution in the realm of computer forensics.

title: Mining Massive Hierarchical Data Using a Scalable Probabilistic Graphical Model
Abstract: This paper proposes an innovative approach to mine massive hierarchical data using a scalable probabilistic graphical model, which efficiently integrates traditional frequent itemset mining (FIM) and hierarchical depth-first search (HDFS) into a novel probabilistic graphical model framework. The resulting paradigm, termed as PHDGM, leverages the power of probabilistic reasoning to accurately capture intricate patterns and relationships hidden within the hierarchical data, thereby overcoming traditional FIM and HDFS limitations. By casting HDFS into a probabilistic graphical model, the current paper develops an ingenious strategy that not only retains the benefits of FIM but also empowers data mining processes with the ability to explore complex hierarchies more efficiently. The computationally scalable and probabilistically robust approach enables seamless integration with big data platforms, rendering existing data mining tools obsolete. Through comprehensive experimental results and thorough theoretical analysis, the paper demonstrates the exceptional effectiveness and efficiency of PHDGM in extracting meaningful and interpretable patterns from massive hierarchical data, thereby significantly advancing the frontiers of high-performance data mining applications. By eradicating the existing bottlenecks associated with FIM and HDFS, the proposed PHDGM has profound implications for multitudes of high-value applications encompassing data analysis, data mining, and decision-making across various sectors, including business, medicine, energy, and complex systems management.

title: Visually Indicated Sounds
Abstract: This paper delves into the phenomenon of visually indicated sounds, where visual cues from an environment, gesture, or interaction, influence an individual's perception and interpretation of sounds. Recent studies have shown that the brain is highly attuned to multimodal sensory inputs, often giving precedence to sensory information from one modality over another, thereby giving rise to phenomena such as inter-sensory congruence and sound-propagation illusions. Investigating the ways in which visual information can alter the perception, localization, and intensity of sounds is crucial for understanding the complex interplay between our senses and the role it plays in shaping our subjective experience of the world. By exploring the neural correlates of visually indicated sounds through interdisciplinary approaches that combine psychology, neurophysiology, and machine learning, this research seeks to provide new insights into the mechanisms driving multisensory integration and how it affects our understanding of sounds in various contexts. The implications of this research can have far-reaching consequences for the development of more effective communication and interaction technologies, highlighting the importance of considering the nuanced dynamics between our senses in creating more immersive and engaging user experiences.

title: A Simple Baseline for Travel Time Estimation using Large-Scale Trip Data
Abstract: This paper proposes a simple yet effective baseline model for travel time estimation using large-scale trip data. In recent years, the increasing availability of location-enabled devices and ride-hailing services has led to a surge in the collection of trip data, offering unprecedented opportunities for travel time estimation. However, most existing travel time estimation models are complex and often suffer from high computational costs, rendering them impractical for real-world application. To address this limitation, this work focuses on developing a simple baseline model that leverages basic spatiotemporal information from trip data. Our approach employs a straightforward methodology that combines spatial smoothing and temporal interpolation techniques to estimate travel times. The model is highly interpretable and computationally efficient, allowing it to be easily integrated into various transportation systems and applications. Results demonstrate that our baseline model achieves competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art models, with notably faster computation times. title: Q-caching: an integrated reinforcement-learning approach for caching and routing in information-centric networks
Abstract: Q-caching, an integrated reinforcement-learning approach for caching and routing in information-centric networks, proposes an innovative framework that concurrently optimizes caching placement and routing decisions to improve network performance. By leveraging the inherent adaptability of reinforcement-learning (RL) techniques, this approach enables network nodes to dynamically adjust caching and routing strategies in response to changes in network traffic patterns and user requirements. The Q-caching framework integrates a caching module that determines the optimal placement of content across nodes based on predicted demand, while a routing module utilizes RL to adaptively select the best path for content transmission, taking into account factors such as network congestion, cache availability, and latency. By optimizing both caching and routing in a unified framework, Q-caching aims to significantly improve the efficiency and responsiveness of information-centric networks, particularly in scenarios involving high-volume content dissemination, such as video streaming and online gaming. Through extensive simulations and analytical studies, this research demonstrates the efficacy of Q-caching in enhancing network performance, reducing latency, and improving overall user experience, making it a promising solution for next-generation networks.

title: Approximate Hubel-Wiesel Modules and the Data Structures of Neural Computation
Abstract: This research paper delves into the complex realm of neural computation, exploring the theoretical frameworks that underlie perceptual processing in the brain. Specifically, it investigates the conceptual relationships between the seminal models of Hubel and Wiesel - pioneers who laid the foundational work in understanding the neural basis of visual perception. The paper introduces the novel concept of approximate Hubel-Wiesel modules, where modules are treated as entities exhibiting partial, degenerate, or biased versions of the standard hubel-wiesel architecture. By using techniques drawn from deep neural networks and the statistical mechanics of discrete Hopfield networks, researchers develop a rigorous theoretical framework for studying the microstructure of the visual cortex, enabling the identification of specific patterns of organization and behavior in neuronal populations. Furthermore, the approximate modules are contextualized in relation to existing data structures of neural computation, including the traditional Wilson-Cowan model and recently proposed variants of attractor neural networks. The empirical exploration of these connections reveals new insights into how neural population dynamics can give rise to computationally powerful hierarchical structures, fostering an interdisciplinary perspective that blends mathematical modeling with empirical data emanating from neurophysiology and neuroanatomy. Ultimately, this research aims to contribute to a deeper, quantitative understanding of neural information processing in the visual system, with particular emphasis on its intrinsic computational architectures.

title: Knowledge and Influence of MOOC Courses on Initial Teacher Training
Abstract: This study explores the impact of Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs) on initial teacher training, with a focus on knowledge acquisition and influence on practice. The increasing popularity of MOOCs has led to questions about their potential to enhance teacher education and improve teacher quality. To investigate this, 150 novice teachers who enrolled in MOOCs as part of their initial training program were surveyed. The results show that participants reported a significant increase in their knowledge and understanding of teaching and learning principles, particularly in areas such as instructional design, classroom management, and technology integration. The influence of MOOCs on participants' practice was also notable, with many reporting changes in their teaching methods and approaches, particularly in the use of technology and differentiated instruction. However, some participants reported difficulties in applying MOOC content in the classroom due to lack of support and limited access to technology. Furthermore, the study highlights the potential of MOOCs to reach a wider audience and provide opportunities for teachers to develop their skills and knowledge at their own pace. The findings of this study contribute to a better understanding of the role of MOOCs in initial teacher training and highlight the need for further research and development in this area to ensure that MOOCs are integrated effectively into teacher education programs.

title: Full-scale Cascade Dynamics Prediction with a Local-First Approach
Abstract: This study demonstrates significant advancements in predicting the full-scale cascade dynamics of complex systems by proposing a novel local-first approach. Conventional computational efforts often focus on achieving large-scale accuracy, which can hinder the ability to predict catastrophic cascading failures that arise from localised disturbances. Our local-first approach initially focuses on the microscopic dynamics of local interactions before upward propagation of information and material to predict the temporal and hierarchical cascading signatures that arise from these micro-failure events. Through a specially designed distributed sensor and actuator (DSA) system, we collected real-world data that characterises localised deviations from nominal states in over 500 micro-scale networks of interest. By leveraging machine learning, generative models, and simulated time-series forecasting, we have developed the ability to build robust multi-scale predictors that estimate and predict the emergence of cascading failures from localised perturbations. By exhibiting accurate, higher-order generalisability and predictive performance compared to existing methods, our novel local-first approach significantly expands the scope for anticipating cascading failures in complex systems like grids, social networks, transportation systems, and financial systems.

title: GELATO and SAGE: An Integrated Framework for MS Annotation
Abstract: The annotation of genomic sequences is a fundamental step in the discovery of functional elements, which ultimately aids in deciphering the intricate mechanisms governing organism development and disease susceptibility. However, the identification of these elements is a computationally intensive and laborious task due to the vast complexity of genomics data. To address this challenge, we propose GELATO and SAGE, an integrated framework for single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP)-enhanced annotation of genomic sequences. Our method provides a multi-faceted approach combining novel gene synthesis, advanced machine learning algorithms, and a genome-specific model-driven approach to enhance the discovery of functional genomic elements. GELATO leverages the advantages of the Gene Regulatory Network (GRN) to identify the probable regulatory interactions between sequences and regulatory regions. SAGE subsequently uses these predicted interactions to predict candidate functional elements, providing an accurate and efficient annotation of genomic sequence variations. Our experiments demonstrate that GELATO and SAGE significantly outperform existing methods in annotating novel genomic elements and identifying potential off-target effects associated with genome editing technology. The framework also proves to be cost-effective, scalable, and reliable for analyzing large-scale genomic data. Overall, the GELATO and SAGE approach presents a reliable solution for interpreting genomic sequences, advancing our understanding of the intricate relationships between sequence and function.

title: Convexified Modularity Maximization for Degree-corrected Stochastic Block Models
Abstract: Convexified modularity optimization represents a pivotal approach to community detection in complex networks, particularly suited for Stochastic Block Models (SBMs). Under the degree-corrected stochastic block model, networks are comprised of multiple densely connected clusters (or blocks), each characterized by distinctly different nodes with specific connection patterns. Utilizing the modularity score, a measure that quantifies the density of within-cluster links relative to links between clusters, community detection is often achieved through optimization. However, the inherent non-convexity of this modularity maximization task severely hampers the efficacy and scalability of available algorithms, primarily due to local optima stagnation and computationally intensive iterations. To this end, a convexified version of the modularity score is proposed, which not only ensures computationally efficient optimization but also guarantees global optimality under certain constraints. This transformed modularity score is formulated through a concave-convex procedure that integrates the effects of within-cluster density and between-cluster sparsity into a single objective function. An intricate derivation of this convexified objective function enables large-scale community detection in high-dimensional networks without suffering from performance degradation resulting from local optima or extensive computational complexity, signifying significant advancements in the field of network structure analysis.
