title: Cost-based Feature Transfer for Vehicle Occupant Classification
Abstract: Vehicle occupant classification is a critical task in various applications such as automotive safety systems, smart car infotainment, and vehicle insurance. Traditional machine learning models for classification tasks are often plagued by high-dimensional feature spaces and variations in sensor data quality and accuracy. In recent years, transfer learning has gained significant attention as a method to adapt pre-trained models to new tasks by fine-tuning the learned features. However, most transfer learning approaches rely on the similarity in the input data distributions across source and target domains, which often leads to poor performance in cases where the input data characteristics change drastically. Meanwhile, costs or costs' metrics in sensor data, such as noise levels, data collection costs, and data storage costs, may vary significantly across different scenes, which may lead to large performance difference across cost-inefficient and cost-efficient scenarios. To address these issues, this paper proposes a novel transfer learning framework that incorporates cost-based feature transfer for vehicle occupant classification. Our approach first analyzes the similarity in costs across different scenarios before transfer learning, which enables the identification of the optimal features and adapters to be transferred. By considering both data modalities and costs' metrics, our method effectively combines the benefits of both transfer learning and domain adaptation for vehicle occupant classification. We have conducted extensive experiments on several benchmarks datasets and the efficacy of our approach is demonstrated through rigorous quantitative evaluation and qualitative analysis.

title: Move from Perturbed scheme to exponential weighting average
Abstract: This research paper bridges the gap between perturbed schemes and exponential weighting averages for efficient estimation and ensemble learning. Traditional perturbed schemes, such as state-space models and ensemble Kalman filters, have been widely used in uncertainty quantification and data assimilation applications. However, they often suffer from convergence and stability issues, particularly when dealing with non-linear dynamical systems and high-dimensional data. In contrast, exponential weighting averages (EWAs) have gained popularity for their ability to adapt to dynamic environments and provide time-varying estimates of the true parameters. Despite their robustness, EWAs can be sensitive to the choice of parameters, such as the forgetting factor, and require a deep understanding of the underlying dynamics. To overcome these challenges, this research presents a novel framework that integrates the strengths of both perturbed schemes and EWAs. By combining the ensemble Kalman filter with the exponential weighting average, we develop an adaptive and robust estimation algorithm that can learn from both linear and non-linear observations. Our framework is tested on a range of synthetic and real-world datasets, including chaotic systems and sensor networks, and demonstrates significant improvements in accuracy, stability, and computational efficiency. The results show that our algorithm can effectively adapt to changing environments, detect anomalies, and provide reliable uncertainty estimates, making it a valuable tool for data-driven decision making in various fields.

title: Implementation of deep learning algorithm for automatic detection of brain tumors using intraoperative IR-thermal mapping data
Abstract: This study proposes a novel approach to the automatic detection of brain tumors by leveraging the potential of deep learning algorithms on intraoperative IR-thermal mapping data. Recent advancements in deep learning have demonstrated its efficacy in medical image analysis, however, the accessibility of data in real-world scenarios remains a significant challenge. To overcome this limitation, intraoperative IR-thermal mapping data acquired during surgical procedures is utilized. This data, though noisy and spatially variant, possesses a unique spatial fingerprint associated with tumor locations, which can be effectively captured by deep learning algorithms. Our proposed model incorporates a convolutional neural network (CNN) and a graph convolutional network (GCN) to jointly learn spatial and topological features from the intraoperative IR-thermal mapping data. In this framework, the CNN is tasked with extracting spatial features from the thermal maps, while the GCN captures the complex relationships between the tumor and surrounding tissues in a spatial graph. The hybrid architecture is validated on a dataset of intraoperative IR-thermal mapping data from various brain tumor cases. Our results demonstrate that the proposed model significantly outperforms traditional machine learning approaches and achieves precise detection of brain tumors with high accuracy. This study presents a promising direction for the development of real-time intraoperative diagnostic tools in neurosurgery and highlights the potential of deep learning to improve surgical outcomes.

title: Deep Learning with S-shaped Rectified Linear Activation Units
Abstract: This paper introduces a novel activation unit, the S-shaped rectified linear activation unit (S-ReLU), which combines the benefits of ReLU and sigmoid functions. S-ReLU addresses the vanishing gradient issue associated with traditional ReLU activation, while also providing piecewise linearity, which is essential for deep neural networks. In traditional ReLU, negative input values are mapped to zero, resulting in a vanishing gradient when propagated backward. In contrast, S-ReLU modifies ReLU to produce an S-shaped curve, where even the smallest negative input values produce a non-zero gradient. This feature enables the network to learn more complex relationships and avoids the dying ReLU issue. Experiments conducted on a range of deep learning benchmarks demonstrate that S-ReLU yields improved performance and convergence times compared to ReLU and softmax activation units. The results show that S-ReLU provides better preservation of detailed features, robustness to outliers, and efficient training times, making it a promising alternative to traditional activation units in deep neural networks. title: FAASTA: A fast solver for total-variation regularization of ill-conditioned problems with application to brain imaging
Abstract: FAASTA, a fast solver for total-variation regularization of ill-conditioned problems, presents an efficient method for addressing complex imaging reconstruction challenges. This algorithm leverages the core concept of total-variation minimization to constrain solutions to ill-conditioned inverse problems, thereby mitigating the impact of noise and artifacts in the reconstructed images. By exploiting the fast iterative shrinkage-thresholding algorithm (FISTA) as its propulsion engine, FAASTA seamlessly converges to globally optimal or, at the very least, more desirable suboptimal solutions within a few iterations. One significant advantage FAASTA boasts is its capacity to dramatically accelerate restoration procedures in the context of brain imaging, where computational efficiency is paramount. In contrast to conventional convex programming heuristics that have shown potential only when heavily optimized, experimental evaluations demonstrate FAASTA delivers meaningful and reliable restoration capabilities without the excessive overhead typically associated with iterative models. title: On the Differential Privacy of Bayesian Inference
Abstract: This abstract discusses the differential privacy of Bayesian inference, a statistical approach used for Bayesian model selection. With the proliferation of machine learning in high-stakes applications, such as healthcare and finance, ensuring the privacy of sensitive data has become a pressing concern. However, traditional Bayesian inference methods, which rely on posterior distributions and likelihood functions, are inherently sensitive to data from individual examples, thereby failing to provide any meaningful notion of differential privacy. We investigate this problem by casting Bayesian inference as a process of iterative posterior updates, each of which operates on a data vector to compute the likelihood of the model parameters. Our work demonstrates that by suitably controlling the number and quality of the iterations, as well as the scaling of the likelihood, we can recover accurate Bayesian inference results while also providing differential privacy. Our approach ensures that changing a single data entry cannot alter the resulting posterior distribution in any meaningful way, as it modifies the output sufficiently so that no adversary can infer whether the data was changed from the output of the Bayesian model. We provide theoretical guarantees for our approach and demonstrate its practical viability on a range of synthetic and real-world data sets. The core challenge lies in balancing the competing demands of accuracy and privacy, and our research contributes to a better understanding of how Bayesian inference can be adapted for differentially private statistical estimation.

title: Seeing through the Human Reporting Bias: Visual Classifiers from Noisy Human-Centric Labels
Abstract: This study addresses the fundamental challenge of human reporting bias in machine learning classification tasks, particularly those relying on visual features. The subjective nature of human labeling creates noisy data, which can significantly impact the performance and generalizability of trained models. By meticulously examining the consequences of human-centric labels, we uncover a profound phenomenon – the misalignment between human perception and the objective truth. This dichotomy hinders the development of accurate visual classifiers, as they learn to optimize for human-defined categories rather than the underlying true labels. To mitigate this issue, we propose a novel approach that leverages a hybrid framework combining self-supervised and supervised learning techniques. By pre-training visual classifiers on large-scale unlabeled datasets and subsequently fine-tuning them with human-centric labels, our model can effectively capture the nuances of human reporting bias and adapt to the ground truth. Our extensive experiments demonstrate the efficacy of this approach, showcasing improved accuracy and robustness across various visual classification tasks. The implications of our findings have far-reaching consequences for the development of reliable and trustworthy machine learning systems, underscoring the necessity for more nuanced and human-centric data collection and annotation strategies.

title: Multi-Instance Visual-Semantic Embedding
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel multi-instance visual-semantic embedding framework for efficient and robust visual representation learning. The proposed framework, termed as MS-Embed, represents each image as a set of instances, where each instance corresponds to a specific region or object within the image. MS-Embed seamlessly integrates instance-aware feature extraction with semantic-aware embedding, allowing it to model the relationships between different instances and their semantic labels. The framework is enabled through a dual-encoder architecture, comprising a feature extractor and an embedding network. The feature extractor captures spatial and temporal features from each instance, while the embedding network generates a dense semantic representation that encodes the instance-specific information. By aggregating instance features via a learnable attention mechanism, MS-Embed establishes a hierarchical embedding space where images are juxtaposed with their instance-wise representations. Our experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of MS-Embed on various benchmark datasets, including visual recognition, image classification, and instance-level object detection tasks. Notably, MS-Embed achieves superior performance and efficient processing, rendering it a compelling solution for image representation learning. By pushing the boundaries of instance-semantic interaction, MS-Embed bridges the gap between instance-level knowledge and high-level visual understanding, paving the way for future advancements in computer vision research.

title: Facility Deployment Decisions through Warp Optimizaton of Regressed Gaussian Processes
Abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to optimizing facility deployment decisions using a combination of regrssed Gaussian processes and warp optimization. The primary goal is to address the complexity of facility deployment problems, which often involve multiple, conflicting criteria and large numbers of potential solution space. To tackle this challenge, we employ a regrssed Gaussian process to model the relationships between facility locations and their corresponding performance metrics, such as travel distances, storage capacities, and operational costs. We then utilize a derivative-free optimization algorithm, specifically designed for high-dimensional search spaces, to efficiently explore the solution space and identify near-optimal facility configurations. Warp optimization, a recently developed methodology, is leveraged to construct a manifold that captures the intrinsic geometric structure of the objective function, thereby allowing us to navigate the search space more effectively and avoid local optima. The efficacy of the proposed approach is extensively evaluated using several case studies, each with increasing complexity, and involving varying numbers of facilities and performance metrics. Our results demonstrate that the regrssed Gaussian process-warp optimization hybrid outperforms state-of-the-art metaheuristics, such as simulated annealing and genetic algorithms, in terms of solution quality, computational efficiency, and scalability. title: Transformed Residual Quantization for Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search
Abstract: This abstract discusses a new approach to approximate nearest neighbor search through the application of transformed residual quantization. The proposed method leverages the concept of transformed residuals to efficiently reduce the dimensionality of high-dimensional vectors, thereby facilitating the search process. By utilizing learned transformations, the residual information between the input vectors and the centroids is effectively captured, leading to a more accurate representation of the underlying data structure. The transformed residuals are then quantized using a dedicated quantizer, allowing for approximation without significant information loss. Experimental results indicate that the transformed residual quantization technique can significantly reduce the time complexity of the search operation without sacrificing too much accuracy. title: What Happens to a Manifold Under a Bi-Lipschitz Map?
Abstract: A bi-Lipschitz map is a type of homeomorphism that preserves the geometry of a manifold up to a multiplicative constant. In this paper, we investigate the effects of a bi-Lipschitz map on the topological and geometric properties of a manifold. We first examine how a bi-Lipschitz map affects the dimension and connectedness of a manifold, demonstrating that these invariants are preserved under such maps. We then consider the effects of a bi-Lipschitz map on the metric structure of a manifold, showing that it induces a canonical distance function that is Lipschitz equivalent to the original distance function. This canonical distance function is essential in defining the Lipschitz regularity of the manifold, which is a fundamental concept in modern geometry and analysis. We also explore the relationship between bi-Lipschitz maps and quasi-isometries, demonstrating that the latter can be viewed as a limiting case of bi-Lipschitz maps. Furthermore, we analyze how a bi-Lipschitz map affects the geometric invariants of a manifold, such as curvature and volume, and provide examples to illustrate these effects. Throughout this paper, we utilize a combination of topological, geometric, and analytical techniques to provide a comprehensive understanding of the impact of bi-Lipschitz maps on manifolds. Our results have implications for various areas of mathematics, including differential geometry, geometric topology, and geometric analysis.

title: Predicting the Co-Evolution of Event and Knowledge Graphs
Abstract: The co-evolution of event and knowledge graphs represents a complex and dynamic phenomenon where the structure and content of both graphs interact and influence each other over time. As event graphs capture the dynamics of the real world, such as news articles, social media posts, and sensor readings, they can drive updates to knowledge graphs, which encompass structured information about entities, their relationships, and concepts. Conversely, knowledge graphs inform the entity and relationship identification in event graphs, improving their accuracy and completeness. To tackle this interdependence, we propose a novel framework that integrates graph neural networks (GNNs) and graph attention mechanisms to model the co-evolutionary process. The framework leverages event graphs to identify knowledge graph updates and adapts these updates to knowledge graph embeddings using GNNs. Our approach also incorporates graph attention mechanisms to identify the most relevant entities and relationships in both graphs, facilitating a more accurate and efficient co-evolution process. We evaluate our framework on several benchmarks, demonstrating its ability to outperform state-of-the-art methods in predicting knowledge graph updates and event graph content, highlighting its potential in applications such as knowledge graph maintenance, event prediction, and information retrieval. title: On Distributed Cooperative Decision-Making in Multiarmed Bandits
Abstract: Distributed cooperative decision-making in multiarmed bandits is a critical problem in various fields including communication networks, sensor networks, and online advertising. In contrast, distributed multiarmed bandit algorithms have multiple agents or learners that cooperate with each other to make decisions, sharing information and coordinating their actions. This paper explores the problem of cooperative decision-making in distributed multiarmed bandits, where multiple agents with limited information and communication constraints work together to maximize a common reward. We investigate two scenarios: (1) a fully connected network where all agents can share information freely, and (2) a partially connected network where agents can only communicate with their neighbors. We propose novel distributed algorithms that balance exploration and exploitation, and show that they achieve higher cumulative rewards compared to non-cooperative methods. Our results demonstrate the benefits of cooperation in distributed multiarmed bandits, suggesting that agents can improve their individual rewards by sharing information and learning from each other. Additionally, we investigated the relationship between CLASS-EP subscales and students' self-reported attitudes towards experimental physics, perceived understanding of experimental physics concepts, and reported frequency of performing hands-on experimental activities. A sample of 500 students enrolled in experimental physics courses participated in the study. Our results showed that CLASS-EP exhibited a satisfactory fit with the reported eight-factor structure, although slight modifications were suggested for some subscales. Furthermore, our analysis revealed moderate-to-strong correlations between CLASS-EP subscales and students' attitudes towards experimental physics and their perceived understanding of experimental physics concepts. These findings provide evidence for the validity of CLASS-EP as a tool for assessing students' epistemologies about experimental physics, while also highlighting the need for further refinement and calibration to improve its predictive power. title: Information-Theoretic Bounded Rationality
Abstract: This paper investigates the application of information-theoretic principles to the theory of bounded rationality in decision-making under uncertainty. Bounded rationality, as introduced by Herbert Simon, refers to the limitations in humans' ability to process and utilize information, leading to suboptimal decision-making. Information-theory, pioneered by Claude Shannon, provides a mathematical framework for quantifying information and its transmission. By combining these two concepts, this research presents a novel approach to modeling and analyzing decision-making processes with imperfect information. We introduce a decision framework based on conditional entropy, which measures the uncertainty associated with a decision-maker's choices. This framework enables us to quantify and compare the noise in different decision processes, providing insights into the efficiency and optimality of bounded rational decision-making strategies. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach through a series of simulations and case studies, involving both simple decision-making tasks and more complex scenarios, such as probabilistic allocation problems and probabilistic multi-armed bandits. The proposed framework offers a novel method for analyzing and optimizing decision-making strategies under uncertainty, which has far-reaching implications for fields such as economics, behavioral science, and artificial intelligence. title: GraphConnect: A Regularization Framework for Neural Networks

title: Sparse Coding with Fast Image Alignment via Large Displacement Optical Flow
Abstract: Sparse coding has been widely employed in image processing and computer vision tasks, including image denoising, compressive sensing, and feature extraction. Currently, the state-of-the-art algorithms achieve this alignment using various interpolation techniques, which involve patch-wise refinement and may lead to inaccurate results. To overcome this limitation, this paper proposes a novel approach called RARENet, which integrates sparse coding with fast image alignment via large displacement optical flow. RARENet leverages a hierarchical structure to recursively estimate the displacement between patches, reducing the computational cost while maintaining accurate alignments. The proposed approach achieves state-of-the-art performance in both synthetic and real-world image datasets, showcasing its potential in applications such as video compression, computer vision, and biomedical imaging. title: Backward and Forward Language Modeling for Constrained Sentence Generation
Abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive investigation of constrained sentence generation through the lens of backward and forward language modeling. title: Revisiting Differentially Private Regression: Lessons From Learning Theory and their Consequences
Abstract: Differentially private regression remains a crucial yet challenging problem in machine learning, as it involves ensuring that the disclosure of sensitive information about individual data points does not compromise their privacy. title: Kernel principal component analysis network for image classification
Abstract: Kernel principal component analysis network has garnered significant attention in the realm of image classification for its exceptional ability to capture complex patterns and relationships within the data. However, conventional PCA-based approaches are often limited by their linear nature, which restricts their ability to model non-linear relationships. To address this limitation, a novel kernel principal component analysis network is proposed, which combines the strengths of PCA with the power of kernel methods. This network is trained to learn a non-linear representation of the input data in a higher dimensional feature space, allowing it to capture intricate patterns and relationships that are not accessible through conventional PCA-based approaches. By utilizing a kernel function to transform the input data into a higher dimensional space, the network can accurately model complex non-linear relationships and correlations within the data. Experimental results on various benchmark datasets demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed kernel PCA network in achieving state-of-the-art performance in image classification tasks. Furthermore, the network's ability to learn robust and discriminative features enables it to generalize well to unseen data, making it a promising approach for real-world image classification applications. Overall, the proposed kernel PCA network has the potential to revolutionize the field of image classification by providing a powerful and effective tool for modeling complex patterns and relationships within image data.

title: A Mathematical Theory of Deep Convolutional Neural Networks for Feature Extraction
Abstract: Deep convolutional neural networks have revolutionized the field of computer vision by significantly improving the performance of feature extraction tasks. However, the lack of a comprehensive mathematical framework to understand and analyze these networks has hindered the development of more efficient and robust feature extraction algorithms. This paper presents a novel mathematical theory aimed at filling this gap, providing a rigorous and interpretable framework for understanding the behavior of deep convolutional neural networks in feature extraction tasks. By leveraging techniques from partial differential equations, harmonic analysis, and linear algebra, we develop a mathematical model that captures the key characteristics of convolutional neural networks, including layer-wise feature extraction and fusion, spatial and channel-wise attention mechanisms, and residual connections. Our theory is grounded in the concept of a "feature map manifold," a high-dimensional space that encodes the dynamics of feature extraction in deep neural networks. We demonstrate that our mathematical framework can be used to predict the behavior of convolutional neural networks in various tasks, such as image classification, object detection, and image segmentation. The proposed theory offers a foundational understanding of deep convolutional neural networks and provides a powerful tool for designing and optimizing feature extraction algorithms in various machine learning applications.

title: The Limitations of Optimization from Samples
Abstract: This work delves into the fundamental limitations of optimization from samples, a widely used strategy for making decisions under uncertainty. Optimization from samples is commonly employed in machine learning, data-driven decision-making, and statistical inference. While it has been instrumental in tackling various real-world problems, it suffers from several inherent limitations. One of the primary concerns is that optimization from samples relies on empirical risk minimization, which assumes that the optimal decision rule is the one that minimizes the average misclassification rate or expected loss over a finite number of samples. However, this assumption is problematic when the data-generating distribution is inherently complex, high-dimensional, or rapidly changing. Furthermore, optimization from samples is notoriously vulnerable to overfitting, wherein the estimated decision rule is excessively specialized to the randomly selected training samples. As a result, the decision rule fails to generalize well to unseen data, leading to poor out-of-sample performance. This work aims to elucidate these limitations and explore alternative approaches to decision-making under uncertainty that do not rely on optimization from samples. By investigating the fundamental trade-offs inherent in optimization from samples, this work aims to shed light on the need for novel, robust strategies that can mitigate these limitations and improve the accuracy and reliability of data-driven decision-making.

title: Using machine learning for medium frequency derivative portfolio trading
Abstract: This study focuses on the application of machine learning techniques in managing medium frequency derivative portfolios. The growing complexity and high risk inherent in derivative trading have made it essential to develop a sophisticated and data-driven approach for portfolio optimization. By integrating machine learning algorithms with medium frequency derivative trading strategies, the proposed system aims to improve portfolio performance, reduce risk, and enhance overall market agility. The machine learning models, trained on historical market data, are designed to identify patterns and correlations in market trends that may not be apparent through traditional analysis methods. These models can generate buy and sell signals, allowing portfolio managers to make informed investment decisions in real-time. The research assesses the performance of various machine learning models, including decision trees, random forests, and neural networks, in different market conditions to identify the most suitable approach for medium frequency derivative portfolio trading. The findings of this study demonstrate the potential of machine learning in improving portfolio returns, reducing trading costs, and enhancing overall portfolio stability, offering a valuable contribution to the field of derivative trading and investment portfolio management.

title: A new robust adaptive algorithm for underwater acoustic channel equalization
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel robust adaptive algorithm for underwater acoustic channel equalization, which is a crucial component in underwater communication systems. The algorithm is designed to address the challenges posed by the highly time-varying and multipath characteristics of underwater acoustic channels, which significantly impede reliable communication. The proposed scheme, termed as Deep Learning-based Adaptive Filter (DLAF), integrates a deep neural network with a novel adaptive filtering mechanism to mitigate channel impairments. The DLAF employs a hierarchical structure comprising multiple layers of deep neural networks, each responsible for adaptively filtering and learning the channel characteristics. By leveraging the inherent ability of deep neural networks to learn complex patterns in data, the DLAF is able to efficiently update the filter weights and adapt to the changing channel conditions in real-time. Extensive simulations and experimental results demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed DLAF, outperforming conventional adaptive filtering schemes in terms of bit error rate, convergence speed, and robustness. The DLAF is also capable of operating in a variety of underwater environments, including shallow and deep water, and is suitable for use in various underwater communication applications, such as marine sensors, underwater vehicles, and offshore communications. Overall, the proposed DLAF represents a significant advancement in underwater acoustic channel equalization and will play a crucial role in enabling reliable and efficient underwater communication.

title: Poseidon: A System Architecture for Efficient GPU-based Deep Learning on Multiple Machines
Abstract: Poseidon is a novel system architecture designed to efficiently manage parallel GPU-based deep learning computations on multiple machines. By providing a scalable and fault-tolerant framework, Poseidon optimizes the training process of deep neural networks while minimizing resource utilization and energy consumption. This architecture introduces a hierarchical job management system that dynamically allocates tasks across a cluster of machines, balancing workload redistribution and load optimization to meet the requirements of individual computing nodes. A dynamic data transfer and caching mechanism is also implemented to reduce data movement between nodes and enable efficient data parallelism. Furthermore, Poseidon incorporates a distributed memory allocation scheme to minimize memory fragmentation and optimize memory usage, which is critical in large-scale deep learning computations. Additionally, a global synchronization protocol is introduced to manage synchronization and coordination among computing nodes and ensure data consistency, thus avoiding bottlenecks and ensuring high-precision results. By leveraging these novel architectural features and optimizations, Poseidon facilitates efficient, high-throughput, and scalable deep learning computations on large clusters of machines, enabling researchers to perform extensive studies on complex AI problems that would be infeasible with existing architectures.

title: Discriminative Subnetworks with Regularized Spectral Learning for Global-state Network Data
Abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to discriminative subnetwork discovery in global-state network data by combining regularized spectral learning with insights from network embedding techniques. Despite the wealth of existing research on embedding methods for network analysis, prior work often overlooks the utility of discovering low-dimensional subgraphs that hold distinctive patterns and anomalies. Our proposed method, Spectral Subnetwork Selection (SSS), leverages the concept of regularized spectral learning to adaptively construct discriminative subnetworks that best represent salient features in global-state network data. By modeling the subnetwork discovery as a constrained optimization problem, we use a novel combinatorial objective function that captures the relationships between node proximities and spectral correlations in the input network. To further improve the robustness and interpretability of SSS, we incorporate an interpretable scoring function that evaluates the statistical significance of discovered subnetworks. Empirical evaluations on a comprehensive set of benchmark networks from diverse domains demonstrate that SSS significantly outperforms state-of-the-art subnetwork discovery methods in terms of both accuracy and scalability, highlighting the utility of our approach for uncovering complex global patterns and anomalies in network data with incomplete information. We also demonstrate the applicability of SSS to real-world applications such as anomaly detection and node classification.

title: Regularized Estimation of Piecewise Constant Gaussian Graphical Models: The Group-Fused Graphical Lasso
Abstract: This paper presents a novel method for the regularized estimation of piecewise constant Gaussian graphical models, where we exploit the structure-based priors to simultaneously identify multiple regions with constant correlations and the associated graphical model for each region. Traditional high-dimensional graphical models estimation generally assumes a constant correlation structure throughout the entire sample space and can be applied to each region separately, leading to poor performance and overfitting in the presence of piecewise constant structures. By formulating a group-fused graphical lasso, we succeed to introduce both spatial and structural regularization penalties, which can automatically identify the pieces and promote sparsity and edge consistency within and across regions. We develop an efficient optimization algorithm for solving the resulting optimization problem efficiently. Through extensive numerical studies and real-world applications with synthetic and real-world datasets from both Gaussian and non-Gaussian settings, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in identifying piecewise constant structures, and compare its efficacy in recovering true sparse and piecewise constant graphical models against existing methods. Our results also show that this new approach retains robustness under various challenges, such as non-Gaussianity, spatial autocorrelation, and low sample size settings.

title: Long-Baseline Neutrino Facility (LBNF) and Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE) Conceptual Design Report Volume 2: The Physics Program for DUNE at LBNF
Abstract: The Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE), to be located at the proposed Long-Baseline Neutrino Facility (LBNF) site, aims to advance our understanding of neutrino physics, improve the determination of fundamental neutrino parameters, and explore beyond-standard-model phenomena in neutrino interactions. DUNE's detailed physics program consists of a comprehensive set of studies encompassing neutrino oscillation and interaction studies, beyond-standard-model physics searches, and precision measurements of neutrino properties. Initially, the dominant focus of the experiment will be neutrino oscillation measurements with unprecedented precision, complementing existing and future oscillation experiments to establish a baseline for future discoveries. Additionally, DUNE will explore beyond-standard-model physics through measurements of neutrino interactions that could exhibit unique properties predicted by frameworks beyond the Standard Model of particle physics. With its unique detector technologies and 3-megaton liquid-argon time-projection chamber, DUNE will strive to achieve world-leading sensitivity in several key measurements, including the neutrino mass hierarchy and the CP-violating phase delta. The precise measurement of neutrino-argon cross sections and the systematic uncertainties will also significantly contribute to the precision of DUNE measurements.

title: Morphological Inflection Generation Using Character Sequence to Sequence Learning
Abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to morphological inflection generation by leveraging the capabilities of character sequence-to-sequence learning models. Morphological inflection refers to the process of generating various forms of a word based on its grammatical context, such as plural or tense forms. Traditional approaches to inflection generation rely on rule-based systems or machine learning models trained on token-level or word embeddings. However, these methods often fail to capture the complexities of morphology, particularly in languages with rich inflectional systems. In contrast, our proposed method adopts a character sequence-to-sequence architecture that directly models the relationships between input words and their corresponding inflected forms. By doing so, it can learn nuanced patterns and irregularities in the language, allowing for more accurate and flexible generation of inflected words. Our approach is specifically designed to handle the characteristics of morphological inflection, including phonological, orthographic, and semantic processes. We evaluate our model on a range of morphologically complex languages, demonstrating improvements in accuracy and robustness over state-of-the-art baselines. The results show that character sequence-to-sequence learning offers a promising direction for addressing the challenges of morphological inflection generation, with potential applications in natural language understanding, machine translation, and text processing tasks.

title: Expectation propagation for continuous time stochastic processes
Abstract: Expectation propagation (EP) is a popular inference method in Bayesian statistics that provides an efficient way to approximate complex posterior distributions. However, EP, as originally formulated, is limited to discrete-time systems and batch data. In this study, we extend the EP framework to accommodate continuous-time stochastic processes. We develop a novel continuous-time EP (CT-EP) algorithm that utilizes a signal-processing perspective to update particle weights and propagates expectations through a continuous-time Markov state-space model. The proposed method does not require discretization of the continuous-time system, allowing for a more accurate representation of the underlying dynamics. We demonstrate the effectiveness of CT-EP for various scenarios, including simulations involving linear Gaussian systems and nonlinear stochastic processes. We also present illustrations with real-world datasets, showcasing the application of CT-EP to continuous-time signal processing and state estimation tasks. Our results indicate that CT-EP is a promising approach for solving inference problems in continuous-time systems, offering improved performance and flexibility compared to traditional batch Bayesian estimation methods. Overall, the CT-EP algorithm provides an important step towards adapting Expectation Propagation to real-world signal processing and control applications that involve continuous-time stochastic processes.

title: Bayesian anti-sparse coding
Abstract: This abstract provides an overview of a novel Bayesian anti-sparse coding technique that aims to model data distributions where high-dimensional signals exhibit anti-sparsity, a phenomenon characterized by the presence of both sparse and dense components. Traditional sparse coding methods, such as dictionaries or overcomplete bases, fail to capture this diversity and may lead to suboptimal representation and learning outcomes. To address this limitation, the proposed Bayesian anti-sparse coding method leverages a hierarchical prior distribution that can adapt to diverse densities by incorporating both sparse and dense features. The prior distribution is composed of a sparse component that is based on a Laplace (double-exponential) distribution and a dense component based on a normal distribution. The competition between these two components induces a robust estimation of the anti-sparse nature of high-dimensional data, enabling more accurate and interpretable representations of complex data structures. A variational Bayes approach is employed to learn the model parameters, allowing for efficient computation of the posterior distribution of the model parameters. This method has been validated on various data sets of varying complexity, demonstrating its ability to learn accurate and interpretable representations in scenarios where traditional sparse coding methods fail.

title: Demonstration of quantum advantage in machine learning
Abstract: Our research paper delves into the concept of quantum advantage in machine learning, a phenomenon where quantum computers outperform their classical counterparts in solving specific machine learning tasks. By leveraging the unique properties of quantum bits (qubits), such as superposition and entanglement, we aim to demonstrate the superiority of quantum machine learning algorithms over their classical counterparts. We explore the realm of supervised and unsupervised learning, developing novel quantum algorithms that can efficiently solve complex problems such as linear regression, clustering, and classification. Our work is built upon the foundation of recent breakthroughs in quantum supremacy experiments and the development of quantum circuits for machine learning tasks. We provide a comprehensive comparison of the performance of our quantum algorithms with their classical counterparts, showcasing the exponential speedup gained through the use of quantum parallelism. Furthermore, we discuss the implications of our research on the future of machine learning, highlighting the potential for quantum computers to revolutionize the field and tackle complex problems that are currently intractable. Our results demonstrate a clear quantum advantage in machine learning, paving the way for the development of quantum AI systems that can tackle real-world problems more efficiently than their classical counterparts.

title: Asymptotic Behavior of Mean Partitions in Consensus Clustering
Abstract: This paper explores the asymptotic behavior of mean partitions in consensus clustering, a methodology used to obtain a stable partition from multiple clustering results. We develop a framework that generalizes consensus clustering under a common statistical framework and establish theoretical bounds on its asymptotic behavior. Through the lens of information-theoretic tools, we derive the mean partition of the consensus clustering and its corresponding variance. Our results reveal that the mean partition converges to the underlying ground truth as the number of clusterings increases, but with a rate that varies with the level of noise and diversity among individual clusterings. Specifically, we show that the rate of convergence depends on the mutual information between individual partitions and the ground truth, and demonstrate that a high level of mutual information between clusterings significantly accelerates the convergence. Furthermore, we also derive bounds on the variance of the mean partition that incorporate the diversity among individual clusterings, highlighting the potential trade-offs between partition diversity and convergence rate. Our findings demonstrate the mathematical underpinnings of consensus clustering and provide new insights into the asymptotic behavior of mean partitions.

title: Face Hallucination using Linear Models of Coupled Sparse Support
Abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of face hallucination using linear models of coupled sparse support. Face hallucination aims to generate a high-resolution face image from its low-resolution counterpart, which has extensive applications in video surveillance, biometric recognition, and human-computer interaction. Traditional face hallucination methods rely heavily on non-linear models, such as convolutional neural networks (CNNs), which may suffer from over-smoothing and lack of local detail. In contrast, this paper proposes a novel approach based on linear models, specifically coupled sparse support (CSS) learning. CSS integrates the strengths of sparse coding and dictionary learning to capture local patterns in low-resolution faces and project them onto a high-resolution face space. A linear model estimates the mapping between the low-resolution and high-resolution face spaces, enabling the recovery of detailed facial features. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed CSS-based approach in face hallucination, outperforming state-of-the-art non-linear models on several benchmarks. Moreover, the paper analyzes the stability and sensitivity of the CSS model to various regularization parameters, highlighting its robustness and ease of adaptation to different face hallucination scenarios. Overall, this work presents a novel linear model for face hallucination, providing a computationally efficient and interpretable solution for high-quality face reconstruction.

title: Can Pretrained Neural Networks Detect Anatomy?
Abstract: Deep learning techniques relying on pretraining with large datasets have led to significant advancements in the field of medical imaging, where accurate identification and segmentation of anatomical structures are critical for diagnosis and treatment planning. Recent research has demonstrated the potential of using pre-trained neural networks to automatically detect and segment various anatomical structures from medical images, including organs and tissues. This study aims to investigate the feasibility of employing pre-trained neural networks to detect anatomy in a range of common medical imaging modalities, including computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and ultrasound (US). Specifically, we evaluate the performance of several pre-trained models fine-tuned on a large dataset of annotated medical images covering a diverse set of anatomical regions and imaging modalities. Our results show that pre-trained neural networks can be successfully adapted to detect anatomy with high accuracy, outperforming traditional machine learning approaches and demonstrating strong potential for deployment in clinical settings. However, we also highlight the need for careful model selection, image preprocessing, and validation protocols to ensure accurate and robust performance in real-world scenarios. Furthermore, our findings suggest that pre-trained neural networks can serve as a valuable tool for guiding clinicians and radiologists in the interpretation of medical images, potentially leading to improved diagnostic accuracy and patient outcomes.

title: Energy Consumption Forecasting for Smart Meters
Abstract: This study presents an innovative approach to energy consumption forecasting for smart meters, leveraging the integration of machine learning algorithms, temporal-spatial data, and internet of things (IoT) infrastructure. By combining daily weather forecasts, historical energy consumption data, and near real-time smart meter readings, our proposed model can accurately predict energy demand at a granular level. Specifically, the model utilizes a hybrid ensemble approach, incorporating both deterministic and probabilistic forecasting methods, such as ARIMA, LSTM, and GRU, to capture short-term and long-term patterns in energy consumption. Our proposed framework also accounts for temporal variations, spatial dependencies, and seasonal effects through the integration of geographic information systems (GIS) and spatial analysis techniques. The model's performance is evaluated using a comprehensive dataset collected from various smart grids across different regions, demonstrating a significant improvement in forecasting accuracy compared to traditional methods. Moreover, our study explores the impact of IoT sensors, such as weather stations and sensors monitoring local electricity grid capacity, on the forecasting model's performance, highlighting the synergistic benefits of integrating these sensors with our proposed framework. title: Complexity and Approximation of the Fuzzy K-Means Problem
Abstract: The Fuzzy K-Means (FKM) problem is a fundamental clustering algorithm that extends the classical K-Means by incorporating fuzzy membership degrees to the clusters. This problem has numerous applications in various fields, such as image analysis, bioinformatics, and data mining, where the data points may exhibit partial memberships to multiple clusters. However, the FKM problem is known to be computationally complex, belonging to the NP-hard class, making it challenging to solve optimally for large-scale real-world data sets. To address this computational difficulty, various approximation algorithms have been proposed to efficiently find high-quality solutions. Despite the extensive research in this area, the design of approximation algorithms for FKM remains an open question, and the performance guarantees of existing algorithms are often limited by tight bounds. This paper presents a comprehensive study on the complexity and approximation of the FKM problem. Specifically, we examine the theoretical properties of the FKM problem, investigate the trade-offs between the approximation ratio, the computational efficiency, and the clustering accuracy of different approximation algorithms. We also develop a new polynomial-time approximation algorithm for the FKM problem, which achieves a significantly improved approximation ratio compared to existing algorithms. Our results provide new insights into the computational complexity of the FKM problem and shed light on the design of efficient and effective approximation algorithms for this problem.

title: Operator Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Spaces
Abstract: The theory of Operator Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Spaces (ORKHS) has gained significant attention in recent years due to its far-reaching implications in a wide range of fields, including machine learning, signal processing, and control systems. The concept of ORKHS is an extension of the classical Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Spaces (RKHS) theory to the realm of operators, enabling the development of novel methods for solving complex problems in functional analysis, partial differential equations, and image processing. By employing operators as the core building blocks, ORKHS provides a unified framework for modeling and analyzing problems involving interactions between functions and operators. A key feature of ORKHS is its ability to incorporate prior knowledge and domain-specific information through the incorporation of reproducing kernels, leading to improved adaptability and generalizability of models. Furthermore, ORKHS has been found to offer new insights and perspectives on classical problems, such as inverse problems, uncertainty quantification, and inverse imaging problems, enabling the construction of efficient and stable solutions. This paper aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the current state of ORKHS research, focusing on its theoretical background, practical applications, and future research directions, with the ultimate goal of facilitating the adoption of ORKHS in various fields and promoting its continued development as a powerful tool for solving complex problems.

title: A novel Bayesian strategy for the identification of spatially-varying material properties and model validation: an application to static elastography
Abstract: This paper presents a novel Bayesian strategy for the identification of spatially-varying material properties and model validation in the context of static elastography. Static elastography is a medical imaging technique that employs mechanical compression to differentiate between soft tissue types, with potential applications in disease diagnosis and monitoring. However, the accurate identification of material properties is crucial for effective tissue classification and poses significant challenges due to the complex interplay between material properties and imaging parameters. To address this issue, we introduce a Bayesian framework that integrates Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods with a physics-based forward model, enabling the estimation of spatially-varying Young's modulus and viscosity in parallel. The proposed strategy employs a hierarchical Bayesian representation that accounts for both material heterogeneity and measurement uncertainties, thereby enhancing the accuracy and reliability of material property estimates. We demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed methodology through comprehensive numerical simulations, which confirm its ability to accurately capture spatial variations in material properties and reproduce known tissue characteristics. Furthermore, we evaluate the sensitivity of the proposed strategy to various sources of uncertainty, including measurements noise, model parameter values, and model assumptions. The results highlight the potential of the proposed Bayesian strategy as a framework for tackling the challenges associated with static elastography and its broader applications in biomedical imaging.

title: Domain Adaptation and Transfer Learning in StochasticNets
Abstract: Domain adaptation and transfer learning have emerged as crucial concepts in the realm of neural networks, particularly in stochastic models, to address the challenges of adapting to new and varied data distributions. The core idea behind stochastic nets is to capture the underlying stochastic processes that govern the behavior of complex systems, thereby facilitating efficient and accurate modeling of dynamics across diverse domains. However, stochastic models often suffer from the limited availability of labeled data in specific application domains, hindering their applicability in real-world scenarios. This is particularly problematic when domains exhibit significant variability in data distributions, leading to poor generalizability of models. Domain adaptation and transfer learning techniques offer promising solutions to this dilemma by enabling the adaptation of pre-trained stochastic nets to novel target domains with minimal labels. Specifically, this research explores the efficacy of various domain adaptation and transfer learning strategies in stochastic nets, including multi-task learning, adversarial training, and meta-learning. Experimental results on diverse stochastic models, such as stochastic recurrent neural networks and stochastic convolutional neural networks, demonstrate the potential of these approaches in enhancing the robustness and generalizability of stochastic nets across multiple domains. Overall, this research contributes to a deeper understanding of the capabilities and limitations of stochastic nets in the context of domain adaptation and transfer learning, thereby paving the way for their widespread adoption in real-world applications.

title: Deep Poisson Factorization Machines: factor analysis for mapping behaviors in journalist ecosystem
Abstract: Deep Poisson Factorization Machines propose a novel factor analysis approach to model complex behaviors within a journalist ecosystem. This innovative methodology combines the strengths of Poisson Factorization Machines, which is adept at modeling high-cardinality categorical features and mitigating the issue of curse of dimensionality, with the flexibility of deep learning. By incorporating a neural network-based feature extraction layer, Deep Poisson Factorization Machines are able to learn complex interactions and latent factors from the interactions of journalists, enabling a deeper understanding of their behaviors and preferences. The proposed model also leverages the Poisson likelihood function to account for the inherent sparsity and non-negative nature of interaction counts in the journalist ecosystem. Furthermore, it offers an interpretable representation of the behavior, providing insights into the relationships between journalists' writing topics, collaborators, and other relevant factors. A comprehensive evaluation of the proposed model on various datasets demonstrates its superiority over traditional methods in capturing the nuanced behavior patterns of journalists, offering a valuable tool for media monitoring and content creation applications. title: Learning the Preferences of Ignorant, Inconsistent Agents
Abstract: We present a novel approach to learning the preferences of ignorant and inconsistent agents from observational data. In many real-world scenarios, such as modeling users' behavior in e-commerce or recommendation systems, we are faced with agents that possess incomplete knowledge, exhibit conflicting preferences, or employ strategies that are not immediately apparent. Our method, centered around preference elicitation, involves developing a framework that can adequately capture the uncertainty inherent in the agents' actions and interactions. This framework leverages a Bayesian non-parametric approach to modeling the agents' preferences, allowing for online learning and adaptation to unexpected behavior. The proposed algorithm also incorporates a novel method for sampling uncertain agent interactions, thereby mitigating the impact of inconsistencies and incompleteness. We empirically evaluate our approach on simulated and real-world datasets, demonstrating its ability to accurately infer the agents' preferences, even when confronted with significant uncertainty and inconsistency. Furthermore, our analysis highlights the benefits of utilizing our method in preference elicitation tasks, where it exhibits improved accuracy and robustness compared to existing approaches. Overall, our contribution provides a compelling framework for understanding and modeling the behavior of ignorant and inconsistent agents, with broad applications in fields such as AI, cognitive science, and decision theory.

title: Relay Backpropagation for Effective Learning of Deep Convolutional Neural Networks
Abstract: Relay backpropagation is a novel optimization technique that has been proposed to alleviate the vanishing gradients problem inherent in deep neural networks, which severely limits the depth that can be achieved in deep learning models. Despite the success of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) in a multitude of image classification and object detection tasks, traditional backpropagation remains a major bottleneck in large-scale deep learning. The traditional backpropagation algorithm relies heavily on the accumulation of local gradients, which results in exponentially diminishing signal-to-noise ratios as the depth of the network increases. This results in a loss of representational power and severe degradation in learning capabilities. To alleviate this problem, relay backpropagation introduces a new relay layer in the network architecture, which is positioned between the convolutional and fully connected layers. The relay layer extracts and accumulates global spatial features from the entire convolutional layer, facilitating effective signal propagation and learning. The efficacy of the relay backpropagation technique has been demonstrated through extensive experimental evaluations on popular benchmark datasets such as ImageNet and CIFAR-10, resulting in significant accuracy improvements. This is attributed to the improved representation capacity and optimization efficiency provided by the relay layer. Further experimental evaluations substantiate the benefits of relay backpropagation over state-of-the-art optimization techniques. The proposed technique shows great promise for the development of deeper, more efficient, and highly accurate CNNs for large-scale image classification and object detection tasks.

title: Successive Ray Refinement and Its Application to Coordinate Descent for LASSO
Abstract: The Successive Ray Refinement (SRR) algorithm has been explored as a means to enhance the efficiency of optimization methods, particularly in the context of sparse regression tasks such as the Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO). This paper delves into the integration of SRR with Coordinate Descent (CD), a popular optimization technique for LASSO problems. By leveraging the SRR approach to iteratively refine directions within the current iteration of CD, the constrained subproblem in LASSO can be addressed more accurately. The SRR-CD hybrid methodology eliminates the need for explicit regularization parameters and by-construction supports efficient proximal calculations, resulting in significant computational speedup. Our theoretical analysis reveals that SRR-CD attains the optimal performance in solving the LASSO equation of linear regression. We corroborate its efficacy via a series of numerical experiments comparing SRR-CD against CD, LARS, and GLMNET, exhibiting superior performance relative to all these methods, such as convergence speed, residual errors, support recovery, and average solution costs. Notably, SRR-CD shows remarkable adaptability to an extensive array of noise models, from IID to structured constraints, without configuring extra tuning parameters. Our results indicate that SRR-CD offers a significantly compelling framework for tackling high-dimensional regression tasks where both statistical accuracy and optimization speed are critical.

title: A hidden confining world on the 750 GeV diphoton excess
Abstract: Recent observations by the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) have ignited interest in a 750 GeV diphoton excess, which, despite being a statistically significant phenomenon, remains inadequately explained within the Standard Model of particle physics. This anomalous production of collimated gamma-rays, first reported in 2015, has not been reproducible in subsequent experiments. A plethora of theoretical models have been proposed to elucidate this feature, ranging from supersymmetric versions of the Standard Model to theories involving extra dimensions and compactified spaces. Among these interpretations, certain models posit the existence of a hidden sector harboring new particles that are confined by strong interactions. These "dual photons" (γ*γ') mediate a force capable of communicating between the Standard Model sector and the hidden sector through the presence of a scalar mediator. Our research aims to investigate the theoretical viability of such a hidden confining world, specifying string-theoretic realizations amenable to LHC-inspired searches for quantum chromodynamics (QCD)-inspired hidden sector interactions. This study endeavors to (1) develop novel methods for categorizing the diverse array of strong-interaction-confining phenomenology applicable to hidden-sector theories with scalar, vector, and possibly fermionic mediators; (2) construct the expected dynamical signatures in search of evidence supporting the existence of this hidden confining world; and (3) determine whether the 750 GeV diphoton excess aligns with the features postulated by the hidden confining world hypothesis, and evaluate the potential for experimental verification of this theoretical concept.

title: A Survey of Available Corpora for Building Data-Driven Dialogue Systems
Abstract: This study provides a comprehensive overview of the diverse range of corpora utilized in building advanced data-driven dialogue systems. As the demand for human-like conversational AI has grown, the importance of developing high-quality training data has become increasingly evident. To this end, researchers have created numerous datasets and corpora tailored to various dialogue-related tasks, including conversational dialogue, multi-turn conversation, person-to-person conversation, human-to-humanship dialogue, and virtual human dialogue. These corpora encompass an array of formats, styles, and domains, each serving as a crucial component in enhancing the performance of dialogue systems. Through a detailed analysis of existing literature and corpus descriptions, this paper identifies a total of 235 datasets and corpora for dialogue-oriented research. Several critical trends and patterns were observed, including the rapid increase in multilingual and visually grounded dialogue datasets, growing focus on challenging and nuanced task-centric evaluations, and an escalating call for publicly available and more robust metadata. A thorough categorization of the surveyed corpora reveals a notable scarcity of cross-disciplinary and real-world dialogue datasets, however, our research offers a comprehensive overview of the current landscape and highlights pressing issues and future research directions in the field of dialogue system development.

title: Oracle inequalities for ranking and U-processes with Lasso penalty
Abstract: This paper establishes oracle inequalities for ranking and U-processes when employing the Lasso penalty. The Lasso penalty has been extensively used in the context of high-dimensional estimation to reduce model complexity and promote sparsity. These oracle inequalities provide a precise characterization of the performance of the Lasso when applied to ranking and U-processes, which are essential tools for functional data and empirical process theory. The properties of the Lasso, such as the rate of convergence and the stability of the estimator, are investigated through various types of oracle inequalities. By analyzing the intersection of high-dimensional statistics and empirical process theory, we establish the connection between the Lasso estimator and the best linear rank-based estimator, allowing us to derive sharper bounds for the uniform deviation risk. Furthermore, we demonstrate the applicability of our results by analyzing the convergence rates of the Lasso in the context of functional ranking and asymptotic properties of the cross-validated estimator. These findings have significant implications for the use of Lasso-based methods in high-dimensional estimation and empirical process theory, especially when dealing with functional data and ranking problems. Our results provide a comprehensive analysis of the performance of the Lasso, and its application to ranking and U-processes has the potential to lead to improved inference procedures and model selection strategies in various fields of study.

title: TermPicker: Enabling the Reuse of Vocabulary Terms by Exploiting Data from the Linked Open Data Cloud - An Extended Technical Report
Abstract: This extended technical report describes TermPicker, a novel approach to enable the reuse of vocabulary terms by leveraging data from the Linked Open Data (LOD) cloud. TermPicker's primary goal is to provide a comprehensive and efficient method for identifying and annotating relevant terms in a given domain, thereby facilitating their reuse in various applications, such as data integration, semantics-based search, and knowledge graph construction. The proposed framework relies on graph-based representations of LOD datasets, which are used to create a multilayered network of interconnected vocabularies. By analyzing this network, TermPicker can identify term clusters and concepts, as well as infer relationships between terms, ultimately enabling the discovery of relationships and concept hierarchies that may be difficult to discern manually. The report outlines the architecture and key components of TermPicker, including its term annotation and cluster analysis modules, as well as its user interface. A thorough evaluation of TermPicker's performance and scalability is also presented, demonstrating its effectiveness in handling large-scale datasets and outperforming traditional term extraction techniques. The outcomes of this research have significant implications for the research community and industry practitioners working in the areas of knowledge representation, information retrieval, and data integration, underscoring the potential of TermPicker as a valuable tool for improving the efficiency and effectiveness of vocabulary term reuse.

title: Probabilistic Programming with Gaussian Process Memoization
Abstract: This paper explores probabilistic programming with Gaussian Process (GP) memoization, providing a novel framework for efficiently utilizing GP-based models in probabilistic programming. GP memoization allows for the caching of previously computed GP evaluations, adaptively constructing a probabilistic memory to reduce redundant computation. In probabilistic programming, memoization can be applied to construct a dynamic memory, tailored to the exact requirements of the problem, thus mitigating the computational burden associated with GPs. The proposed approach incorporates GP memoization within a probabilistic programming language, leveraging lazy evaluation to ensure seamless integration and reducing the need for explicit memory management. This framework is demonstrated using a Bayesian linear regression problem, showcasing significant speedup and efficiency over naive GP-based approaches. Furthermore, the paper rigorously analyzes the trade-offs between memoization and the loss of probabilistic semantics, highlighting the tension between computational efficiency and accuracy in probabilistic learning. Additionally, the authors extend the framework to support hierarchical and more complex probabilistic models, showcasing its generality and applicability to real-world problems. The contributions of this paper provide a practical and efficient means of utilizing GPs within probabilistic programming, opening up new avenues for applications where inference needs to be performed.

title: Spacetime-constrained oblivious transfer
Abstract: This study investigates the concept of spacetime-constrained oblivious transfer (STC-OT), a novel approach to secure multiparty communication in distributed environments, where two or more parties exchange sensitive information. STC-OT enables an authorized sender to transfer a selected message to a recipient, while keeping the message's content concealed from any eavesdropper within a predetermined spacetime constraint. The latter refers to the maximum allowed propagation delay and sensitivity to noisy environments, affecting the message's transmission through spacetime. This work demonstrates that by utilizing the spacetime constraints, a sender can securely transmit sensitive information to a trusted recipient in a way that minimizes the vulnerability to adversarial eavesdropping, theft, and manipulation. Through an in-depth analysis of the fundamental principles underpinning STC-OT, a set of parameters and constraints are established, providing a comprehensive framework for optimizing secure information exchange. In addition to the theoretical contributions, this research delivers two novel protocols for implementing STC-OT in real-world scenarios: a quantum key distribution (QKD) protocol, utilizing entangled photon states and efficient non-destructive measurements, and a post-quantum protocol operating in the realm of lattice-based cryptography. By addressing real-world security concerns and offering innovative solutions to mitigate various attacks on sensitive information, this study illuminates new avenues for enhanced confidentiality, integrity, and security in distributed and open communication systems.

title: Deep-Spying: Spying using Smartwatch and Deep Learning

This paper proposes and explores a novel concept of wireless eavesdropping using smartwatches via deep learning, coined as Deep-Spying. By leveraging the ubiquitous presence of smartwatches among individuals, adversaries can utilize them as an unobtrusive and stealthy platform to intercept and extract sensitive information from cell phones. A binary classification deep neural network is designed and implemented to detect the presence of secure Wi-Fi connections on the victim's device, allowing the smartwatch to effectively eavesdrop on and intercept data flowing between the victim's smartphone and the secure Wi-Fi network. A comprehensive performance evaluation using various attack scenarios and deep learning architectures is presented to demonstrate the effectiveness and potential consequences of the developed technique. Furthermore, a thorough analysis of the root causes behind the attacks, specifically highlighting the impact of user privacy and platform insecurity, is conducted, and recommendations for addressing these vulnerabilities are provided. The results show that the proposed method successfully compromised various target devices, effectively casting doubt on the promises of wearable devices as secure gateways in IoT-communication networks. title: Classification of weak multi-view signals by sharing factors in a mixture of Bayesian group factor analyzers
Abstract: This study develops a novel statistical framework for the classification of weak multi-view signals by leveraging the factor sharing mechanism in a mixture of Bayesian group factor analyzers (BMGFAs). In many real-world applications, such as video surveillance, brain-computer interfaces, or network anomaly detection, data are often represented as multiple views, which can be complementarity or informatively redundant, but sometimes noisy and weak. To address the challenges posed by weak signals and limited information availability in these scenarios, we propose a BMGFA model that allows for the factor alignment of subspaces across views while preserving the sparse structure of weak signals. The developed framework enables automatic identification of informative subspaces, factor alignment, and estimation of high-dimensional mean vector and covariance matrix. Experimental results on various benchmark datasets demonstrate the robustness and efficacy of our proposed method against competing state-of-the-art methods, including superior performance on weak signal scenario and more accurate signal classification with noisy observations. Moreover, the empirical study shows the parameter inference can be efficiently handled through the development of a Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm. The BMGFA framework shows promise for real-world applications involving weak signal analysis.

title: Bayesian Covariance Modelling of Large Tensor-Variate Data Sets $\&$ Inverse Non-parametric Learning of the Unknown Model Parameter Vector
Abstract: The high dimensionality of tensor-variate data sets poses significant challenges in statistical inference, particularly in model parameter estimation. Conventional Bayesian methods often struggle with the computational complexity and non-identifiability issues stemming from the intricate dependency structure inherent in multivariate data. This research presents an innovative Bayesian framework for covariance modelling of large tensor-variate data sets, enabling the development of sparse and structured prior distributions for the covariance matrix. By leveraging the Hilbert space structure, our framework facilitates efficient computation of the posterior distribution, guaranteeing scalability to massive datasets while preventing over-fitting. To further resolve the non-parametric complexity challenge, we introduce an inverse non-parametric learning approach for modelling the unknown model parameter vector. This novel technique reconstructs the parameter vector by mapping the empirical data-driven loss function onto the parameters estimated from the probabilistic Gaussian process prior. Our results demonstrate that the proposed framework effectively captures complex underlying interactions and provides both robust and probabilistic estimation of model parameters. When applied to synthetic and real-world large tensor-variate datasets, this framework exhibits superior performance compared to existing methods. Our findings shed new light onto the potential applications of Bayesian inverse non-parametric learning in large-scale multivariate data analysis.

title: An Empirical Comparison of Neural Architectures for Reinforcement Learning in Partially Observable Environments
Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has experienced significant advancements in tackling complex tasks in various real-world scenarios, particularly in environments characterized by partial observability, where agents have to make informed decisions based on incomplete information. This empirica paper conducts an in-depth study of state-of-the-art neural architectures employed for solving RL problems with partial observability. A systematic comparison of fully-connected networks, convolutional neural networks, Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, multilayer perceptron networks, and graph convolutional networks is undertaken to investigate their strengths and weaknesses in various scenarios. We utilize a set of benchmark environments from the partially observable environments suite, which simulates a diverse set of real-world challenges, such as monitoring intrusion alert systems, navigating through partially observable grids, and learning to adapt to uncertain states. The results reveal significant variations in performance among different architectures, often leading to large discrepancies in terms of convergence speed, mean reward, and termination time. Additionally, we incorporate sensitivity analysis and in-depth explorations to identify parameters critical for optimal generalization and robustness. Through our findings, we demonstrate that choosing the most suitable neural architecture for solving RL tasks in partially observable environments is contingent upon the specific characteristics of the task at hand. By offering actionable insights into factor selection and potential pitfalls, this study contributes to the advancement of effective neural architectures for complex RL tasks and sheds light on future directions for exploratory research.
