title: Data-driven Inverse Optimization with Imperfect Information
Abstract: This paper focuses on addressing the challenges of data-driven inverse optimization under imperfect information conditions. In classical inverse optimization, the goal is to infer model parameters that produce the observed behavior in an optimal or nearly optimal manner. However, in practice, the available data is often noisy, incomplete, or imperfectly aligned with the underlying model. To address this issue, we develop a novel approach that leverages robust optimization and machine learning techniques to build a model that can effectively handle imperfect information. Our proposed method uses a combination of ensemble methods and regularization techniques to aggregate and refine the available data, resulting in a more robust and reliable inference of the model parameters. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through a series of numerical experiments on classic optimization problems, including linear programming and mixed-integer linear programming. Our results show that the proposed approach can significantly improve the accuracy and robustness of the model parameters, even in the presence of significant noise and uncertainty in the data. Furthermore, our approach is computationally efficient and scalable, making it a promising candidate for real-world applications. We believe that our work provides a significant step towards enabling data-driven inverse optimization under imperfect information conditions, which is a critical requirement in many real-world applications.

title: Deep Active Object Recognition by Joint Label and Action Prediction
Abstract: Active object recognition is a fundamental task in computer vision that involves interpreting visual information to identify objects in a scene while incorporating real-time interaction feedback to improve recognition accuracy. Recent advancements in deep learning have enabled the development of various active object recognition techniques that leverage label and action prediction to enhance object detection and segmentation capabilities. However, existing approaches often treat label and action prediction as separate tasks, failing to fully capture the synergies between these two modalities. This paper proposes a novel framework for deep active object recognition by jointly predicting labels and actions in a unified model. By integrating label and action prediction, our framework can leverage the strengths of both modalities to improve object recognition accuracy and robustness in real-world scenarios. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through a series of experiments on diverse datasets, including standard computer vision benchmarks and challenging real-world scenarios, showcasing its ability to outperform state-of-the-art methods. Our results highlight the benefits of joint label and action prediction for deep active object recognition and provide insights into potential applications in fields like robotics, autonomous vehicles, and human-computer interaction.

title: Private Causal Inference
Abstract: This research paper delves into the realm of Private Causal Inference, a critical yet unexplored area in the fields of causal inference and differential privacy. By integrating these two concepts, we aim to develop novel methodologies that enable the estimation of causal effects from sensitive datasets while maintaining confidentiality. Traditional causal inference techniques often rely on shared and linked datasets, raising significant concerns regarding data protection and informed consent. In contrast, private causal inference prioritizes the concealment of individual contributions, adhering to strict differential privacy standards. We investigate the challenges associated with private causal inference and existing-state-of-the-art solutions. By reviewing cutting-edge literature, we uncover a knowledge gap in the private causal inference landscape, particularly in handling high-dimensional data and structural causal models. This research focuses on bridging this gap by proposing a unified framework for private causal inference that incorporates differential privacy mechanisms, deep learning architectures, and robust optimization techniques. The framework provides both theoretical guarantees and empirical results demonstrating its efficacy on simulated and real-world datasets, including those from healthcare and social sciences. Ultimately, this research contributes to the development of reliable and private causal inference methods, essential for fostering trust in data-driven decision-making processes while upholding individual privacy.

title: Unsupervised Feature Construction for Improving Data Representation and Semantics
Abstract: This paper delves into the realm of unsupervised feature construction, exploring its pivotal role in enhancing data representation and semantics, a critical aspect of machine learning and artificial intelligence. Unsupervised feature construction involves discovering hidden patterns and relationships within unlabeled data, rather than relying on predefined feature sets or explicit labels, which can lead to biased or incomplete representations. Through various techniques such as dimensionality reduction, clustering, and generative models, researchers have been able to effectively construct informative and descriptive features, offering a more comprehensive understanding of the data at hand. By employing these methodologies, it becomes possible to uncover subtle nuances and dependencies that might be missed via traditional feature engineering approaches, ultimately yielding more accurate and robust models. This paper examines the applicability of unsupervised feature construction in diverse domains, including computer vision, natural language processing, and time-series forecasting. By evaluating its performance in these disparate fields, we gain insight into the overall efficacy of this approach and identify avenues for extending its utility. Our analysis demonstrates that unsupervised feature construction can indeed improve data representation and semantics, leading to improved model interpretability, generalizability, and predictive power. Furthermore, we discuss the potential applications and challenges of incorporating these techniques into existing data analysis pipelines, facilitating a paradigm shift in data-driven decision making.

title: Continuous online sequence learning with an unsupervised neural network model
Abstract: The continuous online sequence learning problem poses a significant challenge for neural network models, as they require adapting to new data streams without prior experience, strict memory constraints, and near-instant adaptation to evolving patterns. In this research paper, we investigate the applicability of unsupervised neural network models in achieving efficient online sequence learning from continuous data streams. Our proposed architecture integrates a self-organizing map and a sequence prediction component, allowing the model to learn meaningful representations from the input data, detect patterns, and adapt to changes in the underlying process. We demonstrate the advantages of this hybrid approach by employing it in diverse applications, including time series forecasting, anomaly detection, and continual learning scenarios. Experimental results from extensive simulations validate the robustness of our proposed model, showcasing its capabilities for efficient adaptation and processing of online sequential data. Our model is computationally lightweight, requires minimal memory, and can operate incrementally without any prior knowledge of the sequence distribution or characteristics, making it highly suitable for real-world scenarios. By leveraging its adaptability and real-time sequence processing capabilities, this model can be widely applied in various fields, including finance, energy, and healthcare, to improve data-driven decision making, predictive analytics, and autonomous intelligence.

title: Sign learning kink-based (SiLK) quantum Monte Carlo for molecular systems
Abstract: The development of accurate and efficient methods for simulating molecular systems is crucial for advancing our understanding of chemical reactivity and optimizing materials properties. Sign learning kink-based (SiLK) quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) is a relatively new approach that combines the rigorous accuracy of QMC with the computational efficiency of machine learning. By leveraging the kink signed difference measure, SiLK QMC can adapt to the underlying Hamiltonian and efficiently locate the sign problem, thereby significantly reducing the computational cost associated with large-scale QMC simulations. In this work, we implement and test the performance of SiLK QMC for a range of molecular systems, including potential energy surfaces, thermodynamic properties, and spectroscopic signatures. Our results show that SiLK QMC achieves high accuracy and efficiency compared to traditional deterministic and stochastic QMC methods, demonstrating its potential for simulating complex molecular systems. Furthermore, we investigate the transferability of the learned sign learning model across different molecular configurations and examine its limitations in capturing highly non-analytic regions of the potential energy surface. The findings of this study contribute to the development of novel QMC methods for tackling challenging problems in quantum chemistry and materials science.

title: Large Scale Business Discovery from Street Level Imagery
Abstract: Business discovery and expansion into new markets have always been a crucial aspect for large-scale companies seeking growth and increased revenue. However, traditional business intelligence methods relying on data collection through questionnaires and on-site surveys often come with significant costs and risks. The advent of street-level imagery presents a novel approach to business discovery by leveraging satellite, aerial, or mobile camera imagery to collect data on businesses and their activities at a massive scale. This allows businesses to identify market trends, study competitor activity, and understand consumer behavior using both structured and unstructured data from images. Techniques such as object detection, image classification, and text recognition can be applied to extract insights from the collected imagery. As such, leveraging street-level imagery represents a valuable tool for businesses, enabling the deployment of data-driven strategies to identify and capture new opportunities. In this paper, we explore the potential of using street-level imagery for large-scale business discovery and shed light on the technical and practical challenges associated with this approach.

title: Numerical Demultiplexing of Color Image Sensor Measurements via Non-linear Random Forest Modeling
Abstract: This study delves into the realms of computational vision, specifically focusing on color image sensor measurements, and proposes a novel numerical demultiplexing approach through non-linear random forest modeling. Traditional demultiplexing techniques often rely on linear models, failing to accurately capture the complex interactions between the color filter array (CFA) and the spatial and spectral characteristics of the imaged scene. The proposed non-linear random forest-based demultiplexing method is designed to effectively address this limitation by leveraging the strengths of both machine learning and image processing techniques. By casting demultiplexing as a non-linear regression problem, our method effectively evaluates a range of color filter arrays via extensive simulation results and various non-linear demultiplexing models, including decision trees and random forest ensembles, producing markedly improved predictions that restore color images to their original full-color state, producing improved peak signal to noise ratios (PSNR) while also evaluating computational costs. Moreover, our experiments highlight the significance of the accuracy metric used in conjunction with the complexity measure of the analysis. Most notably, when subjected to a computationally demanding color filter array size, such as 10x10, the results from random forest regression demonstrate a two-fold reduction in computational complexity and achieve significantly improved color accuracy compared to traditional methods, yielding remarkable qualitative and quantitative improved results that advance the understanding and application of numerical demultiplexing and computer vision.

title: Signal Recovery on Graphs: Fundamental Limits of Sampling Strategies
Abstract: This abstract for the research paper revolves around the recovery of signals on graphs. The inherent complexity of representing signals on graph-structured data poses significant challenges to widely used signal processing techniques. Existing numerical methods often rely on oversampling to compensate for the loss of orthogonality between the eigenvectors of the graph Laplacian, severely limiting the applicability of these methods to large-scale networks. Investigating these challenges, this research explores the fundamental limits of sampling strategies for signal recovery on graphs. It provides theoretical analysis of the signal reconstructability under different sampling schemes, including uniform and adaptive sampling. The work contributes a rigorous framework to determine the minimum number of samples required to reconstruct a signal on a given graph. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework, and validation on various types of graphs and signal recovery applications highlights its potential to overcome the limitations of conventional methods and make graph-based signal processing more tractable and efficient. By characterizing the fundamental trade-offs between sampling efficiency and signal accuracy, the proposed work advances the theoretical foundations of signal recovery on graphs and offers a principled approach for improving existing algorithms.

title: Multiregion Bilinear Convolutional Neural Networks for Person Re-Identification
Abstract: The person re-identification (re-id) task addresses the challenge of associating the same individual across different cameras and non-overlapping views within a common scene. This is extremely important in surveillance and monitoring applications. Traditional methods often rely on extract local features like edge information and interest points, which might not capture the precise global appearances of individuals. However, owing to their reliance on local features, these typical methods may be less effective in overcoming the variations stemming from pose, viewpoint, illumination, occlusion, and overall intra-scene appearance shifts. In response, a Multiregion Bilinear Convolutional Neural Network (MR-B-CNN) has been introduced in this research paper. The proposed method builds upon the novel bilinear convolution operation, permitting the integration of local and global information about the individual image within a hierarchical architecture of parallel processing streams. A weighted average pooling approach has been employed to capture the spatial distribution of the individual. MR-B-CNN learns scale-invariant person representation at multiple spatial regions and captures more discriminative information about distinct global appearances by leveraging correlation between parallel outputs from different spatial regions. Experimental results have been presented to demonstrate the efficacy of MR-B-CNN in handling a wide variety of scenes, viewpoints, and pose variations.

title: Feature Representation for ICU Mortality
Abstract: This study investigates effective feature representation methods for predicting ICU (Intensive Care Unit) mortality, a critical decision-making task in healthcare. ICU mortality prediction is a challenging problem due to high variability in patient conditions, noisy and incomplete data, and the complexity of the decision-making process. Current approaches rely heavily on manual feature engineering, which can lead to information loss and biased representations. To address this limitation, we explore different feature representation techniques, including deep learning-based methods and traditional machine learning algorithms, specifically tailored for ICU mortality prediction. We evaluate the performance of various feature representation techniques using publicly available datasets, such as MIMIC-III and eICU, and compare them with state-of-the-art methods. Our results show that deep learning-based feature representation methods outperform traditional approaches in terms of prediction accuracy and robustness to noisy data. Furthermore, we identify key factors influencing ICU mortality, such as laboratory values, vital signs, and comorbidities, and demonstrate their importance in predicting patient outcomes. The developed feature representation models are applied in a real-world clinical setting, demonstrating potential to improve the accuracy of ICU mortality predictions and inform personalized treatment strategies.

title: A Theoretically Grounded Application of Dropout in Recurrent Neural Networks
Abstract: Dropout, a regularization technique inherently designed for fully connected networks, has been applied to recurrent neural networks (RNNs) with moderate success; however, the theoretical underpinnings of this application remain unclear. This paper aims to bridge the theoretical gap by providing a coherent framework for dropout in RNNs. We first establish a formal relationship between dropout in RNNs and traditional formulations of the technique. Then, leveraging the theory of randomly projected distributions, we derive asymptotic bounds on the expected value of the output distribution of dropout variants applied to RNNs, demonstrating improved generalization performance. Furthermore, we analyze the effect of dropout on the forward and backward passes in RNNs and present an efficient, residual-based implementation of dropout that dynamically copes with RNN architectures as well as varying dropout rates. This novel approach yields improved performance and learning rate stability throughout the course of training, according to our extensive experimental results, displaying its adaptability to a variety of RNN models and tasks. Experimental results show improved results in RNNs in terms of model performance and for model and training stability. Finally, this analysis and development set forth the groundwork, highlighting the necessity of consideration of dropout in the further theoretical and practical exploration of RNNs as well as this exploration contributes in helping the users to choosing optimal dropout rate for their requirement

title: Blockout: Dynamic Model Selection for Hierarchical Deep Networks
Abstract: Deep learning models have become integral in various applications due to their ability to learn complex patterns and relationships within data. However, these models often suffer from high computational costs and large memory requirements, making them challenging to deploy in resource-constrained environments. To address this issue, this research proposes a novel approach called Blockout, which aims to dynamically select the most suitable model to utilize in hierarchical deep networks. By identifying non-significant layers and modifying the network architecture accordingly, Blockout enables the efficient use of computational resources while maintaining comparable performance to the original model. The proposed approach consists of three key components: a significance analysis module, a pruning module, and a dynamic model selection module. The significance analysis module detects the contribution of individual layers to the model's performance, which informs the pruning module to eliminate non-significant layers. The dynamic model selection module then selects the most suitable model configuration based on the current input and available computational resources. Through a comprehensive evaluation on various deep learning tasks, the proposed Blockout approach demonstrates its ability to achieve comparable or even superior performance to the original models on a wide range of applications, while significantly reducing the computational costs and memory requirements. The success of Blockout paves the way for the development of more efficient and adaptable deep learning models for real-world applications.

title: Learning Games and Rademacher Observations Losses
Abstract: This paper delves into the realm of learning games, where players strategically interact with each other and the environment to achieve a desired outcome. Inspired by the radiance model in deep learning, we exploit the notion of Rademacher observations-related losses to develop a novel framework for analyzing gameplay dynamics. By extending the loss function concept to learning games, we can assess the impact of individual player actions on the overall outcome, providing valuable insights into key factors influencing the game's trajectory. The Rademacher observations-related losses serve as a basis for our exploration, as they enable us to quantify the predictability of player interactions and the resulting game state changes. We demonstrate the efficacy of this framework by applying it to various learning game scenarios, including competitive and cooperative settings, and compare its performance with existing methods. Through a combination of theoretical analysis and empirical evaluations, this research underscores the potential of incorporating Rademacher observations losses into the study of learning games, allowing for more nuanced understanding of gameplay patterns and informing the development of more effective learning strategies. Overall, this work contributes to a deeper comprehension of the complex relationships between player actions, game dynamics, and outcomes in learning game environments.

title: Fine-grained Categorization and Dataset Bootstrapping using Deep Metric Learning with Humans in the Loop
Abstract: This paper presents a novel framework that combines deep metric learning with human-in-the-loop evaluation to address the challenges of fine-grained categorization and dataset bootstrapping. Fine-grained categorization involves distinguishing between subtle differences in object classes, requiring large and diverse datasets. However, collecting and annotating such datasets is a time-consuming and costly process. The proposed framework utilizes a co-learning approach, where a deep metric learning model is initially trained on a small, noisy, and uncurated dataset. The model's performance is then evaluated by humans in the loop, who provide feedback in the form of label correction and data augmentation. This feedback is used to update the model's weights, and the process is iteratively repeated to refine the model's accuracy. Furthermore, the framework incorporates an active learning strategy to select the most uncertain samples from the dataset, ensuring that human evaluators focus on the most informative instances. The effectiveness of the proposed framework is evaluated on several fine-grained categorization benchmarks, demonstrating significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods. The results also highlight the potential of the framework for dataset bootstrapping, where the initial dataset can be expanded through active learning and human-in-the-loop evaluation, leading to improved model performance and reduced annotation costs. Overall, the proposed framework offers a promising solution for fine-grained categorization and dataset bootstrapping, leveraging the strengths of deep metric learning and human evaluation.

title: Learning a Hybrid Architecture for Sequence Regression and Annotation
Abstract: This paper presents a hybrid architecture for sequence regression and annotation tasks, capable of handling both continuous and categorical regression problems. The proposed architecture combines a state-of-the-art transformer-based model with a recurrent neural network (RNN) to effectively learn complex temporal relationships and incorporate contextual information. The hybrid architecture leverages the strengths of both transformer and RNN components by enabling the transformer to focus on capturing long-range dependencies in sequences while the RNN module attends to local and intermediate-level relationships. The architecture's performance is evaluated on three widely used benchmarks for sequence regression and annotation tasks. The results demonstrate the superiority of the proposed hybrid architecture over existing methods, achieving state-of-the-art performance on these challenging problems. Notably, the hybrid model outperforms standalone transformer and RNN models on regression tasks involving both continuous and categorical predictions, showcasing its adaptability to diverse problem setups. Furthermore, an ablation study reveals that the synergy between the transformer and RNN components is crucial for the model's overall performance, highlighting the benefits of a hybrid approach. This work contributes to the advancement of sequence regression and annotation research by providing a versatile and high-performing architecture that can be applied to a broad range of applications, including speech processing, natural language processing, and recommender systems.

title: DNA-Level Splice Junction Prediction using Deep Recurrent Neural Networks
Abstract: This research delves into DNA-level splice junction prediction, a crucial step in understanding the complex process of alternative splicing in human genes. Alternative splicing, which accounts for nearly 70% of human genes, results in a vast array of transcript variants, ultimately giving rise to a multitude of proteins with diverse functions. However, the underlying mechanisms and patterns governing alternative splicing are not yet fully comprehended. Recent studies have highlighted the potential of deep learning architectures, particularly deep recurrent neural networks (RNNs), in accurately predicting splice junctions. In this investigation, we explore the efficacy and practicability of employing deep RNNs to predict splice junctions at the DNA level. By leveraging large-scale datasets and advanced deep learning techniques, we investigate the predictive performance of our proposed model across various genomic features, including sequence motifs, conservation scores, and chromatin landscape properties. Our experimental results demonstrate the potential of deep RNNs in capturing subtle patterns associated with splice junctions, thereby contributing to a deeper understanding of the intricate processes driving alternative splicing and providing valuable insights for the design of novel genetic therapies, diagnostic tools, and functional genomics research. Overall, this work exemplifies the immense potential of deep learning in deciphering the intricacies of RNA splicing, enabling the discovery of novel splice junctions and shedding light on the complex relationships governing genome function and regulation.

title: A Novel Minimum Divergence Approach to Robust Speaker Identification
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel minimum divergence approach to robust speaker identification in noisy environments. The approach incorporates a modified Gaussian mixture model (GMM) with a novel objective function based on Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence. By minimizing the divergence between the expected and actual distributions of speaker models across different environments, the proposal improves the robustness and accuracy of speaker identification under various acoustic conditions. To further enhance the performance, the system incorporates a new type of acoustic features, namely spectral features obtained through spatially smoothed Short-Time-Fourier-Transform (STFT) magnitude spectrograms, which better capture the speaker-specific spectral characteristics. Furthermore, it combines the soft-label maximum likelihood linear regression (MLLR) with a generalized probabilistic inference framework, enabling better adaptation to the variability in speaker models induced by noise and reverberation. This modified MLLR is employed to estimate the transformation between speaker models obtained from adaptation and clean data. Experimental results on two benchmark databases show significant improvements in terms of equal error rate, false acceptance rate, and false rejection rate compared to state-of-the-art techniques. The proposal demonstrates a robust speaker identification framework that can be applied in real-world applications, including security, surveillance, and human-computer interfaces, with enhanced accuracy and reliability. Overall, the proposed minimum divergence approach provides a unique and effective way to robust speaker identification in challenging environments by leveraging the novel divergence-based objective function, spectral features, and probabilistic inference framework.

title: Streaming Kernel Principal Component Analysis
Abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to implementing kernel principal component analysis (KPCA) in distributed streaming environments, where large-scale data is continuously generated and needs to be processed. Existing KPCA algorithms are primarily designed for batch processing and often suffer from high computational and storage overhead when applied to streaming data. To address this issue, we propose a streaming KPCA (SKPCA) algorithm that leverages online kernel approximation techniques to efficiently process data streams. By utilizing a combination of kernel feature maps and dimensionality reduction, SKPCA is able to extract meaningful features from the data in real-time, enabling effective anomaly detection, classification, and representation learning. We evaluate SKPCA on several large-scale datasets and demonstrate its ability to handle complex data streams with varying distribution properties. Our results show that SKPCA outperforms state-of-the-art algorithms in terms of computational efficiency, memory usage, and feature extraction accuracy. Furthermore, SKPCA is scalable and can be easily parallelized to accommodate large-scale streaming environments, making it a promising solution for real-time data analysis and machine learning applications. The algorithm's ability to adapt to changing data distribution properties and its applicability to various domains, such as finance, healthcare, and IoT, make it a valuable tool for a wide range of industries and research communities.

title: Morpho-syntactic Lexicon Generation Using Graph-based Semi-supervised Learning
Abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to generating morpho-syntactic lexicons, which are essential resources for natural language processing tasks such as machine translation, part-of-speech tagging, and syntactic parsing. Traditional methods often rely on handcrafted lexicons, which can be time-consuming and prone to Human error. To address this limitation, we propose a graph-based semi-supervised learning framework for automatic morpho-syntactic lexicon generation. Our model leverages a joint representation learning framework that integrates word embeddings, morphological features, and syntactic dependencies into a unified graph representation. The graph is then used to predict the morpho-syntactic properties of words, such as part-of-speech tags, morphological features, and dependency relations. To handle the scarcity of labeled data, we incorporate a semi-supervised learning framework that leverages both labeled and unlabeled data to improve prediction accuracy. Our empirical evaluation on a range of languages, including English, Spanish, and Arabic, demonstrates the effectiveness of our approach, achieving significant improvements in morpho-syntactic lexicon accuracy compared to state-of-the-art baselines. Additionally, our model requires relatively fewer labeled instances, making it a more efficient and cost-effective solution for linguistic resources development. The proposed approach has the potential to revolutionize the way morpho-syntactic lexicons are generated, enabling more accurate and efficient natural language processing tasks.

title: Multiple penalized principal curves: analysis and computation
Abstract: Principal curves and surfaces are non-linear dimensionality reduction techniques that have been widely used in various fields for their ability to capture complex geometrical structures in data. However, traditional principal curves may fail when dealing with noisy or high-dimensional data, as they can be heavily influenced by outliers and are sensitive to the choice of parameters. To address these limitations, we develop a novel framework for multiple penalized principal curves. Our approach involves penalizing the principal curves using L1 and L2 norms, enabling them to resist the influence of noisy data points while retaining their ability to capture meaningful structures. Furthermore, we propose a new algorithm for computing multiple penalized principal curves using alternating minimization, which efficiently balances the trade-off between curve smoothness and capture of underlying data features. Our theoretical analysis demonstrates the statistical consistency and asymptotic convergence of the proposed algorithm. Through extensive numerical experiments and simulations, we showcase the efficacy of our framework in uncovering complex data structures and outperforming state-of-the-art methods, particularly in the presence of outliers and high-dimensional noise. Overall, our contribution provides a robust and efficient methodology for non-linear dimensionality reduction applications, paving the way for its adoption in various fields, such as image processing, bioinformatics, and financial analysis.

title: A Light Touch for Heavily Constrained SGD
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel adaptation of Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) to improve its performance on heavily constrained optimization problems. The constraint on heavily constrained problems can lead to inferior performance, poor convergence, or even becoming stuck in local minima due to the non-convexity of the loss function, as these types of problems involve a large number of variables with many constraints. The authors develop a 'light touch' strategy, dubbed LitSGD, which gives a limited touch to a constrained space to enhance exploration of the search space while adhering to predefined constraint boundaries. LitSGD distinguishes itself by gradually introducing 'soft' constraints into the SGD method through a smart initialization and gradual enforcement of constraints directly in the learning process. By adaptively adjusting the constraint adherence strength influenced by a dynamic soft-thresholding technique, LitSGD is able to efficiently maneuver intricate landscapes. Furthermore, LitSGD introduces lightweight and parameter-efficient methods for constraint-aware exploration. Empirical results demonstrate that LitSGD significantly outperforms the original SGD and state-of-the-art competitors on various benchmarks, outperforming especially those most concerning scenarios often encountered with complex optimization problems involving diverse networks, synthetic datasets and heavy noise. This technique offers a framework for integrating SGD with constraint enforcement, potentially leading to the development of novel solutions with a vast range of real-world applications and diverse academic research directions.

title: Relative Density and Exact Recovery in Heterogeneous Stochastic Block Models
Abstract: This paper investigates the relationship between relative density and exact recovery in heterogeneous stochastic block models, a class of network models which generalize traditional Stochastic Block Models by allowing different numbers of communities or clusters within the network. We introduce a novel perspective on the phase transition of exact recovery, tying it to the behavior of the relative density of the strongest community, which we define as the ratio of the within-community edge probability to the between-community edge probability. By leveraging this perspective, we demonstrate that the phase transition of exact recovery is intimately connected to the spectral radius of the block matrix, and that when this ratio exceeds the smallest non-trivial eigenvalue of the block matrix, exact recovery becomes possible regardless of the sample size. On the other hand, we show that if this ratio is less than the smallest non-trivial eigenvalue of the block matrix, exact recovery is impossible even in the large sample regime, indicating a fundamental limitation on our ability to recover the true cluster assignments from network data. Our results provide new insights into the conditions under which exact recovery is possible in heterogeneous stochastic block models, shedding light on the interplay between relative density, spectral structure, and recovery performance.

title: Deep Learning Stock Volatility with Google Domestic Trends
Abstract: This research investigates the potential for utilizing Google Domestic Trends data to inform deep learning models in predicting stock volatility. By leveraging the vast and comprehensive nature of search query data, our study aims to examine the correlation between user search queries and financial market behavior. We employ a deep learning approach, incorporating Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) and Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) architectures, to forecast stock volatility based on Google Domestic Trends data. Our hypothesis is that by analyzing search query patterns and volumes, we can identify historical trends and correlations that can be used to predict future market movements. To test this hypothesis, we collect a dataset of Google Domestic Trends data and corresponding stock volatility from leading financial indices, which we then use to train and evaluate our deep learning models. Our results indicate that deep learning-based models can indeed capture meaningful patterns in Google Domestic Trends data and use them to accurately forecast stock volatility. Furthermore, our study reveals that the incorporation of Google Domestic Trends data enhances the predictive capability of traditional financial models, suggesting that integrating external online data streams can significantly improve the accuracy of stock volatility forecasting. Our findings have implications for investors, traders, and financial institutions seeking to leverage big data analytics to inform their investment decisions.

title: Strategies for Training Large Vocabulary Neural Language Models
Abstract: Neural language models have been instrumental in driving advancements in natural language processing, with large vocabulary models being particularly effective in capturing complex linguistic patterns. However, training such models is a computationally expensive and resource-intensive task, often requiring substantial computational resources and time to achieve optimal performance. This paper investigates strategies for training large vocabulary neural language models, with a focus on efficient and scalable approaches. We explore the utility of techniques such as checkpointing, gradient accumulation, and mixed precision training, which have been shown to significantly reduce the computational requirements of model training. Additionally, we examine the impact of model parallelization and data parallelization strategies on the efficiency of training large vocabulary models. Our results show that a combination of these techniques can lead to substantial reductions in training time and computational costs, making it possible to train more complex and accurate language models than previously feasible. Furthermore, we propose a novel approach to parallelizing language model training, which leverages recent advances in distributed computing and asynchronous training methods. This approach allows for more efficient utilization of computational resources and can be scaled to large datasets and complex models. The insights and strategies presented in this paper will enable researchers and developers to train more effective and efficient large vocabulary neural language models.

title: Increasing the Action Gap: New Operators for Reinforcement Learning
Abstract: The action gap problem in reinforcement learning (RL) remains a significant challenge, limiting the effectiveness of RL agents in real-world applications. By definition, the action gap occurs when the optimal action under the policy does not match the optimal action under the model's predicted distribution, leading to suboptimal performance. In this paper, we propose novel operators to decrease the action gap, thus enhancing the overall performance of RL agents. Our approach involves the introduction of two new operators, named the adaptive expected Q-value adjustment operator, and the selective Boltzmann exploration operator, which aim to bridge the gap between the model's prediction and the policy's behavior. By combining these operators with existing exploration-exploitation strategies, we demonstrate significant improvements in solving the action gap problem. Furthermore, we conduct extensive experiments on a range of benchmark tasks, including high-dimensional continuous control, to validate the efficacy of our proposed operators. Our results show that the action gap can be effectively reduced, leading to improved RL agent performance across various scenarios. The key contribution of our work lies in providing a new, effective, and implementable approach to tackling the action gap problem, thereby enhancing the capability of RL agents to operate in real-world environments.

title: Energy-Efficient Classification for Anomaly Detection: The Wireless Channel as a Helper
Abstract: Anomaly detection in wireless networks is increasingly crucial to prevent security breaches and optimize network performance, especially given the ever-expanding deployment of IoT devices and wireless communication infrastructure. Existing anomaly detection methods rely heavily on machine learning algorithms, which often require significant computational resources and power consumption, thus compromising network efficiency. This study introduces an energy-efficient classification approach for anomaly detection that leverages the inherent characteristics of wireless channels. By harnessing the received signal strength (RSS) and its fluctuations, our method identifies potential anomalies within the wireless channel itself, adapting to variations in network conditions and topology. This approach is based on a novel combination of statistical analysis and machine learning, utilizing robust features extracted from the wireless channel's unique properties. The proposed method not only detects anomalies in real-time but also reduces the computational overhead associated with traditional machine learning-based approaches, thus achieving superior energy efficiency. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in a variety of network scenarios, showcasing its potential as a self-sustaining and efficient anomaly detection mechanism for wireless networks. The proposed classification model can be easily integrated into existing network architectures, paving the way for energy-efficient anomaly detection in future wireless communication systems.

title: Data Driven Resource Allocation for Distributed Learning
Abstract: The effective allocation of computational resources in distributed learning environments has become increasingly crucial with the proliferation of large-scale machine learning applications. However, the heterogeneous and dynamic nature of these environments poses significant challenges in optimizing resource allocation decisions. This paper presents a data-driven approach to resource allocation in distributed learning, which leverages historical resource utilization data, learning task characteristics, and performance monitoring metrics to inform allocation decisions. The proposed framework utilizes a novel data-driven resource allocation model that integrates a combination of regression-based and reinforcement learning-based techniques to proactively allocate resources and adapt to changing computational demands. The evaluation of the proposed framework demonstrated significant improvements in learning accuracy, reduction in average job completion time, and efficient utilization of resources compared to traditional allocation strategies. Additionally, the performance of the proposed framework was shown to be robust and scalable across a range of distributed learning scenarios. The results highlight the potential of data-driven approaches in optimizing resource allocation and improving the overall efficiency and effectiveness of distributed learning systems. Furthermore, the presented framework can be easily extended to accommodate different types of resources and learning tasks, making it a valuable tool for resource-constrained environments.

title: Feature-Level Domain Adaptation
Abstract: Domain adaptation has emerged as a crucial technique in machine learning for addressing the challenges associated with training models on a source domain when the target domain differs significantly. The development of robust feature-level domain adaptation methods has become a pressing need in many real-world applications, including but not limited to healthcare, finance, and autonomous systems, to enable seamless adaptation of deep neural network models across different domains. Despite the existing literature providing several solutions, a significant knowledge gap remains in understanding the effects of various domain adaptation techniques at the feature level. The primary objective of this research is to scrutinize the application of feature-level domain adaptation techniques in mitigating the domain gaps. Key contributions of this research include a comprehensive review of existing literature on domain adaptation at the feature level, highlighting the weaknesses and gaps in the existing solutions, followed by a qualitative analysis of five popular techniques, namely maximum mean discrepancy, correlation alignment, additive noise, geodesic flow kernel and inter- adversarial adversarial training. Furthermore, an algorithmic framework, called DA-Swarm, which leverages the mechanisms of particle swarm optimization, a swarm intelligence technique, to eliminate the issue of hyperparameter tuning, will be proposed. Through extensive experiments on several benchmarking datasets, a comprehensive assessment of the performance of various domain adaptation techniques at the feature level, as well as the proposed DA-Swarm methodology, will be conducted to validate the research findings and investigate the impact of the suggested framework on reducing the performance gap between source and target domains. The findings of this research not only shed light on the critical role of feature-level domain adaptation in developing more generalizable machine learning models but also contribute to the improvement of existing techniques and the development of innovative solutions for real-world applications.

title: Causal and anti-causal learning in pattern recognition for neuroimaging
Abstract: This paper delves into the realm of pattern recognition for neuroimaging, exploring the dichotomy between causal and anti-causal learning approaches. Recent advancements in machine learning have seen the emergence of novel techniques that aim to uncover the underlying causal relationships between brain activity and the external world. However, these causal methods often succumb to a fundamental challenge: the issue of causality identification. By contrast, anti-causal learning methods deploy a more data-driven strategy, focusing on correlational patterns between brain activity and task variables. We argue that both types of learning are essential for comprehensive understanding in neuroimaging pattern recognition; yet, their current integration remains a subject of debate. This paper endeavors to bridge the knowledge gap between the two paradigms. Through a systematic review of existing research, we dissect the methodologies and theoretical underpinnings of both causal and anti-causal learning methods. Next, we provide novel insights by conceiving a unified framework, leveraging strengths from each paradigm to develop a more inclusive framework for neuroimaging tasks. Our research sets the stage for a deeper comprehension of neural processing mechanisms and motivates future research directions, transcending the dichotomy between causal and anti-causal approaches to illuminate the intricate relationships between brain and behavior. The findings of this paper hold significant implications for the design of innovative neuroimaging protocols and have substantial potential to catalyze substantial breakthroughs in brain-computer interfaces, neurotherapy, and neuroprosthetics.

title: From One Point to A Manifold: Knowledge Graph Embedding For Precise Link Prediction
Abstract: This paper delves into the realm of knowledge graph embedding for precise link prediction, aiming to bridge the gap between the existing methods and the vast complexities of real-world knowledge graphs. Traditional knowledge graph embedding methods have been successful in encoding entities and relationships using euclidean space, but they fail to capture the nuances of non-linear relationships inherent in many real-world knowledge graphs. To address this limitation, we propose a novel framework based on the concept of manifold learning, where the knowledge graph is embedded in a non-linear space. Our framework, dubbed "Manifold-KE," leverages the power of manifolds to capture the curvature and non-linearity of relationships in the knowledge graph. By embedding entities and relationships in a high-dimensional non-linear space, Manifold-KE is able to capture a wider range of relationships, leading to improved link prediction performance. We conduct extensive experiments on various benchmark datasets, and the results demonstrate the superiority of Manifold-KE in terms of precision and recall. Furthermore, our method is able to effectively handle missing links and noisy data, making it a robust tool for knowledge graph completion tasks. The proposed framework opens up new avenues for research in knowledge graph embedding and link prediction, with potential applications in real-world domains such as information retrieval, question answering, and recommender systems.

title: On Deep Representation Learning from Noisy Web Images
Abstract: The advent of web images has led to a significant shift in the landscape of visual data, offering access to immense repositories of visual data. However, the incorporation of these noisy web images into deep neural networks poses a significant challenge due to their inherent variability in quality, context, and annotation. In this paper, we explore a set of techniques designed to enhance the representation learning capabilities of deep neural networks when trained on noisy web images. By incorporating novel regularization methods, transfer learning strategies, and adaptive annotation schemes, our approach enables deep representational models to better estimate the underlying data distributions and disentangle the effects of noise. Our proposed method leverages the inherent relationships between visual attributes and contextually rich descriptions to inject robustness and descriptive power into the deep representations. Using a diverse set of benchmark datasets, we demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in improving the robustness and accuracy of deep image classification tasks. Our results show significant improvements in noise robustness and accuracy, as well as a reduction in the sensitivity to overfitting, thereby accentuating the potential of web images in deep representation learning applications.

title: Predicting links in ego-networks using temporal information
Abstract: This research paper proposes a novel approach to predicting links in ego-networks, focusing on the incorporation of temporal information to enhance model accuracy and reliability. Ego-networks, also known as personal networks, encompass the set of relationships that an individual has with others, including friends, family, acquaintances, and colleagues. The study utilizes a comprehensive dataset comprising ego-networks with a time dimension, capturing the evolution of these relationships over time. The proposed framework leverages machine learning techniques to develop a high-accuracy linkage prediction model that can account for temporal patterns, user context, and the dynamics of ego-network evolution. Furthermore, the proposed framework is capable of providing an explanation of the predictions, highlighting the key factors and the temporal characteristics that influence the formation of new relationships. The methodology employed entails the identification of missing links based on past relationships, future predictions adjusted for temporal changes, and overall network behavior. The study demonstrates superior predictive performance compared to traditional methods, using metrics such as precision, recall, and F1 score. Additionally, the temporal component allows for insight into the power of long-term relationship and the most effective periods for new link formation. The research has far-reaching implications for social network theory, digital social media platforms, and artificial intelligence, all of which rely heavily on the accurate prediction of relationships within the online and offline world.

title: Learning optimal nonlinearities for iterative thresholding algorithms
Abstract: Iterative thresholding algorithms, such as ISTA, FISTA, and ADMM, have been gaining popularity in various machine learning and signal processing tasks, including compressive sensing, image recovery, and deep learning, due to their fast convergence rates and efficient implementations. However, the choice of nonlinearities and proxy functions in these algorithms often relies on heuristics or common practices, which may not always lead to optimal convergence speeds. In this paper, we propose a novel framework to learn optimal nonlinearities for iterative thresholding algorithms through a carefully designed optimization process. Our approach is based on the lens of spectral properties of the Jacobian matrices of the nonlinearities, which are responsible for the convergence behavior of the algorithms. By injecting neural network learnability into the design of these nonlinearities, we propose a neural network-aided approach to learn optimal nonlinearities that adapt to specific problems and convergence criteria. We demonstrate the versatility and effectiveness of our framework on a wide range of problems, including compressive sensing, image recovery, and deep learning-based tasks, showcasing its potential in accelerating convergence and improving performance of iterative thresholding algorithms. Our results highlight the importance of optimizing nonlinearities for faster and more reliable convergence, demonstrating that machine learning can be effectively used to improve the performance of traditional algorithms.

title: Pileup Subtraction and Jet Energy Prediction Using Machine Learning
Abstract: Pileup subtraction is a critical technique used in high-energy colliders to account for the energy deposited by multiple protons scattering off a target nucleus, also known as pileup events. However, the traditional pileup subtraction methods can introduce uncertainties and biases, which can significantly affect the precision of jet energy measurements. In this paper, we explore the application of machine learning (ML) techniques to improve the accuracy of pileup subtraction and jet energy prediction. By leveraging the power of ML, we can effectively identify and remove pileup contaminants, leading to improved jet energy resolutions and reduced bias. We deploy a range of ML algorithms, including neural networks and decision trees, on large Monte Carlo generated datasets to quantify their performance. Our results show that the ML-based methods can achieve better pileup subtraction and jet energy prediction compared to traditional techniques. Notably, the ML-based methods can accurately reproduce the underlying jet energy distribution, even in high pileup environments. We also investigate the robustness of the ML-based methods against variations in pileup density and jet cone sizes. Our findings have significant implications for the improvement of jet energy measurements, particularly in the high-luminosity LHC upgrades, where pileup conditions are expected to be extremely challenging.

title: Hyper-Heuristic Algorithm for Finding Efficient Features in Diagnose of Lung Cancer Disease
Abstract: This research paper presents a novel application of hyper-heuristic algorithms to identify the most informative features in lung cancer diagnosis. The study utilizes a comprehensive dataset of lung cancer patients to train and validate a hyper-heuristic based feature selection method that maximizes the accuracy of predictive models while minimizing the dimensionality of the feature space. By exploring a wide range of candidate metaheuristics, including greedy randomised adaptive search procedure, iterated local search, and simulated annealing, the proposed framework iteratively searches for the optimal subset of features that effectively distinguish between malignant and benign cases. The experimental results demonstrate a significant improvement in classification performance compared to existing feature selection methods, with the top-performing model achieving an accuracy of 96.2% and an AUC-ROC of 0.995. The proposed hyper-heuristic method is also shown to outperform state-of-the-art algorithms, including sequential floating forward selection and correlation-based feature selection, in terms of both diagnostic accuracy and computational efficiency. Furthermore, the study provides insightful analysis on the statistical significance of the identified features, highlighting the importance of several biomarkers in distinguishing between early-stage and advanced-stage lung cancer cases. Overall, this research contributes to the development of a practical and efficient feature selection approach for lung cancer diagnosis, paving the way for more effective early detection and treatment strategies.

title: Linear Models of Computation and Program Learning
Abstract: This study delves into the realm of linear models of computation and their application in program learning. By leveraging the theoretical foundations of linear logic, which provides a formal framework for reasoning about linear resources, we can develop a deep understanding of the computational processes underlying program execution. We propose that by modeling computation as a process of transforming and manipulating linear resources, we can create more efficient and interpretable learning algorithms for programs. This interdisciplinary approach combines insights from computer science, logic, and mathematics to shed new light on the problem of program learning, where the goal is to infer the execution properties of a program from a set of observations. Our approach focuses on learning linear models of computation, which can be used to identify the distribution of resources (e.g., memory or computation) invoked by different program behaviors. By leveraging these linear models, we can develop more accurate and interpretable program learning models. The use of linear logic and linear models of computation also opens up avenues for leveraging the vast existing literature on linear systems, optimization, and control theory to improve the learning processes and efficiency of program learning algorithms, paving the way for more effective and scalable program analysis tools.

title: Semantic-enriched Visual Vocabulary Construction in a Weakly Supervised Context
Abstract: The construction of a visual vocabulary is an essential step in visual recognition and image classification. In a weakly supervised context, where only image-level annotations are available, the task becomes more challenging. Traditional methods rely on predefined object categories and pre-trained models, which may not capture the subtle nuances of the visual data. This paper proposes a novel approach to constructing a semantic-enriched visual vocabulary in a weakly supervised context. Our method, dubbed SVE-Voc, leverages Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) and attention mechanisms to learn a hierarchical representation of visual features and meaningful concepts from the unlabelled images. By incorporating metalearned graph augmentation strategies, SVE-Voc adapts to the evolving graph structure and scales to large unlabelled datasets. Our framework also incorporates a concept discovery module that exploits neighbourhood correlations to automatically recognize novel objects within the graph, enriching the existing vocabulary. By integrating these components, we achieve state-of-the-art performance in zero-shot image classification, object discovery, and graph-based clustering on several benchmark datasets, outperforming traditional weakly supervised methods and demonstrating the efficacy of SVE-Voc. These results highlight the potential of SVE-Voc as a versatile tool for visual recognition in real-world scenarios where human-annotated data is scarce. Our method contributes towards pushing the frontiers of visual vocabulary construction and empowering applications that demand robust, flexible, and scalable visual representation learning.

title: Relaxed Linearized Algorithms for Faster X-Ray CT Image Reconstruction
Abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to accelerate X-ray Computed Tomography (CT) image reconstruction using relaxed linearized algorithms. Existing algorithms for CT image reconstruction are computationally intensive, limiting their application in real-time image reconstruction scenarios such as fluoroscopy and interventional procedures. To address this challenge, we propose a set of relaxed linearized algorithms that leverage the sparsity of the reconstruction problem to achieve significant computational speedups. The proposed algorithms introduce a series of relaxations to the classical linearized optimization problem, allowing for faster convergence rates and reduced computational complexity. Specifically, we develop a hierarchical scheme that scales the optimization problem from fully linearized models to iteratively relaxed versions, leading to efficient and accurate image reconstruction. Our analysis shows that the proposed hierarchy preserves the convergence guarantees of the original optimization problem, while significantly reducing the computational cost. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through comprehensive simulations and experiments on real CT data, showcasing a 5-10 fold speedup compared to state-of-the-art methods. This study highlights the potential of relaxed linearized algorithms for accelerating CT image reconstruction, enabling real-time analytics in various medical imaging applications.

title: About the tensorial nature of the Christoffel symbols, or lack thereof
Abstract: The Christoffel symbols, a fundamental concept in differential geometry and general relativity, have long been perceived as components of a connection on a manifold, yet their tensorial nature remains a subject of debate despite their widespread application in theoretical physics. This paper delves into the tensorial properties of Christoffel symbols, aiming to clarify their mathematical structure and identify any discrepancies with the prevailing understanding. By leveraging advanced differential geometric techniques, including the Koszul's interpretation of the Christoffel symbols and the association of connections with the Jacobi-Levi-Civita bracket, this investigation reveals a profound distinction between the Christoffel connection and the canonical connection on a manifold, shedding light on the inherent non-tensorial features of the Christoffel symbols. The proposed research provides novel insights into the properties of Christoffel symbols, challenging the current paradigm and offering a revised understanding of the connection between manifolds and the curvature tensors associated with them. Furthermore, the investigation's findings have significant implications for the development of differential geometric theories, as well as their applications in theoretical physics, particularly in Einstein's theory of gravity. This paper contributes to the fundamental understanding of Christoffel symbols, a crucial aspect of differential geometry and general relativity, by reconciling their mathematical essence with their operational properties, henceforth providing a more comprehensive understanding of their non-tensorial nature.

title: On non-iterative training of a neural classifier
Abstract: This abstract elucidates the notion of non-iterative training in neural classifiers, a paradigm that diverges from traditional training methods reliant on iterative refinement. The proposal of non-iterative training is centered around expediting the training process by bypassing the iterative refinement of model parameters, thereby streamlining the learning process. By eschewing the need for repeated passes to converge towards an optimal set of model parameters, the approach mitigates computational overhead related to conventional incremental refinement. Instead, non-iterative training methods opt to optimize model performance in a singular pass through the training dataset, resulting in impressive acceleration of the training process while maintaining high predictive accuracy. This paper delves into a novel non-iterative training regime, leveraging insights from theoretical machine learning to devise a method that maximizes margin between classes in the feature space, while minimizing the impact of regularization on the loss function. Our evaluation indicates that this approach delivers performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods, while offering significant speedup over conventional iterative training models. This research validates the efficacy of non-iterative training in neural classifiers, pointing towards its potential as a viable alternative to the current paradigm. By embracing non-iterative training, the prospect of faster and more efficient model development holds promise for numerous applications in areas as diverse as natural language processing, computer vision, and time-series forecasting.

title: Dropout Training of Matrix Factorization and Autoencoder for Link Prediction in Sparse Graphs
Abstract: This study proposes a hybrid approach for link prediction in sparse graphs by integrating dropout training with matrix factorization (MF) and autoencoder (AE). Dropout training is a regularization technique commonly used in neural networks to prevent overfitting. However, its application in graph-based methods, such as MF and AE, is less explored. We introduce dropout variants for MF and AE, and demonstrate their effectiveness for link prediction in sparse graphs. The MF model employed is based on the principle of non-negative matrix factorization (NMF), and the AE model uses a neural network architecture with a stacked structure. We incorporate dropout into these models by randomly dropping out a fraction of the node features and/or link interactions during training. The proposed approach, referred to as dropout MF-AE, leverages the strengths of both MF and AE for effective link prediction. Experimental results on several benchmark datasets, including Cora, CiteSeer, and PubMed, show that dropout MF-AE outperforms state-of-the-art methods, including the original MF and AE, in terms of link prediction accuracy. Furthermore, the study reveals that the optimal dropout rate for MF-AE varies across datasets, and suggests that a simple yet effective way to choose the dropout rate is based on the observed training and testing accuracy on a validation set. Overall, this research makes a significant contribution to the field of graph-based machine learning by providing a new framework for link prediction in sparse graphs.

title: Multimodal, high-dimensional, model-based, Bayesian inverse problems with applications in biomechanics
Abstract: This manuscript addresses the challenge of accurately solving high-dimensional model-based Bayesian inverse problems, particularly in the context of biomechanics. It focuses on multimodal problems that involve a variety of input and output data types, requiring the integration of diverse algorithms and analytical techniques. The proposed framework provides a unified approach to solving such problems, combining the use of Bayesian inference with models of varying complexity. This methodology is particularly well-suited to applications in biomechanics, where high-dimensional data is frequently encountered and model accuracy is critical. By leveraging the strengths of Bayesian statistical methods and advanced computational techniques, the proposed approach enables the estimation of biomechanical system parameters from a combination of different data sources, including experimentally-derived data, subject-specific imaging modalities, and in silico simulations. Throughout the manuscript, the presented methodology is demonstrated using real-world examples, highlighting its potential to advance the field of biomechanics and facilitate the development of more accurate, personalized models of human movement and behavior. title: Semisupervised Autoencoder for Sentiment Analysis
Abstract: This research paper presents a novel semisupervised autoencoder approach for sentiment analysis on text-based datasets. Traditional sentiment analysis methods rely heavily on labeled data, but in real-world scenarios, annotating large datasets is a time-consuming and expensive process. To address this issue, we propose a semisupervised autoencoder that leverages both labeled and unlabeled text samples to improve model performance. Our approach employs a bidirectional autoencoder architecture that consists of an encoder and a decoder, where the encoder maps input text to a low-dimensional representation, and the decoder reconstructs the original text. The autoencoder is trained on labeled data to learn domain-specific features, while unsupervised loss functions are used to regularize the model and prevent overfitting. The proposed method combines the merits of both labeled and unlabeled data, utilizing the annotations to focus on sentiment-relevant features and the unlabelled data to refine the model's generalization capabilities. Our extensive experiments on several benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed semisupervised autoencoder performs competitively with the state-of-the-art supervised sentiment analysis methods, while also outperforming traditional semisupervised approaches. This work shows the potential of using semisupervised learning techniques in sentiment analysis applications, where limited labeled data may be available.

title: Teaching the Foundations of Data Science: An Interdisciplinary Approach
Abstract: The integration of data science into educational curricula has become increasingly important as the field continues to grow and shape various aspects of modern society. However, challenges arise in crafting an effective teaching strategy that addresses the multidisciplinary nature of data science, encompassing concepts from statistics, computer science, domain-specific knowledge, and communication skills. To overcome these obstacles, this paper proposes an interdisciplinary approach to teaching the foundations of data science, incorporating a hands-on, project-based methodology that encourages students to engage with real-world problems and apply theoretical principles in a practical context. By emphasizing teamwork, critical thinking, and iterative learning, students develop a comprehensive understanding of data science concepts and their applications, including data visualization, machine learning, and data mining. The proposed framework incorporates a 'flipped classroom' approach, leveraging online resources and technologies to facilitate student access to educational materials outside the traditional classroom setting. Through collaborative assignments and peer review, students refine their communication and presentation skills, ultimately synthesizing theoretical knowledge with practical problem-solving skills. By adopting this interdisciplinary approach, educators can equip students with the diverse skill set required to thrive in the rapidly evolving field of data science.

title: Memory-based control with recurrent neural networks
Abstract: This paper explores the application of recurrent neural networks (RNNs) in memory-based control systems, paving the way for more robust and adaptive control methods. Traditional control strategies often rely on mathematical models of the system to be controlled, which can be difficult to obtain, especially in complex or nonlinear systems. Conversely, RNNs can learn from experience and adapt to changes in the system, enabling more flexible and efficient control schemes. Memory-based RNNs, in particular, possess an internal memory mechanism that can store information about past events and use it to inform present and future control decisions. By leveraging this ability, memory-based RNNs can learn to overcome limitations such as limited model knowledge, non-stationarity, and partial observability, common in many control problems. This research systematically investigates the performance of memory-based RNN controllers in various application domains, including model-free control of nonlinear systems, autonomous vehicle navigation, and industrial process control. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of memory-based RNNs in achieving superior control performance and robustness compared to traditional control methods, highlighting their potential to push the boundaries of achievable control performance in a wide range of applications. Experimental comparisons and simulations further validate the theoretical advantages of memory-based RNNs, providing valuable insights for their practical implementation in various control systems.

title: Near-Optimal Bounds for Binary Embeddings of Arbitrary Sets
Abstract: This paper explores the fundamental problem of minimizing the binary embedding dimension of arbitrary sets, which underlies many learning algorithms and data analysis applications. Given a finite set of points in ℝ^d, a binary embedding is a mapping of these points to {±1}^k that approximately preserves their pairwise distances. Our study extends the well-known ϵ-sampling techniques, which offer almost optimal bounds for d-dimensional Euclidean spaces, by introducing new theoretical frameworks for more general metric spaces, graphs, and set structures. These frameworks incorporate and generalize existing results, thereby providing new insights into binary embeddings. We shall establish near-optimal bounds for the embedding dimension of subsets of ℝ^d, and the impact of ϵ-sampling on the binary representation of these point sets. Moreover, our results are applicable to richer data sets, including graphs and data structures of unknown intrinsic dimension. We investigate both ℓ_p-metric spaces for p in {1, ∞} and ∞-distance graphs. By leveraging random subsampling and near-neighbour information, we develop efficient embedding algorithms that achieve these near-optimal bounds in polynomial time with respect to key parameters. We then illustrate our results through detailed examples that showcase the impact of our findings on practical learning tasks and data analysis.

title: We Are Humor Beings: Understanding and Predicting Visual Humor
Abstract: This paper delves into the intriguing aspect of humor, specifically visual humor, to better comprehend its underlying mechanisms and provide a framework for predicting its manifestations. Despite its omnipresence in everyday life, human humor remains a complex and poorly understood phenomenon, often reduced to simplistic explanations or boiled down to individual preferences. However, visual humor presents a more tangible aspect of humor, making it a prime subject for scientific examination. By analyzing a variety of visual stimuli, including memes, cartoons, and comics, this study aims to extract the key features that contribute to their humor. Machine learning techniques are employed to identify the underlying patterns and relationships between visual elements, such as shapes, colors, and textures, and their perceived humor. The results reveal that certain combinations of these features are associated with higher levels of humor, including incongruity, exaggeration, and surprise. Furthermore, the study demonstrates the potential of the proposed framework to accurately predict the humor of unseen visual stimuli, paving the way for the development of a humor-related AI system. The implications of this research are vast, with potential applications in areas such as comedy writing, advertising, and even social media content creation, where understanding and leveraging visual humor can significantly enhance user engagement and satisfaction.

title: Automatic Incident Classification for Big Traffic Data by Adaptive Boosting SVM
Abstract: This study focuses on the automatic classification of incident types in large-scale traffic data using an Adaptive Boosting Support Vector Machine (AdaBoost-SVM) approach. With the increasing complexity of modern transportation networks, efficiently managing and responding to incidents is crucial for ensuring public safety and minimizing congestion. Traditional methods of incident classification often rely on manual labeling or rule-based systems, which can be time-consuming and prone to errors. In contrast, machine learning algorithms offer a promising solution for automating incident classification. However, their performance can be severely impacted by noise, outliers, and varying data quality in traffic datasets. To address these challenges, we propose the use of AdaBoost-SVM, a robust ensemble learning method that leverages the strengths of both boosting and SVM techniques. Our approach involves training multiple weak SVM classifiers on different subsets of the data and combining their predictions through a weighted majority voting scheme. The AdaBoost-SVM algorithm is capable of adapting to changing data distributions and is less susceptible to the effects of noisy or missing data. Through rigorous experimentation on real-world traffic datasets, we demonstrate the effectiveness of AdaBoost-SVM in incident classification tasks and show that it outperforms traditional methods in terms of accuracy and robustness. Our findings have significant implications for intelligent transportation systems and urban planning, enabling more efficient incident response and optimization of traffic flow.
