title: Data-driven Sequential Monte Carlo in Probabilistic Programming
Abstract: This abstract discusses the integration of Data-driven Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) algorithms within the framework of Probabilistic Programming (PP), a novel approach to Bayesian inference. By leveraging the strengths of both Data-driven SMC and PP, researchers aim to create a more efficient and adaptive inference engine capable of handling complex, high-dimensional probability models. The proposed methodology begins with a probabilistic programming language, allowing users to specify intricate probabilistic models in a declarative, high-level syntax. Data-driven SMC is then employed to selectively focus on regions of the state space with the highest probability, thereby improving the efficiency and accuracy of the inference process. Through the use of recursive Bayesian updates and machine learning-inspired learning rates, the algorithm adjusts its sampling strategy in real-time, responding to the complexities of the given problem. By coupling the adaptability of Data-driven SMC with the convenience of PP languages, this approach offers an exciting new direction for researchers seeking to tackle challenging problems in machine learning, computer vision, and associated domains. Initial experiments demonstrate promising results, highlighting the potential of this combined approach to provide faster convergence times, improved posterior approximations, and enhanced interpretability of uncertain quantities in complex probabilistic models.

title: Nuquantus: Machine learning software for the characterization and quantification of cell nuclei in complex immunofluorescent tissue images
Abstract: The characterization and quantification of cell nuclei in complex immunofluorescent tissue images hold immense significance in understanding various biological and pathological processes. However, traditional manual counting or analysis methods are often inefficient, prone to human error, and time-consuming. This is where machine learning-based solutions, such as Nuquantus, come into play. Nuquantus is a novel machine learning software designed to automate the estimation of cell nuclei characteristics, providing accurate and reliable quantitative analysis of immunofluorescent images. The software leverages a combination of deep learning algorithms, convolutional neural networks, and modern computer vision techniques to identify and segment individual cell nuclei, as well as assess their morphological and morphometric properties. By integrating data from multiple imaging modalities and processing algorithms, Nuquantus facilitates the high-throughput analysis of large-scale tissue imaging datasets, enabling researchers to unravel the complexities of cell-cell interactions and dynamical behavior in complex biological environments. With its ability to improve accuracy, reduce computational time, and provide high-quality outputs, Nuquantus is poised to revolutionize the field of tissue image analysis and has the potential to reveal novel insights into cellular processes that underlie various diseases, including cancer.

title: Origami: A 803 GOp/s/W Convolutional Network Accelerator
Abstract: This paper presents a novel origami-based design for a convolutional network (CNN) accelerator, pushing the envelope of deep learning acceleration power efficiency. By leveraging the intrinsic structural properties of origami, researchers have developed an innovative approach that integrates multiple processing elements and memory units into a compact, foldable structure. The proposed origami CNN accelerator, named OrigamiNet, delivers an unprecedented 803 GOP/s/W performance while reducing the area footprint by up to 35% compared to traditional planar implementations. At its core, OrigamiNet employs a hierarchical network architecture that combines folded 2D arrays of processing elements (PEs) with adaptable interconnects, enabling efficient data flow and minimizing latency. The result is a scalable and modular design that accommodates complex neural network workloads, showcasing a maximum processing capacity of 256 GOP/s and 4.2Mb of on-chip memory. Mathematical modeling shows that OrigamiNet's 3D structural properties yield a 23x reduction in power consumption compared to a traditional 2D implementation with similar processing capabilities, making it a highly attractive solution for next-generation edge AI and real-time processing applications. Initial experimental results using a custom 65nm test chip demonstrate the efficacy of OrigamiNet's innovative design, indicating its significant potential for disrupting the field of deep learning acceleration.

title: Small-footprint Deep Neural Networks with Highway Connections for Speech Recognition
Abstract: The recent advancements in deep learning have led to the development of smaller footprint deep neural networks that can efficiently handle real-world speech recognition tasks. This study proposes a novel approach to designing small-footprint deep neural networks with highway connections for speech recognition. Building upon the highway network concept, our proposed architecture incorporates recurrent highway networks (RHN) with a combination of time-delay neural networks (TDNN) and convolutional neural networks (CNN). The RHN component enables efficient parameter sharing among different time steps, allowing for a more compact model. In addition, we explore the use of adaptive weighting schemes to dynamically control the flow of information within the highway connections, effectively balancing the trade-offs between accuracy and model complexity. Our experimental results on the widely usedWall Street Journal (WSJ0) and Librispeech datasets demonstrate that the proposed small-footprint RHN-TDNN-CNN architecture achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming existing compact models in terms of both accuracy and computational efficiency. By reducing the number of parameters and operations required, our approach opens up new avenues for implementing deep neural networks on resource-constrained devices, providing new opportunities for real-world speech recognition applications. Our study sheds light on the potential of combining different network architectures and dynamic adaptability techniques to create efficient and accurate models for speech recognition tasks.

title: Decoding index finger position from EEG using random forests
Abstract: This study presents a novel approach to decoding the position of the index finger from electroencephalography (EEG) signals utilizing random forests, a type of ensemble learning method. Despite the increasing interest in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) and the various techniques employed to decode finger movement and position, developing an accurate and efficient algorithm remains a significant challenge. The work builds upon existing studies that have used machine learning algorithms to decode finger position from EEG signals but focuses on the specific task of identifying the index finger position, often considered a more complex and nuanced movement. A dataset of EEG recordings was collected from 20 subjects as they performed a series of finger movement tasks, including holding the index finger in steady positions. Random forests were then trained to decode the index finger position from the EEG signals, and the accuracy of the classification system was evaluated using various metrics. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of random forests in accurately detecting the position of the index finger, with an average accuracy of 85% and a significant improvement over traditional machine learning algorithms. Furthermore, this study's findings have important implications for the development of BCIs that can enable individuals with paralysis or prosthetics to interact with devices and communicate more effectively.

title: Watch-Bot: Unsupervised Learning for Reminding Humans of Forgotten Actions
Abstract: Watch-Bot is an innovative robotic system designed to provide reminders to humans about forgotten actions, aiming to improve human productivity and reduce procrastination. Through an unsupervised machine learning framework, the Watch-Bot learns from humans' behavior and social context to identify patterns and anomalies in daily routines. This model enables the Watch-Bot to autonomously detect instances when a human has forgotten to perform a task or action, and subsequently remind them of their forgotten responsibilities. By leveraging human feedback and reinforcement learning, the Watch-Bot adapts to users' varying needs and learning rates, maximizing the system's effectiveness and human acceptability. A key contribution of our work is the development of a novel multi-task learning architecture, which balances the system's ability to learn about human responsibilities with its capacity to adapt to changing social contexts. Our evaluation results demonstrate that Watch-Bot can accurately detect forgotten actions and provide effective reminders, leading to significant improvements in human productivity and task completion rates. Furthermore, our study highlights the potential of using unsupervised learning techniques to develop assistive robots that understand and respond to human needs in context-dependent environments. The Watch-Bot system has significant implications for the development of future assistive robots, wearable devices, and smart home systems that aim to augment human cognition and improve quality of life.

title: Preconditioned Stochastic Gradient Descent
Abstract: This research paper explores the concept of preconditioned stochastic gradient descent (SGD), a stochastic optimization technique that has garnered significant attention in recent years due to its ability to efficiently train large-scale machine learning models. Preconditioned SGD introduces a novel way of adapting the step size of the SGD algorithm by incorporating a preconditioner matrix that scales the gradient steps based on their magnitude, thereby improving convergence rates and enabling more stable learning processes. The preconditioner matrix is calculated using a set of sampled gradients from previous iterations, allowing the algorithm to adapt to changing model landscapes as training progresses. This paper theoretically analyzes the convergence properties of preconditioned SGD and provides an empirical study of its effectiveness on benchmarks such as image classification and language modeling. The results show that preconditioned SGD outperforms standard SGD in terms of convergence speed and accuracy, making it a particularly valuable method for training deep neural networks. Furthermore, the paper investigates the choice of preconditioner and its impact on the algorithm's performance, demonstrating that a more efficient preconditioner selection criterion can be derived based on the spectral properties of the Hessian matrix of the loss function. Overall, the work presented in this paper aims to advance the understanding of preconditioned SGD and its applications in high-dimensional machine learning tasks.

title: Understanding Human-Centric Images: From Geometry to Fashion
Abstract: This paper delves into the realm of understanding human-centric images, emphasizing the transformative journey from computational geometry to the sophisticated realm of fashion. By analyzing the existing literature and research, we present a comprehensive overview of the current state of human-centric image processing, highlighting the pivotal role of geometry in driving advancements in this field. The integration of geometric principles with computer vision has led to the development of various algorithms and techniques aimed at enhancing the accuracy and effectiveness of image analysis. These innovations have far-reaching implications for applications such as object recognition, segmentation, and tracking, ultimately enabling more informed decision-making in fields like retail, healthcare, and security. Furthermore, we explore the intersection of human-centric images with fashion, illustrating how insights from image processing can inform product design, garment construction, and textile estimation. By applying statistical models and geometric transformations, we demonstrate the potential of combining computer vision with fashion expertise to create innovative designs and prediction models, providing a paradigm shift in how we conceptualize and understand human-centric images. Ultimately, this paper highlights the growing significance of interdisciplinary approaches that marry geometry and fashion, fostering the development of more natural and intuitive human-computer interfaces.

title: Fighting Bandits with a New Kind of Smoothness
Abstract: This research develops a novel attack strategy for battling bandit problems, focusing on the concept of "smoothness" in adversarial settings. Traditionally, bandit algorithms are based on a "greedy" approach where an optimal sequence of decisions is determined through exploration and exploitation. However, the problem with this strategy is that it often fails in cases where the bandit's behavior is not necessarily smooth. In contrast, our approach is centered around a new form of smoothness, coined as 'alpha-smoothness', which allows for a more sophisticated understanding of the bandit's behavior and enhances the power of conventional algorithms. By leveraging the mathematical framework of dynamic programming, we propose a new algorithm called ASMOOTH, which outperforms the standard Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) method. The efficacy of ASMOOTH is demonstrated through extensive experiments in both theoretical and empirical evaluations. Furthermore, we extend the ASMOOTH algorithm to tackle more complex problems, such as bandit feedback functions with an additional layer of randomness, and provide an error bound for our algorithm. Our results clarify the conceptual distinction between "classic" and "alpha-smooth" bandit models and underscore the importance of considering new smoothness measures for enriching problem-solving efficiency in adversarial settings. Ultimately, our research contributes to the development of novel methods for challenging problems in decision-making and provides insights into a more comprehensive study of bandit strategies for real-world applications.

title: Learning Deep Features for Discriminative Localization
Abstract: This paper delves into the realm of discriminative localization, a critical aspect of computer vision that seeks to identify and highlight the most relevant regions within an image that are responsible for a particular prediction or classification. While conventional approaches often rely on handcrafted features that lack semantic meaning, our work focuses on generating deep features that are both rich in information and intrinsically tied to the image content. With the advent of deep learning techniques, it has become increasingly feasible to acquire features of unprecedented depth and complexity from Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). However, traditional methods typically rely on network outputs, neglecting the underlying spatial relationships and localization information that are essential for a thorough understanding of an image. To rectify this, we explore a novel approach for learning discriminative localization features, where input images are scrutinized by multiple scales of resolution and information. The resulting feature maps serve as the foundation for a spatial class activation mapping framework, providing a compelling visual explanation of their relative importance. We demonstrate the efficacy of our technique through comprehensive evaluation on widely used datasets, including ImageNet and PASCAL VOC, showing notable improvements over state-of-the-art localization methods in terms of precision and interpretability. By shedding light on the decisions made by deep networks, our framework paves the way for the development of more reliable, transparent, and explainable models that can inspire greater trust in the decisions of these powerful systems. Additionally, our research opens up new avenues for a range of applications that heavily rely on image understanding, such as autonomous driving, medical diagnosis, and surveillance systems.

title: Modeling Eating Behaviors: the Role of Environment and Positive Food Association Learning via a Ratatouille Effect
Abstract: This study aims to investigate the interplay between environment and positive food association learning on eating behaviors, utilizing a novel framework inspired by the 'Ratatouille Effect' phenomenon where a rat forms a strong emotional bond with a human chef and consequently develops a refined palate. Utilizing an interdisciplinary approach that integrates behavioral, neurobiological, and environmental psychology theories, this research involves a mixed-methods investigation of infant rats reared in simulated human environments, subjected to distinct culinary experiences, and exposed to varying sensory stimuli. The results showed that infant rats that experienced positive and novel food associations in a simulated home environment exhibited increased interest in exploring diverse, nutrient-rich food options and simultaneously underwent significant changes in their gut microbiota composition and brain chemistry. Moreover, these rats demonstrated reduced neophobia (fear of new foods) and enhanced consumption of previously unpalatable foods under the influence of a highly palatable odor. Conversely, those reared in an environment devoid of positive food associations or novel culinary experiences developed neophobic tendencies and a preference for high-calorie, nutrient-poor food items. These findings underscore the profound impact of early life experiences on the establishment and regulation of eating behaviors, highlighting the need to reimagine our understanding of food selection and obesity risk in humans and raising important questions about how early-life exposure to diverse culinary experiences can shape long-term eating behaviors and overall well-being.

title: A machine learning approach to anomaly-based detection on Android platforms
Abstract: Anomaly-based detection plays a crucial role in securing mobile devices against various types of threats, including malware, ransomware, and intrusion attacks. Android, being one of the most popular mobile operating systems, is a prime target for such threats. Traditional approaches to mobile security focus on signature-based detection, where the device's antivirus software scans for predefined patterns of known malicious code. However, this approach has several limitations, including the need for constant signature updates and the inability to detect zero-day attacks. In contrast, anomaly-based detection uses machine learning algorithms to identify and isolate unusual patterns of behavior that may indicate a security threat. This approach has shown promising results in various studies, especially when combined with rich feature sets derived from system logs, network traffic, and user behavior. This paper presents a novel machine learning approach to anomaly-based detection on Android platforms, leveraging a combination of Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and Gradient Boosting Machines (GBMs) to identify suspicious activity in real-time. The proposed system is implemented using a dataset of over 10,000 Android apps, including both benign and malicious examples, and achieves a detection rate of 95% with a false positive rate of 2%. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach in securing Android devices against evolving mobile threats and suggest its potential for real-world adoption in mobile security applications.

title: Policy Gradient Methods for Off-policy Control
Abstract: This paper delves into the realm of reinforcement learning, focusing on the efficacy of policy gradient methods in off-policy control scenarios. Policy gradient methods are a class of algorithms that learn to improve a policy by iteratively updating its parameters in the direction of the gradient of the expected cumulative reward. However, applying these methods in off-policy settings, where the policy used to generate the observed data differs from the policy being optimized, poses significant challenges. The discrepancy between the behavior policy and the target policy can lead to biased gradient estimates, rendering the learning process inefficient or even unstable. To address this issue, we explore several variants of policy gradient methods that are capable of handling off-policy data, including the Actor-Critic method, the Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) algorithm, and the Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) algorithm. By theoretically analyzing and empirically evaluating the performance of these methods, we provide insights into their strengths and weaknesses in off-policy control contexts. The experimental results demonstrate that while each method exhibits unique characteristics, they all achieve impressive performance in various robotic control tasks, with some variants outperforming others in specific situations. This study highlights the promise of policy gradient methods in off-policy control applications and provides a foundation for further research in this area, paving the way for more efficient and robust reinforcement learning algorithms.

title: Deep Relative Attributes
Abstract: Deep Relative Attributes proposes a novel approach to capturing and querying visual attributes of objects in images, videos, and 3D models. By treating attribute representation as a spatial network constructed from spatially relative attributes, the framework reaps the benefits of modeling complex attribute relationships, tackling domain adaptability challenges, and accelerating the learning process. Unlike traditional approaches centered around learning absolute attribute-visual-patch associations or category-attribute relationships, Deep Relative Attributes exploits spatial dependencies of an object's surface properties to infer contextual and non-local attribute influences, establishing connections between different parts, expressions, and attributes of an object's visual representation. Conventional methods concentrate on tasks such as attribute discovery, attribute evaluation, image classification, object detection, image captioning, and retrieval tasks, while maintaining applicability across diverse domains and datasets. This work broadens the accessibility of visual attribute-based representations and their applications by proposing an inventive combination of relative spatial attributes with differentiable reasoning steps. In addition to the superior learning effects and improved cross-domain performance achieved by employing relative spatial attributes, the discussed deep learning model has garnered a compelling architectural design and its inference capability's vast scalability.

title: Stack Exchange Tagger
Abstract: Stack Exchange Tagger utilizes a collaborative approach to improve text classification and tagging, drawing from a vast pool of expertise available on the platform. This research examines the potential of leveraging community-driven knowledge to enhance tagging accuracy and efficiency. By analyzing the collective efforts of users in categorizing questions and answers on Stack Exchange, we can identify patterns and relationships that can inform the development of more effective tagging models. Our study focuses on several key aspects, including the impact of user participation on tagging quality, the role of community expertise in tag suggestion, and the potential for Stack Exchange's semantic network to inform tagging decisions. Through a combination of quantitative and qualitative analysis, we explore the benefits and limitations of harnessing the collective intelligence of Stack Exchange users to improve text classification and tagging. Our results demonstrate that community-driven approaches can significantly enhance tagging performance, particularly when combined with traditional machine learning techniques. Moreover, our study highlights the importance of understanding the social and collaborative dynamics that underlie the Stack Exchange platform, as these factors have a profound impact on the quality and reliability of user-generated tags.

title: True Online Temporal-Difference Learning
Abstract: True Online Temporal-Difference (TD) learning aims to address the limitations of traditional TD methods by adapting to new data in real-time, making it a crucial framework for complex reinforcement learning tasks that require continuous updates. This study presents a detailed analysis of the True Online TD learning paradigm, particularly focusing on its applicability to high-dimensional state and action spaces, as well as its ability to handle non-stationary environments. The primary contributions of this work are the development of a novel online TD learning algorithm that adaptively adjusts the learning rate based on the observed data distribution, thereby ensuring faster convergence rates and improved stability. Furthermore, our approach introduces a novel exploration strategy that balances exploitation and exploration by considering the predictive uncertainty of the Q-function estimates, allowing for efficient exploration-accumulation-trade-offs in complex environments. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of the proposed algorithm over state-of-the-art TD methods on a range of benchmark tasks, including high-dimensional control problems and complex game environments. The results showcase the efficacy of True Online TD learning in enabling efficient and effective reinforcement learning in real-world scenarios, where access to data is continuous and unpredictable. Our findings suggest that True Online TD learning can be a promising framework for developing robust and adaptive reinforcement learning agents that excel in dynamic and uncertain environments.

title: Deep Learning-Based Image Kernel for Inductive Transfer
Abstract: Inductive transfer in deep learning aims to leverage knowledge from one domain to improve performance in another, often related, domain. However, current state-of-the-art methods lack adaptability to unseen, out-of-distribution data, resulting in reduced transferability of learned representations. This paper addresses the problem of inductive transfer by proposing a novel deep learning-based image kernel, specifically designed to facilitate domain adaptation through an iterative process of feature learning and kernel construction. Our approach, termed "Deep Domain-Adaptive Kernel" (DDAK), leverages the strengths of both deep neural networks and traditional Mercer kernels to learn an optimal feature representation that preserves domain-invariant information from the source domain. DDAK employs a two-stage architecture, comprising a deep neural network for feature learning and a separate kernel construction module that refines the learned features to create an optimal kernel. Through an iterative process, our architecture adapts to the target domain by refining the kernel, enabling the model to learn from richer, domain-specific representations. Extensive experiments on multiple datasets demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed method in inductive transfer, showcasing its superior performance over existing transfer learning approaches. By mitigating the out-of-domain data challenge and leveraging the potential of deep neural networks, our method makes significant contributions to the field of inductive transfer, and its application has a wide range of implications for multimodal learning, visual transfer, and domain adaptation.

title: Learning the Correction for Multi-Path Deviations in Time-of-Flight Cameras
Abstract: This research paper addresses the critical challenge of multi-path deviations in Time-of-Flight (ToF) cameras, which compromises the accuracy of 3D reconstruction and generates aberrant results in various applications. ToF cameras have gained popularity in recent years due to their ability to capture depth information simultaneously with RGB data. However, the multi-path problem arises when multiple light rays traverse the same path, causing signal interference resulting in inaccurate distance measurements and rendering the depth information unreliable. Existing methods use sophisticated algorithms and calibrations to counter this issue but are either computationally expensive, cannot be generalized to various scenarios, or require substantial manual intervention. To bridge this gap, this research proposes a novel correction method based on graph-based optimization and machine learning algorithms that identify, isolate, and effectively mitigate multi-path deviations. The proposed approach combines local motion estimation to detect moving objects with graph-based processing to eliminate competing signals, followed by machine learning-based refinement to adapt to diverse environments and optimal noise reduction techniques. By evaluating the proposed method on various datasets under diverse conditions, this paper demonstrates a significant enhancement of 3D reconstruction accuracy and robustness, enabling reliable performance in real-world settings, and outperforming existing techniques, thereby opening avenues for the widespread adoption of ToF cameras in various applications.

title: Big Data Scaling through Metric Mapping: Exploiting the Remarkable Simplicity of Very High Dimensional Spaces using Correspondence Analysis
Abstract: The explosive growth of digital data has led to the increasing challenges of data storage, visualization, and analysis, particularly in very high-dimensional spaces where traditional analytical methods tend to fail due to the curse of dimensionality. This paper explores a novel approach to conquer this challenge by leveraging the remarkable simplicity of high-dimensional spaces using metric mapping, a technique borrowed from correspondence analysis. Our proposed method, denoted as Scalable Mapping (SM), uses distance-preserving transformations, integrated with dimensionality reduction techniques, to map high-dimensional data onto low-dimensional manifolds, facilitating more tractable and insightful visualizations and analyses. By carefully analyzing the properties and complexities of high-dimensional spaces, we identify key opportunities for exploiting the metric structure and symmetries inherent in these spaces to significantly enhance scalability and efficiency. Through a combination of theoretical derivations, computational experiments, and use cases, this research aims to demonstrate the power and potential of SM for liberating Big Data from its cumbersome high-dimensional shackles and enable more effective data-driven decision making and knowledge discovery in a variety of applications, ranging from scientific research to business intelligence and threat detection in computational security and beyond. By exploiting the latent structure of high-dimensional data, this research aims to show a compelling scale-up capacity for real-world data sets, opening up fresh opportunities and insights with high-dimensional data.

title: Online Visual Analytics of Text Streams
Abstract: This research paper explores the concept of online visual analytics of text streams, focusing on the real-time extraction of insights from rapidly evolving data sources. Text streams, also known as text event streams, are generated from various sources such as social media platforms, news feeds, and online forums. Analyzing these streams enables organizations to gauge public sentiment, monitor trends, and anticipate future events. The paper delves into the challenges associated with processing and visualizing massive text data streams efficiently, emphasizing the limitations of traditional batch-oriented methodologies. Online visual analytics employs innovative techniques to facilitate dynamic and interactive data exploration, incorporating advanced visualization methods, machine learning, and natural language processing. A comprehensive framework is proposed to optimize text stream processing, incorporating data preprocessing, feature extraction, and visualization components. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed framework in facilitating real-time text stream analysis, with substantial reductions in processing latency and enhancements in data quality. Future work focuses on extending the framework to handle broader data types and integrating it with other data analysis systems to create a unified analytics environment. The exploration of this novel field has the potential to transform business decision-making processes and revolutionize the way organizations interact with vast amounts of unstructured text data.

title: Distributed Optimization with Arbitrary Local Solvers
Abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to distributed optimization that leverages arbitrary local solvers to facilitate decentralized and scalable problem-solving in complex systems. The proposed method, dubbed Distributed Aggregated Gradient (DAG), empowers devices to exploit their locally available optimization solvers to concurrently solve portions of the overall optimization problem. By utilizing each device's unique computational capabilities and optimizing its local objective function, the DAG algorithm allows for more efficient and adaptive decision-making. Such a decentralized approach enables optimal allocation of computation resources and facilitates real-time adaptations in response to shifting system demands or objective functions. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that the DAG algorithm converges to the optimal solution at a rate of up to O(1/T), where T represents the total number of iterations. Furthermore, numerical experiments on a range of synthetic and real-world examples confirm the Dag algorithm's robustness, stability, and efficiency, with significantly improved convergence rates over existing distributed optimization methods. The proposed framework has far-reaching implications for a variety of applications, including but not limited to, large-scale machine learning, network optimization, and autonomous systems.

title: Tracking Idea Flows between Social Groups
Abstract: This study explores the complex dynamics of idea flows between social groups, shedding light on the intricacies of how knowledge and innovations are disseminated, adopted, and transformed across different social contexts. By leveraging insights from social network analysis, diffusion theory, and actor-network theory, we develop a comprehensive framework for tracking idea flows across various social groups, including networks, communities, and organizations. Our research reveals that idea flows are shaped by multiple factors, including social proximity, cognitive alignment, and structural holes within social networks. We also investigate the role of social influencers and opinion leaders in facilitating or hindering idea flows, highlighting the importance of their positions, networks, and communication styles in shaping knowledge diffusion processes. Our findings suggest that idea flows are often non-linear, multidirectional, and context-dependent, emphasizing the need to move beyond simplistic diffusion models and adopt a more nuanced understanding of the complex social processes at play. Through a mixed-methods approach combining surveys, interviews, and network analysis, we demonstrate the practical applicability of our framework to inform policy-making, innovation management, and organizational development. Ultimately, this research aims to promote a deeper understanding of idea flows and their transformative potential, underscoring the importance of social contexts in shaping the trajectory of innovations and knowledge creation.

title: L1-Regularized Distributed Optimization: A Communication-Efficient Primal-Dual Framework
Abstract: This work proposes a communication-efficient distributed optimization framework for solving large-scale machine learning problems, focusing on the use of L1 regularization. The proposed framework incorporates a novel adaptive primal-dual method, driven by a decentralized architecture that ensures efficient data sharing among participants. By leveraging the properties of the L1 regularization term, the designed framework enables distributed optimization solutions that possess interpretable and robustness characteristics. Extensive numerical experiments conducted on diverse machine learning benchmarks, including image classification, regression, and clustering tasks, demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in achieving high accuracy, accurate model selection, and improved scalability. Key performance metrics, such as communication overhead, computation times, and the distribution of regularization terms across machines, are thoroughly analyzed to explain the success of the proposed framework. Moreover, by quantifying the theoretical convergence properties of the L1-regularized adaptive primal-dual method, the researchers establish a solid foundation for the design and analysis of communication-efficient distributed optimization algorithms. Overall, the proposed distributed L1-regularized optimization framework is proven to be an efficient, reliable, and scalable solution for large-scale machine learning applications, where communication-efficient data processing and decision-making are essential.

title: Quantum Privacy-Preserving Data Mining
Abstract: Quantum computers, with their vast potential for processing vast amounts of data, present a formidable challenge to traditional data mining methods. As quantum computers begin to penetrate the realm of encrypted data, security and privacy become exponentially more complex concerns. Traditional quantum key distribution methods have limitations in addressing the intricacies of data mining, particularly where data is continuously being generated and updated. In this context, privacy-preserving data mining is crucial to maintaining confidentiality and anonymity while enabling data analysis and modeling. This paper delves into the efficacy of quantum private queries, which are an essential mechanism in the development of quantum- secure data mining systems. A comparison of quantum private queries with contemporary data mining frameworks illustrates their capacity for sophisticated confidentiality-preserving data aggregation and clustering, while ensuring data analysis is carried out without infringing on individual privacy. Adopting quantum-safe encryption and leveraging quantum noise's non-interoperability properties with classical cryptography has shown to bolster quantum private query efficiency and security. However, this requires cross-layered cryptographic systems and reevaluating our understanding of key exchange protocols. Novel data mining protocols and techniques utilising quantum private queries emerge as crucial for the development of scalable privacy-preserving data mining systems under the veil of evolving quantum computing. By deepening our comprehension of quantum safe protocols for quantum key distribution, practical applications will arise in big data mining, supporting a new equilibrium between insights and individual freedom and data confidentiality.

title: Cloud-based Electronic Health Records for Real-time, Region-specific Influenza Surveillance
Abstract: This study proposes a cloud-based electronic health records (EHR) system for real-time, region-specific influenza surveillance. The system is designed to utilize the widespread adoption of cloud computing and electronic health records to create a scalable and flexible platform for tracking and analyzing influenza trends. By leveraging a cloud-based architecture, the system can aggregate and analyze EHR data from a multitude of institutions, medical facilities, and laboratories, providing a comprehensive view of influenza activity across regions. This is achieved through a multi-layer cloud computing approach, comprising a public cloud for scalability and reliability, a private cloud for secure and compliant data storage, and a hybrid cloud for real-time data processing. The system utilizes a machine learning-based algorithm to analyze EHR data and enable real-time inferences, detecting patterns, trends, and outliers that can be linked to influenza outbreaks. The result is a tool for epidemiologists, healthcare professionals, and policymakers to track and manage influenza activity in real-time, facilitating data-driven decision-making, targeted interventions, and optimized resource allocation. Furthermore, the system incorporates a mobile application for patients and healthcare providers to report symptoms, reinforcing the system's real-time surveillance capabilities.

title: The Power of Depth for Feedforward Neural Networks
Abstract: Feedforward neural networks (FNNs) have gained immense prominence within the realm of artificial intelligence, primarily utilized for image classification, object detection, and segmentation tasks. Despite the robustness achieved by FNNs, their performance can be effectively enhanced through strategic modifications to the architecture. Specifically, augmenting the depth of FNNs has been postulated to be beneficial. In an effort to further comprehend the influence of depth on the performance of FNNs, a comprehensive review of existing literature was conducted, focusing on the theoretical underpinnings and empirical experiments. It is now widely acknowledged that an increase in depth allows for more complex feature representations to be learned, thereby leading to improved generalization performance. Furthermore, depth also allows for the construction of hierarchical feature representations, comprising local features learned from early layers to more abstract features extracted in deeper layers. Nonetheless, increasing depth also concurrently increases the risk of vanishing gradients, leading to degradation in performance. Research has demonstrated that techniques such as residual connections, batch normalization, and weight initialization can be employed to mitigate this issue, thereby achieving improved performance with progressively deeper architectures. The underlying rationale behind the augmented performance of deep FNNs pertains to the superior representational capacity and integration of spatial and hierarchical features learned through deeper layers, yielding better contextualization of data. Moreover, various studies have experimentally validated that augmenting depth can significantly enhance the performance of FNNs over a wide range of benchmarks.

title: RNN Fisher Vectors for Action Recognition and Image Annotation
Abstract: RNN Fisher Vectors for Action Recognition and Image Annotation effectively integrate Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and Fisher Vectors to advance state-of-the-art performance in human action recognition and image annotation tasks. The incorporation of RNNs enables the model to capture temporal relationships within videos, providing a more comprehensive understanding of actions and events. Fisher Vectors, derived from the probabilistic generative model Gaussian Mixture Models, encode high-level features into compact yet informative representations, allowing for improved discriminability and robustness to variations in illumination, pose, and occlusions. By combining the strength of RNNs and Fisher Vectors, the proposed RNN Fisher Vectors model achieves superior performance in benchmark action recognition datasets compared to existing approaches. Furthermore, the model's adaptability and robustness are demonstrated through successful annotation tasks, where it effectively labels and categorizes images into meaningful semantic groups. The proposed RNN Fisher Vectors approach can be particularly useful in various real-world applications, including surveillance, healthcare, and consumer electronics, where accurate and efficient action recognition is crucial for decision-making and automation. This work also contributes towards the development of more robust and scalable computer vision methods, enabling seamless integration with other AI systems and paving the way for more intelligent and context-aware applications.

title: Active Distance-Based Clustering using K-medoids
Abstract: This paper proposes an improvement to the traditional K-medoids algorithm through the incorporation of active distance-based clustering techniques. Active distance measures are designed to adapt to changing data distributions, allowing the K-medoids algorithm to effectively group data points in clusters with varying densities and shapes. The proposed Active Distance-Based K-medoids (ADBK) clustering algorithm combines a novel distance metric, based on the concept of the Hausdorff distance, with the classical K-medoids update rule, employing a sophisticated data representation using density-based clusters. Furthermore, the algorithm incorporates a mechanism that controls the level of exploration and exploitation by suitably determining the radius of the local neighborhoods, thus striking a balance between global patterns and local optima. The key benefit of ADBK lies in its ability to adapt to data outliers and anomalies, thereby increasing the robustness and scalability of the K-medoids algorithm. Experimental results on a wide range of synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the superiority of ADBK over existing clustering methods in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency. Additionally, the impact of changing data distributions on the clustering performance of ADBK is investigated, highlighting its potential to handle real-time clustering applications. Overall, this research aims to provide a novel and efficient method for clustering high-dimensional data using active distance-based techniques.

title: Quantum assisted Gaussian process regression
Abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to Gaussian process regression by leveraging the principles of quantum computing. Quantum-assisted Gaussian process regression (QAGR) combines the strengths of both quantum and classical machine learning methods to provide superior performance and scalability. The research demonstrates how the quantum circuit can serve as a surrogate model to efficiently compute the Gaussian process's posterior distribution at a fraction of the computational cost of classical methods. By utilizing a variety of quantum-inspired preprocessing techniques and quantum hardware, our QAGR algorithm is capable of significantly reducing the time complexity of traditional Gaussian process regression, making it more suitable for real-world applications. The experimental results demonstrate that QAGR outperforms classical Gaussian process regression in terms of prediction accuracy and runtime, while also showcasing the ability to handle large-scale datasets with an exponential number of data points. Additionally, this work highlights the potential of integrating quantum computing into the Gaussian process framework, enabling the prospect of quantum-accelerated machine learning in high-impact applications, such as materials science, finance, and complex systems modeling, where Gaussian process regression is traditionally used.

title: Sparse Generalized Principal Component Analysis for Large-scale Applications beyond Gaussianity
Abstract: Sparse Generalized Principal Component Analysis (SGPCA) represents a novel computational paradigm for efficient dimensionality reduction of large-scale datasets. It extends the realm of traditional Principal Component Analysis (PCA), overcoming limitations associated with Gaussianity by incorporating non-Gaussian distributions and sparse structures inherent within the data. Here, components captured through SGPCA methodology specifically preserve principal directions while accommodating sparse loadings, leading to an increased ability to capture underlying patterns. A key aspect of SGPCA involves detecting independent components from structured data, leveraging the existence of non-sparse, redundant components over informative sparse ones. By extracting sparse and sparse non-Gaussian components, the proposed algorithm adeptly captures variances while maintaining computational efficiency due to low-rank matrix factorization. Consequently, SGPCA significantly outperforms standard PCA, particularly on datasets exhibiting non-linear properties. Computational simulations and empirical investigations demonstrate the efficacy and real-world applicability of SGPCA on comprehensive benchmark data sets, revealing its robust estimation, and adaptability to situations where traditional models prove unsuitable.

title: Active Sampler: Light-weight Accelerator for Complex Data Analytics at Scale
Abstract: Active Sampler represents a cutting-edge approach to accelerating complex data analytics at scale, addressing the ever-increasing demands of modern data-intensive applications. By leveraging a novel combination of clustering and active learning techniques, our proposed system intelligently selects and accelerates the most critical data subsets, resulting in drastic reductions in processing times and subsequent energy consumption. Utilizing a lightweight parallelization framework, we enable seamless integration with a broad spectrum of computing platforms, from edge devices to high-performance clusters, granting flexibility and scalability to data analytics workloads. Empirical evaluations on multiple datasets and hardware configurations validate the efficacy of our approach, demonstrating accelerations ranging from 2 to 12 times over baseline execution times, while ensuring accurate results and minimal additional overhead. Our study presents a thorough analysis of the Active Sampler's performance, highlighting its robustness to parameter variation and robustness guarantees, alongside comprehensive discussions of its application in fields such as machine learning, data fusion, and real-time analytics. As the modern data processing landscape continues to evolve, the Active Sampler provides a versatile, scalable, and efficient solution, poised to unlock new frontiers in complex data analytics at scale.

title: Minimal Perceptrons for Memorizing Complex Patterns
Abstract: This research delves into the realm of artificial neural networks with a focus on a simplified form of perceptron known as minimal perceptrons, specifically examining their capacity for memorizing complex patterns. Contrary to traditional perceptrons which involve multiple layers of neurons and complex activation functions, minimal perceptrons are comprised of a single layer of threshold neurons and are primarily defined by a restrictive set of permissible weights. The study aims to investigate the theoretical and practical implications of this simplification on the network's ability to store and recall intricate patterns, measuring the effects on learning performance and pattern memorization capabilities. Through model simulations and a focused comparison with other prevalent machine learning architectures, the findings of this research aim to provide critical insights into the optimal application of minimal perceptrons in real-world scenarios, weighing the trade-offs that emerge due to reduced network complexity. By elucidating the roles and limitations of minimal perceptrons in capturing complex patterns, this research ultimately seeks to advance the understanding of the delicately interwoven relationship between model complexity and learning performance in the realm of artificial neural networks. The proposed research has significant implications for theoretical neural networks, cognitive psychology, and computer science applications, such as data storage and pattern recognition, and is likely to stimulate debate on the most effective measures for balancing model complexity and accuracy.

title: Efficient Deep Feature Learning and Extraction via StochasticNets
Abstract: StochasticNets have recently emerged as a powerful architecture for deep feature learning and extraction, which can efficiently handle complex datasets and achieve high accuracy in various machine learning tasks, such as image classification, object detection, and segmentation. In this work, we investigate the use of StochasticNets for deep feature learning and extraction, focusing on their ability to adaptively learn feature representations from data. Our contribution lies in proposing a novel framework, coined Adaptive Stochastic Feature Learning (ASFL), which jointly trains a set of StochasticNets in parallel, each with a different depth, width, and stochasticity. This allows ASFL to efficiently explore the optimal feature space and learn task-specific representations. Through extensive experiments on various benchmark datasets and tasks, we demonstrate the effectiveness of ASFL in improving the robustness, generalizability, and accuracy of deep feature learning and extraction. We also provide a detailed analysis of ASFL's performance on various computational resources, showing its ability to scale to large datasets and complex architectures. Furthermore, our study reveals the importance of stochasticity in deep feature learning and extraction, showcasing the potential of StochasticNets to revolutionize the field of deep learning and AI research. Overall, our work provides a comprehensive understanding of the power and capabilities of StochasticNets in deep feature learning and extraction, paving the way for future research in this exciting area.

title: A Bayesian Generalized CAR Model for Correlated Signal Detection
Abstract: This paper presents a novel Bayesian framework for the detection of correlated signals in complex data sets, overcoming the limitations of traditional generalized Compo-sitional Autoregressive (CAR) models. By incorporating a Bayesian approach, we integrate prior knowledge and uncertainty, enabling more accurate signal detection and estimation in spatially correlated data. Our proposed Bayesian Generalized CAR (BG-CAR) model accounts for both spatial autocorrelation and non-stationarity in the data, accommodating a range of different signal types and variances. We develop an efficient and scalable Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm for posterior inference, allowing fast and accurate posterior analysis of the model parameters. The proposed model exhibits superior performance in terms of signal detection accuracy and robustness compared to existing methods in simulations with both Gaussian and non-Gaussian correlated signals, as well as in real-world examples. We demonstrate the applicability and flexibility of the BG-CAR model in a variety of fields including environmental science, biology, and economics, showing its potential as a powerful statistical tool for correlated signal detection in various data-driven applications. Our results highlight the value of Bayesian approaches in overcoming data complexity and achieving reliable inferences in high-autocorrelation data, thus contributing to the advancement of signal detection methodology and its applications in interdisciplinary research.

title: Improving Human Activity Recognition Through Ranking and Re-ranking
Abstract: Human Activity Recognition (HAR) has become an essential component of various applications, including healthcare, sports, and smart homes. While significant progress has been made in the field, its performance can be hindered by issues such as noise, complexity, and heterogeneity of sensor data, leading to inaccurate activity recognition, inefficient ranking, and poor re-ranking techniques. As a result, identifying optimal ranking and re-ranking strategies becomes a pressing need to enhance the overall accuracy and reliability of activity recognition systems. This study aimed to address this challenge by investigating the potential benefits of ranking and re-ranking techniques in improving the performance of HAR systems. A thorough survey of existing methods and their limitations in handling complex activity recognition tasks was conducted, followed by the development of a novel ranking and re-ranking framework that leverages machine learning and deep learning techniques to select and re-prioritize activities based on their importance and certainty. Experimental evaluations were performed using a diverse set of public HAR datasets, demonstrating substantial improvements in activity recognition accuracy and ranking stability. Our findings indicate that this proposed framework can efficiently address the aforementioned limitations and uncertainties in activity recognition, paving the way for the development of more reliable and effective systems that can accurately classify and predict human activities in various real-world scenarios.

title: Understanding Customers' Evaluations Through Mining Airline Reviews
Abstract: This study examines the application of text mining techniques to analyze airline reviews and evaluate customer opinions on flight quality, service quality, and overall customer experience. By leveraging a large dataset of reviews from various airlines, this research develops a text mining framework to identify key features associated with customer satisfaction and dissatisfaction. The framework incorporates techniques such as natural language processing, sentiment analysis, and topic modeling to extract meaningful insights from the text data. The results indicate that flight quality, service quality, and overall customer experience are the primary determinants of customer satisfaction, while aspects such as flight delay, in-flight meal quality, and crew behavior significantly impact passenger dissatisfaction. Furthermore, the study reveals that customers' opinions and preferences vary across different airlines, travel classes, and routes, suggesting that airlines should develop tailored strategies to address specific customer concerns and improve their overall experience. The findings of this research provide actionable insights for airlines to enhance customer satisfaction, improve service quality, and ultimately increase revenue and market share. This study contributes to the growing body of research on text mining and sentiment analysis in the airline industry, while also providing a practical framework for airlines to monitor and respond to customer feedback.

title: Deep Feature Learning with Relative Distance Comparison for Person Re-identification
Abstract: This paper presents a novel deep feature learning approach for person re-identification by utilizing relative distance comparison. Conventional deep learning methods for person re-identification rely heavily on the use of Batch Normalization (BN) and Distance Supervision (DS) losses to enhance feature discriminability and robustness. However, these methods often focus on inter-class separation rather than capturing the underlying structural patterns and relationships between frames, leading to suboptimal performance in cases where the intra-class variations are significant. To address this limitation, we propose a new approach that incorporates a relative distance comparison mechanism into the deep feature learning framework. Specifically, we introduce a distance-aware fully connected network (DA-FCN) that aggregates both the magnitude and relative position of inter-frame distances to guide feature learning. This technique enables the model to implicitly learn the spatial structure and contextual relationship between frames, leading to improved robustness to variations in pose, viewpoint, and expression. In addition to this novel component, we also introduce a novel identity-wise triplet loss (IW-TL) function that enforces relative consistency of distance within each identity cluster, further enhancing the model's ability to generalize well across different scenarios. Through comprehensive experiments on various challenging person re-identification benchmarks, our proposed method demonstrates superior performance and competitive results, showcasing its effectiveness and robustness in handling real-world scenarios.

title: Macroeconomic Dynamics of Assets, Leverage and Trust
Abstract: The macroeconomic dynamics of assets, leverage, and trust are complex and interdependent phenomena that have far-reaching implications for financial markets, economic growth, and social stability. This research examines the intricate relationships between these variables, investigating how asset prices, leverage ratios, and trust levels influence one another and shape macroeconomic outcomes. We employ a dynamic macroeconomic model to analyze the interactions between assets, leverage, and trust, taking into account the differences in asset types, leverage structures, and trust scenarios. Our results show that the composition of assets plays a critical role in shaping the macroeconomic dynamics, with equity assets exerting a more significant influence on leverage and trust than debt assets. We also find that leverage ratios have a nonlinear impact on asset prices and trust levels, with moderate leverage levels fostering economic growth but excessive leverage contributing to financial instability. Furthermore, our research reveals that trust levels are responsive to changes in asset prices and leverage ratios, with high levels of trust promoting economic stability but low levels of trust exacerbating financial crises. Overall, our study provides new insights into the macroeconomic dynamics of assets, leverage, and trust, highlighting the need for policymakers to adopt a more nuanced and asset-specific approach to financial regulation and macroeconomic management.

title: Learning algorithms at the service of WISE survey
Abstract: The WISE (Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer) survey, conducted between 2010 and 2011, has generated a vast amount of data on the infrared light emitted by celestial objects in the universe, providing valuable insights into the composition, size, shape, distance, motion, and interactions of these objects. However, the sheer volume of this data poses significant challenges for astronomers, making it difficult to extract meaningful information without the aid of sophisticated learning algorithms. This study investigates the application of machine learning and deep learning techniques to the WISE survey data, focusing on image and spectroscopic analysis. A range of learning algorithms, including Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), and Gradient Boosting Machines (GBMs), are employed to identify and classify objects, predict their physical properties, and map their distributions within galaxy clusters and other cosmological structures. The performance of these algorithms is evaluated in terms of accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score, and their results are compared with those obtained from traditional astronomical methods. Furthermore, this study explores the potential of transfer learning and active learning to enhance the efficiency and effectiveness of the learning algorithms. By harnessing the power of machine learning and deep learning, this research aims to unlock new insights into the universe, enabling astronomers to better understand its evolution, composition, and behavior. Ultimately, the findings of this study have the potential to enhance our understanding of the cosmos and shed new light on the mysteries of the universe.

title: Words are not Equal: Graded Weighting Model for building Composite Document Vectors
Abstract: This paper presents a novel graded weighting model for constructing composite document vectors that effectively captures the nuanced importance of each word within a document. Unlike traditional term frequency-inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) based models that assign equal importance to words, our proposed model takes into account the varying degrees of significance of words in a document. We introduce a graded weighting function that estimates the importance of each word based on its contribution to the overall semantic content of the document. This function is composed of two key components: a term frequency component that captures the co-occurrence patterns of words, and a local co-occurrence component that measures the proximity of words within a document. The combination of these components allows for the identification of high-impact words that significantly contribute to the document's meaning, and low-impact words that are not as informative. Our model is then applied to a range of natural language processing tasks, including document classification, clustering, and topic modeling, where it demonstrates superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods that rely on equal weighting. The experimental results illustrate the effectiveness of our graded weighting model in identifying the most informative words and constructing more accurate document vectors, leading to improved performance in downstream tasks.

title: Distilling Knowledge from Deep Networks with Applications to Healthcare Domain
Abstract: This paper delves into the realm of knowledge distillation, a technique aimed at extracting meaningful insights and knowledge from complex deep neural networks. The primary objective of our research is to explore ways of applying knowledge distillation to the healthcare domain, where accurate and interpretable diagnoses are critical. By leveraging the strengths of both traditional and deep learning methods, we aim to develop an innovative framework for extracting valuable knowledge from pre-trained neural networks. This framework will empower healthcare professionals to gain deeper insights into medical decision-making processes, thereby facilitating more informed and accurate diagnoses. Furthermore, our research will also explore the deployment of knowledge distillation techniques for optimizing medical imaging analysis, where the complex relationships between image features and diagnostic outcomes can be distilled into actionable knowledge. Through the successful integration of knowledge distillation with healthcare applications, we aim to improve patient outcomes, streamline clinical workflows, and reduce diagnostic uncertainty. Our work will make significant contributions to both the machine learning and healthcare communities, enabling knowledge-driven healthcare delivery that is more effective, efficient, and grounded in scientific evidence.

title: Evolution of Privacy Loss in Wikipedia
Abstract: This study delves into the evolution of privacy loss in Wikipedia, examining the disparities in user data protection and control over their digital footprint on the platform. By utilizing a longitudinal dataset spanning over a decade, the research showcases an alarming trend of users' increasing vulnerability to data breaches, leaks, and unauthorized data usage. The analysis suggests that Wikipedia's privacy policies, while initially designed to promote free and open information exchange, have not evolved at the same pace as threats to user data. Factors such as increased demands for user profiling and targeted advertising have led to a compromise in users' trust and sense of security on the platform. Furthermore, the study explores the structural issues within Wikipedia's modus operandi that contribute to the accelerated erosion of user privacy. This includes the platform's fundamental reliance on voluntary user contributions and the inherent limitations of its decentralized governance model. By tracing the trajectory of Wikipedia's evolving approach to user data, this research attempts to bridge the theoretical divide between data protection and information sharing, emphasizing the need for an immediate shift towards more robust and proactive measures.

title: A Unified Approach to Error Bounds for Structured Convex Optimization Problems
Abstract: This paper presents a unified approach to deriving tight error bounds for a wide class of structured convex optimization problems, encompassing both linear and nonlinear programming models. By casting these problems into a canonical form, we establish a novel framework for analyzing the convexity and smoothness properties of the resulting optimization landscapes. Specifically, we introduce a generalized notion of strong convexity that accounts for both linear and nonlinear data structures, enabling us to extend well-known error bound results from smooth convex optimization to the more general structured convex setting. Our approach leverages techniques from convex analysis, including Bregman divergences and proximal operators, to provide a unified treatment of error bounds for various problem formulations, including those encountered in machine learning, signal processing, and sensor networks. Through a series of case studies, we demonstrate the efficacy and versatility of our framework, illustrating its power in deriving tight error bounds for high-dimensional optimization problems that arise in a range of applications, including sparse signal recovery, matrix completion, and supervised learning. Our unified approach obviates the need for ad hoc error bound analyses, providing a systematized methodology for analyzing the convergence properties of optimization algorithms for structured convex problems. As such, this research contributes a valuable reference for the optimization community, enabling researchers and practitioners to tackle more challenging problems with greater confidence and precision.

title: Prediction of grain boundary structure and energy by machine learning
Abstract: This study explores the application of machine learning techniques to predict grain boundary structure and energy, which remain significant challenges in understanding and manipulating materials properties at the nanoscale. Grain boundaries are intricate interfaces between crystalline regions that play a crucial role in dictating material performance, influencing properties such as strength, toughness, and corrosion resistance. However, due to their inherent complexity, traditional computational methods often fall short in accurately describing grain boundary topologies and energies. In this work, we leverage the power of supervised learning and generative models to develop accurate predictions of grain boundary structure and energy. Our machine learning framework incorporates a large dataset of pre-characterized grain boundaries, using a combination of descriptors and neural network architectures to learn high-dimensional patterns and relationships that govern grain boundary behavior. The results demonstrate the capability of our approach to predict grain boundary structure and energy with high fidelity, providing valuable insights into the underlying mechanisms that govern material behavior at the nanoscale. Furthermore, our model enables the accelerated exploration of grain boundary space, facilitating the rational design of materials with tailored properties and opening new avenues for the development of high-performance materials and technologies.

title: Mined Semantic Analysis: A New Concept Space Model for Semantic Representation of Textual Data
Abstract: Mined Semantic Analysis: A New Concept Space Model for Semantic Representation of Textual Data, offers a novel approach to the analysis of textual data by leveraging machine learning and semantic modelling. This concept space model employs a combination of word embeddings and graph-based clustering algorithms to identify context-dependent entities and relationships in text data, thus capturing nuanced semantic representations that traditional bag-of-words models often neglect. By integrating mined data from varied sources, the proposed model effectively sidesteps the limitations imposed by domain-specific or corpus-specific embeddings, delivering a more comprehensive and adaptable understanding of text semantics. Furthermore, this model allows for the discovery of latent semantic structures by means of community detection and spectral-based clustering techniques, thereby delineating the topological nuances inherent in large-scale text networks. Through extensive evaluation on multiple benchmark datasets, the model demonstrates remarkable improvements in both performance and interpretability, validating the efficacy of mined semantic analysis for a range of natural language processing and cognitive computing applications. Moreover, this research contributes to the development of an open-source knowledge base framework, enabling knowledge engineers and data scientists to easily incorporate and extend the model to suit their specific needs. The results of this study have far-reaching implications for multidisciplinary fields such as artificial intelligence, information retrieval, and cognitive science, where semantic representation of textual data is of paramount importance.

title: Integral Concurrent Learning: Adaptive Control with Parameter Convergence without PE or State Derivatives
Abstract: Integral Concurrent Learning (ICL) has emerged as a promising approach for addressing the challenge of adaptive control in complex systems, which typically demands a prior knowledge of the system's parameters or explicit measurements of state derivatives. Conventional adaptive control methods either fail to achieve robust stability with poor parameter convergence or compromise it for the sake of minimization of a suitable Lyapunov function to warrant learning. The method investigated here seeks to ameliorate this trade-off by considering concurrency as a key design consideration. ICL integrates integral adaptation laws with concurrent update conditions, offering enhancements in robustness, parameter convergence, and diminished or complete elimination of the persistent excitation (PE) requirement as well as the need for explicit state derivative measurements. This synergy enables ICL to be adaptive, robust, and concurrent - properties quintessential for dependable control of uncertain dynamic systems where convergence to accurate parameter values often have significant implications. Furthermore, the simultaneous adaptation process endows ICL schemes with more flexibility and better performance prospects than traditional Integral Adaptive Control (IAC) schemes, especially for plants having limited or no persistently exciting inputs. This development seems poised to enrich the repertoire of control strategies for uncertain systems thereby contributing significantly to the control science of uncertain dynamic systems.

title: Cross-Validated Variable Selection in Tree-Based Methods Improves Predictive Performance
Abstract: This study investigates the potential of cross-validated variable selection in tree-based methods for enhancing predictive performance. Traditional tree-based models such as decision trees and random forests rely heavily on the selection of relevant features for building the predictive model. However, the limitations of existing feature selection techniques, including stepwise regression and correlation analysis, are becoming increasingly evident as data complexity increases. Furthermore, variable selection is often treated as a separate step from model development, which may not accurately capture the inherent interactions between features and the complex relationships between variables. In response, this study introduces a novel approach that embeds cross-validation into the variable selection process within tree-based models. The proposed method, denoted as CV-TS, systematically evaluates a subset of variables within each fold of the cross-validation loop, thereby allowing for the selection of the most informative features while avoiding overfitting and model instability. The results of experiments conducted on a range of real-world datasets suggest that CV-TS significantly outperforms traditional tree-based methods in terms of predictive accuracy and model interpretability, highlighting the potential of this innovative approach for advancing machine learning applications in fields such as medicine, finance, and climate modeling.

title: Scalable Modeling of Conversational-role based Self-presentation Characteristics in Large Online Forums
Abstract: This research proposes a novel scalable modeling approach for capturing conversational-role based self-presentation characteristics in large online forums. The internet has revolutionized the way individuals interact with each other online, leading to the emergence of vast online communities where individuals express themselves in unique and diverse ways. In these online forums, individuals often assume various roles, such as experts, entertainers, and supporters, to exhibit their self-presentation characteristics. However, manually analyzing large online forums for these conversational-role based characteristics is a daunting task due to the sheer volume of data. Our proposed approach leverages deep learning technologies, particularly graph neural networks (GNN), and hybrid collaborative filtering to model user self-presentation characteristics in a scalable manner. We create a graph-based representation of online forums, where each user is a node containing their role-specific conversation behavior and interaction patterns with other users. Our GNN-based model learns the semantic and structural properties of the graph to infer user self-presentation characteristics. The proposed approach is validated through extensive experiments on a large-scale online forum dataset. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in accurately capturing user self-presentation characteristics and outperforming state-of-the-art methods. The scalable model provides valuable insights for researchers, developers, and administrators to design more effective tools for understanding user behavior and optimizing online community experience.

title: The p-filter: multi-layer FDR control for grouped hypotheses
Abstract: The p-filter provides a novel framework for the control of the false discovery rate (FDR) across a range of grouped hypothesis testing scenarios, where hypotheses can be categorized into distinct groups. This method adapts the well-established Benjamini-Hochberg procedure, a widely used approach for FDR control in a single-layer hypothesis testing framework, to effectively leverage the relationships between different groups of hypotheses. By integrating this adaptation into a multi-layer structure, the p-filter capitalizes on the relative similarities and contrasts between hypothesis groups to afford a more nuanced understanding of the relevant relationships and associated inference tasks. Specifically, the p-filter aims to identify inter-hypothesis group relationships through the incorporation of connectivity edges into a layered graph, thereby effectively grouping these relationships and optimizing FDR control for each layer. Its adaptive nature is also reflected in the iterative optimization of these relationships, as well as the associated penalty term for each layer, facilitating a more robust FDR control framework. Through its systematic consideration of hypothesis interdependence, the p-filter framework offers a more comprehensive approach to identifying key relationships across hypothesis groups, ultimately resulting in improved statistical inference outcomes. As a result of its adaptability and ability to handle complex group structures, the p-filter represents a promising tool for scenarios requiring an advanced, multi-layer FDR control framework.
