title: Boosted Sparse Non-linear Distance Metric Learning
Abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to non-linear distance metric learning, referred to as Boosted Sparse Non-linear Distance Metric Learning (BSNDML). The BSNDML technique leverages an ensemble learning framework to boost the performance of sparse non-linear distance metrics. In contrast to traditional linear distance metrics, BSNDML explores the complex relationships between data points by incorporating higher-order features and non-linear projections. The proposed method starts by using a boosting framework to select and combine a set of base distance metrics, each of which is learned using a sparse non-linear approach. This sparse non-linear distance metric learning is achieved through a combination of L1 regularization and non-linear transformations, such as radial basis functions and polynomial functions. To improve the efficiency of the algorithm, a subset of informative features is selected using recursive feature elimination. Furthermore, to adapt to the dynamic nature of data distributions, the BSNDML method incorporates a learning rate schedule and regularization parameter adjustment mechanism. Experimental results on several benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of BSNDML in boosting the performance of sparse non-linear distance metrics and improving the efficiency of feature-based distance metric learning. The results show that the proposed approach outperforms state-of-the-art distance metric learning methods in terms of the classification accuracy and convergence speed.

title: Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition
Abstract: Deep residual learning has revolutionized the field of computer vision by significantly improving the performance of image recognition tasks. This paper delves into the intricacies of residual networks, exploring their unique architecture and its implications on image classification. The residual learning framework allows direct feature transformation through a skip connection to bypass redundant feature learning, thereby improving the scalability of deep neural networks. By creating a residual mapping function that learns the difference between the input and the desired output, the model can learn more complex and abstract representations of the input data, leading to better generalization and performance. The introduction of residual connections has led to the development of various residual network variants, including ResNet-50 and ResNet-101, which have achieved state-of-the-art results in many benchmark datasets, including ImageNet. The ability to train residual networks with fewer iterations while achieving better performance has also made them more feasible for large-scale image classification tasks. This paper examines the recent developments in residual learning, its empirical successes, and its limitation, discussing the challenges and opportunities for future research directions in this area. Furthermore, it investigates the impact of residual learning on different types of neural network architectures, including convolutional networks, recurrent networks, and transformer networks, and explores their potential applications in image recognition, segmentation, and generation tasks.

title: VRFP: On-the-fly Video Retrieval using Web Images and Fast Fisher Vector Products
Abstract: Our proposed system, VRFP, addresses the challenge of on-the-fly video retrieval on large-scale databases by introducing a novel method that leverages the strengths of web images and fast Fisher vector products (FV). The advent of deep learning and computer vision has spurred the development of various video retrieval approaches, but existing methods often rely on computationally expensive and tedious indexing processes, hindering real-time video search capabilities. To overcome this limitation, VRFP employs a hybrid framework that uses web images to pre-train a Fisher vector model, which is then fine-tuned on the target video dataset. The fast FV algorithm accelerates the computation of feature representations, allowing for efficient video indexing and matching. Moreover, we propose an innovative saliency-based query expansion technique that identifies important regions within query images to improve the relevance of retrieved videos. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of VRFP, showcasing its ability to support fast and accurate video searching on massive datasets. By bridging the gap between web images and video analysis, VRFP offers a scalable and efficient solution for on-the-fly video retrieval, paving the way for wide adoption in various applications, including video surveillance, content-based video search, and multimedia information retrieval.

title: Convolutional Monte Carlo Rollouts in Go
Abstract: In the realm of combinatorial games, Go has remained an elusive challenge for artificial intelligence due to its abstract nature and vast potential moves. Current tree search algorithms often stumble upon time complexity and inefficiencies when dealing with the game's exponential branching factor. This paper introduces a novel approach that hybridizes Monte Carlo Rollouts with Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) to overcome these challenges. The proposed CNN-based Monte Carlo rollout method is built around a hierarchical state representation and uses a specially designed convolutional architecture to efficiently extract features from the game board. The CNN provides a more concise and task-relevant representation of the state, enabling the rollout policy to explore the vast Go search space more effectively. To evaluate the efficacy of the proposed method, we conducted a series of simulations on standard Go benchmarks using various opponents and search budgets. Our results demonstrate that the Convolutional Monte Carlo Rollouts significantly outperform state-of-the-art tree search algorithms like AlphaZero, achieving unbeatable winning percentages even in resource-constrained settings. This breakthrough enhances AI capabilities in the world of Go and potentially sets the stage for its application in other complex board games.

title: Adaptive Neural Control for Mobile Robots Autonomous Navigation
Abstract: This research paper explores the development of adaptive neural control strategies for mobile robots' autonomous navigation. Autonomous navigation poses significant challenges due to the dynamic and uncertain nature of the environment, including obstacles, varying terrain, and sensor noise. To address these challenges, this study proposes a novel adaptive neural control framework that integrates artificial neural networks with model predictive control. The proposed framework leverages the high-dimensional mapping capabilities of neural networks to learn the spatial relationships between the robot and its environment, while adaptively adjusting the control inputs to optimize navigation performance. Extensive simulation and real-world experiments were conducted using a wheeled mobile robot with a range of sensors, including lidars, cameras, and IMUs. The results demonstrate the superiority of the proposed adaptive neural control framework over traditional model-based approaches, showcasing improved navigation efficiency, accuracy, and robustness in various scenarios, including obstacle avoidance, terrain following, and dead-end detection. Moreover, the proposed framework's ability to learn from experience and adapt to changing environments enables the robot to improve its navigation performance over time, making it a promising solution for various robotic applications, from warehouse logistics to search and rescue operations. The developed framework also has the potential to be extended to more complex robotic systems, such as humanoid robots and drones, enabling them to navigate and interact with their environment in a more robust and efficient manner.

title: Guaranteed inference in topic models
Abstract: This paper tackles the challenge of guaranteed inference in topic models, a central problem in unsupervised natural language processing and machine learning. Topic models aim to discover underlying topics or themes in large document collections, but inference in these models has traditionally been approached using approximate methods, such as variational inference, that provide uncertain or probabilistic estimates of topic parameters. To address the limitations of current topic model inference methods, we develop a framework for guaranteed inference, where the inference goal is to find the optimal topic parameters that maximize a given quality metric. Our approach combines techniques from convex optimization and machine learning to derive a set of tractable algorithms that can scale to large document collections. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our guaranteed inference methods using a range of standard topic models, including Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) and Non_negative Matrix Factorization (NMF). Through extensive experiments on benchmark text datasets, we show that our methods consistently outperform state-of-the-art approximate inference algorithms and provide guaranteed bounds on the optimal topic assignments. The results highlight the potential of our framework for reliable and efficient topic modeling in a wide range of applications, particularly in high-stakes domains where accuracy and interpretability are critical.

title: Inference in topic models: sparsity and trade-off
Abstract: Inference in topic models, a widely used technique in natural language processing and information retrieval, involves recovering the underlying topic structure from a large corpus of documents. A major challenge in this process is in finding an optimal balance between goodness of fit and model complexity, particularly where sparsity plays a crucial role in facilitating interpretable results. This research explores the interplay between sparsity and trade-off in inference in topic models, focusing on the implications of sparsity-inducing penalties for achieving more accurate and reliable topic assignments. Building on recent advances in sparse inference methods, such as the Sparse Variational Bayes (SVB) algorithm, our work investigates how adapting these methods to align with sparse topic structures can lead to significant improvements in the fidelity of topic assignments and provide better interpretability of results. Experimental evaluations are conducted on a range of benchmark datasets to assess the effectiveness of the proposed approach and provide insights into its generalizability across different text corpora and topic models. Overall, this study aims to shed light on the value of sparsity in topic model inference, in terms of enabling more interpretable and accurate topic modeling results.

title: Norm-Free Radon-Nikodym Approach to Machine Learning
Abstract: This research proposes a novel machine learning framework that reconciles existing analytical and probabilistic approaches by leveraging the norm-free Radon-Nikodym derivative. The core hypothesis is that machine learning models can be viewed as transformations between probability spaces, thereby allowing the incorporation of diverse domain knowledge and mathematical structures. By bypassing traditional norms and metric assumptions, this framework enables flexible and robust learning processes that transcend the constraints of Euclidean geometry and well-defined probability measures. The norm-free Radon-Nikodym derivative provides a rigorous foundation for modeling distribution shifts, non-stationarity, and non-linearity, which are ubiquitous in real-world machine learning applications. To demonstrate the efficacy of this approach, several probabilistic and non-probabilistic machine learning algorithms, including those based on optimal transport, information geometry, and variational inequalities, are adaptively framed within this norm-free paradigm. The theoretical analysis and experimental results suggest that the proposed approach offers improved generalizability, robustness, and interpretability in diverse applications spanning classification, clustering, regression, and reinforcement learning. Furthermore, the computational efficiency of the norm-free approach allows for scalability and parallelization in high-dimensional data and big data settings. Overall, this research provides a fresh perspective on the foundations of machine learning and offers a unifying framework that transcends current methodological silos.

title: Gated networks: an inventory
Abstract: Gated networks have garnered significant attention in recent years due to their exceptional performance in modeling sequential data and dealing with the vanishing gradient problem. This paper aims to provide a comprehensive inventory of various types of gated networks, their architectures, and their applications in different fields. We begin by introducing the concept of gated networks and their predecessors, highlighting their limitations and the motivations behind the development of modern gated networks. The paper then delves into a detailed examination of the most popular types of gated networks, including Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs), and Gate Recurrent Unit with Learnable Gates (GRU-LG) networks. We investigate their architectures, training procedures, and modes of operation, providing an in-depth understanding of the mechanisms underlying these networks. Furthermore, the paper explores the applications of gated networks in natural language processing, speech recognition, time series prediction, and other fields, highlighting their ability to outperform traditional recurrent neural networks. Additionally, we discuss the recent advancements in gated network architecture design, including attention-based gated networks and transformers, which have significantly improved their performance on various tasks. Through a thorough analysis and comparison of different gated network architectures, this paper provides a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners seeking to understand and leverage the capabilities of gated networks in their applications.

title: Can small quantum systems learn?

Abstract:

The question of whether small quantum systems are capable of learning remains a topic of ongoing debate within the fields of quantum computing and quantum information science. Recent advances in quantum simulation and quantum control have made it possible to study the learning dynamics of small quantum systems, such as superconducting qubits, trapped ions, and ultracold atomic gases. These experiments have shown that small quantum systems can indeed exhibit learning-like behavior, including adaptation to changing environments and recall of previously learned information. However, the extent to which these phenomena can be described by deterministic quantum mechanics remains unclear. Furthermore, the trade-offs between accuracy, complexity, and robustness that arise when scaling up quantum learning systems to larger, more practical sizes continues to be an open challenge. In this research, we investigate the emergence of learning in small quantum systems and explore the underlying mechanisms that give rise to these phenomena. By combining experimental and theoretical approaches, we demonstrate that small quantum systems can learn through the coherent interaction of multiple degrees of freedom, suggesting a new paradigm for quantum computation and information processing. Our results have significant implications for the development of quantum technologies, including quantum information storage, processing, and communication.

title: Predicting proximity with ambient mobile sensors for non-invasive health diagnostics
Abstract: This study proposes a novel approach to non-invasive health diagnostics using ambient mobile sensors for predicting individual proximity. By leveraging the extensive availability of mobile devices and their pervasive sensor infrastructure, we can capitalize on the ambient sensing capabilities of smartphones and wearable devices to anticipate how individuals interact with their environment. Our research focuses on applying machine learning algorithms to data harvested from mobile sensors such as GPS, accelerometer, and proximity sensors in relation to the social and environmental contexts. We explore the notion that humans establish mobile-sensing 'atlas' of behaviors by capturing data-related to movement patterns and further contextual data such as people, weather, and daily routines. Through these analyses, we can glean substantial insights into health markers that distinguish healthy versus unhealthy behaviors, offering real-time alerts and predictive features to promote proactive health maintenance. Our approach aligns with the notion of 'artificial listening' that combines AI techniques with sensor enabled and mobile-based health analytics. In conducting this study, we compare machine learning methods to establish optimal health thresholds based on data from diverse populations, thereby improving health outcomes by promoting personalized well-informed decision making regarding disease prevention strategies. The findings of our research hope to unlock a wide range of mobile-enabled monitoring possibilities, ultimately providing advanced services promoting the prevention of diverse disorders, ranging from accidents to cardio vascular issues etc.

title: Deep Learning Algorithms with Applications to Video Analytics for A Smart City: A Survey
Abstract: Deep learning algorithms have revolutionized the field of video analytics, transforming the way cities approach urban planning and public safety through the creation of smart cities. This survey aims to provide a comprehensive examination of the most recent and promising deep learning methods applied to video analytics in a smart city setting. From object detection to action recognition and scene understanding, various deep learning techniques, including Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), and Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), are being explored for their potential to address the complex challenges faced by cities, such as traffic management, crime detection, and crowd monitoring. The applications of these algorithms are vast, ranging from smart surveillance systems that utilize computer vision to track and identify individuals in real-time, to intelligent traffic management systems that leverage video analytics to optimize traffic flow and reduce congestion. Furthermore, this survey delves into the importance of data annotation, pre-processing, and scalability in deploying these algorithms in real-world settings, highlighting the need for a robust infrastructure to support the successful integration of deep learning-based video analytics in smart cities. Through this comprehensive survey, we seek to provide a clearer understanding of the current state of deep learning-based video analytics and identify the key areas that require further research and development to create a more sustainable and livable smart city.

title: RSG: Beating Subgradient Method without Smoothness and Strong Convexity
Abstract: We propose a new stochastic gradient algorithm that is capable of beating the subgradient method in terms of convergence rate without requiring the smoothness and strong convexity conditions. This result is significant because previous state-of-the-art algorithms that were able to achieve faster convergence rates under less stringent assumptions were typically much more complicated, requiring additional parameters or approximating certain functions that are difficult to compute. In contrast, our proposed algorithm is simple, easy to implement, and computationally efficient. We establish the theoretical convergence rate of our algorithm using a novel analysis that leverages the properties of stochastic gradient methods in conjunction with a carefully designed projection step. Our analysis shows that our algorithm converges at a rate of O(1/k) in the expected function value, which matches the state-of-the-art rate for this class of problems. We also provide extensive numerical experiments that illustrate the efficacy of our algorithm on a range of synthetic and real-world datasets, and show that it outperforms the subgradient method in most cases. Furthermore, our algorithm has comparable performance to other competitive methods that do require strong convexity, but with a much simpler implementation and lower computational cost. Overall, our results demonstrate that beating the subgradient method without smoothness and strong convexity is possible, and provide a promising direction for future research in stochastic optimization.

title: Gamma Belief Networks
Abstract: Gamma belief networks, a variant of traditional Bayesian belief networks, have emerged as a powerful tool for modeling complex systems and uncertainties in decision-making processes. This research delves into the theoretical underpinnings, computational challenges, and real-world applications of gamma belief networks, while revisiting the foundational principles of Bayesian networks and exploring their mathematical and algorithmic intricacies. Through in-depth analysis of the gamma distribution's unique properties, such as its ability to closely approximate other probability distributions and handle truncation and skewness issues, the research shows how gamma belief networks can be successfully applied to diverse domains like finance, ecology, medicine, and engineering. By adopting probabilistic modeling approaches and leveraging the computational power of exponential family distributions, gamma belief networks have the potential to provide significant benefits in predictive analytics, risk assessment, and decision support systems. This study aims to comprehensively explore the strengths and limitations of gamma belief networks, compare them with traditional Bayesian networks and probabilistic graphical models, and evaluate their computational efficiency and scalability in handling large and complex networks, ultimately guiding their effective integration into real-world applications and expanding the scope of decision support systems.

title: Partial Reinitialisation for Optimisers
Abstract: Partial Reinitialisation for Optimisers tackles a critical issue in stochastic optimisation, where the choice of initialisation scheme and learning rate can significantly impact the convergence and performance of the optimisation algorithm. Traditional methods often either randomly initialise parameters or employ a global strategy that assumes a uniform learning rate for all parameters, which might not be suitable for complex or non-linear problems. Recent developments in partial reinitialisation methods aimed to dynamically adjust the learning rate based on the model's progress, but these methods can be computationally expensive and may not always capture the optimal learning rate. This study proposes a novel partial reinitialisation framework, dubbed PARO (Partial Adaptive Restart Optimiser), which selectively restarts the learning process for specific parameters or groups based on their relative progress and learning rate requirements. PARO strives to strike a balance between exploration and exploitation by exploiting the evolving structure of the objective function. Through empirical evaluations on a diverse range of benchmark problems, including synthetic and real-world datasets, PARO is shown to outperform or match state-of-the-art methods in terms of convergence speed and solution quality, whilst also offering a more interpretable and efficient optimisation process. The insights and findings in this study provide valuable guidelines for the development of future optimisation algorithms and techniques that could further enhance the efficiency and effectiveness of machine learning and artificial intelligence systems.

title: Learning measures of semi-additive behaviour
Abstract: This research paper delves into the realm of semi-additive behaviour, where the relationship between variables in a system is neither purely additive nor completely non-additive. It explores the various learning measures that can be employed to evaluate and quantify semi-additive systems, highlighting commonalities and differences between these measures. Semi-additive behaviour, where the sum of the parts in a system does not exactly equal the whole due to interactions or dependencies, is exhibited in a wide range of fields and applications, including biology, economics, and physics. Despite its prevalence, existing methodologies often fail to accurately capture and analyze semi-additive interactions, leading to potential misinterpretations and biases in decision-making processes. To address this knowledge gap, this paper examines existing learning measures used to identify and quantify semi-additive behaviour, including machine learning techniques, information-theoretic approaches, and statistical methods. Findings indicate that no single measure can comprehensively characterize semi-additive behaviour due to its inherent complexity, often requiring the combination of multiple techniques to obtain accurate insights. Consequently, this research contributes to the development of novel and hybrid learning measures tailored to the specific needs of semi-additive systems, paving the way for more robust and data-driven decision-making in complex, interactive environments.

title: Minimally Supervised Feature Selection for Classification (Master's Thesis, University Politehnica of Bucharest)
Abstract: This study focuses on a minimally supervised feature selection method tailored for classification problems, with a primary objective of identifying the most relevant features from a large dataset with minimal prior knowledge or labels. In current machine learning frameworks, feature selection methods often require extensive labeled data or sophisticated domain-specific knowledge to achieve optimal performance, which hampers their applicability and scalability to real-world, diverse datasets. Conversely, the proposed minimally supervised feature selection framework provides an efficient and flexible alternative for large-scale datasets by leveraging unlabeled data and meta-learning techniques. The approach integrates both unsupervised and supervised learning processes to identify the most informative features. Specifically, it starts by employing clustering algorithms to categorize the data into subgroups and subsequently select a subset of distinguished features based on their consistency across clusters. Then, a sparse classification model is utilized to further refine the selected features and improve predictive performance. Experimental evaluations are conducted on a variety of benchmark datasets to validate the efficacy and generalizability of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the minimally supervised feature selection approach outperforms comparable unsupervised baseline methods and achieves competitive performance with traditional supervised methods, thus offering a promising solution for challenging classification problems in various domains.

title: On Variants of k-means Clustering
Abstract: This abstract delves into the realm of k-means clustering, an extensively utilized unsupervised learning algorithm in machine learning and data analysis. The k-means algorithm, by its nature, partitions the data into distinct clusters, with each cluster represented by its centroid (mean) value. However, in real-world applications, data often exhibits high dimensionality, complex structures, and varying densities, posing challenges for traditional k-means to efficiently and accurately cluster the data. Against this backdrop, several variants of k-means clustering have emerged, aiming to address these limitations and enhance the clustering process. The partitioning around medoids (PAM), fuzzy c-means (FCM), Birch, DBSCAN, and k-medoids algorithms are among the variants discussed in this paper. These algorithms employ diverse strategies to mitigate the shortcomings of k-means, including employing alternative distance metrics, addressing noise and outlier sensitivity, and handling high dimensional data. The paper systematically examines the theoretical underpinnings and empirical performances of these variants, providing an in-depth analysis of their strengths, limitations, and applications. Furthermore, it compares and contrasts the performance of these variants using various benchmark datasets, thereby serving as a comprehensive resource for data analysts and researchers wishing to deploy k-means variants in their clustering tasks. By shedding light on the merits and demerits of these variants, this research aims to equip practitioners with the knowledge necessary to choose the most suitable k-means variant for their specific data analysis and machine learning endeavors.

title: Get More With Less: Near Real-Time Image Clustering on Mobile Phones
Abstract: Mobile devices have become increasingly powerful, enabling complex algorithms to be executed on behalf of their users, yet many image processing techniques designed for desktop environments still linger far behind in terms of computational efficiency and adaptability. Taking on the challenge of facilitating image clustering, a valuable image understanding task, on the limited hardware resources typically found in mobile devices remains crucial for ubiquitous and on-demand image analysis. This paper focuses on identifying and eliminating unnecessary computations within traditional image clustering techniques to further optimize the entire process and allow faster cluster formation. Embracing the demand for energy-efficient solutions, a local similarity criterion, namely, the Feature Similarity Index (FSI), is thoroughly examined and contrasted to validate the need for accelerated data processing. By integrating well-known and highly efficient approximation techniques to produce high-quality FSI approximations while omitting redundant computations, and performing an essential study of various well-attested algorithms devoted to significantly leveraging reduced constraints, our empirical testing confirms significant performance gains in terms of speed while saving precious memory within practical fieldwork on a real near real-time cluster formation environment. Our experiment outcomes shed light on optimized algorithmic modifications tailored for minimalistic devices with significant time efficiency benefits as well.

title: Efficient Distributed SGD with Variance Reduction
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel distributed stochastic gradient descent (SGD) algorithm with variance reduction for minimizing a large-scale objective function. The main challenge in distributed SGD is the high variance of stochastic gradients, which leads to unnecessary iterations and poor overall convergence rates. To address this issue, we leverage recent advancements in variance reduction techniques, including SAGA and SVRG, to develop a unified algorithm for distributed optimization. Our approach adaptively controls the variance reduction parameters based on the iteration count and local variance estimates, resulting in a highly efficient and scalable algorithm. Furthermore, we introduce a novel technique to accurately estimate the local variance in a distributed setting, which enables our algorithm to adapt to changing local gradient statistics and speed up the convergence process. We theoretically analyze the convergence properties of our algorithm and demonstrate its competence through extensive experimental evaluations on a range of large-scale datasets, including ImageNet and CIFAR-10. Our results show significant improvements over existing distributed optimization methods, highlighting the potential of our algorithm in accelerating the training of large-scale machine learning models.

title: Stochastic Interpretation of Quasi-periodic Event-based Systems
Abstract: This paper presents a novel stochastic interpretation framework for quasi-periodic event-based systems, which enables the analysis and verification of complex behaviors in such systems. Quasi-periodic event-based systems, characterized by a periodic basis signal with small perturbations, are ubiquitous in modern engineering applications, including digital communications, control systems, and real-time embedded systems. However, traditional analytical methods often fail to capture the uncertainties and variability inherent in these systems, leading to conservativeness and a lack of robustness. Our stochastic interpretation framework leverages concepts from stochastic calculus and probability theory to model and analyze quasi-periodic event-based systems as stochastic processes, capturing the random and time-varying nature of their behaviors. We define a probabilistic semantics for quasi-periodic event-based systems based on a stochastic basis signal, providing a platform for stochastic model checking, verification, and validation. Our approach enables the analysis of rare events and uncertainty propagation in these systems, facilitating the development of more reliable and robust designs. Furthermore, we demonstrate the practical applicability of our framework through case studies and experiments in digital communication systems, showcasing its potential to improve the performance and reliability of such systems. Overall, our stochastic interpretation of quasi-periodic event-based systems provides a powerful tool for addressing the challenges of stochastic analysis and verification in complex engineering applications.

title: Advances in quantum machine learning
Abstract: Quantum machine learning has emerged as a revolutionary field that exploits the principles of quantum mechanics to enhance the performance and efficiency of machine learning algorithms. This paradigm-shifting approach holds significant promise in addressing the limitations of traditional machine learning, which often rely on classical computational methods. The advent of quantum computing and quantum processing units (QPUs) has enabled researchers to develop quantum-inspired algorithms and quantum models that can efficiently tackle complex data sets and tasks. Notably, quantum techniques such as quantum k-means, quantum support vector machines, and quantum neural networks have been proposed and demonstrated to outperform their classical counterparts in various tasks, including clustering, classification, and regression. Furthermore, quantum machine learning algorithms have the potential to break through the barriers of the curse of dimensionality and the noise-tolerance problem, enabling efficient processing of high-dimensional data and robustness against noise and errors. Despite these promising results, significant challenges remain in developing practical quantum machine learning applications, including the need for scalable and fault-tolerant quantum computing architectures, effective quantum noise reduction strategies, and accurate software tools for quantum circuit synthesis and optimization.

title: Where You Are Is Who You Are: User Identification by Matching Statistics
Abstract: This study explores the concept of user identification through matching statistics, proposing that an individual's geographic location and associated statistical data can uniquely define their identity. By leveraging geographic information systems (GIS) and data analytics techniques, researchers have the ability to collect and analyze vast amounts of information related to an individual's location, including demographics, socioeconomic factors, and behavioral patterns. The idea is that this information can be used to create a unique statistical profile, which can serve as a form of identification. The research aims to investigate the feasibility and accuracy of this approach, examining whether it is possible to match individuals with their corresponding statistical profiles and determine the level of uniqueness of these profiles. Additionally, the study seeks to address potential concerns related to data privacy and security, as well as the potential applications and limitations of this method in various fields, such as law enforcement, marketing, and social sciences. The results of this research have significant implications for our understanding of personal identity and the role of location in shaping individual characteristics. By providing a comprehensive analysis of the concept of user identification through matching statistics, this study contributes to ongoing discussions about the intersection of technology, geography, and identity.

title: Embedding Label Structures for Fine-Grained Feature Representation
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to fine-grained feature representation by leveraging label structures for embedding in an unsupervised manner. The conventional methods typically rely on a fixed representation for each class, which may not capture the intricate relationships among classes, especially in fine-grained settings where classes may share similar characteristics. Addressing this limitation, the proposed approach applies a graph-based embedding method that incorporates label relationships as a structural constraint, allowing the learned representations to capture the nuanced differences between classes. The core idea is to construct a graph called the label structure graph, where each node corresponds to a class, and two nodes are connected by an edge if their classes are semantically related. By leveraging this graph structure, the proposed method learns to embed classes in a high-dimensional space where their distances accurately reflect their semantic proximity. The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in improving the fine-grained feature representation, leading to significant performance improvements on several benchmark datasets for image classification tasks. With its interpretability and ability to capture the inherent structure of labels, the proposed method has the potential to revolutionize the field of fine-grained feature learning and representation. The study's novel contribution lies in its unique perspective on label relationships and its applicability to various domains where the class hierarchy is known.

title: Multi-Player Bandits -- a Musical Chairs Approach
Abstract: This abstract delves into the concept of Multi-Player Bandits, a game-theoretic framework for non-stationary environments where multiple agents autonomously decide their actions while collecting rewards. By modeling this scenario with Musicals Chairs, we formulate a combinatorial problem that exemplifies the challenges in Multi-Player Bandits. We provide a novel algorithm, called Player-Action-Fairness (PAF) algorithm, which effectively handles the non-stationarity of the environment and the asynchronous nature of the players' actions, resulting in fairness among players, given the dynamically changing environment. The PAF algorithm achieves this through a two-stage approach: first, by maximizing the reward of each player individually, and then, by ensuring players' fairness through a fairness metric. We further demonstrate the convergence of the PAF algorithm to a Nash equilibrium from arbitrary initial conditions through mathematical analysis. A comprehensive experimental validation of the algorithm is performed on a suite of benchmark multi-player bandit problems, demonstrating comparable or superior performance of the PAF algorithm to existing approaches. Our results highlight the effectiveness of the Musical Chairs analogy in Multi-Player Bandits, providing insights into the mechanisms of autonomy, fairness, and convergence that underlie such systems.

title: Bigger Buffer k-d Trees on Multi-Many-Core Systems
Abstract: Modern multi-many-core systems have become a key factor in driving scientific and technological innovation. However, these systems pose significant challenges when it comes to algorithms that require large amounts of memory and synchronization, such as k-d trees, commonly used in various fields like computer graphics, machine learning, and nearest neighbor search. This research paper explores the possibility of building bigger buffer k-d trees on multi-many-core systems to improve the efficiency of these algorithms. Our proposed approach utilizes a combination of hardware techniques, including large memory compartments, simultaneous multi-threading, and cache coherence management, to accommodate large buffer sizes. Additionally, a novel software design based on parallel and concurrent insertion and deletion of points from the k-d tree is presented to improve the overall performance. An evaluation of our proposed method on a number of benchmarks and datasets is conducted, demonstrating significant improvements over the original bufferless k-d tree algorithm. Results show that our approach can achieve up to two orders of magnitude performance increase, scalability up to 256 cores, and efficient memory usage. The proposed bigger buffer k-d tree on multi-many-core systems is a promising solution for applications requiring large-scale k-d tree operations, enabling more efficient and effective use of these algorithms.

title: Convergence of Entropic Schemes for Optimal Transport and Gradient Flows
Abstract: This abstract explores the convergence properties of entropic regularization methods for solving the optimal transport problem and gradient flow equations, which are fundamental in studying the behavior of physical and social systems. By incorporating an entropic term into the classical cost function of optimal transport, the regularized problem can be approximated using numerical methods such as stochastic gradient descent. However, ensuring the convergence of these schemes to the original transport problem is crucial. We analyze the convergence rate and the effects of varying parameters, including the regularization strength and the resolution of the numerical grid. Additionally, we investigate the efficiency of these schemes in approximating gradient flows, which are used to model the evolution of physical and biological systems. Our framework leverages tools from convex analysis, fluid mechanics, and mathematical statistics to establish a general theoretical underpinning for the convergence of entropic schemes. We provide numerical examples that demonstrate the behavior of these schemes in practice, showcasing their versatility and accuracy in solving nonlinear partial differential equations.

title: Affinity CNN: Learning Pixel-Centric Pairwise Relations for Figure/Ground Embedding
Abstract: This paper introduces Affinity CNN, a novel neural network architecture that capitalizes on the inherent strengths of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to learn pixel-centric pairwise relations, thereby enabling effective figure/ground embedding. The proposed approach leverages prior works on pairwise potentials and dilated spatial pyramid pooling, integrating them to efficiently model object region relationships. Affinity CNN incorporates a novel pairwise affinity module, designed to compute high-quality relationships between pixels across different scales and spatial hierarchies, thus capturing inherent visual dependencies. This helps to establish more robust correspondences between image regions, and consequently, facilitates better segmentation and object discovery. Furthermore, the model incorporates a multi-resolution embedding mechanism, allowing for the exploration of various spatial scales, resulting in an enriched figure/ground embedding that transcends the limitations of conventional pixel-wise representations. A thorough evaluation on various benchmark datasets demonstrates that Affinity CNN achieves superior performance in figure-ground segmentation, object detection, and top-down recognition tasks. The results showcase the efficacy of the proposed architecture in capturing sophisticated object relationships and visual hierarchies, underscoring its potential to contribute towards groundbreaking advancements in various computer vision applications. By effectively capturing pixel-centric pairwise relations, the proposed approach paves the way for innovative applications in areas such as object discovery, scene understanding, and image manipulation, laying the groundwork for comprehensive vision-based analysis and synthesis.

title: A Novel Regularized Principal Graph Learning Framework on Explicit Graph Representation
Abstract: This paper presents a novel regularized principal graph learning framework, which endeavors to extract underlying graph patterns in both explicit and implicit relationships between various entities. By employing a manifold-based representation, the developed model can effectively capture non-linear dependencies within a graph. The proposed framework, referred to as GraphEigenReg, is built upon a unique interplay between two crucial components, namely, the principal graph learning module and a novel regularizer term. The principal graph learning module primarily focuses on discovering the dominant graph topology through dimensionality reduction, while the novel regularizer term ensures the robustness of the extracted graph against noise contamination and redundancy. Notably, the GraphEigenReg framework involves an amalgam of spectral graph theory and harmonic analysis. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first attempt to incorporate the theory of harmonic analysis into the domain of graph learning. Consequently, the resulting principal graphs exhibits superior interpretability and accuracy, especially in distinguishing discriminative and non-discriminative edges in the underlying graph. Our extensive experimental evaluations on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate the efficacy and superiority of the GraphEigenReg framework over several state-of-the-art graph learning algorithms.

title: Perfect Recovery Conditions For Non-Negative Sparse Modeling
Abstract: This research delves into the optimization of recovery conditions for non-negative sparse modeling, a paradigmatic technique employed in signal processing, machine learning, and image analysis. Through careful analysis of existing literature, the study identifies that exact recovery conditions for commonly used sparse models, such as the non-negative least squares (NNLS) and the non-negative Lasso, remain a subject of ongoing research. Notably, the conventional exact recovery conditions are frequently achieved in contexts with i.i.d. measurement matrices, i.e., Gaussian measurements. However, practical signals and measurements typically exhibit structured sparsity, resulting in significantly challenging recovery scenarios. In light of these issues, the proposed research aims to establish a more comprehensive understanding of recovery conditions for non-negative sparse modeling. Specifically, the study employs a range of theoretical instruments and computational experiments to elucidate when non-negative sparse recovery is successful and the range of reliable algorithmic choices for various sparse structures, including polyhedral sparsity patterns. Furthermore, techniques to ensure accuracy in such recovery under weaker models of measurements, often encountered in applications such as image denoising and audio editing, are carefully examined. By refining the recovery conditions and improving computational performance, this research enables more widespread and robust adoption of non-negative sparse modeling, ultimately facilitating real-world applications in signal processing and its allied fields.

title: Window-Object Relationship Guided Representation Learning for Generic Object Detections
Abstract: This work presents a novel, Window-Object Relationship Guided Representation Learning for Generic Object Detection (WORGL) methodology, which leverages the interplay between windows and objects in images to enhance detection performance on diverse generic object classes. By analyzing the interactions between windows, objects, and contexts, our model effectively learns to recognize and differentiate between various types of objects and their relationships. Specifically, the WORGL framework includes a window-object relationship learning module, which captures intricate interactions between windows, objects, and contexts. This allows the model to generate features that are more informative and robust for object detection tasks. We propose an object query driven window sampling strategy that effectively samples windows centered at object queries to focus the model's attention on regions of high object likelihood. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that WORGL outperforms state-of-the-art methods in detection metrics such as precision, recall, and F1-score on challenging datasets such as PASCAL VOC 2007, 2012, and COCO 2017. Furthermore, our approach shows superior performance under real-world conditions, with high robustness to object appearance variations, occlusions, and significant background clutter. Overall, our research provides a compelling case for the effectiveness of the WORGL model in tackling generic object detection tasks, paving the way for its potential applications in robotics, surveillance, and smart vision systems.

title: Distributed Training of Deep Neural Networks with Theoretical Analysis: Under SSP Setting
Abstract: This abstract explores the distributed training of deep neural networks under the strong sparsity pattern (SSP) setting-the scenario where the weight of a neural network follows a strong topological structure, which can be leveraged to optimize performance. By examining the most recent algorithmic approaches and theoretical analyses in the context of distributed deep learning, we investigate the feasibility of meeting critical performance standards of large-scale models within a parallel computing framework based on distributed training. Current studies on the efficiency of parallelization techniques, notably those based on data and model parallelization, are detailed, as well as state-of-the-art practices for effectively handling the communication overhead inherent to parallel computation. To address model convergence and communication efficiency, this study assesses notable distributed optimization algorithms, focusing on convergence rates and time complexities. By evaluating the role of a key variable - the SSP structure's properties on key properties of the optimization algorithm like convergence rate of some specific algorithms used to achieve global optimality. We conclude by investigating and evaluating possible optimization settings specifically targeted at the SSP structural property of the neural networks, showing a trade-off between performance optimization and complexity and exploring applications in areas where such efficiency is critical, enabling the training of larger and more complex models.

title: Reinforcement Control with Hierarchical Backpropagated Adaptive Critics
Abstract: Our research endeavors to extend the realm of classical reinforcement learning by introducing a Hierarchical Backpropagated Adaptive Critics (HBAC) framework, aimed at overcoming the limitations associated with prevalent single-agency and multi-agent reinforcement control methods. Within the proposed HBAC paradigm, self-organizing neural critics are intertwined with hierarchical decision-making architectures, synergizing to effectively navigate complex, dynamic environments where single policy optimization or even multi-policy coordination may falter. By employing hierarchical learning protocols and adaptive critics, the HBAC framework is capable of disentangling the hierarchy between complex behaviors and subsequently identifying value function update objectives that diverge and converge recursively across multiple scales of abstraction. Consequently, the HBAC design unlocks a novel method for fine-grained value function representation and policy development, positioning it as a superior alternative in domains involving complex high-dimensional action spaces and rapid, ephemeral environment evolution. Demonstrated efficacy in the HBAC framework's potential to tackle nuanced control tasks within dynamic game environments, particularly those posing exceptional challenges for conventional policy and action updates based reinforcement control methods, is reinforced by empirical evidence stemming from critical multi-agent testing procedures.

title: Speeding Up Distributed Machine Learning Using Codes
Abstract: This abstract focuses on the crucial issue of accelerating distributed machine learning (DML) using modern codes that can efficiently partition, process, and synchronize data amongst nodes in a cluster. To achieve scalability, speed, and reliability, the current approach in DML centers around minimizing communication and computation redundancy through the implementation of codes designed from coding theory. Low-Density Parity-Check (LDPC) codes, Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC) codes, and Reed-Solomon codes have been relatively considered due to their error correction capability, which is specifically beneficial in overcoming computation node failures within the distributed computation cluster. The primary target in our research is investigating novel code designs optimally matched to specific data types and machine learning algorithms, ultimately facilitating significant speed-up through minimized communication and increased parallel processing, balancing the system efficiency and fault tolerance. An exhaustive comparative evaluation of commonly used codes and implementation frameworks is utilized to develop efficient and low-latency schemes addressing potential bottlenecks in the existing topologies with scalable fault tolerance.

title: Extremum Seeking-based Iterative Learning Model Predictive Control (ESILC-MPC)
Abstract: This paper presents an innovative control strategy integrating extremum seeking and model predictive control to optimize system performance in the presence of uncertainty and nonlinearity, leading to the development of the Extremum Seeking-based Iterative Learning Model Predictive Control (ESILC-MPC) framework. By combining the capabilities of extremum seeking, which enables efficient identification of optimal operating conditions, and model predictive control, which allows for real-time optimization of system behavior based on predictions of future states, the proposed ESILC-MPC framework leverages iterative learning control to adaptively refine predictive models and enhance control performance over time. The robust and high-performance closed-loop dynamics enabled by ESILC-MPC are suitable for applications involving real-time optimization, performance maximization, and disturbance rejection in complex, nonlinear, and uncertain systems. This study demonstrates rigorous theoretical foundation and comprehensive validation results illustrating the efficacy of ESILC-MPC in overcoming the challenges faced by traditional nonlinear control methods. Furthermore, the proposed framework is demonstrated to outperform existing iterative learning model predictive control methods through simulations and experiments, thereby showcasing its ability to serve as a cutting-edge solution for real-world systems demand of high precision and reliability in demanding industrial settings with a significant degree of adaptability to varying operational scenarios.

title: Deep Speech 2: End-to-End Speech Recognition in English and Mandarin
Abstract: Deep Speech 2 is a pioneering approach to end-to-end speech recognition, revolutionizing the field by leveraging deep learning techniques to improve the accuracy of speech-to-text systems in both English and Mandarin languages. This study delves into the design and implementation of a novel neural network model that efficiently handles the complexities of speech recognition, including pronunciation, vocabulary, and phonetic variations. Unlike traditional hybrid models, which rely on hand-crafted features and statistical machine translation, the proposed Deep Speech 2 model learns to represent speech signals directly from raw audio inputs, eliminating the need for explicit feature extraction and alignment steps. The model's architecture is founded on a multi-stream convolutional neural network (CNN) and recurrent neural network (RNN), which work in tandem to capture temporal and spatial patterns in speech signals. Through extensive experimentation and evaluation on a wide range of speech datasets, including Librispeech and AISHELL-1, the study demonstrates the efficacy of Deep Speech 2 in achieving state-of-the-art performance for both English and Mandarin languages, outperforming previous models in terms of word error rate (WER) and phoneme recognition accuracy. Furthermore, the study sheds light on the importance of exploring domain-specific architectures and training objectives to further improve the performance of end-to-end speech recognition systems in low-resource languages and scenarios involving noisy or degraded audio.

title: Selective Sequential Model Selection
Abstract: This work presents a novel approach to model selection that enhances the accuracy and efficiency of statistical modeling by incorporating sequential decision-making under uncertainty. A selective sequential model selection framework is developed, where the sequential selection of predictive models is optimized based on an adaptive and data-driven evaluation of their performance. A key contribution of this framework is the incorporation of model selection criteria that account for both goodness-of-fit and the potential for overfitting, enabling accurate identification of models that strike an optimal balance between these competing objectives. The proposed framework leverages state-of-the-art techniques from Bayesian model selection and sequential decision theory, and utilizes recent advances in Markov chain Monte Carlo and variational inference methods to facilitate efficient and approximate computation of model likelihoods and posterior probabilities. A range of experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the selective sequential model selection framework across diverse datasets and applications, including time-series forecasting, regression tasks, and unsupervised clustering problems. Results show significant improvements in predictive performance, model interpretability, and computational efficiency compared to traditional model selection strategies. Furthermore, this work provides a comprehensive theoretical foundation for sequential model selection and offers a set of practical guidelines for implementing this framework in various statistical modeling contexts.

title: Deep Learning for Single and Multi-Session i-Vector Speaker Recognition
Abstract: Deep learning techniques have revolutionized the field of speaker recognition, significantly outperforming traditional machine learning methods. This paper investigates the application of deep learning for single and multi-session i-vector speaker recognition, which is a popular approach for speaker authentication. The i-vector representation extracts speaker-specific information from the cepstral domain and serves as an input to the speaker recognition system. In the context of single-session speaker recognition, deep neural networks (DNNs) trained with large-scale datasets have achieved state-of-the-art performance. However, with limited data available, multi-session speaker recognition poses a significant challenge due to the variability in speaking styles and acoustic conditions across different sessions. To address this, we propose a novel approach that combines a feed-forward neural network (FFNN) with a fully connected neural network (FCN) to model the speaker's intra-session variability and inter-session variability, respectively. Our method leverages the strengths of both DNNs and i-vectors, achieving promising results on the NIST SRE dataset and the VoxCeleb benchmark. Furthermore, we conduct extensive experiments to evaluate the performance of our proposed method under various conditions, including sessions with and without noise, and varying lengths of training and test sessions. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, which outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques in several cases, and improves the robustness of speaker recognition in the presence of noise and variability.

title: Gibbs-type Indian buffet processes
Abstract: The Indian Buffet Process (IBP) is a Bayesian nonparametric prior that represents a distribution over subsets of a ground set via stick-breaking, providing a flexible and probabilistic modeling framework for numerous applications in data analysis, particularly in unsupervised learning and clustering tasks. Despite its successes, two primary limitations of traditional IBPs restrict their broader adoption: the restrictive modeling assumption that each item in the ground set is independently observed, and the impractical computations involved in its inference process due to its complexity. This necessitates the development of more expressive and computationally efficient variations of the traditional IBP. In response to these challenges, the Gibbs-type Indian Buffet Process (GtIBP) has emerged as a promising extension of the IBP, which incorporates shared components across items, such as structured or clustered data, while leveraging efficient Gibbs sampling-based inference strategies to facilitate scalable and reliable computation. The GtIBP's robust modeling capabilities and adaptable computational framework have made it a versatile tool in a wide array of applications, including semi-supervised learning, clustering, and topic modeling, with implications for numerous disciplines and industries.

title: Breaking the log n barrier on rumor spreading
Abstract: This paper explores the challenge of breaking the log n barrier on rumor spreading in a network, where n represents the number of nodes within the network. Traditional epidemic spreading models, such as the Independent Cascade and the Linear Threshold models, have been widely used to study the spread of information in networks. However, these models often fail to capture the unique characteristics of real-world networks and result in information spreading at a logarithmic rate. Recent advancements in information diffusion models have shown that, under specific conditions, it is possible to achieve a super-logarithmic spread rate, allowing information to spread faster. This paper aims to identify the conditions under which this can be achieved and to derive new algorithms that can break the log n barrier. By analyzing the structure of real-world networks and using insights from machine learning and graph theory, the authors develop a novel rumor-spreading algorithm that can efficiently spread information in a network while minimizing the spread of misinformation. The results show that this algorithm can achieve a significantly faster spread rate than traditional epidemic spreading models, with applications in areas such as social network analysis, information diffusion, and rumor control.

title: Deep Exemplar 2D-3D Detection by Adapting from Real to Rendered Views
Abstract: This paper presents a novel deep learning-based approach for detecting objects in 2D images by leveraging 3D object information. The proposed method, coined as Deep Exemplar 2D-3D Detection, adapts from real-world views to rendered views, effectively bridging the gap between the two modalities. By utilizing a combination of feature generators and shape-aware discriminators, the model simultaneously predicts 2D bounding boxes and 3D object parameters. To address this challenging task, the proposed framework incorporates a conditional Generative Adversarial Network (cGAN) module, which enables the model to capture both photometric and geometric variations between real and rendered views. Through a novel two-stage training process, the cGAN module is first trained to predict 3D shapes from real images, and then fine-tuned to refine the 3D predictions and generate corresponding rendered views. This approach allows the model to adapt to the complex visual transformations and occlusions present in real-world images. Experiments on several benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, achieving state-of-the-art results for 2D-3D detection and demonstrating its potential for a wide range of applications, including robotics, autonomous driving, and augmented reality. Overall, the proposed method significantly advances the state-of-the-art in 2D-3D detection, showcasing the value of adapting from real to rendered views for improved object detection performance.

title: High-Dimensional Gaussian Copula Regression: Adaptive Estimation and Statistical Inference
Abstract: This paper delves into the realm of high-dimensional Gaussian copula regression, a statistical framework that combines the strengths of Gaussian processes and copula theory to model complex relationships between variables. In the high-dimensional setting where the number of covariates exceeds the sample size, traditional regression methods often suffer from the curse of dimensionality, leading to poor estimation and inference. The proposed approach adapts to this challenge by employing a copula-based framework that permits flexible modeling of complex dependence structures between variables. The key innovation lies in the development of adaptive estimation procedures for the copula parameters, which leverage recent advances in high-dimensional statistics and optimization techniques. These procedures enable consistent and computationally efficient estimation of the copula parameters, even in the presence of strong dependence between covariates. Furthermore, the paper develops a comprehensive framework for statistical inference, including the derivation of confidence intervals and hypothesis tests for the model parameters. Extensive simulations and real-data applications demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach in high-dimensional regression settings, showcasing its potential for tackling complex problems in finance, biology, and other fields.

title: Explaining NonLinear Classification Decisions with Deep Taylor Decomposition
Abstract: The Deep Taylor Decomposition (DTD) is a novel neural network interpretation technique that enables insight into the nonlinear classification decisions made by deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs). Traditional Taylor decomposition methods, while effective for linear models, fail to provide meaningful interpretations for the complex decision boundaries of deep CNNs. DTD bridges this gap by employing a recursive decomposition strategy that leverages the hierarchical structure of CNNs. Through this decomposition, DTD identifies the intermediate feature representations that contribute most significantly to the classification outcome, shedding light on the complex interactions between local image features and the network's learned representations. A comprehensive evaluation of DTD shows its ability to uncover the dominant features driving the classification decisions of deep CNNs, while also highlighting the need to consider these intermediate representations when diagnosing errors or optimizing network performance. Our results demonstrate the practical value of DTD in uncovering insightful patterns within the decision-making process of deep CNNs, representing a step towards creating more transparent and accountable AI decision-making systems. By peeling back the layers of the complex neural architecture, DTD allows users to probe the inner workings of CNNs, facilitating the development of more accurate and more interpretable models.

title: Hankel Matrices for Weighted Visibly Pushdown Automata
Abstract: This paper provides a novel approach to studying Weighted Visibly Pushdown Automata (WVPA) using Hankel matrices. Our work primarily focuses on the theoretical and computational aspects of this application, covering the automatic construction of Hankel matrices for the recognized weighted languages of WVPA, through algorithms provided and justified by new models presented in the text. The use of Hankel matrices in this context aids in the synthesis of the automata, enabling subsequent state minimization procedures. The significance of Hankel matrices in this topic pertains to the theoretical frameworks behind many applications of formal languages to computer science, including particularly compiler design and regular expression matching, where pushdown storage structures predominate, due to the need for context-free memory allocation. By introducing Hankel matrices and their use as a succinct representation of recognizable weighted languages accepted by WVPA, we establish an understanding of new potentiality of these matrices to solve certain long-standing problems. title: Learning Discrete Bayesian Networks from Continuous Data
Abstract: The process of learning discrete Bayesian networks from continuous data remains a significant challenge in the field of machine learning and artificial intelligence. Conventional approaches for learning Bayesian networks rely on discrete variables and cannot effectively handle continuous data, resulting in a significant loss of information and decreased accuracy. To address this issue, various methods have been developed to discretize continuous variables, but these methods are often unreliable and not universally applicable. Recent advancements in dimensionality reduction techniques have shown promise in overcoming these limitations by enabling the effective handling of high-dimensional continuous data. This research paper proposes an innovative framework for learning discrete Bayesian networks from continuous data, incorporating a novel multi-resolution dimensionality reduction technique for effective ordinal discretization of continuous variables. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach demonstrates superior performance compared to existing methods in learning accurate and interpretable discrete Bayesian networks from continuous data. Furthermore, the developed framework is shown to be computationally efficient and scalable for large-scale datasets, opening new avenues for its applications in data-driven decision-making and predictive modeling in various fields, including computer vision, healthcare, and finance.

title: Online Gradient Descent in Function Space
Abstract: Online gradient descent in function space is a variant of the gradient descent algorithm tailored to optimize objective functions over an infinite-dimensional space of functions, a crucial scenario in applications such as machine learning on manifolds and physics-informed neural networks. The algorithm, which typically iterates over a Hilbert space equipped with an inner product and a compatible norm, is designed to handle high-dimensional and non-Euclidean geometries, rendering traditional gradient-based methods inadequate. This novel approach adopts a parameterization of the function space via a finite-dimensional basis consisting of the initial hypothesis with additional hierarchical layers that incrementally refine its quality. By leveraging the functional gradient and its orthogonal projection onto the finite-dimensional space supported by the basis, the algorithm updates iteratively the function parameters to achieve convergence to the optimal solution within this parameter space, mitigating noise and facilitating generalization. Experiments with the algorithm reveal superior performance and robustness in complex nonlinear problems when data-driven regularization is employed. Despite its rich theoretical underpinnings, this work initiates investigations into the convergence rates of the algorithm to understand its scaling with problem size and number of layers, essential for harnessing the full potential of online gradient descent in function space within high-dimensional nonlinear optimization applications.

title: Online Crowdsourcing
Abstract:
Online crowdsourcing has revolutionized the way businesses and organizations operate, leveraging the collective abilities and talents of virtual crowds to achieve specific goals. This study delves into the world of online crowdsourcing, examining the dynamics of how virtual workers collaborate, contribute, and interact with each other and with clients. Our research reveals that online crowdsourcing platforms, such as Upwork, Freelancer, and Fiverr, have created new opportunities for individuals and micro-enterprises to participate in the global economy, breaking down geographical barriers and increasing access to a global talent pool.

Through a mixed-methods approach combining quantitative and qualitative data collection and analysis, we investigate the impact of online crowdsourcing on business outcomes, including productivity, cost savings, and quality of work. Our results indicate that online crowdsourcing can be an effective strategy for businesses seeking to augment their internal resources, accelerate project completion, and improve work quality. However, we also identify challenges such as communication breakdowns, quality control, and worker burnout, highlighting the need for platform providers and clients to implement measures to address these issues. Furthermore, our study explores the concept of online community, examining how virtual workers form relationships, develop trust, and build cohesion within online environments. Our findings suggest that online crowdsourcing platforms can foster a sense of community, enabling workers to collaborate, share knowledge, and support one another in their work. As online crowdsourcing continues to grow in popularity, our research contributes to the development of more effective platforms and policies that prioritize worker well-being, community building, and business success.

title: Fast spectral algorithms from sum-of-squares proofs: tensor decomposition and planted sparse vectors
Abstract: Our work bridges the gap between theoretical sum-of-squares interpretations of polynomial-time algorithms and their implementation in practice, producing 'fast' spectral approximation methods. A sum-of-squares (SOS) proof serves as a tool for establishing a wide range of optimization algorithms being efficient. The robustness and significance of SOS techniques inspired us to explore their implications toward fast low-rank tensor decomposition algorithms and on the recovery of planted sparse vectors in linear inverse problems. Our main contribution lies in the development of algorithms having connections to polynomial identity testing - based hardness which convert SOS certificates into computationally and considerably efficient approximation bounds. This conversion allows computing polynomial approximations of certain vector or tensor components with reliable results within a short span of time. We put forward a novel connection, both theoretically and through simple approximation insights, where tensor decomposition turns out to be equivalent to efficient sum-of-squares certificates and in addition, apply it toward planted sparse signal recovery that plays a key aspect of several areas of science and engineering. The key novel contribution hereby is turning over the robust approximations and SOS proofs' utility onto the fast practical use. As an end result, the developed algorithms are more efficient not merely in their time complexity, but also significantly easier to compute within practical scope.

title: Learning to Point and Count
Abstract: This study investigates the development of pointing and counting skills in young children, a fundamental building block of cognitive and linguistic abilities. Researchers have long recognized the importance of these skills for language acquisition, social communication, and problem-solving. However, the exact developmental pathways and underlying mechanisms governing pointing and counting remain poorly understood. Drawing on evidence from cognitive psychology, linguistics, and education, this research examines the role of social interaction, cultural context, and individual differences in shapping early pointing and counting abilities. Using a longitudinal design and mixed-methods approach, we analyzed data from 200 children, aged 12-36 months, who engaged in regular pointing and counting activities with their caregivers. Our findings reveal significant associations between pointing and counting skills, social interaction, and cultural context. Specifically, we show that children's pointing and counting abilities are predictive of later language development, and that social interaction with caregivers plays a critical role in facilitating these skills. Importantly, our results also highlight the significance of cultural context in shaping early pointing and counting abilities, and suggest that caregivers' use of pointing and counting behaviors can have a lasting impact on children's cognitive and linguistic development. These findings have important implications for early childhood education and parental interventions aimed at promoting language acquisition and cognitive development in young children.

title: Direct Intrinsics: Learning Albedo-Shading Decomposition by Convolutional Regression
Abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to learn albedo-shading decomposition from a single image, which is a fundamental task in computer vision and deep learning. The proposed method is based on a convolutional regression model that leverages a direct intrinsics framework to accurately predict the albedo and shading components from a given image. By directly learning the albedo-shading decomposition, this approach eliminates the need for temporal information or specialized hardware, making it more accessible and efficient for practical applications. The model is trained using a large-scale synthetic dataset that includes various objects, materials, and lighting conditions, allowing it to generalize well to real-world scenarios. The experimental results demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method over state-of-the-art approaches, achieving higher accuracy and robustness in albedo and shading estimation. Furthermore, the method is shown to be effective in a variety of applications, such as material recognition, object segmentation, and reflectance manipulation. Overall, this paper presents a significant advancement in the field of computer vision, offering a reliable and efficient solution for albedo-shading decomposition from a single image, with applications in graphics, computer vision, and machine learning. The proposed method has the potential to revolutionize the way we analyze and understand the visual properties of objects in images and videos.
