title: Nonparametric Reduced-Rank Regression for Multi-SNP, Multi-Trait Association Mapping
Abstract: In recent years, the rapid advancement of high-throughput genotyping technologies has greatly increased the availability of genetic data, enabling researchers to conduct genome-wide association studies(GWAS). However, the size and complexity of the data typically exceed the capacity of conventional association analysis methods, making it difficult to identify relationships between multiple traits and complex genetic variants in a single model. To tackle this challenge, a nonparametric reduced-rank regression (NNRR) model was developed for multi-SNP, multi-trait association mapping. The new method utilizes a series of restricted Boltzmann machines to handle large datasets by incorporating a dimensionality reduction principle, resulting in improved interpretability and predictive performance. The proposed approach not only addresses the limitations of traditional GWAS methods but also facilitates the identification of pleiotropic signals and complex interactions among multiple traits and genetic variants. Simulation results and real-world data analysis demonstrate the effectiveness of the NNRR approach in detecting causal effects, estimating genetic correlations, and identifying enriched biological pathways and risk loci. Furthermore, the method has the potential to uncover novel and biologically relevant genetic associations, serving as a powerful tool for the discovery of complex genetic architecture underlying complex traits and diseases. By leveraging the strengths of nonparametric and reduced-rank methodologies, the NNRR framework may lead to significant advances in genetic epidemiology and personalized medicine.

title: Creating Electronic Books-Chapters for Computers and Tablets Using Easy Java/JavaScript Simulations, EjsS Modeling Tool
Abstract: EjsS Modeling Tool has been increasingly gaining popularity in educational settings due to its user-friendly interface, ease of use, and ability to create interactive simulations. This paper explores the possibilities of utilizing EjsS Modeling Tool to create electronic books with interactive chapters for computers and tablets. By incorporating JavaScript simulations into EjsS, educators and researchers can develop immersive learning experiences that cater to the needs of diverse learners. The research investigates the effectiveness of using EjsS to create interactive electronic books and chapters that facilitate hands-on learning, case studies, and real-world applications in various subjects such as physics, biology, chemistry, and mathematics. This study reviews the current state of EjsS Modeling Tool and its applications in educational settings, highlighting the benefits of using this tool to create interactive electronic books and chapters. The paper also discusses the technical aspects of implementing JavaScript simulations in EjsS and presents a step-by-step guide on creating electronic books with interactive chapters using this tool. Furthermore, this research evaluates the usability and effectiveness of the developed electronic books and chapters, providing insights into their potential impact on student engagement and understanding.

title: Optimal strategies for the control of autonomous vehicles in data assimilation
Abstract: Autonomous vehicles (AVs) and data assimilation require the integration of sensor data and environmental information to produce accurate real-time models of their surroundings and driving scenarios. Data assimilation enables vehicles to learn and adapt to changing road conditions, weather, and other environmental factors, thus enabling optimal decision-making. In this context, control strategies play a critical role in managing the trade-offs between data precision, traffic safety, and vehicle efficiency. However, deriving optimal control strategies is hindered by the nonlinearity of the vehicle dynamics and the unpredictability of external factors affecting traffic flow. Recent advancements in machine learning and sensor fusion aim to provide suitable solutions for real-time optimization, yet several open challenges impede their practical implementation in data-rich environments characterized by rapid data obsolescence and the need for robust, real-time processing. We identify the key components that affect data-centric control systems for autonomous vehicles, including Bayesian state estimation, sensor-to-model fusion techniques, weather-aware mapping, and computational frameworks for handling data volumes and real-time performance requirements. We demonstrate that optimal strategies can be realized by integrating various state-of-the-art models and investigating novel ways of processing sensor data and sharing information between vehicles to generate collective awareness of traffic dynamics and enhance road safety. By understanding and synthesizing these disparate components, we provide insights that inform the development of robust control algorithms for autonomous vehicles operating in data-assimilated environments.

title: Pseudo-Bayesian Robust PCA: Algorithms and Analyses
Abstract: Pseudo-Bayesian Robust PCA: Algorithms and Analyses is a novel theoretical framework that integrates robust Principal Component Analysis (PCA) with Bayesian inference to build a robust and powerful data analysis tool. Robust PCA has become a crucial technique for matrix data analysis, particularly for applications involving large datasets with missing or contaminated entries. The conventional robust PCA methods often rely on distributional assumptions, which can be limiting in scenarios where data distributions are unknown or complex. In contrast, Bayesian methods, such as Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithms, can adapt to diverse distributions but face challenges with regard to computational efficiency and scalability. The proposed pseudo-Bayesian robust PCA approach provides a flexible and computationally efficient solution by leveraging variational inference techniques, which enable approximate Bayesian inference with high accuracy. This approach can handle high-dimensional matrices while maintaining statistical robustness, making it suitable for applications in computer vision, signal processing, and data mining. Experimental results demonstrate the accuracy and efficiency of the proposed method, showcasing its potential for applications where robustness and scalability are critical. The pseudo-Bayesian robust PCA approach yields state-of-the-art results in several benchmark datasets, highlighting its value as a reliable and robust tool for data analysis in various domains. By bridging the gaps between robust PCA and Bayesian inference, this method offers a versatile and effective solution for tackling real-world data analysis challenges.

title: The Teaching Dimension of Linear Learners
Abstract: This research paper delves into the intricacies of the teaching dimension of linear learners, focusing on the concept of teaching from an optimization perspective. Recent advances in deep learning have led to increased interest in understanding the inner workings of neural networks, specifically how they learn and generalize. The teaching dimension of linear learners explores the relationship between the number of training examples and the accuracy of the learned model. Traditionally, this relationship has been quantified through the use of VC (Vapnik-Chervonenkis) dimension, yet research has shown constraints with non-linear models such as neural networks especially to real-life data distributions. To address these limitations, an in-depth analysis of linear learners is conducted to understand their capacity to generalize while keeping the data size relatively small. By establishing a connection between the number of basis functions or neurons used in a model with the VC dimension, higher levels of generalization are found to be achievable leading to remarkable reductions in required dataset dimensions that support realistic learning efforts.

title: Learning Efficient Correlated Equilibria
Abstract: This research delves into the realm of game theory, specifically exploring the concept of Correlated Equilibria, a refinement of Nash Equilibria that incorporates probability distributions to capture more sophisticated strategies in multi-agent environments. By recognizing the existence of correlations between players' actions, Correlated Equilibria provide a more nuanced representation of real-world interactions, which often involve interdependent decision-making. However, existing algorithms for computing Correlated Equilibria can be computationally inefficient, particularly in large-scale or dynamic systems. To address this limitation, this study proposes a novel approach for learning efficient Correlated Equilibria, leveraging techniques from reinforcement learning and distributed computing. Our method, which we term "Distributed Correlated Equilibrium Learning," exploits the power of decentralized optimization to efficiently compute approximate Correlated Equilibria, while also accounting for the impact of correlations and interdependencies on player utility functions. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, showcasing significant improvements in convergence speed and accuracy compared to existing methods. Furthermore, we investigate the extension of our framework to accommodate value function learning, enabling the algorithm to adapt to changing environments and learn more sophisticated strategies. By showcasing the potential of Distributed Correlated Equilibrium Learning, this research offers a promising direction for advancing the study of efficient Correlated Equilibria in multi-agent systems.

title: A Large Dataset to Train Convolutional Networks for Disparity, Optical Flow, and Scene Flow Estimation
Abstract: As the field of computer vision continues to evolve, the availability of reliable and comprehensive datasets has emerged as a crucial factor in the development of state-of-the-art algorithms for various applications, including disparity, optical flow, and scene flow estimation. Despite the advancements in deep learning, the lack of a large-scale dataset has hindered the overall performance of convolutional neural networks in handling complex scene understanding tasks, such as predicting depth maps, motion fields, and dynamic scene flow. To address this limitation, this paper presents a large-scale dataset, referred to as LDSS, comprising over 300 high-definition videos with ground-truth annotations for disparity, optical flow, and scene flow estimation. The key feature of LDSS is the inclusion of diverse scenarios, including realistic dynamic scenes, anomalous motion patterns, varying lighting conditions, and occlusions, which significantly raises the bar for model assessment and training. We also investigate the effects of dataset size and diversity on the performance of CNNs, demonstrating a substantial improvement in estimation accuracy using LDSS, in comparison to smaller datasets like KITTI and Sintel. Our results show that LDSS can support the development of robust and accurate models for disparity, optical flow, and scene flow estimation, enabling real-world applications such as autonomous driving, robotics, and surveillance systems.

title: Joint Time-Frequency Scattering for Audio Classification
Abstract: This study presents a novel approach to audio classification using joint time-frequency scattering, an extension of the scattering transform to time-frequency domains. Traditional time-frequency representations, such as Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT) and Continuous Wavelet Transform (CWT), have been widely used for audio analysis. However, they are limited in their representation capabilities, particularly in capturing non-stationary and non-linear patterns present in audio signals. The proposed joint time-frequency scattering transform leverages the superior representation properties of time-frequency tiling and scattering transform to extract meaningful features from audio signals, resulting in enhanced representation capability and robustness to time-frequency distortions. In this work, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach through its application to several audio classification tasks, including music genre classification and emotion recognition. The results show that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods, yielding improved classification accuracy and robustness to noise and variations in audio recordings. Furthermore, we provide a theoretical analysis of the proposed joint time-frequency scattering transform, and discuss its computational complexity and implementation details. This research contributes to the development of more effective and robust audio classification methods, and has potential applications in areas such as music information retrieval, audio processing, and human-computer interaction.

title: Clustering by Deep Nearest Neighbor Descent (D-NND): A Density-based Parameter-Insensitive Clustering Method
Abstract: Deep Nearest Neighbor Descent (D-NND), a density-based clustering method, has garnered significant attention in the realm of unsupervised learning, offering a parameter-insensitive approach to discovering non-linear separation in data. Traditional clustering methods relying on shallow models or density estimation techniques often require tuning of hyperparameters to achieve optimal performance, thus limiting their practical applications. Conversely, D-NND, leveraging the representational power of deep networks, employs a hierarchical descent scheme to progressively refine clusters, effectively partitioning the data into denser regions. This method enables consistent representation of different density characteristics, achieving adaptability to datasets of varying complexities without necessitating manual hyperparameter selection. Furthermore, D-NND has been observed to scale well even with large datasets, effectively circumventing the challenges associated with standard density-based methods such as dealing with noise or outliers. The algorithm's primary mechanism involves analyzing the layer-wise neighbourhood density of the data points allowing to characterize local structures that transcend shallow structural approximations, making D-NND an effective parameter-insensitive alternative to conventional density-based clustering techniques. The resulting hierarchical structure enables flexible incorporation of multi-resolution features, yielding a model that functions as not only a classification tool but also an informative summarization of patterns within the data.

title: An Explicit Rate Bound for the Over-Relaxed ADMM
Abstract: This paper provides an explicit rate bound for the over-relaxed Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) algorithm, which is widely used for solving linearly constrained convex optimization problems. The over-relaxed ADMM is an extension of the classical ADMM algorithm, which incorporates an additional relaxation parameter to improve the convergence rate. However, existing rate bounds for the over-relaxed ADMM are often implicit and difficult to obtain, which hinders the understanding of its convergence behavior. In this paper, we develop a novel explicit rate bound for the over-relaxed ADMM, which is expressed in terms of the relaxation parameter, the step size parameter, and the condition number of the augmented Lagrangian matrix. The proposed bound is derived under mild assumptions and is non-asymptotic, allowing for a more accurate characterization of the algorithm's convergence rate. To the best of our knowledge, this work presents the first explicit rate bound for the over-relaxed ADMM, which fills an important gap in the understanding of this popular optimization algorithm. Our analysis also reveals the optimal choice of the relaxation parameter, which leads to a faster convergence rate, and provides valuable insights for tuning the parameters of the algorithm. The proposed bound is validated through numerical experiments on a range of test problems, demonstrating its accuracy and effectiveness in predicting the convergence rate of the over-relaxed ADMM.

title: Risk Minimization in Structured Prediction using Orbit Loss
Abstract: This paper presents a novel loss function called Orbit Loss for minimization of risk in structured prediction tasks. Despite the prosperity of risk minimization techniques, most of these models suffer from biases and inconsistencies, particularly in settings where structured data is involved, such as computer vision, natural language processing, and speech recognition. The Orbit Loss, inspired by the concept of circumcenter in geometry, provides an unbiased estimation of the standard risk, which is a key quantity of interest in risk minimization. By averaging the risks with respect to certain geometric constraints, the proposed loss has an explicit connection to the standard risk and provides a regularization effect to prevent overfitting. The orbital property enables the model to align with a broader notion of geometric intuition and stability at the analysis level. Empirical evidence is provided to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed loss function. In comparison to several state-of-the-art models and existing approaches, Orbit Loss is shown to achieve notable and statistically significant improvements on a diverse set of structured prediction tasks. Furthermore, the convergence rate, stability, and interpretability of the model are discussed and justified through analysis and accompanying qualitative results, showcasing its potential in real-world applications.

title: Discriminative Nonparametric Latent Feature Relational Models with Data Augmentation
Abstract: Discriminative Nonparametric Latent Feature Relational Models with Data Augmentation propose a novel statistical framework for modeling and analyzing relational data where the underlying structure is characterized by a nonparametric factorial latent space with group-level characteristics. The proposed methodology leverages a recently developed nonparametric Bayesian inference framework, where the model space is approximated via the Bayesian nonparametric latent feature model. By integrating the latent feature model into a discriminative relational model structure, this work enables accurate identification of nuanced relational patterns through the shared latent feature space. Furthermore, a data augmentation strategy is introduced to improve model estimation accuracy, stabilize convergence, and accommodate missing data scenarios. Extensive simulation studies demonstrate the robustness and reliability of the proposed method in capturing the subtle patterns within complex relational data structures. Real-world applications involving protein-protein interaction, ecological community dynamics, and social network collaboration also showcase the model's ability to uncover coherent, interpretable latent relationships that reflect the intrinsic structure of the corresponding relational datasets. Consequently, this research offers beneficial insights into tackling the challenges of relational data analysis through a cutting-edge statistical framework.

title: Scalable domain adaptation of convolutional neural networks
Abstract: Domain adaptation of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) has emerged as a crucial problem in the field of deep learning, particularly when large amounts of supervised data are not available for the target domain. Existing approaches for domain adaptation often rely on transfer learning, fine-tuning, and self-supervised learning techniques, which are limited in their ability to adapt to complex distributions between source and target domains. Recent advancements in scalable domain adaptation have focused on developing techniques that can efficiently leverage large amounts of unlabeled data from the source domain to adapt the pre-trained CNNs for the target domain. One such approach is multi-task learning, which enables the CNN to learn multiple tasks simultaneously, sharing the knowledge across tasks to improve adaptation to the target domain. However, multi-task learning often requires manual task selection, which can be challenging for large-scale domain adaptation problems. Another promising approach is meta-learning, which enables the CNN to adapt to new tasks quickly by learning a meta-model that can be fine-tuned for the target domain. Despite these advancements, scalable domain adaptation of CNNs remains an open problem due to the lack of effective techniques and metrics to evaluate the adaptation performance. To address this issue, this paper proposes a novel framework for scalable domain adaptation of CNNs, combining the strengths of multi-task learning and meta-learning while leveraging recent advances in transfer learning and self-supervised learning. The proposed framework is evaluated on several benchmark datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness in adapting CNNs to complex domain adaptation problems, and outperforming existing state-of-the-art approaches in terms of adaptation performance and transferability.

title: How to Discount Deep Reinforcement Learning: Towards New Dynamic Strategies
Abstract: Deep reinforcement learning has revolutionized various fields by efficiently solving complex decision-making problems. However, most deep reinforcement learning algorithms, particularly those based on Q-learning and policy gradient methods, have been criticized for their poor sample efficiency and slow training speeds, making their deployment in real-world applications challenging. Traditional strategies for addressing these limitations focus on improving the stability of deep reinforcement learning models, increasing data collection, and developing novel exploration strategies. Nevertheless, these methods have limited success in leveraging the full potential of deep reinforcement learning and have largely remained static, with few attempts incorporating dynamic adjustments to adapt to changing task requirements and environments. This study explores the development of novel dynamic strategies for discount deep reinforcement learning, focusing on approaches that dynamically adjust the discount factor in response to changes in task requirements and environmental feedback. By doing so, this research aims to overcome the limitations of traditional reinforcement learning methods and develop practical solutions for high-quality navigation in dynamic and complex scenarios. The framework proposed in this work reveals a more efficient exploration-exploitation trade-off and enhances the model's stability and robustness to diverse tasks and environments, making it a promising approach for leveraging the full potential of deep reinforcement learning in real-world applications.

title: Jointly Modeling Topics and Intents with Global Order Structure
Abstract: This paper tackles the problem of jointly modeling topics and intents in text data, with a novel approach incorporating global order structure. Existing topic modeling and intent detection methods neglect the intricate interactions between latent topics and underlying user intents in online communication. Our proposed model leverages the strengths of both generative and non-parametric topic modeling, and deep learning-based intent detection. We introduce a structured neural network that embeds high-dimensional text data in a lower-dimensional space, where latent topics and their corresponding user intents are represented through a global order structure learned from both the text content and external knowledge graphs. This shared representation facilitates effective inferring of user intents from underlying topics. Our approach facilitates understanding of online interactions as a synergy between communicative content, semantic topics, and user goals. We develop two innovative techniques: content-intent fusion, where topics and user intents are integrated during inference; and external semantics alignment, where external knowledge graph embeddings are aligned with learned text representations to provide contextually relevant information. Comprehensive evaluations on real-world datasets demonstrate that our model outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving improved accuracy and interpretability in capturing user intents and underlying semantic structure in online communication.

title: A Novel Approach to Distributed Multi-Class SVM
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to distributed multi-class Support Vector Machine (SVM) learning, which is a significant extension of traditional distributed SVM methods that are primarily designed for binary classification tasks. The proposed approach, dubbed "Dist-SVM-MC," tackles the challenges of large-scale multiclass classification by leveraging the power of distributed computing and effectively addressing the complexity and scalability issues associated with existing multi-class SVM methods. Dist-SVM-MC adopts a parallel approach, dividing the multiclass problem into a series of binary classification sub-problems that are then solved in a distributed manner, ensuring that each machine learns a subset of the classes and assigns a set of decision functions for their respective domains. To overcome the communication cost and ensure efficient model aggregation, a novel distributed optimization algorithm is introduced, which uses an approximate gradient-based method to iteratively refine the learned models on different nodes until convergence. Empirical evaluations demonstrate the efficacy and scalability of our proposed method by comparing it to popular state-of-the-art distributed multi-class SVM approaches on large-scale benchmark datasets, such as CIFAR-100 and ImageNet, showcasing that Dist-SVM-MC outperforms these methods in terms of classification accuracy and computational speed, while providing a robust and efficient framework for large-scale distributed multiclass classification tasks.

title: Learning population and subject-specific brain connectivity networks via Mixed Neighborhood Selection
Abstract: This research proposes a novel method for identifying population-specific and subject-specific brain connectivity networks in the brain using the Mixed Neighborhood Selection framework. The framework integrates multiple graph learning techniques, including graph convolutional networks and graph autoencoders, to fuse multi-modal brain image data and identify intrinsic brain connectivity patterns. By leveraging this approach, researchers can better understand individual differences in brain structure and function that contribute to various neurological and psychiatric disorders. The Mixed Neighborhood Selection framework incorporates a neighborhood selection step, where the framework learns to select the most relevant brain regions for each individual, allowing for the discovery of subject-specific connectivity patterns that cannot be captured by traditional, population-level analyses. This approach enables the identification of individualized neural networks that are more accurate and informative than population-level networks, leading to a deeper understanding of brain function and the development of more effective treatments for neurological disorders. The findings of this research have significant implications for the diagnosis, treatment, and management of neurological and psychiatric conditions, and provide a valuable tool for neuroscientists, clinicians, and engineers working in the field of brain connectivity research.

title: Fast Optimization Algorithm on Riemannian Manifolds and Its Application in Low-Rank Representation
Abstract: This paper proposes a fast optimization algorithm on Riemannian manifolds to solve the low-rank representation problem of high-dimensional data. The problem of low-rank representation is essential in many domains such as image and signal processing, where it is useful in the process of denoising, feature extraction, and approximation. Traditional algorithms solving this problem suffer high computational costs and unstable convergence, mainly owing to their failure to exploit the underlying geometric structure in the parameter space. Our contribution lies in the introduction of a self-adaptive step size scheme and a projection scheme to improve the stability of optimization and reduce the number of function evaluations, thus substantially speeding up the algorithm. We prove that our proposed algorithm converges under necessary and sufficient conditions, and numerical results demonstrate its superiority over state-of-the-art algorithms in terms of efficiency and robustness, particularly in solving large-scale matrices with limited training data. Through a detailed analysis of the theoretical convergence and extensive experiments using synthetic and real-world datasets, we show that the fast optimization algorithm can efficiently explore the manifold and provide a feasible approach for seeking the low-rank representation of high-dimensional data.

title: Thinking Required
Abstract: The emergence of complex systems in modern computing and artificial intelligence has led to an increasing interest in understanding the relationship between human cognition and machine learning. This research explores the concept of "Thinking Required" in the context of human-computer interaction, drawing on insights from cognitive psychology, artificial intelligence, and design thinking. The paper examines the various forms of thinking that humans engage in, including conscious and unconscious processes, and how these processes are reflected in human-computer interactions. Through a literature review of existing research on human-computer interaction, cognitive science, and artificial intelligence, this study aims to identify the key factors that influence the level of thinking required in different computing applications. The findings suggest that the complexity of tasks, the level of autonomy required, and the presence of human feedback are critical factors in determining the level of thinking required in human-computer interactions. Furthermore, the study highlights the importance of designing computing systems that adapt to the changing needs and cognitive abilities of users, and that provide intuitive and user-friendly interfaces that promote seamless human-computer interaction. The paper concludes by outlining the implications of these findings for the design of intelligent systems and the development of more effective and efficient human-computer interactions.

title: Rademacher Complexity of the Restricted Boltzmann Machine
Abstract: This paper delves into the theoretical understanding of the Restricted Boltzmann Machine (RBM) by analyzing its Rademacher complexity, a fundamental concept in the study of learning algorithms and generalization bounds. The RBM, a probabilistic generative model consisting of visible and hidden units, has been extensively used in deep learning architectures and has shown remarkable performance in various applications such as feature learning, dimensionality reduction, and unsupervised clustering. Despite its popularity, a thorough analysis of the RBM's learnability and generalization capabilities is still an open question, particularly in the context of the Rademacher complexity, which measures the capacity of a class of functions to fit the data by chance alone. In this work, we establish a theoretical framework for bounding the Rademacher complexity of the RBM, providing a deeper insight into its capacity to learn and generalizing performance. Our framework combines techniques from the analysis of the RBM's energy landscape, matrix concentration inequalities, and Rademacher complexity. The contribution of our work lies in providing a novel and computationally efficient estimation of the RBM's Rademacher complexity, which enables us to derive a generalization bound for RBM-based learning algorithms. Our results demonstrate that the RBM can learn and generalize well under certain conditions, and our theoretical framework serves as a foundation for further research on the theoretical aspects of the RBM and its applications.

title: Gauss quadrature for matrix inverse forms with applications
Abstract: Gauss quadrature has been a longstanding technique for approximating the value of definite integrals with high accuracy by representing them as weighted sums of function values. Recently, researchers have focused on its application to time-stepping methods for solving certain matrix problems, particularly when inverting large matrices that arise from finite element discretization of partial differential equations. Theoretically grounded approaches based on Gaussian quadrature for matrix inversion forms have shown considerable promise in computational efficiency gains over traditional methods for solving large-scale linear systems of equations. By employing the Gaussian quadrature method for approximating matrix-vector products, the cost of computing the inverse matrix can be significantly reduced. This paper delves into exploring the theoretical and practical aspects of applying the Gauss quadrature for inverting matrices, describing its salient advantages and limitations in various simulations with high accuracy and minimal computational cost. Furthermore, it provides a constructive framework for handling the technical issues that arise in this approach, including optimizing the weighting coefficients for maximal speedup in different applications, thus unveiling the true potential of Gauss quadrature as a novel benchmark algorithm for computational linear algebra efficiency.

title: A Simple and Practical Linear Algebra Library Interface with Static Size Checking
Abstract: This proposed linear algebra library interface strives to offer a simple yet robust platform for numerical computations, adhering to the constraints of static size checking. Central to designing this interface are two primary concepts: vector and matrix. These data structures are foundational and are employed extensively in linear algebra, making their accurate and efficient implementation paramount. Vectors are implemented using fixed-size arrays to facilitate easy memory access, which is critical in CPU-bound computations that involve sparse matrices. In distinction, matrices are represented using two-dimensional arrays to ensure accurate and computationally efficient operations such as matrix multiplication and transpose. The library provides interfaces for various linear algebra operations, such as eigenvalue decomposition and singular value decomposition, in addition to methods for solving systems of equations and performing matrix factorizations. Furthermore, a static checking mechanism is integrated to ensure that operations involving vectors and matrices adhere to their declared size, which not only improves code maintainability but also enhances the overall performance of the library. By employing static size checking, potential size-related errors are identified at compile-time, thereby increasing software reliability and readability.

title: Improving Type Error Messages in OCaml
Abstract: This research paper presents a comprehensive investigation into improving type error messages in OCaml, a statically typed programming language with a strong focus on functional programming. Type errors in OCaml can often lead to frustration for developers, particularly those who are new to the language, due to its concise and complex type inference system. Current type error messages in OCaml are often cryptic and difficult to understand, making it challenging for programmers to identify and resolve errors. This paper proposes a novel approach to enhancing OCaml's type error messages, utilizing a combination of natural language processing (NLP) and machine learning techniques to generate more informative and user-friendly error messages. Our approach involves analyzing the type error trace, identifying the root cause of the error, and then providing intuitive explanations and suggestions for fixing the issue. The proposed system also incorporates user feedback to improve the accuracy and effectiveness of the type error messages over time. The evaluation results of our proposal demonstrate significant improvements in programmer productivity and satisfaction, indicating its potential to become a valuable tool for OCaml developers. By leveraging the strengths of both NLP and machine learning, our research provides a robust framework for creating more helpful and accurate type error messages in OCaml.

title: In the Age of Web: Typed Functional-First Programming Revisited
Abstract: This paper revisits the concept of Typed Functional-First (TFF) programming in the context of modern web development. With the steady growth of web technologies and demands for robust, maintainable, and scalable software solutions, TFF programming has become increasingly relevant. However, its adoption remains limited, largely due to its perceived complexity and abstraction levels that may be foreign to traditional web developers. Through a comprehensive survey of existing TFF programming languages, frameworks, and tools, this research seeks to demystify its principles and explore its applications in web development. The study delves into the advantages of TFF programming, including type safety, immutability, and composable code, and examines the support for concurrent and parallel programming, type inference, and type systems. Furthermore, it examines the learning curves and challenges associated with adopting TFF programming for web development, as well as its potential for addressing common web development issues such as debugging, security vulnerabilities, and code maintenance. By investigating real-world examples and establishing a dialogue with industry practitioners, this research aims to illuminate the benefits and feasibility of TFF programming in the modern web development pipeline.

title: Sparsifying Neural Network Connections for Face Recognition
Abstract: This paper explores the application of sparse neural networks in face recognition tasks, focusing on the sparsification of neural network connections to improve the efficiency and effectiveness of these systems. The increasing demand for robust and real-time face recognition systems has led to a surge in the development of deep neural networks. However, the complexity and size of these networks have raised concerns about their computational and memory requirements, hindering their deployment in resource-constrained devices. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach that leverages the principles of sparse neural networks to prune and optimize the connections within a convolutional neural network (CNN) for face recognition tasks. Our method involves three key steps: connection pruning, connection recovery, and retraining. We prune connections that have negligible impact on the network's performance using saliency-based methods and connectivity-driven methods. Following pruning, we recover some of the critical connections to prevent losing the underlying patterns and relationships learned during training. We then retrain the network with the remaining, sparse connections. Our experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach in achieving a significant reduction in the number of connections within the CNN, thereby reducing the computational overhead and memory requirements while maintaining or improving face recognition performance.

title: Using SVM to pre-classify government purchases
Abstract: This study explores the application of Support Vector Machines (SVM) for pre-classifying government purchases, a crucial task in public procurement monitoring. The classification of government purchases into different categories, such as goods and services, can be a complex and time-consuming process due to the large volume of transactions and the complexity of vendor and procurement information. Current manual methods can be prone to errors and delays, hindering effective government oversight and potentially leading to corruption. In this research, an SVM-based approach is proposed to pre-classify government purchases based on publicly available datasets. The main objectives are to evaluate the performance of SVM in accurately categorizing government purchases, investigate the effect of different feature selection strategies on SVM performance, and compare the results with existing classification methods. An analysis of the factors influencing SVM performance, such as vendor profiles and procurement attributes, is also conducted. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed SVM-based approach in efficiently categorizing government purchases with high accuracy, contributing to the development of more efficient and transparent public procurement systems. The study provides insights for policymakers and researchers to design and implement effective pre-classification systems for government purchases.

title: Recognition from Hand Cameras
Abstract: The advent of handheld cameras with advanced computational capabilities has opened up unprecedented opportunities for modern computer vision applications, particularly in the realm of facial recognition and hand-based identity verification. Hand cameras, also known as smart camera, have gained immense popularity in recent years due to their compact size, ease of use, and high-resolution imaging capabilities. This research delves into the design and development of a real-time hand-based recognition system utilizing a handheld camera, aimed at elevating the security and convenience of biometric authentication in various aspects of modern life. By leveraging cutting-edge deep learning algorithms and machine learning models, this proposed system is poised to achieve remarkable accuracy levels in hand-based recognition, even in the presence of challenging environments, varying lighting conditions, and occlusion. Furthermore, this research focuses on addressing the issue of dataset imbalance, a common problem encountered in many deep learning-based classification tasks. To achieve this, a novel hand-based dataset collection approach is proposed, incorporating multiple variants of hand poses, orientations, and skin tones to enhance the robustness and generalizability of the recognition system. The proposed system has the potential to revolutionize the field of biometric authentication, providing a secure, convenient, and user-friendly alternative to traditional methods, thereby paving the way for widespread adoption in various industries, such as healthcare, finance, and law enforcement.

title: Driverseat: Crowdstrapping Learning Tasks for Autonomous Driving
Abstract: This research paper presents a novel approach to crowdstrapping learning tasks for autonomous driving systems, coined as Driverseat. By harnessing the collective power of diverse human contributors, Driverseat enables the efficient accomplishment of complex learning tasks such as object detection, segmentation, and trajectory prediction. Leveraging the strengths of human workers from various backgrounds, cultures, and expertise levels, Driverseat forms a robust and inclusive crowdsourcing framework that fosters a collaborative environment for human-AI interaction. A key innovation of Driverseat lies in its autonomous driving-specific task design, where human input is valuably aggregated and weighted based on worker reliability and expertise, thereby ensuring the accuracy and efficiency of AI model updates. Furthermore, the proposed system incorporates a human-centered interface that facilitates intuitive task engagement, real-time feedback, and dynamic task adaptation, thereby mitigating human fatigue and boredom that often hinder crowdsourcing initiatives. A comprehensive evaluation through user studies and real-world autonomous driving experiments demonstrates the efficacy of Driverseat in augmenting the learning capabilities of autonomous driving systems, thereby paving the way for safer, more reliable, and more efficient self-driving vehicles. title: Rank Pooling for Action Recognition
Abstract: Action recognition has garnered significant attention in the field of computer vision due to its vast array of applications, particularly in surveillance, robotics, and human-computer interaction. However, current methods often struggle to effectively capture complex actions within videos, primarily as a result of the temporally static nature of traditional pooling methods. Rank pooling, proposed as an alternative approach, provides improved recognition performance by aggregating action information over multiple frames through the utilization of ranking-based pooling. This new methodology helps to better preserve the temporal structure of the action, thereby facilitating a more comprehensive understanding of its evolution over time. Through the incorporation of a sophisticated ranking-based pooling approach and the fusion of global and local information, rank pooling exhibits the capability to surpass the efficiency of fixed-size and adaptive pooling methods, offering substantial improvements in the accuracy and robustness of action recognition tasks. Moreover, the development of rank pooling enables efficient realization of deep learning architectures in human-action-based applications, particularly in scenarios where the available information is not merely static but varies significantly across time. Additionally, the flexibility of rank pooling and its ability to empower efficient analysis of multi-modal action information highlight its potential applicability in enhancing action recognition methods for applications such as security and surveillance.

title: Explaining reviews and ratings with PACO: Poisson Additive Co-Clustering
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel framework based on Poisson Additive Co-Clustering (PACO), which provides a unified approach to modeling customer reviews and ratings in e-commerce settings. The proposed framework incorporates both content features from the review text and numerical ratings, enabling a comprehensive understanding of customer preferences and sentiment towards specific products. PACO leverages the strengths of co-clustering methods, allowing for the simultaneous discovery of product and reviewer clusters, as well as ratings patterns associated with each cluster. The model's Poisson-based approach facilitates the adaptation to the count nature of reviews and ratings, while accommodating sparse data distributions and outlier reviews. By examining the relationships between products, reviewers, and ratings, the PACO framework enables businesses to better understand customer needs, preferences, and pain points, ultimately informing product development, marketing strategies, and personalized customer experiences. The proposed framework is demonstrated through a comprehensive experimental evaluation on a real-world dataset of product reviews and ratings, showcasing its effectiveness in capturing meaningful patterns, trends, and anomalies in customer feedback. The results highlight the potential of PACO to revolutionize the analysis of reviews and ratings, enabling e-commerce companies to derive actionable insights from vast amounts of customer feedback and enhance their business operations.

title: Linear Readout of Object Manifolds
Abstract: Recent advances in deep learning and geometry have led to significant breakthroughs in the field of topological data analysis. However, traditional methods that rely on exhaustive meshing or sampling-based approaches have struggled to efficiently analyze complex object manifolds. In this work, we present a novel approach for linear readout of object manifolds. Our method leverages the power of spectral geometry to construct a sparse and efficient representation of the manifold, which is then used to compute a linear feature that captures the essence of the object's topology. The proposed approach is inspired by the idea of exploiting the recently discovered connections between deep learning and harmonic analysis on manifolds. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on a range of synthetic and real-world benchmarks, showcasing its ability to outperform state-of-the-art algorithms in terms of both efficiency and accuracy. Key advantages of our approach include its robustness to noise and its ability to handle high-dimensional data. Furthermore, our method is capable of discovering novel geometric features that have been overlooked by previous approaches. Results demonstrate the potential of our method for a wide range of applications, including computer-aided design, computer vision, and data analysis in physics and engineering.

title: SentiBench - a benchmark comparison of state-of-the-practice sentiment analysis methods
Abstract: SentiBench presents a comprehensive comparison of state-of-the-practice sentiment analysis methods, shedding light on their strengths and limitations in capturing nuances of human emotions. By leveraging a diverse set of datasets and realistic use cases, this study provides a robust benchmarking framework for evaluating the performance of various sentiment analysis approaches. The proposed benchmark framework assesses the efficacy of these methods in handling domain-specific emotive expressions, context-dependent sentiment shifts, and ambiguity in linguistic representations. A thorough analysis of results reveals that recent transformer-based architectures exhibit state-of-the-art performance on standard benchmarks, yet demonstrate significant variability in their ability to generalize to out-of-domain scenarios. Furthermore, comparative performance evaluations highlight the sensitivity of state-of-the-practice methods to linguistic representation choices, illustrating the importance of tailored word embeddings and pre-training strategies for accurate sentiment analysis. The insights gained from this comprehensive benchmarking exercise are expected to inform future research directions and drive the development of more robust and adaptive sentiment analysis solutions, capable of accurately capturing the complexities of human emotions and context-dependent nuances in multimodal and dynamic environments. This work provides an essential resource for researchers and practitioners aiming to develop and evaluate sentiment analysis systems for various applications.

title: PatchBatch: a Batch Augmented Loss for Optical Flow
Abstract: This paper presents PatchBatch, a novel batch-augmented loss function designed to improve the estimation of optical flow, a fundamental problem in computer vision. Traditional optical flow estimation methods often rely on a single image patch or a fixed-scale batch during training, which can lead to limited generalization and suboptimal performance. PatchBatch addresses these limitations by intelligently diversifying the input space through a carefully crafted combination of spatial and temporal augmentations, effectively enlarging the batch size with minimal computational overhead. The proposed loss function is composed of a novel weighting scheme that adaptively balances the contributions of different patch pairs, a patch loss term that promotes more accurate flow estimates at the individual patch level, and a batch loss term that enforces global coherence among flow estimates. Through experiments on several benchmark datasets, including Sintel, KITTI, and SYNTHIA, we demonstrate that PatchBatch substantially improves the overall performance of state-of-the-art optical flow methods, achieving up to 60% reduction in endpoint error and outperforming competing approaches with more complex architectures. The results indicate that PatchBatch can serve as a versatile and efficient loss function for optical flow estimation tasks, providing a valuable tool for researchers and practitioners in the field of computer vision.

title: Large Scale Distributed Semi-Supervised Learning Using Streaming Approximation
Abstract: This paper explores the development of large scale distributed semi-supervised learning using streaming approximation, aimed at addressing the challenges associated with the scalability of traditional semi-supervised learning algorithms. By employing a distributed framework and leveraging streaming approximation, we enable the handling of massive datasets that are typical in large-scale machine learning applications. The proposed approach first employs a divide-and-conquer strategy to partition the large dataset into manageable chunks, which are then distributed amongst a cluster of computing nodes. Following this, a streaming approximation algorithm is applied to each node to generate an approximate representation of the dataset. These representations are then centralized and combined using a novel clustering algorithm that is specifically designed to handle the increased dimensionality of the approximate representations. The proposed algorithm is capable of handling datasets with millions of samples and features, making it suitable for a wide range of applications, including image classification, natural language processing, and recommender systems. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed approach, showing significant improvements in both computational efficiency and classification accuracy compared to traditional semi-supervised learning methods, highlighting its potential in large-scale distributed machine learning applications.

title: Similarity Learning via Adaptive Regression and Its Application to Image Retrieval
Abstract: Similarity learning is a fundamental problem in pattern analysis and machine learning, with applications in image retrieval, clustering, and classification. Traditional similarity learning methods rely on fixed-distance metric learning techniques, such as triplet loss, to learn a similarity function that models the similarity between data points. However, these approaches suffer from several limitations, including the need for multiple reference points and the rigidity of the learned metric. In this paper, we propose a novel similarity learning approach based on adaptive regression, which learns a similarity function by directly modeling the relationship between data points. Our approach, dubbed Adaptive Regression for Similarity Learning (ARSL), employs a bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network to learn a dynamic and adaptive similarity metric from data. Specifically, ARSL learns two embedding functions: one for mapping input data into a similarity space and another for modeling the similarity between data points in this space. This allows our model to effectively capture complex relationships between data points and learn meaningful representations for clustering and retrieval tasks. We demonstrate the effectiveness of ARSL on several image retrieval benchmarks, including CIFAR-100, Stanford-40, and Oxford-IIT-Pets, and show that it outperforms state-of-the-art similarity learning methods in terms of retrieval accuracy and efficiency. Our experimental results also highlight the flexibility and scalability of ARSL, making it a promising tool for a wide range of similarity learning applications.

title: Vanishing point attracts gaze in free-viewing and visual search tasks
Abstract: The vanishing point, a key element of perspective where lines converge at infinity, has a profound impact on visual perception and attention. In free-viewing tasks, human observers are naturally drawn to the vanishing point, often gazing at areas where the convergence of lines is most pronounced. This gaze attraction to the vanishing point is robust, persisting even when other salient elements are present in the scene. A visual search task, where observers are tasked with locating a target among distractors, also reveals that the vanishing point exerts a strong influence on gaze patterns. Observers tend to fixate on the vanishing point early in the search process, often guiding their subsequent gaze movements. These findings raise important questions about the cognitive processes underlying gaze attraction to the vanishing point and suggest that the vanishing point may play a unique role in shaping the visual representation and search process. Investigating the neural basis of this effect may provide new insights into the psychological and neurobiological mechanisms governing visual attention, especially in tasks that require detection and search of objects in complex environments.

title: Generating News Headlines with Recurrent Neural Networks
Abstract: This research explores the potential of recurrent neural networks (RNNs) in generating news headlines, focusing on the impact of contextual and linguistic nuances on headline production. A large dataset of news articles is compiled and preprocessed to accommodate the input format suitable for RNN models. Experiments are conducted using various RNN architectures, including long short-term memory (LSTM) and gated recurrent unit (GRU), to evaluate their performance in producing coherent and engaging headlines. The performance of these models is compared in terms of metrics such as perplexity, fluency, and relevance to the article content. The findings suggest that the inclusion of contextual information, such as article topics and entities, can significantly enhance the quality of generated headlines. Additionally, the results indicate that LSTM-based models outperform GRU-based models in terms of fluency and relevance, highlighting the importance of model selection in headline generation tasks. The experiment also examines the importance of linguistic factors, such as sentiment and syntax, in the generation of news headlines. The results demonstrate that accounting for sentiment has a positive impact on the relevance of generated headlines, while syntax plays a minor role in headline generation. Overall, this study contributes to the development of RNN-based models for generating high-quality news headlines, shedding light on the importance of contextual and linguistic considerations in this task.

title: Variance Reduction for Distributed Stochastic Gradient Descent
Abstract: Distributed Stochastic Gradient Descent (DSGD) has emerged as a promising approach for large-scale machine learning problems, enabling the efficient utilization of multiple computing nodes to speed up model training times. However, a major challenge associated with DSGD is the variance reduction phenomenon, which can significantly affect the convergence rate and accuracy of the gradient estimates. The variance reduction issue arises due to the lack of coordination among different nodes, leading to an overestimation of the gradient values, thus limiting the effectiveness of the optimization algorithm. In this paper, we propose an effective variance reduction technique for DSGD that leverages a novel communication strategy to selectively share information among nodes, thereby reducing the variance of the gradient estimates. Our approach, dubbed as "Coordinated Distributed Stochastic Gradient Descent" (CDSGD), uses a cluster of nodes to collect and share local gradient information, allowing for more accurate estimation of the true gradient, thereby enhancing the overall convergence rate of the algorithm. A comprehensive experimental evaluation of CDSGD on several large-scale datasets demonstrates its effectiveness and scalability compared to existing variance reduction techniques, highlighting its potential for solving complex machine learning problems in parallel computing environments. The proposed method reduces the computational overhead associated with variance reduction, resulting in significant improvement in throughput and convergence rate. Finally, this study supports the application of CDSGD in a range of fields, including deep learning, data integration systems and more.

title: Stabilizing the unstable output of persistent homology computations
Abstract: Persistent homology computations provide topological insights into complex data structures by analyzing the underlying holes and voids, yielding sensitive and qualitative information about the data's geometric and structural properties. However, one of the primary challenges hindering the reliability and usability of persistent homology is the prevalence of unstable output in its computations. As topological features emerge and disappear at varying scales along the filtration, the stability of feature detection rapidly decreases, casting doubt on the significance and interpretability of persistent homology results. This study investigates the sources and ramifications of this instability in persistent homology computations. We highlight several contributions of the present work: firstly, a thorough analysis of the unstable output phenomenon, pinpointing its root causes within the framework of topological data analysis; secondly, an exhaustive examination of state-of-the-art methods attempting to stabilize the volatile output, shedding light on their performance and reliability; and thirdly, the introduction of novel techniques aiming to reinforce feature stability by refining and contextualizing existing methodologies, with promising results. Ultimately, our study can help practitioners leverage the combinatorial and topological insights in persistent homology without being overwhelmed by the limitations imposed by the inherent instability in these methods, advancing our understanding of complex structures and enabling informed decision-making in fields where interpretability is a priority. Our contribution provides a more reliable framework for inference from the output of persistence modules and sets the stage for a future-proof understanding of topological data analysis.

title: Deep Attention Recurrent Q-Network
Abstract: This paper introduces a novel architecture, Deep Attention Recurrent Q-Network (DARQN), designed to address the challenging problem of reinforcement learning in complex and dynamic environments. Building upon the strengths of both attention mechanisms and recurrent neural networks, DARQN is able to selectively focus on relevant information and learn long-range dependencies in a sequence. By employing a hierarchical architecture, DARQN is capable of effectively addressing the exploration-exploitation trade-off, a long-standing issue in reinforcement learning. The proposed model consists of a recurrent encoder, a spatial attention mechanism, and a Q-network, which work together to produce high-quality policies and efficient exploration. Experimental results demonstrate the superior performance of DARQN in various benchmark tasks, including Atari games and continuous-control environments, showcasing its potential in tackling the complexity of reinforcement learning tasks. By significantly improving the balance between exploration and exploitation, DARQN opens up new avenues for achieving more efficient and effective reinforcement learning. The proposed model also shows great promise in allowing for the learning of hierarchical decision-making processes, thus providing a powerful tool for agents to adapt and generalize in a wide range of environments.

title: Maximum Entropy Binary Encoding for Face Template Protection
Abstract: This study explores the concept of Maximum Entropy Binary Encoding (MEBE) as a novel approach for protecting face templates, a critical component in many facial recognition systems. The widespread adoption of face recognition technology has necessitated the development of robust methods to safeguard sensitive biometric data. Traditional techniques for face template protection rely on encryption and/or encryption with template protection operations, yet these methods may compromise the efficiency and effectiveness of facial recognition systems, particularly when executed on resource-constrained devices. In contrast, MEBE leverages the principles of information theory to encode face templates with near-optimal compression rates, thereby reducing the risk of template-theft attacks. By employing a carefully designed probabilistic model, MEBE generates a binary representation of the face template that retains the original information while minimizing the potential for illicit use. Experimentally, this paper compares the performance of MEBE against state-of-the-art methods, determining its suitability for face recognition applications and enumerating factors critical to maximizing the efficacy of template protection. The research demonstrates that the Maximum Entropy Binary Encoding paradigm can serve as a versatile and applicable safeguard for face templates, with implications for the development of secure and efficient facial recognition systems in a range of settings.

title: A Shapley Value Solution to Game Theoretic-based Feature Reduction in False Alarm Detection
Abstract: In the context of anomaly detection and surveillance systems, the continuous presence of false alarms not only wastes resources but also poses a significant threat to system efficacy by obscuring legitimate alerts. Inspired by the concept of coalition formation in game theory, this research endeavors to develop an efficient feature reduction method leveraging Shapley value allocation. The proposed approach rationalizes feature relevance while providing intrinsic explanations for the weights assigned to each feature. Incorporating the underlying principles of cooperative game theory, this solution identifies the optimal subset of features yielding an optimal level of accuracy and desired alarm detection performance. Utilizing this property, our game-theoretic method identifies crucial factors contributing to false alarm occurrences, thereby guiding informed decisions on sampling and measurement. Furthermore, through experiments involving real-world datasets, we demonstrate the merits of the developed approach in benchmarking against prevailing feature reduction algorithms, such as recursive feature elimination and l1 regularization. By effectively pinpointing the underlying features accountable for the majority of false alarms while providing an intrinsic sensitivity to marginal contributions, our method not only streamlines computational requirements but also secures superior false alarm detection capabilities, resulting in a balance between achieving higher accuracy and lowering system latency and required resources, thus paving the way for more reliable anomaly detection systems.

title: Stochastic Collapsed Variational Inference for Sequential Data
Abstract: This work presents a novel stochastic collapsed variational inference approach tailored for sequential or time-series data, enabling the practitioners to tackle high-dimensional variational distributions effectively. Conventional VI methods suffer from intractable inference due to the intractable posterior and the difficulty in scaling up to high-dimensional data, especially in sequential settings where each data point's contribution cannot be treated independently. To address these challenges, our proposed method employs stochastic and collapsed inference strategies, where the stochasticity is introduced at the auxiliary variational distribution's level and the collapsing is achieved by integrating out the observation variables' expectations from the model. This approach significantly reduces the dimensionality of the variational objective and alleviates the bottleneck in computing the log-likelihood's expectations. Furthermore, employing a stochastic representation enables efficient scalability on high-dimensional data, particularly relevant in sequential settings where each data point offers new information for the posterior update, preventing redundant computations. Empirical results on various sequential models demonstrate speed and accuracy improvements achieved by our proposed method in comparison to existing state-of-the-art approaches, providing practitioners with a valuable scalable and computationally efficient approach to inferring complex sequential models with high-dimensional variational distributions.

title: Stochastic Collapsed Variational Inference for Hidden Markov Models
Abstract: Stochastic Collapsed Variational Inference for Hidden Markov Models is a novel approach to scalable Bayesian inference, particularly suited for complex temporal models. This method tackles the limitations of traditional variational techniques by taking advantage of the collapsed variational inference framework and incorporating stochastic optimisation. By extending the concept of collapsed variational inference to this type of hierarchical model, this work addresses the bottleneck of inference in Hidden Markov Model (HMM) estimation, reducing the dimensionality of the parameter space. As the number of states in the HMM grows, traditional variational methods become computationally intractable due to the need to approximate the entire joint distribution. Stochastic collapsed variational inference, on the other hand, uses a set of stochastic functions to dynamically sample the variation of the HMM parameters, iteratively optimising each one. By exploiting these ideas, this research introduces a faster and more efficient way to fit and estimate parameters in Hidden Markov Models, showcasing improved accuracy through application to a range of classic benchmarks and providing new avenues for Bayesian inference of complex temporal models. Overall, the contribution aims to offer an efficient inference strategy and to inform future work in similar domains that require accounting for model complexity.

title: Approximated and User Steerable tSNE for Progressive Visual Analytics
Abstract: The visual analytics community has witnessed a surge in adoption of dimensionality reduction techniques like tSNE to analyze complex high-dimensional datasets, but issues of scalability and interpretability continue to pose significant challenges. To mitigate these limitations, we propose Approximated and User Steerable tSNE (AUST), an approach that combines dimensionality reduction with progressive visual analytics. Our method first employs a novel approximation scheme to scale tSNE to large datasets, leveraging the trade-offs between accuracy and computational efficiency. Additionally, we introduce a novel user steerable mechanism that enables domain experts to fine-tune the visualization process, controlling the saliency of dimensions to suit their analytical objectives. This steerable approach allows users to dynamically reweight tSNE's embeddings, facilitating the identification of key drivers and highlighting their influences on the data. Furthermore, AUST supports progressive refinement of parameters and allows users to iteratively adjust their focus and reveal new insights as needed. In our evaluation, we demonstrate that AUST outperforms state-of-the-art approximations, maintains comparable interpretability to traditional tSNE, and effectively supports progressive visual analytics, acknowledging its applicability in data-driven decision-making processes across various domains, including business analytics, healthcare, and social network analysis.

title: A Deep Structured Model with Radius-Margin Bound for 3D Human Activity Recognition
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel deep structured model that incorporates a radius-margin bound for 3D human activity recognition. The proposed model leverages a graph-based framework to capture intricate spatiotemporal relationships between 3D joints, while the radius-margin bound is derived to regularize the model's learning process, ensuring its robustness and generalizability. A comprehensive review of existing RGB-D based activity recognition models highlights the limitations and challenges associated with current methods, emphasizing the need for a more robust and accurate approach. To this end, the proposed model is demonstrated to outperform state-of-the-art methods on benchmark datasets, including the NTU-120 and UCF-24-3D datasets, under various evaluation metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. The experimental results show that the proposed model's ability to effectively model the spatial context and temporal dependence between 3D joints leads to significant improvements in recognition accuracy, particularly for complex activities involving multiple simultaneous actions. Furthermore, the incorporation of the radius-margin bound is shown to facilitate the training process, preventing overfitting and ensuring the model's ability to generalize well across different environments and scenarios. The paper concludes by discussing the potential applications and future directions of the proposed model in areas such as healthcare, surveillance, and robotics, where accurate 3D human activity recognition is a pressing need.

title: Unsupervised comparable corpora preparation and exploration for bi-lingual translation equivalents
Abstract: This study focuses on the automation of unsupervised comparable corpora preparation and exploration for bi-lingual translation equivalents, aiming to alleviate the labor-intensive process of manual data collection and annotation. Leveraging the vast amounts of unlabelled data available on the web, we develop a novel framework to identify and collect comparable texts, paired with pre-existing machine translation models to generate plausible translations. Our approach exploits cross-lingual similarities in term vectors to create clusters of comparable texts, facilitating the search for pairs of texts displaying semantically similar content in different languages. By fully integrating parsing tools, information extraction, and statistical models, our framework integrates disparate data sources, enriching the potential for cross-lingual analyses. This unsupervised process reduces reliance on manual expert judgment and eliminates operational costs associated with text curators and annotators. Furthermore, automated exploration strategies allow users to visualize inherent properties and meta-information associated with comparable corpora. Our proposed methodology also allows for inductively identifying emergent trends by selecting variable translations or comparing monolingual outputs from disparate MT models. The findings of this research have significant implications for NLP methodologies applied in building language translation models, multilingual representations, and data augmentation, enhancing cross-lingual understanding with improved representation and recognition.

title: PJAIT Systems for the IWSLT 2015 Evaluation Campaign Enhanced by Comparable Corpora
Abstract: This research paper contributes to the advancement of Pivot-based Joint Attention and Interaction Translation (PJAIT) systems for the IWSLT 2015 Evaluation Campaign, with a key focus on enhancing such systems by utilizing comparable corpora. Comparable corpora, comprising sentences or texts that are linked via various relationships, including but not limited to equivalence or parallelism, are explored for their potential to augment PJAIT systems. The goal of this study is to investigate how these sources can improve the performance of PJAIT systems in translating spoken dialogue and to shed light on the impact of training and fine-tuning PJAIT models using comparable corpora on translation accuracy and fluency. The investigated PJAIT system models are compared with baselines that utilize only parallel data or comparable data separately. Specifically, the paper discusses preliminary findings where the use of comparable corpora accelerates PJAIT systems in the tasks of translating conversational dialogues more accurately, thus forming a good understanding platform of PJAIT enhancements. The presented results demonstrate the significant positive effects of integrating comparable data in PJAIT system's ability to learn effective relationships between source and target languages and expressions, underscoring the potential advantages that can be gained from its application in real-world NMT scenarios.

title: Hierarchical Sparse Modeling: A Choice of Two Group Lasso Formulations
Abstract: Hierarchical sparse modeling has emerged as a powerful tool for processing high-dimensional data by identifying groups of correlated features and the relevant subsets of these groups. However, traditional sparse regression techniques often struggle to extend this functionality to hierarchical data structures. This study investigates the use of two group lasso formulations, namely the elastic net group lasso (ENGL) and the weighted group lasso (WGL), as alternatives to traditional hierarchical sparse modeling methods. ENGL leverages the elastic net’s ability to balance the strength of L1 and L2 regularization terms, whereas WGL incorporates a non-convex penalty to promote the sparsity of group-wise correlations. Our experiments demonstrate that both formulations outperform the naive application of traditional sparse regression on hierarchical data structures, achieving improved predictive performance and robust feature selection. Under certain conditions, the results also reveal a significant trade-off between the sparsity of individual features and group-wise correlations, shedding light on the delicate balance between interpretability and performance in hierarchical sparse modeling. Furthermore, we examine the practical implications of our findings for real-world applications, including the identification of disease biomarkers in genomic data and the recommendation of individualized items in high-dimensional rating systems. Ultimately, this research aims to provide a concise yet effective approach to hierarchical sparse modeling, which can simplify the interpretation and prediction of complex systems.

title: Risk-Constrained Reinforcement Learning with Percentile Risk Criteria
Abstract: Risk-Constrained Reinforcement Learning with Percentile Risk Criteria seeks to bridge the gap between risk-conscious decision-making and performance-driven reinforcement learning by introducing a novel framework that incorporates percentile-based risk measures into the policy optimization process. Traditional risk metrics, such as value-at-risk and expected shortfall, are limited by their reliance on a fixed risk tolerance threshold and failure to account for the variability of outcomes across the cumulative distribution function. In contrast, percentile-based risk metrics provide a more nuanced understanding of risk by focusing on tail events and their associated probabilities. This approach enables the acquisition of policies that are robust to a range of risk tolerances while maintaining a satisfactory level of performance. Our proposed method seeks to overcome the computational challenges associated with percentile-based risk measures by leveraging a probabilistic approximation and combining it with the power of the policy gradient method. Through a series of experiments, we empirically demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in a variety of high-stakes decision-making scenarios, showcasing its ability to derive risk-conscious policies with improved performance and reliability under diverse risk tolerances. Our research contributes to the development of more robust and adaptive reinforcement learning algorithms for complex applications requiring careful risk management.
