title: Guarding against Spurious Discoveries in High Dimensions
Abstract: High-dimensional data has become increasingly prevalent in modern statistical inference, posing significant challenges for detecting true signals amidst a background of spurious associations, often labeled as false discoveries. Guarding against such spurious discoveries is crucial in a wide range of applications, including genomics, medical imaging, and social network analysis. Our research paper attempts to address this issue by developing novel methodologies to more accurately identify true discoveries in high dimensions. Building upon the foundations of false discovery rate (FDR) control and its various extensions, our approach combines a modified version of the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure with a data-driven dimensionality reduction technique to eliminate spurious associations prior to the stage of multiple testing. To control FDR, we then employ a sophisticated resampling-based approach that leverages the power of ensemble methods to better capture the underlying distribution of test statistics. Additionally, we provide guidance on the theoretical and empirical construction of FDR-controlling ensemble-based procedures, highlighting their potential advantages over traditional multiple testing correction methods. In the high-dimensional setting, our proposed methods enable the reliable identification of true discoveries while preventing numerous spurious associations from clouding the interpretation of results. Simulation studies and real-world applications showcase the efficacy of our methodologies in curbing spurious discoveries and improving the signal-to-noise ratio in high-dimensional data analysis.

title: A Package for the Automated Classification of Periodic Variable Stars
Abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive package, designated as AstroClass, for the automated classification of periodic variable stars. By employing a hybrid approach combining machine learning techniques with traditional astronomical methods, AstroClass enables astronomers to efficiently identify and categorize variable stars based on their periodic behavior. The package incorporates a sophisticated feature extraction module that extracts a range of descriptors from light curves, including amplitude, period, duty cycle, and others. These descriptors serve as input to a machine learning model that has been trained on a large dataset of periodic variable stars, including eclipsing binaries, delta Scuti stars, and other types. The model utilizes a deep neural network architecture, allowing it to learn complex patterns and relationships in the data that would be challenging to identify using traditional methods. The AstroClass package has been extensively tested on a variety of datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness in accurately classifying periodic variable stars with a high degree of precision. By leveraging the power of machine learning and traditional astronomical methods, AstroClass offers a valuable tool for astronomers seeking to characterize the behavior of periodic variable stars and advance our understanding of their astrophysical properties. The package is designed to be highly adaptable and scalable, allowing researchers to easily incorporate new data and features as they become available, and enabling the community to continue to build on and improve the software in the future.

title: Creation of a Deep Convolutional Auto-Encoder in Caffe
Abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive overview of creating a deep convolutional auto-encoder (CAE) framework in Caffe with a particular emphasis on image degradation and restoration tasks. Convolutional auto-encoders have been widely used in image processing for their ability to efficiently learn and represent complex features of images. The proposed framework utilizes a deep convolutional neural network architecture for both the encoder and the decoder components. The encoder employs convolutional and pooling layers to extract hierarchical representations of images, while the decoder utilizes transposed convolutional and upsampling layers to reconstruct the original image. Our implementation makes use of Caffe, a leading deep learning framework, with customized variations of pre-existing Caffe layers such as conv, pooling, and fully connected layers. Through extensive experimentation and empirical evaluation, we demonstrate the efficacy of our CAE framework on a range of Benchmark image degradation datasets and show its effectiveness in image denoising, inpainting, and superresolution tasks. The numerical results show significant improvements in comparison with existing CAE-based solutions. Furthermore, our approach serves as a reliable and efficient tool for researchers and practitioners requiring the creation of robust computer vision systems for various applications. Although it appears that our methods is capable of resolving many difficulties in various research tasks we'd also like to conduct more rigorous and extensive techniques to expand the limitations and increase the operational performance of the proposed method.

title: Extracting Biomolecular Interactions Using Semantic Parsing of Biomedical Text
Abstract: Biomolecular interactions play a crucial role in various biological processes and diseases, yet their complexities and vast scales associated with traditional experimental methods hinder comprehensive understanding and data analysis. Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) and machine learning have sparked a surge of interest in leveraging text data for extracting biomolecular interactions. This study proposes a novel approach utilizing semantic parsing of biomedical text to disentangle intricate biomolecular relationships. Our framework utilizes a deep learning architecture to parse biomedical texts into a structured representation, which includes entities, relationships, and specific interaction types. By integrating a domain-specific lexicon and knowledge graph, we can accurately detect various types of biomolecular interactions, such as protein-protein, protein-DNA, and protein-RNA. The parsed interactions are then evaluated using gold standard datasets and compared with existing NLP-based methods, exhibiting significant enhancements in accuracy and completeness. Furthermore, our approach enables the creation of an immersive and expandable knowledge graph of biomolecular interactions, allowing researchers to explore complex relationship networks and uncover novel insights into biological pathways and disease mechanisms. By merging NLP techniques with domain expertise, this study demonstrates the potential for semantic parsing to facilitate cutting-edge discovery in the field of biomolecular interactions.

title: State of the Art Control of Atari Games Using Shallow Reinforcement Learning
Abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive study on the application of shallow reinforcement learning techniques for controlling Atari games, a classic benchmark for developing AI and reinforcement learning algorithms. Historically, controlling Atari games was an incredibly challenging problem, even for state-of-the-art models, with success rates often limited to a few percent. To bridge this gap, researchers have been actively exploring various reinforcement learning architectures and algorithms. We explore the potential of shallow reinforcement learning models, which are less computationally demanding than their deep counterparts, in tackling this problem. Our proposed approach utilizes a variation of Q-learning, incorporating experience replay and the incorporation of epsilon-greedy exploration strategy to mitigate overfitting and improve data efficiency. The proposed approach is evaluated against several popular Atari games, including Pong, Breakout, and Space Invaders. Our experimental results reveal that the shallow reinforcement learning model achieves significant improvements in terms of success rates, with several models surpassing 90% success rates on Pong, over 85% on Breakout, and close to 70% on Space Invaders. By exploiting the computationally efficient nature of shallow reinforcement learning models, we successfully address a major limitation of existing Atari game control methods, paving the way for further explorations in this space, and significantly advancing the state of the art in this field.

title: Reuse of Neural Modules for General Video Game Playing
Abstract: This research paper explores the feasibility of reusing neural modules in the context of general video game playing, a problem that requires agents to navigate and interact with diverse games without prior knowledge of their mechanics. By adopting a modular approach to neural network design, we aim to develop an architecture that can be leveraged across various games, reducing the need for extensive game-specific training and allowing for more efficient learning. The proposed approach involves identifying and reusing neural modules that are capable of learning domain-agnostic skills, such as spatial reasoning, motor control, and decision-making, which can be composed and fine-tuned to adapt to novel games. Our research focuses on developing a framework that enables the identification, reuse, and combination of these neural modules, leveraging techniques such as transfer learning, meta-learning, and modular neural network architecture design. The proposed system is trained on a variety of games from distinct genres, with the goal of evaluating the generalization capabilities of the learned neural modules. Results demonstrate the potential of reusing neural modules for general video game playing, showcasing improved performance, reduced training time, and better adaptability compared to traditional monolithic architectures. Our research provides insights into the design of efficient neural network architectures for general game playing, with potential applications in areas such as artificial intelligence, game development, and robotics. By reusing and adapting neural modules across diverse tasks, we can unlock more efficient and robust artificial intelligence systems with broader applicability.

title: Learning the Semantics of Manipulation Action
Abstract: Our understanding of manipulation actions, such as picking up and placing objects, often relies on qualitative and subjective assessments. However, with the growing interest in human-robot collaboration, there is a pressing need for a more precise and objective comprehension of these actions. Research in robotics and computer vision has made significant strides in identifying and classifying manipulation actions, yet these systems typically rely on a manual labeling process that requires extensive expert knowledge. This restricts their scalability and generalizability to diverse environments and object populations. To address these limitations, we propose a novel approach that learns the semantics of manipulation actions through a self-supervised framework. Our method integrates information-theoretic techniques and visual grounding to jointly learn a probabilistic model of object properties and object-manipulator interactions. This framework allows our system to recognize and reason about manipulation actions in a structured and interpretable manner, leveraging visual and sensory information in real-time. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through extensive experiments on a range of manipulation tasks, involving various objects and environments. Our results show that our system outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy and generalizability, highlighting the potential of our approach for applications in human-robot collaboration, robotic assembly, and object recognition.

title: Neuron's Eye View: Inferring Features of Complex Stimuli from Neural Responses
Abstract: This abstract delves into the realm of decoding neural responses to infer the features of complex stimuli. The longstanding challenge of understanding neural representations has been addressed through the integration of theoretical frameworks and empirical evidence obtained from various neural recording techniques. By analyzing the responses of individual neurons and populations, researchers have uncovered a wealth of information about the perceptual features and attributes that underlie neural processing. This research has far-reaching implications for our understanding of complex neural dynamics and has led to significant advancements in fields such as neuroscience, artificial intelligence, and machine learning. Building on this foundation, recent studies have been focused on identifying and deciphering the underlying features of complex stimuli, such as those encountered in vision and audition. To achieve this goal, researchers have employed advanced signal processing techniques and machine learning algorithms to extract meaningful information from neural activity patterns. These methods have enabled the inference of a range of features, including spatial and temporal structure, object identity, and semantic content. By revealing the intricate dance of neural activity underlying complex perception, this research aims to provide a comprehensive 'neuron's eye view' of how the brain constructs our experience of the world.

title: Max-Pooling Dropout for Regularization of Convolutional Neural Networks
Abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to regularization techniques for Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) by integrating Max-Pooling and Dropout to enhance network robustness and generalizability. Max-Pooling allows for the reduction of spatial dimensions in feature maps, enabling the capture of higher-level features and facilitating the downscaling of resolutions, while maintaining critical information. However, this reduction leads to the loss of important details. Dropout, another regularization method, aims to prevent overfitting by randomly setting neurons to zero during the training phase, effectively breaking neuron dependencies. However, standard Max-Pooling followed by standard Dropout may eliminate vital information contained within the feature maps. Consequently, we exploit the synergistic combination of Max-Pooling and Dropout to reduce overfitting and promote feature learning through sparse sub-networks, which lead to more robust feature representation. Our study provides evidence that this integrated technique offers improved accuracy with a decreased risk of overfitting in various computer vision tasks, and helps to bridge the gap between state-of-the-art accuracy and robustness attributes expected from a neural network model.

title: Locally Adaptive Translation for Knowledge Graph Embedding
Abstract: Knowledge Graph Embedding (KGE) models have become a crucial component in a wide range of applications including question answering, link prediction, and recommender systems. However, traditional KGE models often suffer from limited scalability and expressiveness, particularly when dealing with complex and dynamic knowledge graphs. To address these challenges, this paper introduces a novel approach called Locally Adaptive Translation (LAT) for KGE. LAT builds upon traditional translation-based KGE models but incorporates an adaptive learning mechanism that allows for the local refinement of entity and relation embeddings based on the neighborhood of each entity. This local adaptability enables LAT to better capture nuanced, context-dependent relationships within the knowledge graph. The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of LAT in improving the accuracy of entity classification and relation prediction tasks compared to state-of-the-art KGE models. Furthermore, the proposed method shows promising scalability properties and can be easily integrated into distributed computing frameworks for large-scale knowledge graph applications. The ablation studies also confirm the importance of the locally adaptive translation mechanism in achieving improved performance. Overall, the presented LAT approach presents a feasible and scalable solution for handling complex knowledge graphs while maintaining high accuracy in KGE tasks.

title: Proposition of a Theoretical Model for Missing Data Imputation using Deep Learning and Evolutionary Algorithms
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel theoretical model for missing data imputation that synergistically combines the strengths of deep learning and evolutionary algorithms. The increasing complexity of real-world datasets has made missing data imputation a significant challenge in various fields, including but not limited to, health sciences, finance, and climate research. The proposed model, termed as DeepEvolutionary Imputation Model (DEIM), employs a hybrid approach by integrating a deep neural network with an evolutionary algorithm to effectively handle missing data imputation. The deep neural network is utilized to extract complex patterns and feature interactions from the data, while the evolutionary algorithm is used to optimize the model's parameters and architecture through the process of evolution. The DEIM model also incorporates a novel mechanism to handle outliers and noisy data, ensuring that the imputed values are both accurate and reliable. Experimental results demonstrate that the DEIM model outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of imputation accuracy and robustness. Furthermore, the proposed model is also evaluated on various real-world datasets, showcasing its flexibility and generalizability. The findings of this research provide valuable insights into the design and development of effective missing data imputation models, enabling the trustworthy analysis and utilization of incomplete datasets. By integrating deep learning and evolutionary algorithms, the DEIM model offers a promising solution for missing data imputation in various applications, paving the way for more accurate and reliable data-driven decision-making.

title: Staple: Complementary Learners for Real-Time Tracking
Abstract: This paper introduces the concept of complimentary learners for real-time object tracking, addressing the limitations of traditional deep learning-based approaches in navigating complex and dynamic environments. Complimentary learners are AI models that learn to predict the object's movement and interaction with the surroundings, combining their predictions with those generated by a primary tracking model to enhance robustness and accuracy. This novel framework leverages knowledge distillation, ensemble learning, and transfer learning to develop joint tracking models with improved handling of partial occlusions, lighting variations, and pose changes. The proposed model is evaluated against popular real-time tracking benchmarks, showcasing improved performance on occluded and pose-changing sequences, demonstrating its efficacy in challenging scenarios. By harnessing the strengths of multiple models, the complimentary learners provide a viable solution for achieving high-quality real-time tracking with robustness to various environmental factors and object conditions. Despite its potential, the approach can be further optimized and generalized to address the specific demands of various applications, including robotics, surveillance, and video analytics.

title: Neural Generative Question Answering
Abstract: This study proposes a novel approach to neural generative question answering, a task that aims to generate coherent and context-specific responses to user queries. The integration of neural generative models and question answering (QA) systems is gaining increasing attention in the field of natural language processing. The key challenge lies in effectively modeling the underlying linguistic and contextual relationships that govern human communication. Our proposed method leverages pre-trained language models to develop a generative QA framework that not only retrieves relevant context but also synthesizes new information based on user queries. By combining a transformer-based encoder with a variational autoencoder (VAE) for response generation, our model learns to capture the semantic and syntactic structures inherent in human language. We experiment with various datasets to evaluate the performance of our proposed method against state-of-the-art QA systems. The results demonstrate improved response consistency and coherence, indicating that our approach is conducive to generating human-like responses to user queries. Furthermore, our study contributes to the broader landscape of neural generative models by exploring their applications in realistic and interactive dialogue settings. The insights gained from this research provide valuable guidance for developing practical QA systems that not only provide accurate answers but also engage users in meaningful and contextual conversations.

title: Q-Networks for Binary Vector Actions
Abstract: Q-Networks for Binary Vector Actions have garnered significant attention in the realm of deep reinforcement learning due to their ability to effectively handle high-dimensional action spaces. Nevertheless, their direct application to scenarios involving binary vector actions may not necessarily exploit their full potential. This is because binary vector actions are intrinsically low-dimensional and thus do not align with the traditional premise of Q-Networks, which are designed for handling high-dimensional action spaces. The problem becomes even more pronounced when discrete and high-dimensional action spaces are present, as this leads to highly inflated Q-Network architectures with unwieldy Q-tables that fail to generalize well. Aiming to formulate a solution that leverages the unique characteristics of binary vector actions while still working with Q-Networks, we propose an innovative approach by incorporating hierarchical structures into the Q-Network architecture. The enhanced architecture enables Q-Networks to effectively traverse hierarchical representations of binary vector actions, thus allowing them to capture long-range dependencies present in these representations. This approach not only reduces the intrinsic dimensionality of the action space but also promotes better interpretability of the learned Q-values. Our simulation results demonstrate that this enhanced Q-Network architecture exhibits improved learning efficiency and generalization capabilities over its non-hierarchical counterparts, especially in complex domains involving binary vector actions.

title: Toward a Taxonomy and Computational Models of Abnormalities in Images
Abstract: The classification and detection of abnormalities in images is a complex task that has significant applications in various fields such as computer vision, medical imaging, and more. In recent years, research has aimed to develop taxonomy and computational models that can effectively categorize and identify image anomalies. Despite the growing body of literature on image analysis, there remains a lack of standardized frameworks for abnormal image detection and classification. This research identifies the primary goals of an image anomaly taxonomy, including defining normal and abnormal objects, understanding anomaly appearance, and devising a hierarchal categorization framework. The development of a computational model to accompany the taxonomy requires integrating both hand-crafted and learned feature extraction and local and global decision-making architectures. Furthermore, the proposed taxonomy would encompass aspects such as abnormal image detection, reasoning, and quality metrics that can facilitate the benchmarking of computational models. By consolidating the related research and outlining the features of an image anomaly taxonomic framework, the results provide a foundation for the development of automatic image recognition and inspection systems that effectively handle anomalies and abnormalities.

title: Fixed-Point Performance Analysis of Recurrent Neural Networks
Abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive performance analysis of fixed-point recurrent neural networks (RNNs) for efficient implementation on embedded systems with limited resources. The analysis focuses on the trade-off between network performance and hardware costs, highlighting the impact of fixed-point data representation on the quality of results. A comparative study is conducted on several fixed-point RNN variants, including scaled perceptrons, tanh RNNs, and ReLU RNNs, to evaluate their accuracy and convergence rates in various learning tasks. The results demonstrate that fixed-point RNNs can achieve competitive performance with their floating-point counterparts, while reducing memory usage and computational requirements by up to an order of magnitude. Furthermore, the study explores the effects of precision, scaling factors, and activation functions on the network's performance and energy efficiency. To ensure reliable quantization, a novel quantization framework is proposed, combining bit-width adaptation and scaling factor learning to optimize the fixed-point representations. The proposed framework is integrated into a deep learning framework, demonstrated on several benchmark datasets, and compared to state-of-the-art quantization methods. The analysis provides insights into the fixed-point performance bottlenecks and offers a unified framework for optimizing the representations, paving the way for efficient RNN implementation on resource-constrained edge devices. The proposed framework can be extended to other deep learning models and applications, such as speech recognition, natural language processing, and time series prediction.

title: What can we learn about CNNs from a large scale controlled object dataset?
Abstract: The increasing popularity of deep learning CNNs has led to their widespread application in object recognition and image classification tasks, outperforming traditional methods in accuracy and precision. However, despite its widespread adoption, the process of training and fine-tuning CNNs remains daunting due to the complexity of the data and algorithms involved, particularly when it comes to adapting to new and unseen object classes with limited labeled data. This study aims to investigate what can be learned from training and testing CNNs on a large-scale, controlled object dataset, comprised of images of various objects, each annotated with precise bounding boxes and labels. By analyzing the performance of various CNN architectures on this dataset across different learning modes (supervised and self-supervised), we aimed to explore the following questions: What are the salient architectural features that improve CNN performance? Can CNNs learn transferable object representations efficiently? How do the effects of dataset size and density impact CNN performance? Our investigation involved designing experiments to highlight the interplay between CNN architecture, learning strategy, and dataset properties, and the findings provide insights into the architectural features and learning strategies that contribute to improved CNN performance in object recognition tasks.

title: An Online Unsupervised Structural Plasticity Algorithm for Spiking Neural Networks
Abstract: This paper presents a novel online unsupervised structural plasticity algorithm for spiking neural networks designed to enable efficient, adaptive, and scalable neural reorganization. The proposed algorithm, termed synaptic-and-trophic-spater (STSP), leverages a biologically-inspired approach by incorporating synaptic and trophic signals, allowing spiking neural networks (SNNs) to self-organize and adapt in response to the ever-changing environment. By leveraging the interplay between synaptic and trophic signals, STSP enables each neuron to receive feedback about the strength of its outgoing connections, enabling more robust weight updates that promote neural reorganization. STSP also incorporates an efficient, online framework for estimating the trophic signal, circumventing the need for offline simulations, thereby facilitating real-time implementation of SNNs. We demonstrate the efficacy of STSP on several benchmark tasks, including Neurortonal travel, reaching, and generating, showcasing improved generalizability and adaptability of SNNs. Furthermore, we present extensive experimental results indicating that STSP enables more substantial neural reconfiguration than established online unsupervised learning methods, offering a promising framework for building highly adaptive and dynamic SNNs that can efficiently engage in real-world tasks and applications.

title: Predicting and visualizing psychological attributions with a deep neural network
Abstract: This study presents a novel approach to predicting and visualizing psychological attributions using a deep neural network. Current attribution theories in psychology primarily focus on identifying the underlying reasoning processes and mental variables that influence human judgments and behaviors. However, these theories often struggle to provide actionable insights and tangible visual representations of these complex processes. To address this limitation, this research employed a deep learning-based approach, specifically a convolutional neural network (CNN), to model psychological attributions in a data-driven manner. The proposed framework utilizes a combination of semantic and spatial encoding techniques to map attributions onto a geometric space, enabling both predictive modeling and visual representation of these complex mental constructs. Through targeted experimentation and validation, the presented approach demonstrated superior predictive performance compared to traditional attribution models. Results also revealed the benefits of using the proposed deep CNN framework for visualizing attributions, yielding intuitive visualizations that facilitate a deeper understanding of the intricate relationships between attributions, context, and behavior. By providing a more comprehensive and actionable representation of psychological attributions, this work has implications for the development of more effective decision-making strategies, and sheds light on the potential of deep learning in modeling complex psychological phenomena.

title: Adjusting for Chance Clustering Comparison Measures
Abstract: Chance clustering, a phenomenon that arises from analyzing a large dataset with numerous variables, poses significant challenges in correctly identifying meaningful patterns and differences between groups. Traditional comparison measures, such as the adjusted Rand index and mutual information, are used to assess clustering algorithms, but these measures are not immune to the effects of chance clustering. To address this issue, recent studies have proposed various adjustment methods to enhance the robustness of these measures. However, the development of more effective adjustment techniques continues to be an area of active research. This study aims to investigate and compare the performance of different adjustment methods on chance clustering-based comparison measures. A comprehensive analysis of the strengths and limitations of five prominent adjustment techniques – randomization tests, propensity score adjustment, spectral clustering, entropy-based adjustment, and permutation tests – is presented in this work. The analysis includes a simulation study that evaluates the impact of chance clustering on the conventional and adjusted Rand indices, as well as mutual information. The results are applied to a real-world dataset, where the effectiveness of the adjustment methods is assessed. Overall, the findings provide valuable insights into the efficiency and reliability of the proposed adjustment techniques and emphasize their importance in overcoming the pitfalls of chance clustering when comparing clustering algorithms.

title: Predicting the top and bottom ranks of billboard songs using Machine Learning
Abstract: This study explores the application of machine learning algorithms in predicting the top and bottom ranks of Billboard songs. By analyzing a comprehensive dataset of Billboard chart performances spanning over two decades, the research aims to identify the key factors influencing song rankings. A multitude of machine learning models, including random forests, gradient boosting, and neural networks, are trained and compared to evaluate their accuracy in predicting chart performance. The features used for training the models include song attributes, artist characteristics, and music industry-wide metrics such as genre, release date, and label affiliation. The study reveals that the combination of machine learning algorithms and comprehensive datasets presents a feasible and potentially accurate approach to predicting Billboard song rankings. Notably, the performance of deep learning models, particularly convolutional neural networks, exhibits exceptional accuracy in predicting top-tier chart performances. Conversely, ensemble models consisting of multiple algorithms are found to better predict bottom-rank songs, indicating differential patterns and responses to chart performance predictions. Overall, the findings suggest that a data-driven approach integrating machine learning and music industry insights holds promise for predicting Billboard song rankings, providing music industry stakeholders with valuable forecasting tools to inform marketing strategies, artist development, and content creation decisions.

title: MXNet: A Flexible and Efficient Machine Learning Library for Heterogeneous Distributed Systems
Abstract: MXNet is a high-performance, open-source machine learning library that enables the efficient execution of deep neural networks on various types of hardware systems. Its flexibility and extensibility make it a popular choice for distributed computing environments, where it can be used to build heterogeneous systems consisting of diverse hardware components such as GPUs, CPUs, and specialized accelerators. The library's modular architecture and array-based computation model allow for seamless integration of different programming languages, frameworks, and execution engines, making it an ideal platform for multi-modal and multi-task deep learning applications. MXNet's automatic differentiation and gradient computation capabilities also facilitate the rapid prototyping and deployment of complex neural architectures, which can be trained on massive datasets using its asynchronous and parallelized optimization methods. As a result, MXNet has been widely adopted in various applications, including computer vision, natural language processing, and speech recognition, where its ability to scale to millions of users and learn from vast amounts of data enables sophisticated and accurate predictive models. With its continued development and community-driven innovation, MXNet remains a critical component of modern artificial intelligence and deep learning ecosystems.

title: CrossCat: A Fully Bayesian Nonparametric Method for Analyzing Heterogeneous, High Dimensional Data
Abstract: This paper introduces CrossCat, a novel, fully Bayesian nonparametric method for handling complex, high-dimensional data characterized by inherent variability in scale and structure. Available methods for dealing with this type of data are often rigid and unable to adapt to the unique features of diverse datasets, leading to suboptimal results. CrossCat, on the other hand, models these datasets using a flexible and hierarchical Bayesian nonparametric framework that accounts for the different sources of variability and allows for the identification of non-linear relationships. By adopting a modular approach and explicitly modeling the interactions between sub-problems, CrossCat avoids the need for strong model assumptions and can accommodate diverse data structures, dimensions, and scales. This allows for simultaneous analysis of varying types of data and the determination of underlying patterns and relationships. An empirical evaluation of CrossCat using a range of real-world datasets, including those originating from finance, medicine, and environmental science, demonstrates its ability to flexibly model data characteristics, untap relevant insights, and outperform existing methods. The proposed methodology supports more accurate and comprehensive inferences, and allows researchers to explore diverse aspects of data under a unified framework, ultimately paving the way for the more effective utilization of complex data sets in applied domains.

title: MERLiN: Mixture Effect Recovery in Linear Networks
Abstract: MERLiN overcomes the limitations of traditional linear models on network analysis by incorporating complex mixture interactions, providing a more comprehensive understanding of system dynamics in complex networks. Through detailed mathematical derivations, MERLiN is formulated to account for both direct and indirect influences within a network, enabling the accurate recovery of interactions between entities. This model is shown to be effective in distinguishing between different types of complex systems, including sparse and dense networks, as well as homophilous and heterophilous interactions. The recovery of mixture effects in MERLiN is facilitated through non-linear and polynomial regression techniques, highlighting its ability to handle non-linearity in the relationships between entities. Comparative analysis with existing methods for mixture recovery in linear networks demonstrates the robustness and accuracy of MERLiN in identifying network characteristics. Furthermore, the flexibility of MERLiN allows for its application to diverse fields, including social network analysis, recommender systems, and biological systems. The implementation and evaluation of MERLiN indicate its potential as a powerful tool for modeling and understanding the intricate behavior of complex systems.

title: K2 Variable Catalogue II: Machine Learning Classification of Variable Stars and Eclipsing Binaries in K2 Fields 0-4
Abstract: The K2 Variable Catalogue II leverages machine learning techniques to improve upon its predecessors by reclassifying variable stars and eclipsing binaries in the K2 fields 0-4. This enhancement is crucial for the accurate determination of physical parameters, such as temperatures, radii, and orbital periods, for these enigmatic astrophysical phenomena. By capitalizing on the extensive dataset compiled during the K2 mission, the reclassification process identifies hitherto ambiguous or misclassified instances, thereby refining our understanding of variable and binary star populations within the surveyed fields. The efficacy of the machine learning paradigm is demonstrated through a comparison of classification outcomes against well-established catalogues, revealing reasonable concurrency. This approach successfully selects targeted subsets of interest from within the vast catalog of light curves, which can be utilized for comprehensive studies on stellar evolution, stellar structure, and time-domain astrometry. Additionally, the K2 Variable Catalogue II contributes to future undertakings, such as characterizing properties of exoplanet hosts and calibrating distance–luminosity relationships by incorporating the newly generated catalogues into a unified framework for cataloguing variable stars and binary systems.

title: An attractor neural network architecture with an ultra high information capacity: numerical results
Abstract: This research paper presents a groundbreaking architectural design for an attractor neural network (ANN) with a theoretically predicted ultra-high information capacity. The proposed architecture leverages the principles of multistability, non-linearity, and global sensitivity to create complex network topologies that can efficiently accumulate and store large amounts of information. Using a combination of analytical and computational methods, including information-theory-based measures and numerical simulations, the authors demonstrate the exceptional information-capacity capabilities of the proposed ANN architecture. The results show that the network can accumulate information at a rate significantly higher than traditional neural networks, with the capacity to represent and process vast amounts of complex patterns. Furthermore, the proposed architecture exhibits robust stability and predictable behavior, even under conditions of significant internal and external noise. The numerical results presented in this study demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed ANN architecture for real-world applications where high-capacity information processing is crucial, such as image and signal recognition, data compression, and natural language processing. The innovative ANN design outlined in this paper is expected to revolutionize the field of artificial neural networks and their applications in various domains, and may also have fundamental implications for our understanding of biological neural networks and their functionalities.

title: Prototypical Priors: From Improving Classification to Zero-Shot Learning
Abstract: This work focuses on leveraging prototypical priors to elevate classification performance and expand into the realm of zero-shot learning. Prototypical priors imbue deep neural networks with an intrinsic understanding of the intrinsic structure of the data by constructing latent representations that respect the underlying manifold geometry. Through extensive experimental validation on a variety of benchmark datasets, we demonstrate that incorporating prototypical priors significantly enhances classification accuracy, particularly in scenarios where the training data undergoes partial domain shifts, is influenced by outliers, or exhibits changing modalities. Moreover, we discover that this improved understanding of data geometry enables the model to learn a more consistent embedding space. Consequently, when paired with a separate, closed-world classification stage, the resulting prototypical prior-based system achieves competitive and often superior performance in zero-shot learning tasks, including those where none of the depicted classes are present during training. The presented methodology is general enough to be combined with various popular embeddings, attesting to a versatile application. We provide empirical support for the effectiveness of integrating prototypical priors to solve both supervised classification and unsupervised zero-shot learning problems through rigorous comparison with established state-of-the-art architectures.

title: Building Memory with Concept Learning Capabilities from Large-scale Knowledge Base
Abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to building memory systems with concept learning capabilities by leveraging large-scale knowledge bases. Inspired by the human ability to acquire knowledge and reason about abstract concepts, we propose a neural memory architecture that can learn to represent and reason about concepts from large-scale knowledge bases. Our approach, dubbed "Concept Memory Network" (CMN), integrates knowledge representation, reasoning, and learning mechanisms to form a comprehensive memory system. CMN is trained on a massive knowledge base of entities, their relationships, and attributes, enabling it to learn abstract concepts and their relationships. To evaluate CMN, we conduct experiments on a range of tasks, including entity recognition, relation extraction, and concept-based reasoning. Our results demonstrate that CMN outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on these tasks, achieving significant improvements in accuracy and efficiency. Furthermore, we show that CMN can learn to reason about complex concepts, such as "a person is a type of entity" and "a person has a profession", and generalize to new, unseen relationships and attributes. Our findings suggest that CMN has the potential to serve as a robust and scalable memory system for applications that require reasoning about abstract concepts from large-scale knowledge bases, including question answering, natural language processing, and expert systems. Overall, this work marks a significant step towards building memory systems that can learn and reason about concepts, and has far-reaching implications for the development of intelligent systems that can understand and reason about the world.

title: Kalman-based Stochastic Gradient Method with Stop Condition and Insensitivity to Conditioning
Abstract: This abstract presents a novel Kalman-based stochastic gradient method that incorporates a stop condition and mitigates the effects of conditioning, resulting in improved convergence rates and increased computational efficiency. Traditional stochastic gradient descent techniques often rely on line search or backtracking to establish a stopping criterion, which can lead to reduced performance in instances where the gradient estimation error dominates the convergence behavior. Conversely, the proposed approach utilizes a Kalman filter to dynamically estimate the uncertainty associated with the gradient estimates, allowing for adaptive adjustments to the learning rate and incorporating a stop condition based on the confidence level of the gradient estimates. Furthermore, the Kalman-based method effectively alleviates the impact of conditioning by imposing a regularization term on the Hessian matrix, promoting matrix properties that facilitate faster convergence rates, even in the presence of singularity or near-singularity. The developed methodology has implications for a wide range of applications, including machine learning, signal processing, and control systems, where stochastic gradient methods are widely employed. Numerical experiments and theoretical analyses demonstrate the efficacy of the Kalman-based stochastic gradient method in achieving superior convergence performance and stability compared to state-of-the-art optimization algorithms, while exhibiting robustness to conditioning and computational efficiency.

title: Deep Reinforcement Learning with Attention for Slate Markov Decision Processes with High-Dimensional States and Actions
Abstract: Deep reinforcement learning has made significant strides in tackling complex decision-making problems, particularly in high-dimensional state and action spaces. However, existing methods often struggle to generalize across various situations and contexts due to their inflexibility and lack of understanding of the underlying dynamics. To address this limitation, this paper proposes a novel framework that combines the strengths of attention mechanisms with deep reinforcement learning for slate Markov decision processes. By leveraging attention mechanisms, our framework enables the agent to selectively focus on relevant information within high-dimensional state and action spaces, thereby improving its knowledge about the environment. This selective focus also enables the agent to develop a better understanding of the sequential dependencies between actions and states, which is critical for making informed decisions in dynamic environments. Our approach is experimentally validated using a range of benchmark problems with high-dimensional states and actions, demonstrating superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our attention-based framework is particularly effective in scenarios where the complexity and uncertainty of the environment pose significant challenges to traditional reinforcement learning methods. By providing a more adaptive and robust framework for decision-making, our approach has far-reaching implications for a wide range of applications, including recommendation systems, robotic control, and autonomous vehicles.

title: Bayesian Matrix Completion via Adaptive Relaxed Spectral Regularization
Abstract: This paper presents a Bayesian framework for matrix completion problems via adaptive relaxed spectral regularization. The problem of matrix completion arises when we are given only a subset of entries from a larger matrix, with the goal of estimating the remaining missing values based on the observed entries. Conventional approaches to matrix completion typically focus on finding low-rank factorizations of the matrix, but they often fail to capture complex structures and relationships within the data. To overcome these limitations, we propose a Bayesian matrix completion method that incorporates adaptively relaxed spectral regularization to identify informative low-dimensional subspaces from the observed entries. Our approach uses a prior distribution that allows for missing entries in the matrix and adapts to the degrees of freedom present in the observed entries to eliminate noise. By performing Bayesian inference using the proposed adaptive relaxed spectral regularization, our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on various synthetic and real-world datasets compared to existing methods, including matrix factorization-based approaches. The computational efficiency and robustness of our method make it suitable for handling large-scale matrix completion applications with missing entries arising from various domains such as recommender systems and image inpainting.

title: Effective LSTMs for Target-Dependent Sentiment Classification
Abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive exploration of the effectiveness of Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks in tackling the challenge of target-dependent sentiment classification, an essential task in natural language processing. Target-dependent sentiment classification involves identifying the sentiment expressed towards a specific target within a given sentence, which can be a person, place, organization, or even an idea. Traditional approaches have predominantly relied on feature engineering and rule-based methods, which are often time-consuming and tend to yield shallow insights. In contrast, we propose leveraging the power of LSTMs, a type of Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) proficient in learning temporal dependencies within sequential data. Our contribution lies in designing and implementing novel architectures for LSTMs, specifically tailored to the complexities of target-dependent sentiment classification. The proposed models seamlessly integrate the LSTM component with other state-of-the-art techniques, including multi-task learning, attention mechanisms, and sub-word level representation. Empirical evaluations on several benchmark datasets demonstrate the impressive performance of our proposed models, significantly outperforming existing approaches in various settings. The experimental results provide valuable insights into the capabilities and limitations of LSTMs in addressing the intricacies of target-dependent sentiment classification, with far-reaching implications for downstream applications in areas such as text analysis, opinion mining, and hate speech detection.

title: Correlated fluctuations in strongly-coupled binary networks beyond equilibrium
Abstract: Strongly-coupled binary networks, such as those found in biological systems, materials science, and social networks, are ubiquitous in nature, wherein nodes interact through binary variables. Contrary to traditional wisdom that focused on equilibrium properties, recent experiments have revealed the emergence of correlated fluctuations in such systems, which are characteristic of nonequilibrium phenomena. These correlated fluctuations are of fundamental interest as they can arise from a variety of non-equilibrium processes, including internal feedback, structural properties, and spatial correlations. Our paper investigates the presence of correlated fluctuations in strongly-coupled binary networks, focusing on both stationary and transient regimes. Using a combination of analytical and numerical approaches, we specifically explore the dynamic and static correlations between individual binary variables, examining the effects of different coupling mechanisms, system sizes, and external driving signals. Our results demonstrate the existence of correlated fluctuations in both static and dynamic settings, highlighting the importance of non-equilibrium processes in determining the emergent behavior of these complex systems. By establishing a connection between the structural properties of the networks and the correlated behavior of individual nodes, we gain a deeper understanding of the mechanisms driving the emergence of correlated fluctuations, providing insights that can be applied to a wide range of natural and artificial systems.

title: Interactive audio-tactile maps for visually impaired people
Abstract: This research paper explores the development and implementation of interactive audio-tactile maps for visually impaired individuals. The study aimed to investigate the potential of incorporating audio and tactile elements into traditional maps to enhance navigation and wayfinding abilities for visually impaired people. A mixed-methods approach was employed, combining both qualitative and quantitative data collection and analysis methods. Participants with varying levels of visual impairment were recruited to test and evaluate the interactive audio-tactile maps. A pre-designed experimental setup allowed participants to navigate through a series of trials, with and without the use of the maps, to assess their performance and perceived difficulties. Results showed significant improvements in navigation accuracy and reduced anxiety levels when using the interactive audio-tactile maps compared to traditional maps. Furthermore, thematic analysis of participant feedback highlighted the importance of clear audio cues, tactile markers, and user-friendly interface design in creating an effective and accessible navigation experience. The findings have implications for the design and development of inclusive and accessible maps and navigation systems, ultimately contributing to the promotion of mobility and independence for visually impaired individuals. By providing a more intuitive and enjoyable navigation experience, the interactive audio-tactile maps can empower visually impaired people to explore their surroundings with greater confidence and independence.

title: Occlusion-Aware Human Pose Estimation with Mixtures of Sub-Trees
Abstract: Occlusion-Aware Human Pose Estimation with Mixtures of Sub-Trees is a novel approach to addressing the challenging task of estimating human pose in occluded images. The majority of current human pose estimation techniques rely heavily on precise and complete detection of body parts, which often fail when confronted with partial occlusion or complex backgrounds. This limitation motivated the development of a new model that proficiently addresses these challenges, especially in scenes with partial human body occlusions. The proposed system employs a mixture of sub-trees (MST) to establish a more robust hierarchy of human body parts, accounting for variations in pose and intensity of occlusions. An inventive architecture, called MixTree-NET, is designed to combine the outputs of multiple MSTs, taking advantage of their complementary characteristics and selectively utilizing their strengths while rectifying their limitations to produce superior human pose estimates. The MixTree-NET model incorporates an adaptively weighted reinitialization strategy, which enables it to dynamically weigh and reassign important body parts based on the degree and location of occlusion, thus leading to more accurate pose estimation. Thoroughly evaluated on various benchmark datasets with occluded test images, the presented model conclusively demonstrates improved pose estimation skills in the face of heavy occlusions, reducing error rates by 13-18% with respect to state-of-the-art techniques. As such, Occlusion-Aware Human Pose Estimation with Mixtures of Sub-Trees can efficiently be used in a wide variety of applications, including computer vision, human-computer interaction and robotics.

title: Approaches for Sentiment Analysis on Twitter: A State-of-Art study
Abstract: This study presents a comprehensive state-of-the-art review on various approaches for sentiment analysis on Twitter data. With the ever-increasing popularity of social media platforms, particularly Twitter, and the vast amounts of emotional and sentiment-rich data generated on the platform, there is a growing need for effective sentiment analysis techniques. Despite its significance, sentiment analysis on Twitter poses unique challenges due to the short length of tweets, the use of informal language, and the presence of noise, sarcasm, irony, and figures of speech. Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) and deep learning have led to the development of several techniques for sentiment analysis on Twitter, including rule-based approaches, machine learning-based methods, and deep learning models. This study reviews these approaches in detail, highlighting their strengths and limitations, as well as their applications and performances on various sentiment analysis tasks. It also discusses the current challenges and future directions in the field, including the need for more robust and domain-specific models that can handle nuances of language and cultural differences. Our study aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the current state of the art in sentiment analysis on Twitter, identifying key trends, gaps, and opportunities for further research and development.

title: Simulations for Validation of Vision Systems
Abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive review of simulation-based methods for validating vision systems, encompassing a wide range of applications in fields such as robotics, computer vision, and autonomous systems. With the rapid advancement of vision technology, accurate and efficient validation of vision systems has become increasingly essential to ensure their reliability and performance in real-world scenarios. To address this need, simulation-based validation has emerged as a crucial tool for vision system engineers and researchers. The review focuses on the various types of simulations used for validating vision systems, including physical simulations, virtual reality simulations, and computer-aided design (CAD) simulations. It also discusses the different approaches employed for simulating complex real-world environments, such as photorealistic rendering, dynamic lighting, and realistic object interactions. Furthermore, the paper examines the key challenges and limitations associated with simulation-based validation, such as the need for high-quality simulation data, the importance of accurate physics modeling, and the requirement for efficient simulation algorithms. By presenting a detailed analysis of the current state-of-the-art in simulation-based validation of vision systems, this review aims to provide valuable insights for researchers and engineers working in this area, enabling them to develop more effective and reliable vision systems capable of meeting the demands of modern applications.

title: Bag Reference Vector for Multi-instance Learning
Abstract: This research explores the development and application of a novel Bag Reference Vector (BRV) framework for Multi-instance Learning (MIL). MIL enables the classification of cases where an instance is associated with a bag and labeled accordingly, with some instances within the bag being relevant and others being irrelevant. The BRV approach incorporates a set of reference vectors that capture key distributional characteristics of instance representations in each bag, thereby facilitating accurate aggregation of instance-level features to bag-level representations. By leveraging BRV to focus on the underlying distribution patterns within each bag, the proposed method aims to enhance the predictive performance of traditional MIL models. The key contributions of this study include the theoretical formulations of BRV, as well as empirical evaluations on several benchmark datasets that demonstrate its superiority in comparison to existing state-of-the-art MIL methods. The devised framework also provides explicit model interpretability and the ability to seamlessly incorporate domain knowledge. Results show that the novel reference vector-based approach leads to significant improvements in terms of classification accuracy and interpretability, highlighting its potential as a versatile tool for various real-world applications where MIL-based methods have been adopted to classify irregularly structured data.

title: Fast Low-Rank Matrix Learning with Nonconvex Regularization
Abstract: This paper investigates fast low-rank matrix learning with nonconvex regularization, a problem that has garnered significant attention in recent years due to its widespread applications in signal processing, computer vision, and machine learning. The problem involves recovering a low-rank matrix from a set of observations or measurements, with the goal of minimizing the difference between the observed and underlying matrices. However, the low-rank constraint is nonconvex, and solving this problem efficiently requires developing novel algorithms that can exploit the underlying structure of the problem. In this work, we propose a new class of algorithms that employ nonconvex regularization to learn low-rank matrices. Our approach integrates tools from approximation theory, optimization, and matrix analysis to develop efficient and effective algorithms that can be tuned to the specific properties of the problem. We provide a theoretical analysis of the proposed algorithms, demonstrating their convergence properties and ability to recover low-rank matrices under various conditions. We also present extensive experimental results on synthetic and real-world datasets, showcasing the efficacy of our approach in various applications, including image recovery, motion analysis, and compressed sensing. Our results suggest that the proposed approach can be a valuable tool for practitioners seeking to recover low-rank matrices efficiently and effectively.

title: Neural Enquirer: Learning to Query Tables with Natural Language
Abstract: Neural Enquirer proposes an innovative approach to effortlessly interact with databases using natural language queries, bridging the gap between human communication and machine understanding. By conceptualizing the process of querying tables as a sequence prediction task, the authors aim to leverage state-of-the-art neural networks to both understand the human intent expressed in natural language and locate the precise data requested from a given relational database. They delve into various aspects to design their proposed model, starting with accurately segmenting the data tables into unified structures, pre-processing the structured data using graph-structured representation learning, and concurrently training an ensemble of sequence-to-sequence models to learn the optimal question answering strategies. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of Neural Enquirer in facilitating efficient and human-like querying experiences, underpinning its promising potential for practical applications in numerous data-driven environments. Compared to existing systems that demand technical knowledge of structured query languages, the presented method enables users without comprehensive programming expertise to effectively formulate and retrieve relevant data slices from vast datasets in a user-friendly and conversational interface.

title: Modeling Human Understanding of Complex Intentional Action with a Bayesian Nonparametric Subgoal Model
Abstract: Human understanding of complex intentional action plays a vital role in numerous tasks, including artificial intelligence, robotics, and psychology. Currently, existing models often struggle to capture the nuances of intentional action, particularly when they involve multiple subgoals and context-dependent transitions between them. To address this limitation, this research proposes a Bayesian nonparametric subgoal model for modeling human understanding of complex intentional action. The proposed model is grounded in a novel application of Bayesian nonparametric inference to a dynamic subgoal-oriented framework, allowing for the discovery of arbitrary subgoals and context-dependent conditional dependencies among them. By leveraging the inherent flexibility of Bayesian nonparametric models, the proposed framework provides a structured way to incorporate prior knowledge, context, and uncertainty in a single probabilistic framework. This enables the model to accurately capture the subtleties of human reasoning around complex intentional action, facilitating its application to a variety of tasks including those involving social reasoning, sequence modeling, and policy optimization. Furthermore, the proposed framework sidesteps the need for manual subgoal identification, decision tree construction, or other structured approaches that are often prone to errors and biases. The model's ability to balance exploration and exploitation has the potential to greatly augment our understanding of complex intentional action and inform the development of more advanced artificial intelligence systems.

title: Triplet Spike Time Dependent Plasticity: A floating-gate Implementation
Abstract: This paper presents a novel framework for implementing triplet spike time dependent plasticity (tSTDP), a biological neural model crucial for learning and memory, using floating-gate (FG) memristive devices. In particular, we focus on the implementation of tSTDP on FG-based synaptic arrays, demonstrating the feasibility and efficiency of FGs in accurately reproducing the intricate dynamics of synaptic plasticity observed in biological neural networks. Building upon prior research on FG-based synaptic array implementation, we extend the model to capture the complex temporal interactions between three spiking events, hence, enabling the effective learning and storage of temporal patterns and sequential memory. Our approach leverages the intrinsic FG characteristics to create a synaptic plasticity model that dynamically adjusts synaptic weights based on the relative timing of pre- and postsynaptic spike events, accurately emulating the synaptic rearrangements observed during tSTDP. A detailed theoretical analysis and experimental verification, using a prototypical FG-based neuromorphic system, demonstrate the proposed implementation's conformity with the hallmark properties of tSTDP and the corresponding learning mechanisms. The presented findings offer a compelling and scalable platform for integrating FG-based tSTDP components in hybrid neuromorphic architectures for efficient and information-rich neural data processing applications.

title: A New Statistical Framework for Genetic Pleiotropic Analysis of High Dimensional Phenotype Data
Abstract: The increasing availability of high-dimensional phenotype data has enabled the investigation of complex genetic relationships, including pleiotropy, where a single gene influences multiple phenotypes. However, the existing statistical frameworks for genetic pleiotropic analysis are often biased towards the discovery of single phenotype associations and lack the capacity to capture the intricate and nuanced pleiotropic relationships between genes and phenotypes. To address this limitation, this study proposes a new statistical framework that leverages the capabilities of dimensionality reduction and machine learning techniques to accurately identify pleiotropic genes with high impact on multiple associated phenotypes. The framework utilizes a set of novel penalized regression methods that exploit the inherent correlations between the phenotypes to enhance the power of the analyses and protect against the inflation of false positives. By leveraging these advanced statistical techniques, the proposed framework provides a comprehensive solution for the genetic pleiotropic analysis of high-dimensional phenotype data and offers researchers a powerful tool for exploring the complex relationships between genes and phenotypes. This study demonstrates the application and validation of the proposed framework on representative datasets, showcasing its ability to accurately identify pleiotropic genes and phenotypes, and highlighting its potential to accelerate the discovery of novel genetic variants associated with complex diseases. The findings of this study have significant implications for the development of personalized medicine and the advancement of precision health initiatives.

title: Probabilistic Integration: A Role in Statistical Computation?
Abstract: Probabilistic integration has emerged as a powerful tool in statistical computation, enabling the application of probabilistic principles to integrate complex functions and compute expectations over highly nonlinear and high-dimensional spaces. This work presents an in-depth exploration into the role of probabilistic integration in statistical computation, investigating its potential applications, advantages, and limitations in various fields, including machine learning, Bayesian inference, and uncertainty quantification. By leveraging advanced sampling and neural network architectures, probabilistic integration methods such as Monte Carlo (MC) sampling and quasi-MC (QMC) are shown to accurately and efficiently compute expectations, even in cases where traditional numerical integration methods fail. Furthermore, the ability of probabilistic integration to seamlessly handle non-explicit probability densities and compute expectations of complex functions makes it an attractive choice for high-stakes decision-making applications. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of applying probabilistic integration to real-world problems in areas such as global sensitivity analysis, function approximation, and probabilistic neural networks, showcasing its potential to revolutionize statistical computation and probabilistic modeling.

title: The Indian Spontaneous Expression Database for Emotion Recognition
Abstract: The Indian Spontaneous Expression Database for Emotion Recognition is a comprehensive dataset aimed at advancing research in affective computing and emotional intelligence. As the first-of-its-kind dataset to capture the nuances of emotional expressions in an Indian context, it is a valuable resource for researchers, developers, and practitioners working in the field of emotion recognition and related areas such as human-computer interaction, social robotics, and computer vision. The dataset contains a diverse range of spontaneous expressions depicting eight basic emotions (happiness, sadness, fear, surprise, anger, disgust, anticipation, and neutral) in a collectivist and diverse cultural setting. Using audiovisual modalities, we gathered over 15,000 samples from approximately 1,500 participants, each categorized into one of the eight emotion classes. The dataset includes additional metadata such as speaker demographics, text annotations (for emotional intensities and arousal levels), and facial action units providing multiple layers of expressiveness analysis. This rich dataset with extensive metadata has the potential to address several methodological and context-dependent limitations in existing emotion databases and stimulate novel research in affective computing. By leveraging this dataset, researchers can investigate the generalizability of existing emotion recognition algorithms, develop new models tailored to the Indian cultural context, and further understand the intricacies of human emotions, thereby significantly advancing the field of affective computing and related applications.

title: Mean-Field Inference in Gaussian Restricted Boltzmann Machine
Abstract:
Gaussian Restricted Boltzmann Machines (GRBMs) have gained significant attention in modeling complex probabilistic distributions due to their ability to efficiently approximate higher-order correlations between variables. However, inference in GRBMs is computationally challenging, involving intractable marginal probabilities over the hidden variables. A number of approaches have been proposed to approximate the inference problem, such as mean-field approximation and Expectation Propagation (EP). Among these methods, mean-field inference stands out as a popular choice due to its tractability and interpretable results. 

In this work, we explore the application of mean-field inference in GRBMs, highlighting its strengths and limitations in approximating the posterior of the model parameters. Our approach leverages the quadratic nature of the GRBM's energy function to derive a closed-form mean-field update rule. We then leverage stochastic optimization techniques, such as Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD), to update the mean-field parameters. 

We analyze the convergence behavior of our proposed mean-field inference method, demonstrating its ability to learn accurate representations of the data distribution under various simulation scenarios. Furthermore, we compare the performance of our method against other state-of-the-art inference approaches, showcasing its effectiveness in terms of both computational efficiency and model interpretability. Our results underscore the potential of mean-field inference in GRBMs, highlighting its potential as a viable solution for large-scale probabilistic modeling applications.

title: Innovation Pursuit: A New Approach to Subspace Clustering
Abstract: This research paper proposes an innovative approach to subspace clustering, a crucial aspect of high-dimensional data analysis, by introducing a novel framework that navigates the complexities of disparate feature attributes and variable data distributions while ensuring interpretability and computational efficiency. Building on existing subspace clustering methods, our approach incorporates a hybrid learning paradigm that leverages the strengths of both deep learning and traditional clustering algorithms. The proposed method integrates a deep neural network-based feature extractor with a probabilistic subspace clustering model, enabling it to capture non-linear relationships and multiple modes of data in high-dimensional spaces. The framework is formally defined through a variational inference framework that provides a probabilistic representation of clusters and their correlations with both the input features and the underlying data distribution. Empirical evaluations on a range of benchmark datasets demonstrate the superiority of our approach over existing methods in terms of clustering accuracy, robustness to outliers, and interpretability of results. Furthermore, the scalability of our approach is demonstrated through experiments on large-scale datasets and parallelized computations on GPU architectures. Our new method offers a fresh perspective on subspace clustering by addressing long-standing challenges in this field and holds promise for applications in various domains, including computer vision, bioinformatics, and recommender systems.

title: Compressive hyperspectral imaging via adaptive sampling and dictionary learning
Abstract: Compressive hyperspectral imaging via adaptive sampling and dictionary learning is a novel approach to acquiring and reconstructing hyperspectral data with reduced measurement requirements, thereby enhancing sampling efficiency, reducing data acquisition time, and mitigating storage and processing challenges. This paper presents an adaptive sampling scheme that determines the sampling locations and precoding rates in real-time, leveraging a sparse representation prior from dictionary learning. The proposed approach is based on a collaborative optimization framework, where the sampling strategy and dictionary update process are jointly optimized to minimize the per-pixel estimation error using a normalized mean squared error. This fusion of adaptive sampling and dictionary learning enables efficient compressive imaging, outperforming state-of-the-art methods in both denoising and compression tasks. The efficacy of the proposed approach is demonstrated through simulations using benchmark datasets and hyperspectral imagery acquired from a hyperspectral camera. Results show that the adaptive sampling strategy achieves superior reconstruction accuracy with significantly reduced measurements, exceeding up to 92% compression ratio while maintaining comparable peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) values, thereby validating its promising potential for real-world hyperspectral imaging applications. This work paves the way for future studies on compressive sensing and dictionary learning to further optimize the reconstruction process and enhance the accuracy of hyperspectral imaging under limited measurement conditions.

title: Estimating Learning Effects: A Short-Time Fourier Transform Regression Model for MEG Source Localization
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach for estimating learning effects in Magnetoencephalography (MEG) source localization by developing a Short-Time Fourier Transform Regression (STFTR) model. The STFTR model incorporates time-frequency analysis using short-time Fourier transform to quantify the changes in brain activity over time in a more precise manner. By applying this time-frequency filtering to MEG signal analysis, we aim to capture the dynamic learning process, which can provide valuable insights into neural plasticity. Traditional methods for source localization often rely on static signal estimation, which may not accurately represent the dynamic patterns in brain activity associated with learning. In contrast, the STFTR model can reveal the temporal and spectral dynamics of MEG signals, allowing for the estimation of learning effects in a more accurate and robust manner. Our approach incorporates both linear and nonlinear regression components to capture the complex relationship between MEG signal changes and learning performance. By applying the STFTR model to MEG source localization, we demonstrate its potential for improving the estimation of learning effects and providing new perspectives in understanding neural plasticity and its underlying mechanisms.
