title: Zero-Shot Event Detection by Multimodal Distributional Semantic Embedding of Videos
Abstract: This work presents a novel approach to zero-shot event detection in videos by leveraging multimodal distributional semantic embeddings. Unlike traditional event detection methods that rely on extensive annotated datasets and computational resources, our proposed model can generalize to novel events without requiring any explicit supervised learning. By jointly modeling the visual, audio, and text modalities of a video, we create a unified semantic space that captures the underlying distributional patterns of events. Our model is based on the premises of distributional semantics that words and events with similar distributional properties tend to have similar meanings. We learn semantic embeddings for videos and events through a combination of multimodal fusion and graph-based neural networks, which enables the model to capture both intra-modal and cross-modal relationships between videos and events. By leveraging the compositional nature of semantic embeddings, we can effectively transfer knowledge across different semantic spaces, allowing our model to generalize to unseen events with unobserved visual, audio, and textual features. We evaluate our approach on several benchmarks in the zero-shot event detection task, demonstrating significant performance gains over state-of-the-art methods. Our results suggest that our proposed model is a promising solution for real-world video analysis applications that require scalable and interpretable event detection capabilities.

title: Optimal whitening and decorrelation
Abstract: This research paper delves into the optimization of whitening and decorrelation processes, fundamental techniques in data processing and dimensionality reduction. Traditionally, whitening transforms and independently identifiable components (IDCs) such as principal components analysis (PCA) and independent components analysis (ICA) are utilized to decorrelate multivariate datasets, thus reducing noise and redundancy information to improve the accuracy and robustness of data-driven applications. However, these approaches often struggle to identify global optima due to their reliance on iterative methods that can be local, heuristics that do not guarantee optimum solutions, or lack a clear and well-defined criterion for evaluating optimal decorrelation. In this work, we develop a nonlinear information-theoretic approach that combines mutual information, auto-correlation, and entropy measures to identify optimal whitening and decorrelation transforms. We demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed framework through its application to synthesize multidimensional signals and real-world datasets, highlighting its potential to outperform state-of-the-art ICA-based solutions. Furthermore, our analysis showcases the robustness of our optimisation framework against parameter distortions and irregularities in the problem domain, enabling its successful deployment across various contexts and paradigms. By formally leveraging probabilistic and information-theoretic insights, our novel formulation lays the groundwork for more advanced data processing frameworks that effectively navigate the complexities arising from high-dimensional data characteristics and constraints, thus paving the way for vast potential and scalability in numerous fields including signal processing, machine learning, data analysis and communications.

title: Actions ~ Transformations
Abstract: This paper delves into the intricate dynamics of 'actions' and their profound influence on individual transformations. By scrutinizing various socio-cultural contexts, the study seeks to establish a comprehensive framework for understanding how actions shape, rather than merely reflect, transformations within individuals. It is observed that actions, whether intentional or unintentional, serve as conduits for altering an individual's worldview, influencing their behavior, and redefining their sense of identity. A vital aspect of the research involves examining the interplay between internal agency and external forces that drive actions, thus contributing to transformative processes. Further exploration of the role of emotions, power dynamics, and social norms in shaping actions and transformations is also undertaken. The theoretical underpinnings of the study draw on sociological and philosophical perspectives, including embodiment theories, hermeneutics, and existentialism. The research draws on ethnographic data from diverse cultural settings, supplementing these with a critical analysis of existing literature on action, agency, and transformation. The goal of this study is to provide a nuanced understanding of actions as transformative processes, rather than mere consequences, which will ultimately inform the development of more effective transformative strategies in various fields, including education, social work, and personal development.

title: Microclustering: When the Cluster Sizes Grow Sublinearly with the Size of the Data Set
Abstract: Microclustering, an emerging technique in clustering algorithms, aims to group similar data points together while accounting for the limitations of traditional clustering methods when dealing with massive datasets. In the scenario where cluster sizes grow sublinearly with the size of the data set, existing clustering techniques often face challenges in maintaining the integrity of the clusters and incurring an increased computational cost. Against this backdrop, microclustering emerges as a viable solution that can effectively tackle the above-mentioned issues by dividing data points into smaller clusters, known as microclusters. These microclusters convey valuable information related to the original clusters, including their density, shape, and other critical attributes. Therefore, by employing microclustering, practitioners can effectively address the trade-off between density-based methods and partitioning methods while maintaining its computational efficiency and scale to massive datasets. The intrinsic structure and compactness of microclusters make them suitable for various applications, including data summarization, density estimation, and statistical analysis. Additionally, microclustering's efficacy is bolstered by its adaptability towards handling diverse types of data and noise, rendering it a versatile tool for data analysts and researchers working with large datasets. Research in microclustering yields interesting benefits but also brings forth new challenges and opportunities that necessitate a deeper investigation into its theoretical foundations and practical applications.

title: Learning Semantic Similarity for Very Short Texts
Abstract: This paper delves into the realm of learning semantic similarity for very short texts, a crucial aspect in various natural language processing (NLP) tasks such as intent detection, text classification, and question answering. Traditional semantic similarity models have often struggled with very short texts due to the scarcity of contextual information, leading to suboptimal performance and reduced accuracy. To address this challenge, we propose a novel approach that leverages graph-based neural networks and graph attention mechanisms to capture the latent semantic relationships between words in very short texts. Our model, dubbed Very Short Text Semantic Similarity Learning (VSTSSL), is trained on a large corpus of short text pairs with related and unrelated labels, which enables it to learn a representation space that preserves semantic similarity. Experimental results on benchmark datasets show that VSTSSL outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving significantly improved accuracy in tasks involving very short texts, such as detecting intent and classifying text. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the model's performance is robust across different lengths and complexities of very short texts. These findings have significant implications for the development of more efficient and accurate NLP models that can handle very short texts, a crucial aspect of real-world applications where user inputs are often brief and fragmented.

title: Active Learning for Delineation of Curvilinear Structures
Abstract: Active learning for delineation of curvilinear structures focuses on the development of efficient algorithms and techniques to accurately identify and outline curvilinear features from various types of data, such as medical images, geographic information, and engineering surveys. The existing traditional supervised learning approaches often require an enormous amount of annotated data, particularly for curvilinear structures, which can be time-consuming and costly to obtain. Active learning presents a promising solution by strategically selecting a subset of samples to annotate, thereby reducing the overall annotation burden while preserving or even improving the accuracy of the model. This study explores the application of active learning techniques in delineating curvilinear structures, including active learning-based sampling methods, uncertainty-based sampling strategies, and deep learning-based approaches. We conducted experiments on several datasets with different characteristics, such as image resolution, noise level, and structural complexity, and evaluated the performance of various active learning algorithms using various evaluation metrics, including precision, recall, and IoU. The results demonstrate that active learning can significantly reduce the annotation burden while achieving comparable or even better delineation accuracy compared to traditional supervised learning methods, making it a viable solution for various applications in fields like medicine, geospatial analysis, and engineering design.

title: Recognizing Semantic Features in Faces using Deep Learning
Abstract: This study focuses on the application of deep learning techniques to recognize semantic features in faces, which are essential for facial expression understanding and emotion recognition tasks. Traditional facial attribute recognition approaches have been mainly focused on low-level features such as local appearance or hand-crafted features, often requiring additional processing steps for feature extraction. However, these methods may lose crucial contextual information present in faces. To overcome this limitation, we employ convolutional neural network (CNN) based architectures to learn hierarchical representations of facial features directly from raw face images. Our proposed network, named Face Semantic Feature Network (FSFN), consists of multiple residual blocks and attention mechanisms to selectively focus on important regions of facial images. A novel training scheme is also introduced to take full advantage of facial attribute annotations and to preserve the semantic meaning of recognized features. This new approach exhibits superior performance over existing methods in both intrapersonal and interpersonal facial expression recognition tasks. A comprehensive experimental evaluation is conducted using various benchmarks to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed FSFN model, which shows significant improvement in accuracy and robustness. The insights gained from this study could have a positive impact on developing more sophisticated human-computer interaction and facial analysis systems.

title: Duelist Algorithm: An Algorithm Inspired by How Duelist Improve Their Capabilities in a Duel
Abstract: This study introduces a novel algorithm inspired by the human behavior of duelists, investigating how they improve their capabilities in a duel-based competition. The Duelist Algorithm (DA) draws upon game theory and machine learning principles, simulating the process by which duelists adapt, learn, and refine their strategies to outperform their opponents. The researchers identified two key aspects to the behavior of duelists: their ability to quickly assess and learn from their opponents' moves, and their capacity to adjust their tactics in real-time in response to changing circumstances. Based on these insights, the DA was designed to leverage a self-model predictive imitation learning approach, marrying strategic and intuitive learning methods to optimize its performance. The DA's advanced game tree search and opponent modeling capabilities enable it to learn optimal actions from historical data and simultaneously adapt to a dynamic, shifting environment. As a result, the DA demonstrates improved performance in dueling simulations, surpassing baseline algorithms in terms of both efficiency and overall effectiveness. Furthermore, this study provides novel insights into the principles underlying human decision-making and strategic learning in competitive environments, offering significant implications for fields such as gaming, conflict resolution, and strategic planning.

title: Implicit Location Sharing Detection in Social Media from Short Turkish Text
Abstract: This study focus on the detection of implicit location sharing in the context of social media from short Turkish texts, an issue that has been understudied in the literature despite being widespread on various online platforms. Implicit location sharing can occur when users inadvertently disclose their geographical location through context-specific information in the text, images or videos they share, which can potentially put them at risk of cyber threats or physical harm. However, detecting such cues demands specialized knowledge of the nuances of language, context, and culture, making it challenging to develop an automated system for identifying implicit location disclosures. Therefore, this research aims to design and develop an effective Turkish language model to identify implicit location sharing cues in short social media texts. By adopting a deep learning approach to Natural Language Processing, the proposed system will utilize techniques such as sentiment analysis, named entity recognition and topic modeling to detect nuanced implicit location sharing cues, particularly those related to geographical locations, time-of-day, and temporal references, which are particularly relevant in Turkish language usage. Furthermore, this research will utilize machine learning and bootstrapping techniques to continuously improve and update the fine-tuned model. Ultimately, this study is expected to contribute significantly to enhancing the detection of implicit location sharing on Turkish-language social media platforms, thereby mitigating the risks associated with this practice.

title: Hybrid Approach for Inductive Semi Supervised Learning using Label Propagation and Support Vector Machine
Abstract: The growing demand for semi-supervised learning has led to the development of various methods that leverage both labeled and unlabeled data for training machine learning models. Among these, inductive semi-supervised learning has demonstrated great promise in adapting to new, unseen data. This study proposes a hybrid approach for inductive semi-supervised learning that combines label propagation and support vector machine. The proposed method utilizes the strengths of both techniques to efficiently classify new, unlabeled instances while avoiding over-fitting to the available labeled data. Specifically, the approach starts with label propagation to obtain a predictive model of the unlabeled data based on their similarity to the labeled instances. Subsequently, the support vector machine model is trained on the labeled data and the propagated labels to obtain a robust classification boundary. Experimental results on several benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed hybrid approach substantially outperforms label propagation and support vector machine in isolation, as well as existing inductive semi-supervised learning methods. Furthermore, the approach demonstrates its ability to generalize well to new, unseen instances, thereby establishing it as a viable solution for real-world applications. The findings of this research contribute to the existing body of work on semi-supervised learning by providing a novel, efficient, and accurate method for inductive semi-supervised learning.

title: Centroid Based Binary Tree Structured SVM for Multi Classification
Abstract: This paper presents a novel framework for multi-class classification by introducing a centroid-based binary tree structured Support Vector Machine (SVM). The proposed method capitalizes on the strength of binary classification in SVM while addressing its shortcomings in multi-class scenarios. The binary tree structured approach is employed to reduce the complexity of multi-class classification by recursively partitioning the problem into a series of binary classification tasks. To improve the efficacy of the binary tree structured SVM, we introduce the concept of centroids, which are the representative points of the classes. These centroids are used to cluster the classes and partition the binary tree, resulting in more accurate and efficient classification. The proposed method is demonstrated to outperform existing multi-class classification approaches, including one-vs-one and one-vs-rest SVM, on various benchmark datasets. Experimental results show that the proposed approach significantly improves the accuracy of multi-class classification, with an average gain of 5-10% across different datasets. Furthermore, the binary tree structured approach leads to a significant reduction in computational complexity, making it an attractive solution for large-scale multi-class classification problems. The paper concludes by highlighting the benefits of the proposed method and its potential applications in real-world classification tasks.

title: A machine learning-based selective sampling procedure for identifying the low energy region in a potential energy surface: a case study on proton conduction in oxides
Abstract: This study presents a machine learning-based selective sampling procedure that efficiently identifies the low-energy region in a potential energy surface, with a case study on proton conduction in oxides. The proposed method utilizes a combination of machine learning algorithms and cheminformatics techniques to rapidly sample the energy landscape and isolate the most relevant configurations. By integrating a graph neural network with the universal force field, the approach aims to accurately predict the potential energy surface and capture the critical conduction pathways in oxides. The selective sampling procedure is designed to adaptively adjust its focus based on the predicted energies and derivatives, ensuring a systematic exploration of the energy landscape. The methodology is demonstrated on a series of oxides, including silica, alumina, and zirconia, and validated against established computational methods and experimental data. The results show that the machine learning-based selective sampling procedure effectively identifies the low-energy region in the potential energy surface, providing valuable insights into the mechanisms of proton conduction in oxides. This approach has the potential to accelerate the discovery of materials with high proton conductivity and other energy-related applications, and can be extended to address other challenges in materials science and chemistry.

title: Object-based World Modeling in Semi-Static Environments with Dependent Dirichlet-Process Mixtures
Abstract: Object-based World Modeling in Semi-Static Environments with Dependent Dirichlet-Process Mixtures is a novel approach to creating robust and adaptive environmental representations. This model leverages machine learning and probabilistic techniques to generate representations of structured environments that change gradually over time. A key component of this approach is the incorporation of Dependent Dirichlet-Process (DDP) mixtures, which enable the efficient modeling of complex, hierarchical structures in these environments. By using DDP mixtures, the model can effectively capture the dependencies and relationships between objects and regions within the environment, allowing for more accurate predictions and tracking of changes over time. Furthermore, the model is designed to handle semi-static environments, where small changes occur gradually, rather than undergoing drastic or abrupt transformations. This allows for a more efficient and realistic representation of changing environmental conditions. The proposed approach is demonstrated through a series of experiments on image datasets and real-world sensory data, showcasing its ability to adapt to and learn from incremental changes in the environment. Comparisons with existing approaches highlight the strengths of the DDP mixture-based model in handling complex, real-world scenarios. The results demonstrate the potential of object-based world modeling for applications in robotics, autonomous vehicles, and surveillance systems, where environmental adaptability and incremental learning are critical components.

title: Attribute2Image: Conditional Image Generation from Visual Attributes
Abstract: Our research presents a novel conditional image generation framework called Attribute2Image that enables the automatic creation of images from detailed visual attributes. By leveraging recent advancements in deep learning and generative models, Attribute2Image seeks to bridge the gap between the physical and digital worlds, empowering users with the ability to specify their desired image attributes and obtain a corresponding image as the output. The framework is trained on a substantial dataset of attribute-tagged images, facilitating the extraction of intricate relationships between the image features and the specified attributes. To account for the complexities inherent in image generation, we develop a hierarchical attribute representation, which dynamically adapts to the specific attribute categories being processed. Our approach comprises an attribute decoder that translates the input attributes into high-dimensional feature vectors, a feature generator that synthesizes and details the image features, and a discriminator that evaluates the generated images according to their adherence to the specified attributes. Throughout extensive experiments and comparisons with state-of-the-art models, we demonstrate the efficacy and effectiveness of Attribute2Image in accurately capturing a wide range of attribute categories, producing high-quality images that not only resemble real-world instances but also exhibit sufficient variability and diversity. The success of our framework constitutes a crucial step towards the development of personalized and creative content, contributing to various fields such as digital art, advertising, and augmented reality.

title: Protein secondary structure prediction using deep convolutional neural fields
Abstract: Deep convolutional neural fields have shown significant advancements in processing complex biological data, making them a promising candidate for improving protein secondary structure prediction. Traditional methods often rely on handcrafted features and simplified models, resulting in limited accuracy for certain protein sequences. This research aims to bridge the gap by employing deep convolutional neural fields to dynamically learn features from the primary amino acid sequence, capturing its spatial and temporal nuances. Our proposed model exploits a multi-layer, hierarchical architecture to capture both local and global dependencies within the protein sequence, leveraging its ability to process variable-length input sequences with high precision. The framework is trained on a reliable dataset, integrating state-of-the-art techniques for data preprocessing and model optimization. To evaluate its performance, the model is validated on widely used benchmark datasets, including CASP and SCOP, and yields competitive results, significantly outperforming established methods. Furthermore, through ablation studies, the effects of various hyperparameters and architectural modifications on the model's performance are extensively analyzed, providing valuable insights for future improvements. The innovative approach presented in this research not only provides a robust, interpretable model for predicting protein secondary structures but also aids in better understanding the fundamental principles governing protein folding and dynamics.

title: Efficient learning algorithm for quantum perceptron unitary weights
Abstract: This work proposes an efficient learning algorithm for quantum perceptron networks involving unitary weights, which is an advancement in quantum computing that aims to mimic the effectiveness of classical neural networks while capitalizing the inherent strengths of quantum mechanics such as super-position and interference. The algorithm for training quantum neural networks involves finding a unitary matrix that maximizes the overlap between target and learned output states, especially for specific training data. This leads to defining conditions for unitary weights to minimize generalization error of quantum perceptron based on convex optimization techniques and unitary invariance of quantum expectations. Furthermore, efficient numerical methods are developed to tackle the high dimensionality associated with the many output qubits of the perceptron model, reflecting aspects of matrix based optimization that enables us to find optimal parameters on certain unitary matrices of perceptrons. Our proposed unitary based learning algorithm involves finding weight matrices approximating optimal criteria using block diagonal structure in representation of quantum neural network perceptron, employing recent numerical techniques that permits large scales matrix optimizations for learning effectiveness of certain quantum applications. Our ongoing and prospective practical experiments on efficient quantum algorithms could show quantum speed up with efficiently learned quantum perceptron networks.

title: Labeling the Features Not the Samples: Efficient Video Classification with Minimal Supervision
Abstract: This paper presents an innovative approach to video classification that overcomes the challenges of limited annotated data and class imbalance in the domain. By rethinking the conventional labeling strategy, the proposed method, dubbed 'feature labeling,' assigns labels directly to the semantic features extracted from the video sequence, rather than the input samples themselves. This subtle yet profound distinction allows for the efficient capture of complex spatiotemporal relationships in the data, yielding a more robust and generalizable model. The key idea is to assign labels to the features based on their collective understanding, thereby inducing a structured representation of the data that is inherently more comprehensive and accurate than sample-wise labeling. To evaluate the performance of the proposed approach, a series of comprehensive experiments were conducted on benchmark video classification datasets, including UCF-101, HMDB-51, and Kinetics. The results demonstrate a significant improvement in classification accuracy and robustness against occlusions, lighting variations, and other forms of data corruption. Furthermore, a detailed analysis of the learned feature representations shows that the feature labeling strategy triggers a more seamless and informative representation of semantically related features, providing strong evidence for the effectiveness of the proposed method.

title: Loss Functions for Top-k Error: Analysis and Insights
Abstract: This paper delves into the realm of loss functions designed to handle top-k errors in classification tasks, where the focus is on the most confidently predicted labels rather than individual class predictions. The top-k error measurement is used to evaluate the performance of machine learning models in multi-class classification scenarios, and it has been gaining attention in recent years due to its ability to provide a more comprehensive understanding of model performance. A wide range of loss functions have been proposed to optimize the top-k error, including the Hinge loss, Margin loss, and Cross-Entropy loss with ranking constraints. However, understanding the strengths and weaknesses of these loss functions is crucial for guiding the choice of suitable loss functions for specific tasks. Our analysis reveals that the design of loss functions is highly dependent on the task requirements and that each loss function has its unique characteristics and limitations. Furthermore, this research explores the impact of different hyperparameters on the performance of various loss functions, providing valuable insights into how loss function design affects model performance. Ultimately, this study aims to provide a systematic understanding of existing loss functions for top-k error and to serve as a foundation for the development of new, more effective loss functions tailored to the specific needs of different applications.

title: Fast k-Nearest Neighbour Search via Dynamic Continuous Indexing
Abstract: The development of efficient k-Nearest Neighbour (k-NN) search algorithms is a fundamental challenge in numerous fields, including computer vision, pattern recognition, and database query processing, due to their widespread application in similarity search operations. Traditionally, exact methods for k-NN search rely heavily on scanning through the entire dataset, leading to high time complexities and significant computational overheads. Consequently, these approaches often fail to scale efficiently with large, high-dimensional, and sparse datasets, degrading their applicability in real-world applications. This study focuses on the design and evaluation of dynamic continuous indexing techniques for accelerating k-NN search. Specifically, our approach employs a novel adaptive indexing strategy to selectively and strategically maintain fragments of the data space in an i-vector-based indexing structure, dubbed dynamically continuous index (DCI). DCI dynamically adjusts its partitioning and aggregation schemes based on the query and data distribution, ensuring that the most relevant and contiguous data points are readily accessible, thus reducing unnecessary comparisons. This research demonstrates through extensive experiments that the DCI-based k-NN search remarkably outperforms state-of-the-art indexing methods in terms of execution times and scalability, showcasing its potential to tackle high-dimensional spatial data in performance-critical applications.

title: A New Approach for Scalable Analysis of Microbial Communities
Abstract: The rapid advancement of high-throughput sequencing technologies has generated an unprecedented amount of data in the field of microbiome research. However, the complexities of analyzing these large datasets and extracting meaningful insights have become a significant challenge. Traditional computational methods often rely on heuristic approaches that can be inaccurate and computationally expensive, limiting their scalability to large microbial community datasets. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach for scalable analysis of microbial communities based on a probabilistic generative model, coupled with a parallelized algorithmic framework. This integrated methodology leverages the strengths of both machine learning and sequence analysis techniques to efficiently infer the composition and functional dynamics of microbial communities from vast datasets. By combining the computational efficiency of a fully probabilistic generative model with the parallel computing capabilities of modern architectures, our approach enables rapid analysis of large microbial community datasets, including metagenomic, metatranscriptomic, and amplicon sequencing data. This scalable framework is empowered by a software implementation that can handle massive datasets while ensuring flexibility and interpretability of results, making it a powerful tool for microbiome researchers and clinicians seeking to unlock the secrets of complex microbial ecosystems.

title: Taxonomy grounded aggregation of classifiers with different label sets
Abstract: This research explores the concept of aggregating classifiers with diverse label sets through the lens of taxonomy-grounded approaches. Traditional methods for combining multiple classifiers rely heavily on assumptions of identical label spaces, but in real-world scenarios, different classifiers might utilize distinct label sets. The proposed framework integrates decision theory, taxonomy-based classification, and label inconsistency handling to identify the optimal aggregation strategy. By constructing a hierarchical taxonomy, classifiers with disparate label sets can be effectively paired to jointly learn from their respective outputs, resulting in improved accuracy and robustness. The robust taxonomy-based classifier aggregation strategy is able to handle the limitations imposed by label differences, such as partial or imperfect matching between label sets, by incorporating node proximity, label consistency, and decision boundary alignment metrics. The empirical evaluation of the proposed framework on several benchmark datasets demonstrates a notable increase in classification accuracy and robustness over state-of-the-art approaches. Furthermore, the method is validated through large-scale experiments and demonstrated to be particularly beneficial in complex, multi-class classification scenarios with high levels of label ambiguity.

title: Highly Scalable Tensor Factorization for Prediction of Drug-Protein Interaction Type
Abstract: This study proposes a novel approach to tensor factorization that offers improved scalability for large-scale prediction of drug-protein interaction (DPI) types. Building upon traditional matrix factorization models, our highly scalable framework employs an optimized hybrid factorization technique to extract latent features from DPI tensors, representing drugs, proteins, and their interactions in a compact and meaningful manner. By integrating computational-efficient techniques with powerful learning-based methods, our framework enables accurate prediction of DPI types and tackles the scalability challenges associated with state-of-the-art models. We achieve high accuracy on existing benchmarks, such as the Kiba and DrugBank datasets, while maintaining excellent scalability, by implementing parallelization and distributed computing techniques. Furthermore, an extensive ablation study is carried out to evaluate the significance of the proposed hybrid factorization approach and various optimization strategies, significantly demonstrating its efficacy and providing critical insights into the interplay between DPI latent features and interaction types. Moreover, we explore the interpretability and transferability of our model by visualizing relevant latent factor loadings and investigating the generalizability of our framework to diverse pharmaceutical datasets. The proposed framework showcases substantial progress in DPI prediction, streamlining the drug discovery process and enhancing our understanding of intricate biomolecular interactions.

title: Extracting Traceability Information from C# Projects
Abstract: The integration of traceability information into software development projects remains a crucial aspect of ensuring the longitudinal understanding of changes, issues, and dependencies of various components within a system. Despite the widespread adoption of version control systems and code repositories, manually extracting and organizing traceability information continues to present significant challenges, particularly for large-scale, complex projects developed using object-oriented programming languages. This research focuses on investigating the feasibility of automating the extraction of traceability information from C# projects. A novel framework is proposed, leveraging the syntax and structure of C# code to identify and extract connectivity information among classes, methods, and variables. The framework utilizes a combination of static code analysis, graph-based modeling, and information retrieval techniques to produce a comprehensive and accurate representation of the project's dependency structure. A set of metrics is developed to evaluate the framework's performance, including precision, recall, and coverage, against a set of manually collected gold-standard data. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in extracting traceability information from C# projects, with precision and recall values exceeding 90% and coverage of over 95%. This research contributes significantly to the advancement of traceability-driven development methodologies, enabling developers and project managers to better manage complexity, improve collaboration, and reduce the risk of downstream impacts associated with changes or defects.

title: Sequential visibility-graph motifs
Abstract: Our study introduces the concept of Sequential Visibility-Graph Motifs (SVGMs), a novel approach to examining dynamic sequences and their structural properties. By constructing visibility graphs from sequential datasets and employing motif analysis techniques, we aim to identify recurring and statistically significant patterns embedded within these sequences. These motifs, which capture both spatial and temporal relationships, are critical in uncovering the underlying mechanisms driving system behavior. We propose a systematic framework for the detection and analysis of SVGMs, leveraging a combination of graph-based data mining and statistical hypothesis testing. Through extensive experiments on a variety of synthetic and real-world data sets, we demonstrate the efficacy and versatility of our method in identifying meaningful patterns and relationships, such as the temporal organization of anomalous events and the effects of context-dependent interactions on system dynamics. By providing new insights into the structural and temporal properties of dynamic sequences, our findings have far-reaching implications for research in complex systems, data science, and pattern discovery. This work not only contributes to the ongoing development of visibility graph analysis but also pioneering motif analysis techniques, thus opening up new avenues for the investigation of complex phenomena across various domains.

title: Transfer Learning in Brain-Computer Interfaces
Abstract: This paper delves into the realm of brain-computer interfaces (BCIs), specifically exploring the application and efficacy of transfer learning within this domain. With the increasing availability of high-quality neural data and the advent of powerful deep learning architectures, the potential for improving BCI performance is multifaceted. Transfer learning has emerged as a critical technique, enabling the acceleration of training and adaptation to new data distributions, thereby reducing the need for extensive, task-specific annotation and data collection. By leveraging pre-trained models and fine-tuning them on BCI-related tasks, researchers have witnessed enhanced performance and a reduction in the gap between existing and ideal neural interfaces. This study aims to offer an in-depth examination of the current state of transfer learning in BCIs, with a particular emphasis on the selection of suitable neural data, architecture choice, and the transferability of models across different tasks. The findings presented in this research demonstrate the adaptability and potential of transfer learning in the context of BCIs, sparking new avenues for further investigation into the augmenting and augmentation of human-computer interactions through neural engineering. By navigating this novel intersection of neural data analysis and transfer learning, future BCI applications will be optimized, leading to tangible advancements in cognitive rehabilitation, neuroengineering, and other fields reliant on efficient human-neural interfaces.

title: Towards Dropout Training for Convolutional Neural Networks
Abstract: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have obtained impressive performance in various computer vision tasks by effectively learning hierarchical features from visual data. However, these networks are computationally intensive and require vast amounts of data as well as training resources to reach optimal performance. One common approach to addressing these limitations is introducing dropout, a regularization technique by which neurons in the network are randomly dropped out during training with a certain probability, hence preventing co-adaptation and overfitting. This property of dropout has the effect that features learned by each hidden unit are more diverse, therefore improving robustness to certain kinds of data variability. In this research study, the researchers extend the dropout technique to CNNs with the primary objective of reducing overfitting and enhance the capability of neural networks in image classification tasks. This is pursued by proposing a novel framework called ST-Dropout that combines features of spatial attention and dropout, such that the ST-Dropout framework identifies feature maps with the highest relevance and selectively applies dropout to these maps, reducing unnecessary computations and improving the inference efficiency of the entire network. The analysis is done using multiple state-of-the-art deep CNN architectures and extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed ST-Dropout variant yields a better balance of accuracy and training speed.

title: MOCICE-BCubed F$_1$: A New Evaluation Measure for Biclustering Algorithms
Abstract: This paper introduces a novel evaluation measure, MOCICE-BCubed F$_1$, for assessing the performance of biclustering algorithms in identifying co-expressed genes across different conditions from gene expression data. Biclustering is a crucial technique for uncovering complex relationships between genes and conditions in high-dimensional datasets. However, quality assessment of biclustering results remains a challenging task, as existing evaluation metrics often lack specificity, sensitivity, or robustness. MOCICE-BCubed F$_1$ synthesizes the advantages of modification of CO-ocurrence CIentistic evaluation (MOCIE) and BCubed F$_1$ approaches to provide a more comprehensive and balanced evaluation framework. The proposed measure combines precision, recall, and specificity scores to identify both coherent biclusters and spurious matches, it further weights results to focus on coherent biclusters with significant and discernible signals while dismissing weak and ubiquitous ones. In comparison with other biclustering evaluation measures, MOCICE-BCubed F$_1$ showcases superior performance in accurately detecting valid biclusters and correctly rejecting invalid ones. The computational efficiency and easy implementation of MOCICE-BCubed F$_1$ make it an invaluable addition to the arsenal of biclustering quality assessment tools. An extensive set of experiments utilizing various biological datasets as well as synthetically generated datasets validates the efficacy and robustness of the proposed MOCICE-BCubed F$_1$ measure for biclustering evaluation.

title: LSTM Neural Reordering Feature for Statistical Machine Translation
Abstract: This research explores the application of Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural networks in statistical machine translation (SMT) to improve phrase reordering. Traditional phrase-based SMT models have limitations in handling long-distance dependencies in target languages, resulting in suboptimal translations. To mitigate this, the proposed LSTM Neural Reordering Feature integrates an LSTM network into the SMT framework to predict and reorder input sentences. The LSTM model is trained on a parallel corpus to learn contextual relationships between words and phrases, thereby identifying more suitable positions for translations of complex phrases in the target sentence. The resulting reordered input sentences are used to re-score the translation models, thereby integrating the LSTM predictive power into the SMT framework. A key aspect of this research is the use of a trainable weights component that enables the model to adapt to different transfer settings, making it a versatile tool for various SMT applications. Experiments using Chinese-to-English and English-to-Chinese translation tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach in achieving better BLEU scores compared to traditional SMT systems. Through this study, evidence supports the potential of integrating deep learning models into SMT pipelines to improve translation quality, especially when handling challenging reordering tasks, making machine translation more accurate and reliable.

title: Learning Using 1-Local Membership Queries
Abstract: This study investigates the applicability and limitations of using 1-local membership queries, which provide a simplified yet effective alternative to traditional query models, in learning and classification tasks. A key challenge in traditional query models lies in estimating the proximity to the boundary, typically accounting for both negative and positive instances. Building upon this understanding, a 1-local membership query model focuses specifically on class instances in close proximity to the instance of interest. Investigating this simplified yet useful method, the presented research aims to provide a deeper understanding of its functionality and suitability for various machine learning tasks. An in-depth analysis of data-driven classification methods revealed that incorporating 1-local membership queries can significantly enhance the predictive accuracy of current machine learning algorithms, especially when working with sparse and high-dimensional datasets. Through experiments on several benchmark datasets and evaluation metrics, the research demonstrates the potential value of these refined local query models, providing new insights into their capabilities. The presented findings further highlight the importance of proper selection of training sets and the efficient utilization of class-specific domain knowledge when applying the 1-local query model.

title: Covariance-domain Dictionary Learning for Overcomplete EEG Source Identification
Abstract: This paper presents a novel framework for EEG source identification by leveraging covariance-domain dictionary learning for overcomplete representation. Current methods often struggle to accurately distinguish multiple sources in EEG signals due to the limited spatial resolution and sensitivity to noise and artifacts. Our approach utilizes a covariance-domain dictionary learning algorithm that allows for flexible and redundant representations of the source signals, thereby improving the sparse coding capabilities. By manipulating the dictionary in the covariance domain, we can better capture the intrinsic structures of the EEG sources, including both the spatial and temporal characteristics. The proposed framework involves a two-stage process, where the first stage constructs a covariance-domain dictionary from a set of training data, and the second stage uses this dictionary to sparsely represent the EEG signals. The resulting sparse representation is then used to identify the number of sources and their associated locations in the brain. The proposed algorithm is evaluated using simulated and real EEG data, demonstrating improved performance in source identification and localization compared to traditional methods. The results showcase the potential of covariance-domain dictionary learning for addressing the overcomplete representation challenge in EEG source identification.

title: Optimal Estimation and Completion of Matrices with Biclustering Structures
Abstract: This research paper delves into the realm of optimal estimation and completion of matrices characterized by biclustering structures. Biclustering is a technique popular in data mining and machine learning that aims to identify groups of elements in two dimensions, rows and columns, that exhibit similar patterns. The task of estimating and completing biclustered matrices is crucial in various fields, including data imputation and matrix completion. However, existing methods often struggle to handle noisy and incomplete data, leading to reduced accuracy and instability in the biclustering process. The proposed method, denoted as BC-ECM, combines elements of biclustering with Expectation Maximization (EM) algorithm principles to yield robust and efficient performance. BC-EMC captures the complex relationships within and between biclusters, thereby achieving greater accuracy and reliability in estimating and completing biclustered matrices. The approach also facilitates the detection of clusters at multiple scales and adapts to varying degrees of noise in the data. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of BC-EMC on synthetic and real-world datasets, underscoring its potential as a reliable tool for biclustered matrix estimation and completion problems.

title: Inferring Interpersonal Relations in Narrative Summaries
Abstract: This study investigates the challenge of inferring interpersonal relations in narrative summaries, aiming to design and evaluate a model that can accurately predict relationships between characters in stories. Recent advances in natural language processing and machine learning have led to the development of sophisticated models for understanding narrative structures and character interactions. However, existing approaches often fall short in capturing the nuances of human relationships, which are crucial for creating rich and engaging narrative summaries. Our proposed model exploits semantic and syntactic features of language to identify subtle cues indicative of interpersonal relationships, such as dialogue, actions, and emotional expressions. By integrating graph-based representations and deep learning techniques, our model is able to accurately predict the relationships between characters in a story, outperforming existing baselines in terms of precision and recall. In addition to its theoretical contributions, our model has practical applications in various fields, including narrative analysis, text summarization, and recommender systems. The evaluation of our model on a diverse set of narratives demonstrates its effectiveness and robustness, suggesting that it can be a reliable tool for inferring interpersonal relations in narrative summaries and potentially enable the development of more sophisticated narrative analysis and text summarization systems.

title: Multilingual Language Processing From Bytes
Abstract: This paper delves into the realm of multilingual language processing, primarily focusing on the decoding and comprehension of text data in various languages. With an exponential growth in global multilingual communication, efficient language processing mechanisms have become increasingly significant. Traditional approaches to handling multilingual text still rely heavily on manually created and domain-specific natural language processing (NLP) tools and resources, resulting in substantial limitations when adapting models to diverse linguistic settings. Therefore, this research proposes a novel deep learning framework that learns task-agnostic, byte-level representation for text encoding, effectively enabling zero-shot multilingual processing. The model incorporates a byte-wise embedding module based on a novel fusion strategy, which processes the input text data as a sequence of Unicode code points. This distinctive architecture enables seamless transfer of the multilingual model to additional languages without retraining, extending state-of-the-art language diversity in zero-shot settings by a notable margin when evaluated across 45 languages and an extensive set of benchmarks. By offering efficient, robust, and domain-independent text processing capabilities, the proposed architecture has the potential to revolutionize the field of multilingual natural language processing, empowering a wide array of applications such as machine translation, text classification, and multilingual dialogue systems.

title: Decoding Hidden Markov Models Faster Than Viterbi Via Online Matrix-Vector (max, +)-Multiplication
Abstract: This abstract explores the potential for significantly improving the computational efficiency of Hidden Markov Model (HMM) algorithms by leveraging online matrix-vector (max, +)-multiplication. Traditional algorithms, such as the Viterbi algorithm, rely on dynamic programming-based approaches that suffer from high computational overhead due to repeated re-computations of matrices and vectors. In contrast, online matrix-vector (max, +)-multiplication offers a paradigm that enables the efficient computation of matrix-vector products with guaranteed sublinear time complexity. By exploiting these parallels, we develop an online algorithm that enables faster computation of HMM inference tasks, including maximum a posteriori state sequences. This algorithm utilizes online matrix-vector (max, +)-multiplication to iteratively maintain an approximation of the matrix-vector product and adapt to changing conditions, thus circumventing the need for the more expensive re-computations. Comprehensive experimental evaluations on a variety of datasets demonstrate that our algorithm substantially outperforms state-of-the-art HMM algorithms, including the Viterbi algorithm. We also demonstrate potential impact areas across speech processing, bioinformatics, and natural language processing domains, where the tractability provided by our approach can facilitate large-scale HMM-based applications.

title: "I got in trouble": A case study of faculty "doing school" during professional development
Abstract: The concept of "doing school" is often used in educational research to describe individuals embodying the norms, values, and social structures of schooling. However, little attention has been paid to how faculty members navigate and interact with this concept during professional development. This case study explores the phenomenon of faculty "doing school" during professional development training, with a focus on the teacher-educators' experiences and perceptions. Drawing from observation notes, interviews, and reflective journaling, this research examines the tensions and contradictions that emerge when faculty members strive to balance their professional and pedagogical identities. Findings suggest that faculty participants are often caught between the desire to demonstrate their expertise and the need to construct knowledge in a collaborative and reflective manner. As a result, some participants exhibit behaviors that reflect traditional notions of schooling, such as seeking authoritative validation and prioritizing hierarchical relationships. Conversely, others embody more nuanced and scaffolded approaches to learning, which prioritize social support, open communication, and self-directed inquiry. This research sheds light on the complexities of faculty professional development and highlights the importance of acknowledging and challenging the dominant norms and power dynamics that shape teaching and learning.

title: HH 1158: The lowest luminosity externally irradiated Herbig-Haro jet
Abstract: HH 1158, a Herbig-Haro jet, showcases distinct characteristics that diverge from its counterparts, primarily due to its exceptionally low luminosity and unique environment. By conducting a comprehensive investigation, this study delves into the spectral emission, spatial morphology, and dynamical behavior of HH 1158. Multi-wavelength data obtained from the Herschel Space Observatory and the Spitzer Space Telescope provide valuable insights into the jet's physical properties, shedding light on the radiation mechanisms and jet-disk interactions. Hints of a curved morphology in the submillimeter and near-infrared spectral ranges are observed, suggesting differences in the physical processes governing this jet compared to its higher luminosity counterparts. Our analysis aims to determine the radiative efficiencies and energy sources driving the observed behavior of HH 1158 and its counterparts. Spectroscopic observations have so far identified several emission lines, primarily originated from H2, a characteristic indicative of an interacted with a nebular material jet. These data establish a promising foundation for a better comprehension of low-luminosity externally irradiated Herbig-Haro jets and their dynamics.

title: Optimization theory of Hebbian/anti-Hebbian networks for PCA and whitening
Abstract: This abstract delves into the realm of Hebbian/anti-Hebbian networks and their optimization theory, specifically focusing on their application in Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and whitening. Hebbian and anti-Hebbian learning rules are employed in neural networks for unsupervised learning, where the former represents a process of strengthening the connections between neurons that are co-active and the latter represents a process of weakening the connections between neurons that are co-active. Due to their unique contributions, Hebbian/anti-Hebbian networks have emerged as essential tools in the field of neural information processing and dimensionality reduction. In this research, we investigate the optimization of Hebbian/anti-Hebbian networks for two critical data processing tasks: PCA and whitening. PCA is a widely used technique for dimensionality reduction and feature extraction, while whitening is a process that seeks to standardize the covariance of input data, leading to improved separability of features. Through a rigorous examination of optimization methodologies and their implementations on Hebbian/anti-Hebbian networks, we aim to elucidate the theoretical foundations and practical implications of these networks in PCA and whitening. Our work contributes to the understanding of these networks and their potential applications in machine learning and cognitive science.

title: Universality laws for randomized dimension reduction, with applications
Abstract: This paper explores the universality of laws governing randomized dimension reduction in high-dimensional data settings. With the aim of developing a deeper understanding of the theoretical underpinnings of such methods, we investigate the convergence of randomized feature maps towards the kernel-based feature maps. A key contribution of this work lies in establishing sufficient conditions for the universality of randomized linear operators, thereby providing a unified framework for analyzing various randomized dimension reduction algorithms. Our results demonstrate that as the size of the random projections increases, the empirical distribution of the projected data converges to the distribution obtained by applying the kernel-based feature map. Furthermore, we examine the implications of these findings for a range of applications, including k-means clustering, support vector machines, and k-nearest neighbors. By bridging the gap between the theory and practice of randomized dimension reduction, this research provides a comprehensive understanding of the inherent properties of such methods, enabling the development of more efficient, accurate, and scalable algorithms for high-dimensional data analysis. Overall, our study sheds light on the fundamental laws governing randomized dimension reduction, providing a foundation for the design of more robust and effective dimensionality reduction techniques.

title: A Normative Theory of Adaptive Dimensionality Reduction in Neural Networks
Abstract: This abstract explores the concept of adaptive dimensionality reduction in neural networks through a normative theoretical framework. The dimensionality reduction problem, in which high-dimensional input data are mapped to a lower-dimensional representation while preserving essential information, is a critical consideration in deep learning architectures. Current approaches to dimensionality reduction in neural networks, such as bottleneck layers and sparse representations, are often driven by empirical considerations and do not adequately capture the intrinsic structure of the data. This paper presents a normative framework for understanding adaptive dimensionality reduction in neural networks, which is grounded in the principles of information theory and symmetric group actions. By framing dimensionality reduction as a group action and leveraging the mathematical tools of information theory, our framework provides a principled approach to the problem, allowing for both the reduction of redundancy in the input data and the preservation of essential information. The developed theory is demonstrated to possess several desirable properties, including optimality and stability, and is evaluated through numerical experiments on various benchmark datasets. The key contributions of this work include a novel theoretical framework for understanding adaptive dimensionality reduction in neural networks, as well as practical algorithms and methods that leverage this framework to improve the performance of deep learning architectures.

title: A General Framework for Constrained Bayesian Optimization using Information-based Search
Abstract: This paper presents a novel general framework for constrained Bayesian optimization using information-based search. In Bayesian optimization, searching for the optimal solution within the feasible region is often challenging due to the presence of constraints that may limit the exploration of the search space. Existing frameworks typically rely on regularization techniques to handle constraints or employ costly objective evaluations to assess the feasibility of candidate solutions. However, these approaches can be computationally expensive and may not be scalable for large-scale optimization problems. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel information-theoretic approach that leverages measures of uncertainty and entropy to construct an efficient search strategy for constrained optimization problems. By modelling the distribution of feasible solutions, our framework uses the Kullback-Leibler divergence to construct a "probability-based" search direction that adapts to the geometry of the feasible region. The proposed framework is flexible and can be easily integrated with various Bayesian optimization algorithms, making it a valuable tool for a wide range of constrained optimization applications, including design optimization, machine learning hyperparameter tuning, and resource allocation. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through a series of experiments on benchmark problems and real-world applications, showcasing its potential to improve the efficiency and effectiveness of constrained optimization methods.

title: Modeling Dynamic Relationships Between Characters in Literary Novels
Abstract: This research paper presents a novel approach to modeling dynamic relationships between characters in literary novels using a combination of natural language processing (NLP) and graph theory. The proposed framework, termed Literary Nexus, aims to capture the complexities of human relationships by analyzing the interactions between characters throughout the narrative. By leveraging a large corpus of literary novels, the framework identifies and categorizes various relationship types, such as friendship, love, and rivalry, and tracks their evolution over the course of the story. The graph-based representation enables the detection of subtle patterns and relationships that are difficult to identify through traditional NLP techniques. Specifically, the framework employs a variant of the Markov chain model to capture the probabilistic nature of character interactions and a centrality measure to assess the relative importance of each character within the narrative. The efficacy of the proposed framework is demonstrated through a comprehensive evaluation on a dataset of over 100 novels, showcasing its ability to accurately model dynamic relationships between characters and provide new insights into the narrative structure and character development. Overall, the Literary Nexus framework offers a novel and computationally efficient approach to analyzing complex narrative structures, with potential applications in literary analysis, computational storytelling, and natural language processing.

title: Cost-aware Pre-training for Multiclass Cost-sensitive Deep Learning
Abstract:
Recent advancements in deep learning have led to significant improvements in various computer vision tasks, including multiclass classification. However, deploying these models in real-world applications is still challenging due to the high computational and memory requirements. Furthermore, the rising concern of environmental impact, computational power, and energy consumption necessitates more cost-effective solutions. 
Cost-effective pre-training techniques for deep learning models have generated considerable interest in recent years, aiming to find a middle ground between performance and computational costs. However, current cost-aware pre-training methods either focus solely on model knowledge distillation or rely heavily on pre-computed knowledge graphs. This study proposes a novel multiclass cost-sensitive deep learning framework that incorporates a cost-aware pre-training strategy while leveraging a self-recursive weighted learning approach to adaptively balance the trade-off between computational costs and classification performance. The method relies on sample-batch level reinforcement learning to discover a near-optimal selection of pre-training weights that reduce memory footprints without significantly compromising the accuracy of the multiclass classification task. By evaluating the proposed framework under various scenarios and datasets, this research demonstrates its potential to improve the cost-effectiveness of multiclass cost-sensitive deep learning models and its versatility in settings that range from battery-constrained IoT devices to cloud-based high-performance computing architectures.

title: Behavior Discovery and Alignment of Articulated Object Classes from Unstructured Video
Abstract: Behavior discovery and alignment of articulated object classes from unstructured video have garnered significant attention in the realm of computer vision and machine learning, allowing for the extraction of meaningful representations and patterns from unorganized video data. The core challenge posed by this task emanates from the high dimensionality and complexity inherent in understanding the multiple parts and configurations of articulated objects, making it imperative to develop efficient algorithms that can effectively capture their characteristics and disentangle the intricate relationships between their joints and limbs. This research seeks to propose a novel approach for the discovery and alignment of articulated object classes by introducing a unified framework that integrates multi-level graph convolution networks with attentional hierarchies to sequentially capture the spatial and temporal patterns within the articulated objects. The proposed method leverages the distinct structures of articulated objects, incorporating spatial and temporal relationships, and learning to distinguish between different configurations and behaviors. Moreover, the framework incorporates a robust temporal alignment module, allowing for synchronization and realignment of the extracted behaviors in spite of potential variations and inconsistencies in data sources. The evaluations conducted on a variety of benchmarks demonstrate the competitiveness of the proposed approach, achieving state-of-the-art performance in action recognition and articulated object alignment tasks, and offering a step forward in the understanding and modeling of articulated objects in the wild.

title: Scalable and Accurate Online Feature Selection for Big Data
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to scalable and accurate online feature selection for big data, addressing the pressing need for efficient processing of vast amounts of complex datasets. Existing feature selection methods often suffer from poor scalability and accuracy due to their naive assumption of independent data points and features. By contrast, our approach leverages the power of incremental learning to dynamically adapt to the changing data streams and extract relevant features in real-time. Our method, dubbed FastOnlineFS, employs a combination of random forest-based feature importance calculation and a modified mutual information-based feature selection criterion to efficiently identify the most informative features. The proposed approach is modular and can be easily integrated into existing big data processing frameworks, such as Apache Spark or Hadoop, to provide real-time feature selection capabilities. Extensive experiments on diverse big data datasets demonstrate the superiority of FastOnlineFS in terms of both accuracy and scalability, outperforming state-of-the-art online feature selection methods by a significant margin. Furthermore, our approach exhibits robustness to concept drift and data heterogeneity, making it an attractive solution for real-world applications, such as real-time prediction, anomaly detection, and decision support systems, where data streams are dynamic, noisy, and high-dimensional.

title: On Learning to Think: Algorithmic Information Theory for Novel Combinations of Reinforcement Learning Controllers and Recurrent Neural World Models
Abstract: Algorithmic information theory provides a framework for quantifying the complexity of information in the world, and recent advances in reinforcement learning have shown that agents can learn to interact with complex environments by approximating the world's dynamics with neural networks. In this research, we explore the application of algorithmic information theory to the design of novel combinations of reinforcement learning controllers and recurrent neural world models. By leveraging results from algorithmic information theory, we develop a principled approach to selecting controllers and world models that together minimize the complexity of the information being learned. Specifically, we use the concept of Kolmogorov complexity to define an information-theoretic objective for the composite agent, which we then optimize using a combination of model-based reinforcement learning and gradient-based optimization. We evaluate our approach on a variety of tasks, including a complex robotics environment and a stochastic control problem, and show that our agent achieves significantly better performance than agents using traditional, data-driven approaches. Our results demonstrate the potential of algorithmic information theory to drive the development of more efficient and adaptive reinforcement learning agents, and highlight the importance of considering the complexity of information in the design of artificial intelligence systems.

title: Design of Kernels in Convolutional Neural Networks for Image Classification
Abstract: Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have revolutionized the field of image classification with their remarkable ability to learn hierarchical features from images. One critical component of CNNs is the design of kernels, which slides over the input image to capture local patterns and edges. The choice of kernel design has a significant impact on the performance of CNNs, as it determines the type of features that the network can learn. This paper proposes a novel approach to designing kernels in CNNs, which involves a combination of traditional filter design techniques and machine learning strategies. Our approach, dubbed "AutoKer," uses a reinforcement learning framework to optimize the weights of the kernels, enabling the network to automatically learn the most effective features for a given classification task. We demonstrate the effectiveness of AutoKer on several benchmark image classification datasets, including CIFAR-10 and ImageNet, and achieve state-of-the-art performance. Our results show that AutoKer outperforms traditional kernel design methods, such as Gaussian filters and hand-crafted features, and provides a new paradigm for designing kernels in CNNs. The paper also highlights the potential of AutoKer to adapt to diverse image classification tasks and provides a wide range of applications, including efficient real-time image classification and object detection in surveillance systems.

title: Fine-Grained Classification via Mixture of Deep Convolutional Neural Networks
Abstract: This research paper delves into the realm of fine-grained classification, a challenging task that involves distinguishing between highly similar classes of objects. Mixture of Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (MixDCNN) is proposed as an elegant solution to this problem. By ensembling multiple DCNNs, each trained on a specific subset of the classes, the MixDCNN can leverage the strengths of individual networks while mitigating their weaknesses. The proposed approach is founded on the principle that classification problems with numerous fine-grained categories can be efficiently resolved by progressively concentrating on more informative features. Through an extensive analysis of the component networks, the MixDCNN can learn to activate relevant subsets of networks for novel classes not seen during training, while suppressing irrelevant components to minimize overfitting. Experimental results on benchmark datasets, such as CUB-200-2011 and Stanford Cars, demonstrate superior performance of the MixDCNN compared to standalone DCNNs. The efficacy of the proposed method is further validated through ablation studies that investigate the impact of various design choices, including the number of constituent networks, convolutional filter configurations, and the method used to combine the component outputs. By providing a novel paradigm for leveraging ensemble methods in the realm of fine-grained classification, the paper aims to bridge the gap between theoretical advances in DCNN architecture and practical applications.

title: Non-adaptive Group Testing on Graphs
Abstract: Non-adaptive group testing has become increasingly popular in recent years as a powerful tool for high-throughput screening of sparse, defective sets within large populations. However, most existing group testing algorithms rely on random linear bipartite graphs, which can be restrictive, especially when the graph structure is given. Inspired by the real-world applications, such as testing defective components in complex systems, sensing faults in parallel circuits and contagious diseases in a population, which typically exhibit complex graph structures, we explore non-adaptive group testing on weighted and unweighted graphs. This paper provides a comprehensive treatment of this problem and proposes algorithms to determine the optimal sizes of test groups, thereby minimizing test requirements and speeding up the discovery process. We investigate different types of graphs, including cycles, cliques, paths, grids and more, to develop efficient methods for identifying defective sets with different patterns of defectiveness. Our methods can be applied to real-world applications, such as test and verify in complex systems, the optimal setting of various types of sensors and the tracking and spread of diseases through contact within a population.

title: Predicting diverse M-best protein contact maps
Abstract: Predicting diverse M-best protein contact maps is an essential task in understanding protein structure and function, as these maps reveal crucial information about the spatial arrangement of amino acids within a protein. However, calculating M-best contact maps experimentally is computationally intensive and often unfeasible for larger proteins. In this study, we develop a novel deep learning-based framework, dubbed MProMap, to predict diverse M-best contact maps efficiently. Our approach combines a self-attention mechanism with a graph neural network to capture both local and global residue-residue interactions, which are critical for accurately modeling protein contacts. Furthermore, we introduce a novel regularization strategy to alleviate overfitting and ensure that the predicted contact maps remain diverse. Evaluated on a benchmark dataset of 20 proteins, our method achieves a high accuracy of 80.2% in identifying the top M-best contact maps and effectively explores protein contact space, generating up to 11 diverse solutions per protein. Notably, MProMap also enables the prediction of previously unknown protein contacts, shedding new light on protein architecture and function. Ablation studies and visualizations of predicted contact maps highlight the strengths of our method, demonstrating its potential as a valuable tool for structural biology and protein design applications.

title: Asynchronous adaptive networks
Abstract: The critical properties of modern complex networks, such as resilience, adaptability, and fault tolerance, can be effectively harnessed through the development and analysis of asynchronous adaptive networks. This research explores the design and behavior of such networks, which are capable of dynamically adapting their structure and function in response to changing environmental conditions. Central to the study of asynchronous adaptive networks is the examination of the interplay between the spontaneous emergence of adaptability and the predesignated adaptation mechanisms encoded into the system. The results demonstrate that, by encoding a small number of specified adaptation rules within the network, the network is capable of exhibiting emergent behavior that is comparable to complex dynamical systems observed in nature. Furthermore, the study also reveals that the asynchronous adaptive network paradigm can be effectively applied to diverse real-world applications, including decentralized control, distributed sensing, and collective intelligence. By characterizing the overall behavior of these networks, the findings have significant implications for the development of adaptable and resilient network systems that can efficiently respond to a wide range of scenarios, from environmental changes to intentional attacks. A new class of models is proposed that captures the temporal dynamics and decentralized interactions within these networks, providing valuable theoretical insights and quantitative predictions for further analysis and optimization.
