title: Proximal gradient method for huberized support vector machine
Abstract: This paper presents a novel application of the proximal gradient method for solving the Huberized Support Vector Machine (HSVM) optimization problem. The HSVM is a robust variant of the Support Vector Machine (SVM) that incorporates a Huber loss function to handle outliers and noisy data, thereby improving the overall generalization performance of the model. However, solving the HSVM optimization problem involves the minimization of a complex non-smooth and non-convex objective function, which makes it computationally challenging. To address this challenge, we propose the proximal gradient method, an iterative optimization algorithm that combines the benefits of both gradient descent and proximal mappings. We start with a warm-up step that applies the gradient descent method to a softened version of the Huber loss, followed by an iterative proximal gradient method that leverages the proximal mapping of the Huber loss. Each iteration involves the computation of the gradient of the soft loss and the proximal mapping of the Huber loss, and the application of an Armijo rule for step-size selection. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method through a series of experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets, comparing its performance with existing methods such as gradient descent and stochastic gradient descent methods for HSVM. Our results show that the proximal gradient method outperforms existing methods in terms of convergence speed and solution accuracy, making it a promising approach for solving HSVM optimization problems.

title: Alternating direction method of multipliers for regularized multiclass support vector machines
Abstract: The Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) has emerged as an efficient and versatile optimization technique for solving complex machine learning problems. In this research paper, we propose to investigate the application of ADMM for regularized multiclass Support Vector Machines (SVMs) and explore its efficacy in handling large-scale datasets. Traditional multiclass SVM formulations involve solving a quadratic programming problem which can be computationally expensive and difficult to scale for large datasets. To address this challenge, we incorporate ADMM as an efficient optimization algorithm to solve the regularized SVM problem. ADMM breaks down the problem into more manageable sub-problems, each of which can be solved efficiently. Our objective is to analyze the convergence properties of ADMM for regularized multiclass SVMs and demonstrate its applications on benchmark datasets. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of various ADMM parameters on the optimization process. By employing the augmented Lagrangian method and leveraging the sparsity of the problem, ADMM enables efficient parallelization, resulting in considerable computational savings. We show that ADMM-based SVMs can achieve superior performance in classification accuracy compared to traditional methods. This study contributes to the development of efficient optimization techniques for large-scale machine learning problems and demonstrates the potential of ADMM for solving regularized multiclass SVMs.

title: Stability of similarity measurements for bipartite networks
Abstract: This study investigates the stability of similarity measurements for bipartite networks, highlighting the need for robust and consistent methods to capture the inherent structure within these complex systems. Bipartite networks abound in various fields, including social network analysis, economic exchanges, and protein-protein interactions, representing relationships between two distinct types of entities. The similarity between entities in bipartite networks has been extensively studied, with various metrics proposed to measure this similarity, including the Jaccard index, cosine similarity, and resource allocation index. However, no comprehensive analysis has been conducted to evaluate the stability of these similarity measurements across different network configurations, entity distributions, and parameter settings. To address this gap, we generate thousands of synthetic bipartite networks and systematically vary network characteristics such as size, density, and in-degree and out-degree distributions. We then compute the similarity between entities using various metrics and evaluate their stability using metrics such as consistency and variance. Our results reveal that the stability of similarity measurements is highly dependent on the network characteristics and the choice of similarity metric. For instance, the Jaccard index is highly stable in networks with dense entities, while the cosine similarity is more robust in networks with sparse entities. Our findings have significant implications for the development of robust similarity metrics and provide insights into the inherent limitations of current similarity measurement approaches.

title: Hierarchical Invariant Feature Learning with Marginalization for Person Re-Identification
Abstract: Person Re-Identification (Re-ID) is a critical challenge in computer vision, benefiting from the recent advances in deep Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). However, most existing methods focus on learning discriminative features from individual scenes without effectively exploiting their hierarchical structures. Additionally, the marginalization technique has begun to be widely employed in fields including computer vision and robotics, but its application to hierarchical feature learning for Re-ID has not been studied thoroughly. In this research, we propose a Hierarchical Invariant Feature Learning with Marginalization approach for Re-ID, designated as HIFM-ReID. This method involves learning invariant features across an entire hierarchy of camera views through multi-level fusion. The marginalization process incorporates the intra-class relationships learned at different scales to foster robustness to within-class variations. By aggregating hierarchical features and leveraging the marginalization technique, our approach can efficiently model complex variations that are beneficial for more accurate inter-camera person surveillance across novel viewpoints and locations. Comprehensive experiments on several well-established Re-ID benchmarks demonstrate the efficiency of HIFM-ReID over state-of-the-art methods under diverse evaluation conditions, and we believe that our solution makes positive contributions to the surveillance fields due to the obtained results and thorough theoretical analysis.

title: Aspect-based Opinion Summarization with Convolutional Neural Networks
Abstract: Aspect-based opinion summarization is a crucial task in natural language processing that aims to extract and summarize opinions regarding specific aspects of a product, service, or entity from large volumes of text data. Traditional methods rely heavily on manual feature engineering and handcrafted rules, which can be time-consuming and less effective in handling complex and nuanced opinions. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have been explored in the field of text analysis due to their ability to capture local patterns and features in data. This paper proposes a novel approach to aspect-based opinion summarization using CNNs, where a multi-perspective convolutional module is designed to jointly model the contextual representation of words and the aspect-related features from the text data. The model incorporates an attention mechanism to highlight the most relevant parts of the text and weights the importance of different aspects. Experimental results on several benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, achieving significantly higher accuracy and F1-score compared to state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, ablation studies and qualitative analysis provide insights into the impact of different components on the overall performance of the model, contributing to a deeper understanding of the advantages and limitations of incorporating CNNs in aspect-based opinion summarization.

title: Coresets for Kinematic Data: From Theorems to Real-Time Systems
Abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive investigation of coresets for kinematic data in real-time systems, bridging the gap between theoretical foundations and practical implementations. We introduce novel techniques for constructing coresets, which are compact representations of large kinematic datasets, preserving essential properties and transformations. These coresets are essential for efficient computation in real-time systems, enabling accurate prediction, simulation, and visualization of complex kinematic movements. Our theoretical contributions include several key theorems, establishing the necessary conditions for coresets to maintain structural stability under various transformations, such as rotation, scaling, and translation. By leveraging these theorems, we develop scalable algorithms for coreset construction, compatible with a wide range of kinematic datasets and real-time constraints. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of our approach over existing methods, highlighting significant performance gains in terms of computation time and memory usage. Moreover, we showcase several real-world applications of our coresets in real-time systems, including human motion capture, robotic arm control, and virtual reality. Our work opens new avenues for developing efficient kinematic data analysis systems, capable of handling complex movements and interactions in real-time, with potential impact on fields such as robotics, computer vision, and gaming.

title: Machine Learning Sentiment Prediction based on Hybrid Document Representation
Abstract: This paper presents an innovative hybrid approach to machine learning sentiment prediction, focusing on the integration of various document representation techniques to enhance the accuracy of sentiment analysis. The proposed method leverages the strengths of word embeddings, topic modeling, and graph-based embedding methods to create a hybrid document representation that captures both local and global contextual information. By combining the strengths of these individual approaches, the proposed method aims to address the limitations of current sentiment analysis approaches, including the need for large quantities of labeled training data and the tendency to suffer from semantic drift and data sparsity. The proposed approach is evaluated on a benchmark dataset, where it achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods. Experiments demonstrate that the hybrid document representation is effective in capturing subtle nuances in sentiment, particularly in situations where sentiment expressions are ambiguous or context-dependent. A detailed analysis of the results reveals that the hybrid approach outperforms traditional methods in terms of sentiment classification accuracy, F1-score, and macro-F1 score, establishing the significance of the proposed approach in the realm of machine learning sentiment prediction. The results also highlight the importance of combining multiple document representation techniques to leverage their collective strengths and achieve more accurate sentiment analysis outcomes.

title: Position paper: a general framework for applying machine learning techniques in operating room
Abstract: In recent years, the operating room (OR) has become a crucial environment where technology and machine learning (ML) techniques can significantly enhance patient care and improve clinical outcomes. Despite the numerous benefits that ML can bring to the OR, there is currently no comprehensive framework that outlines the general principles and best practices for its successful implementation. This paper aims to fill this knowledge gap by providing a framework for applying ML techniques in the OR. Our proposed framework, known as MOUZE (Monitoring Outcomes through Unsupervised Zooning Essentials), takes into account the unique environment of the OR, where efficiency, reliability, and accuracy are paramount. MOUZE is designed to identify the opportunities for ML adoption, select appropriate ML algorithms and tools, integrate these tools into the existing workflows, evaluate their effectiveness, and integrate feedback into the continuous improvement cycle. Through comprehensive case studies and expert interviews, we validate the MOUZE framework and demonstrate its feasibility in various OR scenarios. Our findings suggest that with the right approach and careful implementation, ML can not only improve patient safety and recovery times but also streamline clinical workflows and enhance the overall efficiency of the OR. By adopting the MOUZE framework, healthcare institutions can maximize the benefits of ML and make it an essential component of modern OR operations.

title: Non-judgemental Dynamic Fuel Cycle Benchmarking
Abstract: This study presents a comprehensive framework for non-judgemental dynamic fuel cycle benchmarking, aiming to facilitate a more objective and transparent evaluation of fuel cycle systems. Traditional benchmarking approaches are often plagued by subjective assumptions, biased comparisons, and incomplete assessments, which can lead to misleading conclusions and hinder informed decision-making in the nuclear industry. Addressing these limitations, this research develops a dynamic fuel cycle benchmarking methodology that accounts for the complexities and variability of real-world fuel cycle operations. The proposed framework is founded on a multi-criteria assessment approach, incorporating indicators that capture the full scope of fuel cycle performance, including economic efficiency, environmental sustainability, safety, security, and waste management. Additionally, the study introduces a novel scoring system to evaluate fuel cycle systems, taking into consideration the time-dependent and non-linear nature of these complex systems. Through a series of case studies and comparisons, the research demonstrates the efficacy of the proposed methodology in providing a nuanced and context-specific analysis of fuel cycle systems. The findings of this study contribute to the development of more effective policies and strategies for the deployment of advanced fuel cycles, ultimately promoting a more sustainable and responsible nuclear energy landscape. By removing the subjective element from fuel cycle benchmarking, this research ensures that performance evaluations are grounded in facts and objective criteria, thereby enhancing the transparency and credibility of decision-making processes in the nuclear industry.

title: Sparse Coral Classification Using Deep Convolutional Neural Networks
Abstract: The analysis of patterns and textures on coral samples can assist researchers in the classification of sparse coral groups. However, traditional machine learning methods might fall short in achieving high-precision coral classification due to the intricate details and variations in coral morphology. In an attempt to overcome these limitations, this paper implements a deep convolutional neural network (CNN) to classify and differentiate sparse coral groups based on microscopic images obtained using a scanning electron microscope (SEM). The proposed CNN architecture utilizes a combination of convolutional layers, activation functions, and a pooling strategy to filter through the subtle patterns present in coral samples. An extensive dataset consisting of 150 microscopy images of 10 distinct species of coral was used to fine-tune the model's performance, thus ensuring its robustness in real-world applications. Experimental results demonstrated the efficacy of the proposed system by achieving a high accuracy rate of 95% in correctly classifying coral species. The novel contribution of this study lies in its effective deployment of deep learning techniques for the identification of delicate coral structures, thus paving the way for automated coral classification systems in marine conservation and research applications.

title: Computational Pathology: Challenges and Promises for Tissue Analysis
Abstract: Computational pathology has emerged as an innovative approach to tissue analysis, transforming the field of pathology by integrating computer science, data analysis, and machine learning algorithms. Despite the significant challenges facing this emerging field, including the acquisition of high-quality digital images, variations in tissue composition, and data generalizability, computational pathology holds tremendous promise for cancer diagnosis, patient stratification, and personalized medicine. Recent advancements in computer vision, image analysis, and machine learning techniques have enabled fast and accurate identification of morphological features, such as changes in cellular morphology and architecture, thereby facilitating the analysis of tissue samples. The application of computational pathology in cancer diagnosis has shown improved diagnostic accuracy, reduced turnaround time, and enhanced patient outcomes. However, several challenges remain to be addressed, including the validation of analytical performance, the regulatory framework for implementing digital pathology systems, and the need for transparent and explainable models. Furthermore, the effective integration of computational pathology in clinical practice will require a multidisciplinary approach, involving pathologists, computer scientists, and clinicians. Despite these challenges, the potential of computational pathology to revolutionize the field of pathology and transform patient care makes it an exciting and rapidly evolving area of research.

title: Write a Classifier: Predicting Visual Classifiers from Unstructured Text
Abstract: This research paper delves into the pressing challenge of establishing a robust connection between unstructured text and visual data within the realm of computer vision. A classifier that can proficiently infer visual classifiers from unstructured text is pivotal in applications such as image classification, object detection, and scene understanding. Current methods for extracting visual classifiers from text have limitations in their ability to generalize across various datasets and domains, resulting in performance degradation when applied to real-world scenarios. In response to these challenges, we propose an innovative approach that integrates the strengths of deep learning, transfer learning, and multimodal learning. Our novel framework, dubbed VisualTextClassifier, leverages Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) in conjunction with a pre-trained convolutional neural network (CNN) to create a unified model that can effectively process and classify unstructured text into corresponding visual classifiers. This multi-modal framework incorporates techniques such as prompt engineering and knowledge distillation to further enhance the model's interpretability and robustness. A comprehensive evaluation of our approach is conducted on benchmark datasets, demonstrating significant improvements in classification accuracy and robustness compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. The proposed VisualTextClassifier strategy opens up new avenues for efficient text-to-visual classification and has wide-ranging implications for artificial intelligence applications, particularly in scenarios where access to visual data is limited.

title: Event Specific Multimodal Pattern Mining with Image-Caption Pairs
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel event-specific multimodal pattern mining framework, which leverages the synergy between image and text modalities to discover latent patterns inherent to specific events in a dataset. The framework utilizes image-caption pairs, which provide a natural alignment of visual and linguistic content, allowing for the exploration of complex relationships between images and their corresponding text descriptions. By incorporating deep learning techniques and multimodal fusion methods, the framework effectively captures both low-level features and high-level abstractions from visual and textual data, facilitating the identification of event-specific patterns. These patterns are then analyzed to discern underlying trends and correlations that can inform the development of robust event detection and prediction models. Experimental results, evaluated using a range of event-specific pattern recognition and retrieval tasks, demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed framework in extracting meaningful patterns from multimodal data. Furthermore, the study demonstrates the benefit of incorporating the proposed framework with traditional feature-based and pattern mining approaches, highlighting its potential applications in event-driven applications, such as surveillance systems, predictive maintenance, and emergency response systems, where timely and accurate event detection is critical.

title: Autoencoding beyond pixels using a learned similarity metric
Abstract: This research presents an advancement in autoencoding by focusing on a learned similarity metric that extends beyond pixel-based representations. Traditional autoencoders operate under the constraint of reconstructing pixel data, often at the cost of lacking semantic understanding of the encoded representations. By leveraging a learned similarity metric, our approach decouples the process of encoding and decoding, enabling the autoencoder to capture nuanced relationships between data points. Our proposed framework employs a novel similarity-based loss function that optimizes the autoencoder to preserve semantic meaning and contextual relationships within the encoded space. Through the incorporation of a learned similarity metric, our method allows for autoencoding of diverse data modalities, including but not limited to images, videos, texts, and graphs. The proposed framework is demonstrated to achieve state-of-the-art performance on a variety of benchmarks, showcasing its flexibility and generalizability across various application domains. We also present a theoretical analysis of the learning process, shedding light on the effect of the learned similarity metric on the autoencoder's ability to capture informative representations. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach is capable of producing high-quality encodings that are transferable, compressible, and interpretable, marking a significant step forward in the development of versatile autoencoding techniques.

title: Learning Local Image Descriptors with Deep Siamese and Triplet Convolutional Networks by Minimising Global Loss Functions
Abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to learning local image descriptors using deep Siamese and triplet convolutional networks by minimizing global loss functions. The proposed architecture combines the strengths of both Siamese and triplet networks to effectively generate discriminative and informative local features that can be used for image matching and retrieval tasks. The method employs a global loss function that considers the pairwise similarity and relative distance between feature embeddings, leading to a more robust and generalizable approach to learning local descriptors. Experimental results on standard benchmarks such as Oxford Buildings, Paris Street View, and Holidays datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed architecture in achieving state-of-the-art performance compared to existing techniques. The results highlight the ability of the network to learn semantically meaningful features that capture the underlying structure of the images, leading to improved matching accuracy and robustness against variations in scale, viewpoint, and illumination. Furthermore, the proposed approach can be easily applied to various computer vision tasks that rely on feature-based methods, including image retrieval, object recognition, and 3D model registration. By minimizing global loss functions, this work offers a flexible and efficient framework for learning local image descriptors that can be adapted to various application domains.

title: Denoising and Completion of 3D Data via Multidimensional Dictionary Learning
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel framework for denoising and completing 3D data via multidimensional dictionary learning. The proposed approach leverages the concept of sparse representation and dictionary learning, which is an efficient and effective technique for data analysis and processing. In the context of 3D data, the multidimensional dictionary learning method is capable of capturing the intrinsic structure and patterns in the data, allowing for robust denoising and completion. The framework consists of two stages: the first stage learns a multidimensional dictionary from the corrupted 3D data, and the second stage uses the learned dictionary to represent the data in a sparse and parsimonious manner. The denoised and completed 3D data are then obtained by thresholding the sparse representation. The proposed approach is evaluated on various 3D datasets, including medical images and 3D models, and the results demonstrate its effectiveness in removing noise and filling in missing data. The method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques in terms of both quantitative and qualitative metrics, and is proven to be robust to different noise levels and corruption scenarios. Furthermore, the proposed method is shown to be computationally efficient and scalable to large 3D datasets, making it a suitable candidate for real-world applications in computer vision, medical imaging, and 3D modeling.

title: Exploiting Local Structures with the Kronecker Layer in Convolutional Networks
Abstract: This work proposes an innovative approach to enhancing the representational capabilities of convolutional networks (CNNs) by incorporating a novel layer, dubbed the Kronecker layer. The Kronecker layer leverages local structures within CNNs to enable the extraction of more robust and informative features from input data. By explicitly modeling the spatial correlations within local regions, the Kronecker layer is capable of capturing fine-grained patterns and details that conventional convolutional layers often overlook. To achieve this, the proposed layer utilizes the Kronecker product of local feature maps, thereby allowing the model to explore an exponentially larger solution space and identify more complex relationships within the input data. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that the incorporation of the Kronecker layer significantly boosts the performance of various CNN architectures on a range of benchmark tasks, including image classification, object detection, and segmentation. Notably, the proposed approach is shown to outperform state-of-the-art methods in several regimes, particularly when faced with noisy or partial observations. Moreover, the expressiveness and flexibility of the Kronecker layer enable it to adapt to diverse application domains, underscoring its potential as a general-purpose component for augmenting the power of CNNs.

title: LIBSVX: A Supervoxel Library and Benchmark for Early Video Processing
Abstract: LIBSVX is a comprehensive open-source library for supervoxel-based early video processing. The library provides an extensive range of algorithms and techniques for segmenting images and videos into supervoxels, which are volumetric image pixels that capture spatial and temporal relationships. Supervoxels have emerged as a crucial component in various video processing tasks, such as object tracking, optical flow estimation, motion segmentation, and event detection. LIBSVX offers a combination of popular algorithms, including the Simple Linear Iterative Clustering (SLIC) algorithm, the Efficient Graph-Based Video Segmentation (EGBVS) algorithm, and the Segmentation of Video Data with Slanted-Christiansen-Elliptical Regions (SCE) algorithm, among others. The library also includes functions for post-processing supervoxels, such as visualizing and filtering the segmentation results. To facilitate the evaluation of supervoxel-based early video processing methods, LIBSVX provides a benchmarking framework with publicly available video datasets, including the KITTI raw dataset, the Weizmann Horse dataset, and the Mushroom dataset. The benchmarking framework allows researchers to compare the performance of different supervoxel algorithms and explore the correlations between supervoxel features and various video processing tasks. Overall, LIBSVX offers a valuable resource for researchers and developers working in the field of early video processing.

title: Actor-Action Semantic Segmentation with Grouping Process Models
Abstract: Actor-Action Semantic Segmentation with Grouping Process Models is an innovative approach to understanding complex human behaviors in videos. This research paper presents a novel deep learning architecture that combines actor-action semantic segmentation with grouping process models, enabling effective analysis of human actions in dynamic environments. By incorporating the concept of grouping process, our proposed framework assigns meaningful labels to actors and actions, allowing for a more comprehensive understanding of social behaviors and interactions. The grouping process is achieved through a graph-based reformulation, where nodes represent actors or actions and edges denote dependencies between them. This representation facilitates the learning of actor-action semantics, capturing the relationships between different actions and the actors performing them. The proposed framework is evaluated on several benchmark datasets, demonstrating state-of-the-art performance in actor-action semantic segmentation tasks. The experimental results highlight the effectiveness of the proposed approach in improving the accuracy and robustness of human action recognition in crowded scenes and complex scenarios. Furthermore, the paper demonstrates the potential applications of the proposed framework in various domains, such as human-computer interaction, surveillance systems, and human behavior analysis.

title: Combined statistical and model based texture features for improved image classification
Abstract: The traditional approach to image classification often relies on hand-crafted features, which may not generalise well across various textures and image modalities. Recently, there has been an upsurge in the exploration of deep learning architectures for feature extraction, yielding remarkable performance in various tasks. However, deep learning models often require a large amount of annotated data for reliable performance, which is often not feasible in practice, especially when handling novel or unseen data. Therefore, there is a pressing need for a hybrid approach that seamlessly combines the strengths of statistical and model-based texture features with the adaptability of deep learning models. In this paper, we present a novel approach that uses a statistical analysis of texture features, obtained from the gray-level co-occurrence matrix (GLCM), to augment the feature representation learned from a deep neural network. This is achieved by incorporating the salient texture features of the GLCM, computed using the Haralick texture measures, into a pre-trained convolutional neural network (CNN). Our two-stage feature learning approach not only leverages the powerful feature learning capabilities of deep learning models but also benefits from the quantitative analysis provided by statistical texture features, thereby enhancing the robustness and generalisability of the image classification system. Comprehensive experimental results on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate the accuracy and efficiency of the proposed approach, thereby underscoring its potential for real-world applications in image classification tasks.

title: Robust Scene Text Recognition Using Sparse Coding based Features
Abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to robust scene text recognition using sparse coding-based features. The proposed method utilizes a sparse representation of characters to develop a robust and accurate text recognition system. Given the variability in scene text images, our approach incorporates a deep sparse coding-based feature extractor that can effectively capture the essential details of characters. This robust feature representation is achieved through the use of an iterative shrinkage-thresholding algorithm that emphasizes the sparse features and discards the noise. Additionally, a sliding window-based technique is employed to progressively extract features from each pixel within the character region. To address the challenges associated with varying font styles, light conditions, and noise pollution, we leverage two main modules in our framework: the Sparse-Based Feature Learning and Text Recognition modules. The Sparse-Based Feature Learning module utilizes a stacked sparse coding structure to learn the compact and discriminative features of characters. The Text Recognition module employs a sequence-to-sequence model and attention mechanism to accurately recognize the text sequences. To evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed approach, extensive experiments are conducted on the STS benchmark dataset with reported state-of-the-art results. The encouraging results demonstrate the robustness and accuracy of our proposed scene text recognition method, making it a promising solution for real-world scene text understanding applications.

title: A framework for robust object multi-detection with a vote aggregation and a cascade filtering
Abstract: This paper presents a novel framework for robust object multi-detection, which leverages a vote aggregation mechanism and a cascade filtering module to achieve accurate and efficient object localization in complex scenes. The proposed framework enhances the object detection pipeline by integrating a multi-scale feature extraction module, a region proposal network (RPN), and a feature pyramid network (FPN) to capture both global and local features of objects. The RPN generates candidate regions, while the FPN refines these candidates by aggregating features at different scales. A vote aggregation mechanism is then employed to accumulate votes from different scales, leading to more robust object detection results. Furthermore, a cascade filtering module is introduced to prune false positives and missed detections, thereby improving the overall detection accuracy. The proposed framework is particularly effective for detecting objects of varying sizes and orientations in cluttered environments, where traditional object detection methods often struggle. Extensive experiments on popular object detection benchmarks, including PASCAL VOC and COCO, demonstrate the superiority of the proposed framework over state-of-the-art approaches in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency.

title: Visually Indicated Sounds
Abstract: A novel and interdisciplinary area of research is being explored, which delves into the phenomenon of 'Visually Indicated Sounds.' This complex and multifaceted study seeks to understand the intricacies of how visual cues in our environment can influence the perception and interpretation of sounds. Building upon the theories of synesthesia, cross-modal correspondences, and sensory substitution, the research aims to investigate the neural mechanisms underpinning the association between visual stimuli and auditory perception. By employing a range of methodologies including behavioral experiments, neuroimaging techniques, and computational modeling, the study will examine how different visual features such as color, shape, and movement contribute to the creation of sound percepts. The findings of this research have the potential to contribute significantly to our understanding of the fundamental relationship between sensory modalities and provide insights into the neural basis of sound perception, perception of music, and possibly even language processing. Preliminary studies have already demonstrated that visual stimuli can influence sound localization, affect the perception of music emotion, and modulate the auditory system's sensitivity to sound patterns, highlighting the vast scope of this phenomenon.

title: MRF-Based Multispectral Image Fusion Using an Adaptive Approach Based on Edge-Guided Interpolation
Abstract: This research presents a novel adaptive approach for fusion of multispectral images using the Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) framework based on Markov Random Fields (MRFs). The proposed method is aimed at combining multispectral and panchromatic images to generate high spatial and spectral resolution images, thereby improving the spatial details of the fused image while preserving the spectral information of the source images. The key innovation lies in the incorporation of edge-guided interpolation technique to estimate the likelihood map, which serves as the basis for iteratively refining the fusion result through the MAP framework. In contrast to traditional MRF-based fusion approaches, the adaptive approach facilitates a more precise estimation of the optimal fusion weights, thereby improving the accuracy of the fused image. A detailed evaluation of the proposed method is performed using a range of benchmark multispectral images, demonstrating its superiority over existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of visual quality, quantitative metrics, and computational efficiency. The results show significant improvements in the edge preservation and detail enhancement capabilities of the fused images, making the approach an attractive option for a wide range of applications, including remote sensing, environmental monitoring, and precision agriculture.

title: Graph entropies in texture segmentation of images
Abstract: Graph entropies, particularly those derived from graph-based image representation, have garnered significant attention in the realm of texture segmentation of images. The primary motivation behind this interest lies in the capacity of graph entropies to capture intricate dependencies between neighbouring pixels, thus providing a more accurate representation of the underlying texture structure. In this context, this research paper aims to present a comprehensive investigation into the application of various graph entropies for image texture segmentation, with a special emphasis on their potential to outperform contemporary methods in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency. Building upon the principles of graph theory and information entropy, we propose to explore several graph entropies, including the Shannon entropy, Renyi entropy, Tsallis entropy, and graph topological entropy, and to systematically analyze their performance in segmenting various textures, including microscopic tissue structures, natural materials, and man-made surfaces. Utilizing a range of classical and state-of-the-art segmentation algorithms as benchmarks, the proposed study seeks to demonstrate the efficacy of graph entropies in extracting object features, reducing dimensionality, and enhancing the quality of segmentation outcomes. By developing and evaluating novel graph entropy-based methods, this research aims to provide a noteworthy contribution to the field of image texture segmentation, while also shedding more light on the theoretical foundations governing the link between graph entropies and image texture analysis. Additionally, the insights gained from this investigation will pave the way for further exploration of graph-based techniques in the broader domain of image processing applications.

title: Outlier Detection In Large-scale Traffic Data By Naïve Bayes Method and Gaussian Mixture Model Method
Abstract: This study aims to investigate the application of machine learning methods for detecting outliers in large-scale traffic data. Two prominent algorithms, Naïve Bayes method and Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) method are employed to identify and classify anomalous data points that significantly deviate from the expected patterns. The Naïve Bayes method, known for its simplicity and speed, is used to calculate the probability of an observation belonging to each class, and the algorithm with the highest probability is selected. On the other hand, the GMM method is utilized to model the underlying distribution of the data points, and the observation with the lowest posterior probability is identified as an outlier. To evaluate the performance of these methods, a comprehensive analysis of various metrics, including sensitivity, specificity, precision, and F1-score, is conducted. Additionally, the impact of parameter selection and data preprocessing on the detection rate of outliers is also explored. The results are compared with each other and the challenges associated with the implementation of these methods in real-world traffic data are discussed. A case study is presented to demonstrate the applicability of these methods in real-world scenarios, showcasing their potential to provide valuable insights into traffic flow patterns and enable data-driven decision making for optimizing traffic management systems. The findings of this study contribute to the development of efficient and accurate methods for outlier detection in large-scale traffic data, ultimately enhancing the overall performance of intelligent transportation systems.

title: Statistical and Computational Guarantees for the Baum-Welch Algorithm
Abstract: The Baum-Welch algorithm, a widely used expectation-maximization approach for estimating parameters in hidden Markov models (HMMs), has been a cornerstone in the field of machine learning and signal processing. Despite its popularity, the theoretical foundations of this algorithm have been largely unstudied. This research provides a comprehensive analysis of the statistical and computational guarantees of the Baum-Welch algorithm, shedding light on its convergence properties, sample complexity, and the quality of the estimated parameters. We establish a rigorous framework for understanding the algorithm's behavior, providing non-asymptotic bounds on estimation error and sample complexity. Our results demonstrate that the Baum-Welch algorithm converges to the global maximum likelihood estimate under mild assumptions on the data distribution and the HMM architecture. We also provide experiments on various synthetic and real-world datasets, showing that our theoretical predictions align with practical performance. Furthermore, we derive algorithms for achieving faster convergence and reducing the computational cost of the Baum-Welch algorithm, leading to improved applicability in resource-constrained settings. Our research provides a solid foundation for understanding the theoretical properties of the Baum-Welch algorithm and offers practical insights for improving its performance, advancing the state-of-the-art in HMM parameter estimation and related applications.

title: Improving Facial Analysis and Performance Driven Animation through Disentangling Identity and Expression
Abstract: This research aims to significantly enhance facial analysis and performance-driven animation by tackling the long-standing challenge of disentangling identity and expression in facial dynamics. Despite numerous advances in computer vision and computer graphics, accurately separating these two intertwined aspects of facial behavior remains a major roadblock in developing realistic and controllable facial animation systems. Existing methods often struggle to dissociate the inherent characteristics of a person's identity from their transient emotional expressions, resulting in mixed or erroneous results. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a novel approach, Identity-Expression Disentanglement (IED), which utilizes advanced deep learning architectures and carefully designed multimodal fusion strategies to extract identity and expression features from facial data. Through extensive experiments using a large-scale dataset of facial videos, our results demonstrate that IED can effectively disentangle identity and expression, leading to substantial improvements in facial analysis and performance-driven animation. The proposed method has broad implications for various applications, including virtual humans, social robotics, and human-computer interaction. Our goal is to enable more natural and engaging interactions between humans and machines by providing a solid foundation for understanding and modeling the intricacies of facial behavior.

title: Data Driven Robust Image Guided Depth Map Restoration
Abstract: This paper presents a novel data-driven approach for robust image-guided depth map restoration, focusing on the challenging scenario where the input depth map is severely degraded due to various noise sources or inaccurate initial estimates. By leveraging the complementary strengths of both image and depth modalities, our method not only recovers the missing depth information but also exploits the spatial correlations and structural regularities within the image domain to refine the restored depth map. To effectively integrate the depth and image information, we propose a deep neural network architecture that consists of a depth estimator, an image-based refinement module, and a fusion mechanism. The depth estimator leverages the degraded depth map and an optional reference image to generate a coarse depth estimate, while the image-based refinement module employs convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures to capture detailed depth variations from the input image. The fusion mechanism is then designed to combine the coarse depth estimate and the refined image features to produce a final, high-quality depth map that balances both structural and photometric fidelity. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of our approach over existing methods, showcasing improved depth map accuracy, robustness, and perceptual quality under a wide range of scenarios, including low-light conditions, heavy noise, and mixed domain settings. The proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance, offering promising prospects for real-world applications in computer vision, robotics, and autonomous systems.

title: Part-Stacked CNN for Fine-Grained Visual Categorization
Abstract: This paper presents a novel deep learning approach, termed Part-Stacked CNN, for fine-grained visual categorization tasks. Traditionally, CNNs have been primarily applied to image categorization tasks, which often involve distinguishing between broad classes, such as dogs versus cats. However, fine-grained visual categorization requires the discrimination of subcategories within classes, such as distinguishing between various breeds of dogs. To address this challenge, we proposes a hierarchical CNN architecture that leverages both low-level visual features and mid-level part-based representations. The architecture incorporates adaptive gating mechanisms that selectively combine the outputs of multiple CNN branches, each trained on different spatial scales and part-based representations of the input image. The resulting Part-Stacked CNN architecture is evaluated on several benchmark fine-grained visual categorization datasets, including CIFAR-10, Stanford Cars, and Stanford Dogs. Notably, the proposed approach achieves competitive performance with state-of-the-art methods and demonstrates superior robustness to variations in pose, viewpoint, and illumination. We conduct comprehensive ablation studies to investigate the contribution of each component of the architecture and demonstrate its interpretability and generalizability to unseen datasets and tasks. Overall, our Part-Stacked CNN framework provides a valuable step towards addressing the challenges of fine-grained visual categorization and has the potential to be used in a wide range of real-world applications, such as surveillance systems and autonomous vehicles.

title: A Multiresolution Clinical Decision Support System Based on Fractal Model Design for Classification of Histological Brain Tumours
Abstract: This study presents a novel multiresolution clinical decision support system (CDSS) that employs a fractal model design to classify histological brain tumors. The system integrates fractal analysis of histological images, feature extraction using wavelet transform, and machine learning-based classification techniques to analyze and diagnose brain tumors. By leveraging the inherent fractal structure of tumors, the proposed methodology enables efficient classification and identification of brain tumor grades and types. A comprehensive evaluation of the system is conducted using a dataset of diverse histological brain tumor images, and the results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed CDSS in obtaining high accuracy rates. The multiresolution analysis enables accurate classification of tumors with varying complexities and resolutions, thereby facilitating optimal diagnosis and treatment plans. The development of this CDSS has the potential to significantly improve the efficiency and accuracy of clinical decision-making processes in neurooncology, leading to better patient outcomes and reduced mortality rates. Furthermore, the fractal-based approach is highly flexible and adaptable to different types of medical imaging data, making it a promising tool for application in various clinical domains. Overall, this study makes significant contributions to the field of medical image analysis and CDSS development, as it offers an innovative and effective solution for classifying histological brain tumors.

title: Texture measures combination for improved meningioma classification of histopathological images
Abstract: This study presents a novel approach to melanoma-free meningioma classification of histopathological images by combining texture measures. Unlike conventional techniques that utilize a single texture analysis metric, our proposed method leverages the synergy of various features from different texture elements to provide a more accurate diagnosis. We employed a multi-level framework that extracts multiple texture features from different levels of image analysis, including morphological and spatial features, and both local and global texture characteristics. These features were selected based on their relevance to meningioma classification, as established via comprehensive literature review and feature selection algorithms. The extracted features were then combined using carefully designed classification models that handled feature redundancy and nonlinearity, forming the proposed combination-based framework. We evaluated the proposed approach using a sizable dataset of meningioma histopathological images with corresponding clinical annotations. Experimental results demonstrate that our scheme outperformed existing meningioma classification approaches, including those individually incorporating texture features, with improved generalizability and robustness. Furthermore, the proposed model's ability to explicitly handle non-linear interactions between texture features highlights its potential in accommodating more complex biological processes in tissue imaging, thus enabling a better understanding of meningioma pathophysiology and facilitating the development of precision medicine for this prevalent brain tumor.

title: Assessment of texture measures susceptibility to noise in conventional and contrast enhanced computed tomography lung tumour images
Abstract: This study investigates the susceptibility of various texture measures to noise in conventional and contrast-enhanced CT (Computed Tomography) lung tumor images. Texture analysis is a widely used method for characterizing tissue properties in medical images, and its application in CT imaging has shown promise for differentiating between different types of tumors and assessing tumor aggressiveness. However, noise in CT images can significantly impact texture analysis results, potentially leading to inaccurate diagnoses. Despite its growing importance, there is a lack of comprehensive understanding of how texture measures respond to noise in CT images. In order to address this knowledge gap, we employed a range of texture analysis techniques (first order statistics, Haralick texture features, and morphological features) and added different levels of Gaussian noise to standard image datasets of lung tumors acquired using conventional and contrast-enhanced CT. Our results indicate that certain first-order statistics and Haralick features are highly susceptible to noise, while morphological features remain relatively robust. Additionally, we observed differences in noise susceptibility between conventional and contrast-enhanced CT images, which highlights the need for considering the type of imaging modality used when applying texture analysis to CT images. These findings provide valuable insights into the noise susceptibility of texture measures in CT imaging, enabling more accurate and reliable analysis of lung tumor images.

title: A Combined Deep-Learning and Deformable-Model Approach to Fully Automatic Segmentation of the Left Ventricle in Cardiac MRI
Abstract: Our proposed study introduces a novel fully automatic segmentation framework combining the strengths of deep-learning and deformable-model techniques to achieve high-precision segmentation of the left ventricle (LV) in cardiac MRI images. In recent years, deep-learning methods have made significant strides in image segmentation tasks, but their performance often deteriorates in the presence of complex anatomical structures or irregular boundaries. On the other hand, deformable models have been shown to be robust in handling such scenarios, but their computational efficiency is typically limited. To bridge this gap, our approach utilizes a convolutional neural network (CNN) as a preprocessing step to generate an initial segmentation, followed by a physics-based deformable model that adaptively refines the segmentation. The CNN is designed to capture the global appearance and spatial context of the LV, while the deformable model focuses on the local refinement and captures fine-scale anatomical details. By integrating these two complementary mechanisms, our approach is able to effectively handle variations in LV morphology and improve the robustness of segmentation across different cardiac MRI datasets. Validation results on a large-scale cardiac MRI database demonstrate the efficacy and efficiency of our proposed approach, achieving state-of-the-art performance in LV segmentation with a compute time that is several orders of magnitude faster than existing deformable-model methods. Overall, our combined deep-learning and deformable-model approach offers a promising solution for fully automatic LV segmentation in cardiac MRI images with high accuracy and efficiency.

title: Sparse Reconstruction of Compressive Sensing MRI using Cross-Domain Stochastically Fully Connected Conditional Random Fields
Abstract: This abstract presents a novel approach to reconstruct sparse MRI images using cross-domain stochastically fully connected conditional random fields (FD-SCRF) in compressive sensing (CS) frameworks. Traditional CS-based MRI reconstruction techniques focus on iterative algorithmic methods incorporating natural sparse prior and exploiting intra- and inter-slice correlations with spatial domain transformations which makes them computationally expensive and not suitable for real-time applications. Our proposed framework incorporates a deep learning-based CRF model that captures cross-domain dependencies between low-dimensional MRI patches in a spatially sparse fashion. This FD-SCRF seamlessly combines both spatial and non-local regularization within a unified energy function facilitating flexible and efficient integration of domain-specific and domain-agnostic feature encoding schemes leading to state-of-the-art sparse image recovery outcomes. Extensive experiments conducted on various MRI datasets demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed framework, achieving improved reconstructions in both visual quality and quantitative metrics. Notably, our FD-SCRF model manifests remarkable flexibility by adaptively learning from diverse sets of MRI modalities, thereby providing a versatile tool for MRI reconstruction and segmenting in various research settings. As the primary contribution, the proposed FD-SCRF yields improved accuracy, robustness, and flexibility allowing real-world applications of CS-based MRI reconstruction.

title: Learning Transferrable Knowledge for Semantic Segmentation with Deep Convolutional Neural Network
Abstract: Semantic segmentation is a fundamental task in computer vision, where images are partitioned into their constituent objects and parts. Despite significant advances in this field, the performance of deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) often degrades drastically when adapting to domain shifts, i.e., when the training and test datasets come from different distributions. This is primarily because CNNs learn highly task-specific features, which may not generalize well to unseen data. To overcome this limitation, this work focuses on learning transferrable knowledge for semantic segmentation using deep CNNs. By analyzing the challenges associated with transfer learning in the context of semantic segmentation, we propose a novel framework that enables the transfer of knowledge across different domains. Our framework, dubbed as Domain-Independent Features (DIF), leverages the concept of multi-head attention to identify domain-agnostic features that can be exploited for transfer learning. In addition, we propose a novel unsupervised domain adaptation method that learns to adjust the weights of the pre-trained network to better suit the target domain. Experimental results on several benchmarks demonstrate the efficacy of our framework in achieving state-of-the-art performance across a range of domain shift scenarios, showcasing its potential in real-world applications where access to diverse datasets is often restricted.

title: Truncated Max-of-Convex Models
Abstract: The Truncated Max-of-Convex Models represent a novel framework for solving complex optimization problems by incorporating truncated max functions to reduce dimensionality and explore hidden patterns within data. By leveraging the properties of convex functions, this approach is capable of handling intricate relations between variables and discovering unique solutions that might be overlooked by conventional methods. The proposed Truncated Max-of-Convex Models adapt traditional convex optimization techniques by incorporating max functions to identify essential features that contribute significantly to the solution. This framework utilizes a computationally efficient truncated max function to truncate the convex combinations, thereby reducing the complexity of the overall optimization problem. This allows for improved scalability and efficiency, especially when dealing with high-dimensional data. Furthermore, the integration of the max function enables the exploitation of structural properties, facilitating the identification of sparse solutions that exhibit crucial characteristics. Empirical investigations demonstrate the efficacy of this approach in tackling a wide range of optimization tasks, including feature selection, sparse coding, and clustering. The insights gained from these studies highlight the Truncated Max-of-Convex Models' potential as a robust and powerful tool for solving intricate optimization problems across diverse domains, where efficient and accurate solutions are paramount.

title: G-CNN: an Iterative Grid Based Object Detector
Abstract: G-CNN is a novel iterative grid-based object detector that tackles the challenge of detecting objects in complex images with disparate shapes and sizes. Unlike traditional single-shot detectors that often struggle with classifying contexts such as fragmented objects, the proposed G-CNN leverages grid-based architecture to hierarchically group and filter candidate regions. This hierarchical structure boosts the model's robustness towards images with multiple instances of complex scenes. By evolving from a fixed-size grid in traditional sliding window methods to an adaptable grid size in the proposed G-CNN, object detection efficiency can be significantly improved, especially for images containing numerous similarly-sized yet distinct objects. Furthermore, the G-CNN's grid-based approach fosters an environment that promotes interaction between candidate objects through iterative filtering, fostering accurate separation and detection of connected objects. Moreover, despite its high computational expense due to iterative processing, G-CNN's performance in terms of detection accuracy can be further optimised through the utilization of a range of computationally-optimised grid-based techniques such as shared memory and parallel computing on GPU-based systems. In this work, G-CNN was found to outperform existing state-of-the-art detectors on challenging datasets, demonstrating its superior object detection performance in scenarios with complex scenes, particularly those containing a multitude of interacting objects.

title: Fast Acquisition for Quantitative MRI Maps: Sparse Recovery from Non-linear Measurements
Abstract: This paper proposes an innovative approach for the rapid acquisition of quantitative MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) maps using sparse recovery from non-linear measurements. The increasing demand for quantitative MRI applications, such as analyzing complex brain disorders and monitoring treatment efficacy, necessitates faster and higher-resolution scanning techniques. Conventional MRI acquisition methods can be time-consuming due to the requirement of multiple images taken under different conditions. To address this limitation, we develop a novel framework that imposes sparsity constraints on the MRI signals, taking into account the inherent non-linear relationship between the received MRI signals and the tissue properties. Utilizing tools from compressed sensing and non-linear reconstruction, our proposed method optimizes the sparsity-promoting basis pursuit algorithm to minimize the l1 regularization term. By incorporating a non-linear regularizer that accounts for the physical measurement model, our approach accurately recovers high-fidelity quantitative MRI maps from limited and noisy measurements, eliminating the need for multi-shot acquisitions. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method using several numerical experiments and real-world data sets, showcasing superior reconstruction performance and reduced acquisition times compared to conventional methods. These findings suggest that our technique holds great promise for a wide range of quantitative MRI applications, where fast and accurate data acquisition is paramount.

title: Adaptive Object Detection Using Adjacency and Zoom Prediction
Abstract: This paper proposes an adaptive object detection framework that leverages adjacency and zoom prediction to efficiently handle diverse object sizes, orientation, and scales. The proposed framework consists of two primary components: an adjacency module and a zoom predictor. The adjacency module predicts the presence and locations of adjacent objects to a target object, which enables the detection model to focus on contexts that improve accuracy and reduce redundant computations. The zoom predictor predicts the optimal zoom level for each target object, taking into account object sizes, scales, and contextual factors. By applying a novel zooming scheme based on the predicted zoom levels, the detection model can adaptively learn object features and improve detection accuracy across various object sizes and contexts. The proposed framework is evaluated on the COCO and PASCAL VOC datasets, demonstrating significant improvements in terms of Average Precision (AP) and mean Average Precision (mAP) compared to state-of-the-art models. Furthermore, the framework is shown to improve detection speed through efficient sampling and computation of object features based on predicted zoom levels and adjacency relationships. This research presents an innovative approach to adaptive object detection, offering a potential solution to the challenging problem of detecting objects of various sizes and contexts in complex scenes.

title: On the Automated Synthesis of Enterprise Integration Patterns to Adapt Choreography-based Distributed Systems
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to automate the synthesis of Enterprise Integration Patterns (EIPs) to adapt choreography-based distributed systems. In the context of service-oriented architecture, choreographed interactions among services can lead to complex systems, making it difficult to maintain their stability and scalability due to the constant need for reconfiguration and adaptation to changing business requirements and technological advancements. Current adaptation approaches often rely on manual configuration and hard-coding of adaptation rules, leading to increased development time, brittleness, and the potential for human error. Our proposed approach utilizes a novel combination of search-based optimization and model-driven engineering techniques to automatically synthesize EIPs that can adapt to dynamic changes in system functionality and environmental conditions. This allows for the creation of adaptive and resilient distributed systems that can operate in the presence of uncertainty and variability, while minimizing the need for manual intervention and ensuring that systems adapt in accordance with the defined design principles and quality-of-service constraints. Our solution was implemented in, and experimented with, a case study involving a multi-service platform for supply chain management; the results demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of our approach in efficiently discovering and deploying EIPs that adapt distributed systems to meet diverse and dynamic requirements within the given constraints.

title: A Latent-Variable Lattice Model
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel statistical model for understanding complex relationships and patterns in high-dimensional data. The latent-variable lattice model (LVL) is designed to capture the intricate connections between multiple variables, facilitating a deeper understanding of their underlying structures. By integrating aspects of both graph-based and factor-based models, LVL represents a significant advancement in modeling methodologies. The lattice structure, which forms the backbone of the model, allows for the efficient exploration of multiple latent variables, thereby providing a rich representation of the underlying data. By doing so, LVL has the potential to address several long-standing challenges in statistical modeling, particularly in the context of large-scale datasets. The model can accommodate different types of data, including continuous and categorical variables, and is capable of incorporating external knowledge or expert information. To evaluate its performance and robustness, LVL is applied to various simulated data as well as real-world datasets from biology and social sciences. Comparison with state-of-the-art models further validates the utility and effectiveness of the proposed approach, highlighting its potential as a powerful tool for analyzing and interpreting complex data relationships. The results demonstrate the model's ability to unravel the intricate connections between multiple variables, providing valuable insights that can inform decision-making in diverse fields.

title: Recovering 6D Object Pose and Predicting Next-Best-View in the Crowd
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to recovering the six-dimensional (6D) object pose and predicting the next-best-view in densely crowded environments using a combination of computer vision, robotics, and machine learning techniques. Our approach focuses on addressing the challenges of accurate object pose estimation and optimal viewpoint selection in the presence of multiple objects and dynamic backgrounds. We introduce a multi-task learning framework that leverages both pixel-wise and feature-based representations to estimate the 6D object pose with high precision. A novel viewpoint selection strategy is also developed to prioritize the most informative viewpoints, taking into account the object's occlusion, visibility, and motion history. Our method utilizes a lightweight convolutional neural network (CNN) to predict the next-best-view based on a set of predefined viewpoints, considering factors such as object's pose, shape, and appearance. The approach is evaluated on a challenging benchmark dataset containing diverse scenes, objects, and crowds, showing consistent improvements in pose estimation accuracy and viewpoint selection effectiveness compared to state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, we demonstrate the applicability of our method in autonomous navigation and surveillance scenarios, showcasing the potential of our approach in real-world deployments. Overall, our proposed method provides a robust and efficient solution for 6D object pose recovery and next-best-view prediction in crowded environments, reflecting recent advancements in computer vision and machine learning.

title: Convolutional Architecture Exploration for Action Recognition and Image Classification
Abstract: This research paper delves into the realm of computer vision, specifically focusing on the exploration of convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures for two fundamental tasks: action recognition and image classification. Despite the widespread adoption of pre-trained models such as VGG16 and ResNet50, ongoing developments in CNN design continue to push the boundaries of performance and efficiency. A comprehensive analysis of the existing literature reveals a diverse array of architectures, each designed to address specific challenges inherent to the tasks at hand. To bridge this knowledge gap, this study proposes a novel architecture, coined 'ActionNet,' which leverages an innovative combination of residual learning, attention mechanisms, and spatial pyramid pooling to enhance the capture of spatial and temporal features. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets, including the widely recognized UCF101, HMDB51, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet, demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed ActionNet architecture in comparison to state-of-the-art models. Notably, the results showcase a significant gain in accuracy, averaging 5-7% improvement across various datasets, underscoring the potential of the proposed approach in achieving superior performance while minimizing computational overhead. The research also presents a framework for automatating structure tuning, an essential step in harnessing the full potential of CNNs, and provides valuable insights into the design decisions that underpin the success of the ActionNet architecture.

title: A Deep Generative Deconvolutional Image Model
Abstract: This research presents an innovative Deep Generative Deconvolutional Image (DGDI) model that combines the strengths of deep learning and deconvolutional techniques to generate highly realistic and diverse images. Inspired by the versatility of deconvolutional neural networks, the DGDI model comprises four primary components: an encoder network designed to capture the essential features of image data, a deconvolutional network responsible for generating novel patterns, a discriminator network used to enforce the realism of the generated images, and a generator network that combines the outputs of the encoder and deconvolutional networks. Through a series of experiments, the effectiveness of the DGDI model is demonstrated by comparing its performance to several state-of-the-art generative adversarial networks (GANs) on various evaluation metrics, including image quality, diversity, and mode coverage. The experiments show that the proposed DGDI model outperforms the baseline GANs in terms of generating high-quality and diverse images. Furthermore, the model's ability to recognize and leverage meaningful patterns in the image data leads to improved image fidelity and reduced mode collapse. The DGDI model also exhibits a higher level of interpretability and controllability compared to traditional GANs, making it a promising tool for various computer vision applications, such as image generation, object recognition, and image-to-image translation. Overall, the DGDI model provides an efficient and effective approach to image generation, showcasing its potential as a valuable asset in the field of computer vision research.

title: Plug-and-Play Priors for Bright Field Electron Tomography and Sparse Interpolation
Abstract: This work presents a novel approach to plug-and-play priors for bright field electron tomography and sparse interpolation, addressing the challenges of noise, missing data, and high dimensionality in reconstructing 3D images from limited-angle projections. By leveraging the recent developments in machine learning and sparse representation, we introduce a unified framework that integrates multiple priors, each tailored to capture distinct structural features of the dataset. The framework consists of a hybrid of traditional sparse modeling methods, such as Total Variation (TV) and nonlocal total variation regularization, with deep learning-based architectures, such as the convolutional neural network (CNN) and the sparse coding network. These hybrid priors are designed to effectively capture noisy and missing data artifacts, while promoting sparsity and structural consistency in the reconstructed images. Our proposed method demonstrates excellent performance in bright field electron tomography, where it achieves state-of-the-art reconstruction quality and robust recovery of features and structures from limited data. Furthermore, the plug-and-play property of the proposed priors enables seamless integration into existing tomographic reconstruction pipelines, making it easy to try different priors and adapt them to specific datasets and applications. Our results demonstrate the potential of machine learning-based priors in transforming the field of bright field electron tomography and sparse interpolation, enabling more accurate and efficient recovery of high-quality images.

title: Mid-level Representation for Visual Recognition
Abstract: Visual recognition has long been a cornerstone of computer vision, with the primary goal of accurately identifying and categorizing visual content. Despite the significant advancements made by deep neural networks in recent years, the focus on leveraging mid-level representations within these networks has led to a new wave of discovery. Mid-level representations, which encompass a range of cognitive intermediate-level features including object segments, parts, and shapes, are crucial for navigating complex visual hierarchies and facilitating high-level contextual understanding. However, previous approaches to generating mid-level representations often rely on complex and computationally expensive methods such as graph-based techniques or attention-based mechanisms. In contrast, this research contributes to the development of a novel mid-level representation, called Hierarchical Part-based Representation (HPR), which utilizes a hierarchical and coarse-to-fine processing framework. HPR distinguishes itself by capturing detailed spatial hierarchies, robust relationships between components, and efficient processing despite the reduced computational resource requirement. Our proposed HPR framework extensively evaluated using a series of challenging visual tasks across various datasets demonstrates improved visual recognition performance, efficiency, and robustness, setting the foundation for real-world deployment of mid-level visual recognition systems. By examining both the accuracy and efficiency of the proposed framework, this work paves the way for exploring more autonomous object and scene categorization within real-world applications.

title: Do Less and Achieve More: Training CNNs for Action Recognition Utilizing Action Images from the Web
Abstract: This paper explores the potential of leveraging action images sourced from the web as a supplementary training dataset for achieving greater performance in action recognition using convolutional neural networks (CNNs). The primary objective of this work is to investigate whether action images gathered from the internet, which may be obtained from various publicly accessible sources, can aid in training CNNs that excel at categorizing human actions or activities. To accomplish this goal, a novel web dataset was constructed comprising action images scraped from publicly available image and video hosting platforms, photo and video sharing websites, as well as web communities. Utilizing this dataset alongside an existing benchmark dataset specially tailored for human action recognition enabled the development of more robust CNNs that are adept at classifying action sequences. Experimental results demonstrate that inclusion of web action images significantly enhances the classification accuracy of CNN models, highlighting the contribution of these images in fostering improved action recognition. Furthermore, this study examines fundamental influencing factors like data quantity, image quality, as well as action specificity on the learning and performance of these CNNs. Through an in-depth evaluation of these contributing elements, the findings of this paper provide actionable recommendations for training CNNs utilizing web action images, hence promoting the practical application of action recognition in a wide array of domains, including surveillance systems, sports analytics, and content-sensitive advertising systems.

title: SR-Clustering: Semantic Regularized Clustering for Egocentric Photo Streams Segmentation
Abstract: SR-Clustering: Semantic Regularized Clustering for Egocentric Photo Streams Segmentation is a novel method designed to tackle the challenges of segmenting egocentric photo streams, which are characterized by their temporal and spatial context. The majority of existing image segmentation techniques are not well-suited to handle the dynamic and cluttered nature of egocentric photo streams, where objects may appear and disappear across multiple frames. To address this issue, the proposed SR-Clustering method incorporates a semantic regularization term that encourages the discovery of clusters that are not only spatially coherent but also semantically consistent. By leveraging a deep semantic feature extractor, the proposed model captures the intrinsic relationships between objects and scenes in the egocentric photo stream, thereby leading to improved clustering performance. Through a series of experiments on benchmark datasets, the results demonstrate that SR-Clustering outperforms state-of-the-art techniques in terms of clustering accuracy, precision, and recall. Furthermore, the incorporation of semantic regularization has been found to effectively mitigate the impact of temporal discontinuities and object variability on the clustering results. The success of SR-Clustering lies in its ability to simultaneously consider spatial and semantic aspects, making it an attractive option for a wide range of egocentric photo stream analysis applications.
