title: Is Hamming distance the only way for matching binary image feature descriptors?
Abstract: This study investigates the efficacy of Hamming distance in matching binary image feature descriptors and explores alternative methods to assess its supremacy in the field of image recognition and object detection. Despite being widely adopted, the limitations of Hamming distance in handling partial matching and dealing with occlusions have raised inquiries about the feasibility of alternative solutions. To this end, this research compares the performance of Hamming distance with other metrics, such as cosine similarity, Euclidean distance, and Manhattan distance, in matching binary feature descriptors. A comprehensive evaluation is carried out on various benchmark datasets, including Caltech-101, PASCAL VOC, and ImageNet, to assess the robustness and accuracy of each distance metric. The experiments demonstrate that while Hamming distance remains a competitive method, other metrics, particularly cosine similarity, can offer comparable or even superior performance in certain scenarios, especially when dealing with partial matching and occlusions. The findings of this research provide valuable insights into the strengths and weaknesses of different distance metrics and highlight the importance of considering alternative methods in the design of binary feature descriptors for image recognition and object detection applications. The implications of this study are substantial, as they can inform the development of more robust and accurate image feature descriptors and contribute to the advancement of computer vision technology.

title: Computational Models for Multiview Dense Depth Maps of Dynamic Scene
Abstract: This research paper explores and reviews various computational models used for generating multiview dense depth maps of dynamic scenes, focusing on the field of computer vision and 3D reconstruction. The development of multiview dense depth maps involves the accurate recovery of depth information from multiple cameras, allowing for 3D scene modeling and reconstruction. Traditional methods, such as stereopsis, structure from motion (SfM), and structure from stereo (SfStereo), have limitations in handling dynamic scenes and high-level occlusions. To address these challenges, recent approaches have employed computational models, including deep learning-based models, variational methods, and graph-based methods. The paper delves into the theoretical underpinnings and practical applications of these models, highlighting their strengths and weaknesses. Additionally, it discusses the importance of considering dynamic scenes, occlusions, and object motion in the modeling process. By providing a comprehensive overview of existing and emerging techniques, the paper aims to facilitate the understanding and improvement of multiview dense depth maps for various applications, including autonomous vehicles, robotics, and video surveillance. The research contributes to the advancements in 3D scene reconstruction and understanding, which is crucial for the development of intelligent systems.

title: Learning to Point and Count
Abstract: The development of language skills, particularly in the areas of pointing and counting, is a crucial milestone in a child's early cognitive development. However, the mechanisms and cues that facilitate this process remain poorly understood. This study aims to investigate the process of learning to point and count in young children, with a focus on the interplay between attention, perception, and executive functions. We implemented a participatory, longitudinal design, wherein forty children aged 2-3 years were enrolled in a language-learning program, which emphasized pointing and counting skills. Using a combination of behavioral observations, eye-tracking technology, and neural imaging (fMRI), we monitored the children's progress and brain activity throughout the 12-week program. Our results showed that improvements in pointing and counting abilities were correlated with increased activity in regions of the brain associated with attention, language processing, and executive functions. We also found that the children's attentional abilities, particularly their capacity for sustained attention, played a critical role in predicting their learning outcomes. Furthermore, we observed a significant increase in the neural connectivity between language and attention networks, suggesting that the process of learning to point and count may involve the reorganization of neural circuits. These findings have important implications for the design of language-learning interventions and highlight the importance of attentional abilities in facilitating language acquisition.

title: SSD: Single Shot MultiBox Detector
Abstract: The Single Shot MultiBox Detector (SSD) is a state-of-the-art real-time object detection architecture that has gained significant attention in recent years. Unlike traditional detectors that rely on two-stage architectures involving region proposal networks (RPNs) and classification networks, SSD operates as a single neural network that predicts detection boxes and class probabilities simultaneously. This architecture eliminates the need for candidate bounding boxes generation making it more efficient and reducing computational requirements. In this paper, we delve into the working mechanism of SSD, its strengths, and weaknesses. Through extensive experiments on a range of popular benchmark datasets including PASCAL VOC and ImageNet, we explore the effectiveness of various hyperparameters and techniques such as data augmentation and learning rate schedules in optimizing the SSD performance. We find that the SSD detector delivers impressive detection accuracy, comparable to some of the most advanced deep learning architectures, while achieving detection speeds of up to 59 frames per second, making it an attractive choice for real-time object detection tasks. Furthermore, we identify key challenges and potential avenues for improving the SSD framework such as handling large variations in scale and aspect ratio, and addressing class imbalance issues. Our investigation provides valuable insights into the underlying mechanisms of SSD and serves as a foundation for developing more efficient and effective real-time object detection systems.

title: Direct Intrinsics: Learning Albedo-Shading Decomposition by Convolutional Regression
Abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to the albedo-shading decomposition problem through the direct estimation of image intrinsic properties using deep convolutional regression. By directly predicting albedo and shading values without relying on intermediate representations, the proposed method overcomes limitations inherent to previous decomposition methods. Through a convolutional neural network architecture, the model learns to decompose input images into their constituent albedo and shading components, allowing for more accurate and robust estimation of intrinsic image properties. The network's architecture is designed to progressively focus on local, medium, and long-range spatial structures within the input images, enabling the model to capture detailed and intricate patterns that are critical for accurate decomposition. The proposed approach is evaluated on a variety of benchmarks and real-world scenes, demonstrating state-of-the-art performance and visual quality. The direct estimation of albedo and shading values also enables applications in computer vision tasks such as reflectance-aware image and video editing, material recognition, and scene understanding. By directly predicting albedo-shading decomposition without intermediate representations, this novel approach enables more efficient, accurate, and robust estimation of intrinsic image properties, unlocking new possibilities for computer vision research and applications.

title: Pseudo-Bayesian Robust PCA: Algorithms and Analyses
Abstract: This study presents a novel approach to robust Principal Component Analysis (PCA) by incorporating pseudo-Bayesian techniques, resulting in a robust and efficient method for high-dimensional data analysis. Pseudo-Bayesian Robust PCA integrates Bayesian inference principles with a robust estimationalgorithm to accommodate outliers and anomalies in the data. By leveraging the strengths of both Bayesian and robust PCA, this approach offers improved robustness, accuracy, and stability compared to standard PCA methods. The proposed algorithm utilizes a weighted least squares formulation to optimize the underlying probabilistic model, ensuring that outliers have minimal impact on the data reconstruction. Experimental evaluations on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method in recovering the true underlying structures and improving robustness against noise and corruption. Furthermore, theoretical analyses establish the statistical consistency and convergence properties of the pseudo-Bayesian Robust PCA, underpinning its reliability and applicability in a wide range of applications. By providing a theoretically grounded robust PCA method, this research contributes to the advancement of data analysis techniques, enabling more accurate and reliable extraction of meaningful patterns and structures from high-dimensional data.

title: Simple Baseline for Visual Question Answering
Abstract: A Visual Question Answering (VQA) model typically seeks to understand the content of an image and then respond to a question about the image. Developing a simple baseline for VQA is crucial for understanding the fundamental components of these models and assessing the contribution of more complex ideas to improved performance. This work proposes a simple baseline for VQA that leverages a conventional Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) for image encoding, paired with an existing natural language processor, such as long short-term memory (LSTM) or Transformers, for question analysis and response generation. The proposed baseline builds upon earlier models, incorporating ideas from various architectures while mitigating the complexity of integrating them. Preliminary results, achieved on multiple benchmark datasets, suggest performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods, albeit lower when high-performing models are specifically customized for the given datasets. While other baselines have largely focused on different elements of the architecture, or made the architectures more complex, this proposed model improves the efficiency of these processes. Detailed performance metrics are analyzed at each step, providing a comprehensive understanding of how performance shapes itself at this specific task involving image encoding, token inputs, question formulation, answer sampling, and overall effectiveness of predictive representations without over-engineering tasks with potentially redundant layers or data formats.

title: A Large Dataset to Train Convolutional Networks for Disparity, Optical Flow, and Scene Flow Estimation
Abstract: Research on deep learning for computer vision tasks, particularly for estimating disparity, optical flow, and scene flow, has grown significantly in recent years, leading to the development of sophisticated algorithms and models. However, the availability of large, diverse, and high-quality training datasets remains a major challenging aspect of this field, mainly due to the difficulties associated with annotating and collecting such datasets. In this study, we propose a large-scale dataset for training convolutional neural networks to estimate disparity, optical flow, and scene flow, aiming to bridge the gap between the advances made in these tasks and the quality of available training datasets. Our dataset comprises a comprehensive collection of challenging and diverse visual scenes and includes approximately 20 million training images with corresponding disparity, optical flow, and scene flow annotations. Each image is accurately annotated with dense disparity, optical flow, and scene flow fields, making it an ideal resource for training and evaluating deep neural network models for solving these tasks. To facilitate seamless integration of our dataset into existing research ecosystems, we provide our dataset in a widely accepted format along with supporting tools and baselines to simplify the evaluation process.

title: In-situ multi-scattering tomography
Abstract: This study introduces a novel approach to in-situ multi-scattering tomography, a non-invasive imaging technique aimed at reconstructing multiphase flow dynamics within porous media. Employing a combination of experimental methods and numerical simulations, researchers have successfully translated the principles of traditional visible and near-infrared imaging techniques to operate within the X-ray radiation regime. By leveraging this multi-scale approach, previously inaccessible flow regimes within complex, real-world systems can be visualized. Initial results suggest that this in-situ imaging technique can yield both high spatial and temporal resolution, facilitating a comprehensive understanding of multiphase flow processes at the macroscopic level, as well as at microscopic scales. Computational models are developed to further elucidate the transport mechanisms involved in the multi-scattering process, providing theoretical foundations for image reconstruction algorithms. These methods ultimately enable researchers to accurately visualize turbulent flow phenomena and quantify distribution of phases within disordered porous media, addressing a long-standing challenge in various scientific disciplines, including chemical engineering, petroleum engineering, and environmental science. Further refinement and validation of the in-situ imaging system is expected to significantly enhance fundamental knowledge and engineering applications in these fields, especially for the prediction and optimization of industrial processes, such as enhanced oil recovery, carbon sequestration, and contaminant transport remediation.

title: Clustering by Deep Nearest Neighbor Descent (D-NND): A Density-based Parameter-Insensitive Clustering Method
Abstract: Clustering by Deep Nearest Neighbor Descent (D-NND) is a novel density-based parameter-insensitive clustering method that leverages the capabilities of deep learning to effectively partition high-dimensional data into meaningful clusters. This method extends the traditional Nearest Neighbor Descent (NND) algorithm by incorporating a deep neural network to selectively preserve the local density features and suppress noise in the data. Unlike traditional clustering methods that are often sensitive to hyperparameters and prone to noise, D-NND is designed to be insensitive to these parameters and robust against outliers. The deep neural network component in D-NND adapts the feature extraction and dimensionality reduction process to the given dataset, enabling the algorithm to automatically capture the complexity of the data distributions. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of D-NND in comparison to popular clustering algorithms, such as K-means and DBSCAN, across various datasets and configurations. Furthermore, the parameter-insensitive nature of D-NND makes it particularly appealing for applications where parameter tuning is challenging or time-consuming. Overall, Clustering by Deep Nearest Neighbor Descent offers a promising clustering approach that is capable of handling complex high-dimensional data with minimal human intervention.

title: Unification of Force and Substance
Abstract: The concept of unification, a fundamental principle in physics and philosophy, has long been a topic of interest and debate among scholars. The unification of force and substance is a novel approach that attempts to integrate the two fundamental aspects of the universe, which have traditionally been treated as separate entities. By exploring the intricate relationships between fundamental forces and the properties of matter, this research aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of the underlying structure of the universe. It proposes a theoretical framework that combines the principles of quantum mechanics and general relativity, two theories that have been successful in explaining various phenomena but have limitations when applied together. The framework posits that forces and substances are interconnected and interdependent, and that the properties of one influence the characteristics of the other. Through a critical analysis of existing theories and experimental results, this research identifies potential areas of convergence and divergence, and develops a revised understanding of the nature of reality. By illustrating the interconnectedness of forces and substances, this study offers a paradigm shift in our understanding of the universe, highlighting the intricate web of relationships that govern the behavior of matter and energy at all scales.

title: On The Continuous Steering of the Scale of Tight Wavelet Frames
Abstract: This paper delves into the theoretical foundations and practical implications of continuous steering in the context of tight wavelet frames. A wavelet frame is an orthonormal decomposition of a function or a signal, with the ability to zoom in, zoom out, or tilt at various angles, making it essential in numerous applications, such as signal processing, image compression, and pattern recognition. However, traditional wavelet frames suffer from a limited angular resolution, restricting their capability to capture complex structures in signals. Continuous steering provides an enhanced angular resolution by shifting the frequency response of a wavelet frame. By adjusting the steering parameter, one can adapt to various features of a signal, thus improving the effectiveness of analyses. This paper investigates the mathematical theories behind the continuous steering of tight wavelet frames, examines various methods for implementing steerable wavelet frames, and demonstrates the potential applications of these steerable wavelet frames in image processing, data denoising, and signal classification. Moreover, this study provides algorithms for steering the scale of tight wavelet frames, aiming to promote research on the theoretical and practical implications of continuous steering in the field of wavelet analysis.

title: Visualizing Deep Convolutional Neural Networks Using Natural Pre-Images
Abstract: Deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have garnered significant attention within the computer vision community, driven by their impressive performance in image classification, object detection, and segmentation tasks. The inherent complexity of these networks poses an essential question: how do specific input stimuli elicit specific outputs through the network's convolutional and pooling operations? One approach to uncovering this process is through the use of pre-images, which are reconstructed inputs designed to produce a specific output. In the context of deep CNNs, natural pre-images are generated by reversing the network's forward pass, effectively solving for an input image that the network would produce a desired output for. This technique allows researchers to visualize the underlying structure of the network, gain insights into the relationships between inputs and outputs, and better understand how images are processed through the network's various layers. By leveraging natural pre-images, researchers can more effectively diagnose and debug their models, identify potential biases, and develop more robust architectures. Furthermore, the ability to reverse-engineer the CNN's forward pass enables the creation of novel pre-processing techniques that can be used to enhance the input data and improve overall performance. This visualization tool holds significant potential for advancing the field of deep learning and pushing the boundaries of computer vision applications.

title: Scalable domain adaptation of convolutional neural networks
Abstract: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have achieved remarkable success in various computer vision tasks; however, their performance often degrades when adapting to new domains or datasets due to the lack of shared knowledge between the source and target domains. To address this issue, domain adaptation methods have been proposed to minimize the domain shift between the source and target domains. Nevertheless, existing domain adaptation techniques for CNNs often suffer from scalability issues, particularly when dealing with large datasets or when attempting to adapt multiple source domains to a target domain. Furthermore, most existing methods focus on a single source domain adaptation or require additional source data, which may not be feasible in many practical scenarios. This study aims to develop a scalable domain adaptation framework for CNNs that can effectively adapt multiple source domains to a target domain with limited shared data. Our proposed framework incorporates a novel multi-task learning approach that can learn shared features between multiple source domains and simultaneously discriminate the target domain data. The framework also leverages a unified loss function that balances the adaptation effects from different source domains. Extensive experiments on various domain adaptation tasks demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed framework in adapting to new domains with minimal shared data, showcasing its potential in real-world applications where data collection and access are limited.

title: Hyperspectral Chemical Plume Detection Algorithms Based On Multidimensional Iterative Filtering Decomposition
Abstract: This research paper presents a novel approach to hyperspectral chemical plume detection using multidimensional iterative filtering decomposition algorithms. The work focuses on developing a robust and efficient method to detect and track effluent plumes in complex environments, such as chemical spills or nuclear accidents. A key aspect of the proposed approach is the utilization of multidimensional iterative filtering decomposition, which enables the identification of subtle spectral patterns in hyperspectral imagery. The newly developed algorithm is demonstrated to achieve superior performance in distinguishing between substance presence and absence, compared to state-of-the-art alternatives. A multidimensional iterative filtering decomposition is implemented in a 2-stage configuration, enabling spatial and spectral refinement. Experimental results using real hyperspectral datasets and simulations validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, exhibiting higher accuracy, precision, and robustness in detecting chemical plume contaminations. The contributions of this research lie in the development of multidimensional iterative filtering decomposition algorithms adapted for hyperspectral chemical plume detection, providing a platform for enhanced monitoring and surveillance in various chemical and environmental sensing applications.

title: Fast Optimization Algorithm on Riemannian Manifolds and Its Application in Low-Rank Representation
Abstract: This paper focuses on developing a novel optimization approach for low-rank representation on Riemannian manifolds, which efficiently solves the challenging non-convex problem of representing high-dimensional data as a linear combination of a few basis elements. The existing methods for low-rank representation either fail to converge or experience slow convergence rates due to the non-convexity of the manifolds. To address these limitations, we propose RiemOpt, a randomized Riemannian optimization algorithm that adaptively allocates computational resources to efficiently reduce the rank of the representation. RiemOpt exploits the geometry of the Riemannian manifold by iteratively applying a projected gradient descent method with a random initialization strategy. Theoretical analysis is provided to demonstrate the convergence of the proposed algorithm, showing that it achieves O(1/k) convergence rate in terms of function value. Extensive numerical experiments on real-world datasets, including image and text, demonstrate the efficiency of RiemOpt in comparison with existing state-of-the-art methods, indicating that our approach can effectively approximate low-rank representations on complex Riemannian manifolds. Moreover, RiemOpt maintains low computational costs, making it suitable for large-scale data applications where computational efficiency is essential. These results establish RiemOpt as a promising optimization tool for low-rank representation on Riemannian manifolds and its applications in various fields.

title: Sparsifying Neural Network Connections for Face Recognition
Abstract: This research explores sparsifying neural network connections for enhancing face recognition performance while reducing computational complexity and model size. Traditional neural networks often have a large number of parameters, leading to high computational requirements, which can hinder their deployment on resource-constrained devices. Recent advancements in sparse neural network learning aim to alleviate this issue by identifying and removing redundant connections, resulting in a more compact and efficient model. By leveraging techniques such as sparse connectivity, quantization, and pruning, our method selectively removes insignificant connections among neural network layers, thereby obtaining a more interpretable, efficient, and accurate face recognition model. Experimental results demonstrate the feasibility of the proposal, with significant reductions in model size, number of parameters, and computational operations required for face recognition, alongside only minor accuracy degradation. Furthermore, this work provides a comprehensive comparison of sparse neural network learning strategies, including the relative trade-offs between computation requirements, model size, and recognition accuracy. Overall, this research contributes to the design of more agile and efficient neural networks for face recognition, bringing them closer to deployment on edge devices and mobile platforms. title: Recognition from Hand Cameras
Abstract: This paper presents a comparative analysis of hand camera-based recognition systems, exploring the feasibility of using off-the-shelf mobile devices to recognize and classify human gestures, hand postures, and objects. The research focuses on the development of a robust and efficient hand camera-based recognition system, capable of adapting to various lighting conditions and user contexts. By leveraging machine learning algorithms and computer vision techniques, the system extracts and processes hand-related features from captured images and videos. A comprehensive evaluation of the proposed system is conducted using a dataset comprising diverse hand imagery, including isolated hand gestures, complex hand movements, and objects manipulated with the hand. The results show that the proposed system achieves high accuracy rates for hand posture recognition, outperforming existing approaches in certain scenarios. Furthermore, the system demonstrates its ability to adapt to variations in user appearance, lighting conditions, and environments. However, certain limitations, such as reduced recognition accuracy under low-light conditions and limited robustness to occlusions and hand occlusion, are identified. To mitigate these issues, potential improvements to the system are proposed, including the incorporation of additional sensors, enhanced recognition algorithms, and more comprehensive training datasets. This research contributes to the body of knowledge on hand camera-based recognition systems, providing insights into their design, development, and application in various fields. title: Fixation prediction with a combined model of bottom-up saliency and vanishing point
Abstract: This study presents a novel fixation prediction model that integrates bottom-up saliency and the concept of vanishing point to simulate human visual fixation behavior. By combining these two distinct computational modules, the proposed model is able to capture both the automatic capture of attention by salient regions in the scene and the impact of topological and depth cue information provided by the vanishing point. The bottom-up saliency module, based on machine learning algorithms, generates a probability map of potential fixation locations within the image, while the vanishing point-based module accounts for the direction and distance of lines that converge at a vanishing point, providing critical depth and context information. The multi-stage training process and model comparisons demonstrate the effectiveness and superiority of the proposed model in accurately predicting human fixations compared to traditional bottom-up or vanishing point-based models. Experiments conducted on a comprehensive dataset comprising diverse, real-world scenes and human fixation records confirm the robustness and generalizability of the proposed model across scenarios, revealing a high degree of consistency with real-world human fixation behavior. The results underscore the potential of the proposed combined model for enhancing the performance of applications reliant on accurate fixation prediction, such as autonomous vehicle navigation, video analytics, and assistive technologies for individuals with visual impairments.

title: Rank Pooling for Action Recognition
Abstract: Action recognition is a vital task in the field of computer vision, particularly in applications such as surveillance, human-computer interaction, and content-based video retrieval. However, existing deep learning methods have limitations in handling large spatial extents and performing feature pooling. To address this issue, a novel rank pooling approach, called rank-spatial pyramid pooling (RSPool), is proposed to extract spatial hierarchy information and improve action recognition performance. RSPool aggregates features through two ranking objectives: a saliency ranking objective that identifies discriminative regions, and a spatial ranking objective that highlights critical spatial hierarchies. To realize RSPool, a dual-task loss is designed to balance these two objectives, and a two-stage architecture is adopted to progressively refine spatial hierarchies. Extensive experiments on severalbenchmark datasets demonstrate that RSPool significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving 94.9%, 94.4%, and 75.6% accuracy on the UCF-101, HMDB-51, and kinetics-400 datasets, respectively. Moreover, our method demonstrates high robustness and generalizability, even when training on a smaller subset of the dataset or with fewer frames. The efficacy of RSPool makes it a promising approach for action recognition tasks in various applications and scenarios. We also analyze the effectiveness of different rank pooling components, which provides valuable insights into the importance of spatial hierarchies in action recognition.

title: PatchBatch: a Batch Augmented Loss for Optical Flow
Abstract:
A Batch Augmented Loss for Optical Flow is a novel approach to improving the accuracy and robustness of optical flow estimation tasks in computer vision. Optical flow estimation is a fundamental problem in computer vision that involves computing the motion of pixels between two consecutive frames of a video sequence. Traditional methods often rely on a data-driven approach, where a loss function is defined as the difference between predicted and ground-truth flow fields. However, such methods tend to suffer from mode collapse, where the model converges to a suboptimal solution due to learning a limited set of modes. 

To address this issue, we propose a novel loss function called PatchBatch, which combines the advantages of local and global consistency losses. PatchBatch loss function is designed to capture both local and global motion patterns in a video sequence, thus it significantly improves the estimation accuracy and robustness of optical flow. Our PatchBatch loss function incorporates a batch-based approach, where the model is trained with a batch of randomly sampled patches from the input frames. Each patch is processed independently, and the resulting flow fields are then aggregated using a global consistency loss. This hierarchical approach allows the model to learn both local and global motion patterns, leading to more accurate and robust optical flow estimation results. 

We extensively evaluated our PatchBatch loss function on several benchmark datasets, including the Middlebury and KITTI datasets. The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in improving the accuracy and robustness of optical flow estimation. Compared to state-of-the-art methods, our PatchBatch loss function achieves significant improvements in terms of both qualitative and quantitative metrics.

title: The Next Best Underwater View
Abstract: Recent advancements in underwater exploration technology have significantly enhanced our ability to visually interact with and understand marine ecosystems. The Next Best View underwater, which has garnered considerable attention, not only facilitates improved site interpretation but also has a profound impact on marine archeological preservation and underwater salvage efforts. This concept suggests that we are constantly searching for a new, untouched, and unexplored underwater location, which would result in a significant shift in our collective understanding of the world beneath the ocean's surface. The continuous pursuit of superior image and data quality has led researchers and engineers to collaborate and share expertise to make it into reality. Furthermore, it has pushed for improvements in sonar technology, AI-driven data analysis, submersible navigation systems, and even 3D geolocation mapping software. The underwater observations that are currently being captured and analyzed offer new insights into biological diversity, marine life interaction, water ecosystem circulation patterns, marine plant growth and extinction possibilities. So our drive for breathtaking new underwater views will have a major influence on marine engineers's attempts to defend the world's ocean floor, encourage higher preservation, and support research initiatives for decades to come.

title: Image reconstruction from dense binary pixels
Abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to image reconstruction from dense binary pixels, aiming to tackle the limitations of classical reconstruction methods. Traditional methods often require precise pixel locations, which can be hindered by the density of the binary pixels. The proposed method leverages a deep learning framework to reconstruct high-quality images from highly overlapping binary pixels. A custom-designed network architecture is developed, which consists of two main components: a binary pixel aggregator and an image refiner. The binary pixel aggregator is responsible for gathering and compressing the dense binary pixel information, while the image refiner utilizes this compressed information to produce a high-resolution image. To address the high-density issue, the network is trained using a novel loss function that focuses on preserving the overall structure and texture of the input image. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach in reconstructing images from dense binary pixels, outperforming state-of-the-art methods in terms of both quantitative and qualitative metrics. Moreover, the proposed method exhibits robustness to variations in the density of the binary pixels, showcasing its potential for real-world applications in computer vision and image processing. The code and datasets used in this research are publicly available to facilitate further exploration and improvement of the proposed approach.

title: Vanishing point attracts gaze in free-viewing and visual search tasks
Abstract: This study investigates the phenomenon where participants involuntarily fixate the vanishing point in scenes, particularly during free-viewing and visual search tasks. The concept of a vanishing point lies at the intersection of visual perception, cognition, and neuroscience, where converging parallel lines meet at a single point on the horizon. Previous research has established that humans have an inherent tendency to perceive lines extending to infinity, which demands active visual processing to resolve the depth discontinuity. Using a combination of experiments and statistical analysis, this study examines the influence of scene composition, attentional factors, and individual differences on gaze allocation in the presence of vanishing points. Results show a robust and widespread attraction of gaze to the vanishing point in both free-viewing and visual search tasks, regardless of the scene's contents or complexity. Furthermore, we observe a significant correlation between the vanishing point's visibility and the proportion of fixations directed towards this location. This research provides insight into the essential components of human visual processing, highlighting the fundamental role of the vanishing point in guiding gaze during everyday visual exploration. The findings have implications for our understanding of the psychology of gaze and the neural mechanisms that underlie visual perception.

title: A Restricted Visual Turing Test for Deep Scene and Event Understanding
Abstract: This paper introduces a novel framework for evaluating the capabilities of deep neural networks in understanding complex visual scenes and events. Building on the traditional Turing Test, which assesses a machine's ability to exhibit intelligent behavior equivalent to, or indistinguishable from, that of a human, we propose a Restricted Visual Turing Test specifically designed for deep scene and event understanding. This test objective is to evaluate the ability of a model to identify the "what" (scene semantics) and "why" (event dynamics) aspects of a presented visual scenario, challenging the model to generalize to unseen situations. To achieve this, we employ a multi-task learning approach, training the model to simultaneously predict scene classifications, object locations, and temporal activity patterns. Our framework integrates inter- and intra-task consistency constraints to ensure that the model's understanding of scene and event is both accurate and coherent. By exploiting common object-centric and semantic representations, we provide a more comprehensive assessment of deep models' capacity to grasp complex visual scenes and events. Experimental results and analysis on benchmark datasets demonstrate the efficacy and reliability of our proposed Restricted Visual Turing Test in evaluating deep models' visual understanding.

title: Maximum Entropy Binary Encoding for Face Template Protection
Abstract: This study aims to enhance the security and privacy of face recognition systems by developing a Maximum Entropy Binary Encoding (MEBE) method for face template protection. With the growing prevalence of biometric authentication, the storage and transmission of face recognition templates have become significant concerns due to their vulnerability to unauthorized access and potential misuse. Existing methods for face template protection have limitations, such as increased storage requirements or compromise between security and computational efficiency. MEBE addresses these limitations by encoding face templates in compact binary representations that preserve the discriminative information of the original templates. The proposed method leverages the maximum entropy principle to optimize the encoding process, resulting in robust and secure binary face templates that are resistant to various attacks. The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of MEBE in defending against template attacks, including template imitation and template theft attacks, while achieving lower storage costs and comparable computational efficiency compared to state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, the investigation of the proposed method's robustness under different attacks and its adaptability to various face recognition systems demonstrates its potential as an efficient and universal approach for ensuring the security of face recognition systems.

title: A Shapley Value Solution to Game Theoretic-based Feature Reduction in False Alarm Detection
Abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to game theoretic-based feature reduction in false alarm detection by leveraging the Shapley value concept from cooperative game theory. The proposed method, referred to as SHAP-RED, seeks to identify the most impactful features in a dataset that contribute to the detection of false alarms. By modeling the feature contribution as a cooperative game, SHAP-RED employs the Shapley value to assign unique weights to each feature, representing their relative importance in the detection process. The weight values are then used to eliminate the least contributing features, leading to reduced dimensionality and decreased computational complexity. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that SHAP-RED significantly improves the performance of existing false alarm detection systems, achieving higher detection accuracy and lower false alarm rates. A critical analysis of the method reveals its potential to mitigate the limitations of traditional feature reduction techniques, such as over-reliance on correlation-based measures or high dimensionality reduction. Furthermore, the interpretability of SHAP-RED is ensured through the insightful Shapley value weights, providing valuable information on the specific features driving the false alarm detection outcomes. The results of this study contribute to a deeper understanding of game theoretic-based feature reduction and can have a significant impact on the design of more efficient and accurate false alarm detection systems.

title: Approximated and User Steerable tSNE for Progressive Visual Analytics
Abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (tSNE) called Approximated and User Steerable tSNE for Progressive Visual Analytics. In the context of visual data analysis, tSNE is a powerful non-linear dimensionality reduction technique for high-dimensional data, but its computationally expensive nature makes it difficult to use in interactive visual analytics environments, where instantaneous feedback is required. The introduced approximation method addresses this limitation by interleaving the computation of tSNE with user interactions, incrementally building the feature representations on demand, based on the user's focus of interest. A key feature of the approach is the user's ability to steer the approximation process by selecting specific data points as anchors for the tSNE computation. This allows the user to control and focus the dimensionality reduction on areas of interest in the data, while adaptively reducing computational effort where it is not necessary. Furthermore, an interactive visualization interface is presented to facilitate the progressive analysis process, displaying a real-time representation of the model's approximation progress, together with informative metrics and controls to assist the user in guiding the process. Eventually, the proposed approach enables the real-time exploration and analysis of large, complex data sets, promoting deeper insights through dynamic and user-driven visual data analysis.

title: A Deep Structured Model with Radius-Margin Bound for 3D Human Activity Recognition
Abstract: This abstract explores the development of a novel deep structured model tailored for 3D human activity recognition. Recognizing human activities from 3D data is a challenging task, as it involves processing complex spatiotemporal patterns across various modalities. Current techniques often rely on hand-crafted features and shallow architectures, limiting their ability to generalize across diverse scenarios. In contrast, our proposed model combines the benefits of deep learning and structured data modeling to learn abstract representations of human activities directly from raw 3D data. To further enhance its performance, we introduce a radius-margin bound, a variant of the classical Rademacher complexity bound. This bound provides a robust theoretical guarantee for the model's generalization performance, allowing it to learn a subset of the data that is most representative of the underlying activity classes. We extensively evaluate our model on several benchmark datasets for 3D human activity recognition, demonstrating its superiority over state-of-the-art approaches in terms of accuracy, robustness, and computational efficiency. By tapping into the rich structural information present in 3D data, our model presents a promising solution for a range of applications, including surveillance, healthcare, and human-computer interaction, where accurate and efficient human activity recognition is critical. With its unique combination of deep learning and structured data modeling, along with the theoretically grounded radius-margin bound, our model offers a compelling alternative for the challenging task of 3D human activity recognition.

title: Creation of a Deep Convolutional Auto-Encoder in Caffe
Abstract: This paper explores the development and implementation of a deep convolutional auto-encoder in the Caffe platform. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and their variants have been wildly successful in image classification, object detection, and image segmentation. Auto-encyoders, which are essentially unsupervised CNNs that learn to map input data onto a lower-dimensional latent space and back to the input space, have found applications in dimensionality reduction, data denoising, and anomaly detection. The proposed deep convolutional auto-encoder in Caffe incorporates multiple convolutional layers, convolutionaltranspose layers, and pooling layers to form a more complex representation of the data in both the encoder and decoder paths. This architecture allows for the efficient encoding and reconstructing of high-dimensional data through a learned lower dimensional latent space and provides the capability to preserve spatial hierarchies. The performance of the proposed model is evaluated using standard auto-encoder metrics such as reconstruction loss, and other image quality assessment metrics. Notably, the model is experimented with various hyperparameters to optimize performance and compared with baseline models to demonstrate its effectiveness in preserving structural details, visual appearance, and capturing the underlying statistical properties of the data while significantly reducing their dimensionality. The contribution of this study is significant as it enhances deep convolutional auto-encoder's performance in preserving both the semantic and numerical details of images effectively when compared against its peers in this area of study.

title: Motion trails from time-lapse video
Abstract: Motion trails from time-lapse video capture the essence of dynamic scenes by highlighting the paths left behind by moving objects. Recent advancements in computer vision and deep learning have led to the development of various algorithms and techniques for detecting and analyzing these motion trails, enabling researchers to study various phenomena such as crowd behavior, traffic flow, and environmental patterns. However, the existing methods often rely on manual annotations, which are time-consuming and prone to errors. Moreover, conventional time-lapse videos might not provide a comprehensive understanding of motion trajectories, as they typically neglect the underlying spatiotemporal relationships. This research aims to bridge the gap by proposing a novel approach for automatically detecting motion trails from time-lapse videos, taking into account both spatial and temporal dimensions. The algorithm, based on a convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture, utilizes a combination of optical flow and feature extraction to accurately identify and represent motion trails in the format of probabilistic Gaussian processes. This approach facilitates the formation of a higher-level understanding of motion patterns, which can be applied to various fields for surveillance, transportation planning, and environmental monitoring purposes. The proposed method is evaluated on a dataset of diverse time-lapse video sequences, demonstrating its effectiveness in recovering the underlying motion trails with high accuracy and robustness.

title: Learning the Semantics of Manipulation Action
Abstract:
This paper explores the problem of understanding the semantics of manipulation actions within a computer vision and robotics framework. Manipulation actions, such as grasping and placing objects, are ubiquitous in daily life and critical to the success of various robotic applications. 

We present a deep learning-based approach to predict the semantics of manipulation actions by learning visual and tactile representations from a large dataset of object interactions. Our approach utilizes a combination of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and graph neural networks (GNNs) to encode the spatial and spatial-temporal features of manipulation actions. 

Additionally, we propose a novel metric learning method to assess the semantic similarity between manipulation actions, enabling robots to discern between alternative actions with identical visual outcomes. 

Through extensive experiments on a challenging benchmark dataset, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in predicting manipulation action semantics with high accuracy. Moreover, our proposed metric learning method enables robots to resolve ambiguities in manipulation actions, such as different grasping styles with the same visual outcome. 

Our work has far-reaching implications for developing intelligent robots that can reason about manipulation actions, generalizing across various environments and objects. By providing a deeper understanding of manipulation action semantics, we aim to bridge the gap between visual and tactile perception, ultimately enabling robots to interact with the physical world in a more intuitive and human-like manner.

title: ASIST: Automatic Semantically Invariant Scene Transformation
Abstract: ASIST aims to bridge the gap between the static nature of existing scene understanding models and the dynamic requirements of real-world applications by enabling scene transformation across various contexts. The primary objective of ASIST is to develop an automatic and semantically invariant approach to scene transformation, where scene-based models can generalize across different environmental conditions, object configurations, and viewpoints. This research introduces a novel paradigm that leverages the power of deep learning and scene graph-based representations to achieve scene transformation. Specifically, ASIST employs a two-stage approach, where a unified scene graph representation is first established, followed by a transformation module that reconfigures the scene graph to accommodate the target scene characteristics. The proposed method exploits the underlying structural relationships between scene elements, including object-object and object-scene interactions, to ensure invariant semantic preservation during transformation. Through extensive experiments on a variety of benchmarks, the results demonstrate the effectiveness of ASIST in delivering semantically invariant scene transformations, with applications in areas such as augmented reality, scene understanding, and robotics. The outcomes of this research have the potential to revolutionize the field of scene understanding, enabling more robust and adaptable scene-based models that can navigate and interact with complex and dynamic real-world scenarios.

title: Computational Imaging for VLBI Image Reconstruction
Abstract: Recent advancements in Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) have enabled the creation of ultra-high-resolution images of celestial objects, revolutionizing our understanding of the universe. However, achieving high angular resolution in VLBI comes at the cost of increased computing resources and complexity, particularly in image reconstruction. This has motivated the exploration of novel computational imaging techniques to enhance the quality and speed of VLBI image reconstruction. Computational imaging has emerged as a promising paradigm, leveraging algorithms and software-defined acquisition to optimize imaging performance. By leveraging computational imaging principles, such as machine learning-based de-noising and phase correction, and sparse sampling in Fourier space, researchers have demonstrated improvements in image quality and reconstruction time. This paper presents a comprehensive review of state-of-the-art computational imaging techniques for VLBI image reconstruction, including the theoretical foundations, algorithmic implementations, and experimental results. We also explore the application of machine learning and other modern signal processing techniques to enhance imaging performance. Our results show that computational imaging can significantly reduce the computational complexity and enhance the quality of reconstructed images, paving the way for future VLBI missions with unprecedented angular resolution and sensitivity. Computational imaging for VLBI thus holds significant promise for advancing our understanding of celestial objects, from fundamental astrophysics to cosmology.

title: Neuron's Eye View: Inferring Features of Complex Stimuli from Neural Responses
Abstract: Neural responses to complex stimuli have long been a source of fascination for neuroscientists, yet extracting meaning from these responses remains a daunting task due to their inherent complexity. By adopting a multifaceted, inclusive approach that considers electroencephalography (EEG) and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data, this research aims to uncover the intricate features of complex stimuli that underlie neural responses. Utilizing machine learning algorithms that integrate both temporal and spatial patterns, we successfully decode neural representations of stimuli from primary visual cortex (V1) to higher-order sensory areas, including the lateral occipital complex (LOC) and the fusiform gyrus (FG). Through an innovative combination of signal processing, dimensionality reduction, and neural decoding techniques, the proposed approach overcomes long-standing challenges in neural encoding research by teasing apart the underlying neural dynamics driving perception and cognition. By capturing the intricate structure of neural activity elicited by increasing complexity of visual stimuli, we gain novel insights into the hierarchical processing of visual information and pave the way for better understanding of neural representations in other modalities, including auditory and somatosensory processing.

title: Model Validation for Vision Systems via Graphics Simulation
Abstract: Effective validation of vision systems is a crucial step in ensuring the accuracy and reliability of robots, drones, and other automated systems dependent on computer vision for navigation and task execution. However, traditional methods of model validation often involve expensive and time-consuming physical testing or tedious manual data annotation, which can limit the scope and frequency of validation. To address this challenge, this research explores the potential of graphics simulation as a validating tool for vision systems. By leveraging the latest advancements in computer graphics and simulation technology, it is possible to create highly realistic virtual environments that mimic real-world scenarios, allowing developers to extensively test and validate their vision systems in a controlled and repeatable manner. The proposed methodology involves the development of a custom graphics simulation framework that integrates physics-based rendering and advanced simulation engines to create photorealistic and dynamic environments. This framework can be used to simulate a wide range of scenarios, from simple object recognition tasks to complex scene understanding and state estimation problems. Through extensive testing and validation of vision systems on this simulated platform, researchers can ensure the accuracy and robustness of their algorithms and identify potential areas for improvement before deploying them in real-world applications.

title: Max-Pooling Dropout for Regularization of Convolutional Neural Networks
Abstract:
This study introduces a novel regularization technique for Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) by combining max-pooling and dropout methods. The conventional design of max-pooling layers relies primarily on retaining specific spatial features, whereas conventional dropout reduces overfitting by randomly eliminating units during training. However, max-pooling comes with potential drawbacks of losing spatial information and limiting the representation power of neural networks. As for dropout, it can potentially worsen the representation when used simultaneously with convolution operations in their original forms. This study presents an alternative to the existing dropout methods by modifying max-pooling to incorporate dropout strategy, increasing the representation power, and reducing the risk of overfitting in CNNs. We propose Max-Pooling Dropout (MPD), a simple yet effective solution that adaptively pools and drops samples during the training process. Through this adapted random sampling strategy at the max-pooling operation, the gradients and spatial spatial information flows within layers become increasingly resistant to overfitting issues that impact both the model's efficiency and its robust representations. 

Our experimental results indicate that MPD outperforms various state-of-the-art regularization techniques in multiple benchmark datasets and evaluation metrics. The achieved balance of retained spatial information, increased model complexity, and enhanced generalization ability highlight the potential of MPD as a viable and versatile regularization method for CNN architectures. The experimental setup, including a comprehensive evaluation, provides a rigorous assessment of MPD's effectiveness in diverse CNN settings and underscores its potential to become a significant regularization technique for enhancing the performance of future generative and discriminative models. Experimental results show that MPD may render lesser regularization losses in comparison to existing techniques, as a result, using this methodology may possibly acquire  better classifications.

title: Sublabel-Accurate Relaxation of Nonconvex Energies
Abstract: Nonconvex Energies have garnered increasing attention in the fields of image and signal processing, computer vision, and materials science due to their ability to capture complex, high-order interactions and phenomena. However, conventional methods for minimizing such energies often face challenges in achieving desirable, accurate ground-truth estimates due to poor local minima. Developing methodologies for sublabel-accurate relaxation of nonconvex energies stands at the forefront of tackling this challenge, which has significant implications for real-world applications, such as image deblurring, texture denoising, and phase retrieval tasks. Recent advances in variational methods, partial differential equations (PDEs), and specific formulations within a convex-concave framework hold promise for pursuing reliable, sublabel-accurate relaxation; an outcome that is expected to significantly boost the accuracy of existing algorithms and allow them to compete with state-of-the-art, deep learning-based techniques. In this manuscript, we will outline an innovative workflow for addressing this critical problem by incorporating new, refined formulations of the variational approach with efficient computational tools and iterative optimization strategies. These novel additions will not only enhance the global convergence properties of the proposed methods but also significantly reduce their computational complexity and outperform prevailing alternatives, particularly in the realm of multi-label and high-dimensional imaging, allowing them to uncover finer, detailed structures of interest.

title: Staple: Complementary Learners for Real-Time Tracking
Abstract: This paper introduces a novel real-time tracking approach, leveraging complementary learners to efficiently and accurately detect and pursue targets in complex and dynamic environments. The proposed framework combines the strengths of multiple neural network architectures, each optimized for specific tasks such as object detection, feature learning, and uncertainty estimation. This allows for robust and adaptative tracking, capable of handling variability in lighting, occlusion, and target appearance. A key component of the framework is the 'Tracker-Ensemble' module, which trains and integrates complementary learners using a weighted voting scheme, where each network's confidence in detection is used to weigh its contribution to the final tracking decision. The approach enables real-time tracking by exploiting the parallelization potential of deep learning models and leveraging recent advances in transfer learning and knowledge distillation. The effectiveness of the proposed framework is demonstrated through extensive experiments on various benchmark datasets, showing significant improvements in tracking accuracy, stability, and computational efficiency compared to existing methods. Additionally, the proposed approach demonstrates adaptability to new unseen scenarios through self-ensembling and adversarial training techniques, showcasing its potential to be used in real-world applications involving complex tracking scenarios, such as intelligent transportation systems, surveillance systems, and robotic perception systems.

title: Toward a Taxonomy and Computational Models of Abnormalities in Images
Abstract: Abnormalities in images arise frequently in various computational tasks, including object detection, image classification, and image segmentation, whose performance can be compromised by the presence of such anomalies. Despite the growing importance of image analysis in real-world applications, there is a lack of systematic understanding and modeling of these abnormalities, which hinders the development of effective strategies for their detection and mitigation. This paper contributes to addressing this gap by presenting a taxonomy of images anomalies, encompassing common types such as image tampering, defects, noise, and artifacts. Our taxonomy is informed by a thorough review of existing literature and takes into account the impact of different types of anomalies on image processing algorithms. Furthermore, this paper proposes a set of computational models designed to capture the essence of various image anomalies, including generative adversarial networks (GANs) for simulating noise and defects, convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for detecting tampering and artifacts, and transfer learning-based models for adapting to new anomaly types. The proposed models are evaluated using a range of benchmark datasets and performance metrics, and their results demonstrate the potential of our approach for improving image analysis under abnormal conditions. By providing a comprehensive framework for understanding and addressing image anomalies, this research aims to promote more robust and reliable image processing systems.

title: What can we learn about CNNs from a large scale controlled object dataset?
Abstract: This research explores the potential of a large-scale controlled object dataset to provide novel insights into the behavior and limitations of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). By leveraging a dataset featuring 100 objects with 100,000 samples each, we conducted extensive experiments to investigate various aspects of CNNs, including object recognition, feature extraction, and generalizability. Our findings indicate that as the object variety increases, the frequency of misclassified images decreases significantly, particularly beyond a certain threshold of 20 distinct objects. Furthermore, we observed that CNNs tend to overfit certain features present in the majority of objects, which reduces their capacity to generalize across novel objects. By examining the correlation between feature activations and object features extracted from the dataset, our analysis suggests that CNNs primarily focus on color, texture, and shape cues, whereas size and material play a relatively minor role in object distinction. However, our results also indicate that these feature-specific capabilities can lead to impaired generalization when encountering unseen objects with similar features. Such findings support the notion that large-scale controlled object datasets can be employed to probe the fundamental characteristics of CNNs and their applicability in practical object recognition scenarios, ultimately contributing to the development of more robust and adaptable object classification models.

title: Predicting and visualizing psychological attributions with a deep neural network
Abstract: This study investigates the application of deep neural networks in predicting and visualizing psychological attributions. Psychological attributions are enduring dispositions that influence an individual's perception and interpretation of various social situations, and their accurate prediction can be instrumental in understanding human behavior. Traditional methods for predicting attributions have been limited by their reliance on linear models and simplistic feature representations, which often fail to capture the complex patterns and relationships present in attribution data. To overcome these limitations, this research employs a deep learning approach that leverages the power of neural networks to model nonlinear relationships and hierarchical feature representations. Our framework combines a deep neural network with a visualization tool to enable both accurate prediction and intuitive interpretation of attribution patterns. We evaluate our approach using a comprehensive dataset of psychological attributions and demonstrate its superiority over traditional methods in terms of prediction accuracy and interpretability. The proposed framework has significant implications for fields such as social psychology, sociology, and marketing, where understanding human behavior and motivation is crucial for decision-making and strategy development. By providing a more accurate and insightful understanding of psychological attributions, this research contributes to the development of more effective interventions and policies aimed at promoting positive social change.

title: Prototypical Priors: From Improving Classification to Zero-Shot Learning
Abstract: Prototypical priors, a class of prior distributions based on the prototypical neural network, have recently garnered significant attention in the machine learning community for their ability to improve the performance of deep classification models. These priors are trained jointly with the downstream task to adapt to the data distribution, resulting in improved robustness and generalizability. Notably, the flexibility of prototypical priors makes them a suitable choice for handling increasing amounts of category imbalances in classification tasks. However, their application is not limited to traditional classification problems, as they have also demonstrated potential in more complex and challenging scenarios such as few-shot learning. In this context, prototypical priors can be pushed to their limits by being combined with other methods for few-shot learning. With further developments, prototypical priors may be able to adapt to zero-shot learning, where the model is tasked with classifying examples from novel categories without seeing any examples during training, potentially representing a novel direction in deep learning applications. This paper will delve into the theoretical foundations and applications of prototypical priors, including their extension to zero-shot learning scenarios, aiming to unlock their full potential in machine learning endeavors.

title: Trending Chic: Analyzing the Influence of Social Media on Fashion Brands
Abstract: The rise of social media has dramatically altered the fashion landscape, enabling brands to directly engage with consumers and shape the direction of the industry. This study investigates the influence of social media on fashion brands, exploring how these platforms have transformed the way brands communicate their aesthetic, interact with customers, and establish their reputation. A mixed-method approach combining quantitative data from social media analytics tools and qualitative data from in-depth interviews with fashion industry experts reveals the complexities of the relationship between fashion brands and their online presence. Findings suggest that social media has become a crucial component of a brand's marketing strategy, allowing them to project a consistent visual identity and build strong relationships with their target audience. However, the study also highlights the potential pitfalls of social media, including the risk of brand damage through hashtag mismanagement and the challenge of maintaining a cohesive tone across multiple platforms. Furthermore, this research identifies key strategies for fashion brands to maximize their social media impact, such as leveraging user-generated content, collaborating with influencers, and utilizing Instagram Reels for storytelling. Ultimately, this study provides a comprehensive understanding of the interplay between social media and fashion, shedding light on the opportunities and obstacles that brands face as they navigate this rapidly evolving landscape.

title: Occlusion-Aware Human Pose Estimation with Mixtures of Sub-Trees
Abstract: This paper introduces a novel method for occlusion-aware human pose estimation, addressing the long-standing challenge of accurately detecting body joints in the presence of partial occlusions. Our proposed approach leverages the concept of mixtures of sub-trees (MST) to model the complex dependencies between body joints and joints that may be occluded. We start by generating a sequence of potential human poses, each represented as a sub-tree of the body joint hierarchy, where nodes represent joints, edges represent parent-child relationships, and weights assign relative likelihoods to each limb segment. These sub-trees are then mixed using a probabilistic framework that accounts for both structural and contextual dependencies, allowing our model to explicitly capture and reason about occlusions. We adopt a two-stage architecture, where the first stage generates a set of possible human poses and the second stage refines these poses to account for the visibility of each joint. Experimental results on the challenging COCO dataset demonstrate state-of-the-art performance, with significant improvements over baseline methods on measures of precision, recall, and AP at multiple IoU thresholds. Our approach exhibits robustness to a wide range of occlusion scenarios and highlights the importance of explicitly modeling structural and contextual dependencies in human pose estimation. The proposed approach provides a flexible and interpretable framework for detecting body joints, particularly in complex scenarios, offering valuable insights for applications in computer vision and robotics.

title: Simulations for Validation of Vision Systems
Abstract: The increasing complexity of modern vehicles has created a substantial need for sophisticated vision systems to ensure the safety and efficiency of road traffic. However, validating these complex systems remains a significant challenge. Computer-based simulations emerge as an efficient solution to verify the performance and reliability of vision systems in virtual environments before actual deployment. This method allows researchers to systematically test and analyze the behavior of these systems across diverse scenarios and operating conditions, reducing the need for physical prototypes and lowering the risks associated with field testing. To capitalise on the potential of simulations in vision systems validation, this study outlines the theoretical framework, experimental design, and computational tools required to create a comprehensive simulation environment. By leveraging the strengths of hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) and model-in-the-loop (MIL) simulation methods, the proposed framework facilitates flexible experimentation, comprehensive analysis, and thorough verification of vision systems, ensuring maximum precision, reliability, and reproducibility in virtual testing environments. The results of this study demonstrate the efficacy of simulation-based testing for validating vision systems and serve as a guideline for the development of innovative and efficient testing methodologies in automotive electronics and other fields of application.

title: Weighted Schatten $p$-Norm Minimization for Image Denoising and Background Subtraction
Abstract: Weighted Schatten $p$-Norm Minimization is a novel approach for image denoising and background subtraction in video sequences. The method relies on formulating the denoising problem as a minimization of the weighted Schatten $p$-norm of the noise covariance matrix, which is introduced to reflect the importance of different noise variances across the frequency domain. This is particularly beneficial in dealing with complex noise patterns and non-Gaussian noise distributions frequently encountered in real-world video sequences. The weighted Schatten $p$-norm minimization approach allows for an efficient estimation of the noise variance at each spatial location, thereby accurately modeling the noise covariance matrix. The proposed technique is shown to be robust to varying noise levels and backgrounds through a combination of simulation and experimental results. A step-wise approach is outlined to solve the optimization problem, involving low-rank approximation of the noise covariance matrix, weighted nuclear norm minimization, and thresholding. In addition, an extended background subtraction framework is introduced by incorporating the weighted Schatten $p$-norm minimization-derived noise covariance matrix, demonstrating enhanced performance in accurately detecting background objects and regions of interest. The results demonstrate promising performance of the proposed weighted Schatten $p$-norm minimization approach for image denoising and background subtraction, making it a compelling alternative to existing state-of-the-art methods in video processing and analysis applications.

title: Fast Low-Rank Matrix Learning with Nonconvex Regularization
Abstract: This paper introduces a novel fast low-rank matrix learning approach incorporating nonconvex regularization, which efficiently retrieves accurate solutions for various applications including computer vision, signal processing, and data analysis. The core idea is to optimize low-rank matrix factorization by leveraging nonconvex regularization techniques that promote robust and sparse representations. Conventional low-rank optimization methods often rely on convex relaxation, which may compromise the accuracy or lead to over-smoothing. In contrast, our proposed method circumvents these drawbacks by using a deep neural network framework to iteratively refine the low-rank factorizations with nonconvex regularization terms, thereby preserving the intricate structure and detail of the original data. Our approach allows for scalable computation and yields state-of-the-art results in terms of both precision and speed for various applications such as image and signal denoising, inpainting, deblurring, and matrix completion. Experimental comparisons with existing state-of-the-art low-rank optimization methodologies demonstrate the efficacy of our method, showcasing its potential to efficiently retrieve high-quality solutions for a broad range of problems.

title: A Literature Survey of various Fingerprint De-noising Techniques to justify the need of a new De-noising model based upon Pixel Component Analysis
Abstract: This abstract presents a comprehensive literature survey of various fingerprint de-noising techniques, highlighting the need for a new de-noising model based on pixel component analysis. Fingerprint de-noising plays a critical role in identifying individuals accurately, as it directly influences the performance of automatic fingerprint recognition systems. Traditional techniques, such as those based on filters, smoothing, and singular value decomposition, have limitations in improving the signal-to-noise ratio of fingerprints. In recent years, deep learning-based approaches have gained significant attention, with convolutional neural networks and autoencoders being widely explored for de-noising fingerprints. However, these methods often require large amounts of clean data for training and may not perform well in cases of severe noise contamination. Moreover, many existing techniques focus on restoring the original fingerprint image, rather than accurately preserving the essential features and minutiae necessary for recognition. Given the variability in fingerprint characteristics, and the numerous challenges associated with de-noising, there is a need for a novel approach that incorporates pixel component analysis to effectively separate noise from essential features. This paper aims to provide a detailed analysis of existing de-noising techniques and to propose a new framework that utilizes pixel component analysis for accurate and efficient fingerprint de-noising, thereby justifying the need for such a model to enhance the overall performance of fingerprint recognition systems.
