title: The Indian Spontaneous Expression Database for Emotion Recognition
Abstract: The Indian Spontaneous Expression Database for Emotion Recognition (ISED4ER) is a comprehensive annotated multimodal dataset designed to capture the nuances of Indian emotions, representing a significant step towards improving the accuracy of emotion recognition systems. ISED4ER incorporates a diverse range of expressions, encompassing various linguistic, geographical, and socio-economic groups, thus addressing the limitation of current datasets which predominantly comprise of emotions from Western cultures. The dataset includes both facial expressions and speech, leveraging audio and video modalities to analyze the complexities of human emotions in a more contextual and intuitive manner. Facial Action Units, Emotion Intensity, and acoustic features are the primary attributes extracted from the multimedia recordings, allowing for a multi-faceted understanding of emotions. Moreover, the dataset incorporates situational and contextual information related to the emotions expressed, providing meaningful cues that a system can utilize to perform real-time emotion recognition and deepen its insight into the human emotional landscape. This extensive annotation of Indian emotions enables the development of culturally relevant models, mitigating the risk of creating artificial assistants that may behave unfavorably in situations where cultural nuances play a critical role, such as in the context of multilingual and multicultural environments. By tapping into this dataset, researchers and industry practitioners can mitigate the cultural bias in emotion recognition systems and bring us closer to achieving accurate and culturally adapted models that attend to the underlying complexities of human emotion, particularly for populations with diverse emotional expressions.

title: Innovation Pursuit: A New Approach to Subspace Clustering
Abstract: This research paper, titled "Innovation Pursuit: A New Approach to Subspace Clustering," proposes an innovative method for identifying clusters within high-dimensional datasets that exist on non-linear subspaces. Conventional subspace clustering algorithms frequently suffer from issues such as the number of clusters being unknown and outliers. By harnessing the strengths of both the traditional clustering methods and the active subspace learning approach, our approach, dubbed the "Innovation Pursuit Algorithm," systematically discovers the embedding subspaces where high-quality clusters reside and efficiently identifies the clusters within the subspaces. To tackle the ill-posed discovery of hidden subspaces, the research introduces the novel concept of continuous optimization. Unlike traditional subspace detection techniques, the proposed innovation pursuit model discovers the best-fitting axes for a high-dimensional subspace by iteratively optimizing the model's objective function. The experiments conducted on multiple datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the new algorithm in unveiling precise subspace clusters and evaluating performance using conventional clustering metrics such as the Normalized Mutual Information (NMI) and the Adjusted Rand Index (ARI), our innovation pursuit approach achieves superior outcomes compared to other state-of-the-art subspace clustering paradigms. This end-to-end optimization and the model's ability to dynamically adjust the clustering boundaries in high-dimensional space enhance its versatility in clustering a diverse set of datasets, ultimately making it a promising solution in realistic real-world applications and clustering tasks.

title: Compressive hyperspectral imaging via adaptive sampling and dictionary learning
Abstract: Compressive hyperspectral imaging has emerged as a promising technique to reduce data acquisition and storage requirements, while maintaining the information richness of hyperspectral data. However, existing methods often rely on either structured sampling patterns or fixed-size dictionaries, which may not be optimal for capturing the underlying spatial and spectral characteristics of the scene. This paper proposes a novel compressive hyperspectral imaging framework that combines adaptive sampling and dictionary learning to effectively reduce the dimensionality of hyperspectral data. The approach involves first acquiring a sparse representation of the data using an adaptive sampling pattern, which is intelligently designed based on the local spatial and spectral variations of the scene. Subsequently, a dictionary learning module is employed to discover the most relevant spatial and spectral features from the adaptively sampled data, thereby generating a low-dimensional representation of the hyperspectral data. The proposed framework is demonstrated to outperform existing methods in terms of both compression ratio and reconstructed image quality, as evaluated on a range of hyperspectral datasets. Through this work, we aim to provide a more efficient and effective approach to compressive hyperspectral imaging, with potential applications in remote sensing, surveillance, and medical imaging. The proposed method may serve as a valuable starting point for future research endeavors focusing on the development of more efficient and accurate compression techniques for hyperspectral imaging.

title: Zero-Shot Event Detection by Multimodal Distributional Semantic Embedding of Videos
Abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to zero-shot event detection using multimodal distributional semantic embedding of videos. The proposed method tackles the limitation of existing event detection models that heavily rely on labeled data and pre-defined ontology, making it challenging to adapt to new, unseen events. Our approach combines visual and audio features extracted from videos to learn a unified representation space, leveraging the distributional semantic model (DSM) to represent the subtle semantic relationships between events. By mapping both the visual-audio embedding and text-based DSM to a shared semantic space, our zero-shot event detection framework enables the identification of novel events without explicit labels. This is achieved through the proposed event embedding learning algorithm, which computes the similarity between video representations and the pre-trained DSM, to yield a meaningful, yet linearized vector representation of events. The effectiveness of our zero-shot event detection method is demonstrated through experiments on various benchmark datasets, showcasing superior performance compared to state-of-the-art baselines in terms of accuracy and adaptability. By allowing the system to learn from the semantic understanding of events, and then applying this understanding to recognize unseen events, our approach has the potential to revolutionize event detection in a wide range of real-world applications, including surveillance, sports analysis, and media monitoring.

title: Actions ~ Transformations
Abstract: Abstract: Actions ~ Transformations delves into the fundamental relationship between actions and their transformative power in various aspects of human life, from social dynamics and personal growth to technological innovation and artistic expression. It presents a comprehensive exploration of the complex interplay between human actions and the profound impact they produce, encompassing both micro-level changes within individuals and macro-level transformations of entire societies. Through an in-depth analysis of numerous case studies, the research investigates the intricate mechanisms by which actions influence and shape reality, revealing insights into the capacity of human agency to drive change and create new possibilities. By examining the reciprocal relationship between actions and transformations, the study provides a nuanced understanding of the dynamic interdependence between human behavior and the outcomes that arise from it. It sheds light on the multifaceted nature of action and transformation, exemplifying how transformative power can be leveraged to foster positive social change, ignite innovation, and catalyze individual growth. Ultimately, the research strives to offer a profound and holistic understanding of the transformative potential of human actions, equipping readers with the knowledge and tools to harness this potential and navigate the ever-evolving landscape of human experience.

title: Active Learning for Delineation of Curvilinear Structures
Abstract: Active learning for delineation of curvilinear structures in images has garnered significant attention in recent years due to its vast applications in fields like medical imaging, remote sensing, and autonomous vehicles. The delineation of curvilinear structures, which typically includes edges of buildings, roads, and objects, presents a challenging task due to their non-linear nature and varying levels of complexity. Traditional supervised learning approaches require a large set of expert-annotated training data, which can be time-consuming and expensive to obtain. To address this limitation, active learning methods have been proposed to intelligently select the most informative samples from the unlabeled pool that are closest to the decision boundary. These selected samples are then annotated by human experts, reducing the overall annotation time and cost. However, the performance of active learning methods largely depends on the choice of the acquisition function, which determines the sampling strategy. Current acquisition functions for active learning are often designed with flat-top distributions or use random sampling strategies, neglecting the spatial coherence of natural images. In this study, we propose an active learning framework that leverages spatial coherence and sampling priorities to select the most informative samples from the unlabeled pool. Our approach uses a Bayesian framework to model the uncertainty of the classifier and incorporates a hierarchical segmentation-based acquisition function to prioritize the selection of spatially coherent samples. Experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, which improves the delineation accuracy by up to 15% compared to state-of-the-art methods.

title: Recognizing Semantic Features in Faces using Deep Learning
Abstract: This study aims to bridge the gap in current facial recognition systems by recognizing and extracting semantic features from human faces, thereby enabling a more in-depth understanding of facial representations and emotions. Traditional facial analysis methods primarily focus on physical characteristics, neglecting the intricate connections between facial expressions, emotions, and other contextual factors. In contrast, the proposed system utilizes cutting-edge deep learning techniques to uncover the underlying semantic features of faces. A novel neural network architecture is designed, which integrates the processes of face representation, emotional analysis, and context interpretation in a unified framework. This network is trained on a vast dataset of diverse facial images, annotated with corresponding emotional and contextual labels. The experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed system, showcasing improved facial expression classification accuracy, more nuanced emotional understanding, and enhanced contextual awareness. Furthermore, the study highlights the potential applications of semantic feature extraction in various fields, including human-computer interaction, affective computing, and facial analysis for clinical diagnosis. Overall, this work contributes significantly to the development of more advanced and human-centric facial analysis systems capable of understanding the complexities of human emotions and social interactions.

title: MMSE Estimation for Poisson Noise Removal in Images
Abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to minimally invasive removal of Poisson noise from images using the Modified Mini-Sum Algorithm (MMSE) Estimation. The presence of noise in images severely affects the accuracy of image segmentation, object detection, and other computer vision tasks, necessitating efficient noise removal techniques. However, existing noise removal methods often fail to provide optimal results, especially in scenarios with high levels of Poisson noise. To address this challenge, this research proposes a framework that combines the strengths of the MMSE Estimation and the Mini-Sum Algorithm to estimate the noise parameters in noisy images. The MMSE Estimation methodology is theoretically conducive to removing Poisson noise, while the Mini-Sum Algorithm facilitates better convergence rates compared to traditional methods. In this approach, the noisy image is partitioned into small blocks, and the MMSE Estimation is used to determine the parameters of the Poisson noise within each block. The parameters are then refined using the Mini-Sum Algorithm to obtain a more accurate noise map, which is finally subtracted from the original image to obtain a noise-reduced result. The proposed approach has been extensively tested on various images with different noise levels, and the experiments demonstrate that it outperforms existing state-of-the-art noise removal methods in terms of both subjective visual quality and objective evaluation metrics. The superior performance of the MMSE estimation for Poisson noise removal makes it a highly attractive solution for a variety of applications in image processing and computer vision.

title: Continuous and Simultaneous Gesture and Posture Recognition for Commanding a Robotic Wheelchair; Towards Spotting the Signal Patterns
Abstract: This paper delves into the development of an advanced system for continuous and simultaneous gesture and posture recognition to command a robotic wheelchair. The proposed system aims to recognize a multitude of hand gestures and postures to empower individuals with motor disabilities to navigate their surroundings efficiently and independently. An exhaustive review of existing gesture recognition and wheelchair control systems is conducted, highlighting their limitations in areas such as robustness, ease of use, and accuracy. To address these concerns, a machine learning-based approach is employed utilizing a combination of computer vision and inertial sensors. Specifically, a convolutional neural network (CNN) is implemented to detect hand gestures through visual recordings, while a deep learning-based approach is used to recognize postures by analyzing inertial data. The proposed system is further enhanced by incorporating real-time signal processing to filter out noise and anomalies. Extensive experiments and simulations are conducted to evaluate the system's accuracy, precision, and reliability in various environments and scenarios. The obtained results demonstrate significant advancements in terms of recognition accuracy and robustness compared to existing systems, paving the way for the widespread implementation of the proposed system in real-world applications, including robotic wheelchairs for individuals with motor disorders. The research contributes to the development of user-friendly, efficient, and reliable control systems that cater to the needs of individuals with motor impairments.

title: Double Sparse Multi-Frame Image Super Resolution
Abstract: This paper presents a novel Double Sparse Multi-Frame Image Super Resolution (DSMFISR) framework that leverages a double sparse representation to significantly improve image super resolution. By tapping into the inherent sparsity within an image, the framework exploits both spatial and frequency domain redundancies to reconstruct high-quality images from low-resolution input frames. The proposed DSMFISR model combines a sparse dictionary learning framework and a multi-frame based residual learning paradigm to capture the temporal dependencies between successive frames. It then utilizes a double sparse reconstruction method, which exploits the combined sparsity of the sparse dictionaries learned from different domains to reconstruct the high-resolution image. Such a representation not only enables efficient representation of high-frequency details but also facilitates robust and stable image formation. Experimental results demonstrate that DSMFISR outperforms state-of-the-art image super-resolution methods in terms of peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) and structural similarity index (SSIM). Furthermore, the proposed framework is computationally efficient and scalable, making it a viable solution for real-time super-resolution applications, such as video surveillance and augmented reality systems.

title: The MegaFace Benchmark: 1 Million Faces for Recognition at Scale
Abstract: The MegaFace benchmark presents a monumental breakthrough in face recognition technology by assembling a massive face dataset consisting of over 1 million images of 84 thousand distinct individuals. This unprecedented scale of data allows researchers and developers to train and evaluate their facial recognition systems in a manner that was previously unattainable. To create the MegaFace benchmark, a massive collection of social media images and photos from various sources were synthesized, followed by an extensive filtering process aimed at removing duplicates, individuals in similar poses or expressions, and images of poor resolution or with partial occlusions. The resulting dataset comprises a vast range of demographic characteristics, age groups, and lighting conditions, thereby enabling more accurate and robust evaluations of facial recognition algorithms. Employing the MegaFace benchmark, our evaluations demonstrate that state-of-the-art systems significantly struggle with identifying faces in a large, noisy, and varied dataset, underscoring the need for further research and improvement to address the limitations of current facial recognition technology. The MegaFace benchmark paves the way for the development of more advanced, real-world applicable face recognition systems capable of handling diverse and complex scenarios.

title: Attribute2Image: Conditional Image Generation from Visual Attributes
Abstract: Attribute2Image: Conditional Image Generation from Visual Attributes deals with the problem of generating images based on their semantic attributes. The task involves learning a conditional distribution over images given a set of predefined attributes such as object presence, identity, color, pose, and more. Recent advances in deep learning have led to a surge in interest in conditional image synthesis, with techniques such as Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), Variational Autoencoders (VAEs), and encoder-decoder architectures being employed for this purpose. These models can learn complex relationships between attribute-label pairs, enabling the generation of diverse and realistic images that meet the specified attributes. One of the key challenges in this field is the limited availability of large-scale attribute-labelled image datasets, which often focus on specific application domains such as facial attributes or interior design. Furthermore, the generated images often suffer from mode collapse, leading to limited diversity in the output. To address this, researchers have proposed various post-processing techniques such as mode regularizers, and diverse training objectives. This study aims to explore the latest approaches in Attribute2Image, including conditional GANs, VAEs, and combinations of these models. It further investigates the role of mode regularizers and diverse training objectives in enhancing the diversity and realism of generated images. Through a comprehensive evaluation on several benchmark datasets, this research seeks to shed light on the strengths and limitations of existing attribute2image models and provide insights into avenues for future research in this exciting area of conditional image synthesis.

title: Rethinking the Inception Architecture for Computer Vision
Abstract: The inception architecture, introduced in 2014, marked a significant milestone in the field of computer vision by revolutionizing the way images were processed using deep neural networks. However, over the years, this architecture has undergone numerous modifications and refinements, raising questions about its fundamental principles and optimal configuration. This paper proposes a comprehensive reevaluation of the inception architecture, illuminating both its strengths and weaknesses, and shedding light on the potential directions for future enhancements. By dissecting the various components of the inception architecture, including the inception layer, concatenation, and pooling operations, our analysis reveals both unnecessary redundancies and missed opportunities for optimization. We demonstrate how the architecture could be improved by eliminating these inefficiencies, introducing novel connections between feature maps, and optimizing the parameter update rules to better leverage the local and global spatial information contained within images. Furthermore, through a series of extensive experiments on a range of benchmark datasets, we empirically validate the efficacy of our proposed modifications, verifying that the optimized architecture achieves state-of-the-art performance while exhibiting improved efficiency and interpretability. Overall, this work underscores the potential for rethinking the inception architecture to unlock new frontiers in image recognition and lays the groundwork for future research in this area.

title: Labeling the Features Not the Samples: Efficient Video Classification with Minimal Supervision
Abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to video classification that deviates from the traditional paradigm of labeling the samples while allowing the features to be automatically learned by the model. By focusing on the structural properties of the videos and leveraging the dynamics of the object interactions, we propose a technique that minimizes the need for extensive manual annotation. Our method, which we term "Labeling the Features Not the Samples" (LFNS), empowers the model to learn meaningful and robust feature representations from the video data without relying heavily on pre-defined labels. The LFNS framework is designed to optimize a global similarity metric between the learned feature representations, effectively distilling the intrinsic patterns within the video content. To achieve this, we introduce a learning objective function that encourages the model to cluster similar videos together based on their feature embeddings, while maintaining a large margin between dissimilar videos. Through a series experiments on benchmark datasets for various video classification tasks, we demonstrate the effectiveness of LFNS in achieving state-of-the-art results while requiring significantly less manual annotation compared to existing methods. These results highlight the potential of LFNS to facilitate efficient video classification with minimal supervision, making it a promising solution for large-scale video analysis applications in the real-world scenarios.

title: Efficient Edge Detection on Low-Cost FPGAs
Abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to enhance the edge detection capability of low-cost Field-Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs), significantly improving their image processing performance. By developing a spatial domain-based edge detection algorithm tailored to the inherent parallelism of FPGAs, we demonstrate the potential for optimal block-cipher architecture optimization, thereby leveraging the optimal potential of System-On-Chip(SoC) in image processing. The novel approach allows for parallelization of image processing at both block-level and pixel-level, thereby advancing the edge detection accuracy to be up to 15% and 25% more accurate when utilizing block cipher architecture embedded in FPGA's. Due to resource constraints, the requirement for using highly complex algorithm to advance this processing rate is practically overcome, thanks largely to using of micro-programmable Architecture of FPGA hardware device. Specifically, the presented method using edge detection algorithms adapts readily to various potential applications including digital zoom functionality, feature extraction for Machine Learning algorithms, and various vision-based intelligent vehicle and surveillance system applications. The experimental results using images from various diverse test scenarios show an average of 20% power consumption reduction when comparing our approach with conventional methods of image processing. Overall, our optimized image processing strategy paves the way for more affordable and portable edge detection devices based on low-cost FPGAs without trading off performance.

title: Loss Functions for Top-k Error: Analysis and Insights
Abstract: Top-k error, a measure of model accuracy where only the k most confident predictions are considered, has become increasingly important in various machine learning tasks, ranging from image classification to natural language processing. However, loss functions that can directly optimize the top-k error are still under development. Most existing methods either optimize the cross-entropy loss or modify the cross-entropy loss to account for the top-k error. Recent studies have proposed alternative loss functions, such as the cross-entropy loss with top-k regulation and the soft-top-k loss, which aim to directly minimize the top-k error. In this work, we analyze the properties and behaviors of various loss functions for top-k error, exploring their theoretical foundations, advantages, and limitations. We provide insights into the mechanisms of the top-k error and its relationship with commonly used loss functions, including the binary cross-entropy loss and the mean squared error. By exploring different formulations and variations of the top-k error, we aim to provide a comprehensive understanding of the currently available loss functions and to shed light on potential areas for improvement. Our analysis will contribute to the development of more effective and accurate methods for training machine learning models with top-k error constraints.

title: Accelerated graph-based nonlinear denoising filters
Abstract: This abstract presents accelerated graph-based nonlinear denoising filters designed to efficiently remove noise from noisy signals and images, while preserving their underlying structures and features. The proposed filters leverage graph signal processing techniques to model and analyze the noisy data, and utilize nonlinear operations to effectively remove noise. By efficiently combining these techniques, the filters are capable of achieving high denoising performance while minimizing computational complexity. To accelerate the filters, the work adopts a greedy optimization approach, which reduces the computational time by a significant factor compared to traditional methods. Experimental results demonstrate that the accelerated filters exhibit comparable denoising performance to the state-of-the-art methods, while achieving execution times that are multiple orders of magnitude faster. The proposed filters are thus suitable for real-time processing applications where high-speed noise removal is crucial. The work provides a comprehensive comparison of various acceleration techniques, including parallelization, model pruning, and hardware acceleration, and highlights their trade-offs and limitations in the context of graph-based nonlinear denoising filters. The findings of this research contribute to the development of efficient and scalable denoising solutions for a wide range of applications, including image and signal processing, computer vision, and Internet of Things (IoT).

title: On Optical Flow Models for Variational Motion Estimation
Abstract: Optical flow models have become increasingly important for variational motion estimation due to their ability to capture complex and dynamic motion in visual scenes. This paper explores the development and comparison of state-of-the-art optical flow models for variational motion estimation, focusing on their performance and applicability in real-world scenarios. We examine a range of architectures, including physically grounded models, neural network-based models, and hybrid approaches that combine the benefits of both. Our objective is to provide a comprehensive analysis of the strengths and weaknesses of these models, considering factors such as accuracy, computational efficiency, and model interpretability. To evaluate their performance, we use a variety of datasets that exhibit different types of motion, including both smooth and jerky movements, as well as occlusions and discontinuities. We also investigate the impact of model regularization and optimization techniques on performance, including the use of different loss functions and learning rates. Our experimental results demonstrate the superiority of certain models over others, depending on the specific application and dataset. Furthermore, we identify key challenges and opportunities for future research in the development of optical flow models for variational motion estimation, highlighting the potential for further advancements in applications such as video surveillance, robotics, and autonomous vehicles.

title: Towards Dropout Training for Convolutional Neural Networks
Abstract: This research delves into the concept of dropout training for convolutional neural networks (CNNs), with a primary focus on utilizing this technique to enhance performance and prevent overfitting. An investigation into the existing architecture of CNNs reveals that they are generally susceptible to overfitting, where the model becomes too specialized in training data, thereby failing to generalize well to new and unseen data. The traditional approach to mitigate this issue involves applying various forms of regularization and weight decay during training. In contrast, this study explores the application of dropout, an interesting technique where a randomly selected subset of neurons is removed during training, thus indirectly enforcing weight decay and facilitating more robust feature representation across different classes. This work aims to evaluate the potential benefits of applying dropout to CNNs, specifically focusing on how this may impact the overall performance and generalizability of the model in various applications, including image classification tasks. A comprehensive analysis is provided, encompassing both theoretical perspectives and empirical evaluations using several benchmark datasets, to demonstrate the efficacy of incorporating dropout into the CNN architecture and highlighting associated insights into the improvement in both performance and robustness of these models.

title: Fast and High Quality Highlight Removal from A Single Image
Abstract: This paper presents a novel approach for fast and high-quality highlight removal from a single grayscale or color image. Highlight removal is a challenging task, particularly when dealing with complex and varied highlight patterns, such as reflections, glares, or overexposure. Existing methods often rely on sophisticated algorithms, iterative processing, or extrinsic data, such as additional images or user interaction, which can increase the processing time and complexity. Our proposed approach leverages a trainable neural network architecture that incorporates a combination of spatial and contextual features to effectively model and eliminate highlights. The network is designed to process images in a single pass, without requiring iterative refinement or additional input, thereby providing a fast and efficient solution. We evaluate the effectiveness of our method on a diverse dataset and compare its performance to state-of-the-art methods, demonstrating significant improvements in terms of highlight removal accuracy, structure preservation, and computational efficiency. The proposed approach has the potential to be applied in various real-world image processing applications, such as digital legacy image editing, surveillance, medical imaging, and mobile device image processing, where fast and accurate highlight removal is essential.

title: Analyzing Classifiers: Fisher Vectors and Deep Neural Networks
Abstract: Fisher Vectors and Deep Neural Networks have emerged as two prominent techniques in the realm of classifier analysis, with each offering distinct advantages in dealing with complex data distributions. This paper delves into an in-depth comparison of these two methodologies, exploring their theoretical underpinnings, computational complexities, and practical applications. By leveraging the power of latent features and statistical modeling, Fisher Vectors manage to capture higher-order information from the data, thereby enhancing the discriminative capacity of classifiers. In contrast, Deep Neural Networks have been widely acclaimed for their ability to learn hierarchical representations of data, culminating in state-of-the-art results in various supervised learning tasks. However, the architectural complexity and training requirements of Deep Networks pose significant computational challenges, underscoring the need for hybrid approaches that can synchronize the merits of both Fisher Vectors and Deep Neural Networks. An empirical evaluation of the two techniques, employing standard benchmark datasets and protocols, reveals that Fisher Vectors demonstrate higher flexibility and interpretability in comparison to Deep Neural Networks. Conversely, Deep Networks achieve superior performance and robustness at the cost of computational feasibility. The disparity between these findings sparks a compelling discussion on the optimal usage of Fisher Vectors and Deep Neural Networks, highlighting the importance of methodological synergy and contextual applicability in achieving optimal classification results.

title: Implicit Sparse Code Hashing
Abstract: Implicit Sparse Code Hashing has emerged as a promising approach for efficient and effective image retrieval tasks. However, traditional implementations often focus on reducing computational complexity while compromising the quality of the retrieved results, due to their reliance on explicit sparse representations. This work proposes a novel Implicit Sparse Code Hashing (ISCH) framework that leverages deep neural networks to learn compact and discriminative binary codes from large-scale image datasets. By adopting a differentiable loss function, ISCH is able to implicitly learn sparse codes without explicitly enforcing sparsity constraints. The proposed approach employs a learnable embedding module to assign salient semantic features to binary codewords, resulting in a significant improvement in retrieval accuracy. Moreover, the lack of sparsity-enforcing term in the loss function allows ISCH to adapt to a wide range of datasets, making it a versatile solution for various image retrieval applications. Comprehensive experiments on several benchmark datasets demonstrate the outstanding performance of ISCH in comparison to existing state-of-the-art hashing methods. Notably, ISCH achieves an average precision of 90.2% on the CIFAR-100 dataset, outperforming the second-best method by a margin of 10.1%. The results showcase the potential of ISCH in harnessing the representational power of deep neural networks for efficient and accurate image retrieval tasks.

title: Dynamic Parallel and Distributed Graph Cuts
Abstract: The increasing complexity of visual data has led to a significant rise in the demand for efficient graph cut algorithms that can handle large-scale data processing. Dynamic parallel and distributed graph cuts have emerged as a promising approach to address the computational challenges associated with these algorithms. This research paper presents an in-depth analysis of dynamic parallel and distributed graph cuts and explores their applications in vision enhancement, camera calibration, and 3D reconstruction. We propose a novel framework for implementing dynamic parallel and distributed graph cuts using a multi-GPU architecture and a peer-to-peer communication model to improve the scalability and performance of these algorithms. The proposed framework utilizes a two-stage graph cut approach, where the first stage involves parallelizing the algorithm at the node level and the second stage involves distributing the cut between nodes to further improve performance. We demonstrate the efficiency and effectiveness of the proposed framework through a series of experiments and benchmarks on real-world datasets. Our results show significant performance improvements over state-of-the-art methods, particularly for larger input sizes, making dynamic parallel and distributed graph cuts a powerful tool for tackling real-world computer vision applications. Furthermore, our framework enables real-time processing of 3D reconstruction and camera calibration tasks, opening up new avenues for applications in robotics, autonomous vehicles, and medical imaging. Overall, this research contributes to the development of high-performance graph cut algorithms that can handle the increasing demands of visual data processing.

title: Sparseness Meets Deepness: 3D Human Pose Estimation from Monocular Video
Abstract: This paper investigates the fusion of 3D human pose estimation and dense video information, exploring the potential for sparsity-aware architectures to enhance deep neural networks in capturing this information. The increasing demand for complex human pose estimation tasks has led to the development of deep 3D architectures, which struggle to integrate diverse information effectively. Presently available methods emphasize on enhancing the deep networks' capability by stacking additional layers to include prior knowledge related to temporal context, while often disregarding temporal coherence. This paper presents a novel approach where 2D and 3D representations are assimilated through an ultra-dense, sparsity-inducing design that prioritizes efficient 3D estimation, supported by progressive fusion of spatial-hierarchical context. To evaluate the effectiveness of this novel approach, it is applied to standard benchmarks featuring complex monocular video human pose estimation tasks, with subsequent comparative analysis. Results show significant improvements in various evaluation metrics and demonstrate the potential of sparsity-aware deep architectures for 3D human pose estimation. Furthermore, an ultra-dense network is introduced and analyzed separately that optimizes efficiency for a chosen training set, leading to interpretability gains and reduced compute cost without a significant impact on model performance. This research aims to provide a critical understanding of the theoretical and practical implications of using ultra-dense, sparsity-aware architectures in 3D human pose estimation for real-world applications.

title: Proposed Approximate Dynamic Programming for Pathfinding under Visible Uncertainty
Abstract: Approximate Dynamic Programming (ADP) has been extensively utilized for pathfinding in various domains, but a significant challenge remains in dealing with visible uncertainty where obstacles' positions are partially known or changing over time. In this study, we propose an ADP framework for pathfinding under visible uncertainty, comprising four primary components: a hierarchical graph, an uncertainty-aware value function, an exploration strategy, and a reactive navigator. The hierarchical graph is constructed using an incremental graph expansion algorithm to accommodate changing obstacle positions and ensure efficient exploration of the environment. The uncertainty-aware value function is formulated as a mixture of discrete and continuous representations to capture the probabilities of different outcomes and their corresponding costs. The exploration strategy utilizes an ε-greedy policy in conjunction with a Gaussian process-based model to improve the trade-off between exploration and exploitation. The reactive navigator is designed to adapt online to new information and changing obstacle positions. Our proposed ADP framework is evaluated against state-of-the-art pathfinding approaches using multiple scenarios of varying complexity. Results demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework in achieving near-optimal solutions under visible uncertainty while efficiently adapting to changing environments. We believe that this research not only provides a novel solution for pathfinding under uncertainty but also opens up avenues for applying ADP in a broader range of applications.

title: Full-density multi-scale account of structure and dynamics of macaque visual cortex
Abstract: This research paper presents a comprehensive investigation into the intricacies of macaque visual cortex structure and dynamics at multiple scales, using full-density multi-scale approaches. By combining state-of-the-art neuroimaging and electrophysiology techniques, we reveal a hierarchical organization of neural circuits that accommodate the diverse assortment of visual stimuli encountered in naturalistic environments. The high-resolution longitudinal mapping of local tissue structure, using diffusion-based MRI and histological assessments, yields critical insights into the intricate spatial architecture of different areas within the visual cortex. Furthermore, the functional dynamics of neural populations are characterized through a systematic analysis of voltage-sensitive dye imaging and high-density single-unit recordings in awake, freely-behaving macaques. Our results demonstrate distinct dynamic regimes - from short-term theta oscillations to long-term beta activity - that modulate neural processing of simple and complex visual features. The combination of these structural and dynamic characterizations enables a precise understanding of how individual neural populations contribute to the emergent properties of visual information processing, thereby facilitating insights into visual perception and cognition. By fostering a deeper comprehension of the fundamental neural processes underpinning visual cortex function, our research paves the way for the development of more effective therapies for visual impairments and neurological disorders, with far-reaching implications for both basic research and translational applications in human visual neuroscience.

title: Behavior Discovery and Alignment of Articulated Object Classes from Unstructured Video
Abstract: Behavior discovery and alignment of articulated object classes from unstructured video presents a promising approach for automatic analysis of visual data, enabling applications in areas such as sports analytics, surveillance systems, and human-computer interaction. Existing methods have largely relied on hand-engineered features and discriminative learning, which are often limited in their ability to generalize across different domains and object configurations. To address these challenges, state-of-the-art techniques employ generative adversarial networks (GANs) and variational autoencoders (VAEs), where the former can model complex structures of articulated objects and the latter can capture high-dimensional distributions of their motion patterns. However, accurate alignment of these object classes remains a difficult task due to vast pose and shape variabilities, and these alignment frameworks rarely generalize across objects. We propose a novel framework for behavior discovery and alignment, which employs a combination of VAEs, unsupervised learning, and hierarchical processing to provide a more comprehensive understanding of articulated object behavior from unstructured video data. By harnessing the strength of VAEs in modeling high-dimensional spaces and leveraging unsupervised learning for capturing generalized knowledge, our approach can effectively learn object classes from a few examples and accurately extract and visualize their intrinsic characteristics, facilitating more intuitive analysis and practical applications.

title: Design of Kernels in Convolutional Neural Networks for Image Classification
Abstract: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have achieved remarkable success in image classification tasks due to their ability to effectively capture spatial hierarchies of images. A crucial component of CNN architectures is the design of kernels, which are small windows that scan input images to extract features. The choice of kernel design significantly impacts the performance of CNNs, as it determines the type and quantity of features that can be learned. This research focuses on investigating and improving the design of kernels in CNNs for image classification tasks. We explore different kernel configurations, including various filter sizes, kernel depths, and activation functions, to understand their impact on feature learning and classification accuracy. Our study reveals that the choice of kernel design is highly problem-dependent and requires a trade-off between the level of abstraction, feature quality, and computational efficiency. We propose a novel kernel design framework that incorporates a hierarchical kernel architecture, which enables the network to learn multi-scale features and adapt to the complexity of images. Through comprehensive experiments on popular image classification datasets, we demonstrate that our proposed kernel design framework significantly improves classification accuracy and robustness, outperforming state-of-the-art architectures. The findings of this research contribute to the understanding of kernel design in CNNs and provide valuable insights for designing more effective and efficient architectures for image classification tasks.

title: Fine-Grained Classification via Mixture of Deep Convolutional Neural Networks
Abstract: Fine-grained classification is a challenging task in computer vision, where objects share similar features but belong to distinct categories. Conventional approaches have shown limitations in tackling the subtleties of these distinctions, leading to poor performance on fine-grained datasets. Recent advancements in deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have positively impacted the field, but the inherent complexities of fine-grained classification continue to hinder the development of more accurate and robust models. In an attempt to overcome these challenges, researchers have explored the concept of incorporating multiple CNNs to pool and integrate their strengths. Mixture of deep CNNs, a novel approach, leverages the ability of individual networks to focus on different aspects of the input imagery and combines their outputs to generate a refined classification. By configuring and aggregating outputs from a variety of CNNs, this method diminishes the influences of any individual network's weaknesses, leading to enhanced recognition capabilities. Employing both visual and feature-level fusion strategies, the proposed methodology effectively captures the complexities of fine-grained objects in multiple domains. Experimental results demonstrate significant improvements over current state-of-the-art models, achieving top-tier performance on fine-grained benchmarks and substantiating the efficacy of the proposed architecture in resolving the intricacies of fine-grained classification tasks. The performance improvements achieved by the mixture of deep CNNs represent an encouraging step towards the development of highly accurate and reliable models for real-world fine-grained classification applications.

title: Incidental Scene Text Understanding: Recent Progresses on ICDAR 2015 Robust Reading Competition Challenge 4
Abstract: This abstract provides a comprehensive overview of the recent advancements in incidental scene text understanding, specifically focusing on the ICDAR 2015 Robust Reading Competition Challenge 4. In challenge 4, the primary goal is to accurately recognize text present in natural scenes, such as street signs, advertisements, and graffiti, often under adverse conditions including various fonts, sizes, orientations, and levels of distortion. Recent progresses in the field are driven by the emergence of deep learning techniques, which have significantly improved the state-of-the-art in scene text recognition. These techniques, including convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and recurrent neural networks (RNNs), have been tailored to address the unique challenges of scene text recognition, such as handling variable text regions, restoring distorted text, and dealing with text background occlusions. This paper presents a detailed review of the recent state-of-the-art methods addressing challenge 4, including architectures, training techniques, and evaluation protocols. Also, key findings and limitations of the current approaches are discussed. Furthermore, we explore various potential future research directions in incidental scene text understanding, with a focus on integrating scene understanding, object detection, and high-level reasoning capabilities to tackle more comprehensive and complex scene understanding tasks.

title: Hierarchical Invariant Feature Learning with Marginalization for Person Re-Identification
Abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to person re-identification, a task of growing importance in intelligent surveillance systems and biometric applications, by introducing a hierarchical invariant feature learning model with marginalization. The goal is to develop an algorithm capable of effectively matching people across non-overlapping camera views, despite variations in illumination, pose, and occlusion. To this end, we construct a hierarchical latent space where each level is dedicated to learning invariance to certain factors, such as viewpoint and resolution, through a sparse autoencoder. Inspired by the idea of marginalization in probabilistic inference, we incorporate an additional level that learns to integrate multiple sources of evidence into a single, more robust representation. By exploiting the structural relationships between different types of data, we demonstrate that our proposed model successfully captures both global and local patterns essential for person re-identification, achieving superior performance over state-of-the-art baseline methods in benchmark datasets such as Market-1501 and DukeMTMC-ReID. Experimental results show that the integration of hierarchical invariant feature learning with marginalization technique significantly boosts recognition accuracy, especially when the probe and gallery sets have large variations. Overall, our work provides a paradigm shift in deriving powerful and robust features through marginalized hierarchical learning, paving the way for real-world applications of person re-identification.

title: Coresets for Kinematic Data: From Theorems to Real-Time Systems
Abstract: This paper tackles the challenge of analyzing large kinematic datasets by introducing coresets - a condensed representation of the dataset that preserves the essential information necessary for downstream tasks such as motion classification, clustering, or regression. We present a rigorous theoretical framework for efficient coreset construction, focusing on maintaining a faithful representation of the original data distribution while significantly reducing its size. Extending the classical coresets framework to handle high-dimensional kinematic motion data requires addressing the underlying geometric, topological, and connectivity properties of the space. Our contribution is a novel combination of machine learning, geometric algebra, and computational geometry techniques to develop efficient coreset algorithms with provable guarantees and scalable implementations. We demonstrate the practical feasibility of our approach on real-world movement datasets from robotic systems, medical research, and animation applications. Our real-time system implementation showcases flexible and accurate coresets that can be effortlessly utilized in any scenario where computational efficiency and meaningful information extraction are necessary, paving the way for both automatic anomaly detection and task-efficient data analysis.

title: Sparse Coral Classification Using Deep Convolutional Neural Networks
Abstract: This abstract presents a novel framework for sparse coral classification utilizing deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs). The decreasing coral cover and habitats due to environmental degradation have rendered coral classification an essential task in marine conservation. Traditional manual methods have proven to be time-consuming and prone to human error, highlighting the need for an efficient and accurate automated classification system. Our proposed framework employs a transfer learning-based approach, utilizing a pre-trained VGG16 CNN architecture fine-tuned on a custom dataset of sparse coral images. The dataset comprises 10,000 sample images collected from various locations worldwide, representing different coral species and environmental conditions. To enhance the model's adaptability, data augmentation techniques were applied, including random rotations, color adjustments, and Gaussian noise addition. An interesting finding of this research is the effectiveness of incorporating spatial pyramid pooling (SPP) layer in the VGG16 architecture, which resulted in a significant improvement in classification accuracy. The proposed framework achieved an impressive accuracy of 95.97%, surpassing existing state-of-the-art methods. This innovative approach has the potential to streamline coral classification processes, facilitating marine conservation efforts and enabling timely detection of coral reef degradation. The efficient and accurate classification of sparse corals paves the way for applications in habitat monitoring, species identification, and research-based studies, ultimately contributing to the preservation of marine ecosystems.

title: The Multiverse Loss for Robust Transfer Learning
Abstract: This paper introduces the Multiverse Loss, a novel framework for robust transfer learning that adapts knowledge from diverse universes or environments to improve the performance of a target model. The Multiverse Loss enables a learner to evolve with multiple instance-space flows simultaneously by mining both the source and target domains, resulting in improved generalizability across diverse unseen data. Inspired by the concept of multiverse theories, the Multiverse Loss constructs multiple instance-space flows that capture a broader range of possible environments encountered by the target model, leveraging diversity to boost its robustness. By adapting this framework to the learner, the Multiverse Loss facilitates transfer learning over environments with changes in instances or environment dynamics, including noise, outliers, or covariate shifts, effectively bridging the gap between source and target distributions. Empirical results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed Multiverse Loss in adaptively learning from knowledge across multiple universes, showcasing its superiority over traditional single-domain learning in complex, multi-faceted decision-making tasks, where transferability is especially valuable, such as reinforcement learning, few-shot learning, or semi-supervised learning scenarios.

title: On-line Recognition of Handwritten Mathematical Symbols
Abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive study on the development and evaluation of an on-line handwritten mathematical symbol recognition system. The proposed system is capable of accurately identifying a wide range of mathematical symbols, including alphanumeric characters, arithmetic operators, and mathematical functions. To achieve this, we employed a machine learning-based approach, specifically employing a deep neural network architecture to classify the symbols. The system utilizes a feature extraction process to identify relevant characteristics of the handwritten symbols, including the shape, size, and orientation of the symbols, as well as their position on the page. We also considered the significance of writer-dependent variations in symbol writing styles, accounting for individual differences in symbol handwriting patterns. The system's performance was evaluated using a dataset of handwritten symbols gathered from a large user base, consisting of both text-based mathematical expressions and mathematics problems requiring symbol recognition. Results demonstrate the system's high recognition accuracy, with overall recognition rates exceeding 95% for commonly used symbols. Furthermore, we conducted a detailed study of the symbols most frequently misrecognized by the system, highlighting a set of highly discriminative features that could improve overall performance. The present study contributes significantly to the field of on-line handwritten mathematical symbol recognition, demonstrating the feasibility of developing automated systems for math-based applications, including online mathematics education, mathematical problem-solving tools, and symbolic computing environments.

title: Sparseness helps: Sparsity Augmented Collaborative Representation for Classification
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to classification problems by leveraging the concept of sparsity, termed as Sparsity Augmented Collaborative Representation (SACR) for Classification. The traditional Collaborative Representation-based Classification (CRC) method relies heavily on the choice of representation coefficients, which can be unstable and prone to overfitting due to the large number of features in high-dimensional datasets. To address this challenge, SACR incorporates sparsity regularization into the representation learning framework. This sparse penalty term encourages the model to select a subset of most relevant features for classification, thus reducing overfitting and improving generalization performance. Theoretical analysis and experiments demonstrate that SACR achieves better robustness against noise and outliers compared to the original CRC. Furthermore, empirical results on benchmark datasets, including handwritten digits, facial expression recognition, and hyperspectral image classification, show that SACR outperforms state-of-the-art classification methods in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency. The proposed method's capability to adapt to various scenarios and its scalability make it a promising solution for real-world classification problems, especially those involving high-dimensional and large-scale datasets. Overall, the SACR approach provides a novel and effective framework for feature selection and classification, offering improved performance and robustness compared to existing methods.

title: MidRank: Learning to rank based on subsequences
Abstract: This work proposes MidRank, a novel approach to learning-to-rank based on subsequences. By capturing the essence of subsequences, MidRank learns to effectively rank items in a more nuanced and informative manner, overcoming the limitations of traditional sequence-based approaches. The key innovation of MidRank lies in its use of self-supervised learning to identify subsequences that exhibit strong correlations with the overall ranking of items, thereby reducing the reliance on hand-engineered features or large-scale annotation efforts. Through a series of rigorous experiments, we demonstrate that MidRank outperforms state-of-the-art techniques in various ranking tasks, achieving significant improvements in terms of ranking accuracy, robustness, and interpretability. Our evaluation covers a range of scenarios, including text-based ranking, graph-based ranking, and recommender systems. Theoretical analysis reveals that MidRank's performance is closely tied to its ability to uncover informative subsequences that capture the underlying ranking dynamics. Furthermore, a comprehensive ablation study provides insights into the design choices and hyperparameters of MidRank, allowing for easier adaptation and fine-tuning of the model for specific tasks and domains. By providing a powerful framework for learning to rank from subsequences, MidRank has far-reaching implications for various applications, including information retrieval, recommender systems, and data-intensive decision-making.

title: Sliding-Window Optimization on an Ambiguity-Clearness Graph for Multi-object Tracking
Abstract: This abstract presents a novel approach to multi-object tracking by introducing a sliding-window optimization on an ambiguity-clearness graph. The proposed method leverages the concept of ambiguity-clearness graph, which encodes the relationships between different object hypotheses and their corresponding confidence levels. The sliding-window optimization framework is designed to iterate over the graph, incrementally refining object trajectories and enhancing the accuracy of association. A key component of the approach is the introduction of a context-aware modality, which considers the spatial and temporal correlations between objects in the scene. This enables the model to effectively filter out ambiguous hypotheses and prioritize clear object associations. The method demonstrates significant improvement over state-of-the-art approaches in terms of accuracy, robustness, and computational efficiency. Experiments conducted on a range of challenging multi-object tracking benchmarks, including those involving rapid scene changes, occlusions, and high-density crowds, demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach. By incorporating a principled mechanism for learning object representations from video data, the method offers a scalable and efficient solution for real-world multi-object tracking tasks, making it an attractive choice for applications in surveillance, robotics, and autonomous driving.

title: Applying deep learning to classify pornographic images and videos
Abstract: Recent advances in deep learning have led to the development of sophisticated algorithms capable of efficiently and accurately identifying visual content. This study explores the application of deep learning techniques to classify pornographic images and videos. Building upon previously proposed detection systems, our research aims to overcome existing limitations by incorporating novel architectures and evaluation protocols. We leverage the efficacy of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and recurrent neural networks (RNNs) to learn complex patterns and temporal dependencies within multimedia content. A comprehensive dataset comprising a diverse assortment of images and videos, carefully curated and annotated to ensure representation of both explicit and non-explicit materials, is employed for training and validation purposes. This dataset serves as a foundation for the development and evaluation of two separate models: a CNN-based classifier optimized for image content analysis and an RNN-based approach tailored for video analysis. Furthermore, the performance of these models is compared and contrasted, highlighting the strengths and limitations of each method. The findings of this study offer valuable insights into the capabilities and challenges associated with the application of deep learning to classifying pornographic content, shedding light on the complexities of this sensitive topic. By distilling these insights, we aim to contribute to the ongoing development of effective and responsible detection systems, ensuring their future deployment in a manner that prioritizes user safety, respect individual privacy, and adheres to relevant regulatory frameworks.

title: Real-Time Depth Refinement for Specular Objects
Abstract: Real-Time Depth Refinement for Specular Objects investigates an efficient and accurate method for refining depth maps of complex specular objects in real-time applications. The current stereo matching techniques struggle with high-frequency details and inconsistencies in challenging environments, resulting in fragmented and inaccurate depth maps. Specular surfaces cause primary difficulties due to their high albedo, making it difficult for depth estimation algorithms to distinguish the reflection from the true surface geometry. This paper proposes a hybrid approach combining a cost aggregation-based stereo matching algorithm with a physically-inspired specular surface priors, referred to as PhySpecStereo. PhySpecStereo enhances the robustness and accuracy of the depth refinement process by introducing a priors-based term to incorporate the spatial and angular consistency of the reflected light rays. Experiments conducted on high-resolution images show significant improvements in depth map quality, measured in terms of accuracy, stability, and time complexity. PhySpecStereo technique can achieve a mean accuracy of 1.08% while maintaining an efficient processing speed of 17ms, outperforming existing algorithms in handling specular surfaces with high-frequency details. By incorporating insights from optical physics, this method not only provides a substantial leap in depth estimation quality but, with minimal increase in computational latency, further realises real-time deployment of PhySpecStereo in augmented reality and autonomous systems.

title: Loss Functions for Neural Networks for Image Processing
Abstract: This paper delves into the fundamental role of loss functions in optimizing neural networks for image processing tasks, a crucial aspect of artificial intelligence. The widespread adoption of neural networks has led to significant advancements in image processing, including segmentation, restoration, and classification. However, the choice of loss function significantly impacts the performance of these models, as it defines the objective function to be minimized during training. A comprehensive review of various loss functions commonly employed in image processing tasks, including mean squared error (MSE), mean absolute error (MAE), cross-entropy loss, and edge detection metrics, such as the structural similarity index (SSIM) and peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) is presented. Furthermore, a detailed analysis of the properties of these loss functions and their suitability for specific image processing tasks is provided. Recent developments in loss function design, including the incorporation of explicit regularizers and the use of adversarial training methods, are also explored. Despite the abundance of research on loss function design, there is still a need for more effective loss functions that balance the trade-off between preservation of detailed features and robustness to outliers and noise. The key takeaway of this paper is that a loss function should be carefully chosen and adapted to the specific task at hand, taking into account the trade-off between competing factors, including data sets, models, and downstream applications.

title: Structured learning of metric ensembles with application to person re-identification
Abstract: The task of person re-identification remains a challenging problem in computer vision due to the high inter-class variations and limited instance information. One potential solution is to utilize metric ensembles, which combine multiple feature extractors with different properties to capture the variability of human subjects. However, traditional ensemble-based methods suffer from the limitation of assigning fixed importance scores to individual components, often leading to sub-optimal performance. To overcome this issue, we propose a novel metric ensemble learning framework that leverages structured learning techniques, enabling the efficient exploration of ensemble structures through a careful initialization of the ensemble weights and a learned importance score for each individual component. Our framework consists of two primary components: an initialization step that leverages a series of transfer learning-based pre-weighting schemes and a learned ensemble selection objective that captures the essence of both the inter-component variability and the instance-level variability of person re-identification. We showcase our method on several benchmark datasets, including CUHK-SYSU, Market-1501, and DukeMTMC, demonstrating its ability to achieve state-of-the-art performance - boosting the ranking accuracy by up to 5.5% in comparison to prior state-of-the-art techniques. By systematically exploring the efficient ensemble construction method, our structured learning approach significantly closes the inter-class variability gap in person re-identification, setting a new direction for future research.

title: TennisVid2Text: Fine-grained Descriptions for Domain Specific Videos
Abstract: TennisVid2Text aims to advance the state-of-the-art in video-to-text generation, particularly for domain-specific videos such as tennis matches. The proposed approach focuses on fine-grained descriptions that capture the nuances and complexities of the game. Beyond generating generic event descriptions, TennisVid2Text endeavors to create detailed accounts of the actions unfolding on the court. To achieve this, the model is trained on a large dataset of annotated tennis videos, incorporating temporal relationships between action events, player movements, and contextual information. The research investigates how to leverage both visual and audio cues from the videos to inform the generated text. Additionally, TennisVid2Text addresses the challenge of temporally aligning the generated text with the video footage. A comprehensive evaluation is conducted to assess the model's performance in capturing the richness and complexity of tennis matches, including its ability to recognize various shot types, player interactions, and strategic maneuvers. By exploring the efficacy of TennisVid2Text in generating domain-specific descriptions, the research seeks to demonstrate the model's potential for application in sport analytics, fan engagement, and video summarization, ultimately contributing to the advancement of video-to-text generation in various domains.

title: Iterative Instance Segmentation
Abstract: This paper introduces a novel iterative instance segmentation approach that significantly improves upon state-of-the-art models by addressing their limitations in terms of computational efficiency, segmentation accuracy, and adaptability to diverse real-world scenarios. Our proposed method, dubbed "Iterative-Cut," employs a two-stage framework, where the first stage initiates instance segmentation by greedily partitioning the input image into a set of initial segments. The second stage then iteratively refines these initial segments through a series of adaptive and learned cuts, which eliminate high-density noise and merge adjacent segments that are likely to belong to the same object. Our model is theoretically grounded in the concept of graph cuts and deep learning-based semantic reasoning, making it capable of exploiting complex contextual information and spatial dependencies within the input image. Through extensive experiments on several challenging benchmark datasets, including PASCAL VOC, COCO, and Cityscapes, we demonstrate that our Iterative-Cut approach consistently outperforms existing instance segmentation models in terms of both mAP and segmentation accuracy, while achieving a significant reduction in computational cost. Moreover, our experimental results also show that Iterative-Cut generalizes well across different object scales, shapes, and textures, making it a compelling solution for real-world instance segmentation tasks that require robustness and efficiency in the face of high variability in image content.

title: Distributed Machine Learning via Sufficient Factor Broadcasting
Abstract: The proliferation of distributed computing has necessitated the development of efficient machine learning (ML) frameworks that can scale across multiple machines while maintaining model accuracy. Distributed Machine Learning via Sufficient Factor Broadcasting (SFB) offers a promising approach by exploiting low-dimensional factorizations to efficiently learn complex models through iterative updates. SFB relies on the assumption that the ML objective can be rewritten in a factorized form, enabling additive updates that preserve model properties. The core idea of SFB lies in broadcasting partial updates across machines, leveraging a sufficient factorization of the data or objective to facilitate synchronization without excessive communication overhead. By focusing on additive updates, SFB can mitigate the vanishing or exploding gradient problems often associated with large-scale optimization. Moreover, the factorized representation of the data can be factored to minimize data transfer, further reducing communication bottlenecks. Throughout this work, we delve into the theoretical foundations of SFB, exploring its convergence properties and its relative efficiency compared to centralized learning strategies. We evaluate the performance of SFB on several landmark ML datasets, gauging its scalability and parallelization capabilities across diverse problem domains, including image classification, natural language processing, and recommender systems. Our results confirm that SFB presents a viable distributed learning paradigm, providing a fertile ground for future optimizations and applications in the realm of big data analytics and machine learning. By pushing the boundaries of communication-efficient ML algorithms, SFB paves the way for efficient large-scale model learning on distributed computing platforms.

title: An analysis of the factors affecting keypoint stability in scale-space
Abstract: This abstract presents a comprehensive investigation into the factors influencing keypoint stability in scale-space, a fundamental concept in image analysis and computer vision. Scale-space theory provides a framework for interpreting local image structure at multiple scales, allowing for the detection and description of features such as edges, corners, and blobs. However, keypoint stability remains a challenging problem, particularly in the presence of image noise, occlusions, and varying lighting conditions. To address this issue, this study undertakes a thorough analysis of the key factors affecting keypoint stability, including image scale, filtering techniques, feature descriptor choice, and keypoint location variability. By employing a combination of theoretical models, computational simulations, and empirical experiments, we identify the optimal configurations of these factors to maximize keypoint stability and robustness. Our results demonstrate the significance of scale-space representation, the impact of feature descriptor choice, and the role of filtering techniques in achieving stable keypoint detection in real-world images. The findings of this study provide valuable insights for the development of more reliable and robust keypoint detection algorithms, with potential applications in object recognition, image matching, and 3D reconstruction. By improving keypoint stability, our research aims to lay the groundwork for more accurate and efficient computer vision systems.

title: An Introduction to Convolutional Neural Networks
Abstract: Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have revolutionized the field of computer vision by significantly enhancing image classification, object detection, and feature extraction tasks. These neural networks are inspired by the structure and function of the human visual cortex, consisting of alternate layers of convolutional and pooling operations that enable feature extraction and spatial hierarchical abstraction. The abstract convolutional and pooling layers extract complex features from images, allowing CNNs to achieve state-of-the-art performance on various tasks. The key aspect of CNNs is its unique architecture, which incorporates learnable convolutional filters that scan the input image in both the horizontal and vertical directions, creating feature maps. The pooling layer reduces the spatial dimensions of the feature maps, enabling the network to efficiently process large images. By stacking these layers, more abstract and discriminative features are learned from the input data, leading to improved performance in a wide range of applications, including image classification, segmentation, object detection, and more. The mathematical simplicity, computational efficiency, and robustness of CNNs have made them a reliable choice for building machine learning models in computer vision. As research in CNNs continues to advance, it is expected to have a significant impact on various fields, leading to the development of more accurate, robust, and efficient deep learning models for image processing and analysis.

title: Towards Automatic Image Editing: Learning to See another You
Abstract: The advancement in digital technology has led to a significant increase in image editing applications, allowing users to enhance and modify images with ease. However, manual image editing can be time-consuming and often requires extensive expertise, limiting its accessibility to the general public. To address this issue, this paper explores the concept of automatic image editing, focusing on learning to recognize and correct imperfections in individuals within an image. By leveraging deep learning techniques, our research proposes an innovative approach that enables machines to identify and rectify common flaws, such as facial blemishes, uneven skin tone, and inconsistent lighting. The proposed system integrates a dual-stage framework combining Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to classify and generate realistic, photorealistic images. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed system exhibits impressive results in detecting and correcting various facial imperfections, making it a potent tool for applications such as portrait enhancement, cosmetic analysis, and even forensic image processing. Furthermore, this study sheds light on the potential of artificial intelligence in augmenting human capabilities, promoting effortless and expedited image editing that revolutionizes the way we perceive and interact with digital images. By making image editing more accessible, our work aims to democratize creative expression and unlock new possibilities in various fields, from art to industry.
