title: A Computational Model for Amodal Completion
Abstract: Amodal completion is a cognitive process that enables humans to perceive and understand visual scenes by filling in missing information, even when it is occluded from view. This process is crucial for efficient and effortless perception of the visual world. Existing models of amodal completion are mainly biological, and there is a scarcity of computational counterparts that can accurately simulate this phenomenon. In this study, we aimed to develop a computational model that replicates the human perception of amodal completion. By integrating insights from psychology, neuroscience, and artificial intelligence, we created an algorithmic framework that is capable of reconstructing occluded shapes and silhouettes in the image. Our model leverages deep learning techniques, such as convolutional neural networks (CNNs), to capture the essence of amodal completion and create realistic predictions of occluded objects. We have evaluated our model on a variety of image datasets, including those with complex scenes and occluding objects. The results show promising alignment with human performance in identifying completed shapes and silhouettes. The proposed model not only constitutes a novel advancement in the field of machine vision but also sheds light on the underlying computational mechanisms of human amodal completion. By facilitating the understanding of this cognitive process, our model has the potential to significantly improve the performance of computer vision systems in various real-world applications.

title: The Scale-free Network of Passwords : Visualization and Estimation of Empirical Passwords
Abstract: This research paper provides a comprehensive analysis of the scale-free network formed by passwords, where a password is represented as a node and its connections to other passwords within a database are treated as edges. By employing advanced visualization techniques, we demonstrate the degree distribution and clustering coefficient of the network, revealing the inherent characteristics of the password space. We observe that the network is dominated by a few highly connected nodes while the majority of nodes exhibit fewer connections, resembling a scale-free network. The analysis extends to estimating the empirical password space using various models, such as the Barabasi-Albert model and the Watts-Strogatz model. Key findings reveal that the password network exhibits a higher average path length and clustering coefficient compared to random networks, underscoring the challenge of uniformly distributing password complexity. Furthermore, our study highlights the importance of understanding password entropy and the significant difference between typical and average-case password spaces, indicating that password cracking can be a multi-scale problem. The research sheds light on the dynamics of password networks and sheds significant insights into the structure and behavior of password complexity, paving the way for more robust password authentication systems.

title: Unsupervised decoding of long-term, naturalistic human neural recordings with automated video and audio annotations
Abstract: This study presents a novel, unsupervised approach for decoding long-term, naturalistic human neural recordings with concurrent automated video and audio annotations. By leveraging recent advances in machine learning and neural data analysis, we aimed to identify predictive markers of neural activity in response to rich, multifaceted environmental stimuli. Our method utilizes a combination of denoising autoencoders, random forests, and k-means clustering to identify distinct population-level neural patterns in response to key events, such as speech, visual stimuli, and motor actions. These patterns are then combined with automated video and audio annotations, allowing for a more comprehensive understanding of the neural correlates of human behavior. We apply this framework to two large datasets of human neural recordings, one from an epilepsy monitoring unit and the other from a naturalistic setting, with concurrent video and audio recordings. Our results demonstrate the ability of this unsupervised approach to uncover repeatable, neural patterns predictive of specific audiovisual events, thereby providing a foundation for developing clinically relevant, neural decoding tools. Furthermore, this work highlights the potential for leveraging large-scale neural datasets to map human cognition and behavior with unprecedented detail, ultimately contributing to a deeper understanding of the neural basis of human experience and behavior.

title: Recurrent Instance Segmentation
Abstract: Recurrent instance segmentation has emerged as a promising approach to tackle the challenges of detecting and tracking individual objects within videos or image sequences. This method extends the standard instance segmentation framework by incorporating temporal information and learning spatiotemporal features. A recurrent instance segmentation framework typically consists of two main components: a segmentation module that performs pixel-level classification and boundary detection, and a tracking module that updates object correspondences across frames. Nevertheless, the high intra-class variability, background interference, and limited frame rates can significantly impede the performance of these frameworks. To mitigate these issues, advanced methods often rely on multimodal inputs, convolutional neural networks (CNNs) with gating mechanisms, and adversarial training to enhance data representation and robustness. The evaluation of recurrent instance segmentation systems often employs metrics such as intersection over union, average precision, and the ratio of true positives to total positives, among others. Experimental results have demonstrated the effectiveness of recurrent instance segmentation in various applications, such as human-object interaction, autonomous driving, and medical image analysis. However, further research is necessary to address open challenges, including object occlusion, varying object scales, and limited training data, to ensure reliable and efficient operation in diverse scenarios.

title: Exploring Person Context and Local Scene Context for Object Detection
Abstract: Object detection has long been a cornerstone of computer vision, with extensive research efforts focusing on developing robust and efficient methods for identifying and localizing objects within images. Recent advancements in convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have significantly improved object detection performance, but traditionally, such methods have relied heavily on global representations of images, often neglecting the nuanced contextual information present in local scenes. This paper delves into a crucial aspect of object detection, exploring the interplay between person context and local scene context to better understand how human presence and surrounding visual cues can synergistically improve object detection capabilities. Through a novel multi-task learning framework, we develop an integrated approach that leverages contextual information from both person and scene perspectives, incorporating spatial relationships and object features to refine object detection outcomes. Experimental results on benchmark datasets, including Cityscapes and PASCAL VOC, demonstrate the efficacy of this approach in enhancing object detection accuracy, particularly in situations involving person-centric scenes and complex local contexts. Our findings contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of contextual influences on object detection, highlighting the importance of considering human-centric and scene-specific factors in the pursuit of robust visual perception. The proposed framework showcases a promising direction for object detection research, suggesting that contextual awareness can serve as a vital pillar in the development of more accurate and inclusive object detection systems.

title: Tracking Motion and Proxemics using Thermal-sensor Array
Abstract: This research endeavors to advance the realm of human-computer interaction and social behavior analysis by developing and integrating a thermal-sensor array into a motion tracking and proxemics monitoring system. Driven by the notion that traditional tracking methods often fail to capture subtle changes in user behavior, particularly in dynamic environments, the proposed approach leverages the thermal signatures of individuals to infer their spatial interactions and social cues. By measuring the unique thermal patterns emitted by the human body, the system can discern subtle variations in proximity, orientation, and movement patterns, thereby enabling rich, multi-faceted insights into human behavior. In contrast to existing camera-based or Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU)-based systems, which often struggle with ambiguous or unstructured scenes, thermal signatures provide a robust and reliable means of capturing socio-spatial data in various environments. To evaluate the efficacy of the proposed system, we conduct a series of experiments, showcasing its capabilities in accurately tracking the movements and proxemics of participants in both controlled and unstructured settings. By integrating thermal sensor arrays into a human-computer interaction framework, our research aims to unveil new avenues for intuitive, spatially-aware interfaces, as well as powerful tools for monitoring and understanding human behavior.

title: Unsupervised Deep Feature Extraction for Remote Sensing Image Classification
Abstract: This paper proposes an unsupervised deep feature extraction approach for remote sensing image classification, leveraging the strengths of self-supervised learning and convolutional neural networks (CNNs). Traditional deep learning methods rely heavily on large-scale labeled datasets, which are often scarce and expensive to acquire in remote sensing applications. In contrast, our proposed method, dubbed "Auto-SfM," employs a self-supervised paradigm to learn robust and transferable features from unlabeled remote sensing images. The Auto-SfM framework integrates a sequence-to-sequence architecture with a novel spatial feature mapping mechanism, enabling the model to learn hierarchical representations of complex spatial patterns and textures in remote sensing images. Through a series of experiments on multiple benchmark remote sensing datasets, we demonstrate that Auto-SfM can efficiently extract discriminative features without labeled data, achieving state-of-the-art or competitive performance in various remote sensing image classification tasks. Additionally, our results show that the learned features exhibit strong transferability across different sensors, seasons, and locations, suggesting their applicability in real-world remote sensing applications. Overall, our work contributes to the development of effective, efficient, and data-efficient methods for remote sensing image classification, with far-reaching implications for a wide range of applications, including crop classification, land cover monitoring, and environmental change detection.

title: Higher Order Conditional Random Fields in Deep Neural Networks
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel integration of higher-order conditional random fields (CRFs) into deep neural networks for structured prediction tasks, aiming to leverage the strengths of both modeling paradigms. The higher-order CRF provides an effective way to model complex interactions between latent variables, while the deep neural network architecture enables efficient learning of low-level features. Here, we equip a deep neural network with a higher-order CRF module, enabling the network to capture nuanced contextual relationships between decision variables. A key challenge lies in efficiently computing the complex CRF partition functions, which scale exponentially with the number of latent variables and iterations. To address this issue, we introduce a probabilistic relaxation of the higher-order CRF that can be marginalized in a hierarchical manner, allowing for a significant reduction in computational complexity. We evaluate our proposed model on several structured prediction tasks, including image segmentation and speech recognition, demonstrating state-of-the-art performance and efficiency. Our results highlight the benefits of integrating higher-order CRFs with deep neural networks, particularly in complex scenarios where accurate modeling of conditional dependencies is crucial. The flexibility and scalability of the proposed architecture make it a promising approach for a wide range of applications in computer vision, natural language processing, and other areas of machine learning.

title: An open access repository of images on plant health to enable the development of mobile disease diagnostics
Abstract: An open access repository of images on plant health to enable the development of mobile disease diagnostics can significantly enhance the efficiency and effectiveness of disease management strategies in the agricultural sector. Existing plant health diagnostic frameworks often rely on in-person consultations, which can be time-consuming and resource-intensive. An open access repository of images would empower farmers, extension agents, and researchers to rapidly identify plant health issues using mobile devices, thereby facilitating timely and targeted interventions. This study proposes the development of a comprehensive image repository featuring high-quality images of various plant species and their associated diseases, drawing on the expertise of experienced horticultural specialists and entomologists. Integration with artificial intelligence algorithms will be critical to enable mobile applications to quickly match images to potential diseases, reducing misdiagnosis and enhancing the accuracy of diagnostic outcomes. Furthermore, the developed repository will provide users with access to curated image collections, disease management recommendations, and targeted extension resources. Research partners from diverse backgrounds, including industry, academia, and community organizations, will collaborate to refine the repository and application, ensuring broad adoption and transformative impacts on agricultural productivity and sustainability. This novel approach will provide critical support to smallholder farmers and commercial growers, ultimately contributing to improved crop yields, reduced economic losses, and a more resilient food system.

title: Pedestrian Detection Inspired by Appearance Constancy and Shape Symmetry
Abstract: Pedestrian detection remains a challenging task in computer vision, particularly in scenarios involving varying illumination, scales, and occlusions. This research explores the utilization of appearance constancy and shape symmetry principles as novel features in a pedestrian detection framework. Inspired by human perception and its ability to recognize and track features despite changing contexts, our approach formulates appearance constancy as a consistent texture pattern and trains deep neural networks to encode this invariant pattern across different images and poses. Shape symmetry, on the other hand, refers to the bilateral or radial oppositional relationships between visual elements, reflecting the balanced proportions of human faces, body, and gait patterns. Our method integrates shape symmetry features into the network architecture to enhance the robustness against partial occlusions. A sophisticated framework integrating these features is presented, comprising multiple convolutional neural networks (CNNs) operating in parallel to detect humans at different pose angles, while also learning features from varied pedestrian footprints in complex environments. Through in-depth evaluation and analysis on benchmark datasets, this research demonstrates the significant efficacy of the proposed method in detecting pedestrians efficiently and accurately, with a considerable improvement in performance over state-of-the-art algorithms. By combining traditional cognitive principles with modern deep learning architectures, this work sheds new light on pedestrian detection, enabling more practical and scalable solutions for real-world applications.

title: Learning to detect video events from zero or very few video examples
Abstract: Deep learning has made significant advancements in event detection for videos, but most methods rely on extensive annotated datasets for training. However, collecting and labeling large-scale video datasets is an arduous task that may not always be feasible. Therefore, the ability to learn from very few or zero video examples is a crucial aspect in the development of video event detection systems. This study focuses on exploring effective methods for learning to detect video events with minimal supervision. We propose an approach that combines meta-learning and few-shot learning techniques to adapt to new video events with limited examples. By leveraging the strengths of both meta-learning and few-shot learning, our approach can efficiently learn to detect novel video events from scratch and improve its performance with limited additional data. Our method involves meta-training an initial model on a diverse range of video events and then fine-tuning it on a small number of target video examples. We also incorporate domain adaptation techniques to address the variation in video data across different sources. Experimenting on two benchmark datasets, we demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in detecting video events with minimal supervision, achieving superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods. Our work opens up new avenues for the development of video event detection systems that can learn from few or zero examples, showcasing significant potential in real-world applications such as surveillance, event analysis, and video editing.

title: A Short Survey on Data Clustering Algorithms
Abstract: Data clustering is a fundamental aspect of machine learning and a crucial task in data analysis, involving the grouping of objects in a data set based on their similarities and differences. Despite its importance, the complexity and inherent diversity of data have led to numerous data clustering algorithms being proposed and implemented. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of some of the most commonly used data clustering algorithms, highlighting their strengths, limitations, and application domains. Starting with the basics of traditional hierarchical agglomerative clustering and divisive clustering, the paper delves into more advanced techniques such as k-means clustering, DBSCAN, and k-medoids. The differences between these algorithms, including their time complexities, memory requirements, and sensibilities to outliers, are carefully examined. Furthermore, the paper digs deeper into newer-generation clustering algorithms like density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise, clique-based clustering, and spectral clustering, highlighting their benefits in handling complex and large-scale datasets. A comparison of the performance of these various clustering algorithms on sample datasets and empirical evidence supports their varying levels of effectiveness in different contexts. Overall, this paper aims to bridge the gap between theory and practice by providing a concise yet informative review of data clustering algorithms, serving as a valuable resource for researchers, practitioners, and students alike, making informed decisions when selecting the most suitable algorithm for their applications.

title: Calculate distance to object in the area where car, using video analysis
Abstract: This research paper contributes to the field of autonomous vehicle technology by developing a video analysis-based method to calculate the distance to objects in the surroundings of a car. The proposed approach relies on computer vision techniques to process video frames captured by a monocular camera installed on the vehicle. By leveraging the motion cues and spatial relationships between the vehicle and surrounding objects, the method can accurately estimate the depth of objects within a range of several meters. The proposed algorithm exploits state-of-the-art computer vision techniques, such as optical flow, feature point tracking, and structure from motion, to reconstruct the scene in 3D space. To further enhance the accuracy and robustness of the method, a robust outlier rejection scheme is implemented to filter out depth anomalies and noisy estimates. Experimental results, obtained using a dataset of real-world video sequences captured under various lighting conditions, demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method in calculating accurate object distances. Comparison with existing methods shows a significant improvement in accuracy, particularly in scenarios with limited fiducial markers or variable background. The paper concludes by highlighting the potential applications of the proposed method in various areas, including autonomous driving, traffic monitoring, and smart cities. Overall, the proposed video analysis-based method represents a promising approach to developing accurate and efficient distance estimation systems for cars in traffic scenarios.

title: PASCAL Boundaries: A Class-Agnostic Semantic Boundary Dataset
Abstract: This paper proposes PASCAL Boundaries, a comprehensive class-agnostic semantic boundary dataset, carefully crafted to facilitate the development of robust object boundary estimation models. Leveraging the PASCAL VOC 2012 dataset, which contains diverse categories of objects, including animals, vehicles, and indoor scenes, we create a unique dataset that highlights the commonalities and nuances of object boundaries across various classes. The resulting dataset comprises approximately 7,755 samples, each annotated with a precise boundary contour that distinguishes the object from its background. To capture the rich geometric and topological characteristics of object boundaries, we also introduce a novel annotation scheme, which includes boundary segmentations and a manually curated boundary dissimilarity matrix. This extensive and well-curated dataset allows researchers to investigate essential questions in object boundary estimation, such as the universality of object boundary representations and the variability of boundary shapes across different object classes. By providing a reliable benchmark for evaluating object boundary estimation algorithms, PASCAL Boundaries contributes to the advancement of visual understanding and facilitates the development of more robust, accurate, and generalizable computer vision models.

title: Video Tracking Using Learned Hierarchical Features
Abstract: This paper presents an advanced video tracking algorithm that utilizes a learned hierarchical feature representation to improve the accuracy and robustness of object tracking in videos. The proposed approach employs a convolutional neural network (CNN) to learn high-dimensional hierarchical features that capture the complex spatial and temporal patterns in videos. A structured output regression layer is employed to predict the object location and size at each time step, while a temporal smoothing module is incorporated to ensure the continuity of the tracking results across frames. The hierarchical features learned by the CNN are progressively decoded to update the tracking state, allowing the algorithm to infer the object's 3D motion and occlusions. The proposed approach outperforms state-of-the-art tracking algorithms in various challenging scenarios, including rapid motion, illumination changes, occlusions, and low-quality video sequences. The experimental results show that the learned hierarchical features provide a more robust and accurate representation of the object's motion, leading to improved tracking performance. Our approach is also computationally efficient and can be seamlessly integrated with other computer vision tasks, such as object recognition and scene understanding.

title: Principal Basis Analysis in Sparse Representation
Abstract: Principal Basis Analysis (PBA) is an innovative framework for analyzing sparse representation, which lies at the intersection of dimensionality reduction and feature extraction. In PBA, the original dataset is represented through a new set of bases, whereas retaining only a sparse subset of the most important features based on the L0 or L1 norm to reconstruct individual samples. Our research endeavors to improve upon existing methods by incorporating a more efficient iterative algorithm that selects the dominant basis components that significantly contribute to sparse reconstruction. By refining these bases and enhancing their interpretability, researchers can now develop more extensive models for data classification, regression, and clustering applications. Throughout our experimental research, we apply PBA to various real-world datasets to critically evaluate its performance compared to the existing methods in terms of feature extraction efficiency, dimensionality reduction effectiveness, and applicability across different problem domains. The notable outcome of PBA presents a hierarchical structure to the data by preserving more inherent patterns and relationships, demonstrating promising potential for its adoption in hierarchical clustering, and supervised or unsupervised feature learning, demonstrating potential beneficial uses in real world environments.

title: Context-aware CNNs for person head detection
Abstract: This paper explores the development of context-aware Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) for the task of person head detection in complex scenes. Traditional CNN-based approaches often suffer from limited contextual understanding, leading to misplaced or missed detections. To address this limitation, we propose a novel context-aware CNN architecture that effectively leverages contextual information to improve person head detection accuracy. The proposed architecture integrates a robust object proposal generation module and a multi-scale feature fusion module to capture both global and local contextual cues. Additionally, a novel component-based head-oriented feature extraction module is designed to focus on the person's head region, enhancing the detection performance. To evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, an extensive experimental study was conducted on various challenging benchmark datasets, including the Caltech Pedestrian benchmark, Citypersons, and the PASCAL Person Part Segmentation dataset. Results demonstrate that the proposed context-aware CNNs significantly outperform state-of-the-art methods, achieving substantial improvements in accuracy (1-5%) and robustness across diverse scenarios, making it a promising solution for real-world person head detection applications. Furthermore, the proposed approach offers a trade-off between accuracy and computational cost, rendering it suitable for implementation in real-time systems with varying computational resources.

title: Shape and Symmetry Induction for 3D Objects
Abstract: This research article delves into the realm of 3D object processing, specifically exploring novel methods for shape and symmetry induction. The ability to accurately infer shape and symmetry properties of 3D objects is crucial in various fields, including computer graphics, robotics, and biology. Current techniques rely heavily on computational complexity, limiting their efficiency and applicability to real-world scenarios. To bridge this gap, we introduce a new framework that combines traditional shape modeling with recent advancements in deep learning and geometric processing. Our proposed approach, dubbed Geo-Symmetry, leverages a hierarchy of learned features to capture subtle shape properties and symmetry cues, enabling the efficient recovery of accurate shape models and symmetry axes. Through a series of experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets, we demonstrate the effectiveness of Geo-Symmetry in preserving the underlying shape geometry and symmetry of complex 3D objects, while significantly reducing computational requirements compared to state-of-the-art methods. By pushing the boundaries of shape and symmetry induction, this research has far-reaching implications for the development of efficient and robust shape analysis and modeling techniques, enabling breakthroughs in applications ranging from object recognition and manipulation to 3D modeling and simulation.

title: Weakly Supervised Object Boundaries
Abstract: Deep learning-based approaches have revolutionized the field of computer vision, achieving state-of-the-art performance in object detection and segmentation tasks. However, most existing methods require dense and labor-intensive annotations, which can be impractical for large-scale applications. In contrast, weakly supervised object boundaries aim to adapt object detection and segmentation to scenarios where only image-level labels or coarse bounding boxes are provided. This approach can significantly reduce annotation costs and allows for efficient deployment in real-world scenarios. In this paper, we investigate recent advancements in weakly supervised object boundaries and explore their potential in applications such as scene understanding, object tracking, and autonomous vehicles. We review various methods that leverage different techniques, including attention mechanisms, transfer learning, and multi-task learning, to predict object boundaries from weak annotations. We discuss the challenges and limitations of current approaches, including the need for robust optimization algorithms and more effective weak supervision strategies. Furthermore, we present a comprehensive evaluation of existing methods on several benchmark datasets, highlighting the strengths and weaknesses of each approach. Our analysis and comparison provide insights into the state-of-the-art in weakly supervised object boundaries and identify potential research directions for improvements in accuracy and scalability.

title: LocNet: Improving Localization Accuracy for Object Detection
Abstract: LocNet: Improving Localization Accuracy for Object Detection is a critical component in various applications such as autonomous vehicles, surveillance systems, and robotics, where accurate object detection is essential for decision-making. However, the existing object detection methods often focus on classification and leave the localization aspect under-explored. Recent studies have shown that localization metrics, such as mean Average Precision (mAP), are improving but still remain inaccurate. This is primarily due to the lack of robust and systematic approaches for estimating object boundaries, which plays a crucial role in achieving accurate localization. To address these limitations, we propose a novel deep learning-based framework, called LocNet, that focuses specifically on improving localization accuracy for object detection tasks. By incorporating a spatially-aware U-Net architecture and a boundary-aware loss function, LocNet is able to effectively capture subtle object boundaries and refine its predictions based on contextual information. Through extensive experiments on popular object detection benchmarks, including PASCAL VOC, COCO, and KITTI, our results show significant improvements in localization accuracy, with a mean average precision gain of up to 5.3% compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, LocNet demonstrates its ability to generalize well across various object detection tasks, making it a robust and efficient solution for real-world applications.

title: Bayesian Identification of Fixations, Saccades, and Smooth Pursuits
Abstract: This research contributes significantly to the field of oculomotor studies by developing an innovative Bayesian approach to identify fixations, saccades, and smooth pursuits accurately from electrooculogram (EOG) data. The presented method leverages a deep understanding of the probabilistic nature of these eye movements and combines it with the robustness of machine learning techniques. A comprehensive mathematical framework is developed to model the EOG signals and their corresponding eye movements. This model is then utilized to design a novel Bayesian classification system that effectively distinguishes between fixations, saccades, and smooth pursuits based on their respective kinematic characteristics. The proposed approach efficiently handles the irregularities in EOG signals due to muscle activities and other noise sources, allowing for precise identification of eye movements across various natural viewing scenarios. Notably, the results demonstrate a significant reduction in classification errors compared to existing methods, highlighting the potential of the Bayesian approach in addressing complex oculomotor phenomena. Furthermore, this research offers valuable insights into the underlying mechanisms of oculomotor control and provides a powerful tool for neuroscientists and engineers to investigate neurodegenerative diseases and other neurological disorders affecting eye movement functions. The effectiveness of the proposed method is scrutinized using both simulated data and real-world EOG recordings from a large-scale dataset. The presented findings underscore the superiority of the Bayesian identification method and pave the way for its application in a wide range of fields, including neuroscience, vision research, and clinical diagnosis.

title: Searching for Objects using Structure in Indoor Scenes
Abstract: Object detection in structured indoor scenes is a significant problem in the field of computer vision, with various applications in robotics, autonomous navigation, and augmented reality. Current approaches primarily rely on learning-based methods that involve training deep neural networks on large datasets, which can be time-consuming and require significant computational resources. This paper presents a novel framework for object detection using structure in indoor scenes, leveraging the inherent geometric properties of the environment to aid the detection process. The proposed approach builds upon the concept of hybrid representations, combining 2D images with 3D structure information to create a more comprehensive understanding of the scene. A graph-based data structure is introduced to efficiently represent the indoor environment, enabling the detection of objects of varying sizes and shapes. The approach is experimentally evaluated on benchmark datasets and shown to achieve state-of-the-art performance in terms of accuracy and efficiency. The proposed framework demonstrates the effectiveness of incorporating structure information in indoor scenes for object detection, opening up new possibilities for applications in robotics, computer-aided design, and building information modeling. The approach also shows promise in edge computing, where it can be utilized to efficiently process visual information in real-time, facilitating real-world applications of the system.

title: Mouse Pose Estimation From Depth Images
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to mouse pose estimation from depth images. Traditional pose estimation methods rely heavily on 2D images, which often suffer from missing depth information, view dependence, and sensitivity to camera movements. In contrast, depth images provide rich spatial information about the environment, allowing for more accurate and robust pose estimation. The proposed method combines a novel depth feature extraction technique with a spatial-temporal graph convolutional network (ST-GCN) architecture to estimate the mouse pose accurately. The method first extracts a set of depth features, including the mouse's position, size, and orientation, from the depth image. These features are then fed into the ST-GCN, which models the spatial and temporal relationships between the mouse's parts to estimate its pose. The ST-GCN architecture employs a hierarchical graph structure to capture the subtle relationships between the mouse's body parts, while the spatial-temporal convolutional layers allow the network to learn long-range dependencies in the sequence. The proposed method is evaluated on a publicly available dataset, and the results show significant improvement over state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy and robustness. The proposed method has applications in computer vision, robotics, and human-computer interaction, where accurate pose estimation is crucial for autonomous systems and user interface design.

title: Picking a Conveyor Clean by an Autonomously Learning Robot
Abstract: The aim of this research is to investigate the efficient cleanup of a conveyor belt by an autonomously learning robot, aimed at enhancing productivity and minimizing downtime in industrial settings. The robot's learning algorithm, a blend of reinforcement learning and imitation learning techniques, enables it to adapt to and learn from various scenarios involving different types and amounts of debris accumulation on the conveyor belt. The proposed robot's navigation system, based on sensors and real-time computer vision, ensures accurate and efficient motion control as it navigates around the conveyor belt, identifies debris locations, and classifies them based on size and material. The system's effectiveness is further augmented by an intelligent decision-making module that optimizes cleanup priorities to ensure the fastest possible restoration of production operations while maintaining spillage within predetermined limits. To evaluate the proposed solution, an extensive simulation study is conducted, comparing its performance against traditional mechanical cleaning methods in a variety of environments and scenarios, taking into account production capacity, equipment wear, and maintenance costs.

title: Fine-Grain Annotation of Cricket Videos
Abstract: This study presents a fine-grain annotation framework for cricket videos, focusing on the identification and classification of detailed events within the game, such as the type of shot played, the fielder involved, and the outcome of the delivery. Using a combination of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, we propose a multi-task learning approach to tackle this problem, incorporating labeling schemes and linguistic features. A comprehensive annotation dataset was created, comprising over 200 hours of cricket video recordings, which was exhaustively labeled with the required fine-grained events. By leveraging parallel annotations, we aimed to achieve improved annotation efficiency and accuracy, while enabling precision that addresses the nuances of cricket scoring. Using in-domain and cross-domain train-test splits, we conducted a rigorous evaluation of the proposed framework, examining its performance under various scenarios involving different data scenarios and metric-based assessments. Our experimentally validated framework can efficiently annotate cricket videos, with high annotation precision, broad applicability, and usability in subsequent process of automated indexing, search, and summarization of cricket video databases, ultimately enriching the experience of fans, coaches, and analysts alike, while advancing research on sports video analysis and multimedia platforms.

title: DenseCap: Fully Convolutional Localization Networks for Dense Captioning
Abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to dense image captioning, a task that generates a list of captions corresponding to specific objects or locations within an image. The proposed method, DenseCap, consists of a fully convolutional localization network that detects multiple objects or locations, and a conditional random field (CRF) that generates detailed captions for each detected object or location. The network is trained using a combination of object detection and image captioning annotations, and is evaluated using the DenseCap-Eval benchmark, a new evaluation metric that measures the quality and diversity of dense captions. The results show that DenseCap outperforms state-of-the-art models in terms of captioning accuracy and provides more diverse captions than previously published methods. The approach is particularly effective for scenes with multiple objects or people, and is also robust to variations in object pose and composition. Furthermore, the use of a fully convolutional network allows for efficient inference and enables the generation of dense captions in real-time for various applications, including image and video processing, robotics, and autonomous driving. The proposed method opens up new possibilities for dense image captioning and has the potential to be applied to a wide range of computer vision tasks.

title: Constrained Deep Metric Learning for Person Re-identification
Abstract: Constrained deep metric learning is an essential technique used to improve the performance of person re-identification (ReID) systems. These systems are designed to match images of the same individual across multiple cameras. Given the large variations in human poses, illumination conditions, and occlusions, existing deep metric learning methods often suffer from overfitting issues. Here, we present a novel method called Constrained Deep Metric Learning for Re-ID (CDML_R), which simultaneously addresses the problems of data imbalance, person identity uncertainty, and overfitting in the target dataset. CDML_R combines a deep learning-based framework with traditional constraints such as triplet-based ranking losses, to learn a more robust and efficient embedding representation conducive to accurate person re-identification. Our experimental results demonstrate that integrating a constraint-based loss function significantly improves the performance on benchmark datasets. By alleviating class imbalance and the "negative sample" issue with traditional approaches, our model improves precision as well as recall, robustness, as well as f1-score thereby leading to superior performance metrics over several challenging PReID datasets. Our experiments exhibit results of the impact that introducing various constraints and analyzing the implications of such constraints highlight its robust performance advantages of our proposed model.

title: The Limitations of Deep Learning in Adversarial Settings
Abstract: Deep learning models have achieved remarkable successes in a wide range of applications, from image recognition to natural language processing. However, a significant limitation of these models lies in their vulnerability to adversarial attacks, which involve intentionally crafted inputs designed to cause the model to produce incorrect or misleading outputs. In this research, we investigate the limitations of deep learning models in adversarial settings, exploring the fundamental reasons behind their susceptibility to attacks and showcasing the challenges faced in developing robust models that can reliably function in the presence of malicious inputs. Through a comprehensive analysis of existing literature and experimental evaluations on various deep learning architectures, we identify the key limitations that make these models vulnerable to adversarial attacks, including the reliance on shallow features, the sensitivity to input manipulations, and the inadequate regularization techniques used in training. Our study further highlights the difficulties in developing models that can effectively resist and recover from adversarial attacks, emphasizing the need for new theories, algorithms, and strategies that can enhance the robustness of deep learning models against such threats. Ultimately, our research contributes to a deeper understanding of the limitations of deep learning in adversarial settings, pointing towards new research directions and investigation opportunities for the development of safer and more reliable AI systems.

title: Constrained Structured Regression with Convolutional Neural Networks
Abstract: Structured regression is a type of regression task where the prediction is not just a single number but a structured output such as image segmentation, object detection, and depth estimation. However, when dealing with real-world applications, the structured regression task often comes with multiple constraints such as sparsity, smoothness, and non-negativity, which essentially make the task more challenging. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have achieved remarkable success in structured regression tasks due to their powerful feature learning capabilities and translation equivariance. However, the standard CNNs fails to incorporate the domain-specific constraints inherently, resulting in poor performance or even degenerate solutions. In this paper, we propose a constrained structured regression framework with CNNs, tailoring to the constraints using a differentiable regularizer. We demonstrate that the proposed differentiable regularizer effectively captures the domain-specific constraints and facilitates the recovery of the desired solution in the absence of explicit labels. Furthermore, we conduct extensive experiments on various structured regression tasks, such as depth estimation and image denoising, and show that the proposed framework outperforms the baseline methods. The outcomes of this study will not only advance the state-of-the-art techniques for structured regression tasks but also provide a unified framework to address the constraints in real-world applications.

title: Top-Down Learning for Structured Labeling with Convolutional Pseudoprior
Abstract: This paper explores the application of top-down learning for structured labeling with convolutional pseudopriors, investigating the integration of prior knowledge with deep learning techniques. The conventional bottom-up approach to convolutional neural networks involves hierarchically decomposing the input image to achieve finer detection and segmentation, relying heavily on spatial features and domain knowledge encoded in the network architecture. In contrast, the proposed top-down approach leverages a broader perspective by incorporating prior knowledge as an additional input to the network, effectively adding a high-level representation of the problem's solution space. Here, the convolutional pseudoprior is introduced, which learns the affinity between nodes in a graph, effectively encoding the structural relationships essential for structured prediction tasks like image segmentation and object recognition. By integrating the pseudoprior computed from a fully connected representation of the problem into the convolutional neural network, this approach enhances the network's ability to capture contextual scene information and long-range dependencies within the image. Experiments conducted on benchmark datasets reveal the effectiveness of this top-down learning paradigm, demonstrating improved performance over state-of-the-art methods under challenging conditions. The experiments also explore the robustness of the proposed method when considering noisy prior information and varying degrees of complexity in the input images.

title: Learning Visual Predictive Models of Physics for Playing Billiards
Abstract: This study presents a novel approach to learning visual predictive models of physics for playing billiards, leveraging the power of deep learning to simulate the dynamics of the game. By incorporating insights from the world of physics into the design of deep neural networks, we develop a visual predictive model that accurately predicts the trajectory of balls on a billiards table. The proposed model, based on a combination of perception and action components, uses a spatial reasoning module to understand the underlying physical laws governing the motion of balls and a controller module to plan and execute shots. Through extensive experimentation on a large and diverse dataset of billiards games, we demonstrate the efficacy of our model in accurately predicting ball positions, velocities, and bounces, as well as its ability to generate novel and effective shots in response to different game scenarios. Our results show that the visual predictive model of physics can serve as a powerful tool for teaching billiards, enabling learners to develop a deeper understanding of the underlying physical principles that govern the game and improving their shot-making skills through data-driven practice. Furthermore, we discuss the broader implications of our work for simulating and predicting the behavior of complex physical systems, with potential applications in fields such as robotics, computer vision, and artificial intelligence.

title: Where To Look: Focus Regions for Visual Question Answering
Abstract: Visual question answering (VQA) has become a prominent area of research in artificial intelligence, with significant advancements in recent years. However, despite these advancements, the current state-of-the-art models still struggle with identifying the relevant regions of an image that are crucial for providing accurate answers to visual questions. This is particularly evident in tasks that require a multi-step approach, where the model needs to focus on specific regions within the image to arrive at the correct answer. The key challenge lies in determining the optimal focus regions for a given question. The traditional approach of computing attention maps and selecting regions based on the highest activation values often does not lead to optimal results, as it fails to capture the complex interplay between image features and question semantics. To address this limitation, this paper proposes a novel approach for identifying focus regions by learning a visual-question attention model that takes into account contextual information and hierarchical representations of the image. Our approach first generates a hierarchical representation of the image using multi-scale feature extraction, followed by the estimation of context-aware attention maps that weigh the importance of different image regions for answering the question. The proposed framework is extensively evaluated on benchmark VQA datasets, including VQA-1.0 and VQA2.0, demonstrating significant improvements over state-of-the-art models. The findings of this study provide valuable insights into the importance of focus regions in VQA and highlight the effectiveness of our proposed approach in achieving accurate and efficient visual question answering results.

title: Pushing the Boundaries of Boundary Detection using Deep Learning
Abstract: Boundary detection is an essential task in image and signal processing with a wide range of applications in areas such as medical imaging, robotics, and autonomous vehicles. However, existing boundary detection techniques often rely on simplistic and hand-engineered features, restricting their ability to generalize to novel and complex scenarios. Recent advancements in deep learning have shown great potential in addressing this limitation by learning high-level features that are adaptive to the underlying data distribution. This study aims to push the boundaries of boundary detection using deep learning by exploring and integrating various state-of-the-art architectures and techniques. We have developed a novel convolutional neural network (CNN) that leverages the strengths of both fully convolutional networks (FCNs) and encoder-decoder frameworks to achieve more accurate and robust boundary detection. Our proposed network, referred to as Boundary-CNN, incorporates a novel attention mechanism to selectively focus on informative regions and improve localization accuracy. Additionally, a transfer learning framework is introduced to adapt the pre-trained model to various data distributions and reduce the need for extensive and data-specific fine-tuning. Comprehensive experiments on several benchmarks demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, achieving superior performance over state-of-the-art methods and more generalizable results. This work has the potential to revolutionize the field of boundary detection and pave the way for a wide range of applications in computer vision and signal processing.

title: CNNdroid: GPU-Accelerated Execution of Trained Deep Convolutional Neural Networks on Android
Abstract: This paper presents CNNdroid, a groundbreaking framework for executing trained deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) on Android devices equipped with GPU acceleration. By leveraging the processing capabilities of the graphics processing unit (GPU), CNNdroid offers a significant improvement in the execution speed of complex deep learning tasks on mobile platforms, thereby reducing latency and energy consumption. The framework is specifically designed to address the inherent limitations of existing approaches, which rely on software-based CPU execution and lack hardware-acceleration. To achieve this, CNNdroid employs a novel neural network architecture, tailored to optimize weight quantization, model pruning, and knowledge distillation. By exploiting the vast processing resources of the GPU, this framework substantially accelerates inference times for a broad range of CNN-based applications, such as image classification, object detection, and facial recognition. To further enhance the efficiency of CNNdroid, developers can extensively configure and fine-tune the execution flow, trading off model complexity, precision, and latency based on their specific performance requirements. Furthermore, this paper demonstrates CNNdroid's scalability and reliability through comprehensive experiments on various Android devices, showcasing the immense potential of this framework in realizing practical and widespread adoption of deep learning-based features on mobile platforms, thereby creating novel use cases for cognitive computing-driven Android applications.

title: Recombinator Networks: Learning Coarse-to-Fine Feature Aggregation
Abstract: This paper introduces Recombinator Networks (ReNets), a novel Paradigm for learning coarse-to-fine feature aggregation within deep neural networks. By leveraging the dual objectives of coarse-to-fine feature representation, ReNets seamlessly integrate the complementary strengths of multi-scale representation learning and high-dim manifold perception. The proposed architecture boasts several key advancements. Firstly, a Recombinator layer is introduced, enabling the flexible combination of features from multiple scales and representations. This layer dynamically controls the extent to which coarse and fine features interact, fostering highly adaptive and discriminative feature representations. Secondly, an effective learning strategy is developed, which incorporates two novel objectives: correspondence maximization and contextual robustness. Correspondence maximization is designed to capture salient feature correspondences across different scales and representations, while contextual robustness encourages the model to express fine-grained details by iteratively refining its feature representations. Our evaluations on diverse benchmarks demonstrate superior performance to existing state-of-the-art techniques, affirming the efficacy of the ReNet paradigm for various vision tasks, including image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation, as well as its adaptability to emerging applications such as 3D scene understanding.

title: Node Specificity in Convolutional Deep Nets Depends on Receptive Field Position and Size
Abstract: This study examines the role of node specificity in convolutional deep neural networks (CNNs) and its relationship to receptive field (RF) position and size. A key aspect of CNN modeling is the investigation of node specificity, which refers to the degree to which individual neurons within a layer respond to specific input features. Recent research has suggested that node specificity can significantly impact the performance and behavior of CNNs. However, the mechanisms underlying node specificity and its interaction with RF geometry have yet to be fully elucidated. In this study, we investigated the effects of RF position and size on node specificity in CNNs using a novel methodology combining node activation patterns and RF geometry analysis. A systematic analysis of activation patterns across layers and nodes was conducted to establish the relationships between node specificity and RF properties. The findings reveal that node specificity in CNNs is dependent on both the position and size of the receptive field. RF size was found to have a critical impact on node specificity, with larger RFs associated with lower node specificity. Conversely, the position of the RF within the network was found to be a more nuanced factor, with nodes in earlier layers exhibiting higher node specificity than those in later layers. These results have significant implications for understanding the behavior of CNNs and provide insights into the importance of considering RF geometry when designing deep learning models.

title: Rendering refraction and reflection of eyeglasses for synthetic eye tracker images
Abstract: This abstract investigates the development of a novel rendering framework that replicates the complex light interactions produced by eyeglasses during synthetic eye tracker image generation. Accurate simulation of refraction and reflection in eyeglasses is crucial for creating realistic eye-tracking data, particularly for applications in computer vision, robotics, and virtual reality. Current rendering techniques often rely on simplistic heuristics or inaccurate approximations of light-bending through lenses, leading to unreliable results. To address this limitation, our research proposes a computationally efficient method for simulating eyeglass-induced optical effects using ray tracing and real-time shading techniques. Our approach utilizes a data-driven model to handle irregular lens geometries and dynamic lighting conditions, ensuring that the rendered eyeglass reflections and refractions closely match in vivo observations. The established rendering framework is evaluated against a comprehensive dataset of images captured with various eyeglasses under diverse lighting conditions. Results demonstrate a consistent improvement in fidelity and accuracy, highlighting the potential for our technique to enhance the creation of realistic and reliable synthetic eye tracker images that closely mimic human visual behaviors. The presented methodology is anticipated to have far-reaching implications for fields that heavily rely on synthetic eye tracking, advocating for its adaptation as a gold standard in the development of next-generation visual interaction technologies.

title: NetVLAD: CNN architecture for weakly supervised place recognition
Abstract: NetVLAD, a novel deep learning architecture emerges as a significant advancement in computer vision, particularly in the realm of weakly supervised place recognition. This CNN-based model uniquely leverages a concept called Local Aggregation of CNN features, allowing it to effectively capture the spatial information that is crucial for place recognition tasks. Unlike its predecessors, NetVLAD is capable of learning compact and structured aggregations of features from a neural network, thus bypassing the need for manually engineered vocabularies. Moreover, this framework remarkably outperforms traditional image-based models by learning mid-to-high level semantic features that are significant for environment recognition. While dealing with scenes captured under various visual conditions such as differing illuminations, poses, and observation angles, the model adeptly adapts to these variations and demonstrates enhanced robustness. Grounded in a comprehensive review of existing approaches to weakly supervised place recognition, NetVLAD stands out as a cutting-edge architecture showcasing state-of-the-art performance in benchmark challenge outcomes. By identifying a clear indication of its effectiveness in numerous evaluation tests and datasets, this study presents a compelling argument for integrating the NetVLAD model into real-world applications involving scene-based place recognition systems.

title: Face Alignment Across Large Poses: A 3D Solution
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel 3D face alignment technique, specifically designed to handle large pose variations, a longstanding challenge in the field of face analysis. The existing 2D face alignment approaches struggle to accurately tackle large pose changes, often resulting in deviations and reduced accuracy. In contrast, this 3D solution leverages a multi-source deep learning architecture that efficiently combines geometric and photometric information to align and register facial landmarks in 3D space. By accounting for the complex face geometry and the diverse pose variations, the proposed method achieves highly accurate alignment across an unprecedented range of pose angles, including extreme head rotations and orientations. The approach utilizes a hierarchical network structure, starting from coarse-to-fine registration, to ensure high resolution alignment and robustness. Furthermore, to validate the effectiveness of our proposal, a comprehensive evaluation on several benchmark datasets is conducted, including standard 2D datasets and large pose 3D datasets, demonstrating state-of-the-art performance in all scenarios. The experimental results show significant improvements over the competing methods and highlight the potential of the proposed 3D alignment framework for various applications in computer vision, such as face recognition, facial expression analysis, and avatars creation, where reliable face registration under large pose variations is essential.

title: Improving the performance of the linear systems solvers using CUDA
Abstract: This abstract presents a comprehensive study on enhancing the efficiency of linear systems solvers using the NVIDIA CUDA architecture. With the increasing demand for high-performance computing in various fields such as scientific simulations, machine learning, and data analytics, optimizing numerical linear algebra routines is essential to achieve real-time results. Traditional CPU-based linear systems solvers often struggle to meet the performance requirements of these applications due to the limitations of serial processing. In contrast, the massively parallel architecture of CUDA enables unprecedented scaling of thread-level concurrency, making it an ideal platform for boosting linear systems solvers. This research focuses on the design, implementation, and optimization of CUDA-based linear systems solvers for various problem sizes and matrices. A detailed analysis of the performance improvement is presented through a combination of theoretical derivations and experimental evaluations. The experimental results demonstrate significant speedup over CPU-based solvers, with the CUDA implementation delivering a performance boost of up to several orders of magnitude for certain problem sizes. Additionally, the developed code is implemented using error-free matrix operations, memory-efficient data structures, and optimal memory access patterns to ensure reliability and portability. The results of this study demonstrate the potential of CUDA-based linear systems solvers in achieving real-time performance for large-scale linear systems and open up new avenues for its adoption in various computational domains.

title: DeePM: A Deep Part-Based Model for Object Detection and Semantic Part Localization
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel deep learning-based model, referred to as DeePM, designed to tackle object detection and semantic part localization tasks simultaneously. DeePM follows a part-based approach, representing complex objects as compositions of their constituent parts. By adopting a split-attention mechanism, DeePM enables effective part localization by paying localized attention to distinct object parts. The proposed architecture is composed of a part-aware encoder and a part-embedding network, which effectively capture the complex relationships between object parts and facilitate semantic part localization. The DeePM model also employs a hierarchically stacked convolutional neural network architecture to efficiently capture hierarchical representations and contextual dependencies across object parts. To evaluate DeePM's performance, extensive experiments are conducted on the COCO, PASCAL VOC, and Pascal Person-Part datasets. The results demonstrate DeePM's strong performance in object detection and semantic part localization, outperforming state-of-the-art part-aware detectors. The proposed DeePM model is also evaluated using metrics such as per-class recall, object part intersection over union, and qualitative evaluation. The effectiveness of DeePM is further validated through ablation studies and comparisons with existing models, showcasing its robustness and scalability across various object detection and part localization tasks.

title: What Happened to My Dog in That Network: Unraveling Top-down Generators in Convolutional Neural Networks
Abstract: This research paper delves into the mysteries of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), specifically focusing on the behavior of top-down generators within them. A top-down generator refers to a mechanism where the network uses lower-resolution features to guide its decision-making process at higher resolutions. This occurrence raises significant questions, including the implication of abandoning traditional, bottom-up CNN architectures in favor of a more hierarchical approach. By peering into the inner workings of these models, researchers can gain a better understanding of how they process visual data and how various processes interact to generate a final prediction, such as identifying an object within an image. Our work centers on the concept of how different top-down generator strategies impact the performance of both classification and object detection tasks within a given CNN. To achieve this, we employ a combination of analytical and empirical methods to model, analyze, and visualize various network architectures. Furthermore, we explore the implications of these findings in the broader context of deep learning research, with consideration for the ability of CNNs to replicate complex visual processing tasks witnessed in the human brain. By providing insights into the top-down generation process, this research aims to bridge the gap between theoretical understanding and successful practical application of these powerful models.

title: Multi-Scale Context Aggregation by Dilated Convolutions
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel deep learning framework based on multi-scale context aggregation (MSCA) via dilated convolutions to better capture the complex patterns and relationships within visual data. By leveraging the concept of dilated convolutions, MSCA is able to efficiently extract and integrate context information at multiple scales, allowing for the development of more robust and accurate models. In this work, the MSCA framework is explored in the context of image classification and semantic segmentation tasks, where the incorporation of dilated convolutions significantly improves model performance compared to traditional convolutional neural networks (CNNs). The effectiveness of the proposed approach is demonstrated through a range of benchmark datasets and comparisons with state-of-the-art models. Furthermore, an in-depth analysis of the MSCA framework provides insights into the role of dilated convolutions in enhancing model performance, shedding light on the intrinsic mechanisms underlying the integration of context information at multiple scales. The findings of this study have significant implications for the broader field of computer vision, highlighting the potential of MSCA via dilated convolutions to revolutionize the development of next-generation visual recognition models. Overall, this work contributes to a deeper understanding of how to effectively aggregate context information within deep neural networks, paving the way for future advancements in image understanding and visual representation learning.

title: Adapting Deep Visuomotor Representations with Weak Pairwise Constraints
Abstract: Our method focuses on adapting existing deep visuomotor representations for new tasks with limited data and weak pairwise constraints. In many real-world scenarios, robots are often required to learn new tasks from demonstrations provided by a human teacher or learn from a small dataset. However, the paucity of data, scarcity of high-quality demonstrations, and limited understanding of the visuomotor representations' adaptability hinder the development of effective transfer learning methods. Consequently, robots face significant challenges in acquiring the necessary visuomotor skills for adapting to varying environments, objects, and situations. Utilizing a combination of learnable probabilistic structured learning networks and learned prior structural knowledge in both the demonstration space and task space allows our method to learn transferable representations from limited pairwise constraints. Furthermore, by incorporating weak and general pairwise constraints, our algorithm facilitates knowledge transfer and adaptation across a broad range of tasks with minimal data supervision. The proposed approach demonstrates improved performance in learning new tasks via our in-depth study and evaluation of multi-task representation transferability, where we show improved performance in several challenging benchmark tasks. Through our method, robots can adapt to new tasks with much reduced need for large datasets and extensive retraining.

title: Multi-Volume High Resolution RGB-D Mapping with Dynamic Volume Placement
Abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to multi-volume high-resolution RGB-D mapping, addressing the limitations of existing methods that often compromise on resolution or coverage when dealing with large environments. Our method, called dynamic volume placement, allows for flexible and adaptive processing of RGB-D data, enabling high-resolution mapping even in scenarios with high levels of occlusion or dynamic objects. The key innovations lie in the development of a probabilistic framework for jointly optimized volume placement and mapping, which leverages the strengths of machine learning and computer vision techniques. Our model is capable of capturing complex environments and handling diverse spatial relationships between objects, exploiting insights from attention mechanisms to concentrate on regions of interest and dynamically alter the placement of mapping volumes. In addition, we propose an efficient greedy algorithm to accommodate real-time volume placement and updating during mapping. Extensive evaluations on various challenging RGB-D datasets demonstrate notable improvements over current state-of-the-art methods, with our approach successfully achieving high-resolution reconstruction and accurate localization across scenarios of varying complexity. The dynamic volume placement paradigm has the potential to revolutionize the field of RGB-D mapping, offering a more flexible, efficient, and effective solution for mapping real-world environments with unprecedented versatility.

title: Auxiliary Image Regularization for Deep CNNs with Noisy Labels
Abstract: Deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have made significant strides in various computer vision tasks, but their performance heavily relies on the quality of the labels, particularly in the presence of noisy or incorrect labels. Auxiliary image regularization is a novel approach to mitigate the impact of noisy labels by incorporating an auxiliary task or objective into the training process, thereby improving the robustness and generalization capabilities of the network. By encouraging the network to focus on a secondary task or objective, auxiliary regularization can be harnessed to effectively reduce overfitting, stabilize training, and improve the overall convergence of the model, even when faced with unreliable or noisy labels. However, designing an effective auxiliary regularization scheme poses a significant challenge, as the choice of the auxiliary task and its corresponding loss function significantly impact the performance of the network. In this work, we present a comprehensive exploration of various auxiliary regularization schemes, each designed to exploit different properties of the noisy labels, including label ambiguity, label noise, and label distribution shift. Our experiments, conducted on several benchmark datasets with varying levels of noisy labels, demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed auxiliary regularization approaches in improving the robustness and accuracy of CNNs in the presence of noisy labels. We also provide a systematic analysis of the effects of auxiliary regularization on the model's convergence trajectory, highlighting the trade-offs between regularization strength and classification accuracy. Ultimately, our work paves the way for the development of more robust and adaptive CNNs that can generalize effectively to real-world scenarios where noisy or unreliable labels are inevitable.

title: Visual Word2Vec (vis-w2v): Learning Visually Grounded Word Embeddings Using Abstract Scenes
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel method for learning Visually Grounded Word Embeddings using Abstract Scenes, dubbed as Visual Word2Vec (vis-w2v). The aim is to capture the semantic meaning of words through their visual representations in abstract scenes, rather than relying on traditional text-based word embeddings. The vis-w2v approach leverages a combination of vision and language to create a more robust and generalizable model. A dataset of abstract scenes is created, where each scene is annotated with a set of words that are visually related to the scene's abstract concept. The vis-w2v model is trained on this dataset using a deep learning architecture that incorporates both convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and recurrent neural networks (RNNs). The output of the model are high-dimensional vectors that represent the visual meaning of each word. These vectors can be used for various natural language processing tasks, such as text classification, information retrieval, and question-answering. The proposed approach is evaluated on a set of benchmark datasets, and the results demonstrate significant improvements over traditional word embeddings methods. The vis-w2v model is also shown to capture nuanced semantic relationships between words, such as synonyms, antonyms, and hyponyms. The contributions of this work are threefold: (1) a novel method for learning visually grounded word embeddings using abstract scenes, (2) a new deep learning architecture that combines CNNs and RNNs to model visual-language relationships, and (3) a potentially groundbreaking approach to improving the performance of various NLP tasks.

title: Fine-grained pose prediction, normalization, and recognition
Abstract: Fine-grained pose prediction, normalization, and recognition have become increasingly important in computer vision, allowing for a deeper understanding and analysis of human and object positions within complex scenes. This research proposes a novel deep learning approach that integrates both pose prediction and normalization to enhance the accuracy of fine-grained recognition tasks. By using a two-branch architecture, the proposed model is capable of learning both the global and local representations of objects or human poses, enabling it to capture subtle differences in pose that are often lost in traditional recognition models. The normalization component is designed to align the pose predictions across the entire dataset, thereby reducing the effect of pose variability and improving the robustness of the model. Furthermore, this research introduces a new normalization technique that leverages Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to generate pose-normalized images, allowing for a more comprehensive and unbiased representation of the underlying object or human class. Experimental results on several benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in fine-grained pose prediction and recognition tasks, indicating its potential for real-world applications in areas such as surveillance, human-computer interaction, and autonomous vehicles.

title: ReSeg: A Recurrent Neural Network-based Model for Semantic Segmentation
Abstract: This paper proposes ReSeg, a novel Recurrent Neural Network (RNN)-based model for semantic segmentation tasks in computer vision. Existing convolutional neural network (CNN) based segmentation models tend to fail in handling complex and sequential data due to their static spatial structure, where each location receives input information independently without considering the temporal or spatial dependencies. To address this limitation, our proposed ReSeg model is designed to effectively explore the spatial context by employing a convolutional LSTM module that integrates the spatial information in the receptive field. The proposed model consists of an encoder, which extracts hierarchical features and progressively refines feature representations through contextual dependency by stacked convolutional LSTM units. The refined feature maps are then processed through a channel-wise attention mechanism to weight the importance of spatial locations, making it possible for deep features to learn category-specific contextual representations. Contrastive to existing methods that emphasize the spatial or recurrent information alternatively, our proposed ReSeg comprehensively leverages cross-modal interactions to emphasize correlations across visual hierarchies and produces superior segmentation results by exploiting spatiotemporal dependencies that more closely resemble real-world interdependencies, leading to outstanding performance in various benchmark datasets such as PASCAL VOC and Cityscapes. By incorporating recurrent connections in the convolutional neural networks, our ReSeg aims to outshine classical approaches that focus only on deep spatial hierarchies in computational complexity, complexity in encoding temporal dependencies.
