title: SceneNet: Understanding Real World Indoor Scenes With Synthetic Data
Abstract: SceneNet is a synthetic indoor dataset designed to push the boundaries of scene understanding in the real world, ultimately addressing the limitations of traditional datasets populated with scarce real-world scenes and annotations. The proposal of SceneNet stems from the evidence that indoor scenes possess great diversity and complexity, whether it's a simple hotel lobby or a cluttered home office, they possess an intricate visual hierarchy. Exploiting computer-generated imagery to populate SceneNet, large quantities of diverse scenes can be synthesized while also precisely controlling the composition, layout, and objects within every scene. As it has high detail and variety, datasets like SceneNet furnish a golden opportunity for the enhancement of scene recognition models, encouraging the development of more adaptable and resilient AI systems. Potential applications for SceneNet include training data for machine perception and computer vision tasks, providing researchers and developers with a robust dataset that closely approximates real-world complexity. SceneNet combines visual diversity in scenes with a high degree of customization, which in turn allows for improved and high quality outcomes in various applications. By leveraging the vast and detailed capabilities of SceneNet, we can move one step closer to establishing scene understanding as a cornerstone of AI research. This work showcases a compelling premise that further investigates SceneNet, especially in terms of applications in real-world indoor settings.

title: Learning High-level Prior with Convolutional Neural Networks for Semantic Segmentation
Abstract: Our research paper delves into the realm of semantic segmentation using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), with a primary focus on learning high-level prior knowledge to improve model performance. Semantic segmentation involves assigning meaningful labels to pixels in an image, a task that is essential in various computer vision applications such as autonomous driving, medical image analysis, and image editing. Traditional approaches to semantic segmentation rely heavily on low-level features learned by CNNs, which are often inadequate to capture complex contextual relationships between pixels. To address this limitation, we propose a novel framework that integrates high-level prior knowledge into the conditional random field (CRF) model for pixel-wise prediction. Our approach involves learning a hierarchical representation of the scene from high-level abstract features to local spatial representations, allowing the model to incorporate domain-specific prior knowledge and contextual information. We achieve this by augmenting the feature maps extracted from the CNN with higher-level semantic features learned through multi-resolution representation and object interactions. Experiments conducted on several benchmark datasets, including PASCAL VOC and Cityscapes, demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in achieving state-of-the-art performance and outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods in semantic segmentation tasks. By integrating high-level prior knowledge into the CNN, our method exhibits superior flexibility and adaptability, rendering it more suitable for various semantic segmentation applications.

title: End-to-end Learning of Action Detection from Frame Glimpses in Videos
Abstract: Action detection from videos has been a longstanding problem in computer vision, with applications in surveillance, activity recognition, and robotics. Existing approaches to action detection typically involve a two-stage process: a bottom-up detection of local events such as optical flow or motion boundaries, followed by a top-down classification to determine the type of action being performed. However, these approaches have several limitations. Firstly, they are computationally expensive due to the need for offline pre-processing to detect local events. Secondly, they often require hand-engineered features and large amounts of annotation data, making them challenging to scale to large and complex datasets. Furthermore, state-of-the-art action detection models rely heavily on i.i.d. (independent and identically distributed) image representations that fail to capture the temporal dynamics of human action. To address these challenges, we propose an end-to-end learning framework for action detection from frame glimpses in videos. Our approach utilizes a convolutional recurrent neural network to learn a spatio-temporal representation of the input video that captures the essence of the action being performed. By using a state-of-the-art video frame glimpse strategy, we focus on extracting contextual information from videos. This allows the model to perform end-to-end learning without requiring any off-line feature detection, making it more efficient and scalable. Evaluation on several benchmark datasets demonstrates the potential of our method to outperform existing approaches in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency.

title: Ask Me Anything: Free-form Visual Question Answering Based on Knowledge from External Sources
Abstract: This research proposes a novel approach to free-form visual question answering (VQA) that leverages knowledge from external sources to expand the scope of applicable questions and provide more informative and accurate answers. The proposed method, Ask Me Anything (AMA), is a state-of-the-art hybrid model that integrates the strengths of traditional VQA architectures with the ability to draw upon a vast repository of external knowledge. By incorporating pre-trained language models and knowledge graphs, AMA is capable of addressing questions that are ambiguous, abstract, or require in-depth domain-specific knowledge. The model's ability to access and fuse information from diverse sources enables it to provide more accurate and comprehensive answers, outperforming existing VQA models on a range of benchmark datasets. The contributions of this research include the development of a robust and scalable framework for integrating external knowledge into VQA systems, as well as the introduction of a novel dataset and evaluation protocol that assesses the model's ability to reason and answer complex questions. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of AMA in handling a wide range of visual question types, paving the way for its deployment in real-world applications such as artificial intelligence-powered customer support, medical diagnosis, and educational tools.

title: Gradual DropIn of Layers to Train Very Deep Neural Networks
Abstract: The efficiency of training very deep neural networks (VDPNNs) is heavily dependent on the training process. Traditional methods of training such networks by stacking layers linearly are highly time-consuming and memory-intensive, leading to expensive computational costs. In this research, we explore a novel technique for training VDPNNs, which focuses on introducing a gradual drop-in of layers. This technique allows for an initially reduced network with fewer layers to be trained first, and then additional layers are gradually added at each epoch. This incremental training approach empowers us to take advantage of the pre-trained knowledge of the previously added layers as a supervision signal for the subsequent layers. The main contribution of our research lies in the design of novel, layered incremental learning strategies that promote efficient training. By applying our approach on a range of benchmark datasets like ImageNet, CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, our results indicate a significant reduction in training time and a noticeable decrease in the memory required, making it an attractive solution for real-world applications. Our findings show that this novel technique enables training of deep neural networks on high-end data in a restricted time frame, suggesting potential applications in real-world scenarios that require quick solutions.

title: Real-Time Anomaly Detection and Localization in Crowded Scenes
Abstract: This abstract presents a novel approach to real-time anomaly detection and localization in crowded scenes, leveraging the synergy between computer vision and machine learning techniques. The increasing proliferation of surveillance cameras in public spaces has necessitated the development of efficient and accurate anomaly detection systems, particularly in scenarios where they can potentially prevent crimes or mitigate harm. In crowded scenes, conventional methods often struggle to discern genuine anomalies from the overwhelming background noise, resulting in high false positive rates and excessive manual intervention. Our proposed framework incorporates a multi-stage architecture that initially employs a variant of the popular YOLOv7 object detection algorithm to track pedestrians and extract features related to their movement patterns. These features are then fed into a Gaussian Mixture Model-based anomaly detector, allowing for the identification of unusual behaviors and crowd dynamics. The detection outcomes are subsequently refined through the application of a Kalman filter-based technique, which provides enhanced spatial localization and reduced variance in the estimates of anomaly coordinates. By integrating these components, our framework achieves both optimal detection accuracy and localizable precision in real-time, addressing the primary limitations of existing solutions in crowded environments and paving the way for widespread adoption in real-world applications. Key experiments and analysis are conducted using a series of benchmarks and datasets, showcasing the efficacy of our approach in a range of complex scenarios.

title: Real-Time Anomalous Behavior Detection and Localization in Crowded Scenes
Abstract: This paper contributes to the field of video surveillance by proposing an efficient and robust method for real-time detection and localization of anomalous behavior in crowded scenes. The proposed approach leverages a deep learning-based framework that incorporates a novel combination of attention mechanisms and spatial-temporal pyramid pooling to effectively identify abnormal activities. The method begins by generating a background model using a background subtraction technique to capture the normal patterns and movements in the scene. A convolutional neural network (CNN) is then employed to detect anomalous behaviors in real-time, where the CNN is trained on a large-scale anomaly detection dataset to learn the characteristics of abnormal events. The localized spatial and temporal information is extracted using the spatial-temporal pyramid pooling technique, enabling the model to accurately pinpoint the spatial coordinates of the anomalies and contextualize them temporally. Furthermore, to improve the efficiency and real-time processing capabilities of the proposed method, a hierarchical attention mechanism is introduced that prioritizes the most relevant areas of the frame and suppresses non-informative areas, thus preventing unnecessary computational overhead. Extensive experiments on various benchmark datasets demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method, achieving higher accuracy and efficiency compared to state-of-the-art approaches. The results suggest the potential of the proposed method in widespread adoption in real-world surveillance applications, such as public security monitoring and crowd analysis.

title: Semantic Segmentation of Colon Glands with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks and Total Variation Segmentation
Abstract: This study focuses on developing a novel technique for accurate and automatic segmentation of colon glands in histopathological images using deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and total variation segmentation. The proposed method leverages the strengths of CNNs and total variation regularization to refine the segmentation results. Initially, a CNN-based model is trained on a large dataset of colon gland images to learn the features and patterns representative of glandular structures. The trained model is then used to predict gland masks, which are subsequently refined using total variation regularization to minimize the effect of noise and spurious segments. The algorithm is tested on a diverse set of histopathological images of the colon, including those with varying degrees of tissue damage, inflammation, and glandular atrophy. Results show a significant improvement in accuracy and segmentation quality compared to state-of-the-art methods, with a median Dice coefficient of 85% and an average Hausdorff distance of 15 pixels. Furthermore, the proposed method demonstrates robustness to changes in image intensity, staining, and resolution, making it a reliable tool for histopathological analysis and tissue characterization. The method's ability to accurately segment glandular structures opens up new avenues for cancer diagnosis and prognosis, enabling early detection and treatment planning. The method's feasibility for clinical applications is also addressed, highlighting the potential for widespread adoption in medical imaging analysis.

title: Screen Content Image Segmentation Using Sparse-Smooth Decomposition
Abstract: The paper presents an innovative approach to screen content image segmentation employing sparse-smooth decomposition, an adaptive technique that optimizes the decomposition process to achieve superior segmentation performance. By leveraging sparse and smooth representations of images, this method effectively dissects complex visual structures and artifacts inherent to images captured on screens, overcoming challenges associated with standard image processing techniques. Combining sparse and smooth decomposition techniques, the proposed approach successfully untangles densely packed and interlaced visual components typical of screen content images, significantly enhancing the accuracy of image segmentation. Through comparative analysis with traditional image segmentation methods, this research demonstrates substantial improvements in precision and reliability, showcasing the effectiveness of sparse-smooth decomposition for distinguishing objects within diverse screen content images. The study outlines the underlying mathematical framework, evaluates the performance of the proposed method on a range of datasets, and discusses future avenues for expansion, underscoring its utility for various screen-based applications, including digital image manipulation and visual analytics. Ultimately, this groundbreaking research initiative highlights the transformative potential of sparse-smooth decomposition in advancing the field of image segmentation and boosting the capacity for efficient object extraction from complex visual data.

title: Zoom Better to See Clearer: Human and Object Parsing with Hierarchical Auto-Zoom Net
Abstract: This paper proposes an innovative approach to human and object parsing by introducing Hierarchical Auto-Zoom Network (HAZN), a novel paradigm that leverages auto-zoom strategies to achieve improved parsing accuracy. By utilizing a hierarchical zooming framework, HAZN iteratively zooms in and out of target regions to refine object boundaries and capture subtle contextual cues that are crucial for accurate parsing. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on fixed or manually pre-defined zoom levels, HAZN dynamically adjusts its zooming strategy based on the complexity of the input scene and the specific parsing task at hand. The proposed architecture consists of a set of zooming modules, each operating at different spatial resolutions, which collaborate to provide a comprehensive understanding of the scene. Extensive experiments on challenging human and object parsing benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of HAZN over state-of-the-art methods, showcasing improved performance, robustness, and computational efficiency. Through its seamless integration of hierarchical zooming and auto-zoom techniques, HAZN offers a more nuanced and adaptive understanding of visual scenes, fostering innovative applications in computer vision research and practice.

title: Convex Sparse Spectral Clustering: Single-view to Multi-view
Abstract: Convex sparse spectral clustering has gained popularity in recent years due to its ability to handle high-dimensional data effectively. However, traditional methods rely heavily on the availability of multiple views or modalities, which are not always feasible in real-world applications. This paper proposes a novel framework for single-view to multi-view convex sparse spectral clustering, leveraging the power of low-rank and sparse representation techniques. The framework first extracts features from a single view using a convex sparse relaxation, promoting the recovery of both the principal components and sparse coefficients. Utilizing this representation, the framework then derives a convex formulation for multi-view spectral clustering, ensuring that the clustering solution is both coherent and parsimonious. A primal-dual optimization algorithm is developed to solve the resulting minimax problem, which is guaranteed to converge to a global minimum under mild conditions. Comprehensive experiments on various datasets and comparative analyses with state-of-the-art methods demonstrate the efficacy and efficiency of the proposed framework, achieving superior clustering accuracy and speed. By bridging the gap between single-view and multi-view spectral clustering, the proposed framework offers a promising solution for practical applications where multiple views are scarce or not available.

title: Data-dependent Initializations of Convolutional Neural Networks
Abstract: This study explores the role of data-dependent initializations in enhancing the performance of convolutional neural networks (CNNs). Current methods of initializing weights for CNNs are often based on theoretical assumptions and uniform or random distributions, which may not be optimal for all datasets and network architectures. We propose a novel approach to initialize CNN parameters in a data-dependent manner, leveraging the statistical properties of the training data to inform the choice of initial weights. Specifically, we demonstrate that a data-dependent initialization scheme, which generates initial weights as a function of the training data's mean and covariance, outperforms traditional methods in a range of benchmark image classification tasks. Our results indicate that this approach can adaptively adjust the level of complexity and regularization in the network to better suit the characteristics of the training data, leading to improved generalization performance and reduced overfitting. We also investigate the effect of hyperparameters on the performance of data-dependent initializations and provide a comprehensive analysis of the benefits and limitations of this approach. Our findings have significant implications for the development of more effective CNN architectures and shed light on the importance of incorporating data-driven insights in the initialization process.

title: Unsupervised learning of object semantic parts from internal states of CNNs by population encoding
Abstract: This study proposes a novel methodology for learning object semantic parts from the internal states of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) through population encoding, a type of unsupervised learning. By applying this approach, CNNs are capable of decomposing complex visual objects into abstract semantic parts, providing insight into the internal representation and decision-making process of the network. The proposed method leverages the output of various convolutional and pooling layers to capture different aspects of object appearance and structure, enabling the network to learn and represent semantic parts in a hierarchical manner. Furthermore, the population encoding technique allows for the exploration of the complex internal states of CNNs, facilitating the identification of relationships and correlations between semantic parts. Through extensive experiments on datasets from various domains, including object recognition and scene understanding, this research demonstrates the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed method in discovering meaningful object semantic parts from internal CNN states. The results show that the learned semantic parts exhibit spatial consistency, hierarchy, and semantic meaningfulness, offering new avenues for understanding the internal workings of CNNs and developing more interpretable and explainable AI systems. The developed methodology contributes to the field of computer vision and deep learning by providing a novel and automatic way to analyze and interpret the internal states of CNNs.

title: TransCut: Transparent Object Segmentation from a Light-Field Image
Abstract: This paper presents TransCut, a novel method for transparent object segmentation from light-field images. Light-field photography captures the directional lighting of a scene, enabling the reconstruction of both the object's shape and the intensity of the light it reflects. However, separating transparent objects from their backgrounds in light-field images remains an open challenge, particularly when the transparent objects have intricate details and thin structures. Existing methods struggle with achieving a precise segmentation due to the occurrence of non-uniform illumination and the difficulty of distinguishing between material boundaries and refractive boundaries. Our proposed TransCut method addresses these deficiencies by employing a generative approach to model the appearance of transparent objects from different viewpoints, effectively disambiguating their material and refractive boundaries. We first create a synthetic dataset of transparent objects with their ground truth segmentations and correspondences, which enables the training of our model using a self-supervised framework. The key contribution of our method lies in the introduction of a novel coherence-aware loss function that enforces spatial and angular consistency between the reconstructed transparent objects from multiple viewpoints, thereby facilitating robust segmentation. We demonstrate the efficacy of our TransCut method through extensive quantitative and qualitative evaluations on both synthetic and real-world light-field image datasets, showcasing its superiority over state-of-the-art approaches in achieving highly accurate and detailed segmentations of transparent objects. Our results offer promising avenues for applications in light-field image processing and biomedical imaging.

title: Mapping Images to Sentiment Adjective Noun Pairs with Factorized Neural Nets
Abstract: This study introduces a novel approach to map images to sentiment-based semantic pairs, consisting of adjectives and nouns, utilizing factorized neural networks. The proposed model, Image-Sentiment Factorization Network (ISFN), leverages the capabilities of neural networks to perform multidimensional sentiment analysis and semantic matching. The ISFN architecture is centered around a hierarchical factorization of sentiment adjective-noun pairs, where the model learns to map images to a probability distribution over these pairs. This factorization is further facilitated by employing a probabilistic neural network, known as the Variational Autoencoder (VAE), which enhances the model's ability to capture complex relationships between visual features and sentiment-based semantic pairs. Through a series of experiments on benchmark datasets, such as ImageEmotion and AVA, the effectiveness of the ISFN is demonstrated in terms of accuracy and robustness in image-sentiment matching tasks. The results show that the ISFN outperforms existing state-of-the-art models, highlighting the importance of incorporating sentiment-based knowledge into image representation learning. The proposed approach paves the way for applications in a wide range of fields, such as computer vision, human-computer interaction, and artificial intelligence, where understanding the sentiment and meaning of visual content is crucial for making informed decisions and generating appropriate responses.

title: Fidelity-Naturalness Evaluation of Single Image Super Resolution
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel dual-criterion approach for evaluating the fidelity and naturalness of single-image super-resolution (SISR) outputs. Currently, no uniform evaluation metric combines both fidelity and naturalness assessments to gauge the overall quality of SISR results. Our proposed dual-criterion evaluation metric, coined fidelity-naturalness score (FNS), assesses both the visual fidelity of the upsampled output to the reference high-resolution image and its naturalness, i.e., how well the output aligns with human perception of real-world scenes. We achieve this by leveraging two state-of-the-art quality assessment metrics, structural similarity index and visual information fidelity, to estimate the fidelity and naturalness of SISR outputs, respectively. Our experiments on five benchmark image datasets demonstrate that FNS significantly outperforms existing evaluation metrics, including peak signal-to-noise ratio, mean squared error, and structural similarity index, in determining the quality of SISR outputs. Furthermore, FNS rankings closely match human judgments of SISR output quality, suggesting its potential as a robust and informative quality metric for SISR evaluation. By providing a more comprehensive evaluation framework, FNS enables researchers and practitioners to develop more effective SISR methods that prioritize both fidelity and naturalness, thus advancing the state-of-the-art in this field.

title: Ground-truth dataset and baseline evaluations for image base-detail separation algorithms
Abstract: This study aims to address the critical need for standardized ground-truth datasets and comprehensive baseline evaluations in the field of image base-detail separation algorithms. The lack of universally accepted evaluation metrics and datasets has hindered the advancement of these algorithms, thereby impeding their practical applications in various fields, such as image and video processing, computer vision, and graphics. Therefore, we develop a set of open-source ground-truth datasets for image base-detail separation, utilizing a range of natural images with varying base-detail configurations and levels of complexity. Our proposed datasets are designed to be easily accessible and extensible, allowing researchers to evaluate and compare the performance of their algorithms with high accuracy. To facilitate this process, we also conduct a comparative evaluation of six state-of-the-art algorithms using our newly created datasets and established evaluation metrics. Our results not only demonstrate the importance of standardized ground-truth datasets in facilitating fair comparisons among algorithms but also provide valuable insights into the strengths and limitations of each method. By sharing our findings and datasets with the research community, we hope to accelerate the development of image base-detail separation algorithms, ultimately paving the way for their widespread adoption in real-world applications. Our study sets a foundation for future research and development in this area by providing a much-needed benchmark for evaluating the performance of image base-detail separation algorithms.

title: An Immersive Telepresence System using RGB-D Sensors and Head Mounted Display
Abstract: Our research focuses on designing an immersive telepresence system utilizing RGB-D (Red, Green, Blue, and Depth) sensors and head-mounted display technology. The proposed system aims to enhance remote communication and collaboration experiences by providing users with a high degree of presence and immersion in a remote environment. By leveraging the capabilities of RGB-D sensors, the system can accurately capture and recreate the depth information of a remote scene, enabling users to perceive their surroundings in a more natural and intuitive manner. The integration of head-mounted display technology further amplifies the sense of immersion, allowing users to seamlessly interact with the remote environment and engage with others in a more realistic and engaging way. To validate the effectiveness of our system, we conducted a series of user studies, which demonstrated significant improvements in user engagement, sense of presence, and overall satisfaction with the remote communication experience. The results of our research can be applied to a wide range of industries, including education, healthcare, and remote work, where immersive telepresence can greatly enhance collaboration, productivity, and overall user experience. Our findings contribute to a better understanding of the role of RGB-D sensors and head-mounted display technology in creating immersive and interactive telepresence environments.

title: Learning visual groups from co-occurrences in space and time
Abstract: This paper introduces VGC, a novel approach to learning visual groups from co-occurrences in both spatial and temporal contexts. Traditional computer vision methods for object categorization primarily focus on attributes of individual objects, overlooking the intricate relationships among objects in a scene. However, scenes are often comprised of multiple objects that frequently co-occur in space and time, forming complex patterns and associations. The proposed VGC model leverages these spatial and temporal relationships to identify and learn visual groups, a novel concept capturing objects that typically co-occur together. By exploiting these co-occurrences, VGC succeeds in uncovering semantic relationships that were previously missed or abstracted away. Our method employs an unsupervised learning framework that discovers densely co-occurring objects and then associates them to infer meaningful visual groups. Using a combination of dense spatial pyramids and temporal pooling, we design a feature extraction mechanism to efficiently represent these co-occurring patterns, which are then categorized using a metric-based clustering technique. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and generalizability of our approach in learning accurate and transferable visual groups, even under varying tasks and conditions, signifying the potential for real-world applications in scene understanding, image segmentation, and activity recognition, among others.

title: The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Noisy Data for Fine-Grained Recognition
Abstract: Fine-grained recognition tasks, which require distinguishing between subtle variations in objects or patterns, have long been a challenging problem for machine learning algorithms. The performance of current state-of-the-art models heavily relies on the quality and quantity of the training data. Conversely, the effectiveness of noisy or imperfect data for fine-grained recognition tasks has been largely overlooked. In this research, we uncover the "unreasonable effectiveness" of noisy data for fine-grained recognition by exploring the benefits and mechanisms underlying its use. Our analysis reveals that noisy data not only provides valuable information for robustness and generalization but also reduces the impact of overfitting and domain gap issues commonly associated with fine-grained recognition tasks. We demonstrate that models trained on noisy data outperform their clean-data counterparts on several popular fine-grained recognition benchmarks, including the CUB-200-2011, Cars196, and Stanford Dogs datasets. Furthermore, we propose a novel data augmentation technique that leverages the properties of noisy data to generate pseudo-labels and improve model performance. Our study offers new insights into the intriguing relationship between noisy data and fine-grained recognition and provides a framework for future research on the unsupervised learning of transferable representations from imperfect data.

title: Recognizing Activities of Daily Living with a Wrist-mounted Camera
Abstract: Recent advancements in computer vision and machine learning have opened new avenues for automatic recognition of daily activities, enabling the development of intelligent assistive technologies for elderly care, patient monitoring, and disability support. This study presents an innovative approach to recognizing activities of daily living (ADLs) using a wrist-mounted camera, addressing the need for more unobtrusive and wearable monitoring systems. By leveraging a convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture, our proposal captures and analyzes visual data from the wrist-mounted camera to identify a comprehensive set of ADLs, including personal grooming, meal preparation, and navigation. The proposed system combines both object-based and action-based representations of the visual data, enabling accurate classification of ADLs under various environmental conditions and user activities. This research demonstrates a reliable and efficient ADL recognition system that utilizes wearable sensors, paving the way for the development of more integrated and scalable health monitoring applications. The proposed system's potential to improve the quality of life for individuals with disabilities and the elderly is demonstrated through various experiments and comparisons with existing state-of-the-art approaches, showcasing its promise as a trustworthy and robust solution for real-world ADL recognition applications.

title: Images Don't Lie: Transferring Deep Visual Semantic Features to Large-Scale Multimodal Learning to Rank
Abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to multimodal learning to rank by leveraging the power of deep visual semantic features. Deep learning has revolutionized the field of computer vision, enabling accurate image classification, object detection, and scene understanding. However, its integration with traditional ranking methods lags behind, mainly due to the semantic gap between high-level visual features and user preferences. To address this issue, we propose a technique to transfer deep visual semantic features from one domain to another, specifically for large-scale multimodal learning to rank applications. Our method, dubbed Visual-Learning-Rank (VLRS), relies on a combination of transfer learning and ranking-based frameworks to derive a compact yet informative representation of images. By utilizing the latent semantic space of convolutional neural networks (CNNs), VLRS captures subtle yet discriminative visual patterns, which are then used to enhance the ranking capabilities of multimodal systems. Comprehensive experiments on standard benchmarks, including the proposed V-Rank and the widely recognized Roter, showcase the effectiveness of VLRS in lifting the state-of-the-art performance in large-scale multilingual image retrieval and ranking scenarios. By narrowing the semantic gap between visual features and user preferences, VLRS unlocks novel possibilities for large-scale multimodal applications, promising valuable insights into the unseen and unexplored realms of multilingual image search and ranking. Theoretical analysis and empirical evaluations highlight the broad applicability and competitive performance of VLRS in this cutting-edge research area.

title: Training CNNs with Low-Rank Filters for Efficient Image Classification
Abstract: Deep neural networks have become ubiquitous in image classification tasks, but their effectiveness often comes at the expense of computational resources and memory requirements. Recent advances in deep learning have shown that training convolutional neural networks (CNNs) with low-rank filters can significantly reduce these costs without compromising accuracy. However, the majority of existing methods focus on modifying the architectures or filters of pre-trained models, which can be both time- and resource-intensive. This paper presents a novel framework for training CNNs from scratch using low-rank filters, which we term LowRank-CNN. By leveraging the properties of low-rank matrices, our method efficiently learns compact and discriminative filter representations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of LowRank-CNN in various image classification benchmarks, including CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet, comparing its performance to state-of-the-art methods. Our experiments show that LowRank-CNN achieves comparable accuracy to existing approaches while reducing the number of model parameters and computational requirements by up to 50%. Furthermore, we show that our method can be easily integrated into existing optimization algorithms and can be deployed on both GPUs and CPUs, making it a promising solution for real-world image classification tasks. Overall, our work provides a more efficient and scalable approach to training CNNs, with significant implications for the development of future deep learning architectures.

title: Superpixel Convolutional Networks using Bilateral Inceptions
Abstract: Superpixel Convolutional Networks using Bilateral Inceptions propose a novel methodology that integrates the merits of superpixel-based representations with the advanced feature extraction capabilities of deep neural networks. Traditionally, superpixel algorithms have been utilized in image processing tasks as pre-processing steps, resulting in a more compact and semantically meaningful representation of images. However, the discriminative power of superpixels can be further enhanced by employing them as a fundamental unit within deep neural networks. This innovation leverages the concept of bilateral inceptions, which combines bilateral filtering, a technique that reduces noise by averaging two images (one blurred and one sharp), with inception-inspired modules to achieve a more robust superpixel-based feature representation. The proposed network framework for image classification exploits these advanced superpixel features to yield improved performance. To demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed model, comprehensive experiments are conducted on popular benchmark datasets, showcasing its superior accuracy and efficiency over state-of-the-art superpixel-based and deep neural network architectures. Key challenges associated with integrating superpixel representations into deep neural networks are robustly addressed through this framework, enabling the development of more efficient and accurate image analysis systems that benefit from the strengths of both methodologies. By combining the respective capabilities of superpixels and deep neural networks, the proposed network paves the way for innovative applications in image classification and computer vision.

title: Hand Pose Estimation through Semi-Supervised and Weakly-Supervised Learning
Abstract: Hand pose estimation is a fundamental task in computer vision, essential for various applications such as gesture recognition, human-computer interaction, and robotics. However, traditional supervised learning approaches face significant challenges in achieving robust hand pose estimation due to the sheer complexity of the hand's anatomy, the variability in posing, and the requirement for large amounts of annotated training data. To alleviate these issues, this study explores semi-supervised and weakly-supervised learning methods for hand pose estimation. In particular, we investigate the effectiveness of self-supervised learning, using autoencoders and contrastive learning to pretrain convolutional neural networks (CNNs) on unlabeled hand images. Additionally, we propose a strategy that involves leveraging weak labels, such as hand region proposals and hand pose class labels, to facilitate learning from limited amounts of annotated data. Through a comprehensive evaluation on several benchmark datasets, we demonstrate the potential of these approaches in achieving high-accuracy hand pose estimation results, outperforming traditional supervised learning methods in many cases. Furthermore, we provide an in-depth analysis of the effects of different pretraining schemes, data quality, and label types on the performance of the proposed semi-supervised and weakly-supervised learning methods, providing valuable insights for future research in this area.

title: Semantic Diversity versus Visual Diversity in Visual Dictionaries
Abstract: This study examines the interplay between semantic diversity and visual diversity in visual dictionaries, focusing on their reciprocal effects on user engagement and cognitive load. The experimental design consists of a 2x2 between-participant factorial task that manipulated the level of semantic diversity (high, low) and visual diversity (high, low) in a visual dictionary. The results show significant main effects of both semantic diversity and visual diversity on user engagement, with high semantic diversity leading to increased exploration and low visual diversity increasing perceived text congruence and comprehension of target concepts. However, a critical observation was that while visual diversity negatively impacted navigation and user experience for users encountering high semantic diversity content in the same visual dictionary, users finding low-semantic diversity content accessed visual dictionary visually with little to no navigation burden. Hierarchical regression analyses also indicate that the model should predict, user experience measured in terms of ease of navigation as the significant mediator for the interaction effect between semantic diversity and visual diversity in visual dictionary, which in turn predicted user engagement as an outcome measure. This research contributes to a better understanding of how balancing semantic and visual diversity can impact user experience in visual dictionaries and has implications for the design of effective, multimodal visual aids for learning and communication.

title: Multi-view 3D Models from Single Images with a Convolutional Network
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel methodology for reconstructing multi-view 3D models from a single monocular image, utilizing a convolutional neural network architecture. The core idea revolves around an encoder-decoder framework, which efficiently captures and learns the underlying 3D features from the given input image. The proposed network leverages a set of sparse 3D keypoints as guidance, which are detected by a separate but learned module. By incorporating these keypoints and leveraging symmetry and perspective constraints, the network effectively generates viewpoints for a 3D model corresponding to these keypoints. These viewpoints collectively form the described 3D model, which further enables the determination of occlusion relationships and spatial geometries. Validation studies show that the proposed method outperforms existing monocular multi-view reconstruction methods, consistently providing results that are more reflective of real-world scenarios in terms of the resulting geometric accuracy, structural completeness, and viewpoint coherence. Moreover, the proposed method does not necessitate any user-defined correspondence or calibration step, which commonly constitute significant challenges for the existing approaches, especially when limited data is available. The approach therefore presents a robust, general-purpose solution for generating accurate 3D models from non-calibrated monocular images.

title: Direct Prediction of 3D Body Poses from Motion Compensated Sequences
Abstract: This study introduces a novel framework for direct prediction of 3D body poses from motion-compensated sequences. Building upon recent advancements in deep learning and computer vision, we propose a neural architecture that leverages the synergy between convolutional and spatial neural networks to achieve high-accuracy 3D human pose estimation from 2D skeletal data. By fusing the motion-compensated sequences with an adaptive 3D model-based learning approach, our model is able to effectively capture the intricacies of human motion and accommodate variations in body shape, size, clothing, and pose. The proposed framework not only improves upon existing 2D-based pose estimation methods by enabling 3D pose prediction but also mitigates limitations associated with marker-based systems. The comprehensive evaluation of our method on multiple publicly available datasets, including Human3.6M, MPI-INF-3DHP, and MSCOCO, demonstrates its robustness and accuracy in diverse motion scenarios. The results show significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods in terms of the average precision and accuracy metrics. Furthermore, the time-efficient and real-time-capable architecture of our model enables real-world applications in fields such as video analysis, robotics, sports analytics, and human-computer interaction. Overall, our proposed framework offers a promising solution for direct prediction of 3D body poses from motion-compensated sequences, opening up avenues for cutting-edge research in computer vision and human pose estimation.

title: Top-k Multiclass SVM
Abstract: This paper presents an exhaustive investigation into the convergence and efficiency of top-k multiclass support vector machines (SVMs), a class of algorithms uniquely capable of handling large-scale multi-class classification problems with a huge number of classes. Although conventional multiclass SVMs offer reasonably good performance, their training efficiency and scalability degrade sharply with an increase in the number of classes, rendering them ineffective for real-world applications with more than a thousand classes. In this work, we systematically explore top-k multiclass SVMs with polynomial, linear, and radial basis function (RBF) kernel functions and investigate their theoretical convergence rates using established learning machinery. Our analysis reveals novel convergence results for top-k multiclass SVMs, showcasing their impressive optimization capabilities for diverse kernel functions. To further promote their broad industrial applicability, we provide efficient training and prediction algorithms for top-k multiclass SVMs, leveraging modern algorithmic techniques and scalable data structures to tackle extensive dataset sizes. Through a comprehensive set of empirical experiments on several applications domains, including text categorization, image classification, and network node classification, we demonstrate the efficacy of top-k multiclass SVMs as a fundamental component in solving tasks that require accurate classification of vast numbers of classes. By consistently outperforming state-of-the-art baselines, the presented top-k multiclass SVM methods offer significant usability gains for researchers and practitioners aiming to unravel intricate real-world data.

title: Deep End2End Voxel2Voxel Prediction
Abstract: Deep End-to-End Voxel-to-Voxel Prediction has garnered substantial attention in recent years due to its vast potential to transform various medical imaging applications, including computer-aided diagnostics, image denoising, and image reconstruction. The traditional approach to voxel-based prediction relies on decoupling the spatial and intensity information within images, which often necessitates complex data transformations and compromises on reconstruction accuracy. To address these limitations, researchers have focused on developing end-to-end architectures that enable the entire prediction pipeline to be learned concurrently. This computationally intensive task demands sophisticated design and optimization strategies, one of which includes leveraging the capabilities of deep neural networks. Inspired by the efficacy of deep learning in processing sequential and hierarchical data structures, a novel voxel-to-voxel prediction approach has been proposed, which employs a lightweight attention mechanism and a deformable convolutional architecture. The resulting framework is capable of efficiently processing three-dimensional inputs, extracting spatial contextual features, and making voxel-wise predictions. However, the convolutional structure used in the proposed model is still computationally expensive for handling complex volumetric data. Therefore, our investigation aims to design a superior model for voxel-to-voxel prediction that leverages parallel computing and adaptively selects high-level and spatial feature representations to better exploit hardware capabilities, thereby enhancing processing efficiency while maintaining accuracy. The significance of this research lies in its potential to provide a holistic automated medical image analysis solution that enables faster and more accurate diagnostic outcomes with fewer human interventions.

title: Personalizing Human Video Pose Estimation
Abstract: Human video pose estimation is a fundamental computer vision problem that enables the prediction of 3D human pose from 2D video frames. Despite recent advancements, existing methods often struggle to capture inter-personal pose variations, yielding inaccurate predictions for individuals with distinctive body shapes or motion styles. Personalizing human video pose estimation can address this limitation by learning subject-specific pose representations. This research proposes a novel framework for personalized pose estimation, which leverages a subject-agnostic video-embedding-based approach and a subject-specific personalization module. The subject-agnostic module is trained on a large-scale dataset to learn robust 3D pose representations from video inputs, while the subject-specific module is designed to refine these representations for each individual, accounting for person-specific pose variations. Our proposed framework is evaluated on several benchmark datasets, demonstrating significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy and robustness. Furthermore, a comprehensive qualitative analysis demonstrates that the personalized approach eliminates pose prediction errors that occur due to cross-person variations, making it particularly suitable for applications where pose estimation is critical, such as surveillance, gaming, and human-computer interaction. Results show that personalized human video pose estimation has a promising potential to address long-standing challenges in human pose estimation.

title: Stories in the Eye: Contextual Visual Interactions for Efficient Video to Language Translation
Abstract: Video-to-language translation has gained significant attention in recent years, driven by advances in deep learning and increased availability of large-scale video datasets. However, translating visual information into natural language efficiently remains a challenging task, particularly for tasks that demand contextual understanding and nuanced nuance, such as describing a scene in a video. Current approaches often rely on manual annotation of regions of interest (RoIs) or spatial attention mechanisms to focus on specific parts of the image or frame. However, this can be time-consuming and limit the capabilities of the model. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to address this issue by leveraging contextual visual interactions in the form of "stories in the eye," a concept borrowed from scene understanding in images, where objects interact and influence each other's presence and attributes. This approach allows for more flexible and accurate modeling of complex visual relationships, enabling the model to recognize patterns and intentions that might be missed by focusing on individual objects or regions alone. By combining this new approach with state-of-the-art encoder-decoder architectures, we demonstrate significant improvements in efficiency and accuracy for video-to-language translation tasks, opening new possibilities for applications in media analysis, film summarization, and more. Our work makes a significant contribution to the field by providing a new framework for video-to-language translation that prioritizes contextual visual interactions.

title: Tracklet Association by Online Target-Specific Metric Learning and Coherent Dynamics Estimation
Abstract: Our research proposes a novel tracklet association method that integrates online target-specific metric learning with coherent dynamics estimation to robustly estimate multi-object trajectories in various complex and dynamic environments. The proposed method, referred to as O-TSML-CDE, learns object-specific distance metrics in real-time using online learning techniques, allowing the model to adapt to changing environmental conditions and varying object observations. By associating tracklets and modeling inter-object interactions, O-TSML-CDE can effectively mitigate the effects of occlusions, clutter, and varying appearance changes that commonly plague multi-object tracking tasks. Furthermore, the incorporation of coherent dynamics estimation helps to refine the estimated object locations by accounting for the smooth and physically plausible motion patterns governed by the laws of physics. To evaluate the efficacy of O-TSML-CDE, extensive benchmark experiments are conducted on several challenging multi-object tracking datasets, including the MOTChallenge, KITTI, and EuroCity-person benchmarks. Results indicate significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods, demonstrating the robustness and reliability of O-TSML-CDE in real-world scenarios. With its ability to adapt to dynamic environments and its consideration of object interactions, O-TSML-CDE presents a promising tracklet association approach for various applications, including autonomous driving, surveillance, and robotics.

title: Recurrent Semi-supervised Classification and Constrained Adversarial Generation with Motion Capture Data
Abstract: This study proposes a novel framework for recurrent semi-supervised classification and constrained adversarial generation with motion capture data. The primary challenge lies in effectively leveraging a limited amount of labeled data while incorporating unlabeled data and realistic synthetic samples generated by adversarial networks to enhance model performance. To address this challenge, this study introduces a Recurrent Gaussian Mixture Model (RGMM) that integrates a mixture of Gaussian distributions to model complex motion patterns, with each component belonging to different classes. The proposed model is able to capture the long-term dependencies within motion capture sequences while effectively utilizing both labeled and unlabeled data. Furthermore, this study introduces a constrained adversarial generation framework that leverages the RGMM to generate realistic motion capture sequences under certain constraints. The generated samples are then used to augment the training set, while ensuring that the resulting classifier maintains class-conditional normality. Experimental results demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed framework in comparison to existing state-of-the-art methods, showcasing improved generalization and robustness in classification tasks with motion capture data. The proposed framework has significant implications for various applications, including human action recognition, motion prediction, and medical diagnosis, where precise analysis and interpretation of human motion patterns are critical.

title: DeepCut: Joint Subset Partition and Labeling for Multi Person Pose Estimation
Abstract: DeepCut: Joint Subset Partition and Labeling for Multi Person Pose Estimation is an efficient and accurate approach for multi person pose estimation that overcomes the limitations of existing methods. Traditionally, multi person pose estimation algorithms consist of two stages: subset partition and labeling. Subset partition involves segmenting a single image into different human body parts, while labeling involves assigning a class and a specific pose to each detected part. In DeepCut, these two stages are intelligently combined into a single model that iteratively segments the image into smaller subsets of pixels and assigns a class to each detected body part simultaneously. The model achieves this by using a multi-task loss function that includes both a partition term and a labeling term. The network uses a U-Net architecture and a feed-forward neural network structure to efficiently process a large number of images and body parts in real-time. In extensive qualitative and quantitative evaluations, including a complex multi person pose estimation dataset, DeepCut produces accurate and faster results compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, demonstrating its potential in various applications such as human-computer interaction, healthcare, and security. the network's robustness and flexibility, along with its reduced computational requirements, can potentially provide unprecedented performance in video data analysis and surveillance systems, further revolutionizing the field of computer vision.

title: Multi-Contrast MRI Reconstruction with Structure-Guided Total Variation
Abstract: This study develops a novel multi-contrast MRI reconstruction framework, leveraging the combination of structure-guided total variation (TV) and state-of-the-art deep learning techniques to optimize image quality and robustness. In MRI scanning, acquiring multi-contrast images can provide rich anatomical information, but the diverse data sets often suffer from noise artifacts and inconsistent quality. To address these challenges, the proposed approach employs an anatomically aware, structure-guided TV regularization that incorporates prior knowledge of tissue anatomy and spatial coherence. By effectively leveraging prior anatomy and reducing noise, the structure-guided TV regularizer enables the enhancement of low-contrast MRI features and structural details. The developed deep learning-based reconstruction model was trained on publicly accessible datasets and achieved impressive results on generalization and adaptation to real-world images. Specifically, quantitative experiments on a wide range of multi-contrast datasets revealed significant improvements in texture preservation, noise reduction, and tissue delineation. Comprehensive visual comparisons further highlighted the methods' ability to restore fine structures and subtle anatomical details. By concurrently enhancing image resolution, quality, and depth of field, the proposed approach offers vast potential for clinical applications and research studies that rely on fast, high-resolution, and noise-suppressed MRI data.

title: Towards Arbitrary-View Face Alignment by Recommendation Trees
Abstract: This study presents a novel approach to address the challenge of arbitrary-view face alignment, where a given face image is aligned to a reference view, especially when the input face image has extreme pose or non-frontal view. The introduced Recommendation Tree-based method, RT, learns to navigate the face alignment problem by predicting the series of face landmark transformations in a hierarchical and incremental manner. Unlike other methods that typically rely on a predefined set of poses or a predetermined transformation path, RT exploits the self-similarity among different poses of an object to recommend the most effective transformations to achieve the desired alignment view. Built upon the strengths of Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) and Transformer-encoded 3D models, RT is highly adaptable and can leverage multi-scale information for higher accuracy. Qualitative evaluations on benchmark datasets and visual comparisons demonstrate that RT can recover face appearances from arbitrary views more robustly, reducing the reliance on manual annotation of the target pose and yielding promising prospects for facial analysis and various applications involving face image recognition. Furthermore, RT exhibits comparable or superior performance to state-of-the-art methods on popular benchmark datasets, showcasing the effectiveness of Recommendation Tree-based face alignment.

title: TEMPO: Feature-Endowed Teichmüller Extremal Mappings of Point Clouds
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel framework, TEMPO, which stands for Feature-Endowed Teichmüller Extremal Mappings of Point Clouds, aimed at establishing correspondences between point clouds while accurately preserving intrinsic geometry and semantic features. By leveraging the powerful representation capabilities of point cloud features and the flexibility of Teichmüller extremal mappings, TEMPO tackles the challenges of feature-aligned point cloud matching in a unified and coherent manner. The approach combines the merits of traditional methods that focus solely on shape correspondence and those that consider both shape and feature similarity, thereby ensuring that the established mappings not only preserve the structural coherence of the input point clouds but also capture their semantic attributes. The proposed framework entails four key components, including a feature-aware point set registration method, a Teichmüller extremal mapping for establishing correspondences between the feature-aligned point sets, an attribute-preserving mapping for mapping semantic attributes between the input point clouds, and an evaluation metric for assessing the goodness of the established mappings. Experimental results on a variety of point cloud datasets derived from different domains demonstrate the effectiveness and versatility of TEMPO in performing feature-aligned point cloud matching, and show its potential in applications like computer-aided design, scene understanding, and robotics. Overall, the TEMPO framework provides a scalable and flexible tool for accurately solving a fundamental problem in geometry processing and feature alignment.

title: Crowd Behavior Analysis: A Review where Physics meets Biology
Abstract: This review delves into the intricate intersection of physics and biology in crowd behavior analysis, a rapidly evolving field with significant implications for urban planning, emergency response management, and social sciences. From the mechanical models of crowd flow and the Navier-Stokes equations to the adaptive behavior of individuals and the emergence of complex collective phenomena, we extensively surveyed the existing literature to reveal the multi-disciplinary nature of this field. Our analysis comprehensively covers various experimental and theoretical approaches to understanding crowd dynamics, including data-driven models, agent-based simulations, and statistical physics techniques. Furthermore, we explore the applications of these approaches in analyzing real-world crowd scenarios, such as evacuation simulations, urban congestion management, and crowd control during public events. The interplay between physics and biology in crowd behavior analysis has led to the development of novel insights into the self-organization and collective intelligence of human crowds, often yielding counterintuitive and surprising results. By providing a comprehensive review of the current state of knowledge in crowd behavior analysis, this paper aims to bridge the gap between theoretical and practical developments, stimulate further interdisciplinary research, and promote the innovative application of crowd behavior analysis in diverse domains, ultimately contributing to safer, more efficient, and more livable cities.

title: ElSe: Ellipse Selection for Robust Pupil Detection in Real-World Environments
Abstract: This study focuses on developing an improved pupil detection technique for real-world environments, addressing the challenges posed by non-frontal faces, varying lighting conditions, and background complexity. The proposed method centers on ellipse selection, leveraging the properties of the iris region and the elliptical shape of pupils, to enhance the robustness of pupil detection. By applying a novel pre-processing technique that reduces noise and improves edge detection, the method generates an initial set of potential ellipse candidates within the region of interest. Subsequent refinement involves elliptical shape based matching, which employs techniques such as edge-directed refinement and boundary constraint to discard non-elliptical shapes. In addition, the implementation of an adaptive thresholding mechanism for ellipse classification helps eliminate false positives. The effectiveness of the developed technique is demonstrated through extensive experiments on challenging datasets, showcasing improved detection accuracy and robustness compared to state-of-the-art methods. By integrating the ellipse selection strategy into the pupil detection pipeline, this research makes significant contributions to the advancement of automatic pupil detection systems, enabling wider applications in fields such as biometric identification, emotional analysis, and driver monitoring. The proposed approach is a critical advancement in dealing with the complexities of real-world pupil detection and facilitating the development of more reliable and efficient systems.

title: Acceleration of the PDHGM on strongly convex subspaces
Abstract: The Parallel Douglas-Rachford Hybrid Projection Gradient Method (PDHGM) is a widely used optimization algorithm for minimizing the sum of multiple norms of vectors, with each norm corresponding to a subspace of the Euclidean space.  While it has been shown to converge to the optimum for strongly convex optimisation problems on Euclidean spaces, the convergence rate seriously deteriorates for PDHGM when these strongly convex subspaces have a small intersection, such as in the case of k-subspaces for small values of k.  To accelerate the PDHGM for such problems, this work proposes a novel approach based on a combination of local and global information of the strongly convex subspaces, at the intersections, and globally.  We show that by leveraging these pieces of information, the convergence rate of the PDHGM can be significantly improved, and that under certain regularity conditions, the proposed approach achieves a linear convergence rate.  Furthermore, we demonstrate the efficacy of our method through numerical experiments using a variety of structured optimisation models, including polyhedral approximations of strongly convex bodies, nuclear norm regularized least squares, and a constrained rank minimization problem. The experiments indicate a substantial reduction in computation time over existing algorithms for several problem classes, demonstrating the value of our proposed acceleration scheme.

title: A dense subgraph based algorithm for compact salient image region detection
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel dense subgraph-based algorithm for compact salient image region detection, which significantly improves the accuracy and efficiency of existing methods in identifying visually distinctive regions within an image. The proposed algorithm leverages the dense subgraph hypothesis, which posits that salient regions often contain densely connected pixels, and integrates it with a graph-based approach to effectively capture the local and global structures of image data. The architecture is comprised of two primary components: an image representation module that transforms the input image into a dense graph, and a novel Salient Region Detector (SRD) that identifies regions with high saliency scores using a multi-scale analysis of graph adjacency matrices. The theoretical advantages of the proposed method are further validated through a comprehensive set of experiments on six benchmark datasets and comparisons against state-of-the-art algorithms. Results indicate that the proposed dense subgraph-based algorithm consistently outperforms existing models in terms of both detection accuracy and computational efficiency, underscoring its potential to serve as a reliable and efficient backbone for various downstream applications, including image segmentation, object recognition, and content-aware image/video analysis. The method's interpretability and generalizability are also demonstrated through detailed visualizations and evaluations on diverse image categories and scenarios, ultimately providing a cohesive framework for enhanced salient image region detection.

title: Compression of Deep Convolutional Neural Networks for Fast and Low Power Mobile Applications
Abstract: This abstract presents a comprehensive study on the compression of deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs) for efficient deployment on low-power mobile devices. The exponential growth in the size of DCNNs has led to significant computational requirements and power consumption, making their widespread adoption on mobile devices challenging. To address this issue, this research focuses on developing novel compression techniques for DCNNs that can preserve their accuracy while significantly reducing their memory footprint and computational complexity. The proposed method involves a two-stage approach: (1) a neural architecture search is conducted to identify the essential connections and weights within the DCNNs, and (2) a quantitative analysis is performed to evaluate the impact of different pruning and quantization strategies on the model's performance and power consumption. Experimental results on various image classification tasks demonstrate that the proposed compression techniques can achieve a significant reduction in model size and computational requirements, leading to 2-4 times faster inference times and 50-70% reduction in power consumption, making them suitable for mobile applications. The proposed method not only provides significant improvements in model compression but also offers insights into the design and optimization of DCNNs for mobile devices.

title: WIDER FACE: A Face Detection Benchmark
Abstract: The widespread adoption of Facial Recognition Technology (FRT) has been hindered by the dearth of efficient and large-scale face detection benchmarks. Existing face detection datasets are often limited by their small size, narrow demographic scope, and inconsistent annotation, leading to biased and unreliable performance evaluations. In response, Yang, Liu, and Luo proposed the WIDER FACE dataset as a comprehensive and inclusive benchmark for face detection algorithms. This new dataset compiles over 20,000 images acquired from theWorld Wide Web, covering a diverse range of face occlusion, pose, scale, and expression variations. With a focus on capturing real-world complexities, WIDER FACE includes challenging scenarios such as faces in the crowd, partial occlusion, and varying lighting conditions. The dataset is further annotated with fine-grained labels, ensuring a high level of accuracy and consistency in performance evaluation. By leveraging the WIDER FACE dataset, face detection research can move beyond controlled laboratory settings and focus on tackling the complexities of real-world applications, ultimately paving the way for more practical and effective deployments of FRT in multimedia processing and computer vision domains.

title: Integrating Deep Features for Material Recognition
Abstract: This research presents a novel approach to material recognition by integrating deep features from multiple domains to improve the accuracy and robustness of material classification models. In recent years, deep learning techniques have been widely adopted for visual recognition tasks due to their exceptional performance in capturing complex patterns and features. However, the effectiveness of these models heavily relies on the domain-specific datasets and architectures used to train them. Our research aims to bridge this gap by proposing a multi-domain feature integration framework that combines the strengths of different deep learning models to improve material recognition performance. We leverage the saliency information from attention networks and the convolutional neural network (CNN) representations to propose a coherent framework that enables joint learning of discriminative features across multiple domains. Furthermore, to alleviate the limited availability of large-scale domain-specific datasets, we develop an approach to knowledge graph-based data augmentation that can adaptively expand the training set to cover diverse and expansive materials. The proposed framework is thoroughly evaluated on a range of texture-based material recognition datasets, demonstrating its superiority over state-of-the-art models in both accuracy and generalizability to unseen materials. The framework's ability to integrate diverse features and augment the training dataset makes it a valuable tool for a wide range of applications in material processing, robotics, and computer vision.

title: Bidirectional Warping of Active Appearance Model
Abstract: The Active Appearance Model (AAM) has been a crucial tool in image analysis for its ability to establish a parametric representation of object shape and appearance, facilitating precise tracking and pose estimation. However, in practice, the bidirectional warping of AAMs becomes challenging due to limitations in its capacity for accurately handling self-intersections and deformations resulting from transformations that cannot be represented linearly. Recent studies have focused on improving AAM's bidirectional warping capability through incorporation of various constraints and innovative warping methods. This paper presents an exhaustive review of these efforts, and introduces a novel approach integrating the characteristics of both linear and non-linear warping methods to effectively tackle the problem of bidirectional warping in AAMs. The proposed method is formulated as a multi-linear blend of conventional linear interpolation and non-linear warping that incorporates variable weightings to adaptively determine the extent to which either linear or non-linear warping should be applied based on the characteristics of the input data. A comparative evaluation of the performance of the proposed approach with existing methods, including their limitations in handling specific types of transformations, demonstrates a significant improvement in the ability to bidirectionally warp instances belonging to the AAMs in question, thus contributing to enhanced efficiency and robustness in image analysis tasks that necessitate accurate pose estimation and facial animation.

title: A Simple Hierarchical Pooling Data Structure for Loop Closure
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel hierarchical pooling data structure for efficiently resolving loop closure in mobile robots. Loop closure is a fundamental problem in simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) that involves detecting when a robot revisits a previously explored location, typically from a different angle or scale. Existing methods for loop closure detection often rely on computationally expensive feature detection and matching techniques, which can hinder real-time navigation applications. Our innovative pooling data structure uses a hierarchical approach, integrating local edge invariant features at multiple scales, resulting in a compact and robust representation of the environment. The proposed data structure is optimized for efficient storage and retrieval of features, facilitating fast matching and loop closure detection. Unlike traditional methods that store and compare every feature with every other, the hierarchical pooling data structure enables incremental learning and feature sharing through its inherently compact design, reducing the computational complexity and mitigating the curse of dimensionality. Our experimental results demonstrate that the proposed hierarchical pooling data structure outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy, speed, and online learning capabilities, showcasing its potential in improving loop closure detection for various mobile robot applications.

title: DOC: Deep OCclusion Estimation From a Single Image
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel Deep OCclusion Estimation (DOC) algorithm that accurately predicts the extent of occlusions in a given image. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have revolutionized the field of computer vision, enabling the automatic estimation of complex scene properties from a single image. However, estimating accurate occlusions from a single image remains a challenging problem. Most existing methods rely on multi-image inputs, which are not always available, or simple threshold-based methods that may not capture the complexity of real-world occlusions. The proposed DOC algorithm addresses this gap by leveraging the power of deep learning to develop a robust and accurate occlusion estimation framework that operates on a single image. Our approach involves training a CNN to predict the occlusion segmentation map from the input image, using a novel combination of spatial and contextual information. We demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed algorithm on a suite of benchmark datasets and provide extensive qualitative and quantitative evaluations. The results show that our DOC algorithm significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of precision, recall, and F1-score. Furthermore, the proposed algorithm provides a novel insight into the relationship between occlusion and contextual information, paving the way for improved understanding and modeling of complex occlusion behaviors in real-world scenes.

title: Deep Metric Learning via Lifted Structured Feature Embedding
Abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to deep metric learning via lifted structured feature embedding, which enables the learning of more discriminative and robust features for comparison-based tasks such as person re-identification and image retrieval. By integrating the notion of structure and invariance into the context of deep networks, our proposed framework is capable of capturing complex relationships within feature distributions and abstracting away nuisance factors, thus leading to enhanced model robustness against variations in pose, lighting, and occlusion. The core innovation lies in the introduction of a lifted structured feature embedding module, which is composed of a series of learnable projection and pooling components designed to effectively aggregate high-order interactions between features. This enables the network to learn hierarchical and distributed representations of visual information, which can be utilized for more efficient and accurate comparison of feature vectors. Through extensive experiments on several benchmarks, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed approach in achieving state-of-the-art performance over the existing methods, thus providing a compelling proof-of-concept for its applicability in various real-world applications requiring robust and discriminative feature learning. Our results underscore the value of integrating structured and invariant representations into deep metric learning, and provide insights into the design of more powerful and flexible feature comparison architectures.
