title: Learning to decompose for object detection and instance segmentation
Abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach for learning to decompose objects into constituent parts, a crucial task in object detection and instance segmentation. Most existing architectures rely on fixed-sized feature extractors or multi-stage refinement pipelines to produce structured outputs, which often struggle with varied object compositions and orientations. In contrast, our proposed framework, dubbed Object Decomposition Network (OD-NET), learns to simultaneously detect and segment objects alongside their constituent parts through a single end-to-end learning process. By incorporating a part-aware skip connection mechanism and a structural part-aligning loss, OD-NET is able to adaptively decompose objects into interpretable and coherent parts. Evaluations on standard benchmarks reveal significant improvements in object detection and instance segmentation performance, particularly in scenarios with complex object structures and varying part compositions. Furthermore, OD-NET's interpretability and robustness under different views and poses are demonstrated through qualitative and quantitative analysis. By capturing the complex relationships between objects and their parts, our framework offers a more comprehensive understanding of scene understanding tasks and serves as a step towards more reliable and explainable perception systems. With its flexible and adaptable architecture, OD-NET has the potential to be applied in a wide range of computer vision applications, including autonomous driving, robotics, and industrial inspection, where accurate object composition and structural understanding of the environment are critically important.

title: Learning Representations from EEG with Deep Recurrent-Convolutional Neural Networks
Abstract: The extraction of informative representations from electroencephalography (EEG) signals has become a crucial aspect in neuroscientific research and brain-computer interface (BCI) development. Traditional signal processing techniques rely heavily on hand-engineered features, which can be time-consuming and inefficient, thereby limiting their real-world applications. Recent advancements in deep learning have led to the development of sophisticated neural network architectures, such as the deep recurrent-convolutional neural network (DRCNN), which have been successfully employed in various domains, including speech recognition, image classification, and natural language processing. In this study, we investigate the potential of DRCNN in learning representations from EEG signals, characterized by their complex and non-stationary nature. The proposed framework integrates the strengths of convolutional and recurrent neural networks to capture both spatial and temporal dependencies within EEG signals. Empirical results on publicly available datasets demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in extracting meaningful and informative representations from EEG signals, leading to improved classification accuracy and enhanced interpretability of neural activity. Furthermore, the generalizability of our proposed framework is evaluated across different electrode configurations and subjects, highlighting its potential in real-world BCI applications and paving the way for future research directions. Overall, our study provides a cogent argument for the employment of deep neural networks in EEG-based BCI systems, where our method emerges as a promising solution for enhancing the interpretability and reliability of neural decoding results.

title: Fast Metric Learning For Deep Neural Networks
Abstract: This paper presents an investigation into the realm of fast metric learning for deep neural networks, a critical yet unforgiving component of deep learning applications, particularly those involving facial recognition, image classification and clustering tasks. As deep neural networks undergo significant computations to calculate distances between data points and network-derived representations, an efficient metric learning approach holds a premium position in real-world applications, given its influence on the complexities and deployment difficulties seen in large-scale datasets. Currently, deep metric learning techniques either introduce overfitting through considerable hyperparameter tuning or forego the accuracy gained from these parameters in favor of computational efficiency, ultimately sacrificing critical discriminative power necessitated in robust applications. In aligning the convergence times and loss measures obtained by regular methods to learning speedup principles, a novel approach of embedding a temporal gradient magnitude and derivative computation within deep network layers aims to retain significant high-performance capabilities. After validating deep metric learning networks using the given method on MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets, results show that neural networks trained with the incorporation of novel speedup methods enable highly robust convergence and discriminative power corresponding to deep metric learning techniques, but yielding significant improvements compared to time-complexity focused approaches. The success obtained in high accuracy through temporally-induced model learning leads to potential realization approaches for large-scale applications and solutions relying on computing efficiency.

title: A convnet for non-maximum suppression
Abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS) using a deep Convolutional Neural Network (CNN). Traditionally, NMS is performed as a post-processing step after object detection, where low-confidence detections are removed to eliminate duplicates. However, this approach can lead to potential loss of detection accuracy and visual information. Our proposed CNN-based NMS aims to incorporate the context of the surroundings of objects into the suppression process, rather than solely relying on the confidence or scores of individual detections. The proposed network architecture consists of a backbone CNN for feature extraction, followed by multiple sub-networks for context-aware feature refinement and final suppression. The network is trained on a comprehensive dataset of annotated images, emphasizing the diversity of object appearances, sizes, and occlusion levels. The validation results demonstrate that our CNN-based NMS outperforms traditional NMS methods in detection precision and recall, while also maintaining the efficient processing speed required for real-time applications. By leveraging deep learning capabilities and incorporating contextual information, our approach offers improved object detection and a more comprehensive understanding of scene content, paving the way for enhanced applications in computer vision, robotics, and surveillance systems.

title: Unsupervised Representation Learning with Deep Convolutional Generative Adversarial Networks
Abstract: This paper delves into the realm of unsupervised representation learning using deep convolutional generative adversarial networks, shedding light on the mechanisms driving these architectures in self-learning tasks. The upsurge in deep learning techniques and the vast amounts of data available has made it possible to pursue unsupervised representation learning with unprecedented success. Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have proven themselves as particularly effective, with Deep Convolutional Generative Adversarial Networks (DCGANs) exhibiting superlative performance in capturing subtleties in images in a dataset, enabling novel applications in image-based domain adaptation and transfer learning. In this paper, an in-depth survey of existing deep unsupervised representation learning techniques employing DCGANs is conducted to appraise the role of different optimisation strategies and architectures in enabling them to learn high-level, data-invariant features in images. Through our experiments and ablation studies, it is shown that incorporating convolutional neural networks (CNNs) with diverse loss functions and regularisation methods plays a pivotal role in developing DCGANs capable of producing features that capture high-level abstractions of images. Our experimental results demonstrate the strong ability of DC-GANs in generating robust cross task and domain representations in images, thereby enhancing their applicability in numerous applications, including semi-supervised classification, clustering, and data imputation. Overall, our work provides a comprehensive understanding of the various design aspects and constituent components that must be considered when constructing DCGANs for unsupervised representation learning.

title: Delving Deeper into Convolutional Networks for Learning Video Representations
Abstract: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have revolutionized the field of computer vision by achieving state-of-the-art performance in image recognition, object detection, and segmentation tasks. A natural extension of image processing is video analysis, which has garnered significant attention in recent years due to its vast applications in surveillance, entertainment, robotics, and healthcare sectors. Video data, however, poses unique challenges due to its high-dimensional nature, varied temporal dynamics, and sparse sampling rates. To address these challenges, research in video representation learning has been actively pursued, focusing primarily on the use of 2D and 3D CNNs to extract informative features from video frames. Despite achieving promising results, these approaches often fail to fully capture the spatial-temporal relationships between frames, leading to suboptimal video representation learning. Recent studies have proposed various modifications to traditional CNN architectures, including the use of convolutional layer modifications, spatial-temporal graph convolutional networks, and hierarchical feature extraction. Despite these efforts, there remains a significant gap in the current understanding of video representation learning, particularly in terms of developing CNN architectures that can effectively integrate spatial and temporal information to produce robust and informative video representations. This research endeavors to systematically analyze and optimize spatial-temporal CNNs for learning accurate and compact video representations, with the ultimate goal of developing a foundational framework for various video analysis applications.

title: A Controller-Recognizer Framework: How necessary is recognition for control?
Abstract: This research paper delves into the realm of human-computer interaction by proposing a Controller-Recognizer Framework that harmoniously integrates control and recognition components to optimize user experience. By extensively examining the current state of the art in human-computer interaction, the study identifies an essential yet often overlooked question: How necessary is recognition for control? Through an extensive review of existing literature on human-computer interaction, artificial intelligence, and machine learning, the researchers pinpoint the limitations of conventional control systems that rely solely on user input. The proposed framework, built upon the principles of cognitive science and user-centered design, highlights the potential of recognition-aided control to provide users with more intuitive and efficient interaction with digital systems. Empirical experiments conducted to validate the framework demonstrate significant improvements in user performance, satisfaction, and usability when recognition is integrated into control systems. The results of this investigation shed light on the critical role that recognition plays in augmenting control, with profound implications for the development of more sophisticated and user-friendly interfaces. By systematically examining the interplay between control and recognition, the research provides valuable insights into the creation of more effective and engaging human-computer interactions that are grounded in a deep understanding of human cognition and behavior.

title: First Step toward Model-Free, Anonymous Object Tracking with Recurrent Neural Networks
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to anonymous object tracking, a long-standing problem in the field of computer vision that remains to be adequately addressed, particularly in scenarios where only a limited amount of information is available about the target objects. The primary focus of this work is to develop a model-free tracking system using Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) that can effectively track objects across multiple frames without relying on any prior information such as object classes, locations, or appearance features. This will be achieved by designing a RNN-based tracker that automatically learns to maintain a set of trackers for each object of interest. Leveraging the capability of RNNs in handling sequential data and learn dynamic patterns, the proposed tracker will be able to adapt to changes in the visual appearance of objects between frames, thereby enabling robust tracking performance even in scenarios with non-rigid objects, partial occlusions, and target disappearances. Furthermore, the proposed system will also be designed to be fully anonymous, meaning it does not require any object-specific information, labels, or correspondence between frames. The proposed approach will be evaluated on various challenging benchmarks to demonstrate its effectiveness in tracking objects across multiple frames without any prior knowledge about the objects. By eliminating the need for model-specific training and enabling the development of a fully anonymous tracking system, the proposed work significantly advances the current state-of-the-art in object tracking research.

title: Deep Manifold Traversal: Changing Labels with Convolutional Features
Abstract: Deep manifold traversal is a technique employed in artificial intelligence and machine learning to navigate through high-dimensional data with intrinsic dependencies, catering specifically to tasks like anomaly detection and unsupervised learning. The emerging phenomenon of deep manifold traversal, incorporating convolutional features in varying dimensions to traverse through data manifolds, has captured significant attention in recent years. This traversal technique's potential in understanding complex relationships within high-dimensional data can provide valuable insights for applications. By integrating convolutional neural networks and techniques like variational autoencoders, deep manifold traversal can model and extrapolate geometric structures, uncovering hidden patterns and facilitating the ability to traverse through the feature space according to underlying topology. Exploiting this approach can not only analyze high-dimensional data existing in deep manifolds with non-linear relationships but also devise unique algorithms for feature engineering. This can result in the generation of robust models for manifold learning, characterizing abstract knowledge more effectively in data-driven areas of research, consequently inspiring studies that explore label transformation, merging it with supervised learning protocols, and convolutional deep learning paradigm transformation with labels.

title: QBDC: Query by dropout committee for training deep supervised architecture
Abstract: Deep supervised learning architectures have seen widespread adoption across various domains due to their ability to effectively learn complex patterns and relationships within datasets. The cornerstone of these architectures lies in their ability to incorporate human-in-the-loop feedback and adapt to ambiguities in pre-defined objectives, addressing limitations inherent in traditional loss function-based optimizations. However, manually specifying annotation protocols, designing objective criteria, and identifying optimal model configurations for these complex setups can be arduous and computationally expensive. To address these challenges, a novel approach referred to as Query by Dropout Committee (QBDC) is proposed. By harnessing the adaptive and error-resilient nature of dropout regularization, the QBDC paradigm leverages an ensemble of models to iteratively refine the query space by interrogating input samples at critical junctures in training. These interrogations facilitate adaptive enrichment and pruning of samples based on their respective predictive importances, enabling an auto-tuning mechanism for convergence and efficiency. This learning setup promotes both active and passive interaction modalities, balancing supervisor engagement and model exploration. Such synergy between adaptive feedback accumulation and guided sampling facilitates accelerated discovery of the most informative instances, yielding improved accuracy and efficiency with minimal engineering and tuning. Furthermore, this paradigm alleviates the rigors of obtaining costly expert feedback by allowing for self-catalyzed identification of critical training data, catalyzing convergence rates and optimizing usage of expert feedback.

title: Learning to Generate Images with Perceptual Similarity Metrics
Abstract: This paper explores the application of perceptual similarity metrics in deep neural networks to generate photorealistic images. Traditional image synthesis methods primarily rely on pixel-wise Euclidean distance metrics for evaluation, which often fail to capture the nuances of human vision. On the other hand, perceptual similarity metrics such as the Inception Score (IS) and the Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) have proven effective in assessing the visual quality of generated images. Our research delves into the integration of these metrics within a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) framework, aiming to improve image generation capabilities and ensure that the produced images exhibit photorealistic features. By leveraging the power of perceptual similarity metrics, we design a novel loss function that combines the advantages of adversarial training and perceptual evaluation. The experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed method in generating high-quality images that are both visually appealing and perceptually similar to real-world examples. Moreover, we conduct an extensive analysis of the ablation study, architectural variations, and sensitivity to hyperparameters to provide insights into the performance and limitations of our approach. Our contributions to the field of image synthesis include a better understanding of the role of perceptual similarity metrics in evaluating and enhancing image realism.

title: Feature-based Attention in Convolutional Neural Networks
Abstract: This research delves into the realm of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and explores the concept of feature-based attention. Traditional CNNs have achieved impressive results in computer vision tasks, but often struggle with scenes of clutter, irrelevant details, and variations in object scaling. To overcome these limitations, a feature-based attention mechanism is introduced, which selectively focuses on the most relevant visual features in each image. By dynamically allocating attention weights to the learned features, this mechanism enables CNNs to learn hierarchical representations of images more robustly. The key contributions of this research include devising a novel attention module that fuses multi-scale features from different layers of the network, exploiting instance-level attention weights that adapt to diverse image contexts, and demonstrating the theoretical understanding of how attention weights contribute to image classification performance. Comprehensive experiments conducted on several benchmark datasets showcase the efficacy of the proposed feature-based attention mechanism, yielding significant improvements over state-of-the-art CNN architectures on both image classification and object detection tasks. The empirical results not only validate the strength of feature-based attention but also provide insights into its potential in overcoming limitations of traditional CNNs.

title: Geodesics of learned representations
Abstract: This paper delves into the mathematical analysis of geodesics in the context of learned representations, bridging the gap between geometric learning theory and feature embeddings learned from data. A geodesic in a metric space is the shortest path between two points under that specific geometry and is typically utilized to explain how features of similar classes or objects group together. In recent years, learned representations have garnered significant attention, especially for their success in computer vision and natural language processing tasks. These learned representations form a feature space whose geometry is often opaque and may contain geometric structure that we are eager to uncover. By constraining the learned representations within a geometric framework, we propose new insights into understanding discriminative features within those spaces. We utilize the properties of geodesics to study the topological properties of learned representations, studying the relative distance between points that are naturally grouped together by the encoding.  The primary question we address is how to analyze and understand the embedding that a neural network learns from data and what this analysis can tell us about the task that the network is trying to accomplish. Along the way, we also survey key findings in neural networks and information geometry, which form the foundation of our analysis. Our novel contribution lies in uncovering the specific properties of these learned representations, in comparison to fixed Euclidean spaces, and demonstrating their practical applications in real-world tasks.

title: Manifold Regularized Deep Neural Networks using Adversarial Examples
Abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to manifold regularization in deep neural networks, leveraging adversarial examples to enhance model generalizability and robustness. Traditional methods of regularization focus on the weights and the local structure of the dataset, whereas our approach considers the global manifold structure in feature space. We achieve this by utilizing adversarial examples as penalization terms in a regularized loss function, which encourages the model to learn meaningful representations that are robust to perturbations in the input space. Our framework benefits from the theoretical connection established between adversarial training and manifold regularization, providing a principled way to incorporate manifold regularization into deep neural networks. Through extensive experiments on several benchmark datasets, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in improving the model's robustness, generalizability, and calibration. We observe significant improvements in accuracy and other key performance metrics compared to the baseline models, particularly on datasets with complex manifold structures. Moreover, our approach is computationally efficient and can be seamlessly integrated into existing deep learning frameworks, making it an attractive solution for a wide range of applications. Overall, the proposed method highlights the potential of adversarial examples in enhancing the robustness and generalizability of deep neural networks, and its significance in promoting safe and reliable AI systems.

title: Unsupervised Learning of Visual Structure using Predictive Generative Networks
Abstract: This paper delves into the realm of unsupervised learning of visual structures by leveraging predictive generative networks, a novel approach that tackles the challenges of image understanding in the absence of labeled data. The proposed method relies on a self-supervised paradigm where the network is trained to predict the likelihood of a sequence of frames within a video, accounting for both the spatial and temporal relationships between visual features. By doing so, the model learns to infer the underlying visual structures, including contextual relationships between objects, spatial hierarchies, and coherent dynamics, in a data-driven and probabilistically sound manner. Our framework employs a recursive generative model, predicated on a predictive variational autoencoder, which progressively refines the representation of visual data by iteratively inferring and generating likelihood distributions over the observed frame sequences. This architecture enables the model to hierarchically decompose the visual structure, tracing key spatial and temporal features through the sequence. Through a series of both qualitative and quantitative evaluations on a collection of benchmark datasets, our results demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed predictive generative network in accurately capturing various aspects of visual perception, showcasing the versatility and scalability of the approach, while emphasizing its potential as a foundational tool in computer vision and neuroscience.

title: Efficient inference in occlusion-aware generative models of images
Abstract: Our work proposes novel architectures and algorithms for efficient inference in occlusion-aware generative models of images. Traditional generative models often rely on explicit occlusion handling, which can be computationally expensive and may not accurately capture real-world occlusions. In contrast, our occlusion-aware generative models leverage the strengths of unsupervised learning to naturally incorporate occlusions into the generative process. We present a new family of probabilistic graphical models, including a Bayesian network and a Markov random field, that can effectively model and reason about pixel-wise occlusions in images. These models are designed to efficiently capture the complex relationships between occluded and non-occluded regions, allowing for robust and flexible inference. To facilitate efficient inference, we derive novel algorithms for approximate Bayesian inference and expectation-maximization (EM) that exploit the graphical structure of our models. Our experimental results on various datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our occlusion-aware generative models and inference algorithms, showing improved performance in tasks such as missing data imputation, image completion, and image synthesis. By efficiently leveraging occlusion information, our models open up new avenues for applications in computer vision, including object tracking, scene understanding, and image denoising.

title: Order-Embeddings of Images and Language
Abstract: Order-embeddings of images and language provide a promising approach for capturing the underlying structure of multimodal data and enabling effective pairwise relationships between visual and textual representations. Recent advancements in multimodal learning have led to a renewed interest in order-embeddings, as they allow for learning compact embeddings of visual and textual sequences that preserve the relative order of elements within each modality. This abstraction is crucial for downstream applications such as image-text retrieval, image captioning, and visual question answering, where understanding the semantic relationships between different parts of the image and text is vital. In this study, we present an extensive empirical analysis of state-of-the-art order-embedding methods for images and text, examining their performance both in isolation and when combined to learn multimodal order-embeddings. By utilizing a range of benchmark datasets covering various tasks, including visual and textual similarity metrics, we find that incorporating order-embeddings significantly outperforms traditional learning methods, especially when dealing with input sequences of varying lengths. Our investigation into the representation properties of order-embeddings further reveals their capacity to learn modality-specific feature hierarchies, including low-level visual and high-level linguistic representations. We also analyze the impact of hyperparameters and architecture choices on the effectiveness of order-embeddings, providing novel insights and practical recommendations for downstream applications.

title: FRIST - Flipping and Rotation Invariant Sparsifying Transform Learning and Applications
Abstract: This paper presents the development and analysis of FRIST, a novel framework for learning flipping and rotation invariant sparsifying transforms, which enables efficient representation and recovery of signals in various applications. Typically, signals in real-world scenarios exhibit symmetric or rotational properties, but traditional sparsifying transforms fail to fully exploit these characteristics. FRIST addresses this limitation by introducing a novel flipping and rotation invariance constraint, which is seamlessly integrated into the standard sparsifying transform learning framework. The proposed method uses a combination of data augmentation techniques, such as mirroring and rotation, to generate additional training samples that account for signal symmetries, thereby boosting its ability to generalize to novel visual patterns. As a result, FRIST achieves state-of-the-art performance in image and signal recovery tasks, demonstrating its effectiveness in various application domains including image and signal processing, computer vision, and machine learning. The paper provides a comprehensive theoretical analysis and extensive experimental evaluation of FRIST, showcasing its speed, scalability, and compatibility with various learning frameworks. The robustness and accuracy of FRIST are examined on a wide range of datasets, including images, signals, and biomedical samples, highlighting its versatility in tackling diverse applications. By providing a flexible, efficient, and robust framework for flipping and rotation invariant sparsifying transform learning, FRIST has the potential to transform the field of data analysis and representation, paving the way for future breakthroughs in various interdisciplinary domains.

title: How much data is needed to train a medical image deep learning system to achieve necessary high accuracy?
Abstract: The advent of deep learning algorithms has revolutionized the field of medical imaging, enabling accurate diagnosis and treatment of various diseases. However, a crucial question remains: how much data is required to train a medical image deep learning system to achieve high accuracy? The complexity of medical imaging data, comprising multimodal images and various anatomical structures, necessitates a large-scale dataset to ensure that the model can generalize well across diverse populations and clinical scenarios. While the generalizability of deep learning models has been extensively studied, the exact amount of data required to achieve high accuracy in medical image analysis remains unclear. This study investigates the relationship between data size and model performance using a comprehensive review of 50 recent studies, involving a total of 170 datasets. We analyze the performance metrics of each dataset, examining the impact of data size on accuracy, precision, and recall. Our results reveal a non-linear relationship between data size and model performance, highlighting the vast discrepancies in data requirements for different imaging modalities and disease diagnoses. Furthermore, we identify key factors influencing data efficiency, including data augmentation, domain adaptation, and transfer learning. Our findings have critical implications for the development of medical image deep learning systems, emphasizing the need for standardized, large-scale datasets and effective data augmentation strategies to ensure accurate and robust model performance.

title: Robust Classification by Pre-conditioned LASSO and Transductive Diffusion Component Analysis
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel robust classification framework, which combines the strengths of pre-conditioned LASSO (PC-LASSO) and transductive diffusion component analysis (T-DCA) to improve the accuracy and robustness of machine learning models. The proposed approach addresses the limitations of existing classification methods by incorporating prior knowledge and transductive learning capabilities. Specifically, PC-LASSO is employed to identify the most relevant features from the raw data, while T-DCA is used to adapt the classifier to the specific data distribution of the test set. The combination of these two techniques enables the model to capture the abstract relationships between features and adapt to the data characteristics, thereby enhancing its robustness against noise and outliers. The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach on several benchmark datasets, including image classification and text classification tasks. Compared to state-of-the-art methods, the proposed framework exhibits significant improvements in classification accuracy and robustness, particularly in scenarios with limited training data or high noise levels. Additionally, the proposed approach shows promising results in feature selection and dimensionality reduction, making it a valuable asset for high-dimensional datasets. Overall, the proposed robust classification framework provides a reliable and efficient solution for accurately identifying patterns in complex data distributions, thereby facilitating real-world applications in various fields.

title: Unsupervised Deep Embedding for Clustering Analysis
Abstract: This research paper proposes an unsupervised deep embedding framework for clustering analysis, effectively addressing the limitations of traditional clustering algorithms. The increasing availability of high-dimensional data has made it increasingly challenging for existing clustering methods to effectively identify meaningful subgroup structures. Existing deep learning-based clustering methods often rely on supervision from labeled data, which may not be feasible in many real-world applications. Our proposed framework, called Deep Embedding Clustering (DEC), seeks to resolve this issue by leveraging self-supervised learning techniques to learn robust and informative embedding representations of the input data. The proposed method consists of an autoencoder-based component that learns a dense and low-dimensional representation of the input data, and a clustering component that groups the embedded data points into distinct clusters. DEC leverages a novel loss function that incorporates both clustering assignment and data reconstruction error, allowing it to efficiently explore and exploit underlying manifold structures in the data. By applying DEC to various benchmark datasets, we demonstrate its superiority over existing clustering algorithms in terms of clustering accuracy, stability, and robustness to noise and outliers. Our work addresses a critical gap in the literature on deep learning-based unsupervised clustering and has significant implications for various fields, such as data robotics, sensor networks, and bioinformatics, where unsupervised clustering analysis is crucial for data understanding and decision-making.

title: face anti-spoofing based on color texture analysis
Abstract: This research paper delves into the design and implementation of an advanced face anti-spoofing system based on color texture analysis. Conventional facial verification systems are vulnerable to various types of spoofing attacks, including 2D and 3D printouts, photos, and videos, which can pose significant security risks. In response to this challenge, we propose a novel approach that harnesses the power of color texture analysis to differentiate between real and fake faces. Our system utilizes a deep learning-based framework that extracts and analyzes the color textures present in facial images to determine their authenticity. The proposed system consists of two primary components: a color texture extraction module and a spoof detection module. The former utilizes a combination of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and texture analysis techniques to extract and represent facial texture features, while the latter utilizes a support vector machine (SVM) classifier to determine the authenticity of the facial image. In our experiments, we evaluate the performance of the proposed system on public benchmarks, including the CASIA-V5 and the REPLAY-ATTACK datasets. The results demonstrate that our system achieves competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art face anti-spoofing methods, with mean average precision (MAP) values ranging from 93.1% to 96.5%. The proposed system also exhibits efficient processing times, making it suitable for real-world face authentication applications. Our research highlights the effectiveness of color texture analysis in face anti-spoofing and provides valuable insights into the design of robust facial verification systems.

title: Why M Heads are Better than One: Training a Diverse Ensemble of Deep Networks
Abstract: The concept of training multiple models simultaneously has garnered significant attention in the realm of artificial intelligence, with the goal of harnessing the benefits of diversity and ensembling in deep neural networks. This research expedition explores the notion that training a diverse ensemble of deep networks can lead to improved performance and robustness compared to training individual models in isolation. Our inquiry delves into the mechanisms by which multiple models can collaborate to compensate for each other's weaknesses, resulting in enhanced overall accuracy and generalizability. A comprehensive analysis of the trade-offs between model diversity and ensemble performance is presented, shedding light on the intricate balancing act between maintaining diversity and minimizing the risk of overfitting. We introduce a novel technique for training a diverse ensemble of deep networks, which leverages a decentralized approach to mitigate interference between models and foster healthy competition. The experiments, conducted on a variety of benchmark datasets, demonstrate the superiority of our approach in several aspects, including accuracy, robustness, and efficiency. The findings of this research suggest that training a diverse ensemble of deep networks can be a highly effective strategy for improving the performance and reliability of deep learning systems, and thus has significant implications for a broad range of applications in computer vision, natural language processing, and beyond.

title: Spatio-temporal video autoencoder with differentiable memory
Abstract: This paper introduces a novel spatio-temporal video autoencoder architecture that incorporates differentiable memory to effectively model and learn short-term temporal dependencies and spatial hierarchies within video sequences. The proposed architecture, dubbed dif-MemVAE, leverages a spatial transformer module to fuse multi-scale spatial features from the input video frames, followed by a temporally-aware encoder that captures local dependencies using a hierarchical recurrent neural network (RNN) stack. Importantly, dif-MemVAE incorporates a differentiable memory component that enables the model to selectively retain or discard contextual information across time steps, thereby adapting to varying temporal scales and complexities. This memory mechanism also allows for efficient inference through a novel backward memory update scheme, which effectively reduces the computational complexity of the model while preserving its expressiveness. Through experiments on four benchmark video datasets (CIFAR-100-Videos, MNIST-V, UCF-101, and HMDB-51), we demonstrate that dif-MemVAE achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of both predictive accuracy and temporal representation learning, outperforming competing methods that rely on hand-designed temporal features and requiring minimal supervision during training. The proposed architecture exhibits promising results for a range of video-based applications, including video prediction, anomaly detection, and activity recognition.

title: Robust Convolutional Neural Networks under Adversarial Noise
Abstract:
This research delves into the realm of deep learning security by exploring the robustness of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) under the menace of adversarial noise. Adversarial attacks, where well-crafted input data are designed to mislead the model, pose a significant threat to the veracity of computer vision systems, including image classification and object detection tasks. As CNNs remain a cornerstone of computer vision due to their vast applications, the vulnerability of these networks to adversarial noise becomes a critical concern that necessitates a comprehensive understanding. 

Most current research efforts focus on developing novel attack strategies or improving the robustness of the models through modifications to their architectures or through data augmentation techniques. However, the overarching question of whether it is possible to create a universal defense mechanism against all forms of adversarial attacks remains a pressing issue. The key aim of this study is to comprehensively investigate the state-of-the-art defense techniques, develop a robust framework for evaluating model robustness, and propose novel methods to fortify CNNs against a wide variety of attacks. A comprehensive analysis of the trade-offs between the model's accuracy, robustness, and computational complexity will be performed to provide insights that could be used to inform practical engineering solutions for building more reliable and trustworthy vision systems that are impervious to malicious manipulations. The ultimate goal of this research is to bring the development of robust CNNs under adversarial noise to the threshold of practical applicability.

title: Foveation-based Mechanisms Alleviate Adversarial Examples
Abstract: The foveation-based vision system has gained significant attention in recent years due to its potential in addressing complex computer vision challenges, particularly those posed by adversarial examples. Adversarial examples are malicious inputs designed to mislead machine learning models, resulting in incorrect predictions. Traditional machine learning approaches often fail to mitigate these examples, leading to compromised model reliability and trustworthiness. Foveation, a mechanism emulating the human visual system's ability to focus on salient regions of an image, offers an innovative solution to tackle this issue. By leveraging the precision of a foveated attention mechanism combined with saliency-based methods, a model can effectively identify and emphasize vital information in the visual data. This enables the development of more robust and resilient models capable of withstanding adversarial attacks. The foveation-based mechanisms, once seamlessly integrated into machine learning frameworks, can provide significant improvements in adversarial robustness, thereby mitigating the risks associated with model vulnerabilities. This study investigates and showcases the effectiveness of foveation as a mechanism to alleviate adversarial examples and improve model reliability in computer vision applications.

title: Density Modeling of Images using a Generalized Normalization Transformation
Abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to density modeling of images through a Generalized Normalization Transformation (GNT). Building on the concept of generalized norms, GNT extends the traditional normalization techniques used in image processing to incorporate a more flexible and adaptive approach, allowing for the representation of complex image distributions. The proposed GNT formulation is based on the generalized inverse and Frobenius norm, which provides a more robust and efficient way to normalize images. Experimental results show that GNT outperforms existing normalization techniques, such as batch normalization and instance normalization, in tasks like image denoising and super-resolution. Furthermore, the GNT is evaluated on various datasets, including ImageNet and CIFAR-10, demonstrating its ability to generalize well across different image domains and applications. The proposed method has also been shown to improve the stability and convergence of deep neural networks, facilitating their use in more complex image processing tasks. Overall, the introduction of GNT as a novel approach to image normalization provides a new perspective on the representation and analysis of image data, with the potential for far-reaching impact in fields like computer vision, image processing, and machine learning.

title: Faster method for Deep Belief Network based Object classification using DWT
Abstract: This study proposes a novel and optimized approach to enhance the object classification performance of Deep Belief Networks (DBNs) using Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT). Traditional DBNs suffer from high computational complexity and time-consuming training processes, which hinder their adoption in real-world applications. The proposed method integrates DWT with DBN for feature extraction and dimensionality reduction, leading to a significant reduction in the number of parameters and training time. The DWT is applied to the input images to decompose them into multiple frequency sub-bands, capturing the local and global features of the objects. The developed approach is computationally efficient and extracts robust features that are used to train the DBN. Extensive experimental evaluations on well-known image datasets, including CIFAR-10 and MNIST, demonstrate that the proposed method achieves improved accuracy and reduction in dimensionality. The results show that the proposed DWT-based DBN outperforms various state-of-the-art object classification methods in terms of accuracy, training time, and computational complexity. The proposed approach is particularly beneficial for applications where speed and efficiency are crucial, such as real-time object recognition, surveillance, and autonomous driving systems. The study contributes to the optimization of DBNs for object classification tasks by leveraging the strengths of DWT for efficient feature extraction and dimensionality reduction.

title: Asymmetrically Weighted CCA And Hierarchical Kernel Sentence Embedding For Image & Text Retrieval
Abstract: Our research proposes an innovative approach to improve image and text retrieval performance by integrating Asymmetrically Weighted Canonical Correlation Analysis (AW-CCA) and Hierarchical Kernel Sentence Embedding (HKSE). Traditional correlation-based methods often fail to capture the essence of complex multimedia data, leading to suboptimal retrieval results. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel framework that combines the strengths of AW-CCA and HKSE. AW-CCA is used to model the unequal importance of features in image-text pairs, while HKSE is employed to encode text embeddings in a structured and interpretable manner. Specifically, we propose a multi-level hierarchical structure to capture semantic relationships between words and their contexts. The output of HKSE is then fed into an AW-CCA module, which allows for asymmetric weight assignment to preserve the contextual information. This complementary fusion enables the model to learn enhanced representations of images and texts that are more sensitive to the nuanced features and relationships within the data. Experimental results on standard benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, achieving state-of-the-art performance in image-text retrieval metrics. The proposed framework exhibits robustness and adaptability, outperforming existing methods in various retrieval scenarios. By leveraging the strengths of AW-CCA and HKSE, our approach sets a new benchmark for image-text retrieval and offers promising avenues for future research in multimedia data analysis.

title: Convolutional Clustering for Unsupervised Learning
Abstract: This paper proposes an innovative convolutional clustering approach for unsupervised learning, aimed at identifying meaningful patterns and structures in complex datasets. Building upon the strengths of deep learning and clustering algorithms, our method leverages convolutional neural networks to transform raw data into a feature space that is amenable to clustering. By exploiting the spatial hierarchies and local dependencies present in images and other high-dimensional data, our convolutional clustering framework is designed to capture subtle variations and patterns that may be missed by traditional clustering methods. A novel objective function is defined, which combines the principles of clustering and deep learning to effectively learn discriminative features from the input data. Through a series of experiments on benchmark datasets, including MNIST, CIFAR-10, and STL-10, our method demonstrates state-of-the-art performance in terms of clustering accuracy, purity, and runtime efficiency. Furthermore, the interpretability of the learned features is demonstrated through visualization and dimensionality reduction techniques, providing valuable insights into the underlying structure of the data. With its impressive performance and scalability, our convolutional clustering approach has the potential to revolutionize the field of unsupervised learning and become a powerful tool for data analysis and pattern discovery in a wide range of applications.

title: Multimodal sparse representation learning and applications
Abstract: Multimodal sparse representation learning has emerged as a promising technique for improved representation and analysis of complex data coming from multiple sources. By exploiting the discriminative power of sparse models, researchers have successfully tackled various challenges in tasks such as image classification, object recognition, and image denoising. This paper delves into the theoretical foundations and empirical applications of multimodal sparse representation learning, including its connection with traditional sparse and non-sparse methods. We discuss the strengths and limitations of existing approaches, highlighting the benefits of leveraging multimodal data representations that combine information from multiple sources. Furthermore, a comprehensive review of current state-of-the-art methods and techniques is presented, encompassing both dictionary learning and sparse coding methods. This encompasses various applications, including image classification, object recognition, image denoising, and activity recognition. We also delve into the implementation of multimodal sparse representation learning algorithms, providing insights into potential enhancements for future applications. A real-time implementation of multimodal sparse representation on biomedical images is demonstrated, showcasing its potential in enhanced image quality and disease diagnosis. Our analysis provides valuable insights into the advancements in multimodal sparse representation learning, shedding light on its future perspectives and areas for further investigation.

title: Towards Open Set Deep Networks
Abstract:
Abstract:
Deep learning has revolutionized the field of computer vision, achieving remarkable performance in various tasks such as image classification, object detection, and segmentation. However, traditional deep networks often assume that the test data belongs to the same distribution as the training data, which may not always be the case in real-world applications. This limitation can lead to catastrophic performance degradation when encountering out-of-distribution (OoD) or open-set data, i.e., data that falls outside the recognized classes. Open-set recognition is a fundamental problem that has received significant attention in recent years, with various approaches proposed to handle this challenge. Towards this end, this paper focuses on the development of deep networks capable of accommodating OoD data while maintaining high accuracy on known classes. We propose an innovative solution by introducing a novel criterion, the Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD), to differentiate between known and unknown classes based on the kernel-induced feature space. Furthermore, we develop a two-stage framework, consisting of a classification module for known classes and a novelty detection module for OoD inputs. Our proposed method is evaluated on several benchmarks, demonstrating superior performance and robustness compared to state-of-the-art approaches. Moreover, we examine the sensitivity of our model to hyperparameter settings and kernel choices, providing insights into its adaptability and reliability. The results obtained indicate that the proposed open-set deep network is a powerful tool for addressing the limitations of traditional deep learning models in real-world applications involving unknown or novel data classes.

title: Automatically selecting inference algorithms for discrete energy minimisation
Abstract: The development of inference algorithms for discrete energy minimisation has become increasingly prominent in the fields of computer vision, machine learning, and artificial intelligence. As the complexity of visual tasks continues to grow, so does the need for flexible and efficient inference algorithms to solve them. In this work, we propose a novel approach for automatically selecting inference algorithms for discrete energy minimisation based on the characteristics of the specific problem instance. Our approach uses a combination of machine learning techniques and computational graph analysis to identify the most suitable inference algorithm. We implement a variety of popular inference algorithms, including Graph-Cuts, Dual Decomposition, and the First-Order and Second-Order Operator-Cheung-Demyanov (FCOS and FECOS) algorithms, and evaluate their performance on a range of benchmark datasets. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed approach achieves state-of-the-art performance, often significantly outperforming traditional algorithm selection methods. Furthermore, our approach is flexible and can be easily extended to accommodate new inference algorithms and problem instances, providing a scalable and efficient solution for discrete energy minimisation problems in a variety of applications. By selecting the most effective inference algorithm for a given problem instance, we demonstrate substantial reductions in computational cost and improved accuracy, opening up new possibilities for tackling large-scale visual tasks.

title: What Players do with the Ball: A Physically Constrained Interaction Modeling
Abstract: This study investigates the physically constrained interaction between soccer players and the ball, focusing on the trajectories and dynamics of the ball during various types of passes and control movements. An extensive review of existing literature reveals that understanding player-ball interactions is crucial for analyzing techniques, identifying player characteristics, and informing coaching strategies. To address this, we develop a physically constrained interaction model that simulates the interactions between the ball, the player, and the environment, incorporating factors such as player speed, kinematics, ball spin, and aerodynamics. Our model is then validated through comparative analyses with empirical data from professional soccer matches, including trajectory tracking and player kinematics. The study also explores the relationships between player statistics, such as passing ability and dribbling skills, and the physical properties of the ball, such as air resistance and restitution coefficient. Additionally, we examine how variations in these physical properties and player characteristics affect the performance of passes and control movements, providing insights into the optimization of player skills and ball design. By shedding light on the physically constrained interaction between players and the ball, this research contributes to a deeper understanding of the physics behind soccer techniques and the development of more effective training strategies and ball designs.

title: Coreset-Based Adaptive Tracking
Abstract: This paper presents an adaptive tracking algorithm that utilizes a coreset-based approach for efficient learning and adaptation. In many real-world applications such as object tracking, task planning, and sequential prediction, the underlying data distribution often undergoes significant changes over time. However, the adaptability of existing tracking algorithms is limited due to their sensitivity to noise and large-scale changes in the environment. Our proposed algorithm, referred to as Coreset-Adaptive Tracker (CAT), exploits the benefits of coresets, a widely used technique in machine learning for reducing the dimensionality of large datasets while preserving their essential information. By employing coresets and an incremental learning framework, CAT enables efficient tracking in environments with non-stationary dynamics. The proposed algorithm assigns importance weights to each data sample based on its information gain, allowing it to adaptively select relevant data points from the streaming data. Through extensive experiments on various benchmark datasets, this work demonstrates the robustness and adaptability of CAT, showcasing its potential as a powerful tool for real-world tracking and prediction applications. In comparison to state-of-the-art trackers, CAT exhibits improved performance and efficiency in handling sudden changes in environments, making it a compelling solution for the emerging class of adaptive tracking problems.

title: Quantitative Analysis of Particles Segregation
Abstract:
This study aims to conduct a comprehensive quantitative analysis of particle segregation, a ubiquitous phenomenon in granular materials and industrial processes, such as powder flow, bulk material handling, and pharmaceutical manufacturing. Particle segregation can significantly compromise the quality and safety of final products, resulting in undesirable outcomes, customer dissatisfaction, and ultimately financial losses for industries involved. Despite its importance, the mechanisms governing particle segregation are not yet fully understood and current models are often unable to accurately predict the occurrence and extent of segregation in various scenarios.

Through a combination of experiments, numerical simulations, and statistical analysis, we investigate the impact of particle size, shape, surface properties, and initial packing conditions on segregation patterns during material flow. Our results reveal that particle size and shape play a crucial role in determining the level of segregation, while surface properties, such as friction and cohesion, also significantly influence segregation patterns. Furthermore, we demonstrate that initial packing conditions have a dramatic impact on segregation, highlighting the importance of addressing packing conditions in practical applications.

Our findings have far-reaching implications for the development of more accurate models of particle segregation and the design of segregation-averse systems and equipment. By providing insights into the underlying mechanisms of particle segregation, this study can inform improvements in industrial processes, leading to improved product quality, reduced costs, and enhanced safety. Ultimately, our research aims to contribute to the development of targeted strategies for mitigating particle segregation and optimizing the efficiency and effectiveness of material handling and processing operations.

title: Semi-supervised Learning for Convolutional Neural Networks via Online Graph Construction
Abstract: This paper presents a novel semi-supervised learning framework for Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) that leverages online graph construction to efficiently adapt to new and unlabelled data streams. Our proposed method, coined as OSN, capitalizes on the inherent geometric structure present in the data by incrementally assembling an adjacency matrix that highlights the intrinsic relationships among data points. OSN harnesses an adaptive mechanism to determine the importance of each edge in the evolving graph, ensuring that only influential relationships are maintained. The incorporation of this dynamic graph structure enables the CNN model to effectively distinguish between noise and meaningful connections, thereby facilitating robust identification of patterns and informing more informed predictions. Through a series of extensive experiments, we demonstrate that OSN consistently outperforms state-of-the-art semi-supervised learning algorithms on various benchmark datasets, often in a much more efficient manner. Furthermore, we showcase OSN's flexibility and adaptability by seamlessly integrating it with transfer learning techniques to tackle previously unseen domains with minimal additional overhead. Our findings conclusively validate the merit of online graph construction in semi-supervised learning for CNNs, underscoring its potential to yield substantial performance gains while reducing the need for exhaustively annotated training data.

title: Principled Parallel Mean-Field Inference for Discrete Random Fields
Abstract: This work presents a principled approach to parallel mean-field inference on discrete random fields, leveraging the stochasticity of Gaussian graphical model approximations to develop a scalable and accurate algorithm for probabilistic inference. By exploiting the mean-field assumption, the proposed framework enables the computationally expensive inference steps to be separated and distributed across multiple processing units, while maintaining the consistency and accuracy of the obtained estimates. The core contributions of this research lie in the novel formulation of parallelizable message passing schedules and the derivation of an efficient, distributed algorithm for computing variational lower bounds. Empirical evaluations demonstrate the systematic improvement in inference speed with minimal loss of accuracy achieved through principled parallelization, bringing forward a robust method for tackling numerous machine learning and computer vision tasks. Application domains include discrete Markov Random Fields, Bayesian image segmentation, and computer vision tasks, such as object recognition and image denoising. By combining rigorous mathematical derivations, scalable design principles, and empirical testing, the new approach is poised to set a new benchmark for the community in large-scale discrete inference problems, contributing to advancements in applied probabilistic reasoning and data-intensive research.

title: Variable Rate Image Compression with Recurrent Neural Networks
Abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to variable rate image compression utilizing recurrent neural networks (RNNs). The proposed method leverages the strengths of RNNs to achieve adaptive bitrates by learning complex patterns in images, enabling highly effective and efficient compression. The architecture of the RNN-based compressor takes into account the statistical properties of image data, allowing for the allocation of bits in a manner that balances between rate and distortion. A two-stage process forms the backbone of the proposed method, where the first stage involves the application of RNNs to the image, generating a compact representation of the original data. Subsequently, this representation is further processed using a variant of the Huffman coding algorithm, which dynamically adjusts the bitrate allocation to meet the needs of different image content. The efficacy of the proposed approach is demonstrated through a comprehensive comparison with existing state-of-the-art image compression methods, including JPEG-LS and various deep learning-based techniques. Experimental results show that the RNN-based compressor achieves significant reductions in bitrate without compromising essential image quality metrics such as peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) and structural similarity index (SSIM). The study showcases the potential of RNNs in designing adaptive image encoders and decoders that can work seamlessly with modern multimedia applications and storage systems, ensuring a scalable and efficient compression framework.

title: Learning Deep Structure-Preserving Image-Text Embeddings
Abstract: This research work focuses on developing a novel framework for learning effective image-text embeddings that preserve the underlying structural relationships between images and their corresponding text descriptions. Existing image-text embedding methods typically suffer from lacking the ability to capture the hierarchical structure of the image and the text, leading to suboptimal performance in various downstream tasks such as image retrieval, text-to-image synthesis, and visual question answering. Our proposed framework tackles this limitation by incorporating a deep structure-preserving mechanism, which enables the captured embeddings to maintain the nuanced relationships between images and texts. By leveraging a combination of a hierarchical attention mechanism and a graph-based structure-preserving module, our framework can accurately capture the hierarchical structure of both images and texts, thus facilitating more effective and efficient information exchange between visual and linguistic modalities. Comprehensive experiments on several benchmark datasets demonstrate that our proposed framework achieves state-of-the-art performance on various image-text tasks, showcasing its effectiveness and robustness in modeling intricate structural relationships between images and texts. Furthermore, our framework also facilitates faster convergence and improved stability during the training process, highlighting its practical significance in real-world applications. Overall, our work offers a significant step forward in the field of image-text embedding and has the potential to inspire new research directions in the future.

title: Structured Depth Prediction in Challenging Monocular Video Sequences
Abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive study on developing a structured depth prediction model that robustly handles challenging monocular video sequences. With the widespread adoption of single-camera systems in numerous applications, accurately estimating depth from monocular videos has become an increasingly important task. The proposed framework leverages advances in both convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and geometric reasoning to tackle the limitations of traditional depth estimation approaches, such as relying on simplistic heuristics and failing to capture underlying structural properties of scenes. Our structured depth prediction model utilizes a novel two-branch architecture, which combines a CNN-based encoder with a geometry-aware decoder, to predict scene depth and structure from video frames. Through a set of experiments on both publicly available and custom-generated datasets, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in dealing with difficult scenarios, such as occlusions, motion blur, and illumination changes. By incorporating contextual information from neighboring frames and leveraging scene geometry, our framework yields significantly more accurate depth predictions compared to state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, our model has the potential to be applied to various real-world applications, including autonomous driving, robotics, and surveillance, where precise depth information is crucial for ensuring safe and reliable decision-making processes.

title: Convolutional neural networks with low-rank regularization
Abstract: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have achieved remarkable success in various image classification tasks by leveraging their ability to extract hierarchical features. However, overparameterization is a key challenge that complicates the training and application of these models. To address this issue, low-rank regularization has been widely employed in machine learning, which has been shown to reduce the model's capacity while also facilitating the exploration of meaningful features. Inspired by this motivation, this research delves into the integration of low-rank regularization into CNN architectures to produce more efficient and trainable models. A thorough analysis of theoretical implications and computational experiments is undertaken to understand the effects of low-rank constraints on CNNs. The studies reveal that the incorporation of low-rank regularization into the model significantly reduces the overestimate of model complexity and minimizes overfitting. Consequently, CNNs equipped with low-rank regularization exhibit superior performance on image classification tasks while retaining the ability to adequately extract relevant features from images. The study also discusses the implementation and computational feasibility of incorporating low-rank regularization into CNNs using deep neural network frameworks.

title: Deep Learning for Tactile Understanding From Visual and Haptic Data
Abstract: Deep learning models have progressively enabled computers to comprehend and interpret sensory data from various modalities, including visual and haptic inputs. However, achieving a comprehensive understanding of tactile interactions by synthesizing data from different sensory streams remains an open challenge. In the realm of touch-based interactions, extracting meaningful cues and correlating visual and haptic patterns poses a significant research dilemma. This study focuses on developing techniques and frameworks that employ deep neural networks to infer and infer understanding of tactile experiences from a synergistic fusion of visual and haptic modalities. An extensive analysis is conducted to investigate the feasibility of leveraging deep learning algorithms in discovering correlations between visual representations, haptic patterns, and tactile perception. Our research objective is twofold: (1) devising innovative deep learning architectures that can efficaciously process and analyze both visual and haptic data streams, and (2) exploring novel data-driven approaches to enhance tactile understanding by augmenting sensory input modalities. Our study outcomes are envisioned to span a wide range of applications, from robotics and computer graphics to robotics-assisted surgical procedures, and virtual reality technologies. Ultimately, our work aims to contribute substantially to the advancement of tactile understanding from combined visual and haptic modalities and facilitate widespread adoption across diverse fields.

title: Compact Bilinear Pooling
Abstract: This paper presents an in-depth examination of the Compact Bilinear Pooling (CBP) technique, a prominent approach for aggregating pairwise feature interactions in deep neural networks. CBP is widely utilized in various Computer Vision applications, including image classification, object recognition, and scene understanding. By projecting the features of two input components onto lower-dimensional spaces, CBP effectively captures higher-order feature interactions. However, this procedure is computationally expensive and memory-intensive, making it challenging to deploy in real-time applications. Our research aims to resolve these limitations by proposing a lightweight and adaptable architecture for the CBP module. By employing a more efficient projection method and introducing a novel pooling strategy, we significantly reduce the computational complexity of the original CBP formulation. We integrate this compact CBP module into a state-of-the-art image classification framework and extensively evaluate its performance on the ImageNet dataset, showcasing substantial gains in both inference speed and accuracy. The proposed framework exhibits highly competitive results without compromising the original functionality of the CBP module, providing a feasible solution for its adoption in resource-constrained environments and enabling the integration of this powerful pooling technique into real-world applications.

title: What Objective Does Self-paced Learning Indeed Optimize?
Abstract: Self-paced learning has become increasingly popular in various educational settings, leveraging the unique abilities of each individual to progress through material at their own speed and timeframe. The key benefit of self-paced learning lies in its capacity to optimize flexibility, enabling learners to focus on areas where they need improvement, thereby improving overall knowledge retention. By allowing learners to allocate time more efficiently, self-paced learning also optimizes learner autonomy, potentially leading to a decrease in stress and anxiety levels associated with a traditional, one-size-fits-all classroom environment. Further, self-paced learning optimizes learner motivation, as learners feel a greater sense of agency and control in their learning experience. Another objective that self-paced learning optimizes is access to information, as learners can progress through the learning content at a pace that suits their needs and abilities, fostering greater understanding and deeper conceptualization of complex topics. Apart from these benefits, research has also shown that self-paced learning optimizes the efficiency of educational resources, reducing teacher workload and enabling more effective learning outcomes. Thus, considering these observations, it can be argued that self-paced learning indeed optimizes a multitude of objectives, with flexibility standing at the forefront. This indicates the immense potential of self-paced learning in transforming the way we approach education, moving towards a more learner-centric, personalized experience.

title: A Hierarchical Deep Temporal Model for Group Activity Recognition
Abstract: This paper introduces a novel Hierarchical Deep Temporal Model (HDTM) for effective group activity recognition. In real-world group activity settings, human behaviour is typically complex, social, and hierarchical in nature, involving a sequence of sub-activities that contribute to the overall activity. Existing deep learning based approaches have limitations in modeling hierarchical and temporal relationships among such sub-activities, often resulting in poor recognition performance. To address this issue, HDTM incorporates a hierarchical architecture that represents the group activity as a sequence of nested sub-activities, each represented by a set of temporal features. A multi-task learning framework is also utilized to jointly learn spatial and temporal hierarchies, as well as discriminative temporal relationships among sub-activities. Comparative evaluation on five challenging benchmark datasets demonstrates the effectiveness of HDTM in recognizing group activities with improved accuracy and interpretability. The proposed model performs competitively with existing state-of-the-art methods while providing a more intuitive understanding of group activities. Additionally, experimental analysis reveals that the spatial hierarchy plays a crucial role in enhancing the accuracy of HDTM. This study contributes towards developing more accurate and versatile hierarchical models for group activity analysis, leveraging their widespread applications in healthcare, social media, and surveillance systems.

title: Active Object Localization with Deep Reinforcement Learning
Abstract:
Active Object Localization with Deep Reinforcement Learning is a crucial problem in computer vision, which involves identifying the location of objects within an image or scene. This problem is particularly challenging due to the high variability in object appearances, poses, and backgrounds. Traditional methods have focused on discriminative approaches, where the object location is determined based on a pre-trained model that extracts features from the image. However, these methods often suffer from the limited domain knowledge embedded in the pre-trained models, leading to suboptimal performance in diverse and complex scenarios.

In contrast, this work explores a novel approach to Active Object Localization using Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL). Utilizing the principle of reinforcement learning, this approach learns to actively query image regions to collect semantic information, thereby progressively localizing the object of interest. By incorporating an experience replay mechanism, we can leverage past experiences to adapt to changing environments and accumulate knowledge, enabling the agent to generalize better across diverse object distributions. The proposed method leverages an Actor-Critic architecture to simultaneously explore the environment and select informative regions, thereby balancing between exploitation and exploration. With extensive experiments and evaluations on various benchmark datasets, we demonstrate the efficacy of our method in achieving state-of-the-art performance, while showcasing adaptability and robustness in confronting complex imaging conditions, including large occlusions, viewpoint changes, and illumination variations.

title: ABC-CNN: An Attention Based Convolutional Neural Network for Visual Question Answering
Abstract: The proposed model, ABC-CNN, presents a novel approach to the task of visual question answering by integrating the efficacy of convolutional neural networks with the attention mechanism. A distinctive characteristic of this model lies in its ability to learn selective and localized representations within input images, thus serving to improve performance in the realm of visual question answering. Utilizing a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) component that enables the selection of spatial regions of interest, coupled with an attention-based recurrent neural network (RNN), the generator transforms input information into a more comprehensive, attention-based contextual representation. A unique convolutional filter bank structure is implemented with the goal of fully capturing visual content and robustly capturing contextual information while avoiding potential overfitting. An extensive evaluation of the proposed ABC-CNN model on benchmark datasets like VQA 2.0, VQA 2.0-V2, VQA 2.0-V3, and VQA 2.0-Open, reveals a considerable increase in test accuracy compared to traditional visual question answering models. Ultimately, the innovative architecture enables the effective collaboration of spatial and contextual features in solving multi-step and multi-relation reasoning tasks within visual question answering scenarios.
