title: Sequential estimation of intrinsic activity and synaptic input in single neurons by particle filtering with optimal importance density
Abstract: This paper presents a novel approach for sequential estimation of intrinsic activity and synaptic input in single neurons by employing a particle filtering method with an optimal importance density. The accurate estimation of synaptic input and intrinsic activity is crucial for understanding the neural code and neural computation, and has important implications for the development of neuroprosthetic devices and brain-machine interfaces. The proposed method is based on a probabilistic model that represents the uncertainty in the estimation of neural activity and synaptic input. By iteratively updating the particles with an optimal importance density, the method is able to efficiently sample the posterior distribution of the neural activity and synaptic input. The results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency. The method is validated on simulated and in-vitro neural data, and is shown to be robust to variations in the neural activity and synaptic input. The proposed method has the potential to be used in a variety of applications, including neuroprosthetic devices, brain-machine interfaces, and neural decoding. The approach presented in this paper provides a novel solution to the problem of sequential estimation of intrinsic activity and synaptic input in single neurons, and has the potential to advance our understanding of neural computation and the neural code. Overall, the results of this paper demonstrate the potential of the method to be used in a range of applications involving neural activity decoding.

title: Feature Learning based Deep Supervised Hashing with Pairwise Labels
Abstract: This paper presents a novel feature learning-based deep supervised hashing framework that incorporates pairwise labels to efficiently learn effective hash functions for large-scale image retrieval tasks. The proposed framework, denoted as DSHP (Deep Supervised Hashing with Pairwise Labels), aims to tackle the limitations of existing hashing methods, which typically rely on expensive pairwise comparisons or simply employ pairwise labels as additional supervision signals without capturing their intrinsic semantic relationships. DSHP leverages a deep neural network architecture to learn a compact image representation that preserves the fine-grained semantic information of images. Meanwhile, a novel pairwise label learning strategy is designed to effectively capture the intrinsic semantic relationships between image pairs, which is leveraged to adaptively weight the pairwise similarity. By incorporating these two components, DSHP can efficiently learn hash functions that not only reduce the computational overhead of feature comparisons but also preserve the semantic similarity between images. Experimental results on several benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of DSHP, outperforming state-of-the-art hashing methods in terms of information retrieval accuracy and retrieval efficiency. Additionally, extensive ablation studies and visualized feature maps provide insights into the strengths of DSHP, highlighting its ability to capture subtle semantic differences between images.

title: When Naïve Bayes Nearest Neighbours Meet Convolutional Neural Networks
Abstract: The convergence of multiple machine learning paradigms has been a subject of increasing interest, with the potential for enhanced predictive accuracy and robustness. This study introduces a novel framework that seamlessly integrates the strengths of Naïve Bayes Nearest Neighbours and Convolutional Neural Networks, creating a powerful hybrid model for image classification tasks. The proposed approach leverages the locality-preserving properties of the Naïve Bayes Nearest Neighbours algorithm to identify informative features, which are then utilised to initialise the parameters of a Convolutional Neural Network. This process enables the network to learn richer and more abstract representations of the data through multiple layers of convolution and pooling operations. Experimental results obtained on benchmark image datasets demonstrate the significant improvement in classification accuracy when using the proposed hybrid approach, compared to adopting either methodology in isolation. Notably, the study showcases a substantial reduction in test error rates, alongside enhanced handling of complex feature distributions and diverse data variations. Furthermore, thorough analyses of the model's behaviour provide insights into the interplay between the Naïve Bayes Nearest Neighbours and Convolutional Neural Network components, underscoring the potential for future research directions. This investigation has far-reaching implications for the development of image classification models in various applications, and contributes to a deeper understanding of the interplay between disparate machine learning techniques.

title: Hand-Object Interaction and Precise Localization in Transitive Action Recognition
Abstract: Transitive action recognition, the understanding and interpretation of complex human activities involving object manipulation, remains a significant challenge in computer vision. Key to this challenge is the accurate detection and localization of hands and objects in the scene, as well as the precise tracking of the interaction between them. In this paper, we investigate the relationship between hand-object interaction and precise localization in transitive action recognition, utilizing a deep learning approach to model this complex scenario. Our proposed framework combines a hand-tracking model with an object-detection model, to accurately identify and localize both the interacting hands and objects in the scene, facilitating the successful recognition of transitive actions. Through extensive experiments and comparative analysis with existing state-of-the-art methods, we demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in achieving superior performance on challenging benchmark datasets, such as the Transitive Action Recognition dataset and the MPII Cooking Dataset. We find that the precise localization and accurate tracking of hand-object interaction play a critical role in the successful recognition of transitive actions, and our framework achieves state-of-the-art performance in this domain. The results suggest that the integration of hand-tracking and object-detection models offers significant performance gains in the recognition of complex human activities involving object manipulation.

title: Towards Vision-Based Deep Reinforcement Learning for Robotic Motion Control
Abstract: Vision-based deep reinforcement learning has emerged as a promising approach for robotics, enabling robots to learn complex motion control tasks through trial and error. However, existing deep reinforcement learning methods often rely on simulators or external sensors, limiting their applicability to real-world scenarios where visual feedback is unreliable or noisy. This research proposes a novel vision-based deep reinforcement learning framework for robotic motion control that leverages raw visual observations as the primary input source. The framework is based on a deep neural network architecture that combines a perception module for feature extraction with a policy network for action prediction. The perception module is designed to be robust to visual noise and variations, while the policy network learns the optimal control policy through trial and error. The proposed framework is evaluated using a robotic pushing task, where the robot learns to push objects in a cluttered environment by interacting with the environment and receiving visual feedback. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in achieving robust and efficient motion control, outperforming traditional control methods and existing deep reinforcement learning approaches that rely on external sensors or simulators. The proposed framework has the potential to revolutionize robot learning by enabling robots to learn complex motion control tasks in real-world environments.

title: ProNet: Learning to Propose Object-specific Boxes for Cascaded Neural Networks
Abstract: ProNet proposes a novel object detection method that addresses the limitations of traditional cascaded neural networks by learning to propose object-specific boxes. Unlike existing region proposal networks (RPNs) that rely on generic anchor boxes, ProNet generates highly specific and precise bounding boxes that significantly improve the efficiency and accuracy of subsequent neural networks. Leveraging a combination of architectural innovations and optimization techniques, ProNet generates refined object proposals without requiring extensive offline computation or laborious human annotation. Consequently, the cascaded object detector that follows ProNet achieves 3.6% AP boost over its anchor-box-based counterpart, as well as a considerable speedup of 2.5x inference time, demonstrating the practical applicability of ProNet in real-world object detection applications. This work contributes significantly to the advancement of effective and efficient object detection approaches, empowering the widespread adoption of object detection technology across various fields, from autonomous driving to surveillance and robotics, by taking a crucial step forward in reducing the complexity of object detection pipelines and identifying a clear roadmap for developing future generation object detection systems. The method was evaluated comprehensively using various benchmarks, covering a wide range of object categories, under various data augmentation schemes, and on diverse hardware platforms.

title: Shearlet-Based Detection of Flame Fronts
Abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to flame front detection utilizing shearlets, a mathematical tool for image representation that combines the advantages of wavelets and curvelets. Traditional detection methods often rely on visual processing techniques, which can be severely limited by low contrast scenarios, poor camera quality, or heavy noise in images. In contrast, the shearlet transform enables the efficient representation of anisotropic features, namely, the singularities and edges present in flame fronts. We develop an efficient algorithm that leverages the properties of shearlets to locate and classify flame fronts within images. This algorithm involves a three-stage process: initially, image preprocessing is applied to enhance the visibility of the flame front, followed by a shearlet-based transform that captures the directional features of the flame front. The transformed data is then used to identify the locations and shapes of the flame front, ensuring robust detection and object classification in diverse scenarios. The effectiveness of the proposed approach is demonstrated through a series of experiments, which show a significant improvement in detection accuracy when compared to existing methods, even in low image quality or noisy conditions. This research contributes to the advancement of accurate flame front detection technology and its potential applications in various fields, including combustion engines, steel production, and wildfire monitoring.

title: Automatic Content-Aware Color and Tone Stylization
Abstract: This paper presents a novel deep learning-based approach to automatic content-aware color and tone stylization, which enables users to achieve precise control over the aesthetic style of their images. Leveraging the power of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and conditional generative adversarial networks (Conditional GANs), our method effectively intrudes the subtle nuances of artistic styles onto individual images while preserving their original content. A key novelty of our approach lies in its ability to generate diverse stylized variants from a given image, allowing users to browse and select the most preferred stylization outcome. To this end, we develop a multi-resolution framework that efficiently adapts to variations in image texture, contours, and backgrounds, ensuring consistent stylization across all regions of the image. Our method also includes an intuitive and interactive UI that facilitates real-time exploration and adjustment of stylization parameters. Empirical evaluations on a range of representative images demonstrate that our approach surpasses state-of-the-art methods in terms of flexibility, robustness, and visual quality, making it an attractive solution for content creators seeking rapid and versatile image stylization capabilities. By harnessing the full potential of deep learning and neural imaging, this research provides a fundamental contribution to the field of image processing, paving the way for widespread applications in the realms of fine art, product design, graphic design, and media arts.

title: Grounding of Textual Phrases in Images by Reconstruction
Abstract: This research paper investigates the challenge of grounding textual phrases in images through the strategy of image reconstruction. With the proliferation of multimodal data, deep learning models have become increasingly adept at extracting meaningful representations from images. However, grounding textual phrases in images remains a notorious problem, with models often struggling to accurately correlate words and their corresponding visual contexts. To address this challenge, we propose a novel approach that leverages the power of image reconstruction to align images with textual phrases. Specifically, we present a novel framework, Image-Phrase Reconstruction (IPR), which generates images that best match a given textual phrase. IPR achieves this by utilizing a dual encoder-decoder architecture, where the encoder extracts a high-level representation of the image, and the decoder synthesizes an image from the extracted representation. Through extensive experimentation on various benchmarks, including MSCOCO, Flickr30k Entities, and Conceptual Captions, we demonstrate the efficacy of IPR in accurately grounding textual phrases in images. The results show a substantial improvement over state-of-the-art models in terms of phrase grounding accuracy, highlighting the potential of image reconstruction as a key component in multimodal models. Moreover, we provide an ablation study to understand the contribution of individual components in the IPR framework, further shedding light on the importance of image reconstruction for phrase grounding tasks.

title: Deep Multimodal Semantic Embeddings for Speech and Images
Abstract: Advances in deep learning have led to the development of multimodal learning architectures that enable effective fusion of different data modalities to capture rich contextual information. Multimodal semantic embeddings, in particular, have garnered significant attention in recent years due to their ability to learn robust and transferable representations that bridge the gap between various modalities. This paper presents a novel approach to constructing deep multimodal semantic embeddings for speech and images, leveraging the synergy between these two modalities to capture higher-level semantic concepts. Our proposed method, termed Multimodal Embedding Fusion (MEF), utilizes convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and recurrent neural networks (RNNs) to learn hierarchical representations of speech and images. The CNN module is designed to capture spatial features and geometrical structures from images, while the RNN module is employed to model temporal patterns and sequential dependencies in speech. The learned embeddings are then jointly optimized to maximize mutual information between the two modalities. We evaluate the effectiveness of MEF on several benchmark datasets, demonstrating state-of-the-art performance in multimodal classification and retrieval tasks. The experimental results validate the robustness of MEF in capturing discriminative features from both speech and image modalities, paving the way for its potential applications in multimedia analysis, human-computer interaction, and cognitive studies.

title: Online Principal Component Analysis in High Dimension: Which Algorithm to Choose?
Abstract: This abstract delves into the realm of high-dimensional data, where traditional Principal Component Analysis (PCA) faces significant computational challenges. Online PCA has emerged as a powerful tool to address these challenges by allowing for incremental learning and processing of large datasets. In high-dimensional settings, the choice of online PCA algorithm becomes crucial, as each option has its unique strengths and weaknesses. This study provides a comprehensive comparison of various online PCA algorithms, including online eigendecomposition, Randomized SVD, and incremental PCA, to determine their effectiveness in high-dimensional data. We evaluate the performance of these algorithms in terms of feature extraction, dimensionality reduction, and computational efficiency through extensive simulations and experiments on real-world datasets. The results show that the choice of algorithm heavily depends on the specific characteristics of the data, such as its dimensionality, sparsity, and noise level. Furthermore, our study highlights the importance of regularization techniques in enhancing the stability and accuracy of the algorithms. We also investigate the impact of batch sizes and learning rates on the performance of the algorithms, providing valuable insights into the hyperparameter tuning process. Overall, this research provides a thorough analysis of online PCA algorithms in high-dimensional settings, aiming to guide researchers and practitioners in selecting the most suitable algorithm for their specific applications.

title: Piecewise Linear Activation Functions For More Efficient Deep Networks
Abstract: Deep neural networks have revolutionized the field of artificial intelligence, surpassing human-level performance in various tasks. However, these networks suffer from inefficiencies due to the use of traditional activation functions, which can lead to exploding or vanishing gradients during backpropagation, hindering the learning process. To mitigate these limitations, researchers have turned to alternative activation functions that promote more efficient learning and stability. One such activation function is the piecewise linear function, which combines the benefits of linear and non-linear properties. This study explores the concept of piecewise linear activation functions for deep networks and evaluates their impact on network performance and efficiency. By employing different piecewise linear functions, we investigate how these alternatives improve backpropagation stability and reduce the need for complex weight initialization, thereby reducing the risk of exploding or vanishing gradients. Additionally, we assess the computational efficiency of these piecewise linear functions, demonstrating their advantages in term of accelerated convergence and lower energy consumption. Our results show that these novel piecewise linear activation functions are ideally suited for deep networks, and we believe they have the potential to become a crucial component in the construction of efficient and robust deep learning systems.

title: A Continuous Max-Flow Approach to Cyclic Field Reconstruction
Abstract: A continuous max-flow approach is proposed for reconstructing cyclic fields from sparse measurements, aiming to bridge the gap between traditional grid-based and model-free reconstruction methods. By treating the cyclic field reconstruction as a mapping between two spaces, the approach leverages the max-flow theory to find the optimal flow without discretizing the domain or imposing any specific assumptions on the field's behavior. The max-flow formulation allows for efficient computation and avoids the need for manually tuning parameters or employing iterative refinement techniques. A key contribution is the development of a novel mass-conserving extension of the continuous max-flow approach, ensuring that the reconstructed field adheres to the fundamental principles of incompressibility and the conservation of mass. By incorporating physical constraints and respecting the topological properties of the domain, the proposed method yields a more realistic representation of the cyclic field. Numerical experiments and comparisons with existing methods demonstrate the efficacy and robustness of the continuous max-flow approach in reconstructing complex cyclic flows from incomplete data. This work opens up new avenues for model-free and flexible reconstruction of cyclic fields, offering substantial potential benefits for various fields, including fluid dynamics, image processing, and data assimilation.

title: Complete Dictionary Recovery over the Sphere I: Overview and the Geometric Picture
Abstract: This work presents a novel approach to the problem of dictionary recovery in signal processing, specifically over the sphere of diagonal matrices. Traditional methods often rely on heuristics or specific structure assumptions about the dictionary, leading to suboptimal results or failure in practise. By shifting the focus to the geometric picture formed by the set of signal examples and the dictionary, the authors generate a complete algorithm for recovering the unknown dictionary from a noisy set of measurements. This algorithm leverages the geometric properties of the dictionary and incorporates tools from convex optimization, particularly from second-order cone programming and semidefinite programming. By manipulating the problem through a series of intermediate variables, the authors construct an algorithm that efficiently converges to the optimal dictionary. A significant advantage of this method is its geometric insight into dictionary recovery which interprets the problems as finding the closest subspace to a set of points that adheres to certain geometric properties. Key steps include normalising the set of signal examples, reconstructing the closest subspace, and normalising the reconstructed dictionary to ensure it lies on the sphere.

title: Hierarchical Recurrent Neural Encoder for Video Representation with Application to Captioning
Abstract: This abstraction delves into a novel hierarchical recurrent neural encoder framework specifically designed for representing video content. The proposed architecture effectively leverages the inherent hierarchical nature of video data by incorporating a two-level recursive neural network, with a lower-level encoder responsible for processing localized video segments and a higher-level encoder tasked with capturing the contextual and long-term dependencies present within the video. By engaging the lower-level encoder to extract spatial and temporal features from individual frames and then integrating these features utilizing a recurrent neural network, the proposed architecture yields richer and more nuanced representations of video content. Furthermore, this framework facilitates the modeling of temporal dependencies, allowing for the capture of sequential relationships within the video sequence. In the context of video captioning, the proposed hierarchical recurrent neural encoder framework achieves state-of-the-art results due to its ability to effectively capture the intricate temporal and contextual relationships within a video sequence. Experimental results indicate that the proposed approach consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, demonstrating the potential of this hierarchical recurrent neural encoder framework for a range of video-related tasks, including captioning, action recognition, and event detection.

title: God(s) Know(s): Developmental and Cross-Cultural Patterns in Children Drawings
Abstract: This study explores the concept of children's drawings as a developmental and cross-cultural benchmark for understanding their perceptions and expressions of the divine. Through a qualitative analysis of drawings submitted by children aged 4 to 12 from diverse ethnocultural backgrounds, the research sheds light on the complex and dynamic relationship between children's understanding of God and their cognitive, emotional, and social development. The findings suggest that children's drawings of God exhibit both universal and culturally specific patterns, reflecting their exposure to various religious and spiritual traditions. The study reveals that children's representations of God evolve from abstract and animistic depictions to more complex and anthropomorphic forms as they mature cognitively and socially. The results also highlight the significance of parental and cultural influences on children's conceptions of God, underscoring the role of social and cultural context in shaping their understanding of the divine. By examining the intersection of children's drawings, developmental psychology, and cross-cultural religious studies, this research contributes to our understanding of how children construct and express their beliefs about God and the role that these beliefs play in their emerging sense of self and place in the world. The study's findings have implications for religiosity, education, and child development, underscoring the importance of acknowledging and respecting the diverse ways in which children experience and express their spirituality.

title: A Directional Diffusion Algorithm for Inpainting
Abstract: This study proposes a novel directional diffusion algorithm for image inpainting, a task that aims to restore missing regions in images by synthesizing new data consistent with the surrounding environment. Traditional inpainting algorithms rely heavily on feature extraction and matching techniques, but they often struggle to capture the intricate details and structures present in real-world images. In contrast, our proposed algorithm incorporates a directional diffusion process that takes advantage of the spatial correlations and structural patterns inherent in images. By iteratively diffusing information from the surrounding regions towards the missing areas, our algorithm effectively adapts to the local image features and produces more realistic and cohesive inpainted results. Our approach is based on a deep neural network architecture that learns to predict the optimal diffusion patterns for a given image and inpainting mask. Through extensive experiments on various datasets, we demonstrate that our algorithm outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of both qualitative and quantitative metrics. Notably, our algorithm exhibits exceptional performance in filling large regions with complex boundaries and textures, making it a suitable solution for real-world image inpainting applications. The contributions of this study lie in the development of a novel directional diffusion algorithm and its successful demonstration on a range of challenging image inpainting tasks.

title: Visual7W: Grounded Question Answering in Images
Abstract: Visual7W, proposed as a visual common sense question answering task, extends the question answering capabilities in images by grounding questions in scenes, objects, or events presented within images. The task involves evaluating comprehensive understanding through retrieving the most relevant question relevant image information regarding image stimuli. It aspires towards providing more nuanced understanding by asking open-ended questions that include seven different question types: what, where, when, who, why, how, and in what context. This not only involves understanding object properties but also considering the relationships and spatial configurations between objects present within a scene, as well as scene understanding, entity actions, and causality between entities, thus demanding richer common sense and more versatile knowledge. By enabling accurate answering capabilities for images, Visual7W presents an intriguing yet challenging domain that needs further exploration, contributing greatly in developing a cognitive model which facilitates more robust, adaptable, and versatile visual question answering. This groundwork may also culminate in breakthrough advancements toward more intelligent and interactive interfaces and potentially contributes to pushing the boundaries of unsupervised, self-supervised, reinforced, as well as few-shot learning techniques in various relevant research disciplines and practical applications.

title: A GMM-Based Stair Quality Model for Human Perceived JPEG Images
Abstract: This research presents a novel quality model for staircases in JPEG compressed images based on the Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM). The proposed GMM-based stair quality model aims to quantify the perceived quality of staircases in JPEG compressed images from a human perspective. Existing quality metrics often fail to capture the artifacts introduced by JPEG compression, such as ringing and stair-step effects, which significantly impact the perceived quality of staircases. The proposed model employs a GMM algorithm to accurately capture the textures and patterns present in staircases, and incorporates this information into a comprehensive quality metric. By analyzing a wide range of JPEG compressed images, the results demonstrate that the proposed model achieves higher correlation with human perceived quality than existing quality metrics, including the widely used SSIM and PSNR. Moreover, the GMM-based model is able to effectively distinguish between different types of staircases, including smooth, textured, and linear patterns, and can detect subtle artifacts introduced by JPEG compression that would be missed by other quality metrics. Overall, the proposed model provides a reliable and accurate way to assess the perceived quality of staircases in JPEG compressed images, making it a valuable tool for image compression and quality assessment applications.

title: Multimodal MRI Neuroimaging with Motion Compensation Based on Particle Filtering
Abstract: This study presents a novel multimodal MRI neuroimaging framework that incorporates motion compensation based on particle filtering to address the fundamental challenge of motion artifacts encountered in functional MRI (fMRI) scans. The proposed approach integrates three key modalities, namely, T1-weighted anatomical imaging, multi-band Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI), and blood-oxygenation-level-dependent (BOLD) functional imaging, to provide a comprehensive understanding of brain structure and function. Particle filtering, a Bayesian estimation technique, is harnessed to model and predict subject motion, facilitating accurate real-time estimation of motion parameters and enabling informed data correction. The resultant method is extensively evaluated on both simulated and real fMRI data against state-of-the-art techniques, demonstrating significant reductions in motion artifact-induced signal distortions and improved accuracy in detecting subtle neural activations. The efficacy of the proposed framework is further validated through applications in assessing white matter integrity using DWI and characterizing cognitive networks with temporally-resolved BOLD signals. The developed technique shows vast potential for improving the sensitivity and specificity of fMRI-based diagnoses, as well as guiding tailored neurostimulation protocols in various neurological disorders. The proposed multimodal MRI neuroimaging framework with motion compensation is a significant advancement in the field of neuroimaging, offering improved data quality and robustness under real-world imaging conditions, ultimately contributing to a deeper understanding of the intricate neural mechanisms underlying human cognition and behavior.

title: Computational Pathology: Challenges and Promises for Tissue Analysis
Abstract: Computational pathology, an interdisciplinary field that combines computer science, machine learning, and pathology, has emerged as a revolutionary approach to analyzing and diagnosing tissue samples. Despite its promising potential, computational pathology is not without its challenges. One of the primary hurdles is the sheer complexity and variability of tissue structures and patterns, which can lead to inaccurate and inconsistent results. Moreover, the integration of high-dimensional microscopic images, genomics, and clinical data presents significant computational and analytical challenges. Current deep learning-based approaches have shown impressive results in detecting specific cancer types and biomarkers, but the reliability and generalizability of these models remain uncertain. However, the field holds great promise for improving diagnostic accuracy, reducing false positives and negatives, and streamlining the pathology workflow. Emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence-powered digital pathology platforms, computational annotations, and machine learning-based decision support systems are rapidly advancing the field. Furthermore, ongoing research focuses on standardizing imaging and annotation protocols, improving model interpretability, and addressing issues of explainability, fairness, and bias in AI-driven diagnosis. As computational pathology continues to evolve, it is likely to revolutionize the field of pathology, enabling precision medicine, and improving patient outcomes.

title: Write a Classifier: Predicting Visual Classifiers from Unstructured Text
Abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to visual classification using unstructured text, aiming to bridge the gap between text and visual representations. Despite the abundance of visual data in various domains, manual annotation of class labels remains a tedious and time-consuming task. The proposed classifier relies on leveraging text data as a proxy to infer the class labels of visual images. This is achieved by training a deep neural network to learn the associations between text features and visual features. The proposed method utilizes an embedding-based technique to convert text data into a compact, continuous representation. This embedding is then combined with visual features extracted from the image using convolutional neural networks (CNNs). The resulting text-visual fusion is fed into a fully connected network for visual classification. The proposed approach is evaluated on various benchmark datasets, demonstrating its efficacy in accurately predicting class labels with minimal annotation. The results are compared against state-of-the-art visual classification methods, highlighting the potential of text-visual fusion for visual classification tasks. Furthermore, the study investigates the effectiveness of incorporating pre-trained language models and transfer learning for visual classification, revealing promising improvements in classification accuracy. The contribution of this work lies in providing a comprehensive solution for automatically extracting class labels from text, offering significant time and cost savings in annotating visual data.

title: Selecting Near-Optimal Learners via Incremental Data Allocation
Abstract: This paper presents an incremental data allocation framework designed to efficiently select near-optimal learners from a pool of candidates. The key challenge faced by decision-makers arises from the exponentially increasing number of possible learner combinations, which hinders the ability to exhaustively search for the optimal solution. To address this challenge, the proposed framework leverages a smart data allocation strategy, which iteratively allocates training data to learners based on their performance and diversity. By allocating data in a manner that maximizes the information gain for subsequent learners, the framework systematically explores the solution space and refines the candidate pool. A carefully crafted objective function is used to evaluate and compare learner combinations, enabling decision-makers to select the most effective learners for a given task. Through a theoretical analysis and experimental evaluation on multiple datasets, we demonstrate the efficiency and effectiveness of the proposed framework in selecting near-optimal learners. Empirical results show that the framework achieves significant improvements in predictive performance over traditional iterative search approaches, while reducing the overall search time by an order of magnitude. Our findings highlight the potential of incremental data allocation strategies in scaling up machine learning tasks with growing data sizes, making the proposed framework a valuable asset for decision-makers seeking to optimize their learner selection process. The proposed framework has far-reaching implications for the machine learning community, facilitating the exploration of complex learner spaces and enabling the discovery of high-performing models.

title: An (MI)LP-based Primal Heuristic for 3-Architecture Connected Facility Location in Urban Access Network Design
Abstract: This paper proposes an (Mixed-Integer)LP (Linear-Programming)-based primal heuristic for optimizing the 3-architecture connected facility location problem in urban access network design. Urban access networks are characterized by a high degree of complexity, with multiple levels of services, varying connectivity requirements, and complex urban infrastructures. The introduction of a 3-architecture model, comprised of macrocells, microcells, and picocells, has brought a level of complexity to the traditional facility location problem (FLP). Traditional solution methods and heuristics are often inadequate in handling the intricacies of this multi-architecture scenario. The proposed LP-based primal heuristic aims to address this issue by quickly generating feasible solutions using an LP relaxation of the problem. This relaxation formulates the facility location and capacity allocation aspects as a mixed-integer linear program (LP), enabling the utilization of mature LP solvers for obtaining near-optimal solutions within reasonable computational times. The developed heuristic integrates two-phase approaches: first, for the mixed-integer LP formulation, we directly solve it with the optimization solver, and second, we create a new round of local search to find a near-optimum solution to the solution. By evaluating the effectiveness of our methods on reference benchmarks, we demonstrate improvements and enhancements over existing solution methods and show its utilization as a powerful alternative for quickly solving the connected facility location problem under the constraints of 3-architecture urban access networks.

title: Evolving Non-linear Stacking Ensembles for Prediction of Go Player Attributes
Abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to the prediction of go player attributes through the development and application of evolving non-linear stacking ensembles. The proposed method leverages the strengths of ensemble learning and evolutionary computation to build a robust predictive model that can handle complex relationships between go player attributes and performance outcomes. A key component of this approach is the evolution of non-linear stacking ensembles, which allows the model to adapt to the underlying structure of the data and to identify the most relevant features for prediction. The evaluation of the proposed method is conducted through a series of experiments on a dataset of professional go players, with the results showing significant improvements in prediction accuracy compared to baseline machine learning models. Furthermore, the proposed method is able to identify the most influential factors contributing to go player performance, providing valuable insights for coaches, trainers, and analysts. The approach is also demonstrated to be highly flexible and extensible, allowing for easy incorporation of new features and datasets. Overall, the evolving non-linear stacking ensemble method presented in this paper offers a promising solution for the prediction of go player attributes, and its applicability extends to other domains where complex relationships between variables need to be modeled. The proposed method not only improves predictive accuracy but also provides actionable insights for stakeholders in the domain of go.

title: Bayes-Optimal Effort Allocation in Crowdsourcing: Bounds and Index Policies
Abstract: Our research investigates the problem of optimal effort allocation in crowdsourcing, which aims to minimize the total cost of task completion by assigning a suitable amount of work to each worker, taking into account their reporting costs and uncertainty in task difficulty. We consider a Bayesian agent who knows the underlying distributions of worker capabilities and task difficulties, but whose objective differs from that of a benevolent crowd employer. We provide a fully general characterization of the optimal effort allocation strategy in this setting, derived from the problem's formulation as a partially observable Markov decision process. The key insights gained through this analysis include the identifiability of the optimal effort allocation to be a function of a worker's value of information and the potential value of perfect information for the employer and the global knowledge gap between workers. Furthermore, we generalise results known for simple scenarios and propose more accurate measures for assessing effort allocation. Such results facilitate the design of sampling strategies for enhancing worker engagement, decision making for coordinating multiple employers within crowdsourcing models, and understanding the complexities that arise when integrating advanced analytics in such economies.

title: Benders Decomposition for the Design of a Hub and Shuttle Public Transit System
Abstract: This paper explores the application of Benders Decomposition, a mathematically rigorous and computationally efficient optimization technique, to the design of a hub and shuttle public transit system. The hub and shuttle system is a common transit model used in many cities worldwide, where passengers are transported to and from a central hub using high-frequency shuttles, and then transferred to other parts of the city via connecting trunk lines. By applying Benders Decomposition, we are able to decompose the complex problem of hub and shuttle design into two interlinked subproblems: (1) the assignment problem of determining the optimal hub locations and shuttle routing, and (2) the linear programming problem of determining the optimal service schedules and capacities for the hub and trunk lines. Through our decomposition approach, we develop a novel iterative algorithm that alternates between solving the assignment problem to determine the new variables in the linear programming problem, and solving the linear programming problem to determine the optimal solution values. The proposed algorithm is demonstrated on several large-scale hub and shuttle network instances, and the computational results show significant improvements in solution quality and computation time compared to traditional approaches. The results of this study provide valuable insights into the design of efficient and cost-effective hub and shuttle systems, and highlight the potential of Benders Decomposition as a powerful tool for solving large-scale complex optimization problems in public transportation.

title: A Notation for Markov Decision Processes
Abstract: Markov decision processes (MDPs) are a fundamental framework for modeling sequential decision-making under uncertainty in a wide range of fields, including artificial intelligence, operations research, and control systems. However, analyzing and solving MDPs can be computationally challenging due to their complex representation of sequential decisions and probabilistic outcomes. To facilitate more efficient and scalable analysis of MDPs, this paper introduces a novel notation that transforms MDPs into a graph-based representation, enabling the application of graph-based algorithms and techniques to solve MDP-related problems. The proposed notation, which we term the Markov Decision Process Graph (MDPG), provides a compact and intuitive way to represent MDPs, while preserving the underlying structure and dynamics of the original process. By leveraging the properties of graph theory, the MDPG notation enables the straightforward application of algorithms for graph breadth-first search, depth-first search, shortest path, and cycle detection, among others. This enables the efficient computation of key MDP-related metrics, such as the value function, policy gradients, and reachability probabilities. The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of the MDPG notation through various applications, including classical MDP problems, reinforcement learning, and control theory, and highlights its potential for speeding up MDP analysis and solving via graph-based methods.

title: Nonparametric Bayesian Factor Analysis for Dynamic Count Matrices
Abstract: This paper introduces a Bayesian nonparametric framework for factor analysis on dynamic count matrices, a novel application in the context of discrete-valued data. Prior existing work on factor analysis has focused on continuous-valued data and has largely overlooked discrete data for which no apparent additive or multiplicative structure exists. To bridge this gap, we have harnessed the strengths of nonparametric Bayesian methodologies, the Dirichlet process, and novel advancements in point process theory to create a dynamic Bayesian nonparametric factor model. This approach allows for simultaneously capturing unobserved patterns across different units and multiple time points within count matrices, while effectively modeling their discrete nature. Our model also considers a dynamic aspect by incorporating time-dependent weights which enable us to adaptively allocate significance to different patterns across time. By leveraging recent advancements in Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) inference with and without centered kernel Bayes factors for automatic model selection, our proposed framework provides a robust and flexible Bayesian nonparametric solution for the challenging task of dynamic factor analysis on discrete-valued data, ultimately providing vital insights for understanding the latent structures of observational count matrices over time.

title: Evaluating Go Game Records for Prediction of Player Attributes
Abstract: This study delves into the realm of Go, a centuries-old board game with deep complexity and strategic depth, to develop novel methods for predicting player attributes based on their gameplay records. By leveraging Go game records, we aim to uncover underlying patterns and relationships that reflect a player's skills, decision-making processes, and overall gameplay style. Our research focuses on the importance of utilizing various types of game records, including match outcomes, move sequences, and time management, to distill and quantify player attributes such as strategy, spatial reasoning, and tactical skills. A hybrid approach that integrates traditional statistical analysis and cutting-edge machine learning techniques is proposed to mine the rich data encoded within Go game records. Our approach first employs graph-based representation and network analysis to detect subtle patterns and topological structures hidden in the game data, followed by feature extraction and dimensionality reduction using techniques like autoencoders and t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE). By evaluating the predictive accuracy of our proposed methods, we demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of using Go game records to forecast player attributes and provide insights into the characteristics of expert-winning strategies. This research contributes to a better understanding of the Go domain and offers potential applications in areas like coaching, player development, and competition analysis, ultimately promoting the growth and improvement of the Go player community.

title: Simple, Robust and Optimal Ranking from Pairwise Comparisons
Abstract: The task of ranking objects from pairwise comparisons has numerous applications in fields ranging from recommender systems to social network analysis and decision-making processes. Current ranking methods, such as Borda's method and the rating scale model (RSM), often suffer from several limitations including inability to handle ties and ambiguity in the optimal ranking solution. To address these concerns, this research proposes a novel method to obtain simple, robust, and optimal rankings from incomplete and noisy pairwise comparison data. Our method, dubbed as Simple, Robust, and Optimal Ranking (SOR), builds upon the recent advancements in data-driven ranking techniques and introduces several novel concepts such as a probabilistic interpretation of rankings and an efficient algorithm for computing the optimal ranking. Through an extensive empirical evaluation on both synthetic and real-world datasets, we demonstrate that SOR outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of ranking simplicity, robustness to noise and ties, and optimality of the resulting rankings. Furthermore, SOR is found to be computationally efficient and scalable, making it a viable solution for large-scale ranking applications. Our results not only contribute to the development of more reliable and interpretable ranking methods but also shed light on the theoretical foundations of ranking from pairwise comparisons.

title: Modeling Variations of First-Order Horn Abduction in Answer Set Programming
Abstract: This research delves into the realm of first-order logic and its applications in Answer Set Programming (ASP), a declarative problem-solving paradigm rooted in non-monotonic reasoning. Specifically, it investigates variants of first-order Horn abduction within the ASP framework. Abduction is a form of inference where, given a set of observations and a theory, we seek to identify the underlying premises responsible for the observed facts. First-order Horn abduction generalizes the concept to accommodate quantification and negation. By modeling these variations in ASP, we can effectively capture complex real-world scenarios and harness the power of computing answer sets to solve abduction problems. The proposed approach provides a novel framework for representing and solving abduction problems, featuring enhancements in expressivity, efficiency, and soundness over existing methods. By integrating the concepts of first-order logic, abduction, and ASP, our model enables the sound and feasible computation of abduction solutions, facilitating its applications in knowledge representation, artificial intelligence, and data analysis. The work presents novel ASP encodings for several abduction variants, utilizing non-ground abductive theories, prioritized premise abduction, and constraint-based abduction. Empirical studies demonstrate the efficacy and scalability of our approach in solving scenarios of various complexities, thereby underscoring its potential for broad applicability in real-world problem domains.

title: Closing the Gap Between Short and Long XORs for Model Counting
Abstract: Model counting, a crucial aspect of many probabilistic reasoning tasks, has witnessed significant advancements in recent years. However, XOR constraints, which are integral to the problem, remain a significant challenge. This is owed to the fact that short XORs are efficiently handled by many model counting algorithms, whereas long XORs cause exponential blowups, rendering such approaches ineffective. As a result, there has been ongoing research to close the gap between short and long XORs, aimed at developing efficient model counting techniques capable of handling constrains of varying lengths. In this context, the development of specialized XOR enumeration procedures, adaptive algorithms, and formulation of XOR constraints in terms of smaller ones, have shown promise. Theoretical studies have also made strides in analyzing existing algorithms under the lens of XOR lengths, demonstrating the intricate interplay between constraint lengths and computational complexity. Our work builds upon this foundation by exploring a novel methodology that decouples the algorithmic limitations of traditional model counting approaches from the inherent complexity of long XORs, thus paving the way for significant advances in the field. This novel approach not only yields substantial computational performance benefits but also fosters further understanding of the intricacies involved in handling XOR constraints of varying lengths.

title: Learning Natural Language Inference with LSTM
Abstract: This study investigates the application of Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks to learning natural language inference tasks. Natural language inference involves determining the relationship between a premise statement and a hypothesis statement, typically classifying the relationship as either entailed, countered, or neutral. Current state-of-the-art models often fail to generalize well to unseen data and rely heavily on careful manual feature engineering and task-specific tuning. In contrast, LSTMs are capable of learning complex temporal patterns within sequences, a desirable property for models attempting to capture the nuances of language. In this work, we explore the incorporation of LSTMs as a means of capturing contextual dependencies within the premise and hypothesis statements. To do so, we compare the performance of multiple LSTM architectures, including a simple bidirectional LSTM and two multi-task LSTM variants, against strong baseline models on a variety of multiple-choice question answering datasets. Experimental results suggest that LSTMs can achieve comparable accuracy to state-of-the-art models on these tasks, particularly when fine-tuned on the datasets of interest. Additionally, the incorporation of LSTMs allows us to define models that learn natural language inference without manually engineering intermediate representations or relying heavily on hand-crafted rules, marking a significant step towards truly learning-based models of language.

title: Internet of Things for Residential Areas: Toward Personalized Energy Management Using Big Data
Abstract: The rapidly increasing adoption of IoT devices in residential areas has led to a significant improvement in energy efficiency and personalized energy management. This study explores the feasibility of leveraging big data analytics to optimize energy consumption in residential areas. By integrating sensors, smart home devices, and wearables, a comprehensive IoT system is designed to collect and analyze data on occupants' habits, energy usage patterns, and environmental factors. The system employs machine learning algorithms to learn the preferences and behavior of individual occupants, enabling real-time adjustments to energy supply and demand. The proposed system not only reduces energy waste but also enhances occupant comfort and convenience. This research emphasizes the importance of data analytics in interpreting complex patterns of energy consumption and identifies the key drivers of energy usage in residential areas. By adopting a personalized approach to energy management, this IoT-based system can help minimize energy demands, promote eco-friendliness, and achieve reduced energy consumption while preserving occupant satisfaction.

title: Combining Fuzzy Cognitive Maps and Discrete Random Variables
Abstract: This study proposes an innovative approach that integrates the capabilities of Fuzzy Cognitive Maps (FCMs) with Discrete Random Variables (DRVs) to analyze and model complex, dynamic systems in a more comprehensive and flexible manner. FCMs, a graphical representation of causal relationships between variables, are widely used to model cognitive processes and make predictions in a variety of domains. However, FCMs are criticized for their inability to handle uncertainty and randomness inherent in real-world systems. To address this limitation, we incorporate Discrete Random Variables, which enable the incorporation of probability distributions and random events into the FCM framework. The proposed approach allows for the modeling of both certain and uncertain relationships between variables, capturing the dynamic and non-linear behavior of complex systems. The methodology is demonstrated through a case study involving a supply chain network, where the FCM-DRV approach is applied to analyze the impact of various disruptions and stochastic events on the system's performance. The results show that the proposed approach can effectively predict and mitigate the effects of uncertainty, improving the overall reliability and robustness of the supply chain network. This research contributes to the advancement of FCMs by incorporating stochastic elements, enabling the analysis of complex systems under uncertainty and paving the way for more realistic and robust modeling of real-world problems.

title: Interactive Discovery of Coordinated Relationship Chains with Maximum Entropy Models
Abstract: This paper presents a novel approach for interactive discovery of coordinated relationship chains using maximum entropy models, enabling users to explore and identify complex patterns in multivariate data. By constructing a network of predictive relationships, the proposed method facilitates the comprehension of interconnected factors that influence each other's behavior, uncovering dynamic interactions and causal pathways. The maximum entropy model is utilized to accurately capture the probabilistic nature of these interactions, taking into account prior knowledge and observational data. Through an intuitive interface, users can iteratively refine their query and explore different aspects of the data, making discoveries about relationships and driving insights. The proposed system incorporates context-aware filtering, ranking, and aggregation to simplify the analysis of large-scale datasets and provide actionable results. The methodology leverages efficient algorithms to scale for real-world data volumes, facilitating the exploration of high-dimensional data spaces. In addition, the work includes an evaluation framework for assessing the effectiveness of the system using real-world data. This research contributes to the development of interactive data analysis tools that can facilitate informed decision-making and enhance our understanding of complex phenomena, thereby providing valuable insights into the mechanisms governing coordinated relationships.

title: On the Foundations of the Brussels Operational-Realistic Approach to Cognition
Abstract: The Brussels Operational-Realistic Approach to Cognition (BORAC) theory has evolved to provide a comprehensive framework for understanding human cognition, emphasizing the importance of integrating contextual, experiential, and intentional factors. This research delves into the foundational components of BORAC, examining its ontological and epistemological foundations, as well as its methodological and theoretical underpinnings. A key aspect of this research is the exploration of BORAC's conceptualization of action, perception, and context, and how these concepts are interlinked to form a cohesive understanding of cognition. By critically examining the existing literature on BORAC and its theoretical frameworks, this study aims to shed light on the theoretical significance and practical implications of the approach. The findings of this research demonstrate that BORAC's operational-realistic perspective offers a novel understanding of human cognition, one that highlights the dynamic interplay between agent, environment, and action. This, in turn, has significant implications for various fields, including cognitive science, robotics, and artificial intelligence, where developing adaptive and flexible systems that can operate in complex and dynamic environments is a pressing concern. Overall, this research provides a deeper understanding of the theoretical foundations of BORAC and highlights its potential as a framework for developing more sophisticated and realistic models of human cognition.

title: Taming the Noise in Reinforcement Learning via Soft Updates
Abstract: This research proposes a novel approach to address the instability and noise inherent in reinforcement learning (RL) by seamlessly integrating soft updates into the training process. Existing methods primarily focus on maintaining a trade-off between exploration and exploitation, often sacrificing stability for the sake of convergence speed. However, the interplay between the dynamics of the environment and the greedy nature of RL agents can result in sudden fluctuations and noise, compromising overall performance and affecting the learning process. The proposed method seeks to mitigate this issue by introducing a soft update regimen that tactfully adjusts the model parameters, suppressing large updates and promoting stability while still allowing convergence. An empirically-driven decision-making approach, rooted in the knowledge gained from the soft updates, enables the agents to seamlessly navigate complex environments without succumbing to noise-related issues. The research demonstrates the efficacy of this novel approach through comprehensive experiments on various challenging RL benchmarks, showing significant improvements in convergence speed and performance, with a notable reduction in environment noise sensitivity. By highlighting the feasibility of soft updates in mitigating noise, this work has the potential to enlighten the future development of reliable RL-based solutions for real-world applications.

title: Conditional probability generation methods for high reliability effects-based decision making
Abstract: This paper presents an in-depth examination of conditional probability generation methods and their applications in high-reliability effects-based decision making. The complexities of uncertainty in decision-making processes, particularly in high-stakes scenarios such as defense and nuclear power, pose significant challenges to achieving effective and reliable outcomes. Traditional probability methods often fail to capture the intricacies of uncertain scenarios, leading to suboptimal decision support. In response, we explore five state-of-the-art conditional probability generation methods, including Monte Carlo simulations, Bayesian networks, Dempster-Shafer theory, possibility theory, and set-valued conditional probability. Each method is thoroughly evaluated in a simulated scenario, with critical performance metrics, including accuracy, reliability, and computational efficiency, analyzed. Furthermore, the findings demonstrate the advantages of employing conditional probability generation in combination with effects-based decision making, resulting in enhanced adaptability, responsiveness, and ultimately improved decision reliability. We discuss the results and insights gained from this research, highlighting key takeaways for potential users and future research directions to further enhance high-reliability decision making in complex and dynamic environments.

title: Mining Massive Hierarchical Data Using a Scalable Probabilistic Graphical Model
Abstract: This abstract presents a novel approach to efficiently mine massive hierarchical data by leveraging a scalable probabilistic graphical model. With the proliferation of big data and complex knowledge graphs, the task of extracting meaningful patterns and relationships from hierarchical data has become increasingly crucial. However, existing methods often suffer from high computational costs, scalability issues, and inaccurate results due to the sheer size and complexity of the data. To address these challenges, we propose a probabilistic graphical model that incorporates a hierarchical structure and a scalable inference framework. Our model, dubbed HPHMM, combines the strengths of Hierarchical Hidden Markov Models (HHMMs) and Probabilistic Graphical Models (PGMs) to efficiently capture the hierarchical relationships and dependencies within the data. We employ a novel factorized inference algorithm that scales linearly with the data size, allowing for real-time analysis of massive hierarchical datasets. Experimental results on large-scale datasets demonstrate the efficacy of HPHMM in discovering hidden patterns, Hierarchical relationships, and anomalies compared to state-of-the-art methods. The scalability and accuracy of HPHMM make it a promising tool for applications involving massive hierarchical data, such as recommendation systems, social network analysis, and genomics. Our research contributes to the development of more efficient and effective methods for mining complex hierarchical data, enabling new insights and discoveries in various domains.

title: GELATO and SAGE: An Integrated Framework for MS Annotation
Abstract: GELATO and SAGE are two comprehensive tools designed to facilitate the task of manual annotation in mass spectrometry (MS) data analysis, a crucial step in understanding biological pathways and disease mechanisms. This integrated framework combines the strengths of both tools to provide a more efficient and accurate annotation experience. GELATO serves as a powerful expert system, equipped with in-depth knowledge of protein structures and biochemical pathways, allowing users to identify known structures. In contrast, SAGE, a neural network-based model, provides the complementary ability to predict structures with high specificity, even for those that are novel or absent from existing databases. By integrating these capabilities, the GELATO and SAGE framework enhances the annotation process with two key benefits: an increased number of predicted structures and improved accuracy of outcomes. Furthermore, this framework has been engineered to leverage the availability of large-scale MS data repositories and to facilitate collaborative effort among users, enabling a broader, more accurate annotation of biological datasets. Additionally, the tool has been developed to ensure flexibility and scalability, making it beneficial for both research and industrial applications.

title: Regularized Orthogonal Tensor Decompositions for Multi-Relational Learning
Abstract: In the realm of multi-relational learning, tensor decompositions have garnered significant attention as a means to reveal the underlying patterns and relationships within complex data structures. However, traditional tensor decomposition techniques often fall short in capturing the nuances of relational data, as they typically fail to account for the varying strengths and directions of relationships. This limitation can lead to suboptimal performance and poor ability to generalize to unseen relationships. To circumvent this issue, this paper proposes novel regularized orthogonal tensor decomposition methods for multi-relational learning. Our approach combines the strengths of tensor decompositions with the robustness of regularization techniques, allowing for the incorporation of relational invariants and the preservation of structural properties in the data. Specifically, we develop two regularization schemes, leveraging both structural and graph-theoretic interpretations of relational data. Through a deep exploration of these regularized methods, we demonstrate their efficacy in enhancing the accuracy, robustness, and interpretability of multi-relational learning. Experimental results on a range of benchmark datasets confirm the superior performance of our proposed methods, highlighting their potential to revolutionize the way we analyze and learn from complex relational data.

title: Using Data Analytics to Detect Anomalous States in Vehicles
Abstract: The rapid proliferation of connected and autonomous vehicles has led to an unprecedented availability of sensor data, which can be leveraged to enhance vehicle safety and reliability through predictive maintenance and real-time monitoring. This research proposes an innovative approach to detecting anomalous states in vehicles using advanced data analytics techniques. By integrating machine learning algorithms with large-scale vehicle sensor datasets, our developed framework significantly improves the detection of unusual system behavior, enabling early intervention and minimizing the risk of catastrophic failures. Utilizing a Gaussian Mixture Model clustering algorithm to identify unusual data patterns, our approach demonstrates superior performance in detecting anomalies compared to traditional methods, with an accuracy of up to 95% in real-world scenarios. Furthermore, a comprehensive empirical evaluation is conducted to assess the impact of various parameters, including sensor sampling frequency, model complexity, and algorithmic noise tolerance. The study highlights the profound potential of our framework in providing invaluable insights for vehicle maintenance scheduling, enabling prophylactic measures to be taken against impending anomalies. Overall, the framework presented here represents a tangible step forward in harnessing data analytics for safer, more efficient, and more reliable vehicles.

title: Device and System Level Design Considerations for Analog-Non-Volatile-Memory Based Neuromorphic Architectures
Abstract: Analog-non-volatile-memory (ANVM)-based neuromorphic architectures have gained significant attention in recent years for their potential to mimic the human brain, offering enhanced processing efficiency, low power consumption, and accelerations for complex artificial neural networks (ANNs) workloads. This study delves into the critical device and system-level design considerations for realizing a functional and efficient ANVM-based neuromorphic architecture. The analysis focuses on the requirements for the building blocks, such as synapse and neuron designs, that dictate the overall performance and functionality of the architecture. In particular, the feasibility and limitations of nanoscale materials (e.g., memristor, phase-change memory) are examined for prospective ANVM formulations. Furthermore, the consideration of system-level aspects, for instance, memory array architecture, peripheral circuitry and programming schemes, is assessed to understand the impact of these factors on system reliability and scalability. System-level studies such as power modeling, thermal considerations, and memory yield are also explored as key enablers to tackle real-world neuromorphic processor design application challenges, including artificial vision, audio processing, neuromorphic engineering, computing reliability, ultra-low power consumption and non-volatile data retention while ensuring acceptable operating speeds across real-world workloads and large-scale deployment. By presenting these technical and computational considerations, this work serves as a foundation to develop neuromorphic systems that can efficiently mimic the strengths of human brain, effectively unlocking exciting possibilities for AI-based applications across multiple industries.

title: Toward a Research Agenda in Adversarial Reasoning: Computational Approaches to Anticipating the Opponent's Intent and Actions
Abstract: This paper contributes to the development of a research agenda in adversarial reasoning, with a focus on computational approaches for anticipating the opponent's intent and actions. It is grounded in the understanding that effectiveness in strategic situations often relies on the capacity to forewarn and counter adversaries. By scrutinizing various adversarial contexts, including competitive games, decision-making under uncertainty, and autonomous systems, we identify key concepts, theories, and computational techniques essential for advancing adversarial reasoning. To develop and deepen understanding of these concepts, the research agenda is structured around three core research thrusts: predictive modeling, reasoning about intentions, and adaptive decision-making. Predictive modeling addresses methods for forecasting the opponent's behavior at multiple time steps while considering their goals, preferences, and the environment. Reasoning about intentions involves analyzing and explaining observed actions, behaviors, and policies to infer their underlying intent. Adaptive decision-making focuses on the development of policies that adapt to unfolding situations and learn from the opponent's moves. Through empirical studies and theoretical contributions, this research agenda aims to offer in-depth insights and solutions to long-standing challenges in adversarial reasoning, ultimately bridging the current knowledge gap between theoretical foundations and practical methods.

title: Multi-Level Cause-Effect Systems
Abstract: This research delves into the intricate workings of Multi-Level Cause-Effect Systems, exploring the complex interactions between various components and levels of influence in producing an outcome. By combining insights from systems theory, network science, and non-linear dynamics, this study examines the critical relationships that govern the behavior of cause-effect processes across multiple scales. It identifies key drivers of emergent behavior, including nonlinear feedback loops, hierarchical dependencies, and temporal synchronizations, and provides a framework for understanding the dynamics of cascading effects within these systems. Through a multi-disciplinary approach, incorporating concepts from ecology, economics, sociology, and complex systems research, the investigation clarifies the underlying mechanisms by which minor changes can initiate chain-reaction effects, potentially leading to unforeseen and far-reaching consequences. Based on simulations, empirical data analysis, and case studies, the research aims to contribute to the development of more resilient models for predicting system behavior and mitigating risks associated with destructive feedback loops and unintended consequences. Ultimately, the goal is to provide a deeper understanding of the intricate cause-effect relationships within Multi-Level Cause-Effect Systems, informing strategies for management, policy-making, and decision-making in the face of growing complexity.

title: Probabilistic Model-Based Approach for Heart Beat Detection
Abstract: This paper presents a probabilistic model-based approach for heart beat detection, which is a fundamental task in cardiac signal processing. Cardiac signals recorded from various sensors, such as electrocardiograms (ECGs) and photoplethysmograms (PPGs), exhibit a high degree of non-linearity and variability. In order to accurately detect heart beats from these complex signals, a robust and efficient algorithm is required. We propose a probabilistic model-based approach that leverages the principles of machine learning to identify the patterns and characteristics of heart beats. The approach is based on a Hidden Markov Model (HMM) that utilizes the temporal dependencies and correlations among the features extracted from the cardiac signals. Our method systematically evaluates the relationships between the signal features and the likely presence of a heart beat, enabling the accurate identification of R-peaks and onsets of heart cycles. By using a probabilistic model, our approach can effectively address the challenges of variability and irregularity inherent in cardiac signals, thereby improving the detection accuracy and robustness. Results from experiments on publicly available benchmark datasets demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed approach, showing a notable improvement in heart beat detection accuracy compared to existing methods. Furthermore, the flexibility of the probabilistic model-based approach allows for easy adaptation to various cardiac signal modalities and scenarios, conferring potential benefits in diverse clinical and real-world applications.

title: RDF2Rules: Learning Rules from RDF Knowledge Bases by Mining Frequent Predicate Cycles
Abstract: RDF2Rules is a novel approach that leverages frequent predicate cycles discovered from RDF knowledge bases to infer new rules. By extracting the underlying structures inherent to the knowledge graph, RDF2Rules aims to automate the process of generating useful rules from large-scale RDF datasets, thereby reducing the complexity and time-consuming nature of manual rule extraction. The approach comprises two primary stages: pattern discovery and rule extraction. Initially, the methodology relies on a novel graph mining algorithm to identify frequent predicate cycles within the RDF knowledge base, which are considered as patterns that co-occur frequently together. Subsequently, the extracted patterns are utilized to generate potential rules by incorporating transitive and symmetric properties of the associated predicates. Experimental results demonstrate that RDF2Rules is capable of discovering meaningful and accurate rules that accurately capture the underlying relationships within the knowledge graph, and significantly outperform traditional rule mining approaches in terms of coverage, precision, and recall. The effectiveness of RDF2Rules is further validated by its successful application on several standard benchmark datasets, showcasing its potential for enhancing the capabilities of knowledge graph querying systems and facilitating the realization of more informed decision-making processes in numerous real-world applications, including semantic web services and artificial intelligence systems.

title: Measuring pattern retention in anonymized data -- where one measure is not enough
Abstract: Anonymized data has become a cornerstone of various applications in the realms of machine learning, data science, and data sharing, as it enables the preservation of sensitive information while still allowing for insightful analysis. However, a common challenge that arises when working with anonymized data is accurately measuring its quality. One of the critical aspects of evaluating anonymized data is assessing the retention of the underlying patterns present in the raw, non-anonymized dataset. Although numerous metrics have been proposed to quantify pattern retention, such as the distortion metric and pattern distortion average, using only one measure might be insufficient due to the complexity of patterns in real-world data. This study delves into the underpinnings of current measures and highlights their limitations. We also propose a multi-metric approach that incorporates both the distortion metric and Kolmogorov complexity, allowing for a more nuanced understanding of the pattern retention in anonymized data. By implementing a real-world dataset, the results of this study demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed multi-metric approach in identifying the limitations of existing methods and providing a more accurate representation of the retention of patterns in anonymized data. This contributes to the development of more robust strategies for data anonymization, ultimately leading to higher fidelity insights and more informed decision-making processes.
