title: Deep Reinforcement Learning in Large Discrete Action Spaces
Abstract: Deep Reinforcement Learning in Large Discrete Action Spaces has garnered significant attention in recent years due to its vast potential applications in real-world problems. However, the primary constraint limiting the widespread adoption of these models is the curse of dimensionality, which emerges when agents are faced with a large number of possible actions to take in an environment. In such cases, computational costs increase exponentially as model size and time complexity grow. The state-of-the-art approaches based on deep learning attempt to address this limitation by leveraging neural networks and actor-critic methods. This paradigm has been proven to be effective in environments where the number of possible actions is relatively small or manageable. Nonetheless, direct application of deep actor-critic methods results in poor learning performance and sample efficiency when there are infinitely many possible actions available. Conversely, some research studies suggest the inherent property of fully connected neural networks and the issue of function approximation in environment spaces as major factors in learning inefficiencies in environments with expansive action spaces. It can thus be said that developing effective techniques to efficiently handle problems with enormous action spaces holds the key to unlocking the full potential of deep reinforcement learning. In this work, researchers evaluated and implemented existing methods with the primary intention of yielding meaningful research contributions and improvement in sample efficiency for reinforcement learning applications. Our solution leverages advanced exploration-exploitation frameworks designed specifically for environments featuring a significantly large number of possible actions, which should yield substantial improvements in simulation and sample efficiency for users.

title: Composite Bayesian inference
Abstract: This paper presents an in-depth exploration of composite Bayesian inference, a relatively unexplored area in the realm of statistical learning. The advent of composite Bayesian models has enabled researchers to bridge the gap between the Bayesian and frequentist paradigms, providing a more nuanced understanding of the underlying uncertainty and variability associated with complex data-generating processes. By integrating the strengths of both paradigms, composite Bayesian models can effectively handle the challenges posed by high-dimensional data, non-linearity, and uncertainty-driven decision-making. The proposed framework combines elements from both Bayesian inference and frequentist model selection, resulting in a more robust and interpretable approach to uncertainty quantification. This work demonstrates the viability of composite Bayesian inference for a range of real-world applications, including image classification, regression analysis, and time-series forecasting. A comprehensive evaluation of the proposed method using synthetic and real-world datasets reveals its competitive performance against state-of-the-art approaches. The theoretical underpinnings of composite Bayesian inference are grounded in a novel derivation of the marginal likelihood using a reparameterized posterior and a novel application of Laplace's method. Through this work, we provide a concrete formulation of composite Bayesian inference, along with a set of practical recommendations for implementation, thereby paving the way for a new generation of Bayesian-informed statistical learning techniques. Our results underscore the potential of composite Bayesian inference to transform the landscape of statistical modeling and decision-making, underlining its value as a versatile and theoretically well-motivated approach to uncertainty quantification.

title: The Max $K$-Armed Bandit: PAC Lower Bounds and Efficient Algorithms
Abstract: The Max $K$-Armed Bandit is a fundamental problem in online learning and optimization, where the goal is to identify the arm with the maximum reward given a limited number of samples. In this work, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the Max $K$-Armed Bandit problem, focusing on the trade-off between exploration and exploitation. We derive computationally tight lower bounds on the sample complexity required to find the optimal arm with a given level of confidence, specifically under the Pac Bayesian framework. Our lower bound, which scales as $\Omega(K \log 1/\delta)$, reveals the inherent difficulty of the problem when the number of arms $K$ is large and holds even for algorithms with oracle access to the maximum arm. On the other hand, we propose an efficient algorithm that achieves a sample complexity scaling as $O(K \log 1/\delta)$, providing a matching upper bound for the Pac Bayesian setting. The key to our algorithm is a novel use of the "explore-then-commit" principle, combined with an advanced analysis that exploits the structural properties of the Max $K$-Armed Bandit problem. As a bonus, we extend our analysis to the setting of finite-armed bandits, where the arms have multiple features and the rewards depend on these features in a structured manner. Our results demonstrate the limitations and possibilities of the Max $K$-Armed Bandit problem, shedding new light on the interplay between exploration and exploitation in this fundamental problem.

title: Representation and Coding of Signal Geometry
Abstract: Signal geometry encompasses a wide array of mathematical concepts and computational tools employed in representing, analyzing, and processing signals with intricate spatial structures. The representation and coding of signal geometry are pivotal in various signal processing applications, such as computer vision, image and video compression, and geographic information systems. This research delves into the fundamental principles and modern techniques for encoding and representing signal geometry, with a focus on advancing the state of the art in signal geometry-based methods for handling complex signals. We explore the theoretical aspects of geometric representations, including geometric transformations, differential geometry, and topological properties, which provide essential frameworks for modeling the intricate patterns and structures found in various signals. Furthermore, this study examines several coding techniques for signal geometry, such as geometric image coding, variational methods, and deep learning-based approaches, which enable efficient and robust transmission and storage of geometrically rich signals. Our research provides new insights and methods for representing and coding signal geometry, contributing to the development of cutting-edge signal processing and computer vision applications that can accommodate and analyze complex spatial structures. The proposed techniques are evaluated using comprehensive experiments and demonstrations, emphasizing the potential of signal geometry-based methods in real-world applications.

title: Randomized Social Choice Functions Under Metric Preferences
Abstract: This study delves into the realm of randomized social choice functions, specifically under the context of metric preferences. Traditional social choice functions focus on aggregating individual preferences into a collective decision, often with a reliance on ordinal or cardinal utility representations. However, in scenarios where preferences can be represented as numerical distances or metrics, such as travel times or aesthetic judgments, new complexities arise. The incorporation of randomized selection mechanisms offers a means to address these challenges by providing a nuanced framework for evaluating and aggregating diverse viewpoints. Our research explores the behavioral implications of employing metric preferences within randomized social choice functions. We examine the conditions under which such selection mechanisms yield stable and consistent outcomes, considering scenarios where individual preferences exhibit varying levels of noise and ambiguity. Furthermore, we investigate the effects of different distance functions on the emergent behavior of the randomized social choice functions, seeking to identify which metric-based preferences produce the most desirable aggregation outcomes. The resulting analysis contributes to a deeper understanding of how randomized social choice functions can effectively accommodate and integrate diverse, metrically represented individual preferences.

title: Selecting the top-quality item through crowd scoring
Abstract: Crowd scoring has emerged as a promising approach for selecting high-quality items in various domains, such as e-commerce, product design, and decision-making. This research delves into the concept of crowd scoring, examining its underlying mechanisms and the factors influencing its effectiveness in identifying top-quality items. By leveraging insights from behavioral economics, social psychology, and computer science, our investigation reveals that crowd scoring relies on the accumulation of ratings and reviews from a large number of individuals, each contributing their subjective evaluation of the item. We explore how the diversity, accuracy, and consistency of these ratings collectively impact the quality of the crowd score. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of biases and psychological factors, such as confirmation bias and anchoring effect, that can skew the crowd score and compromise its reliability. Additionally, we develop a novel framework for identifying optimal scoring mechanisms that minimize the influence of biases and maximize the prediction accuracy of the crowd score. The empirical evaluation of our framework demonstrates its superior performance in selecting high-quality items compared to existing methods, validating its potential as a reliable tool for decision-making in various applications.

title: Adaptive Ensemble Learning with Confidence Bounds
Abstract: This paper presents an investigation into the development of adaptive ensemble learning models that incorporate confidence bounds. By combining multiple machine learning models with diverse decision-making strategies, we can leverage the strengths of individual models while mitigating their weaknesses. However, one of the primary challenges in ensemble learning lies in selecting the most effective combination of models, given that model performance may degrade as additional models are included. Furthermore, accuracy is not always the sole importance, as the reliability of predictions within a given confidence threshold remains a significant concern. To address these issues, we propose an adaptive ensemble framework that dynamically adjusts the weights assigned to individual models based on their performance on past datasets. Additionally, this framework incorporates confidence bounds to guarantee a predetermined level of prediction accuracy, thereby enabling real-world applications in high-stakes decision-making scenarios such as medical diagnosis, financial risk assessment, and autonomous vehicle navigation. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through comprehensive experiments on a range of benchmark datasets and real-world tasks, and show that it consistently outperforms existing ensemble learning methods. The results highlight the potential of our adaptive ensemble framework to provide reliable and accurate predictions in a variety of settings, making it a valuable contribution to the advancement of machine learning and artificial intelligence.

title: A Learning Algorithm for Change Impact Prediction
Abstract: This research proposes a novel machine learning-based approach, referred to as ChangeImpactPredictor, that aims to predict the effects of organizational changes on employees, teams, and business processes. By leveraging a hybrid framework combining both traditional and deep learning techniques, the algorithm is designed to capture complex patterns and relationships within organizational change data. The proposed model utilizes a two-stage architecture, where the first stage involves the extraction and processing of historical data related to organizational changes, employee behaviors, job satisfaction, team performance, and business outcomes. In the second stage, a deep learning neural network is employed to model the dynamic interactions among these factors and predict the impact of future changes on various organizational aspects. Through evaluation using a comprehensive dataset comprising real-world organizational change scenarios, the study demonstrates the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed algorithm in accurately predicting change-related effects on employees and organizations. The ChangeImpactPredictor has the potential to provide valuable insights and recommendations for business leaders, change managers, and HR professionals to minimize disruptions, maximize employee engagement, and optimize organizational success during periods of change.

title: The ERA of FOLE: Foundation
Abstract: The advent of the Foundation of Land Equity (FOLE) era has heralded a transformative shift in the global landscape, imparting profound implications for real estate markets, governments, and citizens alike. At its core, FOLE seeks to reframe the traditional notion of land ownership by emphasizing the importance of underlying foundation rights in driving economic growth, promoting social equity, and fostering community resilience. This novel paradigm posits that secure foundational properties are essential for stimulating local development, particularly in contexts beset by inadequate infrastructure and resource constraints. By empowering local communities to reclaim control over foundational assets, FOLE fosters a more collaborative and inclusive approach to urban planning, thereby reconciling competing interests and priorities. Emerging research suggests that FOLE could significantly enhance land tenure security, facilitate more equitable access to basic amenities, and amplify the capacity of jurisdictions to adapt to future environmental and social challenges. Furthermore, the FOLE era has also witnessed a proliferation of experimental initiatives and innovative pilot projects, both locally and globally, seeking to operationalize the principles of FOLE in practice. As the world continues to grapple with pressing questions of environmental sustainability, social justice, and economic resilience, the FOLE movement presents a compelling vision for reconciling these competing imperatives through the lens of foundational values and practices.

title: A Deep Generative Deconvolutional Image Model
Abstract: This paper presents a Deep Generative Deconvolutional Image Model (DG DIM), a novel approach to image generation and reconstruction. The model combines the strength of deconvolutional neural networks with that of generative adversarial networks (GANs) and variational autoencoders (VAEs) to learn complex patterns and structures in high-dimensional images. The proposed model consists of two parallel streams: a generator stream that leverages a series of transposed convolutional layers and activation functions to upsample the input noise and gradually increase the spatial dimensions while preserving the semantic content of the original image; and a discriminator stream that adopts a multi-resolution architecture with feature extractors inspired by VGG networks to assess the quality and authenticity of the generated image. During training, the two streams continually interact, with the generator attempting to produce realistic and informative images and the discriminator critically evaluating and guiding the generator towards optimal performance. Our results demonstrate that the DG DIM achieves impressive image generation and reconstruction capabilities even with limited training data, offering state-of-the-art performance on popular benchmark datasets such as CelebA-HQ and ImageNet. By integrating cutting-edge concepts from computer vision, machine learning, and deep learning, this study expands our understanding of image representation and generation and brings forth promising applications in areas such as computer vision, remote sensing, and robotics, along with artistic image generation and image editing.

title: Heuristic algorithms for finding distribution reducts in probabilistic rough set model
Abstract: The probabilistic rough set model has gained significant attention in recent years due to its potential in handling uncertainty and incomplete information in decision-making processes. However, the computation of distribution reducts, which are a crucial aspect of this model, has proven to be computationally expensive and time-consuming. Heuristic algorithms have been proposed as a means to expedite this process by providing efficient solutions. This research aims to explore and evaluate the performance of various heuristic algorithms, namely genetic algorithm, particle swarm optimization, and simulated annealing, for finding distribution reducts in probabilistic rough set models. The proposed framework employs a combination of statistical and machine learning techniques to compare the efficacy of these algorithms. The implementation of each algorithm is conducted on a range of datasets with varying characteristics to assess their scalability and robustness. The results demonstrate that each heuristic algorithm exhibits unique strengths and weaknesses, and that the choice of algorithm depends on the specific requirements of the problem. Furthermore, the study highlights the benefits of using hybrid approaches that incorporate elements of multiple algorithms to obtain optimal solutions. The research contributes to the development of efficient methods for finding distribution reducts and provides valuable insights for researchers and practitioners working in the fields of data mining, machine learning, and decision-making under uncertainty.

title: SR-Clustering: Semantic Regularized Clustering for Egocentric Photo Streams Segmentation
Abstract: SR-Clustering: Semantic Regularized Clustering for Egocentric Photo Streams Segmentation is a novel clustering approach that tackles the problem of segmenting egocentric photo streams into coherent groups. Egocentric photo streams typically consist of a collection of images taken by a person during their daily activities, exhibiting diverse scenes, objects, and people. The existing clustering methods often fail to capture the semantic meaning and context within these streams, leading to fragmented or irregular segmentation results. To address this challenge, the proposed SR-Clustering framework integrates a semantic regularization term into the traditional clustering objective function, allowing for more accurate and meaningful segmentation. This regularization term is achieved by incorporating a pre-trained convolutional neural network (CNN) with fine-grained visual features that capture scene, object, and action information from the images. By combining the clustering objective with the CNN's semantic representation, SR-Clustering enables the discovery of coherent photo groups that reflect not only visual similarities but also semantic connections and relevance within each group. Experimental results on public benchmark datasets demonstrate the superiority of SR-Clustering, exhibiting higher precision, recall, and F1-score compared to state-of-the-art clustering algorithms, thus highlighting its potential for effective and meaningful segmentation of egocentric photo streams in various real-world applications, including activity recognition, social media analysis, and human-computer interaction.

title: Implementing a Bayes Filter in a Neural Circuit: The Case of Unknown Stimulus Dynamics
Abstract: This paper presents an integration of principles from machine learning and neuroscience to formulate a novel approach to inferring stimulus dynamics in neural circuits. Building on the Bayesian framework, we develop a Bayesian filter compatible with the structural properties and computational representations used by neural systems, with the goal of addressing unknown stimulus dynamics. Our implementation of a Bayes filter mimics the functions and interactions of the processes occurring in neural circuits when processing sensory information. Specifically, we model the neural activity in the neural circuit as a state-space representation, where the hidden states are associated with the neural activity encoding the stimulus. The model leverages local computations within the neural circuit to recursively refine estimates of the current stimulus, while approximating the hidden state through an efficient update mechanism that updates the top-down prior under each new sensory evidence. By employing techniques such as on-line approximations of the Kalman gain and Gaussian smoothing parameter through neural hebbian learning, we optimize this method within a simulated neuroscience environment to generate predictions of the stimulus from noisy and delayed neural activity. Our proposed framework contributes to the development of algorithms for Bayesian estimation of neural signals in the context of unpredictable stimuli, offering new avenues for understanding information processing in the brain.

title: Keeping it Short and Simple: Summarising Complex Event Sequences with Multivariate Patterns
Abstract: This study explores the development of effective methods for summarizing complex event sequences using multivariate patterns. The vast majority of existing summarisation techniques struggle to capture the nuanced and often non-linear structure of real-world event sequences, leading to inaccurate and incomplete summaries. To address this shortfall, we introduce a novel approach that leverages multivariate patterns to succinctly represent complex event sequences. Our proposed method involves first identifying the most salient patterns within the sequence, using a combination of dimensionality reduction and clustering techniques. These patterns are then used to construct a concise and meaningful summary of the sequence, highlighting key events, trends, and relationships. We evaluate the efficacy of our approach using a range of synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrating its ability to outperform existing summarisation techniques in terms of both accuracy and interpretability. The results of this study have important implications for a variety of applications, including decision support, event monitoring, and complex systems analysis. By providing a more insightful and actionable summary of complex event sequences, our proposed method has the potential to significantly enhance the quality of decision-making and knowledge discovery in these domains.

title: Beauty and Brains: Detecting Anomalous Pattern Co-Occurrences
Abstract: The intricate relationship between beauty and intelligence has been debated and studied extensively in various fields, including psychology, sociology, and neuroscience. However, the underlying mechanisms and patterns governing this connection are not yet fully understood. This paper explores the concept of anomalous pattern co-occurrences as a novel approach to identifying trends and anomalies in the relationship between beauty and intelligence. By applying statistical and machine learning techniques to a large-scale database of facial images, cognitive abilities, and personality traits, we were able to detect anomalous patterns in the co-occurrences of physical attractiveness and high cognitive abilities. Our results show that these anomalous patterns are not random and are instead driven by specific underlying factors, such as cultural and economic influences, social status, and genetic predispositions. Furthermore, we found that these anomalous patterns can be predictive of future success and well-being, highlighting the importance of considering the complex interplay between beauty and brains in real-world applications. This study offers a valuable contribution to the existing literature on beauty and intelligence, shedding new light on the intricate dynamics of this multifaceted relationship.

title: News Across Languages - Cross-Lingual Document Similarity and Event Tracking
Abstract: This paper explores the concept of news across languages through the lens of cross-lingual document similarity and event tracking. The proliferation of news articles in multiple languages on the internet has made it increasingly difficult to track events and understand related information across different linguistic boundaries. To address this challenge, we propose a novel approach to cross-lingual document similarity, harnessing the power of deep learning techniques and word embeddings to bridge the language gap. Our approach utilizes a pairwise similarity metric to measure the similarity between embeddings of news articles in different languages. Our evaluation metrics comprise various cross-lingual document similarity tasks, such as ranking and classification. Furthermore, we extend our approach to event tracking by identifying events and their corresponding entities through a knowledge graph-based architecture. Our experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in cross-lingual document similarity and event tracking, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines in several evaluation metrics. We believe that the proposed approach can be applied to various real-world applications, including cross-lingual information retrieval, news recommendation, and crisis management. The presented work offers a promising direction for developing tools that can traverse language barriers and foster global understanding of news-related information.

title: Evaluation of Time-Critical Communications for IEC 61850-Substation Network Architecture
Abstract: The increasing demand for reliable and efficient operation of modern substations necessitates the integration of advanced communication technologies, such as time-critical communications, into substation network architectures. IEC 61850, a standard for substation automation, specifies the requirements for substation communication and control systems. However, the integration of time-critical communications within the IEC 61850 substation network architecture remains a complex task due to its specific constraints and requirements. The paper focuses on evaluating the suitability of existing communication protocols, namely Ethernet-IP (EtherCAT) and IEEE 1588v2, for supporting real-time applications in IEC 61850 substation networks. It discusses the characteristics of these protocols, their typical applications, and their performance in meeting the strict timing requirements of time-critical communications. A comparative analysis of these protocols is presented to assess their suitability for different time-critical communication scenarios in IEC 61850 substation networks. Furthermore, simulation-based experiments are used to validate the analytical results and to identify potential challenges associated with integrating time-critical communications within IEC 61850 substation networks. The findings of this research provide essential guidelines for the design and implementation of efficient and reliable time-critical communication systems within IEC 61850 substation networks.

title: On the Differential Privacy of Bayesian Inference
Abstract: This abstract explores the concept of differential privacy in the context of Bayesian inference, a fundamental methodology in statistical modeling and machine learning. The increasing reliance on data-driven decision-making and the subsequent concern for individual privacy have sparked a renewed interest in developing Bayesian inference frameworks that incorporate differential privacy. Our research delves into the limitations of existing approaches, which often fail to ensure effective privacy protection due to the inherent dimensionality and complexity of Bayesian models. To bridge this gap, we propose a novel framework that integrates differential privacy into Bayesian inference through a game-theoretic formulation. By modeling the privacy-utility tradeoff as a maximin problem, our approach enables the derivation of optimal Bayesian learning strategies that balance the accuracy of inference against the privacy risks associated with data disclosure. Empirical studies on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the efficacy of our framework, exhibiting significant improvements in differential privacy guarantees compared to state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, our framework is amenable to various Bayesian inference settings and can be easily extended to accommodate more complex models and data scenarios. The contributions of this work include a comprehensive analysis of differential privacy in Bayesian inference, the development of a novel framework for integrating privacy and inference, and a suite of empirical results showcasing the practical relevance and advantages of our approach.

title: Restricted Predicates for Hypothetical Datalog
Abstract: Restricted Predicates for Hypothetical Datalog have emerged as a highly effective approach to tackling the complexities and uncertainties inherent in real-world applications, particularly in knowledge graph reasoning and data integration tasks. However, traditional hypothetical Datalog systems suffer from various limitations, including the evaluation of hypothetical queries on large-scale datasets, which often involve expensive computational costs and result in significant performance degradation. To address these issues, this research explores the notion of restricted predicates, a novel concept that enables the selective evaluation of hypothetical queries based on specified constraints. The core idea revolves around the introduction of a restricted predicate learning framework, which incorporates a set of predefined logical rules and constraints to filter out unnecessary data and reduce the search space. Through the incorporation of machine learning techniques and logical rule-based systems, the proposed approach seeks to provide a more efficient and scalable method for processing hypothetical queries in Datalog systems. By utilizing the restricted predicates, this research aims to significantly enhance the performance of knowledge base systems, allowing users to extract meaningful insights and relationships from large-scale data repositories while minimizing computational complexity and query overhead. As a result, this work has the potential to transform the landscape of knowledge graph reasoning and data integration, enabling more accurate and efficient analysis of complex data and applications.

title: An Evaluation of Yelp Dataset
Abstract: This research paper presents an in-depth evaluation of the Yelp dataset, a comprehensive collection of user-generated reviews for various businesses across different categories and locations. The Yelp dataset is a rich source of unstructured text data, providing a unique opportunity to explore and analyze online review sentiments, user behavior, and business performance. By leveraging natural language processing (NLP) and machine learning techniques, this study aims to uncover the patterns and trends in the Yelp dataset, shedding light on the dynamics of online reviews and their impact on businesses. Specifically, the evaluation focuses on the demographics of reviewers, review topics, sentiment analysis, and the relationship between review ratings and various business attributes such as location, category, and hours of operation. The results of this study contribute to a better understanding of online review phenomena, informing business strategies for managing their online reputation and improving their services. Furthermore, the analyzed insights can be applied to develop more effective review generation and filtering algorithms, benefiting both reviewers and businesses alike. By quantifying the factors that influence review ratings and sentiments, this research endeavors to provide actionable recommendations for businesses to optimize their performance in the competitive landscape of online reviews.

title: Addressing Complex and Subjective Product-Related Queries with Customer Reviews
Abstract: This research paper delves into the rising trend of product-related queries on review platforms, where individuals pose complex, subjective, and open-ended questions, seeking understanding and affirmation from peers. The constant growth of e-commerce and the democratization of product information has led to such interactions becoming increasingly common. Understanding customers' behaviors and preferences in these scenarios can be pivotal in enhancing product offerings, satisfaction, and loyalty. Further, it can aid in developing effective product description, categorization, and recommendation systems that cater to diverse consumer needs. We propose a novel research framework that systematically studies such queries and reviews across multiple product domains, incorporating sentiment analysis, topic modeling, and network analysis to reveal invaluable insights. By examining the structural properties of reviews and identifying key query clusters, we aim to uncover underlying preferences, concerns, and expectations. Ultimately, the results can guide manufacturers to tweak product features, product categorization, and customer engagement strategies to better match consumers' emerging needs and perceptions. Our findings, we anticipate, will not only facilitate informed customer-choice processes but also help brands gauge their market performance more accurately by accounting for complex feedback voices from diverse consumers.

title: Information-Theoretic Bounded Rationality
Abstract: The concept of bounded rationality, first introduced by Herbert Simon in 1957, highlights the limitations of human decision-making processes under uncertainty and complexity. Traditional models of decision-making assume that individuals possess perfect knowledge, unlimited information processing capacity, and zero cognitive biases. However, real-world decision-making is often subject to practical limitations such as cognitive constraints, scarcity of information, and temporal constraints. To bridge this gap, information-theoretic approaches have emerged as a powerful tool for characterizing and modeling bounded rationality. Information-theoretic measures, such as entropy, mutual information, and conditional entropy, can be used to quantify the uncertainty and information exchange in decision-making processes. This paper explores the application of information-theoretic principles to bounded rationality, examining how individuals make decisions when facing uncertain and rapidly changing environments. By leveraging insights from information theory, we develop a framework for modeling bounded rationality that captures the essence of human decision-making, including cognitive biases, limited attention, and time constraints. Our approach enables a more nuanced understanding of the interplay between information and decision-making, shedding light on the intricate mechanisms that govern human choice under complexity and uncertainty. By analyzing real-world decision-making scenarios and computational models, we demonstrate the efficacy of our framework in better capturing the essential features of bounded rationality, ultimately enhancing our understanding of how individuals navigate and adapt to dynamic environments.

title: Multivariate Time Series Classification Using Dynamic Time Warping Template Selection for Human Activity Recognition
Abstract: This research proposes an innovative approach for human activity recognition using dynamic time warping (DTW) template selection in multivariate time series classification. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and recurrent neural networks (RNNs) have achieved impressive results in activity recognition, but suffer from high computational complexity and poor performance on diverse and long temporal sequences. To address this issue, we design an optimization framework that selects the most representative DTW templates from a large template set. These templates are created by clustering similar time series patterns using k-means and then applying DTW to compute the similarity matrix. Next, we utilize a greedy approach to select the most informative templates that capture the characteristic patterns of each activity. The selected templates are then used as inputs to a support vector machine (SVM) to classify human activities. Our experimental results on publicly available datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of classification accuracy and computational efficiency. Furthermore, we investigate various template selection techniques, including random forest and entropy-based methods, to provide a comprehensive comparison of their performance. Overall, our framework offers a promising solution for real-time human activity recognition in resource-constrained environments.

title: Constrained Sampling and Counting: Universal Hashing Meets SAT Solving
Abstract: Constrained sampling and counting problems involve generating and enumerating solutions that satisfy given constraints or properties. These problems have a wide range of applications in various fields, including cryptography, artificial intelligence, and data analysis. Traditional approaches to addressing these problems often rely on exponential-time algorithms, limiting their scalability. This research aims to develop novel, efficient solutions by bridging the gap between constrained sampling and universal hashing, and stochastic satisfiability (SAT) solving. Specifically, we introduce a new framework that leverages universal hashing to efficiently construct SAT formulas from given constraints, which are then solved using SAT solvers. Our approach exploits the strengths of each component to efficiently sample and count solutions, achieving significant performance gains over existing methods. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our approach on a variety of challenging constrained sampling and counting problems. By providing a hybrid framework that combines the power of universal hashing and SAT solving, this research addresses a significant gap in the existing literature and opens up new avenues for tackling complex constrained sampling and counting problems. Our proposed approach has the potential to impact a broad range of applications, including probabilistic verification, machine learning, and data-intensive research areas.

title: Remote Health Coaching System and Human Motion Data Analysis for Physical Therapy with Microsoft Kinect
Abstract: A remote health coaching system for physical therapy harnessing the capabilities of Microsoft Kinect is presented, focusing on human motion data analysis to aid rehabilitation and patient recovery. This novel system enables healthcare professionals to remotely monitor patients and provide personalized feedback and coaching, thereby bridging the accessibility gap of physical therapy services. The Microsoft Kinect, with its depth sensing capabilities and motion tracking functionalities, serves as a non-invasive and cost-effective tool in capturing and analyzing essential human movements. The integration of Kinect technology with a remote health coaching system empowers healthcare professionals to accurately assess gait, balance, and other movement patterns, facilitating the development of customized rehabilitation plans tailored to each patient's specific needs. The analysis of motion data reveals valuable insights on subtleties in gait patterns, thereby allowing healthcare professionals to identify nuances and bottlenecks in the rehabilitation process, thereby accelerating patient recovery and reducing the risk of relapse. Additionally, this digital system enables the continuous tracking and analysis of patients' progress over time, presenting prospects for monitoring responses to therapy and offering improved quality-of-life outcomes through a multidisciplinary approach.

title: Serifos: Workload Consolidation and Load Balancing for SSD Based Cloud Storage Systems
Abstract: This abstract provides a comprehensive exploration of workload consolidation and load balancing in solid-state drive (SSD) based cloud storage systems. The research focuses on the Greek island of Serifos as a metaphorical case study for optimizing resource utilization and ensuring high service availability in cloud storage environments. Traditional HDD-based storage systems are becoming increasingly obsolete due to their limitations in terms of data access times and energy efficiency, prompting the adoption of SSD technology which promises higher performance and lower latency. However, integrating SSDs into cloud storage infrastructure can lead to thermal dissipation issues and non-uniform resource utilization across servers, necessitating workload consolidation and load balancing to ensure optimal performance. Our research proposes an adaptive, policy-driven workload consolidation framework that utilizes a multi-level load balancing algorithm to dynamically allocate workloads across multiple SSD servers. By simulating real-world workloads and benchmarking performance metrics, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework in achieving higher throughput, lower latency, and reduced energy consumption in SSD-based cloud storage systems. Furthermore, a robust experimental evaluation on a real-world dataset further validates our findings and highlights the practical implications of implementing such workload consolidation and load balancing strategies in future-proof cloud storage infrastructure.

title: Towards Integrated Glance To Restructuring in Combinatorial Optimization
Abstract: This research paper delves into the realm of combinatorial optimization, a critical area in computer science and mathematics that deals with finding the optimal solution to a problem that has a finite number of potential solutions. Combinatorial optimization has numerous applications in logistics, scheduling, network flow, and resource allocation, among others. Traditional combinatorial optimization algorithms often struggle with large-scale instances due to their computational complexity, which renders them impractical for real-world applications. This study focuses on developing an integrated glance approach to restructuring combinatorial optimization problems, with an aim to enhance efficiency and scalability. By leveraging machine learning and metaheuristic techniques, the proposed integrated glance approach is able to identify problem structure and reformulate the problem in a more tractable form. This restructuring enables the application of more efficient algorithms and heuristics, leading to a significant reduction in computation time and improved solution quality. Experimental results on a variety of benchmark instances demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed integrated glance approach, showcasing its potential to revolutionize combinatorial optimization and paving the way for its applications in complex real-world problems. The study contributes to the development of more robust and efficient algorithms for combinatorial optimization, with far-reaching implications for various fields that rely on these techniques.

title: A Mathematical Theory of Deep Convolutional Neural Networks for Feature Extraction
Abstract: This paper establishes a rigorous mathematical foundation for deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) in the context of feature extraction. Building upon the theory of convolutional filters and the Fourier analysis of discrete signals, we derive a general framework for understanding the behavior of deep CNNs. By leveraging the wavelet theory and the properties of filter banks, we demonstrate the hierarchical representation of features through nested convolutional filters. Our mathematical formulation reveals the inherent regularization mechanisms present in deep CNNs, enabling the removal of redundant filters and contributing to improved generalization performance. Furthermore, we introduce a methodology for systematic filter design based on linear algebraic techniques, which facilitates efficient and computationally scalable architectures. The proposed theory is validated through a series of experiments involving synthetic and real-world data. In these experiments, the theoretical framework consistently outperforms state-of-the-art deep learning models in terms of feature extraction quality, computational efficiency, and real-time processing capabilities. Ultimately, our results provide a solid foundation for developing more sophisticated, data-efficient, and interpretable deep CNN architectures, promising new breakthroughs in the field of artificial intelligence.

title: Test-Driven Development of ontologies (extended version)
Abstract: This extended version of the Test-Driven Development (TDD) of ontologies research paper presents a comprehensive framework for the automated development of ontologies, ensuring their semantic accuracy, and data consistency while minimizing human errors, commonly resulting in suboptimal performance of knowledge management and artificial intelligence systems. By leveraging the principles of Test-Driven Development, this framework establishes a systematic approach to ontology construction, emphasizing rigorous testing and continuous iteration to improve ontology quality. The research evaluates the efficacy of TDD methods in ontology development through the implementation of a case study involving the creation of an event ontology, using a commercial tool as the development environment and a set of predefined testing environments to validate the ontology's accuracy. The case study is supported by various evaluation metrics to quantify the improvements in ontology quality thanks to the application of TDD principles. Moreover, a comparative study with the traditional development approach is conducted to highlight the advantages of TDD, such as reduced development time, increased data consistency, and improved semantic accuracy, thus making it an appealing option for large-scale ontology engineering projects. Furthermore, the study provides insights into the challenges faced while applying TDD in ontology development, informing a significant roadmap for the integration of TDD techniques into existing ontology engineering workflows.

title: Ontology-driven Information Extraction
Abstract:
This research paper explores the application of ontology-driven information extraction techniques in enhancing the efficiency and accuracy of information retrieval processes from unstructured and semi-structured data sources. Despite the advancements in natural language processing and machine learning, extracting relevant and accurate information from vast amounts of textual data remains a significant challenge. The proposed approach leverages the power of ontologies to provide a semantic framework for capturing and representing domain-specific knowledge, thereby facilitating the extraction of meaningful insights from unstructured data.

The ontology-driven information extraction technique used in this study integrates the extraction of entities, relationships, and concepts from raw text data using a combination of rule-based and statistical methods. The proposed system utilizes a domain-specific ontology to guide the extraction process, enabling it to capture subtle relationships and nuances that are often lost in traditional keyword-based approaches. Experiments conducted on a range of datasets and use cases demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach in extracting accurate and relevant information from unstructured data sources.

The results of this study not only demonstrate the potential of ontology-driven information extraction techniques but also highlight their applications in various domains, including information systems, knowledge management, and business intelligence. The paper provides an overview of the technical framework and design principles underlying the proposed approach and presents a comprehensive evaluation of its performance and scalability. Overall, this research contributes to the advancement of information extraction technologies and provides a robust methodology for exploiting the potential of large-scale unstructured data sources for informed decision-making.

title: Can Pretrained Neural Networks Detect Anatomy?
Abstract: This study investigates the ability of pretrained neural networks to detect anatomical components in medical imaging datasets. Deep learning models have achieved remarkable success in various computer vision tasks, including object detection and segmentation in medical images. However, the extent to which these pretrained models can be applied to specific medical imaging tasks, such as identifying anatomical structures, remains unclear. In this research, we evaluate the performance of various state-of-the-art neural network architectures, including ResNet, U-Net, and VGG, that have been pretrained on large datasets like ImageNet. We test these models on several medical imaging datasets, including chest X-rays, brain MRIs, and abdominal CT scans, and assess their ability to detect specific anatomical structures, such as lungs, bones, and organs. Our results show that while these pretrained models can achieve reasonable performance on certain tasks, their performance can be variable and sensitive to the specific imaging modality and anatomical structure in question. We also investigate the impact of fine-tuning the models on our medical imaging datasets and compare the results to models trained from scratch. The study provides insights into the potential and limitations of utilizing pretrained neural networks for anatomical detection in medical imaging and has implications for efficient and effective model deployment in clinical settings. Overall, the findings of this study contribute to the growing understanding of the strengths and weaknesses of deep learning in medical imaging applications and shed light on the potential for targeted fine-tuning to improve performance on specific tasks.

title: A Planning based Framework for Essay Generation
Abstract: This research aims to develop a novel planning-based framework for automated essay generation, which focuses on synthesizing coherent and informative essays from user prompts. The proposed framework, titled the "E-GEN" (Essay Generation and Evaluation Network), combines the strengths of symbolic planning and connectionist learning to effectively manage the complex relationships between propositions, themes, and essay structures. By applying planning-based methods to natural language generation, the E-GEN framework enables the creation of high-quality essays with a desired tone, style, and coherence. A key aspect of the framework is its ability to model composition-level knowledge and predicate reasoning in essay generation. Using a novel planning formalism and a graph-based approach, the E-GEN framework can concurrently plan, reason, and translate the generated plans into specific linguistic expressions. Furthermore, to evaluate the performance of the E-GEN framework, a comprehensive comparison with existing machine learning-based essay generation systems is presented, utilizing standard benchmarks and metrics. The results demonstrate the superior performance of the E-GEN framework in generating coherent and engaging essays with well-structured evidence, effectively capturing the essence of essays with respect to their input text prompts. The findings of this study provide important insights into the application of planning-based AI techniques for extended text generation tasks. Ultimately, this research contributes to a deeper understanding of the intricate collaboration between natural language generation and planning, highlighting the potential for significant improvements in the quality and coherence of generated essays.

title: Quadripolar Relational Model: a framework for the description of borderline and narcissistic personality disorders
Abstract: This study proposes the Quadripolar Relational Model (QRM) as a novel understanding of borderline and narcissistic personality disorders, enabling the explanation of the complex interplay between emotional expression, attachment, conflict resolution, and personality dynamics. The model posits that borderline personality disorder (BPD) and narcissistic personality disorder (NPD) exist within a four-dimensional plane, characterized by varying levels of emotional regulation, self-identity, attachment patterns, and relational conflict management. The first axis represents the emotional regulation of oneself and others, spanning from emotional intensity to flat emotional expression. The second axis captures self-identity, incorporating a range of self-soothing mechanisms and emotional availability. The third axis focuses on attachment styles, switching between secure, anxious, and avoidant attachment patterns. Finally, the fourth axis addresses modes of conflict resolution, including conflict-avoidance, competition, or respectful dialogue. Together, these four dimensions interact to produce distinct patterns of personality traits and behavioral responses, facilitating an unbiased, multidimensional view of borderline and narcissistic personality disorders. By providing a unified structure for analyzing these complex conditions, the QRM offers valuable implications for diagnosis, treatment, and prevention strategies.

title: On Voting and Facility Location
Abstract: This study explores the optimization of facility location and voting systems to ensure equitable and efficient resource allocation, service coverage, and citizen engagement. Focusing on the intersection of voting systems and facility location problems, we aim to identify and address the challenges associated with synchronizing voter turnout, poll site accessibility, and facility utilization with location decisions. A data-driven approach is employed, combining geospatial analysis and mathematical modeling to optimize facility locations considering voting patterns, demographic characteristics, and geographical accessibility. The research framework incorporates spatial optimization techniques and network analysis to evaluate the overall impact of facility locations on voting outcomes and resource allocation. The outcomes of the study are intended to provide actionable insights and recommendations for local and national policymakers, election administrators, and urban planners to enhance voter turnout, ensure inclusive participation, and optimize resource utilization in the context of facility location decisions. The research also aims to contribute to a more nuanced understanding of the complex relationships between voting systems, facility location, and civic engagement, thereby informing evidence-based policy and decision-making at the local, state, and national levels.

title: Modeling Progress in AI
Abstract: The advent of artificial intelligence (AI) has revolutionized the way we approach complex problems, transforming industries and reshaping our daily lives. As AI continues to advance at an unprecedented pace, modeling progress in AI has become a crucial aspect of understanding its impact and potential future applications. Recent breakthroughs in areas such as deep learning, natural language processing, and computer vision have led to significant improvements in AI model performance, enabling them to tackle increasingly complex tasks with high accuracy. This has resulted in applications ranging from intelligent virtual assistants and image recognition systems to autonomous vehicles and personalized medicine. However, as AI models become more sophisticated, understanding their behavior, decision-making processes, and limitations has become increasingly important. This necessitates the development of robust AI modeling techniques and frameworks that can accurately capture the intricacies of AI systems and facilitate effective communication between developers, stakeholders, and end-users. Furthermore, modeling progress in AI also involves exploring new areas of research, such as real-world data-driven representations, fairness, and explainability, which are critical for ensuring AI systems that are transparent, accountable, and socially beneficial. By examining the trajectory of AI progress, this study aims to provide a comprehensive framework for understanding the evolution of AI modeling and its implications for future applications and societal well-being.

title: Learning the Preferences of Ignorant, Inconsistent Agents
Abstract: This paper presents an exploration into the pressing challenge of modeling and learning the preferences of agents that operate under conditions of ignorance and inconsistency, often encountered in real-world decision-making scenarios. Most preference learning algorithms rely on access to idealized information about the agent's preferences, assuming a level of rationality and consistency that is frequently not present in practice. However, in many cases, the actual preferences of these agents remain unknown or are difficult to infer. The authors propose a novel approach that accounts for the agent's ignorance and inconsistency by incorporating a probability distribution over possible preference models. This approach involves using a probabilistic graphical model, where the nodes represent different preference models and the edges capture the inconsistencies between them. The model learns to infer not only the agent's true preferences but also the strengths of the inconsistencies between the learned models, thereby enabling the adaptation to new observations and changes in the agent's behavior. By leveraging the insights from this work, systems interacting with agents will be able to learn their preferences more accurately and make informed decisions in real-world settings. The approach is demonstrated through a series of experiments on synthetic and real-world data, showcasing its ability to handle missing and contradictory information, and provide a reliable and flexible method for modeling the preferences of complex, real-world agents.

title: A Survey of Available Corpora for Building Data-Driven Dialogue Systems
Abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive survey of available corpora for building data-driven dialogue systems, discussing their characteristics, use cases, and challenges associated with their curation and integration. Corpora play a pivotal role in the development of data-driven dialogue systems, as they serve as the foundation for training and fine-tuning the systems to generate coherent, context-specific, and human-like responses. The survey encompasses a wide range of dialogue corpora, including user-to-system, user-to-user, task-oriented, and open-domain datasets, each with its unique characteristics, strengths, and limitations. Our analysis reveals that these corpora vary significantly in terms of size, complexity, and domain specificity, necessitating careful consideration of corpus selection and customization for specific application tasks. We also examine the challenges associated with corpus curation, including data quality issues, annotation complexity, and data privacy concerns. Furthermore, we discuss the role of active learning, dataset augmentation, and transfer learning in addressing the limitations of current corpora and improving the performance of data-driven dialogue systems. The findings of this survey aim to inform the development of more effective and efficient data-driven dialogue systems that can interact with humans in a more natural and intuitive manner.

title: Probabilistic Programming with Gaussian Process Memoization
Abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to probabilistic programming with Gaussian process memoization, enabling efficient and accurate inference for complex probabilistic models. Gaussian processes are a powerful tool for modeling uncertainty in regression and classification tasks, but their high computational cost has limited their application in large-scale probabilistic programming. We propose a memoization strategy that caches the results of Gaussian process evaluations, allowing for the reusability of computations and a significant reduction in inference time. Our approach leverages a hierarchical and adaptive caching mechanism to balance the trade-off between memory usage and computational efficiency. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through a series of empirical evaluations on benchmark tasks, including Bayesian linear regression and probabilistic classification. Our results show that memoization of Gaussian process evaluations leads to a substantial speedup in inference time, with a median reduction of 95% for large datasets. Furthermore, we explore the application of our method to more complex probabilistic models, including Gaussian process classification and Bayesian neural networks with Gaussian process layers. Our findings highlight the potential of memoization to widen the adoption of Gaussian processes in large-scale probabilistic programming and demonstrate the necessity of efficient and adaptive caching strategies for high-performance probabilistic inference.

title: A thermodynamical approach towards multi-criteria decision making (MCDM)
Abstract: A thermodynamical approach towards multi-criteria decision making (MCDM) offers a unique framework to evaluate complex decision problems by harnessing the principles of thermodynamics, which describe the behavior of systems in terms of their energy interactions. This proposed theoretical framework unifies various decision-making techniques, such as TOPSIS, ELECTRE, and PROMETHEE, within a thermodynamical paradigm. By adopting entropy and exergy metrics, it becomes possible to quantify the intrinsic uncertainty and potential quality of choices. Information theory and its associated concepts, like the Shannon entropy, are used to account for the vagueness and ambiguity associated with decision inputs. In the given MCDM model, the key components are thermal efficiency, exergy destruction rates, and potential temperature differences that serve as quantifiable indicators for alternative evaluation. The MCDM approach is computationally implemented, ensuring an accurate and efficient decomposition of multi-dimensional choice problems. Prior to direct decision-making recommendations, this thermodynamical adaptation scrutinizes any probability distribution with probability limits to evaluate an optimal solution. Considering typical issues associated with traditional MCDM models, the application of thermodynamic laws may improve decision accuracy in circumstances of uncertainty, offering enhanced interpretative insights into complex multi-parameter decision scenarios.

title: An Empirical Comparison of Neural Architectures for Reinforcement Learning in Partially Observable Environments
Abstract: This paper presents an empirical comparison of diverse neural architectures for reinforcement learning (RL) in partially observable environments. State-of-the-art RL algorithms often rely on complex neural networks to learn control policies, but designing architectures suitable for partially observable environments remains a challenging task. We compare the performance of eight neural architectures, each combining different forms of processing units, such as convolutional layers, recurrent neural networks, and graph convolutional networks. These architectures are evaluated on four partially observable environments, including GridWorld, Lunar Lander, CartPole, and MiniGrid, using a comprehensive set of benchmarks. Our results show significant variations in the performance of different architectures across environments and task complexities. We observe that, in general, models with a greater capacity to process sequential and spatial information (notably graph-convolutional networks and recurrent neural networks) tend to outperform models with a greater focus on general function approximation (such as multilayer perceptrons). Conversely, non-recurrent models with lightweight processing units (like sparse, 1D convolutional networks) are more effective in certain environments where increased model capacity can decrease performance. Our investigation aims to provide valuable insights for researchers and practitioners to select the most suitable neural architecture for RL in partially observable settings and highlights the need for further exploration into designing and optimizing RL models for complex, real-world scenarios.

title: Blind, Greedy, and Random: Ordinal Approximation Algorithms for Matching and Clustering
Abstract: This paper presents a comparative study of Blind, Greedy, and Random approximation algorithms for solving complex optimization problems in matching and clustering contexts. In the realm of matching problems, we investigate the performance of Ordinal Blind (OB), Ordinal Greedy (OG), and Ordinal Random (OR) algorithms as they attempt to maximize the weight of assigned edges. The experimental results reveal that the Blind algorithm exhibits exponential memory size requirements but possesses worst-case guarantees for approximation performance. Conversely, the Greedy algorithm outperforms its Blind counterpart by being more computationally efficient and memory-friendly in return for weaker theoretical guarantees. On the other hand, the Random algorithm's performance is unpredictable, showing the potential to output optimal or near-optimal solutions for challenging problem instances but failing to maintain consistency. Our analysis highlights the practical trade-offs between these algorithms in matching problems. Furthermore, we adapt the Blind, Greedy, and Random algorithms to tackle clustering problems in the ordinal domain, where the goal is to optimize both similarity and gap penalization. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of these algorithms in clustering settings, where they outperform baselines and state-of-the-art approaches in various scenarios, especially when dealing with massive and sparse datasets.

title: Deep Active Object Recognition by Joint Label and Action Prediction
Abstract: Deep Active Object Recognition by Joint Label and Action Prediction revolves around the development of effective and efficient methods that can accurately recognize and classify objects in complex and dynamic environments. Traditional approaches in object recognition rely heavily on static features and do not account for the temporal relationships between objects and their actions. This research aims to bridge this gap by introducing a novel framework that integrates deep learning techniques with active perception principles to predict both the label and the action of an object in real-time. The proposed framework utilizes a hierarchical neural network architecture, comprising of a sequence prediction module and a reasoning module, to analyze video sequences and predict the most likely label and action of an object. The sequence prediction module leverages convolutional recurrent neural networks (CRNNs) to capture spatial and temporal features, while the reasoning module exploits graph neural networks (GNNs) to model the relationships between objects and their actions. In-depth experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate the superiority of the proposed framework over state-of-the-art methods, showcasing significant improvements in accuracy and efficiency. This work has far-reaching implications for applications in robotics, autonomous vehicles, and human-computer interaction, where accurate object recognition and action prediction are critical for informed decision-making.

title: Unsupervised Feature Construction for Improving Data Representation and Semantics
Abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of improving data representation and semantics through the application of unsupervised feature construction techniques. In many real-world scenarios, complex data often lacks clear and well-defined labels, hindering the ability of standard machine learning algorithms to extract meaningful insights. Consequently, there is an increasing need for developing and applying unsupervised feature construction methods capable of transforming raw data into higher-level abstractions that capture inherent structures and semantics. Our proposed method, autoencoder guided feature construction (AEFC), combines the strengths of autoencoders with topological data analysis to automatically generate meaningful features that facilitate better understanding and representation of the data. We evaluate the performance and effectiveness of AEFC through extensive experimentation on a diverse set of datasets, including high-dimensional images, biological sequence data, and network topologies. Our results demonstrate the efficacy of AEFC in discovering and revealing latent patterns, correlations, and relationships within complex data that are otherwise difficult to discern using traditional supervised methods. Furthermore, the resulting features extracted by AEFC are more robust and less prone to overfitting compared to those derived from standard autoencoders. This study contributes to the development of advanced unsupervised feature construction techniques and paves the way for the application of these approaches in various domain-specific applications, such as data mining, knowledge discovery, and decision-making processes.

title: Differential Evolution with Event-Triggered Impulsive Control
Abstract: Differential Evolution with Event-Triggered Impulsive Control is a novel optimization technique that leverages the salient features of event-triggered control and impulsive control strategies to create a powerful hybrid optimization method. By introducing impulsive control in a controlled and event-triggered manner, the proposed technique is capable of fine-tuning the search process and enhancing the exploitation capabilities of traditional differential evolution methods. The core idea behind this approach is to trigger impulsive interventions only when necessary, resulting in a reduction in computational complexity while ensuring the robustness of the optimization process. Utilizing mathematical modeling and simulation techniques, researchers have demonstrated that the proposed method outperforms traditional differential evolution in various optimization scenarios, including those with large-scale and complex problems, where the event-triggered mechanism effectively leverages existing knowledge to eliminate unnecessary iterations and accelerate the convergence process. Furthermore, the proposed method is robust against uncertainty and noise, making it a suitable candidate for real-world applications. This research provides novel insights into the field of event-based control and presents a potentially game-changing optimization tool that is likely to have significant impacts on fields such as engineering, economics, and logistics.

title: Signal Representations on Graphs: Tools and Applications
Abstract: Signal Representations on Graphs: Tools and Applications is a rich area of research at the intersection of signals, graphs, and learning theory, aiming to develop a unified framework for generalizing signal processing concepts from regular grids to graph-structured data. In recent years, numerous graph signal processing (GSP) tools and applications have been introduced to bridge the gap between traditional signal processing and graph-based data, enabling efficient analysis, filtering, and classification on non-Euclidean domains. This paper surveys the state-of-the-art GSP tools, including graph Fourier transforms, graph filters, and PageRank-like methods, highlighting their applications in computer vision, network science, and machine learning. We also delve into the recent advancements in graph signal sampling, graph neural networks, and graph signal denoising, demonstrating the potential for enhanced information extraction and pattern discovery on graph-structured data. Furthermore, we examine the theoretical underpinnings of GSP and its relationships with classical signal processing concepts, laying a foundation for rigorous design, analysis, and optimization of GSP tools and techniques. By reviewing the current landscape and discussing open challenges in GSP, we envision new possibilities for tackling complex problems in structural analysis, energy networks, brain connectivity analysis, and numerous other domains, ultimately benefiting from the transformative potential of graph signal processing.

title: Feature Representation for ICU Mortality
Abstract: The accurate forecasting of Intensive Care Unit (ICU) mortality remains a significant concern in clinical settings, where timely interventions can have a substantial impact on patient outcomes. Traditional clinical features have proven to be insufficient in capturing the complexity of ICU data, leading researchers to explore more sophisticated machine learning approaches. Feature representation is a crucial step in these endeavors, where intricate patterns within high-dimensional data are distilled into meaningful representations that facilitate informed decision-making. This study delves into the exploration of novel feature representation techniques specifically tailored for ICU mortality prediction, leveraging a range of state-of-the-art algorithms to distill key temporal and spatial characteristics from patient data. Supervised learning architectures, incorporating attention mechanisms and graph neural networks, are employed to capture the intricate dynamics between diverse clinical metrics, vital signs, and time-series trends. Empirical results reveal the superiority of these novel feature representations in outperforming traditional methods, demonstrating improved predictive accuracy and robustness in the presence of noise and uncertainty. Further investigation is conducted to explore the interpretability and transferability of these models, shedding light on the contributing factors to ICU mortality and guiding clinical practice toward more personalized and effective interventions.

title: Solving stable matching problems using answer set programming
Abstract: Stable matching problems have been extensively studied in the context of various real-world applications, such as medical residency allocation, organ transplantation, marriage markets, and school admissions. However, their computational complexity and the need for efficient solutions have remained significant challenges. Answer set programming (ASP) offers a promising paradigm for addressing these challenges. The primary contribution of this research lies in presenting a novel solution to stable matching problems using ASP. By employing the logical foundations of ASP, we demonstrate the feasibility of modeling instability conditions and associated conflict resolution using answer set solvers. Our approach is based on encoding the stable matching problem as an ASP program, which enables the calculation of stable matchings. Moreover, we develop an ASP-based framework that enables the computation of all possible stable matchings, not just one. We empirically evaluate the computational efficiency of our ASP-based framework using real-world datasets that exhibit increasingly large scales. Furthermore, we show that our ASP-based approach not only supports efficient computation of stable matchings but also yields more flexibility for modeling and handling real-world constraints and perturbations. Ultimately, the presented ASP-based framework emerges as a potential solution for tackling stable matching problems and contributes to the development of more scalable and versatile decision-support tools for allocation problems and other related domains.

title: Symphony from Synapses: Neocortex as a Universal Dynamical Systems Modeller using Hierarchical Temporal Memory
Abstract: This research presents a novel approach to modelling dynamic systems by leveraging the hierarchical organization and temporal processing capabilities of the neocortex. Inspired by the symphony of interactions present in the brain, we explore the idea of applying Hierarchical Temporal Memory (HTM) to model complex dynamical systems. By representing the neocortex as a distributed, adaptive, and hierarchical system, we demonstrate how HTM's property of self-organization can be used to extract meaningful patterns and relationships from raw sensory data. Our approach, called Cortex-HTM, utilizes a hierarchical architecture with spatial and temporal memory cells to identify and predict patterns in data. This is achieved through a process of recursive grouping and pruning of neurons, similar to how the neocortex maintains and refines its topological representations. We evaluate Cortex-HTM on a variety of complex dynamical systems, including chaotic attractors, neural networks, and financial time-series data. Our results show that Cortex-HTM is able to accurately model and predict the behavior of these systems, often outperforming state-of-the-art methods. This work has significant implications for our understanding of the neural basis of cognition and perception, as well as for the development of novel artificial intelligence and machine learning architectures. By investigating the symphony of interactions present in the brain, we gain insights into the fundamental principles of dynamical systems modelling and make strides towards the creation of more adaptive and intelligent AI systems.

title: Smart Data Pricing Models for Internet-of-Things (IoT): A Bundling Strategy Approach
Abstract: The emergence of the Internet-of-Things (IoT) has led to the proliferation of connected devices, giving rise to the need for innovative pricing models that can effectively manage network resources while catering to diverse user requirements. This research proposes a novel bundling strategy approach to develop smart data pricing models for IoT networks. The approach integrates artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) techniques with game theoretical frameworks to create dynamic pricing models that adapt to changing network conditions and user behaviors. By analyzing the relationships between device types, usage patterns, and user preferences, the proposed model bundles services in real-time, offering customized pricing plans that reflect the value of data transfer and network quality. The bundling strategy not only improves network efficiency and revenue maximization but also enhances user experience through personalized offers and increased transparency. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed approach in optimizing data pricing and network usage, promoting a more sustainable and fair IoT ecosystem. The developed smart data pricing models can be deployed in various IoT applications, including smart cities, industrial automation, and home automation, to create a more efficient and user-centric IoT environment.
