title: BayesDB: A probabilistic programming system for querying the probable implications of data
Abstract: BayesDB is a novel probabilistic programming system that empowers users to explore the probable implications of data, underpinning their ability to make informed decisions in a wide array of applications. By harnessing the power of Bayesian inference, BayesDB allows users to define probabilistic models of complex phenomena, systematically analyzing the propagation of uncertainty from uncertain observations to derived conclusions. At its core, BayesDB provides a SQL-like interface for querying probabilistic databases, facilitating seamless integration with existing data management systems and intuitive exploration of the probabilistic relationships within the data. This intuitive interface enables users to compose complex queries involving conditional probabilities, model updates, and evidence accumulation, thereby discovering key patterns, correlations, and causal relationships that would be difficult to uncover using traditional data analysis techniques. Moreover, BayesDB's probabilistic nature allows it to gracefully handle missing data and tolerate noisy or uncertain inputs, yielding more robust and scalable inferences than conventional methods. Through its commitment to the SQL paradigm and probabilistic reasoning, BayesDB offers a powerful tool for probabilistic data analysis, analysis of complex systems and causal relationships, supporting a broad spectrum of applications in medicine, climate modeling, finance, engineering, sociology, politics, and numerous other fields.

title: Conditions for Normative Decision Making at the Fire Ground
Abstract: Normative decision-making at the fire ground encompasses a broad range of situational factors, decision-maker traits, and communication dynamics that interplay to determine the effectiveness of firefighter performance and safety in critical incidents. Research has long acknowledged the high-stress environment typical to firefighting, where decision-makers often find themselves concurrently dealing with life threats and objective-setting. Limited consensus, however, has been achieved in the field regarding what constitutes optimal conditions for normative decision-making within fire ground scenarios. This study sought to address the persistent knowledge gap by examining the role of situational factors, such as communication, clear objectives, and situational awareness, in conjunction with firefighter decision-maker traits like training, experience, and decision anxiety levels. Empirical investigation revealed that open communication, clear objectives, and a controlled situational setting were significantly linked to normative decision-making performances in the fire ground. Moreover, results indicated that decreasing decision anxiety and bolstering experiential knowledge of decision-makers positively influenced performance. These findings contribute to the critical discourse surrounding firefighter performance and shed light on actionable strategies that can be implemented to address situational challenges, bolster communication dynamics, and mitigate the impacts of decision anxiety at the fire ground.

title: Increasing the Action Gap: New Operators for Reinforcement Learning
Abstract: The action gap, a discrepancy between the optimal policy in the simulation and the one obtained in the real world, has long hindered the deployment of reinforcement learning (RL) methods in complex environments. To bridge this gap, the focus has been shifted towards developing new operators that can learn more efficiently and effectively without relying heavily on exhaustive exploration, which often proves to be computationally expensive and time-consuming. This work proposes novel variants of several established RL algorithms that focus on mitigating the action gap through more informed exploration and by emphasizing the robustness of the learned policies. By introducing the concept of 'action-prior' and 'pre-conditioned value iteration', we aim to systematically select the most informative actions and reduce the reliance on trial-and-error exploration, thereby reducing the uncertainty attached to policy updates. Additionally, we also present a hybrid framework combining exploration patterns and iterative value refinement to effectively tackle real-world RL tasks. By characterizing these new operators, we demonstrate the ability to bridge the action gap efficiently, providing evidence for the applicability of value iteration and exploration methods for achieving near-optimal policy learning. Furthermore, we empirically validate our proposals using comprehensive benchmark evaluations, illustrating the potential of our approach in real-world RL settings.

title: From One Point to A Manifold: Knowledge Graph Embedding For Precise Link Prediction
Abstract: Knowledge graph embedding has been a crucial approach in addressing the link prediction task in various real-world applications, including but not limited to, recommender systems, question answering, and recommendation systems for users. Traditional transductive methods and various supervised embeddings have been shown to achieve good results in several such tasks, but usually fails when information jumps beyond pairwise relationships, where knowledge graphs turn to manifolds. They get much more complex to model as it gets virtually impossible to build upon simple pairwise relationships. A new approach to this issue lies in introducing generalized manifolds using our potential distribution in real space, preserving information beyond the traditional pairwise network relationships. In this paper, we focus on our new manifold learning approach for link prediction in knowledge graph embedding by adopting techniques like deep neural networks for manifold optimization problem and embedding different concepts such as symmetry, similarity and distance preservation effectively. This provides general framework that captures beyond pairwise and offers much better optimization. Our approach is highly capable of providing optimal node positioning within the embedding space, even though knowledge graph may become significantly dense and complex. Furthermore, our optimized strategy is shown to perform fairly well for larger and non-linearly structured diverse data coming from standard benchmark datasets and applications. By exploring different cases with our approach showing highly robust framework over popular competitive embedding algorithms, this paper offers deeper insights for researchers working on link prediction in a knowledge graph with its dynamic manifold structure.

title: Hyper-Heuristic Algorithm for Finding Efficient Features in Diagnose of Lung Cancer Disease
Abstract: This study develops and applies a hyper-heuristic approach to optimize the feature selection process in the diagnosis of lung cancer disease, utilizing an ensemble of machine learning models to identify the most relevant radiomic features from CT scans. By combining multiple feature selection methods, the proposed hyper-heuristic algorithm efficiently identifies the optimal subset of features that provide the highest classification performance for lung cancer diagnosis. The study commences with an extensive review of existing feature selection methods in the context of lung cancer diagnosis and highlights the limitations of conventional approaches. Following this, the proposed hyper-heuristic approach is formally introduced, incorporating a novel weighted committee approach to effectively combine the strengths of multiple feature selection methods. A comprehensive experimental study with a large-scale radiomics dataset is conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed hyper-heuristic algorithm, deploying widely used machine learning classifiers, including Random Forest, Support Vector Machine, and Convolutional Neural Network. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed hyper-heuristic approach significantly improves the feature selection process, enhancing classification accuracy, area under the ROC curve, and area under the precision-recall curve by up to 20%, 25%, and 15%, respectively, compared to state-of-the-art feature selection methods. The findings of this study provide a novel insight into hyper-heuristic-based feature selection in lung cancer diagnosis, highlighting the potential for improved diagnostic accuracy and efficiency in medical imaging applications.

title: Semantic-enriched Visual Vocabulary Construction in a Weakly Supervised Context
Abstract: The vast amount of visual data generated by image and video capture technologies necessitates the development of robust techniques for image and video analysis. In this paper, we investigate the problem of constructing a semantic-enriched visual vocabulary in a weakly supervised context, where the supervision is limited to textual annotations. To this end, we propose a novel framework that leverages the power of deep learning-based feature extractors, such as convolutional neural networks (CNNs), to capture the underlying patterns in the visual data. Our approach employs a combination of multiple CNNs pretrained on large-scale vision datasets to obtain a compact and robust visual vocabulary, which is further enriched by incorporating semantic information from the textual annotations. We propose a systematic method to measure the semantic similarity between images and the textual annotations, thereby enabling the construction of a meaningfully organized visual vocabulary. Experimental results on several benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework in achieving state-of-the-art performance in various vision tasks, including image classification, object detection, and image segmentation. Furthermore, our framework is evaluated using metrics such as recall, precision, and mean average precision, which underscores its usefulness in Weakly supervised settings with limited label availability.

title: Sentence Entailment in Compositional Distributional Semantics
Abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to modeling sentence entailment in compositional distributional semantics, a framework that combines the principles of distributional semantics with the compositional semantics of formal logic. We reformulate the task of sentence entailment as an event-attribute matrix (IAM) similarity problem, enabling the computation of entailment relationships between sentences through a compositionally invariant representation. Our approach capitalizes on the recent advances in the expressiveness and numerical stability of non-equivalence functions, facilitating the modeling of subtle and nuanced entailment relationships between sentences. We also leverage state-of-the-art techniques for semantic decomposition and alignment, which are essential components in capturing the compositional structure of natural language. The empirical evaluations demonstrate the efficacy of our method in capturing entailment relationships between sentences, indicating significant improvements over existing baseline models. Furthermore, our method exhibits a remarkable level of componence, making it well-suited for incremental and compositional reasoning. Overall, this study contributes significantly to the field of compositional distributional semantics, providing a novel and robust framework for modeling sentence entailment. The extension of this work to more complex scenarios, such as inference and question answering, holds immense promise and highlights the significant potential of this approach in addressing key challenges in natural language processing.

title: Data-driven Sequential Monte Carlo in Probabilistic Programming
Abstract: The paper "Advancements in Bayesian Inference: A Data-driven Sequential Monte Carlo Approach in Probabilistic Programming" presents an innovative method for augmenting probabilistic programming (PP) with data-driven sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) algorithms. This fusion enables the community to exploit the power of flexible probabilistic modeling in PP, while capitalizing on the robust uncertainty quantification abilities of SMC methods. The proposed data-driven SMC framework focuses on adaptively sampling the proposal distributions, thereby fostering robust particle representation in complex, high-dimensional posterior distributions, prevalent in real-world problems. By embedding various data-driven strategies for proposal distribution refinement, particularly focusing on utilizing Bayesian model Evidence, and the corresponding convergence rate analysis, the integration offers improved exploration capabilities and model selection capacity in Probabilistic Programming. Furthermore, the methodology also exploits the SMC capabilities for augmenting model parameter exploration and Bayesian prediction tasks. Empirical evaluations on diverse datasets demonstrate significant performance improvements over conventional PP-based methods in terms of Bayesian model estimation and uncertainty quantification. Nonetheless, a detailed study of the computational complexity and scalability of the presented data-driven SMC framework is warranted to facilitate practical implementation, potentially enabling this powerful tool-set to be used efficiently for various operational applications with potential impact on real-world data analysis.

title: An Event Calculus Production Rule System for Reasoning in Dynamic and Uncertain Domains
Abstract: This paper introduces an Event Calculus Production Rule System (ECPRS) that tackles the complexities of dynamic and uncertain domains by integrating the Event Calculus and Production Rules in a unified framework. Traditional production rule systems are effective for reasoning in static domains, but they struggle to adapt to rapidly changing domains and uncertain circumstances. The Event Calculus, on the other hand, is powerful for representing temporal dynamics, but its computational complexity and procedural encoding can be limiting. To address these challenges, ECPRS leverages the Event Calculus's temporal reasoning capabilities within the modular and flexible architecture of production rule systems. This integration enables ECPRS to support robust and efficient reasoning in dynamic and uncertain domains. Specifically, ECPRS captures novel and situation-specific knowledge using weighted Event Calculus axioms and production rules, which leverages ontological and non-monotonic reasoning to mitigate the effect of uncertainty and variation. The proposed framework is implemented in a novel computational model that demonstrates its efficiency, flexibility, and scalability by solving test cases and comparing them to benchmark models. The results indicate that ECPRS can successfully incorporate novel information, handle intricate interactions between event relationships, and accurately generate temporally consistent conclusions under uncertainty.

title: Origami: A 803 GOp/s/W Convolutional Network Accelerator
Abstract: This paper proposes an Origami-based Convolutional Network Accelerator, optimizing existing deep learning architecture in terms of high-throughput, low-power, and scalability. A cutting-edge folded architecture is presented, enabling designers to reduce significantly the area and power consumption while increasing the throughput by about 9.3x, approaching peak 803 GOp/s/W, a first in computational neuromorphic computing. Conventional 2D architectural techniques fail to match Origami's achievements, therefore demonstrating its superior scalability. Original memory hierarchy, power management, and thermal modeling architectures are tailored, with an initial assessment against conventional designs resulting in a substantial ten-fold savings in power. What drives Origami's efficiency is the non-uniform interconnection via arrays of synapses set up in each folded origami layer, in conjunction with a hierarchical access pattern that serves a hierarchical storage and network in real time. In essence, this accelerates most of the convolutional processing in a large ConvNet model. Origami can now execute a much wider range of deep neural networks at unprecedented levels of power per performance. We project that future designs will not merely achieve improvements tied to the increase in chip density but also reach lower frequencies thanks to careful design and precision in the origami layers, redefining practical mobile implementation of our deepest AIs.

title: Evaluation of Pose Tracking Accuracy in the First and Second Generations of Microsoft Kinect
Abstract: This study aims to evaluate the pose tracking accuracy of the first and second generations of Microsoft Kinect, two pivotal devices in the realm of motion capture and depth sensing technologies. The Microsoft Kinect has revolutionized human-computer interaction by enabling users to control electronic devices and interact with virtual environments using intuitive body movements. Our evaluation focuses on the precision and reliability of the pose tracking capabilities of both generations, examining the inherent limitations and variations that might influence their performance. A comprehensive dataset of various physical activities and gestures has been captured using both devices to systematically compare and contrast their pose tracking accuracy. Our findings indicate that while both generations exhibit robust performance across a range of gestures, the second generation of the Kinect outperforms the first generation in certain scenarios, with a notable increase in accuracy and a decrease in tracking latency. The insights gained from this comparison can provide valuable guidance for developers and researchers considering the selection of a suitable motion capture technology for their applications.

title: Building and Measuring Privacy-Preserving Predictive Blacklists
Abstract: This research presents an innovative approach to creating and evaluating privacy-preserving predictive blacklists for preventing cyber threats. The proposed system aims to maintain a balance between the accuracy of threat detection and the protection of user data by employing cutting-edge techniques from machine learning and data privacy. To achieve this objective, we utilize a secure multi-party computation (SMPC) protocol that enables collaborative blacklisting among participating organizations without compromising sensitive user information. By using SMPC, our system ensures that local threat indicators are combined in a way that preserves the anonymity of individual contributors, making it challenging for adversaries to identify specific users. Furthermore, our blacklisting strategy incorporates a context-aware machine learning model that takes into account various factors, including user behavior, network activity, and device characteristics. The evaluation of our system demonstrates its ability to efficiently detect malware and other cyber threats with a high degree of accuracy, while maintaining an acceptable trade-off between false positives and false negatives. The contributions of this research include the design of a novel privacy-preserving blacklisting framework, an adaptive decision-making process for context-aware threat detection, and an empirical assessment of the proposed system's effectiveness in real-world scenarios. Our findings have meaningful implications for the development of trustworthy cybersecurity solutions that prioritize user data protection while ensuring the mitigation of emerging cyber threats.

title: Policy Gradient Methods for Off-policy Control
Abstract: This work investigates the application of policy gradient methods in off-policy reinforcement learning for control tasks, focusing on the theoretical and empirical aspects of these algorithms. Policy gradient methods are a class of model-free reinforcement learning algorithms, where the policy is updated towards maximizing a performance objective. In contrast, off-policy methods learn from a sequence of experiences gathered by following different policies. This combination enables learning directly from exploratory data without incurring the high cost of policy iteration. We delve into the key principles that underlie off-policy policy gradient methods, such as maximizing expected returns, constructing effective advantage functions, and estimating gradients from samples of data. Experimental results on benchmark control tasks demonstrate the improved sample efficiency and robustness of these algorithms when executed in an off-policy paradigm, showcasing the potential of this framework for complex, high-dimensional control problems. Furthermore, we advance theoretical understanding by characterizing the convergence properties of off-policy policy gradient methods, assuming weak conditions on the data distribution. Our findings highlight the efficacy and flexibility of these algorithms for real-world reinforcement learning applications, ranging from robotics to game playing, where effective control is indispensable. Overall, this work strives to bridge the theoretical and empirical gaps in the study of off-policy policy gradient methods, with implications for their increased adoption and development in a wide range of control tasks.

title: Using Linear Constraints for Logic Program Termination Analysis
Abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to logic program termination analysis based on linear constraints, which enhances the existing methods by providing a more precise and efficient analysis of recursive functions in logic programs. By formulating termination as a linear constraint solving problem, our approach efficiently checks the well-foundedness of the semantic entailments for given clause indexing functions, thereby establishing a direct connection between the termination analysis and the corresponding linear constraints. The key idea revolves around using an iterative framework that traverses the clause indexing graph while introducing new constraints, leading to a precise characterization of the terminating behavior of the logic programs. The proposed method incorporates classic termination tools like narrowing and memoization while also addressing some of the inherent complexities associated with non-linear clause variables. This approach has been implemented and experimentally evaluated on several standard termination benchmarks, demonstrating significant improvement in both accuracy and efficiency, thereby highlighting its capabilities as a valuable addition to the existing termination analysis tools. Overall, the linear constraint-based approach showcased in this paper presents a more refined methodology for terminating behavior, paving the way for the wider adoption of proof-based systems in logic programming environments.

title: True Online Temporal-Difference Learning
Abstract: This study presents a novel approach to temporal-difference (TD) learning, focusing on the development of a true online TD learning algorithm that can efficiently learn from interactions with an environment without relying on offline batch refinement or reliance on pre-defined episodic structures. In the context of online reinforcement learning, TD learning has proven to be an effective method for learning value functions in a variety of complex environments. However, existing TD learning algorithms often employ offline batch processes or model parameter updates, which can limit their adaptability in dynamic settings and impair their ability to capitalize on immediate learning opportunities. To address these limitations, we introduce the novel True Online TD (TOTD) algorithm, which incorporates a temporal-difference update scheme that is specifically designed for online settings. Unlike other online TD methods, the proposed algorithm possesses two key features that distinguish it from its offline counterparts: the absence of pre-defined episodic structures and the elimination of offline batch refinement. This allows the TOTD algorithm to operate in a more flexible and adaptive manner, capitalizing on immediate learning opportunities in online environments. The effectiveness of the TOTD algorithm is rigorously established through extensive numerical experiments and comparisons with existing online TD methods, which demonstrate its potential to achieve superior performance in a variety of challenging environments.

title: The Rationale behind the Concept of Goal
Abstract: The concept of a goal has been an essential component of human motivation, behavior, and achievement, with numerous theories and models proposed to explain its underlying mechanisms. Despite the abundance of research on goal theory, the rationale behind the concept of a goal continues to be an enigma, with various approaches offering distinct yet often overlapping perspectives. This paper provides a comprehensive analysis of the concept of a goal, examining the philosophical, psychological, and sociological underpinnings that shape our understanding of goals. Through a meticulous review of both empirical and theoretical studies, we uncover the multifaceted nature of goals, including their cognitive, emotional, and motivational components. Our analysis reveals that goals are not merely arbitrary targets or desired outcomes, but rather complex constructions that reflect our values, identities, and relationships. Furthermore, we highlight the dynamic interplay between goal pursuit, self-concept, and social context, demonstrating how goals are shaped and influenced by individual and collective factors. By synthesizing insights from diverse fields, this paper offers a nuanced understanding of the concept of a goal, illuminating the intricate web of psychological, social, and philosophical processes that underlie goal-directed behavior.

title: Query Answering over Contextualized RDF/OWL Knowledge with Forall-Existential Bridge Rules: Decidable Finite Extension Classes (Post Print)
Abstract: This research investigate knowledge representation and reasoning capabilities required for answer query over dynamically enriched RDF/OWL knowledge bases, adopting novel extensions of Finite Model Reasoning over Decidable Finite Extension Classes that incorporate Forall-Existential Bridge Rules, a powerful reasoning technique in logic programming and knowledge representation. Theoretical grounding is established by developing first-order and higher-order representations of semantic interpretations that are guaranteed to preserve satisfiability and correct answer query result. Consequently, existing algorithms for answer query over finite RDFS/OWL DL ontologies are enhanced with bridge rules, creating novel systems for contextualized query answering that obtain precise and scalable satisfaction results. Further, the theoretical analysis of bridge rules extension of Decidable Finite Extension Classes guarantee correctness of the system's output even for infinite extensions. Subsequently, the practical side of the extension is emphasized with algorithms designed for reasoning under these extensions. Results from set-theoretic and computational experiences with complex knowledge bases indicate that the proposed extension leads to notable increase in answering competency and satisfiability preservation levels while maintaining the guaranteed decidability within finite satisfaction levels.

title: Deep Feature Learning with Relative Distance Comparison for Person Re-identification
Abstract: This paper presents a novel person re-identification approach that employs deep feature learning and relative distance comparison for improving the accuracy and robustness of matching individuals across non-overlapping cameras. The proposal involves a two-stage pipeline: in the first stage, multiple convolutional neural networks (CNNs) extract a collection of multi-scale and diverse deep features from input images; in the second stage, a relative distance comparison mechanism, based on the principles of triplet loss, is used to compare the derived features and learn discriminative pair-wise relationships for each probe-gallery pair. To accomplish this, an adaptive triplet sampling strategy is developed to dynamically regulate the level of difficulty and diversity during the learning process, ensuring that the CNN and the relative distance comparison module jointly learn a robust and transferable person embedding. Experimental results and comparisons with nine state-of-the-art methods demonstrate the superiority of the proposed approach on six benchmark datasets, indicating its ability to cope with variations in illumination, pose, occlusion, and camera viewpoints. Furthermore, the robustness and adaptability of the proposed framework to varying environments and settings are underscored by its satisfactory performance under realistic factors such as appearance, viewpoint, and occlusion changes. Through an integrated evaluation of metrics and experiments, this work solidifies the viability of our proposal for applications requiring accurate and efficient person re-identification in scenarios of varying complexity.

title: Hierarchical Quantification of Synergy in Channels
Abstract: This research delves into the hierarchical quantification of synergy in channels, a topic of paramount importance in various fields such as signal processing, information theory, and decision-making. By exploring the concept of synergy, which refers to the interaction of multiple components resulting in an outcome greater than the sum of their individual contributions, the study provides a comprehensive framework for quantifying and analyzing synergistic effects within channels. The proposed hierarchical approach systematically categorizes synergy into different levels, including joint occurrence, conditional mutual influence, and collective enhancement, to assess the intricate relationships between channel components. By applying advanced statistical and mathematical techniques, such as time-frequency analysis and graph theory, the research aims to reveal the hidden patterns and regulations of synergy in complex channel systems. The findings of this research have far-reaching implications for various applications, including signal processing, data compression, decision-making, and even social network analysis. Furthermore, the developed framework has the potential to enhance our understanding of complex systems and their behavior, ultimately shedding light on the intricate mechanisms underlying synergy in channels. The research also provides valuable insights into the development of new methods and algorithms for analyzing and quantifying synergistic effects in various fields of study. By uncovering the principles governing synergy in channels, this research contributes significantly to the advancement of knowledge in the fields of signal processing, information theory, and decision-making, and holds potential applications in numerous disciplines, including engineering, computer science, and social sciences.

title: Subsumptive reflection in SNOMED CT: a large description logic-based terminology for diagnosis
Abstract: This research paper delves into the realm of Subsumptive reflection in SNOMED CT, a vast and complex Description Logic-based terminology used for diagnosing medical conditions. SNOMED CT (Systematized Nomenclature of Medicine Clinical Terms) is the most comprehensive clinical terminology in existence, enabling efficient and unambiguous communication among healthcare professionals. However, its vast size and intricate structure pose significant challenges in navigating and applying its content effectively. This paper investigates the concept of Subsumptive reflection in the context of SNOMED CT, where a concept is subsumed by one or more parent concepts, leading to a hierarchical representation of medical knowledge. To address the need for effective reasoning and explanation in SNOMED CT, this study proposes a novel framework that leverages Description Logic (DL) for Subsumptive reflection, thereby allowing for the establishment of logical relationships between subsuming and subsumed concepts. The significance of this contribution lies in its potential to facilitate knowledge-based reasoning, improve query performance, and enhance the overall quality of diagnostic decision-support systems. The proposed framework is not only theoretically sound but also demonstrates a remarkable improvement in scalability, thanks to the native support for DL-based reasoning in popular ontology management systems like OWL 2. The impact of this work transcends the realm of medical informatics, as it showcases the potential for DL-based reasoning to be applied in various knowledge-intensive domains where Subsumptive reflection is essential. Ultimately, this research provides a substantial contribution to the advancement of SNOMED CT, facilitating more accurate and effective use of its vast knowledge base in clinical decision-making.

title: Convolutional Monte Carlo Rollouts in Go
Abstract: Recent advancements in artificial intelligence have led to significant improvements in Go playing algorithms, with Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) and its variants emerging as prominent solutions. However, these methods often rely on tree search procedures that can be computationally expensive and not well-suited for games with complex symmetries and long planning horizons, such as Go. This paper introduces Convolutional Monte Carlo Rollouts (CMCR), a novel approach that combines the strengths of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) with MCTS to efficiently explore the game tree and predict the outcome of rollout simulations. In CMCR, a CNN is used to approximate the value function and predict the quality of potential moves, while a Monte Carlo sampling mechanism is employed to gather a set of diverse rollout sequences that can be used to assess the accuracy of the CNN predictions. By leveraging the properties of convolutional neural networks, CMCR greatly reduces the computational complexity of tree search and is able to handle positions with long planning horizons more efficiently than traditional MCTS methods. Our experiments demonstrate that CMCR is capable of achieving state-of-the-art results in Go-playing, with stronger performance on the LishuiGo and KGS datasets compared to popular MCTS variants, while maintaining competitive runtimes.

title: Mobile Robots Adaptive Control Using Neural Networks
Abstract: This study explores the potential of neural networks in implementing adaptive control strategies for mobile robots, facilitating real-time adjustments in response to dynamic environmental conditions. As mobile robots are increasingly employed in various applications, such as exploration, manipulation, and transportation, the need for adaptive control systems that can compensate for unforeseen events and changing situations becomes imperative. The conventional control methods often rely on predefined rules and limited learning capabilities, rendering them inadequate for handling complex dynamic environments. In contrast, neural networks possess inherent aptitudes for unsupervised learning, self-organization, and dynamic adaptation, making them a suitable choice for designing adaptive control systems for mobile robots. This research focuses on investigating the feasibility and efficiency of employing neural networks in conjunction with various control architectures to enhance the adaptability and learning capabilities of mobile robots. Theoretical frameworks, simulation studies, and experimental implementations will be utilized to evaluate the performance of the proposed adaptive control systems under diverse scenarios, including changes in terrain, environmental conditions, and task requirements. By leveraging the advanced learning abilities of neural networks, this study aims to develop robust and resilient adaptive control strategies for mobile robots, thereby paving the way for their increased acceptance in a multitude of applications.

title: Diversity and Intelligence in Multi-robot Teams
Abstract: The performance of multi-robot teams is significantly enhanced by variety in their composition, revealing a correlation between diversity and intelligence in these teams. This paper delves into the intricacies of diversity and its impact on collective decision-making, problem-solving capabilities, and adaptability in multi-robot environments. By incorporating robots with distinctly differing parameters such as sensorimotor traits, learning mechanisms, and predefined tasks, the investigations explore the interplay between individual variability and collective intelligence. This intersection of diversity and intelligence becomes apparent in various contexts including adaptive multi-robot responses to dynamic scenarios, cooperative foraging strategies, and even in team repair mechanisms following member removal. Researchers employ advanced analytical techniques, complemented by extensive simulation and real-world experiments to quantify the extent to which diverse population compositions influence the emergence and robustness of intelligent collective behaviors. Furthermore, contributions made here to understanding collective dynamics demonstrate how deliberately constructing diverse multi-robot assemblages could efficiently accelerate the development of adaptive, intelligent team behaviors valuable in practical applications ranging from emergency response scenarios to infrastructure inspection, underlining the indispensable role of diversity in the augmentation of robot intelligence in various operational contexts.

title: Predicting proximity with ambient mobile sensors for non-invasive health diagnostics
Abstract: Ambient mobile sensors have revolutionized non-invasive health diagnostics by providing a novel approach to monitoring physiological signals without direct invasiveness. This study focuses on developing a predictive model that utilizes proximity data from ambient mobile sensors to forecast health conditions. By leveraging machine learning algorithms, the proposed model analyzes the spatial relationships between individuals and ambient sensors to infer underlying physiological states. The study explores the feasibility of using sensors' proximity data to diagnose health conditions, such as blood glucose monitoring, seizure detection, and stress level prediction. The predictive model utilizes a combination of sensor proximity features and contextual data, such as environmental factors and user behavior, to enhance predictive accuracy. The results of the study demonstrate that the proposed model can accurately predict health conditions based on proximity data from ambient mobile sensors, with an average accuracy of 85% for blood glucose levels and 90% for stress level prediction. The model's performance is comparable to or even exceeds that of traditional invasive diagnostic methods, highlighting the potential of ambient mobile sensors for cost-effective and non-invasive health diagnostics. The study contributes to the development of a mobile health monitoring system that utilizes ambient sensors to enable proactive healthcare and preventive measures, thus improving overall health outcomes.

title: Learning measures of semi-additive behaviour
Abstract: This paper contributes to the understanding of semi-additive behavior in individuals, which is a crucial aspect of complex cognitive processes such as planning, decision-making, and problem-solving. Semi-additive behavior refers to the phenomenon where the outcome of two tasks combined is not strictly additive, resulting from cognitive processes such as interference, resource competition, or contextual factors. We propose a new framework for modeling semi-additive behavior based on a combination of cognitive load theory and threshold models of decision-making. Our framework assumes that the total cognitive load associated with performing two tasks depends on their individual load and interaction effects, which are capture through a set of parameters such as resource sharing, interference, and contextual dependencies. We also introduce a set of measures, including the semi-additive scaling factor, the cognitive interaction effect, and the contextual dependency coefficient, to quantify the degree of semi-additive behavior in individuals. These measures are derived from the principles of our proposed framework and are validated through a set of experiments where participants perform different tasks under varying conditions. Our results demonstrate that the proposed measures provide a reliable and consistent estimate of semi-additive behavior, and their relationship with individual differences in working memory capacity and decision-making style is also explored. The implications of our findings for understanding individual differences in semi-additive behavior and for the development of more effective training programs and interventions are also discussed.

title: ShapeNet: An Information-Rich 3D Model Repository
Abstract: ShapeNet is a comprehensive 3D model repository with unprecedented information richness, offering a significant advancement in the field of three-dimensional computer vision and related disciplines. Launched in 2015, ShapeNet has allowed researchers and developers to access and utilize a massive dataset consisting of over 3 million 3D models belonging to a wide range of categories, including buildings, furniture, vehicles, and man-made objects. One of the key features of ShapeNet is its hierarchical category structure, where models are organized according to their subcategory and superclass, facilitating efficient retrieval and querying. The repository's extensive metadata, including object names, part names, materials, textures, and object attributes, offers unparalleled information richness and enables users to engage in detailed data analysis, categorization, and learning. ShapeNet's influence is multifaceted, supporting applications in computer-aided design, robotics, computer vision, and artificial intelligence, demonstrating its relevance and importance in current and future technological innovations. Furthermore, ShapeNet serves as a benchmarking dataset for evaluating the performance of various machine learning models and algorithms, fostering advancements in areas such as object recognition, part decomposition, and scene understanding. Through its unique design and vast dataset, ShapeNet has revolutionized the landscape of 3D model representation, facilitating future breakthroughs in the field of computer vision and beyond.

title: A Novel Regularized Principal Graph Learning Framework on Explicit Graph Representation
Abstract: This study proposes a novel regularized principal graph learning framework tailored for explicit graph representation, which effectively balances the structural and attribute information of nodes in an optimal manner. Traditional methods of graph learning often fail to capture the intricate relationships between attributes and structural connectivity, resulting in suboptimal graph representations. Our proposed framework incorporates principal graph learning into the graph signal processing domain by combining the strengths of manifold learning and regularization techniques. Specifically, we introduce a novel sparsity-inducing regularization term to drive the graph signal to capture local geometry and disentangle node attributes, thereby achieving a more interpretable and robust graph representation. A concurrent proximal alternating direction method of multipliers is designed to efficiently solve the proposed optimization problem, ensuring the computational scalability of our framework. Comprehensive experiments on a variety of benchmark datasets demonstrate the superiority of our approach in terms of accuracy, robustness, and efficiency. The results of this research contribute significantly to the field of explicit graph representation and offer new insights into the relationships between node attributes and structural connectivity, opening up new avenues of research in graph signal processing, manifold learning, and regularized optimization methods. Our framework is demonstrated to be particularly effective in applications involving spectral domain analysis and dimensionality reduction.

title: Setup of a photomultiplier tube test bench for use at LHAASO-KM2A
Abstract: This abstract outlines the setup and development of a photomultiplier tube (PMT) test bench for use in the Low Energy Antimatter with Shower Array (LHAASO) - Kuangmu-2A (KM2A) experiment. The LHAASO-KM2A is a large-scale Cherenkov telescope located in the Yangbajain region of Tibet, China, designed to study cosmic rays and gamma-ray bursts. A crucial component of this experiment is the PMT, used in the digital muon detectors to record and time the arrival of muon particles triggered by high-energy gamma-ray showers. However, the performance and calibration of these PMTs are critical to the accuracy and efficiency of the telescope's observations. Therefore, the development of a test bench is essential for evaluating the electrical and optical characteristics of PMTs. This test bench facilitates the measurement of the PMTs' gain, dark count rate, threshold, and timing jitter in response to varying light levels. It is comprised of a custom-built chassis, powering and control systems, and a data acquisition module. By providing a controlled environment to measure the PMTs' performance, this test bench will play a significant role in ensuring the optimal functioning of the LHAASO-KM2A telescope. The results of the PMT calibration process, including the characterization of their performance and subsequent optimization of their settings, will significantly enhance the overall sensitivity of the telescope to detect high-energy events in the universe.

title: Architecture of the LHCb muon Frontend control system upgrade
Abstract: The forthcoming upgrade of the Large Hadron Collider beauty (LHCb) muon frontend control system is a critical task that demands a robust and highly scalable design to meet the increasing data storage and processing demands of the forthcoming Runs 3 and 4 of LHCb. The existing control system is based on a VME bus architecture which has shown to be limiting in terms of scalability and data throughput. The new architecture aims to eliminate the VME bus abstraction layer and instead employ a modern, field-programmable gate array (FPGA)-based system with a distributed architecture that utilizes Ethernet protocols for communication between peripherals and the central processing units. This upgrade will leverage the power of custom-developed firmware running on FPGAs to efficiently readout data from detector systems, perform real-time processing, and communicate the results to the offline reconstruction and analysis systems in a highly configurable and fault-tolerant manner. Furthermore, a flexible architecture supporting the heterogeneous environment of diverse hardware and software components will be implemented, making it easy to integrate with the online and offline systems while minimizing computational resources requirements and allowing for seamless testing and validation. The success of this upgrade will ultimately result in the recovery of a significant portion of lost physics from the LHC Run-1 and Run-2 datasets and will pave the way for enhanced performance in the forthcoming data-taking campaigns, elevating the overall efficiency and physics reach of the LHCb experiment.

title: Learning Discrete Bayesian Networks from Continuous Data
Abstract: Learning discrete Bayesian networks from continuous data poses significant challenges due to the need to discretize the continuous variables and preserve the inherent structural and probabilistic relationships within the data. In this paper, we propose an innovative approach to directly learn discrete Bayesian networks from continuous variables by adopting an unsupervised feature learning method to identify the most informative and pertinent discrete intervals for each continuous variable. This is achieved through a novel combination of autoencoders and binning techniques, which allows us to automatically select the optimal binning strategy for each variable. Our approach enables the identification of representative discrete intervals that preserve the probabilistic relationships between variables, thereby facilitating the accurate learning of discrete Bayesian networks. Through experiments on various synthetic and real-world datasets, we demonstrate the efficacy and robustness of our approach in comparison to existing methods that rely on manual or uniform binning strategies. The results show that our approach yields more accurate discrete Bayesian network models with improved predictive performance and higher statistical significance. Furthermore, the learned discrete intervals are found to be interpretable and provide valuable insights into the underlying structure of the data, making our approach particularly appealing for applications in machine learning, bioinformatics, and data mining. Overall, our work presents a significant advancement in the field of Bayesian network learning from continuous data.

title: Optical SETI Observations of the Anomalous Star KIC 8462852
Abstract: The star KIC 8462852 has garnered extensive attention due to its unusual and unpredictable dimming patterns, fuelling speculation about its potential to harbor a massive alien structure. This anomaly led to widespread media scrutiny as "Tabby's Star," with many suggesting that it might be evidence of extraterrestrial engineering or even a Dyson Sphere. Although several hypotheses have been proposed to explain the observed dimming, none have been conclusively proven. As its light curves remain unexplained by conventional stellar models, the possibility of anomalous activity, including astrophysical processes or alien technology, cannot be dismissed outright. Consequently, scientists have been conducting Optical SETI (Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence) observations of KIC 8462852 in an attempt to gather evidence for the presence of advanced civilizations. Our research aims to provide a comprehensive analysis of the star's observational data, utilizing both ground-based and space-based telescopes, to ascertain whether any unusual patterns or signals consistent with intelligent origin can be detected. Furthermore, we investigate the detectability limits of the current SETI surveys and discuss potential avenues for future research, aiming to shed light on the enigmatic nature of KIC 8462852 and its importance in our pursuit of understanding the possibility of extraterrestrial life.

title: Sensitivity analysis, multilinearity and beyond
Abstract: This paper delves into the realm of sensitivity analysis, exploring its intricacies and the impact of multilinearity on decision-making processes. Sensitivity analysis is a statistical technique used to understand how different inputs affect the outcome of a model, providing valuable insights into potential risks and opportunities. However, the traditional approach to sensitivity analysis assumes linearity, which may not always hold true in real-world scenarios. The introduction of multilinearity, where relationships between variables are non-linear, compels a reconsideration of the model's sensitivity. The paper examines the implications of multilinearity on sensitivity analysis, discussing its limitations and the potential consequences for decision-making. A new approach to sensitivity analysis is proposed, one that takes into account the complexities of multilinearity, offering a more nuanced understanding of system behavior. Case studies from various fields, including finance, environmental science, and healthcare, are analyzed to illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach. The results demonstrate the importance of considering multilinearity when conducting sensitivity analysis, and highlight the potential benefits of adopting a more comprehensive approach. By reevaluating the interconnectedness of variables, decision-makers can make more informed choices, leading to better outcomes and more effective policy-making. Furthermore, the developed sensitivity analysis provides a foundation for the development of multivariable optimisation techniques for more broad and complex decision-making models in different real-world scenarios.

title: Digital Genesis: Computers, Evolution and Artificial Life
Abstract: The intersection of computers and artificial life has led to significant advancements in our understanding of evolution, developmental biology, and the fundamental mechanisms underlying life. The emergence of digital organisms, virtual environments, and computer simulations has created a novel framework for exploring the dynamics of life, its evolution, and the role of predation, competition, and symbiosis. By utilizing computational tools to model and analyze evolutionary processes, researchers have been able to replicate and expand upon long-standing biological hypotheses, providing insights into the origin and diversification of life. Furthermore, digital organisms have also become increasingly sophisticated, exhibiting complex behaviors, adapting to changing environments, and evolving over time, thereby challenging traditional notions of life and its relation to the digital and the algorithmic. The theoretical implications of digital genesis are far-reaching, inviting a deeper exploration of the intricate relationships between computation, representation, and life, and blurring the boundaries between the natural and the artificial. This research aims to examine the theoretical and methodological implications of digital genesis, its potential to advance our understanding of evolution, and the intersection of biology, computation, and artificial life, shedding new light on the future of life and its relation to the digital.

title: From rules to runs: A dynamic epistemic take on imperfect information games
Abstract: This paper presents a novel dynamic epistemic analysis of imperfect information games, where agents operate in a dynamic environment driven by both strategic actions and epistemic updates. Adapting dynamic epistemic logic to accommodate imperfect information, we introduce a formal framework that captures the evolution of both states of the world and mental states of agents over time. Our system, called "runs," allows for a precise modeling of correlated equilibria, which have been notoriously challenging to achieve in imperfect information games. By incorporating epistemic uncertainty into run-based models, we can study scenarios where agents' beliefs and knowledge influence their decisions, and probabilistic structures, like Nash equilibria, play a crucial role. Our dynamic take provides an insightful look at how epistemic information flows and its recursive implications for strategic decision-making in the face of probabilistic uncertainty. The robustness and flexibility of our framework make it an attractive tool for tackling complex real-world problems, where information is inherently imperfect, and strategic decisions heavily rely on the nuances of epistemic reasoning. Specifically, our results demonstrate that a probabilistic view of imperfect information dynamics does not compromise the game-theoretic foundations of strategy but rather incorporates epistemic and probabilistic elements in the agents' decision-making processes.

title: How to Discount Deep Reinforcement Learning: Towards New Dynamic Strategies
Abstract:
Deep reinforcement learning has made significant progress in recent years, particularly in complex tasks such as game playing and robotic control. Nevertheless, addressing the issue of learning efficiency remains a critical challenge in deep reinforcement learning. The conventional approach of exploiting the same learning rate throughout the training process often leads to suboptimal results due to the risk of overshooting or undershooting in the convergence rate of the policy update. Moreover, the high computational complexity and large action spaces in many real-world applications further exacerbate the difficulty of finding an appropriate learning rate schedule.

In this study, we focus on developing novel dynamic strategies for discounting deep reinforcement learning, aimed at improving the convergence rate and enhancing the overall efficiency of the learning process. Our proposed methods involve adaptive adjustment of the discount factor based on real-time performance monitoring, leveraging both intrinsic and extrinsic forms of regularizing the agent's behavior. A control-theoretic framework is also introduced to understand the dynamics of the discount factor adaptation, thereby facilitating an integrated analysis of the interaction between the agent and its environment.

Empirical evaluations on a range of benchmark environments demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed strategies, showcasing significant improvements in terms of computational efficiency, exploration-exploitation balance, and policy convergence rates, when compared with conventional baseline methods. By pinpointing critical factors influencing the performance of discount deep reinforcement learning, our findings offer new insights and decision-making frameworks for practitioners seeking optimal learning dynamics in various fields of applications.

title: A Novel Approach to Distributed Multi-Class SVM
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel distributed Multi-Class Support Vector Machine (SVM) framework, which leverages the benefits of both model parallelism and data parallelism to efficiently scale up Multi-Class SVMs to large datasets. The proposed approach involves partitioning the SVM model across multiple computing nodes, where each node learns a subset of the classes and a subset of the data. This allows for significant reduction in communication overhead, as each node only needs to exchange a fraction of the model parameters with other nodes. Additionally, the approach enables efficient exploitation of heterogeneous computing resources, such as multi-core CPUs and specialized hardware accelerators. The proposed framework integrates techniques from distributed machine learning and model averaging to ensure convergence and consistency of the model across nodes. Theoretical analysis and experimental evaluations demonstrate the scalability, efficiency, and accuracy of the proposed distributed Multi-Class SVM framework on a wide range of datasets, including image classification, natural language processing, and recommender systems. Compared to existing distributed SVM methods, the proposed approach achieves faster convergence, lower communication overhead, and improved generalization performance, making it a promising solution for large-scale machine learning applications.

title: Thinking Required
Abstract: The transition from a traditional to a technological-based economy has raised significant concerns regarding the impact on the human mind, particularly in relation to thinking required for various tasks and roles. While technology has streamlined processes and increased efficiency, it has also led to a shift in cognitive demands, emphasizing speed and ease over complexity and depth. As a result, individuals are now faced with a unique challenge: to adapt to an environment where critical thinking, creativity, and problem-solving skills are highly valued yet frequently undervalued. This raises the question of whether the current educational system and societal norms are adequately preparing individuals to navigate this changing landscape. Research suggests that the over-reliance on technology has resulted in a decline in cognitive abilities such as attention span, working memory, and the ability to engage in deep thought. Furthermore, the increasing use of automation and artificial intelligence in various industries has rendered some skills obsolete, while others have become more valuable. In this context, there is a pressing need to re-evaluate our understanding of intelligence and cognitive abilities, and to develop new strategies for promoting critical thinking, creativity, and problem-solving skills in individuals. By examining the interplay between technology, education, and cognitive development, this study seeks to contribute to a deeper understanding of the impact of technological advancements on the human mind and to provide insights into the necessary adaptations required to align with the emerging needs of the technological-based economy.

title: Knowledge Sharing in Coalitions
Abstract: In coalition settings, member organizations often possess unique knowledge and expertise, which can significantly contribute to the achievement of collaborative goals and objectives. However, knowledge sharing amongst coalition partners can be a complex and challenging task, requiring careful consideration of contributing factors such as trust, communication, and motivation. This research aims to investigate the dynamics of knowledge sharing in coalitions, examining the antecedents and consequences of various knowledge sharing behaviors. A multiple-case study approach was employed, involving in-depth analyses of four coalitions operating in different sectors, including healthcare, environmental protection, and social services. Data were collected through interviews with coalition representatives and organizational records, and were analyzed using a combination of qualitative and quantitative methods. The findings suggest that trust is a critical factor in facilitating knowledge sharing amongst coalition partners, and that communication and motivation also play important roles in encouraging knowledge exchange. Additionally, the research reveals that coalitions' propensity for knowledge sharing is influenced by their formal structures and informal networks, highlighting the importance of understanding the underlying social and organizational dynamics within coalitions. The study's findings have implications for coalition development and management, suggesting that deliberate efforts to foster trust, encourage communication, and motivate knowledge sharing are essential for successful collaboration and goal achievement.

title: Probabilistic Structural Controllability in Causal Bayesian Networks
Abstract: This study aims to investigate the concept of probabilistic structural controllability in causal Bayesian networks. Controllability in a system refers to the ability to control or influence its behavior by applying a set of external interventions. In this work, a new measure of probabilistic structural controllability is proposed, which incorporates conditional probabilities and probabilistic causal relationships within a Bayesian network. This measure allows for the evaluation of the degree to which control over a target variable can be achieved through a sequence of interventions. By applying this measure to a probabilistic Bayesian network, we can efficiently determine which interventions are most effective in achieving a desired outcome. We utilize graph-theoretical methods to translate the causal relationships within the probabilistic network into a control flow that maximizes the expected probability of the target variable under intervention. Extensive simulations are conducted to compare the results with traditional probabilistic control methods, demonstrating the effectiveness and efficiency of our proposed approach. The research outcomes contribute to improving our ability to manipulate the behavior of complex systems by exploiting the probabilistic causal structure encoded within Bayesian networks. Moreover, our study has important implications for applications in decision-making, where probabilistic inference and control are crucial, such as in healthcare, quality control, and finance.

title: Driverseat: Crowdstrapping Learning Tasks for Autonomous Driving
Abstract: This research paper explores the deployment of decentralized crowd-sourcing strategies to support the creation of accurate and comprehensive datasets for autonomous driving, as embodied by the concept of "Driverseat." By crowdsourcing driving tasks and leveraging diverse human expertise, the aim is to augment the capabilities of neural networks in learning complex driving behaviors and making informed decisions on the road in real-time. Building upon recent breakthroughs in areas such as edge AI, mobile sensor arrays, and concurrent crowdsourcing platforms, the paper outlines a framework that enables cars to dynamically recruit "co-drivers" to assist in situational awareness, environment perception, and pre-planned routes' updations during operation. Furthermore, this approach aims to promote safer, more adaptive, and overall efficient autonomous transportation experiences by mitigating the challenges posed by noisy datasets, dynamic road environments, and unique traffic patterns. By integrating both technological and socioeconomic factors into the decision-making process, Driverseat represents a critical model for balancing machine autonomy and human input within modern infrastructure systems. Critical performance metrics, key edge-case scenarios, and methodologies for maximizing the success of real-world trials are thoroughly analyzed to enhance the groundwork for practical applications of this innovative system.

title: Rank Pooling for Action Recognition
Abstract: Rank Pooling for Action Recognition introduces a novel approach to action recognition in videos by aggregating local descriptors into a concise representation using Rank Pooling, which preserves important frames while discarding the rest due to their lack of discriminative information. Traditional pooling methods such as spatial pyramid pooling or spatial max-pooling suffer from information loss, while also failing to preserve the contextual relationships between frames in a video. The proposed method counteracts this limitation by associating each frame with a rank in the sequence where the highest ranking descriptor presents the most informative frame for the action recognition task while completely discarding low-ranking frames based on their degree of relevance to the event happening in the video. This efficient methodology not only improves upon previous action recognition systems by decreasing computational complexity but also ensures effectiveness with accurate results demonstrated through rigorous experiments. Experiments on several benchmark action recognition datasets reveal how Rank Pooling-based frameworks achieve comparable or improved results over other state-of-the-art methods in terms of recognition accuracy, showcasing this proposed approach's potential applicability in future video-based applications like activity analysis in surveillance systems and monitoring various forms of movement in medical contexts. Additionally, experiments with evaluation metrics such as runtime demonstrate the efficient operating capability made possible by this novel aggregation method.

title: Fast Algorithms for Game-Theoretic Centrality Measures
Abstract: Game-theoretic centrality measures, such as Shapley values and Banzhaf indices, are crucial in identifying key players in cooperative game theory. These measures quantify the contribution of each player to the coalition's overall value, thereby providing insights into player importance and coalition robustness. However, existing algorithms for computing these centrality measures suffer from high computational costs, limiting their adoption in large-scale network applications. The increasing complexity of modern networks necessitates the development of more efficient algorithms for computing game-theoretic centrality measures. This paper presents new fast algorithms for computing Shapley values and Banzhaf indices in cooperative games and networks. By employing novel techniques in parallel computing and recursive decomposition, our algorithms significantly outperform existing state-of-the-art methods, reducing computational time by orders of magnitude. We demonstrate the efficacy of our algorithms on various benchmark networks and games, showcasing their scalability and performance. Our results have far-reaching implications for the adoption of game-theoretic centrality measures in network analysis, coalition formation, and decision-making under uncertainty. By addressing the computational efficiency of these measures, we aim to unlock new insights into the dynamics of complex systems and fuel innovation across various domains.

title: Large Scale Distributed Semi-Supervised Learning Using Streaming Approximation
Abstract:
Large Scale Distributed Semi-Supervised Learning Using Streaming Approximation. 
This research focuses on the development of an efficient and scalable framework for large-scale distributed semi-supervised learning using streaming approximation. In today's era of big data, deploying machine learning models remains a significant challenge, particularly in scenarios where label scarcity and distributional shift are prevalent. Existing distributed semi-supervised learning algorithms often suffer from high computational complexity, prolonged training times, and inadequate incorporation of streaming data. By leveraging a continuous stream of unlabeled data and adapting to non-stationary environments, our proposed framework exploits the benefits of semi-supervised learning while offering real-time updates and reduced computational overhead. We design a distributed pipeline that combines a streaming data generator, a non-parallelizable core algorithm, and a parallelizable approximation module. The framework communicates and synchronizes updates across nodes through a minimal overhead, ensuring the effective utilization of data and computational resources. Through theoretical analysis and extensive experimentation on benchmark datasets and real-world scenarios, we demonstrate the efficacy and scalability of our large-scale distributed semi-supervised learning using streaming approximation framework in addressing the key challenges of big data machine learning, including training speed, model quality, and adaptability to non-stationary environments.

title: A Restricted Visual Turing Test for Deep Scene and Event Understanding
Abstract: This abstract discusses the development and implementation of a novel visual Turing test tailored to assess the deep comprehension of complex scenes and events by artificial intelligence models and humans alike. The proposed test, dubbed Restricted Visual Turing Test for Deep Scene and Event Understanding (RVT-DSEU), sets out to bridge the gap in existing scene understanding benchmarks by placing emphasis on subtle context and dynamic events, and ensuring meaningful interaction through the imposition of spatial and temporal restrictions. The test comprises a series of challenges that range from static scenario identification to the forecasting of event progression based solely on prior knowledge of the setting. In establishing and running a Restricted Visual Turing Test, the key goal is to subject computational models, including deep neural networks, to an exhaustive set of scenarios so as to yield an accurate measurement of their capacity to depict instances of understanding and general knowledge application. Experimental evaluations and comparisons between AI models and humans aim to arrive at a conclusive comparison of their respective aptitudes, in the direction of recognizing, comprehending, and predicting complex scenarios such tests demand.

title: Risk-Constrained Reinforcement Learning with Percentile Risk Criteria
Abstract: This paper presents a novel risk-constrained reinforcement learning (RL) framework that incorporates percentiles of a value function to quantify uncertainty and incorporate risk in decision-making processes. Traditional RL methods aim to maximize expected rewards but often neglect the potential risks associated with exploration and exploitation. In contrast, risk-constrained RL addresses the need for balance between risk and reward by using risk-sensitive metrics such as Value-at-Risk (VaR) or Expected Shortfall (ES). However, these metrics are limiting as they are sensitive to extreme but improbable events and fail to account for more nuanced forms of risk exposure. To address these limitations, our proposed approach uses the percentiles of a value function to calibrate the exploration-exploitation trade-off, allowing the agent to adapt dynamically to the environment and prioritize risk reduction when necessary. The formulation integrates the percentile-based risk constraints into the Markov decision process and employs a meta-learning approach to fine-tune policy iterations. Simulation results on a variety of stochastic environments demonstrate that our approach can adapt to increasing uncertainty by moderating exploratory actions, thus achieving a superior balance between risk, reward, and exploration.

title: A Novel Paradigm for Calculating Ramsey Number via Artificial Bee Colony Algorithm
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel paradigm for calculating the Ramsey number via artificial bee colony (ABC) algorithm, an effective method inspired by the foraging behavior of honeybees. Traditional approaches to calculating the Ramsey number have been largely dominated by brute force and exact methods, which are often impractical for large instances due to their prohibitive running time complexity. However, the adoption of nature-inspired metaheuristics has emerged as a promising approach to solving large-scale optimization problems. Building upon this concept, we propose an ABC model for computing Ramsey numbers, leveraging its unique search mechanism and efficient exploration of solution spaces. The proposed algorithm is implemented in MATLAB R2022a, and its performance is evaluated against existing computational methods, including the well-known Monte Carlo method and the Iterated Local Search (ILS) algorithm. Our numerical results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed ABC-based method, achieving significant reductions in computation time while maintaining competitive accuracy. The findings of this study have important implications for graph theory, optimization problems, and computational complexity, providing a new perspective on calculating Ramsey numbers via artificial intelligence techniques and reiterating the benefits of the ABC algorithm as a viable computational tool for tackling intricate combinatorial problems.

title: Extracting Biomolecular Interactions Using Semantic Parsing of Biomedical Text
Abstract: Advances in biotechnology and computational biology have fueled the rapid growth of volume and complexity of biomedical literature, leading to an exponential increase in available data on biomolecular interactions. However, the human curation of this data remains a daunting task, limiting our understanding and ability to analyze them at scale. Recent developments in natural language processing (NLP) and artificial intelligence (AI) have enabled the integration of machine learning and deep learning techniques to improve the extraction of relevant information from biomedical text. Our research focuses on applying semantic parsing, a key NLP technique, to develop an effective framework for extracting biomolecular interactions from biomedical literature. Through a combination of rule-based and machine learning-based approaches, we have developed a system that can accurately recognize and extract various types of biological entities, including genes, proteins, and their interactions, as well as underlying temporal and spatial relationships. Evaluation results show significant performance improvement against existing state-of-the-art systems, demonstrating the effectiveness and potential application of our method in supporting downstream analyses, such as pathway prediction and protein-protein interaction network construction, beneficial for functional genomics, systems biology, computational pathology and other related biomedical applications.

title: Reuse of Neural Modules for General Video Game Playing
Abstract: The development of artificial intelligence (AI) capable of general video game playing has led to significant advancements in the field of game playing and neural networks. Building upon this progress, our research focuses on the reusability of neural modules to create more efficient and adaptable game playing agents. By modularizing neural networks, we allow individual components to be trained and fine-tuned for specific game tasks, such as object detection and movement planning, while leveraging pre-trained knowledge across various games. This approach enables the creation of a general game playing agent that can be applied to multiple game environments with minimal modification. Our proposed framework, ‘Neural Module Reuse Network’ (NMRR), consists of three main components: a neural module repository containing trained and validated module instances, a module selection mechanism for determining the most suitable modules for a given game, and a module adaptation module for fine-tuning the selected modules to the specific game environment. Through an extensive evaluation of NMRR on a diverse set of video games, we demonstrate its ability to outperform or match the performance of traditional game-specific agents, showcasing the potential of neural module reuse in achieving general game playing capabilities. By eliminating the need for extensive game-specific training, our approach offers a significant reduction in development time and computational resources, paving the way for the creation of more efficient and adaptive AI game playing agents.

title: On the Min-cost Traveling Salesman Problem with Drone
Abstract: The Min-cost Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) is a classic combinatorial optimization problem that has garnered significant attention in recent years due to its applications in logistics and transportation. The traditional TSP involves a single traveling salesman who aims to visit a set of cities and return to the origin while minimizing the total travel cost. However, with the advent of drone technology, the conventional TSP has been extended to include drones that can facilitate the transportation of goods, reduce travel times, and enhance the efficiency of the overall delivery process. The Min-cost TSP with drone involves determining the optimal tour that minimizes the total cost, which encompasses not only the travel costs of the salesman and drones but also the loading and unloading costs associated with the transportation of goods. This problem offers a wide range of practical applications, including package delivery, disaster relief, and medical supplies transportation. In this research, we develop novel metaheuristic and exact algorithms to solve the Min-cost TSP with drone efficiently and provide a thorough analysis of the computational results. Our proposed algorithms are designed to tackle the intricacies of the problem by taking into account the dynamics of drone interactions, wind resistance, and the capacity constraints of cargo holding drones. We compare the performance of our algorithms with existing methods and provide insights into the optimal solution structure, enabling practitioners to develop effective strategies for managing drone-based logistics operations.
