title: What Makes it Difficult to Understand a Scientific Literature?
Abstract: Understanding scientific literature is a crucial aspect of scientific progress, yet numerous challenges hinder its comprehension. This seems often due to the specialized jargon, technical terminology, and highly specialized knowledge required to navigate scientific texts. Research has shown that even experts often have difficulty understanding texts due to factors such as complexity, context dependence, and abstract concepts. Various factors contribute to this complexity, including dense and convoluted writing styles, lack of references to well-known sources, overuse of acronyms and extremely technical vocabulary, confusing syntax, ambiguity, the high volume of detail, non-standardized formatting, lack of clear explanations and many others. This can be compounded by cultural or socio-economic factors that affect an individual's educational background and familiarity with the discipline. The field of science communication has emphasized the importance of clear communication in the dissemination of knowledge. Conversely however, experts do find themselves in difficult situations that might typically demand a vast in-depth understanding of most concepts. Furthermore, despite employing expert-level knowledge and highly sophisticated analysis tools, difficulties in fully understanding and interpreting a given text still arise.  Approaches have been proposed in addressing the nature of these obstacles; including those emphasizing the importance of simplifying scientific writing while maintaining accuracy, developing new algorithms that can automate interpretation, leveraging visual and interactive representations, using contextual information, learning from collective unconscious, offering remedial courses and other tools designed to improve comprehension. However, despite these attempts, many students and lay readers struggle to make sense of scientific literature.

title: Locally Adaptive Translation for Knowledge Graph Embedding
Abstract: This research explores a novel locally adaptive translation method for knowledge graph embedding, addressing the limitations of traditional global translation approaches. Global translation methods often overlook the intricacies of local relationships between entities and their contexts, leading to suboptimal performance in downstream tasks. The proposed locally adaptive translation method employs a graph convolutional network to learn adaptive translation coefficients for each knowledge graph, enabling it to capture the nuances of local relationships. By iteratively refining the translation coefficients based on the graph structure, the method adapts to the diverse local patterns present in the knowledge graph, resulting in more accurate and robust translation results. The proposed method is evaluated on several state-of-the-art knowledge graph embedding benchmarks, demonstrating its superiority over existing global translation approaches in terms of translation accuracy, entity recognition, and downstream task performance. Moreover, the locally adaptive translation method offers an interpretable and controllable approach to knowledge graph translation, enabling users to understand and refine the translation process. The method's local adaptability also allows for efficient translation of large and complex knowledge graphs, making it a promising solution for real-world applications.

title: Proposition of a Theoretical Model for Missing Data Imputation using Deep Learning and Evolutionary Algorithms
Abstract: This abstract highlights the development of a novel theoretical model that leverages the synergy between deep learning and evolutionary algorithms to propose an efficient and accurate approach for missing data imputation. Existing methods for handling missing values in datasets often rely on simplified heuristics or traditional machine learning techniques, which can fail to capture complex patterns in data. To overcome these limitations, our proposed theoretical model combines the strengths of deep learning-based imputation methods with the adaptability and diversity of evolutionary algorithms. By integrating the advanced feature learning capabilities of deep learning models with the evolutionary optimization mechanisms of global optimization algorithms, our model can learn from various patterns in the data and identify the most suitable approach for each specific problem. In this context, we introduce the concept of a hybrid deep learning-evolutionary architecture, which involves the application of evolutionary algorithms to optimize the weights and hyperparameters of deep learning models, thus enhancing their performance in imputing missing values. Our theoretical model offers a comprehensive and flexible framework for missing data imputation tasks, allowing for the integration of diverse imputation strategies and methodologies tailored to the requirements of specific domains and applications.

title: Toward a Taxonomy and Computational Models of Abnormalities in Images
Abstract: This research contributes to the development of a comprehensive taxonomy and computational models for identifying and characterizing abnormalities in images. Advances in image analysis and machine learning have made it possible to automate the detection of various visual anomalies and disorders, but existing research often relies on scattered, application-specific studies, lacking a unified framework. Our research aims to address this gap by proposing a multidisciplinary taxonomy that integrates multiple domains, including medical imaging, computer vision, and cognitive science. The taxonomy categorizes abnormalities into distinct classes based on their origin, manifestation, and impact on the visual system. To support the taxonomy, we develop and evaluate several computational models, incorporating state-of-the-art techniques from deep learning and image processing. These models are designed to detect a range of abnormal conditions, including lesions, tumors, and pathologies, as well as anomalies caused by natural or artificial factors. We also conduct a comprehensive review of relevant literature to identify open challenges and opportunities for future research. Additionally, the efficacy of our taxonomy and models is evaluated through an extensive validation process, involving multiple datasets and real-world applications. Our research presents a significant step toward the establishment of a standardized framework for understanding and modeling abnormalities in images, paving the way for innovative image-based diagnostic tools and enhanced medical imaging practices.

title: Predicting and visualizing psychological attributions with a deep neural network
Abstract: This research paper presents a novel approach to predicting and visualizing psychological attributions using a deep neural network. In recent years, understanding human behavior and decision-making processes has become increasingly important in various fields such as social sciences, marketing, and healthcare. Psychological attributions, which involve the tendency to assign causes or reasons to observed phenomena, play a crucial role in shaping human behavior and interactions. However, manually gathering and analyzing attributions can be a time-consuming and labor-intensive process. Therefore, developing an automated system for predicting and visualizing attributions becomes a pressing need. In this study, we explore the potential of a deep neural network to predict psychological attributions based on text inputs. By utilizing a multi-layer perceptron model and training it on a large dataset of human attributions, we were able to achieve high accuracy in predicting attributions. Furthermore, we developed a visualization tool that allows users to explore and understand the underlying attributions in a more intuitive and user-friendly manner. Our results demonstrate the feasibility of using deep learning models for predicting and visualizing attributions, with implications for various applications in social sciences and beyond. By providing a more efficient and accurate way of understanding human behavior and decision-making processes, this research contributes to advancing our knowledge of psychological attributions and promoting further research in this area. The findings of this study have potential to yield valuable insights into various phenomena, such as human behavior, teamwork, and decision-making.

title: CrossCat: A Fully Bayesian Nonparametric Method for Analyzing Heterogeneous, High Dimensional Data
Abstract: CrossCat is a novel, fully Bayesian nonparametric method developed to analyze complex, high-dimensional datasets characterized by heterogeneity. The proposed approach enables scalable and flexible modeling of variable relationships in the presence of unobserved or latent variables, often resulting from interactions between variables or grouped effects. By leveraging the power of Bayesian nonparametrics, the method naturally and efficiently models the data's complexity, enabling the estimation of probability distributions for the relationships among variables without requiring a pre-specified form. This flexibility allows for the identification of the most influential factors driving the relationships between variables. Moreover, the implementation of CrossCat is computationally efficient, making it suitable for large datasets encountered in various scientific disciplines, including genetics, metabolomics, and social sciences. The performances of CrossCat were evaluated across various simulations and real-world datasets, confirming its strengths in capturing the intricate patterns present in the data. The method demonstrates its ability to provide interpretable and accurate results, making it an attractive addition to the existing statistical toolbox for data analysis in various fields of research. As a result, the proposed method is designed to offer a robust and nonparametric solution for investigating complicated relationships and patterns within high-dimensional datasets, yielding meaningful insights in an increasing number of research areas.

title: A Smartphone-Based Acquisition System for Hips Rotation Fluency Assessment
Abstract: This paper presents a novel smartphone-based acquisition system for assessing hips rotation fluency in individuals. The system leverages the capabilities of modern smartphones to provide a low-cost, user-friendly, and accessible approach to evaluating hip mobility. A comprehensive review of existing methods for hip mobility and flexibility assessment reveals the limitations of traditional techniques, particularly in terms of objectivity and reproducibility. To address these issues, a customized smartphone application was developed to detect and quantify the rotations of the hips through digital video footage. By using a bilateral goniometer-based calibration system, the application enables the accurate measurement of hip rotation angles and velocities. The system was validated through a series of experiments involving a cohort of participants with varying levels of hip mobility. Results demonstrate the high accuracy and reliability of the smartphone-based system in detecting differences in hips rotation fluency between individuals. Compared to existing methods, the proposed system shows a significant reduction in measurement variability and improved test-retest reliability. The implications of this research are substantial, as it enables the widespread adoption of a reliable and low-cost tool for assessing hip mobility in various populations, including patients with musculoskeletal disorders and athletes requiring improved hip flexibility for performance optimization.

title: Building Memory with Concept Learning Capabilities from Large-scale Knowledge Base
Abstract: This research paper presents an innovative approach to building memory models with the ability to learn concepts from large-scale knowledge bases. The proposed method leverages state-of-the-art techniques in artificial intelligence, graph neural networks, and knowledge graph embeddings to enable the model to acquire and retain semantic knowledge from massive datasets. The model aims to capture the intricate relationships between entities and concepts, allowing it to reason and generalize across various domains. To achieve this, we design and train a comprehensive knowledge graph representation, where entities and concepts are encoded with low-dimensional vector representations. These vectors are then used to compute semantic similarity and relatedness, enabling the model to engage in meaningful conversations and answer complex questions. Our evaluation strategy comprises a range of benchmark datasets, including knowledge graphs, question-answering, and concept classification tasks. We demonstrate significant improvements in performance metrics, including accuracy and efficiency, showcasing the potential of our approach in real-world applications. Furthermore, we provide insights into the learned concept representations and relationships, highlighting the model's ability to generalize and reason across different domains. Overall, our contributions offer a novel framework for building memory models with concept learning capabilities, positioning them at the forefront of the knowledge representation and reasoning landscape.

title: Deep Reinforcement Learning with Attention for Slate Markov Decision Processes with High-Dimensional States and Actions
Abstract: Deep reinforcement learning has become an increasingly popular approach for solving complex sequential decision-making problems, particularly in domains with high-dimensional states and actions. However, existing methods often fail to efficiently learn optimal policies in such scenarios due to the curse of dimensionality and the need for sequential exploration. We address this challenge by proposing a novel deep reinforcement learning algorithm for Slate Markov Decision Processes (SMDPs) that incorporates attention mechanisms to focus on relevant information. Our approach, dubbed Attention Slate Q-Network (ASQN), leverages the power of neural attention to selectively highlight important features and actions in the high-dimensional state and action spaces. By doing so, ASQN is able to efficiently reduce the dimensionality of the problem, leading to faster learning and more accurate policy optimization. Furthermore, we incorporate a slate-based exploration bonus to encourage the agent to explore different combinations of actions and exploit the sequential nature of the decision-making process. Experimental results on several benchmark SMDP domains demonstrate the effectiveness of ASQN in learning high-quality policies compared to state-of-the-art baseline methods. Overall, our work presents a promising solution for tackling complex sequential decision-making problems in high-dimensional state and action spaces.

title: Bayesian Matrix Completion via Adaptive Relaxed Spectral Regularization
Abstract: This research paper investigates a novel Bayesian approach to the popular matrix completion problem, a crucial challenge in modern data analysis and machine learning. The matrix completion problem involves recovering a missing-entry matrix from a set of observed entries, often in the presence of large amounts of missing data. We propose a Bayesian matrix completion method that incorporates adaptive relaxed spectral regularization (ARSReg) to learn from the data and adapt to varying levels of noise and missingness. Our method, Bayesian Matrix Completion via Adaptive Relaxed Spectral Regularization (BMCA-ARS), leverages a probabilistic model to characterize the uncertainty in the data and incorporates ARSReg, an adaptive approach that learns the regularization strength and spectral properties of the low-rank structure of the matrix from the data itself. This learning-based framework enables BMCA-ARS to automatically adjust to the varying levels of noise, missing data, and matrix ranks present in different datasets. The resulting method provides state-of-the-art performance on benchmark datasets and adapts well to complex and noisy real-world data scenarios. By estimating the uncertainty in the matrix entries and leveraging ARSReg for low-rank structure inference, BMCA-ARS offers a flexible and robust solution to the matrix completion problem.

title: Querying with Łukasiewicz logic
Abstract: Łukasiewicz logic, a many-valued formal system developed by Jan Łukasiewicz, has been increasingly applied in various AI and data science applications due to its ability to handle uncertainty and vagueness in data. Querying with Łukasiewicz logic has emerged as a powerful approach for querying uncertain and vague knowledge bases. However, implementing Łukasiewicz logic querying efficiently and effectively remains a significant challenge. This paper addresses this challenge by proposing a novel querying framework that leverages the strengths of Łukasiewicz logic while mitigating its computational complexities. Our framework utilizes a hybrid approach that combines the benefits of Lukasiewicz logic with those of propositional logic, allowing for efficient handling of complex queries and scalable performance. The proposed framework is further enhanced with an optimized indexing technique that accelerates query execution. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our framework in querying with Łukasiewicz logic, showcasing significant improvements in query execution time and scalability compared to existing approaches. The proposed framework offers a promising solution for querying uncertain and vague knowledge bases in various applications, including AI, data science, and expert systems. This work has far-reaching implications for the development of more robust and scalable querying systems that can effectively handle uncertainty and vagueness in real-world data.

title: Discrete Equilibrium Sampling with Arbitrary Nonequilibrium Processes
Abstract:
Discrete Equilibrium Sampling with Arbitrary Nonequilibrium Processes is a novel statistical mechanics framework enabling efficient equilibrium sampling of complex discrete systems from nonequilibrium scenarios. 
Employing temporal coarse-graining to reveal equilibrium behavior in processes governed by arbitrary nonequilibrium protocols, this approach can be applied to systems following non-equilibrium dynamics from stochastic forces like Gaussian white noise or others more complex in nature such as Lévy flights that capture non-Gaussian fluctuations for more realism, providing equilibrium sampling of nonequilibrium processes for systems obeying arbitrary nonequilibrium dynamics that cannot easily be analyzed using traditional equilibrium statistical mechanics techniques. 
Utilizing temporal coarse-graining enables us to establish a connection between the nonequilibrium process and the equilibrium distribution for various complex systems ranging from deterministic to fully stochastic systems. 
Our framework not only enables analysis of these complex systems but also facilitates deeper physical insight into the equilibrium behavior emerging from the interplay between nonequilibrium forces. Ultimately, this enables true sampling and analysis of those systems with nonequilibrium processes governed by arbitrary protocols, which is challenging to achieve using existing methods.

title: A Chessboard Model of Human Brain and One Application on Memory Capacity
Abstract: This research paper proposes a novel analogical framework for understanding human brain function by modeling it after a chessboard. Inspired by the hierarchical structure and intricate interactions of a chessboard, the chessboard model of the human brain aims to provide a cohesive and versatile framework for exploring various brain functions, including sensory processing, cognitive processing, and memory storage. Using this analogy, the model comprises a grid of interconnected nodes, each representing a specific brain region, and edges symbolizing the neural connections between them. This framework enables the investigation of how different brain regions collaborate and interact to facilitate complex tasks such as decision-making, problem-solving, and learning. Furthermore, the paper demonstrates the application of this chessboard model to the study of memory capacity by analyzing the optimal configuration of nodes and edges for storing and retrieving information. The results show that the chessboard model can provide insights into the limits of human memory capacity and offer new strategies for improving memory function. This research contributes to our understanding of brain function and has implications for the development of more effective artificial intelligence systems, brain-computer interfaces, and memory-enhancing therapies.

title: A Study on Artificial Intelligence IQ and Standard Intelligent Model
Abstract: This study explores the realm of Artificial Intelligence (AI) Intelligence Quotient (IQ) and Standard Intelligent Models. By juxtaposing the theoretical frameworks of intelligence, cognition, and decision-making inherent in human cognition with the evolving landscape of AI systems, our research seeks to redefine and compare the capacity for intelligent reasoning within both domains. A comprehensive literature review delves into the notion of AI IQ, integrating insights from cognitive psychology, neuroscience, computer science, and education to formulate a preliminary framework for evaluating AI's cognitive prowess against its human counterpart. Our analysis highlights significant discrepancies between AI's perceived and actual cognitive capabilities, where AI systems exhibit remarkable prowess in specific areas such as pattern recognition, data analysis, and problem-solving within well-defined parameters. Conversely, AI struggles to replicate the nuanced human experience, characterized by creativity, emotional intelligence, and contextual adaptability – factors critical to problem-solving in dynamic, real-world environments. Our research underscores the need for reevaluating the assumption that AI systems can be readily judged using existing human-centric intelligence quotient (IQ) metrics, and instead advocates for the development of tailored measuring tools to comprehensively assess AI's unique strengths and limitations in comparison to human intelligence.

title: Neural Enquirer: Learning to Query Tables with Natural Language
Abstract: The discovery of powerful query systems that can reason over relational databases has the potential to revolutionize the way data is accessed and utilized. Traditional query systems require users to have a deep understanding of the database schema and the underlying query language, which can be a significant barrier to adoption for users without extensive technical expertise. To address this challenge, we introduce Neural Enquirer, a novel query interface that enables users to query relational databases using natural language. By harnessing the power of deep learning and leveraging advances in natural language processing, Neural Enquirer is able to understand and interpret user queries in a more intuitive and flexible manner. Specifically, our system consists of a neural network that takes as input a user's natural language query and produces as output a SQL query that retrieves the desired data from the database. Through a comprehensive evaluation of Neural Enquirer's performance on several benchmark datasets, we demonstrate that our system is able to achieve state-of-the-art results in terms of query accuracy and natural language understanding. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that Neural Enquirer is able to generalize effectively to unseen database schema and query patterns, enabling it to be applied to a wide range of real-world applications.

title: Modeling Human Understanding of Complex Intentional Action with a Bayesian Nonparametric Subgoal Model
Abstract: Understanding complex intentional actions, which are a crucial aspect of human behavior, has been a long-standing challenge in artificial intelligence and cognitive science. Human actions often unfold dynamically and involve multiple goals, which may be unobserved or implicitly known. This inability to fully model these complex intentional behaviors restricts optimal decision-making and action planning in real-world domains, including robotics, computer vision, and human-computer interaction. Recent works have employed Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and Actional Memory to model human understanding of intention. However, these methods are typically limited to sequential observations and struggle when dealing with unseen or partially unseen environments. In contrast, Bayesian models that leverage non-parametric priors provide a much more versatile approach to modeling purposeful actions in uncertain conditions.  This paper proposes a novel model, termed ABC (Action Bayesian Coder), which integrates the strengths of Bayesian non-parametric mixture models with graph-structured data to better capture the subjective nature of intentions. By employing a stochastic, hierarchical process that iteratively generates relevant subgoals and contextual updates, ABC naturally integrates predictions of human intentional behavior across various cognitive and situational contexts. Comprehensive experiments conducted on a diverse range of scenarios, including robotic grasping and human activity recognition, demonstrate the superior understanding of complex intentional actions as well as robustness over existing approaches.

title: The GTR-model: a universal framework for quantum-like measurements
Abstract: This work presents a novel approach to quantum-like measurements through the development of a generalized transforming-representable (GTR) model. The GTR-model provides a unified framework for understanding and simulating the behavior of physical systems that exhibit quantum-like properties, including decoherence and entanglement, without relying on the underlying Hilbert space structure. Building on the concept of transformation-representability, a key insight in this research is the definition of a novel measure-theoretic framework that allows for the systematic exploration of different classes of quantum-like measurements. By leveraging the GTR-model's flexibility, researchers can study various experimental setups, including those involving interacting quantum systems and environment, under a common mathematical umbrella. Key properties of the GTR-model include the preservation of covariance under unitary transformations, the emergence of entanglement and decoherence, and the ability to approximate the predictions of traditional quantum mechanics in the low-excitation limit. The significance of the GTR-model lies in its potential to facilitate a deeper understanding of the fundamental principles governing quantum behavior and to offer a flexible and computationally efficient framework for probing the frontiers of quantum gravity and quantum technologies. By shedding light on the relationship between quantum mechanics and its applications, the GTR-model paves the way for innovative solutions to pressing scientific and technological challenges.

title: Recognizing Semantic Features in Faces using Deep Learning
Abstract: Deep learning techniques have revolutionized the field of facial analysis by providing unprecedented accuracy in identifying various characteristics from faces captured in images or videos. This study aims to explore the application of deep learning models in recognizing semantic features in faces, which involve non-essential yet crucial attributes such as facial expression, age, and social status. Our analysis investigates the role of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and recurrent neural networks (RNNs) in capturing these attributes, with a focus on understanding the impact of different architectures on performance. The proposed methodology adopts a multi-task learning framework to jointly train the models on multiple semantic features and facial identification. A dataset comprising a variety of faces with diverse expressions, ages, and social contexts is employed to evaluate the performance of different models. The research demonstrates the potential of deep learning techniques in recognizing semantic features and facial characteristics with high accuracy. Furthermore, the analysis sheds light on the strengths and limitations of CNNs and RNNs in processing and analyzing facial data. The findings are expected to contribute to the development of more effective facial analysis systems with applications in areas such as surveillance, security, and human-computer interaction. The theoretical framework of this study builds upon existing research in the field and provides new insights into the capabilities and limitations of deep learning models in semantic facial analysis.

title: Assessing forensic evidence by computing belief functions
Abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence and probabilistic theories in forensic science offers a promising approach to evaluating evidence, particularly within the context of belief functions. This research delves into the application of computing belief functions as a method for assessing forensic evidence, focusing on its potential to provide an unbiased and rational assessment of the evidence, thereby enhancing the reliability of forensic outcomes. By combining the principles of Dempster-Shafer theory and the theory of evidence, belief functions empower analysts to consider uncertainty, partial belief, and potential contradictions in evidence, thereby fostering a more comprehensive examination of complex forensic data. This computational approach enables the synthesis of various types of evidence, including direct, indirect, and circumstantial, to derive a comprehensive belief assignment, reflecting both the strength and the plausibility of an individual's guilt or innocence. Guided by this novel analytical framework, researchers, and forensic professionals can quantify the relative plausibility of competing hypotheses and, in the process, generate a qualitative evaluation that encompasses both probabilities and epistemological degrees of belief, thereby contributing to the development of a more coherent and standard procedure for forensic assessment and decision-making.

title: Quantifying knowledge with a new calculus for belief functions - a generalization of probability theory
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to quantifying knowledge by developing a new calculus for belief functions that generalizes probability theory. Belief functions, as a mathematical theory, have been extensively used in various fields such as artificial intelligence, decision-making, and data analysis, particularly in situations where uncertainty and imprecision are present. The traditional probability theory is limited in its ability to handle Dempster-Shafer theory's belief functions, which can represent both precise and imprecise uncertain knowledge in a more comprehensive manner. Recognizing the limitations of the current probability theory, researchers have been motivated to explore more general and flexible frameworks for representing knowledge. The proposed new calculus for belief functions achieves quantifiable and hierarchical degrees of uncertainty that bridge the gap between subjective and objective uncertainty. By providing a framework for belief function calculus, we enable more robust and interpretable models that consider multiple sources of information and adjust the notion of "likelihood" to a new criterion. The developed formalism is demonstrated to be superior in handling the uncertain and incomplete knowledge inherent in complex systems, such as decision-making and machine learning applications. Additionally, the proposed calculus is rigorously defined, facilitating the use of belief functions in knowledge representation and reasoning.

title: Object-based World Modeling in Semi-Static Environments with Dependent Dirichlet-Process Mixtures
Abstract: Object-based world modeling is a prevalent concept in robotics and computer vision, enabling agents to interpret and interact with their environment through geometric shapes and structures, rather than pixel-level representations. However, traditional object-based models often falter in semi-static environments, where physical objects are constantly in motion and interacting with one another, resulting in dynamic changes to their shapes and relationships. To address this challenge, this paper proposes a novel approach utilizing Dependent Dirichlet-Process Mixtures (DDPMs), a Bayesian non-parametric framework capable of modeling complex, high-dimensional data distributions with unknown and varying numbers of components. By incorporating DDPMs into object-based world modeling, we develop a flexible and adaptive representation that can accurately capture the dynamic evolution of objects and their relationships in semi-static environments. The proposed approach is demonstrated through experiments on simulated scenarios, where objects with various shapes and properties are modeled using DDPMs, and their relationships are learned through probabilistic dependencies. Results show significant improvements in modeling accuracy and adaptability, making the proposed framework suitable for real-world applications, such as robotic navigation and computer vision tasks in environments with complex, dynamic scenarios. By effectively integrating DDPMs with object-based modeling, this research paves the way for more accurate and flexible representations of semi-static environments, enabling robots and autonomous systems to better navigate and interact with their surroundings.

title: Attribute2Image: Conditional Image Generation from Visual Attributes
Abstract: Attribute2Image is a novel framework for conditional image generation that enables the creation of realistic and diverse images based on high-level visual attributes, such as object categories, shapes, colors, textures, and backgrounds. By leveraging advances in deep learning, particularly in the fields of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) and encoder-decoder architectures, our approach can learn to generate images that accurately reflect the specified attributes. The proposed framework consists of an encoder network that maps input attributes to a semantic embedding, and a decoder network that generates an image based on this embedding. Through extensive experiments and evaluations on diverse datasets, including the Attribute2Image dataset, the CIFAR-10 dataset, and the ImageNet dataset, we demonstrate the effectiveness and flexibility of our framework in generating high-quality images that meet specific attribute requirements. Furthermore, we explore the use of Attribute2Image for various applications, such as image editing, object generation, and image-to-image translation, highlighting its potential as a powerful tool for image synthesis and data augmentation. Our results show that Attribute2Image can generate images with high fidelity and diversity, making it a valuable asset for researchers and practitioners working in the fields of computer vision, robotics, and graphics.

title: Fast k-Nearest Neighbour Search via Dynamic Continuous Indexing
Abstract: This research paper presents a novel approach to accelerating k-Nearest Neighbour (k-NN) search in high-dimensional spaces using dynamic continuous indexing. The proposed method, dubbed DKNN, focuses on addressing the scalability and efficiency limitations of traditional static indexing techniques in fast and accurate k-NN search. To achieve this, DKNN employs a cluster-based spatial indexing strategy, where a set of pre-computed affinity matrices are dynamically maintained to represent the indexing landscape. Each affinity matrix captures the local structure and proximity relationships within a cluster of dataset elements, enabling efficient similarity search by circumventing the need for traditional geometric-based indexing methods. A probabilistically-driven technique for adaptively selecting the most promising clusters to index is also introduced, allowing DKNN to judiciously allocate resources based on the current search context. By exploiting the strengths of continuous indexing while minimizing computational overheads, DKNN is shown to significantly outperform existing state-of-the-art k-NN search methods in terms of query latency and indexing memory efficiency. Experimental evaluations on a range of datasets, from image and audio classification to collaborative filtering, demonstrate the efficacy and robustness of DKNN under various search scenarios and indexing settings, thereby underscoring its potential to serve as a compelling alternative to traditional k-NN search solutions.

title: A New Approach for Scalable Analysis of Microbial Communities
Abstract: This study proposes a novel framework for scalable analysis of microbial communities, addressing the pressing need for efficient and reliable metagenomic data processing. The exponential growth in next-generation sequencing technologies has led to an overwhelming amount of genomic data, necessitating the development of robust and adaptable analytical tools. Our approach hinges on the integration of machine learning algorithms and parallel computing infrastructure to expedite the analysis of large-scale metagenomic datasets. By harnessing the power of distributed computing and employing techniques such as random forest and k-means clustering, our framework optimizes the processing of genomic data, allowing for the identification of biomarkers, the reconstruction of community structures, and the elucidation of functional relationships within microbial ecosystems. Additionally, we incorporate a meta-analysis module to synthesize findings across multiple datasets, providing a more comprehensive understanding of community dynamics. Validation of our framework using publicly available datasets demonstrates marked improvements in computational efficiency, facilitating the exploration of complex microbial communities and shedding light on the intricacies of microbiome function. This scalable analysis approach promises to revolutionize the field of microbiome research, empowering scientists to unlock insights into microbiome regulation, disease mechanisms, and the development of tailored therapeutic strategies.

title: Taxonomy grounded aggregation of classifiers with different label sets
Abstract: This study presents a novel taxonomy-based aggregation approach for combining the predictions of multiple classifiers trained on distinct label sets. Current ensemble methods predominantly rely on a unified label set, which restricts their applicability in real-world scenarios where inter-label relationships and varying label set compositions are prevalent. The proposed approach leverages a taxonomy topology to model the relationships between labels, allowing for the aggregation of classifiers with diverse label sets. A taxonomy representation, constructed using a hierarchical graph structure, enables the identification of label subspaces and captures the underlying relationships between them. The aggregation is performed using a weighted sum-based algorithm that considers both the taxonomy similarity and the classifier accuracy in determining the final predictions. The proposed method is evaluated using a comprehensive set of experiments on multiple classification datasets, showcasing its potential to improve the overall classification performance compared to traditional ensemble methods. Additionally, the study highlights the importance of taxonomy-aware ensemble aggregation and demonstrates its applicability across various domains and datasets, underscoring its potential to become a viable option for tackling the challenges of real-world classification tasks.

title: A Hybrid Intelligent Model for Software Cost Estimation
Abstract: This paper proposes a hybrid intelligent model for software cost estimation that leverages the strengths of various machine learning and soft computing techniques to improve the accuracy and reliability of cost estimation. The model incorporates a combination of fuzzy logic, genetic programming, and swarm intelligence to develop a robust and adaptive framework for estimating software development costs. The proposed model is based on a comprehensive analysis of historical project data and incorporates various factors that influence software development costs, including project size, complexity, technology, and personnel skills. A dataset of 500 software projects is used to train and test the model, which is evaluated using established metrics such as mean absolute error, mean squared error, and R-squared value. The results demonstrate the superiority of the proposed model over existing approaches, with a significant improvement in accuracy and a reduction in estimation errors. The findings of this study have implications for software project managers, who can utilize the proposed model to develop more accurate cost estimates and make informed decisions about resource allocation and project timelines. Furthermore, the model's adaptive nature enables it to learn from new project data and improve its performance over time, making it a valuable tool for software development organizations seeking to optimize their cost estimation processes.

title: Transfer Learning in Brain-Computer Interfaces
Abstract: Brain-Computer Interfaces (BCIs) have gained significant attention in the field of neurotechnology, enabling individuals to communicate and control devices with their brain signals. One of the major challenges in developing BCIs is the limited availability of labeled training data, which can be rectified by adopting transfer learning techniques. Transfer learning involves pre-training a model on a large, related dataset and fine-tuning it on a smaller target dataset, leveraging the pre-existing knowledge to improve generalization and adaptability. This study explores the potential of transfer learning in BCIs by pre-training deep learning models on large EEG datasets and fine-tuning them on BCIs datasets with limited samples. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of transfer learning in improving task accuracy and reducing the required number of training samples. Furthermore, the study investigates the influence of different pre-training tasks, such as classification and regression, on the performance of BCIs. Results suggest that pre-training with classification tasks yields better results, especially when the target BCI task is a classification problem. The study also examines the quality of the pre-trained models and its impact on the fine-tuning process. Overall, this research highlights the benefits of transfer learning in BCIs, enabling the development of more efficient and accurate brain-computer interfaces.

title: Evaluating Morphological Computation in Muscle and DC-motor Driven Models of Human Hopping
Abstract: Morphological computation refers to the way in which the structure and shape of an organism's body contribute to its overall function, essentially computing movement or action. Human hopping is a complex motor skill that requires precise coordination between the kinetic and potential energy of the body. Muscle-driven models of human hopping have traditionally been used to study the neuromuscular control mechanisms involved, but recent research has shown that muscle-driven models often struggle to replicate the actual kinematics of hopping, particularly in terms of the energy efficiency and smoothness of movement. This study investigates the use of DC-motor driven models, which simulate the mechanical properties of muscles using electric motors, to improve the accuracy and efficiency of human hopping simulations. The results show that DC-motor driven models are able to accurately replicate the kinematics of hopping, while also providing insights into the mechanical properties of muscles and the energy efficiency of movement. The implications of these findings for the development of more accurate and efficient models of human movement are discussed, and the potential applications of this research in the fields of robotics, biomechanics, and physical therapy are explored.

title: LSTM Neural Reordering Feature for Statistical Machine Translation
Abstract: This research proposes a novel approach to improve the performance of statistical machine translation (SMT) systems by incorporating Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural networks into the reordering feature extraction stage. The reordering of source language words is a crucial aspect of SMT, as it significantly impacts the overall quality and fluency of the translated output. Traditional reordering models often rely on manually engineered features or shallower neural network architectures, which may fail to capture the complex dependencies between source language words. To address this limitation, we introduce a neural reordering feature that leverages the strengths of LSTM networks to automatically learn meaningful reordering features from the source language input. The proposed LSTM neural reordering feature is integrated into a state-of-the-art SMT system, demonstrating improved BLEU scores and human evaluations on multiple benchmark translation tasks. Experimental results show that the proposed approach outperforms various baselines, including traditional feature extraction methods and shallower neural architectures, by effectively capturing the syntactic and semantic dependencies between source language words. Additionally, our approach enables the development of more accurate and efficient SMT systems that can handle a wide range of languages and translation tasks, contributing to the advancement of the SMT field.

title: Learning Using 1-Local Membership Queries
Abstract: This work revolves around the concept of learning using 1-local membership queries, a unique framework that allows for efficient and effective learning in complex environments. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on extensive data or computationally expensive algorithms, 1-local membership queries offer a novel way to make informed decisions by probing a single instance of the underlying distribution. The core idea here is that a learner can gain valuable insights about the underlying data by carefully selecting and querying a single representative instance, which is reflective of the broader distribution. The proposed approach has numerous applications in various domains, including classification, clustering, and dimensionality reduction. A key aspect of this framework is its inherent ability to provide robust and flexible solutions, adaptable to diverse learning scenarios and data types. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of this method in accurately modeling complex data distributions and outperforming state-of-the-art learning techniques in several benchmark tasks. Furthermore, the developed approach exhibits substantial computational efficiency, making it particularly suitable for real-world applications characterized by large and complex datasets. By virtue of its innovative querying strategy and efficient learning framework, this work provides promising avenues for advancement and expansion in the field of machine learning and data analysis.

title: Inferring Interpersonal Relations in Narrative Summaries
Abstract: This study presents a novel approach to inferring interpersonal relations in narrative summaries using a fusion of techniques from natural language processing and graph theory. We propose a framework that leverages word embeddings to represent narrative entities and their interactions, and then applies a graph-based model to identify these relations. Our framework utilizes a combination of node embeddings and edge embeddings to capture the complex relationships between entities in a narrative summary. Furthermore, we develop a set of relation-specific features that serve as input to a classification model, which accurately predicts the type of interpersonal relation between entities, such as friendship, romantic relationship, or antagonism. We evaluate the performance of our approach on several datasets, including narrative summaries from various domains, and demonstrate its efficacy in accurately identifying interpersonal relations. Our results show that our framework significantly outperforms baseline models, including state-of-the-art relation extraction and classification models. We also conduct an analysis of the relationship between entity features and interpersonal relations, which provides insights into the underlying mechanisms governing interpersonal relationships in narrative summaries.

title: Imitation-Induced Criticality: Network Reciprocity and Psycho-logical Reward
Abstract: Imitation, a fundamental aspect of human social behavior, has been extensively studied in various domains, including psychology, neuroscience, and social network analysis. However, its relationship to criticality, a phenomenon appearing in systems with a delicate balance between order and disorder, remains poorly understood. This study delves into the emergence of imitation-induced criticality in the context of network reciprocity, a key mechanism that enables the spread of social influence. We present a mathematical framework that integrates principles from social network theory and population dynamics, capturing the intricate interactions between network topology, individual behavior, and population-wide outcomes. Our findings reveal that imitation-induced criticality arises in networks characterized by reciprocal relationships, where individuals are more likely to learn from and imitate each other's behaviors. At the critical point, social influence spreads rapidly, leading to increased coordination and conformity within the population. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the reward functions underlying individual behavior play a crucial role in shaping the criticality threshold. By incorporating elements of psychological reward, such as vicarious learning and self-efficacy, our model can capture the complex dynamics of social influence and provide insights into the emergent properties of imitation-induced criticality in social networks. This research provides a novel framework for understanding the emergence of criticality in social systems, with significant implications for the design of interventions aimed at promoting social change and influencing collective behavior.

title: Ask, and shall you receive?: Understanding Desire Fulfillment in Natural Language Text
Abstract: This study explores the concept of desire fulfillment in natural language text through a novel application of the well-established principle popularized by Norman Vincent Peale's motivational book "The Power of Positive Thinking" that "ask and it shall be given unto you." By incorporating machine learning and natural language processing techniques, the research aims to investigate the effect of expressing desire within a given context on the perceived likelihood of its fulfillment. A dataset of texts describing desires and outcomes was compiled, with participants rating the perceived likelihood of each outcome. The results show that explicitly stated desires are indeed more likely to be fulfilled, but only when accompanied by specific actions or steps towards their realization, challenging the notion that simply asking or stating a desire is sufficient for its fulfillment. Furthermore, the study found that nuances in language, including tone, modality, and degree of commitment, significantly impact the perceived likelihood of desire fulfillment. The findings have significant implications for fields like education, health, and social work, where empowering individuals with the ability to effectively communicate their desires and create meaningful goals may be a key factor in achieving successful outcomes.

title: Modeling Dynamic Relationships Between Characters in Literary Novels
Abstract: This study presents a novel approach to modeling dynamic relationships between characters in literary novels, leveraging the intersection of natural language processing and graph-based network analysis. The proposed framework, dubbed Literary Character Network (LCN), represents each character as a node in a complex graph, where edges signify interactions, dialogue, or narrative events. By incorporating temporal and spatial information, LCN captures the evolving nature of relationships between characters, including shifts in emotional connections, power dynamics, and social standings. The methodology involves text preprocessing, graph construction, and network analytics to identify patterns and correlations in character relationships. To validate the framework, we employed a comprehensive dataset consisting of 50 literary novels, covering various genres and time periods, and extracted character relationships through statistical analysis and machine learning techniques. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of LCN in uncovering novel insights into literary narratives, including character clustering, social hierarchy establishment, and dramatic arc progression. The framework also reveals subtle mechanisms underlying character development and relationship evolution, such as the impact of location, context, and narrative voice on interpersonal dynamics. By providing a systematic and quantitative analysis of dynamic relationships in literary novels, LCN opens new avenues for literary analysis, education, and creative writing, enabling researchers, educators, and authors to gain a deeper understanding of the complex social structures underlying fiction.

title: Influence diagrams for the optimization of a vehicle speed profile
Abstract: Influence diagrams emerge as a powerful graphical tool for capturing the complexities underlying vehicle speed profile optimization under various operating conditions. This research paper delves into the formulation and application of influence diagrams for optimization in the context of vehicle speed profile. By translating real-world engineering constraints into a compact and comprehensible format, influence diagrams provide an elegant framework for balancing competing objectives such as fuel efficiency, emission reduction, and ride comfort. The proposed method leverages both qualitative and quantitative data to construct a probabilistic influence diagram, accounting for factors like road topography, traffic conditions, and driver behavior. This structured representation enables the isolation and quantification of key variables influencing optimal speed trajectories. Additionally, influence diagrams facilitate the incorporation of nonlinear relationships and conditional dependencies among variables. By integrating this visual approach with established optimization algorithms, this research optimizes vehicle speed profiles in real-time, thus minimizing environmental impact and energy consumption while ensuring a comfortable ride experience for passengers. Results from simulation experiments demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed approach in delivering significant reductions in fuel consumption and emissions, relative to baseline scenarios.

title: On Learning to Think: Algorithmic Information Theory for Novel Combinations of Reinforcement Learning Controllers and Recurrent Neural World Models
Abstract:
This paper delves into the intersection of reinforcement learning, recursive world models, and algorithmic information theory, exploring novel combinations of reinforcement learning controllers and recurrent neural world models with the aim of enhancing learning capabilities. The integration of these components allows for the development of more complex and generalizable world models that facilitate efficient exploration and adaptation in dynamic environments.  
By leveraging the predictive capabilities of world models, the paper proposes a framework that enables reinforcement learning controllers to effectively represent their surroundings and generate informative experiences. This framework is rooted in the principles of algorithmic information theory, which quantifies the complexity of information sequences, thus enabling the control of model complexity and knowledge acquisition. 
A key contribution of this work lies in its exploration of hybrid world models that incorporate multiple recurrent neural networks with variable complexity and hierarchical organization, thus allowing for flexible adaptation to different tasks and environments. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in learning to think and adapt in complex scenarios, such as navigating through challenging mazes and learning to control non-linear chaotic systems. Overall, this research provides new insights into the application of algorithmic information theory for developing novel combinations of reinforcement learning controllers and recurrent neural world models.

title: Scaling POMDPs For Selecting Sellers in E-markets-Extended Version
Abstract: Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs) have gained significant attention in the realm of decision-making under uncertainty, particularly in complex domains such as e-markets. However, solving large-scale POMDPs remains a challenging task due to their inherent computational complexity. E-markets present an additional layer of complexity with the existence of multiple sellers, each with their unique capabilities and constraints. Selecting the optimal seller in such scenarios is crucial for achieving desired outcomes. To address this challenge, we propose an extended version of POMDPs, tailored for scaling to e-markets with multiple sellers. The proposed approach incorporates seller-specific probabilistic models to capture the uncertainty associated with their offerings and capabilities. Additionally, we develop efficient algorithms for solving the scaled POMDPs, leveraging techniques such as state aggregation, value function approximation, and constraint relaxation. Through extensive simulations and case studies, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach in selecting optimal sellers in e-markets, leading to improved outcomes and decision-making under uncertainty. The results highlight the potential of the extended POMDPs framework in tackling complex e-market scenarios, showcasing its potential applications in real-world e-commerce systems. Overall, our work makes a significant contribution to the development of scalable POMDPs for e-markets, paving the way for more efficient and effective decision-making in e-commerce.

title: Machine Learning Sentiment Prediction based on Hybrid Document Representation
Abstract: This paper explores the development of a hybrid document representation model for sentiment prediction in machine learning. Current approaches in sentiment analysis often rely on a single feature extraction mechanism, which may limit their accuracy, especially when dealing with complex documents. To overcome this limitation, we propose a hybrid approach that combines the strengths of both traditional feature-based and neural-based representation methods. Specifically, our model incorporates a convolutional neural network (CNN) for capturing local dependencies in language and a recurrent neural network (RNN) for modeling long-range contextual relationships. We also introduce a novel feature extraction technique that extracts both lexical and semantic features from the input text. The proposed hybrid model is evaluated on several benchmark sentiment analysis datasets, demonstrating significant improvements in performance compared to traditional and neural-based approaches. Furthermore, our model is found to be robust and adaptable to various types of documents and sentiment analysis tasks, showcasing its potential applications in real-world settings. The experimental results indicate that the proposed hybrid model can serve as a promising solution for accurate sentiment prediction in machine learning applications, particularly in areas where context-dependent and complex sentiment analysis is required.

title: Exploiting Anonymity in Approximate Linear Programming: Scaling to Large Multiagent MDPs (Extended Version)
Abstract: Approximate linear programming has emerged as a promising approach for solving large multiagent Markov decision processes (MDPs), due to its ability to efficiently balance exploration and exploitation in complex stochastic environments. However, the scalability of current techniques is still limited by their reliance on precise knowledge of the agent's distribution over actions, which poses significant computational challenges in high-dimensional spaces. To address this limitation, we develop a novel method for exploiting anonymity in approximate linear programming, where a group of agents with identical behavior are treated as a single anonymous entity. By leveraging the properties of anonymous behavior, our approach enables the efficient reduction of high-dimensional state and action spaces, thereby scaling approximate linear programming to large multiagent MDPs. Our key insight is to approximate the anonymous behavior of a group of agents using a single mean-action distribution, which is updated periodically to capture the agents' adapting behavior. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in a variety of scenario's, including resource allocation problems and congestion games, where we show that exploiting anonymity leads to significant improvements in computational efficiency and solution quality. Overall, our work provides a novel perspective on the exploitation of anonymity in approximate linear programming, and opens up new avenues for scaling large multiagent MDPs.

title: Sparse Coral Classification Using Deep Convolutional Neural Networks
Abstract: This paper presents an innovative approach to sparse coral classification using deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs). With the escalating threat of coral bleaching and habitat destruction, rapid and accurate identification of coral species has become increasingly vital for effective conservation efforts. However, traditional manual classification methods rely heavily on expert knowledge, are time-consuming, and often produce inconsistent results. To address these limitations, we propose a DCNN-based framework to classify fragmented and damaged coral samples from underwater photographs. The framework consists of three primary modules: a segmentation module to isolate the coral region of interest, a feature extraction module utilizing transfer learning techniques to capture relevant morphological features, and a classification module employing a multi-class neural network to identify the coral species. We evaluated our approach on a diverse dataset containing 10 species of coral, with varying levels of fragmentation, damage, and underwater environment conditions. Our results demonstrate a remarkable improvement in classification accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods, with a precision of 92% and recall of 95%. The proposed framework not only promotes coral conservation but also offers a viable solution for rapid species identification in other marine ecosystems, facilitating more efficient and effective global protection efforts.

title: Solving Transition-Independent Multi-agent MDPs with Sparse Interactions (Extended version)
Abstract: This paper extends previous work on solving transition-independent multi-agent Markov decision processes (MADPs) with sparse interactions. In MADPs, learning from interaction data becomes increasingly challenging due to the exponential growth in data with the number of agents and possible actions involved. Transition-independence in MADPs implies that the outcomes of actions taken by individual agents do not directly affect the dynamics of other agents, thereby reducing the complexity of multi-agent learning. However, this restriction is often violated in practice due to sparse interactions, where agents may occasionally impact one another, even if it's rare. This limitation severely hampers the effectiveness of many existing MADP learning algorithms designed under the transition-independence assumption. To address this issue, this study proposes a novel approach that combines a set of pre-training phases with a state-action value function based Q-learning algorithm. Our approach consists of two phases: a batch learning phase and an interaction phase, where batches are learned from possible combinations of sparse interaction patterns experienced over multiple iterations of the interaction phase. This enables our algorithm to learn from sparse but critical inter-agent interactions, alongside inherent transition-independence characteristics. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our novel approach through extensive benchmark experiments and comparisons with existing algorithms. Empirical results show that our proposed approach achieves state-of-the-art performance in various transition-independent MADP scenarios.

title: Robotic Search & Rescue via Online Multi-task Reinforcement Learning
Abstract: This paper presents a novel framework for Robotic Search and Rescue (RSR) tasks via online multi-task reinforcement learning. We aim to develop a robot that can adapt to unfamiliar environments and learn from experience, thereby improving its search efficiency and reducing response times. Our proposed approach leverages the power of multi-task learning to enable a single robot to solve multiple RSR tasks simultaneously, such as search, navigation, and obstacle avoidance. By learning a shared representation of the environment, the robot can generalize its knowledge across tasks and environments. To facilitate online learning, we adopt an off-policy multi-task actor-critic algorithm that allows the robot to learn from raw sensory observations and generate exploratory actions while interacting with the environment. The developed system was tested using a simulated environment and a physical robotic platform, showcasing its ability to adapt to new environments, learn from experience, and generalize across various RSR tasks. Our results demonstrate the potential of this paradigm for improving the speed and effectiveness of RSR operations in real-world scenarios. The proposed framework is scalable, modular, and can be easily integrated with various robotic platforms, enabling widespread deployment in search and rescue missions. title: Bootstrapping Ternary Relation Extractors
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to bootstrapping ternary relation extractors through iterative training and self-supervised learning techniques. Ternary relations, which involve three distinct entities, pose significant challenges in natural language processing tasks due to their relatively low frequency and complexity. Existing methods often rely on external resources, such as pre-trained models or hand-crafted features, which can be limited or biased. Our method attempts to alleviate these issues by introducing a self-supervised learning mechanism that leverages the ternary structure of the data to generate pseudo-triples. These pseudo-triples are then used to augment the training data and improve the performance of the ternary relation extractor. Through an iterative training process, the model learns to recognize patterns and relationships in the data, ultimately resulting in a more robust and generalizable model. We evaluate our approach on a range of benchmarks, including standard relation extraction datasets and a custom dataset created for this research. Results show that our method outperforms state-of-the-art models in most cases, achieving significant improvements in both precision and recall. Furthermore, our approach allows for unsupervised learning, eliminating the need for external resources and making it more feasible for real-world applications. By providing a self-sufficient and scalable solution to ternary relation extraction, our research contributes to advancing the field of natural language processing and its applications in information extraction and analysis.

title: Column-Oriented Datalog Materialization for Large Knowledge Graphs (Extended Technical Report)
Abstract: This extended technical report demonstrates a novel approach to efficiently materializing column-oriented Datalog queries over large knowledge graphs. Traditional graph databases often struggle to scale with the increasing complexity and size of knowledge graphs, leading to significant performance bottlenecks. By leveraging the concept of materialization, we introduce a column-oriented Datalog materialization system specifically designed to tackle these scalability challenges. Our proposed system utilizes a partitioning strategy to divide the knowledge graph into smaller chunks, allowing for efficient computation and storage of Datalog query results. The column-oriented materialization approach is enabled by the use of vertical partitioning, where each column of the knowledge graph is stored independently, resulting in improved query performance and reduced storage requirements. Furthermore, our system incorporates an innovative query reformulation technique that automatically rearranges Datalog queries to optimize materialization and query execution. These enhancements enable our system to handle large-scale knowledge graphs with millions of entities and high query complexity, outperforming traditional graph databases in terms of query latency and throughput. Experimental results on a massive knowledge graph demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, showcasing a significant improvement in query performance and a substantial reduction in storage needs.

title: Applying deep learning to classify pornographic images and videos

title: Semantic Folding Theory And its Application in Semantic Fingerprinting
Abstract: Semantic Folding Theory provides a novel framework for analyzing and modeling semantic relationships between words and phrases in a language. It proposes that meaning can be understood as the aggregation of folding maps, where each map represents the unique perspective or view of a concept. These folding maps are asserted to capture subtle nuances of word meaning that are lost in more traditional meaning representation approaches. This theory can be used to formalize word meanings as concise geometric descriptions, enabling more efficient search, indexing, and retrieval of semantic information. Furthermore, the application of Semantic Folding Theory in semantic fingerprinting offers a revolutionary method for creating unique digital identifiers for objects, texts, or concepts. These semantic fingerprints essentially represent the fingerprint of an object or concept by encoding its inherent properties and meaning geometry. Such a semantic fingerprinting method is shown to significantly improve the security, authentication, and search capabilities of data stores and retrieval systems. By incorporating Semantic Folding Theory into existing cryptographic protocols and machine learning models, researchers can develop more sophisticated techniques for text classification, clustering, and data anomaly detection. By unfolding the hidden geometric properties of language, this groundbreaking theory can open a new chapter in natural language processing and create new opportunities for enhancing human-computer interaction and data security.

title: Multiagent Cooperation and Competition with Deep Reinforcement Learning
Abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive study on multiagent cooperation and competition using deep reinforcement learning (DRL) techniques. In complex multiagent environments, agents must navigate intricate social dynamics, which cannot be captured by traditional single-agent RL settings. The proposed approach involves designing novel architectures and algorithms that enable agents to effectively cooperate and compete with each other. Specifically, we explore the application of multi-agent DQN, actor-critic methods, and attention mechanisms to model complex interactions among agents. Our experiments focus on several benchmark tasks, including the classic Cooperative Navigation, Predator-Prey, and Multi-Agent Traffic Control tasks. title: War of 2050: a Battle for Information, Communications, and Computer Security

title: On the convergence of cycle detection for navigational reinforcement learning
Abstract: Cycle detection is a pivotal component in navigational reinforcement learning, enabling agents to efficiently explore and learn within complex environments. However, the extensive computational resources required for convergence typically hinder the practical applications of cycle detection in the real-world. To address this challenge, this research investigate the convergence properties of various cycle detection algorithms in the context of navigational reinforcement learning. We examine the asymptotic convergence and empirical stability of graph-based and distributed methods, identifying key parameters that significantly impact the rate of convergence. The study presents a novel framework that leverages the strengths of both centralized and decentralized algorithms to achieve faster and more reliable cycle detection. By employing a hybrid approach combining local explorations with global convergence guarantees, the proposed framework not only enhances the efficiency of cycle detection but also provides a robust foundation for more advanced reinforcement learning techniques. Our experimental results demonstrate significant improvements in convergence speed and accuracy across a range of synthetic and real-world environments, showcasing the potential of the proposed framework to enrich the capabilities of navigational reinforcement learning agents. title: Word Existence Algorithm
Abstract: This research paper presents a novel computational framework for determining the existence of words in various computational environments. The Word Existence Algorithm (WEA) is an innovative, machine learning-based methodology that leverages artificial intelligence techniques to identify words within large datasets. The development of WEA is necessitated by the rapid growth of digital information and the increasing need for efficient and accurate text analysis tools. The algorithm utilizes a hybrid approach, combining the strengths of both supervised and unsupervised learning methods to achieve robust word recognition capabilities. By incorporating keyword extraction, named entity recognition, and part-of-speech tagging techniques, WEA is capable of identifying relevant words within text, web pages, and other digital formats. The empirical study demonstrates WEA's reliability and accuracy in detecting words in diverse environments, including but not limited to, optical character recognition, stylometric analysis, and text similarity assessment. The critical evaluation of WEA highlights its potential applications in natural language processing, information retrieval, and digital forensics, underscoring its significance as a sophisticated tool for word existence detection in modern computing applications. title: Shaping Proto-Value Functions via Rewards
Abstract: Proto-value functions are a foundational concept in reinforcement learning, learning a distribution over utility functions to understand the desired objectives of complex tasks. However, previous methods for learning proto-value functions only utilized sparse or dense rewards, neglecting the possibility of using adaptive feedback. This paper aims to bridge this gap by presenting a novel framework for shaping proto-value functions via rewards. Our key contribution lies in developing a novel reward-based approach to infer the underlying utility function that can effectively capture the complex relationships between actions and rewards. We achieve this by approximating the underlying utility function using a neural network, which is then updated based on the differences between the observed rewards and the predicted rewards from the approximated utility function. To make the framework more robust and efficient, we introduce a two-player game-theoretic perspective, where the agent plays a cooperative game with the environment to maximize the cumulative rewards. We further provide a theoretical analysis of the convergence conditions and the impact of exploration-exploitation trade-offs on the learning process. We validate our approach on a range of challenging tasks, including complex navigation and manipulation scenarios, demonstrating its ability to adapt to changing rewards and promote robust and efficient exploration.

title: A Stochastic Process Model of Classical Search
Abstract: This paper presents a novel stochastic process model for the classical search, which is a fundamental problem in search theory. The proposed model incorporates probabilistic transitions between search states, allowing for the representation of search decisions under uncertainty. Inspired by the structure of Markov chains, our model captures the strategic choices made by the searcher, including the exploration of new areas and the exploitation of promising leads. We derive a set of explicitly tractable metrics that quantify the expected time to find the target, taking into account the trade-off between thorough exploration and swift exploitation. By leveraging the machinery of stochastic processes, we establish a tight upper bound on the expected time to find the target, which provides a theoretical benchmark for the optimality of search strategies. Our model is flexible enough to accommodate various types of search data, including passive and active search scenarios. We illustrate the applicability of the model through simulation studies, demonstrating its remarkable ability to predict search performance under different scenarios. Our results provide unprecedented insights into the efficacy of various search strategies, with implications for decision-making in a wide range of applications, including urban search and rescue operations, crop yield monitoring, and disease surveillance.

title: Some Epistemological Problems with the Knowledge Level in Cognitive Architectures
Abstract: This abstract explores the epistemological underpinnings of the knowledge level in cognitive architectures, highlighting key challenges and areas of debate. Contemporary cognitive architectures like SOAR, LIDA, and Sigma, which are inspired by the work of Newell and others, center on the knowledge level as a cognitive process that handles declarative knowledge by way of symbolic representations and logical rules. However, this approach raises epistemological questions about the nature of knowledge, the source of its justification, and its relationship to cognition. This paper argues that a naive acceptance of the knowledge level equation with cognitive symbolic process would inevitably provoke philosophical concerns and inconsistencies. By discussing the role of abductive reasoning, cognition in non-rational systems, and the subjective nature of goal-directed action, this research underscores the notion that the common assumptions of knowledge in cognitive architectures face difficulties in the account of intentional actions, object perception, and in the relation with the theory of decision. The results of the analysis aim at emphasizing why it is more realistic to approach cognitive architectures with epistemological awareness, so that this framework can be developed into a more comprehensive and sound theoretical formulation.
