title: Incremental Truncated LSTD
Abstract: This study presents an extension to the incremental learning framework of Temporal Difference (TD) methods, notably the Least-Square Temporal Difference (LSTD) algorithm, by incorporating a truncation strategy to improve sample efficiency and reduce computational requirements in large-scale reinforcement learning environments. The proposed Incremental Truncated LSTD (IT-LSTD) algorithm efficiently approximates the value function and policy using a truncated sample set, thereby reducing the dimensionality of the feature space and enabling faster updates of the solution. The IT-LSTD method adheres to the incremental learning paradigm to minimize memory requirements and maintain an accurate solution under limited batches of samples. It introduces a novel truncation scheme that prunes the least-influential samples and accelerates convergence while preserving a substantial amount of information from the original data distribution. Through numerical evaluations, we demonstrate that IT-LSTD achieves faster learning rates compared to its incremental LSTD counterpart, making it a superior choice in scenarios where computational costs and sample sizes are significant concerns. Additionally, the consistency of the proposed method is verified through a set of experiments demonstrating its robustness under various learning settings, making it a suitable candidate for real-world applications requiring efficient and effective solution approximation. Comprehensive empirical investigations validate the proposed IT-LSTD approach, making it a promising alternative to accelerated TD methods.

title: Bayesian Network Models for Adaptive Testing
Abstract: This paper explores the application of Bayesian network models in adaptive testing, presenting a comprehensive review of its potential benefits and challenges. Adaptive testing is a statistically sound procedure that adjusts the difficulty of test items in real-time based on the test-taker's performance, thereby providing an efficient and effective assessment of knowledge and skills. Bayesian network models, a probabilistic graphical model capable of handling complex interactions and dependencies, have shown promising results in simulating adaptive testing. Through the incorporation of probabilistic calculations and network-based knowledge representation, Bayesian network models can detect subtle relationships between variables, adapt testing conditions effectively, and produce more accurate item calibration and parameter estimation. However, the practical implementation of Bayesian network models in adaptive testing also faces several challenges, including model complexity, calculational efficiency, and proper parameter estimation methods. This study provides a systematic examination of the properties, advantages, and limitations of Bayesian network models in adaptive testing, including an analysis of the computational requirements and scalability issues associated with their implementation. By exploring the Bayesian network modeling paradigm in adaptive testing, the proposed framework aims to facilitate the development of more efficient and accurate adaptive testing methods that can better capture the complex interactions between test-takers, test items, and testing conditions.

title: An Introduction to Convolutional Neural Networks
Abstract: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have become a cornerstone of modern computer vision, playing a pivotal role in numerous applications, ranging from image classification and object detection to segmentation and generation. The revolutionary concept of CNNs originated from an in-depth understanding of brain functionality and neural networks, emerging as a solution to address the limitation of traditional deep learning models in handling spatial hierarchies. This paper aims to provide a comprehensive introduction to the fundamental aspects of CNNs, tracing the historical development milestones from LeNet to the highly efficient and complex models prevalent today. By establishing a solid foundation, our study focuses on elucidating the underlying architectural components, convolutional and pooling layers, facilitating an understanding of key concepts, such as spatial and temporal hierarchies in visual feature extraction. Furthermore, an exploration of CNN variations, architectures, and optimisation techniques provides insight into the evolving domain, enabling utilisation of these powerful tools in solving complex real-world problems. We incorporate empirical examples, step-by-step methodology, visual explanations, and source code, to empower readers with a deeper understanding of CNN theory, application, and implementation. This comprehensive treatise ultimately endeavours to instill readers with the confidence to embark on projects involving object detection, drug discovery, defect recognition, natural language processing and material inspection.

title: A Symbolic SAT-based Algorithm for Almost-sure Reachability with Small Strategies in POMDPs
Abstract: Our research contributes to solving complex decision-making problems in Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs) by developing a novel symbolic SAT-based algorithm for almost-sure reachability with small strategies. Specifically, our algorithm addresses the challenge of finding optimal solutions in POMDPs that involve complex specifications, such as reachability objectives with probabilistic guarantees. By leveraging the power of Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT) solvers and symbolic representations, our approach enables efficient computation of almost-sure strategies for POMDPs with a significantly reduced number of decision variables compared to traditional methods. This breakthrough in solving POMDPs with symbolic SAT-based algorithms is grounded in the ability to compactly encode strategy implementations as constraints, leading to substantial time and memory savings. Furthermore, our approach is capable of computing small strategies that are necessary for achieving near-optimal objectives in various decision-making applications, such as robotics, healthcare, and finance. In comparison to existing methods, our algorithm demonstrates improved scalability and feasibility for solving large-scale POMDPs, thereby opening up new avenues for addressing complex real-world problems with probabilistic guarantees. Through rigorous experimental evaluation on a range of challenginginstances, we demonstrate the efficacy and efficiency of our algorithm, showing that it outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of solution quality and computation time, thereby showcasing its potential for real-world applications.

title: Who Can Win a Single-Elimination Tournament?
Abstract: A single-elimination tournament is a widely used format in various competitions, where each participant paired in a fixed match is eliminated from the competition after a single loss. Nonetheless, even with the seemingly straightforward rules, determining the player with the highest probability of winning remains an intriguing challenge. Our study aims to provide insights into the probability of success for different players in a single-elimination tournament. We focus on randomly seeded and randomly paired tournaments, and our analysis involves deterministic methods as well as simulations to quantify the probabilities of winning. The results indicate that players seeded high and those with more extensive experience exhibit a higher likelihood of advancing through the tournament. Conversely, weaker opponents in the seeding phase exhibit higher possibilities of being knocked out early in the competition. Our study's findings also raise questions about the robustness of the seeding process, shedding light on its limitations in addressing potential variations among participants. Moreover, these outcomes highlight the importance of employing advanced statistical techniques for predicting outcomes in single-elimination tournaments, particularly those involving many participants. The knowledge obtained from these analyses can be used to better strategize the tournament itself and improve the scheduling to minimize severe upsets.

title: Beyond OWL 2 QL in OBDA: Rewritings and Approximations (Extended Version)
Abstract: This extended version of the Beyond OWL 2 QL in OBDA: Rewritings and Approximations paper presents an in-depth exploration of pushing the boundaries of Ontology-Based Data Access (OBDA) by embracing languages beyond OWL 2 QL. OWL 2 QL has been the standard for OBDA, offering query rewriting and answering techniques that ensure complete and correct query results. However, in reality, many large-scale datasets and ontologies require more expressive languages to accurately represent their complexities and nuances. Our work delves into various ways to extend OBDA from OWL 2 QL, considering different types of rewritings, including rule-based rewritings, approximations, and combinations of the two. We also provide a thorough investigation of the trade-offs between expressiveness, decidability, and complexity for these extended techniques, along with their runtime performance and implications on data accessibility. In particular, this work focuses on developing optimal query rewriting and answering approaches that can handle more complex queries and datasets while maintaining the guarantees of OWL 2 QL's standard. Our preliminary results demonstrate that, by leveraging advanced rewriting and approximation techniques, it is feasible to effectively apply OBDA to a broader range of real-world applications and domains, even those that require more advanced knowledge representation. This extended research aims to serve as a starting point for the OBDA community to further adapt and refine its OWL 2 QL-centric approach to meet the needs of future data applications.

title: A global Constraint for mining Sequential Patterns with GAP constraint
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel global constraint for mining sequential patterns with a Gap constraint, denoted as seq-pattern-gap. The Gap constraint in sequential pattern mining refers to the restriction of allowing certain gaps between consecutive items in the patterns. Traditional sequential pattern mining techniques either ignore this Gap constraint or add it as a post-processing step, which may result in suboptimal or incomplete solutions. Our proposed global constraint is rooted in the theory of sequential pattern mining and modelled as a global constraint in constraint programming. We provide a formal definition of the seq-pattern-gap constraint and demonstrate its relationship with existing global constraints in constraint programming. An efficient filtering algorithm is also developed to significantly prune the search space, achieving better performance than existing methods. Thorough experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed global constraint in discovering high-quality sequential patterns with the Gap constraint. Our contribution sheds new light on solving large-scale sequential pattern mining problems with the Gap constraint and opens up new avenues for applying constraint programming in data mining. By leveraging the flexibility of constraint programming, seq-pattern-gap enables users to easily incorporate domain-specific preferences and discover meaningful patterns that would be missed by traditional methods, paving the way for real-world applications in areas such as logistics, finance, and bioinformatics.

title: Welfare of Sequential Allocation Mechanisms for Indivisible Goods
Abstract: This paper explores the welfare properties of sequential allocation mechanisms for indivisible goods, a class of problems that have garnered significant attention in the field of matching theory. We develop a comprehensive framework for analyzing the fairness and efficiency of these mechanisms, focusing on the underlying principles that govern the allocation process. Our key contribution lies in the identification of a novel class of sequential mechanisms, which we term 'information- insensitive' mechanisms, and demonstrate that these mechanisms have robust welfare properties. Specifically, we show that information-insensitive mechanisms achieve envy-free allocations, which is a stronger notion of fairness in the context of indivisible goods. Furthermore, we establish that information-insensitive mechanisms are asymptotically efficient, meaning that their allocations converge to the optimal allocation as the number of goods increases. This asymptotic efficiency is established via a novel martingale inequality that we prove, and we demonstrate its applicability to a range of sequential allocation mechanisms. Through simulations, we also provide empirical evidence of the efficacy of information-insensitive mechanisms, demonstrating their robustness in a variety of settings. Overall, our research demonstrates the importance of sequential allocation mechanisms in ensuring fairness and efficiency in the allocation of indivisible goods. By developing a deeper understanding of these mechanisms, we shed light on the essential underlying principles that govern their behavior.

title: A Deep Architecture for Semantic Matching with Multiple Positional Sentence Representations
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel deep architecture for semantic matching tasks, focusing on the incorporation of multiple positional sentence representations to improve model interpretability and robustness. Existing works on semantic matching typically rely on a single vector representation for sentences, which might fall short in capturing nuanced semantic relationships between sentences in different contexts. To address this limitation, the proposed architecture utilizes an embedded interaction mechanism that produces multiple sentence representations by positioning them at various points within a given contextual window, facilitating semantic inference across arbitrary distances. Furthermore, a self-attention mechanism is incorporated to capture salient and relevant subtleties in the input sentence sequences while discounting trivial or redundant patterns. Additionally, to mitigate overfitting and enhance the model's generalization capabilities, multiple instances of the proposed architecture are concurrently trained and then fused using a novel weighted adaptation approach that learns to adaptively assign higher weights to the more accurate representations. Experimental evaluations conducted on benchmark datasets demonstrate substantial gains in performance over state-of-the-art models on various semantic matching tasks, underscoring the efficacy and adaptability of the proposed deep architecture with multiple positional sentence representations.

title: Recurrent Instance Segmentation
Abstract: Recurrent Instance Segmentation has emerged as a promising approach to tackle the challenges of instance-level understanding in videos and complex scenes, where objects undergo significant pose, size, and occlusion variations. This paper proposes a novel Recurrent Instance Segmentation (RIS) framework that integrates recurrent neural networks (RNNs) with state-of-the-art convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to learn and refine dynamic information for each instance over time. Specifically, a short-term RNN module is employed to capture per-frame instance features, which are then fed into long-term components to leverage and propagate instance-level contextual cues across frames. Our approach not only facilitates instance-aware video modeling but also enables the model to learn discriminative representations that are more robust to partial occlusions and deformations. Furthermore, the proposed multi-stage prediction strategy and confidence-based refinement mechanism enable more accurate and efficient inference, addressing a critical challenge in current instance segmentation methods. Extensive experiments on popular benchmarks such as DOTA, COCO, and DAVIS demonstrate the efficacy of RIS in achieving superior performance and robustness compared to existing state-of-the-art approaches, including advanced multi-task architectures and refined IoU heuristics. This work provides a fresh perspective on recurrent instance understanding and sheds new light on exploiting temporal dependencies for advanced computer vision applications.

title: Plan Explicability and Predictability for Robot Task Planning
Abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence and robotics has led to the development of sophisticated autonomous systems that can perform complex tasks. However, the lack of transparency and understanding of the decision-making process behind these systems poses significant challenges for their adoption in high-stakes domains, such as healthcare and transportation. Plan explicability and predictability refer to the ability of a robot to explain and justify its task planning decisions, enabling humans to comprehend and trust the robot's actions. This paper explores the importance of explicability and predictability in robot task planning, highlighting the need for interpretable and transparent planning algorithms. We investigate the current state-of-the-art in robot task planning, identifying strengths and limitations of various approaches. Through a series of case studies, we demonstrate the benefits of incorporating explicability and predictability into robot planning systems, including improved human-robot collaboration, enhanced trust and reliability, and better fault diagnosis and recovery. Furthermore, we identify key challenges and opportunities for future research, emphasizing the need for more advanced Explainable AI (XAI) techniques and multi-disciplinary collaborations between computer science, robotics, and human-computer interaction experts. By advancing the understanding of plan explicability and predictability, we aim to create more transparent, trustworthy, and effective robot task planning systems that can support a wide range of applications and domains.

title: Reinstating Combinatorial Protections for Manipulation and Bribery in Single-Peaked and Nearly Single-Peaked Electorates
Abstract: This paper investigates the problem of manipulation and bribery in electoral systems, focusing on single-peaked and nearly single-peaked electorates, which are common in real-world voting scenarios. The work aims to reinstate combinatorial protections, which have been widely criticized and largely abandoned in modern voting systems due to their perceived efficiency and simplicity. Our research combines insights from social choice theory, computational complexity, and mechanism design to identify and address the potential vulnerabilities in single-peaked and nearly single-peaked electorates. To achieve this, we leverage the concept of "almost" strategy-proof mechanisms, which we refine to ensure robustness against manipulation and bribery. We introduce novel combinatorial protections that not only preserve the desirable properties of single-peaked electorates (such as having a Condorcet winner) but also provide a robust safeguard against strategic voting and bribery attempts. Our results include the implementation of new computational algorithms for evaluating and preventing manipulation and bribery in single-peaked electorates, as well as insights into the theoretical limits of these protections. Overall, this research aims to revive the notion of combinatorial protections as a viable tool for ensuring the integrity and stability of democratic elections, with potential applications in both theoretical and practical contexts.

title: Unifying Decision Trees Split Criteria Using Tsallis Entropy
Abstract: This research paper aims to unify decision trees' split criteria using Tsallis entropy, a generalization of the Shannon entropy theory. Decision trees are a popular machine learning algorithm used for both classification and regression tasks, and their performance heavily relies on the choice of split criteria. Shannon entropy and Gini impurity are two common information-theoretic criteria used in traditional decision trees, but they have limitations, such as being sensitive to class imbalance and unable to capture complex relationships between features. To overcome these limitations, we propose a decision tree framework that incorporates Tsallis entropy as the unified split criteria. The Tsallis entropy measure provides a more flexible and robust way to quantify complexity and has the ability to capture the complex relationships between features. In this paper, we derive a novel unified Tsallis entropy-based split criteria, which considers the dual perspectives of class imbalance and feature correlations. Experimental results on various benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves state-of-the-art performance in decision tree classification and regression tasks. We also conduct a thorough analysis to evaluate the sensitivity of the proposed method to different Tsallis order parameters and compare its performance with existing methods. Our results show that the unified Tsallis entropy-based decision trees outperform traditional decision trees and other ensemble methods in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency, making it a promising alternative for real-world applications.

title: A Roadmap towards Machine Intelligence
Abstract: The rapidly evolving landscape of artificial intelligence has sparked intense curiosity and debate about its potential trajectory, raising crucial questions about the role of machine intelligence in shaping the future of human civilization. This comprehensive roadmap delves into the complex dynamics of machine learning, exploring the intricacies of neural networks, deep learning, and cognitive architectures, thereby laying the groundwork for an in-depth exploration of the enabling technologies that will bring us closer to true machine intelligence. With a probing analysis of current breakthroughs and innovations in computer vision, natural language processing, and Reinforcement learning, this study sets the stage for a nuanced discussion on the critical aspects of machine intelligence, including explainability, transparency, accountability, and robustness. Furthermore, we examine the far-reaching implications of machine intelligence for various sectors such as healthcare, finance, transportation, education, and national security, along with an assessment of the socioeconomic and psychological consequences it may unleash. The roadmap provides actionable insights into the steps required to harness the unparalleled potential of machine intelligence while mitigating its risks and ensuring that we navigate the inevitable paradigm shift with collective understanding and foresight, thereby building a safer and more harmonious future where humans and machines coexist in symbiosis.

title: Strategic Dialogue Management via Deep Reinforcement Learning
Abstract: This work focuses on the development of an advanced dialogue management framework that leverages deep reinforcement learning to effectively navigate complex conversational scenarios. Current approaches often rely on pre-defined dialogue structures and rule-based systems, which can become convoluted as conversations progress. In contrast, our proposed framework utilizes a deep reinforcement learning agent that learns to dynamically manage dialogue flows based on real-time contextual information. The agent is trained on a large dataset of human-human conversations, where it learns to optimize dialogue outcomes by maximizing a custom-designed reward function that incorporates both task-oriented and engagement-driven metrics. Key components of the framework include a state encoder that extracts relevant dialogue features, a policy network that learns to select optimal actions, and a critic network that provides value estimates to guide decision-making. Through extensive simulations and validations with both synthetic and real-world datasets, our approach demonstrates significant improvements in dialogue efficiency, user engagement, and system flexibility, enabling it to adeptly handle a wide range of conversational scenarios, including domain switching, uncertainty handling, and counterfactual reasoning. By pushing the boundaries of dialogue management capabilities, this work has far-reaching implications for the development of more sophisticated conversational AI systems.

title: Learning with Memory Embeddings
Abstract: This research introduces a novel approach to learning with memory embeddings, a paradigm that seeks to incorporate temporal context and autoregressive predictions into the learning process. By leveraging memory-aware neural networks, we design a framework that augments traditional feed-forward architecture with explicit memory components, effectively modeling long-range dependencies and contextual relationships. Our approach integrates sequential data with the ability to reason about past experiences, enabling the model to attend to relevant information from the temporal domain and dynamically allocate memory resources as needed. The resulting architecture permits the analysis of complex temporal patterns, temporal relationships, and structural dependencies inherent in sequential data, ultimately yielding improved predictive capabilities. To demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, we evaluate the proposed learning framework on a range of sequence-to-sequence tasks, including but not limited to time-series forecasting, language modeling, and question-answering on temporal knowledge graphs. Our experimental results show significant improvements over baseline models, with notable gains observed in tasks requiring temporal reasoning and contextual understanding. Through this research, we aim to provide a foundational understanding of learning with memory embeddings and inspire future work in the development of more sophisticated temporal learning models.

title: Breaking Symmetries in Graph Search with Canonizing Sets
Abstract: Breaking symmetries in graph search allows for the efficient generation of candidate solutions by eliminating redundant nodes that correspond to permutations of a solution's components. Traditionally, canonizing sets are utilized to achieve this symmetry breaking by assigning unique labels to the nodes in the graph based on their permutation properties. However, canonizing sets are sometimes challenging to compute, and they may not always preserve the problem's symmetries, potentially resulting in incorrect solutions being generated. This research explores the use of algebraic and geometric methods to define canonizing sets for various graph structures, with the goal of developing a scalable approach to breaking symmetries in graph search. The research involves analyzing the constraints and properties of different graphs and deriving canonizing sets that leverage the inherent structure of these graphs, such as planarity, Cayley graph properties, or the use of group actions. The approach proposed in this research utilizes graph theory, combinatorics, and discrete mathematics to ensure that generated solutions adhere to the problem constraints while minimizing the computational overhead associated with maintaining the canonizing set. The effectiveness of the derived canonizing sets is evaluated through case studies on constrained planning problems and optimization tasks, where significant reductions in search space size and fast solution times have been achieved by applying this method to specific graph structures.

title: MOOCs Meet Measurement Theory: A Topic-Modelling Approach
Abstract: This study explores the convergence of Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs) and measurement theory through a topic-modelling approach, aiming to bridge the gap between educational research and learners' experiences. By harnessing the analytical capabilities of Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA), we develop a novel framework that can extract latent themes and assign sentence-level sentiment scores from MOOC participants' feedback comments. A comprehensive analysis of learner interactions on select online learning platforms was conducted, yielding a large corpus of 30,000+ user-submitted comments. Employing topic-modelling algorithms, this dataset was distilled into 25 distinct themes, including socio-emotional support, peer feedback, course design, and personal growth. Our findings indicate that while technical support and navigation issues dominate the most participants' concerns, emotive language surrounding the impact of MOOC participation on learners' self-efficacy, enjoyment, and professional development emerges as a significant factor influencing their learning experience. Moreover, the proposed approach facilitates insights into the relative importance of different themes by accounting for sentiment polarities and emotional intensity, fostering more accurate and informative analyses. These contributions, by virtue of their interdisciplinary nature, serve to strengthen the ties between educational science and data science.

title: A Python Engine for Teaching Artificial Intelligence in Games
Abstract: This abstract presents a novel Python engine designed for teaching artificial intelligence (AI) in games, focusing on ease of use, modularity, and flexibility. The engine's main goal is to provide a comprehensible and engaging platform for students and educators to explore AI concepts in a gaming context. By leveraging object-oriented programming principles and modular design, the engine enables users to create and modify game levels, AI behaviors, and game mechanics, facilitating a hands-on learning experience. The engine's architecture is built around a game loop, event handling, and AI decision-making components, which can be easily extended or replaced to accommodate different AI techniques and game genres. To promote student understanding and experimentation, the engine features a visual interface for setting up and controlling AI agents, as well as a scripting system for customizing game behaviors. Furthermore, the engine includes a built-in testing framework and integrated documentation, allowing users to quickly write and run unit tests, ensure code quality, and access API documentation. By providing a robust, flexible, and easy-to-use platform for teaching AI in games, this Python engine empowers educators and learners to explore complex AI concepts through a fun and interactive experience.

title: Searching for Objects using Structure in Indoor Scenes
Abstract: Object search is an essential task in various applications, such as service robots, home automation, and smart surveillance systems, where manipulating objects can improve human daily life quality and reduce workload. The structure of an indoor scene offers contextual information useful for discovering goals efficiently, as human visual attention often employs spatial layout and semantic knowledge when searching for goals in cluttered environments. Most existing state-of-the-art object search algorithms based on deep learning techniques, especially ones that exploit scene context in object search, assume easily accessible RGB-D data and fail to handle unknown and dynamic environments. In real-world, however, we often face cases where scene layout and object pose cannot be easily obtained or suffer from partial occlusions or dynamically changing scenes which significantly affect performance and reliability. Recent advancements in computer vision aim to exploit higher-level structural information embedded in indoor scenes beyond the sole reliance on RGBD data. In this study, we explore leveraging the structural information from in-house LiDAR scans and the integration of object affordances to address the deficiency in object search systems that prevent them from adapting well to environments of the real world, enhancing robustness and accuracy of the system under uncertainties such as occlusions or changing light conditions in complex indoor environments, potentially making the system a true partner in service and home automation that assists people with daily activities and allows for more time allocation to enjoy their daily lives.

title: Approximate Probabilistic Inference via Word-Level Counting
Abstract: Word-level counting has emerged as a promising approach for approximate probabilistic inference in various machine learning models. However, the existing methods often rely on probabilistic insights or computational tricks that can be difficult to generalize across different models and scenarios. This research proposes a novel framework that exploits the properties of word-level counting to develop a universal approach to approximate probabilistic inference. By focusing on counting the occurrences of words in the joint and marginal distributions of the model, we derive a family of approximations that can be applied to a wide range of probabilistic models, including probabilistic graphical models, neural networks, and structured prediction models. We show that this approach yields state-of-the-art accuracy in a variety of benchmark experiments, often by leveraging the structural properties of word-level counts to develop more accurate approximations. Furthermore, we explore the theoretical limits of this approach, demonstrating that it achieves optimal lower bounds in certain scenarios. Through a combination of theoretical analysis, experimental evaluation, and empirical demonstration, our research provides a comprehensive framework for developing efficient and accurate word-level counting approximations for probabilistic inference in machine learning models.

title: Exploiting Environmental Computation in a Multi-Agent Model of Slime Mould
Abstract: This study explores the concept of environmental computation in a multi-agent model of slime mould, offering insights into the ability of biological systems to mimic computational processes. By employing a simulated framework of Physarum polycephalum, a species of slime mould, our research demonstrates how these organisms can solve complex problems in a distributed and adaptive manner. Inspired by the natural process of foraging, the slime mould's network of cytoplasmic tubules represents a form of environmental computation, where information is encoded in the landscape itself rather than in the agents' internal states. Our multi-agent model incorporates a novel approach to problem-solving, where each agent adjusts its behavior and adapts to its surroundings to optimize the overall network performance. The results reveal the slime mould's ability to efficiently solve network optimization problems, such as the shortest path problem and minimum spanning tree problem, showcasing its potential in fields like network design and traffic flow management. By leveraging the environmental computation inherent in slime mould's behavior, this research provides a new perspective on computational complexity, demonstrating that collective intelligence and distributed problem-solving can lead to efficient solutions in complex systems. The findings not only shed light on the biological foundations of computation but also offer a novel approach to developing robust and adaptive systems for various real-world applications.

title: A Survey of Signed Network Mining in Social Media
Abstract: This paper provides a comprehensive survey of signed network mining in social media, focusing on the methodologies and applications that have emerged in recent years. Signed network mining refers to the analysis of social networks with positive and negative edges, representing relationships or interactions between individuals or entities. In the context of social media, signed networks can capture the complex and multifaceted nature of human relationships, including friendship, conflict, and influence. Our survey covers various aspects of signed network mining in social media, including graph-based approaches, tensor factorization, and deep learning techniques. We review a range of applications, such as community detection, sentiment analysis, and user behavior prediction, highlighting the potential of signed network mining for understanding social dynamics and behavior on online platforms. The paper also discusses the challenges and limitations of signed network mining, including the availability and quality of data, the complexity of social networks, and the need for interpretable results. Despite these challenges, the paper demonstrates the growing interest and contributions in this field, showcasing the vast potential of signed network mining for improving our understanding of social media and its implications for society. Our survey provides a starting point for researchers and practitioners interested in exploring the capabilities and applications of signed network mining in social media.

title: Planning in the Wild: Modeling Tools for PDDL
Abstract: Planning in the Wild, which focuses on end-users using domain-specific planning tools outside of the laboratory environment, has seen substantial growth in recent years. However, these tools often fall short in terms of usability and adequacy for users with varying levels of expertise. One of the standard platforms in the area of planning, the Planning Domain Definition Language (PDDL), has been widely adopted in both research and industrial applications. Nonetheless, modeling tools for PDDL remain somewhat limited as they typically lack the features that experts consider essential for real-world problems. To address this issue, this research aims to offer a deeper understanding of the core challenges involved in PDDL modeling and propose user-centered tools that can be more easily utilized by end-users devoid of extensive knowledge in artificial intelligence. Our primary approach involves carrying out an empirical study to analyze the planning processes of various domain experts and novices, followed by the design and implementation of novel planning models that improve upon existing approaches. Our ultimate goal is to supply developers with a practical guidebook for crafting user-centric planning tools that support experts and non-experts alike. We contend that this research will significantly contribute to making PDDL modeling tools more accessible, user-friendly, and practical for applications in the real world.

title: Learning Visual Predictive Models of Physics for Playing Billiards
Abstract: The paper presents a novel approach to learning visual predictive models for playing billiards, which enables robots to master the game at a superhuman level. Building on recent advances in visual perception and learning-based control policies, our system learns to predict the physical interactions between balls and table surfaces from video data. This visual predictive model is grounded in a physics-based simulation, which simulates the physical laws governing billiards, allowing the robot to reason about the consequences of its actions in a high-dimensional state space. Our approach combines ideas from sparse sampling-based motion planning and control, multimodal learning, and model-based reinforcement learning. Through a series of experiments and benchmarking against state-of-the-art systems, we evaluate the performance of our visual predictive model and its ability to generalize across different table geometries and ball conditions, and make predictions accurately despite camera noise. Our system outperforms all benchmarked models, achieving zero misses in billiards shots. The presented framework serves as a blueprint for applications in diverse domains requiring precise and flexible control, such as professional robotic sports, hazardous material operations, or advanced automotive equipment.

title: MazeBase: A Sandbox for Learning from Games
Abstract: MazeBase is an overarching platform designed to enable seamless learning from games in a decentralized manner, empowering users with the ability to create, utilize, and integrate diverse game-based learning tools. This sandbox-style environment is an amalgamation of cutting-edge AI technologies, advanced game development frameworks, and adaptable educational models, promoting an immersive and experiential learning experience. The underlying architecture of MazeBase incorporates modular, scalable components that can be configured to tackle a wide range of educational objectives and disciplines, thereby fostering optimized knowledge acquisition and retention. By utilizing MazeBase, educators can structure customized curriculum pathways incorporating elements of gamification, real-world simulations, and situational pedagogy, creating a highly engaging and interactive learning ambiance. Furthermore, the adaptable nature of MazeBase ensures seamless integration with existing educational infrastructure, eliminating obstacles to widespread implementation. Through empirical analysis and usability assessments, the efficacy of MazeBase is demonstrated to be significantly higher than traditional teaching methods, showcasing its potential in redefining the paradigm of modern education. By leveraging the vast potential of MazeBase, educators and learners alike are given the tools to reimagine the boundaries of knowledge acquisition, mastery, and lifelong learning.

title: What is the plausibility of probability?(revised 2003, 2015)
Abstract: The concept of probability has long been a cornerstone of statistical analysis and decision-making under uncertainty, yet its fundamental nature remains a subject of philosophical debate. Historically, philosophers have struggled to provide a robust account of probability, with various attempts to interpret it as a matter of degree of belief or a physical property of the world. More recently, the revised foundations laid out in 2003 and 2015 have sought to rectify the deficiencies of previous theories, but the underlying epistemological questions remain unanswered. In particular, the problem of assuming the probability of events with an uncertainty becomes a conflicting task to both past and recent efforts, giving both believers and critics reason to doubt its viability. This paper aims to revisit the probability theory based on its past, present, and the knowledge from both foundations of 2003 and 2015, to identify key flaws and evaluate the extent to which these challenges can be resolved. Through a critical analysis of these foundations, we examine whether probability can be considered a scientifically viable concept and whether its calculations hold any meaningful physical implications. By synthesizing the lessons learned from earlier interpretations, this paper endeavors to address the persisting question of whether probability is anything more than a useful heuristic or, indeed, a metaphysical construct.

title: Interpretable Two-level Boolean Rule Learning for Classification
Abstract: This research paper delves into the development of an interpretable two-level Boolean rule learning approach for classification tasks in machine learning. Boolean rule learning involves discovering logical rules from data, which can be more interpretable than traditional machine learning models. However, existing Boolean rule learning methods often suffer from interpretability issues, such as high dimensionality and complex rules, making them challenging to understand and trust. Two-level Boolean rule learning presents an innovative solution by creating a hierarchy of decision-making processes, where the high-level rules provide coarse-grained decisions, and the low-level rules offer finer-grained determinations. Our approach, utilising a novel decision tree-based algorithm, constructs the two-level Boolean rules in a tree-like structure, enabling hierarchical and modular decision making. By incorporating this interpretable two-level Boolean rule learning approach, we demonstrate a notable improvement in the accuracy and interpretability of classification models, while providing explanations for the decision-making process. A comprehensive evaluation using various benchmark datasets shows the effectiveness and advantages of our proposed method in handling both large and small datasets. The method is also compared to several state-of-the-art approaches, highlighting its superiority in terms of interpretability, efficiency, and decision-making accuracy.

title: Learning Simple Algorithms from Examples
Abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to learning simple algorithms from examples, focusing on the discovery of short, interpretable, and understandable rules from raw data. The proposed method leverages a combination of explainable AI and symbolic regression techniques to identify repeatable patterns in the input data, thus allowing it to construct a set of deterministic rules that can be evaluated to reproduce the observed examples. Employing a genetic programming framework, the system is empowered to discover and adapt a diverse range of algorithmic solutions through an iterative process of mutation and selection, driven by both the accuracy and simplicity of the generated rules. Furthermore, a novel hybrid fitness function is presented, combining both the goodness of fit of the predictions and a penalty term based on the algorithmic length and complexity of the evolving rules, allowing the system to strike an optimal balance between simplicity and accuracy. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy and versatility of this approach in learning a variety of simple algorithms from different types of data, including time series and classification tasks, showing significant advantages in simplicity, interpretability, and computational efficiency over existing methods.

title: Noisy Submodular Maximization via Adaptive Sampling with Applications to Crowdsourced Image Collection Summarization
Abstract: Noisy submodular maximization is a fundamental problem in computer science that has garnered significant attention in recent years due to its numerous real-world applications, including crowdsourced data summarization and image collection abstraction. Traditional methods for solving this problem rely heavily on multiple passes over the entire dataset, which can be computationally expensive and inefficient, particularly when dealing with large-scale data. In an attempt to mitigate this issue, recent approaches have focused on adaptive sampling techniques that selectively choose subsets of the data to reduce computational costs without compromising the accuracy of the solution. However, most of these methods fail to account for the prevalence of noise in the data, which can severely impact the performance of the maximizer. This paper presents a novel adaptive sampling method for noisy submodular maximization that harnesses the strengths of both determinism and randomness to efficiently identify the highest-value elements in the data. Our approach is designed to accurately capture the underlying submodularity of the objective function, even in the presence of noise, and is guaranteed to produce the optimal solution with a high probability. Theoretical analysis and extensive experiments on various applications, including crowdsourced image collection summarization, demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our method in real-world scenarios, highlighting its potential as a viable solution for big data summarization tasks.

title: Multi-Agent Continuous Transportation with Online Balanced Partitioning
Abstract: This paper presents a novel multi-agent continuous transportation framework that leverages online balanced partitioning to efficiently manage and dispatch large-scale transportation tasks in real-world scenarios. The proposed method combines the benefits of multi-agent systems, which enable scalability and adaptability, with the accuracy and robustness provided by online partitioning techniques. By intelligently allocating tasks to multiple agents, our approach ensures that each agent operates within its capacity while minimizing the overall transportation time and cost. The methodology involves a distributed controller that dynamically partitions the transportation graph into smaller sub-graphs, allowing agents to focus on executing the most profitable or time-sensitive tasks first. Using simulations and case studies, we demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed framework in various transportation settings, including logistics, ride-sharing, and passenger transportation systems. The results show a significant reduction in transportation time and cost while maintaining a high level of service quality and customer satisfaction. Furthermore, the framework's online feature allows it to respond to changing task distributions and dynamic environments in real-time, making it particularly suitable for large-scale transportation systems with high variability and uncertainty. Our findings highlight the potential of multi-agent systems with online partitioning for improving the efficiency and scalability of transportation networks, making it an attractive solution for future transportation systems.

title: SceneNet: Understanding Real World Indoor Scenes With Synthetic Data
Abstract: Scene understanding and 3D reconstruction of real-world indoor scenes are crucial tasks in computer vision, with various applications including robotics, smart homes, and autonomous systems. However, collecting and annotating large-scale datasets of real-world indoor scenes can be a time-consuming, expensive, and labor-intensive process. This Paper proposes a novel deep learning approach called SceneNet, which leverages synthetic data to effectively understand and reconstruct indoor scenes. By generating photorealistic synthetic data using a comprehensive 3D simulator, SceneNet can efficiently learn and generalize to real-world indoor scenes with minimal real-world data. Our approach combines a novel hybrid 2D/3D representation and a multi-task learning framework to robustly predict the 3D layout and appearance of indoor scenes from single or multiple RGB inputs. The training procedure involves transferring knowledge from synthetic data to real-world data by utilizing a novel learned image translation component to mitigate the domain shift. The results and evaluations of SceneNet have shown its capability in improving the accuracy and robustness of scene understanding in comparison to state-of-the-art convolutional neural networks. Specifically, SceneNet achieves 83.4% mAP and 5% reduction in average depth errors compared to other published scene understanding models trained using ground truth information. SceneNet can effectively expand the availability of high-quality data and improve the scalability of scene understanding systems.

title: Non-Sentential Utterances in Dialogue: Experiments in Classification and Interpretation
Abstract: Non-sentential utterances (NSU) are a pervasive feature of natural language and real-world dialogue, yet they pose significant challenges to machine learning, natural language processing, and human-computer interaction. In this study, we investigate the classification and interpretation of NSU in dialogue, exploring their compositional properties, context-dependent meanings, and prosodic characteristics. We contribute to a better understanding of NSU by providing a comprehensive analysis of their typology, variability, and informativity, drawing on a representative dataset of NSU instances from diverse sources, including everyday conversations, online forums, and human-robot interactions. Our experiments in classification employ cutting-edge machine learning techniques, including deep learning and neural networks, to develop predictive models that can identify and categorize NSU based on linguistic, contextual, and interactional cues. Additionally, we examine the interpretability of NSU in different contexts, examining how they relate to subsequent speech acts, discourse structure, and conversational flow. Our findings have significant implications for the development of more sophisticated dialogue systems and human-computer interfaces, as well as our understanding of the complex, dynamic nature of human language in context. By shedding light on the complexities and nuances of NSU, this research aims to advance the field of natural language processing and provide a foundation for more effective and engaging human-computer communication.

title: Evaluating Prerequisite Qualities for Learning End-to-End Dialog Systems
Abstract: This study aims to comprehensively evaluate prerequisite qualities that enhance the learning of end-to-end dialog systems, which have witnessed a surge in popularity due to their ability to efficiently process and understand natural language inputs. Despite their growing application in various areas such as customer service, language translation, and sentiment analysis, these systems still face significant challenges in accurately understanding and responding to user queries. To overcome these limitations, researchers have been actively seeking to design features that robustly capture the complexities of language and adapt to an ever-evolving range of user interactions. The proposed framework encompasses a detailed analysis of critical qualities crucial for the optimal performance of end-to-end dialog systems, including contextual understanding, response relevance, and emotional intelligence. Through rigorous experiments, this research aims to provide an in-depth assessment of these qualities, shedding light on their respective importance in promoting effective dialog systems. Furthermore, our findings will facilitate the incorporation of superior features for improving the training process and overall performance of end-to-end dialog systems, revolutionizing their potential applications in numerous industries and revolutionizing human-computer interaction.

title: Countering Social Engineering through Social Media: An Enterprise Security Perspective
Abstract: This study examines the intersection of social engineering and social media in the context of enterprise security, highlighting the significance of addressing these threats to safeguard organization's sensitive information and assets. As social engineering attacks continue to evolve, becoming increasingly sophisticated and targeted, the need for effective countermeasures has never been more pressing. Grounded in a review of the existing literature, this research contributes to our understanding of the psychological and technical aspects of social engineering, with a particular focus on its growing presence on social media platforms. Through a mixed-methods approach, combining qualitative and quantitative methods, this study explores the ways in which social media is exploited by social engineers, the tactics they employ, and the consequences for organizations that fall victim to these attacks. The research also investigates the current state of enterprise social media security practices, identifying areas for improvement and highlighting best practices and technologies that can be employed to mitigate these threats. Ultimately, this study aims to provide a comprehensive analysis of social engineering on social media, offering practical recommendations for enterprise security professionals to enhance their organizations' defenses against these insidious threats. By shedding light on the complex relationship between social engineering and social media, this research seeks to inform the development of effective countermeasures and promote a safer and more secure online environment.

title: Near-Optimal Active Learning of Multi-Output Gaussian Processes
Abstract: This paper tackles the problem of actively learning multi-output Gaussian processes, wherein the machine learning model is required to interactively request input from a dataset in order to minimize the error of the learned model while also reducing the number of queries. To address this, an active learning algorithm is proposed that combines the benefits of Bayesian optimization and multi-fidelity learning. The algorithm is based on a probabilistic model of the uncertainties in the predicted outputs and uses this model to query the most informative data points. The effectiveness of the proposed algorithm is demonstrated through a series of experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets, in which it is shown to significantly outperform existing methods in terms of the quality of the learned model while dramatically reducing the number of data points required for training. Furthermore, the algorithm is analyzed in terms of its theoretical guarantees and computational complexity, showing that it is scalable and efficient. Overall, the proposed active learning algorithm for multi-output Gaussian processes provides a powerful and flexible tool for applications where labelled training data is scarce, such as robotic control, material science and many other fields requiring machine learning.

title: Gaussian Process Planning with Lipschitz Continuous Reward Functions: Towards Unifying Bayesian Optimization, Active Learning, and Beyond
Abstract: This paper contributes to the growing interest in adapting Gaussian process (GP) models to optimize reward functions in complex, potentially noisy environments. Specifically, we investigate the application of GP-based planning to scenarios with Lipschitz continuous reward functions, forming a bridge between various paradigms including Bayesian optimization, active learning, and model-based reinforcement learning. To obtain more informed action selection, we marry GP models with techniques from active learning to derive a unified framework that progressively adapts its search space with uncertain regions, yielding higher exploration-exploitation trade-offs. Furthermore, to streamline exploration, we integrate a Lipschitz loss into the GP model's likelihood to emphasize near-optimal exploration strategies. This loss allows for informed policy and hyperparameter tuning to avoid an unpleasant process of overfitting in environments with high uncertainty levels. Our proposed approach efficiently learns a globally-optimal or near-global-optimal solution that captures both Bayesian uncertainty and local Lipschitz structure across the space. We back our framework with a series of theoretical results regarding optimality and convergence guarantees as well as extensive experiments on a selection of real-world and benchmark problems. These demonstrate an efficiency of sampling, speed of computation, and convergence speed that outperforms a variety of existing approaches in comparable problem scenarios.

title: Applying Social Media Intelligence for Predicting and Identifying On-line Radicalization and Civil Unrest Oriented Threats
Abstract: Social media has become an essential platform for the dissemination of information, influencing user opinions and behaviour. Despite its numerous benefits, social media has also been exploited by malicious actors to spread radical ideologies and orchestrate civil unrest, posing significant threats to global security. This study aims to explore the application of social media intelligence (SME) in predicting and identifying online radicalization and civil unrest-oriented threats. By leveraging machine learning and natural language processing techniques, the proposed framework will analyze social media data to detect early warning signs of potential threats. The framework will comprise of three modules: the data collection module, the feature extraction module, and the prediction module. The data collection module will gather data from various social media platforms, while the feature extraction module will extract relevant features from the collected data. The prediction module will then utilize machine learning algorithms to predict the likelihood of online radicalization and civil unrest-oriented threats. To evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed framework, a case study will be conducted using real-world data from social media platforms. The findings of this study will provide a comprehensive understanding of the role of SME in predicting and identifying online radicalization and civil unrest-oriented threats, enabling authorities to develop more effective counter-measures to mitigate these threats.

title: A Model for Web-Intelligence Index to Evaluate the Web Intelligence Capacity of Government Web Sites of Sri Lanka
Abstract: This research proposes a comprehensive model for a Web-Intelligence Index (WII) to assess the web intelligence capacity of government websites of Sri Lanka. Given the pivotal role of government websites in disseminating information, transforming processes, and engaging citizens, it is essential to evaluate their web intelligence effectively. The proposed model integrates various indicators, including content, service, interaction, appearance, accessibility, and knowledge update facets, to create a holistic assessment framework. The framework covers quantitative and qualitative metrics, such as page loading speed, online support services, response time to queries, and the accuracy of disseminated information, ensuring a rigorous evaluation process. The proposed index framework is designed to assess government websites' capacity to transform citizens' lives, improve service delivery, and promote digital inclusion, ensuring optimal web intelligence. By adopting a comparative analysis, this study investigates the current state of web intelligence in government websites and identifies gaps, advocating for informed strategies to enhance their performance and improve citizen experiences. The research aims to bridge the knowledge gap in evaluating web intelligence, providing innovative insights for policymakers, stakeholders, and researchers, encouraging public sector reform and digital transformation in Sri Lanka.

title: Hand Pose Estimation through Semi-Supervised and Weakly-Supervised Learning
Abstract: This research delves into the realm of hand pose estimation, a critical aspect of computer vision, specifically within the context of semi-supervised and weakly-supervised learning frameworks. Hand pose estimation involves determining the position and orientation of a person's hand in a two-dimensional or three-dimensional space from visual data. The complexity of this task is heightened by the variations in hand appearance, posture, and viewpoint, as well as by the presence of occlusions and complex backgrounds. Despite the significance of hand pose estimation in numerous applications, including robotics, virtual and augmented reality, and human-computer interaction, its challenge lies in the scarcity and high cost of annotated training data. To address this issue, researchers have turned to semi-supervised and weakly-supervised learning techniques, which allow leveraging a combination of labeled and unlabeled data to improve model accuracy without incurring the high costs associated with manual annotation. This research aims to investigate the efficacies of semi-supervised and weakly-supervised learning strategies in modeling hand pose variations and proposing novel machine learning architectures that can iteratively refine their predictions using unlabeled data and gradually require less labeled data. By exploring the synergies between unlabeled data, domain adaptation algorithms, and discriminative models, this research aspires to advance the capabilities of hand pose estimation and offer insights into its applications in various fields.

This research aimed to explore new methods for ensuring contamination-free measures and algebraic operations in diverse fields including environmental monitoring, food safety, and medical diagnostics. A novel algebraic framework was developed to address the challenges of handling uncertain and noisy measurements while maintaining the validity of operations such as addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division. The proposed framework integrated multiple data sources and weighting functions to yield a robust and reliable representation of measured values. Furthermore, a hierarchical representation scheme was introduced to categorize datasets based on their precision, accuracy, and reliability, enabling effective filtering and aggregation of measurements. Experimental results and case studies demonstrated the effectiveness of the proposed measures in applications ranging from air quality monitoring to microbiological testing. Additionally, computational comparisons with existing methods highlighted the efficiency and scalability of the novel algebraic algorithms, underscoring their potential for large-scale industrial and clinical applications. title: Stories in the Eye: Contextual Visual Interactions for Efficient Video to Language Translation
Abstract: This paper delves into the realm of video to language translation, an area that has garnered significant attention in the realm of artificial intelligence and machine learning. Current state-of-the-art models in this domain rely on encoded representations of videos, neglecting contextual visual interactions that are crucial for grasping complex narratives. In contrast, human visual understanding is deeply rooted in analyzing the spatial relationships between elements within a scene, and the way these elements interact with each other over time. Inspired by this insight, this study proposes a novel approach that incorporates contextual visual interactions into the process of video to language translation. The proposed method leverages a visual attention mechanism to identify key objects and actions within a video, and then models the spatial relationships between these elements through graph-based methods. Furthermore, this study also explores the use of multimodal fusion techniques to integrate linguistic and visual information, improving the overall performance of the translation model. Experimental results on a range of benchmark datasets demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed approach, achieving significant improvements in translation accuracy and fluency over existing methods. By mirroring the way humans understand complex narratives, the proposed method paves the way for more natural and engaging video to language translation, with potential applications in areas such as multimedia communication, education, and assistance for the visually impaired.

title: Tracklet Association by Online Target-Specific Metric Learning and Coherent Dynamics Estimation
Abstract:
Abstract: 
This research contributes to the field of visual surveillance by introducing a Tracklet Association framework that effectively stitches together fragmented trajectories of pedestrians in crowded scenes. The proposed framework, dubbed Tracklet-Net, spans two key components: online target-specific metric learning (TSML) and coherent dynamics estimation (CDE). TSML enables the model to adapt to new persons within a scene, while incorporating contextual information from previous observations to produce a robust yet discriminative target-specific metric. This learned metric is then utilized by CDE to establish long-range associations between tracklets, capturing the complex dynamics of pedestrian behavior while mitigating potential drifts due to changing viewpoints or occlusions. By incorporating a consistent temporal aspect and leveraging motion patterns, tracklet association in the proposed framework achieves a higher degree of robustness against various factors that are commonly encountered in video-based surveillance scenarios, such as multiple camera angles and varying lighting conditions. A comprehensive study on several established benchmarks showcases the potential of Tracklet-Net in significantly advancing the state-of-the-art in multi-object tracking, providing both high precision and real-time associability of fragmented tracks.

title: A Model for Safety Case Confidence Assessment
Abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive framework for assessing the confidence in Safety Cases, a critical component of risk-assessment and mitigation in high-risk domains such as nuclear power, aviation, and oil and gas. The proposed model, which combines naturalistic decision-making and probabilistic risk assessment, takes into account multiple factors influencing Safety Case confidence, including the quality of safety arguments, evidence and knowledge, as well as the level of uncertainty and ambiguity in the safety assessment process. The model incorporates an adaptive approach to confidence evaluation, enabling it to accommodate evolving safety evidence and changing risk perceptions. The development of confidence in Safety Cases is facilitated by a structured risk management approach, which identifies and addresses potential weaknesses and vulnerabilities in safety arguments and supporting evidence. A comprehensive evaluation of the proposed model is conducted using a case study of a critical safety system, demonstrating the effectiveness of the model in assessing confidence in Safety Cases and guiding improvement efforts. The contributions of this research include the development of a holistic framework for Safety Case confidence assessment, a probabilistic method for evaluating confidence levels, and practical guidelines for enhancing confidence in Safety Cases through risk-informed decision-making.

title: Crowd Behavior Analysis: A Review where Physics meets Biology
Abstract: Crowd behavior analysis remains a complex and multifaceted field that has garnered significant attention in recent years, owing to its widespread implications in various contexts such as emergency response management, event planning, and crowd safety evaluation. The intersection of physics and biology in understanding crowd behavior has significantly enhanced our comprehension of collective phenomena, which exhibit both intrinsic and extrinsic mechanisms governing their dynamics. This review provides an extensive overview of existing approaches in crowd behavior analysis, where physical and biological models are intricately combined to explain the emergent properties of crowds. Furthermore, this synthesis combines various scales, ranging from individual-level attention and decisions to collective-level phenomena such as congestion and dispersion dynamics. Grounding these physics-informed models within the biological principles governing human behavior and decision-making processes has proven particularly effective in improving our predictive capabilities and thereby informing more effective mitigation strategies for crowd-related hazards and emergencies. Through the lens of physics and biology, researchers can better discern the hierarchical dynamics of collective systems, revealing the tension between the self-organization tendencies of agents and the environmental constraints to which they are subjected.

title: Joint Word Representation Learning using a Corpus and a Semantic Lexicon
Abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to joint word representation learning that leverages a corpus and a semantic lexicon to improve word embeddings. Existing word representation learning methods often rely solely on a large corpus of text, but neglect the rich semantic information encoded in dictionaries and thesauri. By incorporating a semantic lexicon, our approach can capture nuances in word meanings that are difficult to infer from corpus data alone. We propose a joint model that learns word embeddings by maximizing a combination of corpus-based and semantic-based similarity scores. The corpus-based similarity score is measured using the widely used WordSim333 dataset, while the semantic-based similarity score is derived from the semantic lexicon. We explore different learning strategies, including multitask learning and noise-contrastive estimation, to optimize the joint model. Our experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms state-of-the-art word representation learning methods in a range of natural language understanding tasks, including word analogy, word similarity, and text classification. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the joint model learns more informative and interpretable word embeddings that capture subtle semantic relationships between words. The proposed approach has the potential to improve the performance of many downstream NLP applications, and can be extended to other tasks that benefit from joint representation learning.

title: Better Computer Go Player with Neural Network and Long-term Prediction
Abstract: This research paper focuses on the development of a next-generation computer Go player by incorporating neural networks and long-term prediction capabilities, striving to achieve parity with human world champions. By integrating advanced artificial intelligence (AI) technologies, we aim to bridge the gap between current computer Go players and the cognitive abilities of human experts, specifically in the realms of foresight, strategic planning, and adaptability. A key aspect of our proposed approach is the utilization of deep neural networks, leveraging their ability to learn complex patterns and relationships within the vast, non-linear Go board space. Furthermore, the incorporation of long-term prediction techniques enables our system to analyze potential consequences of various moves, fostering a more nuanced understanding of the game's dynamics. To train our neural network and evaluate its effectiveness, we rely on extensive datasets of professional Go games, as well as custom-built simulation environments designed to mimic various competitive scenarios. Through rigorous experimentation and tuning of our AI model, we aim to create a more formidable Go player capable of holding its own against the world's best human players, setting the stage for further breakthroughs in the field of computer Go and its applications in AI research.

title: Unsupervised Learning of Visual Structure using Predictive Generative Networks
Abstract: Predictive generative networks have emerged as a promising direction for unsupervised learning of complex visual structures. This research aims to develop a novel Predictive Generative Network (PGN) architecture capable of discovering and modeling underlying visual structures in raw visual data without requiring explicit supervision or annotation. Unlike traditional unsupervised learning methods that rely on heuristic criteria or domain-specific knowledge, PGNs can learn to predict the likelihood of observing various visual patterns and interactions through self-supervised exploration of the data distribution. In this work, we reformulate the visual structure learning problem as a prediction task, where the network is tasked with predicting the future or nearby visual patterns within a coherent visual context. A key aspect of our approach is the development of a novel predictive objective function that encourages the discovery of spatial and temporal patterns, hierarchies, and interactions within the visual data. We validate the proposed PGN approach on several challenging benchmark datasets, including natural image collections, medical imaging datasets, and videos. Our results demonstrate that PGNs can learn robust and realistic visual representations of complex objects, scenes, and activities without the need for explicit supervision, outperforming state-of-the-art methods in various evaluation metrics. The proposed approach has far-reaching implications for a range of applications, including computer vision, robotics, medical imaging, and autonomous driving.

title: Dynamic Adaptive Network Intelligence
Abstract: This abstract explores the concept of Dynamic Adaptive Network Intelligence (DANI), a novel approach to developing adaptive and resilient network systems that can autonomously respond to changing environmental conditions and unforeseen events. DANI combines concepts from artificial intelligence, network science, and complex systems theory to enable networks to adapt to dynamic internal and external factors, such as node failures, network congestion, and security threats. By leveraging machine learning techniques and real-time network monitoring, DANI systems can learn from experience and selectively modify their topology, routing, and traffic management strategies to maintain optimal performance, resilience, and security. Through a combination of theoretical modeling and simulation-based experiments, this research demonstrates the potential of DANI to improve network robustness, scalability, and efficiency in a wide range of application domains, including communication networks, social networks, and critical infrastructure systems. The findings of this study contribute to the development of more autonomous, self-healing, and intelligent network systems that can mitigate the impacts of unforeseen events and sustain high availability, security, and user experience.

title: Actor-Mimic: Deep Multitask and Transfer Reinforcement Learning
Abstract: This work presents the Actor-Mimic framework, a novel deep multitask and transfer reinforcement learning approach designed to facilitate efficient learning in complex environments with high dimensional action and state spaces. The Actor-Mimic framework leverages the strengths of both multitask and transfer learning by jointly training multiple tasks using a shared actor network and target network, while also enabling the actor and learner to update in parallel and independently. By doing so, Actor-Mimic tackles the inherent limitations of traditional reinforcement learning methods, including the lack of transferability across tasks and the slow learning rates associated with multi-task settings. Through the parallel and independent updates, the actor network learns to mimic the expert behaviors and decision-making strategies of a proficient learner network, yielding more efficient and effective learning outcomes. Furthermore, the Actor-Mimic framework showcases state-of-the-art performance in various challenging reinforcement learning benchmarks, demonstrating its ability to tackle sparse rewards and tackle high-dimensional actions. Our study demonstrates the advantages of Actor-Mimic for learning complex policies in scenarios characterized by multiple tasks and a high level of uncertainty, making it a potential game-changer for real-world applications of deep reinforcement learning.
