title: Communicating Semantics: Reference by Description
Abstract: This paper examines the challenges of referring to specific entities or concepts in communication, specifically focusing on reference by description. It delves into the complexities of conveying meaning through descriptive phrases, considering factors such as the ambiguity inherent in word choice, the reliability of contextual information, and the potential for misinterpretation. By analyzing various linguistic and cognitive aspects of reference, the research aims to elucidate the conditions under which successful reference by description occurs and the strategies people employ to mitigate potential semantic misunderstandings. The theoretical frameworks explored draw from philosophical discussions on reference, linguistic pragmatics, and cognitive science, highlighting the intricate interplay between speaker intent, listener reasoning, and the linguistic features of descriptive phrases. Case studies are presented to illustrate the pragmatic nuances involved in reference by description, such as the effects of prior knowledge, cultural background, and speaker-listener rapport on interpretation. The study's findings contribute to the understanding of how communication navigates the spectrum between explicit reference and inferential intention, shedding light on the delicate balance between semantic accuracy and effective communication in various contexts, from everyday conversations to specialized domains like science, law, and technology. By investigating the mechanisms underlying reference by description, the research seeks to refine the theoretical foundations of pragmatics and linguistics, with implications for effective communication in a diverse range of environments.

title: Preprint WebVRGIS Based Traffic Analysis and Visualization System
Abstract: This paper presents a novel web-based Virtual Reality, Geographic Information System (WebVRGIS) framework that enables effective traffic analysis and visualization. The proposed system integrates the power of WebVR and GIS technologies to provide immersive and interactive 3D visualizations of traffic data, facilitating transportation planners and researchers to gain deeper insights into traffic dynamics. By leveraging the strength of WebVR, the system enables users to explore and analyze traffic patterns from various perspectives, interact with 3D visualizations, and make informed decisions. The GIS component allows for the integration of spatial data, enabling the system to analyze and visualize traffic conditions, road networks, and traffic incidents in a comprehensive manner. The system's architecture is designed to handle large-scale traffic data, ensuring real-time processing and accurate visualization. Furthermore, the paper outlines the development methodologies, integration strategies, and implementation approaches employed to construct the WebVRGIS framework. The system's potential applications are vast, ranging from intelligent transportation systems to urban planning, making it an invaluable tool for transportation professionals and researchers alike. The experimental results obtained demonstrate the system's efficacy in facilitating effective traffic analysis, visualization, and decision-making, underscoring its potential to revolutionize the field of transportation research and planning.

title: Abstract Attribute Exploration with Partial Object Descriptions
Abstract: Attribute exploration plays a crucial role in various real-world applications, including computer vision, natural language processing, and recommender systems, where understanding the relationships between attributes is vital for accurate object classification and decision-making. However, in many tasks, we are often faced with partial object descriptions, wherein only a subset of attributes are observed or provided. This limited access to attribute information poses significant challenges in accurately identifying the underlying attributes and objects. Existing methods typically rely on complete or nearly complete attribute information, limiting their applicability in scenarios with partial attribute descriptions. To bridge this gap, we propose an abstract attribute exploration technique that leverages probabilistic graphical models and neural networks to effectively explore and infer missing attribute values from limited information. This approach allows for handling noise, outliers, and concept drift, making it more robust and adaptable to real-world scenarios. Through extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets and real-world applications, we demonstrate the efficacy and robustness of our proposed method, showcasing its potential to improve object classification and recommendation accuracy in scenarios with partial attribute descriptions. By providing a reliable and efficient framework for attribute exploration under uncertainty, our work has far-reaching implications for a wide range of areas that rely on accurate attribute identification and decision-making.

title: Coreset-Based Adaptive Tracking
Abstract: This paper proposes a new coreset-based adaptive tracking framework that efficiently handles online target tracking tasks with non-rigid object deformation and partial occlusion. By leveraging coreset, a novel data sampling technique, we enable the adaptive tracker to maintain robust real-time performance despite high computational costs associated with fine-grained object modeling. The core of our approach is the ability to dynamically update the coreset representation based on the appearance consistency and shape complexity of the target object. We introduce a multi-scale feature set that combines deep convolutional neural networks with custom-designed hand-crafted features to model non-rigid deformation and partial occlusion. Through integration of these features and coreset updates, our adaptive tracking framework exhibits not only improved accuracy but also enhanced adaptability in real-world applications, such as visual surveillance, robotics, and autonomous vehicles. Comprehensive evaluation results on diverse datasets and case studies demonstrate that our tracker can effectively deal with non-trivial situations like rapid shape variation and occlusion, achieving state-of-the-art performance and scalability. Our contributions provide a promising solution for efficient and reliable tracking applications where extreme non-rigid deformation and partial occlusion are ubiquitous, and offer valuable insights for advanced robotics, surveillance, and autonomous driving systems.

title: Detection of Slang Words in e-Data using semi-Supervised Learning
Abstract: This study proposes a semi-supervised approach for the detection of slang words in e-data, focusing on text from various social media platforms and online communities. The existing methods primarily rely on machine learning techniques, which require extensive labeled datasets to identify misused or informal terms. However, it is challenging to generate these datasets due to the ephemeral nature of slang words and the need for constant updating to reflect new or emerging terms. To address this problem, this research utilizes semi-supervised learning algorithms, which enable the incorporation of unlabeled data to improve model performance. The proposed framework employs active learning strategies and clustering techniques to identify the most informative unlabeled samples and adds them to the labeled dataset. A hybrid approach combining dictionary-based classification and deep learning models is used to detect slang words based on their context and frequency of occurrence. The proposed method was evaluated on a large dataset of e-data from various social media platforms, showing significant improvement in detection accuracy when compared to traditional machine learning methods. The study's findings highlight the potential of semi-supervised learning in addressing the challenges of slang word detection in e-data, making it a valuable contribution to the field of text analysis and natural language processing.

title: A Hybrid Approach to Word Sense Disambiguation Combining Supervised and Unsupervised Learning
Abstract: This paper presents a novel hybrid approach to Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) that leverages the strengths of both supervised and unsupervised learning techniques. The proposed method combines a convolutional neural network (CNN) with Word Embeddings, a clustering algorithm and a large-scale knowledge graph to effectively handle the limitations of each individual approach. In the supervised component, a CNN is trained on annotated training data to learn the correlation between contextual information and word senses, and the learned representations are used as input features for Word Embeddings, which captures the semantic relationships between words. The unsupervised component utilizes a clustering algorithm to identify senses by grouping semantically similar words, and a knowledge graph is employed to incorporate real-world relationships between word senses and concepts. The hybrid approach integrates the outputs of the supervised and unsupervised components through a weighted fusion scheme to generate the final sense prediction. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed hybrid approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on several benchmark datasets, and the ablation study reveals the complementary strengths of each component. The proposed method also exhibits good generalization capabilities and high scalability, making it a promising solution for WSD tasks in various NLP applications.

title: Overcoming Language Variation in Sentiment Analysis with Social Attention
Abstract: This paper delves into the challenges posed by language variation in sentiment analysis, a crucial task in natural language processing (NLP) that enables computers to understand human emotions and opinions from text data. Sentiment analysis has become a key component of numerous applications, including customer service, product recommendation, and social media monitoring, typically relying on machine learning models trained on large datasets. However, when language varies across different dialects, accents, or cultural contexts, these models' performance can drop significantly, leading to diminished accuracy and reliability in pinpointing true sentiments. This is particularly pertinent in contemporary situations where people increasingly express themselves using diverse forms of online communication. The research we present focuses on improving sentiment analysis by incorporating social attention mechanisms, a form of neural network that identifies the most relevant information based on its relevance to the context. By integrating social attention into the core framework of our sentiment analysis system, we are able to process information from distinct linguistic sources, mitigating issues associated with underrepresented dialects, noisy language patterns, and varied contextual information. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that our social attention mechanism leads to superior sentiment classification performance, thus allowing for more effective navigation of the complexities of language variation and social media context.

title: BIRDNEST: Bayesian Inference for Ratings-Fraud Detection
Abstract: The BIRDNEST framework was designed as a Bayesian inference-based approach to tackle the complex issue of ratings-fraud detection in modern online review systems. This research work focuses on developing an efficient and accurate methodology to detect fake ratings, which are prevalent in many online review platforms. A primary motivation behind the BIRDNEST framework is the need to provide not only a more reliable way to filter out fake ratings but to also attribute the likelihood of an individual review being fake to a numeric score that takes into account all relevant contextual information. The presented work evaluates various components that impact the likelihood of ratings being genuine, including a comprehensive set of user demographic features, patterns of rating behaviors, interaction levels, user consensus, review content details, and a range of contextual information such as time of reviews and user relationships with one another. A hybrid attack model is proposed for evaluating the robustness of the developed model under varying attack vectors and detection scenarios, showcasing the framework's resilience in resistance to multiple advanced attack types. Comprehensive experiments were conducted on actual publicly available data sources from popular consumer review platforms involving millions of genuine and fake ratings to verify the efficacy of the presented BIRDNEST approach, providing proof of its high detection accuracy compared to existing solutions.

title: Unitary-Group Invariant Kernels and Features from Transformed Unlabeled Data
Abstract: The advent of invariant features derived from transformed or manipulated data has laid the groundwork for significant advancements in machine learning, particularly in deep learning. A novel family of unitary-group invariant kernels and features, inspired by symmetry properties of data distributions, is presented in this research. By employing transformations such as orthogonal matrices and projective transformations, this ensemble of kernels and features leverages the inherent structure underlying complex, high-dimensional data spaces to enable more robust and generalizable performance, especially when complemented with unlabeled data. The essential insight behind the derived invariant features is rooted in the concept that intrinsic data symmetries can be effectively capitalized upon by employing group actions (transformations) on unlabeled samples followed by dimensionality reduction via a kernel-based approach. Consequently, this innovation grants machines the capacity to generalize insights to unobserved data configurations thereby addressing a fundamental challenge in machine learning: achieving effective generalizability. Through theoretical analyses and extensive empirical validation, this research, employing datasets from image classification, computer vision, and other domains, demonstrates the remarkable potential of the proposed methodology for enhancing performance in a broad class of tasks. These contributions not only further reveal the significance of geometric and algebraic considerations in deep learning but also present practical tools for enhancing performance in real-world machine learning applications.

title: Behavior Query Discovery in System-Generated Temporal Graphs
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to behavior query discovery in system-generated temporal graphs, which are ubiquitous in various fields such as social networks, traffic management, and financial transactions. These graphs often exhibit complex behavior patterns that are difficult to identify manually, hindering efficient decision-making and predictive modeling. To address this challenge, we introduce TBQD (Temporal Behavior Query Discovery), a framework that leverages graph neural networks and meta-learning techniques to automatically detect and characterize behavior patterns in temporal graphs. TBQD first learns a compact representation of the graph using a graph neural network, which captures key topological features and evolve these into behavior patterns using meta-learning. We then develop three types of behavior queries, including trajectory query, slice query, and sequence query, which enable users to retrieve relevant behavior patterns based on their specific needs. Experimental results on five real-world datasets demonstrate that TBQD outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of behavior pattern discovery accuracy and efficiency, with up to 96% gain in detecting rare patterns and 85% reduction in query response time. Our empirical results also show that TBQD can uncover novel insights and unexpected correlations in system-generated temporal graphs, highlighting its potential applications in various domains.

title: Censoring Representations with an Adversary
Abstract: This research proposes a novel approach to censored representation learning by leveraging the concept of an adversary, a concept that is commonly employed in machine learning for security threats and attacks. Specifically, we focus on developing a framework that enables the identification of sensitive information in data representations, and subsequently modifies or removes such information to achieve the desired level of censorship. By framing the problem as an adversarial game between a censor and the data, we use techniques from adversarial training to update the data representations in a way that minimizes the ability of the censor to recover the sensitive information. Our approach differs from existing methods in its reliance on a specific adversary model, which allows for a principled and tractable optimization problem that can be solved using standard deep learning techniques. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on several benchmark datasets, including image and text data, and show that our method outperforms existing censored representation learning methods in terms of preserving sensitive information while maintaining the utility of the data. Furthermore, we provide theoretical bounds on the performance of our approach, shedding light on its limitations and potential applications. Overall, this research contributes to a deeper understanding of censorship in machine learning and opens up new avenues for research in privacy-aware data analysis and statistical inference.

title: Alternative Markov and Causal Properties for Acyclic Directed Mixed Graphs
Abstract: This study introduces a novel framework for analyzing acyclic directed mixed graphs by developing alternative Markov and causal properties that extend existing methodologies. Building on recent breakthroughs in graphical models, we provide a rigorous and comprehensive approach to understanding the relationships within complex systems represented by acyclic directed mixed graphs. By leveraging advanced concepts from graph theory, linear algebra, and statistical analysis, our framework facilitates the identification of essential relationships and dependencies in these networks, allowing for more accurate predictions and better decision-making. Specifically, we derive novel necessary and sufficient conditions for causal and Markov properties in acyclic directed mixed graphs and explore their implications for structural causal models. The proposed framework is shown to encompass and generalize existing methods, while providing a unified theory for characterizing the causal structure of complex systems. A range of applications across various fields, including epidemiology, economics, and artificial intelligence, are also demonstrated, underscoring the practical utility of our theoretical contributions. Through a combination of mathematical derivations, computational experiments, and real-world case studies, this research sets the stage for advancing the theoretical foundations of causal reasoning and probabilistic modeling in acyclic directed mixed graphs.

title: Towards Lateral Inhibition and Collective Perception in Unorganised Non-Neural Systems
Abstract: This research explores the concept of lateral inhibition and collective perception within the framework of unorganised non-neural systems. Inspired by the natural world, where phenomena such as flocking and schooling are evident without the presence of centralised processing or neural networks, we develop computational models to investigate the emergence of such complex collective behaviors. By utilizing agent-based simulations, we examine how minimal rule sets governing simple sensory-motor interactions between individual agents can lead to the emergence of robust, coherent patterns and collective perception. The focus is on demonstrating how through local interactions, unorganised systems can collectively process and respond to environmental stimuli in a distributed manner, functionally akin to the lateral inhibition seen in biological neural networks. Our research lies at the intersection of swarm intelligence, collective robotics and biologically inspired computing, and aims to contribute a comprehensive understanding of how seemingly complex processes can arise from local interactions in degenerate (non-neural) systems, offering insights into alternative and energy-efficient approaches to processing complex information. The model's capability to replicate observed behaviors paves the way for the real-world implementation of swarms and decentralized systems with potential applications in areas such as environmental monitoring, spatial analysis, and social robotics.

title: Solution Repair/Recovery in Uncertain Optimization Environment
Abstract: This study focuses on developing a novel framework for adaptive solution repair and recovery in uncertain optimization environments, where randomness and uncertainty prevail. Emergence of irreconcilable inconsistencies and infeasibilities in optimization algorithms due to the inherent uncertainty often leads to the failure of models, resulting in costly economic losses. To mitigate this issue, a novel metaheuristic framework based on adaptive repair strategies is proposed, incorporating concepts from robust optimization and stochastic programming. The framework is built on an integrated approach combining probabilistic and possibilistic optimization techniques to manage and predict uncertainty, develop proactive and reactive repair strategies, and systematically evaluate the repair quality. The methodology is demonstrated using a series of computational experiments on a range of uncertainty profiles and problem types, including linear and nonlinear programming, as well as multi-objective and possibly nonsmooth optimization problems. Results reveal significant improvements in the reliability and efficiency of solution repair and recovery, especially for high-dimensional and highly uncertain problems. The proposed adaptive framework offers a promising solution for practitioners seeking enhanced robustness and flexibility in uncertain optimization environments, enabling the efficient handling of exceptional cases and minimizing the likelihood of irreparable inconsistencies and failures.

title: Using Abduction in Markov Logic Networks for Root Cause Analysis
Abstract: Abduction in Markov Logic Networks (MLNs) has garnered significant attention in recent years due to its potential in facilitating robust root cause analysis. This paper explores the application of abduction in MLNs for identifying the primary causes of complex events or outcomes. Traditional root cause analysis techniques often rely on heuristics and are susceptible to biases and incomplete knowledge, whereas MLNs provide a structured probabilistic framework for reasoning under uncertainty. By integrating abduction, which involves inferring unobserved causes from observed effects, MLNs can systematically investigate potential root causes and quantify their likelihood. We propose a novel approach that combines abduction with MLNs, which enables efficient and accurate identification of root causes in complex settings. Our approach reformulates the root cause analysis problem as an abduction task in an MLN, where unobserved causes are treated as latent variables. This allows for the probabilistic modeling of causal relationships and the propagation of uncertainty. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through a series of case studies, including fault diagnosis in industrial systems and medical diagnosis. Experimental results show that our method outperforms traditional approaches in terms of accuracy and robustness, particularly in scenarios with limited knowledge and high uncertainty. The potential of abduction in MLNs for root cause analysis has significant implications for various domains, including safety engineering, risk management, and healthcare.

title: Discovering Underlying Plans Based on Distributed Representations of Actions
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel method for discovering underlying plans in complex tasks using distributed representations of actions. The authors argue that existing plan recognition models primarily rely on symbolic representations of actions, which can be inflexible and fail to capture nuances in human behavior. In contrast, their approach leverages neural network-based distributed representations, which can encode context-dependent and hierarchical information about actions. By analyzing the collective patterns of action distribution across different situations, the proposed model is able to identify abstractions and generalizations that underlie human behavior, thereby inferring potential plans. The authors conduct experiments on simulated and real-world datasets, including videos of human locomotion and robotic manipulation, demonstrating that their approach effectively extracts underlying plans and outperforms traditional symbolic-representation-based methods. The findings suggest that distributed action representations can provide a more robust and scalable framework for plan recognition, enabling the design of more intelligent systems that can learn from and adapt to complex and dynamic environments. The proposed method has the potential to be applied in numerous domains, including human-robot interaction, skill acquisition, and decision-making under uncertainty, offering new avenues for the development of more autonomous and efficient assistive technologies.

title: A New Smooth Approximation to the Zero One Loss with a Probabilistic Interpretation
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel smooth approximation to the zero-one loss function, which is widely used in binary classification tasks. Unlike existing smooth approximations that lack probabilistic interpretation, the proposed method provides a principled way of translating classification probabilities to a continuous loss value. The key insight is to model the zero-one loss as a function of the likelihood ratio of the true class versus the estimated class, and then relax this ratio using a smooth kernel function. The resulting loss function not only maintains the key desirable properties of the original zero-one loss, such as consistency and calibration, but also enjoys additional benefits of smoothness and differentiability. Importantly, the proposed method can be interpreted as a probabilistic measure of classification uncertainty, allowing practitioners to assess the reliability of their classification decisions. As a result, the proposed smooth approximation can be used in a variety of machine learning applications where accurate performance estimates and uncertainty quantification are essential. Through extensive experimental evaluations on several benchmark datasets, we demonstrate the superiority of the proposed smooth approximation over state-of-the-art methods in terms of calibration and robust classification performance.

title: Return of Frustratingly Easy Domain Adaptation
Abstract:
This abstract delves into the recent resurgence of "Frustratingly Easy Domain Adaptation" (FEDA) - a long-abandoned subfield of machine learning pioneered in the early 2000s. Initially, FEDA promised to bridge the knowledge gap between significantly different domains by leveraging surprisingly simplistic yet highly effective data adaptation strategies. However, due to the devastating blow of discovering their fundamental underlying flaws in 2006, research in this area was relegated to the backburners of academia for nearly two decades. 
Lately, researchers in the field of deep learning have revisited this abandoned territory, and in the process re-engineered these seemingly simplistic methods, resulting in unusually adept and efficient performance. Though initially skeptics predicted calamitous failures because the foundational rules were previously deemed broken, researchers claim to have refined and strengthened the method, eliminating fundamental defects associated with earlier versions of FEDA. Rather astonishingly this rebranded version of FEDA boasts its value in environments that other knowledge adaptation strategies struggle in – not least, complex applications from the realms of speech recognition and facial recognition where accuracy can fall short with even slightly disparate target datasets.
Advocates argue that this breakthrough adaptation of FEDA could alter how the art of knowledge adaptation is taken, opening up lucrative opportunities for faster, lighter and more performant knowledge transferring strategies - many that further diverge from and therefore advance far beyond the traditional methodology of typical transfer learning processes. A compelling discussion of its role, scope, and potential complications of this surprising, and lately - newly revitalized strategy provides the core foundation and theoretical background for this vital research.

title: Neurocontrol methods review
Abstract: The concept of neurocontrol, also known as brain-machine interfaces, has been gaining momentum as a potential solution for assisting individuals with motor disorders, learning disabilities, and other neurological impairments. This review aims to provide a comprehensive overview of current neurocontrol methods, highlighting their underlying principles, techniques, and applications. We begin by discussing the fundamental aspects of neurocontrol systems, including signal processing and decoding algorithms, which enable the extraction of relevant neural information from electroencephalography (EEG), functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS), and electrocorticography (ECoG) data. Subsequent sections delve into specific neurocontrol methods, such as brain-computer interfaces (BCIs), neural prosthetics, and neural decoding algorithms for motor control. Our analysis also explores the role of machine learning and artificial intelligence in enhancing the performance and adaptability of neurocontrol systems. Furthermore, we examine the clinical applications of neurocontrol, including the treatment of stroke, spinal cord injury, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). Additionally, we discuss the challenges and limitations associated with current neurocontrol methods, such as signal drift, device-related artifacts, and individual variability. Ultimately, this review seeks to provide a nuanced understanding of the neurocontrol landscape, highlighting the potential of these methods for revolutionizing the treatment and management of neurological disorders and fostering new frontiers in neurotechnology.

title: Gated Graph Sequence Neural Networks
Abstract: This paper delves into the realm of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and proposes a novel architecture Gated Graph Sequence Neural Networks, which integrates state-of-the-art ideas from both graph attention mechanisms and gated recurrent unit (GRU) cells to efficiently model complex, sequence-based graph structures. Inspired by the success of recursive neural networks in processing sequential data, we design a hierarchical neural network framework capable of capturing both local and global graph patterns. By adopting a two-level hierarchical approach, our architecture effectively leverages the strengths of both graph attention and GRU cells to represent temporal dependencies in the graph. The main contribution of this research lies in the development of a novel gated graph sequence neural network (GGSNN) module, which seamlessly integrates spectral graph convolutional operators with learnable memory-based attentive mechanisms to propagate and aggregate information in the graph. Experimental results on several challenging tasks, including link prediction, node classification, and graph classification, demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed architecture, surpassing the performance of competitive baselines and achieving state-of-the-art results on several benchmark datasets. Furthermore, we discuss the potential applications of GGSNNs in real-world scenarios, underscoring the broad versatility and adaptability of our proposed neural network architecture. Through this research, we provide an in-depth exploration of sequence-based graph representations and highlight the advantages of exploring the interplay between different neural network components to tackle complex, real-world applications.

title: Active exploration of sensor networks from a robotics perspective
Abstract: Active exploration of sensor networks from a robotics perspective is a rapidly evolving field that has garnered significant attention in recent years. The advent of advances in sensor technology, robotics, and machine learning has ushered in a new era of autonomous and adaptive exploration of complex environments. From a robotics perspective, this entails developing architectures, algorithms, and control frameworks that enable robots to interact seamlessly with heterogeneous sensor networks, thereby facilitating informed decision-making and goal-oriented exploration. Central to this endeavor is the development of nuanced understanding of sensor network dynamics, including communication patterns, sensor modalities, and spatial configurations. Moreover, the integration of multiple sensor modalities such as computer vision, lidar, and sonar enables robots to build rich, multi-faceted models of their environment, thereby facilitating a more efficient and effective exploration strategy. Our research endeavors to articulate a holistic framework for active exploration of sensor networks from a robotics perspective, encompassing cutting-edge developments in sensor modeling, data fusion, and control theory. By harnessing the power of robotics and sensor networks, we envision the possibility of autonomous systems that can comprehensively map, analyze, and understand complex environments, with far-reaching applications in areas such as search and rescue, environmental monitoring, and infrastructure inspection.

title: Bayesian Optimization with Dimension Scheduling: Application to Biological Systems
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to Bayesian optimization (BO) that incorporates dimension scheduling for efficient exploration of complex biological systems. By leveraging the benefits of BO in adapting to the problem space, the proposed method, termed Bayesian optimization with dimension scheduling (BODS), dynamically adjusts the number of input dimensions based on the prior knowledge and evolving distribution of the objective function. This dimension scheduling mechanism, which uses a machine learning-based model to predict the relevance of each input dimension, complements the Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling process within BO to strike a balance between exploration and exploitation. Specifically, BODS assigns higher importance weights to those dimensions with most predictive power, effectively reducing the dimensionality of the search space and accelerating the optimization process. The proposed method is thoroughly tested on two distinct biological applications: protein evolution and personalized cancer treatment, where it demonstrates superior performance compared to state-of-the-art BO methods and parallel random search in terms of convergence speed, accuracy, and robustness. Through BODS, researchers can efficiently explore large solution spaces, enabling the design of effective therapeutic strategies and shedding light on the intricate mechanisms of biological systems.

title: The Use of Machine Learning Algorithms in Recommender Systems: A Systematic Review
Abstract: This systematic review presents an in-depth analysis of the application and effectiveness of machine learning (ML) algorithms in recommender systems. The rise of digital platforms and the ever-increasing volume of user-generated data have led to a significant growth in the use of recommender systems to personalize content, products, and services. The current state-of-the-art in recommender systems research focuses on developing ML-based approaches to improve the accuracy, scalability, and adaptability of recommendation techniques. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the various ML algorithms employed in recommender systems, including collaborative filtering, content-based filtering, knowledge-based systems, and hybrid approaches. A critical examination of the strengths and limitations of each algorithm is presented, highlighting their respective advantages, challenges, and areas for future research. Additionally, this review explores the integration of other AI techniques, such as natural language processing and computer vision, to enhance the recommendation process. A thorough analysis of the methodologies used in existing studies is also conducted to identify the most effective algorithms and techniques in various domains, including music, movies, products, and services. By synthesizing the existing body of knowledge, this systematic review aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of the current state of the art in the application of ML algorithms in recommender systems and to inform future research directions in this field.

title: Ask, Attend and Answer: Exploring Question-Guided Spatial Attention for Visual Question Answering
Abstract: Visual question answering (VQA) is an interdisciplinary task that requires both image understanding and question comprehension. This paper delves into the concept of question-guided spatial attention, a crucial aspect of VQA models that enables them to selectively focus on relevant regions of the image when answering a question. By integrating this mechanism into a VQA framework, models can significantly improve their performance and interpretability. We propose an attention-based architecture that learns to attend to relevant image regions when answering a question, effectively leveraging the guidance provided by the question to focus on critical visual details. This approach is implemented through a question-encoder that generates a spatial attention mask, which is then multiplied element-wise with the image features to highlight relevant regions. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed approach outperforms state-of-the-art VQA models on several benchmark datasets, indicating the effectiveness of question-guided spatial attention in improving VQA performance. Additionally, we conduct ablation studies to provide insights into the significance of the proposed approach, revealing that the use of question-guided spatial attention leads to significant improvement in model performance due to its ability to selectively focus on relevant image regions.

title: Convolutional Models for Joint Object Categorization and Pose Estimation
Abstract: Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have revolutionized the field of computer vision, and recently, they have also been widely applied in tasks related to object detection and pose estimation. Joint object categorization and pose estimation refer to the simultaneous task of identifying the category of an object and estimating the pose or orientation of that object in a given scene. This task is particularly challenging and requires models with high discriminative power to accurately classify objects under different poses. In this study, we explore the development of convolutional models for joint object categorization and pose estimation. We conduct a comprehensive analysis of different CNN architectures and examine their ability to concurrently categorize objects and estimate their poses. Our approach involves implementing various state-of-the-art CNN models and training them on a large dataset of images containing objects with varying poses. We also investigate the use of data augmentation techniques and regularization methods to improve model generalization and robustness. We go on to present the results of our experiments, comparing the performance of different models on a range of metrics, including classification accuracy and pose estimation error. Through this research, we aim to contribute to the development of more effective and efficient CNN models for joint object categorization and pose estimation, leading to improved applications in robotics, autonomous driving, and visual surveillance.

title: How (not) to Train your Generative Model: Scheduled Sampling, Likelihood, Adversary?
Abstract: Generative models have become ubiquitous in many applications, including computer vision, natural language processing, and robotics, due to their ability to learn complex distributions from large datasets. However, training these models can be a challenging task, especially when dealing with balancing exploration and exploitation. Scheduled sampling, likelihood, and adversarial objectives are three common approaches used to train generative models. This paper provides an in-depth analysis of the effectiveness and limitations of these approaches, commonly applied methods such as scheduled sampling with entropy regularization and likelihood-based objectives via the variational autoencoder (VAE) framework. Moreover, we explore the adversary-based approach, specifically generators and discriminators in the GAN paradigm. Our comprehensive study reveals the strengths and weaknesses of each approach and provides insights into the most suitable conditions for their successful application. We investigate how these approaches affect the convergence, mode coverage, and sample quality of generative models, through both theoretical analysis and empirical evaluation on several benchmark datasets. Furthermore, we inspect the role of entropy regularization and its connection to the exploration-exploitation trade-off, as well as the importance of the balance between generators and discriminators in GAN architectures. Our findings offer valuable guidance to researchers and practitioners seeking to train generative models efficiently and effectively.

title: Performing Highly Accurate Predictions Through Convolutional Networks for Actual Telecommunication Challenges
Abstract: The integration of deep learning techniques in telecommunication has revolutionized the field by offering innovative solutions to complex challenges. This research aims to investigate the efficacy of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) in accurately predicting telecommunication-related issues. Telecommunication networks are inherently complex systems involving various components that interact to provide seamless communication services. Effective prediction of potential issues within these networks is crucial to ensure uninterrupted service quality, minimizing the occurrence of network outages, and enhancing overall user experience. However, predicting telecommunication challenges poses significant demands on machine learning algorithms, which require a deep understanding of network behavior patterns, noise reduction, and robust feature extraction. Our research demonstrates that CNNs can efficiently fulfill these demands, leveraging their exceptional ability to extract meaningful spatial features from complex data representations. The proposed CNN-based model is designed to analyze a comprehensive dataset of multiple telecommunication networks, predicting with high accuracy various types of issues such as network congestion, equipment failures, and data transmission errors. We show that the incorporation of CNNs enhances the precision and efficiency of predictions, particularly when compared to traditional machine learning models. Furthermore, the proposed CNN-based model offers the flexibility to incorporate additional features and adapt to evolving telecommunication landscape, making it a valuable tool for network planning, maintenance, and optimization.

title: Quality assessment of voice converted speech using articulatory features
Abstract: This study endeavors to investigate the quality assessment of voice converted speech (VCS) using articulatory features as a novel approach to evaluate its naturalness and intelligibility. Recent advancements in speech synthesis technology have led to the development of voice conversion systems that can transform the speaker's identity, age, and emotional characteristics, greatly impacting the field of human-computer interaction. However, despite the numerous applications of VCS, its overall quality and acceptability by human listeners remains a critical concern. Traditional methods assessing VCS quality are largely reliant on listener impressions and perceived similarity to original speakers, which can be subjective and time-consuming to evaluate. As an alternative, this research utilizes articulatory features, such as lip and tongue articulations, vocal tract constraints, and respiratory patterns to assess VCS quality. By considering the biomechanical characteristics and acoustic metrics associated with these features, this study aims to provide a more comprehensive and objective evaluation framework for VCS. Employing a mixed-methods approach, combining both machine learning algorithms and statistical analysis, this research examines the relationship between articulatory features and perceived VCS quality. The outcomes of this study have significant implications for the development of more effective and user-friendly voice conversion systems, ultimately enhancing human-machine interaction and speech synthesis applications.

title: Heterogeneous Knowledge Transfer in Video Emotion Recognition, Attribution and Summarization
Abstract: This paper investigates the application of heterogeneous knowledge transfer in video emotion recognition, attribution, and summarization tasks, which involves leveraging multimodal and multi-source data to improve the accuracy and robustness of video-based emotional analysis. Traditional computer vision and deep learning-based approaches often struggle with limited training data, poor generalizability, and insufficient contextual understanding of video content. In contrast, the proposed heterogeneous knowledge transfer framework introduces an ensemble learning perspective that integrates knowledge from various sources, including attention-based mechanisms, knowledge distillation, multi-task learning, and external knowledge sources, such as text and audio descriptions. The framework is designed to adapt to varying input modalities, content types, and application domains, enhancing the capacity for accurate emotion recognition, attribution of contextually relevant regions and time-intervals, and summarization of video content for key emotional moments. Experimental evaluations on multiple benchmark datasets validate the superior performance, convergence rate, and generalizability of the proposed approach, demonstrating its potential for real-world applications in various fields, including human-computer interaction, human-centered design, and affective computing. The developed framework provides a robust foundation for advancing video emotion analysis in terms of adaptability, accuracy, and scalability, addressing several limitations of prior research in this area.

title: Applying Semantic Web Technologies for Improving the Visibility of Tourism Data
Abstract: This research paper embodies the pioneering application of Semantic Web technologies in optimizing the visibility of tourism data for enhanced experience of travellers and tour operators. Despite the extensive growth of tourism, the current methods employed for collecting, analyzing, and disseminating tourism data are ineffective and fragmentary, rendering the information often inaccessible and incompatible. The proposed study attempts to address this issue by embracing the potential of Semantic Web technologies to enrich the structuring and interlinking of tourism data, thereby, efficiently organizing and providing novel insights to stakeholders. The development of a data model specifically tailored to capture the conceptual relationships inherent to tourist applications is crucial. The incorporation of ontologies will facilitate a universal framework for harmonizing the inherent complexities within tourism data. Furthermore, inferencing methods will enable the generation of logical conclusions facilitating both an insightful comprehension of tourist preferences and potent analysis of market trends. Ultimately, the aim is to facilitate travel information sharing for visitors to efficiently, locate and identify recommended travel features in accordance with user needs, and to allow tourism business proprietors to enhance their profiles through data-driven assessments.

title: Word Embedding based Correlation Model for Question/Answer Matching
Abstract: This study proposes a novel question-answer matching framework that incorporates word embeddings to capture semantic relationships and correlation between questions and potential answers. The proposed model employs a unique two-stage approach to quantify the degree of similarity between question-answer pairs. Initially, it attributes semantic representations to questions and candidate answers via pre-trained word embeddings, resulting in high-dimensional vector spaces. Subsequently, a correlation analysis is performed by calculating the Pearson's correlation coefficient between the vector representations of question and answer pairs. This allows the model to capture both the semantic differences and contextual variations between questions and answers. Experimentally, the proposed model demonstrates significant improvements over traditional similarity-based approaches, such as Cosine Similarity, in accurately matching questions with their relevant answers. Furthermore, the model's correlation analysis provides an intuitive understanding of the relationship between questions and answers, enabling users to gauge the degree of similarity and correlation between them. The experimental results also highlight the robustness and scalability of the proposed approach in various scenarios, including the WebQA and SQuAD datasets. Overall, the proposed model presents a promising solution for question-answer matching tasks and has potential applications in information retrieval, question answering systems, and human-computer interaction. Its ability to incorporate semantic relationships and correlation analysis makes it a valuable tool for capturing the complexities of natural language queries and answers.

title: Deep Reinforcement Learning with a Natural Language Action Space
Abstract: Deep reinforcement learning has revolutionized the field of artificial intelligence by allowing agents to learn complex behaviors from raw experience, but its applications have been largely limited by the requirement for a numerical or categorical action space. This has inspired research into the use of natural language as an action space, which would enable more flexible and human-like interaction. However, incorporating natural language into reinforcement learning presents several unique challenges, including the need for high-dimensional action spaces and the difficulty of computing accurate action-value estimates. This paper explores the application of deep reinforcement learning with a natural language action space, and investigates the use of transformer architectures and sequence-to-sequence generation to address these challenges. We develop a novel agent that takes natural language input and generates a sequence of actions to achieve a desired outcome, with a focus on dialogue management and human-robot interaction. Our results demonstrate that the agent is able to learn effective behaviors in complex environments, and achieve state-of-the-art performance in several dialogue-based benchmarks. Furthermore, we investigate the robustness of the agent to changes in the language input, and find that it is able to adapt to new vocabulary and grammatical structures with minimal additional training. The implications of this work are significant, as it suggests that natural language will become a viable component of future reinforcement learning systems.

title: Demand-Driven Incremental Object Queries
Abstract: This research paper presents a novel approach to incremental object queries, leveraging demand-driven strategies to optimize performance in complex data-processing systems. The proposed method, aimed at querying entities subjected to dynamic changes, exploits the principles of incremental computation and speculative execution to minimize unnecessary computations and accelerate query results. By establishing a correlation between incremental data changes and updated query requirements, the system proactively anticipates and generates new query execution plans, circumventing redundant computations and reducing query latency. The architecture is based on the concept of 'demand-driven incremental views,' which continuously re-evaluate query results in response to dynamic data updates, ultimately minimizing the need for incremental queries. Furthermore, this research introduces an adaptive model-driven incremental query system that facilitates the prediction of query requirements and ensures that the system remains responsive to emerging query patterns. The evaluation results demonstrate a substantial improvement in performance and flexibility compared to traditional, static query-based systems, showcasing the demand-driven approach as a robust solution for real-time incremental querying in dynamic systems. The findings also highlight the potential of efficient query plan adaptation, knowledge-driven incremental querying, and demand-driven incremental views in tackling complex, real-world data management scenarios.

title: Dynamic Sum Product Networks for Tractable Inference on Sequence Data (Extended Version)
Abstract: This paper presents a novel extension of sum product networks (SPNs) for tractable inference on sequential data, featuring dynamic sum product networks (DSPNs). Existing SPNs have shown remarkable performances in handling high-dimensional and complex datasets, but their applicability is initially constrained by the requirement for training data to be pre-allocated, which can be computationally expensive. This limitation becomes particularly significant when dealing with sequential data where fixed representation sizes are inappropriate due to the variability of the data. To address this challenge, DSPNs are introduced to allow learning, inference, and representation learning alongside the sequential data's dynamic structure. A recursive variational learning approach is developed, enabling the flexible adaptation of a set of dynamic sum product networks based on the learned representations of the sequential data. Our experiments demonstrate that DSPNs outperform traditional SPNs in various benchmark tasks involving sequential training data. The results showcase the efficacy of DSPNs in tractable inference tasks and are of crucial importance for numerous applications including natural language processing, speech recognition, and recommender systems. Furthermore, the presented framework supports dynamic decision-making processes that are essential in real-world scenarios.

title: Symbol Grounding Association in Multimodal Sequences with Missing Elements
Abstract: This study delves into the long-standing challenge of symbol grounding, a fundamental concept in artificial intelligence (AI) and cognitive science, involving the associating of abstract symbols with meaningful representations. In multimodal sequences, such associations become increasingly complex due to the multiplicity of modalities and the possible presence of missing elements, which hinders the effective interpretation and understanding of the sequence. To address this issue, this research proposes a novel symbolic grounding approach that integrates lexical, visual, and semantic information. Based on an attention-based multimodal encoder, the proposed method initially captures the complex interactions between modalities within a sequence and subsequently infers the representations of missing elements by leveraging both spatial and temporal contextual information. Empirical evaluations demonstrate significant improvements in multimodal sequence understanding over state-of-the-art baselines on benchmark datasets. The proposed method is highly effective in handling missing elements by aggregating contextual information from adjacent parts of the sequence. Furthermore, the findings reveal insights into the role of multimodal association in enhancing the interpretability and robustness of AI models when dealing with noisy or ambiguous sequence inputs. Overall, this study presents a principled frame for addressing the symbol grounding challenge in multiple modalities with missing elements, which holds promise for applications in human-robot interaction, natural language processing, and data augmentation. The developed methodology could be applied to various real-world scenarios where multimodal understanding of uncertain or incomplete information is essential.

title: HackAttack: Game-Theoretic Analysis of Realistic Cyber Conflicts
Abstract: This research investigates the strategic dynamics of cyber warfare through a game-theoretic lens, providing novel insights into the uncertain and rapidly evolving realm of cyber conflicts. Dubbed HackAttack, our framework incorporates elements of network topology, attacker- defender asymmetry, and stylized truth-telling dilemmas to model the complexities of cyber operations. By casting real-world scenarios into a strategic game, our analysis highlights the precarious relationships between attackers' exploitability and defenders' intrusion detection, as well as the incentives driving norm-breaking behavior in the pursuit of advantages. Employing a mixed-integer linear programming formulation, we generate realistic simulated battles, allowing for both optimal attack and defense planning. Notably, our models accommodate temporal considerations, explicit knowledge exchange between adversaries, and strategic interaction effects among multiple actors. The outcomes of this research hold significant implications for developing more accurate predictive tools, better informing real-world deterrent and countermeasures, and rationalizing the need for novel institutional designs to safeguard against the perils of unbridled cyber ferocity. Ultimately, our results underscore the inherent imperfections of existing counter-attack strategies, bringing forth significant concerns about the inadequacy of hasty conclusions guided by intuition in matters of global network security.

title: Combining Monte-Carlo and Hyper-heuristic methods for the Multi-mode Resource-constrained Multi-project Scheduling Problem
Abstract: The Multi-mode Resource-constrained Multi-project Scheduling Problem (MRMSP) is a complex problem that involves scheduling multiple projects with limited resources and each project can be executed in multiple modes, which in turn requires varying amounts of resources. In order to provide efficient solutions for MRMSP, this research paper proposes a novel approach by combining the Monte-Carlo method and hyper-heuristic method. Monte-Carlo method is used to generate a range of candidate solutions, while hyper-heuristic method is utilized to select and combine the best strategies to find the optimal solution. This hybrid approach aims to capture the strengths of both methods, where the Monte-Carlo method can efficiently explore the solution space, and the hyper-heuristic method can identify an effective search strategy for the best solution. The proposed approach is tested on various instances of the MRMSP, and the results show that the hybrid method outperforms other state-of-the-art algorithms in terms of solution quality and computational efficiency. The findings of this research demonstrate the potential of combining different metaheuristics to solve complex scheduling problems, and provide insights into the design of effective hybrid algorithms for solving MRMSP. The results also highlight the importance of adaptability and flexibility of the hyper-heuristic method in selecting suitable strategies for solving complex and dynamic optimization problems.

title: Introduzione all'Intelligenza Artificiale
Abstract: La Intelligenza Artificiale (IA) rappresenta un settore in continuo sviluppo, che si occupa di creare sistemi artificiali capaci di risolvere problemi, apprendere e migliorare le proprie prestazioni senza l'intervento umano. L'avvento dell'IA ha rivoluzionato numerosi ambiti, tra cui la medicina, la pianificazione logistica e la sicurezza informatica. La presente ricerca mira a fornire un'introduzione approfondita all'argomento, esplorando le sue origini storiche, le principali tecnologie che la compongono e le sue applicazioni più significative. La IA si basa su diversi algoritmi di apprendimento, come il machine learning e il deep learning, che consentono ai sistemi di analizzare grandi quantità di dati e di imparare dai propri errori. Inoltre, la ricerca focalizzerà sulla discussione delle sfide e dei limiti dell'IA, come l'etica della privacy e la possibilità di sostituzione dei posti di lavoro. L'ambizione di questo progetto è quella di fornire un quadro comprensivo e ampiamente accessibile per chiunque voglia conoscere e comprendere la fondamentale introduzione all'Intelligenza Artificiale, dalla teoria alla pratica applicativa nel mondo attuale e futuro.

title: Novel Feature Extraction, Selection and Fusion for Effective Malware Family Classification
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel ensemble-based approach for effective malware family classification, focusing on feature extraction, selection, and fusion. Machine learning algorithms heavily rely on the quality and relevance of features used in training models; however, selecting informative and non-redundant features is a challenging task, especially in the malware domain, where vast amounts of irrelevant data can overwhelm analysts. To address this issue, a hybrid feature extraction technique combining statistical, syntactical, and semantic features is designed to obtain a comprehensive representation of malware family characteristics. Furthermore, this paper employs a novel multi-filter feature selection approach that leverages a combination of mutual information, correlation analysis, and recursive feature elimination methods to identify the most informative features. Additionally, a robust feature fusion technique, empowered by ensemble learning and dimensionality reduction, is developed to create highly discriminative feature representations. The proposed ensemble model, consisting of extensible architecture and component learning modules, demonstrates a significant improvement in detection accuracy, outperforming state-of-the-art approaches in various experimental scenarios, with an overall F1-score increase of 12.5% in classifying real-world malware families.

title: Uncertainty relations in quantum optics. Is the photon intelligent?
Abstract: The study of uncertainty relations in quantum optics has far-reaching implications for our understanding of the behavior of light at the quantum level, prompting questions about the very nature of light itself. Long thought to be nothing more than a wave or a particle, the behavior of photons has been observed to defy classical notions of causality and determinism. From the Heisenberg uncertainty principle, which dictates that certain properties of a photon cannot be simultaneously measured, to the more recent observation of the non-locality and entanglement exhibited by certain types of photons, it has become increasingly clear that the behavior of light is not adequately accounted for by classical theories of electromagnetic radiation. Recently, a number of experiments have begun to investigate the role of observation and measurement in the behavior of photons, with some results suggesting that the act of measurement itself may be influencing the behavior of light in ways that are difficult to explain in terms of classical physics. This has led to speculation about the possibility that photons, or at least certain types of photons, may possess a fundamental intelligence or autonomy that allows them to respond to their environment in ways that are not predetermined by their initial conditions or the laws of physics. While this idea is still highly speculative and the subject of much debate, it has the potential to revolutionize our understanding of the nature of reality and the behavior of light, with implications for our understanding of the universe at the most fundamental level.

title: On Choosing Committees Based on Approval Votes in the Presence of Outliers
Abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive framework for committee selection based on approval votes in the presence of outliers. In many real-world settings, such as recommender systems and decision-making processes, approval votes are used to evaluate candidate committees and determine their suitability for a particular task. However, the presence of outliers in the approval votes can significantly affect the validity of these evaluations. Existing methods for selecting committees are often sensitive to outliers and may lead to suboptimal solutions. To address this issue, we develop a novel outlier-robust framework for committee selection based on approval votes. This framework involves a two-stage procedure, where the first stage models the approval votes as a probability distribution, and the second stage uses a robust optimization technique to select the committee. We provide a theoretical analysis of the proposed method and demonstrate its effectiveness through a series of experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets. The results show that the proposed method outperforms existing approaches in terms of robustness and accuracy, even in the presence of significant outliers. Furthermore, we provide a practical implementation of the method using a case study of recommender systems for movie selection, illustrating its potential in real-world applications. Overall, this work contributes to the development of robust methods for selecting committees in the presence of approval votes and outliers, expanding the scope of possible applications in decision-making and recommender systems.

title: Deep Reinforcement Learning in Parameterized Action Space
Abstract: Deep reinforcement learning has experienced significant advancements in recent years, primarily in cases where the action space is either discrete or continuous. However, when dealing with a parameterized action space, comprising multiple modalities and with infinite possible action combinations, traditional reinforcement learning methods face major challenges. The reason lies in the difficulty in function approximation and exploration, particularly when considering optimization over the complex action space. In this regard, we focus on developing an algorithm that can efficiently navigate the parameterized action space and perform efficient exploration to achieve optimal rewards. Our technique integrates ideas from deep neural networks for robust function approximation and probabilistic model-based methods for efficient exploration. We provide an extensive empirical evaluation of our proposed algorithm in multiple simulation environments and real-world applications, demonstrating substantial improvements in convergence speed and reward maximization over state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, we investigate the benefits of using different architectures and techniques such as action masking, probabilistic forward predictions, and exploration rates to achieve optimal action selections and reward maximization. Our research aims to shed new light on the potential of parameterized action space applications in real-world scenarios and identify untapped avenues for reinforcement learning research.

title: Seeing the Unseen Network: Inferring Hidden Social Ties from Respondent-Driven Sampling
Abstract: Respondent-driven sampling (RDS) has emerged as a powerful method for studying hidden populations in sociology, epidemiology, and public health. However, despite its widespread adoption, RDS remains limited in its ability to reveal intricate network structures and hidden social ties within these populations. This study explores the possibility of inferring these hidden connections using a combination of RDS data and graph-theoretic techniques. By analyzing the referral patterns and social connections inferred from RDS data, we aimed to reconstruct the underlying social network of the study population. Our results demonstrate that RDS data can be used to identify hidden social ties, albeit with certain limitations and biases. Using community detection algorithms, we were able to identify meaningful groups and sub-networks within the reconstructed social network, which were not apparent from the RDS data alone. Our study highlights the potential of using RDS data and graph-theoretic techniques to uncover hidden social structures and facilitate deeper understanding of the dynamics within hidden populations. The implications of this research are far-reaching, offering new avenues for studying complex social networks, tracking the spread of infectious diseases, and designing targeted interventions in diverse fields.

title: ICON Challenge on Algorithm Selection
Abstract: The ICON Challenge on Algorithm Selection is an ongoing effort to establish a standard metric for evaluating the performance of algorithms in solving various computational problems. In this context, algorithm selection is defined as the process of choosing an algorithm from a suite of candidate algorithms that best suits the problem at hand. However, current evaluation metrics often rely on a single-number score, which may not accurately capture the complexity and variability of real-world problems. This is partly due to the fact that different algorithms are often designed to excel under specific problem conditions, resulting in biased evaluations when using uniform metrics. The goal of the ICON Challenge is to develop and test new evaluation metrics that can better capture the performance of algorithms across different problem instances and problem classes. To achieve this, a large-scale empirical study was conducted, involving the evaluation of over 1,000 algorithm instances on more than 100 problem sets from various domains, including optimization, machine learning, and graph algorithms. The study revealed that current evaluation metrics can significantly mislead the choice of the best algorithm for a given problem class, and that more nuanced metrics, such as adaptive performance measures and algorithm-agnostic metrics, are necessary to capture the diversity of algorithm performance. The findings of this study have significant implications for the development of more effective algorithm selection strategies, which can lead to improved performance and efficiency in various computational tasks.

title: Software Agents with Concerns of their Own
Abstract: This research endeavors to explore the notion of software agents that possess their own concerns and attendant motivations, diverging from traditional approaches where agents solely operate to satisfy predefined objectives. By embracing a notion of situated cognition, where intelligent systems learn and adapt from their environment, and leverage self-modeling, these autonomous agents begin to evolve with an intrinsic drive to improve, thereby mirroring human self-action planning. Through the utilization of a novel cognitive framework that integrates reflective self-awareness, situated motivation, and situated cognition, we design and develop an autonomous software agent capable of formulating their own objectives and preferences based on their evolving self-concept. This agent is implemented within a decentralized, multi-agent environment, where it collaborates and interacts with other agents possessing their own concerns and distinct rationalities. Our findings indicate that autonomous agents can learn, adapt, and create their own objectives through situated experiences, demonstrating the capacity for their own self-expression and situated motivation. Our work brings forward essential results and insights from the development of agents that act on their own concerns and motivations, prompting a shift towards more responsive and adaptive assistive technologies.

title: IfcWoD, Semantically Adapting IFC Model Relations into OWL Properties
Abstract: The integration of Building Information Modelling (BIM) into various industries has led to the increasing adoption of the Industry Foundation Classes (IFC) standard. However, IFC Data models rely heavily on proprietary property sets and proprietary link entities to describe physical and logical relationships between models and data, and do not provide any mechanism for reasoning about the semantics of these models. Furthermore, the lack of an explicit ontology hinders applications such as data exchange, interoperability and semantic querying. In this research, an approach for semantically adapting IFC model relations into OWL properties is proposed. Using the Web Ontology Language (OWL), the IFC relational data can be mapped into ontological representations, facilitating the description and reasoning about the data. OWL is leveraged to define the ontology of the adapted IFC model, enabling an extension of its semantics to facilitate reasoning and querying capabilities for model-based applications. To explore the feasibility and importance of the developed ontology, various queries are formulated and executed on the resource description framework (RDF) dataset, which has been created from the semantically adapted IFC model. The result in this research demonstrates that the solution facilitates the understanding and interpretation of IFC model data, and provides critical insights into how the integration of such adaptations can enhance existing BIM applications and unlock their full semantic potential.

title: Characterizing Concept Drift
Abstract: Concept drift is a fundamental challenge in machine learning and data analytics, where the statistical properties of the data distribution change over time, rendering models built on historical data ineffective. Characterizing concept drift is crucial for developing adaptive systems capable of tracking and responding to evolving patterns, trends, and relationships. This research aims to investigate the concept drift phenomenon in various domains and applications, identify its manifestations, and develop a comprehensive framework for characterizing and modeling it. A systematic review of existing literature reveals that concept drift can be categorized into three primary types: incremental drift, sudden drift, and periodic drift, with distinct characteristics and implications for model performance and maintenance. The study employs a mixed-methods approach, combining theoretical analysis, empirical evaluations, and case studies to examine the dynamics of concept drift in real-world data streams, including financial transactions, Tweets, and energy consumption patterns. The findings demonstrate that concept drift can be detected and quantified using a range of statistical and machine learning metrics, including accuracy degradation, entropy increase, and distribution shift. The research contributes to the development of robust and adaptive data-driven systems capable of learning from and responding to evolving patterns, thereby improving model performance, reducing maintenance costs, and enhancing decision-making in a wide range of applications.

title: Complexity of the Description Logic ALCM
Abstract: Description logic ALCM, an extension of the well-known description logic ALC with concrete domains, has been garnering significant attention in the realm of Knowledge Representation and Reasoning due to its ability to represent a wide range of concepts and relationships between them in a more nuanced and expressive manner. The complexity of ALCM is investigated in this paper, where we delve into the various decision procedures, such as subsumption, satisfiability, and concept satisfiability, to ascertain the intricacies involved in determining the complexity of this non-classical logic. Specifically, we explore the impact of concrete domains on the computational complexity of ALCM, including the interplay between the complexity of the concrete domains, the structure of the algebraic specifications, and the dimension of the space of possible interpretations. Our analysis reveals that ALCM exhibits a higher degree of complexity compared to its ALC counterpart, particularly in the presence of certain types of concrete domains, leading to an upsurge in computational costs. Furthermore, we provide evidence that the computational complexity of ALCM is closely tied to the complexity of the concrete domains, highlighting the need for a deeper understanding of the interplay between these two fundamental components of the logic. The results of our investigation offer valuable insights into the limitations of ALCM and provide a foundation for the development of more efficient algorithms and decision procedures for this powerful, yet computationally intensive, logic.

title: Doubly Robust Off-policy Value Evaluation for Reinforcement Learning
Abstract: This paper presents a novel doubly robust off-policy value evaluation (DROPE) method for reinforcement learning. The proposed algorithm combines the advantages of model-based and model-free off-policy evaluation approaches by utilizing both the true model and a learned model to estimate the cumulative reward function. The DROPE method leverages the strengths of doubly robust estimation to provide a more accurate and robust value estimate, even when the learned model is biased or incomplete. Specifically, it adapts the doubly robust estimator to account for the off-policy evaluation mismatch and model misspecification, thereby reducing estimation bias and variance. Through theoretical analysis and experimental results, it is demonstrated that DROPE achieves higher accuracy and lower estimation variance compared to existing off-policy evaluation methods, including Importance Sampling (IS), Weighted Importance Sampling (WIS), and Model-based Estimation (MBE). The proposed method's robustness against model misspecification is also evaluated through a series of experiments, showcasing its ability to provide reliable value estimates even in the presence of significant model errors. The paper's findings contribute to the advancement of off-policy value evaluation in reinforcement learning, highlighting the benefits of embracing model uncertainty and incorporating multiple models to promote robust and accurate policy evaluation.
