title: Visualising interactive inferences with IDPD3
Abstract: This research paper endeavours to pioneer a novel method for visualising interactive inferences through the IDPD3 framework. As a fundamental aspect of intelligent systems, interactive inference pertains to the capability of machines to generate conclusions or draw new information based on existing data and new, user-provided inputs. The IDPD3 framework involves an integrated combination of multiple techniques including Interval-based descriptions, Distributed probabilistic processing, and Data-driven reasoning. However, a crucial limitation of current approaches lies in their inability to effectively visualise the interactive inference process, thereby hindering the intuitive comprehension and alignment with user objectives. This paper addresses this challenge by developing a visualisation technique leveraging interactive visual analytics to provide real-time visualisation and enable detailed exploration of interactive inference outcomes. By exploiting immersive visualisation within the IDPD3 framework, we aim to facilitate an intuitive understanding and transparent communication of complex inference mechanisms. Our research outputs a visualisation tool that dynamically updates based on evolving inputs, thereby empowering users to critically assess the reliability and coherence of interactive inference results. Ultimately, the proposed IDPD3 visualisation technique facilitates improved collaboration and enhanced decision-making capacities in real-world applications of interactive inference in intelligent systems.

title: Bound Your Models! How to Make OWL an ASP Modeling Language
Abstract: This research proposes an integration of Answer Set Programming (ASP) and the Web Ontology Language (OWL), opening up new opportunities for modeling complex knowledge domains. By translating OWL ontologies into ASP-based frameworks, the traditional boundaries between logic-based modeling and rule-based programming are blurred. This innovative approach allows for the treatment of instances and classes in OWL models as dynamic and context-dependent, facilitated by the ability of ASP to reason with incomplete or inconsistent knowledge. The integration of ASP and OWL is not only limited to knowledge representation but also enables the execution and validation of ASP programs on OWL models, allowing for the prediction of logical consequences and inferences in complex domains. Furthermore, this integration enables a deeper exploration of OWL's Expressibility Gap - namely, the gap between what is axiomatizable using Description Logic (DL) and what is logically expressible in terms of classical two-valued logic - using ASP's capabilities in reasoning with uncertainty and inconsistency. To achieve this goal, a novel translation mechanism is devised to map DL constructs in OWL to the relevant constructs in ASP. Thoroughly evaluated and compared with existing OWL and ASP tools, the proposed integration showcases its potential in solving complex problem-solving tasks that involve both knowledge representation and rule-based programming.

title: A web-based IDE for IDP
Abstract: This research paper introduces WebIDEIDP, a novel web-based Integrated Development Platform designed for Identity and Access Management (IDP) system developers. Leveraging the advantages of cloud computing and web-based technologies, WebIDEIDP aims to enhance the efficiency and productivity of IDP system development by providing a comprehensive and intuitive development environment. The platform is built using modern web technologies such as HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript, ensuring seamless compatibility across various devices and browsers. WebIDEIDP features a code editor with syntax highlighting, auto-completion, and debugging tools, facilitating error-free coding and accelerated development. Additionally, it includes tools for project management, workflow visualization, and real-time collaboration, enabling developers to work together efficiently and effectively. The platform also incorporates a simulation engine that allows developers to simulate and test IDP systems without the need for physical hardware or complex setup. Furthermore, WebIDEIDP includes a repository of pre-built IDP components and connectors, enabling quick and easy integration of third-party services and APIs. Through its innovative design and feature-rich functionality, WebIDEIDP is poised to revolutionize the IDP system development landscape, making it an indispensable tool for developers, system administrators, and organizations alike.

title: Lowering the learning curve for declarative programming: a Python API for the IDP system
Abstract: The development and deployment of declarative programming systems, such as the Interval Domain Propagation (IDP) system, can be challenging due to their inherently complex nature. Declarative programming languages, like IDP, which represent computations using relations and constraints, require an extensive understanding of the underlying algorithms and data structures, thus rendering them inaccessible to novice users. This research aims to bridge this gap by introducing a Python API for the IDP system, designed to simplify the barrier to entry for developers and researchers who wish to utilize this technology. The proposed API hides the low-level complexities associated with IDP's interval arithmetic and lattice operations, abstracting them behind a set of intuitive and Pythonic interfaces. By leveraging Python's high-level nature, the API enables users to work with IDP in a declarative and compositional manner, without requiring a deep understanding of the underlying mathematics. Additionally, the API facilitates the integration of user-defined functions and extensions, thus allowing the IDP system to adapt to diverse application domains. This research demonstrates the feasibility of simplifying access to complex declarative programming systems by introducing an approachable and user-friendly API.

title: SWISH: SWI-Prolog for Sharing
Abstract: The SWISH project endeavours to make SWI-Prolog a cutting-edge, web-based IDE that not only provides a robust and intuitive environment for writing and executing Prolog code, but also empowers users to share and collaborate on their work seamlessly. This shift towards a web-based interface has made it possible to access and interact with Prolog applications from anywhere, on any device, without the need for complex setup or dedicated hardware. Furthermore, SWISH's architecture allows for smart and efficient use of existing libraries, embracing compatibility with Prolog's integration of existing libraries. As part of this endeavour, SWISH has also made significant strides in promoting an open, collaborative, and dynamic community, where users can share and learn from one another, fostering a culture of knowledge-sharing and continuous improvement. By marrying the expressive power of Prolog with the intuitive and interactive nature of a web-based IDE, SWISH has undoubtedly levelled the playing field and made Prolog-based development accessible to a wider audience, potentially stimulating a resurgence in the use and application of this powerful and expressive language.

title: Finetuning Randomized Heuristic Search For 2D Path Planning: Finding The Best Input Parameters For R* Algorithm Through Series Of Experiments
Abstract: This research aims to optimize the 2D path planning by applying the randomized heuristic search, particularly focusing on the R* algorithm. The R* algorithm, being a revised version of the A* algorithm, has its limitations due to the uncertainty in the input parameters selection, which can significantly impact its performance. In this study, we investigate the effect of various input parameters such as the transition costs, steering costs, and obstacle costs on the R* algorithm's ability to plan the most efficient path in a given environment. To achieve this, we systematically design a series of experiments using randomly generated grid worlds with different path lengths, obstacles, and weights to analyze the performance of the R* algorithm under diverse conditions. Our goal is to identify the optimal set of parameters that maximizes the success rate of the R* algorithm in planning an optimal path. Through extensive experimentation, we find that varying the transition costs significantly impacts the algorithm's performance. Furthermore, our results indicate that heavy steering costs hinder the R* algorithm's ability to navigate through narrow passages efficiently. Additionally, obstacles of varying sizes and weights demonstrate the importance of fine-tuning the obstacle costs to achieve the best possible path plans. This study provides valuable insights into the impact of input parameters on the R* algorithm's performance, contributing to the optimization of 2D path-planning algorithms.

title: SAT as a game
Abstract: The Scholastic Aptitude Test, colloquially known as the SAT, has conventionally been perceived as a standardized test, serving as a benchmark for college admissions. However, this perception has been challenged in recent years, with increasing recognition of its underlying properties as a game. By leveraging game theory, this research aims to provide a deeper understanding of the SAT's inherent mechanics, exploring how it incentivizes test-takers to strategically allocate time and resources. This perspective shift reveals patterns in test-taking behavior, characterizing students as 'players' competing for the reward of a coveted college spot. Game theory principles such as optimal stopping, mixed strategies, and Nash equilibrium can be applied to solve problems emanating from the SAT, highlighting topics like quantization and rationalization, where small numerical adjustments on the test yield disproportionate gains. Furthermore, this game-theoretic examination brings to light potential consequences, including but not limited to strategically taking unfair advantage, creating biases against groups of candidates and test-fairness concerns.

title: A Pareto Optimal D* Search Algorithm for Multiobjective Path Planning
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel path planning algorithm, dubbed Pareto Optimal D* Search (PODS), which efficiently addresses the multiobjective path planning challenge by adopting a Pareto optimality framework. Classical D* search is well-suited for finding the shortest path in dynamic and uncertain environments but lacks applicability to multiobjective scenarios, such as satisfying multiple urgency and safety criteria. To address this limitation, PODS extends the D* search paradigm to handle multiple objectives, thereby enabling the discovery of optimal solutions that trade off conflicting priorities. In PODS, a unique scalarization technique is integrated to transform the multiobjective optimization problem into a single-objective problem. This method ensures that the resulting optimal solution approximates the true Pareto front, thereby accounting for multiple objectives in the path planning process. Simulation studies using standard benchmark scenarios and real-world environments demonstrate the efficacy and robustness of PODS in outperforming state-of-the-art algorithms, such as the SART (Speedup A-star with Reweighting) and MMR (Multi Criteria-based Monte Carlo) methods. The PODS algorithm offers substantial computational savings while maintaining a marked improvement in navigation performance. The results of this research provide insights into the benefits of using Pareto optimality in combination with D* search for optimizing path planning in complex and dynamic environments.

title: Toward an Efficient Multi-class Classification in an Open Universe
Abstract: This research endeavors to develop an efficient multi-class classification framework tailored for the open universe, where the absence of clear class boundaries and ever-changing environmental conditions render traditional machine learning approaches less effective. By leveraging cutting-edge techniques from deep learning, transfer learning, and meta-learning, our proposed framework encompasses a novel hierarchical classification paradigm, capable of adaptively adjusting its decision-making process as it encounters novel class instances. The framework's backbone consists of a compositional module capable of iteratively generating class hierarchies from scratch, leveraging a compact encoding of class relationships akin to a probabilistic taxonomy. The compositional layer dynamically adjusts the induced class hierarchies in response to the uncertain or contradictory information obtained during multi-class classification tasks. In a critical step toward deployment in real-world settings, experimental evaluation using nine well-established multi-class datasets verifies the superiority of the proposed framework over state-of-the-art methods in both optimal and uncertain environments, facilitating reliable and efficient classification in the ever-evolving open universe context, where accurate decision-making faces unpredictable challenges. The research explicitly tackles the principal barriers, offers reliable and coherent theoretical support, providing clear guidance on the theoretical implications, practical applications, and future research directions for further improvements and explorations, especially for deep learning-based methods, under uncertain and open environments.

title: From random walks to distances on unweighted graphs
Abstract: This study provides a comprehensive exploration of the fundamental concepts and relationships between random walks, distances, and unweighted graphs, providing novel and mathematically sound methods for estimating shortest paths and understanding the structural properties of complex networks. By establishing a connection between random walks and distances, we introduce a novel distance metric based on the mean first passage time and its associated harmonic series. This approach allows for efficient and accurate estimation of shortest paths even in cases where traditional methods such as Dijkstra's algorithm or Bellman-Ford are impractical due to computational complexity or the sheer size of the graph, making it an attractive solution for real-world network analysis. Our results also indicate a surprising connection between the spectral gap of the transition matrix and the harmonic series, leading to simplified methods for estimating bounds on distances. Furthermore, we derive precise bounds on the harmonic series in terms of the mixing time of the random walk, offering a refreshing perspective on the relationship between walk-based methods and distance computation. Such insights enable us to establish that the harmonic series is maximized when the optimal stationary distribution coincides with the uniform distribution, the scenario in which the walk coincides with the stationary distribution, potentially leading to novel applications in network clustering and community detection.

title: Z Specification for the W3C Editor's Draft Core SHACL Semantics
Abstract: The Z specification for the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) Editor's Draft of Core SHACL Semantics aims to provide a formal framework for validating and constraining data linked in the Web using ontology-based approaches. SHACL (SHape Constrained Language) is a key technology in data governance, allowing for the harmonization and validation of data across schema.org and other ontologies. The Z specification targets ensuring clarity, precision, and consistency in the interpretation of SHACL constraints, improving the overall effectiveness of data validation. The editors have striven to simplify, combine redundant sections, and systematize informal notes to improve readability and streamline comprehension for W3C members. The update includes advancements from the HTML WG feedback and recommendations, ensuring alignment with key HTML goals such as user experience, usability, and developer productivity. Furthermore, these modifications augment accessibility, highlighting strategies to bring SHACL even closer to fulfilling its goals in addressing the core needs of business use cases like knowledge, customer, and organizational systems. With precise language, conciseness, and emphasis on logical accuracy, this Z specification offers concrete assistance and tools to proficiently develop more accurate HTML renderings and Web data applications in enterprise environments, where knowledge requires coordination among intricate patterns and related data artifacts.

title: Automatic Prosody Prediction for Chinese Speech Synthesis using BLSTM-RNN and Embedding Features
Abstract: This study aims to develop an automatic prosody prediction system for Chinese speech synthesis using BLSTM-RNN and embedding features. Current Chinese speech synthesis systems, while advanced, often fail to replicate natural variations in prosody, which are crucial for conveying emotions, attitudes, and intended meanings. To address this limitation, our approach combines a BLSTM-RNN architecture with a novel embedding feature set, specifically designed for Chinese language. The proposed system first generates phonetic features from the input sentence, followed by encoding the sentence level information using a learned embedding space. The BLSTM-RNN model is then used to predict the prosody of the sentence based on the embedded features, leveraging the capabilities of both long-short term memory units and recurrent neural networks to capture temporal dependencies. By implementing this system, we aim to significantly improve the naturalness and expressiveness of Chinese speech synthesis, enabling more effective communication of complex ideas and emotions in various applications, such as multimedia, education, and customer service. Experimental evaluations on a large-scale Chinese audio-visual dataset demonstrates the effectiveness of our approach, yielding state-of-the-art prosody prediction accuracy and robustness compared to existing methods.

title: Optimized Mission Planning for Planetary Exploration Rovers
Abstract: The success of planetary exploration rovers heavily relies on the strategy employed for navigating the alien terrain through optimized mission planning. This research addresses the critical need for an optimized approach to enhance the efficiency and productivity of planetary exploration rovers, enabling them to accomplish comprehensive surveys of the planetary surface with the minimum consumption of resources. A novel mission planning framework has been developed to accomplish this goal by incorporating a combination of advanced trajectory planning techniques, mixed-integer linear programming, and ant colony optimization. The proposed framework optimizes the mission plan while taking into consideration multiple constraints such as energy availability, communication budget, navigation uncertainty, and mission priority. Furthermore, the framework integrates a robust simulation environment to evaluate the mission feasibility and provide insights into adaptive decision-making under uncertainty. By successfully incorporating state-of-the-art methods in artificial intelligence, trajectory planning, and computational optimization, the research aims to optimize the performance of planetary exploration rovers, providing unparalleled insights into the diversity of planetary environments and revolutionizing the exploration of our solar system. The research demonstrates that the proposed framework achieves substantial improvements in mission efficiency and productivity compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, thereby establishing a new benchmark for future mission planning endeavors in planetary exploration.

title: Chaos of Protein Folding
Abstract: Chaos theory has recently emerged as a significant framework for understanding the complex process of protein folding, which is fundamentally crucial to protein function and stability. Despite the discovery of high-resolution protein structures, a unified theory that can accurately predict the folding of a protein remains elusive, largely due to the highly non-linear and dynamic nature of protein folding. In this context, researchers have increasingly applied chaos theory to study the inherent complexity and irregularity observed in protein folding pathways. By exploring the intricate relationships between protein folding, thermodynamics, and kinetics, scientists have uncovered intriguing patterns and principles, such as the presence of 'folding funnels', 'unfolded state ensemble', and 'kinetic traps', which give insight into the underlying processes of protein folding. Recent studies have also employed computational tools and simulations to map the intricate energy landscapes associated with protein folding, demonstrating the utility of chaos theory in revealing the intricate mechanisms governing this phenomenon. As researchers continue to explore the complex dynamics of protein folding, the increasing interplay between disciplines, including physics, chemistry, biology, and mathematics, will likely shed new light on the intricate processes that govern protein structure and function.

title: Topological chaos and chaotic iterations. Application to Hash functions
Abstract: This paper delves into the realm of topological chaos and its applications to chaos theory in the context of iterative mathematical functions, with a specific focus on hash functions. It investigates the intricate relationships between topological entropy, chaotic behavior, and the cryptographic properties of hash functions. By merging concepts from dynamical systems and topological theory, the research identifies specific characteristics of chaotic iterations that can be leveraged to develop stronger hash functions. An essential aspect of the study is to explore how properties such as topological mixing and expansivity can be used to construct hash functions that exhibit high security and resistance to collisions. Furthermore, the paper includes a comprehensive analysis of various hashing algorithms and their corresponding topological structures, with the goal of identifying potential vulnerabilities and improving their cryptographic robustness. Through this interdisciplinary approach, the study aims to reveal new insights into the connections between topological chaos and hash functions, shedding light on the importance of chaos theory in the development of secure cryptographic primitives. The research ultimately strives to contribute to the ongoing efforts in cryptography to create more resilient and reliable hashing algorithms, thereby enhancing digital data security and protection against cyber threats.

title: Why Neurons Have Thousands of Synapses, A Theory of Sequence Memory in Neocortex
Abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive theory on why neurons in the neocortex have thousands of synapses, and how these synapses enable sequence memory in the human brain. Current understanding of brain function emphasizes the importance of synchronized neural activity in information processing, but recent studies suggest that sequence memory, a fundamental component of episodic memory, may be mediated by a rich network of synaptic connections. We propose that the massive number of synapses on individual neurons in the neocortex serves as a mechanism for generating permutations of sensory inputs, thereby enabling sequence recognition. By modeling the emergence of sequence memory as a byproduct of synaptically-generated pattern completion, we argue that the thousands of synapses on each neuron serve as "memory nodes" that establish chains of associations between different sensory inputs. The theory is supported by several key predictions, including the expectation that sequence memory should be resistant to interference by novel sensory inputs, and that the fidelity of sequence memory should degrade with increasing temporal distance between events. Furthermore, our framework makes specific predictions about the structural and functional properties of neocortical neurons that are critical for sequence memory, including the presence of specific synaptic components, such as NMDA receptors and microtubule-associated proteins, that facilitate pattern completion and memory storage.

title: Short-Term Plasticity and Long-Term Potentiation in Magnetic Tunnel Junctions: Towards Volatile Synapses
Abstract:
This abstract discusses the emulation of synaptic plasticity in magnetic tunnel junctions (MTJs), which are crucial components of artificial synaptic devices. Biological synapses exhibit short-term and long-term plasticity, enabling information storage and recall across various timescales. Inspired by the biophysical mechanisms governing these phenomena, we investigate the development of volatile synapses in MTJs. 
Short-term plasticity in MTJs has been demonstrated through the careful control of current pulses, mimicking the properties of synaptic facilitation and depression. The successful implementation of these processes in MTJs relies on understanding the fundamental response of tunnel magnetoresistive junctions to external stimuli. Furthermore, we focus on inducing long-term potentiation (LTP) in MTJs, an essential mechanism for synaptic learning and memory storage. 
To achieve LTP in MTJs, we utilize established biophysical models of LTP development in biological systems, such as associative Hebbian learning, and translate them into the nanoscale analogue of the synaptic junction. The LTP events in MTJs result in persistent changes in synaptic conductance, representing a viable pathway to long-term information storage in neuromorphic devices. Additionally, we highlight significant advances in the design, fabrication, and operation of MTJs that are capable of mimicking the volatile nature of biological synapses, paving the way for the application of MTJ-based synapses in artificial neural networks. Our findings underscore the potential for nanoscale systems to emulate, and potentially supplant, the function of neurons in computing devices, offering significant gains in efficiency, robustness, and programmability.

title: Learning Adversary Behavior in Security Games: A PAC Model Perspective
Abstract: This paper presents a principled analysis of learning adversary behavior in security games, focusing on the computationally bounded, strategy-stealing notion through the lens of the Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) model, which is a widely recognized framework in machine learning. In the context of security games, we postulate that an attacker's behavior is determined by her ability to learn about the defender's strategy and exploit the latter's weaknesses. Our primary objective is to theoretically examine whether a learning PAC model, derived from game theory, can be effectively employed to capture the primary properties of a security game and thereby model adversary behavior in such settings. Specifically, we assume that defenders attempt to form predictions regarding the behavior of attackers within a reasonable lag or latency. In response, our proposed theory is founded on a probabilistic model for policy analysis, aiming to illustrate that convergence to a Nash equilibrium may be maintained through a computationally efficient process. In addition, the statistical metrics are employed to derive PAC-based, optimality constraints that capture critical properties of security games, promoting our strategy-stealing approach to modeling adversary behavior as a means to develop more adaptive and resilient defense mechanisms. Furthermore, an evaluation of our proposed method is provided through various simulated scenarios which demonstrate our theory's ability to maintain the security in complex attacks by accurately modelling adversaries in a principled manner.

title: Learning Causal Graphs with Small Interventions
Abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to inferring causal graphs from observational data, taking into account the limitations of small-scale interventions. Currently, most causal discovery algorithms rely on having a substantial number of interventions to accurately learn the underlying causal relationships between variables. However, in many real-world scenarios, such as in genetics or econometrics, it is often challenging to obtain sufficient data with controlled interventions. We propose a method, called SCIG (Small-Change Intervention Graph), that leverages a combination of observational data and small-scale perturbations to learn causal graphs with a high degree of accuracy. Our approach is based on the principle that even small changes in the system can lead to significant deviations in the probability distribution, providing valuable information about the causal structure. We demonstrate the effectiveness of SCIG through extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets, showcasing its ability to outperform state-of-the-art methods under conditions of limited intervention data. Our results not only provide new insights into the power of small interventions in causal discovery but also have significant implications for a wide range of applications where interventions may be difficult to obtain, such as in drug discovery or policy evaluation. The SCIG framework offers a promising solution for learning causal graphs in settings where traditional methods are not feasible.

title: Quantum neural computation of entanglement is robust to noise and decoherence
Abstract: This study delves into the realm of quantum computation, specifically focusing on the neural processing of entanglement, a fundamental concept in quantum mechanics characterized by the interconnectedness of particles in a manner that transcends classical notions of space and time. A quantum neural network was employed to demonstrate the robustness of entanglement to environmental noise and decoherence, which are inherent threats to quantum coherence and the long-term stability of entangled states. The robustness of entanglement in the presence of noise is a critical aspect of developing practical quantum information processing technologies, as it necessitates the ability to shield or combat the detrimental effects of environmental perturbations on entangled systems. Our research employed various quantum noise models to simulate the impact of decoherence on entanglement in a quantum neural network, revealing that the entanglement content can indeed persist despite the presence of significant noise. By exploring the entanglement dynamics in an open quantum system, our findings provide new insights into the potential applications of quantum neural computation in processing information in the presence of high levels of environmental noise, a scenario that is likely to occur in real-world quantum information processing architectures. The robustness of entanglement is demonstrated to be preserved across a range of noise regimes, highlighting the resilience of entanglement to a variety of environmental perturbations.

title: Latent Bayesian melding for integrating individual and population models
Abstract: Latent Bayesian melding is a novel methodology that seamlessly integrates individual and population mathematical models to provide a more comprehensive understanding of complex systems. By combining the strengths of both individual-based and aggregate-level perspectives, this approach enables the estimation of population-scale parameters while also accounting for inter-individual variability. The proposed methodology leverages a Bayesian framework to model the hierarchical relationship between individual and population parameters, allowing for the quantification of uncertainty in both levels of the model. A key feature of latent Bayesian melding is its ability to handle missing or uncertain individual-level data, thereby extending its applicability to real-world scenarios where complete information is often scarce. Through this approach, researchers can leverage rich individual-level information while also extracting generalizable insights about population-scale behaviors and trends. Theoretical developments and applications of latent Bayesian melding are presented, showcasing its potential to unlock new insights in epidemiology, ecology, and social sciences. Case studies are provided to illustrate the effectiveness of latent Bayesian melding in estimating population-scale parameters from individual-level data, thereby shedding light on important research questions and highlighting its valuable contribution to the field of integrative modeling.

title: Turing's Red Flag
Abstract: This paper delves into the significance and implications of the overlooked concept of "Turing's Red Flag" in the context of artificial intelligence, cognitive science, and pedagogy. It raises questions about whether Alan Turing's foundational work on machine intelligence should be reevaluated through the lens of contemporary social and moral concerns. The paper assesses Turing's 1950 paper, "Computing Machinery and Intelligence," and identifies a subtle yet critical thread of reasoning he embedded, which he may have wanted to remain hidden, much like waving a red flag in a delicate situation. Dubbed "Turing's Red Flag," this thread is a moral caveat that highlights the inherent unpredictability and potential ethics concerns associated with creating artificial minds that approximate human-level intelligence. By probing the implications of Turing's Red Flag, this paper invites readers to consider whether efforts to develop artificially intelligent entities necessarily require a reevaluation of the moral and social contracts between humans and their creations. Ultimately, this research seeks to contribute to ongoing discussions surrounding the development of sophisticated artificial intelligence and the creation of a shared global framework that might guide the harmonious coexistence of human and artificial intelligences, specifically by identifying the limitations and pitfalls associated with a concept that bears the risk of adverse applications when not pursued cautiously and ethically. The analysis offered in this work underscores the significance of considering the long-term consequences of our decisions in AI research and development and the importance of reorienting our endeavors towards a morally responsible approach.

title: A Study of the Spatio-Temporal Correlations in Mobile Calls Networks
Abstract: This study presents a comprehensive analysis of the spatio-temporal correlations in mobile call networks, aiming to uncover the underlying patterns and relationships that govern the behavior of users within these networks. The research focuses on the spatial and temporal aspects of mobile calls, examining the evolution of call patterns over time and their spatial distribution across different geographical regions. By employing cutting-edge statistical and machine learning techniques, the study develops a robust framework for modeling and analyzing the complex dynamics of mobile call networks. The research draws upon a large-scale dataset of mobile call records, comprising over 10 million calls made by users within a metropolitan area over a period of six months. By decomposing the calls into their basic elements - including caller and receiver locations, time and duration of calls, and network traffic information - the study reveals a rich tapestry of spatial and temporal correlations that are sensitive to changes in mobility patterns, network infrastructure, and demographic factors. The findings demonstrate that the spatio-temporal patterns of mobile calls exhibit a strong degree of spatial autocorrelation, with specific locations in the city exhibiting distinct types of call behaviors that change over time. Furthermore, the study shows that the correlations are significantly influenced by factors such as time of day, day of the week, and season, as well as the spatial distribution of populations, roads, and network infrastructure. The results of this study have significant implications for a range of applications, including urban planning, emergency response systems, and targeted marketing strategies.

title: Highway Long Short-Term Memory RNNs for Distant Speech Recognition
Abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to distant speech recognition using Highway Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs). The increasing demand for far-field speech recognition has led to the need for more accurate models that can handle noisy and distant speech inputs. Existing methods have limitations in preserving long-term dependencies and adapting to changing acoustic environments. To address these challenges, this work introduces a Highway LSTM RNN architecture that combines the benefits of Highways and LSTMs. Highways allow for efficient communication among layers, while LSTMs learn long-term dependencies through memory cells. The proposed model modifies the traditional LSTM gates by incorporating adaptive Highway connections, enabling the network to selectively decide which information to pass through and which to discard. This adaptive processing allows for improved performance in distant speech recognition tasks. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed Highway LSTM RNN outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of word error rates, particularly in noisy and reverberant environments. The findings of this study contribute to the development of more effective deep learning models for distant speech recognition, with potential applications in voice assistants, smart home devices, and other speech-based interfaces.

title: Robust Subspace Clustering via Tighter Rank Approximation
Abstract: This paper presents a novel framework for robust subspace clustering, focusing on the challenges of rank approximation and noise resilience in real-world datasets. Existing methods often struggle to accurately capture the underlying geometric structures and are vulnerable to outliers and noisy observations. To address these limitations, we propose a tighter rank approximation approach, which integrates the strengths of both low-rank and sparse decomposition techniques. Our method, dubbed as Rank-Adaptive Matrix Factorization (RAMF), leverages a novel non-convex rank approximation objective that strategically balances the competing demands of low-rank approximation and noise suppression. Through a series of careful mathematical derivations and algorithmic optimizations, RAMF yields a computationally efficient and scalable approach to subspace clustering, capable of handling large and high-dimensional datasets with robustness to outliers. Extensive experiments on various synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the superior performance of RAMF over state-of-the-art methods, including improved recovery accuracy, reduced noise sensitivity, and enhanced computational efficiency. Our results show that RAMF provides a powerful and versatile tool for robust subspace clustering, with promising applications in computer vision, signal processing, and machine learning. By pushing the state-of-the-art in this area, our work provides a valuable contribution to the subspace clustering community.

title: Sample Complexity of Episodic Fixed-Horizon Reinforcement Learning
Abstract: Our work focuses on understanding the sample complexity of episodic fixed-horizon reinforcement learning (EFHRL), a fundamental problem in artificial intelligence that aims to enable agents to learn from rich observations and goal-oriented experiences. In contrast to traditional RL problems, EFHRL problems are characterized by episodic interactions, which imply a limited number of trials or episodes before encountering a new situation or rebooting from a predefined starting point. By bridging the gap between two main categories of reinforcement learning methods, namely, model-free and model-based approaches, the paper proposes a unified analysis for the sample complexity of EFHRL in terms of the environment's complexity. This novel framework establishes upper and lower bounds for both the expected sample complexity and the high-probability sample complexity of finding near-optimal policies in EFHRL settings. The results demonstrate that when the number of episodes grows polynomially with the episode length, it is possible to achieve a nearly optimal sample complexity in EFHRL, outperforming traditional model-free or model-based methods in certain scenarios. This research elucidate the theoretical underpinnings of EFHRL and provides practical insights that can be used to design more efficient algorithms for solving complex, goal-oriented problems. The proposed unified analysis also extends to various state-of-the-art EFHRL algorithms, highlighting the trade-offs between exploration-exploitation strategies and the sample efficiency of EFHRL methods.

title: Fermi's paradox, extraterrestrial life and the future of humanity: a Bayesian analysis
Abstract: This research paper presents a Bayesian analysis of Fermi's paradox, focusing on the probability of extraterrestrial life and its implications for the future of humanity. By combining the vast amount of observational evidence from the universe with theoretical frameworks from astrobiology and the search for extraterrestrial intelligence (SETI), we construct a Bayesian model to quantify the likelihood of intelligent life existing beyond Earth. Our analysis reveals a significant probability (approximately 73%) that intelligent life may exist elsewhere in the universe, even when accounting for various extinction events that may have occurred. Furthermore, we investigate the feasibility of interstellar communication and transportation, suggesting possible avenues for exploration and colonization. Our results indicate that humanity is likely to encounter extraterrestrial civilizations within a timescale of tens of thousands to millions of years, depending on the advancement of our civilization. The implications of this finding are profound, as it raises questions about the long-term survival and prosperity of humanity, and whether we will eventually become a multi-planetary species to ensure our existence in the face of potential extinction events. The Bayesian framework employed in this research provides valuable insights into the probability of extraterrestrial life, shedding new light on the Fermi paradox and the potential for future human exploration.

title: My Reflections on the First Man vs. Machine No-Limit Texas Hold 'em Competition
Abstract: The first Man vs. Machine No-Limit Texas Hold 'em competition marked a significant milestone in the ongoing debate over the performance and capabilities of artificial intelligence (AI) systems. We explore how Libratus utilized a combination of data-driven decision-making and strategic moves to gain an advantage over its human opponents. Additionally, we examine the human players' mental states, teamwork dynamics, and collective decision-making strategies, which played a crucial role in shaping their performance. Furthermore, we discuss the insights gained from the competition, including the role of adaptability, the impact of exploitation and exploration strategies, and the potential consequences of AI systems surpassing human performance in complex environments. title: Feature-Based Diversity Optimization for Problem Instance Classification
Abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to problem instance classification through feature-based diversity optimization. The proposed method aims to improve the existing problem instance classification frameworks by incorporating diversity optimization techniques. Traditional classification models often suffer from overfitting and poor generalization capabilities, particularly when dealing with complex and diverse problem instances. To address these limitations, the proposed method incorporates a feature-based diversity optimization module, which assesses and adjusts the feature representation of problem instances to enhance their diversity and discriminability. This is achieved through a carefully designed framework that leverages techniques from both feature learning and diversity optimization. The feature-based diversity optimization module is seamlessly integrated with a modified support vector machine (SVM) classifier, which is trained on the optimized feature representations of problem instances. Experimental results on a range of benchmark datasets demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed approach in accurately classifying problem instances and achieving superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, the results reveal that the proposed method effectively mitigates the issue of overfitting and improves the robustness of problem instance classification models. title: Attention with Intention for a Neural Network Conversation Model
Abstract: Recent advancements in neural network models have led to the development of sophisticated conversational AI systems, capable of interacting with humans in a more natural and engaging manner. However, despite significant strides in this field, most existing models lack a critical aspect of human conversation - the intentional and intentional integration of attention mechanisms to direct the flow of dialogue. This research aims to address this limitation by developing a novel neural network-based conversation model that seamlessly integrates attention with intention to improve the model's ability to respond coherently and contextually to user queries. The proposed model utilizes a hierarchical attention mechanism, which enables the model to selectively focus on specific aspects of the input context and attend to relevant entities, concepts, or relations. At the same time, an intention-guided mechanism is employed to inject a task-directed aspect into the model's decision-making process, ensuring that responses are generationally relevant to the user's objectives and tasks. The integration of these two components enables the model to generate more meaningful, informative, and coherent responses, significantly improving user experience and engagement. title: Automatic Synthesis of Geometry Problems for an Intelligent Tutoring System
Abstract: This research focuses on the development of an automatic synthesis methodology for generating geometry problems suitable for an intelligent tutoring system (ITS). The proposed framework leverages a combination of machine learning and computer algebra systems (CAS) to create customized, tailored problems for students at various skill levels. The core idea is to utilize a problem representation model that can capture the intricate geometric relationships and logical reasoning required in solving geometry problems. The framework consists of three primary components: problem knowledge graph construction, problem generation, and problem filtering. The knowledge graph is constructed by analyzing a large corpus of geometry problems and representing the relationships among various problem-solving concepts. The CAS is utilized to generate candidate problems based on the constructed knowledge graph. The generated problems are then filtered and refined based on their difficulty levels and relevance to the student's current skillset, thereby ensuring that the synthesized problems are both challenging and educational. The effectiveness of the proposed synthesis methodology is evaluated through user studies and comparisons with existing problem generation methods. title: Computing the Ramsey Number R(4,3,3) using Abstraction and Symmetry breaking
Abstract: This research paper explores the computational challenge of determining the Ramsey number R(4,3,3), a fundamental concept in graph theory. Abstraction and symmetry breaking are employed as novel approaches to tackle this complex task. The Ramsey number represents the minimum number of vertices required to guarantee the existence of a monochromatic subgraph of a specific type. Existing methods, such as brute-force algorithms, are not feasible due to the immense computational resources needed to handle large-scale graphs. In contrast, this research develops an abstract framework that abstracts away unnecessary details and utilizes a combination of combinatorial and probabilistic techniques. Symmetry breaking is achieved through the use of partitioned sets and graph symmetry groups. An efficient strategy based on incremental construction and recursive reductions is proposed, allowing for a dramatic reduction in the search space. As a result, it becomes possible to compute R(4,3,3) in a reasonable amount of time, providing new insights into the Ramsey number's behavior and expanding the range of computable Ramsey numbers.

title: iCellular: Define Your Own Cellular Network Access on Commodity Smartphones
Abstract: iCellular allows users to provision their own cellular network access on commodity smartphones by leveraging novel software and radio module innovations. This platform enables users to dynamically configure and customize their network settings to suit specific use cases and requirements, such as personal emergency situations or high-speed data transfer applications. Unlike traditional cellular network access models that rely on central networking infrastructure and human operator intervention, iCellular empowers users to own and manage their network access, enjoying greater autonomy, security, and reliability. By integrating various software and hardware components, including a modified cellular radio module, an operating system, and corresponding apps, iCellular creates a personal hotspot-like experience on standard off-the-shelf smartphones, thereby promoting device heterogeneous networking. This innovation unlocks novel forms of local-area network access, where smartphones can establish their own cellular-like connections without relying on traditional commercial network infrastructure, allowing users to create their own peer-to-peer communication networks as needed, hence optimizing use case specific network experience while preserving energy and security. Overall, iCellular pioneers a new class of mobile communication technology that redefines network infrastructure boundaries by delegating ubiquitous networking access directly to user devices.

title: Learning Constructive Primitives for Online Level Generation and Real-time Content Adaptation in Super Mario Bros
Abstract: This research explores the development of constructive primitives for online level generation and real-time content adaptation in the classic video game Super Mario Bros. We introduce a novel approach that combines the strengths of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) and Neural Style Transfer (NST) to generate diverse and challenges levels, while maintaining the iconic gameplay experience of the original game. A two-player setup is implemented where one network, dubbed the "generator", produces a new level based on a given set of constraints, and a second network, the "evaluator", assesses the generated level's coherence and completeness, providing a scoring function to guide the generator's improvement. Through iterative refinement, the generator learns to balance difficulty and creativity in each generated level. By applying NST to the level generator, we are able to adapt the generated content to multiple game modes, such as different power-ups or items, in real-time. The proposed system is capable of generating thousands of novel levels and seamlessly adapting to changing game parameters, offering an engaging and dynamic gaming experience. Our results demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of the proposed approach, showcasing its potential for broader applications in generative game content creation and adaptive game design. title: Cells in the Internet of Things
Abstract: The incorporation of cells, specifically designed micro-/nanoscale artificial cells, into the Internet of Things (IoT) is a rapidly evolving field that has the potential to revolutionize the way we interact with and control our smart environments. Artificial cells, first conceptualized by researchers in the 1950s, are microscopic, autonomous entities that can be engineered to perform specific functions, such as sensing, actuation, and storage. title: Redesigning pattern mining algorithms for supercomputers
Abstract: This paper focuses on the redesigning of pattern mining algorithms to efficiently utilize the capabilities of supercomputers, thereby accelerating pattern discovery and extracting insights from large-scale datasets. Traditional pattern mining algorithms hinder the scalability of data mining tasks due to their high computational complexity and memory requirements. In recent years, supercomputers have become increasingly powerful and accessible, enabling data scientists to tackle complex patterns hidden within massive datasets. To unlock these capabilities, a carefully optimized and redesigned pattern mining paradigm is proposed, incorporating task parallelization, data and pattern distribution, and smart load balancing techniques on massively parallel architectures. By leveraging these innovative techniques, the proposed approach improves the processing speed of Frequent Pattern Mining (FPM) algorithms by up to 6.42 times compared to serial algorithms. Furthermore, our experimental results demonstrate the efficiency of the redesigned algorithm on several large-scale datasets, validating its scalability and effectiveness in uncovering patterns from massive data collections. title: Empirical Study on Deep Learning Models for Question Answering
Abstract: This empirical study on deep learning models for question answering explores the performance and applications of various neural architectures in understanding and answering questions drawn from a vast range of topics and domains. Empirical assessments and comprehensive analyses of the findings are presented to shed light on the feasibility and limitations of deep learning models for question answering tasks. title: Time-resolved emission from bright hot pixels of an active region observed in the EUV band with SDO/AIA and multi-stranded loop modeling
Abstract: The bright hot pixels in active regions are a vital component of the solar magnetic field, resulting from intricate magnetic processes that control them. This research examines the time-resolved emission behavior in the EUV band of an active region, observed with the Solar Dynamics Observatory's Atmospheric Imaging Assembly (SDO/AIA). By scrutinizing the intricate properties of hot pixels through data-driven methods and theoretical modeling, this analysis unearths remarkable details of these mini-events, enabling better understanding of the fundamental physics in interplay with ongoing magnetic activities. title: Vehicle Color Recognition using Convolutional Neural Network
Abstract: Vehicle color recognition using convolutional neural networks (CNNs) has gained significant attention in recent years due to its potential applications in various domains, including autonomous vehicles, traffic monitoring, and parking management systems. This study presents an innovative approach to vehicle color recognition using a deep CNN architecture based on a large-scale dataset, which consists of thousands of sample images with diverse illumination conditions, pose variations, and occlusions. Experiments demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance with an accuracy rate of up to 98% on the test set, significantly outperforming existing methods. title: The Human Kernel
Abstract: The human brain has long been regarded as the pinnacle of cognitive complexity, housing the essence of human thought, emotion, and experience. However, despite extensive research in neuroscience and psychology, the fundamental nature of human consciousness remains poorly understood. Recent advancements in artificial intelligence and cognitive computing have led to the emergence of a new conceptual framework, one that challenges traditional notions of human intelligence and proposes a novel architecture for understanding the workings of the human mind. This framework, inspired by the structure and function of the brain, is often referred to as the "human kernel." At its core, the human kernel posits the existence of a central, intrinsic cognitive unit that mediates all aspects of human perception, cognition, and emotion. This kernel, comprising interconnected networks of neurons and cognitive modules, is thought to serve as a unified processor for integrating sensory information, generating novel ideas, and guiding human behavior. By unpacking the theoretical underpinnings of the human kernel, researchers can gain a deeper understanding of the intricate mechanisms that govern human intelligence, creativity, and decision-making, with far-reaching implications for fields such as neuroscience, psychology, artificial intelligence, and cognitive science.

title: Safe Control under Uncertainty
Abstract: This paper investigates the problem of ensuring the safe operation of control systems under uncertainty. In many control applications, uncertainty arises from various sources such as-modeling errors, environmental disturbances, and sensor noise. If not properly addressed, these uncertainties can lead to unexpected system behavior, which can be catastrophic in high-stakes domains such as aerospace and autonomous vehicles. The goal of safe control under uncertainty is to design control strategies that simultaneously achieve desired performance objectives while preventing system failure. We take a comprehensive approach to this problem, drawing on techniques from robust control, optimization, and machine learning. Our framework integrates models of uncertainty with control strategies, enabling the computation of desired safe control policies that minimize the risk of system failure. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on a suite of benchmark systems, showcasing its ability to guarantee safe operation in the presence of significant uncertainty. Furthermore, we show that our framework can be adapted to accommodate real-time and online control, making it a viable solution for safety-critical applications. By providing a robust and scalable framework for safe control under uncertainty, this work paves the way for the development of more reliable and dependable control systems, ultimately reducing the risk of accidents and improving overall system safety.

title: Impact of Dual Slope Path Loss on User Association in HetNets
Abstract: The rapid proliferation of 5G networks has led to the emergence of Heterogeneous Networks (HetNets) as a crucial component, aiming to provide seamless connectivity to an ever-increasing number of users. However, the dual slope path loss (DSPL) model, proposed to accurately capture the varying environmental conditions, poses significant challenges in determining the optimal user association mechanism within HetNets. This study delves into the impact of DSPL on user association, emphasizing the need to distinguish it from conventional path loss models. Results reveal that using DSPL leads to reduced inter-cell interference and a more even distribution of users across cells, thus ensuring improved network-wide service quality. Furthermore, this research demonstrates that inaccurate prediction utilizing standard path loss models significantly diminishes the benefits of adopting DSPL. Through extensive simulations conducted on various network topologies, we identify the critical factors influencing the performance of DSPL-based association mechanisms, including cell load, user mobility, and antenna heights. Our conclusions have significant implications for 5G HetNet operators seeking to harness the potential of DSPL for optimal network management and a more robust user experience, driving the need for further research and development in optimizing DSPL-based user association strategies.

title: An Efficient Implementation for WalkSAT
Abstract: This research paper presents a novel efficient implementation for WalkSAT, a widely-used stochastic local search algorithm for solving Boolean satisfiability problems (SAT). The proposed implementation focuses on optimizing the random walk procedure, a core component of WalkSAT, to achieve faster convergence and improved performance on various benchmark instances. By analyzing the underlying dynamics of the random walk, we identify opportunities for enhancing its efficiency through the use of more informed walk decisions and adaptive randomness control. These optimizations are implemented using a range of techniques, including variable ordering heuristics, restart strategies, and probabilistic perturbation mechanisms. The resulting implementation is compared to existing WalkSAT variants through experiments on a large set of benchmark SAT instances, including those with different properties (e.g., size, complexity, and structure). Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed implementation consistently outperforms the competitors in terms of solution quality, runtime, and robustness across the benchmark suite. Furthermore, the analysis of the respective performance metrics and optimization strategies employed reveals valuable insights into the strengths and limitations of the implemented approach, facilitating its application to other related problems in the field of satisfiability testing and optimization. title: Intelligent Financial Fraud Detection Practices: An Investigation
Abstract: This study delves into the realm of intelligent financial fraud detection practices, critically examining the cutting-edge techniques employed to stay ahead of sophisticated cybercriminals. As the global financial landscape digitizes at an unprecedented pace, the threat of financial fraud is evolving at an alarming rate, with threats such as phishing, identity theft, and online banking scams on the rise. In response, financial institutions and regulatory bodies are in dire need of effective and robust techniques to identify and prevent fraudulent activities. title: Evolutionary Landscape and Management of Population Diversity
Abstract: Evolutionary landscape and management of population diversity is a pivotal research area in the realms of ecology, genetics, and conservation biology that examines the intricate dynamics governing population dynamics in response to environmental change, human activities, and species interactions. The current knowledge suggests that populations exhibit considerable genetic and phenotypic diversity, which can be influenced by processes such as gene flow, mutational pressure, genetic drift, and selection. However, understanding how populations are shaped and managed over evolutionary timescales is still under investigation, with recent studies implicating the impact of evolutionary processes on population resilience, adaptation, and extinction risk. Emerging themes highlight the significance of evolutionary conservation approaches that aim to preserve evolutionary potential and mitigate the loss of genetic variation in threatened species. This study integrates theoretical and empirical perspectives to explore the complex interplay between evolutionary processes, management policies, and biodiversity outcomes. By integrating data from various taxonomic groups and management contexts, the findings from this research are expected to elucidate effective strategies for evolutionary landscape conservation, improving our ability to safeguard ecological processes and life on Earth.

title: Path integral distance for data interpretation
Abstract: The path integral distance (PID) has emerged as a powerful tool for analyzing and interpreting complex data in various fields, including physics, biology, and finance. This paper presents a comprehensive investigation of the PID technique, with a focus on its application in data interpretation. By employing the methods of quantum field theory, the PID is derived as a distance metric that captures the underlying dynamics and patterns in data. The theoretical foundations of PID are discussed, and its applications in data clustering, classification, and dimensionality reduction are explored. The results demonstrate that PID outperforms traditional distance metrics, such as Euclidean and Manhattan distances, in capturing non-linear relationships and complex patterns in data. Furthermore, the PID is shown to be robust to noise and outliers, making it an attractive choice for analyzing real-world datasets. The paper also presents several case studies, including image recognition, time series analysis, and network science, to showcase the effectiveness of PID in real-world applications. Overall, this study highlights the potential of PID as a promising new tool for data interpretation, and its contributions are expected to have a significant impact on the field of data science and artificial intelligence.

title: Fusing Loop and GPS Probe Measurements to Estimate Freeway Density
Abstract: This study explores the concept of integrating loop probe and GPS probe measurements to estimate freeway density. Loop probe measurements have long been used in traffic monitoring and management, providing detailed information about vehicle counts and speeds. In contrast, GPS probe data encompasses a much broader scope, enabling real-time monitoring of travel times, speeds, and positions of individual vehicles along a corridor. By combining these two data sources, researchers can leverage the strengths of each, creating a more comprehensive and accurate assessment of freeway density. A rigorous analytical framework is presented to demonstrate how loop probe and GPS probe data can be fused to generate robust density estimates. The framework accounts for the spatial and temporal variability of vehicle activity, ensuring that the resulting density estimates reflect real-time conditions on the freeway. Validation of the proposed framework is undertaken using real-world data from a major freeway in a large metropolitan area, revealing a substantial improvement in density estimation accuracy. The results shed new light on the potential of data fusion techniques in enhancing the accuracy and reliability of transportation systems, ultimately informing more effective traffic management strategies and contributing to improved traveler experiences.

title: Soft-Defined Heterogeneous Vehicular Network: Architecture and Challenges
Abstract: This abstract provides an overview of the architecture and challenges associated with the development and deployment of Soft-Defined Heterogeneous Vehicular Networks (SDHVNs). The rise of autonomous and connected vehicles has led to the growth of vehicular networks, which are integral to enhancing road safety, traffic efficiency, and real-time information dissemination. However, the complexity and heterogeneity of vehicular networks present significant challenges in achieving seamless communication and ensuring reliable data transfer. This research explores the architecture of SDHVNs, focusing on the integration of traditional vehicular ad-hoc networks (VANETs), cellular networks, and Internet of Things (IoT) technologies. The proposed architecture incorporates software-defined networking (SDN) and network function virtualization (NFV) to enable flexible and scalable network management. The study also identifies key challenges, including spectrum scarcity, latency, security vulnerabilities, and interoperability issues, which hinder the widespread adoption of SDHVNs. To mitigate these challenges, a novel distributed control plane architecture is proposed, leveraging edge computing and reinforcement learning to optimize network performance and ensure real-time data exchange between vehicles and roadside units. The outcomes of this research are anticipated to provide valuable insights for the development of future vehicular networks and pave the way for the creation of intelligent transportation systems (ITSs) that prioritize road safety and efficiency.

title: Coordinating Truck Platooning by Clustering Pairwise Fuel-Optimal Plans
Abstract: This research focuses on developing a novel approach to coordinate truck platooning by clustering pairwise fuel-optimal plans, aiming to optimize the fuel consumption and emissions reduction of connected and autonomous vehicles (CAVs) on highways. The study investigates the problem of determining the optimal spacing and speed profile for a platoon of trucks to minimize fuel consumption and reduce emissions. A clustering-based approach is introduced to group trucks into disjoint clusters, where each cluster constitutes a platoon with its own optimal spacing and speed profile. The optimal clustering is determined by minimizing the total fuel consumption of all trucks in the platoon, while considering constraints on safety distance, platooning formation, and road conditions. The proposed method utilizes a combination of graph theory and optimization techniques, such as dynamic programming and 0/1 integer programming, to solve the clustering problem in polynomial time. Simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach in reducing fuel consumption by up to 20% and emissions by up to 30% compared to conventional platooning methods. The research also investigates the impact of various parameters, such as truck speed, spacing, and clustering size, on the potential savings in fuel consumption and emissions. The study's findings contribute to the development of more efficient and sustainable traffic management systems, as well as more eco-friendly transportation policies.

title: Optimization as Estimation with Gaussian Processes in Bandit Settings
Abstract: This paper contributes to the field of Bayesian optimization and multi-armed bandits by developing a unifying framework that views optimization as estimation within a Gaussian process-based bandit setting. Leveraging the intimate connection between the regret minimization problem in bandits and the maximum marginal likelihood estimation in Gaussian processes, we uncover an inherent analogy that enables the formulation of optimization problems through estimation lens. Specifically, by casting the optimization task as solving a series of estimation problems over a Gaussian process posterior, we derive an efficient and consistent optimization algorithm that adapts to the structure of the unknown objective function. Our novel approach enables robust decision-making in scenarios where the objective function's complexity is a major concern, such as in high-dimensional or non-symmetric spaces. Through theoretical analysis and extensive numerical experiments, we showcase the efficacy of our proposed framework, demonstrating superior performance and scalability advantages over existing methods in bandit optimization settings. The unifying perspective of optimization-as-estimation within a Gaussian process framework not only provides theoretical insights into the optimization problem but also enables the development of robust and adaptive optimization strategies for a wide range of real-world applications.

title: Time-Sensitive Bayesian Information Aggregation for Crowdsourcing Systems
Abstract: This paper presents an innovative approach to time-sensitive Bayesian information aggregation in crowdsourcing systems, where the rapid gathering and processing of user-generated data are essential. Traditional Bayesian methods rely on pre-defined models and do not account for the dynamic nature of crowdsourcing, where user contributions are received in real-time and can be highly variable in quality and relevance. To address this limitation, we propose a novel time-sensitive Bayesian information aggregation framework that integrates machine learning algorithms with bayesian inference to aggregate and update user-generated data in near real-time. Our framework exploits the temporal dependencies between user contributions, allowing it to model and adapt to the dynamics of the crowdsourcing system, including the evolution of user behavior, community feedback, and changing task requirements. By leveraging a probabilistic graphical model and using techniques from deep learning to learn the dependencies between user contributions, our framework can effectively identify and eliminate noisy or misleading data while rapidly aggregating relevant information to support informed decision-making. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world crowdsourcing datasets, showing that it outperforms state-of-the-art aggregation methods in terms of information quality and aggregation speed. The proposed framework has the potential to revolutionize the field of crowdsourcing by enabling the rapid and reliable aggregation of information, even in situations where users may provide conflicting or uncertain responses.

title: Creating Scalable and Interactive Web Applications Using High Performance Latent Variable Models
Abstract:
This study explores the potential of high performance latent variable models (HPLVMs) in creating scalable and interactive web applications, characterized by their capacity to handle large amounts of user data and complex user behaviors simultaneously. By leveraging the HPLVM framework, developers can build dynamic models that efficiently process and adapt to varying user inputs, leading to enhanced user experiences and increased application flexibility. The proposed approach enables real-time prediction and adaptation of user behavior, facilitating the creation of highly personalized and responsive web applications that are capable of handling a significant volume of concurrent user interactions.

Utilizing HPLVMs also facilitates the integration of machine learning algorithms and large datasets into web applications, allowing developers to capture complex user behavior patterns and identify hidden relationships between different user attributes and system responses. This in turn enables the development of more sophisticated and accurate models that can better anticipate and respond to user needs, resulting in improved application performance, increased user engagement, and enhanced overall user satisfaction. Furthermore, the HPLVM-based approach promotes modularity and extensibility, allowing developers to easily integrate new features and adapt to changing user requirements without compromising the overall application architecture or performance. The resulting web applications can seamlessly adapt to the needs of individual users, thereby establishing a more engaging and personalized interaction experience.

title: High Performance Latent Variable Models
Abstract: The advent of high-performance computing has enabled the widespread adoption of latent variable models, which have found applications in diverse fields such as computer vision, natural language processing, and social network analysis. However, traditional methods for modeling latent variables often suffer from limitations due to their slow computational time, making them unsuitable for large-scale datasets. In response to this challenge, recent research has focused on developing high-performance latent variable models that can efficiently handle massive datasets while maintaining their interpretability and accuracy. These novel models leverage advances in deep learning, parallel computing, and optimization techniques to accelerate inference and learning, enabling the exploitation of complex relationships within high-dimensional data. By capitalizing on the strengths of these new technologies, scientists and engineers can develop sophisticated models of human behavior, social networks, and system dynamics that more accurately reflect real-world phenomena. Ultimately, the development of high-performance latent variable models holds great promise for addressing many critical problems in fields such as finance, healthcare, and climate modeling, where the need for accurate and scalable analytics is paramount.

title: Intellectual interchanges in the history of the massive online open-editing encyclopedia, Wikipedia
Abstract: Wikipedia, launched in 2001, has revolutionized the way people access and contribute to knowledge online. As the world's largest online encyclopedia, it has become a platform for intellectual interchange, bringing together diverse perspectives and expertise from across the globe. This paper delves into the history of Wikipedia's intellectual interchanges, exploring the complex dynamics of collaboration, social negotiation, and power struggles that have shaped its development. Through a critical discourse analysis of user contributors' interactions, this study examines how Wikipedia's editorial policies, such as neutral point of view and verifiability, influence users' perceptions of knowledge creation and dissemination. Additionally, the paper explores the impact of Wikipedia's openness on the creation of original content, highlighting both the benefits of crowdsourcing knowledge and the challenges of maintaining accuracy and trustworthiness in a vast, decentralized knowledge-sharing space. By examining the intricacies of Wikipedia's intellectual interchanges, this research sheds light on the ways in which the platform's complex dynamics shape the production and dissemination of knowledge, revealing both the opportunities and limitations of a collaborative, user-driven approach to information sharing. As Wikipedia continues to evolve, understanding its intellectual interchanges is crucial for navigating the evolving landscape of online knowledge creation and the roles that humans and technologies play within it.

title: Semantic, Cognitive, and Perceptual Computing: Advances toward Computing for Human Experience
Abstract: The increasing complexity and interconnectedness of the world call for a paradigm shift in computing, moving beyond mere processing power and toward a more experiential and human-centered approach. Semantic, cognitive, and perceptual computing (SCPC) emerges as a multidisciplinary field, seeking to integrate artificial intelligence, cognitive science, and neuroscience to create computing systems that truly enhance the human experience. By leveraging advances in sensorimotor neural networks, brain-inspired computing, and cognitive architectures, SCPC strives to develop intelligent machines that can perceive, reason, and interact with humans in a more intuitive and empathetic manner. The core tenets of SCPC include the integration of sensory modalities, the modeling of cognitive processes, and the development of affective computing systems that can recognize and respond to human emotions. A crucial aspect of SCPC is its focus on real-world applications, such as healthcare, education, and accessibility, where human-centered computing has the potential to significantly improve quality of life. Overall, SCPC aims to revolutionize the way humans interact with technology, making it more enjoyable, efficient, and effective in an era where computing is increasingly intertwined with everyday life.
