title: Discriminative Predicate Path Mining for Fact Checking in Knowledge Graphs
Abstract: Discriminative predicate path mining plays a critical role in fact-checking for large-scale knowledge graphs, especially in tasks involving truth verification, data repair, and knowledge extraction. In this research, we propose a novel framework that integrates machine learning and graph mining techniques to identify discriminative predicate paths that contribute to truth inference in knowledge graphs. Our approach starts by constructing a background knowledge graph and extracting potential predicate paths associated with each fact to be verified. We then utilize a boosted decision tree-based algorithm to iteratively learn a subset of high-impact predicate paths that are indicative of truth. An ensemble of graph convolutional networks is further leveraged to refine these discriminative paths and capture complex interactions among entities and relationships in the knowledge graph. Extensive experiments on real-world fact-checking benchmarks demonstrate that our proposed framework outperforms state-of-the-art methods, yielding significant improvements in accuracy, F1-score, and area under the precision-recall curve. Moreover, our framework can efficiently scale to large knowledge graphs while being interpretable, which enables effortless identification of the influential relationship patterns leading to truth verification. The proposed approach offers a balanced balance between predicting truth and extracting knowledge for scalable truth verification systems, paving the way for more accurate decisions based on knowledge graphs in complex real-world applications.

title: PERCH: Perception via Search for Multi-Object Recognition and Localization
Abstract:
PERCH: Perception via Search for Multi-Object Recognition and Localization 

This paper proposes a novel end-to-end perception framework called PERCH, which leverages search and multi-object recognition and localization capabilities to parse complex visual scenes. By formulating perception as a search problem, PERCH effectively handles cluttered and diverse environments, leading to enhanced robustness and better scalability. The framework employs a combination of hierarchical and convolutional neural networks to sequentially search for objects within a scene, thereby facilitating accurate localization and identification. Unlike traditional perception approaches that struggle to handle occlusions and overlapping objects, PERCH trains a dynamic graph-based model to reason about relationships between detected objects and the environment, incorporating spatial awareness and contextual knowledge. This holistic understanding enables PERCH to adapt to novel and unseen scenes, yielding state-of-the-art recognition and localization performance on benchmark datasets and real-world test cases. In addition, extensive experiments demonstrate PERCH's exceptional ability to handle challenging scenarios involving partial occlusions, simultaneous activations of multiple objects, and substantial environmental diversity, making it a valuable contribution to the fields of computer vision and artificial intelligence. The proposed framework paves the way for the deployment of intelligent systems that interact with and understand complex visual environments with unprecedented accuracy and reliability.

title: On the Computability of AIXI
Abstract: AIXI is a theoretical model of an artificial intelligence agent proposed by Marcus Hutter, which seeks to maximize the expected sum of rewards over an infinite horizon. Despite its theoretical significance, the computability of AIXI remains an open question. This paper explores the limitations of AIXI's computability, showing that a finite implementation of the agent is not possible under the constraints of a universal Turing machine. We demonstrate that AIXI's computation involves dealing with an uncomputable function, namely the Solomonoff prior, which assigns a probability to each program as a function of its Kolmogorov complexity. However, a machine cannot enumerate all possible programs, including those that produce uncomputable results, hence rendering the computation of AIXI's action uncomputable. This result is achieved through a reduction from the halting problem, where we show that the decidability of AIXI's action is equivalent to the decidability of the halting problem for a universal Turing machine. Furthermore, we examine the implications of this result on the possibility of approximating AIXI's behavior with a computable agent, and discuss the potential applications and limitations of such an approximation in the context of artificial intelligence and machine learning. Overall, our findings have significant implications for the development of artificial intelligence agents that aim to maximize their expected rewards in complex environments.

title: A New Empirical Constraint on the Prevalence of Technological Species in the Universe
Abstract: Recent advances in the detection of exoplanets and the characterization of their properties have sparked interest in the possibility of life beyond Earth, including the likelihood of technological species capable of interstellar communication. The Fermi Paradox, which questions the absence of empirical evidence for extraterrestrial civilizations, has been approached through various frameworks, including the Rare Earth hypothesis and the zoo hypothesis. However, a fundamental challenge in addressing this paradox lies in the empirical constraints on the prevalence of technological species in the universe. Our study contributes to this debate by employing an empirical approach to investigate the likelihood of technological species in our galaxy. Using a combination of data from the Gaia mission, the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite, and the Breakthrough Listen initiative, we develop a novel statistical framework to infer the presence of technological signals in the vicinity of Earth. By comparing our findings with existing estimates of the density of exoplanets and the probability of life, we derive a new empirical constraint on the prevalence of technological species. Our results suggest that the probability of a technological species existing within 100 light-years of Earth is less than 1%. This study provides a critical assessment of the hypothesis that technological species are rare in the universe and contributes to a deeper understanding of the conditions necessary for life to emerge and thrive. The implications of our findings have far-reaching consequences for the development of the field of astrobiology and the search for extraterrestrial intelligence.

title: System Descriptions of the First International Competition on Computational Models of Argumentation (ICCMA'15)
Abstract: The first International Competition on Computational Models of Argumentation, ICCMA'15, brought together researchers from diverse backgrounds to compare and evaluate the performances of various computational argumentation systems. The competition featured several aspects, including the retrieval of valid arguments, evaluation of argument strengths, mining of persuasive arguments, and construction of counterarguments. The system descriptions for participating teams in each task provided a comprehensive overview of the approaches employed to tackle the challenges of argumentation. They highlighted diverse methods, techniques, and strategies applied in the design and implementation of the systems. The argument retrieval task focused on utilizing techniques such as argument graph detection, graph-based methods, knowledge-intensive approaches, and subgraph matching. The argument strength evaluation task incorporated approaches like dynamic weighting methods, ensemble learning, and machine learning-based approaches. Meanwhile, the persuasive argument mining task employed graph-based methods, machine learning techniques, and information retrieval methods. The task of counterargument construction involved various approaches, ranging from deductive reasoning, abductive reasoning, and machine learning-based methods. The evaluation of the participating systems showed promising results, demonstrating improvements in accuracy and performance compared to traditional argumentation systems. Overall, ICCMA'15 provided a critical platform for the evaluation of computational argumentation models, highlighting areas of success and opportunities for future advancements in the field.

title: Social Media Analysis for Product Safety using Text Mining and Sentiment Analysis
Abstract: This study proposes a comprehensive framework for analyzing social media posts to identify potential product safety issues using text mining and sentiment analysis. With the widespread adoption of social media platforms, consumers are increasingly sharing their experiences and opinions about products online, providing valuable insights into product safety. Our framework utilizes natural language processing (NLP) techniques to extract relevant text data from social media platforms, including tweets, posts, and reviews. We then employ text mining methods to identify key terms and concepts related to product safety, such as recalls, defects, and adverse reactions. To analyze the sentiment of the text data, we apply a number of sentiment analysis techniques, including supervised machine learning algorithms and lexicon-based approaches. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework in detecting product safety issues, including food poisoning, product defects, and medical device malfunctions. We also identify areas where social media can serve as an early warning system for product safety risks, allowing regulators and manufacturers to take proactive measures to mitigate potential harm. title: Causal Falling Rule Lists
Abstract: Causal Falling Rule Lists (CFRLs) have been gaining attention in recent years within the realm of causal reasoning and machine learning. This emerging paradigm combines the strengths of symbolic rule learning and probabilistic reasoning to infer cause-and-effect relationships from observational data. This abstract delves into the theoretical underpinnings, applications, and challenges associated with CFRLs. By leveraging the representational power of rule lists and the inferential capabilities of likelihood-based methods, CFRLs have been successful in addressing various tasks, including dimensionality reduction, noise robustness, and explainability. Furthermore, CFRLs have the potential to integrate seamlessly with other popular causal discovery techniques, capturing both structural and probabilistic aspects of causal relationships. However, the introduction of CFRLs also raises several methodological questions, such as model selection criteria, parameter estimation, and interpretability. To address these concerns, a novel fusion framework that incorporates the strengths of domain knowledge and automated rule generation is proposed, and its theoretical justifications are developed using information-theoretic and graphical perspectives. The proposed framework has been demonstrated through simulation studies and empirical evaluations to outperform current benchmark methods in terms of accuracy and robustness, highlighting its promise as a promising new direction in causal learning.

title: Symbolic Neutrosophic Theory
Abstract: The Symbolic Neutrosophic Theory is an extension of the classical mathematical concept of neutrosophy, introduced by Florentin Smarandache as a philosophy-based theory that deals with the concept of indeterminacy and uncertainty. This theory merges the principles of symbolic logic with the neutrosophic concept to develop a novel framework for tackling complex, imprecise, or uncertain phenomena. The theory employs a triplet of numbers [0, 1, t] to represent the uncertain values, considering t as the degree of uncertainty, and re-defined the classical neutrosophic sets to incorporate symbolic representations, enabling the inclusion of both truth and falsity in a single set. The Symbolic Neutrosophic Theory provides a unified approach for representing various forms of uncertainty and inconsistencies in data, thus enabling better handling of paradoxical or contradictory information. This theoretical context is becoming increasingly important in emerging fields of research, including fuzzy ontology, uncertain set theory, and robust decision-making. Furthermore, its applications are already being explored in diverse areas like image processing, medical diagnosis, and finance, and therefore offers intriguing prospects for development of novel algorithms for uncertainty processing and data analysis. As a mathematical theory with profound philosophical roots, it holds vast potential for solving problems in real-world applications where degrees of uncertainty are overwhelming, such as decision-making under uncertainty, as well as many other areas.

title: Comprehensive indicator comparisons intelligible to non-experts: The case of two SNIP versions
Abstract: This paper explores the enhancement of indicator comparisons for non-experts by differentiating between two versions of the Source-Normalized Impact per Paper (SNIP) method, which is used to evaluate the citation impact of scholarly sources. Current index comparisons often involve technical descriptions and complicated metrics, leading to difficulties in comprehension for non-specialists. We contend that intelligibility is a crucial factor in generating trust and understanding among various stakeholders, including researchers, policymakers, librarians, and scientists from other disciplines. By carefully reviewing the mathematical formulations, applications, and theoretical backgrounds of two contrasting SNIP versions, this study aims to provide straightforward comparisons accessible to individuals without an in-depth understanding of citation analysis techniques. Systematic assessments of these versions will include their strengths and limitations, as well as examples of implementation in practice, facilitating greater clarity and transparency in evaluating citation metrics. title: Normalization of Relative and Incomplete Temporal Expressions in Clinical Narratives
Abstract: The normalization of temporal expressions in clinical narratives is a critical task in healthcare text analytics, as it enables the temporal relationship between medical events and conditions to be accurately captured, facilitating the development of predictive models and clinical decision support systems. However, the analysis of relative and incomplete temporal expressions, such as temporal prepositions (e.g., "before," "after," "during") and undefined intervals (e.g., "in the past," "recently"), remains a significant challenge. Recent advances in natural language processing (NLP) techniques have made it possible to address these issues, but a comprehensive analysis of their normalization is needed. This study proposes an approach to normalizing relative and incomplete temporal expressions in clinical narratives, utilizing a combination of rule-based and machine learning methods. The proposed approach leverages syntactic and semantic parsing, temporal relation identification, and knowledge graph representation to identify and normalize temporal expressions. Experimental results on a clinical narrative dataset demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed approach, achieving accurate temporal expression normalization and enabling improved clinical decision-making. The study's findings have significant implications for the development of clinical NLP systems and contribute to improving the accuracy and reliability of healthcare data analytics, supporting more informed and personalized patient care.

title: Holographic Embeddings of Knowledge Graphs
Abstract: Holographic embeddings of knowledge graphs have emerged as a powerful approach to represent complex semantic relationships in large-scale graph-structured data. By modeling knowledge graphs as both entities and attributes using a holographic tensor, these embeddings leverage the principles of gauge invariance and isomorphism invariance to significantly improve upon traditional encoder-decoder architectures. This novel approach leads to the development of more robust knowledge graph completion and recommendation tasks, as well as the generalisation of downstream tasks such as entity disambiguation and property prediction over unseen entity combinations and missing relationships. Theoretical analysis demonstrates the efficacy of holographic embeddings in capturing higher-order generalisations and abstract concepts from the underlying graph structure. Furthermore, an integrated framework combining holographic embeddings with standard deep neural architectures yields dramatically improved performance on numerous benchmarks, outperforming traditional semantic relationship extraction methods. The empirical evaluation of this novel approach on large-scale instances of diverse knowledge graphs, encompassing entities such as products, people, books, and movies, further reinforces the suitability of holographic embeddings for scaling up knowledge graphs while ensuring low latency and real-time entity retrieval operations. Overall, the advent of holographic embeddings marks a substantial evolution in the quest for accurate knowledge graph embeddings, offering breakthroughs in both theoretical depth and practical applicability.

title: Bad Universal Priors and Notions of Optimality
Abstract: In recent decades, the debate on universal priors in decision theory and epistemology has garnered significant attention, with proponents arguing for their crucial role in providing a rational foundation for expectations of uncertain outcomes. However, critics have raised concerns about the potential flaws and pitfalls associated with certain universal prior distributions, contesting their status as optimally justified measures of rational uncertainty. Specifically, this paper aims to explore the detrimental consequences of adopting 'bad' universal priors in decision theory, focusing on their implications for definitions of optimality in rational choice. We contend that certain universal prior distributions, such as those invoking probability distributions centered on the uniform distribution, fail to adequately account for empirical evidence and may lead to suboptimal decision outcomes. Furthermore, their adherence to an overly simplistic conception of rational choice can result in overly broad implications for optimality, compromising the theory's ability to make reliable predictions and provide actionable advice in complex decision-making scenarios. By examining the pitfalls of 'bad' universal priors, our analysis sheds light on the importance of refining our understanding of optimality in decision theory and encourages the development of more sophisticated and nuanced approaches to rational uncertainty that can more effectively account for the complexities of real-world decision-making processes.

title: Hybridization of Interval CP and Evolutionary Algorithms for Optimizing Difficult Problems
Abstract: Interval constraint programming (ICP) and evolutionary algorithms (EAs) are two powerful optimization techniques that have been widely applied to tackle various complex problems in fields such as logistics, finance, engineering, and computer science. However, when dealing with difficult problems, each technique has its own limitations, and merging them could provide a more robust solution. This paper explores the hybridization of interval constraint programming and evolutionary algorithms, with the aim of developing a more efficient and effective optimization method. The proposed approach leverages the strengths of both techniques to overcome their individual weaknesses, allowing for the exploration of a larger solution space while maintaining a structured search process. By incorporating interval constraints and EA operators, the proposed hybrid algorithm can efficiently handle difficult problems with non-linear constraints, noisy objective functions, and complex search spaces. A range of numerical experiments on benchmark problems and real-world case studies demonstrate the effectiveness and scalability of the proposed approach, showcasing its ability to find better solutions and converging towards an optimal solution more efficiently compared to standalone ICP and EA algorithms. title: Change Detection in Multivariate Datastreams: Likelihood and Detectability Loss
Abstract: Change detection in multivariate datastreams has become increasingly complex with the advent of large-scale monitoring systems generating vast amounts of interconnected data. This study explores the challenges and limitations associated with change detection techniques in multivariate datastreams, focusing on likelihood and detectability loss. The conventional likelihood-based approach, widely adopted in multivariate change detection, can suffer from high computational complexity, especially with a large number of variables. This can result in overfitting and difficulty in selecting the optimal hyperspectral window for detection. Furthermore, likelihood ratios are often subject to detectability loss, making it challenging for practitioners to identify genuine anomalies amidst naturally occurring variability. To address these limitations, we propose an innovative approach integrating likelihood with Bayesian non-parametric clustering, thus explicitly accounting for latent relationships and network effects. The adaptation employs kernel-based mixture models, leveraging their capability to identify shifting distributions within the multivariate space, leading to improved detection performance and significantly reduced detectability loss. Empirical assessments, using various datasets across climate and transportation networks, demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in accurately and reliably detecting anomalies amidst unpredictable change regimes.

title: Evaluating the Competency of a First-Order Ontology
Abstract: This paper proposes a framework for evaluating the competency of a first-order ontology, a crucial aspect of ontology development in the field of artificial intelligence and knowledge representation. A first-order ontology is a formal representation of knowledge that consists of a set of conceptual entities, their relationships, and constraints. Evaluating the competency of such an ontology is essential to ensure that it accurately reflects the intended meaning and provides a robust foundation for applications like question-answering systems, natural language processing, and decision-making. To address this challenge, we develop a novel approach that considers multiple dimensions of ontology competency, including suitability for representing domain knowledge, consistency, scalability, and semantic precision. Our framework integrates existing evaluation metrics and proposes new ones, such as interpretability, coverage, and compatibility with other ontologies. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach using a case study of a widely used first-order ontology in the field of bioinformatics, evaluating its competency against various benchmark datasets and applications. The results show that our framework can accurately identify strengths and weaknesses of the ontology, providing actionable insights for ontology developers, users, and appraisers. Overall, this research contributes to a more comprehensive understanding of ontology competency and its evaluation, facilitating the development and deployment of high-quality ontologies in various domains.

title: Improving the Competency of First-Order Ontologies
Abstract: This research paper explores the essential aspects of enhancing the competency of first-order ontologies, which are used to represent knowledge and support reasoning processes in various applications, such as artificial intelligence and semantic networks. First-order ontologies have been widely adopted due to their ability to effectively capture and manipulate complex knowledge structures. However, the limitations and shortcomings of first-order ontologies have sparked intense debate and motivated research into their improvement. This study identifies several challenges associated with first-order ontologies, including their inability to handle non-classical logics, incompleteness, and inefficiencies in querying and inferencing processes. To address these problems, we propose and evaluate a set of ontological extensions that aim to enhance the competency of first-order ontologies. Our approach involves integrating non-classical logics into the ontology framework and developing novel query and inference mechanisms that support expressive queries. We also introduce an innovative methodology for modularizing and scaling ontologies to improve their manageability and efficiency. By addressing these fundamental limitations, our research contributes significantly to the advancement of ontology engineering and the development of robust, intuitive, and effective knowledge representation frameworks. title: SRMR variants for improved blind room acoustics characterization
Abstract: This study proposes a framework for enhanced blind room acoustics characterization, reliant on Sound Reconstruction Metrics Rate (SRMR) variants. Existing SRMR methods have established their efficacy in assessing room acoustics; however, their limitations in addressing real-world scenarios necessitate modifications and extensions. By incorporating novel SRMR variants, this research aims to bridge the gap between theoretical models and empirical data. Utilizing machine learning approaches and spectral features, the proposed SRMR variants can effectively capture the room's interaction with reverberant sound. The developed SRMR metrics adhere to the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) standards and the Concert Hall method, rendering them universally applicable. Key improvements include adaptive temporal filtering for more accurate assessment of early decay time, exploitation of acoustic wavelet transforms for enhanced spatial and temporal analysis, and optimized time and frequency resolution integration for accurate representation of sound energy distribution in the room. Experimental evaluations demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed SRMR variants in diverse acoustical settings, showcasing enhanced accuracy, robustness, and flexibility. This work opens avenues for efficient acoustical analysis, facilitating improved room design, and enhancing listener experience.

title: Layer-Specific Adaptive Learning Rates for Deep Networks
Abstract: Deep neural networks have revolutionized the field of machine learning with their unparalleled performance on a wide range of tasks including image and speech recognition, natural language processing, and game playing. However, deep neural networks often require a vast amount of computational resources and memory, making their training a time-consuming and expensive process. One major factor contributing to the high computational cost of deep neural network training is the use of a single global learning rate that is applied uniformly across all layers of the network. This approach can lead to slow convergence rates, oscillations, and even divergence for deep networks, particularly those with heterogeneous layer thicknesses and activation functions. In recent years, there has been a growing interest in exploring adaptive learning rates that can adjust themselves dynamically according to the layer-specific requirements to facilitate faster convergence and better generalization performance. Inspired by this idea, we propose a novel Layer-Specific Adaptive Learning Rate (LS-ALR) approach for deep networks that adjusts the learning rates of different layers separately based on their layer-specific adaptation rates calculated from a set of carefully designed learning rate adaptation formulas. Our proposed approach, which is inspired by the principles of adaptive learning and control theory, incorporates several key features, including layer-specific learning rate adaptation, adaptive scaling of learning rates, and a novel layer-specific regularization term that promotes more efficient exploration-exploitation trade-offs. Our extensive experimental results on various computer vision and natural language processing tasks demonstrate that our proposed LS-ALR approach can achieve state-of-the-art performance with significant reductions in training time and computational resources. By facilitating adaptive learning across different layers, LS-ALR provides a flexible and computationally efficient way to train deep networks with remarkable performance and faster convergence rates.

title: Narrative Science Systems: A Review
Abstract: Narrative Science Systems have gained significant attention in recent years due to their ability to automate the process of generating valuable insights and narratives from complex data. This review aims to provide an in-depth analysis of the current state of narrative science systems, their applications, and the challenges they pose. We explore the fundamental concepts behind narrative science, including data storytelling, automated content generation, and the use of natural language processing (NLP) and machine learning (ML) techniques. A comprehensive literature review of existing research on narrative science systems reveals that they have been successfully applied in various domains, such as finance, healthcare, and education, leading to improved decision-making and knowledge sharing. However, the review also highlights the limitations and challenges associated with narrative science systems, including the need for high-quality data, the development of more sophisticated NLP and ML algorithms, and the potential for biases in automated narratives. Furthermore, we examine the role of AI in narrative science, including the potential for human-AI collaboration and the importance of transparency and explainability in automated narratives. By discussing the current state of narrative science systems and their applications, this review provides insights into the future directions of this rapidly evolving field, with potential applications in various industries and settings.

title: Scatter Component Analysis: A Unified Framework for Domain Adaptation and Domain Generalization
Abstract: Scatter Component Analysis: A Unified Framework for Domain Adaptation and Domain Generalization offers a novel approach to solving the fundamental problem of learning generalizable models across diverse domains. Traditional methods face significant challenges in adapting to new environments while maintaining performance. To address this issue, the proposed framework integrates ideas from domain adaptation and domain generalization. It leverages the geometry of the induced decision boundaries, aligning it with the target distribution and exploring its impact on predictive performance in the absence of any target data. Central to the solution is the Scatter Component Analysis algorithm, a three-stage process that first identifies informative decision boundaries. Then, it adapts the model by minimizing the difference in their alignment between the source and target domains. The third stage, generalizes the knowledge learned from the source data to target environments by optimizing the decision boundary against the target distribution. A combination of theoretical analysis, experiments, and empirical evaluations show that the proposed method demonstrates substantial improvements over existing domain adaptation and domain generalization approaches in scenarios with limited source data and no target data, thus offering substantial prospects for deployment in real-world applications. Through the proposed framework, Scatter Component Analysis brings about a paradigm shift in the development of robust and transferable models.

title: A synchronous rendering of hybrid systems for designing Plant-on-a-Chip (PoC)
Abstract: This abstract delves into the development of a novel platform for designing and fabricating Plant-on-a-Chip (PoC) systems, a cutting-edge technology that aims to integrate living organisms with microscopic chips for various applications such as plant-based biosensing, bioremediation, and synthetic biology. The proposed synchronous rendering of hybrid systems enables the seamless integration of plant cells, microfluidic networks, and semiconductor chips, allowing for precise spatial and temporal control over plant growth, environmental conditions, and electronic signal processing. By leveraging advanced computer-aided design (CAD) tools and 3D printing techniques, the platform facilitates the development of complex PoC architectures with unprecedented precision, flexibility, and miniaturization. The resultant PoC systems are not only highly efficient and compact but also offer enhanced durability, robustness, and scalability. Furthermore, the proposed platform empowers users to design and simulate various hybrid plant-chip configurations, enabling efficient optimization of system performance, minimizing the environmental impact, and accelerating the realization of next-generation PoC-based technologies. The successful implementation of this novel platform is poised to revolutionize the field of synthetic biology, opening up new avenues for innovative applications in biotechnology, medicine, and sustainability.

title: Inheritance in Object-Oriented Knowledge Representation
Abstract: This paper delves into the complex aspect of inheritance in object-oriented knowledge representation, exploring its theoretical foundations, practical applications, and the challenges faced in its implementation. Inheritance, a fundamental concept in object-oriented programming languages, enables the creation of new objects or classes based on existing ones, thereby promoting code reusability and modularity. However, as we shift our focus to knowledge representation, the concept of inheritance becomes increasingly nuanced, requiring a careful examination of its role in facilitating reasoning, learning, and problem-solving. The paper examines the various forms of inheritance, including single inheritance, multiple inheritance, and hybrid inheritance, and discusses their implications for knowledge representation systems. Furthermore, it delves into the theoretical frameworks that underlie inheritance in knowledge representation, including the semantic net model, description logic, and commonsense knowledge representation. A critical analysis of the challenges associated with implementing inheritance in knowledge representation systems is also presented, including the resolution of conflicts between inherited and specific knowledge, handling exceptions and exceptions, and ensuring robustness and scalability. The paper contributes to the understanding of inheritance in object-oriented knowledge representation by providing a comprehensive overview of the state-of-the-art methods and techniques, highlighting the importance of inheritance in building sophisticated knowledge representation systems.

title: Exploiters-Based Knowledge Extraction in Object-Oriented Knowledge Representation
Abstract: This paper explores the concept of exploiters-based knowledge extraction in object-oriented knowledge representation, which revolves around the identification, extraction, and manipulation of knowledge from existing ontological structures. By constructing a comprehensive conceptual framework and utilizing a systematic approach, researchers can develop and utilize exploiters, which are specialized knowledge fragments that can be employed to reason, derive, and extract specific knowledge from an object-oriented knowledge base. The primary objective of this study is to analyze the adequacy and potential of exploiters as tools for facilitating manual or automatic knowledge extraction within object-oriented knowledge representation environments. It is found that exploiters can play a pivotal role in augmenting the functionality of knowledge-based systems by offering strategic ways for both domain experts and software developers to identify, extract, and manipulate specific knowledge necessary for domain modeling or decision support. Furthermore, the analytical findings of this investigation provide insights into the types of exploiters that can be constructed, their component characteristics, and the associated implications for object-oriented knowledge representation. Overall, the results of this study demonstrate the efficacy of exploiters-based knowledge extraction in providing more accurate, efficient, and effective knowledge extraction capabilities within this knowledge representation framework.

title: Object-Oriented Dynamic Networks
Abstract: Object-oriented dynamic networks represent a paradigm shift in the design and implementation of complex software systems, enabling the efficient modeling and simulation of dynamic, adaptable, and intelligent networks. This paper presents a comprehensive framework for object-oriented dynamic networks, encompassing three primary components: network structure, behavior, and adaptation. The network structure module allows for the creation and configuration of complex network topologies, utilizing object-oriented programming principles to encapsulate network entities and relationships. The behavior module introduces a novel event-driven architecture, permitting the specification of dynamic network behaviors and interactions at a detailed, microscopic level. Adaptable networks are facilitated by the adaptation module, which incorporates machine learning and feedback mechanisms for real-time adjustment and optimization of network performance. A key innovation is the integration of decentralized, autonomic decision-making, allowing for scalable and self-organizing networks. Experimental evaluations demonstrate superior performance, robustness, and flexibility compared to traditional networks, making object-oriented dynamic networks an attractive solution for a wide range of application domains. This research provides an essential foundation for the development of autonomous, adaptive, and self-aware networks in fields such as cybersecurity, transportation systems, and social networks.

title: Universal and Determined Constructors of Multisets of Objects
Abstract: The concept of multisets, which generalizes traditional sets by allowing for repeated elements, plays a crucial role in various mathematical and computational contexts. In this paper, we delve into the realm of universal and determined constructors of multisets of objects. Our investigation focuses on exploring the possibility of constructing multisets with specific properties or constraints through various methods. We begin by examining the applicability of traditional set theories and their limitations in representing multisets, leading us to develop a novel framework for constructing multisets. This involves the introduction of two primary constructors: the universal constructor, which generates a multiset containing all possible elements, and the determined constructor, which creates a multiset based on a given set of rules or constraints. Through a series of mathematical proofs and examples, we demonstrate the utility and versatility of our constructors in various scenarios, including combinatorial problems and computational algorithms. Furthermore, we discuss the implications of our findings on fields such as computer science, mathematics, and artificial intelligence. Ultimately, this research contributes to a deeper understanding of multisets and their role in solving complex problems, paving the way for further explorations and applications in diverse disciplines.

title: Mathematical Foundations for Designing and Development of Intelligent Systems of Information Analysis
Abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive exploration of the mathematical foundations required for designing and developing intelligent systems of information analysis. The rapid proliferation of complex data has led to a significant gap in the development of robust and adaptive analytical frameworks. In response, this research aims to bridge this gap by establishing a solid mathematical foundation for intelligent systems of information analysis. By drawing on principles from linear algebra, topology, algebraic topology, and differential geometry, the proposed framework enables the efficient representation, manipulation, and analysis of large-scale datasets. The mathematical foundation is further reinforced by leveraging concepts from category theory, providing a robust infrastructure for the integration of diverse data sources and analytical techniques. A key contribution of this research is the development of novel analytical models and algorithms that can effectively handle noise, anomalies, and high-dimensional data. The proposed framework is demonstrated through several case studies, showcasing its potential in applications ranging from social network analysis to image processing and natural language processing. The outcome of this research has significant implications for the development of next-generation intelligent systems capable of processing and analyzing complex data, leading to novel insights and actionable knowledge in various domains.

title: Embarrassingly Parallel Variational Inference in Nonconjugate Models
Abstract: Variational inference has emerged as a powerful tool for approximating complex posterior distributions in machine learning models, particularly in nonconjugate settings where direct computation of the posterior is infeasible. Despite its success, variational inference can be computationally expensive, especially when dealing with large datasets, making it a significant bottleneck in many applications. To address this challenge, we propose a novel approach for embarrassingly parallel variational inference in nonconjugate models, leveraging the power of distributed computing to speed up the inference process. Our method relies on a divide-and-conquer strategy, where the global variational objective is decomposed into smaller, independent sub-problems, each of which can be solved in parallel using standard stochastic gradient descent. By leveraging the embarrassingly parallel nature of our approach, we can achieve significant speedup on large datasets, enabling the application of variational inference to problems that were previously intractable. Furthermore, our method allows for the incorporation of user-specified privacy constraints, making it particularly suitable for applications where data privacy is a concern. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through extensive experiments on several benchmark datasets, showcasing its ability to achieve state-of-the-art results with improved computational efficiency.

title: On Arthur Eddington's Theory of Everything
Abstract: This research paper delves into the work of Sir Arthur Eddington, a renowned astrophysicist who proposed a unified theory of physics in the 1920s. Eddington's theory, often referred to as the Eddington Number, aimed to reconcile the principles of general relativity and quantum mechanics, providing a consistent framework for understanding the behavior of matter and energy at various scales. Through an in-depth examination of Eddington's seminal work, 'The Nature of the Physical World' (1928), this study reveals the rationale behind his theory and its key components, including the concept of E-Values and the distinction between two modes of comprehension, one 'fitting' and the other 'fashionable'. The paper also explores the implications of Eddington's theory on our understanding of time and the fundamental forces of nature, shedding new light on the persistent challenges of integrating quantum and relativity theories. As a significant figure in the history of cosmology, Eddington's ideas have had a lasting impact on the development of modern physics, and a closer scrutiny of his Theory of Everything challenges contemporary researchers to revisit and reevaluate the foundation of their current understanding of the universe.

title: Structured Memory for Neural Turing Machines
Abstract: Structured Memory for Neural Turing Machines extends the capabilities of Neural Turing Machines (NTMs) by introducing a novel structured memory architecture that leverages the strengths of both external memory and internal memory. Traditional NTMs rely solely on external memory, which can be prone to noise and limited in scalability. In contrast, our structured memory design combines the benefits of both internal and external memory, resulting in improved computational efficiency and fault tolerance. The proposed architecture is composed of multiple memory layers, each with a distinct memory structure, allowing for efficient information retrieval and manipulation. Our design also incorporates a novel attention-based scheme, enabling the network to selectively access and update specific memory locations, thereby enhancing the structural organization of the memory. Furthermore, we introduce a new memory size adaptation mechanism, which allows the network to dynamically adjust its memory usage based on tasks, further improving overall performance. Using a combination of theoretical analysis and empirical evaluations, we demonstrate the efficacy of our structured memory approach on a range of tasks, including few-shot learning, sequence modeling, and reinforcement learning. Our results show that the proposed structured memory for NTMs achieves state-of-the-art performance in these tasks, underscoring the potential of structured memory architectures for improving the scalability and efficiency of NTMs.

title: UAVs using Bayesian Optimization to Locate WiFi Devices
Abstract: This paper investigates the application of Bayesian optimization in unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) to locate WiFi devices in various scenarios. Bayesian optimization is an efficient global optimization method that uses probability theory and machine learning to find the optimal solution among a wide search space, making it suitable for complex problems. In this study, we use a UAV equipped with a WiFi receiver to perform a survey of a given area. The received WiFi signals are then used to create a signal strength map, which serves as the input to the Bayesian optimization algorithm. Our goal is to locate multiple WiFi devices in the area while minimizing the number of UAV measurements. We develop a novel framework that integrates the signal strength map with Bayesian optimization, enabling the UAV to efficiently scan the area, locate WiFi devices, and determine their corresponding signal strengths. The framework's performance is evaluated in various experiments, including urban and rural environments, and different numbers of WiFi devices. Results show that the proposed approach significantly reduces the number of UAV measurements required and improves the accuracy of the WiFi device locations compared to traditional approaches. Our study indicates that Bayesian optimization can be a valuable tool for UAV-based WiFi device localization, offering a promising solution for various applications, such as search and rescue operations, surveillance, and network planning.

title: A Multilevel Coordinate Search Algorithm for Well Placement, Control and Joint Optimization
Abstract: This paper presents an innovative application of the Multilevel Coordinate Search (MCS) algorithm to the joint optimization of well placement, control, and operations in the context of complex oil and gas reservoirs. The proposed approach is designed to address the inherent complexities and challenges associated with this multifaceted optimization problem, which requires simultaneous consideration of reservoir heterogeneity, uncertainty, and system dynamics. By leveraging the inherent multi-resolution and information-sharing capabilities of MCS, the novel approach efficiently navigates the high-dimensional search space and identifies optimal solutions that balance multiple and potentially conflicting objectives. To this end, the MCS algorithm is integrated with a robust reservoir simulation model and a set of well operation control variables, resulting in a comprehensive optimization framework that can be used to identify near-optimal well placements, operating conditions, and control strategies. The effectiveness of the proposed MCS-based optimization approach is rigorously validated through a comprehensive set of test cases, including synthetic and real-world reservoir examples, and compared to the results obtained using state-of-the-art optimization algorithms. The results demonstrate the practical applicability and superior performance of the proposed MCS-based strategy, which offers significant potential for improving reservoir management and decision-making practices, particularly in the areas of well placement, control, and operations optimization.

title: Asymptotic Logical Uncertainty and The Benford Test
Abstract: This abstract delves into the intricate relationship between asymptotic logical uncertainty (ALU) and the Benford test, two seemingly disparate concepts that converge to reveal novel insights into the nature of randomness and probability in complex systems. ALU is a theoretical framework positing that the uncertainty of a reasoning process may increase asymptotically with the complexity of the situation, while the Benford test is a statistical technique used to identify anomalies in data distributions. Here, we explore the intersection of these ideas by considering how ALU can be applied to a hypothesis-testing scenario using the Benford test as a metric, yielding a novel measure of the asymptotic probability of a hypothesis being true given evidence. Our approach is grounded in the axiomatic treatment of logical uncertainty and the mathematical formalism of the Benford test, resulting in a quantitative measure that can be used to compare and contrast the uncertainty associated with different pieces of evidence in a hypothesis-testing setting. Through rigorous mathematical analysis and simulation-based experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach in identifying anomalies in data distributions and revealing the asymptotic logical uncertainty associated with these anomalies, providing a deeper understanding of the interplay between randomness, probability, and logical reasoning in complex systems.

title: Evaluating Real-time Anomaly Detection Algorithms - the Numenta Anomaly Benchmark
Abstract: The advent of complex systems and growing demands for reliable data-driven decision making in industries such as finance, healthcare, and cybersecurity have necessitated the development of efficient real-time anomaly detection algorithms. Despite the increase in anomaly detection methods, evaluating these algorithms poses significant challenges due to the diverse range of anomalies, benchmarking datasets, and evaluation metrics available. The Numenta Anomaly Benchmark (NAB) is an open-source benchmarking framework designed to provide a comprehensive platform for evaluating anomaly detection algorithms by simulating real-world system behaviors and complexities. In this paper, we evaluate various real-time anomaly detection algorithms based on machine learning and statistical techniques to assess their performance on the NAB. The evaluation involves comparing the algorithms' detection capabilities, precision, recall, and speed in identifying anomalies under different scenarios, including bursty, cyclical, and gradual anomalies. Our findings suggest that certain algorithms perform well under specific anomaly types but fail to deliver comparable performance when faced with varying anomaly patterns. Furthermore, we examine the impact of parameter tuning and hyperparameter optimization on the algorithms' performance, thereby providing actionable insights for practitioners to select the most suitable algorithms for real-world applications. The results of this study contribute to the understanding of current anomaly detection algorithms and provide a foundation for the development of more robust and adaptive real-time anomaly detection solutions.

title: The Inductive Constraint Programming Loop
Abstract: Inductive Constraint Programming (ICP) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for solving complex problems in various domains by exploiting the synergy between symbolic constraints and inductive reasoning. This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of the ICP loop, a fundamental component of ICP systems. We provide a detailed description of the ICP paradigm and its underlying principles, including the iterative process of inductive reasoning, search space exploration, and constraint refinement. Our contribution lies in the formalization of the ICP loop, which enables a more accurate and efficient modeling of the search space and the constraint satisfaction process. We propose a novel method for inducing constraints during the search process, leveraging machine learning techniques to improve the efficiency of the ICP loop. Our approach is evaluated on a set of benchmark problems, demonstrating significant improvements over state-of-the-art ICP systems. The results of this study provide valuable insights for the development of more efficient and effective ICP systems, with potential applications in areas such as artificial intelligence, computer vision, and decision support systems. Furthermore, our work highlights the potential of integrating machine learning techniques with ICP to create more powerful and adaptive problem-solving systems.

title: Data structuring for the ontological modelling of wind energy systems
Abstract: The development of robust and accurate models for wind energy systems is crucial for predicting and analyzing their behavior under various conditions. However, the complexity of these systems and their integration with various technical, environmental, and socio-economic factors presents a significant challenge. This paper explores the application of ontological modelling for the representation and analysis of wind energy systems. Ontologies can provide a structured and explicit representation of the conceptual relationships between different components and factors in wind energy systems, enabling a more comprehensive understanding of their behavior and interactions. Our research focuses on the creation of a data structure that embodies a common framework for storing, retrieving, and integrating data from various data sources related to wind energy systems. We examine the implications of using different data structuring techniques, such as relational databases, graph databases, and knowledge graphs, to represent the ontological model of wind energy systems. Our results indicate that the integration of knowledge graphs provides a suitable framework for representing the complex relationships and networks involved in wind energy systems, offering a sound basis for further analyses of their behavior and performance. The developed data structure can serve as a knowledge sharing platform for wind energy researchers and practitioners, facilitating the exchange of information and expertise.

title: Context-Aware Bandits
Abstract: Our research focuses on addressing the limitations of traditional multi-armed bandit algorithms in dynamic and complex environments, such as those encountered in real-world applications of Context-Aware Bandits. While existing solutions have shown promise in certain contexts, they often fail to account for the nuances of human behavior and preferences, leading to suboptimal decision-making and inefficient resource allocation. To mitigate these limitations, we propose a novel Context-Aware Bandit algorithm, namely, Contextual Upper Confidence Bound (CUCB), which learns to adapt to changing user preferences and situational context. CUCB integrates two key components: a Contextual Gaussian Process (CGP) for modeling non-linear relationships between user behavior, context features, and reward signals, and a Context-Aware Upper Confidence Bound (CAUCB) for balancing exploration and exploitation. Experimental results demonstrate that CUCB outperforms state-of-the-art algorithms in terms of cumulative reward and regret, effectively navigating the trade-off between adaptability, interpretability, and efficiency. Furthermore, we provide empirical insights into the critical factors influencing the performance of Context-Aware Bandits, including the importance of contextual features, user model update strategies, and algorithmic parameters. By shedding light on the interplay between human behavior, context, and learning algorithms, our research contributes to a better understanding of context-aware decision-making and has the potential to inform the design of more effective and user-centric systems.

title: Fast detection of multiple objects in traffic scenes with a common detection framework
Abstract: The increased reliance on autonomous vehicles and traffic management systems necessitates the development of efficient and robust object detection frameworks that can accurately identify multiple objects in complex traffic scenes. However, existing object detection methods, such as YOLO and SSD, are often plagued by high computational overhead, limited scalability, and poor performance in densely occluded scenes. To address these challenges, we propose an innovative common detection framework that leverages a hierarchical, multi-stage architecture to efficiently detect multiple objects in high-density traffic environments. Our approach combines a novel region proposal network (RPN) with a spatially-aware anchor-free architecture to improve object localization and boundary estimation. We also introduce an attention-based semantic alignment module to enhance feature information retrieval and fusion, allowing for more accurate object classification and reduced false positives. Additionally, we implement a parallel processing scheme to accelerate computation and adapt our framework to low-latency applications. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets (e.g., Cityscapes, NuScenes, and KITTI) demonstrate the superior performance and efficiency of our framework compared to state-of-the-art object detection methods, underscoring its potential for real-world adoption in intelligent transportation systems.

title: Influence of network topology on cooperative problem-solving systems
Abstract: Cooperative problem-solving systems are increasingly utilized in various domains, such as robotics, logistics, and data analytics, where groups of agents need to collaborate to achieve complex tasks. The network topology of these systems plays a crucial role in determining their performance, as it affects the communication, coordination, and cooperation among agents. This study investigates the impact of different network topologies on the efficiency and effectiveness of cooperative problem-solving systems. We explore three types of topologies: centralized, decentralized, and hybrid, using both theoretical modeling and experimental simulations. Our results show that centralized networks facilitate faster convergence and higher accuracy, but are prone to single-point failures and bottlenecks. Decentralized networks, on the other hand, offer greater robustness and flexibility, but are often slower and less accurate. Hybrid networks, which combine elements of both, exhibit the best of both worlds, balancing efficiency, accuracy, and robustness. Our findings have implications for the design and organization of cooperative problem-solving systems, highlighting the importance of network topology in determining their performance. We also provide guidelines for selecting the optimal topology based on the specific requirements and constraints of the problem at hand, contributing to the development of more efficient and effective collective intelligence systems.

title: ParallelPC: an R package for efficient constraint based causal exploration
Abstract:
ParallelPC is an R package designed for efficient constraint-based causal exploration, particularly in the context of causal discovery and inference. Building upon the framework of constraint-based causal estimation, this package leverages multiple computation techniques and data parallelization to facilitate the analysis of complex networks and large datasets. The main goal of ParallelPC is to significantly accelerate the computation and scalability of constraint-based causal estimation methods by harnessing the computational power of multi-core processors and distributed computing environments. 

Using the PC algorithm as its core component, ParallelPC integrates several optimization strategies to expedite the calculation of conditional dependence coefficients, thereby speeding up the process of building causal graphs from observational data. These strategies include, but are not limited to, parallelized computation, memoization, edge caching, and constraint pruning, which collectively improve the computational efficiency and robustness of the algorithm. As a result, ParallelPC empowers researchers to efficiently explore large-scale causal networks and generate high-quality causal inferences with minimal data pre-processing requirements. This approach enhances the potential for analyzing complex systems, facilitates collaborative research in causal inference, and extends the utility of parallel computing in machine learning and data science applications.

title: Mining Interesting Trivia for Entities from Wikipedia
Abstract: This research paper delves into the realm of entity-centric knowledge discovery from Wikipedia, focusing on uncovering interesting trivia that can be mined for various entities in the online encyclopedia. The proposed methodology leverages an ensemble approach, combining graph-based techniques, keyphrase extraction methods, and sentiment analysis, to identify not only the factual relationships between entities but also their associated trivia. To improve the efficiency and scalability of the proposed framework, a parallelised implementation is explored using Hadoop MapReduce, enabling the processing of massive Wikipedia datasets. Moreover, a novel entity relevance metric is introduced to identify entities that exhibit intriguing patterns or behaviors, providing users with a strategic starting point for further exploration. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed framework in uncovering a diverse set of interesting trivia, offering new insights into the intriguing aspects of diverse entities in Wikipedia. By making the Wikipedia knowledge graph more accessible and user-friendly, the research aims to facilitate in-depth exploration of complex relationships and emergent trends in the digital realm. Ultimately, the developed framework paves the way for the identification of hidden patterns and relationships that can be instrumental in various real-world applications, including knowledge graph augmentation, information retrieval, and social network analysis.

title: Pseudo-Marginal Slice Sampling
Abstract: Pseudo-marginal slice sampling is an increasingly popular statistical method used to approximate complex Bayesian inferences in a computationally efficient manner. Developed as a variant of traditional slice sampling, the pseudo-marginal slice sampling method leverages the concept of unbiased estimation to update the target distribution using stochastic gradient samples. This approach allows for a more accurate and efficient exploration of the target distribution, especially in high-dimensional spaces where traditional MCMC methods may struggle to converge. By approximating the un-normalized target density using a sequence of unbiased estimates, pseudo-marginal slice sampling enables the incorporation of complex likelihood functions and explores the posterior distribution without suffering from the curse of dimensionality. The technique has been employed in various fields, including finance, machine learning, and epidemiology, to investigate complex posterior distributions, model parameter uncertainty, and explore uncertainty around fitted models. An additional strength of pseudo-marginal slice sampling lies in its applicability to simulating rare events and sensitivity analysis, making it a valuable tool for handling real-world inference tasks where computational resources are limited. This paper aims to investigate the theoretical properties and practical implementation of pseudo-marginal slice sampling as it relates to solving complex statistical problems. Through a comparison to alternative MCMC methods, the investigation evaluates the computational efficiency and statistical accuracy of the pseudo-marginal slice sampling algorithm in various scenarios.

title: On oblivious branching programs with bounded repetition that cannot efficiently compute CNFs of bounded treewidth
Abstract: This paper delves into the intricacies of oblivious branching programs (OBPs) to investigate their inability to efficiently compute Conjunctive Normal Forms (CNFs) of bounded treewidth. Typically, OBPs are employed in computational complexity and circuits for evaluating Boolean functions in a nondeterministic yet oblivious manner, allowing each processor to access input bits in the same order regardless of the input configuration. The treewidth of a CNF is an essential factor in understanding its expressive power in terms of the structure it imposes on the variables in the CNF. By examining OBPs with bounded repetition, the research aims to bridge the knowledge gap between non-deterministic CNF computations and their relation to OBPs. An important study has shown that CNFs of bounded treewidth cannot be efficiently computed by OBPs with bounded repetition, shedding light on a crucial problem in theoretical computer science. This study concentrates on elucidating why this constraint prevents CNFs of bounded treewidth from being efficiently computed by OBPs. We derive examples and insights into the necessary conditions for CNFs of bounded treewidth to be efficiently computed by OBPs with bounded repetition, demonstrating the correlation between structural constraints of the CNFs and the computational capabilities of the OBPs. By understanding why OBPs struggle to handle certain CNFs, we acquire a nuanced perspective on what is required to allow efficient computations in branching programs with potential applications in circuit complexity theory.

title: Attend, Adapt and Transfer: Attentive Deep Architecture for Adaptive Transfer from multiple sources in the same domain
Abstract: Our research focuses on designing an attentive deep architecture for adaptive transfer from multiple sources within the same domain, catering to the complexities of real-world scenarios where multiple sources of knowledge are often available for learning. In these situations, selecting the most relevant and information-rich sources becomes a crucial task that significantly impacts the model's performance. Existing architectures rely heavily on handcrafted selection methods or shallow neural networks to make this selection. However, these approaches lack generalizability and are often unable to effectively leverage the heterogeneity of multiple sources, leading to suboptimal performance. To bridge this gap, we propose a novel architecture that employs an attention mechanism to dynamically weigh the contributions of each source. Our adaptive transfer framework enables the model to selectively focus on specific regions of each source that hold the most relevant information, thereby improving the efficiency and efficacy of learning from multiple sources. Comprehensive experiments on standard benchmark datasets demonstrate the superior performance of our framework compared to state-of-the-art methods, highlighting its utility in diverse applications that involve domain adaptation and transfer learning. By combining the strengths of deep learning and attentive networks, our work offers a compelling solution for tackling the challenges associated with learning from multiple related sources in the same domain.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Asymmetric Information Theory
Abstract: This study delves into the intersection of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Asymmetric Information Theory (AIT), two disciplines that have long been employed in distinct domains but now converge in significant ways. In classical information theory, the capacity of a channel is typically determined without considering the presence of a third party that might interfere in the information transfer flow. However, introducing the concept of non-symmetry or asymmetry in information, along the lines of AIT, one may arrive at different insights where agent bargaining power can override classical efficiency theorems and informational cascades make AI model predictions relatively unreliable when several self-interested actors are involved. This research focuses on the analysis of asymmetric information with AI-driven interfaces in real-life scenarios, with a focus on the outcomes in artificial markets and environments where an imbalance in information exerts a strong impact. A specific experimentation framework and algorithmic treatment make the study of this conjunction practically feasible and allows uncover some analytical results regarding: capacity of channels, influence on fairness of bargaining rights and expected market participation strategies.

title: Gelisp: A Library to Represent Musical CSPs and Search Strategies
Abstract: Gelisp is a comprehensive library designed to facilitate the representation and solution of musical constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs). The library targets researchers and practitioners working in the domain of music information retrieval and automated music theory. By providing a flexible framework for encoding complex musical CSPs, Gelisp enables the exploration of novel applications, such as automatic composition, musical knowledge representation, and music analysis. Key features of Gelisp include a modular architecture, allowing users to easily extend the library with their own plug-ins, as well as a wide range of data structures and algorithms for solving CSPs. Specifically, Gelisp includes several cutting-edge algorithms, such as constraint relaxation and local search, which have been adapted from the field of artificial intelligence to the specific needs of music theory. Additionally, Gelisp incorporates state-of-the-art data structures for efficient representation of musical metadata, including chord progressions, melodies, and harmony theories. Through its intuitive and machine-readable interface, Gelisp enables researchers to define and solve a wide range of musical CSPs, paving the way for novel musical applications and music technology innovations. By providing a robust platform for musical constraint programming, Gelisp has the potential to revolutionize the field of music information retrieval and beyond, unlocking new possibilities for automated music generation, music recommendation, and music theory exploration.

title: Learning optimal quantum models is NP-hard
Abstract: Numerous attempts to find optimal quantum models have been met with great difficulties due to their inherent NP-hardness, meaning the computational resources required increase exponentially with the size of the problem, rendering exact heuristic searches practically inefficient for all but the smallest cases. To address this, a diverse array of approximate methods have been proposed to circumvent the intractability of quantum model learning. Quantum Circuit Learning, which focuses on training a quantum circuit to produce a certain target distribution, and Quantum Variational Neural Networks, which can approximate a wide range of functions, including those that describe quantum phenomena such as interference and entanglement, are notable instances of approximate quantum model learning. These approximate techniques enable model discovery in a vast variety of scenarios but potentially lead to substantial loss of accuracy and high training times, even with low complexity quantum gates or restricted network depth. The problem is that these restrictions result in a sub-optimal exploration of the quantum model space, which makes direct comparison to theoretically optimal results challenging. Deep exploration, regularization techniques and exploiting knowledge from related fields offer potential solutions to optimize approximate model learning. Understanding that practically feasible quantum model learning faces huge challenges stimulates ongoing research in subfields such as optimization concepts, loss function formulations and the search of methods through which the precision can be improved effectively with restricted computational resources giving a way forward to potential breakthroughs and broad applications.

title: Dreaming More Data: Class-dependent Distributions over Diffeomorphisms for Learned Data Augmentation
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to data augmentation, addressing the limitations of traditional techniques by leveraging diffeomorphisms to create class-dependent transformations of the input data. The key insight is to learn a distribution over diffeomorphisms, which are smooth, invertible mappings that can stretch and distort the input data in a way that preserves its underlying structure. By using this distribution to generate new, transformed examples of the data, the model can effectively explore the hypothesis space and reduce overfitting. The authors introduce a new type of diffeomorphism learning algorithm that combines neural networks with geometric constraints to ensure the smoothness and invertibility of the transformations. This allows the model to learn robust and generalizable representations of the data. Experiments on several benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method, achieving significant improvements in test accuracy compared to state-of-the-art data augmentation techniques. Furthermore, the resulting models are more robust to noisy and missing data, and exhibit improved transferability to unseen tasks. By fully exploiting the geometric structure of the data, the approach opens up new avenues for learned data augmentation and has the potential to become a fundamental tool in machine learning research.

title: Bifurcation-based adiabatic quantum computation with a nonlinear oscillator network: Toward quantum soft computing
Abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to adiabatic quantum computation by harnessing the power of bifurcations in nonlinear oscillator networks. Bifurcation-based adiabatic quantum computation (BBAQC) leverages the rich dynamic behavior of oscillator networks to encode and manipulate quantum information in a dissipation-free manner. The proposed framework demonstrates that quantum soft computing can be achieved through the self-organization of coherent oscillations in a many-body system, devoid of the need for explicit quantum control and calibration. A key insight is that bifurcations in the network dynamics can be exploited to create a sequence of adiabatic transformations, which enable the efficient solution of unconstrained optimization problems. Theoretical analysis reveals that BBAQC can be realized using a network of weakly coupled nonlinear oscillators, where each oscillator represents a computational unit that can be thought of as a quantum-inspired 'neuron'. The results also show that the computational performance of BBAQC is robust against imperfections and experimental noise, making it an attractive candidate for the development of emergent quantum technologies. By providing a viable alternative to traditional quantum computing paradigms, BBAQC unlocks exciting prospects for the exploration of quantum-inspired computing on classical hardware, offering a more democratic and autonomous pathway to computational innovation. This work showcases the potential of nonlinear oscillator networks to emerge as quantum-soft computing devices, capable of self-organization and real-time optimization of complex problems.

title: A novel mutation operator based on the union of fitness and design spaces information for Differential Evolution
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel mutation operator for Differential Evolution (DE) algorithms that leverages information from both the fitness and design spaces to enhance exploration-exploitation trade-offs. Current mutation operators in DE typically rely on the difference between population members to generate new offspring, which can lead to premature convergence or slow convergence rates. To address these limitations, our proposed mutation operator, denoted as DE-UD (DE with Union of Differential evolution- Design information), involves integrating differential evolution's distance measure with information related to the design space. A computational framework for DE-UD has been developed, allowing it to access and incorporate local information from the design space. During the evolution process, DE-UD iteratively updates and adapts the search direction to navigate through the design space in a more informed and structured manner. We demonstrate the effectiveness of DE-UD on a benchmark set of test instances, including a range of constrained and unconstrained optimization problems. Experimental results show that DE-UD outperforms or matches the performance of existing DE variants and other state-of-the-art algorithms on most problem instances, indicating its potential to become a widely used operator in evolutionary computation. The proposed framework and results presented in this paper contribute to the field of adaptive mutation operators for DE and provide valuable insights into achieving better balance between exploration and exploitation in evolutionary optimization.

title: Data-Efficient Learning of Feedback Policies from Image Pixels using Deep Dynamical Models
Abstract: This work focuses on developing a data-efficient approach for learning feedback policies from image pixels using deep dynamical models. The primary objective is to endow agents with the ability to learn complex sensing and control behaviors from raw visual observations without exhaustive ground truth data, thereby enabling them to generalize to unseen environments and tasks. Drawing upon recent breakthroughs in deep learning and dynamical systems, we propose a novel framework that integrates aspects of model predictive control, direct model learning, and reinforcement learning to construct feedback policies. By employing a deep dynamical model to predict the one-step future state conditioned on the current state and action, the framework enables the agent to adaptively adjust its policy to maximize a cumulative reward function. Our approach is characterized by its ability to compute actions directly from unstructured image pixels, thereby bypassing the need for pre-defined image descriptors or feature engineering. We demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed framework through extensive experiments on a variety of dynamic scenarios, including robotic grasping and manipulation tasks, and show that it achieves substantial data efficiency improvements compared to standard reinforcement learning methods.
