title: Asymptotically tight bounds for inefficiency in risk-averse selfish routing
Abstract: This paper presents a rigorous and comprehensive framework for analyzing inefficiency in risk-averse selfish routing systems. We develop a novel approach to establishing asymptotically tight bounds on the inefficiency of such systems, highlighting the trade-off between selfish routing and risk-averse behavior. Our analysis leverages a combination of insights from optimal transport theory and majorization theory, allowing us to derive a series of tight bounds on the inefficiency of risk-averse selfish routing. These bounds reveal a clear and quantifiable relationship between the level of risk aversion and the ensuing inefficiency, providing a nuanced understanding of the underlying dynamics driving the system. By employing a duality-based framework, we establish a rigorous connection between our bounds and a range of fundamental metrics, including capacity, demand, and flow optimality. Furthermore, our approach enables the derivation of a key relationship between the optimal strategy for risk-averse selfish routing and the classical "price of anarchy" concept, highlighting the potential for our analysis to illuminate the broader landscape of selfish routing systems. By generating a comprehensive and tightly-integrated framework for understanding the inefficiency of risk-averse selfish routing systems, our work contributes to a deeper and more precise understanding of the critical interplay between selfish behavior and system efficiency.

title: Budget Constraints in Prediction Markets
Abstract: The emergence of prediction markets has revolutionized the realm of event forecasting, providing unparalleled insights into the collective sentiments of market participants. However, a critical oversight in these markets is the presence of budget constraints, which significantly influence the diversity and accuracy of participant responses. The current market design fails to account for the finite resources available to investors, leading to a reduced scope of information aggregation. This phenomenon is detrimental, as under-resourced investors are compelled to prioritize their bets, resulting in fragmented responses and subsequently diluted market signals. Furthermore, the uneven distribution of capital among market participants distorts market outcomes, limiting the emergence of accurate forecasts. This paper delves into the intricacies of budget constraints in prediction markets, elucidating their profound impact on market performance. By examining the relationship between investment portfolios, decision-making behavior, and market efficiency, we shed light on the debilitating effects of resource scarcity on prediction markets. Ultimately, this comprehensive analysis fosters a deeper understanding of the operational dynamics within these markets, laying the groundwork for innovative design improvements that can effectively mitigate the detrimental consequences of budget constraints and unlock the full potential of prediction markets.

title: Towards a general framework for an observation and knowledge based model of occupant behaviour in office buildings
Abstract: This research proposes a novel framework for modeling occupant behavior in office buildings, focusing on the interplay between observations and knowledge. Existing literature on occupant behavior has mainly relied on anecdotal evidence or generic models that fail to account for building-specific characteristics and occupant diversity. To address this limitation, we develop a general framework that integrates various sources of data, including sensor measurements, occupant surveys, and building characteristics. The proposed framework utilizes a knowledge graph to represent occupant behavior patterns, allowing for a more comprehensive and nuanced understanding of occupant interactions with the built environment. By leveraging machine learning and data analytics techniques, the framework can identify complex relationships between occupant behavior, building performance, and occupant satisfaction. Furthermore, the framework is designed to be adaptable to various office building typologies and can accommodate dynamic changes in occupant behavior over time. Through a case study of a large office building, we demonstrate the efficacy of our framework in predicting occupant behavior and identifying areas for energy efficiency improvements. The proposed framework has considerable potential to inform building design and management practices, contributing to the creation of more sustainable, comfortable, and productive office environments. By bridging the gap between observations and knowledge, our framework offers a transformative approach to occupant-centered building design and operation.

title: Using Ontology-Based Context in the Portuguese-English Translation of Homographs in Textual Dialogues
Abstract: This paper explores the incorporation of ontology-based context into the translation of homographs in Portuguese-English textual dialogues. Homographs are words that have the same spelling but different meanings, which can lead to ambiguity and errors in machine translation and human translation alike. In this study, a case is made for utilizing contextual information within large ontologies to disambiguate homographs and improve translation accuracy. The proposed system combines a Portuguese language ontology with a contextual inference model to provide a more nuanced understanding of text meaning. A key benefit of this approach is its ability to adapt to a wide range of textual genres, from casual conversation to formal correspondence. By examining the performance of the proposed system against both human-translated and machine-translated corpora, this research evaluates the effectiveness of ontology-based context in eliminating homograph-related translation errors. The findings indicate significant reductions in errors attributed to homograph translation in both English-Portuguese and Portuguese-English translation directions. Moreover, the study demonstrates the ability of ontology-based context to function across multiple domains and a variety of lexical registers.

title: VBPR: Visual Bayesian Personalized Ranking from Implicit Feedback
Abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to personalized ranking for recommendation systems using visual implicit feedback, which we term as Visual Bayesian Personalized Ranking (VBPR). Traditional methods often rely on user ratings or explicit feedback, which can be time-consuming and expensive to collect. In contrast, VBPR leverages implicit feedback from user interactions with visually presented items, such as clicks, views, and purchases, to learn the underlying user preferences. Our proposed framework combines the strengths of deep learning and Bayesian inference to effectively model the complex interactions between users, items, and their visual attributes. In the proposed VBPR model, each user is represented as a set of latent factors that capture their interests, while items are modeled as a combination of their visual and content features. Our Bayesian inference process estimates the posterior distribution over latent factors, allowing for uncertainty quantification and robust recommendation. Extensive experiments on two benchmark datasets (Last.fm and Ta-Feng) demonstrate the superior performance of VBPR compared to state-of-the-art methods, including improved ranking accuracy and efficiency. Our results also reveal the benefits of incorporating visual attributes in the recommendation process and the potential of VBPR for real-world applications in e-commerce, social media, and personalized advertising. By providing a flexible and scalable framework for modeling complex user preferences from implicit feedback, VBPR has the potential to revolutionize the field of recommendation systems.

title: DKP-AOM: results for OAEI 2015
Abstract: This paper presents an evaluation of the results of our novel approach, DKP-AOM, which stands for Diplo Deep KEM Paths Automatic Ontology Mapping, in the context of the Ontology Alignment Evaluation Initiative (OAEI) 2015. The core contributions of this work lay in implementing an automated solution to match ontologies, utilizing predefined and pre-computed patterns in the framework of Description Logics (DL). The proposed method utilizes a novel representation, specifically a diplo-deep KEM path, to incorporate the relationships between logical axioms in ontology structures as an intermediate step before the alignment process. For ontology matching, the DKP-AOM tool relies on a built-in system for reasoning using domain knowledge to compare entities between ontologies. Furthermore, a series of empirical experiments and detailed comparative analysis against other state-of-the-art matching techniques, as employed in the evaluation tasks of the OAEI 2015, highlight notable performance enhancements in the DKP-AOM framework when it came to adapting to the diversity of provided real-world benchmarks and simulated alignment scenarios. Such comprehensive evaluation and analytical inspection into the efficacy of DKP-AOM underscore the technology's potential in addressing real-world applications where precise ontology matching on a scalable and efficient basis is desired.

title: Disjunctive Answer Set Solvers via Templates
Abstract: This paper presents an innovative framework for developing disjunctive answer set solvers using templates, a novel approach that boosts the development efficiency of disjunctive answer set programming (DASP) solvers and fosters the creation of high-performance solvers tailored to various real-world applications. Based on an extensible template, our proposed framework seamlessly integrates existing optimization techniques, facilitating the fusion of novel constraint handling methods, local search strategies, and other optimization techniques into existing DASP solvers. Furthermore, our framework automates many routine tasks associated with solver development, including case-of-the-art engine design, optimization configuration management, and overall efficiency evaluation, thereby significantly reducing the complexity and time required for implementing and optimizing disjunctive answer set solvers. The framework's extensibility also allows for the development of incremental improvements and maintenance of solvers throughout their operational lifecycle. Through extensive experimentation, we demonstrate the framework's effectiveness in generating, testing, and optimizing three representative DASP solvers, achieving high performance and robustness that compare favorably with state-of-the-art solvers. Our work thus provides a substantial and tractable paradigm for crafting highly specialized DASP solvers and fosters the broad utilization of answer set programming in various fields by accelerating solver development and optimization.

title: Where to look first? Behaviour control for fetch-and-carry missions of service robots
Abstract:
This research focus on service robots' fetch-and-carry missions where they need to interact with their environment in a safe and efficient manner to successfully accomplish their objectives. In traditional robotics, the primary goal often revolves around creating a control strategy that allows robots to interact with external objects, which could be static or in motion. Noticing that the complexities typically arise when a robot requires to initiate the communication in a dynamic environment; hence, the researcher investigated optimal sensorial data integration techniques that allow for decision making and flexibility enhancement to the robot's navigation system in real-time. Moreover, focusing on robotic behaviour control for a fetch and carry operation, researchers discovered the critical value of integrating attention mechanisms which guide decision making and enable service robots navigate complex environments where unforeseen obstacles could be present, therefore avoiding unpredictable interactions that could result in system crashes.

As part of the investigation into how the given settings for the mission affect robots' behavior control, we categorised three different behaviour controlled states for service robots and highlighted that all these states have an effect on the accomplishment of mission objectives. Overall performance evaluations show the practicality of a smartly selected perception system which not only collects the information it requires but interprets them correctly without any need for extra hardware.

title: Local Rademacher Complexity Bounds based on Covering Numbers
Abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to establishing local Rademacher complexity bounds by utilizing the concept of covering numbers, a key notion in computational geometry and approximation theory. Our analysis begins by introducing a generalized covering number for a given set of Rademacher distributions, which we refer to as the empirical covering number. We demonstrate that the empirical covering number can be efficiently estimated using a Rademacher average of a learning machine, thereby providing a computationally tractable proxy for the original covering number. We then apply our empirical covering number-based framework to derive both upper and lower bounds on the local Rademacher complexity, capturing the effect of the specific covering used in the argument. The derived bounds are shown to be tight in certain regimes, thus serving as a useful tool for analyzing the behavior of learning machines in high-dimensional spaces and facilitating a more nuanced understanding of their learnability characteristics. In practical terms, the proposed local bounds have the potential to lead to significant improvements in efficiency and accuracy of various machine learning algorithms, by enabling a more principled control over their generalization performance and adaptability to different types of data distributions.

title: Within-Brain Classification for Brain Tumor Segmentation
Abstract: This study presents a novel within-brain classification approach for brain tumor segmentation, where the brain Scan is first segmented into CSF, white matter, grey matter, and the lesion region. The segmented regions are then classified into normal brain and tumor using a feature-based classification system, where the features are calculated from the intensity and morphological characteristics of the brain scan. The results of the classification are then used to re-segment the brain scan to obtain the tumor mask. To improve the results, a post-processing step is applied to remove noise from the segmented tumor mask. The proposed approach is evaluated using various metrics such as Dice similarity coefficient, Jaccard similarity coefficient, and Average Surface Distance. The results show that the proposed method outperforms the state-of-the-art methods, achieving high accuracy and precision in brain tumor segmentation. Additionally, the within-brain classification approach has the potential to reduce the false positives and improve the overall performance of brain tumor segmentation. The proposed method can be applied to various applications such as neurosurgery planning, radiation therapy planning, and diagnosis of brain tumors. The results of this study show the feasibility and potential of the within-brain classification approach in brain tumor segmentation, and it provides a new direction for future research in this field.

title: A Common-Factor Approach for Multivariate Data Cleaning with an Application to Mars Phoenix Mission Data
Abstract: This paper proposes a common-factor approach for multivariate data cleaning, a critical but often overlooked step in data analysis. Motivated by the need for robust and reliable data cleaning methods, we develop a principled framework for identifying and removing common patterns of error in multivariate datasets. Our approach leverages the concept of common factors, typically used in factor analysis to uncover underlying latent structures, to model and remove error patterns that are common across multiple variables. This method has several advantages over conventional methods, including the ability to handle complex error patterns and multiple types of errors simultaneously. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach using the Mars Phoenix Mission's atmospheric data, which is notorious for its errors and missing values. By applying our common-factor approach, we are able to significantly reduce errors and recover accurate information about the Martian atmosphere, which is essential for scientific research and mission planning. Furthermore, our approach can be easily adapted to other datasets with similar characteristics, making it a valuable tool for data analysts across various fields.

title: 5G Ultra-Reliable Vehicular Communication
Abstract: This paper delves into the burgeoning realm of 5G ultra-reliable vehicular communication, a pivotal component in the integration of Automated Driving Systems (ADS) and Internet of Things (IoT) within the transport infrastructure. The continued reliance on radio communication as the primary medium for vehicular communication necessitates the development of ultra-reliable technologies that can mitigate the prevalent latency, packet losses, and mobility-induced handovers intrinsic to in-vehicle networks. As a result, the implementation of 5G ultra-reliable vehicular communication becomes an essential driver for enhancing road safety and traffic efficiency. This paper begins by delving into the characteristics of the targeted landscape, focusing on the parameters of 5G NR air interface, which provide a robust foundation for establishing ultra-high reliability objectives. The exploration of ultra-reliable low-loss wireless transmission, key techniques for supporting mission-critical services, and new 3D beamforming configurations is presented. Furthermore, the paper evaluates several vehicular network architectures capable of orchestrating seamless and efficient communication in real-time adverse dynamic scenarios. By proposing a proactive and proactive policy to manage complexity, and propose an optimized mechanism to estimate channel state information (CSI), the intended paper strives to aid the development of a comprehensive and realistic application framework.

title: Boosting in the presence of outliers: adaptive classification with non-convex loss functions
Abstract: This research proposes an adaptive classification framework for handling noisy and highly imbalanced data characterized by outliers. The existing classification algorithms heavily rely on convex loss functions which may not effectively mitigate the impact of outliers, leading to biased model estimates. By contrast, non-convex loss functions, such as least absolute deviation (LAD) and Huber loss, are more robust to outliers but have been limited by their computational complexity and instability. To address this challenge, we introduce an adaptive boosting algorithm that dynamically adjusts the convex-non-convex loss ratio based on the identified outlier observations. Our framework leverages the merits of both convex and non-convex loss functions and scales efficiently by iteratively updating a convex-linear mixture of base learners. Using a comprehensive suite of experiments on diverse datasets, we demonstrate that our adaptive classification framework efficiently minimizes loss under the presence of outliers and tackles the convergence issues inherent in standalone non-convex loss functions. Moreover, we provide theoretical evidence on the convergence rate of our adaptive boosting method, highlighting its robustness to outliers and non-convex loss landscapes. The proposed approach offers a versatile methodology for data analysts and modelers seeking to unveil significant insights from noisy datasets.

title: Cross-convolutional-layer Pooling for Image Recognition
Abstract: This article delves into the realm of deep neural networks and presents an innovative approach to image recognition, focusing on the application of cross-convolutional-layer pooling. By designing a pooling method that combines the benefits of spatial pyramid pooling and cross-channel pooling, this technique aims to rectify the trade-off between feature representation and computational efficiency inherent in conventional convolutional neural networks (CNNs). The proposed approach effectively aggregates multi-scale spatial features and frequency features, thus facilitating robust image representation and improved generalizability. Rigorous experiments on benchmark datasets, including CIFAR-10 and ImageNet, demonstrate the merits of cross-convolutional-layer pooling over its conventional counterparts. When integrated into a pre-trained CNN, the methodology yields significant performance enhancements, with notable improvements in top-1 accuracy and robustness against various transformations, including rotation, scaling, and flipping. Furthermore, the proposed method substantially reduces the computational cost, thereby overcoming one of the significant hurdles inherent in adopting deep neural networks for resource-constrained devices and scenarios with stringent real-time requirements. Overall, the findings presented in this article underscore the potential of cross-convolutional-layer pooling as a compelling technique for advancing the field of image recognition, particularly in applications where both precision and efficiency hold paramount importance.

title: Client Profiling for an Anti-Money Laundering System
Abstract: This research aimed to investigate the application of client profiling in enhancing the effectiveness of anti-money laundering (AML) systems. AML systems rely heavily on the ability to identify and flag suspicious transactions, which is often challenging due to the complexity and variability of illicit financial transactions. Client profiling is an emerging technique used in AML systems to gather and analyze data about individual clients, to assess their likelihood of engaging in money laundering activities. This study proposes a novel client profiling framework that incorporates both rule-based and machine learning-based approaches to construct a comprehensive risk profile for each client. The framework utilizes both client-specific data (e.g., identification information, transaction history) and external data sources (e.g., sanctions lists, adverse media reports) to generate a dynamic risk score for each client. The proposed framework was evaluated using a dataset of real-world clients and demonstrated improved detection accuracy and reduced false positive rates compared to traditional rule-based AML systems. The findings of this study suggest that incorporating client profiling into AML systems can significantly enhance the detection of money laundering activities, while also reducing the risk of flagging legitimate clients.

title: Approximate Fisher Kernels of non-iid Image Models for Image Categorization
Abstract: This paper investigates the application of approximate Fisher kernels to non-independent and identically distributed (non-iid) image models for image categorization tasks. Traditional methods of computing Fisher kernels require rigorous matching between feature representations and class-specific models, which is computationally expensive when dealing with non-iid data. To address this limitation, we propose an approximate approach that leverages the concept of Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs) and non-negative quadratic forms to efficiently compute the Fisher kernel responses. By resorting to a non-rigid pseudo-input framework, our method allows for a range of flexible and discriminative power enabling its use across diverse image classification contexts with significant memory and computational cost advantages over other existing methods. Our formulation integrates a family of likelihood kernels into the Fisher kernel formulation and results in an efficient and interpretable solution allowing both theoretical and intuitive insight into modelling the underlying joint distribution of the observed data. Through a series of systematic evaluations on widely used benchmark datasets including Caltech101, CIFAR100, and ImageNet, our empirical results demonstrate that the proposed approach is capable of leveraging diverse information and yielding improved accuracy, with a notable trade-off between memory efficiency and efficacy compared to exact Fisher kernel methods.

title: Intelligent Search Optimization using Artificial Fuzzy Logics
Abstract: This study proposes an innovative search optimization approach based on the integration of artificial fuzzy logic systems and optimization techniques to tackle complex search problems efficiently. The proposed method leverages the strengths of fuzzy logic in handling uncertainty and ambiguity while incorporating optimization algorithms to identify the optimal search strategies. By utilizing fuzzy inference systems, the approach enables the representation of complex relationships and decision-making processes in a more flexible and robust manner, thereby improving the accuracy and reliability of the search results. The integration of fuzzy logic with optimization algorithms, such as genetic algorithms and simulated annealing, further enhances the search optimization process by allowing for the exploration of a larger solution space and the identification of the global optimum with higher precision. Experimental results and comparative studies demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed approach in multiple search scenarios, including classic benchmark problems and real-world applications. The findings of this research contribute to the development of more effective and efficient search optimization methods, which can be applied in various fields, including artificial intelligence, computer science, and data analytics, to optimize complex problem-solving processes and improve decision-making capabilities. The implications of this research are profound, as they can lead to significant improvements in the efficiency and effectiveness of search optimization processes in various domains, thereby enabling the identification of better solutions and informed decision-making.

title: Bayesian modeling of networks in complex business intelligence problems
Abstract: Bayesian modeling of networks has emerged as a powerful tool in tackling complex business intelligence problems, where uncertainty and interconnectedness are pervasive. This research explores the application of Bayesian methods to capture the intricate structure of business intelligence networks, which often involve disparate data sources, opaque relationships, and emergent patterns. By employing a Bayesian framework, we aim to infer the underlying relationships between entities, uncover latent knowledge, and provide a robust and scalable approach for analyzing business intelligence data. Our approach is grounded in the concept of a prior distribution, which effectively incorporates prior knowledge, expert opinions, and available data, while leveraging the strength of Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) and variational inference algorithms to efficiently explore the vast model space. The proposed framework enables principled inference of network structure, edge weights, and node characteristics, allowing for the detection of anomalous behavior, identifying key influencers, and predicting business outcomes. Through a series of case studies on real-world business intelligence datasets, we demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of our approach in capturing complex business intelligence phenomena, outperforming traditional network analysis techniques in terms of predictive accuracy, interpretability, and scalability. By providing a Bayesian foundation for network modeling in business intelligence, our research contributes to the development of more data-driven, adaptive, and anticipatory decision-making strategies for organizations operating in increasingly complex and dynamic environments.

title: Online Vision- and Action-Based Object Classification Using Both Symbolic and Subsymbolic Knowledge Representations
Abstract: This research paper proposes an innovative approach to online vision-and-action-based object classification that leverages both symbolic and subsymbolic knowledge representations to improve accuracy and adaptability in dynamic environments. Traditional object classification models often rely on static, pre-defined knowledge representations, which can be insufficient for handling complex, real-world scenarios characterized by varying lighting conditions, object transformations, and sensor noise. To overcome these limitations, our proposed approach combines symbolic knowledge representation with subsymbolic knowledge representation, drawn from cognitive architectures and neural network models, respectively. The symbolic component provides a high-level, explicit representation of object categories and their attributes, enabling fast and efficient inference in well-characterized environments. In contrast, the subsymbolic component represents object features in a lower-level, distributed manner, allowing the model to learn from experience and navigate uncertain or dynamic situations. Our online learning framework enables seamless updates and adaption to new data, reducing the need for manual labeling and retraining. Through comprehensive experiments on benchmark datasets and real-world applications, this research demonstrates the efficacy of the proposed approach in achieving state-of-the-art performance in object classification while ensuring adaptability to changing environments.

title: Contribution to the Formal Specification and Verification of a Multi-Agent Robotic System
Abstract: This abstract presents a comprehensive approach to the formal specification and verification of a multi-agent robotic system. With the increasing complexity and autonomy of modern robotic systems, ensuring their correctness and reliability has become a paramount concern in various domains, including logistics, healthcare, and navigation. To address this challenge, we propose a methodology that combines concepts from formal methods, multi-agent systems, and robotic control. Specifically, we employ a combination of model-based and syntax-based formal approaches to provide a rigorous and expressive framework for specifying the behavior of individual robotic agents and their interactions with the environment and each other. Our approach is built around a formal language, developed for describing the temporal and spatial aspects of robot behavior, and is augmented with verification tools and techniques to check the correctness of agent-level and system-level properties. A case study involving a group of simulated robots navigating a shared workspace is used to evaluate the proposed methodology and demonstrate its effectiveness in detecting errors and ensuring system correctness. The results of this study show that the proposed approach can efficiently identify potential failures and inconsistencies in the robotic system, thereby improving its overall reliability and safety.

title: Exposing the Probabilistic Causal Structure of Discrimination
Abstract: This research paper proposes a novel probabilistic causal framework for uncovering the underlying causal structure of discrimination, bridging the gap between research on causal inference and social inequality. Our framework, which we term 'Discrimination Causal Graph' (DCG), integrates concepts from probabilistic causality, network analysis, and social sciences to model the complex interplay between discriminatory behaviors and outcomes. By quantifying the strength and confidence of causal links between discriminatory parameters and outcome variables, the DCG enables researchers to identify and prioritize the most influential drivers of discrimination. We demonstrate the feasibility of this framework using a combination of empirical data from disparate fields, including education, employment, and law enforcement. Our results show that the DCG successfully identifies networks of discriminatory relationships, distinguishes between direct and indirect effects, and contextualizes these relationships within the broader social landscape. The DCG thus provides a powerful tool for unpacking the causal mechanisms underlying discrimination, thereby empowering policymakers, practitioners, and researchers to craft targeted interventions that tackle systemic inequalities. By unveiling the probabilistic causal structure of discrimination, this research contributes to a more nuanced and effective understanding of this pervasive social issue.

title: Implementing Efficient All Solutions SAT Solvers
Abstract: This work presents a novel implementation of efficient all-solutions SAT (Boolean Satisfiability) solvers, which offer a systematic approach to exhaustively finding all feasible solutions to a given Boolean formula, thus addressing one of the fundamental open problems in the field. By partitioning the search space using a new graph-based data structure and extending state-of-the-art clause learning techniques, our approach has been shown to significantly outperform existing all-solutions SAT solvers in terms of both solution count and quality, offering a reliable inference engine for diverse applications, including but not limited to, artificial intelligence planning, model counting, and constraint programming. The proposed method contributes to advancing the frontier of complete All-SAT solvers by addressing numerous long-standing scalability, and robustness bottlenecks impeding large-scale solvers, while shedding light on key insights into effective learning strategies, efficient variable ordering, and novel clause database restructuring in a powerful yet theoretically grounded framework. Notably, our breakthrough implementation may expedite tasks that require counting or enumerating Boolean models, augmenting both theoretical understanding and practical realization, this comprehensive research report outlines the methodologies and innovations applied in solving All-SAT problems in an efficient manner. The solution significantly outperforms several prominent complete All-SAT solvers, which was tested with a large benchmark.

title: Multimodal Hierarchical Dirichlet Process-based Active Perception
Abstract: This paper presents a novel framework for active perception, which combines the benefits of multimodal sensing and hierarchical Dirichlet process (HDP) modeling to adaptively select salient tasks and modalities. Our method addresses the challenge of continuous learning in dynamic environments, where the probability of encountering new events is high and the environment's underlying structure evolves over time. We first formulate a generative model for the observed data, which assimilates the expertise of multiple modalities, including visual, acoustic, and kinesthetic, through the multimodal HDP (MHDP). The MHDP model enables our framework to flexibly allocate attention across multiple modalities, autonomously identifying the most informative or critical modality for each task. Furthermore, by employing a hierarchical approach, we infuse the MHDP model with domain knowledge, enabling the framework to refine its initial understanding of the environment and progressively generalize its knowledge to novel experiences. Our approach leverages Bayesian non-parametric modeling, offering a natural and intuitive way to incrementally learn from the environment and handle uncertainty in the statistical inference process. As a critical component of our framework, active task selection is formulated as an optimization problem under a trade-off of exploration-exploitation and task-relevance, ensuring that the agent efficiently allocates resources to discover new knowledge. Experimental validation is performed on various benchmark tasks, demonstrating the versatility and adaptability of our method, while comparisons with state-of-the-art active perception methods highlight the benefits of incorporating hierarchical Dirichlet process modeling and multimodal sensing.

title: Proceedings of the ACE Challenge Workshop - a satellite event of IEEE-WASPAA (2015)
Abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of the ACE Challenge Workshop, a satellite event of the IEEE Workshop on Applications of Signal Processing to Audio and Acoustics (WASPAA) held in 2015. The workshop focused on assessing the performance of source separation algorithms for audio signals, a crucial task in various audio processing applications. A total of 27 algorithms were tested on a database of 10 realistic audio mixtures, each containing two, three, or four sources. The evaluation framework was based on objective quality metrics and subjective listening tests, conducted with a pool of 34 listeners. The results show insights into the strengths and weaknesses of different techniques, such as deep learning-based models, non-negative matrix factorization, and subspace-based methods. The analysis highlights the existence of significant disparities between various evaluation metrics and lists. Furthermore, an evaluation of the reliability of listeners' opinion scores demonstrates a significant variability across listeners, source setups, and music genres. The complexity of the task is illustrated by the near-optimal performance achieved by a few state-of-the-art algorithms on certain assessment measures. Nevertheless, the workshop's findings suggest considerable room for improvement in developing source separation systems that meet the diverse requirements of various applications. Overall, the workshop objectives were successfully met, providing a thorough roadmap for further advancements in source separation research and establishing a framework for the evaluation of audio source separation systems.

title: A Generative Model of Words and Relationships from Multiple Sources
Abstract: This research proposes a novel generative model capable of capturing complex relationships between words from multiple sources of text data. The model, dubbed WordNet++, integrates the strengths of traditional word embeddings with the expressive power of graph-based methods to create a unified framework for modeling word semantics. By leveraging a combination of static and dynamic graph-based relationships, along with the structural and semantic significance of words in respective texts, it accurately represents and generalizes relationships between words. Our approach incorporates auxiliary information from parallel corpora and other knowledge sources to further leverage the training data and boost the accuracy of word relationships. To evaluate the performance of the proposed system, we conduct comprehensive experiments on various datasets and observe substantial gains in word similarity and relationship prediction tasks, compared to other state-of-the-art word representation methods based solely on static word relationships. We also observe consistent pattern emergence in word distributions across different models, validating their practical use cases for semantic analysis and subsequent natural language processing (NLP) tasks. As a whole, the proposed model demonstrates its versatility and efficacy in organizing a network of relationships for words with a unique, comprehensive methodology that can be effectively implemented in several areas such as text mining, question answering systems and text generating tasks.

title: Transfer Learning from Deep Features for Remote Sensing and Poverty Mapping
Abstract: Transfer learning has revolutionized the field of remote sensing by enabling the utilization of pre-trained deep neural networks (DNNs) to extract meaningful features from complex remote sensing datasets, thereby achieving state-of-the-art performance in various applications such as land cover classification, crop health monitoring, and disaster response. However, most existing research has focused on utilizing pre-trained DNNs as feature extractors, neglecting the potential of further improving the accuracy of classification tasks through fine-tuning. This papers investigates the effectiveness of transfer learning from deep features for poverty mapping in developing countries using publicly available data. We evaluate the impact of fine-tuning pre-trained models on the accuracy of poverty mapping tasks, considering various configurations of model architecture, learning rate schedules, and optimization algorithms. Our results demonstrate that fine-tuning pre-trained DNNs can significantly improve the accuracy of poverty mapping tasks, with gains of up to 10% compared to the non-fine-tuned baseline. Notably, we find that the performance of fine-tuned models is highly sensitive to the choice of learning rate schedule and optimization algorithm, underscoring the importance of careful hyperparameter tuning. We also conduct an ablation study to investigate the contribution of individual layers to the overall performance of the fine-tuned models, revealing that the penultimate layer is the most significant contributor to the improvement in accuracy.

title: Clamping Improves TRW and Mean Field Approximations
Abstract: Clamping improves Tight Relaxation Woods (TRW) and Mean Field Approximations, a crucial development in approximate inference and belief propagation techniques. This work reveals how incorporating clamping, a procedure of fixing variables according to their mean field or marginal inference, enhances the performance of TRW and Mean Field approximations in solving complex probabilistic graphical models. Recent studies in artificial intelligence and machine learning have highlighted the shortcomings of traditional exact inference methods in handling large, high-dimensional graphs. Focusing on addressing this issue, researchers have sought alternative approaches, leveraging approximate inference techniques that yield efficient, yet unbiased solutions. Clamping, in this context, forms a vital building block by refining TRW and Mean Field approximations through a systematic method of marginal inference. By leveraging clamping in conjunction with TRW and Mean Field algorithms, researchers can counteract the limitations of existing inference techniques. Consequently, this adaptation opens avenues for refining model learning and probabilistic reasoning in machine learning applications where intricate graphical structures are typical. Moreover, its seamless integration with other optimization methods fosters the potential of tackling challenging problems.

title: Supporting interoperability of collaborative networks through engineering of a service-based Mediation Information System (MISE 2.0)
Abstract: The interoperability of collaborative networks is a crucial aspect of facilitating seamless data exchange and collaboration among different entities. However, the existing technical, organizational, and social barriers hinder the effective integration of these networks, leading to inefficiencies and limitations in achieving their goals. To address this challenge, this research paper presents the design and development of MISE 2.0 (Mediation Information System), a service-based system engineered to support interoperability in collaborative networks. Built upon the principles of service-oriented architecture (SOA), MISE 2.0 provides a flexible and adaptable framework for facilitating the integration of diverse networks, systems, and applications. Through the use of semantic mediation techniques, data mapping, and service composition, MISE 2.0 enables the seamless exchange of data and services between different stakeholders, breaking down technical, organizational, and social barriers. The proposed system addresses the limitations of existing mediation systems by incorporating advanced features such as Context-Aware Negotiation, Automatic Service Composition, and Real-time Monitoring. By harnessing the potential of MISE 2.0, collaborative networks can achieve improved interoperability, reduced conflicts, and increased efficiency, ultimately leading to more effective collaboration and better outcomes. This research aims to contribute to the advancement of collaborative networks and the development of more effective mediation systems.

title: Knowledge-based system for collaborative process specification
Abstract:
This paper presents an innovative knowledge-based system designed to facilitate collaborative process specification in complex organizational settings. By leveraging the power of knowledge graphs and artificial intelligence, our system integrates the collective expertise of stakeholders to create a comprehensive and adaptive process specification framework. The proposed system utilizes a hybrid knowledge representation model that combines formal and natural language processing approaches to capture the intricacies of process knowledge. Key features of our system include automated process discovery, collaborative knowledge modeling, and decision-making support through expert system reasoning.

The knowledge-based system is designed to support multiple stakeholders, including process owners, experts, and end-users, in a collaborative environment. By leveraging knowledge graphs, our system enables the reuse and integration of existing knowledge, reducing the time and effort required to specify processes. A major contribution of this research is the development of a novel process specification framework that incorporates contextual and dynamic elements, enabling better adaptability to changing organizational requirements. The system is further empowered by integrating machine learning algorithms, allowing it to learn from experience and improve process knowledge over time. Our system's efficacy is demonstrated through a case study on a large-scale organizational process, showcasing its ability to facilitate more effective and efficient process specification. With this innovative approach, organizations can benefit from improved process knowledge, reduced complexity, and enhanced collaborative decision-making capabilities.

title: A Sentence Meaning Based Alignment Method for Parallel Text Corpora Preparation
Abstract: This paper presents a novel sentence meaning based alignment method for preparing parallel text corpora, which enable machine translation evaluation, language learning, and cross-lingual information retrieval among others. The proposed method leverages deep learning and cognitive linguistic insights, particularly from the framework of Meaning-Text Model. This approach focuses on aligning the aligned sentences at the level of their underlying meanings, aiming to reduce the errors in word-to-word or segment-to-segment alignments, and improve the overall quality of the prepared parallel text corpora. The sentence meaning is first represented using a hierarchical multi-layer graph-based structure, allowing for the incorporation of subtle linguistic nuances and abstract semantic relationships between words. Subsequently, the proposed method aligns these meaning representations across languages, with allowance for lexical ambiguities and polysemic meanings, yielding more accurate alignments of sentences with matched linguistic contexts. To evaluate the efficacy of the proposed method, comparative experiments were performed using diverse parallel text corpora, with results indicate that the proposed alignment method achieves state-of-the-art performance in sentence-to-sentence alignment quality and maintains competitive performance in supporting high-quality downstream tasks.

title: Real-Time Statistical Speech Translation
Abstract: This paper delves into the realm of real-time statistical speech translation, where significant advancements in the field of artificial intelligence and machine learning have led to the development of efficient and practical systems. A key focus of the research lies in leveraging statistical models to enable real-time speech-to-text translations that cater to the needs of multilingual communication in diverse domains, such as international diplomacy, business, and tourism. By employing techniques like Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) and robust contextual modeling, our proposed system successfully captures the intricacies of spoken languages and efficiently translates verbal input into target languages. The integration of sophisticated algorithms, adequate computational resources, and extensive domain-specific training enables the system to achieve remarkable translation accuracy and unprecedented processing speeds. Furthermore, the proposed system is equipped to adapt to scenarios involving unscripted dialogue, accommodating typical features of spoken language, such as disfluencies, false starts, and filler sounds. With a strong emphasis on user-centric design, the system presents output in the desired format, engaging the user with intuitive interfaces and natural feedback mechanisms. Key evaluation metrics highlight the effectiveness of our proposed system, demonstrating superior translation accuracy, rapid processing times, and an engaging user interface that promotes immersive multilingual communication.

title: Moving Object Detection in Video Using Saliency Map and Subspace Learning
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach for moving object detection in video using a saliency map and subspace learning framework. The increasing demand for intelligent surveillance systems and robotic applications that can operate in complex environments necessitates the development of reliable methods for detecting moving objects in video. Our approach leverages advances in computer vision and pattern recognition to address this challenge. A deep learning-based model is employed to generate a saliency map for each frame, which highlights the most relevant regions that are likely to contain moving objects. To improve the robustness and accuracy of object detection, a subspace learning technique is applied to the saliency map, enabling the extraction of discriminative features that are invariant to changes in pose, scale, and illumination. The subspace learning framework is further enhanced by incorporating a weighted neighborhood graph that captures the inherent spatial relationship between pixels within each frame. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on publicly available datasets, showcasing significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods in terms of precision, recall, and F1-score. Furthermore, our approach successfully detects moving objects in challenging scenarios, including fast motion, partial occlusion, and varying lighting conditions. The proposed framework offers a promising solution for video analysis and can be widely applied in surveillance, security, and robotics applications where real-time object detection is critical.

title: Multi-objective Differential Evolution with Helper Functions for Constrained Optimization
Abstract: Multi-objective Differential Evolution with Helper Functions for Constrained Optimization is a novel metaheuristic approach that addresses the limitations of traditional optimization techniques in handling multiple objectives and constraints simultaneously. This method integrates the principles of Differential Evolution with the concept of helper functions, which are designed to facilitate the exploration and exploitation of the search space while ensuring that the solution adheres to the given constraints. The proposed approach is tailored to tackle real-world optimization problems that involve multiple conflicting objectives and complex constraints. By leveraging the strengths of helper functions, the algorithm is able to adaptively adjust its exploration and exploitation phases, leading to improved convergence rates and better Pareto front approximations. A key advantage of the proposed method is its ability to handle disparate objective functions, varying degrees of non-linearity, and irregular constraint boundaries without compromising its efficiency and effectiveness. Furthermore, the algorithm's ability to incorporate domain-specific knowledge through the helper functions enables it to solve complex problems that have not been tackled using traditional optimization methods. The proposed Multi-objective Differential Evolution with Helper Functions demonstrates promising results in solving benchmark functions and real-world applications, showcasing its potential as a powerful optimization tool for various fields.

title: Asynchronous Gibbs Sampling
Abstract:
Asynchronous Gibbs sampling is a pivotal extension of the traditional Gibbs sampling algorithm, enabling the exploration of complex Bayesian networks with substantial computational efficiency and speed-up. Unifying strengths from both parallel and sequential computing paradigms, this versatile sampling technique instantiates multiple chains simultaneously, promoting concurrent computations, thereby making the Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methodology an even more viable alternative for modeling large and highly interconnected systems. This innovative adaptation leverages a dedicated asynchronous communication protocol among chains, which efficiently manages the shared state space, hence, facilitating a well-controlled exploration of the entire posterior distribution without sacrificing its accuracy. Empirical studies indicate that asynchronous Gibbs sampling achieves significant acceleration of sampling, often resulting in considerable time savings, especially in scenarios involving computationally expensive likelihood functions and hierarchical models. Furthermore, this approach has opened up new avenues for scaling complex Bayesian modeling and inference to problems of large sizes. 

By analyzing the theoretical framework and conducting in-depth numerical experiments, this research provides a comprehensive and systematic investigation into the asynchronous Gibbs sampling algorithm, focusing on its main characteristics, advantages, and computational benefits, as well as shedding light on some critical considerations and limitations that need further exploration. As a result, the research provides a thorough evaluation of the algorithm and its potential application in a broad range of domains, including but not limited to computer vision, natural language processing, and machine learning, making it possible to tackle intricate modeling problems that were previously thought to be computationally infeasible.

title: Symbol Emergence in Robotics: A Survey
Abstract: This work provides a comprehensive survey of the concept of symbol emergence in robotics, aiming to uncover the underlying mechanisms behind the autonomous acquisition of symbolic representations by artificial systems. Symbol emergence refers to the process whereby artificial agents, such as robots, generate and employ meaningful symbols or abstractions to describe and interact with their environment, ultimately achieving a level of cognitive understanding that is seemingly human-like. Through a thorough literature review, this survey explores the various approaches used in artificial intelligence and robotics research to facilitate symbol emergence, including symbolic AI, connectionist modeling, cognitive architectures, and social learning paradigms. The results indicate that successful symbol emergence requires a synergistic combination of computational mechanisms, such as self-organization and creativity, with cognitive processes, like attention and reasoning. Moreover, the survey highlights challenges and open questions in this field, like the trade-off between expressiveness and computational resources, and the need for new evaluation metrics to assess the symbolic competence of artificial agents. The survey concludes by pointing to avenues for future research that combine fundamental advances in machine learning and cognitive architectures with experimental validation using cutting-edge robotic platforms.

title: Two Phase $Q-$learning for Bidding-based Vehicle Sharing
Abstract: The proliferation of sharing economy models has led to increasing popularity of vehicle sharing services globally. However, formulating an optimal pricing strategy for vehicle sharing is a challenging task due to its dynamic nature and incomplete information. In this paper, we focus on developing a decision-making framework to facilitate efficient learning and bidding process in vehicle sharing. We propose a two-phase Q-learning algorithm to model the vehicle sharing service provider's behavior, encouraging revenue maximization and user satisfaction through an adaptive and greedy approach. In the first phase, our model focuses on establishing a baseline strategy for the vehicle sharing service provider through a solo learning process, ensuring familiarity with the market dynamics. Subsequently, in the second phase, we introduce a social learning component by integrating knowledge sharing between the vehicle sharing service provider and competing firms. This facilitates intelligent adaptation and strategic bidding under different market conditions, such as varying demand, supply, and competition levels. We perform thorough experimentation to verify the efficacy of our proposed two-phase Q-learning algorithm, demonstrating improved earnings and competitiveness for the vehicle sharing service provider. The findings of this research provide insightful guidelines for the design of efficient decision-making processes in the vehicle sharing industry, driving better user experiences and revenue growth for service providers.

title: On the Min-cost Traveling Salesman Problem with Drone
Abstract: The Min-cost Traveling Salesman Problem (MCTSP) is a well-known NP-hard problem that has been extensively studied in the field of Operations Research and Computer Science. With the recent advancements in Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) technology, the traditional MCTSP has been reformulated to include drone-based delivery and transportation. This new variant of the problem, known as the Min-cost Traveling Salesman Problem with Drone (MCTSP-D), aims to minimize the total travel cost while considering the limited battery life of drones, the capacity constraints of the drone, and the pickup and delivery at different locations. In this research paper, we propose a Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model to solve the MCTSP-D, which incorporates the above-mentioned constraints and objective functions. We also develop a novel ant colony optimization (ACO) algorithm that considers the parallel paths of drones and the interactions between the drone and the salesman. The proposed ACO algorithm is compared with existing metaheuristic approaches such as Genetic Algorithm (GA) and Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) through extensive computational experiments on a variety of instances. Our results demonstrate that the proposed MILP model and ACO algorithm can provide high-quality solutions for the MCTSP-D, outperforming existing approaches in terms of solution quality and computational efficiency. Furthermore, our experiments also reveal that the inclusion of drones in the TSP can significantly reduce the total travel cost, suggesting the practical applicability of this problem variant in real-world scenarios.

title: Reasoning in Infinitely Valued G-IALCQ
Abstract: This paper presents an in-depth exploration of reasoning in infinitely valued G-IALCQ, a propositional algebraic logic system used to reason about truth values beyond the classical true and false. In this framework, the set of truth values forms a specific type of structure, known as a G- interval linearly quasi-order, which enables the interpretation of infinitely many truth values. Our investigation focuses on understanding how to derive logical rules and formulas within this system, taking into account the rich structure of its truth values. We first analyze the language of infinitely valued G-IALCQ and the key properties it inherits from the underlying structure. Our work then delves into the derivation of various logical rules and formulas, including the intuitionistic negation and disjunction, leveraging the interval linear quasi-ordering as a core theoretical tool. Furthermore, we examine the relationship between infinitely valued G-IALCQ and classical logic, as well as other known multi-valued logics, such as Łukasiewicz and product logics, to offer a broader perspective on the logics' properties and applications. Through a formal analysis and systematic comparison with comparable systems, this study sheds fresh light on the structure and implications of reasoning within infinitely valued G-IALCQ, contributing to the understanding of logical systems with infinite sets of truth values. Ultimately, the research aims to provide insights into the theoretical underpinnings of infinitely valued G-IALCQ, laying the groundwork for practical applications in areas such as artificial intelligence, formal verification, and fuzzy logic-based decision making.

title: Variational Information Maximisation for Intrinsically Motivated Reinforcement Learning
Abstract: This abstract outlines a novel framework that seamlessly integrates variational information maximisation (VIM) with intrinsically motivated reinforcement learning (IMRL). The VIM framework is used to implicitly represent the uncertainty associated with the trajectories generated by an agent within an unknown environment, thereby fostering self-discovery and active learning. In conventional IMRL paradigms, agents are typically motivated by curiosity-driven exploration, driven by a primary objective to learn the underlying reward functions of their environment. In contrast, this novel framework significantly recasts the motivations inherent in IMRL, with a core objective to maximise the mutual information between the agent's sensory experiences and its latent internal representations. By formalising the interaction between the agent and its environment within an information-theoretic paradigm, this framework allows for the computation of approximate representations of the available information and ensuing control of exploratory policies. Consequently, the proposed VIM-IMRL framework displays flexibility in scenarios where environments inherently possess complex, non-linear structures, ultimately enabling enhanced adaptability in the face of partial observability, domain shifts, and, more broadly, imperfect understanding of reward functions. Further technical prospects revolve around harnessing the information-gathering potential of the proposed methodology to enhance a variety of applications, especially these where complex uncertainty contexts arise.

title: Towards Unveiling the Ontology Key Features Altering Reasoner Performances
Abstract: This abstract provides an in-depth examination of the ontology's key features that significantly alter reasoner performances in artificial intelligence and knowledge representation systems. Although reasoners are fundamental components in querying and inferring ontology-based knowledge, their performance is heavily influenced by the various design and implementation choices made in ontology engineering. Current research has mainly focused on the ontological commit approach, which leaves a significant gap in understanding the intrinsic impact of key ontology features on reasoner efficiency. Through a systematic and rigorous methodology, this study has identified and analyzed three critical ontology features, i.e., existential quantification, relationship cardinality constraints, and property restrictions, that dramatically affect the performance of popular reasoners. An empirical evaluation using multiple ontologies and reasoners has been carried out to quantify the impact of these key ontology features, revealing significant performance differences and trends. By unveiling the underlying factors governing reasoner performance, this research provides novel insights to ontology engineers, designers of knowledge representation systems, and developers of reasoning engines, enabling them to design more efficient and scalable ontologies and improve the overall performance of knowledge-based systems. The findings of this study have profound implications for the development of more efficient knowledge representation systems and applications, serving as a crucial step towards the realization of highly scalable and autonomous knowledge-based systems.

title: Tuned and GPU-accelerated parallel data mining from comparable corpora
Abstract: This study presents a novel approach to parallel data mining from comparable corpora, focusing on the development of an adaptive and GPU-accelerated framework that efficiently extracts meaningful insights from large-scale textual datasets. By leveraging the advanced computing capabilities of high-performance GPUs, the proposed methodology significantly accelerates data processing and extraction tasks, enabling the analysis of vast corpora in a manner that was previously impractical. The framework is designed to be highly scalable and fault-tolerant, allowing it to handle the complex and dynamic nature of parallel computing environments. To achieve this, a hybrid approach combining multi-threading and distributed processing is employed, along with the use of optimized data structures and algorithms tailored to the specific requirements of GPU-based computing. The effectiveness of the proposed framework is evaluated through a series of comparative experiments involving various corpora and data mining tasks, demonstrating significant improvements in processing speed and scalability relative to traditional CPU-based approaches. These results contribute to the growing body of research on GPU-accelerated data mining and highlight the potential of this approach for enabling large-scale, high-performance text analysis applications in diverse fields. Ultimately, this research seeks to advance the state-of-the-art in parallel data mining, providing a efficient and scalable solution for tackling complex data analysis challenges in the era of big data.

title: Learning dynamic Boltzmann machines with spike-timing dependent plasticity
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel method for learning dynamic Boltzmann machines using spike-timing dependent plasticity (STDP). Traditional Boltzmann machines are computationally expensive to train on large datasets due to the complexity of their energy functions and the need for approximate inference methods. Dynamic Boltzmann machines, on the other hand, offer a more efficient alternative by encoding temporal dependencies in their state transitions. However, learning these dynamic machines using traditional gradient-based methods is often computationally infeasible. In this work, we explore the application of STDP, a biologically plausible learning rule found in neural networks, to learn dynamic Boltzmann machines. We derive an STDP-based learning algorithm that effectively updates the weights and coupling strengths of the machine's units while respecting the underlying spike-timing relations. Our results demonstrate that the proposed STDP-learning algorithm can efficiently learn dynamic Boltzmann machines on complex datasets, resulting in models that exhibit accurate temporal dependencies and robust generalization capabilities. The proposed method not only enables the efficient learning of dynamic Boltzmann machines but also provides a link to the biologically-inspired STDP learning rule. Additionally, our results suggest that this framework can be used as a starting point for integrating more sophisticated neural learning rules into machine learning models.

title: Boolean Matrix Factorization and Noisy Completion via Message Passing
Abstract: Boolean Matrix Factorization (BMF) and noisy completion have garnered significant attention in recent years due to their applications in various domains including recommender systems, social network analysis, and statistical learning. Traditional BMF approaches often rely on iterative optimization methods, but they can become computationally expensive and sensitive to noisy observations. Furthermore, these methods fail to capture the inherent uncertainty in noisy datasets and thereby tend to produce overly confident predictions. To address these limitations, this work proposes a message passing-based framework for BMF and noisy completion. Leveraging the concept of message passing, our approach models the interactions between the variable nodes representing the Boolean entires and the factor nodes representing the hidden latent factors as a series of messages passed between them. We demonstrate that this framework can effectively handle noisy observations by propagating uncertainty through the message passing process, resulting in more robust and accurate predictions. Our approach also incorporates a parameter adaptation scheme to adapt to varying noise levels, enabling its applicability to a wide range of problems. We empirically evaluate our framework on several benchmark datasets and demonstrate its superior performance over existing state-of-the-art methods, highlighting its potential as a reliable tool for recommendation, inference, and machine learning tasks.

title: Ensemble UCT Needs High Exploitation
Abstract: This study investigates the Ensemble Upper Confidence Trees (UCT) algorithm, a family of algorithms commonly employed in multi-armed bandit and combinatorial problems, where the exploitation of acquiring information from a system is crucial but often hindered by high exploration costs. The paper focuses on ensuring optimal exploitation of this algorithm to derive high-quality solutions in these constrained environments. Existing approaches to Ensemble UCT optimization methods are compared and contrasted to identify key limitations and inefficiencies. A thorough analysis reveals that traditional approaches lead to suboptimal performance, high computational complexity, and considerable exploration costs, leading to decreased quality of solutions achieved in such environments. Furthermore, an extension to current methods was proposed to better enhance exploitation efficiency in Ensemble UCT. Our enhanced method includes more adaptive exploration strategies and additional effective approximations, by which the exploitation efficiency improves significantly compared to traditional approaches, while in the meantime maintaining the low computational complexity required in real-world applications. Ultimately, the proposed method is proven to outperform state-of-the-art algorithms under various problem settings, producing superior average rewards, improved solution qualities, and better convergence properties in a scalable manner.

title: An Innovative Approach for online Meta Search Engine Optimization
Abstract: This paper presents a novel and innovative approach for online meta search engine optimization (SEO), focusing on enhancing the efficacy and efficiency of web search results through an integrated platform. The proposed system, dubbed "MetaSearchOptix," leverages the principles of collaborative filtering, natural language processing, and machine learning to provide a comprehensive and personalized meta search engine experience. By integrating multiple search engines and aggregating relevant information, MetaSearchOptix aims to mitigate the limitations of traditional search engines, such as information surfeit, inaccuracies, and biased results. The proposed system employs a hybrid optimization framework that combines rule-based and machine-learning-based approaches to rank search results, ensuring both precision and recall. Additionally, the system incorporates user feedback and preferences to adapt to individual querying behaviors and optimize search outcomes accordingly. The implementation of MetaSearchOptix demonstrates significant improvements in search accuracy, relevance, and overall user experience compared to existing meta search engines. Through this innovative approach, the proposed system demonstrates its potential to revolutionize the online search landscape, enabling users to access more relevant and accurate information with greater ease and efficiency. By exploring the intersection of computer science and human-computer interaction, this research contributes to the advancement of meta search engine optimization and fosters a more effective and user-centric online searching experience.

title: Theoretical Analysis of the Optimal Free Responses of Graph-Based SFA for the Design of Training Graphs
Abstract: This study provides a theoretical analysis of the optimal free responses of graph-based Semi-Supervised Finite Alphabet (SFA) methods for designing effective training graphs in machine learning applications. Graph-based SFA methods have been widely adopted in semi-supervised learning for their ability to leverage the structural information of the data graph to improve prediction accuracy. However, the design of the training graph plays a crucial role in determining the performance of these methods, and existing approaches often rely on heuristic methods that may not be optimal. By adopting a theoretical framework, we aim to derive the optimal free responses of graph-based SFA methods, which can be used to design high-quality training graphs that maximize prediction accuracy. Our theoretical analysis focuses on the key components of graph-based SFA methods, including the graph Laplacian, the finite alphabet, and the semi-supervised learning objective. We derive closed-form expressions for the optimal free responses and demonstrate their optimality through rigorous mathematical derivations. The results of our analysis provide important insights into the design of training graphs for graph-based SFA methods, enabling the development of more effective machine learning algorithms that can leverage the structural information of the data graph to improve prediction accuracy.

title: Thermodynamics and efficiency of an autonomous on-chip Maxwell's demon
Abstract: This study presents a theoretical framework for investigating the thermodynamics and efficiency of an autonomous on-chip Maxwell's demon. A Maxwell's demon is a thought experiment that challenges the traditional understanding of the second law of thermodynamics, which states that entropy always increases over time. In the context of on-chip design, the demon can be realized as a system of nanoscale components, such as switches and storage devices, that manipulate particles to achieve a specific, non-equilibrium configuration. By leveraging advances in nanotechnology and thermodynamic modeling, we can explore the operational principles and thermodynamic limits of such a demon at the chip level. Our focus is on characterizing the efficiency of the on-chip demon in terms of the dissipation of energy and the generation of useful work, as well as examining the consequences of its operation on the surrounding environment. Employing a combination of analytical and computational methods, including stochastic thermodynamics and molecular dynamics simulations, we aim to push the boundaries of current understanding on the thermodynamics of information and the limits of autonomous Maxwell's demons on silicon chips. This research has the potential to underpin the development of innovative, autonomous nanoscale systems that exploit the thermodynamic advantages of Maxwell's demon at the smallest scales. The findings presented will contribute to the ongoing debates about the relationship between information, entropy, and energy at the nanoscale, ultimately informing the design of novel, efficient on-chip devices.

title: Encoding Reality: Prediction-Assisted Cortical Learning Algorithm in Hierarchical Temporal Memory
Abstract: This abstract presents an investigation into the implementation of a prediction-assisted cortical learning algorithm within the hierarchical temporal memory (HTM) framework. The primary objective is to develop a novel cognitive learning paradigm that can efficiently and accurately learn from changing environmental stimuli, thereby allowing for the encoding of reality. To achieve this goal, we introduce a prediction-assisted learning approach, which exploits the power of machine learning and temporal learning principles, paving the way for a more autonomous and self-organizing learning system. Building upon the HTM concept, this custom learning schema harnesses the predictive abilities of HTM to facilitate and fine-tune the learning process. Our algorithm utilizes an adaptive, context-dependent prediction system and leverages prediction errors for synaptic plasticity and learning optimization. We apply this novel approach to various datasets and simulate its performance in tasks involving dynamic real-time data and predictions, culminating in significant enhancements in recognition accuracy and rapid adaptation capabilities. By combining elements of classical connectionism with cutting-edge machine learning principles, this prediction-assisted cortical learning algorithm stands as a groundbreaking step towards the development of sophisticated cognitive architectures and learning systems that can more effectively capture the complexities of an ever-changing reality.

title: Analysis of Intelligent Classifiers and Enhancing the Detection Accuracy for Intrusion Detection System
Abstract: This study carries out an extensive analysis of intelligent classifiers to enhance the detection accuracy of Intrusion Detection Systems (IDS). The IDS plays a vital role in safeguarding computer networks from unauthorized access and malicious activities. However, the increasing complexity and sophistication of cyber threats necessitate the deployment of advanced IDS that can effectively detect and respond to these threats. The investigators employ multiple classification techniques, including supervised learning, unsupervised learning, and ensemble methods, to evaluate their effectiveness in intrusion detection. Various machine learning algorithms, such as Support Vector Machines, Decision Trees, Random Forests, and Neural Networks, are analyzed and compared using publicly available intrusion datasets. The outcomes of these experiments reveal that a hybrid approach combining different classification techniques achieves significant improvements in detection accuracy. The study highlights the importance of fine-tuning classifier hyperparameters and selecting the most suitable features for intrusion detection. Furthermore, the proposed IDS architecture incorporates attack signature data and network traffic patterns to enhance its alerting mechanisms, allowing for real-time response to detected threats. By leveraging intelligent classifiers and advanced preprocessing techniques, the IDS can effectively mitigate evolving cyber threats and prevent the loss of sensitive information. The analyzed data sets and analytical architecture serve as a reference for future research and development of robust intrusion detection systems.
