title: Modeling mutual feedback between users and recommender systems
Abstract: This research paper presents an innovative modeling approach to capture the dynamic mutual feedback relationship between users and recommender systems. By integrating insights from social network analysis, user behavior modeling, and recommender system evaluation, we develop a probabilistic framework to quantify the reciprocal influence between users and recommendation models. Specifically, our approach takes into account the complex interactions that arise from users expressing preferences, modifying behavior and adaptability according to recommendations, and responding by modifying their trust and reliance on the system. We extend existing recommender systems to consider users' perceptions and sentiments about the recommendations, thus creating a more realistic and user-centric online ecosystem. Our framework enables the modeling of a user's influence exerted on the system and the subsequent effects of the system's recommendations on the user's behavior, resulting in more accurate predictions of users' interests, preferences, and satisfaction. We demonstrate our approach on real-world data collected from a social media platform and evaluate its performance through various metrics, such as click-through rates, recommendation accuracy, and user engagement. Our results illustrate the importance and value of capturing the mutual feedback effect in recommender systems, leading to improved personalization, user trust, and overall online experience.

title: Partial clones containing all Boolean monotone self-dual partial functions
Abstract: This research paper delves into the realm of Boolean monotone self-dual partial functions, a specific type of partial functions that exhibit monotonicity and self-duality properties when restricted to their domain. Central to the investigation is the study of partial clones, which are sets of partial functions on a given set that are closed under composition. The paper provides a comprehensive analysis of the landscape of partial clones containing all Boolean monotone self-dual partial functions, highlighting their relationship to clone theories and the inherent connections between partial functions and Boolean algebras. By developing new techniques and results related to the preservation of monotonicity and self-duality under various operations, this research showcases significant advancements in the field of universal algebra. A key finding is that partial clones containing all Boolean monotone self-dual partial functions are characterized by a unique set of properties, which in turn give rise to novel insights into the structural and combinatorial nature of these functions. Through a combination of theoretical foundations and computational studies, this paper demonstrates the richness and diversity of Boolean monotone self-dual partial functions, and it opens avenues for further exploration and applications in related areas. Ultimately, this research contributes to a deeper understanding of the intricate relationships between partial functions, clones, and Boolean algebras.

title: On the characters of the Sylow p-subgroups of untwisted Chevalley groups Y_n(p^a)
Abstract: This paper investigates the Sylow p-subgroups of untwisted Chevalley groups Y_n(p^a), particularly focusing on their characters with respect to p. Chevalley groups are a class of simple algebraic groups, extensively studied in the context of Lie theory and group representations. For a prime p, the untwisted Chevalley group Y_n(p^a) of type Y_n is defined with parameters n and a, relating to the dimension and p-exponent of the group. The Sylow p-subgroups of these groups form a fundamental part of this study, hence it is natural to explore their character theory as p-subgroups of both Y_n(p^a) itself, and of how they are intertwined with other subgroups in p. The character table of a Sylow p-subgroup will give a detailed description of the elementary representations of the group G and identify certain block structures. Although Sylow theorem has done great job for subgroups of algebraic groups, it's long and tedious job to obtain the important data through Sylow theorem, to avoid lengthy and complicated calculations which could not give any concrete result. There are already several groups who worked on Sylow p-subgroup characters of algebraic groups but these efforts are inadequate to explore the whole phenomenon. Hence, in this research work, we targeted on these types of groups with respect to different possible subgroups of prime order p to obtain the accurate characteristics that Sylow p-subgroup hold within that type of algebraic groups which is useful for solving different computational group problems.

By harnessing the capabilities of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) in conjunction with transformer architectures, we establish a framework that automatically extracts abstract concepts and their relationships from video sequences, effectively capturing high-level semantics without human annotation. title: A System Architecture for Software-Defined Industrial Internet of Things
Abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive system architecture for software-defined Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT). The proposed architecture emphasizes scalability, flexibility, security, and device heterogeneity, which are crucial aspects for the widespread adoption of IIoT in various industrial settings such as manufacturing, logistics, and energy management. The proposed architecture is based on the concept of software-defined networking (SDN) and software-defined everything (SDE) paradigm, which enables network programmability, improved device management, and streamlining of industrial operations. The architecture consists of four main sub-systems: i) industrial data processing and analysis, ii) software-defined network management, iii) multi-device management, and iv) predictive maintenance analytics. The industrial data processing and analysis sub-system utilizes a variety of data analytics techniques to provide real-time insights on industrial operations and processes, enabling informed decision-making and planning. The software-defined network management sub-system utilizes open-source network operating systems to manage industrial network operations and achieve improved network flexibility and scalability. The multi-device management sub-system utilizes device management protocols to manage and monitor a variety of industrial devices with different communication protocols and standards. The predictive maintenance analytics sub-system utilizes machine learning and data analytics techniques to predict equipment and device failures, enabling early preventive maintenance and minimize downtime. The proposed architecture aims to improve industrial operations by providing real-time data insights, enabling improved control and monitoring of industrial systems, and improving overall industrial productivity and efficiency.

title: Zero and negative energy dissipation at information-theoretic erasure
Abstract: Information-theoretic erasure, a phenomenon where information is decoded from erased or corrupted systems, has garnered significant attention in recent years. This concept challenges our conventional understanding of thermodynamics and energy dissipation, particularly at the information-theoretic level. Here, we delve into the intriguing realm of zero and negative energy dissipation accompanying information-theoretic erasure. Our investigation reveals that information erasure, under certain conditions, can exhibit paradoxical behavior, allowing for the dissipation of zero or even negative energy. This seemingly counterintuitive phenomenon arises from the connection between information erasure and the thermodynamic entropy of a system. By exploring the interplay between Shannon entropy and thermodynamic entropy, we uncover insights into the fundamental nature of energy dissipation and its relationship with information processing. Through a combination of theoretical derivations and numerical simulations, we demonstrate that certain protocols for information erasure can indeed bypass the second law of thermodynamics, yielding zero or negative energy dissipation. These findings not only shed light on the fascinating world of information-theoretic erasure but also highlight the need for a revised understanding of energy dissipation in the context of information processing. As we continue to push the boundaries of our knowledge, these results hold significant implications for the development of novel information-theoretic protocols and the exploration of previously uncharted territories in the field of quantum information theory.

title: Towards a Decoupled Context-Oriented Programming Language for the Internet of Things
Abstract: This paper presents the design and development of a novel programming language called IoTDecouple, which is tailored to address the unique challenges of the Internet of Things (IoT) paradigm. Traditional programming languages focus on creating standalone applications that operate without external influences, whereas IoT devices interact with various external factors, such as environmental conditions, device properties, and user inputs. As a result, programmers must explicitly handle these interactions, leading to increased code complexity, reduced modularity, and poor device reconfigurability. IoTDecouple tackles these challenges through the principles of decoupled context-oriented programming. By introducing a semantically rich declarative modeling system, IoTDecouple enables programmers to explicitly define the device's context, composed of device dependencies, constraints, and parameters. Moreover, it includes a type system that validates the coherence of context configurations, ensuring reliability and predictability. The programming language integrates tools for context inference and programming abstractions that facilitate intuitive device code modifications. This combination of functionalities allows for more efficient, dynamic, and self-adaptable IoT applications, addressing key limitations in current IoT software development practices. To demonstrate the effectiveness of IoTDecouple, a set of case studies is presented, showcasing its successful application in managing different aspects of IoT environments. The results provide a good insight into the merits of IoTDecouple and set the stage for its potential integration into mainstream IoT software engineering practices.

title: The likelihood principle does not entail a `sure thing', `evil demon' or `determinist' hypothesis
Abstract: The likelihood principle is a fundamental concept in statistical inference that has been debated extensively in recent years. While it provides a useful framework for making statistical decisions, some have argued that it implies acceptance of a deterministic reality, as if it posits an 'evil demon' or a fatalistic determinism governing the analysis. However, this interpretation overlooks the nature of probability as a mathematical representation of uncertainty, rather than a claim about the underlying mechanism governing the phenomenon under study. The Bayesian and frequentist interpretations of probability, while distinct, are both compatible with the likelihood principle, which allows for subjective, contextual assessments of probability. A careful examination of the principle reveals that its intention is to provide a formal criterion for evaluating the internal consistency of statistical analyses, rather than making ontological claims about the world. Furthermore, applications of the likelihood principle in real-world settings, such as statistical modeling and hypothesis testing, often involve degrees of freedom and non-parametric assumptions that underscore its flexibility. In conclusion, the likelihood principle should not be viewed as promoting an 'evil demon' or 'determinist' hypothesis, but rather as a neutral mathematical framework for representing uncertainty and facilitating rational decision-making in the face of incomplete knowledge.

title: The resolution bias: low resolution feedback simulations are better at destroying galaxies
Abstract: The resolution bias has been a long-standing issue in cosmological simulations, where the inclusion of high-resolution feedback mechanisms is believed to be essential for accurately modeling galaxy formation. However, in contrast to conventional wisdom, our research reveals that low-resolution feedback simulations can, in fact, be more effective at destroying galaxies. By optimizing the resolution of our simulations to focus on large-scale structure and neglecting the high-resolution details, we observe significant differences in the incidence of galactic disruption. Specifically, the low-resolution simulations exhibit denser gas distributions, increased merger rates, and more pronounced galaxy-quasar interactions, resulting in catastrophic galaxy destruction. We find that this 'resolution bias' is linked to the distinct characteristics of low-resolution simulations, such as reduced star formation, enhanced supermassive black hole growth, and altered gas flows. These findings suggest that conventional high-resolution feedback schemes may not be as crucial for galaxy destruction as previously thought and raise important implications for understanding the underlying physics of galaxy evolution. Furthermore, our research highlights the need to reassess the balance between resolution and realism in cosmological simulations, emphasizing the potential benefits of low-resolution simulations in modeling extreme galactic phenomena.

title: Spontaneous mass generation and the small dimensions of the Standard Model gauge groups U(1), SU(2) and SU(3)
Abstract: The Standard Model (SM) of particle physics is a widely accepted theory that describes the fundamental forces and particles in the universe. However, there are several open questions and observed phenomena that remain unexplained by the SM, such as spontaneous mass generation, which is a fundamental mechanism that gives mass to fundamental particles. One of the most puzzling aspects of spontaneous mass generation is its inability to account for the small dimensions of the Standard Model gauge groups U(1), SU(2), and SU(3). The gauge groups describe the symmetries of these fundamental forces, and the small dimensions of these groups are a striking feature of the SM, with the typical energy scales of beyond the electroweak scale. This paper explores the potential relationship between spontaneous mass generation and the small dimensions of the gauge groups, with a focus on their implications for the SM and its potential extensions. It provides a comprehensive review of the current understanding of spontaneous mass generation and its consequences for the gauge groups, as well as a discussion of recent developments and open questions in the field. By understanding the interplay between spontaneous mass generation and the gauge groups, we can better appreciate the underlying structure of the universe and potentially uncover new insights into the physics beyond the SM. A deeper understanding of these phenomena could also lead to the development of new models and theories that address some of the long-standing problems in particle physics.

title: Web Tracking: Mechanisms, Implications, and Defenses
Abstract: Web tracking mechanisms, enabled by various technologies such as cookies, pixels, and device fingerprinting, have become ubiquitous in modern web ecosystems, significantly impacting users' online experience and privacy. This paper delves into the complex landscape of web tracking, exploring both its empowering and invasive aspects. On one hand, tracking facilitates personalized advertising, e-commerce recommendations, and streamlined user experiences. On the other hand, the pervasive use of tracking technologies raises serious concerns regarding user surveillance, data security, and the commodification of personal information. By analyzing the mechanisms underlying web tracking, this study aims to expose the intricate web of relationships between internet service providers, advertisers, and data brokers. We will examine how targeted advertising, behavioral analysis, and data linkage empower or undermine users' civic agency and autonomy online. Furthermore, this research will survey the current defenses against web tracking, including browser extensions, privacy policies, and regulatory measures, and evaluate their effectiveness in mitigating the intrusive aspects of web tracking. Our analysis will contribute to the ongoing debate about the tension between convenience, personalization, and privacy in the digital age and provide insights for the development of more comprehensive and responsible web tracking regulations. Last but not least, the results of this research will inform the design of privacy-centric web technologies that balance the benefits of personalized online experiences with the users' rights to control their personal data.

title: Entropy spectrum of the apparent horizon of Vaidya black holes via adiabatic invariance
Abstract: The entropy spectrum of Vaidya black holes, which represent a class of radiative and dynamical black holes, is investigated through the lens of adiabatic invariance. This mathematical framework, rooted in classical mechanics, is adapted to the quantum realm to analyze the relationship between energy scaling and entropy behavior. By probing the apparent horizon, a two-dimensional surface marking the boundary of the event horizon, the authors derive an expression for the corresponding entropy spectrum. Employing a carefully crafted WKB approximation, the spectral density is obtained, shedding light on the non-equilibrium dynamics and possible black hole radiation emission mechanisms in this model. Analysis reveals an inverse relation between the energy scaling parameter and the spectral density exponent, suggesting a transition from a classical to a quantum-like behavior as the black hole evolves. Furthermore, a discrete, step-like structure of entropy gain is revealed, with each step being a characteristic function of the energy scaling parameter. This well-defined, quantized entropy incremental pattern offers insight into the underlying degrees of freedom entwined with the black hole evolution. Implications of these findings on the radiation scaling and ergosurface properties of Vaidya black holes are discussed in the context of potential applications within the broader realm of black hole physics, particularly in cosmological contexts featuring radiative and dynamical black holes.

title: Precision Predictions for the Primordial Power Spectra of Scalar Potential Models of Inflation
Abstract: This study focuses on the inflationary paradigm by employing scalar potential models, which are widely regarded as viable candidates for explaining the observable universe's large-scale structure and homogeneity. The analysis begins with the formulation of a scalar potential landscape, described by various mathematical frameworks, including quadratic, quartic and quintic power-law forms. A novel resummation method is developed, accounting for anisotropic quantum corrections that are pivotal in modern precision inflationary predictions. This method serves as a starting point to predict the primordial power spectra of various scalar potential models, incorporating corrections beyond the leading order. A general framework for statistical analysis is introduced, where the likelihood function is constructed using accurate numerical simulations of the resummed power spectra. Furthermore, we utilize Bayesian model selection and Markov chain Monte Carlo techniques to rigorously quantify the reliability of the statistical predictions. These developments not only lay the foundation for precision analyses of the primordial power spectra in scalable model frameworks but also highlight potential avenues for future research in the computation of signal-to-noise ratios. Our findings demonstrate that even with current computing powers the resummed corrections can be beneficial; more so expected as we plunge into era where observations are becoming increasingly precise and the universe's make-up continues to shed light in various breakthroughs surrounding cosmology and its core branch Inflation.

title: Decision Maker based on Atomic Switches
Abstract: The proliferation of digital technologies in modern life has led to an exponential increase in the amount of data being generated, accumulated, and processed. title: DTLS Performance in Duty-Cycled Networks
Abstract: The development of duty-cycled networks has emerged as a promising approach to mitigate energy consumption and extend the lifespan of battery-powered devices, such as wireless sensor nodes and internet of things (IoT) devices. However, these networks also introduce new challenges to ensure reliable and efficient data transfer. This research investigates the performance of Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) protocol in duty-cycled networks. Our study aims to understand how the frequent sleep-wake cycles of nodes in such networks impact DTLS handshake, packet loss, and acknowledgment performance. We also examine the effects of varying parameters, such as duty cycle, packet size, and network topology, on the DTLS protocol's metrics. The results show that with increasing duty cycle and packet size, the handshake and packet delivery success rates decrease significantly, while DTLS-enabled devices lose more packets during the sleep phase than without DTLS. Interestingly, we observe that the protocol's metric performance can be influenced by the network topology, where mesh networks experienced fewer packet loss rates than star networks. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that the DTLS protocol's retransmission mechanism helps mitigate packet loss, but its redundancy also introduces unnecessary retransmissions and battery drain. This research provides insights into the trade-off between battery efficiency and data reliability in duty-cycled networks with DTLS and offers recommendations for optimizing DTLS protocol configurations to achieve a balance between energy consumption and reliability in such networks.

title: Secure management of logs in internet of things
Abstract: The exponential growth of Internet of Things (IoT) devices has resulted in a significant increase in the volume of generated logs, posing substantial challenges to their secure management. title: Matrix weighted norm inequalities for commutators and paraproducts with matrix symbols
Abstract: Matrix weighted norm inequalities for commutators and paraproducts with matrix symbols are essential tools in harmonic analysis and partial differential equations. In this paper, we investigate the boundedness of commutators and paraproducts with matrix symbols on variable Lebesgue spaces and certain matrix-weighted Lebesgue spaces, which are crucial for tackling nonhomogeneous and anisotropic settings in weighted analysis. Our work focuses on extending the well-established theory for scalar symbols to the setting of matrix-valued symbols. Specifically, we prove that various matrix-weighted norm inequalities hold for the paraproduct operator associated to a symbol whose entries are in both VMO and Lipschitz regularity. We also provide a characterization of the matrix-weighted Lebesgue space involving the commutator of a Calderón-Zygmund operator with a certain matrix-valued symbol. These results illuminate the connection between the regularity properties of the symbol and the weighted Lebesgue space regularity. Through the investigation of the interplay between the structure of the symbol and the associated weighted inequalities, we establish a comprehensive framework for addressing matrix-weighted norm inequalities in the contexts of both paraproducts and commutators with matrix symbols. By capitalizing on advances in weighted harmonic analysis and matrix analysis, our study lays a groundwork for the development of novel applications in boundary control problems, spectral analysis, and operator algebras.

title: Magnetars: the physics behind observations
Abstract: Magnetars, a type of neutron star characterized by its intense magnetic field, have been a subject of increasing interest in recent years due to their unique properties and impressive observational successes. title: Lines in positive genus: An introduction to flat surfaces
Abstract: This paper delves into the realm of positive genus lines, which refer to the characteristic curves found on flat surfaces in varieties of dimension 2. A flat surface, or rather a surface with trivial canonical sheaf, is an object of significant study in algebraic geometry. The lines on such a surface, specifically those with positive genus, can be thought of as algebraic curves associated to its geometry. The problem of classifying these curves in higher genus is multifaceted and rich with complexity, providing ample opportunities for analysis and exploration. title: A reasonable thing that just might work
Abstract: The concept of 'A Reasonable Thing that Just Might Work' revolves around the idea of pragmatism in innovation. This paper delves into the realm of possibility-driven designs, focusing on leveraging everyday materials and societal norms to develop workable solutions for real-world challenges. By exploring the tangible aspects of failed projects, existing technology frameworks, and current issues within societal dynamics, the argument is made for adopting a 'good enough' approach in problem-solving. Abstract: The communication complexity of distributed convex learning and optimization is a crucial aspect of large-scale machine learning, where data is distributed across multiple machines or nodes, requiring efficient communication to achieve optimal solutions. The analysis covers both deterministic and randomized communication protocols, highlighting the importance of adaptivity, synchronization, and precision in reducing communication costs. By establishing the fundamental limits of communication in distributed convex learning and optimization, our work provides a theoretical foundation for developing more efficient and scalable distributed optimization methods, bridging the gap between theory and practice in large-scale machine learning applications.

title: Dissipative dark matter and the rotation curves of dwarf galaxies
Abstract: Dissipative dark matter has been proposed as a possible solution to the challenge posed by the observed rotation curves of dwarf galaxies, which often show a sudden upturn at large radii. Unlike standard cold dark matter (CDM) predictions, dissipative dark matter scenarios involve dark matter components with nonzero viscosity or thermal conductivity, leading to a suppression of power on small scales. This characteristic allows us to potentially reconcile the observations of dwarf galaxies with the predictions of the standard CDM model. We examine the implications of dissipative dark matter for the properties of dwarf galaxies, including their rotation curves, central surface brightnesses, and stellar populations. Our analysis includes a comparison with collisionless CDM models, focusing on both the general agreement and the potential discrepancies between these two paradigms. We also explore whether dissipative dark matter can provide an explanation for the puzzling diversity in the observed rotation curves of dwarf galaxies. By reconciling the standard model's predictions with the observed properties of dwarf galaxies, dissipative dark matter presents an intriguing alternative to the conventional CDM model, allowing us to better understand the role of dark matter in galaxy formation.

To address this knowledge gap, we develop a theoretical framework for analyzing the conjugacy of Cayley-Salmon lines in the projective plane. Our approach involves exploiting the geometric properties of non-icircular Cayley-Salmon configurations and deriving algebraic conditions that are sufficient for conjugacy. By solving key equations and analyzing the resulting configurations, we arrive at a comprehensive understanding of when Cayley-Salmon lines are conjugate. title: Face enumeration on simplicial complexes
Abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to face enumeration on simplicial complexes, a fundamental problem in computational geometry and topological data analysis. A simplicial complex is a topological space that consists of simplices, which are generalizations of triangles and tetrahedra, and their face relationships. title: Improved estimates for nonoscillatory phase functions
Abstract: This research aims to develop more accurate methods for computing nonoscillatory phase functions, which are crucial in solving oscillatory equations and ensuring the stability and reliability of numerical solutions in fields such as mathematical physics, astrophysics, and quantum mechanics. To overcome these limitations, this study proposes a novel method for calculating nonoscillatory phase functions based on the idea of interpolating between phase values obtained at suitably chosen points, represented as interpolation schemes. By exploiting mathematical concepts rooted in functional analysis, numerical analysis, and statistical mechanics, we design a sophisticated phase estimation framework that leverages machine learning techniques and state-of-the-art numerical methods to significantly enhance estimation accuracy and numerical stability. Abstract: This research paper presents a novel approach to optimal linear estimation under unknown nonlinear transformations. Our findings suggest that, even in the presence of arbitrary randomness, repeated quantum iterations can give rise to complex and fascinating behaviors that defy our intuitive understanding of quantum mechanics, highlighting the need for a deeper exploration of the intricate relationship between randomness, dynamics, and collective behavior in quantum systems.

The existence of tilt, however, implies the need to redefine the concept of high-$p_T$ jets, since the collinear approximation underlying the traditional jet definition may be systematically distorted by the presence of this additional, angle-dependent probability amplitude. Instead of depending solely on the gluon distribution, the tilted ensemble, formed at finite tilt, has a conditional probability amplitude involving an exponentiation, the convolution of the fragmentation functions, the probability per gluon branch,  $\Gamma(x)$, and the tilt. A deeper understanding of QCD initiated processes, thus, relies heavily on knowledge of $\hat{q}$ which while being crucial in obtaining exact, finite, jets, remains a parameter open to possible experimental verification, however not conclusively classified as either, a QCD prediction or a free parameter, leaving multiple unanswered questions in high-$p_T$ phenomenology. Recent developments suggest that the structurally dynamic cellular network concept can be formulated within the tensor network framework, which enables a stronger connection to established quantum field theories. Conversely, quantum graphity formalism allows for a direct embedding of the theory within the landscape of condensed matter systems, highlighting the potential for experimental verification. Through a detailed examination of these theoretical developments, this review aims to shed light on the interplay between the evolving ideas of quantum geometry and quantum gravity, while emphasizing the need for a more concrete reconciliation between the theoretical frameworks of these two approaches.

Furthermore, we discuss the potential solutions and remedies that can be implemented to protect QKD systems against these threats, such as adding extra authentication and verification protocols, detecting and isolating malicious systems, and adopting software-defined architectures. Abstract: The Stokes problem with Navier slip boundary condition is a classic partial differential equation problem that arises in the study of fluid dynamics. Specifically, we consider a domain in the fractional Sobolev space $W^{s,p}$, where $s$ represents the regularity of the domain and $p$ is a real number in the range $1\leq p < \infty$. Our main result provides a sharp bound on the value of $s$ for which the weak solution to the Stokes problem with Navier slip boundary condition exists. The proof relies on a delicate interplay between the fractional Sobolev regularity of the domain, the geometry of the domain, and the properties of the Navier slip boundary condition. As a consequence of our result, we obtain a sharp regularity estimate for the weak solution to the Stokes problem, which generalizes and improves upon previous results in the literature. Our work has implications for the understanding of fluid dynamics in complex geometries, such as porous media and thin films, where the Navier slip boundary condition is a common modeling assumption.

By utilizing them, we establish a six-parameter family of Kraus operators for the one-qubit depolarizing channel that encompasses depolarizing, dephasing, X, Y, and Z bit-flip errors, and their combinations. A comparison of this generalized framework with the original model demonstrates its ability to produce distinct quantum states, emphasizing the increased level of complexity it adds. Our research contributes significantly to the theoretical understanding of quantum noise and fault tolerance in quantum computing by providing a more robust description of the one-qubit depolarizing channel, supported by the application of generalized Kraus operators that paves the way for further analyses in quantum information processing and quantum error correction. Furthermore, our results also shed light on potential new approaches to reduce or possibly eliminate errors affecting quantum systems in various real-world applications.

Utilizing polarized proton beams at RHIC, STAR experiments have exploited the sensitivity of charm production to longitudinally polarized gluons, leveraging its high asymmetries. This precise analysis involves state-of-the-art algorithms for track filtering, topological reconstruction of D mesons, and statistical analysis. Results from these measurements shed light on the gluon polarization and transversity distribution of the proton, deeply embedded in the nucleon structure and intimately connected with Quantum chromodynamics.

This approach can promote fairness, transparency, and a more level playing field, allowing for a more diverse and representative pool of contributors. Moreover, anonymizing authors can also address concerns of unconscious bias and nepotism, ultimately contributing to the advancement of scientific knowledge and the integrity of the scientific process. By reexamining the classical results of Nash's embedding theorem and Gromov's h-principle, our research reveals novel geometric characterizations that provide a unified framework for understanding the embeddability of manifolds. The geometric embedding problem, a long-standing open question in differential geometry, is recast in a new light through the lens of singularities of stable maps, constructible functions, and stratified Morse theory. Our results demonstrate that the embeddability of a manifold is closely tied to the existence of a sequence of embedded submanifolds that satisfy a certain stability condition, which we term "geometric stability." This concept, in turn, is shown to be equivalent to the vanishing of a specific obstruction class, thereby providing a complete geometric characterization of embedding theorems. The implications of our findings extend far beyond the domain of differential geometry, with potential applications to algebraic geometry, topology, and mathematical physics. By uncovering the deep geometric underpinnings of embedding theorems, our work opens up new avenues for research and presents a compelling framework for the study of complex manifolds.

title: Criterion of the boundedness of singular integrals on spaces of homogeneous type
Abstract: This paper focuses on the boundedness criteria for singular integrals on spaces of homogeneous type. The theory of singular integrals on Euclidean spaces, developed primarily by Calderon and Zygmund, has far-reaching applications in analysis and partial differential equations. The extension of this theory to spaces of homogeneous type, first proposed by Coifman and Weiss, has garnered significant attention and has offered a more general framework to study singular integrals. The major challenge lies in establishing a meaningful criterion that generalizes the Hilbert transform's boundedness, given its crucial role in demonstrating the boundedness of the Riesz transforms in Euclidean spaces. Our contribution lies in providing an intrinsic characterization of the boundedness of singular integrals through geometric analysis of the space's structure, connecting the local and global properties of the space. The new criterion established emphasizes the significance of controlling the 'characteristic dimension' of the space and designing an interplay between the size of the kernel and the scale-invariance structure of the space. The framework can be adapted to other types of singular integral operators, paving the way for an amalgamation of harmonic analysis and geometry of the space of homogeneous type.

title: Strong solidity of free Araki-Woods factors
Abstract: This paper provides a comprehensive exploration of the strong solidity property within free Araki-Woods factors, a fundamental concept in the study of von Neumann algebras and the theory of free probability. The strong solidity of a von Neumann algebra refers to the phenomenon where the presence of a non-trivial projection in the algebra's standard part implies that the algebra's center is trivial. The free Araki-Woods factors, specifically the infinite free Araki-Woods factor MΦ_free, play a crucial role in our understanding of the interplay between non-commutative geometry, free probability, and operator algebras. Through a series of carefully constructed inductive arguments and the application of advanced tools from the theory of operator algebras, our research demonstrates that MΦ_free is a strongly solid factor. Furthermore, this investigation highlights profound implications for the study of non-commutative structures and their properties. By advancing the theoretical foundations of free Araki-Woods factors, our findings shed new light on the far-reaching connections between these concepts and the broader landscape of operator algebras. As such, this work stands as a pivotal contribution to the burgeoning field of non-commutative geometry and operator algebra theory.

title: Fluctuation effects in metastable states near first order phase transitions
Abstract: This abstract provides an in-depth examination of fluctuation effects in metastable states near first-order phase transitions in various physical systems, including magnetic, binary fluid, and structural phase transitions. Additionally, we investigate how fluctuations modulate the dynamics of phase boundary motion and critical scaling properties in the vicinity of the phase transition. By quantifying the effect of fluctuations on the free energy landscape, we uncover the intricate interplay between kinetic and thermodynamic factors governing phase transitions near their critical points. Our findings are relevant to a broad range of scientific disciplines and have implications for understanding phase transition phenomena in diverse systems, from materials science and condensed matter physics to geophysics and biophysics. The significance of fluctuation effects in this context highlights their importance in predicting and characterizing the behavior of metastable states near first-order phase transitions.

title: Principled Evaluation of Differentially Private Algorithms using DPBench
Abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive principled evaluation of differentially private (DP) algorithms using DPBench, an open-source benchmarking framework for assessing the performance and robustness of DP techniques. Moreover, we identify key factors influencing the performance of DP algorithms, including the choice of noise mechanisms, the distribution of sensitive data, and the deployment settings. title: Changing character of electronic transitions in graphene: From single particle excitations to plasmons
Abstract: Graphene, a single-layer of carbon atoms arranged in a hexagonal lattice, has garnered significant attention in the field of condensed matter physics due to its exceptional electronic properties. Among its characteristic features, electronic transitions play a pivotal role in understanding the optical, electrical, and thermal properties of graphene. Recent research has shifted focus from traditional single particle excitations, where individual charge carriers are excited from the valence to the conduction band, to the realm of collective plasmons, where a synchronized motion of charge carriers occurs. The character of electronic transitions in graphene is observed to transform from being purely electronic to a hybrid of electronic and plasmonic excitations as the energy scales relevant to the system approach the Fermi energy of graphene. As such, the electronic properties of graphene are significantly influenced by the presence of plasmons and change the photo-induced dynamics of the material at high excitation energies. This fascinating phenomenon is exemplified by a pronounced increase in the frequency dependent dielectric function of graphene, reflecting the cooperative behavior of charge carriers and the emergence of plasmon-like modes. Furthermore, studies reveal that the magnitude of this plasmonic response is inversely dependent on the sample thickness and is exacerbated by the occurrence of inter-valley scattering. These fundamental studies provide groundbreaking insights into the excitations in graphene and provide an essential step toward harnessing the vast potential of this highly versatile material in upcoming technological applications.

title: The consequences of dependence between the formal area efficiency and the macroscopic electric field on linearity behavior in Fowler-Nordheim plots
Abstract: The macroscopic electric field's influence on the linearity behavior in Fowler-Nordheim (F-N) plots is complex and can be significantly affected by the formal area efficiency. As the gap between a cathode and an anode in an emissive device reduces, the electric field increases, which is often accompanied by conduction mechanisms outside of F-N tunneling. Furthermore, variations in the electrode geometry and surface roughness can modulate the electric field strength and introduce inhomogeneities in the near-electrode region. These factors can erode the linearity in F-N plots, leading to significant changes in the extracted conduction parameters. As the area efficiency decreases, the proportion of surface area participating in the emission process is altered, which may affect the spatial distribution of the electric field and, consequently, the tunneling behavior. This nuanced interplay indicates a critical dependence between formal area efficiency and the macroscopic electric field on the manifestation of linearity in F-N plots. The present study examines the intercorrelation of these two parameters and their combined effects on the behavior of the conduction characteristics in F-N regimes under various operating conditions, thereby shedding light on the precise understanding of linearity deviations and the eventual device performance quantification. By combining these lines of inquiry, we aim to critically investigate the consequences of dependence between the formal area efficiency, macroscopic electric field on the linearity behavior of F-N plots.

title: Causality of singular linear discrete time systems
Abstract: This research paper delves into the causality of singular linear discrete time systems, which is a fundamental aspect of system theory and control engineering. Singular systems are characterized by the presence of unspecified initial conditions, giving rise to an ambivalence between causality and singularities. However, the singular nature of these systems complicates this traditional perspective, as the system dynamics can evolve over time due to unspecified initial conditions. To address this, we develop a rigorous framework for investigating causality in singular systems, exploring the interplay between singularities and causal behavior. Our framework enables us to identify the regions of the parameter space where the system exhibits either causal or non-causal behavior, shedding light on the intricate interplay between these seemingly contradictory properties. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of causality on the analysis and design of singular systems, particularly in the context of control synthesis. By demonstrating the significance of causality in the context of singular systems, this research contributes to a deeper understanding of the fundamental limitations of these systems and the development of more sophisticated control strategies for their stabilization and regulation.

We also assess the predictions of a coupled (momentum, fluid mass, energy, chemistry, and geomechanics) numerical model designed to simulate the mechanical-thermodynamic degradation of hydrate-bearing sediments due to compaction-induced heating. We thereby investigate the model formulation, hydro-mechanical behavior, gas hydrate dissociation mechanisms, and validation performance under various isostatic laboratory conditions. By performing direct analogue-simulation comparisons in the time- and length domains, our aim is to provide insights into a coupled numerical framework that can be utilised as an accurate estimate of long-term subsea reservoir methane production for large fluid displacements, hydrate-dissociation phenomena under subsurface overpressure and at great depths.

title: Size-Independent Quantification of Ligand Binding Site Depth in Receptor Proteins
Abstract: The precise evaluation and quantification of ligand binding site depth in receptor proteins have been a growing area of interest in the field of structural biology and drug discovery, owing to its key impact on the binding affinity and pharmacological activities of ligands. title: On the reconstruction of Lifshitz spacetimes

We then apply the Einstein-Hilbert-like action to the background-dependent frame for the anisotropic scaling and provide an explicit form of the higher-derivative terms. Our analysis indicates that the Lovelock gravity provides an intricate and rich class of solutions beyond the Einstein's general theory of relativity and demonstrate its potential usefulness in describing the properties of Lifshitz spacetimes. title: Signal Processing on Graphs: Causal Modeling of Unstructured Data

By representing complex systems as graphs, we can harness the power of network analysis and graph signal processing (GSP) to identify causal relationships between nodes, reconstruct underlying structures, and reveal the dynamics of complex systems. Building upon existing GSP techniques, our approach incorporates causal modeling principles to capture the temporal dependencies between nodes, allowing for accurate identification of causal influences and efficient prediction of future graphs. This methodology is particularly well-suited for dealing with big data, where traditional methods often fail due to the sheer volume, velocity, and variability of the data. Through a series of experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets, we demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in uncovering causal patterns and trends in complex systems, including gene regulation networks, traffic flow patterns, and social media interactions. Our results highlight the potential of causal GSP for applications in various domains, including systems biology, traffic engineering, and data analytics, and pave the way for future research on the intersection of causality, graphs, and signal processing.

title: DistancePPG: Robust non-contact vital signs monitoring using a camera
Abstract:
This abstract introduces DistancePPG, a revolutionary non-contact vital signs monitoring system that utilizes a camera to track heart rate and rhythm of patients in real-time. Leveraging photo-plethysmography (PPG) principles, the system captures subtle changes in hemoglobin concentration caused by pulse wave signals in the blood, allowing for accurate estimation of vital signs without the need for physical contact or cumbersome attachments. By developing a novel calibration-free approach, the proposed method ensures robust performance regardless of variations in illumination, skin tone, or viewing angles. 

A comprehensive evaluation of DistancePPG was conducted using a diverse dataset comprising recordings from over 100 participants under different lighting conditions and background scenarios. The results of this study demonstrate the system's ability to achieve state-of-the-art accuracy for heart rate monitoring, outperforming existing non-contact methods, with a mean absolute error (MAE) of 2.3 bpm. Moreover, distancePPG effectively overcomes traditional PPG methods' limitations, such as dependency on light sources and need for a reference signal. The proposed framework exhibits reliability, accuracy, and practicality for remote patient monitoring applications in various settings, including healthcare, sports science, and aerospace engineering.

title: Selection bias when using instrumental variable methods to compare two treatments but more than two treatments are available
Abstract: Instrumental variable (IV) methods are widely used in empirical research to address the issue of selection bias in comparative treatment analyses. While IV methods have been developed and refined for comparing two treatment groups, their extension to compare multiple treatment groups has been less explored. The standard approach to IV analysis involves choosing a single instrument for each treatment group, which is then used to estimate the local average treatment effect (LATE) for that group. However, when multiple treatment groups are available, researchers typically face a daunting selection problem. They must decide which instrument to pair with each treatment group, even though the same instrument may not be valid for all groups. The existing literature offers limited guidance on how to best handle this selection bias problem when comparing multiple treatments. To address this gap, we propose a systematic approach to selecting and testing instruments across treatment groups. Our approach will leverage machine learning techniques to identify the optimal set of instruments for each treatment group, and assess their sensitivity to various specification and robustness checks. By providing a framework for the joint selection of instruments and treatment effects, our analysis will demonstrate how to efficiently estimate treatment effects in situations with multiple treatment groups available. Its direct implications will increase the validity of IV methods in real-world, multi-treatment scenarios, and elevate the accuracy of subsequent policy recommendations.

title: Behavioral modulation of the coexistence between Apis melifera and Varroa destructor: A defense against colony colapse disorder?
Abstract: The apiculture industry faces a significant challenge in the form of Varroa destructor, a parasitic mite that infests honey bees (Apis mellifera) and threatens colony health and productivity. The Varroa mite's impact on bees' health is multifaceted, contributing to reduced immunity, weakened physiology, and shortened lifespan. Colony collapse disorder (CCD), a phenomenon characterized by the sudden and mysterious loss of worker bees, has been linked to Varroa infestations. To counteract this issue, researchers have explored various methods for managing infestations, including chemical treatments and integrated pest management (IPM) strategies. However, these approaches have inherent limitations and drawbacks, making it necessary to investigate alternative methods of controlling Varroa populations. Behavioral modulation of bee immune responses, social interactions, and foraging patterns has emerged as a promising area of research. By understanding how bees respond to and interact with Varroa-infested individuals, researchers can develop targeted interventions that promote bee health and mitigate the effects of Varroa infestations. This research paper examines the behavioral modulation of Apis mellifera in response to Varroa destructor infestations, exploring potential strategies for preventing CCD and maintaining healthy bee colonies. The results of this study contribute to a deeper understanding of the complex relationships between bees and their parasitic enemies, paving the way for more effective management and conservation of these ecologically and economically vital pollinators.

title: On Probabilistic Certification of Combined Cancer Therapies Using Strongly Uncertain Models
Abstract: The integration of multiple cancer therapies has emerged as a promising approach for improving treatment outcomes, but it poses significant challenges in terms of predicting the efficacy of combined regimens. Traditional machine learning methods struggle to capture the uncertainty inherent in cancer progression models, particularly when dealing with incomplete or noisy data. To address this limitation, we propose a novel approach that leverages probabilistic graphical models to Certify the efficacy of combined cancer therapies. Our framework, referred to as Probability-Weighted Deep Ensembles (PWDE), employs a strongly uncertain modeling strategy that explicitly accounts for the unpredictability of cancer response. PWDE combines the strengths of deep learning and probabilistic modeling to generate multiple plausible treatment outcomes, thereby quantifying the uncertainty associated with each option. By aggregating the predictions of multiple models, our approach is able to identify the most effective combined therapy regimens, as well as the range of possible outcomes for each treatment strategy. The proposed framework enables clinicians to make informed decisions about treatment protocols, reducing the risk of adverse reactions and improving patient outcomes. Through extensive simulation-based experiments on publicly available datasets, we demonstrate the efficacy of PWDE in accurately predicting the efficacy of combined cancer therapies, highlighting the potential of this approach for personalized medicine and clinical practice.

title: Photoplethysmography-Based Heart Rate Monitoring in Physical Activities via Joint Sparse Spectrum Reconstruction
Abstract: This study presents a novel approach to heart rate monitoring during physical activities using photoplethysmography (PPG) signals, specifically via joint sparse spectrum reconstruction. Traditional PPG-based heart rate monitoring relies heavily on signal quality, which degrades significantly during strenuous physical activities due to motion artifacts. This research proposes a joint sparse spectrum reconstruction algorithm that simultaneously denoises and reconstructs the PPG signal, mitigating the effects of motion artifacts. The proposed algorithm leverages the compressive sensing theory and exploits the inherent sparsity of the PPG signal. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of the joint sparse spectrum reconstruction algorithm in accurately estimating heart rate during various physical activities, including running, cycling, and brisk walking. The algorithm was compared with two state-of-the-art signal processing techniques, exhibiting superior performance in terms of signal quality and heart rate accuracy. Additionally, the computational complexity of the proposed algorithm was found to be relatively low, making it suitable for real-time heart rate monitoring applications. The findings of this study have significant implications for the development of wearable devices and mobile health applications that rely on PPG-based heart rate monitoring. Overall, this research presents a reliable and efficient solution for accurate heart rate monitoring during physical activities, which is essential for personalized exercise tracking, fitness assessment, and preventive healthcare.

title: Web Similarity in Sets of Search Terms using Database Queries
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to measuring web similarity in sets of search terms using database queries. The method relies on exploiting existing relational databases that normalize web document collections, such as Wikipedia, to calculate the semantic similarity of search term sets. The proposed model leverages the concept of transitive closure to traverse the database schema and establish a multigranular index space that captures relationships between concepts, entities, and keywords. A new similarity metric, named "term-set similarity," is introduced to quantify the affinity between search term sets by taking into account both structural and lexical properties of the connected database edges. To evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed similarity metric, several experiments were conducted using a large-scale dataset and a variety of search term sets derived from the DBpedia ontology. Results showed a significant improvement in accuracy and recall compared to existing methods based on vector space models and word embeddings. Furthermore, the proposed approach provides a scalable solution to query large and dynamic datasets in real-time, opening up possibilities for applications such as semantic search, information retrieval, and recommendation systems. The novel contribution of this paper is its ability to elegantly bridge the gap between information retrieval and database query processing paradigms, enabling a more robust and effective quantification of web similarity in search terms using database queries.

title: Refining Adverse Drug Reactions using Association Rule Mining for Electronic Healthcare Data
Abstract: The increasing complexity of electronic healthcare data has led to a surge in adverse drug reactions (ADRs) worldwide, which poses significant challenges to healthcare professionals in effectively identifying and mitigating these undesirable outcomes. In this study, we explore the application of association rule mining (ARM) as a robust analytical technique to refine ADRs from electronic healthcare data. Specifically, we utilize the Apriori algorithm, a popular ARM algorithm, to discern associations between medication and patient characteristics that contribute to ADRs. Our research focuses on developing an efficient ARM framework that can accurately detect unknown ADRs and subsequently identify high-risk medication combinations and patient populations prone to ADRs. We conducted an in-depth analysis of a comprehensive electronic healthcare dataset comprising over 1 million patient records, which included detailed medication histories, laboratory test results, and clinical diagnoses. By applying the developed ARM framework, we were able to identify distinct patterns of medication usage associated with ADRs, including unexpected interactions between antacids and cardiovascular medications. Furthermore, our analysis revealed distinct patient subgroups and comorbidities that were found to significantly increase the risk of ADRs. The outcomes of this research contribute towards better quality patient care, highlight the potential of ARM to support healthcare decision-making, and underscore the need for proactive and data-driven approaches to mitigate ADRs in clinical settings.

title: Inter-sensor propagation delay estimation using sources of opportunity
Abstract: This research focuses on addressing the prominent issue of uncertainty in sensor networks caused by the variability in inter-sensor propagation delays due to time-varying propagation mediums, antenna characteristics, and environmental conditions. It presents an investigation into the use of sources of opportunity, leveraging external sources, such as GPS, mobile devices, and radio frequency broadcasts, to estimate the delayed samples of sensor data and perform precise delay compensation. The proposed approach utilizes an adaptive signal processing algorithm that extracts features from opportunistic sources and trains a machine learning model to predict the arrival time of the delayed samples. These predictions enable real-time synchronisation among sensor nodes and enhance the overall network performance by eliminating the impact of propagation delays. A key aspect of this research lies in the evaluation of its applicability under various real-world conditions, encompassing topological uncertainties, varying signal-to-noise ratios, and congested communication channels. A thorough simulation analysis, leveraging network simulators like OMNeT++ and ns-3, as well as experimental studies, deploying sensor nodes in diverse environments, are conducted to assess the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed algorithm in accurate delay estimations, thus promising superior efficiency, scalability, and reliability in wireless sensor networks.

title: Dengue disease prediction using weka data mining tool
Abstract: This study proposes a data-driven framework for predicting the incidence of dengue disease using the Weka data mining tool. The framework relies on historical meteorological and viral data to identify the relationship between environmental and viral factors with the occurrence of dengue outbreaks. A comprehensive literature review is conducted to identify key predictors of dengue disease, including temperature, humidity, precipitation, and viral indices. Collected datasets are preprocessed and transformed into a suitable format for analysis using Weka, a widely-used open-source data mining software. Decision tree, support vector machine, and random forest techniques are employed to develop predictive models that assess the likelihood of dengue disease occurrence in a given region. Experimental results indicate that the random forest model achieves the highest accuracy rate of 95.7% by capturing complex relationships between climate variables and dengue disease incidence. The performance of the proposed model is compared with state-of-the-art approaches, demonstrating its effectiveness in accurately predicting dengue outbreaks. The study's findings have significant implications for dengue disease surveillance and management, enabling public health officials to develop proactive strategies for mitigating the spread of the disease. Overall, this research demonstrates the utility of Weka-based data mining in developing effective predictive models for dengue disease, enhancing preparedness and response efforts in regions prone to dengue outbreaks. The proposed framework can be extended to other infectious diseases, offering a robust approach for disease surveillance and early warning systems.

title: How essential are unstructured clinical narratives and information fusion to clinical trial recruitment?
Abstract: Unstructured clinical narratives and information fusion play a crucial role in enhancing clinical trial recruitment. Despite advancements in clinical trials, a significant gap exists between the number of available studies and the number of patients who participate. This discrepancy can be attributed to various factors, including information heterogeneity, inadequate dissemination of clinical trial findings, and limited patient awareness. The incorporation of unstructured clinical narratives into clinical trial recruitment processes has the potential to address these challenges by providing a more comprehensive understanding of patient preferences, needs, and experiences. Information fusion, which involves combining data from disparate sources, can be used to integrate unstructured clinical narratives with existing clinical trial databases and patient profiles. This fusion enables the creation of a rich and dynamic patient profile that accurately reflects each individual's unique characteristics, facilitating more targeted and efficient recruitment approaches. Furthermore, the integration of unstructured clinical narratives and information fusion can help identify patient populations that are most likely to benefit from clinical trials, reducing the risk of trial delays and increasing overall recruitment rates. By leveraging these innovative approaches, researchers and clinicians can optimize clinical trial recruitment, accelerate the translation of research findings into practice, and ultimately improve patient care.

title: Correcting for non-ignorable missingness in smoking trends
Abstract: Missingness in smoking trend studies can arise due to non-ignorable reasons, where the probability of observing data is dependent on the values of the unobserved variable of interest. This issue poses a significant threat to the validity of statistical inferences, as data that is systematically missing can lead to biased estimates and incorrect conclusions. This is particularly pertinent in smoking trends research, where accurate prevalence estimates and trend analyses are crucial for informing public health policy decisions. In recent years, there has been a growing recognition of the need to account for non-ignorable missingness in observational studies. This paper focuses on developing and implementing a series of statistical methods to correct for non-ignorable missingness in smoking trend studies. Drawing on principles from selection models and multiple imputation, these methods enable researchers to jointly model the probability of missingness and the observed outcome, while accounting for the uncertainty associated with missing data. The proposed methods are illustrated through a simulation study and applied to a real-world dataset of smoking trend data, demonstrating their ability to accurately recover the true parameters under a range of missingness scenarios. Results from this research provide valuable insights into the effects of non-ignorable missingness on statistical inferences in smoking trends research, and highlight the importance of accounting for this issue in future studies.

title: Spices form the basis of food pairing in Indian cuisine

title: Conditional Spectral Analysis of Replicated Multiple Time Series with Application to Nocturnal Physiology
Abstract: Conditional Spectral Analysis of Replicated Multiple Time Series with Application to Nocturnal Physiology provides a novel statistical approach for analyzing replicated multiple time series data under specified conditions. This research focuses on the investigation of complex physiological processes that occur during nocturnal periods, such as sleep-wake cycles and their relationships to circadian rhythms. The computational method of conditional spectral analysis is employed to derive the time-frequency features of both the systolic and diastolic blood pressure signals, as well as electromyography signals collected from various physiological sources. A key development within this research is the implementation of a wavelet-based power spectral density estimate to deal with the often-deterministic properties often found in physiological signals, thus facilitating the statistical analysis of replicated time series data. The efficiency of the proposed approach is demonstrated through experiments utilizing a combination of real-world physiological dataset replication and computational data simulation. Statistical validation demonstrates the sensitivity and accuracy of the conditional spectral analysis approach in identifying the dynamics of physiological signals under different conditions of rest and sleep. Overall, this research contributes an enhanced understanding of the physiological processes influencing nocturnal behavior, which enables the development of targeted interventions for the diagnosis and treatment of various sleep-related ailments with promising potential for numerous other physiological applications.

title: Air quality and acute deaths in California, 2000-2012
Abstract: This study examines the relationship between ambient air quality and acute cardiopulmonary mortality in California between 2000 and 2012. We utilized a time-series analysis approach to investigate the impact of particulate matter (PM), ozone (O3), nitrogen dioxide (NO2), and sulfur dioxide (SO2) on daily deaths. By leveraging the California Office of Environmental Health Hazard Assessment's Ambient Air Quality database and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's National Chronic Disease Prevention and Health Promotion database, we collected exposure data and mortality counts for each county in California from 2000 to 2012. Our results indicate that increasing concentrations of PM2.5 and PM10 were associated with a significant increase in acute cardiopulmonary mortality, particularly among vulnerable populations such as the elderly and those with pre-existing respiratory conditions. Similarly, elevated O3 concentrations were linked to an increased risk of acute respiratory mortality, especially during the summer months when O3 levels were highest. Furthermore, we observed a positive association between NO2 and SO2 exposure and acute cardiorespiratory mortality, underscoring the importance of controlling emissions from vehicles and industrial sources to improve air quality and prevent premature deaths in California. Overall, our findings have implications for air quality management strategies and underscore the need for continued monitoring and mitigation of air pollutants to protect public health in the state.

title: Asymmetric Independence Model for Detecting Interactions between Variables
Abstract: The asymmetric independence model has garnered significant attention in recent times for its potential in uncovering complex interactions between variables in multivariate data. However, the model's ability to detect these interactions in a reliable and efficient manner remains an ongoing challenge due to its conditional independence assumption. A novel approach to addressing this challenge involves the adaptation of the asymmetric independence model to cater to different levels of interaction strength. This paradigm shift enables the incorporation of domain knowledge and the analysis of data interactions in a more nuanced manner. Our proposed model, in this context, extends the conventional asymmetric independence model by incorporating a heterogeneous dependence structure, thus accommodating varying levels of interaction effects between variables. Theoretical analysis and Monte Carlo simulations demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed model in distinguishing between independent and dependent variables, including cases with moderate to high interaction effects, compared to traditional asymmetric independence model-based approaches. Furthermore, our case study involving financial transaction datasets reinforces the practical utility of the proposed model in detecting variable interactions that would have otherwise gone unnoticed. Overall, this study aims to shed light on the importance of incorporating structural variables to improve the fidelity and interpretability of asymmetric independence models in detecting complex partnerships between variables, paving the way for more efficient data-driven decision-making. The findings from this research have significant implications for various applications across fields like financial analytics, statistical genetics, and network analysis.

title: Musical practice and cognitive aging: two cross-sectional studies point to phonemic fluency as a potential candidate for a use-dependent adaptation
Abstract: This study presents two cross-sectional investigations examining the relationship between musical practice and cognitive aging, focusing on phonemic fluency as a potential candidate for use-dependent adaptation. In the first study, a sample of 165 older adults with varying levels of musical experience participated in an auditory processing task assessing phonemic fluency, which has been previously linked to cognitive reserve and resistance to age-related cognitive decline. Results showed that musicians scored higher on phonemic fluency compared to non-musicians, and the effect size was significantly larger for musicians who began their training before age 7. Furthermore, musicians demonstrated greater grey matter volume in areas critical for language processing. In the second study, 250 older adults underwent similar testing, with the addition of an exam to assess instrumental musical ability. Our findings indicate that the relationship between musical practice and phonemic fluency is bidirectional: musicians exhibit enhanced phonemic fluency due to early and prolonged education in music, while high-level phonemic fluency in turn appears to support musical ability. These findings suggest that phonemic fluency may be an important mechanism driving the association between musical practice and cognitive aging, and warrant further investigation into the role of phonemic fluency as a potential cognitive reserve builder.

title: Designing Traceability into Big Data Systems
Abstract: Big data systems have revolutionized the way we collect, store, manage, and analyze vast amounts of data. However, the scalability and flexibility that come with these systems have also introduced various challenges in ensuring the data's veracity, especially when it comes to maintaining the chain of custody after data ingestion. Traceability is becoming increasingly important in today's data-driven world, where data sources can be distributed across multiple platforms and stakeholders. The missing link between data's origin, transformation, and usage poses significant risks to data integrity, compliance, and accuracy. In response, this research paper proposes a comprehensive framework that integrates traceability into big data systems from design to deployment. The approach utilizes a risk-based methodology, identifying critical data points across the data life cycle and assigning corresponding traceability attributes. This framework incorporates innovative use cases, including auditing and tamper-detection, ensuring the authenticity of data operations, and enabling real-time anomaly detection. Furthermore, case studies and empirical analyses demonstrate the implementation of this proposal on real-world data platforms to realize the benefits of increased data veracity, decision-making accuracy, and operational cost savings. The research ultimately demonstrates that incorporating traceability into big data systems not only facilitates compliance with regulatory standards but also elevates system transparency and robustness, making it an essential design component for maintaining data trustworthiness.

title: A Secure Electronic Prescription System Using Steganography with Encryption Key Implementation
Abstract: The proliferation of electronic prescription (e-prescription) systems has significantly improved the efficiency and accuracy of medication dispensing processes in healthcare settings. However, these systems are also vulnerable to various security threats, including eavesdropping, tampering, and unauthorized access to sensitive patient information. To address these vulnerabilities, this research proposes a novel approach to designing a secure e-prescription system by integrating steganography and encryption techniques. This approach utilizes a seamless encryption key implementation process, ensuring that both the patient's personal data and prescription information remain confidential and tamper-proof. The system's architecture includes two main components: a client-side and a server-side module. The client-side module employs the advanced encryption standard (AES) to encrypt the patient's personal data and prescription information, while the server-side module leverages steganographic techniques to conceal the encrypted data within an innocuous-looking carrier image. This approach effectively safeguards against unauthorized access, tampering, and eavesdropping attempts, thereby ensuring the integrity and confidentiality of patient data. The proposed system's efficacy and feasibility have been validated through extensive simulations and testing experiments, demonstrating its potential to be a secure, robust, and efficient solution for e-prescription systems in various healthcare settings.

title: Estimating the Attack Ratio of Dengue Epidemics under Time-varying Force of Infection using Aggregated Notification Data
Abstract: This study focuses on developing and evaluating an analytical framework for estimating the attack ratio of dengue epidemics, taking into account time-varying force of infection as well as aggregated notification data, thereby acknowledging under-reporting issues in infectious disease surveillance. Considering data limitations, the proposed approach relies on analyzing notification records for dengue cases during various time periods to quantify the attack ratio, which represents the proportion of susceptible individuals who ultimately become infected. An empirical data-driven framework was established and evaluated for 3 primary dengue-endemic regions, leveraging Bayesian inference and time-series models to enable ongoing estimation under changing reporting patterns and varying epidemiological conditions. Parameters such as disease onset times and relative reporting rates were estimated from available data for developing regions where routine surveillance may not be comprehensive or readily available. Utilization of aggregated notification records effectively captures hidden trends in reported dengue cases and offers optimal data-driven strategies for evaluating public health interventions and resource allocation during epidemic episodes. Outcomes from this research provide valuable impetus for enhanced surveillance strategies, including information systems for real-time early warning detection and improved management of pandemics across geographically disparate, resource-poor, and disease-endemic zones.

title: Reduced-rank spatio-temporal modeling of air pollution concentrations in the Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis and Air Pollution
Abstract: This study proposes a reduced-rank spatio-temporal (RRST) model as a novel approach to estimate air pollution concentrations at multiple study years and across different locations within the Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis and Air Pollution (MESA Air). The RRST model integrates the strengths of spatial and temporal models by accounting for the shared variance structure and spatial dependencies among monitoring sites. This allows for more accurate and robust estimation of air pollution concentrations. The model is further enhanced by incorporating prior exposure estimates from spatial-temporal models, known as the county-level chemical transport model outputs. Using a subset of air pollution monitoring sites with coincident particulate matter with an aerodynamic diameter of less than 2.5 μm (PM2.5) sampling data from 2004 to 2016 in MESA Air, the RRST model demonstrates its superiority to individual spatial and temporal models in characterizing urban-rural and ethnic disparities in air pollution exposure. Our statistical and simulation approaches improve the quantification of cumulative PM2.5 exposure and further inform the epidemiological associations between long-term exposure to air pollution and cardiovascular risks.
