title: Big Data: Opportunities and Privacy Challenges

title: Software that Learns from its Own Failures
Abstract: Recent advancements in Machine Learning (ML) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) have given rise to the concept of self-correcting software, a key aspect of which involves software learning from its own failures to improve its performance over time. title: Hierarchical models for semi-competing risks data with application to quality of end-of-life care for pancreatic cancer
Abstract: Semi-competing risks data, characterized by the presence of a time-to-event endpoint that can be left-truncated or subject to censoring due to a competing event, poses significant challenges in modeling and inference. Specifically, we propose a joint model for the distribution of time-to-death and the quality of life measure, accounting for the left-truncation and censoring due to the competing event of hospitalization. The proposed hierarchical framework incorporates patient-level and hospital-level covariates, allowing for the exploration of provider-level and patient-level factors that influence the quality of end-of-life care. We demonstrate the efficacy and flexibility of our approach through simulations and an empirical analysis of a real dataset obtained from a retrospective cohort study of pancreatic cancer patients, highlighting the potential for our methods to improve the understanding of the care provided to patients at the end of life. Our findings have implications for healthcare policy and practice, facilitating the design of targeted interventions to enhance the quality of care for patients with pancreatic cancer.

title: Radiation damage effects on detectors and eletronic devices in harsh radiation environment
Abstract: Radiation damage effects on detectors and electronic devices in harsh radiation environments have become a pressing concern for various applications spanning space exploration, nuclear power plants, and high-energy physics experiments. As technological advancements allow for the deployment of detectors and electronic devices in increasingly hostile environments, they are susceptible to the deleterious effects of ionizing radiation. High-energy particles can induce defects, alter material properties, and disrupt the functionality of critical electronic components, compromising the overall performance and reliability of the system. The specific mechanisms by which radiation damage unfolds are complex and depend on the interaction between particles, detectors, and electronic devices. This paper delves into the intricacies of radiation damage phenomena and investigates the synergistic effects that arise from the concurrent action of multiple types of radiation. Furthermore, it examines current theoretical models and experimental findings to contextualize the impact of radiation on modern detector technology, including silicon-based and crystalline semiconductors, as well as emerging materials and thin-film structures. By distilling existing knowledge and illuminating avenues for future research, this piece sheds light on the development of new technologies capable of withstanding and countering the enduring effects of radiation damage, thereby ensuring the continued advancement of sensitive applications in harsh radiation environments.

title: Quantifying replicability in systematic reviews: the r-value
Abstract: This paper explores the concept of replicability in systematic reviews by introducing a new metric, the r-value, which quantifies the consistency of inclusion and exclusion criteria across multiple reviewers. Traditional systematic reviews often struggle with replication due to variations in human judgment, leading to doubts about the reliability of the findings. By establishing a standardized framework for assessing replicability, researchers can assess the robustness of the results and increase confidence in the evidence. The proposed r-value measures the agreement between reviewers using a combination of metrics that take into account the specific inclusion and exclusion criteria of the review question. A systematic review of existing systematic reviews demonstrates the utility of the r-value in improving the transparency and reproducibility of systematic reviews. The results show that the r-value can help identify reviews with low replicability, which in turn allows for the development of strategies to improve the design and conduct of future reviews. Furthermore, the application of the r-value provides a clear and actionable outcome of systematic reviews, and facilitates more collaborative and transparent research processes. Overall, the introduction of the r-value complements the existing systematic review process, promoting the development and eventual adoption of more replicable and reliable systematic reviews.

title: A New Intelligence Based Approach for Computer-Aided Diagnosis of Dengue Fever
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel intelligence-based approach for the computer-aided diagnosis of dengue fever, leveraging advanced machine learning techniques and clinical data analysis to improve diagnostic accuracy. The approach integrates a sophisticated data preprocessing module that incorporates various signal processing and feature extraction algorithms to filter out irrelevant data points, recognize patterns, and extract relevant features from patient symptoms, medical images, and laboratory test results. A hybrid computational framework that combines the strengths of two prominent machine learning paradigms: deep learning and ensemble learning, is employed to develop an intelligent decision support system for dengue fever diagnosis. This system utilizes a multilayer perceptron neural network to analyze complex imaging data from techniques such as MRI and CT scans, while also incorporating the principles of random forests and support vector machines to enhance the robustness and reliability of the diagnostic model. Furthermore, the proposed system also incorporates a novel, self-adaptive mechanism that enables real-time refinement of the diagnostic model based on continuous feedback from medical experts. Rigorous experiments utilizing a large dataset comprising various medical cases, have been conducted to evaluate the efficacy and accuracy of the proposed approach, demonstrating a 95% diagnosis accuracy rate.

title: A Criticism of the Current Security, Privacy and Accountability Issues in Electronic Health Records
Abstract: The rapid advancement and widespread adoption of electronic health records (EHRs) have significantly transformed the healthcare sector, offering numerous benefits such as improved patient outcomes, enhanced care coordination, and reduced administrative burdens. However, concerns regarding the security, privacy, and accountability of EHRs have also been escalating, posing substantial risks to sensitive patient data. A critical examination of the current EHR landscape reveals various vulnerabilities, including insufficient data encryption methods, inadequate firewalls and anti-virus software, and a lack of stringent access controls. Moreover, the increasingly interconnected nature of EHR systems, along with the growing reliance on cloud storage and mobile devices, has created numerous entry points for potential hackers and unauthorized users. The evolving threat landscape, coupled with the limitations of existing regulatory frameworks and lack of enforcement, has created a Perfect Storm that undermines the very essence of patient trust. Furthermore, the complexities surrounding accountability and liability issues, particularly in cases of data breaches and misused information, have left many healthcare providers and individuals ill-equipped to manage the ensuing consequences. This paper aims to critically assess the state of security, privacy, and accountability in EHR systems and explore potential solutions to mitigate these pressing concerns and ensure the integrity of sensitive patient data.

title: Electronic Medication Prescribing Support System for Diagnosing Tropical Diseases

Furthermore, the electronic medication prescribing support system will be integrated with a comprehensive database of tropical diseases, allowing for real-time updates and information sharing among healthcare professionals. title: Sufficient Covariate, Propensity Variable and Doubly Robust Estimation
Abstract: This paper provides an in-depth examination of sufficient conditions for covariate and propensity score variable in estimation of causal effects. We consider the doubly robust estimator of the average treatment effect in the presence of covariates and the propensity score model. A sufficient covariate condition is established, which ensures the identifiability of the treatment effect in the full model and allows for its estimation using any doubly robust estimate. An extension of this condition to the setting of stratification with inverse probability weighting is derived, resulting in a reweighting algorithm for efficient estimation. Furthermore, we investigate the implications of the sufficient covariate condition for the construction of doubly robust estimates using any non-parametric or semi-parametric propensity score component that satisfies certain regularity conditions. Asymptotic results demonstrate the consistency of the doubly robust estimator under the proposed conditions, establishing theoretical support for its use in practice. The findings of this research have significant implications for the design of randomized controlled trials and observational studies, enabling the construction of robust causal effect estimates using minimal modeling assumptions. Theoretical contributions and numerical experiments illustrate the importance of the sufficient covariate condition in reducing bias and improving estimation efficiency.

title: High-Dimensional Longitudinal Classification with the Multinomial Fused Lasso
Abstract: This paper addresses the critical issue of high-dimensional longitudinal classification where numerous features and samples are observed over multiple time points. The proposed method is based on the multinomial fused lasso, which combines sparse feature selection with pairwise dependencies among features to optimize classification performance. By applying the fused lasso penalty to successive differences of the coefficients in a multinomial logistic regression framework, the model can selectively perform soft-thresholding for uncorrelated features while encouraging group-wise sparsity for correlated covariates. The adaptive feature selection and robustness to high-dimensionality of the method are mathematically grounded in the theoretical analysis provided, assuming a certain level of smoothness, a finite set of distinct feature patterns, and a condition on the effective degrees of freedom across time points. Compared to standard sparse regression methods, the efficiency and interpretability of the proposed method are significantly improved, and the improvement in performance is consistently observed in empirical experiments under various settings, including heterogeneous subpopulations and instances of high-dimensionality without feature engineering or recursive feature elimination.

title: Novel Approaches for Predicting Risk Factors of Atherosclerosis
Abstract: Atherosclerosis is a multifaceted cardiovascular disease characterized by the buildup of plaques within arterial walls, ultimately leading to downstream complications such as myocardial infarction and stroke. Despite the rising incidence of this disease, early prediction and diagnosis of atherosclerosis remains a formidable challenge. Traditional risk factor assessment based on age, lipid profiles, blood pressure, and medical history can only provide a probabilistic prediction of disease risk, often failing to account for the interactions and interdependencies between these risk factors. This study aims to investigate the potential for novel predictive models to augment current risk assessment strategies. Utilizing cutting-edge analytical tools and machine learning algorithms, we examine the application of computational methods to patient-derived data, integrating digital information from electronic health records, genomics, proteomics, and wearable devices. The proposed framework combines statistical modeling with ensemble learning to generate robust prediction models that account for intricate interactions between risk factors, including intricate patterns and patient-specific correlations that may be missed by traditional approaches. Preliminary results indicate the potential for improved identification and stratification of high-risk patients, providing clinicians with a more accurate basis for prevention and intervention strategies.

title: Near-critical SIR epidemic on a random graph with given degrees
Abstract: Near-critical SIR epidemic on a random graph with given degrees models a scenario where a disease spreads among individuals connected through a network. We study the dynamics of a susceptible-infected-recovered (SIR) epidemic on a configuration model, a random graph with given degrees, approximating real-world contact networks. By considering both the epidemic threshold and the critical point, we navigate the regime where the disease is not extinct but also not persistent. Utilizing the edge-based mean-field approximation, numerical simulations, and analytical methods, we investigate the effects of the transmission rates, network structure, and population size on the outbreak's trajectory and ultimate fate. The core objective revolves around the identification of critical values of model parameters that separate different regimes of the SIR dynamics, thus facilitating better comprehension and implementation of public health measures in real-world networks with a known degree distribution. By accounting for the population's demographics and the network structure, this study directly translates into significant applications in assessing the vulnerability of various populations to the SIR disease and appropriately allocating healthcare resources. Furthermore, we discuss potential avenues for future research in relation to incorporating additional realistic factors into the SIR model, such as age and community structure, to bolster predictions and interventions in real-world systems.

title: Estimating the effects of water-induced shallow landslides on soil erosion
Abstract: Water-induced shallow landslides are a significant contributor to soil erosion globally, causing widespread environmental damage and economic losses. These landslides occur when intense rainfall triggers the movement of water-saturated soil, leading to the detachment and transportation of soil particles. The effects of water-induced shallow landslides on soil erosion are multifaceted, involving both direct and indirect impacts. Directly, these landslides result in the removal of soil particles, altering landscapes and affecting local hydrology. Indirectly, the effects of these landslides can influence soil properties, such as soil porosity and permeability, which in turn, affect the infiltration rates and surface runoff. This study aims to estimate the effects of water-induced shallow landslides on soil erosion, focusing on the complex interactions between soil properties, hydrological processes, and landslide occurrence. By employing numerical modeling and field experiments, this research explores the spatial and temporal dynamics of soil erosion in response to water-induced shallow landslides. We present a rigorous analysis of the relationships between landslide occurrence, soil properties, and erosion patterns, providing valuable insights into the devastating consequences of water-induced shallow landslides on soil erosion. This work informs local decision-making and informs strategies for mitigating the impacts of these environmental hazards, ultimately promoting sustainable land management practices and minimizing soil erosion risks.

title: Extended Report: Fine-grained Recognition of Abnormal Behaviors for Early Detection of Mild Cognitive Impairment
Abstract: This study focuses on developing a fine-grained recognition system to identify abnormal behaviors indicative of mild cognitive impairment (MCI) in elderly populations. Previous research has led to the development of methods for detecting subtle cognitive changes in the early stages of MCI, primarily relying on conventional cognitive assessments, laboratory tests, and neuroimaging techniques. However, the effectiveness of these approaches is often hindered by the complexity and variability of individual cognitive profiles and the challenges associated with early symptom manifestation. To address this shortcoming, our approach adopts a multimodal and deep learning-based framework that integrates natural language processing and sensor-based behavioral data to comprehensively monitor and analyze the daily activities, speech patterns, and physical mobility of vulnerable elderly subjects. The proposed methodology integrates both traditional feature extraction and neural network-based feature learning, leveraging a fine-grained hierarchy of feature extraction to effectively recognize intricate patterns of altered behavior. Extensive experiments were conducted on three publicly available datasets, namely, the MMSE (Mini-Mental State Examination) dataset, the MoCA (Montreal Cognitive Assessment) corpus, and the Real-world Activity Recognition of People over 65 (RAP-65) dataset. These empirical evaluations have demonstrated that our proposed framework consistently achieves high accuracy in detecting subtle cognitive anomalies and early warning signs of MCI, underscoring the efficacy of fine-grained behavior recognition in facilitating early diagnosis and intervention.

title: Forecasting and Uncertainty in Modeling the 2014-2015 Ebola Epidemic in West Africa
Abstract: The 2014-2015 Ebola epidemic in West Africa poses significant challenges for the development of effective forecasting and countermeasures. However, leveraging mathematical models to forecast and predict the spread of the disease can significantly contribute to the improvement of public health responses. This paper aims to investigate the impact of key model parameters on forecast accuracy and analyze the sources of uncertainty within these models. A range of machine learning algorithms and ordinary differential equation (ODE) models are utilized, focusing on incorporating real-world data into these models to provide more comprehensive and accurate forecasts. We draw upon empirical data from the World Health Organization (WHO) and data sources from affected countries to contextualize the epidemic in West Africa. Research results reveal that predictive models which incorporate variability in population movement and infection source can significantly forecast disease transmission, providing crucial insights for healthcare policymakers on need-targeted control of the disease's spreading. However, widespread discrepancies between predicted and observed cases highlight how uncertainty remains within forecasting systems due to the lack of accessibility of epidemiological data and issues of data quality variability which significantly challenge the development of a reliable predictive forecast.

title: Heart rate and its variability as an indicator of mental health in male prisoners
Abstract: This study investigated the relationship between heart rate and its variability (HRV) and mental health in male prisoners with a focus on identifying potential biomarkers for mental health disorders. Utilizing a cross-sectional design, HRV analysis was performed on electrocardiogram (ECG) recordings of 150 male prisoners with varying levels of psychiatric and behavioral difficulties. The prisoners' mental health status was evaluated through a standardized diagnostic interview and survey. Results indicated that male prisoners with a diagnosis of major depressive disorder or post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) exhibited reduced HRV, characterized by decreased peak-to-peak intervals and standard deviation of normal-to-normal (SDNN) intervals. In contrast, prisoners with anxiety disorders showed a slight increase in HRV. These findings suggest that HRV may serve as a valuable indicator of mental health status in male prisoners, particularly in the context of depression and PTSD. Furthermore, our study highlights the potential utility of non-invasive physiological measures like HRV in predicting mental health outcomes, which could inform the development of targeted interventions and treatment strategies for male prisoners. These findings contribute to a growing body of research exploring the relationship between physiological processes and mental health, with implications for both clinical practice and correctional policies.

title: Open TURNS: An industrial software for uncertainty quantification in simulation
Abstract: Open TURNS is an industrial software developed by EDF R&D for the quantification of uncertainties associated with numerical models. It offers a flexible and powerful framework for uncertainty quantification (UQ) in various fields, including engineering, physics, and more. By leveraging Open TURNS, users can efficiently manage the complexity of high-dimensional models and handle large datasets, allowing for rapid experimentation and a high level of reproducibility. At its core, Open TURNS relies on the concept of random process, which extends the traditional notion of random variables and allows for a more accurate representation of real-world phenomena. This software also supports a wide range of computational methods for UQ, including stochastic analysis, sensitivity analysis, and uncertainty propagation. Additionally, Open TURNS features a comprehensive set of tools for visualizing and analyzing the results of uncertainty simulations, facilitating the interpretation of the uncertainty impact on the system under study. By adopting Open TURNS, industrial professionals and researchers can take full advantage of the computational power available today, gaining valuable insights into the uncertain behavior of complex systems and ultimately making more informed decisions.

title: Direct laser acceleration of electrons in free-space
Abstract: Direct laser acceleration of electrons in free-space has undergone significant advancements in recent years, holding promise for the development of compact, high-energy particle accelerators that could revolutionize various fields including high-energy physics, materials science, and medical applications. This research area has been invigorated by the notion of exploiting optical-frequency electromagnetic radiation, particularly high-power lasers, to propel electrons to relativistic velocities in a matter of centimeters. Conventional radio-frequency or particle-beam-based acceleration technologies pose significant constraints in this regard, often requiring meters-long devices and extensive infrastructure. In contrast, laser-based acceleration techniques potentially enable scalability and miniaturization, augmenting research capabilities and opening up new avenues for practical applications. By focusing laser pulses on a target, creating a high-pressure, energetic plasma, researchers aim to accelerate electrons via a self-modulating plasma wave. This phenomenon counterintuitively exhibits a quasilinear behavior, not intuitively deduced from classical electrodynamics. Recent studies indicate that there exists an intrinsic efficiency-scaling limit, limiting accelerator performance and requiring experimental confirmation of theoretical predictions. Ultimately, refining our understanding of laser-plasma interaction and the propagation of electromagnetic waves in target media will be crucial for optimizing the acceleration process and realizing the full potential of direct laser acceleration of electrons in free-space.

title: Hydrogen Fluoride Capture by Imidazolium Acetate Ionic Liquid
Abstract: Hydrogen Fluoride (HF) capture is a crucial step in various industrial processes, including the production of semiconductors, pharmaceuticals, and uranium enrichment. However, the acidic, highly corrosive nature of HF poses significant challenges in its capture and storage. Ionic liquids (ILs), a class of low-melting point salts composed of organic cations and inorganic anions, have garnered attention for their potential applications in HF capture due to their unique physicochemical properties. In this study, the imidazolium acetate IL was used as a promising material for capturing HF. The IL was synthesized and characterized using a range of techniques, including H-1 nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy and mass spectrometry (MS). The liquid-liquid equilibrium (LLE) of HF with imidazolium acetate IL was investigated, revealing that the IL exhibits an excellent affinity for HF capture. Thermodynamic modeling using the regular solution theory (RST) and the non-random two-liquid (NRTL) model was employed to describe the LLE of the HF-IL system. The results indicate that the NRTL model provides a better description of the LLE of the HF-IL system, while the RST model underestimates the activity coefficients of HF in the IL phase. Kinetic studies of HF capture by imidazolium acetate IL revealed that the capture process occurs rapidly, with a capture rate constant of approximately 1.2·10-3min-1. The effectiveness of imidazolium acetate IL for HF capture was further assessed by evaluating its reusability and chemical stability under acidic conditions.

title: LMest: an R package for latent Markov models for categorical longitudinal data
Abstract: The LMest R package is designed to fit latent Markov models to categorical longitudinal data, providing a flexible framework for modeling complex temporal patterns and structural relationships within the data. Latent Markov models are a variant of the traditional latent class analysis, where the latent states are allowed to change over time. This package extends the capabilities of the standard R statistical software by offering a comprehensive set of tools and algorithms for specifying, fitting, and evaluating latent Markov models. The LMest package enables users to accommodate various types of missing data, including missing at random, and to handle large-scale datasets through parallel processing. Furthermore, the package offers diagnostic and visualization tools to facilitate model assessment and comparison, and it includes a variety of model metrics and fit indices to aid in selecting the optimal specification. The package also enables the estimation of various probability distributions for the transition probabilities, which is particularly useful when analyzing categorical data with an ordinal structure. By incorporating the functionality of the package, researchers and practitioners can efficiently model and analyze complex longitudinal data with multiple categorical variables, facilitating a deeper understanding of the underlying processes and mechanisms governing the patterns of change over time. The LMest package makes it a valuable tool for applied researchers and analysts working with categorical longitudinal data.

title: Editorial: Spatial accessibility of pediatric primary healthcare: Measurement and inference
Abstract: This paper employs a comprehensive and quantitative approach to evaluate spatial accessibility of pediatric primary healthcare services, aiming to provide a deeper understanding of this critical aspect of healthcare delivery to vulnerable populations, namely children. Building on the theoretical underpinnings of the two-step floating catchment area (2SFCA) method and its derivative, the modified 2SFCA (M2SFCA), we develop an innovative spatiotemporal framework for measuring pediatric primary healthcare accessibility across a diverse range of urban and rural settings. Our spatial accessibility measure incorporates a suite of critical attributes, including the number and distribution of pediatric healthcare facilities, population density, transportation networks, and travel time, while also accounting for temporal variations in service hours, wait times, and seasonal demand fluctuations. Through a rigorous validation process using real-world pediatric primary healthcare utilization data from a large metropolitan region, we demonstrate the robustness and applicability of our framework in measuring spatial accessibility disparities. Our findings highlight the importance of spatial considerations in planning equitable pediatric primary care services, informing targeted interventions to address medically underserved areas and promoting better health outcomes among children. The proposed framework offers a valuable tool for policymakers, healthcare managers, and researchers seeking to improve pediatric primary healthcare access and quality in diverse settings.

title: Spatial accessibility of pediatric primary healthcare: Measurement and inference
Abstract: This study explores the spatial accessibility of pediatric primary healthcare services, investigating the accessibility gap between healthcare facilities and vulnerable pediatric populations. title: Oscillometric continuous blood pressure sensing for wearable health monitoring system
Abstract: This paper proposes the implementation of oscillometric continuous blood pressure sensing technology in a wearable health monitoring system. Oscillometry is a non-invasive technique that measures blood pressure by analyzing the oscillations in the arterial blood flow. The wearable device is designed to capture these oscillations using advanced sensing and signal processing techniques, enabling continuous monitoring of blood pressure in real-time. The system consists of a microcontroller unit that processes the raw sensor data from the oscillometric sensor and calculates the blood pressure values based on established algorithms. To ensure accuracy and precision, the device employs machine learning algorithms to filter out noise and interference from the signals, thereby improving the overall reliability of the readings. Moreover, the wearable device integrates with edge computing to enable on-board processing and reduce latency in data analysis, contributing to real-time blood pressure monitoring. The wearable device is designed to be compact, lightweight, and wearable, compatible with a wide range of populations including elderly patients, patients suffering from cardiovascular diseases, and athletes requiring blood pressure monitoring during physical activities. The proposed wearable system demonstrates great potential in revolutionizing remote health monitoring, enabling timely intervention and improving patient outcomes.

title: On Vulnerabilities of the Security Association in the IEEE 802.15.6 Standard
Abstract: The IEEE 802.15.6 standard is designed to provide a framework for secure communication within body area networks (BANs), catering to diverse applications such as health monitoring and medical implants. Despite its notable contributions to the field, the standard's security association, which is responsible for secure data exchange, has not been thoroughly analyzed for potential vulnerabilities. In this research paper, an in-depth examination of the IEEE 802.15.6 standard reveals several shortcomings in the security association. Specifically, the security protocol is found to be vulnerable to attacks such as authentication bypass, key compromise, and replay attacks due to its reliance on fixed keys and a lack of mutual authentication between devices. Moreover, the protocol's susceptibility to side-channel attacks, such as power and interference attacks, poses a significant threat to the confidentiality and integrity of communication within BANs. These findings are significant as they highlight the need for immediate attention to strengthen the security of the IEEE 802.15.6 standard to ensure secure and reliable communication in critical applications. The present study aims to provide a comprehensive analysis and evaluation of the security association in the IEEE 802.15.6 standard, serving as a stimulus for the development of more robust security mechanisms to address these identified vulnerabilities.

title: Functional optoacoustic neuro-tomography (FONT) for whole-brain monitoring of calcium indicators
Abstract: Functional optoacoustic neuro-tomography (FONT) has emerged as a novel imaging modality that enables real-time, whole-brain monitoring of neural activity with unprecedented spatial and temporal resolution. By harnessing the photoacoustic effect, FONT detects the optoacoustic signals generated by light absorption in the brain, allowing for the imaging of calcium indicators in real-time. This capability is particularly significant in functional brain imaging applications, as calcium indicators are widely used to monitor the dynamics of neuronal activity. FONT's combination of non-invasive detection and high-resolution imaging capabilities holds great promise for neuroscience research, enabling the direct observation of neural activity in its native tissue environment. The technology has been shown to provide detailed, high-resolution images of the brain's neural circuits, enabling researchers to observe the intricate dynamics of neural relationships and interactions. Preliminary studies have demonstrated FONT's ability to detect neural activity with high sensitivity and specificity, outperforming traditional modalities such as functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) in many aspects. Furthermore, FONT's non-invasive nature and lack of ionizing radiation make it an attractive alternative to existing imaging modalities, particularly for longitudinal studies and repeated measurements in the same subject. As a result, FONT is poised to revolutionize our understanding of the brain and its function, offering unprecedented insights into the intricate workings of the human brain.

title: Electronic health record phenotyping improves detection and screening of type 2 diabetes in the general United States population: A cross-sectional, unselected, retrospective study
Abstract: This cross-sectional, unselected, and retrospective study evaluated the effectiveness of electronic health record (EHR) phenotyping in detecting and screening type 2 diabetes in the general United States population. The study utilized administrative claims data from a large US health data repository, consisting of over 270 million patient records, to identify individuals who received a diagnosis of type 2 diabetes between 2010 and 2018. The study's primary outcome measure was the comparison of detection and screening rates for type 2 diabetes between EHR-identified cases and cases identified through traditional methods. Phenotyping algorithms in EHR systems detected a statistically significant 26% higher rate of type 2 diabetes cases compared to manual review of medical records, and an additional 17% increase in cases among African American patients. Additionally, the use of EHR phenotyping significantly improved screening rates for type 2 diabetes among high-risk individuals aged 45-64 years old, including those with a family history of the disease. These findings suggest that EHR-based phenotyping can facilitate earlier and more accurate detection of type 2 diabetes, particularly in underserved and high-risk populations, enabling timely interventions and improving patient outcomes. The results of this study highlight the potential of EHR phenotyping to enhance healthcare quality and reduce healthcare disparities in the US.

title: SHM method for damage localization based on substructuring and VARX models
Abstract: The Structural Health Monitoring (SHM) method for damage localization based on substructuring and Vector AutoRegressive eXogenous (VARX) models presents a novel approach to assessing structural integrity under real-world conditions. By partitioning a complex structural system into smaller substructures, this method enables the application of distributed sensing techniques to capture localized characteristics of structural behavior. The VARX model, developed within the framework of Subspace State Space System Identification methods, is then utilized to extract linearly correlated signals from the substructure measurements. These extracted signals are subsequently analyzed using Machine Learning algorithms to identify anomalies indicative of damage localization, considering both the substructure's physical properties and its interactions with neighboring components. Performance evaluation of this approach on both numerical and experimental data reveals substantial accuracy improvements over traditional frequency response-based methods, particularly when dealing with minor damage manifestations. Furthermore, the substructuring-VARX-SHM method is demonstrated to efficiently mitigate the issues associated with structural non-linearity, temperature variability, and environmental factors that often pose significant challenges to real-world damage detection applications. title: Causal inference for ordinal outcomes
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel framework for causal inference when the outcome variable is ordinal in nature. Ordinal outcomes are common in many fields, including health sciences, social sciences, and economics, yet most existing methods for causal inference assume continuous or binary outcomes. The proposed framework, dubbed Ordinal Causal Inference (OCI), extends existing generalized method of moments (GMM) and generalized method of quantile moments (GMQ) approaches to accommodate ordinal outcomes. OCI separates the effect into distinct components; an underlying binary effect, measuring the comparative advantage of being in the reference category of the exposure compared to a benchmark category, and an ordinal effect that captures the differential impact of the exposure across different levels of the ordinal outcome. Through a simulation-based approach and a real-world dataset application from health economics comparing health care modalities affecting self reported pain in post-operative patients, the OCI approach demonstrates improved estimation and inference over existing methods. The paper contributes to the field by providing an accessible and accurate framework for causal inference in ordinal outcomes and shows such inference is critical when making policy decisions in healthcare that can have measurable and substantial impacts for patients.

title: A Taxonomy of Big Data for Optimal Predictive Machine Learning and Data Mining
Abstract: This research paper proposes a comprehensive taxonomy of big data, which is crucial for optimal predictive machine learning and data mining applications. The proposed taxonomy aims to bridge the gap between the diversity of big data sources and the inherent complexity of predictive machine learning and data mining models. Based on the multidimensional characteristics of big data, such as variety, velocity, volume, and veracity, a novel framework is developed to categorize big data into four primary categories: structured big data, semi-structured big data, unstructured big data, and multi-structured big data. These categories are further divided into subcategories to facilitate a more granular and precise analysis. The paper validates the taxonomy through a case study involving real-world datasets, highlighting the practical applicability of the framework. The proposed taxonomy enables data scientists and practitioners to select the most suitable big data characteristics for their predictive machine learning and data mining projects, thus improving the accuracy and efficiency of the models developed. title: Brighter than the sun: Powerscape visualizations illustrate power needs in neuroscience and psychology
Abstract: Power needs in neuroscience and psychology have been a long-standing concern, yet their visualization remains a challenging task, largely due to the complexity of the power requirements and the diverse fields involved. Findings from these studies demonstrate the ability of Powerscape visualizations to reveal dynamic patterns of power usage, facilitate predictions of power imbalances, and identify prospective interventions to mitigate power inequalities in cognitive processes. title: Quadripolar Relational Model: a framework for the description of borderline and narcissistic personality disorders
Abstract: The Quadripolar Relational Model provides a novel framework for understanding and describing borderline and narcissistic personality disorders, two complex psychiatric conditions characterized by pervasive and severe impairments in interpersonal relationships. By integrating insights from psychoanalytic, psychodynamic, and attachment theories, this model proposes that borderline personality disorder (BPD) and narcissistic personality disorder (NPD) can be viewed as relational constructs, rather than discrete and absolute diagnostic entities. The Quadripolar Relational Model posits that each disorder represents a specific configuration of four fundamental relational patterns, including withdrawal-defensiveness, entitlement-manipulation, abandonment-preoccupation, and perfectionism-adversariality. This framework highlights the crucial role of early relational experiences in shaping the development of these disorders, as well as the importance of therapeutic relationships in facilitating recovery and personal growth. An examination of the Quadripolar Relational Model's theoretical underpinnings and clinical applications reveals its potential to inform the development of more effective treatment strategies and improve interpersonal outcomes for individuals with BPD and NPD. The implications of this model for our understanding of psychopathology, attachment, and relational dynamics are also explored, underscoring its value as a theoretical and clinical paradigm for the 21st century.

title: Predicting and visualizing psychological attributions with a deep neural network
Abstract: This research proposes the development and deployment of a deep neural network-based framework for predicting and visualizing psychological attributions. Psychological attributions play a crucial role in human behavior, decision-making, and social interactions, and understanding these attributions can provide significant insights for various domains such as psychology, social sciences, education, and healthcare. However, attributing complex psychological states and behaviors can be challenging due to their subjective and often implicit nature. Existing methods rely heavily on rule-based systems or shallow machine learning models that fail to capture the intricacies of human behavior. To address these limitations, this study presents a comprehensive approach to predicting psychological attributions using deep neural networks, incorporating both textual and visual stimuli. By leveraging multimodal inputs, including text, audio, and visual data, the proposed framework aims to quantify and visualize attributions related to human behavior. The framework consists of two main components: a prediction network that accurately estimates attributions based on input data and a visualization module that generates intuitive and informative representations of the results. To evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed framework, we conducted a series of experiments using annotated psychological attribution datasets, with results demonstrating improved prediction accuracy and visualization efficacy compared to existing methods. The proposed framework shows promise for facilitating more accurate and meaningful analysis of psychological attributions, offering valuable insights for real-world applications in psychology, social sciences, and education.

title: The GTR-model: a universal framework for quantum-like measurements
Abstract: This paper proposes a fundamental shift in our understanding of quantum-like measurements by introducing the Generalized Transform and Reflection (GTR) model. Building upon the foundations of generalized probability theories and non-locality, the GTR model offers a unified framework that reconciles the principles of quantum mechanics and classical statistical inference. By formulating quantum-like measurements as transformations between distinct probabilistic structures, the GTR model reveals a deep analogy between the probabilistic and kinematical aspects of quantum mechanics. This analogy enables a reformulation of the measurement process in terms of simple geometric transformations, allowing for a more intuitive and comprehensive understanding of the underlying structure of quantum dynamics. The GTR model bridges the gap between the mathematical formalism of quantum mechanics and its experimental implementations, providing a novel perspective on the nature of physical reality and the foundations of measurement theory. By exploring the theoretical implications and empirical consequences of the GTR model, this research aims to establish a new paradigm for understanding quantum mechanics and its applications in physics, philosophy, and engineering. The proposed framework has far-reaching implications for our understanding of non-locality, information processing, and the foundations of physical reality.

title: Creation and Evaluation of Software Teams - A Social Approach
Abstract: This paper explores the creation and evaluation of software teams from a social approach, focusing on the collective aspects that contribute to their effectiveness and success. It outlines a comprehensive methodology for assembling and managing software development teams, emphasizing the importance of interpersonal relationships, communication dynamics, and communal motivation. The proposed model incorporates various social theories and framework, including Social Identity Theory, Social Learning Theory, and Group Norms, to provide a structured framework for the formation, development, and sustenance of cohesive software teams. A mixed-methods approach combining surveys, interviews, and case studies is used to validate the effectiveness of the proposed model. The empirical findings suggest that a strong social foundation is essential for software team success, including factors such as shared goals, team workability, and clear communication. The study contributes to the literature by providing actionable insights and practical recommendations for team leaders and managers seeking to create high-performing software teams. Furthermore, it highlights the need for more research on the social aspects of software development, emphasizing the value of a holistic approach that takes into account the diverse psychological, emotional, and relational factors that influence team dynamics. title: Imitation-Induced Criticality: Network Reciprocity and Psycho-logical Reward
Abstract: This study probes the intricate dynamics of imitation-induced criticality in network reciprocity, a phenomenon pivotal in fostering cooperative behavior within groups. By virtue of its reciprocal structure, networks demonstrate striking parallels with biological organisms, conveying reciprocal interactions between members, under circumstances conducive to social learning. Through agent-based modeling, we investigate the dichotomy between reciprocal and one-way interaction networks as mediators of imitation-induced criticality, with a view to bridging the microscopic scale, encompassing the individual's proclivity to imitate behavior, and the mesoscopic, represented by population-level reciprocity networks, thereby yielding profound insights into the behavior of individuals in collaboration. Our modeling framework incorporating psycho-logical and neuro-cognitive reward principles in pursuit of knowledge acquisition in real-world scenarios, thus sheds new light on the factors that conspire to propel a system toward the global instability characteristic of critical points, key elements in unfolding new information, as they convey new rules and norms in conformity with imitated neighbor behaviors.

title: Psychological Types of Brazilian Software Engineering Students
Abstract: This study investigates the psychological types of Brazilian software engineering students, exploring the implications for their professional development and team collaboration. Using the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI), a psychometric instrument that categorizes individuals into 16 distinct personality types based on four dichotomies (Extraversion/Introversion, Sensing/Intuition, Thinking/Feeling, and Judging/Perceiving), this research aims to identify the dominant psychological types among Brazilian software engineering students. A total of 500 students from five major universities in Brazil participated in the study, completing the MBTI questionnaire and providing demographic information. The results showed that the most prevalent psychological types among the participants were INTJ (16.1%), ISTJ (13.1%), and ENTP (10.5%). Additionally, significant correlations were found between certain psychological types and demographic variables such as age, academic performance, and choice of software engineering specializations. The findings suggest that Brazilian software engineering students can be differentiated based on their psychological types, and that tailoring educational and professional development programs to meet the specific needs of each type could enhance their learning experiences and career outcomes. The study's results have implications for educators, researchers, and industry professionals seeking to better understand and support the development of software engineers in Brazil.

title: Adjusted Priors for Bayes Factors Involving Reparameterized Order Constraints
Abstract: This study explores novel applications of reparameterized order constraints (ROC) for the purpose of computing Bayes factors in hierarchical models. In recent years, researchers have leveraged ROC to effectively approximate the otherwise intractable high-dimensional integrals that arise in hierarchical Bayesian models. Central to this work is the concept of ROC priors, which have been demonstrated to yield favorable computational and statistical properties. However, traditional ROC priors are often too diffuse, leading to low power and poor results when applied in hypothesis testing scenarios that necessitate high precision. This research introduces adjusted ROC priors that incorporate additional prior information to bolster the power and precision of Bayes factor analysis. The proposed method takes into account the specifics of each hypothesis test, enabling adjusted ROC priors to be tailored to particular testing scenarios. Employing simulations and empirical analyses, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the adjusted ROC priors in hypothesis testing, showcasing improved power, precision, and stability compared to traditional ROC priors. Furthermore, we apply our methodology to two case studies involving nested data structures and observe significant increases in statistical precision and power, underscoring the benefits of incorporating adjusted ROC priors in hypothesis testing. Overall, the adjusted ROC priors offer a more robust and versatile solution for Bayesian inference and hypothesis testing in the context of hierarchical models, affirming their utility in a range of applications.

title: MOOCs Meet Measurement Theory: A Topic-Modelling Approach
Abstract: This paper explores the intersection of Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs) and Measurement Theory, where we apply a topic-modelling approach to analyse the conceptual frameworks underlying MOOCs. By synthesizing insights from MOOCs researchers and measurement theorists, we build on the notion that MOOCs often employ implicit, unobservable constructs, such as learner engagement or prior knowledge, to inform the design and assessment of their courses. We contend that these constructs can be broadly categorized as "latent variables" that are quantitatively analysable, much like those in Psychological Measurement Theory. Our goal is to demonstrate the feasibility of using topic-modelling techniques, which characterise unstructured text data as mixtures of topics, or latent themes, to profile MOOCs features corresponding to seven prominent measurement theories: Classical Test Theory (CTT), Item Response Theory (IRT), Generalizability Theory (G), Mixed-Effects Models, Rasch's Model, Partial Credit Models (PCM), and Latent Class Analysis (LCA). Through the analysis of over 4,800 peer-reviewed papers on MOOCs from top-tier scholarly databases, we illustrate how topic modelling can reveal interesting correspondences between MOOC design aspects and measurement theoretical precepts and limitations, setting the stage for cross-pollination ideas and theory-informed practices in the field of MOOCs design and evaluation, and suggesting avenues for policy and research directions in education.

title: Influence of Personality Types in Software Tasks Choices
Abstract: This study investigates the impact of personality types on software task choices, aiming to provide insights into the complexities of software development teams. The underlying assumption is that distinct personality traits can significantly influence an individual's approach to software tasks, leading to differing task preferences and performance outcomes. Previous research in the field has often overlooked the intricacies of personality types and their interaction with software development practices. Utilizing the Big Five personality traits (Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, and Neuroticism) and the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI), this study surveys 300 software developers across various industries, gathering data on their personality types and task preferences. Results indicate significant correlations between certain personality types and task choices, such as introverted and analytical individuals favoring tasks requiring attention to detail. Conversely, extroverted and spontaneous developers tend to prefer tasks requiring creativity and collaboration. Furthermore, results suggest that team diversity in terms of personality types is positively associated with team performance and adaptability. However, it also highlights the limitations of team cohesion when divergent personality types are not managed effectively. These findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the role of personality types in software task choices and underscore the importance of considering individual differences in software development teams to achieve optimal performance.

title: Symbol Grounding Association in Multimodal Sequences with Missing Elements
Abstract: This study investigates the concept of symbol grounding in multimodal sequences, focusing on scenarios where certain elements are missing. Symbol grounding is the relationship between abstract symbols and their concrete referents, which is critical for artificial intelligence (AI) systems to understand and interact with the world. Multimodal sequences, comprising multiple types of data such as images, text, and audio, can facilitate more robust and flexible symbol grounding. However, handling missing elements in these sequences poses a challenge, as it requires the AI system to anticipate and infer the absent information. We propose a novel approach using a combination of multimodal encoder-decoder models and multimodal attention mechanisms to address this issue. Our approach learns to recognize patterns and relationships between modalities to predict the missing elements, thereby enhancing the overall understanding and completeness of the multimodal sequence. We evaluate our method on several benchmark datasets, demonstrating significant improvements in prediction accuracy and semantic consistency compared to baseline methods. Additionally, we conduct an analysis of the learned representations and their relevance to real-world applications, providing insights into the effectiveness and limitations of our proposed approach. The findings of this study contribute to the advancement of symbol grounding in multimodal AI, facilitating its practical applications in areas such as image and dialogue processing, and multimodal reasoning.

title: Expressiveness and Understandability Considerations of Hierarchy in Declarative Business Process Models
Abstract: This research delves into the nuances of hierarchy in declarative business process models, focusing on the interplay between expressiveness and understandability. As the business landscape continues to evolve, businesses are increasingly relying on declarative models to capture their operational complexities and manage changing circumstances. However, the incorporation of hierarchy in these models poses significant challenges, particularly in terms of balancing expressiveness and understandability. On one hand, hierarchy enables declarative models to concisely represent intricate processes, thereby promoting flexibility and ease of editing. However, this conceptual complexity often translates into a higher cognitive load for modelers and analysts, potentially hindering the overall understandability of the models. This study aims to contribute to the existing body of knowledge by investigating how different hierarchical structures and notations affect the expressiveness and understandability of declarative business process models. Through a mixed-methods approach combining empirical analysis and systematic literature review, this research identifies key factors that influence the balance between expressiveness and understandability in hierarchical declarative models, and proposes a set of recommendations for model designers and practitioners to strike an optimal balance in their business process modeling endeavors. By shedding light on the intricate relationship between hierarchy, expressiveness, and understandability, this study provides valuable insights into the effective application of declarative models in a range of industries and contexts.

title: Change Patterns for Model Creation: Investigating the Role of Nesting Depth
Abstract: The concept of nesting depth has garnered significant attention in the realm of model creation, particularly within the context of change patterns. title: Context-Content Systems of Random Variables: The Contextuality-by-Default Theory
Abstract: The Context-Content Systems of Random Variables: The Contextuality-by-Default Theory presents a novel framework for understanding the intricate relationships between contextual and inherent properties of random variables. The theory posits that context and content, often seen as distinct and opposing concepts, exist in a synergistic relationship in the realm of probability theory. Contextuality-by-Default Theory provides a quantifiable approach to understanding how contextual information shapes our perception of the content of random variables. By introducing the concept of context-contingent probabilities and the notion of contextual anchors, this theory redefines the way we think about probability, causality, and the role of context in shaping our understanding of the world. Through a comprehensive examination of the relationships between semantic and pragmatic aspects of language, the theory demonstrates how contextual information influences the content of what is communicated. Furthermore, the theory proposes that contextuality is a fundamental aspect of reality, not merely a product of limited information or conscious processing. By shedding light on the intricate dance between context and content, Contextuality-by-Default Theory offers a paradigm shift in our understanding of random variables, probability theory, and the nature of reality itself. Its implications reach far beyond the realm of physics, opening doors to novel perspectives on communication, cognition, and the human experience.

title: God(s) Know(s): Developmental and Cross-Cultural Patterns in Children Drawings
Abstract: This study explores the developmental and cross-cultural patterns in children's drawings of religious figures, examining how children's conceptions of God(s) change across different cultures and stages of development. A mixed-methods approach was employed, combining quantitative data from a global online survey of over 1,000 children's drawings with qualitative analysis of a subsample of 20 participants from diverse cultural backgrounds. Results revealed a clear progression from initial anthropomorphic representations of God(s) in preschoolers to more abstract and complex forms in older children, with significant variations across cultures. Children from collectivist cultures such as Japan and China tended to draw God(s) in more benevolent and supportive roles, while those from individualist cultures like the United States and Australia depicted God(s) as more distant and authoritative.Interestingly, children's drawings from non-Western cultures often depicted God(s) interacting with natural phenomena, underscoring the importance of environmental and spiritual interconnectedness in children's conceptualizations. These findings suggest that children's understandings of God(s) are shaped by a complex interplay of cognitive, cultural, and socio-historical factors, highlighting the need for further research into the development of theological and spiritual cognition across diverse cultural contexts. title: Negative Probabilities and Contextuality
Abstract: Quantum mechanics has long been a subject of fascination due to its seemingly counterintuitive behavior, particularly in the realm of probability and contextuality. The concept of negative probabilities, which are thoughtfully derived from the quantization of charged particles, has been a topic of debate among theoretical physicists. In contrast, contextuality, the existence of states that cannot be described without considering the external context, has been directly linked to non-locality and quantum entanglement. Our research delves into the intricacies of the relationship between negative probabilities and contextuality. We establish a method to demonstrate that quantum mechanics is impossible without negative probabilities for contexts describing the basis of measurement. Furthermore, it is found that any purely contextual model of the observed phenomenon does not lead to the negativity for all type of outcomes with respect to certain context. Our model highlights the interplay between contextuality and negative probabilities, providing a renewed understanding of quantum systems' behavior under various measurement settings. Additionally, the proposed algorithm allows us to rigorously resolve and establish a comprehensive formulation of conditions necessary to satisfy contextuality and negativity, offering a more thorough understanding of quantum measurement and the physical implications of negative probabilities.

title: A new humanlike facial attractiveness predictor with cascaded fine-tuning deep learning model
Abstract: This research introduces a cutting-edge deep learning framework for predicting human facial attractiveness, tailored to replicate human-like aesthetic evaluation. The proposed model adopts a cascaded fine-tuning strategy, where a coarse-to-fine facial feature extraction is performed through a hierarchical architecture comprising multiple convolutional neural network (CNN) modules. Initially, a lightweight pre-trained network is employed for coarse-level feature extraction, leveraging discriminative properties of spatial and textual features. Thereafter, a series of progressively finer-resolution modules are sequentially fine-tuned in a cascaded manner, allowing for hierarchical refinement of facial attributes and subtle feature rendition. Furthermore, a novel multi-task learning strategy is incorporated to amplify the model's sensitivity to context-specific facial aspects, mitigating potential biases inherent in traditional single-task architectures. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that the cascaded fine-tuning framework exhibits superior predictive accuracy, robustness, and generalizability, nearing state-of-the-art human judgments on benchmark datasets featuring diverse ethnic and age demographics. Notably, the proposed predictor outperforms existing automatic facial attractiveness models by facilitating an unprecedented level of nuance and subtlety in capturing human-like beauty evaluations, providing a groundbreaking advancement in computational aesthetics and human-computer interaction research.

title: Finding structure in data using multivariate tree boosting
Abstract: This paper explores the application of multivariate tree boosting as a methodology for extracting underlying structure in complex datasets. A crucial aspect of handling multivariate data lies in identifying intricate relationships between various variables, which guides the formulation of meaningful conclusions and predictions. Multivariate tree boosting, a variant of boosted decision trees that leverages multiple features at each node, is capable of navigating complex high-dimensional data and uncovering patterns that might elude traditional univariate analysis methods. By incorporating ensemble techniques and leveraging the strengths of tree-based models, multivariate tree boosting enables the detection of both linear and non-linear correlations between variables, providing a more comprehensive understanding of the underlying data structure. A key strength of this approach lies in its ability to handle both categorical and numerical features, thereby accommodating dataset heterogeneity and facilitating analysis across diverse domains. The proposed methodology is evaluated through a simulated dataset and a real-world application in collaborative filtering for personalized recommendations, demonstrating significant accuracy improvements over state-of-the-art methods. The results demonstrate the efficacy of multivariate tree boosting as a powerful tool for extracting meaningful structure in complex datasets, facilitating novel insights and informed decision-making across various disciplines.

title: Balancing Type I Error and Power in Linear Mixed Models
Abstract: This study investigates the delicate balance between type I error and power in linear mixed models, a class of statistical methods increasingly used in various fields, including psychology, biology, and medicine. The linear mixed model framework allows for the analysis of complex, multi-level data structures with unequal variances, but it is also more prone to type I errors due to its flexible modeling of covariance structures. As a result, researchers often struggle to maintain an acceptable balance between the probability of rejecting a true null hypothesis (power) and the probability of rejecting a false null hypothesis (type I error). A comprehensive literature review revealed that many widely used linear mixed model procedures in statistical software packages exhibit inflated type I error rates under certain conditions, leading to unnecessary rejections of the null hypothesis and loss of credibility in research findings. To mitigate this issue, we proposed several modifications to two popular linear mixed model estimators, namely REML and ML, and evaluated their performance using simulated data and a real-world dataset from the health sciences. Our results showed that the proposed modifications significantly reduced type I error rates while maintaining acceptable power levels, highlighting the importance of careful specification of covariance structures and optimization of model parameters in linear mixed models to ensure reliable results. Overall, this study aims to provide a better understanding of the interplay between type I error and power in linear mixed models and offers practical recommendations for researchers to optimize their use of these models in hypothesis testing.

title: Corruption and Wealth: Unveiling a national prosperity syndrome in Europe
Abstract: Corruption and Wealth: Unveiling a national prosperity syndrome in Europe presents a comprehensive examination of the intricate relationship between corruption, economic prosperity, and national wealth in European countries. This in-depth analysis delves into the multifaceted dynamics underlying the phenomenon of corruption, exploring how it influences the socio-economic development of nations. By employing a mixed-methods approach, combining empirical data and qualitative research, the study reveals a paradoxical association between corruption and economic growth in European countries. Results suggest that while a moderate level of corruption appears to be correlated with increased economic prosperity, extreme corruption can have devastating effects on a nation's wealth and stability. Notably, the findings indicate that countries characterized by high levels of trust, effective institutional frameworks, and strong governance tend to exhibit lower corruption rates and higher levels of national wealth. Conversely, nations plagued by systemic corruption, inequality, and institutional weakness often struggle to achieve sustainable economic growth. This study seeks to contribute to the understanding of the complex interplay between corruption, economic prosperity, and national wealth, shedding light on the mechanisms that underlie the phenomenon of a national prosperity syndrome in Europe, a framework that highlights the interconnections between corruption, trust, and economic performance.

title: Falsification or Confirmation: From Logic to Psychology
Abstract: In the realm of scientific inquiry, the age-old dichotomy between falsification and confirmation has long been debated by philosophers and researchers alike. Karl Popper's seminal work "The Logic of Scientific Discovery" posited that the ultimate goal of science lies in the pursuit of falsification, wherein theories are rigorously tested to identify their limits and potential vulnerabilities. Conversely, other philosophers, such as Karl Raimund Popper's contemporary, Hans Reichenbach, argued for the complementary importance of confirmation, where evidence is accumulated to support and build upon existing theories. This paper seeks to bridge the methodological divides between these two opposing epistemological perspectives, examining the empirical conditions under which falsification and confirmation respectively serve as the dominant evaluative criteria in scientific validation. By analyzing the methodological logics governing the history of psychology, we aim to elucidate the complex psychological and sociological factors influencing the formulation of hypotheses and the accumulation of evidence in this field. Our analysis will determine whether the dialectical balance between falsification and confirmation demonstrates a paradigmatic oscillation between two mutually reinforcing values or whether, in certain situations, one value does indeed prevail over the other. Ultimately, this paper provides an interdisciplinary examination of how psychological research is shaped by the inherent tensions between the pursuit of validity and the management of uncertainty.

title: From Ambiguity Aversion to a Generalized Expected Utility. Modeling Preferences in a Quantum Probabilistic Framework
Abstract: This research paper bridges the gap between classical expected utility theories and decision-making under uncertainty, proposing a novel quantum probabilistic framework to model preferences when the likelihood of outcomes is quantified with ambiguous probabilities. Specifically, we extend the concept of ambiguity aversion, a pervasive phenomenon in real-world decision-making, to a more general setting where probabilities are uncertain or frequency-defined rather than scenario-based. By harnessing the mathematical structure of quantum mechanics, we develop a quantum probabilistic framework that can capture the inherent coherence of decision-making under ambiguity, allowing for the non-classical phenomenon of state vectors (superposition and entanglement) to be applied to various aspects of uncertainty. Our axiomatic approach encapsulates a diverse range of decision-theoretic scenarios exhibiting ambiguity aversion, such as those in which long-run probabilities are defined, providing concrete illustrations, case studies, and computational methods. Furthermore, we formalize several key implications of quantum probability on decision theory, including a generalized notion of rationality under uncertainty and the non-linearity of ambiguity. Overall, our research provides a cohesive and empirically motivated theory of decision-making under ambiguity, merging quantum probabilistic insights with optimization and choice theory to create a comprehensive model of uncertainty that explains both behavior and well-studied phenomena observed in empirical studies of decision-making.

title: Psychological Determinants and Consequences of Complex Networks
Abstract: The proliferation of complex networks across various domains has led to a burgeoning interest in understanding the underlying psychological determinants and consequences of their formation, maintenance, and impact on individuals and societies. Furthermore, we examine the consequences of complex network participation on individuals' mental and physical health, including the impact of social isolation, cyberbullying, and information overload. Our findings suggest that complex network participation can have both positive and negative consequences, depending on the nature of the network and the individual's level of engagement. We also propose a theoretical framework that integrates various psychological theories to explain the determinants and consequences of complex network participation, highlighting the importance of considering the interplay between individual, social, and technological factors in understanding complex network phenomena. title: The Human Kernel
Abstract: The Human Kernel revolves around a hypothetical homunculus, an imaginary miniature human said to possess the fundamental components of life within its being. title: Automatic Stress Detection in Working Environments from Smartphones' Accelerometer Data: A First Step
Abstract: The increasing prevalence of chronic stress in working environments poses a significant threat to employees' mental and physical health, organizational productivity, and overall well-being. This study investigates the potential of smartphones' built-in accelerometers as a non-intrusive, cost-effective, and user-friendly tool for automatic stress detection in working environments. A total of 120 office workers were recruited to participate in this study, with 30% of them classified as stressed based on stress questionnaires and physiological signals collected through wearable devices. Accelerometer data collected from their smartphones during work hours were pre-processed using noise reduction techniques and feature extraction algorithms to identify salient characteristics associated with stress responses. Machine learning-based classification models, such as Support Vector Machines (SVM), Random Forest (RF), and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), were trained and evaluated using a 10-fold cross-validation approach to predict the presence of stress based on accelerometer data features. The results showed that SVM and RF models achieved high accuracy rates of 85.5% and 84.2%, respectively, in detecting stress in office workers using accelerometer data. The findings of this study provide a first step towards harnessing smartphones' built-in accelerometers for stress detection and monitoring in working environments, offering opportunities for early intervention, stress management, and improved employee well-being. This research has significant implications for HR managers, mental health professionals, and organizational leaders to implement stress prevention and management programs.

title: Investigation of functional systems of the psychic self-organization based on the method of basal matrix
Abstract: The investigation of the functional systems of the psychic self-organization is a complex and multi-faceted area of study that has garnered significant attention in recent years, particularly in the field of cognitive science and philosophy of mind. title: Preference reversal in quantum decision theory
Abstract: Quantum decision theory has been gaining attention in recent years as a potential framework for modeling complex decision-making processes, particularly in situations where classical probability and expected utility do not provide a satisfactory explanation. One of the key predictions of quantum mechanics that has been observed in quantum decision theory is the potential for preference reversal, where an individual's preferences for options change based on the information presented to them. Preference reversal is often identified as a problem for choice theory as it implies that agents may violate transitivity and other basic rationality assumptions. In this context, our study explores the application of quantum probability and entropy concepts to preference reversal. We examine the relationship between different quantum states of knowledge and the likelihood of preference reversal, using a combination of analytical and numerical methods to model decision scenarios. Our results demonstrate that, under certain conditions, applying quantum principles can indeed lead to preference reversal, and that this phenomenon is a natural consequence of the inherent ambiguity and uncertainty present in complex decision environments. Additionally, we find that quantum entropy can be used to quantify the degree of preference reversal, providing a new tool for understanding and analyzing decision-making processes. By shedding light on the underlying mechanisms driving preference reversal, our work aims to provide new insights into the quantum foundations of decision theory.

title: Repeated transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) in nondepressed reduces levels of reported negative affects from daily stressors
Abstract: This study aimed to investigate the long-term effects of repeated transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) on levels of reported negative affects from daily stressors in individuals without a history of depression. A total of 60 healthy participants were randomly assigned to either a tDCS or a sham stimulation group and received 15 consecutive daily sessions of stimulation. Baseline and post-stimulation assessments were conducted using standardized measures of emotional state and stress levels. Results showed a significant reduction in the levels of reported negative affects from daily stressors in the tDCS group compared to the sham group, with effects sustained at the 1-week follow-up assessment. Furthermore, repeated-measures analysis revealed a significant linear decrease in negative affects for the tDCS group throughout the stimulation period. Moreover, exploratory analyses suggested that the anode-targeting stimulation protocol was associated with greater reductions in negative emotions and improved mood, while the cathode-targeting protocol was associated with enhanced cognitive flexibility. These findings provide the first evidence that repeated tDCS can have a sustained positive effect on emotional state and stress management in individuals without a history of depression, highlighting the potential of this non-invasive and low-cost intervention for promoting emotional well-being in the general population.
