Furthermore, we investigate the systematic offset between the dynamical-to-stellar mass ratio (M/L) derived from our data and the values predicted by standard stellar population synthesis models. Our results indicate that M/L is governed by subtle dependencies on the stellar population's metallicity and age gradients, thereby uncovering potential avenues for refining our understanding of galaxy evolution and selection effects in large-scale surveys. title: How much does your data exploration overfit? Controlling bias via information usage

Through a combination of stochastic and information-theoretic methods, novel statistical and algebraic frameworks are introduced to quantify and correct for the infamously insidious effects of data exploration upon ensuing modeling endeavors. title: Extended slow dynamical regime close to the many-body localization transition
Abstract: The many-body localization (MBL) transition marks a fundamental boundary between uncorrelated thermal systems and interacting disordered ones, characterized by localized phases and an extended ergodic regime. However, the onset of the MBL transition is known to be preceded by a dynamically arrested intermediate regime, often referred to as the "slow dynamical regime," where relaxation times diverge and sub-diffusive behavior appears. Exploring the characteristics of this slow dynamical regime has long been recognized as an essential task, given its potential implications for our understanding of both MBL and interacting systems in general. Here, we present evidence for a novel scaling behavior emerging at the onset of the MBL transition, one that distinguishes the slow dynamical regime from the usual single-particle scaling theories applicable in the ergodic phase. Utilizing numerical simulations of the Fermi-Hubbard model with disorder, our results identify key signatures of the slow dynamical regime as the system approaches the MBL transition, providing a framework for understanding the transition mechanisms underlying this long-standing phenomenon. These findings highlight the self-organization features at the MBL transition, critically reinforcing our comprehension of how the boundary between localized and ergodic matter is established. Further, these studies offer insights into the generic dynamical arrest scenarios that unfold when microscopic interactions disrupt ergodicity in complex disordered systems.

title: Classifying orbits in the restricted three-body problem
Abstract: The restricted three-body problem has long been a cornerstone in the study of celestial mechanics, providing a simplified yet crucial framework for understanding the complex interactions between multiple celestial bodies. Despite its relative simplicity, the three-body problem exhibits a surprisingly rich variety of dynamics, encompassing both regular and chaotic motion, stable and unstable orbits, and bound and unbound trajectories. In this context, the classification of orbits assumes paramount importance, as it allows for a precise description of the behavior of the third object and its predicted path of motion. This paper contributes to the ongoing efforts to develop a systematic and comprehensive classification of orbits in the restricted three-body problem, thereby shedding new light on the intricate relationships between the motion of the third object and the fundamental parameters of the problem, such as the mass ratio of the primaries and the energy of the third object.

This study focuses on the CODYRUN building simulation code, a popular tool used for predicting the energy performance of buildings. By creating a virtual mockup of a building's physical environment, CODYRUN simulates various factors that influence energy consumption, including daylighting. In this research, we aimed to evaluate the performance of the daylighting model embedded within CODYRUN by comparing its results with empirical data obtained from real-world buildings. Specifically, we utilized a suite of experimental protocols developed by the International Energy Agency (IEA) and implemented in a series of case studies involving various building geometries, orientations, and climatic conditions. Our analysis unveiled mixed results, with the CODYRUN model exhibiting average discrepancies of up to 20% when compared to actual daylighting performances. However, a detailed examination of the simulations revealed several factors that could contribute to these discrepancies, including limitations in the model's assumptions regarding sky brightness and view factor calculations. These findings have significant implications for building designers and researchers, highlighting the need for improved modeling techniques and encouraging further refinements to the CODYRUN code to improve its predictive capabilities.

title: A novel principal component analysis for spatially-misaligned multivariate air pollution data
Abstract: This paper presents a novel principal component analysis (PCA) method tailored for handling spatially-misaligned multivariate air pollution data, a common issue in environmental monitoring. Existing PCA methods often assume that the data is perfectly aligned in space and time, however, air quality monitoring networks are often irregularly deployed and measurements may not be concurrent. The proposed approach addresses this limitation by developing a novel spatial and temporal alignment procedure that integrates spatial interpolation and temporal synchronization techniques. These procedures involve two stages: the first stage utilizes a scalable spatial interpolation algorithm to fill missing values and estimate measurement values at regular spatial grids, while the second stage employs a robust time-synchronization algorithm to align measurements from different time-series. Following data alignment, the proposed PCA method, named SPATIAL-PCA, is developed and applied to a real-world dataset collected from a network of air quality monitoring stations. SPATIAL-PCA significantly outperforms traditional PCA methods in terms of accuracy and robustness, effectively capturing the spatial and temporal patterns of air pollution variables and revealing correlations that were previously masked by data misalignment. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of SPATIAL-PCA in providing a more accurate and reliable representation of air pollution levels, which can inform decision-making and policy development in environmental protection.

An insurance-led approach can also facilitate the sharing of climate-related risks across geographical and demographic boundaries, creating a more equitable and stable framework for adaptation and mitigation. To achieve this, the paper advocates for the development of novel insurance products and risk models tailored to climate-related hazards, as well as policy reforms to incentivize the uptake of climate-resilient practices and investments. By fostering a symbiotic relationship between insurance, climate change research, and sustainable development, an insurance-led response can help bridge the adaptation gap, unlock new opportunities for climate-resilient economic growth, and create a more climate-resilient society for all. The results revealed that the introduction of oxygen vacancies significantly enhanced the CH4 sensing response and selectivity of SnO2 nanostructures, particularly at low operating temperatures. Furthermore, the role of in-plane and bridging oxygen vacancies in modulating the charge carrier concentration and mobility of SnO2 was elucidated, providing valuable insights into the design and optimization of high-performance SnO2 gas sensors. Additionally, the method employs a distributed trust-region block-coordinate fixed-point algorithm to ensure convergence and stability. Furthermore, a numerical investigation is conducted to demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method for solving diverse unsteady source inversion problems, including those with varying numbers of spatial domain partitions and time snapshots. title: A wide binary trigger for white dwarf pollution
Abstract: The process of pollution of single white dwarfs by heavy elements has been primarily linked to binary mergers involving low-mass companions, such as red giant donors or He WD donors. However, recent detection of a wide binary comprising a contaminated white dwarf and an evolved giant companion, each rotating rapidly and orbiting at a distance of over 100 AU, poses a critical challenge to the prevailing merger origin scenario. Alternative scenarios, including engulfment by the giant companion during Roche lobe overflow, and exchange interactions facilitated by perturbative late-stage stellar encounters or massive planet formation events, are also being considered. This paper presents the impact of unresolved triple and higher order multiplicity on wide binary transformations, an example from the latest detection, including evaluation of mass accretion and redistribution within a system which cannot be computed in advance or handled by standard stellar evolution codes.  Investigations into the interaction histories of these events suggest commonalities that a universally applicable predictive theory can utilize, demonstrating the universal power of a simple physical input.

title: Extreme Dependence Models
Abstract: Extreme Dependence Models are emerging as a crucial tool in finance and risk management to quantify dependencies between extreme variables, such as stock prices, credit ratings, and insurance claims. Traditional statistical models have limitations in capturing these complex relationships, leading to inaccurate assessments of risk and potential portfolio losses. In response, researchers have proposed various classes of Extreme Dependence Models, including Co-VaR, co-regularized extreme value theory, and Hüsler-Reiss models, to better describe and predict extreme events that arise from interrelated assets or variables. These models not only enable the estimation of joint probability distributions of extreme variables but also facilitate the evaluation of jointVaR (Value-at-Risk) and stressed VaR, which are instrumental in regulatory risk management. Furthermore, they assist in detecting potential risk concentrations within and between portfolios, making them particularly valuable for financial institutions and policymakers. Despite their growing significance, Extreme Dependence Models are often afflicted by identification issues, data scarcity, and model specification problems, demanding more robust methodologies and novel computational techniques to mitigate these challenges. This review aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the theoretical and practical aspects of Extreme Dependence Models, highlight their applications in finance, and outline avenues for future research in this burgeoning field, contributing to the continued development and implementation of these models in risk management.

Additionally, we identified patterns in the posted photos indicating correlations between air quality and socioeconomic factors, temporal variations in air pollution, and differences in air quality between cities. These findings suggest that user-generated online photos can be a valuable supplement to traditional monitoring systems, enabling real-time and spatially explicit monitoring of air pollution in major cities. title: The near-infrared radiation background, gravitational wave background and star formation rate of Pop III and Pop II during cosmic reionization
Abstract: The cosmic reionization epoch is marked by the emergance of the first luminous sources capable of ionizing the remaining neutral gas, and Pop III and Pop II stars played pivotal roles in this process. However, the relative contributions of these stellar populations to the near-infrared radiation background (NIRB), gravitational wave background (GWB), and star formation rate (SFR) during this era remain unclear. Utilizing coupled radiation hydrodynamics simulations with physical-motivated models, this research investigates the impact of Pop III and Pop II stars on the NIRB, GWB, and SFR during cosmic reionization. We find that Pop III stars significantly dominate the NIRB, producing a peak amplitude 6 times that of Pop II stars, mainly due to their higher radiative efficiencies and distinct IMF. The Pop III contribution to the GWB is found to be 65% of the total GWB, while Pop II stars account for the remaining 35%, primarily resulting from the different mass distributions and IMF of these stellar populations. Furthermore, Pop III stars exhibit enhanced SFR of 2 orders of magnitude relative to Pop II, driven by their shorter formation timescales and higher gas consumption rates. Our study implies that precise observational identification and analysis of the NIRB, GWB, and SFR in the early universe are essential for distinguishing the presence and characteristics of Pop III stars, thereby enabling a comprehensive understanding of the cosmic reionization process and the evolution of the first stars in the universe.

title: Pushdown Control-Flow Analysis for Free
Abstract: This paper proposes an innovative approach to pushdown control-flow analysis, a crucial step in static program analysis, by extending it to support free variables commonly found in functional programming languages. Our solution is designed to address these challenges by incorporating an extension of pushdown control-flow analysis that can handle nondeterministic paths caused by free variables. This extension is rooted in combining symbolic execution with a novel data-flow approach to manage dynamic memory allocation and function calls that might involve free variables. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our extension using a set of benchmarks that highlight the problematic scenarios with free variables, and the results show significant improvement over existing techniques in terms of precision and efficiency. This approach can be applied to various programming languages that employ free variables, including Racket and Scheme, making it a valuable tool in the field of static program analysis and its applications in compiler design and software verification.

Conventional discretization methods tend to generate ill-conditioned or even singular linear systems, which are difficult to solve accurately and efficiently. To address this issue, we employ the domain decomposition method, dividing the computational domain into smaller subdomains that can be solved separately. By applying a suitable preconditioner to the resulting interface problem, we aim to reduce the overall computational cost and improve the robustness of the numerical solution. We investigate different types of preconditioners, such as additive Schwarz methods and balanced domain decomposition, and analyze their performance using various benchmark problems. The results demonstrate that our approach can achieve significant improvements in terms of convergence rate and computational cost, making it a promising technique for tackling high-frequency Helmholtz problems with absorption. The proposed method is also shown to be scalable to large-scale problems, making it a valuable tool for real-world applications.

A more in-depth examination of polluted population III stars also aids in understanding the cosmic distribution of metals, particularly the synthesis of red giants. This study aims to develop a reliable mathematical model for the prediction of air pollutant abatement in deep street canyons utilizing air scrubbers. The developed model considers parameters such as wind direction and speed, air temperature, humidity, pollutant concentrations, scrubber efficiency, and the overall flow dynamics within the canyon. A case study on a real-world urban environment was conducted, employing primary data from continuous emission monitors and meteorological sensors. The results demonstrate the accuracy and robustness of the proposed model in predicting PM, NOx, and VOC concentration reductions achieved through the use of air scrubbers under different operational scenarios and environmental conditions. title: The non-linear health consequences of living in larger cities
Abstract: The urban health paradox has long been observed, where residents of larger cities tend to exhibit better health outcomes in terms of life expectancy and certain disease prevention, yet experience a disproportionate burden of non-communicable diseases, stress-related disorders, and increased mortality rates compared to their rural counterparts. However, the growing body of evidence suggests that the relationship between urban living and health outcomes is far more intricate, and that larger cities may be characterized by unique non-linear health patterns. While some individuals living in larger cities may experience improved mental and physical well-being, others may be vulnerable to accelerated aging, chronic disease progression, and diminished quality of life as a result of prolonged exposure to stressors associated with urban living, such as air pollution, noise pollution, and social isolation. This study aims to elucidate the non-linear health consequences of living in larger cities, examining the complex dynamics that underlie the association between urban residence and health outcomes, and identifying the subgroups of populations that are most at risk of adverse outcomes. The results of the studied case demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method in obtaining robust designs that exhibit enhanced performance under uncertainty, as well as improved system reliability and resilience. title: The information-complete quantum theory
Abstract: Quantum theory has profoundly impacted the field of physics by providing a comprehensive framework for understanding subatomic phenomena. Despite its remarkable success, developments in the domain have consistently raised the question of whether this framework is exhaustive. Ever since its inception, research into the foundations of quantum mechanics has sought to uncover any possible areas of incompleteness, with attempts to provide more general formulations for predicting the properties of quantum systems. The concept of information-completeness plays a pivotal role in addressing this question, essentially implying that for a complete physical theory, every physical property observable can be reduced to statements about outcomes of experiments in a lab. The conventional understanding of quantum mechanics aligns with this notion, where information is obtainable via measurement of the probabilities of outcomes through the use of wave functions or density matrices. However, in the face of a large amount of real-world phenomena that quantum theory fails to fully model, the question remains whether the general principle of information-completeness is a distinctive feature of quantum mechanics or if it is an inherent property of any possible complete fundamental physical theory. In this paper, we delve into both the historical context and the current status of research related to addressing this pivotal inquiry.

The observability of these systems is crucial for informed decision-making, yet it remains a contentious issue due to the complexity and intricacy of the network interactions. Cognitive Dynamic Systems (CDS) offer a potential solution, as they can adaptively learn and reason about the intricate relationships within these complex systems. This research aims to combine the principles of cognitive dynamic systems with the analysis of stochastic complex networks to enhance observability and provide a more comprehensive understanding of the systems' behavior. By leveraging advanced techniques in machine learning and cognitive computing, the proposed approach aims to develop an adaptive framework that can track and reveal network dynamics, even in the presence of uncertainty and variability. Furthermore, this framework aims to reveal novel nonlinear interactions and predict the occurrence of rare events, greatly expanding the potential applications of complex network observability. This research is expected to contribute significantly to the field of complex systems and have a positive impact on various domains, including social networks, neuroscience, and financial systems, among others by enabling more accurate predictions, interventions, and dynamic control of complex networks. The developed framework is expected to lead to novel insights and applications, bridging the gap between cognitive dynamic systems and stochastic complex networks.

title: Short gamma-ray bursts in the "time-reversal" scenario

Abstract: 
The time-reversal paradigm for short gamma-ray bursts (SGRBs) proposes that these cataclysmic events may originate from the collapse of a neutron star or the merger of two neutron stars, as opposed to the merger of a neutron star and a black hole. According to this hypothesis, a neutron-star merger would induce a prompt accretion of the surrounding matter onto the newly formed object, resulting in a gamma-ray burst. The time-reversal scenario suggests that the matter accretion process would repeat in the reverse order, causing an optical counterpart (the supernova remnant) to become "hotter" as it cools and expands over time. Recent observations of SGRBs, specifically those displaying a late-time rise in optical light, are consistent with this prediction. The time-reversal scenario provides a unique alternative to the traditional collapsar model and offers an explanation for the observed diversity of SGRBs, including those that exhibit both bright optical and radio emission. If the time-reversal paradigm is confirmed, it would significantly modify our understanding of the physics of neutron-star binaries and the cosmic events that give rise to SGRBs. This work presents a detailed exploration of the time-reversal theory and its implications for the observation and understanding of these enigmatic cosmic events.

title: Toeplitz Corona and the Douglas Property for Free Functions
Abstract: This paper provides a comprehensive study on the Toeplitz corona and the Douglas property for free functions. Specifically, we investigate the relationship between these two fundamental concepts in operator theory, which have been studied extensively in the context of compact operators on Hilbert spaces. The Toeplitz corona, introduced by Donald Sarason, is a set of free functions in the unit ball of a free algebra that possess certain analytical and algebraic properties, while the Douglas property is a weaker condition that generalizes the contractive divisor problem of Douglas and Rudin. By combining these concepts, we establish new results on free functions that provide a more nuanced understanding of their algebraic and geometric properties. Our study culminates in the derivation of a new characterization of the Douglas property for subalgebras of free functions, which streamlines the complex interaction between the Toeplitz corona and the Douglas property. This characterization provides a precise description of the boundary behavior of functions in the Toeplitz corona, while also highlighting the central role that the Douglas property plays in the study of free functions. By exploring these connections, we contribute to the ongoing efforts to understand the intricate relationships between operator theory, algebraic geometry, and free analysis.

title: Systematic Review on Project Actuality
Abstract: This systematic review aims to critically examine the concept of project actuality, which refers to the realization and effectiveness of actual project outcomes in alignment with initial project goals, objectives, and expected deliverables. Despite the increasing recognition of project actuality in project management literature, limited attention has been given to the empirical analysis of the factors that contribute to project actuality, the relationships between project factors, and the potential outcomes of successful project actualization. To address this knowledge gap, this review systematically synthesized a vast array of existing research findings from various disciplines, including project management, organizational studies, and operations research. The comprehensive search for literature yielded an enormous collection of relevant studies conducted in various sectors, including construction, information technology, and service industries. Through a rigorous review and critical evaluation of these studies, we identified a range of significant factors that can contribute to project actuality, including project planning, stakeholder engagement, risk management, and team collaboration. The findings of this review also reveal that project actuality is closely linked to project outcomes, such as cost efficiency, time performance, and quality delivery. The results of this systematic review have the potential to inform practitioners, researchers, and policymakers about the key drivers of project actuality and the importance of achieving successful project outcomes in a rapidly changing and competitive business environment.

title: State of the Art of Agile Governance: A Systematic Review
Abstract: Agile governance has emerged as a transformative approach to address the complexities and uncertainties inherent in modern organizational landscapes. This systematic review aims to distill the state of the art of agile governance, synthesizing a vast body of research to provide a comprehensive understanding of its principles, applications, challenges, and implications. Through a meticulous examination of existing scholarly literature, this review identifies the core characteristics, benefits, and limitations of agile governance, as well as its key enablers and inhibitors. The review also investigates the intersections and synergies between agile governance and other frameworks, such as DevOps, lean management, and design thinking, highlighting areas of convergence and divergence. Furthermore, the review provides insights into the critical success factors, risk management strategies, and performance measurement approaches associated with the effective implementation of agile governance. By aggregating the findings from diverse research studies, this systematic review seeks to inform practitioners, policymakers, and scholars about the current state of agile governance, its evolution, and its potential to drive sustainable growth, responsiveness, and innovation in complex organizational settings.

title: A Guide To Deal With Uncertainties In Software Project Management
Abstract: This paper offers a comprehensive guide to navigating uncertainties in software project management, a critical aspect of modern software development. Given the inherently unpredictable nature of software projects, managers are frequently faced with a wide range of uncertainties originating from various sources, including changing stakeholder expectations, emerging technological advancements, and imperfectly predictable user needs. To tackle these challenges effectively, software project managers must leverage effective strategies for mitigating the effects of uncertainty on the project lifecycle. One major obstacle to project completion is delay caused by high uncertainty in any given project. However, significant delays in projects disrupt workflows and impact resources. Therefore, this paper explores various methodologies for handling uncertainties, which include predictive analytics, systems thinking, risk-based management, and human-centered design. These approaches help identify and quantify uncertainties, communicate predicted risks to key stakeholders, set realistic project timelines and budgets, and ensure seamless adaptation to emerging facts during the project lifecycle. Our examination illustrates the importance of uncertainty management in software project management and delves into the intricacies of these methodologies through exploration of real-world case studies.

title: Reverse Engineering of Middleware for Verification of Robot Control Architectures
Abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to the reverse engineering of middleware for the verification of robot control architectures. Middleware plays a crucial role in the development and deployment of robotics systems, acting as an abstraction layer that enables the communication and coordination between various components. However, the lack of transparency and modularity in middleware architectures makes it challenging to analyze and verify their correctness, particularly in safety-critical applications such as robot control. To address this gap, we propose a methodology for the reverse engineering of middleware, focusing on the extraction and analysis of architectural and behavioral models. Our approach leverages model-driven engineering techniques and formal verification methods to ensure the correctness and reliability of the middleware architecture. By applying this approach to a range of robot control architectures, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our methodology in identifying and resolving architectural defects, improving the overall robustness and safety of the system. The presented work contributes to the field of robotics software engineering by providing a systematic and rigorous framework for the verification of middleware architectures, enabling the reliable development of complex robotics systems. Our findings have significant implications for the design and deployment of middleware in robotics, and can be used to improve the consistency and interoperability of various robotics platforms and applications.

title: The Problem of Motion: The Statistical Mechanics of Zitterbewegung
Abstract: The phenomenon of Zitterbewegung, predicted by physicist Werner Heisenberg in 1930, is a type of high-energy particle motion characterized by a rapid oscillatory behavior, often described as a "trembling" or "quivering." While initially overlooked, recent advancements in condensed matter and particle physics have rekindled interest in this intriguing phenomenon, with potential implications for a deeper understanding of the behavior of matter at the quantum level. This paper delves into the statistical mechanics of Zitterbewegung, exploring its underlying mathematical framework and analyzing the statistical properties of this phenomenon in various physical systems. By employing a combination of quantum field theory and statistical mechanics, we derive a framework for understanding the probability distributions and correlation functions associated with Zitterbewegung. Our analysis reveals that the statistical properties of Zitterbewegung are significantly influenced by the symmetries and topological properties of the underlying physical system, leading to novel phenomena such as the emergence of a "Zitterbewegung gap" in certain materials. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that Zitterbewegung can be induced by external perturbations, such as electromagnetic fields, and can exhibit intriguing non-equilibrium behavior. Overall, this work lays the foundation for a deeper understanding of Zitterbewegung and its potential applications in various fields, from condensed matter physics to high-energy particle physics.

title: Contrasting string holography to its optical namesake
Abstract: String holography and optical holography may seem like unrelated concepts, yet they share a common thread - the recording and reconstruction of information in their respective domains. Optical holography, the creation of three-dimensional images from interference patterns, has long been a cornerstone of modern physics, allowing for the capture and reproduction of complex patterns with unprecedented fidelity. String holography, on the other hand, is a theoretical framework within string theory, proposing that the information content of a black hole is encoded on its surface, much like a hologram encodes two-dimensional information onto a flat surface. While the principles may appear analogous at first glance, the underlying theories and applications of these two holographic paradigms are vastly different. Optical holography operates under the constraints of classical physics, leveraging the properties of light to encode and reconstruct images, whereas string holography is a quantum gravity concept, attempting to bridge the gap between the holographic principle and the mysteries of black hole physics. Despite these differences, both approaches underscore the intimate relationship between information and geometry, highlighting the profound implications of holographic thinking in our understanding of the universe. This paper undertake to illuminate these parallels and contrasts between optical and string holography, offering an exploration of the distinct concepts, theories, and applications of these two disparate yet interconnected phenomena.

title: The complexity of satisfaction problems in reverse mathematics
Abstract: This research paper provides a comprehensive exploration of the complexity of satisfaction problems in reverse mathematics, a relatively underexplored area in the realm of mathematical logic. The study aims to classify and characterize the computational complexity of various satisfaction problems arising in reverse mathematics, with a focus on their level of assertiveness and degree of difficulty. By employing a range of mathematical techniques, including low basis theorems and Σn-interpretability, the research seeks to identify explicit upper and lower bounds on the lengths needed to solve various satisfaction problems, revealing intricate relationships between well-established and previously understudied satisfaction problems. The findings of this research possess significant implications for the field of reverse mathematics, where computational complexity is crucial for identifying and proving conservation theorems. Moreover, the research sheds new light on the fundamental connections between satisfaction problems and well-known theorems such as ACA_0 and RCA_0, yielding novel insights into the structure of models of subsystems of second-order arithmetic. By addressing the inherent complexities within satisfaction problems in reverse mathematics, this research ultimately contributes to a more comprehensive understanding of the interplay between computational power and mathematical truth.

title: Transport modeling of sedimenting particles in a turbulent pipe flow using Euler-Lagrange large eddy simulation
Abstract: A computational fluid dynamics approach is proposed to simulate the transport of sedimenting particles in a turbulent pipe flow using the Euler-Lagrange large eddy simulation methodology. This hybrid technique combines the macro-scale features of large eddy simulation, which resolves the large-scale turbulent structures and models the smaller scales using a sub-grid scale model, with the particle motion governed by the Euler-Lagrange method. The Euler-Lagrange approach models the discrete particles as a collection of phase-space correlated random processes, enabling the simulation of the complex interactions between particles and the turbulent fluid flow. A particle-particle and particle-fluid interaction model is developed to account for the influence of individual particles on the flow and the deformation of particle mass distribution due to fluid forces. Numerical simulations are performed in a planar turbulent pipe flow with various sediment particle sizes, concentrations, and positions to examine the effects of turbulence on particle transport and the resulting particle distribution. The results show that the Euler-Lagrange large eddy simulation can effectively capture the complex dynamics of particle-laden turbulent flow, highlighting the merits of the proposed approach for modeling sedimenting particles in various industrial and environmental applications. The computational results are validated using available experimental data, demonstrating the robustness and accuracy of the proposed methodology for quantifying particle transport in turbulent pipe flows.

title: Swift and Fermi observations of X-ray flares: the case of Late Internal Shock
Abstract: The study of X-ray flares in gamma-ray burst (GRB) remnants has revolutionized our understanding of these cosmic events, providing valuable insights into the underlying physical processes. Recent observations by Swift and Fermi satellites have shed new light on the phenomenon of Late Internal Shocks (LIS), a theoretical framework that challenges the traditional model of GRB forward shocks. By analyzing a sample of 50 GRBs, this research paper presents a comprehensive investigation of X-ray flares associated with LIS. The analysis reveals that X-ray flares are indeed a common occurrence in GRBs, with 70% of the sample exhibiting late-time flaring activity. Furthermore, the results suggest that LIS can account for the majority of X-ray flares observed in GRBs, with a correlation between the X-ray flare energy and the rate of internal shock dissipation. The study also finds that the decay of LIS power can be used to constrain the total amount of internal shock dissipation in GRBs. The implications of these findings are far-reaching, with LIS providing a new paradigm for understanding the complex physics of GRB X-ray flares. The results of this study have significant implications for our understanding of the internal dynamics of GRBs, and highlight the importance of high-energy observations in unveiling the underlying mechanisms driving these enigmatic events.

title: Power enhancement of heat engines via correlated thermalization in multilevel systems
Abstract: This work focuses on the power enhancement of heat engines through the concept of correlated thermalization in multilevel systems. By exploiting correlations between energy levels, we demonstrate a novel approach to improve the efficiency and power output of heat engines. Through theoretical analysis and numerical simulations, we identify the conditions under which correlated thermalization can lead to significant power enhancements, particularly at low temperatures. Our results show that by carefully managing the cross-correlation between energy levels, it is possible to transcend the Carnot efficiency limit and reach higher efficiencies than previously thought possible. We identify the role of correlation matrices and show how they affect the thermalization of energy levels in multilevel systems. Furthermore, we demonstrate that correlations can be harnessed to modulate the engine's power output and efficiency in real-time, enabling more flexible and adaptive power management. Our study sheds new light on the behavior of correlated thermalization in multilevel systems, revealing a previously unexplored avenue for enhancing the performance of heat engines. By suggesting new strategies for optimizing power generations, this research contributes to the development of more efficient and sustainable thermal energy conversion technologies.

title: Tunable dichroism and optical absorption of graphene by strain engineering
Abstract: This research paper investigates the tunable optical properties of graphene, a highly sought-after material for its exceptional electrical and thermal conductivity, mechanical strength, and optical transparency. Graphene's dichroism, or the anisotropic difference in absorption of light in different polarizations, can be manipulated through strain engineering, a technique allowing for controlled mechanical deformation of the material. By leveraging the sensitive dependence of graphene's crystal structure on strain, we demonstrate a novel method to fine-tune the dichroism and optical absorption of graphene. Our approach involves the systematic application of mechanical strain to isolate predetermined crystallographic configurations within the graphene lattice, thereby inducing targeted optoelectronic properties. Comprehensive simulations based on density functional theory and experimental verification through Raman spectroscopy and ultraviolet-visible spectroscopy reveal that the strain-induced variations in graphene's dichroism are accompanied by commensurate modifications in its absorption spectra. Notably, our results show that the absorption coefficient in the near-infrared range decreases by over 40% with the application of a 10% biaxial tensile strain, while the dichroism coefficient increases by up to 50% in response to analogous compressive strain. These findings open up new avenues for tailoring the optoelectronic performance of graphene-based devices to suit a range of applications, from ultra-high-speed electronics to compact optical communication systems.

title: Tuning of the electronic and optical properties of single layer black phosphorus by strain
Abstract: Black phosphorus (BP), a layered allotrope of phosphorus, has garnered immense attention due to its unique electronic and optical properties, making it a promising candidate for next-generation electronics and optoelectronic devices. The single layer of BP exhibits tunable and highly anisotropic electronic properties, allowing it to operate as a p-type or n-type semiconductor. However, the inherent instability and sensitivity of BP to environmental factors, such as temperature, light, and moisture, render its applications susceptible to degradation. Strain engineering, which involves the intentional introduction of mechanical strain into BP, has emerged as a viable means to modulate its electronic and optical properties. By applying tensile or compressive strain to single layer BP, its electronic structure and bandgap can be significantly altered, enabling the fine-tuning of its conductivity and optical absorption. Notably, strain-induced changes in BP's electronic properties have been shown to significantly impact its electro-optical responses, including its photoluminescence, photodetection, and photocurrent. Theoretical studies and experimental investigations have provided valuable insights into the strain-dependent evolution of BP's band structure and electronic transport properties, highlighting the potential of strain engineering to elevate BP's performance in optoelectronic and sensing applications.

title: Entanglement-enhanced time-continuous quantum control in optomechanics
Abstract: Quantum control is a crucial aspect of optomechanics, enabling researchers to manipulate and study the behavior of mechanical oscillators in the quantum regime. Emerging as a vital tool in this endeavor is entanglement, the phenomenon where two or more particles become correlated in such a way that the state of one particle cannot be described independently of the others. However, implementing entanglement-enhanced time-continuous quantum control in optomechanics poses significant challenges due to the fragile nature of entanglement. This research investigates the possibility of utilizing entanglement to enhance the precision of quantum control in optomechanics. We achieve entanglement between a mechanical oscillator and a microwave field and demonstrate its potential to improve the accuracy of quantum control protocols. Theoretical and experimental approaches are combined to derive an optimal control strategy that leverages the entangled state, enabling superior cancellation of noise and enhancement of coherent control. Our results show that the entanglement-enhanced control framework raises the precision of quantum control by orders of magnitude, opening new avenues for exploring quantum properties in optomechanical systems and narrowing the gap between theoretical predictions and experimental observations. This study paves the way for further advancements in quantum control and its applications in quantum information processing, quantum simulation, and fundamental studies of quantum mechanics.
